title: To amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to reverse certain energy-related modifications enacted by Public Law 119-21.
ai_summary: This bill would undo several changes that a recent law made to tax breaks related to clean energy. Specifically, it would restore a tax deduction for businesses that make their commercial buildings more energy-efficient, extend a tax credit for builders of new energy-efficient homes through 2032 (rather than letting it expire in mid-2026), give companies more time to build facilities that qualify for a clean hydrogen production tax credit, and restore tax credits for clean electricity production and investment that the recent law had cut back or ended early. The bill also ties the phase-out of the clean electricity production credit to an emissions milestone — meaning the credit would not begin winding down until U.S. electricity generation greenhouse gas emissions drop to 25% of their 2022 levels, or until 2032, whichever comes later. The people most directly affected would be commercial property owners, homebuilders, energy companies, and investors involved in clean hydrogen and electricity projects who would benefit from these restored or extended tax incentives.
ai_headline: Bill would restore clean energy tax credits cut by recent law
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

The bill also sets a specific emissions milestone that must be reached before the clean electricity production credit can begin to phase out.

ai_sections.why: Without this bill, the tax breaks reduced or ended by the recent law would remain unavailable or would expire sooner. With it, eligible businesses and investors would face a different tax landscape when making decisions about energy-related construction and projects.

title: Western Tribal Water Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill updates an existing federal program that helps Native American tribes on reservations get better access to safe drinking water. It adds a new requirement that at least 10 projects funded by the program must be located within the Upper Colorado River Basin, a region that includes parts of Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, and other western states — specifically addressing water infrastructure needs for tribes in that area. It also sets aside $60 million per year for fiscal years 2027 and 2028 to fund the program. The tribes most directly affected are those living on reservations in drought-prone areas of the western United States, particularly those in the Upper Colorado River Basin, such as the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, which the bill singles out as having significant aging water infrastructure in need of repair.
ai_headline: Bill targets tribal water access in Upper Colorado Basin
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and in addition to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

title: No Rogue Jurors Act
ai_summary: This bill would bar the federal government from giving money — through grants, contracts, awards, or any other financial support — to any organization, school, or group that promotes "jury nullification." Jury nullification is when a juror votes to acquit (find not guilty) a defendant even though the evidence shows the law was broken, essentially ignoring the law on purpose. The ban specifically covers training programs, written materials, and outreach efforts aimed at encouraging people to seek jury duty in federal or Washington, D.C. courts with the goal of voting against the evidence or the law. Organizations that run such programs — including any program with a name or framework similar to "Equity & Root Cause Jury Training" — would no longer be eligible for federal funding if this bill becomes law.
ai_headline: Federal funds barred for jury nullification programs
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8485 would cut federal funding to any group that teaches or promotes jury nullification in federal or D.C. courts.

The ban covers training programs, written materials, and outreach efforts that encourage people to seek jury duty in order to vote against the evidence or the law.
ai_sections.who: Any organization, school, or group that runs such programs would lose eligibility for federal grants, contracts, awards, or other financial support. This includes programs similar in name or structure to something called "Equity & Root Cause Jury Training."
ai_sections.why: If passed, groups that currently receive federal funding and run these kinds of programs would have to stop them or give up that funding. Organizations not yet receiving federal money would be blocked from applying for it.

title: Funding Early Childhood is the Right IDEA Act
ai_summary: This bill would set new, higher spending limits for two federal programs that help young children with disabilities get early support services. The first program pays for special education services for children ages 3 to 5, and the bill would authorize spending to grow from $503 million in 2027 to $1.22 billion by 2031. The second program supports early intervention services for infants and toddlers with disabilities and their families, with authorized funding rising from $932 million in 2027 to $1.72 billion by 2031. The children and families who would be affected are those with infants, toddlers, or preschoolers who have disabilities and rely on these federally funded programs for things like therapy, developmental support, and special education. It is important to note that authorizing these spending amounts does not automatically provide the money — Congress would still need to pass separate legislation to actually appropriate the funds.

title: Savings Opportunity and Affordable Repayment Act
ai_summary: This bill would create a new federal student loan repayment option called the Savings Opportunity and Affordable Repayment (SOAR) plan, available to borrowers with federal student loans. Under this plan, borrowers would pay nothing on income up to 250% of the federal poverty level for their family size, then 5% of income above that threshold for undergraduate loans and 10% for other loans (such as graduate loans), with the monthly amount adjusted based on the share of their debt from each category. The government would not charge borrowers for any interest their monthly payment doesn't cover, and half of every payment would go directly toward reducing the loan's principal balance. Borrowers repaying only loans from short undergraduate programs (two years or less) could have their remaining balance canceled after 10 years of qualifying payments, while borrowers with other loans could receive cancellation after 15 years. Two existing income-driven repayment plans — the Pay As You Earn (PAYE) plan and the older Income-Contingent Repayment (ICR) plan — would be phased out for new enrollees two years after the bill becomes law, though current enrollees could generally remain in those plans.
ai_headline: New SOAR plan would cap student loan payments at 5–10%
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8475 creates a new federal student loan repayment plan with income-based payments, no interest buildup, and balance cancellation after 10–15 years.

Borrowers currently in the Pay As You Earn (PAYE) or Income-Contingent Repayment (ICR) plans can generally stay in those plans, but new enrollees would no longer be able to join them two years after the bill becomes law.

title: Territorial Protection and Sovereignty Act
ai_summary: This bill would permanently end the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) program, which currently allows people from certain countries experiencing ongoing crises — such as natural disasters or armed conflicts — to live and work legally in the United States on a temporary basis. The law that created TPS would be completely removed from the books, meaning no new TPS designations could ever be granted in the future. Anyone who already holds TPS when this bill becomes law would have their status canceled immediately on that same day. Those people would then have 60 days to leave the United States, and after that 60-day window closes, they would no longer be considered legally present in the country. The bill affects the hundreds of thousands of foreign nationals currently living in the U.S. under TPS protections from countries such as El Salvador, Haiti, Honduras, Venezuela, and others.
ai_headline: Bill would abolish Temporary Protected Status program
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8460 would end the TPS program permanently and cancel existing TPS protections the same day it becomes law.

Anyone currently holding TPS would lose that status immediately on the day the bill is signed. ai_sections.who: The bill affects hundreds of thousands of foreign nationals currently living in the U.S. under TPS from countries including El Salvador, Haiti, Honduras, and Venezuela, among others.
ai_sections.why: People who currently rely on TPS for the legal right to live and work in the U.S. would lose that authorization immediately. After the 60-day window, those who remain would no longer have legal status in the country.

title: Protect our Pets Act
ai_summary: This bill makes two main changes to federal law to increase protections for animals. First, it raises the maximum prison sentences for "animal crushing" — a federal crime that already exists — so that a first offense can result in up to 10 years in prison and a repeat offense can result in up to 15 years, along with fines in either case. Second, it creates a new federal crime: knowingly abandoning a domesticated animal or committing a violent act that endangers a domesticated animal, when that conduct crosses state lines, involves foreign commerce, or takes place on federal land; the same prison terms and fines apply. The new crime covers domesticated mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians kept as pets or for commercial purposes, but it does not apply to standard veterinary care, farming practices, food slaughter, hunting, fishing, pest control, medical research, acts necessary to protect a person or their property, or euthanasia. These changes would affect anyone in the United States who harms or abandons a domesticated animal in a way that falls under federal jurisdiction, and they increase the legal consequences compared to what current federal law provides.
ai_headline: Bill would stiffen penalties for animal cruelty and abandonment
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8480 raises prison sentences for animal crushing and creates a new federal crime for abandoning or harming domestic pets across state lines.
ai_sections.what: This bill makes two changes to federal law. It increases the maximum prison time for animal crushing to 10 years for a first offense and 15 years for a repeat offense. It also creates a new federal crime for knowingly abandoning or violently harming a domesticated animal when the act crosses state lines, involves foreign commerce, or happens on federal land.
ai_sections.who: This applies to anyone in the United States whose mistreatment or abandonment of a domesticated animal falls under federal jurisdiction. The law covers mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians kept as pets or for commercial purposes.
ai_sections.why: People convicted of animal crushing would face longer prison sentences than current federal law allows. Those who abandon or harm a pet across state lines or on federal land could now face federal criminal charges where none existed before.

title: Support for Ownership and Investment in Land Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill directs the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to create a test program that speeds up the application and approval process for two types of farm loans: loans made directly by USDA to farmers who want to buy land, and loans backed (guaranteed) by USDA when a specially certified private lender is handling them for a qualified borrower. The goal is to cut down the time it takes for farmers to get through the paperwork and approval steps — but importantly, the program cannot waive or change any of the actual loan requirements themselves, only the timing of the application process. USDA must report to Congress every year on how the program is working. The program would automatically end on September 30, 2031. This primarily affects farmers and ranchers who are seeking to purchase farmland and are applying for USDA farm ownership loans, as well as the approved lenders who work with those borrowers.
ai_headline: USDA farm loan applications would move faster under pilot plan
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.

title: Surveillance Accountability Act
ai_summary: This bill would require government agencies to obtain a warrant — a court order based on probable cause — before conducting almost any search that intrudes on a person's privacy, including accessing personal data held by companies like banks, phone providers, or cloud storage services. Importantly, it closes what is sometimes called the "third-party loophole," meaning that just because your data is stored with a private company does not mean the government can get it without a warrant, and the fine print in a user agreement cannot take away that protection. The bill also specifically prohibits warrantless use of facial recognition systems, automated license plate readers, and similar surveillance tools to track people in public spaces. If a government official — including a federal employee — violates these rules, the person whose rights were violated can sue that official in court and may have their legal fees covered. The bill includes narrow exceptions for situations already recognized under the law, such as emergencies, plain-view observations by officers lawfully on the scene, checking government-issued ID during a traffic stop, and truly public information that anyone can freely access online.
ai_headline: Bill would require warrants for government data access
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8470 would require government agencies to get a court warrant before accessing your personal data or using facial recognition to track you.
ai_sections.what: This bill would require government agencies to get a court order before searching personal data, even data stored with private companies like banks or cloud services. It would ban warrantless use of facial recognition, license plate readers, and similar tracking tools in public spaces. Exceptions exist for emergencies, things officers can plainly see, checking ID during a traffic stop, and information that is freely available to anyone online.
ai_sections.who: This bill applies to government agencies and officials, including federal employees, who conduct searches or use surveillance tools. People whose rights are violated could sue the official responsible and may have their legal fees covered.
ai_sections.why: Right now, data stored with a private company can sometimes be accessed by the government without a warrant, and user agreements can be used to allow that access. This bill would change that, meaning government access to personal data and public surveillance would face stricter legal requirements.

title: Workforce Data Enhancement Act
ai_summary: This bill sets up a federal grant program to help states build better systems for collecting, linking, and sharing data about workers, job training programs, and employment outcomes. State agencies — particularly those that run unemployment insurance programs, collect labor market data, or administer job training programs — can apply for these grants individually or team up with other states to share data across state lines. Grant money can be used for things like connecting education records with employment records, improving the accuracy and timeliness of information about in-demand jobs and skills (including those related to artificial intelligence), creating secure digital records that workers can own and share with employers, and training staff to better use workforce data. Groups of states working together, especially those that include at least one state that has never received this type of funding before, are given priority when grants are awarded. The goal is to give workers, employers, and training providers better, more up-to-date information to help match people with jobs and skills that the economy needs.
ai_headline: Federal grants would modernize state workforce data systems
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

ai_sections.tldr: This bill would create a federal grant program to help states build better systems for tracking workers, job training, and employment outcomes.
ai_sections.what: This bill would create a federal grant program for states to improve how they collect, link, and share data about workers, job training programs, and employment outcomes. States could use the money to connect education and employment records, create secure digital records workers can share with employers, improve information about in-demand jobs and skills, and train staff who work with workforce data.
ai_sections.who: State agencies that run unemployment insurance, collect labor market data, or manage job training programs can apply. States can apply alone or team up with other states, and groups that include at least one state that has never received this type of funding before get priority.
ai_sections.why: Without current and connected data, workers, employers, and training programs may have a harder time finding accurate information about available jobs and needed skills. This bill is meant to make that information more complete and up to date.

title: WISE Act
ai_summary: This bill requires that at least 20 percent of the federal water infrastructure loan funds that states receive must be spent on environmentally focused water projects, such as green infrastructure, improvements that save water or energy, or other innovative environmental activities. These funds come through a program where the federal government gives money to states, which then use it to make low-interest loans to communities for water and wastewater projects. The 20 percent requirement only applies if there are enough qualifying project applications available — states are not required to turn away other projects to meet the threshold if demand for green projects falls short. The people most directly affected are state water agencies that manage these funds and the local governments, utilities, and communities that apply for loans to build or upgrade water systems.
ai_headline: Federal water loans to require 20% green spending
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.

ai_sections.tldr: States must use at least 20% of federal water loan funds on green or innovative water projects, if enough qualifying applications exist.
ai_sections.what: This bill sets a 20 percent minimum for how states spend certain federal water infrastructure loan funds. That portion must go toward environmentally focused projects, like green infrastructure, water-saving improvements, or innovative environmental activities. States are not required to meet the threshold if there are not enough qualifying applications to fill it.
ai_sections.who: State water agencies that manage these federal loan funds are directly affected. So are local governments, utilities, and communities that apply for low-interest loans to build or upgrade water and wastewater systems.
ai_sections.why: States will need to track how their loan funds are directed and prioritize green project applications up to the 20 percent threshold. Communities seeking loans for green or innovative water projects may find more funding available to them under this structure.

title: RETAIN Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill makes changes to how military pilots and other aviation officers in the Air Force are paid and retained. First, any aviation officer who has completed more than 8 years of flying service would automatically receive the highest possible monthly aviation incentive pay, instead of potentially receiving a lower amount. Second, the bill expands an existing Air Force pilot retention program by making it easier for pilots to qualify, shortening the required commitment in a written retention agreement from four years to one year, and raising the maximum annual retention bonus that can be offered to up to $100,000 — with the full maximum required to be offered to any pilot who agrees to stay on active duty for at least one additional year. The bill also requires the Air Force to give pilots more flexibility in where they are assigned and to match or beat the bonus amounts and contract terms offered by the Air National Guard and Air Force Reserve, so active-duty pilots are not financially pressured to leave for those branches. The program is also extended through 2031.
ai_headline: Air Force pilot pay and retention bonuses raised
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Armed Services.

ai_sections.tldr: Air Force pilots with 8+ years of flight service would get top incentive pay, and retention bonuses could reach $100,000 a year.
ai_sections.what: This bill changes how the Air Force pays and keeps its pilots. Pilots with more than 8 years of flying service would automatically receive the highest monthly aviation incentive pay. A current retention program would be expanded, with shorter commitment periods, higher bonuses up to $100,000 a year, and a requirement that the Air Force match or beat bonus offers from the Air National Guard and Air Force Reserve.
ai_sections.who: This bill affects Air Force aviation officers, especially active-duty pilots. The Air Force would be required to follow the new pay and assignment rules.
ai_sections.why: Active-duty pilots currently may receive lower incentive pay or face longer commitment requirements than pilots in reserve components. Without these changes, some pilots may choose to leave active duty for the Air National Guard or Air Force Reserve, where terms may be more favorable.

title: Cold War Military Force Repeal Act
ai_summary: This bill would cancel a 1957 law — commonly known as the "Eisenhower Doctrine" — that gave the President standing authority to use U.S. military force and provide military assistance to Middle Eastern countries requesting help against communist aggression during the Cold War. That original law was passed at the height of tensions between the U.S. and the Soviet Union, and this bill would wipe it entirely off the books. In practical terms, repealing it would remove one of the older standing legal authorities that a president could potentially point to when taking military action in the Middle East. The bill would primarily affect the executive branch's legal toolkit for authorizing military operations in that region, though Congress and the President would still have other laws and authorities available to them.
ai_headline: Bill repeals 1957 Eisenhower Doctrine on Mideast force
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8436 would erase a 1957 Cold War law that lets the President use military force in the Middle East without new approval from Congress.
ai_sections.what: This bill would repeal a 1957 law known as the Eisenhower Doctrine. title: Baby Food Safety Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill requires the federal government to set legal limits on four toxic metals — lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury — in baby and toddler food (products marketed for children under 24 months) and in fruit and vegetable purees and juices, with those limits to be reviewed and updated at least every four years. Companies that make or process these foods would be required to regularly test their products for these contaminants, keep detailed records of that testing for at least two years, and use accredited laboratories to conduct the tests; the FDA would also run its own independent testing program. A food product that exceeds the established limits, or whose manufacturer fails to follow the testing and recordkeeping rules, can be declared legally "adulterated," and the FDA would gain clearer authority to order a mandatory recall of such products. The bill primarily affects manufacturers and processors of baby food, toddler food, and fruit/vegetable purees and juices, as well as importers of those products, who must verify that foreign suppliers meet the same standards. Ordinary consumers — especially parents of infants and young children — are the intended beneficiaries of the new safety requirements.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: To amend the Immigration and Nationality Act to provide for a pause on the issuance of H-1B visas until certain limitations on the issuance thereof are implemented.
ai_summary: This bill would immediately stop the issuance of H-1B visas — the work visas most commonly used by U.S. employers to hire foreign workers in specialty occupations like technology and engineering — for three years from the date it becomes law. After that pause, new rules would take effect: the number of H-1B visas allowed each year would be cut from 65,000 to 25,000; each employer would have to pay a $100,000 fee per visa petition; workers could only be paid if they earn at least $200,000 per year; and visas would be awarded to the highest-paid applicants rather than through a lottery. The bill also eliminates the ability of staffing agencies to sponsor H-1B workers, bars the federal government from hiring any nonimmigrant visa holders (directly or through contracts), ends work authorization for foreign students on F, M, and certain J visas (the Optional Practical Training program), and blocks most temporary visa holders from applying to become permanent residents while living in the United States. These changes would affect foreign workers currently in or seeking H-1B status, U.S. employers who rely on those workers, foreign students working legally in the U.S. after graduation, and federal agencies that currently contract with nonimmigrant visa holders.
ai_headline: Bill targets H-1B visas with steep caps and new fees
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Critical Infrastructure Airspace Defense Act
ai_summary: This bill gives private owners and operators of certain critical infrastructure facilities — such as nuclear power plants, electrical substations, transformer stations, and power grid control centers — the legal right to use drone-detection and drone-neutralization technology to protect their sites from threatening unmanned aircraft (drones). Currently, only government agencies and some law enforcement can legally take action against drones in this way, but this bill extends that authority to qualifying private facility owners and their designated security staff or contractors, provided they complete a government-approved training and certification program. Drones seized under this authority can be forfeited under applicable law, and the people taking these actions are shielded from civil or criminal liability as long as they are not grossly negligent or acting with willful misconduct. A grant program is established, with up to $250 million authorized over roughly five years, to help eligible facility owners and operators purchase and install approved counter-drone equipment. The new authority for private owners is temporary, expiring at the end of September 2031.

title: Youth Climate Leadership Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill would require five federal agencies — the Environmental Protection Agency, the Department of the Interior, the Department of Energy, the Department of Agriculture, and the Department of Commerce — to each create a Youth Advisory Council made up of 15 to 25 young people between the ages of 16 and 29 who would advise those agencies on environmental issues affecting young people. At least half of each council's members must come from, live in, or work in communities that have been identified as disadvantaged due to environmental or economic hardships, and members would be drawn from a variety of backgrounds such as business, schools, local governments, and environmental groups. Each council would research environmental topics, write reports, and submit recommendations to its agency at least once a year on issues like climate change, pollution reduction, and environmental fairness — particularly for struggling communities. Each agency would receive up to $250,000 per year from 2027 through 2037 to run its council.

title: PCTEC Act
ai_summary: This bill creates a federal grant program to fund "primary care team education centers" — community-based clinics and health centers where medical, nursing, and other health profession students can get hands-on training alongside practicing healthcare providers. Eligible health care organizations could receive up to $1 million per year for up to five years to do things like pay the salaries of the experienced clinicians who supervise students ("preceptors"), help students with housing or transportation during their training, and bring in additional health workers — such as community health workers or school nurses — as part of the care team. The program prioritizes funding for centers that work in areas with health worker shortages and that help people from disadvantaged backgrounds enter health professions. The bill sets aside funding starting at $10 million in 2027 and rising to $50 million by 2029, and requires the federal government to report annually to Congress on how the money is being used and how many students are being trained. Organizations that already receive certain other federal teaching health center grants would not be eligible for this new funding.

title: Save Willy Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill would create a four-year trial program that sets up a small, dedicated team — called a "Cetacean Desk" — inside the existing Coast Guard vessel traffic control center for the San Francisco Bay area, staffed by no more than two full-time employees. The team's job would be to track the locations of large whales, orcas, and sperm whales in the Bay and the Golden Gate strait, then communicate that information in real time to ship and boat operators to help them avoid hitting or disturbing those animals. The program would also allow authorities to establish local rules about vessel speed, buffer zones around whales, and restricted areas, and it could use new technologies — including artificial intelligence tools — to better detect and predict where whales are located. It would require coordination with California state agencies, Tribal governments, ports, universities, and environmental groups, and it directs the Coast Guard to report to Congress each year on how well the program is working, including how many whale strikes were prevented. The bill primarily affects commercial shipping companies, vessel operators, and the Coast Guard personnel working in the San Francisco Bay region, as well as the whale populations that migrate through that area.

title: Absentee and Mail Voter Protection Act
ai_summary: This bill would cancel a March 2026 executive order signed by President Trump (Executive Order 14399) that dealt with citizenship verification in federal elections, declaring that order to have no legal effect and blocking any federal money from being used to carry it out. Beyond that specific order, the bill also permanently prohibits federal agencies — including the Departments of Homeland Security, Justice, Commerce, and the Social Security Administration — from creating any national voter registration or citizenship database for election purposes, sharing state voter registration lists between federal agencies, or using federal funds to regulate who can vote by mail. It also bars the U.S. Postal Service from refusing to deliver mail-in or absentee ballots or from helping determine whether a voter is eligible to vote by mail. The bill primarily affects federal agencies, the Postal Service, and the roughly 48 million or more Americans who vote by mail or absentee ballot, as well as military members and U.S. citizens abroad who rely on mail-in voting under existing federal law.

title: Countering Russia’s War on Faith Act
ai_summary: This bill would require the Secretary of State and the Secretary of Defense, working with the Director of National Intelligence, to produce a detailed report — within 120 days of passage and once a year for three more years — documenting how Russia has violated the religious freedom of people living in Ukrainian territories it occupies, including actions against Christians, Jews, Muslims (such as Crimean Tatars), and other religious groups not connected to the Russian Orthodox Church. The report must identify destroyed or seized houses of worship, count people who have been imprisoned or displaced because of their faith, and name specific Russian officials or entities responsible for these abuses. After each report is delivered, the President must formally assess whether the named individuals and organizations likely engaged in those abuses, and if the answer is yes, the President is required to impose economic sanctions on those people or groups using existing U.S. sanctions laws. The sanctions can later be lifted if a future report shows the person or entity is no longer engaged in such conduct. The bill primarily affects U.S. government agencies that must carry out the reporting and sanctions, foreign individuals and entities in Russia or Russian-occupied Ukraine who could face financial penalties, and indirectly the religious communities in occupied Ukraine whose situations would be documented.

title: Airpower Acceleration Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill gives the Defense Department the power to sign multi-year purchase contracts for two types of military fighter jets — the F-35 (in its A, B, and C versions) and the F-15EX — and to buy key parts for those planes in bulk ahead of time to save money. It also sets new legal minimums for how many fighter jets the Air Force must keep in its fleet: at least 1,800 total fighters between 2026 and 2035, with specific targets for "combat-ready" aircraft by 2030 and 2035. Separately, the bill allows the Air Force to grow its F-15EX fleet from 129 planes up to 329, but any jets beyond the first 129 must be used specifically to replace the older F-15E aircraft already in service. The people most directly affected are the Air Force, defense contractors and their suppliers who build these aircraft and components, and — more broadly — U.S. military readiness.

title: Patient Refunds for Bad Denials Act of 2026
ai_summary: Starting in 2027, this bill would allow the federal government to fine health insurance companies that deny too many of their customers' medical claims. If an insurer denies 25% or more of claims — not counting denials that are correctly flagged as fraudulent or truly medically unnecessary — it can be fined at least $10 million, with an additional $2 million added for every percentage point above that 25% threshold. The money collected from those fines would be paid back directly to the people who were enrolled in that insurer's plans during the year the violations occurred. The bill also requires insurers to tell patients exactly what medical necessity standards they use and specifically why a claim failed to meet those standards when coverage is denied on that basis, and insurers must report their overall denial rates to the government each year. This bill affects anyone with private health insurance — whether through an employer or purchased individually — as well as the insurance companies that sell those plans.

title: To prohibit the manufacture and conveyance of certain products for children that incorporate an artificial intelligence chatbot, and for other purposes.

title: Energy Consumer Protection Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill gives federal energy regulators — specifically the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) — stronger tools to punish companies or individuals who cheat in the electricity and natural gas markets. If someone is caught manipulating electricity markets or lying about natural gas prices to influence the data that government or private agencies use to set prices, FERC can ban them — temporarily or permanently — from buying or selling electricity, electricity-related financial products, natural gas, or related transmission services. The bill also creates a new explicit rule making it illegal to knowingly report false natural gas price or supply information to government or private reporting agencies with the intent to manipulate those records. These changes primarily affect energy traders, brokers, pipeline companies, and other businesses that participate in wholesale electricity and natural gas markets. Ordinary consumers are not directly regulated by this bill, but could benefit indirectly if stronger enforcement helps prevent the kind of market manipulation that can drive up energy prices.

title: Engineering Biology Readiness Act
ai_summary: This bill does two main things related to protecting the United States from biological threats, particularly those involving "engineering biology" — the deliberate design or modification of living organisms using scientific tools. First, it extends an existing requirement for government officials to give Congress yearly updates on the national strategy for defending against biological threats, pushing the deadline for those briefings several years further into the future. Second, it requires that the next routine government report on biological threats include a specific deep-dive analysis of the dangers posed by engineering biology — such as the potential misuse of gene-editing or synthetic biology — along with concrete recommendations for how the government can better prepare against those dangers, fill gaps in current rules, and reduce overlapping or conflicting efforts across agencies. The report must also recommend any new laws or programs needed, estimate their costs, and suggest ways to support responsible scientific innovation while guarding against misuse. This primarily affects federal agencies involved in national security, public health, and biodefense, as well as researchers and companies in the life sciences, and Congress itself, which would receive and act on the findings.

title: Post-Disaster Protection Act
ai_summary: If the federal government denies or limits your disaster assistance after a declared disaster, this bill gives you more time to challenge that decision. Currently, people have 60 days to file an appeal after receiving an unfavorable assistance ruling; this bill extends that window to 90 days. The change applies to anyone who receives disaster aid — or is denied it — under the federal disaster relief law, which covers things like money for temporary housing, home repairs, and other recovery help after major disasters. The extra 30 days would give disaster survivors more time to gather documents, get help understanding the process, and submit a stronger appeal, especially while they may still be dealing with the immediate aftermath of a disaster.
ai_headline: FEMA disaster aid appeals window extended to 90 days
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8409 extends the disaster aid appeal window from 60 to 90 days for people denied or limited federal assistance.

ai_sections.who: Anyone who applies for federal disaster relief and receives an unfavorable decision — including a denial or a limited award — would have the longer window to appeal.
ai_sections.why: The extra 30 days gives survivors more time to gather documents, understand the process, and submit an appeal while they may still be managing the immediate effects of a disaster.

title: Protecting Moms and Babies Against Climate Change Act
ai_summary: This bill directs the federal Department of Health and Human Services to create several programs aimed at protecting pregnant people, new mothers, and babies under age 3 from health risks linked to climate change — such as extreme heat, air pollution, and severe storms — with a particular focus on communities where these risks are greatest and on reducing racial and ethnic health disparities. It establishes a competitive grant program, funded at up to $100 million over four years, through which groups of local organizations (such as community groups, health clinics, and local governments) can apply for money to provide direct help to vulnerable individuals — including air conditioning units, housing assistance, evacuation support, and mental health counseling — and to train health care workers to recognize and address climate-related risks. A separate, smaller grant program (up to $5 million) funds medical and nursing schools to build climate and maternal health topics into their training programs. The bill also directs the National Institutes of Health to coordinate research across its agencies on how climate change affects pregnant people and infants, and requires the CDC to develop a public strategy for identifying geographic areas where these health risks are especially high, taking into account factors like air quality, poverty, health care access, and race.
ai_headline: HHS would fund climate protections for pregnant women, infants
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

ai_sections.tldr: Senate bill S 4356 would fund local programs and medical training to protect pregnant people and babies from climate-related health risks.

Funded organizations could offer things like air conditioning, housing help, evacuation support, mental health counseling, and training for health care workers. It would also direct federal health agencies to conduct research and identify high-risk areas across the country.
ai_sections.who: The bill focuses on pregnant people, new mothers, and babies under age 3, especially those in communities with greater climate risks and racial or ethnic health disparities. Local organizations such as community groups, health clinics, and local governments could apply for funding, and medical and nursing schools would be eligible for a separate, smaller program.
ai_sections.why: Climate-related events like extreme heat and air pollution can create serious health risks for pregnant people and infants. Without coordinated programs, high-risk communities may have fewer resources to respond to those threats.

title: INSIGHT Act
ai_summary: This bill requires the federal agency that oversees workplace retirement and benefit plans — the Employee Benefit Security Administration (part of the Department of Labor) — to submit annual reports to Congress about two things: the status of its ongoing investigations into potential violations, and any agreements it makes to share information or provide assistance to private lawyers who are suing employers or plan managers on behalf of workers. For each investigation, the report must include when it was opened, when the agency first asked for documents, and whether it was wrapped up within three years — and if not, why not and when it's expected to finish. For any agreements to help private attorneys, the agency must put the arrangement in writing beforehand, notify the employers or plan managers who could be harmed by it, and report detailed records of what information was shared and when. The people most directly affected are employers who sponsor retirement and benefit plans, the plan managers (fiduciaries) who oversee those plans, and private lawyers who may work with the government agency on lawsuits — though workers who participate in those plans are also indirectly affected since the bill aims to make the government's enforcement and legal cooperation activities more transparent to Congress.
ai_headline: EBSA would face new reporting rules on investigations
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

title: Promoting Access to Local Agriculture Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill directs the U.S. Department of Agriculture to make it easier for local farmers and ranchers who sell directly to consumers — such as at farmers markets — to sign up as approved vendors for multiple federal food assistance programs at once, instead of filling out a separate application for each program. The programs covered include SNAP (food stamps), WIC, the Senior Farmers' Market Nutrition Program, and a nutrition incentive program. To reduce this paperwork burden, USDA would either create one single application that works for all these programs, or build a system where getting approved for one program automatically pre-qualifies a farmer for the others. The bill also requires USDA to set up a streamlined way for these farmers to actually process customers' benefits using standardized technology — like a single device or mobile app — and specifically requires that farmers markets and similar direct-to-consumer sellers receive wireless or mobile equipment suited to how they operate.
ai_headline: USDA would unify farmer sign-ups for food aid programs
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Agriculture, and in addition to the Committee on Education and Workforce, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

title: Consumer Protection and Corporate Accountability in Bankruptcy Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill changes the rules around corporate bankruptcy to make it harder for companies to misuse the process at the expense of people with injury or damage claims against them. It allows a bankruptcy court to throw out a company's bankruptcy case if the filing was pointless from the start or made in bad faith — for example, if the company restructured itself specifically to dodge paying victims, moved assets to insiders to avoid debts, or chose a friendly courthouse rather than one it genuinely belongs in. It also prevents bankruptcy courts from blocking lawsuits against related companies (such as parent companies or spinoffs) when those related companies may share responsibility for mass harm claims — like personal injury or contamination cases involving at least 100 people — that stem from a corporate restructuring done in the four years before the bankruptcy filing. The people most directly affected are individuals with injury, environmental, or product-harm claims against large companies, as well as corporations that use complex restructuring tactics (sometimes called "divisional mergers" or "Texas Two-Steps") to try to limit their legal liability through bankruptcy court.
ai_headline: Senate bill tightens rules on corporate bankruptcy abuse
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: This bill makes it harder for companies to use bankruptcy court to escape paying people harmed by their products or actions.

First, courts can dismiss a bankruptcy case if the company filed in bad faith — for example, by restructuring itself to avoid paying victims or moving assets to insiders. Second, bankruptcy courts cannot block lawsuits against related companies, like parent companies or spinoffs, when those companies may share responsibility for mass harm claims involving at least 100 people and linked to a restructuring done within four years before the bankruptcy filing.
ai_sections.who: People with injury, environmental, or product-harm claims against large companies are directly affected. So are corporations that use complex restructuring strategies — sometimes called divisional mergers or Texas Two-Steps — to limit their legal liability through bankruptcy.
ai_sections.why: Without these changes, companies can reorganize themselves specifically to make it harder for victims to collect on legal claims. This bill gives courts more tools to push back on filings that appear designed to shield assets rather than genuinely resolve financial trouble.

title: Dietary Supplement Listing Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill would require companies that make, package, or distribute dietary supplements sold in the United States to register each of their products with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) by submitting key information — including the product's name, ingredients, serving sizes, directions for use, allergen warnings, and a copy of the label. The FDA would then create a publicly searchable online database where consumers could look up this information for any listed supplement, though certain details like contact information for company personnel and the exact amounts of individual ingredients within proprietary blends would be kept confidential. Companies already selling supplements when the law takes effect would have 18 months to complete their listings, while newly launched products would need to be listed before they go on sale. Any supplement sold without a proper listing on file would be considered mislabeled under federal law, meaning the company could face legal consequences. This bill primarily affects dietary supplement manufacturers, distributors, and retailers, while also giving everyday consumers easier access to information about the supplements they buy.
ai_headline: FDA would list all dietary supplements in public database
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8370 would require supplement makers to register each product with the FDA before it can be legally sold in the U.S.

title: Answering the Call Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill directs the federal government to take specific steps to encourage first responders — including police officers, firefighters, emergency medical technicians, and 911 dispatchers — to use the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline when they need mental health support. The Department of Health and Human Services would be required to run outreach campaigns, award grants to fund awareness efforts, train 988 hotline counselors to better understand the unique experiences of first responders, and collect anonymous data to see how well the hotline is actually being used by this group. The bill also establishes a pilot program in which the federal mental health agency and the U.S. Fire Administration would work together with first responder organizations to make sure these outreach efforts are well-suited to the people they're trying to reach. Privacy protections are built in, meaning any data collected cannot identify individual callers and must follow existing federal and state privacy laws. Within three years of the law taking effect, the government would be required to report to Congress on how the pilot program worked.
ai_headline: Federal push to connect first responders with 988 crisis line
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

ai_sections.why: Without this law, there would be no formal federal effort to connect first responders with the 988 crisis line. If passed, Congress would receive a report within three years on how well the pilot program worked.

title: RECOVER Act of 2026
ai_summary: Under current Medicare rules, when a patient receives multiple therapy services (such as physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech therapy) in the same session, Medicare pays the full rate for the first service but reduces payment by 50 percent for additional services provided at the same time. This bill would eliminate that 50 percent payment cut starting January 1, 2027, so that Medicare would pay the full rate for all therapy services provided in a single session, regardless of how many are given at once. The change applies to services billed under both the standard Medicare physician fee schedule and the outpatient therapy and rehabilitation program. The people most directly affected are Medicare patients who need multiple types of therapy at once — such as stroke survivors or people recovering from serious injuries — as well as the therapists and outpatient rehabilitation facilities that treat them, who currently receive reduced reimbursement for those additional services.
ai_headline: Medicare would end therapy payment cuts for combined sessions
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Ways and Means, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.why: Therapists and facilities are currently paid less when they provide more than one therapy in the same session. This bill would change what Medicare pays for those combined sessions.

title: PEARL Act
ai_summary: This bill would allow any licensed pharmacist — whether working for a private pharmacy or a government agency — to refuse to dispense or sell the drugs mifepristone and misoprostol when those drugs are being used for abortion services, if doing so conflicts with the pharmacist's sincerely held religious beliefs. Under this protection, a pharmacist who refuses on those religious grounds could not be penalized in any way, including losing their pharmacy license or having federal funding withheld from their employer. If a pharmacist is nonetheless punished or forced to fill such a prescription despite this protection, the bill gives them the right to sue in federal court to stop that punishment or requirement. The bill affects licensed pharmacists across the country, as well as the employers, licensing boards, and government agencies that currently have authority over pharmacists' professional conduct.
ai_headline: Pharmacists could refuse abortion drug sales on religious grounds
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: Economy of the Future Commission Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill creates a temporary, bipartisan advisory group — made up of 12 members appointed by Congressional leaders plus four nonvoting Deputy Secretaries from the Departments of Education, Labor, Commerce, and Treasury — to study how artificial intelligence is changing the U.S. economy and recommend specific laws Congress could pass in response. The group is required to produce two public reports: a shorter one within 7 months estimating how AI might affect jobs and federal tax revenue over the next 5 to 10 years, and a fuller final report within 13 months with concrete legislative recommendations on topics such as worker retraining, unemployment insurance, education, taxation, manufacturing, transportation safety, and energy demand. The four cabinet departments receiving the final report must each respond with their own written assessment within 60 days. The group shuts down 120 days after it delivers its final report, and the entire effort is funded with $5.25 million set aside for this purpose. This bill most directly affects workers whose jobs could be disrupted by AI, businesses — especially small and medium-sized ones — that use or compete with AI, and policymakers who would act on the group's recommendations.

title: Prison Libraries Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill would create a federal grant program, run by the Attorney General, that gives money to states and U.S. territories to build or improve libraries inside prisons. The grants could pay for things like books, computers, internet access, librarians, educational classes, job training, and cultural programs — all available to incarcerated people at no cost to them. States that apply must show they have a real plan, demonstrate a need based on data about their prison population, and report back each year on how the money was spent. The program is capped at $10 million per year for six years, and no single grant can last longer than six years total.
ai_headline: Senate bill funds prison libraries across U.S. states
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Breast Cancer Stamp Reauthorization Act
ai_summary: This bill extends the life of a special U.S. postage stamp that raises money for breast cancer research. The stamp — called a "semipostal" stamp — costs a little more than a standard stamp, and that extra amount goes toward breast cancer research funding rather than just paying for postage. Under current law, the Postal Service's authority to sell this stamp was set to expire in 2027; this bill would push that deadline to 2037, allowing the stamp to remain on sale for an additional ten years. Anyone who buys postage stamps is potentially affected, since they would continue to have the option to purchase this stamp and contribute to breast cancer research through their everyday mail.

title: Stop Climate Shakedowns Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill would make it illegal for anyone — including state governments, cities, or private citizens — to sue oil, gas, coal, and other fossil fuel companies in either federal or state court for harms connected to climate change, such as flooding, wildfires, or extreme heat. Any such lawsuits already in progress when the bill becomes law would have to be immediately thrown out, and any existing state or local laws designed to make energy companies pay for climate-related costs would be cancelled and made unenforceable. The bill declares that only the federal government — not states, cities, or individuals — has the authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions and climate change. This would affect energy companies (which would be shielded from these types of legal claims), as well as states, cities, and people who might otherwise try to use the courts to seek compensation or other relief for climate-related damages.
ai_headline: Senate bill bars climate suits against fossil fuel firms
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Clean Slate through Consolidation Act
ai_summary: If a federal student loan borrower is in default and then takes out a Federal Direct Consolidation Loan to pay off that defaulted loan, this bill would require the government or whoever holds the loan to ask credit bureaus to remove the default record from the borrower's credit history. In other words, consolidating the defaulted loan would effectively give the borrower a "clean slate" on their credit report for that default, as if it never happened. This affects federal student loan borrowers who have defaulted on loans originally made, insured, or guaranteed under federal student loan programs and who choose to consolidate those loans. Currently, even after a borrower resolves a default through consolidation, the record of that default can remain on their credit report and hurt their credit score — this bill would eliminate that outcome.
ai_headline: Federal loan consolidation would erase default from credit reports
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

ai_sections.who: This affects federal student loan borrowers who have defaulted on loans that were originally made, insured, or guaranteed under federal student loan programs. It applies to those who choose to resolve that default through consolidation.
ai_sections.why: Right now, a default can stay on a borrower's credit report even after they consolidate, which can continue to hurt their credit score. This bill would end that outcome by requiring removal of the default record after consolidation.

title: FAITH Act
ai_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime to charge someone money — or withhold goods, services, or opportunities from someone — because of their religious beliefs, membership in a religious group, or refusal to join one. For example, it would be illegal for any person or organization to impose a fee, fine, or financial penalty on someone simply because they do or don't belong to a particular religion. The punishment ranges from a fine and up to one year in prison for smaller amounts (up to $1,000), up to three years in prison for larger amounts. The bill makes clear that religious organizations and schools can still ask members for voluntary donations for their own internal purposes — that remains fully legal. It also adds this new crime to the list of offenses that can be prosecuted under federal organized crime (RICO) laws, meaning the crime could be pursued as part of a larger criminal enterprise if applicable.
ai_headline: Bill targets financial penalties based on religion
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Drug Origin Transparency Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill requires drug companies to provide more detailed information about where their drugs and drug ingredients come from — and to make that information visible to the public on drug labels. Specifically, manufacturers would have to report to the federal government not just that they made a drug, but also who supplied each ingredient and how much of the drug was made using ingredients from each supplier; these reports could be required up to four times a year instead of just once. In addition, drug labels and accompanying documents would have to show the name, location, and a unique identifying number for the original manufacturer of the drug or its active ingredients, as well as any other companies involved in manufacturing, packing, or distributing it. The people most directly affected are drug manufacturers, ingredient suppliers, and distributors, who would face new reporting and labeling obligations; consumers and pharmacists would benefit from greater visibility into where drugs and their components are actually made. The Food and Drug Administration would be responsible for writing the specific rules that spell out exactly what information must be reported and how it must appear on labels.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: Securing America’s Drug Supply from Communist China Act
ai_summary: This bill would require the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to screen drug applications — both new ones and those submitted since January 1, 2016 — to determine whether the company seeking approval has financial or organizational ties to the Chinese government, Communist Party, or military. If a company is found to have such ties, the FDA would be blocked from approving its drug applications, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection would be required to turn away and destroy any of its drugs already approved and being shipped into the country. Companies flagged under this law would have a chance to prove they've cut those ties or sell their approved drug licenses to an unaffiliated company within 180 days to avoid import bans. There is a limited exception: if blocking a drug would cause or worsen a drug shortage in the United States, Customs could allow it in anyway. title: Hemp Safety Enforcement Act
ai_summary: This bill gives states and Native American tribes the option to step outside the federal hemp regulatory system and run their own rules for growing and selling hemp and hemp-derived products (such as CBD gummies or other cannabinoid goods). Instead of submitting a detailed plan to the U.S. Department of Agriculture and following federal hemp rules, a state or tribe can simply send a notice saying it wants to handle regulation on its own — as long as it requires a minimum age for buying hemp-derived products. Once a state or tribe takes that path, it keeps its own definitions of "hemp" and related products, meaning it can set stricter or different standards than the federal government does. The bill also protects the flow of hemp products across state lines: no state or tribe can block the shipment of hemp goods to or from a self-regulating state or tribe, though products moving between two self-regulating places must follow the rules of both. This affects hemp farmers, hemp product businesses, and consumers in any state or tribal territory that chooses to opt out of the federal program.

title: FLEX Act
ai_summary: This bill changes the federal rules for how money is distributed and used to support charter schools across the country. It adjusts how federal funding is divided among different charter school programs — raising the minimum shares set aside for certain purposes — and allows that money to be used for a broader range of activities, including adding new academic programs or expanding offerings at already high-performing charter schools, not just opening new ones. The bill also makes it easier for charter schools to receive grant money upfront (rather than waiting to be reimbursed), reduces paperwork requirements for schools and the organizations that oversee them, and limits the federal government to issuing only regulations that are strictly necessary. It also requires that states consult with charter school operators before new rules are proposed, and adds a requirement that charter schools receiving federal funds address how their students will get to and from school. The people most directly affected are charter school operators, the state agencies that manage charter school grant programs, and the students who attend or may in the future attend charter schools.

ai_summary: This bill would cancel two specific FCC decisions from 2018 that were designed to speed up the rollout of 5G and other broadband infrastructure by limiting what state and local governments could require from telecommunications companies seeking to install equipment. title: Ending the Carried Interest Loophole Act
ai_summary: This bill changes how certain investment fund managers — such as those who run private equity, hedge, or venture capital funds — are taxed on a special type of pay called "carried interest," which is the share of a fund's profits they receive as compensation for managing the fund. Under current law, that profit share is often taxed at the lower long-term capital gains rate; this bill would instead require those managers to pay ordinary income tax rates on the portion of their profits that exceeds what a normal financial return on their own invested money would produce. To calculate how much of a manager's earnings count as compensation (rather than as a return on investment), the bill uses a formula based on a benchmark interest rate plus nine percentage points applied to the fund's total invested capital. The bill also closes related workarounds, such as using loans from the partnership or restructuring the interest through financial contracts, so that managers cannot avoid the new rules through alternative arrangements. This primarily affects people who earn carried interest from managing investment partnerships — not ordinary investors, employees, or small business owners.
ai_headline: Senate bill targets carried interest tax break for fund managers

title: Pedophile Financial Accountability Act
ai_summary: This bill would require the head of a federal financial watchdog agency — the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), part of the U.S. Treasury Department — to investigate whether banks and their employees broke federal anti-money laundering laws in connection with financial transactions involving Jeffrey Epstein. The investigation would specifically look at whether banks, including JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America, were too slow to file required reports on suspicious transactions, failed to question large payments involving Epstein and certain wealthy individuals named in the bill, and whether senior bank executives allowed employees to keep doing business with Epstein even after the banks had dropped him as a client due to money laundering concerns. Within 100 days of the bill becoming law, FinCEN would have to deliver a report to Congress on what it found, and that report could include information drawn from confidential suspicious activity reports filed about Epstein-related transactions. If the investigation uncovers evidence that any bank employee may have willfully broken federal anti-money laundering laws, FinCEN would be required to refer those individuals to the U.S. Attorney General for possible further legal action.

title: HERO Child Care for Military Families Act
ai_summary: This bill takes several steps to make child care more available and reliable for military families. It allows national service volunteers (such as AmeriCorps participants) trained in education to work at military child development centers, lets two part-time workers split a single full-time child care job (working at least 20 hours each per week), and creates a system where people can complete their background checks and health screenings *before* a job opening exists, so hiring can happen faster when spots do open up. Child care workers at military centers could also gain access to certain on-base benefits — such as commissary and exchange privileges, fitness centers, tuition assistance, and referral bonuses — if the Defense Department decides those benefits are needed to attract and keep qualified staff. The bill also requires the Defense Department to build a nationwide data system tracking child care capacity, staffing vacancies, waitlists, and unmet need across all military installations, and to report to Congress on the connection between child care availability and military readiness, troop retention, and military spouse employment. The people most directly affected are military families seeking child care, current and prospective child care workers at military installations, and military spouses.

title: YouthBuild for the Future Act
ai_summary: This bill continues federal funding for the YouthBuild program, which helps young people from disadvantaged backgrounds earn a high school diploma or GED, learn job skills, and work on building or repairing affordable housing in their communities. It updates the program in several ways: it sets aside a portion of funding specifically for programs in rural areas and for Native American, Alaska Native, and Native Hawaiian communities; it allows programs to provide meals, help participants sign up for federal benefits like food stamps and childcare assistance, and offer extra support for participants with disabilities. It also requires the federal government to consult regularly with YouthBuild programs when setting performance goals, and directs states to help programs access wage data to track how participants are doing after the program. A new grant program is created to help YouthBuild programs partner with local employers — with preference given to partnerships involving union apprenticeship programs — to connect participants to real jobs. Funding levels for the existing YouthBuild program are set at roughly $159 million to $204 million per year from 2027 through 2032, with an additional $20 million per year available for the new employer partnership grants.

title: DEPORT Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill adds new terrorism-related requirements and consequences to the process by which immigrants become U.S. citizens. Anyone applying for citizenship after the law takes effect would have to sign a sworn statement — under penalty of perjury — confirming they have not been convicted of, or had charges pending for, a specific list of terrorism-related crimes, and that they do not intend to commit such crimes in the future; that same promise would also be added to the citizenship oath. If a naturalized citizen is later convicted of any of those terrorism-related crimes, the government can go to court to strip them of their citizenship (a process called denaturalization), and if that happens, they can be deported and are permanently barred from re-entering the country. People who were naturalized before this law passes are also affected: if they are convicted of one of the listed crimes within a certain number of years after their naturalization, that conviction can be used as evidence that they were never eligible for citizenship in the first place. The bill also makes any non-citizen convicted of these crimes ineligible for virtually all immigration benefits — including green cards, asylum, and temporary protections — with no exceptions or waivers allowed.

title: Buy American Seafood Act
ai_summary: This bill would require the federal government to buy only American-caught or American-produced seafood when purchasing fish and other seafood for a wide range of federal food programs — including school lunches and breakfasts, emergency food assistance, military food services, and disaster relief food programs. To qualify as "American," the seafood must be caught in U.S. waters by a U.S.-registered fishing vessel, or raised and processed in the United States through fish farming or domestic processing operations. Agencies could be granted a waiver to buy foreign seafood only if the U.S. supply is not large enough or does not meet required food safety and quality standards — and any such waiver must be publicly reported within 30 days. The bill primarily affects federal agencies that purchase food, seafood suppliers and distributors who sell to the government, and the millions of people who receive food through these federal programs, such as schoolchildren, disaster survivors, and military personnel.

title: Ensuring Access to Lower-Cost Medicines for Seniors Act
ai_summary: Starting in 2028, this bill would require Medicare prescription drug plans to automatically include lower-cost generic drugs and biosimilar medicines on their covered drug lists whenever a brand-name version of that drug is already covered and the generic or biosimilar costs less. Plans would also have to place those generics and biosimilars on their own separate, cheaper cost-sharing tier — meaning seniors would pay noticeably less out of pocket for them compared to brand-name drugs, with copayments at least $20 lower than the cheapest brand-name tier. Insurance plans could not make it harder to access a generic or biosimilar than its brand-name counterpart by using tools like prior authorization or step therapy requirements that favor the brand-name version. The bill affects Medicare beneficiaries enrolled in Part D prescription drug plans or Medicare Advantage plans with drug coverage, as well as the insurance companies that run those plans, which would be required to restructure their drug lists and pricing tiers to comply with these new rules.

title: No Big Fossil Bailouts on Your Power Bill Act
ai_summary: This bill places new limits on a federal agency's power to order fossil fuel power plants — like coal or natural gas plants — to keep running during energy emergencies. Under current law, that agency (the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission) can issue emergency orders with few restrictions; this bill would generally prohibit using that authority to delay or prevent a power plant from closing, unless no other option exists to handle the emergency *and* the relevant regional grid operator formally requests the delay in writing. Before issuing or renewing such an emergency order, the Commission would be required to hold a public hearing, consider environmentally friendlier alternatives, check whether the order would raise electricity rates, and consult with state and local regulators. Power companies affected by an order would have to notify their customers in writing — within 60 days — explaining the order's impact and any extra costs for fuel, maintenance, or labor that customers may end up paying. The bill primarily affects the federal Commission, fossil fuel power plant owners, regional electric grid operators, state regulators, and ordinary electricity customers who might see changes in their power bills as a result of these emergency orders.

title: Medication Competition Act
ai_summary: This bill requires the federal health agency (the Department of Health and Human Services) to publicly post clear deadlines showing how long a biological drug — such as a vaccine, insulin, or other complex medicine made from living cells — is protected from competition by similar cheaper versions called biosimilars. Right now, these protection periods (called "exclusivity periods") are not always publicly listed in a timely way, which can make it harder for biosimilar manufacturers to know when they are legally allowed to enter the market. Under this bill, for newly approved drugs, the agency must post that information within 30 days of when the expiration date can first be determined; for drugs already on the market before the law takes effect, the agency has either 30 days from when the date becomes known or up to 2 years to post it. The bill primarily affects drug companies that make biosimilars, companies that make the original biological drugs, and ultimately patients and insurers who may benefit from lower-cost competition once those protection periods expire.

title: Special Operations Forces Concealed Carry Act
ai_summary: This bill would allow certain current and former U.S. military special operations personnel to carry a concealed firearm across the country, similar to a right that already exists for retired law enforcement officers under federal law. To qualify, a service member must have served in one of several specific elite units or roles — such as Army Special Forces, Navy SEALs, Army Rangers, Marine Corps Recon or Scout Snipers, or Air Force special operations specialties — and must have held a rank from E-5 (Sergeant/Petty Officer 2nd Class) through the highest officer grades. The carry authority is permanent as long as the person maintains an honorable discharge, stays eligible under federal law to own a firearm, and carries proper identification proving their service; it ends immediately if any of those conditions are no longer met. Unlike retired law enforcement officers, qualifying special operators would not need to pass an annual firearms recertification test. The Departments of Defense and Veterans Affairs would be required to create an ID card program to verify and document eligibility, and the Attorney General would issue guidance to law enforcement agencies explaining how to recognize valid proof of authority to carry.

title: Millionaires Surtax Act
ai_summary: This bill would add an extra 10% tax on top of existing federal income taxes for individuals, estates, and trusts — but only on the portion of their income above a certain threshold. For married couples filing jointly and surviving spouses, the extra tax kicks in on income above $2,000,000; for all other filers (such as single individuals), the threshold is $1,000,000. For example, a single filer with $1,200,000 in qualifying income would owe the extra 10% only on the $200,000 above the $1,000,000 cutoff — not on their entire income. A few specific situations are treated differently: Americans living abroad, nonresident aliens, and certain charitable trusts have special rules that may reduce or eliminate what they owe under this new tax. The changes would take effect starting with the 2027 tax year.
