The GAO must also recommend a standard definition for "workforce housing" and analyze how existing or new programs could be adjusted to serve this group.
ai_sections.who: The bill focuses on middle-income households, defined as families earning between 80% and 120% of the median family income in their area. It does not create new programs or send money to anyone.
ai_sections.why: Without a study, Congress lacks a clear picture of where middle-income families are struggling most and which federal tools, if any, could help them. The report gives lawmakers a fact-based starting point if they choose to act later.

press_names: Housing for America's Middle Class Act

title: HOME Expansion Act
ai_summary: This bill makes three main changes to a federal program that helps communities fund affordable housing. First, it allows smaller towns and rural areas that don't already receive a separate type of federal community development funding to use HOME program money to fix or install nearby infrastructure — like water lines, sewer systems, sidewalks, and roads — as long as that infrastructure is directly connected to affordable housing in the area. Second, it raises the maximum price at which a home can be sold and still count as "affordable" under the program, changing the limit from 95% to 110% of the area's median purchase price, which means slightly more expensive homes can qualify. Third, it creates two new exceptions to the income rules for homeowners: military members who are deployed far from home or receive permanent reassignment orders can temporarily have their income requirements waived, and family members who inherit a HOME-assisted home can keep its affordable housing status as long as they live there as their primary residence and take on the original owner's obligations under the program.
ai_headline: Senate bill expands HOME affordable housing program rules
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

ai_sections.tldr: The HOME Expansion Act lets small towns use housing funds for nearby infrastructure, raises the home price limit, and adds income rule exceptions for military and heirs.
ai_sections.what: This bill changes three rules in the federal HOME program, which helps communities fund affordable housing. Small towns and rural areas without certain other federal funding could use HOME money for nearby water lines, sewers, sidewalks, and roads tied directly to affordable housing. It also raises the top sale price a home can have and still count as affordable, from 95% to 110% of the local median purchase price, and creates income rule exceptions for deployed or reassigned military members and for family members who inherit a HOME-assisted home.
ai_sections.who: Small towns and rural areas, military service members who are deployed or permanently reassigned, and family members who inherit a HOME-assisted home are directly affected. Local governments that run HOME program projects would also work under the updated rules.
ai_sections.why: Raising the price limit means homes that cost a little more than before can now qualify as affordable under the program. The military and inheritance exceptions mean fewer people would lose their housing status due to deployment or a family member's death.

title: End Veteran Homelessness Act of 2025
ai_summary: This bill makes several changes to the HUD-VASH program, a federal program that provides rental vouchers and support services to help homeless veterans find and keep housing. It clarifies that case managers — staff who connect veterans to housing, health care, and other benefits — should be assigned only to veterans who actually need that help, and requires that the most vulnerable veterans (such as those with serious mental illness, substance abuse disorders, or physical disabilities) be helped first. The bill also adds new protections so that veterans who decline case management cannot lose their rental vouchers or be evicted solely for that reason, and it allows veterans who don't need case management at all to still use a voucher. Finally, it requires the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of Housing and Urban Development to submit annual reports to Congress tracking how the program is working — including how many vouchers are being used, who is being served, and what barriers exist — and directs the Government Accountability Office to conduct an independent study of the program within one year.
ai_headline: Bill updates rules for HUD-VASH homeless veteran vouchers
last_action_text: Forwarded by Subcommittee to Full Committee by Voice Vote.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 1957 updates the HUD-VASH housing voucher program so veterans can't lose housing aid just for declining case management.
ai_sections.what: This bill changes how the HUD-VASH program works. It requires that the most vulnerable veterans — such as those with serious mental illness, substance use disorders, or physical disabilities — be helped first. It also protects veterans from losing their rental vouchers or being evicted just because they declined case management services.
ai_sections.who: Homeless veterans who receive housing vouchers through the HUD-VASH program are directly affected. Case managers, the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Department of Housing and Urban Development, and the Government Accountability Office all have new responsibilities under this bill.
ai_sections.why: Without these changes, some veterans could lose housing vouchers for reasons unrelated to whether they actually needed case management. Congress would also have less information about how well the program is working, since the reporting requirements are currently not in place.

title: Tribal Conservation Priorities Inclusion Act
ai_summary: This bill changes existing federal farm conservation law to formally include Indian Tribes alongside state and local governments when it comes to identifying and addressing priority conservation needs on agricultural land. Right now, several federal programs — which pay farmers and landowners to adopt environmentally friendly practices like improving water quality, reducing erosion, or protecting wildlife habitat — allow state and local governments to help set the conservation priorities for their areas, but do not explicitly mention tribal governments or tribal lands. This bill adds tribes and tribal lands to those programs so that tribal governments can have the same standing as states and localities in shaping conservation goals for land within their territories. The people most directly affected are tribal governments and people who farm or manage land on tribal lands, who would gain clearer access to these conservation programs and a recognized voice in setting their priorities.
ai_headline: Tribal governments gain standing in USDA farm conservation programs
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Conservation, Research, and Biotechnology.

ai_sections.tldr: This bill would give tribal governments the same official role as states in setting farm conservation priorities on tribal lands.
ai_sections.what: This bill updates federal farm conservation law to formally include Indian Tribes alongside state and local governments. It adds tribes and tribal lands to existing programs that pay farmers and landowners to use environmentally friendly practices on agricultural land.
ai_sections.who: Tribal governments would gain a recognized voice in shaping conservation goals for land within their territories. Farmers and landowners who work on tribal lands would also gain clearer access to these federal conservation programs.
ai_sections.why: Right now, tribal governments are not explicitly named in these programs, meaning they lack the same standing as states and local governments. This bill changes that by putting tribal governments on equal footing when conservation priorities are identified and addressed.

title: Superfund Area Facts and Exposure Act
ai_summary: This bill directs the Government Accountability Office (GAO) — the federal government's independent research and auditing agency — to count how many homes are located within one mile of federally designated Superfund sites, which are places the government has identified as seriously contaminated with hazardous materials. The study must separately count how many of those nearby homes are public housing units. Within six months of the bill becoming law, the GAO must deliver its findings to Congress in a written report. The bill affects anyone who lives near a Superfund site, particularly residents of public housing, and it gives lawmakers factual data about how many people may be living close to these contaminated areas.
ai_headline: GAO ordered to map homes near Superfund sites
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

ai_sections.tldr: Congress would require a federal study counting how many homes—including public housing—sit within one mile of Superfund contamination sites.
ai_sections.what: This bill tells the Government Accountability Office (GAO), the federal government's independent research agency, to count homes located within one mile of federally designated Superfund sites. The count must separately identify how many of those homes are public housing units. The GAO must deliver a written report to Congress within six months of the bill becoming law.
ai_sections.who: This affects people who live near Superfund sites, especially residents of public housing close to those contaminated areas. Lawmakers would receive the resulting data.
ai_sections.why: Congress would have factual numbers about how many people may be living near seriously contaminated sites. That information could inform future decisions about those areas.

press_names: Superfund Area Facts and Exposure Act

title: To designate the facility of the United States Postal Service located at 4431 Main Street in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, as the "Dr. Constance 'Connie' E. Clayton Post Office".
ai_summary: This bill gives an official honorary name to a specific post office building. If passed, the U.S. Postal Service facility at 4431 Main Street in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, would be officially renamed the "Dr. Constance 'Connie' E. Clayton Post Office." Any official government documents, maps, or records that refer to that building would use the new name going forward. The bill does not change how the post office operates, affect its services, or involve any spending — it is purely a naming designation. It mainly affects how that single Philadelphia post office is identified in official government records.
ai_headline: Philadelphia post office renamed for Dr. Connie Clayton
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7532 would officially rename a Philadelphia post office after Dr. Constance "Connie" E. Clayton.
ai_sections.what: This bill would give an official honorary name to the U.S. Postal Service building at 4431 Main Street in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. It would be called the "Dr. Constance 'Connie' E. Clayton Post Office." Official government documents and records referring to that building would use the new name going forward.
ai_sections.who: This bill directly affects how one Philadelphia post office is identified in official government records.
ai_sections.why: The post office would carry a new official name in government documents and maps. The bill does not change how the post office operates or the services it provides.

title: Jaime’s Law
ai_summary: This bill would require background checks for ammunition purchases, extending the same system already used for firearm purchases. Under the bill, when one private individual wants to sell or give ammunition to another private individual, the transaction must first go through a federally licensed gun dealer, importer, or manufacturer, who runs a background check to make sure the buyer is legally allowed to have ammunition. If the buyer is prohibited under federal or state law — for example, due to a felony conviction — the sale cannot proceed. The bill includes exceptions for certain situations, such as temporary transfers between family members, loans at shooting ranges, transfers needed to prevent imminent harm, and use during hunting or fishing when the transferor has no reason to believe the recipient will misuse the ammunition. The bill affects anyone who buys or sells ammunition privately, as well as licensed dealers who would take on the role of processing these checks, and it explicitly states it does not create a national ammunition registry.
ai_headline: Bill would extend background checks to ammunition sales
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7564 would require a background check before any private sale or gift of ammunition, using the same system as gun purchases.
ai_sections.what: This bill would extend background checks to ammunition purchases, including private sales between individuals. The check would be run by a licensed gun dealer, importer, or manufacturer. Some transfers are exempt, such as loans at shooting ranges, transfers between family members, situations to prevent immediate harm, and certain hunting and fishing uses.
ai_sections.who: Anyone who buys or sells ammunition privately would need to follow the new process. Licensed gun dealers would take on the responsibility of running the checks.
ai_sections.why: People prohibited by federal or state law from having ammunition, such as those with felony convictions, could not complete a purchase. The bill states that it does not create a national ammunition registry.

title: United States-Cuba Trade Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill would end the decades-long U.S. trade embargo against Cuba by repealing or removing a wide range of laws and regulations that have restricted trade, travel, and financial dealings between the two countries. If enacted, Americans would be free to travel to Cuba and spend money there without special government permission, U.S. companies could sell goods and services to Cuba and install telecommunications equipment on the island, and money transfers (remittances) to Cuba would no longer be capped at a limited amount. Cuban goods would be treated the same as goods from most other countries when it comes to U.S. import taxes, and U.S. phone and internet carriers could operate between the two countries. The bill also directs the President to pursue negotiations with Cuba over property that was seized from U.S. citizens and over human rights protections, and requires a report to Congress on U.S.-Cuba trade within a year and a half of passage.
ai_headline: Bill would repeal U.S. trade embargo against Cuba
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Foreign Affairs, and in addition to the Committees on Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, the Judiciary, Agriculture, and Financial Services, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7521 would end the U.S. trade embargo on Cuba, letting Americans travel, spend, and do business there freely.
ai_sections.what: This bill would lift the long-standing U.S. trade embargo against Cuba by removing many laws that have blocked trade, travel, and money transfers between the two countries. Americans could travel to Cuba freely, U.S. companies could sell goods and services there, and remittances to Cuba would no longer be capped. Cuban goods would be taxed the same as goods from most other countries, and U.S. phone and internet carriers could operate between the two nations.
ai_sections.who: The bill would affect American travelers, U.S. businesses, phone and internet carriers, and people who send money to Cuba. It also directs the President to negotiate with Cuba on property claims and human rights, and requires a report to Congress within a year and a half of passage.
ai_sections.why: If passed, the rules that have limited contact between the U.S. and Cuba for decades would no longer apply. Americans and U.S. companies would have new legal freedom to travel, trade, and communicate with Cuba.

title: SPARK Act
ai_summary: This bill directs the Small Business Administration (SBA) to create two new programs that support small business incubators and accelerators — organizations that help early-stage businesses grow — specifically in communities that have historically had less access to business resources. The first program would have the SBA sign funding agreements with qualifying organizations (such as nonprofits, community lenders, minority banks, and community colleges) to run 5-year projects offering free mentorship, counseling, and business development services to startups and small businesses, with each funded organization receiving at least $500,000 per year. The second program would give those same types of organizations up to $1 million per year (or up to $500,000 for organizations not in the first program) to pass along as small grants (capped at $20,000 each) or low-interest loans directly to qualifying small businesses — at no fee to the business owner. Both programs are aimed at helping entrepreneurs who are women, racial minorities, veterans, people with disabilities, formerly incarcerated individuals, rural residents, or located in economically distressed areas, and the SBA would be required to track outcomes, report to Congress annually, and set up rules to prevent fraud.
ai_headline: SBA bill targets incubator funding for underserved communities
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship.

ai_sections.tldr: The SPARK Act would create two SBA programs funding incubators and small grants for entrepreneurs in underserved communities.
ai_sections.what: This bill directs the Small Business Administration to create two new programs. The first would fund organizations to offer free mentorship, counseling, and business development services to startups over five-year projects. The second would let those same organizations pass along small grants of up to $20,000 each, or low-interest loans, directly to qualifying small businesses at no cost to the owner.
ai_sections.who: Eligible funding recipients include nonprofits, community lenders, minority banks, and community colleges. The programs are aimed at entrepreneurs who are women, racial minorities, veterans, people with disabilities, formerly incarcerated individuals, rural residents, or located in economically distressed areas.
ai_sections.why: These programs would direct business support resources toward communities that have historically had less access to them. The SBA would be required to track outcomes, report to Congress annually, and set up rules to prevent fraud.
ai_sections.cost: Organizations in the first program would receive at least $500,000 per year. Organizations in the second program could receive up to $1 million per year, or up to $500,000 if they are not also in the first program.

title: Stop Price Gouging in Grocery Stores Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill would place new rules on grocery stores and other retail food sellers, making it illegal for them to charge prices that are far above what those items normally cost — a practice it calls "price gouging" — and also making it illegal for stores to use customers' personal information (such as data gathered by cameras or facial recognition technology) to charge different people different prices for the same item. Stores larger than 10,000 square feet would be required to use traditional physical price tags (like paper stickers or shelf labels) instead of electronic digital price displays. If a store uses facial recognition cameras, it must post a clear sign at the entrance telling customers about it, and any use of a customer's biometric data (like a fingerprint or face scan) requires the customer's written consent and strict limits on how that data can be shared. People who are harmed by these practices can sue the store directly in federal court, state attorneys general can bring cases on behalf of residents, and the Federal Trade Commission would be responsible for enforcing the law and writing the specific rules that define when a price crosses the line into illegal territory.
ai_headline: Senate bill targets grocery price gouging and biometric data use
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

ai_sections.tldr: Grocery stores could face federal rules banning price gouging, personalized pricing based on your data, and most electronic price tags.
ai_sections.what: This bill would make it illegal for grocery stores to charge prices far above normal or to use personal data like facial scans to charge different customers different prices. Stores larger than 10,000 square feet would have to use physical price tags instead of electronic displays. Stores using facial recognition cameras must post a notice at the entrance, and collecting biometric data like fingerprints or face scans would require a customer's written permission.
ai_sections.who: The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the law and set the specific rules defining when a price counts as illegal. State attorneys general could take stores to court on behalf of residents, and individual customers who are harmed could also sue in federal court.
ai_sections.why: Stores that break these rules could face lawsuits from customers, legal action from their state, or enforcement by the federal government. Customers would have new legal tools to challenge pricing practices and the collection of their personal data.

press_names: Stop Price Gouging in Grocery Stores Act

title: After Hours Child Care Act
ai_summary: This bill would create a new federal pilot program, run by the Department of Health and Human Services, to help working parents who have jobs outside normal 9-to-5 weekday hours — such as evening, night, or weekend shifts — find and afford child care. Through the program, grants of between $25,000 and $500,000 would be awarded competitively over five-year periods to child care providers, businesses, or partnerships of those organizations to start new child care programs, expand existing ones, improve facilities, hire staff, or help providers meet licensing and safety requirements. To receive a grant, organizations must cover 25 percent of the costs themselves, with the federal government paying the remaining 75 percent. The program is designed to benefit parents who struggle to find child care during nonstandard hours, with the goal of helping them stay employed, earn promotions, and build savings. At least every two years, the department would be required to report to Congress on how many children were served and how the grants affected child care availability.
ai_headline: HHS pilot would fund odd-hours child care grants
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7498 would fund a federal pilot program giving grants to child care providers who serve parents working evenings, nights, or weekends.
ai_sections.what: This bill would create a federal pilot program run by the Department of Health and Human Services. It would award competitive grants to child care providers, businesses, or partnerships to start, expand, or improve child care options for parents who work outside standard weekday hours.
ai_sections.who: Working parents with evening, night, or weekend shifts who struggle to find child care would be the intended beneficiaries. Child care providers, businesses, and partnerships between those organizations could apply for grants.
ai_sections.why: Without child care during nonstandard hours, some parents may have difficulty staying employed or advancing at work. The program is meant to address a gap in care availability during hours when most providers are closed.
ai_sections.cost: Grants would range from $25,000 to $500,000 and run over five-year periods. Organizations receiving grants must pay 25 percent of costs themselves, with the federal government covering the remaining 75 percent. The Department of Health and Human Services would also be required to report to Congress on program outcomes at least every two years.

title: To amend the Food, Agriculture, Conservation, and Trade Act of 1990 to ensure adequate staffing and resources for the Institute of Tropical Forestry and the Institute of Pacific Islands Forestry.
ai_summary: This bill would require the federal government to maintain minimum staffing levels at two U.S. Forest Service research facilities — the Institute of Tropical Forestry in Puerto Rico and the Institute of Pacific Islands Forestry in Hawaii. Specifically, the Secretary of Agriculture would be required by law to keep at least 50 employees at the Puerto Rico institute and at least 30 employees at the Pacific Islands institute, along with enough resources for both locations to meaningfully carry out their scientific research, demonstration projects, and sharing of forestry knowledge. The bill primarily affects federal agency staffing decisions and the communities, scientists, and land managers in Puerto Rico and the Pacific Islands who rely on the research and expertise these institutes provide. Currently, the law contains no such minimum staffing requirements, so this change would set a legal floor that the government must meet.
ai_headline: Bill sets minimum staffing floors for two Forest Service labs
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7518 would set minimum staff levels at two Forest Service research institutes: 50 in Puerto Rico, 30 in Hawaii.
ai_sections.what: This bill would require the federal government to keep at least 50 employees at the Institute of Tropical Forestry in Puerto Rico and at least 30 at the Institute of Pacific Islands Forestry in Hawaii. It would also require both locations to have enough resources to carry out research, demonstration projects, and sharing of forestry knowledge. Right now, no such minimums exist in law.
ai_sections.who: This bill affects the U.S. Forest Service and the Secretary of Agriculture, who would be legally required to meet the new staffing floors. Scientists, land managers, and communities in Puerto Rico and the Pacific Islands who rely on these institutes would also be affected.
ai_sections.why: Without minimum staffing requirements, these institutes could be reduced in size, which could limit the research and expertise available to people in those regions. This bill would set a legal floor that the government must stay at or above.

title: Airborne Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill creates a new federal tax credit for businesses, public entities, and nonprofit organizations that improve the air quality inside their buildings. Owners of commercial properties, government-owned buildings, and 501(c)(3) nonprofits could claim a credit of $1 per square foot for getting a professional indoor air quality assessment, $5 per square foot for installing or repairing an air cleaning system, and $50 per square foot for upgrading a heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) system — with those per-square-foot amounts jumping to $25 and $250 respectively if the installation work meets federal prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements. To qualify, any air cleaning or HVAC upgrade must be professionally certified as meeting specific industry ventilation standards and must have followed an indoor air quality assessment first. The credit for upgrades is capped at 50 percent of what the taxpayer actually spent on those improvements, and the credit for assessments is capped at the actual cost of the assessment. The bill also directs the Department of Energy to set up a voluntary certification program so property owners can formally verify their buildings meet the required air quality standards.
ai_headline: New tax credits target indoor air quality upgrades in commercial buildings
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7460 offers businesses, governments, and nonprofits a federal tax credit for improving indoor air quality in their buildings.
ai_sections.what: This bill creates a federal tax credit for improving indoor air quality in commercial, government, and nonprofit buildings. Credits range from $1 per square foot for an air quality assessment up to $50 per square foot for an HVAC upgrade, with higher amounts available if the work meets federal wage and apprenticeship rules. Any air cleaning or HVAC upgrade must be professionally certified and must follow an assessment first. The bill also directs the Department of Energy to create a voluntary certification program for buildings that meet the required air quality standards.
ai_sections.who: Owners of commercial properties, government-owned buildings, and 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations may claim the credit. The Department of Energy is directed to set up the voluntary certification program.
ai_sections.why: Tax credits reduce what a qualifying property owner owes in federal taxes. Meeting the higher credit amounts requires following federal prevailing wage and apprenticeship standards during installation work.
ai_sections.cost: Credits for upgrades are capped at 50 percent of what the taxpayer actually spent on those improvements. Credits for assessments are capped at the actual cost of the assessment.

title: SELF DRIVE Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill sets new federal safety rules for cars and trucks that can drive themselves — vehicles equipped with what the bill calls "automated driving systems" (self-driving technology at higher levels of automation). Companies that make or sell these self-driving vehicles in the United States would be required to prepare a detailed "safety case" — a documented explanation of how their system works, what conditions it's designed to handle, how it responds to emergencies and vulnerable people like pedestrians and cyclists, and how it protects against hacking — and must provide that document to federal transportation officials upon request. The bill also creates a national database where manufacturers must report serious crashes involving self-driving systems within a set time window, and requires them to regularly report how many miles their vehicles have traveled with the self-driving system active. States and cities would generally be blocked from creating their own conflicting rules about the design or sale of these vehicles, though they would keep their existing authority over traffic laws, vehicle registration, insurance, and similar matters. The bill also directs federal officials to review existing rules about the security of connected vehicles and report back to Congress.
ai_headline: Federal safety rules set for self-driving vehicles
last_action_text: Forwarded by Subcommittee to Full Committee by the Yeas and Nays: 12 - 11.

ai_sections.tldr: Federal law would set uniform safety rules for self-driving vehicles, blocking states from adding their own design or sales requirements.
ai_sections.what: This bill creates new federal safety rules for vehicles that use automated driving systems. Companies would have to file a detailed safety document covering how their system works, handles emergencies, protects pedestrians and cyclists, and guards against hacking. A national crash database and mileage reporting system would also be created.
ai_sections.who: Companies that make or sell self-driving vehicles in the United States would have to follow these rules. Federal transportation officials would receive and review safety documents and crash reports, and states and cities would lose the ability to set their own rules on the design or sale of these vehicles.
ai_sections.why: Without a single national standard, self-driving vehicle rules vary by state, which this bill would change by placing that authority at the federal level. States would keep control over traffic laws, registration, and insurance, but not over how these vehicles are designed or sold.

title: Disaster Zone Energy Affordability and Investment Act
ai_summary: This bill lets certain businesses that already have unused energy tax credits — credits they earned in prior years but couldn't fully use — sell or transfer those credits to other taxpayers, as long as the business is spending money to operate in an area hit by a federally declared disaster or a governor-declared state disaster that occurred after December 31, 2023. Under current tax law, businesses can "carry forward" unused energy-related tax credits to future tax returns, but those carryforwards generally cannot be sold or transferred to someone else; this bill creates an exception for disaster-affected businesses. The amount that can be transferred is capped at whatever the business actually spends on its operations in the disaster area, and those qualifying expenses must be made within two years after the disaster declaration. This primarily affects businesses — not individual households — that hold unused general business energy credits and are rebuilding or continuing operations in a federally or state-recognized disaster zone.
ai_headline: Disaster-hit businesses could sell unused energy tax credits
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: Businesses in disaster zones could sell unused energy tax credits, up to the amount they spend operating in that area within two years.
ai_sections.what: This bill creates an exception to current tax law that normally prevents businesses from selling or transferring unused energy tax credits. Businesses in federally or governor-declared disaster zones that happened after December 31, 2023 could transfer those credits to other taxpayers. The amount transferred cannot exceed what the business actually spends on operations in the disaster area within two years of the disaster declaration.
ai_sections.who: This applies to businesses, not individual households, that already hold unused general business energy credits. To qualify, those businesses must be spending money to operate in a federally or state-recognized disaster zone.
ai_sections.why: Under current law, unused energy credits can be carried forward to future tax returns but cannot be sold or transferred. This bill would allow disaster-affected businesses to convert those otherwise stuck credits into value by transferring them.

press_names: Disaster Zone Energy Affordability and Investment Act

title: Community Health Center Drug Pricing Protection Act
ai_summary: This bill requires that when community health clinics (known as federally qualified health centers) buy outpatient prescription drugs, they must be charged the discounted "340B" price **at the moment of purchase** — they cannot be made to pay full price upfront and wait for a refund or rebate later. The 340B program is an existing federal program that entitles certain safety-net health providers to buy drugs at significantly reduced prices, but some drug manufacturers have required these clinics to pay higher prices at the register and then seek reimbursement afterward. This bill closes that gap by prohibiting the federal government from signing agreements with drug manufacturers that allow any such "pay full price now, get money back later" arrangement. The people most directly affected are the low-income and underserved patients who rely on federally qualified health centers, since these clinics depend on immediate drug cost savings to stretch their budgets and serve their communities. The rule applies to drug purchases made from the day the law is enacted and also affects agreements with manufacturers that are already in place.
ai_headline: Bill requires upfront 340B discounts at health clinics
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

ai_sections.tldr: This bill requires drug companies to charge community health clinics the discounted 340B price upfront, not after a rebate process.
ai_sections.what: This bill requires that federally qualified health centers pay the discounted 340B drug price at the time of purchase. Drug manufacturers would no longer be allowed to charge full price at the register and refund the difference later. The rule applies to new drug purchases starting on the day the law takes effect and also applies to existing agreements with manufacturers.
ai_sections.who: Federally qualified health centers, which are community health clinics that serve low-income and underserved patients, are directly affected. The patients who rely on these clinics are also affected, since the clinics depend on immediate savings to fund their services.
ai_sections.why: Without upfront discounts, clinics must spend money they may not have and wait to get it back, which can strain their budgets. That strain can affect how well clinics are able to serve their communities.

press_names: Community Health Center Drug Pricing Protection Act

title: Purchased and Referred Care Improvement Act of 2025
ai_summary: This bill strengthens protections for Native American patients who receive health care from outside doctors or hospitals that the Indian Health Service (IHS) has approved and referred them to. Under current law, patients are already not supposed to be billed personally for this care, but this bill makes that protection apply no matter what paperwork a patient may have signed, and it also extends that protection to debt collectors — not just the original provider. The bill also requires the IHS to notify both the patient and the outside provider within 5 business days that the patient owes nothing, and it creates a process for patients who paid out of pocket to be reimbursed by the IHS within 30 days of submitting their paperwork, either online or in person. Finally, the bill replaces the older term "contract health services" with "purchased/referred care" throughout federal health law, and it directs the government to update its manuals, contracts, and official documents to match the new rules within set timeframes.
ai_headline: Senate bill shields Native Americans from IHS referral bills
last_action_text: Committee on Indian Affairs. Hearings held.

ai_sections.tldr: Native American patients referred to outside doctors by IHS cannot be billed personally for that care, even if they signed paperwork saying otherwise.
ai_sections.what: This bill protects Native American patients from being billed for outside medical care that the Indian Health Service approved and arranged. The protection applies even if a patient signed forms, and it covers debt collectors, not just the original provider. Patients who already paid out of pocket can request reimbursement from IHS within 30 days of submitting their paperwork.
ai_sections.who: This bill affects Native American patients who receive care from outside providers referred by the Indian Health Service. It also applies to those outside providers, debt collectors, and the IHS itself.
ai_sections.why: Without this bill, patients could still receive bills or debt collection notices even though existing law was meant to protect them. The bill also creates clearer timelines and a formal process so patients and providers know what to expect.

press_names: Purchased and Referred Care Improvement Act

title: Child Care for Every Community Act
ai_summary: This bill would create a new nationwide government program providing child care and early learning services to all young children who are not yet old enough to be required to attend school. Any eligible child would have a legal right to participate — not just those whose families meet certain income limits — and the federal government would cover at least 90% of program costs, with families who pay fees capped at no more than 7% of their income. Local governments, states, tribal nations, and certain nonprofit organizations could apply to run the program in their area, and they would be required to offer full-day, full-year care that includes health, nutrition, mental health, and family support services alongside education. The bill specifically prioritizes serving low-income children, children with disabilities, children learning English as a second language, homeless children, and children of migrant farmworkers, and it sets rules requiring fair pay for child care workers and meaningful involvement of parents in how programs are run.
ai_headline: Bill would guarantee universal preschool for all U.S. children
last_action_text: ASSUMING FIRST SPONSORSHIP - Ms. Ocasio-Cortez asked unanimous consent that she may hereafter be considered as the first sponsor of H.R. 5658, a bill originally introduced by Representative Sherrill, for the purpose of adding cosponsors and requesting reprintings pursuant to clause 7 of rule XII. Agreed to without objection.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 5658 would give every young child a legal right to child care, with the federal government paying at least 90% of costs.
ai_sections.what: This bill would create a nationwide child care and early learning program open to all children who are not yet old enough to start school. Any eligible child would have a legal right to participate, regardless of family income. Programs would be required to offer full-day, full-year care that includes education, health, nutrition, mental health, and family support services.
ai_sections.who: All young children below school age could take part, with special priority given to children who are low-income, have disabilities, are learning English, are experiencing homelessness, or have parents who are migrant farmworkers. States, local governments, tribal nations, and certain nonprofits could apply to run the program in their area.
ai_sections.why: Because all children are eligible by right, participation would not depend on whether a family meets an income test. Child care workers would be subject to fair pay requirements, and parents would have a formal role in how local programs are run.
ai_sections.cost: The federal government would cover at least 90% of program costs. Families who are charged fees would pay no more than 7% of their income.

title: Protecting Small Businesses from Predatory Website Lawsuits Act
ai_summary: This bill changes the process that people with disabilities must follow before they can sue a private business over an inaccessible website or mobile app. Under the new process, a person would first have to notify the business directly that its site or app is not accessible; if the business doesn't fix the problem within 180 days, the person could then file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Justice, which would have up to 360 days to investigate; only after that entire process is completed — which could take well over a year — could the person file a lawsuit. Importantly, if the Justice Department finds the business is in compliance, or simply fails to reach a decision within its 360-day window, that counts as a final ruling in the business's favor and the person cannot sue. This affects people with disabilities who encounter inaccessible commercial websites or apps, and the private businesses that own or operate those digital properties.
ai_headline: Bill adds DOJ review step before disability web access suits
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
policy_area: Civil Rights and Liberties, Minority Issues

ai_sections.tldr: Before suing over an inaccessible website, a disabled person must complete a process lasting well over a year — and may still lose the right to sue.
ai_sections.what: This bill adds new required steps before a person with a disability can sue a private business over a website or app that is hard or impossible to use. First, the person must notify the business directly. If the business does not fix the problem within 180 days, the person can file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Justice, which then has up to 360 days to investigate before a lawsuit is allowed.
ai_sections.who: This affects people with disabilities who cannot fully use a private business's website or mobile app. It also affects the private businesses that own or run those websites and apps.
ai_sections.why: The full required process can take well over a year before a lawsuit is possible. If the Department of Justice finds the business is in compliance, or does not reach a decision within its 360-day window, that outcome is treated as a final ruling in the business's favor and the person loses the right to sue.

title: ROUTE Act
ai_summary: This bill would allow truck drivers who are 18, 19, or 20 years old to drive commercial vehicles (like large semi-trucks) across state lines under specific conditions, even though federal law currently limits interstate commercial driving to those 21 and older. To qualify, a young driver must already hold a valid commercial driver's license for in-state driving in their home state. The interstate driving allowed under this bill is limited: the driver must stay within 150 miles (as the crow flies) of their home base, must return to that home base and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours, and must take at least 10 hours off before their next work period. This would primarily affect younger adults seeking careers in trucking and the employers — such as freight and delivery companies — who might hire them for regional routes that cross state lines.
ai_headline: Truckers aged 18–20 could haul freight across state lines
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6642 would let drivers ages 18–20 cross state lines in commercial trucks if they stay within 150 miles of their home base.
ai_sections.what: This bill would allow truck drivers who are 18, 19, or 20 years old to drive large commercial vehicles across state lines. Right now, federal law requires interstate commercial drivers to be at least 21. To qualify, a young driver must hold a valid commercial driver's license for in-state driving, stay within 150 miles of their home base, return and be released within 14 consecutive hours, and take at least 10 hours off before their next shift.
ai_sections.who: This bill would affect younger adults who want to work in trucking. It would also affect freight and delivery companies that hire drivers for regional routes crossing state lines.
ai_sections.why: If passed, employers could hire drivers in the 18–20 age range for certain interstate routes they currently cannot legally staff with those workers. Drivers in that age group could access interstate trucking jobs that are currently closed to them under federal law.

title: To designate the facility of the United States Postal Service located at 3135 1st Avenue North in St. Petersburg, Florida, as the "Poul Hornsleth Post Office".

Any government documents, maps, or records that refer to that building would use the new name going forward. ai_sections.who: This bill directly affects only this one postal facility in St. Petersburg, Florida. Postal services, employees, and the general public would not be affected beyond the name change.
ai_sections.why: If passed, official records and references to this building would reflect the new name. No other changes to the facility or its operations would result.

title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Department of Veterans Affairs relating to "Reproductive Health Services".
ai_summary: This resolution would cancel a rule issued by the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) on December 31, 2025, that dealt with reproductive health services. If passed by both the House and Senate and signed into law, the VA rule would be wiped off the books and could no longer be enforced. The resolution does not spell out what the VA rule itself required or allowed — it simply acts to nullify it entirely. Veterans who might have been affected by whatever reproductive health services that VA rule addressed would be the people most directly impacted by this cancellation.
ai_headline: House moves to repeal VA reproductive health rule
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs.

ai_sections.tldr: Congress is voting to cancel a VA rule on reproductive health services issued December 31, 2025, wiping it from the books entirely.
ai_sections.what: This resolution would cancel a rule the Department of Veterans Affairs issued on December 31, 2025, about reproductive health services. It does not change or replace the rule — it removes it completely. If passed by both chambers and signed into law, the rule could no longer be enforced.
ai_sections.who: Veterans who were affected by whatever reproductive health services that VA rule covered would feel this most directly.
ai_sections.why: If the resolution passes, the VA rule disappears and any access or requirements it created would no longer be in effect. If it does not pass, the VA rule stays in place.

title: Gerald’s Law Act
ai_summary: This bill would make veterans eligible for a VA burial allowance if they die at home while receiving VA hospice care, as long as they had previously been receiving care in a VA hospital or VA-connected nursing home. Currently, the burial allowance is available to veterans who die inside those VA facilities, but not to those who transfer to at-home hospice care and pass away there. The change would close that gap so that dying at home — rather than in a facility — does not disqualify a veteran's family from receiving burial assistance. The bill would apply retroactively, as though it had been part of a veterans' health care law passed in 2020.
ai_headline: VA burial benefits would extend to home hospice veterans
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs.

ai_sections.tldr: Veterans who die at home during VA hospice care would still qualify for a VA burial allowance, same as those who die in a VA facility.
ai_sections.what: This bill would extend the VA burial allowance to veterans who die at home while in VA hospice care, if they had previously been receiving care in a VA hospital or VA-connected nursing home. Right now, that allowance is only available when a veteran dies inside a VA facility. The bill would also apply retroactively, as if it had been part of a veterans' health care law passed in 2020.
ai_sections.who: Veterans who move from a VA hospital or VA-connected nursing home into at-home hospice care would be affected, along with their families who handle burial arrangements.
ai_sections.why: Under current rules, a veteran's family can lose access to burial assistance simply because the veteran chose to spend their final days at home rather than in a facility. This bill would remove that distinction.

title: Public Safety Communications Act
ai_summary: This bill creates a new office inside the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), a federal agency that handles communications policy, specifically to focus on public safety communications. The new office would be led by a career government official called the Associate Administrator for Public Safety Communications, who would oversee federal grant programs for Next Generation 9-1-1 (the modernized version of the 911 emergency call system), advise on public safety communications policy, and manage the First Responder Network Authority, which is the organization that runs the nationwide broadband network used by police, firefighters, and other emergency responders. The office would also oversee government research and technology testing aimed at improving how first responders communicate during emergencies. This would primarily affect federal agencies, emergency responders, and local governments that rely on or apply for federal funding related to public safety communications systems.
ai_headline: NTIA would get a new public safety communications office
last_action_text: Forwarded by Subcommittee to Full Committee by Voice Vote.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 1519 creates a new federal office inside NTIA to oversee emergency communications programs and the broadband network used by first responders.
ai_sections.what: This bill sets up a new office inside the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), a federal agency that handles communications policy. The office would be led by a career official called the Associate Administrator for Public Safety Communications. It would manage grant programs for Next Generation 9-1-1, oversee the First Responder Network Authority, and guide research and technology testing for emergency communications.
ai_sections.who: This primarily affects federal agencies, emergency responders such as police and firefighters, and local governments that use or apply for federal funding related to public safety communications.
ai_sections.why: Creating a dedicated office centralizes oversight of emergency communications programs and the nationwide broadband network first responders use. This changes how those programs are managed and who is accountable for them at the federal level.

title: Next Generation 9–1–1 Act
ai_summary: This bill directs a federal official (the Assistant Secretary of the National Telecommunications and Information Administration) to run a grant program that helps states, U.S. territories, and Native American tribes upgrade their 911 systems to "Next Generation 9-1-1" — a modern, internet-based system that can handle not just phone calls but also texts, photos, videos, and other data sent to emergency call centers. Grant money can be used for building and maintaining the new systems, training staff, telling the public how to use the new capabilities, and adding cybersecurity protections, with spending caps on training and administrative costs. To receive a grant, states and tribes must meet several requirements, including designating a single coordinator, submitting an upgrade plan, and certifying that local 911 fees are not being spent on unrelated things — and any entity that provides false information loses eligibility and must return the money. The bill also creates a national cybersecurity center focused specifically on protecting these 911 systems, and an advisory board of 16 public safety professionals (from law enforcement, fire and rescue, emergency medical services, and 911 operations) to advise on how the grants and rules should work. Funding is authorized for fiscal years 2026 through 2030, with no more than 4 percent of appropriated funds going to administrative costs.
ai_headline: Federal grants would fund Next Generation 9-1-1 upgrades
last_action_text: Forwarded by Subcommittee to Full Committee by Voice Vote.

ai_sections.tldr: Federal grants would help states, tribes, and territories upgrade 911 systems to handle texts, photos, and videos—not just calls.
ai_sections.what: This bill creates a federal grant program to help upgrade 911 systems to "Next Generation 9-1-1," a modern internet-based system that can receive texts, photos, videos, and other data—not just phone calls. Grant money can pay for building and maintaining the new systems, training staff, informing the public, and adding cybersecurity protections. The bill also establishes a national cybersecurity center for these 911 systems and a 16-member advisory board of public safety professionals.
ai_sections.who: States, U.S. territories, and Native American tribes can apply for grants, but must meet requirements such as naming a single coordinator, submitting an upgrade plan, and certifying that local 911 fees are used properly. The program is run by the Assistant Secretary of the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, with guidance from an advisory board drawn from law enforcement, fire and rescue, emergency medical services, and 911 operations.
ai_sections.why: Without upgrades, 911 centers may not be able to receive texts, photos, or videos that callers send during emergencies. Entities that submit false information lose eligibility and must return any grant money received.
ai_sections.cost: Funding is authorized for fiscal years 2026 through 2030. No more than 4 percent of appropriated funds may go to administrative costs, and the bill also sets spending caps on training costs.

title: Dietary Supplement Listing Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill would require companies that make, package, or distribute dietary supplements sold in the United States to register each of their products with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and provide detailed information about them, including the product's name, ingredients, serving sizes, directions, allergen warnings, and a copy of its label. Companies with products already on the market would have 18 months to comply, while new products would need to be registered before they go on sale; companies must also notify the FDA within a year if they stop selling a product and update their registration within 30 days if they change a label. The FDA would be required to create a publicly searchable online database where anyone could look up this information, though certain details — like contact information for company owners and the exact amounts of individual ingredients inside proprietary blends — would be kept confidential. A dietary supplement that hasn't been properly registered would be considered "misbranded," meaning it could be treated as an illegal product. This bill primarily affects dietary supplement manufacturers, distributors, and packagers, but also benefits consumers, healthcare providers, and researchers who want easier access to accurate information about what is in the supplements they use or study.
ai_headline: FDA would track and publish dietary supplement data
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. (text: CR S259-260)

ai_sections.tldr: Senate bill S 3677 would require dietary supplement makers to register every product with the FDA before it can legally be sold.
ai_sections.what: This bill would require companies that make, package, or distribute dietary supplements to register each product with the FDA and submit details such as ingredients, serving sizes, directions, allergen warnings, and a copy of the label. Products already on shelves would have 18 months to comply; new products must be registered before going on sale. Companies must also update the FDA within 30 days of a label change and within one year of stopping sales of a product.
ai_sections.who: This bill directly affects dietary supplement manufacturers, distributors, and packagers. Consumers, healthcare providers, and researchers who want accurate information about supplement contents are also affected.
ai_sections.why: A supplement that is not properly registered would be considered misbranded and could be treated as an illegal product. The FDA would be required to maintain a publicly searchable online database of registered products, though some details such as owner contact information and exact amounts within proprietary blends would remain confidential.

title: SHIFT Act
ai_summary: This bill changes how the federal government and regional fishery councils manage fish populations that are moving into new ocean areas due to changing environmental conditions. When fish stocks shift significantly into a new region — whether measured by where the fish are, where fishermen are catching them, or where fishing revenues are going — the government must formally recognize that shift and update who is responsible for managing that fishery, using the best available science to account for ecological changes like habitat and food web effects. The bill also tightens the rules for introducing new types of fishing or fishing gear, requiring a formal analysis showing that any new fishery won't seriously harm fish habitat, existing fisheries, or coastal fishing communities before it can be officially authorized. Every five years, regional councils must review their authorized fisheries and gear and propose any needed updates. The people most directly affected are commercial and recreational fishermen, fishing communities along the U.S. coasts, and the regional councils and federal agencies that manage marine fisheries.
ai_headline: Senate bill tracks fish as stocks shift to new waters
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

ai_sections.tldr: The SHIFT Act requires the federal government to update who manages a fishery when fish populations move into new ocean areas.
ai_sections.what: This bill requires federal agencies and regional fishery councils to formally recognize when fish populations shift into new ocean regions and to update management responsibilities accordingly. It also requires a formal analysis before any new type of fishing or fishing gear can be approved, to check for harm to fish habitat, existing fisheries, or coastal communities. Every five years, regional councils must review their authorized fisheries and gear and propose updates as needed.
ai_sections.who: Commercial and recreational fishermen and coastal fishing communities are directly affected. Regional fishery councils and the federal agencies that manage marine fisheries are also affected.
ai_sections.why: Without these changes, management responsibilities might not keep up when fish populations move due to changing environmental conditions. The new gear and fishery review requirements mean that potential harm to habitats, other fisheries, and fishing communities must be assessed before new fishing activity is authorized.

title: Find It Early Act
ai_summary: This bill would require health insurance plans to cover additional breast cancer screenings — such as 3D mammograms, ultrasounds, MRI scans, and other imaging — at no cost to the patient, meaning no copays, deductibles, or other out-of-pocket charges. The no-cost coverage would apply to two groups: people identified as being at higher risk for breast cancer (including those with dense breast tissue, based on established medical criteria), and people whose doctor determines they need screening based on factors like age, race, ethnicity, or personal or family medical history. The requirement would apply broadly across nearly all types of health coverage, including employer-sponsored plans, individual and marketplace insurance, Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE (military health coverage), and VA health care for veterans. The frequency of covered screenings would follow guidelines set by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network, a medical organization that publishes cancer care standards. The bill would take effect on January 1, 2026.
ai_headline: Insurers would cover extra breast cancer scans at no cost
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Health.

ai_sections.tldr: Starting January 1, 2026, most health plans would be required to cover extra breast cancer screenings at no out-of-pocket cost for higher-risk patients.
ai_sections.what: This bill would require health insurance plans to cover additional breast cancer screenings — including 3D mammograms, ultrasounds, and MRI scans — with no copays, deductibles, or other out-of-pocket costs. How often screenings are covered would follow guidelines set by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network.
ai_sections.who: The no-cost coverage would apply to people at higher risk for breast cancer, including those with dense breast tissue, and to people whose doctor recommends screening based on age, race, ethnicity, or personal or family medical history. The requirement would apply to most types of health coverage, including employer plans, marketplace insurance, Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, and VA health care.
ai_sections.why: People in the covered groups who currently pay out of pocket for additional screenings would no longer have that cost. The bill would take effect on January 1, 2026.

title: Fiscal State of the Nation Act
ai_summary: Every year, the Treasury Department already submits an audited financial report on the federal government's finances to Congress. This bill would require Congress to hold a public joint hearing — with members of both the House and Senate Budget Committees present — where the Comptroller General (the head of the Government Accountability Office, a nonpartisan watchdog agency) would walk lawmakers through the findings of that audit, including information about deficits, surpluses, long-term debt projections, and the government's overall financial health. The hearing must be held within 45 working days of the Treasury submitting its report, must be open to the public and to media coverage, and any member of Congress — not just Budget Committee members — would be allowed to participate. The presentation itself must follow nonpartisan, fact-based standards set by the Government Accountability Office. This bill primarily affects members of Congress and the Comptroller General, though ordinary citizens would benefit from the increased public visibility into the government's financial condition.
ai_headline: Bill requires public GAO briefing on federal finances
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Rules.

ai_sections.tldr: This bill would require Congress to hold a public hearing each year where a nonpartisan watchdog walks lawmakers through the federal government's financial audit.
ai_sections.what: This bill would require Congress to hold a public joint hearing each year to review the federal government's audited financial report. The Comptroller General would present findings on deficits, debt projections, and the government's overall financial health. The hearing must happen within 45 working days of the Treasury submitting its report, must be open to the public and media, and any member of Congress may participate.
ai_sections.who: This bill primarily affects members of Congress and the Comptroller General, the head of the Government Accountability Office. Ordinary citizens would also be affected through greater public visibility into the government's financial condition.
ai_sections.why: Without this requirement, no formal process exists to ensure Congress publicly reviews the Treasury's annual financial audit together. This bill would create a set time and format for that review to happen on the record, in public.

title: Community Passport Services Access Act
ai_summary: This bill would allow public libraries that are organized as nonprofits, charities, or similar non-governmental organizations to officially accept passport applications and keep the fee they charge customers for that service. Right now, that fee-retention authority is limited to certain government offices and the U.S. Postal Service; this bill adds qualifying public libraries to that list. Libraries that were already acting as passport acceptance facilities before this bill becomes law would be formally authorized to collect and keep that fee within 30 days of enactment, as long as they were following State Department rules at the time. The people most directly affected are library patrons who want a convenient local place to submit a passport application, and the libraries themselves, which would gain a new source of revenue from the execution fees they collect.
ai_headline: Nonprofit libraries could soon accept passport applications
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6997 would let nonprofit public libraries accept passport applications and keep the fee they charge for that service.
ai_sections.what: This bill adds qualifying nonprofit public libraries to the list of places officially allowed to accept passport applications and keep the execution fee charged to customers. That authority currently belongs only to certain government offices and the U.S. Postal Service. Libraries already acting as passport acceptance facilities when the bill becomes law would be formally authorized to collect and keep that fee within 30 days, as long as they were following State Department rules at the time.
ai_sections.who: Library patrons looking for a convenient local place to submit a passport application are directly affected. So are the public libraries themselves, which would gain a new source of revenue from the execution fees they collect.
ai_sections.why: Libraries that already offer this service would move from an informal arrangement to an officially recognized one. Libraries not yet offering the service would have a legal pathway to do so and keep the associated fee.

title: Public Integrity in Financial Prediction Markets Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill would make it illegal for a wide range of federal government workers and officials to bet on prediction markets — online platforms where people place wagers on whether specific events will happen — when those bets involve government policy, government actions, or political outcomes. The ban applies to elected members of Congress, their staff, political appointees, and employees of federal agencies. The prohibition specifically targets situations where these individuals either already possess inside government information that the public doesn't have access to, or where their job gives them a reasonable opportunity to obtain such information. For example, a federal employee who knows in advance about an upcoming policy decision before it is announced publicly could not use that knowledge to profit by betting on a prediction market tied to that policy. The core concern the bill addresses is that people with access to non-public government information could have an unfair advantage when betting on political or policy outcomes.
ai_headline: Federal workers would be barred from political prediction market bets
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, and in addition to the Committee on House Administration, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.tldr: Federal workers and officials with access to inside government information could not bet on prediction markets tied to policy or political outcomes.
ai_sections.what: This bill would ban certain federal government workers and officials from placing bets on prediction markets when those bets involve government policy, government actions, or political outcomes. The ban applies specifically when those individuals already have inside government information the public cannot access, or when their job gives them a reasonable chance to get such information.
ai_sections.who: The ban covers elected members of Congress, their staff, political appointees, and employees of federal agencies.
ai_sections.why: Without this rule, people with access to non-public government information could have an unfair advantage when betting on political or policy outcomes. For example, a federal employee who knows about a policy decision before it is made public could use that knowledge to profit on a prediction market tied to that policy.

title: EB–5 Regional Center Program Advisory Committee Authorization Act
ai_summary: This bill creates a new advisory committee inside U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to provide guidance and recommendations on the EB-5 Regional Center Program — the federal program that allows foreign investors to obtain U.S. visas by investing money in American businesses or projects that create jobs. The committee would have up to 35 members drawn from regional centers (the organizations that pool and manage EB-5 investments), city mayors, county and state economic development officials, and federal agencies, and would be organized into subcommittees covering topics like application processing times, job creation, and investment rules. It would meet at least four times a year, submit annual reports to the Secretary of Homeland Security and the USCIS Director, and provide quarterly briefings to Congress — though it could not make recommendations about specific individual visa cases. The people most directly affected are foreign investors seeking EB-5 visas, the regional centers that sponsor investment projects, and the communities — particularly rural areas, high-unemployment areas, and cities of various sizes — where those projects are located.
ai_headline: USCIS would gain an EB-5 investor visa advisory panel
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6992 creates a new advisory committee at USCIS to give guidance on the EB-5 visa investment program.
ai_sections.what: This bill sets up an advisory committee inside U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to give guidance on the EB-5 Regional Center Program, which lets foreign investors get U.S. visas by investing in American businesses that create jobs. The committee would have up to 35 members, meet at least four times a year, report annually to homeland security leadership, and give quarterly updates to Congress. It would not be allowed to weigh in on individual visa cases.

ai_sections.why: Creating this committee gives USCIS a formal channel for outside input on topics like application processing times, job creation, and investment rules. Without such a structure, those perspectives would have no organized way to reach agency leadership or Congress.

title: National Landslide Preparedness Act Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary: This bill extends and updates a federal program aimed at reducing the dangers of landslides across the United States through at least 2030, and increases the dedicated funding for that program from $25 million to $35 million per year, with at least $10 million of that specifically required to go toward buying, installing, and maintaining early warning systems in high-risk areas. It broadens who is included in landslide preparedness efforts by explicitly adding Native Hawaiian organizations and Tribal organizations alongside state and local governments, and it directs the U.S. Geological Survey to create regional partnerships — starting in Alaska — with universities and research organizations that have landslide expertise. The bill also requires the government to assess the specific landslide risks posed by atmospheric rivers (large weather systems that bring heavy rain or snow) and other extreme rain events, and expands the national landslide database to flag areas threatened by factors like drought, erosion, earthquakes, volcanic activity, and thawing permafrost. People most directly affected include residents of landslide-prone communities, emergency managers, state and local officials, Native Hawaiian and Tribal communities, and researchers who study or respond to landslide hazards.
ai_headline: USGS landslide warning program extended through 2030
last_action_text: Reported (Amended) by the Committee on Natural Resources. H. Rept. 119-431, Part I.

ai_sections.tldr: Congress would extend the national landslide preparedness program through at least 2030 and raise its annual funding from $25M to $35M.
ai_sections.what: This bill extends a federal landslide preparedness program through at least 2030. It raises annual funding, requires early warning systems in high-risk areas, and expands a national landslide database to track threats from drought, erosion, earthquakes, volcanic activity, and thawing permafrost. It also requires the government to study landslide risks tied to heavy rain events and atmospheric rivers.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects residents of landslide-prone communities, emergency managers, state and local officials, Native Hawaiian and Tribal organizations, and landslide researchers. Native Hawaiian and Tribal organizations are newly added to the program alongside state and local governments.

ai_sections.cost: Annual funding for the program would increase from $25 million to $35 million. At least $10 million of that each year must go toward buying, installing, and maintaining early warning systems in high-risk areas.

title: Public Health Nursing Act
ai_summary: This bill would direct the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services to build up the nation's public health nursing workforce by giving grants to state, local, and territorial public health departments. Those departments could use the money to recruit, hire, and train licensed registered nurses — covering wages, benefits, and necessary medical supplies like protective equipment — with a focus on placing nurses in underserved communities, mobile health clinics, hospitals, and home visitation programs. Communities that face high rates of chronic disease, infant mortality, or maternal health problems, as well as low-income, rural, and medically underserved areas, would be prioritized for funding. title: Bycatch Reduction and Research Act of 2026
ai_summary: This bill directs the federal government — primarily the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) — to improve research, technology, and financial tools aimed at reducing "bycatch," which is the unintended capture of fish and other marine life (such as salmon) during commercial fishing. NOAA would be required to study how salmon move through Alaskan waters, examine how trawl fishing gear disturbs the ocean floor, and analyze the broader environmental factors affecting fish populations in the Bering Sea, Aleutian Islands, and Gulf of Alaska — sharing findings in public reports within three years. The bill also calls for building a testing facility (a "flume tank") where fishermen, researchers, and government scientists can try out new gear designs that catch fewer unwanted species and cause less seafloor damage, and it sets up a donation-funded assistance fund — managed by the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation — to help commercial fishermen pay for cleaner, more selective fishing gear and technology. Electronic monitoring systems on fishing vessels would be streamlined and made more consistent, and NOAA would be required to post plain-language observer coverage requirements online so the public can see bycatch data for major federal fisheries. The people most directly affected are commercial fishermen operating in Alaskan and other U.S. federal waters, Alaska Native communities, fishing vessel owners, and the researchers and agencies that manage these fisheries.

title: Revitalizing America’s Housing Act
ai_summary: This bill is a wide-ranging housing package that tries to make homes safer, more affordable, and easier to buy or rent across the United States. It would require the federal government to identify rules that make housing more expensive, offer new or expanded tax breaks to encourage building and selling homes in lower-income neighborhoods, and make it easier for communities to convert unused federal land into affordable housing. It expands access to discounted home-buying programs and public housing for groups like police officers, firefighters, emergency medical technicians, veterans, and volunteer first responders, and it directs studies and new reports on issues like housing near toxic waste sites, homelessness, and inspection backlogs in public housing. People most directly affected include first-time and middle-income homebuyers, longtime homeowners looking to sell, renters in public housing, veterans, first responders, residents near contaminated sites, and local governments seeking more flexibility in their housing and zoning rules.
