title: Health Care Fairness for Military Families Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill makes two main changes to TRICARE Young Adult, which is the health insurance program that allows adult children of military service members to stay on their parent's military health coverage. First, it removes a rule that currently cuts off eligibility for young adults who qualify for health insurance through their own employer. Right now, if a military family's adult child is offered job-based insurance at work, they lose access to TRICARE Young Adult even if they don't take that employer coverage. This bill would eliminate that restriction.

Second, the bill removes the separate monthly premium that young adults currently have to pay to be enrolled in TRICARE Young Adult. Under current law, these young adults pay their own premium on top of whatever their military parent already pays for family coverage. This bill would get rid of that extra charge, making the coverage free for eligible young adults just as it is for younger dependents on standard TRICARE plans.

The people most directly affected are adult children of active duty service members, National Guard members, and military retirees who are between the ages of 21 and 26. Currently about 600,000 to 700,000 young adults fall into this general age range within military families. The change would also affect the Department of Defense, which would absorb the cost of coverage that young adults currently pay for themselves through premiums.
ai_headline: Bill would drop premiums and employer rule for military dependents' health plan

title: Stop CCP Money Laundering Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill tells two U.S. government agencies to investigate Hong Kong's financial system and report their findings to Congress. First, the Treasury Department has 180 days to decide whether Hong Kong should be officially labeled a "primary money laundering concern," which is a serious designation that can trigger restrictions on how U.S. banks do business there. Second, within a year, the State Department, working with Treasury and Commerce, must produce a detailed report on whether banks in Hong Kong are being used to move money or send restricted technology to countries like Russia and Iran in ways that break U.S. law.

The report must also look at whether Chinese national security laws passed in 2020 and 2024 have made it harder for banks in Hong Kong to follow standard anti-money laundering rules, such as verifying who their customers really are. It must also cover how well Hong Kong and U.S. authorities are working together to enforce trade and financial penalties.

This bill does not directly ban any transactions or punish anyone right now. It mainly affects government agencies that will have to do the research and write the reports. Down the road, American banks and businesses that operate in Hong Kong could be affected if the investigations lead to new restrictions. U.S. consumers would not feel a direct impact from the bill itself, but the findings could eventually influence broader U.S. trade and financial policy.
ai_headline: Senate bill orders U.S. agencies to probe Hong Kong money laundering ties
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

title: Streamline Transit Projects Act
ai_summary:
This bill would let large local transit agencies take over certain environmental review duties that the federal government currently handles. Specifically, it deals with something called "categorical exclusions," which are routine transit projects that have already been determined to cause little to no environmental harm and therefore do not require a full environmental study. Right now, a federal agency signs off on these determinations. Under this bill, qualifying transit agencies could do that work themselves, as long as they sign an agreement with the federal government and prove they have the staff, legal expertise, and money to handle it properly.

To qualify, a transit agency must serve an urban area with more than 200,000 people and meet certain standards set by the U.S. Department of Transportation. The agency would take on full legal responsibility for making sure environmental rules are followed, and the federal government would no longer be liable for those decisions. The agreement between the agency and the federal government would be reviewed every three years, or every five years for agencies with at least ten years of experience doing this work. The federal government can take back control if an agency is not meeting its responsibilities.

This bill mainly affects large city and regional transit agencies that receive federal funding, as well as the communities those agencies serve. Supporters of this general approach argue it could speed up the start of transit construction projects by cutting down on waiting time for federal approvals. Critics of similar policies have raised concerns about whether local oversight provides the same level of environmental protection as federal review. Everyday riders, local residents near transit projects, and taxpayers who fund public transportation could all be affected depending on how the change plays out in practice.
ai_headline: Large transit agencies could self-approve routine environmental reviews
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

title: Power for the People Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill tries to stop regular electricity customers from paying higher bills because of the growing power demands of large data centers. Right now, when a massive data center connects to the electric grid, the cost of upgrading power lines and other infrastructure often gets spread across all electricity customers in an area. The bill would require data centers to pay for those upgrade costs themselves. It also tells the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to create a special waiting line, called a load queue, that data centers must go through before connecting to the grid. Data centers that bring their own clean energy sources, agree to have their power cut during emergencies, and pay construction workers fair wages would get moved up in that line.

The bill also pushes states to create separate billing categories just for data centers, rather than lumping them in with homes and businesses. Under these special rate classes, data centers could be required to pay minimum charges based on how much power they asked for, sign longer contracts with utilities, and put up more money upfront when applying to connect to the grid. States would have two years to study and decide whether to adopt these rules. The federal government would offer grants and technical help to states working through this process.

The people most directly affected are data center owners and operators, who would face new costs and requirements before connecting to the grid. Ordinary households and small businesses that pay electric bills could potentially benefit if the policy successfully shifts infrastructure costs away from them. Workers building data centers and power facilities could also be affected, since the bill includes requirements around union-friendly labor agreements and apprenticeship programs for data center construction projects.

title: Biological Intellectual Property Protection Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would require American companies and researchers to get a government license before sharing certain biotechnology information with foreign entities from countries considered threats to the United States, like China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea. Specifically, it targets digital files containing the designed sequences of synthetic DNA or RNA — basically the blueprints for lab-created genetic material. Right now, those files can often be sent overseas without any special government approval. Under this bill, the Department of Commerce would have one year to set up that licensing system.

The bill is focused on stopping intellectual property theft in the field of synthetic biology, which is an area of science where researchers design new genetic material for purposes like making medicines, agricultural products, or industrial chemicals. Congress is concerned that when a US company sends its custom DNA or RNA sequence designs to a lab or company in a country like China, that information could end up in the hands of foreign military or intelligence services. The bill does include an exception for certain information that is already considered publicly available or freely shared, so basic scientific publishing would not automatically be affected.

The people most directly affected would be US biotechnology companies, university research labs, and scientists who currently share or sell synthetic biology data with partners, customers, or collaborators in countries flagged as national security concerns. Those organizations would need to apply for and receive a government export license before sending that kind of file. Foreign companies and research institutions in countries of concern would face restricted access to US-designed genetic sequence information.

The Department of Commerce would have one year to build and launch the licensing system. Information already considered publicly available would be exempt from the requirement.

title: AFTER Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill changes the Animal Welfare Act to require federal agencies that use animals in research to have a plan for retiring those animals when the research is done. Right now, there is no federal requirement for what happens to lab animals after they are no longer needed for experiments. Under this bill, any federal research facility would need to create rules, within 90 days of the law passing, that actively try to place healthy retired animals with rescue organizations, animal sanctuaries, shelters, or private individuals who want them as pets. Non-human primates like monkeys would specifically be placed in sanctuaries rather than private homes.

The bill sets clear definitions for what counts as a legitimate sanctuary or rescue organization. For example, a qualifying sanctuary cannot sell animals, breed them, let the public have direct contact with them, or use them for performances. An animal has to be evaluated by a licensed veterinarian and found mentally and physically healthy before it can be retired through this process. The bill also says agencies should look beyond just nearby organizations and consider placing animals with groups anywhere in the country. Common lab rats and mice are not covered by this bill.

The people most directly affected are the employees and administrators at federal research facilities, who would need to create and follow new retirement procedures. Animal rescue groups and sanctuaries that meet the bill's standards could receive retired research animals. Animals used in federally funded research, such as dogs, cats, rabbits, and primates, would have a clearer path to adoption or sanctuary placement. States are also allowed to pass their own stricter animal retirement laws if they choose.

title: No Rewards for January 6 Rioters Act
ai_summary:
This bill would block the federal government from using taxpayer money to pay or reimburse people who were charged with crimes related to the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol. That includes money from the Judgment Fund, which is a pool of federal money used to pay out certain legal claims against the government. The ban would apply even to people who were later pardoned for their involvement. The bill also prevents the creation of any new fund specifically set up to compensate those individuals.

The bill also addresses money that January 6 convicts already paid to the courts, such as fines or restitution. It says the government cannot refund those payments, even if a person's conviction was later reversed or they received a pardon. Any money that might otherwise be returned would instead go to the Architect of the Capitol, the office responsible for maintaining the Capitol building that was damaged during the attack.

This bill would directly affect people who were prosecuted in connection with January 6 and who might otherwise seek government compensation, particularly those who were pardoned and believe they are owed money back. It would also affect federal agencies that handle legal payouts. The bill was introduced in the Senate and has been sent to the Judiciary Committee, meaning it has not yet been voted on or become law.

title: NOPAIN for Veterans Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires the Department of Veterans Affairs to add FDA-approved non-opioid pain medications to its official drug list, called the national formulary. Right now, the VA controls which medications doctors can prescribe to veterans, and new drugs sometimes take a long time to become available through the VA system. Under this bill, once a non-opioid pain medication is approved by the FDA, the VA would have to make it available to veterans within 18 months, or within one year of it qualifying for certain Medicare payment programs, whichever comes first. The VA would have 90 days after the bill becomes law to start following these new rules.

The bill specifically targets non-opioid drugs used to treat pain after surgery or for acute pain conditions. These are medications that work without affecting the brain's opioid receptors, meaning they are not addictive in the same way opioids can be. The goal is to make sure veterans have faster access to these newer pain treatment options as alternatives to opioid-based drugs.

This bill directly affects veterans who receive healthcare through the VA and are dealing with pain management, particularly after surgeries or procedures. It also affects VA doctors, who would have more non-opioid treatment options available to prescribe. The bill includes a note that money from the Cost of War Toxic Exposures Fund, which is set aside for veterans harmed by toxic exposures like burn pits, cannot be used to pay for this program.

title: Restoring Overtime Pay Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill deals with overtime pay rules for salaried workers. Under current federal law, employees classified as executive, administrative, or professional workers can be exempt from overtime pay requirements if their salary meets a certain minimum. This bill would raise that minimum salary level in steps: starting at $45,000 per year when the law takes effect, then rising to $55,000 in 2027, $65,000 in 2028, and $75,000 in 2029. Starting in 2030, the threshold would automatically adjust each year to match the 55th percentile of what full-time salaried workers earn nationally, so it would keep pace with wages over time without needing new legislation.

The bill also changes a rule about job duties. Right now, some workers can lose overtime protections if a large portion of their work involves non-managerial tasks. This bill tightens that rule, requiring that at least 20 percent of a worker's time be spent on genuine executive or administrative duties in order to qualify for the overtime exemption. The idea is to make it harder for employers to classify workers as managers or professionals just on paper while most of their actual work is routine.

This affects salaried workers across many industries, particularly those earning between roughly $35,000 and $75,000 a year who are currently classified as exempt from overtime. It also affects employers, who may need to either raise salaries to keep certain workers exempt or begin paying those workers overtime. Small businesses with salaried supervisors or office workers could see the most significant changes.

last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

title: VISIT USA Act
ai_summary:
This bill would move $160 million from a government account called the Travel Promotion Fund directly to Brand USA, which is a nonprofit organization that markets the United States as a travel destination to people in other countries. The money in that fund comes from fees that foreign visitors pay when they apply to enter the US through the visa waiver program. The bill directs the Treasury Department to make this transfer within 30 days of the law being signed.

Brand USA uses funds like this to run advertising campaigns, attend travel trade shows, and promote American tourism attractions abroad. The bill waives a normal cap on how much can be transferred at once but still requires Brand USA to match the government money with private funding, as existing law already requires. The goal is to encourage more international tourists to visit the US, which supporters argue brings in revenue and supports jobs in the travel and hospitality industry.

This bill would most directly affect Brand USA and the federal Treasury. Indirectly, it could affect businesses in the US tourism industry such as hotels, airlines, and attractions that benefit from international visitors. Foreign travelers who might be influenced by Brand USA marketing campaigns could also be affected. US taxpayers are not directly charged, since the funding comes from fees paid by foreign visa applicants rather than general tax revenue.

title: Title X Abortion Provider Prohibition Act
ai_summary:
Title X is a federal program that pays for family planning services like birth control, STI testing, and health checkups for people with low incomes. This bill would change the rules so that any clinic or health organization performing abortions could no longer receive that federal funding. To keep getting Title X money, a provider would have to certify that it does not perform abortions and does not send any of its own funds to other groups that do. Hospitals are treated slightly differently and can still receive funding as long as they do not pass money along to outside abortion providers.

There are two exceptions built into the bill. An organization can still receive Title X funding and perform abortions if the pregnancy resulted from rape or incest, or if a doctor certifies that continuing the pregnancy would put the woman's life at risk. The bill also requires the federal government to report to Congress each year listing which organizations receive Title X grants and how many abortions were performed under those exceptions.

The people most directly affected are low-income individuals who rely on Title X-funded clinics for basic reproductive health care. If a clinic that currently offers both family planning services and abortions loses its Title X funding, it may have fewer resources to provide other services like contraception and cancer screenings. Organizations such as Planned Parenthood, which receive Title X dollars and also perform abortions, would have to choose between stopping abortion services or giving up the federal funding. Patients in areas where that clinic is the main affordable option could find it harder to access care.

title: Taxing Buybacks from Big Oil Windfalls Act
ai_summary:
This bill would raise the tax on stock buybacks made by large oil and gas companies. Right now, any corporation that buys back its own stock pays a 1 percent excise tax on those purchases. This bill would jump that rate to 25 percent, but only for oil and gas companies that average at least $1 billion in yearly revenue over the prior three years. The higher tax would apply to companies involved in producing, refining, processing, transporting, or distributing oil and natural gas.

The higher 25 percent rate is not permanent. It would automatically stop applying once the national average price of regular gasoline drops below $2.937 per gallon for five weeks in a row. In other words, the extra tax is designed to be a temporary measure that stays in place while gas prices remain above that threshold.

This bill would most directly affect large, established oil and gas corporations that use profits to buy back their own stock. Stock buybacks are a way companies return money to shareholders, often boosting the stock price. Everyday Americans would not pay this tax directly, but some economists argue that higher taxes on corporations can influence business decisions, prices, or investment. Consumers, investors, and workers in the energy industry could all potentially feel indirect effects, depending on how affected companies respond.

title: MAP for Care Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates a voluntary program within Medicare to help people set up advance directives, which are legal documents that spell out what kind of medical care a person wants if they become too sick to speak for themselves. Examples include a living will, which lists specific treatment wishes, or a durable power of attorney for health care, which names someone to make medical decisions on a person's behalf. The government would build an online system where Medicare enrollees could create, store, update, or cancel these documents securely. The program would have to be up and running within five years of the bill becoming law.

The bill sets rules for companies and organizations that want to offer these advance directive services. To be approved, they must meet security and privacy standards, allow near-instant online access to documents, follow each state's laws about what makes an advance directive valid, and survey users every year about their experience. The Medicare website would also post links to official advance directive forms for every state, as well as alternative forms submitted by outside groups, so people can compare options before deciding what fits their situation.

The people directly affected are the roughly 67 million Americans enrolled in Medicare, which mainly includes adults 65 and older as well as some younger people with disabilities. Participation is entirely optional, and the bill makes clear that no one is required to create an advance directive. It also states that the federal program does not override individual state laws on the topic, so existing state rules about what makes these documents legally valid still apply.

title: West Bank Violence Prevention Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would require the President to impose penalties on foreign individuals who commit or support violent acts in the West Bank, a disputed territory between Israel and the Palestinian Authority. Specifically, it targets people who attack civilians, destroy property, seize land, or commit terrorism there. The punishments include freezing any money or assets those people have in the United States and banning them from entering the country. The President would also have to report to Congress every six months on who has been sanctioned and what is happening on the ground in the West Bank.

The bill applies only to foreign persons, not American citizens. It would not block humanitarian aid like food, medicine, or medical supplies from reaching people in the region. The President can waive the sanctions if national security requires it, and sanctions can be lifted if a sanctioned person stops their harmful behavior and provides reliable assurances they will not repeat it.

American residents would not be directly penalized under this bill, but it could affect anyone in the United States who does business with or sends money to a sanctioned person. People with family or financial ties to individuals operating in the West Bank could find those connections complicated if those individuals end up on the sanctions list. The bill was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Foreign Relations Committee, so it has not yet become law.

title: No Settlements for January 6 Law Enforcement Assaulters Act
ai_summary:
This bill would block the federal government from paying any legal settlement money to people who were convicted of assaulting a police officer during the January 6, 2021 Capitol breach. Normally, people can sue the government and receive payment from a federal account called the Judgment Fund if they win or settle a civil lawsuit. This bill would make an exception: anyone with a qualifying assault conviction from that day could not receive that kind of payout, even if they claimed they were harmed during the events themselves or during their prosecution.

The bill targets a specific group of people who meet two conditions at the same time. First, they must have been convicted of assaulting a law enforcement officer in connection with January 6. Second, their lawsuit must be based on harm they say they suffered either during the Capitol events or as a result of being prosecuted for those events. Both conditions have to apply for the restriction to kick in.

This legislation would affect a relatively small number of people who were convicted on assault charges related to January 6 and who have filed or might file civil claims against the federal government. It would not affect the general public, law enforcement officers, or people convicted of non-assault offenses from that day. The bill was introduced in the Senate and has been referred to the Judiciary Committee, meaning it has not yet become law.

title: Stand Strong for Medicare Act
ai_summary:
This bill would add coverage for certain fall prevention products to Medicare for the first time. Specifically, Medicare would pay for items like grab bars, non-slip mats, shower chairs, and bed rails when a doctor or other qualified medical provider writes an order for them. Right now, Medicare does not cover these kinds of home safety products, so seniors who need them must pay out of pocket.

The bill affects people who are on Medicare, which is primarily Americans age 65 and older, as well as some younger people with disabilities. If passed, a Medicare enrollee whose doctor recommends fall prevention equipment could have Medicare help pay for it, rather than covering the full cost themselves. The coverage would take effect 60 days after the bill is signed into law.

The bill also includes a rule that says Medicare payments for these items cannot be reduced through the automatic budget cuts known as sequestration. This is meant to protect the new benefit from being trimmed down through future across-the-board federal spending cuts. The bill was introduced in the Senate in September 2025 and has been sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it would need to be approved before moving forward.

ai_summary:

title: To amend the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 to increase the civil penalties that may be imposed under such Act.
ai_summary:
This bill changes the fines that can be charged to people or companies that break U.S. export control laws. Export controls are rules that restrict selling or sending certain goods, technology, and information to other countries, especially when those items could be used for military purposes or by unfriendly nations. Right now, someone who breaks these rules can be fined up to $300,000 per violation or twice the value of the illegal transaction, whichever is greater. This bill would raise that to $1.2 million per violation or four times the value of the transaction.

The change would apply to any violation that happens on or after the date the bill becomes law. It does not affect past violations. The goal is to make the penalty steep enough to discourage businesses and individuals from trying to illegally export controlled items.

This bill mainly affects businesses, manufacturers, researchers, and individuals who deal in goods or technology that require a U.S. export license. That includes things like advanced electronics, software, weapons components, and certain industrial equipment. Most everyday Americans would not be directly affected, but the law could indirectly impact companies that do international trade, especially those in defense, technology, or manufacturing industries.

title: American Farmers First Act
ai_summary:
This bill does two main things. First, it would block a U.S. government fund called the Exchange Stabilization Fund from being used to financially support Argentina. This fund is managed by the Treasury Department and can be used to help stabilize foreign currencies or financial markets. The bill would ban any new financial deals with Argentina using this fund and would require any existing deals to be ended within 7 days of the bill becoming law. This ban would last until December 10, 2027.

Second, the bill would take whatever money comes back from unwinding those Argentina-related deals and hand it over to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. That money would then be paid out as one-time relief checks to American farmers who grew crops that lost overseas buyers during the 2025 crop marketing year. The Agriculture Secretary would decide which crops qualify based on which ones saw exports drop.

The people most directly affected are American farmers, particularly those who have struggled to sell their crops to foreign customers in 2025. The bill also affects how the Treasury Department can operate the Exchange Stabilization Fund going forward. It does not directly affect average consumers, though U.S.-Argentina financial relationships and farm commodity prices can have broader ripple effects on food supply chains over time.

title: VOTE Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require states to give voters advance warning when their polling place has been changed before a federal election. If a voter's assigned polling place is different from where they voted last time, the state must notify them at least 7 days before Election Day by mail, phone, text, and email if those contact methods are available. If the change happens less than 7 days out and a voter shows up at their old polling place, election officials must make every reasonable effort to still let that person vote.

The bill also requires that closed polling locations post signs on Election Day directing voters to their new polling place, including the address, directions, and contact information for local election officials. States must also post this information on their websites and social media. Areas that use vote centers instead of assigned polling places must notify all eligible voters of all available voting locations at least 2 days before early voting begins. All notices must be provided in languages required under the Voting Rights Act for communities with large non-English-speaking populations.

This bill affects all registered voters across the country who vote in federal elections, meaning elections for President, Senate, and House of Representatives. It also directly affects state and local election officials, who would be responsible for carrying out these notification requirements. The goal is to make sure voters are not surprised or confused by polling place changes, but the bill does not change where polling places can be located or who is eligible to vote.

title: STEADFAST Act
ai_summary:
This bill would end the existing federal program that uses taxpayer money to help fund presidential campaigns. Right now, when people file their taxes, they can check a box to send $3 to the Presidential Election Campaign Fund, which gives money to candidates running for president. The STEADFAST Act would shut that program down completely and redirect the money — along with any leftover funds already in the account — to a new purpose: helping states upgrade and secure their election systems.

The new program would send grants to states, territories like Puerto Rico and Guam, and Washington D.C. to pay for things like new voting machines, cybersecurity improvements, paper ballots, and physical security for election equipment. States would apply for the money through the Election Assistance Commission and would have to report publicly on how they spent it. The size of each state's grant would be based on how many registered voters it has. Vendors hired to do the work would need to be pre-approved by the commission, and companies that have previously donated money to help run elections would be blocked from being approved.

Not every state would be treated equally under this bill. States that use paper ballots with a verifiable paper trail, require photo ID to vote in person, and use federal databases to check that non-citizens are not registered to vote would be moved to the front of the line when grants are handed out. States that do not meet those conditions could still apply but would receive lower priority. The bill affects all U.S. states and several territories, election administrators, voting equipment vendors, and any taxpayers who previously used the presidential campaign checkoff on their tax returns.

title: Modernizing and Improving the National Terrorism Advisory System Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill tells the Department of Homeland Security to come up with a plan to update the National Terrorism Advisory System, which is the official system the government uses to warn the public about terrorism threats. The Secretary of Homeland Security would have one year to write a strategy and send it to Congress.

The strategy would have to look at several things, including who inside DHS is in charge of the system, how alerts are created and ended, how easy they are for the public to find and understand, and how well they reach as many people as possible. DHS would also need to talk to local and state police, tribal governments, emergency responders, and private businesses before finishing the plan. Two years after the bill passes, a government watchdog called the Comptroller General would check in and report to Congress on whether any of this is actually happening.

This bill mainly affects the Department of Homeland Security and the people who work within it, but it also touches state and local law enforcement, emergency responders, and the general public. Everyday Americans could eventually see changes in how they receive terrorism warnings, though this bill does not change the alert system itself right now. It only requires a plan to be written.

ai_summary:
This bill requires the Department of Homeland Security to reorganize a specific internal office called the Engagement, Liaison, and Outreach Office, known as the ELO Office. Within 120 days of the bill becoming law, the Secretary of Homeland Security would have to submit a detailed plan to Congress explaining how to restructure that office, cut any unnecessary positions or programs, and move its core work into a related division called the Partner Engagement directorate. The goal is to make the office run more efficiently, improve how it shares information with law enforcement partners, and reduce duplicated work across different parts of the department.

The bill also places limits on what the Secretary can do with the ELO Office while that plan is being developed. The department cannot grow the office, increase its budget, or create new offices that do the same job until the reorganization plan has been submitted and its launch certified to Congress. This is meant to prevent the department from expanding the very structure it is supposed to be fixing.

The people most directly affected are DHS employees who work in or alongside the ELO Office, since some positions may be reassigned or eliminated. State, local, tribal, and territorial law enforcement agencies that currently receive intelligence support and access to secure information systems through the ELO Office would also be affected, though the bill specifically requires the plan to protect continuity of those services. Ordinary residents would not feel a direct impact, but the changes are intended to improve how federal and local law enforcement agencies work together on national security and public safety matters.

Right now, NTER sits inside the Office of Intelligence and Analysis, which focuses on national intelligence work. The bill would move it to the Office for State and Local Law Enforcement, which is the DHS office that works directly with police departments, sheriffs, and other law enforcement agencies at the state, local, tribal, and territorial level. The move must happen within 180 days of the bill becoming law, and all staff, equipment, and funding tied to the program would transfer along with it.

The bill also changes how the program is paid for. Currently, NTER is funded through the National Intelligence Program budget, which is the pool of money used for national spy and intelligence agencies. The bill says that funding source must stop once the transfer is complete, and DHS would need to find other funding streams, such as state and local preparedness grants or other non-intelligence budget lines, to keep the program running.

The people most directly affected are state, local, tribal, and territorial law enforcement agencies and officials who use NTER training and tools to spot and respond to potential threats of targeted violence in their communities. The bill requires DHS to report to Congress every six months for two years on how the transition is going, so lawmakers can check that the program keeps working without interruption for those local partners.

title: Rural Depositories Revitalization Study Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells federal banking regulators to study why banks and credit unions in rural areas are struggling and what could be done to help them grow and stay financially healthy. The agencies would have one year after the bill becomes law to send their findings to Congress.

People most directly affected would be residents of rural communities who rely on local banks and credit unions for services like checking accounts, loans, and mortgages. Rural areas have seen many bank branches close in recent decades, so this study is aimed at understanding that trend and exploring possible solutions. title: Pandemic Unemployment Fraud Enforcement Act
ai_summary:
During the COVID-19 pandemic, the federal government created special unemployment programs to help people who lost work. Unfortunately, a large amount of money from these programs was stolen through fraud, including identity theft, fake claims, and other schemes. Normally, the government only has about five years to bring criminal charges or sue someone for fraud. This bill would extend that window to 10 years for fraud connected to those pandemic unemployment programs.

The bill applies to anyone suspected of committing fraud against programs like Pandemic Unemployment Assistance, Federal Pandemic Unemployment Compensation, and Pandemic Emergency Unemployment Compensation. This includes crimes like wire fraud, identity theft, money laundering, and filing false claims. One important limit is that the extension does not apply if the original deadline for a case had already passed before this bill becomes law.

This bill mainly affects two groups. First, it affects people who may have committed fraud against these programs, since they could face charges for a longer period of time. Second, it affects federal and state law enforcement agencies, which would have more time to investigate and prosecute these cases. The bill also cancels 5 million dollars in unused pandemic-related funds to help cover its costs.

title: Bureau of Land Management Mineral Spacing Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes the rules for drilling oil and gas on certain lands where the federal government owns less than half of the underground mineral rights but a private landowner owns the surface. Right now, companies need both a federal permit and a state permit to drill in these situations. Under this bill, if the federal government owns less than 50% of the mineral rights below ground, the company would only need a state permit. The company could start work 30 days after submitting that state permit to the federal government, without waiting for federal approval.

The bill also removes several federal review requirements for these drilling projects. They would no longer need to go through the National Environmental Policy Act review process, which typically requires studying environmental impacts. They would also be exempt from checks under the National Historic Preservation Act and the Endangered Species Act. However, the federal government would still collect its share of royalty payments from whatever oil and gas is produced, and federal inspectors could still visit sites to make sure production is reported and measured correctly.

This bill mainly affects oil and gas companies that operate on privately owned land sitting above federally owned mineral deposits, as well as the federal agencies that currently oversee those permits. It could also affect communities and wildlife near drilling sites, since some environmental and historic preservation reviews would no longer apply. The bill specifically does not apply to any Native American or tribal lands.
ai_headline: Bill would strip federal environmental review from some oil and gas permits
last_action_text: Subcommittee Hearings Held

title: Fisher House Availability Act of 2025
ai_summary:
Fisher Houses are free or low-cost temporary homes located near VA and military medical centers. Right now, they are mainly available to veterans receiving VA care and their family members. This bill would expand who can stay in a Fisher House when there are open rooms. Specifically, it would allow active-duty military members and their families to use these facilities on a space-available basis, meaning they can only stay if a room is not already needed by a veteran or their family.

The bill also broadens access in another way. Currently, the focus is on the patient traveling for care. This bill adds situations where a family member of a veteran or active-duty service member is the one traveling far to receive medical care. In those cases, the veteran or service member could stay at the Fisher House too, to support that family member. The key phrase throughout is "space-available," which means veterans and their families still have priority, and these expanded groups only get access to rooms that would otherwise sit empty.

This affects active-duty military members and their families, as well as family members of veterans who need to travel for their own medical care. It also directs the VA to set up rules for how this space-available access will work in practice. Fisher House facilities are donated and built by the Fisher House Foundation, and the VA manages them. The bill does not change any existing benefits for veterans already using these facilities.

last_action_text: Committee on Veterans' Affairs. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

title: Repeal the TikTok Ban Act
ai_summary:
This bill would undo a law passed in 2024 that required ByteDance, the Chinese company that owns TikTok, to either sell the app or face a ban in the United States. That earlier law said TikTok posed a national security risk because a foreign adversary could potentially access American users' data or influence what content people see. This bill would wipe that law off the books entirely and cancel any official government designations that were made under it.

If passed, this would mean TikTok and any other apps that were labeled "foreign adversary controlled applications" under the old law could continue operating in the US without facing a forced sale or ban. It would also apply retroactively, meaning actions already taken under the old law would be treated as if they never happened.

This bill directly affects the roughly 170 million Americans who use TikTok, as well as the companies that own or operate apps that were flagged under the original law. It also affects businesses that advertise on TikTok and creators who rely on the platform for income. The bill was introduced by two members of Congress from opposite parties, and it has been sent to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, where it would need to be approved before the full House could vote on it.

title: Food Date Labeling Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill creates a national standard for the date labels printed on food packaging. Right now, food companies use many different phrases like "Best By," "Sell By," "Expires On," and others, which confuses shoppers about whether food is still safe to eat or just past its peak quality. If this bill becomes law, companies that choose to put a date on their packaging would have to use one of two specific phrases. "BEST If Used By" would mean the food is still safe to eat after that date but might not taste or look as good. "USE By" would mean the food should not be eaten after that date. Companies are not required to include any date at all, but if they do, they must use the correct standard phrase.

The bill affects food manufacturers and grocery stores, since they would need to update their packaging within two years of the law passing. It also affects everyday shoppers, who would see clearer, more consistent labels at the store. The government would also be required to run public education campaigns explaining what the two phrases mean. Infant formula is specifically left out of this bill and keeps its existing, stricter rules.

States cannot create their own different versions of these two label phrases, but they can still pass laws that ban the sale or donation of food after a "USE By" date. States cannot, however, ban the sale of food just because it has passed a "BEST If Used By" date. The bill applies to all meat, poultry, egg products, and other packaged foods regulated by the federal government.
ai_headline: Senate bill would standardize food date labels to two federally defined phrases
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

title: ENFORCE Act
ai_summary:
This bill strengthens federal laws against child sexual abuse material in several ways. It closes a loophole by making it clearer that creating AI-generated or drawn images of child sexual abuse is a federal crime, even when no real child was directly used in the production. It also removes the time limit for prosecutors to bring charges for this type of material, meaning someone can be charged years or even decades after the crime occurred.

The bill also changes how people accused of these crimes are treated before and after a trial. Suspects charged under the updated law would be more likely to be held in jail while awaiting trial rather than released. After serving a prison sentence, offenders would face longer terms of supervised release, meaning more monitoring by authorities once they are out. The bill also requires that illegal images used as evidence stay under government or court control during legal proceedings, rather than being copied and shared in the discovery process.

This bill mostly affects law enforcement agencies, federal prosecutors, and the courts, giving them stronger tools to investigate and punish crimes involving child sexual abuse material. It also affects people convicted of or charged with these offenses, who would face stricter conditions before, during, and after a trial. Advocates for child protection and legal defense attorneys would also be impacted, since the changes shift how these cases are handled throughout the justice system.
ai_headline: Federal bill targets AI-generated child abuse images and removes statute of limitations
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

The bill eliminates the statute of limitations for these offenses, allowing prosecution years or decades after the crime. title: Protecting Americans from Russian Litigation Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would block foreign courts' rulings and arbitration decisions from being enforced in the United States when those rulings stem from someone following American sanctions or export control laws. For example, if a U.S. company stopped doing business with a Russian company because U.S. sanctions required it, and a Russian court then ordered the U.S. company to pay damages, that Russian court order could not be collected on in any U.S. federal or state court. The bill also lets defendants immediately move any such case to federal court, where it must be thrown out.

The bill is aimed at protecting American businesses and individuals who cut ties with sanctioned countries, like Russia, and then got sued in foreign courts as a result. It applies to cases already in progress, not just future ones. There are carve-outs to make sure the bill does not block terrorism victims, people harmed by torture or hostage-taking, or parties who voluntarily agreed to settle disputes in U.S. courts or through U.S.-based arbitration.

People most directly affected include U.S. companies that do or did international business and faced foreign lawsuits after complying with sanctions, as well as foreign entities trying to collect on those overseas judgments inside the United States. American consumers and courts would be indirectly affected since it changes what kinds of foreign legal decisions can be enforced here. The bill was introduced with bipartisan support and has been sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee.

last_action_text: Held at the desk.

title: Protecting Americans from Russian Litigation Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill blocks foreign courts and arbitration panels from using US sanctions as a basis to sue American individuals or companies in US courts. Right now, when the US government puts sanctions on a country like Russia, American businesses sometimes have to cancel contracts or stop doing business with certain people. Those foreign companies or governments can then go to a foreign court or arbitration panel, win a judgment against the American business, and try to collect that money through US courts. This bill would make US courts refuse to recognize or enforce those foreign judgments and awards.

The law applies to any situation where an American person or company broke a contract specifically because they were trying to follow US sanctions or export control laws. If a foreign party tries to bring that kind of case to a US court, the American defendant can have it moved to federal court and thrown out. The title references Russia, but the bill's language covers sanctions against any foreign country, so it would apply broadly wherever US sanctions exist.

This primarily affects American businesses, banks, and individuals who deal in international trade and have faced or could face foreign legal judgments for complying with US sanctions. It also affects foreign companies and governments that might have tried to use US courts to recover money lost because an American partner walked away from a deal due to sanctions. American victims of terrorism and certain other serious crimes are specifically protected and can still pursue their own cases under existing laws.

title: Bank Fraud Technology Advancement Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill tells federal banking regulators to study how well banks and credit unions are using advanced technology, like artificial intelligence and data analytics, to catch and stop fraud. The agencies have 18 months to complete the study and send a report to Congress. The report must cover what fraud-fighting tools are currently being used, how well they work, what is stopping financial institutions from using them more, and whether current rules make it harder or easier to adopt new technology.

A big focus of the bill is on smaller, community-based banks and credit unions. These smaller institutions often cannot afford the same high-tech fraud detection tools that large national banks use. The study must look at whether that puts everyday customers at smaller banks at a disadvantage and explore options like shared services or group buying arrangements that could help smaller institutions access better tools without bearing the full cost alone.

After the study is done, regulators may set up a voluntary pilot program to help community banks and credit unions actually try out some of these advanced fraud detection tools. This program could include shared purchasing deals, technical help, and clearer rules about how to use AI responsibly. The bill affects federal banking regulators, banks, credit unions of all sizes, and ultimately everyday bank customers, since better fraud detection could mean fewer people lose money to scams or identity theft.

title: Build Nuclear with Local Materials Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill tells the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), which oversees nuclear power plants, to start writing new rules that would allow builders to use regular commercial-grade steel and concrete at nuclear plants. Right now, nuclear plants often have to use specially certified materials even for parts of the facility that are not directly connected to nuclear safety, like office buildings, warehouses, or other support structures on the property. The bill would have to be acted on within 90 days of becoming law.

The key distinction in the bill is between "safety-related" and "non-safety-related" structures. Safety-related parts of a nuclear plant, like the reactor containment building, would not be affected and would keep their strict material requirements. Only structures that do not play a direct role in preventing a nuclear accident or protecting the public from radiation would be eligible for the looser standard. The NRC can still require stricter materials for non-safety structures if it finds a specific safety reason to do so.

The bill would most directly affect companies that build and operate nuclear power plants, construction contractors, and material suppliers. Supporters say it could lower construction costs and make it easier to source materials locally. Critics may question whether the line between safety and non-safety structures is always clear. Everyday Americans could be affected if the change influences how quickly or cheaply new nuclear plants can be built, which could in turn affect electricity supply and prices in areas where new plants are developed.

last_action_text: Committee on Environment and Public Works Subcommittee on Clean Air, Climate, and Nuclear Innovation and Safety. Hearings held.

title: Cultural Trade Promotion Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the federal government to do more to help American creative workers sell their products and services in other countries. It updates existing trade laws to include musicians, artists, craftspeople, writers, performers, designers, and others in creative fields when federal agencies plan their export promotion strategies. It also expands protections and export support that previously applied only to American Indian arts and crafts to now include Native Hawaiian arts and crafts as well.

The bill makes a few specific changes. It tells the U.S. Commercial Service, which is the government office that helps American businesses sell abroad, to also focus on very small businesses called microenterprises. It requires trade officials from the Commerce Department and the U.S. Postal Service to work together to find better international shipping options for small and micro businesses. It also adds a permanent seat on the federal Travel and Tourism Advisory Board for someone who represents creative industries.

The people most directly affected are small and independent creative workers, including freelancers, artists, musicians, craftspeople, authors, and small creative businesses across the country, as well as Native Hawaiian artists and cultural workers. Indirectly, it could affect communities where creative industries play a significant role in the local economy, including Native American communities. The bill does not create a new federal agency or spend new money directly; it mainly updates existing programs and committees to pay more attention to this group of workers.

title: Small Business Health Options Awareness Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill requires the Small Business Administration (SBA) to spread the word to small businesses about a health benefits option called an Individual Coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangement, or ICHRA. An ICHRA lets an employer give employees a set amount of tax-free money each month, which workers then use to buy their own individual health insurance plans. Right now, many small business owners may not know this option exists. The bill would have the SBA share information about ICHRAs through its local offices, Small Business Development Centers, its website, social media, and press releases.

The bill does not create a new program or change any existing health insurance rules. It simply directs the SBA to act as an information channel, passing along guidance already developed by federal agencies like the Treasury Department, the Department of Health and Human Services, and the Department of Labor.

Small business owners are the main group this bill targets, since they are often the ones trying to figure out affordable ways to offer health benefits to employees. Workers at small businesses could also be indirectly affected, since learning about ICHRAs might lead their employer to offer this kind of benefit. The bill does not require any business to change what it does — it only aims to make sure small business owners know this option is available to them.
ai_headline: SBA would be required to inform small businesses about a lesser-known health benefit option

title: Integrated Ocean Observation System Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews funding and updates the rules for a network of sensors, buoys, and monitoring systems along America's coasts and oceans. That network collects real-time data on water conditions, weather, tides, and other ocean-related information. The bill keeps the program running through 2030 with $56 million per year and expands its focus to include meteorological, meaning weather-related, observations alongside the existing ocean and coastal monitoring. It also requires that after any major storm, officials must review how well the system's data helped forecasters predict that storm.

The bill also makes sure that regional monitoring stations around the country get a guaranteed share of the funding, with each established regional system receiving at least 7.5 percent of the annual budget. It updates some internal terminology, changing references from a "Council" to a "Committee" to reflect how the program is currently organized, and adds requirements for better data sharing between federal agencies and local regional systems.

This bill most directly affects federal agencies like NOAA, regional coastal monitoring organizations, researchers, and emergency managers who rely on ocean and weather data. It also indirectly affects coastal communities, fishermen, shipping operators, and anyone who depends on accurate storm forecasting and ocean conditions for safety or business decisions.

title: Blast Overpressure Research and Mitigation Task Force Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells the Department of Veterans Affairs to create a special task force focused on blast overpressure injuries. Blast overpressure happens when an explosion sends a powerful pressure wave through the air that can damage the brain and body, even without a visible wound. The task force would be a joint effort between the VA and the Department of Defense, and it must be up and running within 180 days of the bill becoming law.

The task force would have several jobs. It would work to improve medical care and benefits for veterans and active-duty troops who were hurt by blasts, including those with traumatic brain injuries, PTSD, balance problems, hearing or vision loss, and gut or nervous system issues. It would also coordinate research between the VA and the military to make sure scientists are studying the most important questions, and it would help develop better tools to diagnose these injuries, including portable devices that could be used in the field or at home.

Every year, the task force would report to Congress on what it has learned and recommend improvements to how the VA reviews disability claims tied to blast injuries. The people most directly affected are veterans and active-duty military members who have been exposed to explosions during their service, a group that includes many combat veterans as well as troops who train with heavy weapons. The task force is set to automatically end on September 30, 2029.
ai_headline: VA ordered to launch blast injury task force within 180 days
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by Voice Vote.

title: Rural and Municipal Utility Cybersecurity Act
ai_summary:
This bill renews and updates a federal grant program that helps smaller electric utilities improve their cybersecurity. It authorizes up to $250 million over five years, from 2026 through 2030, for the Department of Energy to hand out grants, prizes, and technical assistance. The money is meant to help these utilities buy better security technology, defend against cyberattacks, and share information about threats with other utilities and the government.

The program focuses on smaller and local power providers that often have fewer resources to protect themselves than large private companies do. Eligible recipients include rural electric cooperatives, city- and county-owned utilities, and smaller investor-owned utilities that sell less than 4 million megawatt-hours of electricity per year. Priority goes to utilities that have especially limited cybersecurity budgets, or that provide power to military or other critical defense facilities.

The bill also includes a privacy protection for utilities that participate. Any information a utility shares with the government through this program is kept confidential and cannot be released through Freedom of Information Act requests or similar state public-records laws. This is meant to encourage utilities to openly share details about vulnerabilities or attacks without worrying that sensitive information could become public.
ai_headline: Federal grants target cybersecurity gaps at smaller electric utilities
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

title: SECURE Grid Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires states to update their energy security plans to specifically address the safety and reliability of local power distribution systems. These are the smaller electrical networks, running at lower voltages, that deliver electricity directly to homes, businesses, and neighborhoods. Right now, state energy plans focus more on the larger power grid, so this bill fills a gap by making sure states also plan for threats to the "last mile" of electricity delivery.

The bill expands what states must cover in those plans. States would need to address physical threats like extreme weather and attacks on equipment, cybersecurity threats targeting local power lines and systems, and risks in the supply chain for electrical equipment. States must also outline how they would respond to and recover from those threats. The bill also extends the program's funding authorization from 2025 to 2030, keeping federal support available longer.

The people most directly affected are state energy officials, who must revise their planning documents, and electric utilities, who would be consulted in that process. Equipment suppliers for the power grid are also brought into the conversation. Everyday residents are indirectly affected, since stronger local grid planning could mean faster recovery after storms, cyberattacks, or other disruptions that cause power outages in their communities.

last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

Plans must also outline response and recovery procedures for those threats.

title: Pipeline Cybersecurity Preparedness Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Department of Energy to create a program focused on protecting pipelines and liquefied natural gas facilities from both physical attacks and cyberattacks. The program would work to improve communication and coordination between the federal government, state governments, and the energy industry when it comes to keeping these facilities safe. It also calls for developing new cybersecurity technologies and tools, running test projects to try out security improvements, and creating training programs to build a skilled workforce in this area.

Most of the tools and technologies developed under this program would be available for voluntary use, meaning pipeline and energy companies could choose to adopt them but would not be required to. The bill also makes clear that it does not take away any authority that other federal agencies, like the Transportation Security Administration, already have over pipeline security.

The people most directly affected are workers and companies that operate natural gas pipelines, hazardous liquid pipelines, and liquefied natural gas facilities across the country. More broadly, everyday Americans could be affected indirectly, since these pipelines carry the fuel used to heat homes, generate electricity, and power businesses. Better security for these systems could reduce the risk of disruptions caused by cyberattacks or physical incidents.

title: Energy Threat Analysis Center Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill renews and expands a Department of Energy program focused on protecting the U.S. energy grid from cyberattacks. The program, which was set to expire, would be funded through 2031 instead. The bill also creates something called an Energy Threat Analysis Center, where government officials and energy companies can work together to share information about cyber threats, study how hackers might attack power systems, and develop ways to stop or limit the damage from those attacks.

The bill allows classified and unclassified threat information to be shared between the government and energy companies. Importantly, any information shared through this program is protected from public disclosure laws, meaning it cannot be obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests or similar state laws. The government also keeps full control over who gets help or information through the program, and no company or group is guaranteed access just because others received it.

This affects people and organizations across the U.S. energy sector, including electric utilities, natural gas companies, and other energy providers, as well as the federal, state, tribal, and local governments that work with them. For everyday Americans, the goal is to reduce the risk of cyberattacks that could knock out electricity or disrupt other energy services that people rely on at home and at work.

title: To prohibit the District of Columbia from requiring tribunals in court or administrative proceedings in the District of Columbia to defer to the Mayor of the District of Columbia's interpretation of statutes and regulations, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill is about who gets the final say when there is a disagreement over what a DC law or regulation means. Right now, courts and other official bodies in Washington DC can be required to simply accept the Mayor's or a city agency's interpretation of the law when settling disputes. This bill would ban that practice, meaning judges and other decision-makers would have to read and interpret the law for themselves, rather than automatically siding with the Mayor or agency on what the law means.

This matters because many legal disputes involve questions like "what does this rule actually require?" When a government agency is allowed to define its own rules, it has more power in those fights. Removing that advantage means courts act as a more independent check on the Mayor and city agencies.

This bill would affect Washington DC residents who challenge city government decisions, businesses or individuals in disputes with DC agencies, and the DC government itself, which would lose some of its legal edge in those proceedings. It also repeals a recent DC law that had moved things in the opposite direction. Because Congress has special authority over DC, it can step in and change how DC courts operate in ways it cannot do with state courts.
ai_headline: Bill strips DC Mayor and agencies of automatic win in legal disputes over local rules
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 565.

Judges would instead have to read and interpret those laws independently. The bill also repeals a recent DC law that had moved in the opposite direction.

title: International Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews and updates a longstanding U.S. law aimed at fighting human trafficking in other countries. It keeps key anti-trafficking programs running through 2029 or 2030 and increases the funding authorized for those programs. For example, it raises one major funding level from $65 million to $102.5 million per year. It also extends the International Megan's Law, which requires the government to notify other countries when a registered sex offender plans to travel there.

The bill makes several practical changes to how the U.S. deals with countries that have human trafficking problems. It renames the "Special Watch List" to the "Tier 2 Watch List" to make the system clearer, and it directs U.S. officials at international banks to push for anti-trafficking protections in development projects in high-risk countries. It also clarifies exactly what types of foreign aid can be cut off when a country is failing to address trafficking, while making sure that humanitarian aid, health programs, and food assistance are not interrupted.

The bill also adds new protections for a specific group of vulnerable workers inside the United States: household employees who work for foreign diplomats and international organization staff, holding special A-3 or G-5 visas. It requires the government to expand a national registration program for these workers, inform them of their legal rights annually, and require their employers to report wages. Diplomats who abuse these workers could face visa suspensions or criminal consequences. Congress would also receive more regular briefings on which countries are improving or worsening on trafficking and why waivers from penalties are granted.
ai_headline: U.S. anti-trafficking law extended and expanded through 2029–2030
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Foreign Relations.

It also creates new protections for household workers inside the United States who hold A-3 or G-5 visas and work for foreign diplomats or international organization staff.

title: Scratch Cooked Meals for Students Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would create a pilot grant program run by the U.S. Department of Agriculture to help school districts prepare more meals from scratch using fresh, unprocessed ingredients instead of pre-packaged or heavily processed foods. The program would award competitive grants to school food authorities, meaning the local agencies that manage cafeteria programs. Each grant would last two school years, and up to $20 million per year could be approved for the program from 2027 through 2031. Schools that receive grants could use the money to train cafeteria staff, buy new kitchen equipment, update facilities, pay workers for the extra labor involved, and educate students about food through things like taste tests and cooking lessons.

Not all schools would have equal chances of receiving a grant. The program gives top priority to districts where the most students qualify for free or reduced-price lunch, meaning lower-income communities would be first in line. Priority is also given to school districts that run their own food service rather than outsourcing it to a private company, and to districts where cafeteria workers have or are working toward a union contract or similar labor agreement. Schools that do not yet meet those conditions can still qualify if they commit to meeting them before the grant ends.

This bill mainly affects public school students, school cafeteria workers, and school administrators across the country. Students in lower-income districts stand to benefit the most since those schools are prioritized. Cafeteria employees could see changes in their job duties, training opportunities, and potentially their wages. The bill is currently in the early stages and has only been introduced in the Senate, so it has not become law yet.

title: GROUSE Act of 2026
ai_summary:
The GROUSE Act would create a new federal program that pays private landowners to restore wildlife habitat on their forest land. If a landowner's forest was recently logged, is currently being logged, or was damaged by a natural disaster like a wildfire or tornado, they can apply to sign a contract with the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Under that contract, the government would cover 75 percent of the costs to plant native trees, shrubs, and other vegetation that benefits upland birds and wildlife, such as grouse, quail, and similar species. The contracts last up to five years, and landowners must work with a wildlife biologist or forester to create a habitat restoration plan.

There are limits on how much land qualifies. A landowner can only receive payments for up to 250 acres or 5 percent of their eligible forest land, whichever is smaller. The land must also be at least 10 acres and must be privately owned, non-industrial forest land. The government can also provide hands-on technical help to landowners who need guidance carrying out their restoration plan.

This bill mainly affects small and mid-sized private forest landowners across the country, particularly in rural areas where logging and natural disasters are common. It would also benefit hunters, wildlife enthusiasts, and conservation groups who care about upland bird populations. The program would be run through the USDA and built into the existing framework of the Food Security Act of 1985, which already manages several farmland and conservation programs.

The government would cover 75 percent of costs to plant native trees, shrubs, and vegetation that supports upland birds like grouse and quail. Contracts last up to five years and require a habitat restoration plan developed with a wildlife biologist or forester.

title: African Development Foundation Termination Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would shut down the United States African Development Foundation, a small, independent federal agency created in 1980. The Foundation's main job has been to give grants and loans directly to grassroots community groups and small businesses in African countries to help them grow economically. If this bill becomes law, the Foundation would officially close 120 days after it is signed. No new grants or loans could be issued from the moment the bill is signed, and any unspent government money would go back to the U.S. Treasury. Existing multi-year grants that are already in place would be managed by the State Department until they naturally expire.

The bill also spells out what happens to the Foundation's staff, property, and records. Employees would receive legally required notices about losing their jobs, following standard federal layoff rules. All files, contracts, and other assets would be handed over to the State Department, which would only use them to wrap up whatever is already underway, not to continue the Foundation's work in any new form.

This bill mainly affects the Foundation's roughly 50 or so federal employees, who would lose their positions. It also affects the African community organizations, farmers, and small business owners who currently receive or were hoping to receive funding from the Foundation. American taxpayers are affected in the sense that the agency's annual budget, which has been around 30 to 40 million dollars in recent years, would no longer be spent on this program.
ai_headline: Bill to shut down U.S. African Development Foundation clears path to closure

title: Biological Intellectual Property Protection Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would require U.S. companies and researchers to get a government license before sending digital genetic sequences to certain foreign adversaries. Specifically, it covers synthetic DNA and RNA sequences that were designed by humans or artificial intelligence. The targets are countries the U.S. already considers threats, most notably China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea. The idea is that even sharing a digital file containing a gene sequence could allow a foreign government to copy or steal American biotech research, so the bill adds that kind of data to existing export control rules.

The bill affects biotechnology companies, university research labs, and scientists who work with synthetic biology and might collaborate with or send data to researchers or organizations in those countries. If this becomes law, those groups would need to apply for a federal license before transferring that type of genetic data internationally. There is an exception for information that is already considered publicly available or educational under current export rules, so basic academic publishing would likely not be affected.

The broader goal is to protect American intellectual property in the fast-growing field of synthetic biology, which has commercial, medical, and potential military uses. Congress is expressing concern that foreign governments, particularly China, could use shared genetic design data to advance their own military or industrial programs. The bill does not ban the research itself, just the transfer of certain genetic sequence files to entities connected to countries on the foreign adversary list.
ai_headline: New bill would require licenses to share synthetic gene data with foreign adversaries

title: Abolish Super PACs Act
ai_summary:
This bill would bring Super PACs under the same donation limits that already apply to regular political action committees. Right now, individuals, corporations, and other groups can give unlimited amounts of money to Super PACs. Under this bill, those contributions would be capped. The existing limit for donations to regular PACs is $5,000 per year per donor, and that same kind of restriction would now apply to Super PACs and any committees that funnel money into Super PACs. The bill defines a Super PAC broadly, so groups that pool money to run political ads independently of campaigns would all fall under these new rules.

The bill affects anyone who currently donates large sums to Super PACs, including wealthy individuals, corporations, and other organizations. It would also affect the Super PACs themselves, since they would have far less money available to spend on political ads and other election activities. Candidates for federal office would feel an indirect impact too, since Super PACs often run expensive advertising campaigns that support or oppose specific candidates without directly coordinating with them.

Everyday voters are not directly regulated by this bill, but they would be affected by changes in how elections are funded and what political advertising looks like. The bill was introduced in the Senate in May 2026 and sent to the Committee on Rules and Administration, meaning it has not yet been debated or voted on by the full Senate.
