title: CCP Sanctions Shot Clock Act
ai_summary:
The United States government keeps a list called the Non-SDN Chinese Military-Industrial Complex Companies List. This list identifies companies believed to be connected to China's military. American investors are restricted from putting money into companies on this list. Right now, even when the President's own report identifies a company as qualifying for this list, there is no deadline requiring the Treasury Department to actually add it.

This bill would fix that by creating a one-year deadline. Once the President submits a report naming companies that belong on the list, the Secretary of the Treasury would have up to one year to officially add those companies and update the published list. Think of it like a shot clock in basketball — once the timer starts, the government has to act before time runs out.

This bill mainly affects American investors and financial institutions, since they face restrictions on buying stock or investing in companies that appear on the list. It also affects the foreign companies that might be added, since being placed on the list limits their access to U.S. investment dollars. The bill does not directly impact most everyday Americans, but it could affect people who hold certain mutual funds or retirement accounts that include shares of Chinese companies.

title: South China Sea Strategy Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill requires the U.S. Secretary of State to create a formal written plan, within 180 days of the law passing, for how the United States will handle diplomacy in the South China Sea. The South China Sea is a major waterway in Asia where China, the Philippines, Vietnam, and several other countries have overlapping territorial claims. The plan must lay out U.S. goals for the region, identify which government office is in charge of each goal, and describe how the U.S. will work with nearby countries and allies on issues like trade routes, maritime law enforcement, and avoiding military conflict.

The bill also requires the State Department to report back to Congress within about a year on what programs, policies, and funding would be needed to actually carry out that plan through 2029. A follow-up briefing to congressional committees must happen within 30 days after that report. The strategy document would be made publicly available, though it can include a classified section for sensitive information.

The people most directly affected are U.S. diplomats and government agencies who would carry out the strategy, as well as citizens and businesses that depend on safe shipping lanes through the South China Sea, which carries a large share of global trade. Countries bordering the sea, specifically Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam, would also be involved as partners in the diplomatic efforts described in the plan.

title: To amend title 5, United States Code, to add certain employees of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives to the definition of employees in fire protection activities for the purpose of compensation for certain illnesses and diseases deemed to be proximately caused by employment in fire protection activities.
ai_summary:
This bill changes who qualifies for a specific federal workers' compensation benefit. Right now, federal law gives special protections to employees who work in fire protection, meaning if they get certain illnesses or diseases, the government assumes those health problems were caused by their job. This bill would extend that same protection to two groups of ATF employees: Certified Fire Investigators and members of the National Response Team. These are ATF workers who regularly investigate fires, explosions, and arson scenes, where they can be exposed to smoke, toxic chemicals, and other hazardous materials.

In practical terms, this matters because of how workers' compensation claims work. Normally, a sick worker has to prove their illness was caused by their job, which can be difficult and time-consuming. Under the existing fire protection employee rule, that burden is flipped, and the government is presumed responsible unless proven otherwise. By adding these ATF employees to that category, the bill makes it easier for them to receive compensation if they develop illnesses linked to their work at fire and explosion scenes.

This bill directly affects ATF Certified Fire Investigators and National Response Team members who are federal employees. It would apply to any compensation claims filed after the bill becomes law. It does not affect private sector workers, state or local fire investigators, or other ATF employees not in those two specific roles.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

title: CARE for RPA Crews Act
ai_summary:
This bill deals with how the U.S. military recognizes drone operators who take part in combat. Right now, military members who fight in traditional combat zones can receive a "combat status identifier," which is an official marker on their record showing they engaged in combat. Drone crews, who remotely pilot aircraft and carry out real combat missions from locations that may be far from the battlefield, do not currently receive an equivalent recognition. This bill would require the Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps to create a similar status marker for drone crews within 180 days of the bill becoming law.

This affects military personnel who operate remotely piloted aircraft, commonly known as drones, during combat operations. These service members perform missions that can be just as consequential as those of traditional combat troops, including airstrikes and other combat activities, but their official records do not currently reflect that combat experience in the same way. The new status identifier would give their combat service formal recognition equal in standing to what other combat veterans receive.

The practical impact could include how these service members are evaluated for promotions, benefits, and veteran status recognition, since official military records and combat identifiers often play a role in those decisions. The bill does not specify exact benefits but requires military leadership to design a system that treats drone crew combat service as equally significant to other forms of direct combat participation.
ai_headline: Bill would give drone crews the same combat record status as ground troops
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Armed Services.

Currently, service members who fight in traditional combat zones receive an official marker on their records showing they engaged in combat, but remotely piloted aircraft crews do not receive an equivalent recognition. The new identifier would give drone crew combat service formal standing equal to that of other direct combat participants.

title: NEDD Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill is about drones near nuclear facilities. Right now, federal law bans government agencies from buying or using drones made by certain foreign countries considered security risks, like China. A 2024 defense law already gave some cabinet departments exceptions to that ban for special security purposes. This bill adds the Department of Energy to that list of exceptions, meaning the Energy Secretary could buy and use those foreign-made drones if needed, under specific conditions.

The reason this matters is that the Department of Energy oversees the country's nuclear weapons stockpile and nuclear research sites. The bill also expands the Energy Department's authority to counter drones flying over a broader range of nuclear-related facilities, including places that make non-nuclear parts for nuclear weapons, not just sites that handle nuclear materials directly. This gives the department more tools to protect those locations from drone threats.

Most everyday Americans would not be directly affected by this bill. It mainly changes how the federal government manages security at nuclear facilities. Workers at Energy Department sites, contractors who build nuclear components, and federal security personnel are the groups most directly touched by these changes. The bill was introduced with support from both a Democratic and a Republican senator, and it has been sent to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee for review.

ai_summary:

Some agencies, such as the State Department and Transportation Department, were already given exceptions to that rule so they could use those drones for specific security-related purposes, like detecting or studying drone threats. This bill adds the Secretary of Energy to that list of exceptions.

In practice, this means DOE could buy and operate foreign-made drones that are otherwise restricted, as long as it follows the same rules and reporting requirements the other excepted agencies must follow. The most likely reason is that DOE oversees nuclear weapons sites and national laboratories, which face growing drone threats. Being able to use or study those same drones could help the department figure out how to detect and defend against them.

This bill mainly affects the Department of Energy and the facilities it protects, including nuclear sites like the Nevada National Security Site and national laboratories across the country. title: Epstein Files Transparency Act
ai_summary:
This law requires the U.S. Department of Justice to release its files related to Jeffrey Epstein within 30 days of the bill being signed. That includes records from the FBI and federal prosecutors' offices covering investigations, prosecutions, flight logs, immunity deals, internal communications, and documents about Epstein's detention and death. It also covers records related to his associate Ghislaine Maxwell and any individuals or organizations connected to his criminal network. The documents must be posted online in a searchable, downloadable format so the public can access them.

The law sets clear limits on what the government is allowed to hide. Officials cannot withhold records simply because releasing them would be embarrassing or politically inconvenient. However, they are permitted to redact information that would identify victims, contains child sexual abuse material, could harm an active investigation, or is legitimately classified for national security reasons. Any redaction must be explained in writing and reported to Congress. If something is classified, the Attorney General must try to declassify it or at minimum release a summary of what was withheld.

Within 15 days after the release is complete, the Attorney General must send Congress a full report listing what was released, what was held back, and why. The report must also name any government officials or public figures mentioned in the documents, with no redactions allowed for those names. This law primarily affects the Department of Justice and FBI, but it also directly involves any public figures, government officials, and organizations whose names appear in Epstein-related files, as well as survivors whose privacy protections are written into the law.

title: Section 232 Public Transparency Act
ai_summary:
Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 allows the federal government to investigate whether certain imports pose a threat to national security. If a threat is found, the president can take action such as placing tariffs or other restrictions on those imports. Right now, the reports from these investigations can be kept from the public for a long time, or sometimes are never fully released.

This bill would require the government to publish the unclassified, non-business-sensitive parts of those investigation reports within 270 days of starting an investigation, or when the report is handed to the president, whichever comes first. The idea is to make the process more open so the public can see what findings led to any trade actions taken in the name of national security.

This bill mainly affects businesses that import or export goods, industries that compete with foreign imports, and anyone who wants to understand why the government has imposed certain tariffs or trade restrictions. It also matters to the general public, since Section 232 tariffs can affect the prices of everyday products like steel, aluminum, and the goods made from them.

title: Golden Mussel Eradication and Control Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill creates a federal program to fight the golden mussel, an invasive species that has been spreading into U.S. waterways, starting with the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta in California. A federal task force would work with states, cities, universities, port authorities, and nonprofits to research the mussel's biology, track where it is spreading, and develop ways to stop and remove it. The task force would also be required to publish guidelines within one year for controlling its spread, including setting up inspection stations for boats.

The bill also sets up a competitive grant program, meaning organizations like universities, nonprofits, and local governments can apply for funding to develop new technologies for removing golden mussels from water pipes, boat hulls, fish screens, canals, and other places they attach themselves. Any useful technologies developed through these grants could be shared or licensed to speed up the response effort nationwide.

The people most directly affected include residents and workers near infested waterways, particularly in California, as well as those who manage water infrastructure, fishing operations, and ports. Boaters could face new inspection requirements at watercraft stations. Farmers and communities that rely on irrigation systems or clean water supplies could also be impacted, since golden mussels are known to clog water intake systems and harm ecosystems. The bill proposes spending up to 15 million dollars per year from 2026 through 2030 to fund these efforts.

title: American Sovereignty and Monterey Historic Military Site Study Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Department of the Interior to study Lower Presidio Historic Park in Monterey, California, to find out whether it should become a National Park. The Secretary of the Interior would have three years after funding is approved to complete the study and report the findings to Congress. The study would look at how historically significant the site is, whether making it a National Park is practical and affordable, and what it would cost the federal government to manage it. It would also consider other options, like having state, local, or tribal governments or private groups take a leading role in preserving the site.

The park has a long and layered history. It was home to the Esselen and Rumsen peoples for thousands of years, was explored by Spanish explorers in the 1500s and 1600s, served as California's capital under Spanish and Mexican rule, and was the spot where the U.S. Navy raised the American flag over California in 1846. It later became an active Army post where future Civil War generals served, where the Buffalo Soldiers were stationed before becoming some of America's first national park rangers, and where the Defense Language Institute was eventually established.

This bill directly affects the federal government, particularly the Interior Department, which would carry out the study. It also involves the City of Monterey, which currently leases and operates the park, as well as local Native American tribes and any organizations connected to the site. Regular residents would not face any immediate changes, since the bill only orders a study, not an actual change in the park's status.
ai_headline: Interior Department ordered to study Monterey historic park for national status
last_action_text: Subcommittee Hearings Held

The Secretary of the Interior would have three years after funding is approved to complete the study and report findings to Congress. The study would assess historical significance, practicality, affordability, federal management costs, and alternative preservation arrangements involving state, local, tribal, or private entities.

title: Washington’s Trail—1753 National Historic Trail Feasibility Study Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill tells the Secretary of the Interior to study whether a roughly 500-mile route through Virginia and Pennsylvania should be officially named a national historic trail. The route follows the path that a young George Washington traveled in late 1753, when he was sent by Virginia's colonial governor to deliver a message to French military forces. That mission took place just before the French and Indian War began. Right now, the bill only orders a study to see if the designation makes sense, not the designation itself.

If the trail is eventually designated after the study, it would join the National Trails System, which includes well-known routes like the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail. Designation can bring federal attention, funding, and tourism to the communities along the trail. The route would pass through parts of Virginia and Pennsylvania, so residents, local businesses, and governments in those states could be most directly affected.

The people most likely to notice this bill are history enthusiasts, outdoor recreation groups, local tourism businesses, and state and local governments in western Pennsylvania and Virginia. Federal taxpayers would cover the cost of the study, though feasibility studies like this are generally a small expense. No trail is being built or officially named yet. Congress would need to act again based on the study's findings before anything permanent happens.

title: GEO Act
ai_summary:
This bill deals with geothermal energy, which is power generated from heat stored underground. Right now, companies that want to drill and develop geothermal energy on federal land have to apply for permits and approvals from the government. Sometimes those applications sit without a decision for a long time, especially when there are ongoing lawsuits related to the project. This bill would require the federal government to make a decision, either approving or denying each application, within 60 days after finishing all required environmental and legal reviews. The rule would apply even if a lawsuit is pending, unless a court has specifically put a stop to the project through a judge's order.

The bill affects energy companies and developers who want to tap into geothermal resources on federal land. It also affects the federal agencies, mainly the Department of the Interior, that process these permit applications. Those agencies would now be held to a firm deadline. The bill does not change the rights of people or groups to sue over a project, and it does not give courts any new or reduced power to block projects. A court can still step in and halt things if it chooses to.

Everyday Americans could be indirectly affected if faster permitting leads to more geothermal energy development, which is a source of renewable electricity. People living near proposed geothermal sites or those involved in related legal challenges would be more directly touched by this change. Overall, the bill is narrowly focused on speeding up the government's paperwork and decision-making process for one specific type of energy project.
ai_headline: Federal agencies face 60-day deadline on geothermal permit decisions
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 568.

The deadline applies even when a lawsuit related to the project is pending, unless a court has issued a specific order halting the project.

title: Protecting Veteran Community Care Act
ai_summary:
This bill would make it easier for veterans to get mental health and substance use treatment outside of VA facilities when the VA cannot serve them quickly enough. Right now, the VA's Community Care Program lets veterans see outside doctors under certain conditions, but the bill's sponsors say the VA has been making it too hard for veterans to use that option for mental health care specifically. The bill would add a new rule saying that if a veteran qualifies for a VA Mental Health Residential Rehabilitation Treatment Program but there is no open spot, or if the VA cannot meet its own wait-time standards for that care, the veteran can go to an approved outside treatment program instead and have it covered.

The bill also adds some consumer-style protections. Veterans could not be told they are ineligible for outside care just because no community provider happens to meet the VA's scheduling standards at that moment. If more than one care option is available, the veteran gets to choose which one they want. Outside programs used under this rule would have to be state-licensed and accredited by recognized behavioral health organizations, though the VA could waive those requirements in limited cases where no other option exists.

Finally, the bill requires the VA to start tracking and reporting detailed data on community care requests, including how many were approved, denied, or appealed, with a special focus on mental health requests. It also requires Congress to formally approve any future changes the VA tries to make to the rules that govern when veterans can access outside care, giving Congress more direct oversight over those decisions. Veterans seeking residential mental health or substance use treatment would be most directly affected, particularly those in areas where VA facilities are limited.
ai_headline: Senate bill would expand outside mental health care access for veterans when VA falls short
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Veterans' Affairs.

The bill adds consumer protections, including the right to choose among available options and a ban on denying eligibility solely because no nearby provider meets scheduling standards. Outside programs used under this rule would need to be state-licensed and accredited by recognized behavioral health organizations, with limited VA waivers allowed when no other option exists.

The bill's data-reporting requirement and congressional approval mandate reflect concern that without oversight, access restrictions could be tightened without public accountability.

title: Never Fight Alone Act
ai_summary:
This bill would make it easier for veterans to get mental health and substance use treatment from private, community-based providers when the VA cannot serve them quickly enough. Right now, veterans can sometimes see outside providers through the VA Community Care Program, but the rules have made it hard to use that option for mental health and residential treatment programs specifically. This bill adds a new rule saying that if a veteran qualifies for a VA Mental Health Residential Rehabilitation Treatment Program but cannot get in promptly, or if the VA cannot meet its own wait-time standards for that care, the veteran can go to an approved outside facility and have the VA cover it. It also says the VA cannot deny community care just because outside providers happen to be unavailable either, and it gives veterans a say in choosing between available options.

The bill sets quality requirements for outside mental health and residential treatment facilities, requiring them to be state-licensed and nationally accredited. It also requires the VA to start reporting detailed data each year on how many community care requests were made, approved, denied, and appealed, including a breakdown for mental health services. Additionally, it puts a check on VA bureaucracy by requiring Congress to pass a resolution before the VA can tighten the rules that determine when veterans qualify for community care.

This bill primarily affects veterans who need mental health treatment or help with substance use and are struggling to get timely care through the VA system. It would also affect private mental health treatment facilities that could become eligible VA community care providers, and VA administrators who would face new reporting requirements and limits on their ability to change eligibility rules without congressional approval.

title: ORBITS Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the ORBITS Act of 2025, tries to address the growing problem of space junk orbiting Earth. Right now, there are thousands of broken satellites, rocket parts, and other human-made objects floating in orbit that no longer work. The bill directs NASA to run a competitive program where private companies, universities, and nonprofits can apply for funding to develop and test technology that would actually go up and remove or redirect that junk. The government would publish a public list of the most dangerous pieces of debris within 90 days of the bill passing, and up to $150 million would be available between 2026 and 2030 to support this work.

The bill also directs several federal agencies to update the official rulebook for how satellites should be built and disposed of after their missions end. This updated rulebook would cover things like how to avoid collisions, how quickly old satellites must be brought down, and how to track smaller pieces of debris that are currently too small to monitor. After those rules are updated, agencies like the FCC and FAA would use them to shape future regulations for anyone launching things into space.

The bill affects a wide range of people and organizations. Companies in the commercial space industry, satellite operators, universities, and nonprofit research groups could all apply to participate in the debris removal demonstration program. Anyone who uses technology that depends on satellites, which includes most Americans using GPS, weather forecasts, or internet services, has an indirect stake in this, since space junk poses a real threat to those systems.
ai_headline: NASA would fund private debris removal under new space junk bill
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 440.

The government would also publish a public list of the most dangerous debris within 90 days of passage. Separately, federal agencies would update rules governing how satellites are built, disposed of, and tracked after their missions end.

Anyone who relies on GPS, weather forecasts, or internet services has an indirect stake, since those systems depend on satellites that space debris threatens.

ai_sections.cost: Up to $150 million would be available for the debris removal demonstration program, covering the period from 2026 through 2030.

title: Kenya Merritt Renewing our PACT Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill creates a legal shortcut for certain civilian federal employees who got sick after working near open burn pits overseas. Right now, these workers have to prove their illness was caused by their job, which can be very difficult. The bill would create a "presumption," meaning the government automatically assumes the illness was job-related if the worker qualifies. This matches a benefit that military veterans already received under a 2022 law. The bill is named after Kenya Merritt, likely someone personally affected by burn pit exposure.

To qualify, a civilian federal employee must have worked at least 30 days in a country where the U.S. was running a military operation on or after August 2, 1990. They must also work for one of several specific agencies, such as the Departments of Defense, State, Justice, Homeland Security, or the intelligence community, or be a federal law enforcement officer. The diseases covered by the presumption are the same ones already recognized for veterans, and the list can grow over time as new conditions are added to the veterans program.

The people this affects most are civilian government contractors and federal workers who served alongside the military in places like Iraq and Afghanistan and later developed serious health conditions. It does not cover private sector workers or military service members, who are handled under separate laws. The Department of Labor would manage the program and must report to Congress within one year on how many people are eligible and how the rollout is going.
ai_headline: Federal workers sickened by burn pits abroad gain presumed coverage under HR 8524
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8524 removes the burden of proof for federal civilian workers sickened by overseas burn pits, matching benefits veterans got in 2022.
ai_sections.what: HR 8524 creates a legal presumption that certain civilian federal employees' illnesses are job-related if they worked near burn pits overseas, eliminating the need for workers to individually prove causation. To qualify, a worker must have served at least 30 days in a country where the U.S. was conducting a military operation on or after August 2, 1990, and must be employed by a qualifying agency such as the Departments of Defense, State, Justice, or Homeland Security, the intelligence community, or serve as a federal law enforcement officer. The covered diseases mirror those already recognized for veterans and can expand as that veterans list grows.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects civilian federal employees and federal law enforcement officers who worked alongside the military in overseas locations such as Iraq and Afghanistan and later developed serious health conditions. It does not apply to private sector workers or military service members, who are covered under separate laws.
ai_sections.why: Without the presumption, affected workers face significant difficulty proving a direct link between their illness and their work environment, a standard that has blocked or delayed claims. Extending the presumption aligns civilian workers' legal standing with that of veterans, who received the same protection under a 2022 law.

This bill would make it easier for certain civilian federal employees to get workers' compensation if they got sick after being exposed to burn pits or other toxic hazards while working overseas. Right now, these workers often have to prove that their illness was caused by their job, which can be very difficult. This bill would create a legal "presumption," meaning the government would automatically assume the illness was connected to their work, without requiring the employee to provide direct proof.

The bill covers civilian employees from several federal agencies, including the Departments of Defense, State, Justice, Homeland Security, Treasury, Commerce, and Agriculture, as well as federal law enforcement officers and intelligence community workers. To qualify, a person must have worked at least 30 days in a country where the U.S. was conducting a military operation on or after August 2, 1990. The list of covered illnesses would mirror the same diseases already recognized for military veterans under existing veterans' benefits law, and it would be updated automatically whenever the Department of Veterans Affairs adds new diseases to that veterans' list.

This bill affects civilian federal workers who served alongside the military in places like Iraq and Afghanistan and may have been exposed to the smoke from burn pits, which were large open-air fires used to dispose of waste. It does not apply to military service members, who are covered under separate laws. title: Crime Victims Fund Stabilization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
The Crime Victims Fund is a federal account that pays for services like shelters for domestic violence survivors, rape crisis centers, and support programs for crime victims. It gets its money mainly from fines and penalties paid by people convicted of federal crimes. This bill would add a new source of money to that fund: settlements and penalties collected under the False Claims Act, which is the law used to sue companies or individuals who defraud the federal government. This change would be temporary, running from when the bill is signed through the end of fiscal year 2029.

The bill does include two limits on what False Claims Act money can flow into the fund. First, the portion of any settlement that goes to a whistleblower, meaning the private citizen who reported the fraud and helped bring the case, cannot be deposited into the Crime Victims Fund. Second, money that the government uses to cover its own losses from the fraud is also kept out. Only the remaining penalty amounts would go into the fund.

This bill would mainly affect organizations that receive Crime Victims Fund grants, such as local victim assistance programs, domestic violence shelters, and sexual assault service providers, because it would give them access to more stable or increased funding. It could also affect companies and individuals who settle False Claims Act cases with the government, since more of those settlement dollars would be directed to this specific fund rather than going into the general federal treasury. Ordinary crime victims who use services funded by this account could also benefit if the additional money allows more programs to keep running or expand.
ai_headline: False Claims Act settlements would funnel money to crime victim services through 2029

title: Researching Innovative Shipbuilding and Next-Generation Transit Infrastructure for Durable and Efficient Systems
ai_summary:
This bill tells a federal research group called the Transportation Research Board to study new ways to build the hulls of boats and ferries used for public transportation. Specifically, the study would look at using modern materials like carbon fiber and other composite materials instead of traditional materials like steel or aluminum. The goal is to find out whether these newer materials could make passenger ferries and other water transit vessels more efficient and able to carry more people or cargo.

The bill does not build any ships or spend money on new vessels. It only requires a research evaluation, meaning experts would analyze and report on whether these new designs and materials are worth using. No immediate changes to any existing ferry systems would happen as a result of this bill alone.

The people most directly affected would be researchers at the Transportation Research Board and, down the road, communities that rely on ferries and water buses for daily transportation. Cities and regions with busy waterway transit systems, such as those along major rivers, bays, or coastlines, could eventually benefit if the research leads to better and more cost-effective vessels. Taxpayers who fund public transit systems could also be affected if the findings lead to cheaper or longer-lasting boats in the future.
ai_headline: Federal study ordered on carbon fiber hulls for public ferries
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.

ai_sections.what: HR 8998 directs the Transportation Research Board to evaluate whether modern composite materials such as carbon fiber could replace steel or aluminum in passenger ferry and water transit vessel hulls. The study would result in an analysis and report from experts. No vessels would be built and no existing ferry systems would change as a direct result of this bill.

Communities that depend on ferries and water buses for daily transportation could be affected further down the road if the research influences future vessel decisions.

title: Our Doctors First Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would stop Medicare from paying hospitals and other medical training sites for the cost of training doctors who are not U.S. citizens or nationals. Right now, Medicare helps fund graduate medical education, which is the residency and internship training that medical school graduates must complete before they can practice on their own. This funding helps hospitals afford to run those training programs. Under this bill, only trainees who are U.S. citizens or nationals would count toward the federal payments hospitals receive for running those programs.

The bill sets up a penalty system for hospitals and clinics that break the rule. A first violation would bring a fine equal to 25 percent of the payment that would have gone toward the non-citizen trainees. A second violation would mean a $1 million fine. A third violation would cut off all Medicare graduate medical education funding to that facility for five years, and repeated violations after that would result in ten-year funding cutoffs.

This affects teaching hospitals, clinics, and other facilities that train doctors and currently receive Medicare graduate medical education money. It also directly affects international medical graduates, who make up a significant share of doctors in U.S. residency programs, especially in fields like primary care and in rural or underserved areas. Patients in communities that rely heavily on those doctors could feel an impact if training programs shrink or facilities lose funding.
ai_headline: Medicare would stop funding residency training for non-citizen doctors
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Ways and Means, and in addition to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

Only trainees who are U.S. citizens or nationals would count toward the federal funding hospitals receive for running residency and internship programs. Facilities that violate the rule face a tiered penalty system starting with fines and escalating to full funding cutoffs.
ai_sections.who: Teaching hospitals, clinics, and other facilities that train doctors and receive Medicare graduate medical education funding are directly subject to the bill's requirements and penalties. International medical graduates currently in U.S. residency programs are also directly affected, as are patients in rural and underserved communities that rely heavily on those doctors.

Facilities that lose funding through penalties or repeated violations could face further strain on their ability to run training programs.

A second violation brings a $1 million fine, a third results in a five-year cutoff of all Medicare graduate medical education funding to that facility, and repeated violations after that trigger ten-year funding cutoffs.

title: Elder Pride Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new federal grant program under the Older Americans Act, specifically targeting LGBTQI seniors who live in rural areas. The federal government would make up to $5 million per year available in 2027 and 2028 for states, tribal governments, nonprofits, and local agencies to apply for. The money would be used for outreach, reducing social isolation, improving access to care, and providing sexual health services including HIV-related care to older adults in rural communities.

Organizations that receive these grants could use the funds for things like training local service providers to work more effectively with LGBTQI seniors, building connections between those seniors and community resources, and expanding nondiscrimination policies at organizations that serve older adults. Grant recipients would also be required to work alongside existing local agencies and organizations rather than operating on their own. The bill specifies that grant money must add to existing state and local funding, not replace it.

The people most directly affected would be LGBTQI seniors living in rural parts of the United States, where services of any kind can be harder to reach and where social isolation is often a greater concern. Nonprofits, senior centers, area agencies on aging, and other organizations that serve older adults in rural areas would also be affected, as they would be eligible to apply for this funding. The bill was introduced in the House and referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce, meaning it has not yet become law.

title: GME Transparency Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill requires hospitals that receive Medicare funding to train doctors to report data about the immigration and citizenship status of their medical residents. Medical residents are doctors who have finished medical school and are doing their required hands-on training at a hospital, usually for several years. The bill covers hospitals that get federal Medicare money specifically for these training programs, which is a large share of teaching hospitals across the country. If a hospital refuses to submit the required information, it could lose its Medicare funding for those training programs.

The reported information would be broken down into five categories: US citizens, permanent residents (green card holders), J-1 visa holders (a common visa for international medical graduates doing residency), H-1B visa holders, and others who are lawfully present in the country. The data would be de-identified, meaning individual residents would not be named. Hospitals would have to file this report within 180 days after each fiscal year ends, and then the federal government would send a summary report to Congress within 270 days, with numbers broken down by state.

This bill mainly affects teaching hospitals and the medical residents training in them. The US relies heavily on international medical graduates to fill residency slots, especially in rural areas and specialties with shortages, so this could draw attention to that practice. It does not restrict who can participate in residency programs or change any visa rules. It only creates a new reporting and transparency requirement tied to existing Medicare funding.

title: Vacancy to Value Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill creates a five-year test program run by the General Services Administration (GSA) to sell or give away federal buildings and land that the government is no longer using. Instead of selling these properties at full price, the government could let them go for less than market value if the buyer agrees to turn them into something useful for the surrounding neighborhood, such as affordable housing, health clinics, childcare centers, schools, or job-creating businesses. Buyers must submit a redevelopment plan and start construction within five years, or the government can take the property back.

The bill also sets up a separate grant program through the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to help fund the cost of actually fixing up and building on those properties. Grants could cover things like planning, cleaning up pollution on a site, tearing down old structures, building new ones, or adding infrastructure. Priority for both the property transfers and the grants goes to nonprofit organizations, local governments, tribal governments, public housing agencies, and community land trusts, especially those serving low-income or historically underserved areas.

This bill mainly affects communities that have unused or abandoned federal properties nearby, along with the nonprofits, local governments, and developers who might redevelop them. Residents in those neighborhoods could see new housing or community facilities built on land that was previously sitting empty. After the five-year pilot ends, GSA must report back to Congress on how well the program worked.

title: Promoting Childhood Independence and Resilience Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill tries to protect parents from being investigated or charged with child neglect simply for allowing their kids to do things on their own, like playing at a park, walking to school, riding a bike, running errands, or staying home alone for a short time. It creates a legal definition for these kinds of activities, calling them "reasonable childhood independence activities," and says that allowing a child to do them does not count as child abuse or neglect. It also requires the federal Department of Health and Human Services to study the issue and report back to Congress with recommendations for how states can support parents who give their kids this kind of freedom.

The bill changes two major federal laws that govern child welfare funding. States that receive federal child welfare money would be required to update their plans and train their workers to understand that kids doing age-appropriate things on their own is not a reason to open a child abuse investigation or separate a family. It also says states must put protections in place so that parents cannot face criminal charges, civil penalties, or placement on a child abuse registry just because they let their child walk to school or play outside unsupervised.

This bill would affect parents and guardians across the country, as well as state child protective services agencies, caseworkers, and investigators. Families who have faced investigations or legal trouble for allowing normal childhood activities would be most directly helped. States would need to update their policies and worker training to stay in compliance and keep receiving federal funding for child welfare programs.

title: Worker Rights and Support Act
ai_summary:
This bill would add new federal rules to the Fair Labor Standards Act requiring employers across the country to give workers specific types of breaks. Workers would get at least a 30-minute meal break for every 6 hours worked, at least a 10-minute rest or restroom break for every 4 hours worked, and additional short breaks of up to 20 minutes when a doctor says a worker needs them for a medical condition. The meal break can be unpaid if the worker is fully free from work duties, but rest, restroom, and medical breaks must be paid at the worker's regular rate. If a worker is expected to keep working or stay on-site during a meal break, the employer must pay them at one and a half times their normal rate for that time.

Workers can voluntarily give up their meal break if they choose, but employers are not allowed to pressure them into doing so. The bill also makes violating these rules illegal under existing labor law, which means workers could sue their employers or have the federal government take action on their behalf. States and union contracts that already provide stronger protections than this bill would not be weakened by it.

This bill would affect most private-sector employees and their employers across the United States, particularly workers in industries where breaks are not always guaranteed, such as warehousing, retail, food service, and transportation. It does not currently apply to workers covered by union contracts that set their own break rules, and it would not override state laws that already give workers more protections.

title: SURS Extension Act
ai_summary:
This bill extends a federal support program that helps small, rural, and underserved medical practices participate in Medicare's Quality Payment Program (QPP). The QPP is a system where doctors and other healthcare providers are judged on the quality of care they give Medicare patients, and their Medicare payments can go up or down based on their performance. The SURS program provides extra technical help and resources to smaller or less-resourced practices so they can meet those quality reporting requirements. Without this extension, that support program would have expired. The bill keeps it running through 2031.

The people most directly affected are doctors and healthcare providers who work in small offices, rural areas, or communities that are considered medically underserved. These practices often lack the staff and technology that large hospital systems have, making it harder to handle the paperwork and data reporting that Medicare requires. The SURS program gives them guidance and assistance so they are not at a disadvantage compared to bigger providers.

Indirectly, patients in rural and underserved areas could also be affected. If their local doctors struggle to meet Medicare requirements without support, those providers could face payment penalties or may choose to stop seeing Medicare patients altogether. By keeping this assistance program in place, the bill aims to help ensure that smaller practices can continue serving Medicare patients in communities that already have fewer healthcare options.

title: No Housing Welfare for Illegal Aliens Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes two main changes to federal housing law. First, it ends a long-standing practice called "prorated" housing assistance. Under current rules, if a family has some members who are eligible for federal housing help (like U.S. citizens) and others who are not (like undocumented immigrants), the family can still receive a reduced amount of aid based on how many eligible members there are. This bill would end that. Every single family member, including children, would have to prove they are legally eligible before the family receives any federal housing assistance at all.

Second, the bill would cut off two major federal grant programs — Community Development Block Grants (CDBG) and HOME grants — from cities, counties, states, tribes, or other organizations that operate as so-called "sanctuary" jurisdictions. That means any government or group that limits cooperation with federal immigration enforcement, refuses to hold people in jail at ICE's request, or fails to notify federal authorities before releasing certain immigrants could lose this funding entirely. These grants pay for things like affordable housing construction, neighborhood improvements, and community services in thousands of localities across the country.

The people most directly affected are mixed-immigration-status families who currently receive partial housing assistance, as well as residents of cities and counties that have sanctuary policies, since those local governments could lose significant federal dollars for housing and community development programs. Local governments, nonprofits, and tribes that run housing programs would also face new eligibility requirements tied to their immigration enforcement cooperation.

title: AVERT Future Violence Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Department of Justice to study the connection between animal cruelty and human violence. Specifically, the National Institute of Justice would have three years to research why people commit animal cruelty, what risk factors are involved, and whether harming animals is a warning sign that someone may later commit violence against people. After the study, the agency would send Congress a report with specific recommendations for laws and programs at the federal, state, and local levels.

The bill also creates a voluntary grant program that the Attorney General can offer to states, local governments, tribes, courts, and nonprofits. These groups could use the money to train law enforcement officers, judges, prosecutors, and mental health professionals to better recognize and respond to animal cruelty. Funds could also go toward building better data systems that track animal cruelty cases and toward mental health treatment and rehabilitation programs for people who have committed acts of animal cruelty.

The people most directly affected include law enforcement agencies, courts, animal welfare organizations, domestic violence service providers, and mental health professionals who could receive grant funding and training. Researchers and policymakers would be shaped by the study's findings. Individuals convicted of animal cruelty offenses could be affected by new intervention or diversion programs that result from the bill. The total cost authorized is $4 million, split between the study and the grant program.

title: Affordable Housing and Area Median Income Fairness Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would authorize up to $5 billion per year for each of three existing federal housing programs from 2026 through 2035. The three programs are the HOME Investment Partnerships Program, Community Development Block Grants, and the National Housing Trust Fund. All three already exist and send money to local governments and nonprofits to build or preserve affordable housing. The new funding would only go to areas where the federal government has already recognized that housing costs are unusually high compared to local incomes, a designation called a "high housing cost adjustment."

The bill also directs the Department of Housing and Urban Development to study how "area median income," or AMI, is calculated. AMI is a key number used to decide who qualifies for affordable housing programs and what the maximum rents on subsidized units can be. Critics have argued that the way AMI is currently calculated — often by averaging incomes across large regions that include wealthy suburbs — can inflate the number, which then raises the income cutoffs and allowed rents in cities, making subsidized housing less affordable than intended. The bill requires HUD to start this study within 180 days and deliver a full report to Congress within two years. The bill specifically asks HUD to look at how the wealthy suburbs of Westchester and Rockland Counties affect the AMI calculation for New York City.

This bill would most directly affect low- and middle-income renters living in high-cost cities, local housing agencies, and nonprofit developers who build affordable housing. Landlords with tax-subsidized units would also be affected if AMI calculation rules change, since those rules determine the maximum rents they can charge. Authorizing funding does not guarantee the money will be spent — Congress would still need to pass separate appropriations bills to actually release the funds.

title: POWER Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires the U.S. Department of Energy to track and report to Congress how much electricity and water large data centers are using. Starting two years after the bill becomes law, and every year after that, the Energy Secretary must submit a detailed report covering things like how much water each data center draws from public water supplies, whether they generate their own electricity or buy it from the power grid, and who paid the costs to connect them to the electrical grid. The bill focuses specifically on data centers that were fast-tracked through the federal permitting process under a recent executive order, but it leaves out data centers run by the military and certain government agencies.

The bill affects large, privately operated data centers that received special federal permits to build faster. These are often massive facilities built by major tech companies to power things like artificial intelligence and cloud computing. By requiring this reporting, Congress would have a clearer picture of how much strain these facilities place on local water supplies and the broader electrical grid.

Everyday residents could be indirectly affected, since data centers in their area may be competing for the same water and electricity that homes, farms, and businesses rely on. The bill also looks at who is footing the bill when a data center needs to connect to the power grid, which could matter to utility customers if those costs are passed on to them. The bill does not ban or limit data centers in any way, it only requires the government to gather and share information about their resource use.

title: Physician Education for Fistula Treatment Act
ai_summary:
This bill would allow the U.S. government to fund training programs for OB-GYN doctors and related specialists in the world's poorest countries. The main focus is on a painful childbirth injury called obstetric fistula, which happens when prolonged, difficult labor creates an abnormal opening in a woman's body that causes lifelong incontinence and other serious health problems. The bill would create fellowship and residency programs, as well as training centers, to build up the supply of doctors and midwives who can prevent and surgically repair these injuries. It would be managed through the National Institutes of Health's Fogarty International Center.

The bill also requires the White House to develop a formal 10-year strategy for reducing the shortage of doctors in the poorest countries. That plan would need to cover medical training, community education, research into both the medical and social causes of the problem, and how to build lasting local health care systems. A report on that strategy would be due to Congress within two years, and annual progress reports would be required after that.

This bill does not directly affect most U.S. residents. It is a foreign aid measure aimed at women in very low-income countries, particularly in parts of Africa and Asia where obstetric fistula is most common. U.S. taxpayer dollars would fund the program, but the medical care and training would be delivered abroad. American universities and medical schools could potentially be involved as training partners.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs.

title: REAADI for Disasters Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the REAADI for Disasters Act, aims to make sure that older adults and people with disabilities are better protected before, during, and after disasters like hurricanes, floods, or public health emergencies. Right now, these groups die at higher rates during disasters, often because evacuation warnings are not communicated in accessible formats like sign language or plain language, shelters lack proper accommodations, and emergency plans rarely involve disabled or elderly people in their creation. The bill would require organizations receiving federal disaster funds to follow disability laws, set up advisory committees that include people with disabilities and older adults, and make sure emergency shelters and communications are accessible to everyone.

The bill also creates new federal funding programs. It would set up a Disaster Human Services Emergency Fund with up to $100 million per year to quickly get services like personal care, transportation, housing, and case management to vulnerable people during and after disasters. Separately, it would fund regional training and research centers, run by organizations led by or focused on people with disabilities and older adults, to study what works and train local emergency agencies. Another $300 million per year in grants would help state, local, and tribal agencies build their capacity to serve at-risk people during emergencies.

The bill affects a wide range of people and organizations. People with disabilities and adults 65 and older would have stronger legal protections and more accessible services during disasters. State and local governments, emergency management agencies, nonprofits, and healthcare providers would face new requirements to include these groups in planning and to follow civil rights laws even during emergencies. A national advisory committee would also be expanded to include more voices from the disability community, tribal governments, and rural areas to guide federal policy going forward.

title: Local School Foods Expansion Act of 2025
ai_summary:

It also sets aside $25 million per year from 2026 through 2030 to fund it, with part of that money going to help schools and farmers handle the paperwork and logistics of participating.

The bill adds new priorities for which states get picked to join the program. States that show a commitment to supporting small, local, and socially disadvantaged farmers would be favored, as would states that work with Native American tribal food producers and communities that use traditional foods. States that serve a high share of children from low-income or disadvantaged backgrounds would also get extra consideration. The bill also requires the federal government to study how well the program is working and report back to Congress within four years.

The people most directly affected are students in participating states, who could see more fresh produce in their school meals. School food programs, local and small-scale farmers, tribal agricultural producers, and state agencies would also be involved, since they would need to coordinate to make the program run. Schools and farmers in states not yet in the program could receive help getting ready to apply in the future.

title: To amend title 40, United States Code, to permit commercial filmmaking and photography on the United States Capitol grounds, and for other purposes.

Any money collected from these permits would go into a special Capitol Trust Account used to support the Capitol grounds.

This bill mainly affects professional filmmakers, commercial photographers, and production companies who want to use the iconic Capitol backdrop for commercial projects like advertisements, TV shows, or movies. It also affects the U.S. Capitol Police, who would take on the new responsibility of reviewing and approving permit requests. title: John W. Walsh Alpha-1 Home Infusion Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would require Medicare Part B to cover treatment for Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency, a rare inherited disorder where the body does not make enough of a protein that protects the lungs and liver. The specific treatment is called augmentation therapy, which involves receiving an infusion of that missing protein directly into the bloodstream. Right now, Medicare does not clearly cover this treatment when it is done at home, which can force patients to travel to clinics or pay out of pocket. The bill would change that by officially adding home infusion for this condition to the list of services Medicare Part B covers, starting January 1, 2027.

The bill also sets up a payment system so that home infusion companies can be paid by Medicare for both the supplies needed to deliver the IV treatment and for up to two hours of nursing care during each infusion visit. Medicare would cover 80 percent of the approved cost, meaning patients would generally be responsible for the remaining 20 percent, the same cost-sharing structure used for most other Part B services.

The people most directly affected are Medicare enrollees who have Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency and need regular infusion therapy to manage their emphysema. This is a relatively small group, since the condition is rare, but the change could make treatment much more convenient and affordable for them by allowing care at home instead of a medical facility. Home infusion therapy suppliers and the nurses who provide this service would also be affected, as they would now have a clear Medicare billing pathway for this specific treatment.

title: Access to Breast Cancer Diagnosis Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would require health insurance plans to cover certain breast exams at no cost to the patient. Specifically, it eliminates deductibles, copays, and coinsurance for two types of exams: diagnostic exams, which are used when a doctor notices something unusual and needs a closer look, and supplemental exams, which are extra screenings for people at higher risk due to family history or other factors. These exams can include MRIs, ultrasounds, and diagnostic mammograms. The rule would take effect for insurance plan years starting January 1, 2026.

The bill applies to most private health insurance, including job-based group plans and plans people buy on their own. It also covers older "grandfathered" health plans that were locked in before the Affordable Care Act, which normally do not have to follow newer coverage rules. Plans linked to Health Savings Accounts, known as high-deductible health plans, are also included without losing their special tax status under this bill.

People most directly affected are those who need follow-up breast imaging after an abnormal screening result, or those whose doctors recommend extra screening because of elevated personal risk. Currently, these diagnostic and supplemental exams often come with out-of-pocket costs even when a routine mammogram is fully covered. Insurance companies and employers who offer health coverage would be required to absorb those costs instead of passing them on to patients.
ai_headline: Bill would end out-of-pocket costs for diagnostic and supplemental breast exams

title: To include the Czech Republic in the list of foreign states whose nationals are eligible for admission into the United States as E1 nonimmigrants if United States nationals are treated similarly by the Government of the Czech Republic.
ai_summary:
This bill would add the Czech Republic to a list of countries whose citizens can apply for a special type of US visa called an E-1 visa, also known as a "treaty trader" visa. An E-1 visa allows people from certain countries to come to the United States temporarily to carry out significant trade in goods, services, or technology between their home country and the US. Right now, Czech citizens cannot get this visa because the Czech Republic is not on the approved list. There is one condition: the Czech government must offer the same kind of visa access to American citizens in return.

This bill affects Czech nationals who work in international trade and want to do business in the United States, as well as US companies that trade with Czech partners. Currently, a Czech citizen involved in trade with the US has no clear path to enter the country under this specific visa category. If the bill passes and the Czech Republic holds up its end by giving Americans the same treatment, Czech traders could apply for E-1 status and work in the US temporarily.

The broader impact is relatively narrow. It does not change immigration law in a major way or affect most people. It is mainly relevant to business owners, traders, and companies on both sides that deal in US-Czech commerce. The bill applies equally and only if both countries agree to treat each other's citizens the same way, making it a mutual arrangement rather than a one-sided policy change.

title: FEMA Accountability Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires FEMA to publish a detailed monthly report on how money from the Disaster Relief Fund is being spent. Starting within 60 days of becoming law, FEMA's administrator must send these reports to key congressional committees every month. The reports must cover things like how much money is available, how much has been officially committed to projects, how much has actually been paid out, and which projects have been stuck waiting for a decision for more than 180 days. FEMA must also post each report on its public website within 10 days of submitting it to Congress.

The bill also requires FEMA to create a standardized format for reporting this financial data within 90 days, following federal open data rules. This is meant to make the information easier to understand and compare over time. It also requires FEMA to explain any money that has been held back, delayed, or moved to a different purpose, including when that money is expected to be released.

This bill would directly affect FEMA as an agency, since it creates new reporting requirements. It would also affect state and local governments, tribal communities, and U.S. territories that receive federal disaster aid, since they could track the status of funds meant for their communities. Ordinary residents recovering from declared disasters could also benefit, since the public reporting would make it easier to see whether promised federal money is actually being delivered.
ai_headline: New law would force FEMA to publish monthly disaster fund reports
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Economic Development, Public Buildings, and Emergency Management.

title: PREEMIE Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews federal funding and programs focused on premature births in the United States. The original PREEMIE Act was first passed years ago and has been updated a few times since. This version extends the law through 2029, keeping money flowing to research on why babies are born early, how to prevent it, and how to better care for premature and low birthweight infants.

The bill also makes one important change to a previous requirement. An earlier version of the law said the government "may" create a team of agencies working together on premature birth issues. This bill changes that word to "shall," meaning the Department of Health and Human Services is now required to create that interagency working group within 18 months. On top of that, it directs the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine to bring together a panel of maternal health experts to conduct a study and deliver a full report to Congress within two years. That report must cover the financial costs of premature births, factors that lead to early deliveries, and ways to detect risks sooner.

This bill mainly affects premature babies and their families, pregnant women who may be at risk of early delivery, and the doctors and researchers working in maternal and infant health. It also shapes how federal health agencies spend money and focus their work. It does not directly give money to families or change insurance rules, but the research and programs it funds are aimed at reducing the number of premature births and improving outcomes for babies who are born early.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: Disaster Aid Without Delay Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill targets a specific rule about how FEMA, the federal disaster relief agency, sends out money after a declared disaster. It would ban the Department of Homeland Security from setting a minimum dollar amount that disaster relief funds must reach before they can be approved or sent out. In other words, the government could not hold back aid just because a request falls below some set dollar figure.

Right now, FEMA operates under the Stafford Act, which is the main law that allows the federal government to send money to states, communities, and individuals after major disasters like hurricanes, floods, or wildfires. The bill says that no policy, rule, or internal guidance can create a financial cutoff point that slows down or blocks that money from flowing to people who need it.

This would most directly affect people in areas that have been hit by disasters, particularly smaller communities whose damage costs might not reach a high dollar threshold. It would also affect state and local governments that apply for federal disaster assistance. FEMA itself would face new legal limits on how it manages its internal approval process for releasing funds.

title: Sport Fish Restoration, Recreational Boating Safety, and Wildlife Restoration Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill updates and extends several federal programs that support fishing, boating, and wildlife conservation. First, it extends the funding rules under the Dingell-Johnson Sport Fish Restoration Act through 2031, instead of letting them expire in 2026. This law directs money from taxes on fishing equipment and motorboat fuel to state fish and wildlife agencies. The bill also adjusts how much money can go to interstate fisheries commissions, which are groups of states that work together to manage shared fish populations like striped bass or salmon.

The bill also expands what counts as an allowed use of federal boating infrastructure grants. Right now, those grants help build and maintain docks and facilities for recreational boaters. This bill would add a new category: building or upgrading fueling stations that offer alternative marine fuels, such as biodiesel or fuels made from cooking oil, animal fats, or plant materials. The idea is to give boaters more options beyond standard gasoline or diesel at the marina.

Finally, the bill lowers the federal excise tax on a specific product: portable, battery-powered bait containers that keep live bait aerated. Currently those are taxed at 10 percent at the manufacturer level, the same as most fishing tackle. This bill would cut that tax to 3 percent. People who are most affected by this bill overall include recreational fishermen, boaters, state fish and wildlife agencies, and marina operators across the country.

title: Advanced Wastewater Treatment Assistance Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill creates a federal grant program run by the EPA that would send money to every state to upgrade their wastewater treatment systems. Congress would authorize up to one billion dollars between 2026 and 2030 for these upgrades. The goal is to fund "advanced" treatment, meaning systems that can remove more harmful substances from wastewater than older technology can handle. States and the EPA can each keep up to 1 percent of the funds for administrative costs, and the EPA would set a formula to decide how much each state receives.

There is a significant focus on lower-income and underserved areas. At least 49 percent of the total funding must go toward projects serving disadvantaged communities, small towns, rural areas, or tribal treatment facilities. Normally a state or local government would need to pay at least half the project cost itself, but that cost-sharing requirement is waived entirely for projects serving qualifying disadvantaged communities, meaning those places could receive fully federally funded upgrades.

The bill also requires the EPA to work with the National Academies of Sciences to study how well advanced wastewater technologies remove emerging contaminants, specifically PFAS chemicals (sometimes called "forever chemicals") and nanomaterials. An interim report would be due within three years and a final report within five years. This bill affects local governments and water utilities across the country, particularly in rural, small, and low-income communities that rely on publicly owned treatment systems.

title: SAFE Act
ai_summary:
This bill targets a specific problem in the trucking industry called "chameleon carriers." These are trucking companies that have been caught breaking safety rules, fined, or shut down, and then simply restart under a new company name to avoid their bad record and keep operating. The bill directs the federal government to study how widespread this problem is, including how many crashes, deaths, and injuries these carriers may have caused since 2012.

The bill also requires the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration to build a computer tool that automatically screens applications for new trucking operating licenses. The tool would look for warning signs that a new applicant is actually an old unsafe company in disguise, checking things like shared addresses, phone numbers, equipment, drivers, managers, and insurance history. A human employee would still make the final decision on every application, and the bill specifically says the computer cannot make the final call on its own. Anyone who gets flagged and denied must be told why within 30 days and given a chance to appeal.

This bill mainly affects trucking companies, freight brokers, and equipment providers who apply for federal operating licenses. It would also affect federal regulators who enforce trucking safety rules. For everyday Americans, the goal is safer roads by making it harder for companies with dangerous safety records to quietly restart and continue hauling freight on public highways.

last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.
