The bill raises the pay floor to the highest of the federal minimum, state minimum wage, or local minimum wage. It also requires the VA to replace paper timesheets with an electronic system and to publish yearly program data including participation, demographics, job types, pay, and schools involved.
ai_sections.who: The bill primarily affects veterans and active-duty service members enrolled in school and using VA education benefits, along with their colleges and universities. Nonprofit organizations and state and local governments would also be affected as newly eligible host sites for work-study participants.
ai_sections.why: Expanding eligible job sites and raising the pay floor changes both the pool of veterans who may find suitable placements and the compensation those veterans receive. Annual public reporting would create a documented record of how the program operates and who it reaches.

title: Campaign Finance Transparency Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes new rules for how political campaigns can accept donations online. If you give money to a federal campaign using a credit or debit card on a website or app, the campaign would be required to collect your card's security code (the CVV number on the back) and the ZIP code tied to your billing address. The name on the card must match the name of the person donating. Gift cards and store cards would be completely banned as a way to donate to campaigns. People who live outside the U.S. would need to provide a passport or similar ID to prove they are American citizens or legal permanent residents before their donation can be accepted.

The bill also removes the current $200 threshold for reporting donations. Right now, campaigns only have to report the names and details of donors who give more than $200 total in a year. This bill would require campaigns to report every donor, no matter how small the contribution. It also makes it illegal not just to donate in someone else's name, but to help or assist anyone else in doing so. If a campaign treasurer suspects a donation was made in someone else's name, they would be required to report it to the Federal Election Commission.

This bill affects anyone who donates money to a federal political campaign, as well as the campaigns and political committees that receive those donations. Campaigns would need to update how they collect and verify payment information online. Small donors who currently give under $200 and are not reported publicly would now have their information recorded. The Federal Election Commission would be responsible for writing the specific rules to carry all of this out within 90 days of the bill becoming law.
ai_headline: Online campaign donation rules tightened under new federal bill
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 651.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8720 requires CVV codes, ZIP matching, and full donor reporting for all online federal campaign donations.
ai_sections.what: HR 8720 sets new verification requirements for online donations to federal campaigns, including mandatory collection of the card's CVV code and billing ZIP code, and a name-match requirement between the card and the donor. Gift cards and store cards would be banned entirely as donation methods. The bill also eliminates the current $200 reporting threshold, requiring campaigns to report every donor regardless of contribution size.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects anyone who donates to a federal political campaign online, as well as the campaigns and political committees that receive those donations. People living outside the U.S. would need to provide a passport or equivalent ID to confirm citizenship or legal permanent resident status before a donation can be accepted.
ai_sections.why: Campaigns would need to update their online payment systems to collect and verify new information, and small donors who currently give under $200 without public disclosure would now have their information recorded. Campaign treasurers who suspect a donation was made in someone else's name would be required to report it to the Federal Election Commission, which must issue implementing rules within 90 days of enactment.

title: Strong Communities Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill creates a new grant program within the existing COPS (Community Oriented Policing Services) program, which already provides federal money to help local police departments. Under this new program, local law enforcement agencies could apply for grants to pay for police officers or recruits to attend training schools or academies. The catch is that anyone who receives this training money must agree to work as a full-time officer for at least 4 years within the next 8 years, and they must work close to where they already live, specifically within 7 miles of a home where they have lived for at least 5 years. In rural counties with fewer than 150,000 people, that distance expands to 20 miles. If a person takes the money but does not fulfill the service requirement, they have to pay it back, though the Attorney General can create rules allowing exceptions in special circumstances.

The bill mainly affects local police departments, sheriff's offices, tribal law enforcement agencies, and people who want to become police officers in or near their own neighborhoods. Colleges and universities that run law enforcement training programs could also be involved as partners. The idea is to encourage people who are already rooted in a community to become officers there, rather than moving away after getting their training paid for.

The bill also requires the Attorney General to report to Congress every year on how the money is being used, including how many officers received training and how many stayed on the job afterward. This transparency requirement is meant to help Congress track whether the program is actually working to keep trained officers in local communities.
ai_headline: New federal grants would pay for local police training with a 4-year service requirement
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 3458 adds a COPS grant program funding police training for recruits who agree to serve 4 years within their home community.
ai_sections.what: HR 3458 creates a new grant program under the existing COPS program that funds training academies for police officers and recruits. Recipients must commit to working full-time as an officer for at least 4 years within an 8-year window. Those who do not meet the service requirement must repay the funds, with limited exceptions allowed by the Attorney General.
ai_sections.who: Local police departments, sheriff's offices, and tribal law enforcement agencies are eligible to apply. Prospective officers and colleges or universities that run law enforcement training programs may also be involved.
ai_sections.why: The program targets people already rooted in a community, requiring recipients to work within 7 miles of a home where they have lived for at least 5 years, or within 20 miles in rural counties with fewer than 150,000 people. The Attorney General must report to Congress annually on training recipients and officer retention, giving lawmakers data to assess whether the program keeps trained officers in local communities.

title: The Dalilah Law
ai_summary:
This bill would make it illegal for states to give commercial driver's licenses (CDLs) to people who are not U.S. citizens, green card holders, or holders of certain temporary work visas. A CDL is the special license required to drive large trucks, buses, and other big commercial vehicles. States that do not follow these rules would lose federal transportation funding. The bill also requires that all CDL tests be given only in English, and that applicants must demonstrate English proficiency to qualify.

People who already hold a CDL would have 180 days after the law passes to go through a recertification process. During that process, their immigration status and English proficiency would be checked. Anyone who does not recertify in time, or who does not meet the new requirements, would have their CDL taken away. Anyone who drives a commercial vehicle without meeting these requirements would be permanently banned from ever holding a CDL in the future.

This bill directly affects people currently working or hoping to work as truck drivers, bus drivers, or in other commercial driving jobs who are not citizens, green card holders, or holders of the specific work visas named in the bill. It also affects the trucking and transportation industry broadly, since those employers would have a smaller pool of eligible drivers. State governments would be affected too, since they must update their licensing processes or risk losing federal transportation money.
ai_headline: Bill would bar non-citizen commercial driver's licenses and require English tests
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.

All CDL tests would be required to be given in English, and applicants would have to demonstrate English proficiency. People who currently hold a CDL would have 180 days to recertify under the new immigration and English requirements or lose their license.

It also affects trucking and transportation employers, who would have a smaller pool of eligible drivers, and state governments, which must update their licensing processes to remain compliant.

ai_sections.cost: States risk losing federal transportation funding if they do not update their licensing processes to comply with the bill's requirements.

title: LIGHT Safety Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells the federal government to set a legal limit on how bright car headlights can be. Right now, there is no cap on the maximum brightness of low beam headlights on vehicles sold in the United States. The Department of Transportation would have one year to write and finalize a new rule setting that brightness limit, measured in lumens or a similar unit of light measurement.

The bill is a response to growing complaints that modern headlights, especially those using LED and other newer technologies, are too bright and blind oncoming drivers. Supporters argue that extremely bright headlights create a safety hazard on roads, particularly on two-lane highways where there is no barrier between traffic going in opposite directions.

This bill would affect automakers, who would have to design future vehicles to meet the new standard, and it could also affect vehicle owners if rules eventually apply to aftermarket headlight upgrades. Most directly, it would impact everyday drivers who share the road with vehicles that have very bright headlights. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration would be the agency responsible for determining and enforcing the specific brightness limit.
ai_headline: Federal bill would cap how bright car headlights can be
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7772 requires the Dept. of Transportation to set a maximum headlight brightness limit within one year.

The Department of Transportation would have one year to write and finalize the new rule, with brightness measured in lumens or a comparable unit.
ai_sections.who: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration would determine and enforce the specific brightness limit. Automakers, vehicle owners who use aftermarket headlight upgrades, and everyday drivers who share roads with bright-headlight vehicles would all be affected.
ai_sections.why: There is currently no federal cap on low beam headlight brightness, and complaints have grown that LED and other modern headlight technologies blind oncoming drivers. The bill's supporters contend this creates a safety hazard, particularly on two-lane highways with no barrier separating opposing traffic.

title: Next-Gen Collision Avoidance Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to create a written plan for rolling out a newer, smarter collision-avoidance system called ACAS-X. Right now, most aircraft use an older system to warn pilots when planes get too close to each other. ACAS-X is a more advanced version that uses better technology to reduce the risk of midair collisions. The FAA would have 180 days after the bill becomes law to finish the plan and send it to Congress, and then make it publicly available within 10 days after that.

The plan itself must cover several things: a step-by-step roadmap for getting the technology onto aircraft, what research and testing still needs to happen before it can be officially certified, and how the FAA will work with pilots, airlines, manufacturers, and safety experts during the process. The bill also requires the FAA to coordinate with aviation authorities in other countries so that international standards line up, and to look at how ACAS-X would work with equipment already installed on many planes today.

This bill would mainly affect the FAA, commercial airlines, general aviation pilots, helicopter operators, and companies that make aircraft and avionics equipment. For everyday passengers, the goal is simply safer skies. The bill does not require anyone to install the new system yet — it only requires the FAA to come up with a plan for eventually doing so.
ai_headline: FAA given 180 days to draft rollout plan for advanced collision-avoidance system
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7239 requires the FAA to deliver a written ACAS-X deployment plan to Congress within 180 days of enactment.
ai_sections.what: HR 7239 directs the FAA to create a written plan for deploying ACAS-X, a more advanced aircraft collision-avoidance system than the one currently in widespread use. The plan must include a step-by-step rollout roadmap, remaining research and certification needs, a stakeholder engagement process, international coordination with foreign aviation authorities, and an assessment of compatibility with equipment already installed on aircraft. The FAA must submit the plan to Congress within 180 days of enactment and make it publicly available within 10 days after that.

How the FAA shapes the eventual rollout plan will determine the timeline and scope of requirements that industry and international partners may face later.

title: Whale CHARTS Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill directs the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to build a more detailed, up-to-date system for tracking where whales travel, feed, breed, and give birth in U.S. waters. NOAA would create high-quality maps showing whale locations and migration routes, conduct surveys of whale species that are not well understood, and develop new tools like underwater sound monitors, drones, and satellites to detect whales more accurately. Those maps would be shared publicly online and could eventually be added to navigation systems used on ships and boats.

The bill also sets up a grant program, managed through the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, to fund projects that reduce dangerous run-ins between whales and vessels or fishing gear. Grants could go toward new detection technology, better outreach to mariners, and approaches that help ocean industries and whales share the same waters more safely. Priority goes to projects that also benefit small businesses in fishing, tourism, and boating. Grant money can only flow to U.S.-based people or organizations.

The people most directly affected include commercial shippers, recreational boaters, fishermen, and coastal tourism operators, who would have better information about where whales are located. Researchers, universities, tribes, and local governments could apply for grants. The bill authorizes roughly $18 million over five years for the mapping, survey, and grant programs, and requires NOAA to report to Congress every three years on progress.
ai_headline: NOAA whale tracking maps would go public under $18M bill
last_action_text: Subcommittee Hearings Held

NOAA would produce maps of whale locations and migration routes, survey poorly understood species, and deploy underwater sound monitors, drones, and satellites to improve detection. Those maps would be published online and could be integrated into vessel navigation systems.

title: ADOPT Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill makes certain adoption-related activities a federal crime. Specifically, it targets unlicensed "middlemen" who connect birth parents with prospective adoptive parents for pay, run ads to find children or families for adoption, or give more than $2,500 in financial support to a birth parent before that parent has spoken with a licensed agency or attorney. People who break these rules could face fines up to $50,000 and up to five years in prison. Organizations could be fined up to $100,000 per violation. The law would only apply when the adoption crosses state lines or uses tools like the internet, phone, or wire transfers.

The bill does not ban private adoption. It carves out clear exceptions for licensed adoption agencies, attorneys licensed in the relevant state, government child welfare agencies, and certain nonprofit organizations working under government contracts. Those groups can still run ads, connect families, and provide financial help to birth parents under existing rules. The point is to stop unregulated, for-profit middlemen from operating outside the oversight that licensed professionals face.

This bill affects anyone involved in a private domestic adoption that crosses state lines, including birth parents, prospective adoptive parents, and especially third-party individuals or businesses that try to arrange adoptions for a fee without being licensed or acting as an attorney. It was introduced in the House in November 2025 and referred to the Judiciary Committee, meaning it has not yet become law.
ai_headline: Federal bill targets unlicensed adoption middlemen with fines and prison time
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

The law applies only when the adoption crosses state lines or uses the internet, phone, or wire transfers. Licensed adoption agencies, state-licensed attorneys, government child welfare agencies, and certain nonprofits under government contracts are explicitly exempt.

Licensed professionals and agencies operating under existing oversight are not restricted by this bill.

title: PATH to Education Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new federal grant program to help public transit agencies improve bus and rail service to certain schools. Transit providers could apply for grants to add new bus routes or stops near campuses, run buses more often, or adjust schedules so that students can actually get to and from class. The schools that qualify include community colleges, minority-serving colleges, rural colleges, vocational and technical schools, and Head Start early childhood centers. Transit agencies would have to apply for the money and partner with at least one of these qualifying schools. Priority would go to transit systems serving schools where more than a quarter of students receive Pell Grants, which are federal financial aid awards given to lower-income students.

A separate but similar piece of the bill focuses on rural transit, using a different existing federal program to fund the same kinds of improvements in areas outside cities. Both parts of the bill also specifically help families who use Head Start programs for young children, making it easier for parents to get their kids to and from those early education centers. Funding would start at one million dollars in 2027 and grow to five million dollars by 2031 for each of the two grant programs.

This bill mainly affects college students, especially lower-income ones, who rely on public transportation to get to school. It also affects parents of young children enrolled in Head Start programs, as well as local transit agencies and the schools themselves. People living in rural areas are specifically included through the rural transit portion of the bill.
ai_headline: New federal grants would route more buses to community colleges and Head Start centers
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.

Eligible improvements include new routes or stops, more frequent service, and adjusted schedules. title: VISIT USA Act
ai_summary:
This bill moves $160 million from a government fund called the Travel Promotion Fund directly to Brand USA, which is a nonprofit organization that advertises the United States as a travel destination to people in other countries. The money in that fund was collected from fees that foreign visitors pay when they apply to travel to the US under the Visa Waiver Program. The bill directs the Treasury Department to make this transfer within 30 days of the law being signed, and it bypasses a normal cap on how much money can be moved to Brand USA at one time.

Brand USA would use this money to run marketing campaigns overseas, such as ads and promotions encouraging international tourists to visit American cities, national parks, and other destinations. The bill still requires Brand USA to follow existing rules about matching the government funds with private money raised from businesses in the travel industry, like hotels and airlines.

This bill mainly affects the US travel and tourism industry, including hotels, airlines, restaurants, and attractions that benefit when more foreign tourists visit. It could also affect foreign travelers who might see more advertising about visiting the US. American taxpayers are not directly funding this, since the money comes from fees paid by foreign visitors, but how effective Brand USA's campaigns are could influence how many international tourists come to the US and how much they spend here.

title: Southeast Asian Deportation Relief Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would stop the U.S. government from deporting people from Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam who entered the United States on or before January 1, 2008, and have lived here continuously since then. Even if these individuals have an existing deportation order, the government could not remove or detain them under this law. They would also be eligible for work permits, and those required to check in regularly with immigration officers would only need to do so virtually, once every five years instead of more frequently in person.

The bill also addresses people from those three countries who were already deported or left under a deportation order on or after April 24, 1996. It would allow them to ask the government to reopen their immigration cases, and if they qualify, their deportation orders would be canceled. The U.S. government would even pay for their travel back to the country so their cases could be heard again. People who were deported would be treated legally as if the deportation never happened, which could help them qualify for other immigration benefits.

The people most directly affected are an estimated 15,000 long-term U.S. residents of Cambodian, Laotian, and Vietnamese origin who currently have final deportation orders. Many came as refugees fleeing war and genocide decades ago, arrived as children, and have lived most of their lives in the United States. The bill also affects those who have already been deported and might want to return to have their cases reconsidered.
ai_headline: Bill would halt deportations of 15,000 Southeast Asian long-term residents
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Real Courts, Rule of Law Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would create a brand-new, independent court system specifically for immigration cases. Right now, immigration judges work for the Department of Justice, which is part of the executive branch and reports to the President. This bill would move immigration courts out of the executive branch entirely and set them up as a separate court system under Article I of the Constitution, similar to how the U.S. Tax Court or bankruptcy courts are set up. The new system would have two main levels: trial courts where cases are first heard, and an appellate division that reviews those decisions. Judges at the appellate level would be appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate, while trial judges would be appointed by the appellate court itself, not by a political official.

The bill is designed to give immigration judges more independence from the President and political appointees. Under the current system, the Attorney General can override immigration court decisions and set policies that affect how judges rule. Under this proposal, immigration courts would set their own rules, control their own budget, and judges could only be removed for specific reasons like misconduct or disability, not for political reasons. The bill also requires written opinions explaining decisions, sets up a program to help people understand court procedures, and mandates annual public reports on how the courts are performing.

This bill would directly affect anyone involved in an immigration court case, including immigrants facing deportation, asylum seekers, and their lawyers. It would also affect the roughly 700 current immigration judges, who would transition into the new system during a changeover period of up to four years. The federal government agencies like the Department of Homeland Security that bring cases before immigration courts would also be affected, since they would now be arguing before a truly independent court rather than one housed within their own branch of government.
ai_headline: Bill would move immigration courts out of executive branch control
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, and in addition to the Committee on the Budget, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

title: No Flight, No Fight Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would make it illegal for airlines to ship adult male chickens (roosters) as air cargo in the United States or on international flights. There is one main exception: large commercial farms that earn $350,000 or more per year in farm income can still fly roosters if they provide paperwork proving they qualify. Any airline that accepts a rooster for shipping without that documentation could face financial penalties. The law would take effect six months after it is signed.

The bill's stated reasons include aviation safety, the spread of bird diseases, and concern that fast air transport of roosters makes it easier to move birds for cockfighting, which is illegal in all 50 states. By requiring certification from senders, the bill aims to make it harder to ship roosters for illegal purposes while keeping the door open for the large-scale egg and meat industries that have legitimate reasons to move breeding birds quickly.

This bill mainly affects small rooster owners, breeders, and hobbyists who currently ship birds by air and would no longer be allowed to do so. Large commercial poultry operations meeting the income threshold would mostly be unaffected. Airlines would need to add a new step to their cargo intake process to check paperwork before accepting any rooster shipment. Individual states could also pass their own stricter rules on top of this federal law.
ai_headline: Federal bill would ban rooster air cargo with limited farm exemptions
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation.

Farms earning $350,000 or more per year in farm income may still ship roosters if they submit qualifying documentation. The certification requirement is intended to make illegal rooster shipments harder to complete without blocking legitimate large-scale breeding operations.

title: To amend title 5, United States Code, to restrict the employment in the Federal Government of individuals who are not citizens or nationals, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
HR 9063 would make it harder for non-citizens to work for the federal government. Right now, federal law allows some exceptions that let certain non-citizens, like lawful permanent residents (green card holders), work in federal jobs under specific circumstances. This bill would tighten those rules and limit federal employment more strictly to U.S. citizens and nationals.

The bill affects people who are not U.S. citizens or nationals but currently work for, or are seeking to work for, federal agencies. It would also affect federal agencies that currently hire or have pathways to hire non-citizens in certain roles. U.S. nationals include people from places like American Samoa who owe permanent allegiance to the United States but are not full citizens.

Because the full text of the bill is not available here, some specific details, such as which jobs might still be allowed exceptions or how existing non-citizen federal workers would be handled, are unclear. What is clear is that the bill's main goal is to reduce or eliminate the situations where the federal government can bring on workers who are not citizens or nationals of the United States.
ai_headline: Bill would tighten federal hiring rules for non-citizens
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

Current law allows some exceptions that permit certain non-citizens, such as lawful permanent residents, to hold federal jobs under specific circumstances. This bill would reduce or eliminate those exceptions, though which roles might still qualify and how current non-citizen workers would be handled remain unclear.

title: PRECEPT Nurses Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a $2,000 tax credit for experienced nurses who spend time training new nurses or nursing students. To qualify, a nurse must work at least 200 hours in a year as a "preceptor," which means a mentor who supervises and teaches someone learning the job in a real clinical setting. The credit only applies to preceptors working in areas officially labeled as having a shortage of health professionals, meaning places where there are not enough medical providers to meet community needs. The credit would be available starting in the 2026 tax year and would expire after 2032.

This bill is aimed at addressing a well-known problem in nursing: there are not enough experienced nurses willing or able to take time to train the next generation. Training new nurses takes significant time and effort, and preceptors are rarely paid extra for it. The $2,000 credit is meant to make that commitment more financially worthwhile. To claim it, a nurse would need official paperwork from either a nursing school or their employer confirming they completed the required hours.

The people most directly affected are licensed registered nurses and other qualified healthcare providers who mentor nursing students or newly hired nurses in underserved communities. Nursing students and new nurses in those areas could also benefit indirectly if the credit encourages more experienced nurses to take on training roles. The government would track how many people use the credit each year and evaluate whether it actually increased the number of preceptors by mid-2033.
ai_headline: Bill offers $2,000 tax credit to nurses who train new colleagues in shortage areas
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: DROUGHT Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill changes the rules for a federal loan and financing program called WFIA, which helps pay for water infrastructure projects like pipes, treatment plants, and reservoirs. Right now, the federal government can only cover up to a certain share of a project's cost. This bill creates exceptions that would allow the federal government to cover up to 90 percent of the cost for certain qualifying water projects, meaning local governments or water utilities would only need to come up with the remaining 10 percent themselves.

To qualify for this higher level of funding, a project has to meet at least one of three conditions. First, it must be located in a state or county that has experienced severe drought conditions within the past five years. Second, it must serve a lower-income community where the average household earns at or below 200 percent of the federal poverty level. Third, it must be a project that federal officials consider regionally or nationally significant because it meaningfully improves drinking water supply, promotes water recycling, reduces overall water use, lowers costs for water customers, or provides major public health or environmental benefits. Projects that qualify also get moved to the front of the line when the government is deciding which projects to finance.

This bill would most directly affect state and local governments, water districts, and utilities in drought-prone areas, particularly in the western United States. Lower-income communities that struggle to fund expensive water infrastructure upgrades would also be affected. Everyday residents in those areas could benefit if local governments use the extra federal funding to improve their water systems at lower cost to ratepayers.
ai_headline: Federal water bill would raise government's share to 90% for qualifying projects
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment.

Under current rules, the federal government is limited in how much of a project's cost it can cover. Lower-income communities where households earn at or below 200 percent of the federal poverty level would also be affected.
ai_sections.why: Qualifying projects would be moved to the front of the line for federal financing decisions, changing how limited federal funds are distributed among competing projects. Local governments and utilities in drought-affected or lower-income areas would face a reduced local funding requirement, which could alter how and whether they pursue infrastructure upgrades.
ai_sections.cost: The federal government could cover up to 90 percent of eligible project costs under WFIA, with local governments or water utilities responsible for the remaining 10 percent. Projects serving communities at or below 200 percent of the federal poverty level, in drought-affected areas, or deemed regionally or nationally significant would qualify for this higher federal share.

title: MARINA Act
ai_summary:
The MARINA Act tells the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers how it must handle rent and fees charged to marinas that operate on federal land managed by the Corps. Right now, marina operators pay rent based on a percentage of their total sales. This bill would lower the rent calculation by capping the percentage rate on certain categories of sales, like fuel, boats, food, and beverages, at no more than 1 percent. It also requires the Corps to create one clear, uniform fee schedule for all of its districts, since currently each district can charge marinas different administrative fees with little consistency. Those fees would be capped depending on how complex a given activity is, ranging from $1,000 for routine matters up to $50,000 for large projects requiring multiple government agencies to sign off.

The bill also extends how long marina leases can last. Under current law, lease lengths are set at the Corps' discretion. This bill would require initial leases and first renewals to last at least 50 years, and any renewals after that to last at least 25 years. Additionally, the bill says the Corps cannot require marina operators to pay their workers more than the federal minimum wage as a condition of their lease, unless a separate federal contracting law already requires higher pay.

This bill mainly affects the private businesses that run marinas on Corps of Engineers lakes and reservoirs, which are mostly recreational boating facilities spread across the country. It could also indirectly affect everyday boaters and lakeside visitors who use those marinas. The Corps of Engineers itself would need to rewrite its rules within one year of the bill becoming law.
ai_headline: New bill caps marina rents and sets 50-year leases on federal land
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment.

It caps the rent percentage on categories like fuel, boats, food, and beverages at no more than 1 percent of sales, and requires a single uniform fee schedule across all Corps districts. It also sets minimum lease lengths of 50 years for initial leases and first renewals, and at least 25 years for subsequent renewals.
ai_sections.who: The bill primarily affects private businesses operating marinas on Corps of Engineers lakes and reservoirs across the country. Recreational boaters and lakeside visitors who use those marinas could also be indirectly affected.

title: SMART Kids Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells the U.S. Surgeon General to create official guidelines on how much screen time children should have each day. The guidelines would be based on scientific evidence and would cover six different age groups, from babies under 2 years old all the way up to teenagers aged 16 to 18. The Surgeon General would also have the option to look at whether certain types of screen use, like video chatting with family versus scrolling social media, might be more or less harmful than others. An outside organization without financial ties to the tech industry would help develop the recommendations. The final guidelines must be published online and sent to Congress within one year of the bill becoming law.

The bill does not create any laws, fines, or enforcement rules. It only requires the government to produce and share recommendations, similar to dietary guidelines or vaccine schedules. Parents, schools, and others could choose to follow the advice or not.

This bill would most directly affect parents and caregivers of children under 18, pediatricians and child health professionals, and school administrators. It could also affect tech companies indirectly if the published guidelines draw public attention to screen use habits. Children of all ages are the focus of the health guidance being requested.
ai_headline: Surgeon General ordered to set children's daily screen time guidelines
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8743 directs the Surgeon General to publish evidence-based daily screen time guidelines for children under 18 within one year.
ai_sections.what: HR 8743 requires the U.S. Surgeon General to develop and publish official, evidence-based guidelines on daily screen time for children, covering six age groups from infants under 2 through teenagers aged 16 to 18. The guidelines must be published online and submitted to Congress within one year of the bill becoming law. The bill creates no laws, fines, or enforcement mechanisms — compliance with any resulting recommendations is entirely voluntary.
ai_sections.who: Parents, caregivers, pediatricians, child health professionals, and school administrators would be the most directly affected audiences for the guidelines. Tech companies could be indirectly affected if published guidelines shift public attention toward children's screen use habits.
ai_sections.why: Publishing government-backed screen time recommendations could influence how families, schools, and health providers approach children's daily device use. Because the guidelines carry no legal weight, any changes in behavior would depend entirely on voluntary adoption.

title: Military ADS–B Out Loophole Act
ai_summary:
ADS-B Out is a tracking technology that aircraft are required to broadcast so that air traffic control and other planes can see them on radar. Current FAA rules allow military and other government aircraft to turn off this tracking during a "sensitive government mission," but the rules do not clearly define what that means. This bill would require the FAA to narrowly define "sensitive government mission" so the tracking exemption can only be used during the specific part of a flight where sensitive activities are actually happening, not for an entire flight just because part of it involves sensitive work.

The bill also sets up a system of oversight and accountability. Government agencies that use the exemption would have to file regular reports with the FAA listing each flight where tracking was turned off, including the location, time, and reason. The FAA would then report that information to Congress every six months. If an agency turns off its tracking five or more times in a single month, Congress must be notified within two weeks. The Government Accountability Office would also review how the exemption has been used, and the Transportation Department's Inspector General would conduct annual audits starting three years after the bill passes.

This bill primarily affects federal agencies like the Department of Defense, as well as state, local, and tribal agencies that fly aircraft on sensitive government missions. It does not directly change anything for private pilots or commercial airlines. The goal is to make sure that when government planes go invisible to radar, there is a legitimate and limited reason for it, and that someone is keeping track.
ai_headline: Bill would limit when government planes can hide from radar tracking
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation.

title: Trump Accounts for All Generations Act
ai_summary:
This bill deals with special savings accounts for children called "Trump Accounts." Under a program that currently runs only through 2028, the federal government deposits $1,000 into a savings account for every newborn child in the United States. This bill would make that program permanent so it does not expire, and it would adjust the $1,000 starting deposit over time to keep up with inflation after 2028.

The bill affects every American child born in the United States, since each newborn would receive a government-funded account. The money in these accounts is meant to grow over time and can be used later in life. Parents and others can also add their own contributions to the accounts. The inflation adjustment means the initial deposit amount would gradually increase over the years to match rising prices.

The main practical change this bill makes is removing the expiration date from the existing program and adding the inflation adjustment, so future generations continue to receive accounts of roughly equal real value. Children born today and in the future, along with their families, are the primary people affected.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

The bill also adds an inflation adjustment to the initial $1,000 deposit starting after 2028, so the real value of the account keeps pace with rising prices over time. Parents and others may also contribute their own money to the accounts.

title: Stop Executive Renaming for Vanity and Ego (SERVE) Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would make it illegal to name or rename any federal property after a sitting president while that person is still in office. This includes federal buildings, public lands, and any other government-owned assets. It also bars the use of federal money to carry out any such naming. If any federal property has already been given a sitting president's name by the time this bill becomes law, it would have to be changed back to whatever name was assigned to it by a previous law.

The bill also applies retroactively, meaning it is not just a forward-looking rule. Any recent renamings that have already taken place would need to be undone if the president is still in office when the bill passes.

This bill would primarily affect the executive branch and federal agencies that manage government property, such as the General Services Administration, the National Park Service, and others. It would also affect any communities or facilities connected to federal properties that have been recently renamed. Ordinary Americans would mostly notice this if a local federal building, park, or landmark had recently received a new presidential name and then had to revert to its old one.

last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Economic Development, Public Buildings, and Emergency Management.

title: Parks to People Active Transportation Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new federal grant program run by the Department of Transportation. The program would give money to state and local governments, tribal nations, and regional planning groups to build or improve greenway paths — paved trails and shared walkways designed for walking, biking, and other non-car travel. These paths would need to cross multiple communities, counties, or even state lines, and would be selected through a competitive application process. The federal government would pay up to 80 percent of project costs in most cases, with higher federal shares available for rural areas (90 percent) and very low-income communities (100 percent). The bill authorizes $300 million per year from 2027 through 2031 for these grants.

The program is aimed at connecting communities to parks, public transit, schools, and jobs through trails that people can use without a car. When deciding who gets grants, the Transportation Department would look at factors like community support, safety improvements, and whether the project helps close gaps in existing trail networks. Projects must cost at least $15 million to qualify, though smaller planning and design grants are available for as little as $100,000.

The people most directly affected are residents who live near proposed trail routes, especially in lower-income communities and rural areas that are given priority for funding. Local and state governments, metropolitan planning agencies, and tribal nations are the ones who would apply for the money and manage the projects. Cyclists, pedestrians, and people using wheelchairs or mobility devices would be the primary users of any paths built under this program.
ai_headline: Federal bill would fund multistate greenway trails at up to $300M yearly
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.

title: Thermal Runaway Reduction Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill tells the Department of Transportation to create new safety rules for shipping lithium-ion batteries by truck or other commercial vehicles. The main concern is "thermal runaway," which is when a battery overheats and catches fire in a way that is hard to stop. Within two years of the bill becoming law, the government would require that batteries be shipped at no more than 30 percent of their full charge, since a less-charged battery is less likely to catch fire. The bill also requires the government to create clear rules for how to safely package and move batteries that are already damaged, recalled, or defective.

The bill also sets up a grant program with up to $10 million available for fire testing facilities to study new ways to put out lithium battery fires. Researchers would test tools and methods that work without using certain harmful chemicals known as PFAS. They would also look at how a battery's charge level affects how hard the fire is to fight, and how emergency responders can quickly figure out how charged a battery is during an accident.

Finally, the bill creates a separate grant program to help local fire departments, both volunteer and paid, get the equipment they need to handle lithium battery fires on the road. This includes fire suppression blankets, containment tools, and environmental cleanup gear. The people most directly affected include shipping companies that transport batteries, manufacturers who ship battery-powered products, fire departments across the country, and consumers who could be safer as a result of better-regulated battery transport.
ai_headline: New federal rules would limit battery charge levels during truck shipments
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials.

title: Defending the Human Rights of Palestinian Children and Families Living Under Israeli Military Occupation Act
ai_summary:
This bill would place restrictions on how US financial assistance to Israel can be used. Specifically, it would ban any American funds from being spent to support the military detention of Palestinian children, the destruction or seizure of Palestinian homes and property in the West Bank, or actions that help Israel annex additional Palestinian land. The bill also requires the Secretary of State to report to Congress each year, either confirming that US funds were not used for those purposes or explaining in detail how they were.

The bill also adds new requirements to an existing law, the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, so that the State Department's annual human rights report must include specific information about how Palestinian children are treated in Israeli military detention, how Palestinian property is handled in the West Bank, and whether Israel is following a 2016 United Nations Security Council resolution about settlements. On top of that, the Government Accountability Office would be required to produce yearly reports examining how a special category of US military aid, called offshore procurement funding, has been spent in Israel and whether any of it has been connected to settlement activity.

The people most directly affected are Palestinians living in the West Bank, particularly children who have been detained by Israeli military authorities, and families whose homes have been demolished. It also affects the Israeli government, which currently receives significant US military aid with relatively few restrictions attached. US taxpayers and policymakers are affected as well, since the bill creates new oversight and transparency requirements around how American money is being used abroad.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs.

title: CARGO Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would stop the National Institutes of Health (NIH) from giving money to research projects that use live animals if those projects take place outside the United States. Right now, NIH can send grant money to foreign universities, labs, and organizations for animal research. If this bill becomes law, any research involving live animals would have to happen on U.S. soil, including U.S. territories, in order to receive NIH funding.

The bill's supporters point out that NIH spent about $2.2 billion on foreign animal research between 2011 and 2021, and that NIH does not physically inspect those overseas labs. Foreign organizations currently self-report their own animal welfare information, which Congress argues creates a risk of inaccurate reporting and potential mistreatment of animals.

This bill mainly affects foreign research institutions and universities that currently receive NIH funding for animal studies. It would also affect U.S. scientists who partner with overseas labs on animal research, since those projects could lose NIH support unless the animal work is moved to the United States. Domestic research institutions and labs would be unaffected in terms of their eligibility, though the overall pool of NIH-funded research partners would shrink.

Foreign universities, labs, and organizations currently receive NIH funding for animal research, but this bill would end that eligibility. title: TRACK ICE Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change the rules about flight privacy for planes used by immigration enforcement agencies. Right now, the FAA has a program that lets private plane owners and operators hide their flight information from the public. The TRACK ICE Act would make that privacy protection unavailable for any private aircraft that is flying for ICE or Customs and Border Protection, paid for with federal money, and being used to detain or deport people. In other words, if a private company is getting paid by the government to fly immigration detainees, the public could see the flight data.

The bill also requires the Department of Homeland Security to post detailed flight information online within 72 hours after each deportation or detention flight. That information would include departure and arrival locations, times, the aircraft registration number, and how many people were on board. It would also require demographic details about the people being transported, such as their nationality, age group, and family status, as well as what kinds of physical restraints, like handcuffs or shackles, were used on them during the flight.

This bill most directly affects ICE, Customs and Border Protection, private aviation companies that contract with those agencies, and people who are detained and transported by immigration authorities. It would also affect any member of the public, journalist, or researcher interested in tracking how immigration enforcement flights are carried out. The bill was introduced in the House and has been sent to committee, meaning it has not become law yet.
ai_headline: Bill would strip flight privacy from private planes hired for deportations
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7172 would ban flight-privacy shields for private planes paid by the US government to detain or deport immigrants.
ai_sections.what: HR 7172 would remove FAA flight-privacy protections from any private aircraft contracted by ICE or Customs and Border Protection using federal funds to detain or deport people. It would also require the Department of Homeland Security to publish flight details online within 72 hours of each deportation or detention flight, including locations, times, aircraft registration, passenger counts, demographic information, and types of physical restraints used.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects ICE, Customs and Border Protection, private aviation companies that contract with those agencies, and people detained and transported by immigration authorities. Journalists, researchers, and members of the public who want to track immigration enforcement flights would also be affected.
ai_sections.why: Removing the privacy shield would make flight data for federally funded immigration enforcement flights visible to the public. Mandatory disclosure of restraint use, demographics, and flight logistics could increase public and press scrutiny of how detainees are treated during transport.

title: Stopping Border Surges Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes several changes to immigration law focused on two main areas: how unaccompanied migrant children are handled, and how the asylum system works. For children who arrive at the border without a parent, the bill would require them to be interviewed by officers specially trained to work with child trafficking victims, and it would speed up their court hearings to within 14 days of screening. It also removes a rule that previously gave children from non-neighboring countries more legal protections than those from Mexico and Canada, applying the same faster process to all unaccompanied children regardless of where they come from. Before placing a child with a sponsor, the government would have to share that sponsor's personal information with immigration authorities.

On asylum, the bill tightens the rules in several ways. People who passed through another country on their way to the US would generally have to show they already tried to get asylum there first. The deadline to apply for asylum would shrink from one year to six months after arriving. Asylum seekers would only be allowed to apply if they entered at an official port of entry, not between border crossings. Work permits for asylum applicants would be delayed until one year after filing instead of 180 days, and would expire sooner. People who return to the country they fled could lose their asylum status. Filing a false asylum claim could result in up to 10 years in prison.

This bill primarily affects migrants and asylum seekers at the US border, including families and children traveling without parents. It also affects immigration judges, border officers, and federal agencies like Homeland Security and Health and Human Services that manage migrant cases and child placements.
ai_headline: HR 116 cuts asylum deadlines and tightens rules for migrant children
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, and in addition to the Committee on Foreign Affairs, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 116 shortens the asylum application window to 6 months, limits entry to ports of entry, and speeds up hearings for unaccompanied children.
ai_sections.what: HR 116 tightens asylum rules by cutting the application deadline from one year to six months, requiring applicants to have sought asylum in transit countries first, and restricting applications to those who entered at official ports of entry. The bill also changes how unaccompanied migrant children are processed, requiring specialized interviews, faster court hearings within 14 days, and equal treatment regardless of country of origin. Sponsors receiving migrant children would have their personal information shared with immigration authorities before placement.
ai_sections.who: The bill primarily affects migrants and asylum seekers at the US border, including unaccompanied children and their potential sponsors. It also affects immigration judges, border officers, and federal agencies including Homeland Security and Health and Human Services.
ai_sections.why: People who entered between ports of entry or did not seek asylum in a transit country would be barred from applying under the new rules. Asylum seekers would wait longer for work permits, up to one year after filing, and could lose status if they return to their home country, while false claims could result in up to 10 years in prison.

title: Hemp Enforcement, Modernization, and Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates a new federal system for regulating hemp-derived cannabinoid products, such as CBD oils, edibles, vapes, and lotions. Right now, these products exist in a legal gray area with little consistent federal oversight. The bill puts the FDA in charge of setting safety standards, requiring manufacturers to register with the government, and listing their products. It defines exactly what counts as a cannabinoid hemp product and draws clear lines about what is and is not allowed to be sold. Products that contain too much intoxicating material, contain fully synthetic cannabinoids, or are designed to be absorbed through the skin in a way that enters the bloodstream would be banned outright.

The bill sets specific rules depending on the type of product. Edibles and drinks would have limits on how much intoxicating cannabinoid content is allowed per serving and per package. Vapes and smokable products would need to use prefilled, sealed cartridges and could only contain ingredients approved by the FDA. All products would need clear labels showing cannabinoid content, health warnings, allergen disclosures, and a QR code linking to lab test results. No one under 21 could legally buy any of these products, and companies could face criminal penalties of up to 10 years in prison for serious violations.

This bill affects a wide range of people. Hemp product manufacturers, especially smaller businesses, would need to register facilities, list products, and meet new testing and labeling requirements. Retailers would be required to enforce the age-21 rule. Consumers would get more consistent product information and safety protections. Foreign companies selling these products in the US would also be subject to inspection requirements.
ai_headline: FDA would take charge of hemp cannabinoid products under new federal bill
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7212 puts the FDA in charge of hemp-derived cannabinoid products, banning some outright and requiring age-21 sales, registration, and labeling.
ai_sections.what: HR 7212 creates a new federal regulatory system for hemp-derived cannabinoid products such as CBD oils, edibles, vapes, and lotions, ending the current legal gray area. The FDA would set safety standards, define which products are permitted, and ban those with too much intoxicating content, fully synthetic cannabinoids, or transdermal bloodstream absorption. Edibles and drinks would face per-serving and per-package limits on intoxicating content, while vapes would require prefilled sealed cartridges and FDA-approved ingredients only.
ai_sections.who: Hemp product manufacturers would need to register facilities, list products, and meet testing and labeling requirements, with smaller businesses among those affected. Retailers would be required to enforce a minimum purchase age of 21, and foreign companies selling into the US market would face inspection requirements.
ai_sections.why: All products would require labels disclosing cannabinoid content, health warnings, allergen information, and a QR code linking to lab test results, giving consumers more consistent product information. Companies that commit serious violations could face criminal penalties of up to 10 years in prison.
ai_sections.cost: Companies found in serious violation of the law could face criminal penalties of up to 10 years in prison.
costChips: Criminal penalty up to 10 years prison
