title: Secure Family Futures Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes two tax rules specifically for certain insurance companies, like life insurance companies that sell policies to families. First, it says that when these companies buy bonds or loans (called debt), those investments will no longer be counted as "capital assets" under the tax code. This matters because it changes how gains or losses from those investments get taxed when the companies sell them. The goal is to make it easier for these companies to manage the bonds they hold without facing certain tax complications.

Second, the bill extends how long these insurance companies can carry forward capital losses. Right now, if an insurance company loses money on investments, it can apply that loss to reduce its taxes for up to 5 years into the future. This bill would stretch that window to 10 years, giving companies more time to use those losses as a tax benefit.

The people most directly affected are mid-sized and large domestic insurance companies, particularly those selling life insurance and similar products to ordinary families. Indirectly, policyholders could be affected if these tax changes influence how financially stable their insurance company is or how it prices products. The bill does not change anything for small insurance companies that have made certain tax elections, foreign insurance companies, or Blue Cross Blue Shield type organizations.
ai_headline: Senate bill rewrites debt investment tax rules for domestic insurers
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

ai_sections.tldr: S 1335 reclassifies insurer debt investments and doubles the capital loss carryforward window from 5 to 10 years.
ai_sections.what: S 1335 removes debt investments such as bonds and loans from the definition of capital assets for certain insurance companies, changing how gains and losses on those holdings are taxed. The bill also extends the period during which these companies can apply capital losses against future taxes, stretching the window from 5 years to 10 years.
ai_sections.who: Mid-sized and large domestic insurance companies, particularly life insurers selling policies to families, are directly affected. Policyholders may be indirectly affected if the changes influence their insurer's financial stability or product pricing.
ai_sections.why: Reclassifying debt investments is intended to reduce tax complications when insurance companies sell bonds they hold. Extending the loss carryforward period gives companies more time to offset tax liability with prior investment losses, which could affect company finances and, indirectly, policyholders.

title: Vote Without Fear Act
ai_summary:
This bill would make it a federal crime to knowingly carry a firearm inside or within 100 yards of a federal election site, such as a polling place or a location where ballots are being counted. A basic violation carries a penalty of up to one year in prison, a fine, or both. If someone brings a gun to an election site with the intent to commit a crime, the penalty increases to up to five years. If someone kills another person during such a violation, they face federal murder or manslaughter charges.

There are several exceptions built into the bill. On-duty law enforcement officers and authorized private security guards hired by the building owner may still carry firearms. A person may also have a firearm in their vehicle within that 100-yard zone as long as they do not take it out or display it. People who live, work, or own private property that happens to fall within 100 yards of an election site are also exempt as long as they are otherwise following the law.

This bill would affect anyone who legally or illegally carries a firearm and comes near a federal polling place or ballot-counting location on election days or during vote counting. It does not change gun laws in any other setting. It would apply across the country wherever federal elections are being administered.
ai_headline: Senate bill bans guns within 100 yards of federal election sites
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: S 4121 would make it a federal crime to carry a firearm at or within 100 yards of a polling place or ballot-counting site.
ai_sections.what: S 4121 would make it a federal crime to knowingly carry a firearm inside or within 100 yards of a federal election site, including polling places and ballot-counting locations. A basic violation carries up to one year in prison, a fine, or both. Carrying a firearm with intent to commit a crime at such a site raises the penalty to up to five years, and causing a death during a violation triggers federal murder or manslaughter charges.
ai_sections.who: The bill applies to anyone — with or without a legal permit to carry — who brings a firearm near a federal polling place or ballot-counting location on election days or during vote counting. On-duty law enforcement, authorized private security guards, and people who live, work, or own property within the zone are exempt, as are people who keep a firearm inside a vehicle without displaying it.
ai_sections.why: The bill would create a new category of federal firearms offense tied specifically to election administration sites. Anyone currently accustomed to legally carrying a firearm could face criminal liability on or near federal election sites unless they qualify for one of the stated exemptions.
ai_sections.cost: Violations carry a fine as a possible penalty, either alone or alongside imprisonment, but the bill specifies no fixed fine amount.

title: Association Health Plans Act
ai_summary:
This bill would allow businesses and self-employed people to band together through trade or professional associations to buy health insurance as a group, even if those businesses are in completely different industries. Right now, federal law makes it harder for these "association health plans" to operate broadly. The bill would change that by officially recognizing a qualifying group of employers as a single "employer" under federal benefits law, letting them pool their members together to negotiate and purchase health coverage. To qualify, the association must have been around for at least two years, have at least 51 covered employees total, and must have been created for reasons beyond just buying health insurance.

The bill also includes rules about how premiums can be set. Insurers could charge individual member businesses different rates based on the specific health risk profile of their workers, as long as the overall pricing method is actuarially sound. Self-employed individuals who work at least 10 hours a week in their own business could also join these plans and be treated as both an employer and an employee for coverage purposes. Groups made up entirely of self-employed people would have to pool everyone together and charge each person the same rate.

The bill would mainly affect small business owners, self-employed workers, and trade or professional associations that want to offer health coverage. Supporters would say it gives smaller employers more buying power similar to what large corporations already have. The bill also states that these plans cannot deny coverage due to pre-existing conditions and cannot charge someone more based on their health status, keeping some existing consumer protections in place. It was introduced in the Senate in May 2025 and has been referred to committee.
ai_headline: Senate bill lets small businesses pool together to buy group health insurance
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

ai_sections.tldr: S 1847 lets businesses and self-employed workers join association health plans across industries, with protections against pre-existing condition exclusions.
ai_sections.what: S 1847 would allow businesses and self-employed individuals to join trade or professional associations and purchase health insurance as a group, even across unrelated industries. Federal law currently limits how broadly these association health plans can operate. The bill formally recognizes qualifying employer groups as a single employer under federal benefits law, enabling pooled coverage negotiations.
ai_sections.who: The bill primarily affects small business owners, self-employed workers who work at least 10 hours a week in their own business, and trade or professional associations seeking to offer health coverage. Associations must have existed for at least two years, have at least 51 covered employees total, and must have been formed for purposes beyond purchasing health insurance.
ai_sections.why: Smaller employers could gain collective purchasing power that currently is more accessible to large corporations. Insurers would be permitted to set different premium rates for individual member businesses based on their workers' health risk profiles, as long as the overall method is actuarially sound, which may affect how costs are distributed across members.

title: Protecting First Responders from Secondary Exposure Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill allows federal grant money to be used in a new way: to buy special containment devices for first responders and to train them on how to use those devices. The goal is to protect police officers, firefighters, paramedics, and other first responders from accidentally absorbing fentanyl or other dangerous drugs just by being near them at a scene. This kind of unintended exposure is called "secondary exposure," and it can be seriously harmful or even life-threatening.

Right now, there is already a federal grant program that helps fund law enforcement and public safety efforts. This bill simply adds a new item to the list of things that grant money can be spent on. It does not create a new program or require any new spending on its own. States and local agencies would still have to apply for the grants and choose to use the money this way.

The people most directly affected are first responders across the country, including police officers, EMTs, and firefighters who may come into contact with fentanyl or similar substances on the job. Local and state governments that receive these federal grants would have more flexibility in how they protect their emergency workers. Taxpayers and community members are also indirectly affected, since safer first responders means those workers can continue doing their jobs without being put out of service by accidental drug exposure.
ai_headline: Federal grants could fund fentanyl protection gear for first responders
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 77.

ai_sections.tldr: S 180 lets existing federal grant money pay for fentanyl containment devices and training for first responders.
ai_sections.what: S 180 adds a new allowable use to an existing federal grant program: purchasing containment devices and providing training to protect first responders from accidental fentanyl or dangerous drug exposure. The bill does not create a new program or mandate new spending. States and local agencies would still apply for grants and choose whether to use funds this way.
ai_sections.who: First responders including police officers, firefighters, paramedics, and EMTs are the people most directly affected. State and local governments that receive the existing federal grants would gain more flexibility in how they spend those funds.
ai_sections.why: First responders can be seriously harmed or killed by secondary exposure to fentanyl or similar substances encountered on the job. If first responders are incapacitated by accidental exposure, communities lose emergency service capacity.
ai_sections.cost: The bill does not create new spending or appropriate new funds on its own. It expands what existing federal grant money may be spent on.

press_names: Protecting First Responders from Secondary Exposure Act

title: Keeping Obstetrics Local Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Keeping Obstetrics Local Act, aims to help keep maternity and childbirth services open at hospitals that serve low-income or rural communities. Right now, many of these hospitals lose money on delivering babies because Medicaid pays them less than it actually costs to provide the care. The bill would require Medicaid to pay these hospitals at least 150 percent of what Medicare pays for the same services starting in 2027, and the federal government would cover a larger share of those costs. Small rural hospitals that deliver fewer than 300 babies a year would also receive special yearly payments to help cover the basic costs of keeping a labor and delivery unit open and staffed, even during slow periods.

The bill also expands coverage for pregnant and postpartum people on Medicaid and CHIP. Currently, some states end full coverage shortly after birth. This bill would make 12 months of full benefits after pregnancy mandatory nationwide, not just optional. It also creates new options for states to set up coordinated care programs for pregnant and postpartum patients, and it calls for better Medicaid coverage of services from doulas, midwives, and other maternal health workers, especially in rural areas. Mental health screenings during and after pregnancy would also receive more federal funding support.

The people most affected are pregnant women and new mothers who rely on Medicaid or CHIP, which together cover about 4 in 10 births in the United States. Rural communities and lower-income neighborhoods stand to benefit the most, since they are most at risk of losing local hospital maternity units due to financial pressures. Hospitals serving large numbers of Medicaid patients, as well as the states that run Medicaid programs, would also be directly impacted by the new payment rules and requirements.
ai_headline: Senate bill would set Medicaid floor for maternity pay at rural hospitals
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

ai_sections.tldr: S 2059 would require Medicaid to pay rural and safety-net hospitals at least 150% of Medicare rates for maternity care starting in 2027.
ai_sections.what: The Keeping Obstetrics Local Act would require Medicaid to pay hospitals at least 150 percent of Medicare rates for maternity services beginning in 2027. Small rural hospitals delivering fewer than 300 babies per year would receive additional annual payments to keep labor and delivery units staffed. The bill would also make 12 months of full postpartum Medicaid and CHIP coverage mandatory nationwide.
ai_sections.who: Pregnant women and new mothers on Medicaid or CHIP are the primary population affected, a group that accounts for about 4 in 10 births in the United States. Hospitals serving large Medicaid patient populations, rural communities, and the states that administer Medicaid programs would also face direct changes under the new payment rules.
ai_sections.why: Many hospitals in rural and low-income areas currently lose money on maternity care because Medicaid reimbursements fall below the actual cost of providing those services. Without a payment floor, these hospitals face financial pressure that can lead to the closure of local labor and delivery units.
ai_sections.cost: The federal government would cover a larger share of Medicaid costs for maternity services under the new payment rates. Small rural hospitals would also receive dedicated annual payments to offset the fixed costs of maintaining open labor and delivery units.
costChips: Federal share of maternity Medicaid costs rises
Annual payments for small rural hospitals
Applies to hospitals under 300 births a year

title: Family Vaccine Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill does two main things. First, it writes the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, known as ACIP, directly into federal law. ACIP is the expert group of doctors and scientists that currently reviews vaccines and recommends which ones Americans should get. Right now, ACIP exists through government regulations that can be changed or ignored more easily. This bill would make it a permanent part of federal law, require its meetings to be open to the public, and set rules for who can serve on it. It also requires that if the head of the CDC or other health officials decide to go against an ACIP recommendation, they must publicly explain why and notify Congress within 48 hours.

Second, the bill adds a rule to the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program, which is the federal program that pays people who are seriously harmed by certain vaccines. Specifically, it says that if the government wants to remove a vaccine from the list of vaccines covered by that program, or change what injuries qualify for payment, that decision must be backed by strong scientific evidence. This is meant to prevent those changes from being made for political or other non-scientific reasons.

This bill affects a wide range of people. Families and patients are affected because ACIP recommendations determine which vaccines are covered for free under most private health insurance plans and under Medicaid's Vaccines for Children program. Doctors, nurses, and pharmacists are affected because they follow ACIP schedules in their practices. People who have been injured by vaccines and rely on the compensation program are also directly affected. Essentially, anyone who receives vaccines or pays for health insurance in the United States has a stake in how this committee operates.
ai_headline: Senate bill locks vaccine advisory panel into federal law and shields injury program
last_action_text: Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. Hearings held.

ai_sections.tldr: S 3323 codifies the ACIP vaccine advisory panel into federal law and requires science-based evidence to change the injury compensation program.
ai_sections.what: S 3323 would write the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) into permanent federal law, replacing regulations that can currently be changed or ignored more easily. It requires ACIP meetings to be open to the public and mandates that any CDC official who overrides an ACIP recommendation must publicly explain why and notify Congress within 48 hours. The bill also requires that any changes to vaccines or injuries covered by the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program be backed by strong scientific evidence.
ai_sections.who: Families, patients, doctors, nurses, and pharmacists are affected because ACIP recommendations determine which vaccines are covered free under most private insurance plans and under Medicaid's Vaccines for Children program. People who have been seriously harmed by vaccines and rely on the compensation program are also directly affected.
ai_sections.why: Codifying ACIP into law would make it harder for future administrations to dismantle or bypass the committee through regulatory changes alone. Tying changes to the injury compensation program to scientific evidence standards would limit the ability to make those changes for political or non-scientific reasons.

title: Asunción Valdivia Heat Illness, Injury, and Fatality Prevention Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would require the U.S. Department of Labor to create a new national safety rule specifically protecting workers from heat-related illness and injury on the job. Within one year of passing, the department would have to issue an initial standard. That standard would require employers to provide things like cool drinking water, paid rest breaks in the heat, access to shade or cool spaces, and policies to help workers adjust to hot conditions gradually. Employers would also need to have a written heat safety plan, train workers and supervisors to recognize heat illness, and provide any needed protective gear at no cost to the worker. All required training and materials would have to be available in the worker's language.

The bill covers most workers in the United States who fall under existing workplace safety law. It would especially affect people who work outdoors or in hot indoor environments, such as farm workers, construction workers, warehouse employees, landscapers, and factory workers. Employers in those industries would be responsible for following the new rules, and they could face penalties if they do not. Workers who report violations or safety concerns would be protected from being fired or punished by their employer.

The bill is named after Asunción Valdivia, a California farm worker who died in 2004 after picking grapes for ten hours in extreme heat. Currently, there is no single federal heat safety standard for most workers, though a few states have their own rules. This bill would create one national baseline that applies across the country.

title: Vision Lab Choice Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill deals with vision insurance plans and the rules around how eye doctors can do their jobs. Right now, some vision insurance plans can restrict which labs or suppliers an optometrist uses when making glasses or contact lenses for patients. This bill would make it illegal for vision insurance plans to put those kinds of restrictions on optometrists. In other words, your eye doctor would be free to choose whichever lab or supplier they think is best for you, rather than being forced to use one picked by your insurance company.

The bill also sets rules about contract lengths between optometrists and vision insurance plans. Contracts could last no longer than two years at a time, and the eye doctor would have to agree before any contract gets extended. This gives optometrists more say over the terms of their agreements with insurance companies rather than being locked in indefinitely.

The people most directly affected are optometrists who participate in vision insurance networks, and their patients. If an eye doctor has more freedom to choose labs and suppliers, it could affect the quality, speed, or cost of eyeglasses and contacts that patients receive. The bill applies to both employer-sponsored vision plans and individual vision insurance plans. States still have the power to enforce these rules, and if a state already has its own vision insurance laws, those state laws would generally take precedence.

title: Lower Drug Costs for Families Act
ai_summary:
This bill targets prescription drug price increases by expanding and strengthening a system where drug companies must pay rebates when they raise prices faster than inflation. Currently, these inflation rebates apply mainly to drugs used by Medicare patients. This bill would extend those same rebate rules to cover drugs sold in the commercial market, meaning private insurance plans as well. It would also change the starting point used to measure price increases, moving the base year back from 2021 to 2016. Using an older starting point means more years of price hikes are captured in the calculation, which would generally result in larger rebates owed by drug companies.

The people most directly affected are drug manufacturers, who could owe significantly larger rebates to the federal government under the new rules. Private insurance companies and their customers could also see indirect effects, since the bill attempts to apply pricing pressure beyond just Medicare. The government would collect more rebate money, which could reduce federal spending on drug programs.

For everyday people, the intended effect is lower drug costs over time, though the bill does not directly set prices or cap what anyone pays at the pharmacy. Whether and how much patients actually save would depend on how insurance companies and employers pass along any savings. The bill was introduced in March 2025 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, so it has not yet become law.

title: Bring Our Heroes Home Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates a new system to collect and make public government records about American military members and civilian workers who went missing during wartime, going back to December 7, 1941 (the attack on Pearl Harbor). It would set up a special archive called the Missing Armed Forces and Civilian Personnel Records Collection at the National Archives. Every federal agency, military branch, and government office would be required to search for any records they have about missing personnel, send copies to the National Archives, and make those records available to the public. The default rule is that records must be released unless there is a strong, specific reason to keep them secret.

To oversee this process, the bill creates a five-member independent review board appointed by the President with Senate approval. This board would have real power, including the ability to issue subpoenas, hold hearings, and override a government agency's decision to keep records secret. If an agency wants to withhold or heavily redact a record, it has to explain in writing exactly why, and the harm from releasing it must clearly outweigh the public's interest in knowing. After ten years, nearly everything must be released unless the President personally certifies that specific records still need to be withheld.

The people most directly affected are the families of service members and government workers who went missing in wars from World War II through recent conflicts and never had a full accounting. Researchers, historians, and the general public would also gain access to records that have long been classified or scattered across agencies. Federal agencies, military departments, and the intelligence community would be required to spend significant time and resources locating, reviewing, and turning over these records on strict deadlines.
ai_headline: New law would open wartime missing-personnel records to the public
last_action_text: Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

title: SCREEN Act
ai_summary:
The SCREEN Act would require websites that regularly publish or host pornographic content to use age verification technology before letting anyone access that content. Simply clicking a box to confirm you are an adult would not count. The site would need to use real technology, like checking a government ID or using another digital verification method, to determine whether a user is likely under 18. Websites would have one year after the bill becomes law to put these systems in place. The Federal Trade Commission would be in charge of enforcing the rules, conducting audits, and publishing guidance to help websites comply. Violations would be treated the same as unfair or deceptive business practices under existing FTC law.

The bill applies to any website that regularly makes sexual content available to users and is doing so with the intent to make money, even if that content is not its only source of income. It covers websites operating in the US or specifically targeting US users. These websites must also protect any personal data collected during the age verification process, keep that data only as long as necessary, and make their verification process publicly known. They can hire outside companies to handle verification, but the website itself remains legally responsible.

This bill affects several groups of people. Owners and operators of adult content websites would face new legal requirements and potential fines if they do not comply. Adults who use those websites would need to go through an age verification step before accessing content. Children under 18 would be blocked from accessing the content entirely, which is the bill's main goal. Privacy advocates may also take interest, since the bill involves collecting personal information to verify age, even though the bill does require websites to protect that data carefully.

title: Kids Online Safety Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Kids Online Safety Act, requires social media platforms, online video games, messaging apps, and video streaming services to take specific steps to protect users under age 17. Platforms must turn on their safest privacy and safety settings automatically for minors, rather than making families search for them. They must give kids easy ways to limit who can contact them, turn off features like infinite scrolling and autoplay, opt out of personalized recommendations, and restrict location sharing. Parents get tools to monitor screen time, block purchases, and manage their child's account settings. Platforms also have to respond to safety reports within 10 to 21 days and are banned from showing ads for drugs, alcohol, tobacco, gambling, or cannabis to users they know are minors.

The bill also requires large platforms with over 10 million monthly users to publish yearly public reports, reviewed by outside auditors, describing how many minors use their service, how the platform's design affects kids, and how well their safety tools are working. A new advisory council made up of parents, researchers, educators, youth representatives, and platform representatives would be created to advise Congress on online child safety issues. The government would also study how age verification could be done at the device level without collecting too much personal data.

A separate section of the bill affects all users, not just minors. Any platform that uses hidden algorithms to decide what content people see must clearly disclose that fact and give every user the option to switch to a simpler, non-personalized feed instead. Platforms cannot charge extra or penalize users who choose the non-personalized option. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would both have the power to enforce these rules.

last_action_text: Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

title: DETERRENT Act
ai_summary:
The DETERRENT Act would require colleges and universities to be much more open about money and deals they receive from foreign sources. Schools must report gifts of $50,000 or more from foreign organizations or governments to the Department of Education. For countries or groups considered national security threats, like China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, schools must report every gift no matter how small. Schools would also be completely banned from making contracts or business deals with those high-concern countries and entities unless they get special government permission, which must be renewed every year. All of this information would go into a public, searchable database so anyone can look it up.

The bill also requires colleges to track foreign gifts and contracts received by individual professors and researchers, not just the school as a whole. Faculty at schools receiving over $50 million in federal research funding would have to report any foreign gifts or contracts annually to their own institution. Schools must also have a written plan to watch for possible foreign spying through these financial relationships. Each school covered by this law must appoint a dedicated compliance officer to make sure all these rules are followed correctly.

Schools that break these rules face serious consequences. Fines can range from $50,000 up to twice the value of an unreported gift or contract, and repeated violations can cost a school a percentage of all its federal funding. A school that loses three separate court cases over violations could lose access to all federal student aid programs for at least two years. This bill primarily affects colleges and universities, their professors and researchers, and foreign governments or organizations that currently give money to or do business with American schools.

title: SHIPS for America Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill is a major effort by Congress to rebuild the American shipbuilding industry, grow the U.S. fleet of cargo ships, and expand the workforce of American sailors and shipyard workers. Right now, the U.S. has fewer than 200 large oceangoing ships, and only about 80 of them operate in international trade. Meanwhile, China has over 5,500 ships and builds vessels at a rate roughly 230 times greater than the U.S. The bill says this gap is a serious national security problem, because in a war or major crisis, the country might not have enough ships or trained sailors to move military supplies and keep the economy running. To fix this, the bill creates a new White House advisor called the Maritime Security Advisor, sets up a Maritime Security Trust Fund filled with fees and taxes collected from foreign ships entering U.S. ports, and uses that money to fund shipbuilding programs, loan guarantees for shipyards, and support for commercial fleets that fly the American flag.

The bill also tries to make sure more cargo shipped to and from the United States actually travels on American ships. It increases fees on foreign vessels, especially those connected to China, and strengthens rules requiring that goods paid for with U.S. government money be carried on American ships. It also creates a new program called the Strategic Commercial Fleet to subsidize American shipping companies operating internationally, similar to how the military already pays some ship operators to stay ready for wartime use.

A large section of the bill focuses on people. It aims to grow the number of licensed American merchant mariners, which currently stands at only about 12,000, by offering student loan forgiveness, job training programs, easier pathways for military veterans to become civilian mariners, and more funding for maritime academies. Shipyard workers would also see new training and recruitment programs. The bill affects American shipping companies, shipyards, maritime workers, military planners, and ultimately consumers, since stronger domestic shipping could influence the cost and reliability of imported goods.

title: Stop Antisemitism on College Campuses Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change the rules colleges and universities must follow to stay eligible for federal student financial aid programs. Under current law, schools must meet certain requirements to participate in federal student loans and grants. This bill would add a new requirement: colleges cannot authorize, fund, or support any campus event that promotes antisemitism. The bill uses the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism, which covers hatred toward Jewish people and includes a list of specific contemporary examples.

If a college violates this rule, it could lose access to federal Title IV programs, which include Pell Grants and federal student loans. That is a significant consequence because most colleges depend heavily on that federal funding, and losing it would affect the entire school community, not just those involved in any particular event.

This bill most directly affects college administrators, who would need to screen campus events to avoid losing federal funding. It also affects students at those schools, since a loss of federal aid eligibility could make attending much more expensive or could disrupt their financial aid. Students who organize campus events, free speech advocates, and Jewish students and communities all have a stake in how this law would be applied. The bill was introduced in the Senate in March 2025 and has been referred to committee, meaning it has not yet become law.

title: Repeal the TikTok Ban Act

title: Health Marketplace for All Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new type of health insurance arrangement called a "health marketplace pool." Under current law, only actual employers can offer group health insurance plans to employees. This bill changes that by allowing any organization that forms one of these pools to be treated legally as an employer just for the purpose of offering group health coverage. That means groups of individuals, small businesses, associations, or other organizations could band together to buy health insurance as one large group, potentially getting lower rates that bigger employers usually get.

The pools would have to follow some rules. They cannot turn away members based on health status or pre-existing conditions. They must offer the same coverage to all members, and they can either buy insurance from an insurance company or self-insure. Interestingly, the pools could also offer drug-only plans covering prescription and over-the-counter medications, with no other medical benefits attached. The bill also makes clear that joining one of these pools does not make a member legally responsible as a fiduciary, meaning members would not carry the legal duties that come with managing a traditional employer-sponsored plan.

This bill would most directly affect people who currently lack access to affordable group health insurance, such as self-employed workers, gig workers, freelancers, and employees of very small businesses. It could also affect insurance companies, which might see new customers or new competition. Larger employers and traditional insurance markets could see indirect effects as well. People who already have employer-sponsored coverage or government programs like Medicare and Medicaid would not be directly impacted.

title: Health Savings Accounts For All Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill makes big changes to Health Savings Accounts, which are special tax-free accounts people use to pay for medical costs. Right now, you can only open an HSA if you have a specific type of high-deductible health insurance plan. This bill removes that requirement, meaning anyone could open and contribute to an HSA regardless of what kind of health insurance they have, or even if they have no insurance at all. It also raises how much money you can put into an HSA each year, tying the new limit to the same higher caps used for workplace retirement accounts like 401(k)s. People age 50 and older could contribute even more.

The bill also expands what you can spend HSA money on tax-free. Currently the list covers doctor visits, prescriptions, and similar medical costs. This bill would add vitamins, dietary supplements, gym memberships, and wearable fitness trackers like smartwatches. It also lets you use HSA funds for direct primary care arrangements, where patients pay a flat monthly fee directly to a doctor. Another change allows people to use HSA money for medical expenses that happened before the account was opened, as long as those expenses occurred in the same tax year or the year before the account was set up.

A few other changes are included as well. If you make a paperwork or payroll mistake with your HSA contribution, you can correct it before your tax return is due without a penalty. When an HSA account holder dies, the account can now pass to a child, parent, or grandparent tax-free, not just a spouse. Finally, HSA funds would receive the same legal protections from creditors in bankruptcy that retirement accounts currently enjoy. These changes would affect anyone who currently has or might want an HSA, employers who contribute to employee HSAs, and people managing HSA funds after a family member's death.

title: Health Marketplace and Savings Accounts for All Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes two main changes to health care law. First, it significantly expands Health Savings Accounts, or HSAs. Right now, HSAs are tax-free savings accounts you can only use if you have a specific type of high-deductible health insurance plan. This bill removes that requirement, meaning anyone could open and contribute to an HSA regardless of what insurance they have or whether they have insurance at all. It also raises the amount of money you can put in each year, lets you use HSA funds on vitamins, supplements, gym memberships, and fitness trackers, and allows unused HSA money to be passed on to a child or parent when the account holder dies, not just a spouse. HSA funds would also be protected from creditors in bankruptcy, the same way retirement accounts currently are.

Second, the bill creates a new type of organization called a "health marketplace pool." These pools would allow individuals, self-employed people, and small businesses to band together and buy health insurance as a group, the same way large employers already do. Currently, group health insurance is mainly available through employers. Under this bill, any qualifying organization could form one of these pools and offer group coverage to its members, potentially giving people access to lower group insurance rates even if their employer does not offer coverage.

The people most directly affected would be the roughly 28 million Americans who are uninsured or who buy their own individual health insurance, along with self-employed workers and small business employees who currently lack access to employer-sponsored group coverage. People who already have HSAs would also see expanded options for how they save and spend that money.

title: Great American Healthcare Plan
ai_summary:
This bill makes three main changes to the US healthcare system. First, it expands Health Savings Accounts, which are special tax-free accounts people use to pay for medical costs. It raises how much money you can put in each year, lets more people open one even without a specific type of insurance plan, and allows HSA funds to be spent on more things like gym memberships, vitamins, healthy food, and health-sharing ministries. It also lets unused money from workplace health spending accounts roll over into an HSA, and allows family members like parents or children to inherit an HSA when the account holder dies.

Second, the bill requires hospitals, labs, imaging centers, and insurance companies to publicly post their actual prices for services. This means a hospital would have to show, on a free website, what it charges different insurance companies, what it charges people paying cash, and what the maximum and minimum prices are for each service. Fines would apply to hospitals that refuse to comply, and a senior hospital official would have to sign off saying the posted prices are accurate.

Third, the bill creates a new type of purchasing pool called a Health Marketplace Pool, which would let individuals, small businesses, and other groups band together to buy health insurance as a group, similar to how large employers currently get group rates. It also includes provisions related to cancer drug pricing and expanded access to certain experimental prescription drugs.

These changes would affect nearly all Americans in some way, but particularly people who currently use or are eligible for HSAs, patients trying to compare healthcare costs before receiving care, small business owners and self-employed individuals seeking affordable insurance options, and hospitals and insurers who would face new disclosure requirements.

title: TREY'S Law
ai_summary:
TREY'S Law makes it illegal to enforce nondisclosure or confidentiality clauses in settlements or other contracts that prevent someone from speaking out about the sexual abuse of a child. In other words, if a lawsuit or legal settlement included a "stay silent" rule about child sexual abuse, that rule would now be void and unenforceable. Victims, alleged victims, or anyone with knowledge of such abuse could speak freely without worrying about being sued for violating a contract. The law applies to both new and old agreements, meaning contracts signed years ago are covered too.

The bill does allow some parts of confidentiality agreements to remain valid. For example, a settlement could still keep the dollar amount or payment terms private. What it cannot do is stop a victim or a witness from disclosing that the abuse happened or sharing facts about it. The law also overrides any state laws that would allow these kinds of silence clauses to be enforced, while still allowing states to pass their own laws that give victims even stronger protections.

This bill affects child sexual abuse survivors, witnesses or others who signed confidentiality agreements related to such abuse, and anyone who might try to legally enforce those agreements, such as alleged abusers or institutions. It is relevant in situations like civil lawsuits, out-of-court settlements, or employment agreements where silence about child abuse was made a condition. Supporters and critics alike would likely note it is a significant shift in how binding contracts involving child sexual abuse cases are treated under federal law.

title: Lower Your Taxes Act
ai_summary:
This bill would expand two existing tax credits and create a new monthly child benefit, while also raising some taxes on high earners and corporations to help pay for it.

For working families, the bill roughly doubles the Earned Income Tax Credit, which is a tax break for people who work but earn lower or moderate incomes. It raises the dollar amounts workers can receive, lets more people qualify, and lowers the income level at which the credit starts shrinking. It also removes the minimum age requirement, so workers 18 and older could claim it rather than having to be at least 25. Additionally, people in states that offer their own earned income credit that does not fully refund unused amounts would get extra federal payments to make up the difference.

The bill creates a new monthly child tax credit, paying families $350 per month for each child under 6 and $300 per month for each child aged 6 through 17. These payments would go out automatically each month rather than as a once-a-year tax refund. Families earning above roughly $112,500 to $150,000 per year, depending on filing status, would see reduced payments. To help cover these costs, the bill would raise the tax rate on capital gains income for high earners and increase certain corporate tax rates. The bill primarily affects low- and middle-income working adults, parents with children under 18, higher-income investors, and corporations.

title: Surface Transportation Research and Development Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Department of Transportation to continue and expand several research and technology programs related to roads, highways, and rail through 2031. It renews funding for university transportation research centers, a highway technology program, and an open research initiative that had been set to expire. It also creates a new internal council within the Department of Transportation to better coordinate how the department collects and manages transportation data, with the goal of reducing duplicate work and improving data quality.

The bill also kicks off a few specific studies and plans. It requires the government to study the safety effects of modern LED headlights, including whether bright headlights on cars and trucks create dangerous glare for other drivers, pedestrians, and cyclists. It directs the Federal Highway Administration to develop a national strategy for using reclaimed asphalt pavement, which is old road material recycled into new roads, as a potential cost-saving measure. It also expands rail research to include safety issues with hazardous materials transported by freight trains.

The people most affected by this bill are transportation researchers, university programs that receive federal research grants, state and local transportation departments, and eventually everyday drivers and commuters. The headlight study could lead to new safety rules affecting all car buyers. The recycled asphalt strategy could influence how road construction projects are carried out nationwide. Rail safety additions could affect freight companies and communities near rail lines.

title: Full-Service Community School Expansion Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would expand a federal program called Full-Service Community Schools. These are public schools that do more than just teach classes — they also connect students and families to health care, mental health services, housing help, food assistance, and other support services, all coordinated through the school itself. The bill would set aside large amounts of federal money for this program, starting at $500 million in 2027 and growing to $1 billion by 2031. Schools can apply for planning grants to get started, five-year grants to run the full program, or expansion grants if they already have a program and want to grow it.

To qualify, a school generally needs to have at least 40 percent of its students from low-income families, or be a school that the state has already flagged as needing extra support. Each participating school would be required to hire a community school coordinator — a full-time staff member who organizes all the services and partnerships. The bill also creates leadership teams that include parents, students, teachers, community members, and local organizations, all working together to decide what the school and neighborhood need most.

The people most directly affected would be students and families at low-income schools, especially those dealing with challenges like housing instability, lack of health care, or food insecurity. School districts, nonprofit organizations, local governments, tribal communities, and other community groups would also be involved as partners. Schools in rural areas and on tribal lands are specifically called out for extra attention and priority when grants are awarded.

title: End Solitary Confinement Act
ai_summary:
This bill would ban the use of solitary confinement in all federal detention facilities, including federal prisons, immigration detention centers, and any private facilities that hold people under federal contracts. Currently, officials can lock someone in a cell alone for long periods as punishment or for security reasons. Under this bill, that practice would be largely eliminated. Instead, every person held in a federal facility would be guaranteed at least 14 hours per day outside their cell in shared spaces, with access to programs like education, job training, and mental health treatment. Isolation could only be used briefly in a true emergency, and even then only for a few hours at a time under strict rules. Certain groups, including people under 25 or over 55, pregnant women, people with disabilities or mental health diagnoses, and LGBTQ individuals, could never be placed in isolation at all.

The bill also sets up two layers of oversight. A community monitoring body made up largely of people who have personally experienced incarceration would be able to make surprise visits to any federal facility, interview detainees privately, and publish its findings. A separate Inspector General advisory board would produce annual reports on whether the law is being followed. Facilities and agencies would have to publicly report data every three months on how often and how long people are being isolated.

States and local governments that receive certain federal law enforcement grants would also feel the effects of this bill. They would need to show that their own jails and prisons follow similar rules, or face losing at least 10 percent of that federal funding. People who are harmed by violations of the law could sue in federal court and potentially receive money damages, including for emotional suffering.

title: BLUE Act
ai_summary:
The BLUE Act would make it a federal crime to share personal information about federal law enforcement officers if the person sharing that information intends to physically block, interfere with, or get back at an officer for doing their job. This builds on an existing federal law that already makes it illegal to share private details about certain government workers to threaten or harm them. The new addition specifically covers situations where someone spreads an officer's personal information to disrupt a federal investigation, operation, or legal proceeding.

The bill also expands what counts as protected personal information. Under current law, sharing someone's home address or daily routine is restricted. This bill adds any physical location where a federal law enforcement officer is or is expected to be, whether they are on duty or off duty at the time. So for example, sharing that an officer will be at a specific place at a specific time, with the goal of interfering with their work or retaliating against them, could become a federal crime.

This bill mainly affects federal law enforcement officers, such as FBI agents, DEA agents, and similar federal workers, by giving them additional legal protections against a practice sometimes called "doxing." It also affects anyone who might share such location or personal information about those officers online or elsewhere. Average citizens would only be directly affected if they were involved in sharing that kind of targeted information about a federal officer.

title: Respect Tribal IDs Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill requires all Department of Homeland Security immigration enforcement officers to complete training on how to properly interact with Native American tribal members. The training must be developed within 180 days of the bill becoming law and must be created with input from the Bureau of Indian Affairs and tribal representatives. Officers cannot perform any immigration enforcement duties until they have completed this training, and they must repeat it at least once a year.

The training covers several specific topics: how to recognize official tribal ID documents, how to accept those documents as valid proof of U.S. citizenship, proper behavior when interacting with enrolled tribal members, and the history of how American Indians became U.S. citizens. The training will also include a database of example tribal documents and hands-on practice exercises. Accepted tribal documents include tribal enrollment cards, certificates of degree of Indian blood, tribal census documents, and official letters on tribal letterhead.

This bill mainly affects two groups. First, it affects DHS immigration enforcement officers, who would be required to complete new training before doing their jobs. Second, it affects enrolled members of federally recognized Native American tribes, particularly those living near U.S. borders, who have sometimes had their tribal IDs questioned or rejected during immigration enforcement encounters. The Secretary of Homeland Security must report back to Congress within one year on how the training program is being put into practice.

title: Election Mail Act
ai_summary:
This bill sets new rules for how the U.S. Postal Service and state election offices handle mail-in ballots and other election-related mail for federal elections. First, it requires the post office to process ballots on the same day they arrive at a facility, put a postmark showing the mailing date on every ballot envelope, and carry all election mail at the same speed as first-class mail. It also makes return postage free for completed mail-in ballots, and it bans the postal service from making operational changes that could slow down mail delivery during the 120 days before a federal election. That means no removing mail collection boxes without replacing them and no taking sorting machines out of service during that window.

Second, the bill requires states and local election offices to add trackable barcodes to mail-in ballot return envelopes so voters can follow their ballot through the mail, similar to tracking a package. Election offices must also use special labels and logos on ballot trays to make official ballots easier to identify and prioritize in the mail system. Starting in 2026, any mailed ballot for a federal election that is postmarked by Election Day must be accepted by election officials if it arrives within seven days after the election. title: POLL Act
ai_summary:
The POLL Act would set a federal rule that no voter in a federal election should have to wait more than 30 minutes to cast a ballot. Before each federal election, states would have to publish a public plan explaining how they will keep wait times under 30 minutes. After each election, the federal Election Assistance Commission would review wait times across the country. If voters in a given area waited more than 60 minutes, the Attorney General could step in and require that jurisdiction to follow a remedial plan to fix the problem in future elections. The bill also requires states to have a minimum number of voting machines, poll workers, and other resources at each polling location, with federal standards set by the Attorney General to guide that distribution. If equipment breaks down and causes long delays, poll workers must offer paper ballots right away.

The bill also lets individual voters sue in federal court if they waited more than 30 minutes. A voter could receive at least $50, plus $50 for each additional hour of waiting, along with attorney fees. If a court finds the long wait was caused by intentional vote suppression, those amounts jump to $650 and $150 per extra hour. The bill also bars the top state election official in each state from actively participating in federal political campaigns for any race they oversee, unless they fully recuse themselves from running that election.

This bill would affect all voters who participate in federal elections, meaning elections for President, U.S. Senate, and U.S. House. It would also directly affect state and local election administrators, who would need to meet new planning and staffing requirements. States could receive federal funding, up to $500 million per year, to help cover the costs of meeting these new standards.

title: American Citizens First Act
ai_summary:
This bill would cut off most federal benefits for non-citizens living in the United States. That includes Medicaid (except emergency care), food stamps, housing assistance, federal student aid, and certain tax credits. It would apply to legal immigrants, visa holders, and others who are not U.S. citizens or nationals. It would also allow the government to strip citizenship from naturalized Americans who are convicted of, or found by the Department of Homeland Security to have taken part in, riots, violent protests, property destruction, or actions seen as threatening the constitutional order. Those people could then be deported through a fast-track removal process.

The bill also expands the government's power to quickly deport undocumented immigrants without a full court hearing, removing previous limits based on how long someone has lived in the country. It requires a full security re-screening of Afghan refugees, special immigrant visa holders, and parolees who came to the United States starting January 20, 2021, and freezes new Afghan refugee and visa processing until that review is certified complete. Federal resettlement funding for Afghans would also be paused during that period.

Finally, the bill changes how Temporary Protected Status works. TPS allows people from certain dangerous or disaster-affected countries to live and work in the United States temporarily. Under this bill, TPS for a country's nationals would automatically end if their crime rate, including traffic violations and minor offenses, exceeds the national average by 20 percent or more. This would apply retroactively to TPS designations made after January 2021, specifically naming Afghanistan, Haiti, Venezuela, and Somalia. People currently holding TPS from those countries could lose their protected status as a result.

title: Naturalization Accountability Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes three changes to existing immigration and citizenship law. First, it says that if a naturalized U.S. citizen is convicted of any felony at any time, the government can revoke their citizenship. Under current law, a felony conviction is not automatically a reason to strip someone of citizenship. Second, it removes a five-year time limit that currently exists for revoking citizenship from people who joined certain banned organizations, such as groups considered totalitarian or treasonous, after becoming citizens. Right now, the government only has five years to act; this bill would eliminate that deadline entirely.

The third change deals with criminal penalties for people who obtained citizenship illegally or through fraud. Currently there is a ten-year statute of limitations on prosecuting that specific crime, meaning the government has ten years to bring charges. This bill removes that time limit for one particular offense, which involves illegally procuring naturalization, so prosecutors could bring charges at any point in the future, no matter how long ago the alleged wrongdoing occurred.

This bill primarily affects naturalized U.S. citizens, meaning people who were not born American but went through the legal process to become citizens. It does not affect people who were born as U.S. citizens, since their citizenship cannot be revoked in the same way. People who have a felony conviction after becoming citizens, or who joined certain organizations, would face a greater risk of losing their citizenship under this proposal.

title: Mail Ballot Integrity Act
ai_summary:
This bill would ban states from automatically mailing ballots to all registered voters for federal elections like congressional and presidential races. Right now, some states send every registered voter a mail ballot without them asking for one. Under this bill, that practice would be illegal. Instead, a voter would have to request a mail ballot and sign a statement, under penalty of perjury, confirming they qualify for one.

The bill creates a specific list of people who would be allowed to request a mail ballot. That list includes active-duty military members and their families, people who will be away from their home county on Election Day, voters aged 65 and older, people with certain disabilities, those who are hospitalized, people who are incarcerated but not for a felony, overseas residents, and a handful of other situations. Anyone who doesn't fit one of these categories would need to vote in person.

This bill would affect voters in every state, but it would have the biggest impact in states that currently mail ballots to all registered voters automatically, such as Colorado, Oregon, Washington, and Hawaii. People who currently rely on receiving a ballot without asking for one would now need to take an extra step to request it and prove they qualify. States would also need to update their election systems to comply if the bill becomes law.

title: SCAM Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the SCAM Act, would make it easier for the federal government to strip naturalized citizens of their citizenship. Right now, the government can already take away citizenship in certain cases, but this bill adds new specific reasons and new procedures. Under this bill, if a naturalized citizen joins or helps a terrorist organization within 10 years of becoming a citizen, defrauds a government program out of at least $10,000 within 10 years, or commits a serious felony or espionage crime within 10 years, the government can use that as strong legal evidence to take their citizenship away. The bill also allows the Attorney General, not just federal prosecutors, to bring these cases to court.

If citizenship is taken away under this bill, it would be treated as though the person was never a citizen to begin with, going all the way back to the date they were naturalized. That means the removal of citizenship is backdated, not just effective from the moment of the court decision. After losing citizenship, the person could then be quickly removed from the country through a fast-track deportation process, regardless of how long they have lived here or what their immigration status becomes afterward.

This bill affects only naturalized citizens, meaning people who were born in another country and went through the legal process to become U.S. citizens. It does not apply to people who are citizens by birth. People who could be affected include those convicted of fraud against government programs, espionage, serious crimes, or those found to have ties to terrorist groups, specifically if those actions happened within the first 10 years after they became citizens.

title: Protecting and Preserving Social Security Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes two main changes to Social Security. First, it would switch the way annual cost-of-living raises are calculated for Social Security recipients. Right now, raises are based on a general inflation measure. This bill would create a new price index specifically tracking what people 62 and older actually spend money on, such as healthcare and housing, and use that number instead. The idea is that spending patterns for older Americans are different from the general population, and their annual raises should reflect that.

Second, the bill changes how Social Security payroll taxes work for higher earners. Right now, Social Security taxes only apply to the first roughly $176,000 of a person's wages. This bill would phase out that cap between 2026 and 2031, so that by 2032, all wages above the current limit would be subject to Social Security taxes. This applies to both regular employees and self-employed people. In exchange, those higher earners would also receive a modest additional benefit credit for those extra earnings when they retire, though at a much lower rate than lower earners receive.

The people most directly affected are current Social Security recipients, who could see slightly larger annual raises under the new inflation formula, and workers who earn above roughly $176,000 a year, who would pay more in Social Security taxes starting in 2026. Employers of high earners would also pay more in matching payroll taxes. Lower and middle income workers would see no change in what they pay.

title: Protecting Circuit Boards and Substrates Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates a new federal tax credit equal to 25 percent of what a business spends on printed circuit boards that are made in the United States. Printed circuit boards are the flat green boards found inside nearly every electronic device, from phones and computers to cars and military equipment. Starting with purchases made after December 31, 2025, qualifying businesses can subtract 25 cents from their federal tax bill for every dollar they spend on American-made circuit boards.

The credit applies to businesses that buy or acquire these boards, not necessarily the companies that make them. So if a company assembles electronics and purchases circuit boards manufactured in the US, it can claim the credit. The boards must actually be fabricated, meaning physically produced from raw materials, inside the United States to qualify.

This bill mainly affects businesses across industries that use circuit boards in their products or operations, such as electronics manufacturers, defense contractors, automakers, and technology companies. It could also benefit American circuit board manufacturers, since the tax incentive gives their customers a financial reason to choose domestic suppliers over cheaper foreign ones, particularly from countries like China, which currently dominates global circuit board production.

ai_summary:
This bill would create a special tax on large oil companies during a period of conflict with Iran. Specifically, it targets companies that produce or import more than 100,000 barrels of oil per day. For every barrel of oil they sell above $75 per barrel, they would have to pay a tax equal to 100 percent of that extra amount. For example, if oil is selling at $100 per barrel, the company would owe $25 in tax on each barrel. The tax would stay in place until the President officially declares that fighting with Iran has stopped, the Strait of Hormuz shipping lane is fully open again, and oil prices drop back below $75 per barrel.

All the money collected from that tax would go into a dedicated government fund called the Iran War Gasoline Price Relief Fund. The government would then calculate how much money is in that fund each quarter and divide it up equally among eligible American taxpayers as a rebate, similar to a tax credit. Most U.S. residents who file taxes would qualify. People who are claimed as dependents on someone else's taxes, non-resident foreign nationals, and estates or trusts would not be eligible. The rebate would be refundable, meaning people could receive it even if they owe little or no federal income tax.

This bill mainly affects large oil producers and importers on one side, and everyday American taxpayers on the other. Big oil companies doing business in the U.S. would face significantly higher costs during this period. Individual Americans, by contrast, would receive periodic payments intended to help offset higher gas and energy prices caused by the conflict. U.S. territories like Puerto Rico and Guam would also receive payments through a separate process outlined in the bill.

title: Tax Cut for Striking Workers Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would change the federal tax code so that strike pay is no longer counted as taxable income. Right now, when a union pays its members during a strike or lockout to help replace the wages they are not getting from their employer, that money is treated as regular income and taxed. Under this bill, those payments would be tax-free. The change would apply to payments received starting January 1, 2026.

The bill also makes sure that strike pay would still count as earned income for the purpose of the Earned Income Tax Credit. That matters because the EITC is a tax credit designed to help lower- and middle-income workers, and counting strike pay as earned income means workers would not lose access to that credit just because they were on strike.

This bill mainly affects union members who go on strike or are locked out by their employer and receive financial support payments from their union during that time. It could also affect workers covered under the Railway Labor Act, which covers railroad and airline employees. Workers who do not belong to a union or who do not receive strike benefits from a union would not be directly affected.

title: Enhanced Small Business Growth Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill changes the tax code to give a bigger tax deduction to certain business owners who manufacture physical goods in the United States. Right now, many small business owners can deduct 20 percent of their business income from their taxes under an existing rule called the qualified business income deduction. This bill would raise that deduction to 30 percent for business owners who qualify as domestic manufacturers. To qualify, at least 85 percent of a business's income must come from making physical products, and at least 20 percent of the costs tied to those products must come from labor and overhead expenses inside the United States.

The bill also makes a smaller technical change to how taxable income is calculated for people who itemize their deductions, specifically removing charitable donations from the income figure used to determine the deduction amount. Both changes would take effect starting with the 2026 tax year.

This bill primarily affects self-employed people and owners of pass-through businesses, meaning businesses like sole proprietorships, partnerships, and S-corporations where income is reported on the owner's personal tax return rather than a separate corporate return. The biggest impact would be felt by small and mid-sized manufacturers who make physical goods and do a meaningful share of their production work inside the country. Larger corporations that pay the standard corporate income tax are not affected by this change.

title: Manufactured Housing Community Sustainability Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill creates a new federal tax credit for owners of mobile home parks, also called manufactured housing communities, who sell their property to the residents who live there or to a qualifying nonprofit organization. Specifically, the seller would receive a tax credit equal to 75 percent of the profit they made on the sale. To qualify, the seller must have owned the property for at least two years, and the buyer must agree to keep running it as a manufactured housing community for at least 50 years. Both the buyer and seller have to sign legal documents confirming the deal meets all the rules.

The bill is aimed at encouraging more park owners to sell to residents rather than to commercial real estate investors or developers. When residents buy the land together, they form a cooperative where each household owns a share and votes on community decisions. The bill notes that in resident-owned communities, lot rent increases average less than 1 percent per year, compared to nearly 6 percent per year in commercially owned parks. If the new owner later breaks the 50-year promise and sells the land for another use, they face a penalty tax of 20 percent of the sale proceeds.

The people most directly affected are the roughly 22 million Americans who live in manufactured homes, many of whom are low- and moderate-income households. They currently own their home but not the land underneath it, which makes them vulnerable to rent increases, park closures, and costly forced moves. Park owners considering selling their property are also directly affected, since the tax credit is designed to make selling to residents financially attractive. The bill would take effect for tax years starting after December 31, 2026.

title: Rental Housing Investment Act
ai_summary:
This bill gives tax breaks to people and companies that build new rental housing. Specifically, it lets them write off a large chunk of the building's cost in the first year instead of spreading that deduction out over many years like current law requires. Under normal tax rules, a residential rental building is written off slowly over 27.5 years. This bill would let landlords and developers immediately deduct up to $150,000 per apartment unit when they put a newly built rental property into service. If a developer builds a 10-unit building, for example, they could deduct up to $1.5 million right away.

There is a bigger bonus available for affordable housing. If the property meets low-income housing requirements under existing federal law, the deduction jumps to $250,000 per unit. To keep the benefit fair, there is a clawback rule: if the property stops being used as a rental within 10 years of opening, the owner has to pay back the tax savings. For affordable housing units, that payback window stretches to 15 years. Only newly built properties qualify, not older buildings being bought or renovated.

This bill mainly affects real estate developers, landlords, and investors who build new residential rental properties. It could also indirectly affect renters if the tax incentive leads to more rental units being built, which could ease housing shortages in some areas. It does not directly give money to renters or change rent prices. The bill was introduced in the Senate in March 2026 and has been sent to the Finance Committee, where it would need approval before moving further.

title: Increasing Opportunity For Reindustrialization Act
ai_summary:
This bill expands a program called Opportunity Zones, which currently gives investors a tax break when they put money into certain low-income areas. Right now, states can only designate a limited number of these zones, and the areas must meet income-based requirements. This bill would allow areas containing closed military bases, known as BRAC closures, to also qualify as Opportunity Zones, even if they are not low-income communities.

The bill also makes sure these former military base areas do not count against a state's existing cap on how many Opportunity Zones it can have. In other words, states could add these former base locations on top of their current allowance, not instead of them. This means more investment could potentially flow into communities that lost a military base and the jobs and economic activity that came with it.

The people most directly affected are residents and local governments in communities where a military base was shut down through the official base realignment and closure process. Investors who put money into these newly eligible zones would receive federal tax advantages. It could also affect real estate developers and businesses looking to build or expand in those areas. The bill was introduced in May 2026 and was sent to the Senate Finance Committee for review.

title: MARCH for Military Servicemembers Act
ai_summary:
This bill would remove a section of federal law that restricts the U.S. Department of Defense from using its money or medical facilities to provide abortions. That restriction currently allows military medical facilities to perform abortions only in cases of rape, incest, or when the pregnancy threatens the mother's life. If this bill became law, those limits would no longer be part of the legal code, which could allow the military's medical system to offer abortion services more broadly.

The people most directly affected would be active-duty military members, their dependents, and others who receive healthcare through the military's medical system, such as at base hospitals or clinics. Military families are often stationed in states where abortion access may be limited, so the location of a base can affect what healthcare options are available locally. This bill is aimed at changing what options the military medical system itself could offer, regardless of the state where a base is located.

The bill was introduced in the Senate in May 2026 and sent to the Armed Services Committee, which would need to approve it before it could move forward to a full Senate vote. It has not yet become law.

title: Stars and Stripes Editorial Independence Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill is about protecting the independence of Stars and Stripes, a news organization that has served U.S. military members since the Civil War. Right now, rules protecting its independence exist in military regulations, but those can be changed by the executive branch. This bill would write those protections directly into federal law, making them harder to remove. It requires the Defense Department to ensure Stars and Stripes operates like a professional news outlet, free from censorship, military public affairs influence, or political pressure. It also specifically bans the Defense Department from deliberately hiding unfavorable news about itself. The only allowed exceptions are for information that is classified or that could directly endanger American lives, and even then, both the publisher and a military commander must agree before anything is withheld.

The bill also sets rules about how Stars and Stripes is run day to day. It requires the organization to be led by a civilian with real journalism experience, not a military official. It allows Stars and Stripes reporters to access military bases to cover events, even when commercial reporters cannot. It also says the outlet must be allowed to buy and publish content from outside commercial news sources, and that civilian job candidates cannot be excluded from working there.

The people most directly affected are U.S. military members, Defense Department civilian employees, and their families, especially those stationed overseas or in combat zones who often rely on Stars and Stripes as their main source of independent English-language news. The bill also affects the Defense Department itself, which would face legal restrictions on how much influence it can have over the outlet's reporting.
