title: VA Police Recruitment and Retention Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would stop the Department of Veterans Affairs from lowering the job classifications of its police officers and other law enforcement employees. When a federal position gets "downgraded," the job title and pay grade drop, which usually means the employee earns less money over time. This bill would make that kind of change illegal for VA law enforcement jobs, and it would cancel any downgrades that already happened on or after October 1, 2025, restoring those positions and paying back any wages that were lost.

The bill also applies retroactively, meaning it looks backward in time. If a VA police officer's position was quietly reclassified to a lower pay level between October 2025 and when this bill becomes law, that change would be reversed. The officer would go back to their previous grade and receive any back pay they missed out on during that period.

This bill mainly affects VA police officers and other law enforcement staff who work at VA hospitals, clinics, and facilities across the country. It also limits what the Office of Personnel Management, which oversees federal workforce rules, can do regarding these specific jobs. Veterans who use VA facilities could be indirectly affected, since the bill is aimed at making it easier to recruit and keep qualified security personnel at those locations.

last_action_text: Forwarded by Subcommittee to Full Committee by Voice Vote.

title: Chip Security Act
ai_summary:
The Chip Security Act requires the U.S. Department of Commerce to add security features to advanced computer chips before they are sold or shipped to other countries. Within 180 days of the law passing, any high-powered chip covered by U.S. export rules would need to include location-tracking technology so the government can verify the chip stays where it was approved to go. If a company that exported a chip finds out it has been moved to an unauthorized location, handed to an unauthorized user, or tampered with, they must report that to the government right away.

The law also directs the Commerce Department to study and possibly require additional security features over time, such as tools that could disable or limit a chip that was stolen or smuggled, or methods to confirm what the chip is actually being used for. The department must report its findings to Congress within one year and roll out any approved additional security measures within two years after that. Each year for three years following that, the government must review new security technologies and consider updating the requirements.

This bill mainly affects U.S. companies that manufacture or export advanced semiconductors and AI chips, particularly those already subject to U.S. export controls. It also affects foreign businesses and governments that purchase these chips, since the chips could be monitored for location and usage. Everyday consumers would likely feel little direct impact, though the rules could influence the global supply of high-end chips used in data centers, AI systems, and other advanced computing products.
ai_headline: New law would require location tracking on exported AI chips
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 42 - 0.

title: Grocery, Farm, and Food Worker Stabilization Grant Program Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new grant program run by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The program would send money to unions and membership organizations that represent farmworkers, meat processing workers, and grocery store workers. The money would be used to make direct payments to those workers when a natural disaster or other major disaster strikes and disrupts their jobs or income. Congress would authorize up to $50 million to fund the program.

The workers most directly affected are people who grow and harvest food, work in meatpacking plants, and work in grocery stores. These are jobs that often cannot be done remotely and can be severely disrupted by events like hurricanes, floods, or other large-scale emergencies. The grants would not go straight to individual workers. Instead, they would go to the unions or worker organizations those employees belong to, which would then distribute stabilization payments to members.

Four years after the program starts, the Department of Agriculture would be required to report back to Congress on how the program worked and what impact it had. The bill was introduced in March 2026 and has been sent to the House Agriculture Committee, where it would need to be approved before moving further through the legislative process. It has not yet become law.

title: Farewell to Foam Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would ban the sale and distribution of three specific types of foam plastic products made from expanded polystyrene, starting January 1, 2028. The banned items are foam food containers like cups, plates, bowls, clamshells, and egg cartons; foam packing peanuts used to cushion items during shipping; and foam coolers used to keep things cold. The ban would not apply to foam containers used to ship medicines, medical devices, or biological products like vaccines.

The ban would apply to anyone involved in making, importing, distributing, or selling these products, including restaurants, grocery stores, schools, hospitals, and retail stores. The first time a business breaks the rule, the EPA would send a written warning. After that, fines would kick in, starting at $250 for a second violation, $500 for a third, and $1,000 for each violation after that. Smaller businesses face some limits on how often they can be fined within a seven-day period.

This bill would affect a wide range of people and businesses across the country. Restaurants and food vendors that currently use foam takeout containers would need to switch to other materials like paper, cardboard, or plastic alternatives. Shipping companies and online retailers that use packing peanuts would need to find substitute materials. Consumers who buy foam coolers for picnics or camping would no longer be able to purchase them after the deadline. Manufacturers that currently produce these foam products would need to change or stop that part of their business.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: One Nation, One Visa Policy Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require that any person holding a Chinese passport must have a valid visa before being allowed to enter the United States. Right now, there is a special visa waiver program for the U.S. territory of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands that allows Chinese tourists to visit without getting a visa in advance. This bill would end that exception and block any similar programs from being created or funded in the future.

The bill also specifies that "China" includes Hong Kong and Macau, even though those two places have some separate travel documents and rules. So passport holders from all three of those places would be covered by this requirement.

This mainly affects Chinese tourists, students, business travelers, and others who currently use or might use visa-free entry programs, especially in Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands. It would also affect those U.S. territories economically, since they rely heavily on tourism from China. American businesses and universities that work with Chinese visitors could also feel the impact if the visa process becomes a bigger barrier to entry.
ai_headline: Bill would strip visa-free entry for Chinese passport holders in Guam
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7780 would end visa-free entry for Chinese passport holders in Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands.

The bill would end the existing visa waiver program that allows Chinese tourists to visit Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands without a visa. It would also block any similar programs from being created or funded in the future.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects Chinese tourists, students, and business travelers who currently use or could use visa-free entry, particularly in Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands. American businesses, universities, and the economies of those U.S. territories would also be affected.
ai_sections.why: Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands rely heavily on tourism from China, so ending visa-free entry could have economic consequences for those territories. The added visa requirement could also reduce the number of Chinese visitors reaching American businesses and universities that depend on that travel.
ai_sections.cost: The bill would block future funding for visa waiver programs similar to the one being eliminated.
costChips: Future visa waiver programs blocked from funding

title: SHUSH Act
ai_summary:
This bill would remove silencers (also called suppressors) from the list of heavily regulated items under the National Firearms Act. Right now, buying a silencer requires a $200 federal tax, a background check, a months-long wait for government approval, and registration with the federal government. The SHUSH Act would eliminate all of that, treating silencers the same as ordinary gun accessories like scopes or grips, which anyone legally allowed to own a firearm can buy without extra federal steps.

The bill also has two other notable parts. It would block states and cities from creating their own special taxes or registration requirements for silencers, overriding those local laws. It would also apply the tax refund rules going back to 2015, meaning people who paid the $200 federal tax on silencer transfers after that date could potentially get that money back.

This bill affects several groups. Gun owners who want to buy silencers would face far fewer restrictions and lower costs. Dealers who sell silencers would see a simpler sales process. People living in states that currently ban or heavily restrict silencers could be affected, since the bill would remove some state-level rules, though states could still ban silencers outright through other laws. Federal agencies that currently manage silencer registrations, like the ATF, would have a reduced role in overseeing these devices.
ai_headline: Bill would strip federal registration rules from gun silencers
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Ways and Means, and in addition to the Committee on the Judiciary, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

Silencers would instead be treated like ordinary gun accessories such as scopes or grips. The bill would also block states and cities from imposing their own special taxes or registration requirements on silencers.

title: New Producer Economic Security Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new federal grant program inside the U.S. Department of Agriculture called the New Producer Economic Security Program. The program would send money to organizations like nonprofits, tribal governments, community lenders, and universities, which would then pass that money along to beginning and struggling farmers and ranchers. The help could come as grants, loans, or down payment assistance to help people buy or keep farmland, cover closing costs, fix up soil or water, build infrastructure, or get legal and business advice.

The people this program is designed to help are called "qualified beneficiaries." These are farmers, ranchers, or forest owners who are either brand new to farming, only farm on rented land, have low incomes, or are otherwise considered economically disadvantaged. The bill also gives priority to projects that help farmworkers, support tribal land access, or help families pass farms down to the next generation instead of selling to outside buyers.

The bill authorizes Congress to appropriate whatever funding is needed, but it does not set a specific dollar amount. It also sets up a stakeholder committee to help the USDA decide how to hand out grants fairly. Anyone who runs a farm operation already for more than 10 years and is financially stable would generally not qualify for the direct assistance side of this program.
ai_headline: New USDA grant program targets beginning and low-income farmers
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities, Risk Management, and Credit.

The program would distribute funds through intermediary organizations, including nonprofits, tribal governments, community lenders, and universities, which would then provide grants, loans, or down payment assistance to eligible farmers and ranchers. Allowed uses include buying or keeping farmland, covering closing costs, improving soil or water, building infrastructure, and obtaining legal or business advice.

Farmers who have operated for more than 10 years and are financially stable would generally not qualify for direct assistance.

A stakeholder committee would advise the USDA on distributing grants, which may shape how equitably funds reach intended groups.

costChips: Funding level set by future appropriations

title: Restoring Access for Detainees Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require the federal government to give people held in immigration detention free phone access. Within the first five hours of being detained or moved to a new facility, a detainee would get at least one free call of 10 minutes or more to notify a family member of their location. Each month, detainees would receive at least 200 free minutes to call family. Calls to lawyers, immigration courts, consulates, oversight offices, and certain government agencies would be unlimited and free. Calls to lawyers and oversight officials could not be recorded or monitored unless a court issued a warrant. The bill also says detention facilities can set reasonable rules about when and where calls happen, but they cannot cap time spent talking to a lawyer or count incoming calls against a detainee's free minutes.

The people most directly affected are immigrants held in civil immigration detention, which can include people awaiting deportation hearings or other immigration proceedings. These individuals are not held as part of a criminal sentence. The bill also affects the Department of Homeland Security, which would be responsible for setting up the program and paying for it. The bill points to funding already given to ICE through a recently passed law as the intended source of money.

This bill was introduced in the House and referred to the Judiciary Committee, meaning it has not become law. It essentially tries to bring back a free phone program that existed during the COVID-19 pandemic and later ended, while adding new rules about lawyer calls and family notification.
ai_headline: House bill would give immigration detainees free phone access each month
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Infrastructure Expansion Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill deals with who can be held legally responsible when a construction worker gets hurt on a federal infrastructure project. Right now, some states have laws called "absolute liability" rules, which means that if a worker falls or is injured by a gravity-related hazard on a job site, the property owner or contractor can be held fully responsible no matter what. This bill would end that standard for any project that receives federal money, federal tax breaks, or requires federal permits. Instead, it would replace absolute liability with "comparative negligence," which means a court would look at whether the injured worker also played a role in causing their own injury, such as ignoring safety training, not using provided safety equipment, or being impaired by drugs or alcohol.

The bill would also move these legal cases from state courts into federal courts, and it would override any state laws that conflict with it. So states that currently have stronger protections for injured workers on construction sites would lose the ability to enforce those protections on federally funded projects. Workers' compensation laws, however, would not be affected by this bill.

The people most directly affected are construction workers who do physical labor on federally funded infrastructure projects like highways, bridges, airports, and buildings. Property owners and contractors on those same projects would also be affected, since they would face a different and generally lower level of legal liability if a worker is injured. The bill would apply to any project where federal assistance is accepted starting January 1, 2026.
ai_headline: Federal bill would strip stronger state injury protections from construction workers
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 3548 replaces absolute liability with comparative negligence on federally funded construction projects, overriding stronger state worker protections.
ai_sections.what: HR 3548 would end absolute liability standards for worker injuries on construction projects receiving federal money, tax breaks, or permits, replacing them with comparative negligence. Under comparative negligence, courts would consider whether an injured worker contributed to their own injury, such as by ignoring safety training, refusing provided equipment, or working while impaired. The bill would move these cases from state courts to federal courts and override conflicting state laws, effective for projects accepting federal assistance starting January 1, 2026.
ai_sections.who: Construction workers injured on federally funded infrastructure projects like highways, bridges, airports, and buildings are directly affected, as are the property owners and contractors working on those same projects. States that currently have stronger absolute liability protections for workers would lose the ability to enforce those protections on federally funded projects.
ai_sections.why: Workers in states with absolute liability laws would have reduced legal standing after an injury on a federally funded project, since a court could reduce or limit their recovery based on their own share of fault. Property owners and contractors on federally funded projects would face a generally lower level of legal liability than they currently do in states with absolute liability rules.

title: Congressional Tribute to Constance Baker Motley Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill directs Congress to award a congressional gold medal to Constance Baker Motley, who passed away in 2005. She was a pioneering civil rights lawyer who helped win landmark cases including Brown v. Board of Education, and she later became the first Black woman elected to the New York State Senate, the first woman to serve as Manhattan Borough President, and the first Black woman appointed to a federal judgeship. The medal would be created by the U.S. Treasury Department and presented to her son and niece at a formal ceremony.

The bill also allows the U.S. Mint to produce and sell bronze copies of the gold medal to the public. The cost of making the gold medal comes from an existing U.S. Mint fund, and any money made from selling the bronze copies goes back into that same fund, so there is no additional cost to taxpayers.

This bill directly affects the Motley family, who would receive the medal. It also involves the U.S. Mint, which would design and produce the medals. Members of the general public who are interested in history or collecting could purchase bronze copies. The congressional gold medal is one of the highest honors Congress can give to a civilian, so the bill is essentially a formal national recognition of Motley's lifetime of public service.
ai_headline: Gold medal bill honors trailblazing civil rights lawyer Constance Baker Motley
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

title: Fair Access to Banking Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require large banks, credit unions, and payment card networks to serve any customer whose business is legal under federal law. Specifically, banks with more than $50 billion in assets could not refuse a customer just because of the industry they work in or because of "reputational risk." If a bank does deny someone service, it would have to put the reason in writing, and that reason must be based on specific, measurable financial risk standards, not general opinions about the customer's business or politics. Banks that break these rules could lose access to emergency government lending programs, like the Federal Reserve's discount window, which banks rely on when they need short-term cash.

The bill also covers payment card networks, like Visa or Mastercard, prohibiting them from blocking legally operating businesses from using their systems based on political or reputational concerns. Violations by payment networks could result in financial penalties. The Automated Clearing House network, which handles direct deposits and electronic payments, would also be off-limits to large banks and credit unions that refuse legal businesses.

People or businesses that are wrongly denied banking services could sue the bank directly in federal court without going through a government agency first. If they win, they could receive three times their actual damages plus legal fees. The bill would mainly affect the largest financial institutions and would most directly benefit businesses in industries that have reportedly struggled to get banking services, such as firearms dealers, fossil fuel companies, and certain other legal but controversial sectors.
ai_headline: Large banks would lose Fed emergency lending if they turn away legal businesses
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

Payment card networks like Visa or Mastercard and the Automated Clearing House network would also be prohibited from blocking legally operating businesses on political or reputational grounds.

title: IRA Charitable Rollover Facilitation and Enhancement Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes a tax rule about how people can donate money from their retirement accounts to charity. Right now, Americans age 70½ or older can transfer money directly from an IRA to most charities without paying income tax on that withdrawal. This is called a "qualified charitable distribution." However, current law blocks people from using this tax benefit when donating to a donor-advised fund, which is a special account held at a sponsoring organization that lets donors recommend where their charitable gifts go over time. This bill would remove that restriction and allow IRA charitable rollovers to go into donor-advised funds.

Who would this affect most directly? People age 70½ and older who have traditional IRAs and want to give to charity using a donor-advised fund. These individuals could transfer up to the allowed limit (currently $105,000 per year) directly from their IRA to a donor-advised fund without counting that money as taxable income. Financial institutions and nonprofits that manage donor-advised funds, such as community foundations and large financial firms with charitable arms, would also be affected as they could receive more contributions through this channel.

The bill does not create a new tax deduction. It simply expands an existing one to cover a type of charitable account that was previously excluded. People who do not have IRAs, are under age 70½, or who do not use donor-advised funds would not be directly affected by this change.
ai_headline: IRA charitable rollover ban on donor-advised funds would end under HR 2891
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: In God We Trust Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require the federal government to display the phrase "In God We Trust" on all federal public buildings. The Administrator of General Services, who oversees federal properties, would have one year after the bill becomes law to make sure the motto is placed in a prominent spot on every qualifying building. Federal public buildings include courthouses, office buildings, and similar government-owned or leased facilities across the country.

The bill would affect anyone who works in or visits federal buildings, since they would see the national motto displayed there. It would also require the General Services Administration to spend time and money carrying out the requirement across what amounts to thousands of federal properties nationwide.

"In God We Trust" has been the official national motto of the United States since 1956 and already appears on U.S. currency. This bill would extend that display to federal buildings specifically. The bill was introduced in the House and sent to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, where it would need to be approved before moving further through Congress.

title: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States to limit the number of consecutive terms that a Member of Congress may serve.
ai_summary:
This bill proposes a change to the U.S. Constitution that would set limits on how long members of Congress can serve back-to-back. Senators could serve no more than two consecutive terms (12 years in a row), and House members could serve no more than five consecutive terms (10 years in a row). After hitting that limit, a person would have to wait at least one year before running again. They are not banned from Congress forever, just required to take a break before returning.

Because this is a constitutional amendment, it would not become law just by passing Congress. Two-thirds of both the House and Senate would need to approve it, and then three-fourths of all state legislatures (38 out of 50 states) would have to ratify it within seven years. That is a high bar to clear. The bill also specifies that terms already served before ratification would not count toward the limit, so the clock would start fresh for everyone currently in office.

This would directly affect current and future members of Congress and, by extension, their constituents. Voters in any district or state could find that a long-serving representative they support is required to step aside temporarily. On the other hand, it could open seats to new candidates who might otherwise struggle to unseat an incumbent. The bill does not affect the President or any other federal officeholder.
ai_headline: Proposed amendment would cap consecutive congressional terms at 10–12 years
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

After reaching the limit, a member must wait at least one year before running again. Terms served before ratification would not count toward the new limits.

ai_sections.why: Long-serving incumbents who reach the consecutive-term limit would be required to temporarily vacate their seats, which could affect constituents who support them. title: REVOKE Act
ai_summary:
This bill would allow the government to take away security clearances from former Defense Department employees and retired military members if they lobby on behalf of certain Chinese companies. Specifically, it targets companies that the Defense Department has labeled as Chinese military companies and that also appear on a Treasury Department watchlist. In other words, if a former Pentagon official or retired service member gets paid to represent or advocate for one of these companies in Washington, they would lose their access to classified information. The Defense Secretary can make exceptions for up to 180 days if national security requires it, but must explain that decision to Congress.

The bill affects two main groups of people. The first is former civilian employees of the Department of Defense, such as analysts, managers, or contractors who once worked for the Pentagon. The second is retired or separated military members, like former generals or officers. Both groups are sometimes hired after their government service to work as lobbyists or consultants, which is commonly called the revolving door between government and private industry.

For most everyday Americans, this bill would have no direct impact. Its focus is narrow, targeting a specific group of former government insiders who choose to work for companies on these Chinese military watchlists. Supporters might say it protects national security by reducing the risk that sensitive government knowledge gets used to help Chinese military-linked businesses. Critics might raise concerns about how far the government can go in restricting what private citizens do after leaving public service.
ai_headline: Former Pentagon officials could lose security clearances for lobbying Chinese military firms
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Armed Services.

title: Professional Degree Access Restoration Act
ai_summary:
This bill would undo recent cuts to federal student loan limits for people in graduate and professional school, such as law school, medical school, and master's degree programs. A previous law reduced how much money these students can borrow through federal loans. This bill would bring those limits back up to where they were before that cut took effect.

The main effect is that graduate and professional students would once again be able to borrow more money through the federal loan program to cover the cost of their advanced degrees. Without this change, students who hit the lower borrowing cap may have to turn to private loans, which often come with higher interest rates and fewer borrower protections than federal loans.

This bill directly affects people currently enrolled in or planning to attend graduate or professional degree programs, such as medical, dental, law, or business school. It would not affect undergraduate students. Taxpayers could also be affected, since higher federal loan limits mean the government is taking on more lending. The bill was introduced in the Senate in March 2026 and has been sent to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where it will be reviewed before any further action is taken.

title: Improve and Enhance the Work Opportunity Tax Credit Act
ai_summary:
The Work Opportunity Tax Credit (WOTC) is an existing federal tax break that rewards businesses for hiring people from certain groups who often have a harder time finding jobs. This bill would extend that tax credit through 2030 and make it more generous. Right now, employers can claim 40% of a new hire's first-year wages up to a set limit. This bill raises that rate to 50% and adds a bonus credit for workers who stay on the job for at least 400 hours, encouraging employers to keep these workers longer rather than just hiring and quickly moving on. The wage limits used to calculate the credit would also increase each year with inflation, so the benefit doesn't lose value over time.

The bill also expands who counts as an eligible hire. Currently, food stamp recipients must be under age 40 to qualify; this bill removes that age cap entirely. It also adds military spouses as a new qualifying group, meaning a business that hires the spouse of an active-duty service member can now claim the credit. Special adjustments are made for veterans, long-term welfare recipients, summer youth workers, and workers in agriculture and the railroad industry.

This bill mainly affects two groups: businesses that hire workers from struggling or underrepresented populations, and the workers themselves. Employers in manufacturing, construction, energy, healthcare, and infrastructure are specifically mentioned as targets for outreach. Federal agencies would be required to actively inform business leaders in those fields about the credit. Workers who benefit include veterans, people receiving food assistance, welfare recipients, ex-felons, people with disabilities, and now military spouses.
ai_headline: Tax credit for hiring hard-to-employ workers would rise to 50% under Senate bill
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

A bonus credit would apply when a hired worker stays on the job for at least 400 hours. title: Parents Over Platforms Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires app stores (like Apple's App Store or Google Play) to figure out whether their users are adults or minors when they sign up, and to share that age information with app developers when a user or their parent agrees to it. App stores would also have to give parents the ability to block their child from downloading or using certain apps. App developers, in turn, would be required to use that age information to give minors a different, more restricted experience, and they would be banned from showing personalized ads to anyone identified as under 18. Developers must also get parental consent before letting minors access content the developer has flagged as inappropriate for unsupervised use.

The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules, treating any violations the same way it handles unfair or deceptive business practices, which can result in significant financial penalties. App stores and developers get some legal protection if they make honest, good-faith efforts to follow the law, even if age estimates turn out to be wrong. The bill also overrides any existing or future state laws covering the same ground, making this a single national standard.

The people most directly affected are parents of minors, children and teenagers who use apps, app store operators like Apple and Google, and the companies that build apps. The bill would take effect two years after it becomes law, giving businesses time to build the required systems.

title: Campaign Event Contract Integrity Act
ai_summary:
This bill targets a specific type of financial conflict of interest involving political prediction markets. These are online platforms where people can bet real money on the outcomes of elections and other political events. The bill says that anyone working for or closely connected to a political campaign, party, or political action committee cannot trade these contracts if they have secret inside information about that campaign. This includes staffers, pollsters, consultants, fundraisers, and even family members who act on someone's behalf. They also cannot tip off other people to trade using that inside information, and no one can trade on their behalf as a workaround.

The bill also puts responsibilities on the prediction market platforms themselves. These companies would have to set up systems to spot and stop suspicious trading, keep records, and report shady activity to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which is the federal agency that oversees commodity and derivatives markets. Large traders on these platforms would have to disclose whether they are connected to a campaign or have access to private campaign information. The CFTC would have 180 days to write the specific rules spelling out how all of this works.

People who break the rules could face fines up to $250,000 or three times whatever profit they made, whichever is larger. They could also be banned from these markets and forced to give back any money they gained illegally. The bill does not affect regular researchers, journalists, or anyone trading based only on publicly available information. It mainly affects campaign insiders who might have an unfair advantage over ordinary bettors on political prediction platforms.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.

title: Rural Grants Transparency Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires the U.S. Department of Agriculture to make its rural development grant programs easier to understand and navigate. Right now, small towns, rural nonprofits, and cooperatives often struggle to figure out how to apply for federal grants because the process is complicated and hard to find. The bill directs USDA to create a plain-language "Roadmap" for each grant program, posted on a single website, that explains what the program does, what documents applicants need, how applications are scored, and why applications commonly get rejected. This information must be updated at least four times a year.

The bill also requires USDA to send applicants clear notifications at each step of the process, including a confirmation when their application arrives, a notice if something is missing, and an explanation if they are turned down. If an application is denied, the agency must explain in plain language what hurt the application and how to do better next time. USDA also has to publish a searchable database showing who received grant awards, where projects are located, how much money was awarded, and what the project is for. For competitive grants, the agency must publicly post exactly how applications are scored and what factors carry the most weight.

This bill mainly affects rural communities, small local governments, rural nonprofits, cooperatives, and USDA staff who work in state and local offices. It does not create new grant money or change who qualifies for existing programs. The bill specifically states it must be carried out using resources USDA already has, with no new funding required, and must be fully in place within 180 days of becoming law.

title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Department of Energy relating to "Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Walk-In Coolers and Walk-In Freezers".
ai_summary:
This bill cancels a rule that the Department of Energy issued in December 2024. That rule would have set new energy efficiency standards for walk-in coolers and freezers, which are the large refrigerated storage units commonly used in grocery stores, restaurants, warehouses, and food distribution centers. Congress used a law called the Congressional Review Act, which allows lawmakers to vote to block federal agency rules they disagree with. Once this resolution was signed, the Department of Energy's rule became void and unenforceable.

The people most directly affected are businesses that own or buy walk-in coolers and freezers. Under the canceled rule, manufacturers would have had to build these units to meet stricter energy efficiency requirements, and businesses purchasing new equipment would have had to meet those standards too. Supporters of canceling the rule argued the requirements would raise equipment costs. Supporters of the original rule argued it would lower electricity bills over time and reduce energy use.

Because the rule is now blocked, manufacturers and buyers of walk-in coolers and freezers will continue to follow the older, existing energy standards rather than the newer, stricter ones. This affects a wide range of industries, including supermarkets, restaurants, hotels, and food storage and distribution businesses across the country.

title: No Rigged Grocery Prices Act
ai_summary:
This bill would make it illegal for grocery stores and food delivery apps to use your personal data to charge you higher prices than other shoppers. For example, if a store's software noticed that you live in a wealthier zip code or that you've bought a certain product many times before, it could not use that information to raise the price just for you. The ban applies to large grocery stores of at least 15,000 square feet and to delivery services like Instacart or DoorDash. There are some exceptions, such as loyalty programs you voluntarily sign up for, temporary discounts meant to keep customers, or price differences based on real costs like shipping or taxes.

The bill also adds a couple of consumer protection rules for online grocery shopping. Stores must tell you if an item's availability has changed or if something is sold by weight. Delivery services must get your permission before swapping out an item you ordered for a different one. If a company breaks these rules, the Federal Trade Commission can treat it as an unfair or deceptive business practice and take legal action.

The bill affects everyday shoppers who buy groceries in stores or through delivery apps, as well as the large grocery chains and delivery companies that would need to change how their pricing software works. The bill also requires the Department of Labor to study whether electronic price tags on store shelves are reducing the number of grocery store jobs, though that study has no immediate effect on anyone.

title: Campaign Funds Integrity Act of 2026
ai_summary:

The bill sets real consequences for breaking the rules. Campaigns that violate it could face civil fines through the Federal Election Commission. It could also affect campaign staff or treasurers who manage those funds. Everyday donors are not directly regulated by this bill, but it is designed to protect them by ensuring the money they give to a campaign is used for campaigning and not for speculative financial bets.

title: No U.S. Funding for UNIFIL Act
ai_summary:
This bill would stop the United States from sending any money to UNIFIL, which is a United Nations peacekeeping force that has been stationed in southern Lebanon since 1978. The UN Security Council voted in 2025 to end UNIFIL's mission by December 31, 2026. This bill says that starting October 1, 2027, no U.S. government agency — including the State Department or the military — can contribute any funds to UNIFIL or any organization that replaces it.

The bill also includes a backup rule in case the UN changes course and decides to keep UNIFIL going past December 2026. If that happens, the U.S. would automatically subtract an amount equal to UNIFIL's entire yearly budget from its broader UN peacekeeping payments. Basically, the U.S. would refuse to pay the UN back for whatever UNIFIL costs until the mission ends.

This bill mainly affects U.S. foreign policy and how the country spends money on international peacekeeping. It does not directly impact most Americans in their daily lives, but it could matter to people who follow U.S. involvement in Middle East security or United Nations affairs. UNIFIL currently includes troops from dozens of countries, and the U.S. contributes to its funding as part of its regular UN dues. This bill was introduced by members of both parties, suggesting some bipartisan agreement on the issue.

title: To direct the Secretary of State to take actions with respect to certain foreign affairs matters.
ai_summary:
This bill gives the State Department several new rules and powers related to how it handles maps, flags, foreign aid, technology, and its own staff training. It would ban the State Department from using maps that show the body of water between the U.S. and Mexico as anything other than the "Gulf of America." It also limits which flags can be flown over State Department buildings to a specific approved list, which includes the U.S. flag, flags of other countries, tribal flags, and a few official government flags, but nothing else.

The bill also makes changes to foreign aid. It would stop the State Department from giving grants to nonprofits or international organizations unless those groups follow specific federal rules published in early 2026 that restrict funding related to abortion services and certain gender and diversity programs. It also gives the Secretary of State the legal authority to officially merge USAID, the main U.S. foreign aid agency, into the State Department, potentially eliminating USAID as a separate agency. Additionally, the bill allows small drones under 55 pounds to be used in certain international anti-drug efforts without previous legal restrictions that applied to larger aircraft.

Finally, the bill requires all U.S. diplomats and Foreign Service workers to complete a new training course on what it calls "America First Principles" before they can be posted at any overseas embassy or diplomatic mission. The State Department would also get new flexibility to pursue technology research and development contracts outside the usual competitive bidding process through a pilot program running until 2031. This bill affects U.S. diplomats, foreign aid organizations, USAID employees, and any nonprofits that receive State Department funding.

title: Strategy for Crisis Management Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill requires the Secretary of Defense to create a formal plan for handling potential crises in the South China Sea, specifically situations involving China that could put U.S. interests, people, or allies at risk. The plan would identify the most likely trouble spots in the region and build a detailed "playbook" for each one. Each playbook would lay out step-by-step response options, ranging from military moves to diplomatic and economic actions, and would include an analysis of the costs, risks, and potential humanitarian impacts of each option. The Defense Secretary would have to work with the State Department, Commerce Department, Treasury Department, and other agencies to build these plans.

The bill also requires the Pentagon to update these playbooks at least twice a year to keep them current. Within 120 days of the bill becoming law, the Defense Secretary must report to Congress on progress, and within one year must deliver a full summary of the completed strategy. The reports would be unclassified but could include a classified section for sensitive details.

This bill mainly affects the U.S. Department of Defense and other federal agencies involved in national security and foreign policy. It does not directly change laws or programs that affect everyday Americans at home. However, it could indirectly affect U.S. residents by shaping how the government responds to conflicts in a region that handles a large share of global trade, which can influence prices and economic stability.

title: Aquatic Invasive Species Control and Prevention Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill updates a 1990 law that deals with invasive species in U.S. waters — things like Asian carp, zebra mussels, and other non-native creatures that can damage ecosystems and hurt fishing, recreation, and local economies. It creates two new grant programs: one to fund research into better methods for controlling or wiping out invasive species, and another to fund quick action when a new invasive species is first detected. It also requires the government to develop a national plan for inspecting and cleaning boats at launch sites, set up a monitoring system to track how invasive species move through major waterways like the Chicago Sanitary Ship Canal and the Mississippi River, and study whether existing rules make it harder to respond fast when a new threat shows up.

The bill affects a wide range of people and groups. Boaters and recreational fishers could see new inspection or decontamination checkpoints at boat launches on federal waterways. States, tribal governments, universities, and environmental nonprofits become eligible to apply for the new grant money. Federal agencies like the Fish and Wildlife Service would take on new responsibilities for planning and coordination. Commercial shipping is touched by a small provision encouraging ships to install better ballast water treatment systems, which is one way invasive species hitch rides between waterways.

Overall, the bill authorizes roughly $49.5 million per year through 2031 across all its programs. It does not guarantee that money will actually be spent — Congress would still need to approve the funding each year through the regular budget process. The bill is focused on preventing new invasions and responding more quickly when they happen, rather than changing penalties for individuals or creating new restrictions on everyday recreational use of public waters.

title: Prevent Government Shutdowns Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would make it so the federal government can never fully shut down due to a failure to pass a budget. If Congress misses its deadline to fund the government, money would automatically keep flowing at the same rates as the previous year's budget. This automatic funding would renew itself every 14 days until Congress passes a real spending bill. The goal is to keep federal agencies open and workers paid even when lawmakers cannot agree on a new budget.

To pressure Congress into doing its job faster, the bill adds real consequences for members of Congress and certain White House budget officials when the automatic funding kicks in. During that period, those officials cannot use government money or even campaign funds for official travel, with a few narrow exceptions like returning to Washington or responding to a national security emergency. Congress would also be forced to stay in session and could not take breaks longer than 23 hours, and lawmakers could only vote on a very short list of urgent matters until the budget standoff is resolved.

This bill affects the entire federal government and everyone who depends on it. That includes federal workers who would otherwise be furloughed, military personnel, Social Security and food assistance recipients, national park visitors, and anyone waiting on government services. Members of Congress and White House budget staff would face direct personal restrictions on their activities. Ordinary Americans would mostly feel the effect through continued government services that would otherwise stop during a shutdown.

title: Prevent Government Shutdowns Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill is designed to prevent the federal government from shutting down when Congress fails to pass a budget on time. Right now, if Congress misses the deadline to fund the government, agencies lose their money and must stop most operations. Under this bill, funding would automatically continue at the same rate as the previous year's budget, renewing every 14 days until Congress passes a real spending bill. This keeps government programs and services running without interruption.

The bill also puts pressure on Congress to actually do its job. If the government is running on this automatic funding, lawmakers would not be allowed to vote on most other business until they pass a budget. They also could not take long recesses or adjourn for more than 23 hours at a stretch, and they could not use government funds or even campaign funds for most official travel. The idea is to make a budget standoff uncomfortable enough that Congress is motivated to resolve it quickly.

This bill affects nearly everyone in some way, since it touches all federal programs funded through the normal budget process, including agencies that handle national defense, transportation, health programs, and more. It directly affects members of Congress and their staff, as well as Office of Management and Budget employees, by restricting their travel and limiting what legislation they can work on during a funding gap. People who rely on federal services or work for federal agencies would be the main beneficiaries, since the bill aims to keep those services running even when budget negotiations break down.

title: Colorado Wilderness Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would set aside more than 700,000 acres of land in Colorado as official wilderness areas. That means these lands, mostly managed by the Bureau of Land Management and the U.S. Forest Service, would be permanently protected from development, road-building, and most motorized use. The bill creates more than 25 new named wilderness areas and expands a few existing ones, covering places like the Dolores River Canyon, Redcloud Peak, and Browns Canyon. Some additional areas are labeled "potential wilderness," meaning they could receive full wilderness protection later once certain temporary uses end.

People most directly affected are those who use or work on these lands. Hikers, campers, and wildlife watchers would generally gain more protected land to enjoy. However, off-road vehicle users, mining companies, and energy developers would no longer be allowed to operate in the newly protected areas. Ranchers who currently graze livestock on some of these lands can continue doing so under existing rules. Water rights that were already legally established before the bill passes would not be changed, and existing water facilities like irrigation ditches can still be maintained.

The bill also includes specific rules to make sure military helicopters can still fly over the new wilderness areas for training. Colorado state government keeps its authority over wildlife and fish management. Lands within the wilderness boundaries that are privately owned or owned by Colorado would only become part of the wilderness if the federal government purchases them voluntarily.

title: Mullica River Watershed Wild and Scenic River Study Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill directs the federal government to study the Mullica River watershed in New Jersey to see if it qualifies for official "Wild and Scenic River" designation. That is a federal status that protects certain rivers from development like dams or other construction that could change their natural character. The study would look at the Mullica River and many of its connected streams and tributaries, covering a large portion of the Pinelands region of southern New Jersey. The Secretary of the Interior would have three years to complete the study and report the findings to Congress after funding is provided.

It is important to understand that this bill does not actually designate the river as wild and scenic. It only starts the process of studying whether that designation makes sense. No new restrictions on land use or water use would automatically result from this bill passing. Congress would need to act again after seeing the study results before any formal protections could take effect.

This bill would most directly affect residents, landowners, outdoor recreationists, and local governments in the counties surrounding the Mullica River watershed, which runs through Atlantic, Burlington, and Ocean counties in New Jersey. Environmental researchers, state agencies, and federal land managers would also be involved in conducting the study. Anyone who lives near, works along, or recreates on these waterways could eventually be affected if a full designation follows from the study's findings.

title: WAGES Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill creates a new tax credit for employers who run or participate in official apprenticeship programs registered with the federal government. For every quarter they employ apprentices, qualifying businesses can get back 50 cents for every dollar they spend on apprentice wages, up to $5,000 per apprentice per quarter, plus up to $50,000 per quarter in other program costs like classroom instruction, on-the-job training expenses, and extra pay for experienced workers who mentor apprentices. If the credit is larger than what the employer owes in payroll taxes, the government refunds the difference. The credit only applies to the first two years of each apprentice's participation in a program, and businesses cannot claim it for expenses already covered by other federal programs like the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act.

The bill also makes it easier for employers to give apprentices small awards, like tools or equipment tied to their training, without those gifts being taxed as regular income. The tax-free limit for these kinds of awards is raised to $1,500, or up to $5,000 if the employer has a formal award plan in place.

The people most directly affected are private-sector employers in fields like construction, manufacturing, healthcare, technology, and the skilled trades, as well as workers who want to earn while they learn a profession. Apprentices themselves are not receiving a direct tax break, but the bill is designed to make it cheaper for companies to hire and train them, which could expand the number of apprenticeship slots available. Government agencies are generally excluded from claiming the credit, though colleges, universities, and hospitals run by government entities may qualify.

title: SLUSH FUND Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would create a 100 percent tax on money received from certain legal settlements. Specifically, it targets funds that come from lawsuits filed by a current or former U.S. president, their family members, or businesses they control, when those lawsuits were filed against the federal government or a federal agency. That means if someone receives a payout from one of those settlement funds, the entire amount would be taxed away by the federal government. The bill also makes clear that this money would not count as regular taxable income under normal income tax rules, so only this special 100 percent tax applies. Anyone who deliberately avoids paying this tax faces an additional penalty equal to 50 percent of what they owe.

The bill also requires the people managing these settlement funds to report payments to the IRS and send notices to anyone who receives money, similar to how a bank sends you a tax form. Those reports would also be made available to the public within one month. Managers who fail to file the required paperwork could face a $10,000 fine per violation.

This bill would mainly affect any individual or organization that receives money from a legal settlement fund connected to a lawsuit that a president or their family or affiliated businesses brought against the U.S. government. It would apply to payments made on or after May 20, 2026. Ordinary Americans who have no connection to presidential lawsuits or settlement funds would not be directly affected.

title: Dietary Supplements Access Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change the tax rules so that money spent on dietary supplements counts as a qualified medical expense. That matters because people with Health Savings Accounts (HSAs), Flexible Spending Accounts (FSAs), Health Reimbursement Arrangements (HRAs), or Archer Medical Savings Accounts can already use those accounts to pay for medical expenses with pre-tax dollars. If this bill passes, they could use those same accounts to buy dietary supplements like vitamins, minerals, and herbal products, saving money by not paying income tax on those purchases. There is a cap, though: only up to $500 per year counts ($250 for married people filing taxes separately). Energy drinks, sodas, and similar products are specifically excluded, even if they are marketed as supplements.

This bill would affect people who have employer-sponsored FSAs or HRAs, or who have opened their own HSA, typically through a high-deductible health insurance plan. These account holders could pay for eligible supplements using pre-tax dollars, which effectively reduces the real cost of those products. People without any of these special accounts would not see a direct financial benefit from this bill.

The changes would take effect starting January 1, 2027. The bill was introduced in the Senate and has been sent to the Finance Committee, meaning it has not yet been voted on or become law. It does not require a doctor's recommendation to use the benefit, and it does not change what supplements are legal to sell, only how they are treated for tax purposes.

title: No Tax on Border Patrol Agent Overtime Act
ai_summary:
This bill would make overtime pay earned by U.S. Border Patrol agents tax-free at the federal level. Right now, overtime income is taxed like regular income for most workers. This bill would change the tax code so that certain extra pay Border Patrol agents receive above their base salary would not count as taxable income. That includes things like supplemental pay, premium pay, and standard overtime pay specific to how Border Patrol agents are compensated under federal law.

The change would apply starting with the 2026 tax year. The bill builds on a broader concept already in the tax code called "qualified overtime compensation," which was recently established to exempt some overtime pay from taxes for workers generally. This bill specifically adds Border Patrol agents to that category using the unique pay structure that already exists for them under federal employment law. It does not include hazardous duty pay, which would still be taxed.

This bill directly affects active Border Patrol agents who earn extra pay beyond their base salary. If passed, those agents would take home more of their overtime earnings because that portion of their paycheck would no longer be subject to federal income tax. It would also affect federal tax revenue, since the government would collect less in taxes from that group of workers. The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Finance Committee, so it has not yet become law.

Specifically, it targets pay that goes above their basic salary, including overtime pay, supplemental pay, and premium pay that agents earn under a special federal pay system designed for Border Patrol work. Hazardous duty pay would not be included in the tax break. The change would take effect starting with the 2026 tax year.

The bill does this by adding Border Patrol agent overtime and extra pay to an existing tax code category called "qualified overtime compensation." That category was created to allow overtime earnings to be excluded from federal income tax. This bill expands that existing rule to cover the unique pay structure that Border Patrol agents work under, since their pay is calculated differently than a standard hourly worker covered by regular labor law.

The people directly affected are active Border Patrol agents who receive pay above their base salary. For those agents, this could mean a larger take-home paycheck since that extra pay would no longer be subject to federal income tax. The bill does not affect the general public's taxes, and it does not change Border Patrol staffing levels, enforcement policies, or agency budgets. It is currently in the early stage of the legislative process, referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, and has not yet become law.
ai_headline: Bill would make Border Patrol overtime pay tax-free starting in 2026
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: Freedom from Taxes Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would eliminate several federal taxes that currently apply to certain heavily regulated firearms and accessories covered under the National Firearms Act (NFA). Right now, the NFA requires people to pay a $200 tax when they transfer or make items like silencers, short-barreled rifles, short-barreled shotguns, and machine guns. It also requires dealers and manufacturers of these items to pay a special annual tax. This bill would set all of those taxes to zero, effectively making them free to process.

The bill would also expand an existing excise tax exemption so that it covers all NFA transfers, not just a narrow category. These changes would kick in about 90 days after the law is passed. Importantly, the bill does not change any other NFA rules, such as the background check process, the registration requirement, or the overall list of regulated items. Those rules would remain in place.

This primarily affects gun owners, buyers, and sellers who deal in NFA-regulated items, as well as the firearms dealers and manufacturers who currently pay the special occupational tax. It would also reduce federal tax revenue, since the government currently collects money from each of these transactions and registrations. Average gun owners who only buy standard firearms not covered by the NFA would not be directly affected.
ai_headline: Bill would zero out federal taxes on silencers and short-barreled firearms
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

Changes would take effect roughly 90 days after enactment.

title: Restoring the American Homebuyers Dream Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change a longstanding rule about tax privacy. Right now, the IRS keeps tax information confidential, even for people who file using an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number, or ITIN. ITINs are issued to people who do not have a Social Security number but still pay U.S. taxes. This bill would allow the Department of Homeland Security to submit written requests to the IRS and receive personal information about ITIN holders, including their name, address, filing status, and information about spouses or adult dependents. This would be a significant change to Section 6103 of the tax code, which has traditionally protected all taxpayer data from being shared with law enforcement agencies for non-tax purposes.

The stated goal of the bill is immigration enforcement. The bill's findings section argues that people in the country without legal status have used ITINs to obtain home loans, which the bill's authors claim has contributed to rising housing costs for American citizens. The information shared with DHS could be used to identify and locate individuals for immigration proceedings.

The people most directly affected would be ITIN holders, a group that includes undocumented immigrants but also some legal residents, foreign nationals with U.S. income, and others who cannot get a Social Security number. U.S. citizens would not be affected since they use Social Security numbers, not ITINs. The bill could also affect people who share a tax return with an ITIN holder, such as spouses or adult dependents listed on a filing.
ai_headline: Bill would let DHS request tax data on ITIN holders from IRS
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8920 would let DHS request personal tax data on ITIN holders from the IRS for immigration enforcement.

That information could include names, addresses, filing status, and details about spouses or adult dependents listed on a return. This would be a significant departure from longstanding IRS rules that protect all taxpayer data from being shared with law enforcement for non-tax purposes.

People who share a tax return with an ITIN holder, such as spouses or adult dependents, could also have their information shared. U.S. citizens who file using Social Security numbers would not be affected.
ai_sections.why: The bill's stated purpose is immigration enforcement, and information obtained from the IRS could be used to identify and locate individuals for immigration proceedings. The bill's findings also assert that ITIN holders have used the numbers to obtain home loans, which the authors claim has contributed to rising housing costs, though this framing is the bill authors' own and not an independent finding.

title: Affordable Housing Credit Carryback Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes a tax rule that affects how the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) can be used. Right now, if a business or investor earns this tax credit but cannot use all of it in the current year, they can only carry it forward to reduce future tax bills. This bill would allow them to instead carry the credit back up to five years, meaning they could apply it to taxes they already paid in the past and potentially get a refund.

The main people affected are real estate developers and investors who finance affordable housing projects. These projects can be expensive and unpredictable, so sometimes a developer ends up with more tax credits than they can use in a given year. Being able to go back five years and apply those credits to past tax bills would give them quicker access to cash, which supporters say could encourage more affordable housing construction.

Renters and low-income households are indirectly affected, since the LIHTC program is one of the biggest tools the federal government uses to fund the building of affordable apartments. If the change makes it more financially attractive to invest in these projects, it could influence how many affordable units get built. The bill does not directly change rents, eligibility rules, or housing assistance programs.
ai_headline: Tax credit bill would let affordable housing investors claim past-year refunds
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

This bill would also allow those credits to be carried back up to five years, letting holders apply them to taxes already paid and potentially receive a refund.

This could influence how many affordable housing units get built, though the bill does not directly change rents, eligibility rules, or housing assistance programs.

title: Young Adult Tax Credit Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new monthly tax credit for young adults between the ages of 18 and 24. Starting in 2027, eligible individuals would receive $500 per month, either paid out monthly or as a yearly lump sum. The amount would be adjusted over time to keep up with inflation. Young adults can receive the money directly if they file their own taxes and are not claimed as a dependent by someone else. If a parent or guardian claims an 18-to-24-year-old as a dependent on their taxes, the parent would receive the credit instead. The payments would be sent electronically and cannot be seized by debt collectors or garnished by courts.

To get the credit, a person must be a U.S. citizen, national, or resident between 18 and 24 years old. The IRS would set up an online portal where people can sign up, update their information, and choose between monthly payments or a single yearly payment. If someone receives more money than they are actually entitled to due to fraud or intentional misuse, they would have to pay it back. The portal would be available in multiple languages and work on mobile phones.

The bill also requires the IRS to run a public outreach campaign to make sure people know about the credit, especially those who do not normally file taxes or have bank accounts. U.S. territories like Puerto Rico and American Samoa are also included, with the federal government sending funds to those governments to distribute locally. The bill was introduced in May 2026 and has been sent to the House Ways and Means Committee for review.

title: Modernizing Agricultural and Manufacturing Bonds Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes two main changes to tax rules around government-issued bonds. First, it updates rules for "small issue manufacturing bonds," which are a type of tax-exempt bond that state and local governments can issue to help smaller manufacturers borrow money at lower interest rates. The bill raises the borrowing limits significantly — from $10 million to $30 million per project and from $40 million to $120 million total per company — and ties those limits to inflation going forward so they don't lose value over time. It also expands the definition of "manufacturing" to include facilities that produce certain intangible products, like software or other intellectual property described in the tax code.

Second, the bill changes rules for bonds that help first-time farmers buy land and equipment. Right now, these bonds — which work similarly by letting governments offer lower-cost financing — are capped at $450,000 per farmer. This bill raises that cap to $1 million and removes a separate, lower limit that applied specifically to used farm equipment. It also switches how "substantial farmland" is measured, using the average farm size in a county instead of the median, which can make more land eligible for the program.

The people most directly affected are small and mid-sized manufacturers looking to finance facility expansions or new production, and people trying to buy a farm for the first time. State and local governments that issue these bonds are also affected, since they administer these programs. The changes do not affect everyday consumers directly, but could influence local job markets and agricultural access in communities where these bonds are commonly used.
ai_headline: Senate bill triples borrowing limits for small manufacturers and first-time farmers
last_action_text: Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship. Hearings held.

For manufacturers, the per-project cap rises from $10 million to $30 million, and the per-company total rises from $40 million to $120 million, with both figures indexed to inflation going forward. For first-time farmers, the cap rises from $450,000 to $1 million, the separate limit on used farm equipment is removed, and the measure of qualifying farmland shifts from median to average county farm size.
ai_sections.who: Small and mid-sized manufacturers seeking to finance facility expansions or new production are directly affected, as are people buying a farm for the first time. State and local governments that issue and administer these bonds are also affected.
ai_sections.why: Raising the caps and indexing them to inflation means more projects and purchases could qualify for lower-cost government-backed financing over time. Shifting the farmland measure from median to average county size could make more land eligible for the first-time farmer program.

title: Veterans Suicide Prevention and Care Enhancement Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill tells the Department of Veterans Affairs to create a publicly available list of outside, community-based health care providers who have completed yearly training on veteran suicide prevention. The VA would have 180 days after the bill becomes law to start offering that training and to build the list. Providers who completed a similar training elsewhere can also be included if it meets certain standards. Any provider on the list can ask to be removed if they choose, and the VA must review the list every year to make sure everyone on it is up to date with their training.

The people most directly affected are veterans who receive health care through the VA's Community Care Program, which lets eligible veterans see doctors and providers outside the VA system. With this list, veterans would be able to look up which community providers have specifically been trained to recognize and respond to suicide risk in veterans. Health care providers who participate in the VA's community care network are also affected, since completing the training would determine whether they appear on this list.

The bill also requires the VA to send Congress a report within 180 days, and every year after that, tracking how many providers are on the list, how veterans are using it, and whether it is actually helping veterans access care. Those reports are meant to help Congress understand if the program is working and decide if any changes are needed.

title: Timely Agreements Act
ai_summary:
This bill is about speeding up the process for state-run veterans homes to make purchasing deals with the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). Right now, state veterans homes can propose agreements to buy things like medications and medical equipment through the VA, but there is no set deadline for the VA to say yes or no. This bill would require the VA to approve or reject those proposals within 60 days. If the VA misses that deadline, the proposal is automatically considered approved.

The bill also creates a standard form that state homes can use to submit these proposals, making the process more consistent and easier to navigate. State homes would be able to send proposals in multiple ways, including by mail, email, or fax. A rejected proposal does not prevent a state home from trying again, and the VA can still negotiate revised deals.

The second part of the bill protects state veterans homes from being penalized during inspections if they provide care to eligible veterans without a formal agreement in place. Under current rules, that gap could count against them as a deficiency. This bill says that simply lacking a signed agreement cannot, by itself, be used as a mark against a state home during an inspection. The people most directly affected are veterans living in state-run veterans homes across the country, the staff and administrators who run those homes, and VA officials who manage these agreements.
ai_headline: VA given 60-day deadline to act on state veterans home purchasing deals
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs.

The bill also creates a standard submission form and allows proposals to be sent by mail, email, or fax. ai_sections.why: Currently no deadline exists for the VA to respond to purchasing proposals, leaving state homes in an indefinite waiting period. Without the inspection protection, state homes that provide care to eligible veterans before a formal agreement is signed can face compliance penalties during reviews.

title: Chinese CBDC Prohibition Act of 2026
ai_summary:
China has a digital version of its currency called the digital yuan, which is issued and controlled by the Chinese government. This bill would make it illegal for certain financial businesses in the United States to handle that digital currency in any way. The ban would cover both direct and indirect transactions, meaning these businesses could not touch the digital yuan even if it passes through other steps or middlemen.

The businesses affected are called "money services businesses," which is a broad category that includes places like currency exchanges, check cashing stores, money transfer services such as Western Union, prepaid card providers, and some cryptocurrency exchanges. These are businesses that move or convert money but are not traditional banks. Under this bill, none of them could process, exchange, or transfer China's digital yuan for customers.

Regular Americans would mostly feel this indirectly. If someone wanted to send or receive China's digital yuan through one of these businesses in the United States, they would not be able to. The bill does not appear to restrict what individual private citizens do on their own, but it cuts off the businesses that most people would use to handle such a transaction. The bill was introduced in the Senate in May 2026 and has been sent to the Banking Committee, where it would need to advance before becoming law.
ai_headline: Senate bill would ban money services businesses from handling China's digital yuan
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
