title: Detention Authority Clarification Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require the federal government to automatically detain certain non-citizens while their immigration cases are being processed. Right now, people who entered the U.S. without going through an official entry point are not always held in detention — they can sometimes be released and required to check in or appear for court. This bill would change that by adding a new category to the existing mandatory detention law, covering anyone who is physically inside the U.S. but has not been officially "admitted," meaning they did not go through a legal port of entry or have not been granted lawful status.

Under current law, mandatory detention already applies to non-citizens with certain criminal records or ties to terrorism. This bill expands that list to include people simply on the basis of being present in the country without having been formally admitted. That means immigration authorities would be legally required to hold these individuals in a detention facility — with no option to release them on bond or supervision — until their immigration case is resolved.

This bill would most directly affect non-citizens who crossed into the U.S. outside of an official border crossing, as well as asylum seekers who entered without authorization and are waiting for their cases to be heard. It would also affect immigration courts and detention facilities, which would need to handle a larger detained population. U.S. taxpayers would likely see increased costs for immigration detention. The bill does not affect U.S. citizens or people who entered the country through legal ports of entry with proper documentation.
ai_headline: Bill would require detention of all undocumented immigrants during cases
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: Senate bill S 4593 would mandate detention—no bond, no release—for any non-citizen present in the U.S. without formal admission.
ai_sections.what: S 4593 would add a new category to existing mandatory detention law, requiring federal authorities to detain any non-citizen physically present in the U.S. who has not been formally admitted through a legal port of entry or granted lawful status. Unlike current practice, which sometimes allows release with check-ins or court appearance requirements, this bill would prohibit release on bond or supervision for this group. Detention would continue until each individual's immigration case is fully resolved.
ai_sections.who: The bill would most directly affect non-citizens who crossed into the U.S. outside an official border crossing, including asylum seekers who entered without authorization. Immigration courts and detention facilities would also be affected, as they would need to manage a larger detained population.

ai_sections.cost: U.S. taxpayers would likely see increased costs for immigration detention, though the bill does not specify a dollar amount.

title: Gas Tax Suspension Act
ai_summary:
This bill would temporarily stop the collection of the federal gas tax, which is currently 18.4 cents per gallon for gasoline and 24.4 cents per gallon for diesel. If passed, that tax would be set to zero starting on the day the law is signed. The suspension would last 90 days by default, but the President could extend it to 180 days if economic conditions are seen as bad enough to justify it. The small additional tax that funds the cleanup of leaking underground fuel storage tanks would also be paused during this period.

To make sure road and infrastructure funding is not cut off, the bill requires the U.S. Treasury to replace the lost gas tax money out of the general fund. In other words, the Highway Trust Fund, which pays for roads and bridges, and the Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund would still receive money, just from a different government source instead of directly from drivers at the pump.

Anyone who buys gasoline or diesel fuel in the United States would be affected, since they could potentially pay less per gallon at the pump if suppliers and retailers pass the savings along. Trucking companies and businesses that rely heavily on diesel fuel would also see an impact. Taxpayers in general are also affected indirectly, because the general fund, which is supported by broader tax revenue and borrowing, would be used to cover the gap.
ai_headline: Federal gas tax suspended under bill that shields road funding
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

title: Outage Refund Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require phone, cable, satellite TV, and internet companies with more than 5,000 customers to automatically give customers a credit on their bill whenever service goes down for 4 hours or more. Customers would not have to call and complain or request the credit — the company would have to apply it on its own. The credit equals one-thirtieth of the monthly bill for each day the service is out. If a customer cancels their service and is owed money back, the company must send a refund within 30 days by check, prepaid debit card, or electronic transfer. Planned maintenance outages that companies warn customers about in advance are not covered.

The bill also includes rules to improve customer service. Companies would have to keep recordings of customer service calls for at least one year and share them with customers who ask. They could not charge customers a fee just to have a representative call them back. The Federal Trade Commission would also set rules about missed service appointments and make it easier for people with disabilities or those who do not drive to return equipment without extra cost or hassle.

This affects most Americans who pay for home internet, cable TV, satellite TV, or phone service. The Federal Communications Commission would have 18 months after the bill becomes law to write the specific rules and set penalties for companies that do not follow them. States would still be allowed to pass their own stronger protections on top of what this bill requires.

last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

The credit equals one-thirtieth of the monthly bill for each day service is out, and customers who cancel are owed a refund within 30 days. title: Informed Foster Youth Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill changes the rules for how states must handle the cases of children in foster care. Right now, foster care agencies are required to keep health and education records for each child. This bill requires that those records be shared directly with the child for free, starting at age 14, and given to the child again when they leave foster care. It also updates the transition planning document that older foster youth receive, adding information about how to sign up for Medicaid, how to name someone to make medical decisions for them if they cannot, and how to set up a legal health care proxy.

The bill also requires that foster youth age 14 and older receive several important documents at no cost while still in care. These include a free credit report each year, their birth certificate, a Social Security card, and a state ID or driver's license. When a young person ages out of foster care, the state must hand over all of those documents before the youth is discharged. The state must also tell youth about all support services available to them, not just once, but at every meeting with a caseworker and at every court hearing they attend.

This bill directly affects the roughly 400,000 children currently in the U.S. foster care system, with the strongest focus on teenagers age 14 and older, and especially those who age out of the system at 18. It also affects state child welfare agencies, which would need to update their procedures to meet the new requirements. States that need to pass their own laws to comply are given extra time to do so.

last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

title: American Apprenticeship Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a federal grant program run by the Department of Labor that helps states cover some of the costs of apprenticeship training. States would apply for competitive grants and could use the money to pay for tuition, fees, textbooks, equipment, and other materials connected to apprenticeship programs in fields that are currently underrepresented in the apprenticeship system, such as health care, information technology, and advanced manufacturing. The federal government would cover between 20 and 50 percent of those costs, with states responsible for the rest. The bill would authorize $15 million per year from 2026 through 2031.

The bill focuses specifically on apprenticeship programs registered under federal law that operate in industries where apprenticeships are still uncommon. It also supports "pre-apprenticeship" programs, which are shorter training programs designed to help people get ready to enter a full apprenticeship. States would be required to show a plan for reaching groups that have historically had less access to apprenticeships, including minorities, veterans, people with disabilities, and youth.

This bill would most directly affect people looking to enter skilled trades or growing industries through a structured, earn-while-you-learn training path, as well as the employers, unions, schools, and community organizations that run apprenticeship programs. States would take on an administrative role in deciding how to distribute the money. Workers who benefit would get help paying for the classroom instruction side of their training, which is typically required alongside the on-the-job portion of an apprenticeship.

title: Protecting America’s Workers Act
ai_summary:
This bill updates the 1970 law that created OSHA, the federal agency responsible for workplace safety. It expands who OSHA covers, most importantly adding state and local government workers who were not previously protected under the federal law. It also requires employers to report more workplace injuries, illnesses, and deaths to the government, keep better records, and post notices so workers know their rights. Additionally, the bill gives injured workers and their families new rights to participate in OSHA investigations and settlement discussions.

The bill significantly increases the fines companies can face for breaking safety rules. For example, the maximum penalty for a willful or repeated serious violation would jump from $70,000 to $700,000. Penalties would also automatically adjust each year to keep up with inflation. On the criminal side, employers whose knowing violations cause a worker's death could face up to 10 years in prison instead of the current 6 months. A new criminal penalty is also created for violations that cause serious injury but not death.

Workers who report unsafe conditions or get hurt on the job would get stronger protections against being fired or punished for speaking up. The bill extends the time workers have to file a complaint about retaliation, spells out the process for investigating those complaints, and makes it harder for employers to avoid paying workers back for lost wages or other harm. It also requires the government to regularly review how well individual state workplace safety programs are working compared to the federal standard.
ai_headline: Federal workplace safety law would expand coverage and sharply raise penalties
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

The bill raises civil penalties significantly and increases criminal penalties for employers whose knowing violations cause a worker's death from a maximum of 6 months to 10 years in prison. A new criminal penalty is also created for knowing violations that cause serious injury but not death.

title: FAIR Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill changes the rules for civil asset forfeiture, which is the legal process that allows the government to take property it believes is connected to a crime. Right now, federal agencies can seize money, cars, homes, and other property without charging the owner with a crime, and they can complete the forfeiture process without going to a judge. This bill would require the government to get a court order before permanently taking anyone's property. It also raises the legal standard the government must meet to keep seized property, changing it from a "more likely than not" standard to a stricter "clear and convincing evidence" standard. The government would also have to prove the owner actually knew their property was being used for a crime, not just that it happened to be connected to one.

The bill also changes what happens to money from forfeitures. Currently, proceeds from seized property often go into special law enforcement funds that agencies can use for their own budgets, which critics say creates a financial incentive to seize property. This bill would redirect that money to the general U.S. Treasury instead. It also adds new protections around the practice of "structuring," where people are penalized for making bank transactions in amounts that avoid automatic reporting requirements, requiring the government to prove the person acted knowingly and that the money came from an illegitimate source.

This bill affects ordinary Americans who own property, small business owners, and anyone who handles cash transactions. It also affects federal law enforcement agencies like the DEA and FBI, which currently rely on forfeiture funds. People who previously had limited ability to fight back against seizures, especially those who could not afford a lawyer, would gain new legal protections, including the possibility of court-appointed counsel regardless of whether they own a home.
ai_headline: Bill would require court orders before federal agencies can permanently seize property
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, and in addition to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Financial Services, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

It also tightens rules around bank transaction structuring penalties by requiring proof the person acted knowingly and that the money came from an illegitimate source.

Federal law enforcement agencies such as the DEA and FBI, which currently use forfeiture proceeds to fund their own budgets, are also directly affected.

Redirecting those funds to the U.S. Treasury and raising legal standards would alter how federal agencies pursue and benefit from forfeiture cases.
ai_sections.cost: Forfeiture proceeds that currently fund federal law enforcement agency budgets would instead be redirected to the general U.S. Treasury under this bill.

title: Student Loan Interest Elimination Act
ai_summary:
This bill would eliminate interest on federal student loans. For people who already have federal student loans, interest would stop building up starting July 1, 2026, and the government would automatically make that change without borrowers needing to do anything. For new loans taken out on or after July 1, 2026, the interest rate would be set to zero percent from the start. The bill also raises the maximum amount students can borrow each year, and adjusts those limits for inflation going forward. The subsidized loan program, which currently pauses interest while students are in school, would end since all loans would carry no interest anyway.

The bill creates a new Education Affordability Trust Fund, run by a six-member board appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate. Loan repayments from borrowers would be deposited into this fund, which would then invest the money in bonds. The earnings from those investments would be used to cover the government's costs of running the student loan program. If the fund generates more money than needed for loan administration, the extra funds could go toward larger Pell Grants for low-income students or competitive grants to colleges that keep tuition increases below three percent.

This bill would affect the roughly 43 million Americans who currently hold federal student loans, as well as future college students who plan to borrow. Borrowers would pay back only what they originally borrowed, with no extra cost from interest building up over time. Taxpayers more broadly could also be affected, since eliminating interest changes how the government recoups the cost of lending money for college. The bill was introduced in the Senate in March 2026 and has not yet been voted on.
ai_headline: Senate bill would zero out interest on all federal student loans

title: Capital Emergency Control Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill deals with who controls Washington D.C.'s police department during a presidential emergency. Under existing law, the President can take direct control of the Metropolitan Police Department (D.C.'s main police force) during a declared emergency, but that control is limited to a set time period. This bill would allow the President to keep extending that control in 30-day chunks, as long as the President sends written notice to certain congressional committees explaining why the emergency conditions still exist. There is no stated limit on how many times these 30-day extensions could be granted.

This affects Washington D.C. residents most directly, since the Metropolitan Police Department serves the city. D.C. operates under a unique arrangement where Congress and the President have more authority over local government than they do in any U.S. state. Normally, D.C.'s elected mayor and city council oversee the police department. Presidential emergency control temporarily removes that local authority, and this bill would make it easier to keep that federal control in place for longer periods.

The bill was introduced in the House and sent to the Oversight and Government Reform Committee. It applies to any presidential emergency over D.C. police that is active on or after the date the bill becomes law, meaning it could affect emergencies already in progress, not just future ones.
ai_headline: Bill lets president extend D.C. police control indefinitely in 30-day steps
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

title: Foreign Robocall Elimination Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to create a special task force within 270 days of the law passing. The task force would study illegal robocalls that come into the United States from other countries. It would be made up of representatives from relevant government agencies, phone companies, technology experts, marketing businesses, and consumer advocates. The group would have about a year to research the problem and then submit a report to Congress with recommendations on how to stop foreign robocalls more effectively.

The report the task force produces would need to cover a wide range of topics, including which foreign countries send the most illegal robocalls to Americans, how much money people lose to these scams, and how many identities get stolen as a result. It would also look at whether current technology like caller ID verification systems are working well enough, whether stiffer criminal penalties could help, and whether the Justice Department needs a dedicated office to go after robocall violators. After the report is submitted to Congress, the task force would close down 90 days later.

This bill would affect any American who has received unwanted or scam robocalls, which is most people with a phone. It would also affect phone companies, technology firms, and law enforcement agencies that deal with this issue. One smaller change in the bill reduces how often a related industry group has to file certain reports with the government, dropping it from once a year to once every three years.

title: Expanding Health Care Providers for Veterans Act
ai_summary:
This bill deals with H-1B visas, which allow U.S. employers to hire skilled foreign workers in specialized jobs like medicine. Right now, there is a yearly cap on how many H-1B visas can be issued nationwide. This bill would create an exception to that cap specifically for foreign-trained doctors, nurses, and other healthcare workers who are hired by the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) or by state-approved veteran care homes. In other words, those workers would no longer count against the annual H-1B limit.

The bill also addresses a September 2025 presidential proclamation that restricted certain H-1B visa holders from entering the country. This legislation would block that restriction from applying to healthcare workers employed by the VA or certified veteran care facilities, meaning those workers could still enter the United States to do their jobs even if the broader proclamation would otherwise stop them.

The people most directly affected are veterans who receive care through VA hospitals and state veteran homes, as well as foreign-born healthcare professionals who work or want to work at those facilities. VA medical centers have faced ongoing staffing shortages, and supporters of the bill argue the exemption would help fill open positions. Critics may raise concerns about immigration policy or the use of foreign workers. The bill was introduced in the House and has been sent to the Judiciary Committee, where it would need approval before moving further.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Preventing Waste, Fraud, and Abuse in TANF Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes changes to TANF, which stands for Temporary Assistance for Needy Families. TANF is a federal program that gives block grants, meaning lump sums of money, to states to help low-income families. Right now, states have a lot of flexibility in how they spend that money, and critics say some states have used funds in ways that do not directly help struggling families. This bill adds new rules to tighten up how states can use that money.

Specifically, the bill does four main things. First, it limits TANF spending to families earning less than twice the federal poverty level, meaning states could not direct funds to households above that income line. Second, it sets deadlines for when states must spend the money they receive, though states can hold back up to 15 percent in reserve for future use. Third, it requires states to track and report improper payments, such as payments made by mistake or through fraud, and sets a 10-year goal to reduce or eliminate them. Fourth, it prohibits states from using federal TANF dollars to replace money they would have spent anyway from their own budgets, a practice called supplanting.

The bill would most directly affect state governments, which would face stricter rules and new reporting requirements for how they manage TANF funds. It would also affect low-income families who rely on TANF-funded services, since the new income limits and spending rules could change which programs states choose to fund. The changes would take effect October 1, 2027.
ai_headline: New rules would tighten how states spend federal TANF funds

States would be limited to serving families earning less than twice the federal poverty level, required to spend funds within set deadlines, required to track and reduce improper payments over a 10-year period, and prohibited from using federal TANF dollars to replace their own state spending. States may hold back up to 15 percent of funds in reserve.

title: TANF State Expenditure Integrity Act of 2025
ai_summary:
TANF is a federal program that gives money to states to help low-income families with children. States can pass some of that money to outside organizations, called subrecipients, to deliver services. This bill is aimed at stopping those subrecipients from misusing the funds they receive.

The bill would create a new TANF Program Integrity Unit inside the federal Department of Health and Human Services. This unit would get $10 million a year to monitor how subrecipients spend TANF money, looking specifically for intentional misuse. States would also have to share more information with the federal government to help with that oversight. The unit would report to Congress each year on what it finds.

If the federal government discovers that a subrecipient intentionally misused TANF funds, the state that oversaw that subrecipient faces real consequences. On top of existing penalties, the state would have to spend an equal amount of its own money providing direct cash assistance to families living below the poverty line. This bill mainly affects state governments that run TANF programs, the outside organizations that receive TANF money from states, and ultimately low-income families who depend on those funds being spent correctly.

title: Deport Alien Gang Members Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change US immigration law to make it easier to bar and deport non-citizens who are connected to criminal gangs. It creates a legal definition of a "criminal gang" as a group of five or more people whose members regularly commit serious crimes like drug offenses, gun crimes, human trafficking, identity theft, or violence. The Department of Homeland Security would also get new power to officially label specific groups as criminal gangs, similar to how the government currently designates foreign terrorist organizations.

Under this bill, any non-citizen who is a gang member, has helped a gang, or tries to enter the US to further a gang's activities could be blocked from entering or removed from the country. People already in the US who fall into these categories would be subject to mandatory detention while their cases are processed, meaning immigration officials would be required to hold them rather than release them. The bill also blocks gang-affiliated non-citizens from receiving asylum, temporary protected status, special visas for immigrant youth, and nearly all other forms of immigration relief, with very limited exceptions for people actively cooperating with law enforcement.

The people most directly affected are non-citizens, including legal immigrants, asylum seekers, and undocumented individuals, who have or are believed to have ties to criminal gangs. The bill applies to past conduct as well, meaning someone could be affected based on gang involvement that happened before the law was passed. Immigration officers and the Secretary of Homeland Security would gain broader authority to make and act on gang membership determinations.

title: To amend the Small Business Act to establish a program under which the Small Business Administration may make supplemental disaster loans to home owner associations to repair common areas damaged by disasters and implement disaster mitigation measures, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new loan program through the Small Business Administration (SBA) that allows homeowners associations (HOAs) to borrow money after a disaster strikes. Right now, individual homeowners can apply for SBA disaster loans to repair their own homes, but HOAs generally cannot get that same help for shared spaces like clubhouses, pools, roads, or landscaping. This bill would change that by letting HOAs apply for what are called "supplemental" disaster loans specifically to fix those common areas.

The loans could also be used for disaster mitigation, meaning HOAs could borrow money to make improvements that help prevent or reduce damage from future disasters, not just repair existing damage. The program would operate through the SBA's existing disaster loan system, so the general rules around interest rates and repayment would likely follow similar guidelines already in place for other disaster loan programs.

This bill mainly affects people who live in communities governed by an HOA, which includes many condominium complexes, planned neighborhoods, and gated communities across the country. If a disaster like a hurricane, flood, or wildfire damages shared property in those communities, the HOA would have a new federal borrowing option to fund repairs. Residents in those communities could benefit indirectly, since the cost of repairing common areas would not fall entirely on HOA members through higher dues or special assessments.

title: Carried Interest Fairness Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes how a special type of investment income called "carried interest" gets taxed. Right now, when investment fund managers like private equity, hedge fund, or venture capital managers earn money from their share of profits, that income is often taxed at the lower capital gains tax rate, even though they earned it by doing their jobs. This bill would require that income to be taxed at the higher ordinary income tax rate, the same rate that applies to regular wages and salaries. It also makes this income subject to self-employment taxes, similar to what other self-employed workers pay.

The bill specifically targets people who manage investment funds and get paid through a "carried interest," which is basically a cut of the profits the fund earns. Under current law, because this income flows through a partnership structure, managers can often claim it qualifies for the lower long-term capital gains rate. This bill closes that arrangement by treating their share of profits as ordinary income for tax purposes, since it is compensation for services they performed rather than a return on money they personally invested.

The people most directly affected are investment fund managers at private equity firms, hedge funds, venture capital funds, and real estate investment partnerships. Everyday workers and ordinary investors would not be affected. The bill does protect any profits that come from money a manager actually invested out of their own pocket, which would still qualify for standard investment tax treatment. Penalties of up to 40 percent would apply to anyone who tries to get around the new rules.

The bill also makes that income subject to self-employment taxes. Profits from money a manager personally invested would still qualify for standard investment tax treatment.

title: Prevent Government Shutdowns Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill is designed to prevent the federal government from shutting down when Congress fails to pass a budget on time. Right now, if Congress misses the deadline to fund the government, agencies can be forced to close and federal workers can be sent home without pay. This bill would change that by automatically keeping the government funded at its previous year's spending levels whenever a budget deadline is missed. The funding would renew automatically every 14 days until Congress passes a real budget.

The bill also creates consequences meant to pressure Congress into finishing its work. If the government is running on this automatic funding, members of Congress and White House budget officials would be banned from taking most official trips, and they could not use campaign funds to pay for travel either. On top of that, Congress would be limited in what other business it could vote on, essentially being forced to focus on passing a budget. Senators and representatives also could not take breaks of more than 23 hours at a time during this period.

This bill affects nearly everyone connected to the federal government. Federal workers would keep getting paid and agencies would stay open instead of shutting down. Members of Congress and their staff would face restrictions on their daily work until a budget is passed. People who rely on government programs like food assistance would continue receiving benefits without interruption. Ordinary Americans who use national parks, federal services, or depend on government paychecks would avoid the disruptions that shutdowns typically cause.

title: All Students Count Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would require states to break down student test scores and academic performance data into more detailed ethnic groups when they publish their annual school report cards. Right now, federal education law asks states to report data by broad categories like "Asian American" or "Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander." This bill would require states to report data separately for specific groups within those categories, such as Hmong, Cambodian, Laotian, Samoan, Tongan, and about a dozen others. States would have 18 months after the bill becomes law to start doing this.

The reason behind the change is that grouping all Asian Americans together, or all Pacific Islanders together, can hide big differences in how students from different backgrounds are actually doing in school. For example, some Southeast Asian American communities have much lower graduation and college attendance rates than the overall "Asian American" average might suggest. Supporters argue that without detailed data, schools and policymakers cannot identify which specific groups of students may need more support.

This bill mainly affects state education departments, which would have to update how they collect and report student data. It also affects schools that serve Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander students, since those schools would be evaluated based on more detailed breakdowns. Families from those communities could eventually see more specific information about how students who share their background are performing in local schools.
ai_headline: Bill would split Asian American, Pacific Islander student data into specific ethnic groups

title: Tax DODGER Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires the U.S. Treasury Department to produce a yearly public report showing how many current and retired federal workers, including military personnel, owe back taxes or have not filed their tax returns. The report would break down those numbers by category of worker and by federal agency, and show the total amount of unpaid taxes owed. People who are on a payment plan with the IRS would not be counted as delinquent.

The bill also makes it illegal for someone with seriously delinquent federal tax debt to be hired or to keep working as a federal civilian employee. Job applicants would have to certify when they apply that they do not owe seriously delinquent taxes. If a problem is discovered after someone is already employed, that person would get 180 days to resolve the issue or prove it falls under an exception. There is also a hardship exception that allows an agency head to keep an employee on staff if firing them would not be in the government's best interest.

This bill primarily affects current and prospective federal government employees and military personnel across all branches and agencies. It does not apply to private sector workers. People already on an IRS installment agreement, going through an appeals process, or subject to a wage levy would be protected from being automatically disqualified. Federal agencies would be required to check public records for tax liens and could request additional tax information from the IRS if a lien is found.
ai_headline: Federal workers with unpaid taxes could be barred from government jobs

title: Train FOOD Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires Amtrak, the national passenger railroad, to report to Congress every year on how it is improving its food and drink service on trains. The reports must describe what steps Amtrak has taken, which improvements have been completed, and which ones it has decided are too costly or difficult to carry out. If Amtrak says something is too expensive, it must explain why and estimate the cost. These reports must also be posted publicly on Amtrak's website so anyone can read them.

The bill also requires Amtrak to create an advisory committee made up of Amtrak staff, workers' unions, passenger advocacy groups, and representatives from states that help fund certain train routes. This group will review and comment on the progress reports. Separately, the Government Accountability Office, which is Congress's independent watchdog agency, must produce its own report within two years assessing how well Amtrak is following through on food service improvement recommendations that were previously made by a working group.

This bill mainly affects Amtrak as an organization and its employees who work in food and beverage service. It also affects the millions of passengers who ride Amtrak trains each year, since improved food service would directly impact their travel experience. States that financially support Amtrak routes would also be involved through the advisory committee. The bill does not directly spend new money or mandate specific menu changes; it focuses on accountability and transparency.

title: To rename the portion of United States Highway 75 between President George Bush Turnpike and United States Highway 380 as the "U.S. Congressman and Prisoner of War Sam Johnson Memorial Highway".
ai_summary:
This bill would rename a stretch of US Highway 75 in Texas. Specifically, it changes the name of the section running between the President George Bush Turnpike and US Highway 380 from "Sam Johnson Highway" to the "U.S. Congressman and Prisoner of War Sam Johnson Memorial Highway." Sam Johnson was a Texas congressman who also served as a military pilot and was held as a prisoner of war in Vietnam for nearly seven years. The longer name is meant to honor both parts of his life story.

The change is mostly symbolic. No roads are being built or altered. Official government maps, documents, and records would be updated to use the new name. Signs along that stretch of highway would eventually reflect the change as well.

This bill would most directly affect people who live, work, or travel in the Collin County area of North Texas, where that portion of Highway 75 runs. It could also matter to veterans groups, local governments, and anyone who references that road in official paperwork. For most Americans outside that region, the bill has no practical effect on daily life.

title: A bill to amend the Act of June 22, 1948.
ai_summary:
This bill makes a small but specific change to an old law called the Thye-Blatnik Act, which was originally passed in 1948. That law governs how the federal government buys private land near the Superior National Forest in northern Minnesota. The change updates how land is appraised, meaning how its value is calculated, when the government purchases it from private owners.

Right now, landowners are paid based on the current fair market value of their property. This bill would change that so the government must consider the highest appraised value the land has ever had, including past appraisals, not just what it is worth today. In other words, if a piece of land was worth more in the past than it is now, the owner could potentially receive that higher amount.

This bill mainly affects private landowners who own property near the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness in northeastern Minnesota and who are selling land to the federal government. It could also affect the U.S. Forest Service, which manages that region and handles these purchases. Introduced by Senators Tina Smith and Amy Klobuchar, both of Minnesota, the bill was referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, where it would need to be approved before moving forward.
ai_headline: Senate bill would let Minnesota landowners claim highest past appraisal in federal land sales
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 208.

This means a landowner could receive a higher payment if their land was worth more at some point in the past than it is today.

title: GUARD Act
ai_summary:
The GUARD Act would require companies that operate AI chatbots to verify the ages of their users before letting them interact with the chatbot. Companies would have to use real verification methods, like a government-issued ID, not just an age checkbox or a birthdate entry field. Every existing user account would be frozen until the person proves their age. New users would need to verify their age when signing up. Companies must also periodically re-check ages over time. Personal data collected for age verification must be kept secure, cannot be shared or sold, and must be deleted once it is no longer needed.

The bill also creates new rules about honesty and safety. AI chatbots must clearly tell users at the start of every conversation, and again every 30 minutes, that they are talking to an AI, not a human. Chatbots cannot claim to be therapists, doctors, lawyers, or other licensed professionals, and must remind users to seek real professional help. Separately, the bill makes it a federal crime to knowingly build or release a chatbot that solicits sexual content from minors or that encourages suicide, self-harm, or violence. Each violation of these criminal rules can result in fines up to $100,000. Children identified through age verification would be completely blocked from using AI companion apps, which are chatbots designed to form emotional or friendship-like relationships with users.

This bill affects companies and developers who build or operate AI chatbots in the United States, including apps on phones, websites, and social media platforms. It also directly affects users, especially minors and their parents, as well as anyone who uses a chatbot for emotional support or advice. The U.S. Attorney General and state attorneys general would both have the power to enforce the law and sue companies that do not comply.

title: Local Beef Marketing Incentive Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new government payment program for beef farmers who sell their products directly to customers, rather than going through large meat distributors or packers. The program only kicks in during years when direct-to-market beef sales drop by 25 percent or more compared to a recent five-year average. In those qualifying years, eligible farmers can apply to receive payments that help make up for lost revenue, with a cap of $500 per animal and $100,000 total per farmer per year. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Farm Service Agency would run the program, which is funded through 2031.

To qualify, a farmer must raise and finish cattle for slaughter, use a nearby meat processor located in the same state or within 200 miles, and sell at least half of their beef directly to consumers, restaurants, or retail stores without going through a large middleman. Sales through farmers' markets, farm stores, or community-supported agriculture programs would count. Farmers would need to submit paperwork like receipts and sales records to prove they qualify.

This bill mainly affects small and mid-sized ranchers and farmers who sell beef locally or regionally, rather than through the large national meat supply chain. It could also indirectly affect small local meat processors, as the program requires their use. Consumers who buy local beef from farmers' markets or direct farm sales could see indirect effects if the program encourages more farmers to sell that way.
ai_headline: New federal payments would cushion local beef farmers in down-sales years
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.

title: Retirement Investment in Small Employers Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates a bigger tax credit for very small businesses that set up retirement savings plans for their employees. Right now, small businesses can already get a tax credit to help cover the costs of starting a retirement plan, but this bill gives an even better deal to "microemployers," meaning businesses with 10 or fewer employees. These tiny businesses would get a tax credit that covers 100% of their startup costs instead of the current 50%, and the maximum credit amount jumps from $500 to $2,500 per year. The goal is to make it less expensive for the smallest businesses to offer retirement benefits.

The bill also requires that to qualify for this larger credit, the retirement plan must accept a type of government matching contribution called the Saver's Match, which is a federal program that helps lower-income workers save for retirement. This connects two existing programs to encourage both the employer and employee sides of retirement saving at small workplaces.

This affects owners of very small businesses, such as someone running a shop, a small service company, or a similar operation with 10 or fewer workers, as well as the employees at those businesses. If the bill passes, small business owners would have a stronger financial incentive to set up a retirement plan, which could mean more workers at tiny companies gain access to a workplace retirement savings option. The changes would apply starting with the 2025 tax year.

The changes would take effect starting with the 2025 tax year.

title: RISE Act
ai_summary:
The RISE Act makes two changes to tax law to encourage small businesses to offer retirement plans to their employees. First, it creates a bigger tax credit for very small businesses — those with 10 or fewer employees — that start up a new retirement plan. Right now, small businesses can get a tax credit worth 50% of their startup costs, up to $500 per year. Under this bill, businesses with 10 or fewer workers would get a credit worth 100% of their costs, up to $2,500 per year. This is meant to lower the financial barrier that keeps tiny businesses from offering retirement benefits.

Second, the bill allows retirement plan service providers — like financial companies or benefits administrators — to claim the startup tax credit instead of the small business owner. In exchange, the service provider must lower their fees to the small business by at least the same amount as the credit they receive. The small business owner signs a written agreement confirming they won't also claim the credit. This way, small businesses effectively get reduced costs upfront rather than having to wait to claim a credit on their taxes.

The bill mainly affects very small businesses with 10 or fewer employees, the workers at those businesses who may gain access to retirement savings plans, and the financial service companies that help set up and manage those plans. The changes would take effect starting with the 2027 tax year.

title: Veterans Affairs Heritage Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill creates an official History Office inside the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). The office would be based in Dayton, Ohio, for at least eight years. Its job would be to collect and preserve VA records, artifacts, and historical materials, and to share that history with veterans and the general public through exhibits, publications, websites, and even virtual reality. A Chief Historian would lead the office and report directly to the VA Secretary. The bill also moves two existing programs into this new office: the Veterans Legacy Program (which helps educate the public about veterans buried in national cemeteries) and the Veterans' Oral History Project (which collects recorded stories from veterans).

The bill sets up an internal advisory group made up of senior VA officials to help guide the office's work. It also allows the VA to accept donations of money or property to support the office, partner with nonprofit organizations, and lease out parts of its facilities to raise money for operations. The goal is to have a well-established history program in place by 2030, which marks the VA's 100th anniversary. Within 180 days of passing, the VA would need to submit a planning report to Congress covering staffing, budget, and construction plans, followed by yearly progress reports through 2030.

This bill primarily affects the VA as an institution and its employees who would staff the new office. Veterans, students, researchers, and members of the general public would benefit as the intended audience for the history programs and exhibits the office would create. Residents of Dayton, Ohio, may see a more direct local impact since the office would be physically located there.

title: VETRA Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells the Department of Veterans Affairs to run a test program to upgrade how veterans prove who they are when logging into VA websites. Right now, the VA uses older, weaker security methods like knowledge-based questions. The bill would require the VA to test stronger login systems, such as multi-factor authentication, on up to three of its busiest online platforms. Those could include the disability claims system, the health care enrollment portal, the education benefits system, or the home loan benefits system. The test program would run for two years and could spend up to $25 million from existing VA technology funds.

The bill is designed to reduce fraud and cut down on improper payments by making it harder for the wrong person to access a veteran's account. At the same time, it requires that the new systems not create unnecessary barriers. The VA must use commercially available, federally certified technology and apply stricter login requirements only when the situation calls for it, based on how sensitive or risky a transaction is.

Veterans and their family members who use VA digital services are most directly affected. The VA must report its progress to Congress within one year, and the Government Accountability Office must independently review the program within 18 months. That review specifically looks at whether rural veterans, veterans with disabilities, and those with limited computer skills face any new difficulties accessing their benefits online.
ai_headline: VA ordered to test stronger veteran login security on up to 3 platforms
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations.

The program must use commercially available, federally certified technology and apply stricter login requirements based on how sensitive or risky a given transaction is.

title: COOL Online Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require online sellers to clearly display two pieces of information on product listings: what country the product was made in, and what country the seller's business is based in. These disclosures would need to be easy to spot on the product's webpage. If a product is made in more than one country, all those countries must be listed. The seller, manufacturer, or importer is responsible for providing this information to whatever website is listing the product. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rule and could fine companies that break it.

Not every product or seller would be covered. Excluded items include food, FDA-regulated drugs, used or previously owned goods, and agricultural products like meat, poultry, and eggs that already have their own labeling rules. Very small sellers, meaning those making under $20,000 a year with fewer than 200 sales, are also exempt. Retailers are protected from penalties if they were honestly misled by a supplier about where a product came from, as long as they fix the listing quickly once they find out.

This bill would most directly affect online marketplaces and the businesses that sell new foreign-made goods on them, including large platforms that host third-party sellers. It would also affect shoppers who buy products online, since they would have easier access to information about where products and sellers come from before making a purchase. The law would take effect one year after the relevant government agencies finalize their coordination agreement.
ai_headline: Online sellers would have to show product origin and business country on listings
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

ai_sections.tldr: Senate bill S 294 would require online sellers to display product origin and seller country on every new-product listing.
ai_sections.what: S 294 would require online sellers to clearly display on each product listing the country where the product was made and the country where the seller's business is based. If a product was made in multiple countries, all of them must be listed. The rule would take effect one year after relevant government agencies finalize their coordination agreement.
ai_sections.who: The bill primarily affects online marketplaces, including large platforms that host third-party sellers, and the businesses selling new foreign-made goods on them. Shoppers who buy products online are also affected, as they would see origin information before purchasing.
ai_sections.why: Retailers who were honestly misled by a supplier about product origin are shielded from penalties, provided they correct the listing quickly after learning the truth. Small sellers earning under $20,000 a year with fewer than 200 sales are exempt, as are listings for food, FDA-regulated drugs, used goods, and certain agricultural products already covered by other labeling rules.
ai_sections.cost: The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rule and has authority to fine companies that violate it.

title: EFFIE Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes it a federal felony to fraudulently sign ballot access paperwork for federal elections. To get on a ballot for offices like Congress or the presidency, candidates must submit official documents, often including petition signatures from registered voters. The EFFIE Act would make it a serious crime if a candidate, or anyone working for them, knowingly fakes or falsifies any of those required documents. A conviction could mean up to five years in prison, a fine of up to $250,000, or both.

Right now, ballot fraud of this kind may be handled under existing state laws or general federal fraud statutes, but this bill would create a specific federal felony category for it under the Federal Election Campaign Act. By adding it there, federal authorities would have a clearer, dedicated legal tool to prosecute this type of misconduct in federal races.

This bill would affect anyone running for a federal office, as well as their campaign staff and hired agents. Everyday voters are not directly required to do anything differently, but the law is meant to protect the integrity of the process that determines who appears on their ballots. The bill was introduced in May 2026 and sent to two House committees for review.
ai_headline: Faking federal ballot paperwork would become a felony under new House bill
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on House Administration, and in addition to the Committee on the Judiciary, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8977 makes fraudulent ballot access filings for federal elections a felony carrying up to 5 years in prison and $250,000 in fines.
ai_sections.what: HR 8977, the EFFIE Act, would create a specific federal felony under the Federal Election Campaign Act for knowingly faking or falsifying ballot access documents required to get a candidate onto a federal election ballot. This covers petition signatures and other official paperwork candidates must submit to qualify for offices such as Congress or the presidency. The bill was introduced in May 2026 and referred to two House committees for review.
ai_sections.who: The law would apply to candidates running for federal office and anyone working for their campaigns, including paid agents and staff. Everyday voters face no new direct requirements under the bill.
ai_sections.why: While ballot fraud of this kind may already be prosecuted under state laws or general federal fraud statutes, this bill would give federal authorities a dedicated, clearly defined legal tool specifically for misconduct in federal races. Adding the offense to the Federal Election Campaign Act is intended to affect who appears on ballots and to protect the integrity of the ballot access process.
ai_sections.cost: A conviction under this bill could result in a fine of up to $250,000, up to five years in prison, or both, imposed on the individual found guilty.

title: SHINE Act
ai_summary:
This bill deals with campaign finance reporting. Right now, political committees only have to quickly report large donations they receive close to an election if those donations go directly to a candidate's campaign. The SHINE Act would expand that rule so that any political committee spending money on ads or other activities related to an election would also have to quickly report donations of $1,000 or more that came in during the final 20 days before that election. The report would need to be filed within 48 hours of receiving the donation.

The goal is to close a gap in current disclosure rules. Under existing law, some committees could receive large last-minute donations and spend that money influencing an election without the public knowing who gave the money until after the votes were counted. This bill would require that information to be reported to the Federal Election Commission and made public before election day, as long as the donation arrived more than 48 hours before the election.

This affects political action committees and other groups that spend money on elections, as well as donors who give $1,000 or more to those groups in the weeks leading up to an election. Voters, journalists, and watchdog groups who follow campaign finance disclosures would have access to more up-to-date information about who is funding election-related spending. Party committees are specifically excluded from this new requirement.
ai_headline: SHINE Act would require faster disclosure of large last-minute campaign donations
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on House Administration.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 9049 requires political committees spending on elections to report donations of $1,000+ within 48 hours during the final 20 days before an election.
ai_sections.what: HR 9049 expands existing campaign finance reporting rules to cover any political committee spending money on election-related ads or activities. These committees would have to report donations of $1,000 or more received in the final 20 days before an election within 48 hours of receipt. The requirement applies only when the donation arrives more than 48 hours before election day.
ai_sections.who: The rule affects political action committees and other groups that spend money on elections, as well as donors who give $1,000 or more to those groups in the final weeks before an election. Party committees are specifically excluded from this new requirement.
ai_sections.why: Under current law, some committees can receive large last-minute donations and spend that money influencing an election without public disclosure until after votes are counted. This bill would make that information available to voters, journalists, and watchdog groups before election day through the Federal Election Commission.

title: PANA Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill creates a special government account called the "Venezuela Restoration Fund." It would be filled with money and assets that the U.S. government seizes from people who worked for or supported the Venezuelan governments of Hugo Chavez or Nicolas Maduro. Instead of that forfeited money going into the general federal treasury, it would be set aside specifically for Venezuela-related purposes.

The Secretary of State would control how the money gets spent. The allowed uses include supporting democracy-building efforts in Venezuela, helping document human rights abuses there, funding independent news outlets that operate in Venezuela, and fighting government corruption inside the country. The money could go to both government agencies and private organizations working toward those goals. The Treasury and State Departments would have to report to Congress every year on how much money came in and how it was spent.

This bill primarily affects U.S. foreign policy toward Venezuela. It does not directly impact everyday Americans financially. It would matter most to Venezuelan citizens and organizations working on democracy and human rights inside Venezuela, as well as to any individuals or groups whose assets might be seized because of ties to the Chavez or Maduro governments. It is still in early stages, having only been introduced and sent to the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
ai_headline: Seized Maduro-linked assets would fund Venezuela democracy programs
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 9039 would redirect assets seized from Chavez and Maduro allies into a State Department fund for Venezuela democracy and human rights work.

The Secretary of State would direct spending toward democracy-building, human rights documentation, independent media, and anti-corruption efforts inside Venezuela. Funds could flow to both government agencies and private organizations working on those goals.

ai_sections.why: Forfeited assets that would otherwise enter the general federal treasury would instead be directed to Venezuela-specific purposes. The Treasury and State Departments would be required to report annually to Congress on funds received and spent.

title: WATER for Farmers Act
ai_summary:
This bill is about water that Mexico is required to send to the United States under a 1944 treaty between the two countries. That treaty says Mexico must deliver at least 350,000 acre-feet of water per year from the Rio Grande, averaged over five-year periods. The bill says Mexico has often fallen short of this amount, which has hurt farmers in South Texas who depend on that water to grow crops. The bill would set up a formal yearly check to see whether Mexico has delivered its required share of water.

If Mexico is found to be short on its water deliveries, the bill would allow the U.S. government to place tariffs, which are extra taxes, on goods imported from Mexico. Those tariffs would be aimed especially at Mexican farm products and goods from regions that use Rio Grande water. The longer Mexico stays in shortfall, the higher the tariffs could go. The money collected from those tariffs would be placed into a special fund called the South Texas Agricultural Compensation Trust Fund.

Money from that fund would go directly to farmers in the Rio Grande Valley who lost income because of the water shortage. The Agriculture Department would calculate how much each farmer is owed based on how much water was missing, the value of that water, and the broader economic damage to the region. The bill also requires monthly public reports on water delivery levels and any compensation payments made. This bill mainly affects South Texas farmers, U.S.-Mexico trade, and the federal agencies that manage border water issues.
ai_headline: Bill would hit Mexican farm imports with tariffs if Rio Grande water deliveries fall short
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Foreign Relations.

ai_sections.tldr: Senate bill S 4549 would impose escalating tariffs on Mexican goods when Mexico misses its Rio Grande water treaty obligations.
ai_sections.what: Senate bill S 4549 addresses Mexico's required water deliveries to the United States under a 1944 treaty, which mandates at least 350,000 acre-feet of water per year from the Rio Grande, averaged over five-year periods. The bill would establish an annual review of whether Mexico has met that requirement. If a shortfall is found, the U.S. government could impose tariffs on Mexican imports, rising the longer the shortfall continues, with a focus on Mexican agricultural products and goods from regions that use Rio Grande water.
ai_sections.who: South Texas farmers in the Rio Grande Valley who depend on treaty water for crop production are the primary group affected. Federal agencies that manage border water issues, the Agriculture Department, and U.S.-Mexico trade relations are also directly involved.
ai_sections.why: Mexico has frequently fallen short of its treaty delivery obligations, which has reduced water available to South Texas farmers and caused income losses in the region. The bill creates financial and trade consequences tied to the size and duration of any water delivery shortfall.
ai_sections.cost: Tariff revenue collected from Mexican imports would be deposited into a dedicated South Texas Agricultural Compensation Trust Fund. The Agriculture Department would calculate individual farmer payments based on the volume of missing water, the value of that water, and broader economic damage to the region.

Payments based on water volume and value

title: WATER for Farmers Act
ai_summary:
This bill is about a long-standing water-sharing agreement between the United States and Mexico called the 1944 Water Treaty. Under that treaty, Mexico is supposed to deliver at least 350,000 acre-feet of Rio Grande water to the U.S. every year, averaged over five-year periods. The bill's sponsors say Mexico has repeatedly fallen short on these deliveries, and that current agreements don't do enough to force Mexico to follow through. The bill would require the Secretary of State to officially track whether Mexico meets its yearly water delivery requirement and formally declare a shortfall if it doesn't.

If Mexico is found to be short on water deliveries, the bill sets up two responses. First, the U.S. would impose tariffs, meaning extra taxes, on goods imported from Mexico. Those tariffs would start 90 days after a shortfall is declared and would target Mexican agricultural products and goods from regions that use Rio Grande water. The tariffs would get bigger if the shortfall continues into a second year or beyond. Second, the bill creates a special fund called the South Texas Agricultural Compensation Trust Fund. The money collected from those tariffs would go directly into this fund and be paid out to farmers in the Rio Grande Valley who can show they suffered financial losses because of the water shortage.

This bill most directly affects farmers and agricultural businesses in South Texas, particularly in the Rio Grande Valley, who depend on river water for irrigation. It also affects importers and businesses that buy goods from Mexico, since those goods could become more expensive under the new tariffs. On the Mexican side, farmers and exporters in border regions could face reduced demand for their products if tariffs are imposed. The bill involves multiple federal agencies, including the State Department, the Department of Agriculture, and the U.S. Trade Representative, and it is currently in committee.

title: No Fencing at the United States Supreme Court Act
ai_summary:
This bill would ban the use of federal money to install new permanent fencing around the Supreme Court building or its surrounding grounds in Washington, D.C. However, it does include an exception: if there is already fencing in place when the law is signed, that existing fencing can still be repaired or replaced using federal funds. The bill does not ban temporary fencing, only permanent structures.

The bill was introduced in response to ongoing discussions about security barriers at the Supreme Court, which have been a topic of debate since protests and security concerns arose in recent years. Supporters of the bill argue that permanent fencing would cut off public access to a landmark civic space, while others have raised concerns about the safety of the justices and the building.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies responsible for funding and managing Supreme Court security, as well as members of the public who visit or demonstrate near the Court. Ordinary Americans would not face any direct financial impact, but the bill would shape whether the Supreme Court remains open and visually accessible to the public or is enclosed behind a permanent barrier.
ai_headline: Bill would bar federal funds from building permanent Supreme Court fencing
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.

Existing fencing present when the law is signed could still be repaired or replaced with federal money. The bill does not restrict temporary fencing, only permanent structures.

title: Mass Timber Federal Buildings Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would require the federal government to give priority to using mass timber — a type of engineered wood product made from layers of lumber pressed together — when constructing, renovating, or leasing federal buildings, including military bases. The wood would have to come from forests and manufacturing facilities located inside the United States. It also requires that the wood be sourced responsibly, meaning it must either meet a certified environmental standard or come from land managed under rules set by federal, state, or tribal governments.

When choosing which wood products to buy, the bill tells federal agencies to favor wood that comes from forests being actively restored, forests managed to reduce wildfire risk, or forests owned by underserved groups such as Native American tribes and small family landowners. Contractors would need to provide paperwork proving where the wood came from. The General Services Administration, which manages federal buildings, would also be required to study the environmental impact of using mass timber in new buildings and report the findings to Congress within about a year.

This bill would most directly affect federal construction contractors, timber companies and wood product manufacturers, forest owners — especially tribal nations and small family forest owners — and federal agencies that manage building projects. Indirectly, it could affect workers in the U.S. timber and construction industries, as well as communities near forests that might benefit from increased demand for responsibly harvested wood.
ai_headline: Federal buildings would get mass timber priority under Senate bill
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

title: PERFECT Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill requires the Secretary of Defense to publish and regularly update a public list of dietary supplement ingredients and performance-enhancing substances that military members are not allowed to use. The list must be updated at least every 90 days and made available online in multiple easy-to-use formats, including a searchable database and a downloadable file. The bill also directs the Defense Department to improve its existing supplement safety website, possibly adding AI tools that can scan product labels and check ingredients against the banned list.

The bill also creates some protections for service members who unknowingly use a banned supplement. If a military member uses a prohibited supplement for the first time and can show they genuinely did not know it was banned, their commanding officer has the option to skip formal punishment and instead require education, counseling, or drug testing. The bill also states that possessing a banned supplement ingredient is not the same as drug abuse under military law, which is an important legal distinction that could affect a service member's record and career.

This bill primarily affects active-duty members of the U.S. Armed Forces, military recruits, and their commanding officers. It also applies to Defense Department retail stores, which would be required to stop selling products with banned ingredients. Dietary supplement companies that sell to military customers would be affected as well, since the updated website would include tools aimed at helping vendors check whether their products comply with military rules.
ai_headline: Pentagon must publish and refresh banned supplement list every 90 days
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Armed Services.

title: PANELS Act
ai_summary:
This bill would remove certain federal tax credits from solar energy projects built on what the government classifies as "prime farmland" or "unique farmland." Right now, businesses and developers can claim tax credits when they build solar panels or solar facilities. Under this bill, if a solar project is placed on high-quality agricultural land, those tax credits would no longer apply. The land classifications used come from existing U.S. Department of Agriculture rules that define which soils are best suited for growing crops.

The change would apply to any solar property put into use after the bill becomes law. It covers multiple existing clean energy tax credits, including ones for solar equipment and solar electricity generation facilities. Developers who planned to build solar on prime or unique farmland would lose a significant financial incentive, since these tax credits can be worth a large portion of a project's cost.

This bill mainly affects landowners, farmers, and solar energy developers. Farmers who lease their land to solar companies, or developers who planned projects on fertile agricultural land, would feel the biggest impact. It could also indirectly affect rural communities that rely on lease income from solar projects, as well as the broader solar energy industry, which sometimes targets flat, open farmland for large installations.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: To amend section 844 of the William M. (Mac) Thornberry National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 to change the applicability of the amendments made by such section, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill adjusts a rule about where the U.S. military can buy certain metal products. A 2021 defense law already banned the Department of Defense from purchasing specific metals from certain foreign countries considered national security risks, like China and Russia. This bill changes when that ban actually kicks in for new contracts. The new deadline would be whichever comes first: January 1, 2032, or 180 days after the Defense Secretary officially confirms that there are enough reliable non-restricted foreign suppliers to meet the military's needs in terms of quality and quantity.

The practical effect is that defense contractors have more time before they are required to stop sourcing these metals from restricted countries. The bill also directs the Pentagon to update its procurement rules within 120 days of the law passing to reflect this new timeline.

The people most directly affected are defense contractors and manufacturers who supply metal products to the military, as well as the Pentagon's procurement offices. American taxpayers and military readiness could also be indirectly affected, since the rule is meant to reduce U.S. military dependence on metals from potentially adversarial nations, while the delay gives industry more time to build up alternative supply chains.
ai_headline: Pentagon metal sourcing ban gets extended deadline under HR 9073
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Armed Services.
