title: Digital Asset PARITY Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates new tax rules specifically for cryptocurrencies and other digital assets. Right now, the tax code treats most digital assets the same as stocks, but the rules were written before crypto existed, causing confusion and compliance headaches. The bill addresses several situations: if you use a government-approved stablecoin (a digital coin pegged to one dollar) to make a purchase, you would not owe taxes on any tiny price difference, treating it more like spending cash. The bill also applies "wash sale" rules to crypto, meaning you can no longer sell a digital asset at a loss and immediately buy it back just to claim a tax deduction, the same restriction that already applies to stocks.

The bill sets rules for people who earn crypto by mining or staking, which means using computers or locked-up coins to help run a blockchain network. Those earnings would generally be taxed as ordinary income when received, but miners and stakers could also choose to delay reporting that income for up to five years under a special election, with different tax treatment when they eventually sell. The bill also gives foreign investors a clearer legal safe harbor so that simply trading digital assets does not make them subject to US taxes, and it lets professional crypto traders use a simplified accounting method called mark-to-market already used by securities dealers.

The people most directly affected are everyday Americans who use stablecoins for payments, crypto investors of all income levels, professional crypto traders and funds, miners and stakers, and nonprofits that receive crypto donations. The bill also requires the Treasury Department to study whether small everyday crypto purchases under a certain dollar amount should be exempt from having to calculate and report gains, though it does not create that exemption itself.
ai_headline: New tax bill rewrites crypto rules on trading, mining, and stablecoins
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8899 overhauls how digital assets are taxed, covering stablecoin purchases, wash sales, mining income, and foreign investor rules.
ai_sections.what: HR 8899 creates new tax rules for digital assets, addressing situations the existing tax code was not written to handle. Stablecoin purchases would be treated like spending cash, with no tax owed on small price differences. Wash sale restrictions would apply to crypto, miners and stakers would owe ordinary income tax when they receive earnings but could elect to delay reporting that income for up to five years, and foreign investors would receive a clearer safe harbor from US taxes.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects everyday Americans using stablecoins for payments, crypto investors at all income levels, professional crypto traders and funds, miners, stakers, and nonprofits receiving crypto donations. Foreign investors in digital assets and the Treasury Department, which must conduct a study on small-transaction exemptions, are also involved.
ai_sections.why: Current tax law treats digital assets like stocks despite being written before cryptocurrency existed, creating compliance confusion. Applying these new rules would change reporting obligations and tax timing for a wide range of crypto participants, and the outcome of the Treasury study could eventually affect whether small everyday purchases require gain calculations.

title: To amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to temporarily increase the capital gains exclusion for any qualifying senior who sells a principal residence during a qualifying year, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
When someone sells their home, they normally don't have to pay taxes on a certain amount of profit from that sale. Currently, single homeowners can exclude up to $250,000 in profit from taxes, and married couples can exclude up to $500,000. This bill would temporarily raise those limits to $1,000,000 for eligible seniors who sell their homes between 2027 and 2030. A single senior could shield up to four times more profit from taxes than under current law.

To qualify, a person must be at least 65 years old on the day they sell the home, and they must have owned that specific home for at least 25 years. The home also has to be their main residence. If both spouses qualify, or even just one spouse qualifies, a married couple filing jointly could exclude up to $1,000,000 in profit. The higher limits would only apply during those four tax years and would go back to current levels after 2030.

This bill mainly affects older homeowners who have lived in the same home for a very long time, which often means they have built up significant value in the property over the decades. People who bought their homes after 2002 would not yet meet the 25-year ownership rule during the bill's window. Anyone who does not meet both the age and ownership requirements would still follow the existing $250,000 or $500,000 exclusion rules.
ai_headline: Seniors who've owned homes 25 years could shield $1M in sale profits under new bill
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 9064 would let qualifying seniors 65+ exclude up to $1,000,000 in home-sale profit from taxes between 2027 and 2030.
ai_sections.what: HR 9064 would temporarily raise the home-sale capital gains exclusion to $1,000,000 for eligible seniors during the 2027–2030 tax years. Currently, single filers can exclude up to $250,000 in profit and married couples filing jointly can exclude up to $500,000. After 2030, the limits would return to their current levels.
ai_sections.who: The higher exclusion applies to homeowners who are at least 65 years old on the date of sale and have owned that specific home as their primary residence for at least 25 years. Married couples filing jointly can claim the $1,000,000 exclusion if at least one spouse meets both requirements.
ai_sections.why: Long-term homeowners in this age group often hold properties that have gained substantial value over decades, making the existing exclusion limits less protective against taxable profit. Anyone who does not meet both the age and ownership requirements remains subject to the current $250,000 or $500,000 exclusion rules.

title: Precious Metals Parity Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes a tax rule that affects mutual funds. Right now, mutual funds that want special tax status (called a "regulated investment company") must earn most of their money from certain approved sources, like stocks, bonds, and foreign currencies. Income from precious metals like gold and silver does not currently count toward that requirement. This bill would add gold, silver, platinum, and palladium to the approved list, putting them on equal footing with foreign currencies under the tax code.

In practical terms, this makes it easier for mutual funds to hold physical precious metals without risking their tax status. Currently, a mutual fund that earns too much income from gold or silver could lose its special tax treatment, which would result in higher taxes for the fund. This bill removes that obstacle, allowing fund managers more flexibility to include precious metals in their investment strategies.

This mainly affects mutual fund companies and investment managers who want to offer funds that include physical precious metals. It could also indirectly affect everyday investors who buy shares in those mutual funds, since it may open up more investment options that include gold or silver. Individual investors buying precious metals on their own are not directly affected by this change.
ai_headline: Bill would let mutual funds hold precious metals without losing tax status
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 9060 adds gold, silver, platinum, and palladium to the approved income sources for mutual fund tax status.

Currently, income from precious metals does not count toward that requirement, meaning funds that earn too much from them risk losing their special tax treatment. The bill would put precious metals on equal footing with foreign currencies under the existing tax rule.
ai_sections.who: The change directly affects mutual fund companies and investment managers who want to offer funds that include physical precious metals. Everyday investors who buy shares in those mutual funds could be indirectly affected, as it may open up more investment options that include gold or silver.
ai_sections.why: Without this change, mutual funds that hold physical precious metals can lose their regulated investment company status, resulting in higher taxes for the fund. Removing that obstacle gives fund managers more flexibility in how they structure precious metals offerings.

title: COOL Online Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require online sellers to clearly display two pieces of information on product listings: what country the product was made in, and what country the seller's business is based in. The rule applies to new foreign-made goods that already have country-of-origin marking requirements under existing customs law. Sellers who get that information from a manufacturer or supplier and pass it along in good faith would not be held responsible if that information turns out to be wrong, as long as they act quickly to fix it once they find out.

Not every seller or product would be covered. Small sellers making fewer than 200 sales per year and earning under $20,000 are exempt. Used or secondhand items are also excluded. Foods regulated by the FDA, prescription drugs, meat, poultry, eggs, and other agricultural products covered by separate laws are left out as well. Over-the-counter drugs that already require manufacturer information on their labels would need to show that same business information in the online listing.

The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules and treat violations the same way it handles other unfair or deceptive business practices. The FTC, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, and the Department of Agriculture would be required to work out a shared agreement on how to apply the law consistently. The rules would kick in one year after that agreement is published. This bill mainly affects online retailers and marketplace sellers who sell foreign-made goods, as well as shoppers who would gain more visibility into where products and their sellers come from.
ai_headline: Online sellers would have to disclose product origin and seller location under new bill
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committees on Ways and Means, and Agriculture, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 9057 would require online sellers to display a product's country of origin and the seller's home country on every qualifying listing.
ai_sections.what: HR 9057 would require online sellers to clearly show where a product was made and where the seller's business is based on product listings. The rule applies to new foreign-made goods already subject to country-of-origin marking requirements under existing customs law. Used goods, small sellers with fewer than 200 sales per year and under $20,000 in earnings, and several food and drug categories are exempt.
ai_sections.who: The bill primarily affects online retailers and marketplace sellers who sell foreign-made goods. Shoppers who buy from those sellers would gain more visibility into where products and their sellers come from.
ai_sections.why: Sellers who receive origin information from a manufacturer or supplier in good faith would not be held liable if that information is wrong, provided they correct it quickly once discovered. The FTC would enforce violations under the same standards it applies to unfair or deceptive business practices, with the FTC, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, and the Department of Agriculture required to coordinate on consistent application before rules take effect one year later.

title: Veteran Burial Benefit Correction Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes two changes to the burial benefit the Department of Veterans Affairs pays when a veteran dies from a disability directly caused by their military service. First, it raises the maximum payment from $2,000 to $3,000. Second, it sets up an automatic annual adjustment tied to inflation, specifically the Consumer Price Index, so the benefit keeps pace with rising funeral costs over time instead of staying frozen at a fixed dollar amount.

The people most directly affected are the families of veterans who die from a service-connected disability, meaning a health condition officially linked to their time in the military. Those families can apply to the VA for help covering burial and funeral costs, and this bill would increase how much financial help they could receive. Funeral homes and burial service providers would also be indirectly affected since the benefit influences what families can afford to spend.

The current $2,000 limit has not kept up with the rising cost of funerals over the years. By tying future increases to inflation, the bill aims to prevent the benefit from losing value again the way it has in the past. The bill was introduced in the House and referred to the Committee on Veterans' Affairs, where it would need to pass before moving forward in the legislative process.
ai_headline: VA burial benefit for service-connected deaths would rise to $3,000
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 9055 raises the VA burial benefit for service-connected deaths from $2,000 to $3,000 and adds annual inflation adjustments.
ai_sections.what: HR 9055 raises the maximum VA burial benefit for veterans who die from a service-connected disability from $2,000 to $3,000. The bill also creates an automatic annual adjustment tied to the Consumer Price Index so the benefit keeps pace with inflation over time. The bill has been introduced in the House and referred to the Committee on Veterans' Affairs.
ai_sections.who: Families of veterans who die from a service-connected disability — a health condition officially linked to their military service — are the primary people affected. Funeral homes and burial service providers would also be indirectly affected, since the benefit influences how much families can spend.
ai_sections.why: The current $2,000 limit has not kept up with rising funeral costs over the years. Tying future increases to inflation would prevent the benefit from losing value the way it has in the past.

title: No FED in West Texas Act
ai_summary:
This bill would block the federal government from carrying out a specific land management plan for Muleshoe National Wildlife Refuge, located in west Texas. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service published this plan in February 2023, and it outlines how the refuge could potentially grow or be protected in the future. The bill would prevent the Secretary of the Interior from finalizing, putting into action, or enforcing that plan or anything very similar to it.

Land Protection Plans are tools federal agencies use to identify land near an existing refuge that could someday be added to it, usually through voluntary sales or donations from private landowners. Critics of such plans often argue they could eventually lead to the federal government acquiring more private or state land in a region. Supporters argue they help protect wildlife habitat and that participation by landowners is always voluntary.

This bill mainly affects landowners, ranchers, and farmers in the area around Muleshoe National Wildlife Refuge in Bailey County, Texas, as well as the federal agencies that manage the refuge. It does not shut down the existing refuge itself, it only stops this particular expansion and protection plan from moving forward.
ai_headline: Senate bill would halt expansion plan for Muleshoe wildlife refuge in Texas
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

ai_sections.tldr: S 4412 would bar the Interior Department from finalizing or enforcing a February 2023 land plan for Muleshoe National Wildlife Refuge in Texas.
ai_sections.what: S 4412 would prohibit the Secretary of the Interior from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's February 2023 Land Protection Plan for Muleshoe National Wildlife Refuge. The bill does not close the existing refuge; it only blocks this specific plan and anything substantially similar to it from moving forward.
ai_sections.who: The bill primarily affects landowners, ranchers, and farmers near Muleshoe National Wildlife Refuge in Bailey County, Texas. It also affects the federal agencies responsible for managing the refuge.
ai_sections.why: Land Protection Plans identify nearby private or state land that could potentially be added to a refuge through voluntary sales or donations, which critics argue could lead to expanded federal land acquisition in the region. Blocking the plan would prevent the Fish and Wildlife Service from using it as a framework for any future refuge growth or protection efforts in that area.

title: Protecting American Voters’ Rights Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes one specific change to an existing law called Section 1983, which is a federal law that already lets people sue state and local government officials who violate their constitutional rights. Right now, that law does not clearly cover federal officials. This bill would expand Section 1983 so that Americans can also sue federal officials who violate their constitutional rights related to voting and elections.

In practical terms, if a federal official took an action that a voter believed violated their constitutional voting rights, that voter could take that official to court under this law. Currently, suing federal officials for rights violations requires using different and often more complicated legal paths. This bill would give voters a more direct legal tool to challenge federal actions they believe are unconstitutional when it comes to elections.

This bill would affect any American who believes a federal election or election enforcement official has violated their constitutional voting rights. It would also affect federal officials who oversee elections and enforcement, since they could now face personal lawsuits under this expanded law. The bill was introduced in the House and referred to the Judiciary Committee, meaning it has not become law yet.
ai_headline: House bill would let voters sue federal officials for election rights violations
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
policy_area: Civil Rights and Liberties, Minority Issues

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8858 would expand Section 1983 to let Americans sue federal officials who violate their constitutional voting rights.
ai_sections.what: HR 8858 would expand an existing federal law, Section 1983, which currently allows people to sue state and local government officials for constitutional rights violations. The bill would extend that same legal authority to cover federal officials specifically in cases involving voting and elections. This would give voters a more direct legal path than the more complicated routes currently available for suing federal officials.
ai_sections.who: Any American who believes a federal election or election enforcement official has violated their constitutional voting rights would be affected. Federal officials who oversee elections and enforcement would also be affected, as they could face personal lawsuits under this expanded law.
ai_sections.why: Extending Section 1983 to federal officials would create a new legal avenue for challenging federal actions related to elections that voters believe are unconstitutional. Federal election officials would become personally subject to lawsuits in cases where no such direct legal tool currently exists.

title: A bill to take certain land in the State of California into trust for the benefit of the Pechanga Band of Indians, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill would transfer about 860 acres of federal land in Riverside County, California, from the Bureau of Land Management to trust status for the Pechanga Band of Indians. When land is held "in trust," the federal government holds the title, but the tribe has the right to use and manage it as part of their reservation. The land is currently managed by a federal agency and would become part of the Pechanga Band's reservation if the bill becomes law.

The bill places strict limits on how the land can be used. It must be kept as open space and can only be used to protect and preserve archaeological, cultural, and wildlife resources on the property. No casinos or gaming of any kind are allowed on this land. Existing roads, easements, utility agreements, and water rights that are already in place would remain in effect and would not be changed by this transfer.

The people most directly affected are the Pechanga Band of Indians, a federally recognized tribe based in Temecula, California, who would gain official control over this land. Local residents, neighboring landowners, and anyone with existing agreements tied to that land could also be affected, though the bill specifically protects those existing rights and agreements. Federal land managers at the Bureau of Land Management would no longer oversee this parcel if the bill passes.
ai_headline: Federal land transfer would add 860 acres to Pechanga reservation in California
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Indian Affairs. (Sponsor introductory remarks on measure: CR S1011)

ai_sections.tldr: S 4053 would move 860 federal acres in Riverside County into trust for the Pechanga Band, restricted to open space and cultural preservation.
ai_sections.what: Senate Bill 4053 would transfer approximately 860 acres of Bureau of Land Management land in Riverside County, California, into federal trust status for the Pechanga Band of Indians. The land would become part of the tribe's reservation but must be kept as open space and used only to protect archaeological, cultural, and wildlife resources. Gaming and casino operations are explicitly prohibited on the property, and all existing roads, easements, utility agreements, and water rights would remain in effect.

Local residents, neighboring landowners, and parties with existing agreements tied to the land are also affected, though the bill protects their current rights.

title: A bill to amend the Catawba Indian Tribe of South Carolina Land Claims Settlement Act of 1993 with respect to future membership in the Catawba Indian Nation.
ai_summary:
This bill makes a small but specific change to a 1993 law that settled land disputes involving the Catawba Indian Nation, a federally recognized tribe based in South Carolina. The 1993 law set rules for who could become a tribal member, including a requirement that a person be a direct descendant of someone on an original membership list AND have maintained ongoing political ties to the tribe. This bill would remove both of those extra conditions from the law.

In practical terms, the change means the Catawba Indian Nation would have more freedom to set its own membership rules going forward, without those two restrictions being locked into federal law. Tribes generally have the right to decide who their members are, and supporters of this bill argue that removing these federal restrictions brings the law more in line with that principle of tribal self-governance.

The people most directly affected are individuals who want to enroll as members of the Catawba Indian Nation but have been blocked by the current requirements, as well as the tribe itself, which would gain more control over its own membership decisions. It does not affect other tribes or create any new federal spending. The bill was introduced in the Senate by both senators from South Carolina and was sent to the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs.
ai_headline: Senate bill would free Catawba Indian Nation to set its own membership rules
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Indian Affairs.

ai_sections.tldr: S 3859 removes two federal membership restrictions on the Catawba Indian Nation imposed by a 1993 land-dispute settlement law.
ai_sections.what: S 3859 amends a 1993 federal law that resolved land disputes involving the Catawba Indian Nation of South Carolina. That law required tribal membership applicants to be direct descendants of someone on an original membership list and to have maintained ongoing political ties to the tribe. ai_sections.who: The Catawba Indian Nation, a federally recognized tribe based in South Carolina, would gain authority to set its own membership criteria. Individuals who have been blocked from enrolling under the current requirements are also directly affected.
ai_sections.why: Removing the restrictions would bring the 1993 law closer to the general principle that tribes have the right to determine their own membership. The tribe would have more control over enrollment decisions going forward, without those two conditions being fixed in federal statute.

title: Restoration of Employment Choice for Adults with Disabilities Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes rules about who can be paid less than the minimum wage when they have a disability. Under current law, employers can pay workers with disabilities a lower wage, but there are restrictions meant to protect younger workers and ensure they are informed about other job options first. This bill would remove the age cap that currently limits these lower-wage jobs to workers age 24 and under, allowing employers to pay subminimum wages to adults of any age with disabilities, as long as the worker chooses to accept the job.

The bill also adds a new rule saying that if an employer tries to connect a worker with state job counseling services but the state fails to respond, the employer can move forward with hiring that person at the subminimum wage anyway. It also requires that any paperwork documenting the worker's situation be shared with the employer, not just kept by the state agency.

This bill primarily affects adults with disabilities who work at jobs covered under Section 14(c) of the Fair Labor Standards Act, which are often sheltered workshops or similar programs. It also affects employers who run those programs and state agencies that provide vocational rehabilitation services. Supporters say it expands choices for workers with disabilities, while critics argue it could allow more people to be paid very low wages. The bill was introduced in the House and has been sent to the Education and Workforce Committee.
ai_headline: House bill would let employers pay subminimum wages to disabled adults of any age
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 18 - 15.

The bill also allows employers to proceed with subminimum-wage hiring if the state fails to respond to a required job-counseling referral. Additionally, it requires that documentation of the worker's situation be shared directly with the employer, rather than held only by the state agency.

ai_sections.why: Removing the age cap expands the pool of workers who can legally be paid below minimum wage under Section 14(c). The provision allowing employers to bypass a non-responsive state agency reduces a procedural check that previously delayed or prevented subminimum-wage hiring.

title: Affordable Insulin Now Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would cap how much people with private health insurance pay out of pocket for insulin at $35 per month, starting January 1, 2027. Insurance plans could not make insulin subject to a deductible, meaning you would not have to meet your deductible before the cap kicks in. The $35 cap applies as long as you use an in-network provider or pharmacy. If the negotiated price of your insulin is already lower than $35, your cost would be capped at 25 percent of that negotiated price instead, whichever is less. Any amount you pay still counts toward your annual deductible and out-of-pocket maximum.

The bill also creates a separate program for people who have no health insurance at all. Under this program, doctors' offices and pharmacies could sign up with the federal government to provide insulin to uninsured patients for no more than $35 per month. The government would then reimburse those providers for the difference between $35 and the actual cost of the insulin. Participating providers would not be allowed to bill the uninsured patient for anything beyond that $35.

People most directly affected include the roughly 8 million Americans who use insulin to manage diabetes, whether they are insured through an employer, buy their own plan, or have no insurance at all. Health insurance companies, employers who provide health benefits, pharmacies, and doctors' offices would also need to adjust how they handle insulin pricing and billing to comply with the new rules.
ai_headline: Senate bill caps insulin costs at $35 a month for insured and uninsured Americans
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

ai_sections.tldr: S 4512 would cap insulin costs at $35/month starting Jan. 1, 2027, for both privately insured and uninsured Americans.

If the negotiated price of insulin is already below $35, the patient's cost would instead be capped at 25 percent of that negotiated price. A separate program would allow doctors' offices and pharmacies to provide insulin to uninsured patients for no more than $35 per month, with the federal government reimbursing providers for the difference between $35 and the actual cost.

Insurers and employers would be required to restructure insulin cost-sharing arrangements so that deductibles no longer delay access to the cap.

Payments made by insured patients under the cap still count toward their annual deductible and out-of-pocket maximum.

title: Small Business Wildfire Smoke Recovery Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes one specific change to an existing law called the Small Business Act. Right now, that law allows the Small Business Administration (SBA) to offer disaster loans to businesses that are damaged by things like floods, hurricanes, or wildfires. This bill adds "smoke" to that list, meaning wildfire smoke on its own — even without direct fire damage — would count as a qualifying disaster.

In practical terms, if wildfire smoke forces a small business to shut down or lose customers for days or weeks, the owner could apply for low-interest SBA disaster loans to help recover those losses. Currently, businesses that suffer smoke-related harm but no physical fire damage may not qualify for that help. This bill closes that gap.

The people most directly affected are small business owners in areas that experience heavy wildfire smoke, which tends to hit Western states like California, Oregon, Nevada, and Washington hardest, though smoke can travel across large regions. Customers, employees, and communities that depend on local small businesses could also feel an indirect benefit if those businesses are better able to stay open and recover after smoke events.
ai_headline: Senate bill would let wildfire smoke alone trigger SBA disaster loans
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship.

ai_sections.tldr: S 4532 adds wildfire smoke as a standalone disaster under the Small Business Act, opening SBA loan eligibility to smoke-affected businesses.

Customers, employees, and communities that rely on those businesses could also be indirectly affected.

title: Eastern Band of Cherokee Historic Lands Reacquisition Act
ai_summary:
This bill would transfer ownership of about 76 acres of federal land in Monroe County, Tennessee, along the shores of Tellico Reservoir, into a legal arrangement called a "trust." In a trust, the U.S. government holds the land on behalf of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, meaning the tribe controls and uses the land but the federal government technically owns it. The land includes the Sequoyah Birthplace Museum site, memorials to the Cherokee towns of Chota and Tanasi, and a support property. The bill also gives the tribe permanent easements, which are legal rights to use additional land nearby for walking trails connecting the memorial sites.

The land must be used for cultural and educational purposes, such as operating the Sequoyah museum, honoring Cherokee history, and maintaining memorials where ancestral remains were reburied. The Tennessee Valley Authority, which currently manages the land, would keep certain rights, including the ability to flood parts of the land temporarily, manage water levels in the reservoir, and enter the property for flood control and public health purposes. Any future construction by the tribe near the water would require TVA approval. The bill also clearly prohibits any gambling on these lands.

This bill mainly affects the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, a federally recognized tribe based in western North Carolina, and the Tennessee Valley Authority. It would also affect visitors to the museum and memorial sites. For most other Tennessee residents or the general public, the land would continue to be accessible as a cultural and recreational area, with no gaming allowed.
ai_headline: Federal bill would put 76 acres of Cherokee heritage land in trust
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Indian Affairs.

The bill also grants the tribe permanent easements for walking trails connecting the memorial sites.

title: To remove restrictions from a parcel of land in Paducah, Kentucky.
ai_summary:
This bill deals with a small piece of government land in Paducah, Kentucky. Back in 2012, the federal government gave the City of Paducah about 3.62 acres of land at 2956 Park Avenue, which was part of the Paducah Memorial Army Reserve Center. When the government handed over that land, it included a list of legal strings attached, such as rules about how the land could be used, easements, and other conditions written into the deed. This bill would direct the Secretary of the Interior to remove all of those restrictions.

Once those restrictions are lifted, the City of Paducah would have full control over what it does with the property. Right now, the conditions in the original deed limit the city's options. Removing them would give local officials more flexibility to sell, develop, or repurpose the land however they choose without needing to follow the federal rules that were attached in 2012.

This bill mainly affects the City of Paducah and residents of that area. It does not involve federal money or have any broad national impact. It is a routine type of legislation that Congress sometimes passes to clean up old property transfers and give local governments clear ownership of land that was previously handed down from the federal government.

title: CLEAN Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes it easier and faster to get permission to develop geothermal energy on federal land. Geothermal energy comes from heat inside the earth and can be used to generate electricity. Right now, the government holds sales where companies can bid on leases to develop that energy on public land. This bill would require those sales to happen at least once a year instead of once every two years. It also requires the government to hold a replacement sale in the same year if a scheduled sale gets canceled or delayed, so opportunities are not simply lost.

The bill also sets strict time limits on drilling permit applications. Once a company applies for a permit to drill a geothermal well, the government would have 30 days to tell them if their application is complete or explain what information is missing. Then, once the application is confirmed complete, the government would have another 30 days to issue a final decision. Currently, there are no firm deadlines like this, so the process can drag on for a long time.

This bill mainly affects energy companies interested in developing geothermal projects on federal land, federal land managers at the Department of the Interior, and states where geothermal resources exist, particularly in the western United States. Indirectly, it could affect local communities near potential geothermal projects and anyone who uses electricity, since geothermal is one source of power generation.
ai_headline: Federal geothermal leasing would move to annual sales under HR 1687
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources Subcommittee on Public Lands, Forests, and Mining. Hearings held.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 1687 requires yearly geothermal lease sales on federal land and sets 30-day deadlines on drilling permit decisions.
ai_sections.what: HR 1687 requires the federal government to hold geothermal lease sales on public land at least once a year, up from the current once every two years. If a sale is canceled or delayed, a replacement sale must be held in the same calendar year. The bill also sets two back-to-back 30-day deadlines for processing drilling permit applications: 30 days to confirm completeness and 30 more days to issue a final decision.
ai_sections.who: Energy companies seeking to develop geothermal projects on federal land and federal land managers at the Department of the Interior are directly affected. States in the western United States where geothermal resources exist, nearby local communities, and electricity users are also affected indirectly.
ai_sections.why: More frequent lease sales and firm permit deadlines would reduce the time companies wait to begin development on federal land. Because geothermal is one source of power generation, changes to its development pace could indirectly affect electricity supply in affected regions.

title: American Battlefield Protection Program Amendments Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill makes two main changes to a federal program that helps protect historic American battlefields. First, it extends the Battlefield Acquisition Grant Program through 2036, giving it eight more years of life beyond its current 2028 expiration. Second, it raises the federal share of funding for two grant programs — one for modernizing how battlefields are explained to visitors, and one for restoring battlefield landscapes — from 50 percent to 75 percent. That means grant recipients would need to come up with less of their own money to qualify for federal support. The bill also sets aside up to $2 million per year through 2036 for those two programs.

The bill also directs the National Park Service to study historic sites connected to two wars that currently get less attention: the French and Indian War (1754–1763) and the Mexican-American War (1846–1848). The agency would identify significant sites, assess threats to them, and suggest ways to protect and interpret them — including possibly making some of them official National Park units. The NPS would need to consult with state governors, local governments, tribal nations, and preservation groups during this process and report back to Congress within two years of receiving funding.

The people most directly affected are nonprofit preservation organizations, state and local governments, and tribal nations that apply for battlefield grants, since the cost-sharing change makes it easier for them to qualify. History enthusiasts, local communities near battlefield sites, and future visitors to those sites could also be affected, as the bill aims to better preserve and explain these places for the public.
ai_headline: Federal battlefield grant program extended to 2036 with higher funding match
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources Subcommittee on National Parks. Hearings held.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7618 extends battlefield grants to 2036 and raises the federal funding share from 50% to 75% for two grant programs.
ai_sections.what: HR 7618 extends the Battlefield Acquisition Grant Program eight years, from 2028 to 2036. It raises the federal share for two grant programs — one for modernizing battlefield interpretation and one for landscape restoration — from 50 percent to 75 percent, reducing the match recipients must provide. The bill also directs the National Park Service to study significant sites from the French and Indian War (1754–1763) and the Mexican-American War (1846–1848), assess threats, and suggest protection and interpretation options, including possible designation as National Park units.

ai_sections.why: The higher federal match lowers the financial barrier for eligible organizations seeking grants, which may increase the number or scale of funded projects. The NPS study could lead to formal recognition or protection of sites tied to two wars that currently receive less federal attention.
ai_sections.cost: The bill sets aside up to $2 million per year through 2036 for the battlefield interpretation and landscape restoration grant programs.

title: Crystal Reservoir Conveyance Act
ai_summary:
This bill would transfer ownership of Crystal Reservoir and about 45 acres of surrounding land in Ouray County, Colorado from the U.S. Forest Service to the City of Ouray. The property includes the reservoir itself, Full Moon Dam, related ditches, and all water rights that go with them. The transfer would be free of charge to the city, though Ouray would have to pay for any land surveys needed to complete the deal. The federal government would cover other administrative costs.

In exchange for receiving the land, the City of Ouray must agree to several conditions. The land must be kept as open space forever, with free public access for activities like fishing. No commercial development or major construction is allowed, except what is needed to maintain the dam and reservoir. The city also takes on full responsibility for repairing and maintaining the dam and related infrastructure going forward. If the city ever stops following these rules, the federal government has the right to take the land back.

This bill primarily affects residents of Ouray, Colorado, and anyone who uses Crystal Reservoir for recreation or depends on its water supply. Local taxpayers in Ouray would take on the ongoing costs of maintaining the dam and reservoir. Outdoor enthusiasts would keep free access to the area for fishing and other activities. Water users in the region would see the city gain direct control over the water rights, which would then be managed under Colorado state water law rather than federal oversight.
ai_headline: Federal land transfer gives Ouray, Colorado free ownership of Crystal Reservoir
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

If the city violates these conditions, the federal government retains the right to reclaim the property.

Outdoor enthusiasts would retain free access to the area for activities such as fishing, while the city would gain direct control over the water rights.

title: License to Drill Act
ai_summary:
When a company wants to drill for oil or gas on federal public land, it has to apply for a permit through the Bureau of Land Management, which is part of the Department of the Interior. Right now, applicants pay a fee when they submit that permit application. This bill would extend the deadline for collecting those fees from 2026 to 2037, keeping the program running for roughly another decade.

The bill also changes where that fee money goes. Under current law, only part of the collected fees went into a special fund called the BLM Permit Processing Improvement Fund, which is used to help the agency review and process permit applications faster. This bill directs all of the collected fees into that fund from 2027 through 2037, rather than splitting the money as before.

The people most directly affected are oil and gas companies that want to drill on federal land, since they pay the application fees. The Bureau of Land Management is also affected, because it would receive more funding to handle permit reviews. Indirectly, anyone who lives near or uses federal public lands, or who has an interest in energy production on those lands, could be affected by how quickly or slowly the government processes these drilling permits.
ai_headline: Oil and gas drilling permit fees on federal land extended to 2037
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7831 extends federal oil and gas permit application fees through 2037 and routes all fee revenue into the BLM processing fund from 2027 onward.
ai_sections.what: HR 7831 extends the deadline for collecting oil and gas permit application fees on federal public land from 2026 to 2037. Starting in 2027, all collected fees will go into the BLM Permit Processing Improvement Fund, replacing the previous split arrangement where only part of the fees entered that fund.
ai_sections.who: Oil and gas companies seeking to drill on federal land pay the application fees and are directly affected. The Bureau of Land Management, which reviews and processes those permits, receives the consolidated fee revenue under this bill.
ai_sections.why: Routing all fees into the processing fund could change how quickly the BLM is able to review permit applications. The pace of permit processing affects oil and gas companies, as well as people who live near or use federal public lands where drilling may occur.

title: Geothermal Energy Advancement Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates two new positions inside the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), which is the federal agency that manages public lands. First, it establishes a Geothermal Ombudsman, a single point-of-contact person appointed within 60 days of the law passing. That person's job is to help companies and developers navigate the federal permitting process for geothermal energy projects on public lands, settle disputes between applicants and BLM offices, and work to speed up how long permits take. Second, the bill creates a Geothermal Permitting Task Force, led by that same ombudsman, which can pull in staff from different government offices to help clear backlogs of permit applications. The ombudsman must send Congress an annual report on how well the permitting process is working.

Geothermal energy comes from heat beneath the earth's surface and can be used to generate electricity or heat buildings. Right now, getting a permit to build a geothermal project on federal land can take many years. This bill is aimed at reducing those delays by adding dedicated staff and better coordination across BLM offices. It does not change environmental review requirements or open new land to development on its own.

The bill most directly affects energy companies and developers looking to build geothermal projects on public lands, as well as BLM employees who handle those permits. More broadly, communities near public lands in geothermal-rich states like Nevada, California, Idaho, and Utah could eventually see more geothermal development activity if the permitting process becomes faster. Average Americans are not directly required to do anything under this bill.
ai_headline: BLM gets dedicated geothermal permit office and ombudsman under HR 5631
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 5631 adds a Geothermal Ombudsman and task force inside BLM to cut permitting delays for geothermal projects on public lands.

The ombudsman serves as a single point of contact for companies seeking permits, helps resolve disputes with BLM offices, and must send Congress an annual report on permitting performance. The bill does not change environmental review requirements or open new land to development on its own.

Communities near public lands in geothermal-active states such as Nevada, California, Idaho, and Utah could see increased development activity if permitting speeds up.
ai_sections.why: Geothermal permitting on federal land currently can take many years, and this bill is designed to reduce those delays through dedicated staffing and better coordination across BLM offices. Faster permitting could lead to more geothermal development in regions where that resource exists on public land.

title: Six Assurances to Taiwan Act
ai_summary:
This bill is about a set of promises the United States made to Taiwan back in 1982, known as the "Six Assurances." Those assurances basically said the U.S. would not stop selling Taiwan defensive weapons, would not let China have a say in those sales, would not pressure Taiwan to negotiate with China, and would not take a side on who officially owns Taiwan. The bill would write these assurances directly into law for the first time, making them an official, permanent statement of U.S. policy rather than just a long-standing tradition passed down from one administration to the next.

The bill also creates a new oversight process. If a president ever wants to take any action that goes against those assurances, such as stopping arms sales to Taiwan or pressuring Taiwan to negotiate with China, the president must first notify Congress. Congress would then have 30 to 60 days to review that decision. During that window, no government money can be spent carrying out the action unless Congress specifically approves it. Congress could also pass a resolution blocking the action entirely, and if they do, the president cannot move forward even if he vetoes the resolution and Congress overrides that veto.

The people most directly affected are policymakers in the executive branch, since it limits what a president can do regarding Taiwan without going through Congress first. More broadly, it affects U.S. relations with both Taiwan and China, and it matters to the roughly 23 million people living in Taiwan. American businesses and defense contractors involved in arms sales to Taiwan could also be affected, as could U.S. citizens generally, since Taiwan policy has significant implications for stability in Asia and the broader global economy.
ai_headline: Bill would write 1982 Taiwan arms pledges into permanent U.S. law
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Foreign Affairs, and in addition to the Committee on Rules, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 3452 codifies the Six Assurances on Taiwan into law and requires Congress to approve any presidential action against them.
ai_sections.what: HR 3452 would make the Six Assurances — U.S. commitments made to Taiwan in 1982 — official, permanent law rather than a tradition passed between administrations. Those assurances cover arms sales to Taiwan, preventing China from influencing those sales, and not taking a side on who officially owns Taiwan. The bill also creates an oversight process requiring the president to notify Congress before taking any action that conflicts with the assurances, with a 30-to-60-day review window during which no federal funds can be spent carrying out such an action without congressional approval.
ai_sections.who: Executive branch policymakers are most directly affected, since the bill limits presidential authority over Taiwan policy without prior congressional review. The roughly 23 million people living in Taiwan, U.S. defense contractors involved in arms sales, and the broader public are also affected given Taiwan's role in Asian stability and the global economy.
ai_sections.why: Codifying the assurances removes flexibility the executive branch has historically held to adjust Taiwan policy without legislative input. A president who wants to deviate from the assurances would face a congressional review process, and Congress could pass a resolution blocking the action entirely, even if the president vetoes it and the veto is overridden.

title: Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill makes two changes to US bankruptcy law by raising the debt limits that determine who qualifies for certain types of bankruptcy protection. For small businesses, it raises the ceiling on total debt from the previous limit to $7.5 million, allowing more small businesses to use a faster, cheaper bankruptcy process called Subchapter V, which is designed specifically to help small businesses reorganize and keep operating. For individual consumers, it raises the debt limit for Chapter 13 bankruptcy to $2.75 million, meaning more people with higher debt loads can use this process to set up a repayment plan instead of liquidating their assets.

Chapter 13 bankruptcy lets individuals with a steady income keep their property while paying back debts over three to five years under a court-approved plan. Subchapter V is a similar reorganization option for small businesses. Both are generally seen as more flexible options compared to other forms of bankruptcy. By raising the dollar thresholds, this bill lets people and businesses with more debt qualify for these paths, which they previously could not access.

This bill affects two main groups. First, small business owners whose debts exceed the old limit but fall under $7.5 million now have access to the simpler small business bankruptcy process. Second, individual consumers and married couples with significant debt who previously had too much debt to file Chapter 13 may now qualify. Publicly traded companies and their affiliates are specifically excluded from the small business provision.
ai_headline: Bankruptcy debt limits raised to $7.5M for small businesses, $2.75M for individuals
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 684.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7730 raises bankruptcy debt ceilings so more small businesses and individuals qualify for reorganization plans instead of liquidation.
ai_sections.what: HR 7730 raises the debt limit for small businesses using Subchapter V bankruptcy from the previous ceiling to $7.5 million, and raises the Chapter 13 debt limit for individuals to $2.75 million. Subchapter V is a faster, lower-cost reorganization process designed for small businesses. Chapter 13 allows individuals with steady income to repay debts over three to five years under a court-approved plan while keeping their property.
ai_sections.who: Small business owners with debts under $7.5 million now have access to the Subchapter V process, though publicly traded companies and their affiliates are excluded. Individual consumers and married couples with significant debt loads who previously exceeded the Chapter 13 limit may now qualify under the higher threshold.
ai_sections.why: By raising these thresholds, more debtors gain access to reorganization options rather than being forced into liquidation or other bankruptcy paths. The change expands eligibility without altering the underlying rules of either process.

title: Veteran and Spouse Licensing Flexibility Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would make it easier for veterans and their spouses to keep working in their licensed professions when they move to a new state after leaving the military. Right now, many professional licenses, like those for nurses, electricians, teachers, or cosmetologists, are issued by individual states and do not automatically transfer when someone moves. This bill would require states to accept a valid out-of-state license as good enough to work, as long as the veteran or spouse moves within 36 months of the veteran's discharge date and submits a simple application. If a state cannot process the transfer within 30 days, it must issue a temporary license so the person can keep working in the meantime.

To qualify, the license has to be in good standing, meaning it has never been revoked, is not under investigation, and was not surrendered while the person was in trouble. The veteran or spouse also has to sign a sworn statement saying they meet the new state's rules and that everything in their application is true. States can still run a background check before approving the transfer. Spouses must be named on the veteran's official military discharge paperwork to qualify.

This bill would affect honorably discharged veterans and their spouses who hold professional licenses and relocate after leaving active military service. It would also affect state licensing boards, which would be required to honor those out-of-state licenses rather than putting applicants through a full new licensing process.
ai_headline: HR 5035 would let veterans and spouses transfer licenses across state lines
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 5035 requires states to accept out-of-state professional licenses from honorably discharged veterans and their spouses who relocate within 36 months of discharge.
ai_sections.what: HR 5035 requires states to recognize a valid out-of-state professional license held by an honorably discharged veteran or their spouse, rather than putting them through a full new licensing process. The applicant must submit a simple application and a sworn statement confirming they meet the new state's rules. If a state cannot process the transfer within 30 days, it must issue a temporary license so the person can continue working.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects honorably discharged veterans and their spouses who hold professional licenses and relocate after leaving active military service. It also affects state licensing boards, which would be required to honor qualifying out-of-state licenses.
ai_sections.why: Veterans and military spouses who move across state lines currently risk losing the ability to work in their licensed profession while they complete a full new licensing process in each state. Under this bill, states would be bound by a 30-day processing window and a mandate to accept qualifying licenses, changing how licensing boards handle these applicants.

title: Stronger Communities through Better Transit Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new federal grant program to help pay for the day-to-day operating costs of public transportation systems across the country. Right now, most federal transit money can only be used to buy equipment like buses and trains, not to cover everyday expenses like driver salaries, fuel, and maintenance. This program would authorize up to 20 billion dollars per year from 2025 through 2028 to help transit agencies keep buses and trains running, run them more often, expand their routes and hours, and improve things like scheduling apps, safety, and cleanliness. The federal government would cover up to 50 percent of those costs, though areas with high poverty rates could receive up to 80 percent, and Native American tribes would receive full federal funding.

The bill requires that most of the money go toward communities that are low-income, minority, or otherwise lacking good transit access. Transit agencies that receive the money must survey their riders and local residents at least every two years to find out what improvements people actually want. Agencies must also keep spending at least as much of their own money on transit as they already do, so federal funds add to existing service rather than replacing local spending. The bill also raises the federal share of operating costs for rural transit systems from the current 50 percent to 80 percent.

The people most directly affected include riders of city buses, subway systems, and rural transit services, especially those who depend on public transit to get to work, medical appointments, grocery stores, and schools. Transit agency employees and local governments would also be affected, since the grants would help agencies maintain or expand their workforce and routes without putting as much financial pressure on local budgets.
ai_headline: Federal bill would fund daily transit operations up to $20B a year
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.

Current federal transit funding is largely limited to equipment purchases like buses and trains. The bill would also raise the federal share of rural transit operating costs from 50 percent to 80 percent.

Agencies must maintain their existing local spending levels so federal money supplements rather than displaces current transit budgets.
ai_sections.cost: The program would authorize up to $20 billion per year from 2025 through 2028. The federal government would cover up to 50 percent of operating costs for most agencies, up to 80 percent for high-poverty areas, and 100 percent for Native American tribes.

title: Veterans Protection from Fraud Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill changes federal law to give tougher punishments to people who commit fraud or telemarketing scams when their victims are military veterans. Right now, federal law already has extra penalties for scammers who target elderly people or people with serious disabilities. This bill adds veterans as a third protected group under that same law, meaning a criminal who specifically goes after veterans could face a longer prison sentence or larger fines than they otherwise would.

The bill affects two main groups. First, it affects military veterans across the country, who would gain stronger legal protection if they are deliberately targeted by scammers or fraudulent telemarketers. Second, it affects anyone convicted of fraud or telemarketing crimes, since deliberately targeting veterans would now be treated as an aggravating factor that increases their potential punishment under federal law.

It is worth noting this is an introduced bill, meaning it has been proposed and sent to the House Judiciary Committee but has not yet been voted on or become law. If it passes, federal prosecutors would be able to seek harsher sentences when they can show a scammer intentionally chose veterans as their victims.
ai_headline: Proposed bill would add veterans to federal fraud sentencing protections
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8601 would make deliberately targeting military veterans in fraud or telemarketing scams a federal aggravating factor, increasing potential sentences.
ai_sections.what: HR 8601 would add military veterans as a protected group under existing federal law that already imposes extra penalties for scams targeting elderly people or people with serious disabilities. If a scammer deliberately chose veterans as victims, that would be treated as an aggravating factor, allowing federal prosecutors to seek longer prison sentences or larger fines. The bill has been introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee but has not been voted on or become law.
ai_sections.who: Military veterans nationwide would gain stronger federal legal protection against fraud and telemarketing scams that deliberately target them. Anyone convicted of fraud or telemarketing crimes would face increased potential punishment if prosecutors can show veterans were intentionally chosen as victims.
ai_sections.why: Adding veterans to the existing aggravating-factor statute extends the same sentencing enhancement framework already applied in cases involving elderly victims or people with serious disabilities. Federal prosecutors would have a legal basis to seek harsher sentences when intentional targeting of veterans can be demonstrated.

title: Geo POWER Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Department of Energy to create a new program called the Milestone-Based Geothermal Demonstration Program. Geothermal energy uses heat from inside the Earth to generate electricity, but it has mostly been used in places like the American West where hot rock is easy to reach. This bill focuses on harder-to-reach underground rock formations found in many other parts of the country. The government would give funding to private companies in stages, releasing money only when each project hits specific technical and financial goals, rather than all at once upfront.

The program must fund at least three different projects in at least three different states, and no single company can receive all the awards. Priority goes to areas that currently have little or no geothermal power, including lands belonging to Native American tribes. Projects must show the potential to generate at least 30 megawatts of electricity, which is enough to power tens of thousands of homes. The data gathered from these projects would be made public so future private investors can better understand the risks and opportunities of geothermal energy in new regions.

This bill mainly affects energy companies and developers interested in geothermal technology, the communities and workers in regions where these demonstration projects get built, and Native American tribes on whose land some projects may be sited. Taxpayers fund the program, though no specific dollar amount is set in the bill. If successful, the long-term effect could be broader access to geothermal electricity generation across more of the United States.
ai_headline: Bill would fund staged geothermal projects in at least three states
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute (Amended) by Voice Vote.

title: PUPP Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the PUPP Act of 2025, would create a federal grant program run by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The grants would go to local governments, nonprofits, and homeless shelter organizations to help them build, renovate, or convert buildings into shelters and permanent housing that allow residents to keep their pets. The program would be authorized to spend up to $5 million per year from 2026 through 2030. Grant money could also be used to train staff in pet care and to cover the ongoing costs of housing animals on-site.

Any housing funded by these grants would have to meet certain standards. It would need to offer residents access to supportive services like mental health care, job assistance, and substance use treatment. It would also have to provide basic veterinary care for pets, including vaccines, spay and neuter services, and flea and tick prevention. If services cannot be provided on-site, the housing operator would need to arrange transportation so residents can still access them.

The people most directly affected are homeless individuals and families who have pets such as dogs, cats, rabbits, birds, or small animals. Currently, many traditional shelters do not accept pets, which can lead some people to avoid shelters rather than give up their animals. This bill is also relevant to local governments, nonprofits, and shelter operators who would be eligible to apply for the grants, as well as veterinary providers who might partner with those organizations to deliver animal care.
ai_headline: Federal grants would fund pet-friendly shelters for homeless residents
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Agriculture, and in addition to the Committee on Financial Services, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.why: Because many traditional shelters do not allow pets, some people experiencing homelessness currently avoid shelters rather than give up their animals. This bill would create a funding pathway intended to change that dynamic by making pet-inclusive housing a supported option.
ai_sections.cost: The program would be authorized to spend up to $5 million per year from 2026 through 2030, with funds distributed through USDA grants to eligible local governments, nonprofits, and shelter organizations.

title: Reproductive Rights are Human Rights Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would change what information the U.S. State Department is required to include in its annual human rights reports, which it publishes every year for countries around the world. Right now, those reports cover topics like freedom of speech, torture, and voting rights. This bill would make it a legal requirement to also include a dedicated section on reproductive rights in each country. That section would have to cover things like whether people can access contraception, what abortion laws exist, rates of pregnancy-related deaths, and whether people face coercion or discrimination related to reproduction, such as forced sterilization or forced pregnancy.

The bill focuses entirely on how other countries are reported on, not on changing any U.S. domestic laws or policies. It would require State Department officials to gather input from health organizations, local nonprofits, and other experts when writing those sections. The reports would also need to track whether certain groups, including people with disabilities, LGBTQI+ individuals, and people of different racial or ethnic backgrounds, face unequal access to reproductive health care in each country.

The people most directly affected by this bill would be State Department employees who write these annual reports, since they would have new required topics to research and include. Indirectly, the bill could affect U.S. foreign policy decisions, since these human rights reports are often used to guide aid and diplomatic relationships with other countries. People living in other countries, particularly women, girls, and other groups mentioned in the bill, could also be affected if changes in how the U.S. tracks and reports on these issues influences international pressure or funding.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs.

title: Access to Birth Control Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require pharmacies across the country to fill prescriptions and sell FDA-approved birth control products without unnecessary delays. If a pharmacy has the contraceptive in stock, it must provide it promptly. If it is out of stock, the pharmacy must tell the customer right away and either help transfer the prescription to a nearby pharmacy that has it or order it quickly. The bill also prohibits pharmacy staff from harassing customers seeking birth control, lying about whether a product is available, or refusing to return a valid prescription to a customer.

A pharmacy can still legally refuse to fill a contraceptive prescription in a few specific situations, such as when no valid prescription is presented, when the customer cannot pay, or when a pharmacist has a genuine medical or clinical reason to refuse based on professional judgment. However, a personal or religious objection by a pharmacist is not listed as an acceptable reason for refusal under this bill. States can still keep or create their own laws on this topic, as long as those laws give customers at least as many protections as this federal bill does.

This bill would affect retail pharmacies of all sizes that sell prescription drugs and their employees. It would also affect any customer trying to obtain birth control or related medications, including emergency contraception. Pharmacies that violate the rules could face fines up to $1,000 per day and could be sued by affected customers for damages and legal fees.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: American Lending Fairness Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill deals with interest rate rules for banks and credit unions. Under current federal law, when a bank or credit union makes a loan, it can generally charge the interest rate allowed in the state where it is chartered (licensed), even if the borrower lives in a different state with lower rate limits. Some states have passed laws trying to opt out of this federal rule entirely, but the bill's sponsors say those state opt-outs have been applied too broadly. This bill clarifies that a state can only opt out for loans made by banks and credit unions that are actually chartered in that state, not for loans coming in from out-of-state lenders.

In practical terms, this means a state cannot use an opt-out to block out-of-state banks from charging their home-state interest rates to that state's residents. If a state wants stricter interest rate limits, those rules would only apply to the banks and credit unions the state itself licenses. Out-of-state lenders would still follow their home state's rules.

This bill most directly affects banks, credit unions, and borrowers who take out loans, particularly personal loans, where interest rates vary significantly by state. Borrowers in states with strict interest rate caps might still receive loan offers from out-of-state lenders at higher rates. State governments that have tried to set interest rate limits across the board would see their authority narrowed under this bill.
ai_headline: Bill limits how far states can go in capping out-of-state bank loan rates
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

The bill specifies that a state's opt-out from this federal rule applies only to lenders the state itself charters, not to out-of-state lenders. States that have tried to apply opt-outs broadly would see that authority narrowed.

title: Justice for the Living Victims of Lockerbie Act
ai_summary:
This bill would set up a special government fund to pay compensation to a very specific group of people: Americans who worked for Pan American World Airways on December 3, 1991, were at least 45 years old at that time, and were part of a lawsuit filed against Libya over terrorism. To qualify, a person also had to still be alive as of August 14, 2008. This group is connected to Libyan state-sponsored terrorism, which includes the 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland, and related incidents. The bill would put $42,066,338 into a trust fund, and that money would be split equally among everyone whose claim is approved.

The process would work like this: a federal agency called the Foreign Claims Settlement Commission would announce a claims process within 30 days of the bill becoming law. Eligible people would have 60 days to file a claim. The Commission would then review each claim and decide who qualifies. Approved claims would be sent to the Treasury Department, which would issue payments. If a qualifying person has already died, a legal representative of their estate could file on their behalf.

The people most directly affected are a small, narrowly defined group of former Pan Am employees who survived Libyan terrorism and participated in a specific federal lawsuit in the 1990s. Because the bill sets a fixed total dollar amount divided equally among all approved claimants, the individual payment each person receives depends on how many people successfully file claims. U.S. taxpayers would fund the payments through the federal Treasury.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs.

title: FAIR Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires hospitals that have medical residency training programs to report certain information to the federal government. Specifically, hospitals would need to report how many applicants they received from two types of medical schools, osteopathic (DO) and allopathic (MD), and how many from each group were actually accepted. Hospitals would also need to confirm that they consider applicants from both types of schools, and that if they require a licensing exam score, they accept either the DO exam or the MD exam. If a hospital fails to submit this information, its Medicare payments could be reduced by 2 percent for each year it did not comply, starting in October 2026.

The bill affects two main groups. First, it affects hospitals with residency training programs, which are the post-medical-school training positions that new doctors must complete before practicing on their own. Second, it affects medical school graduates, particularly those from osteopathic medical schools, who have historically faced some barriers when competing for residency spots alongside graduates from traditional allopathic medical schools. The bill does not force hospitals to accept any specific number of applicants from either type of school.

The information hospitals report would be posted publicly online, so applicants, researchers, and the general public could see how different hospitals handle applications from both types of graduates. The bill specifically states it is not creating a quota system or taking over medical education, but rather creating transparency and accountability in the process.

The reported information would be posted publicly online for applicants, researchers, and the general public to view.

title: Providing Veterans Essential Medications Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to help cover the cost of expensive medications for veterans living in state veterans homes. Right now, the VA pays a set daily rate to these state-run nursing facilities for each veteran's care, but that flat payment does not always cover the full cost of high-priced drugs. Under this bill, if a medication costs more than 8.5% of that monthly care payment, the VA must either pay the state home back for that drug or send the medication directly to the facility.

The bill sets a clear definition for what counts as a "costly medication." Specifically, it applies when the average wholesale price of a one-month supply of a drug, plus a 3% transaction fee, goes above that 8.5% threshold. State homes can choose whether they want to be reimbursed in cash or receive the medication directly from the VA.

The people most directly affected are veterans who live in state-run veterans nursing homes and currently need expensive medications as part of their care. State home administrators would also be affected, since they would have a new option to recover costs they may currently be absorbing on their own. The bill does not affect veterans in VA-run facilities or those living independently.
ai_headline: VA bill would cover costly drug expenses at state veterans nursing homes
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Health.

Currently, the VA pays a flat daily rate to these facilities that does not always cover the full cost of high-priced drugs.
