title: LNG Public Interest Determination Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would change the rules for approving exports of liquefied natural gas, commonly called LNG, from the United States. Right now, the federal government can approve LNG export applications fairly quickly, and some approvals skip detailed environmental review entirely. Under this bill, the Department of Energy would be required to study three specific things before approving any LNG export: whether the exports would significantly contribute to climate change, whether they would raise energy prices for Americans, and whether nearby communities, particularly low-income, minority, and rural communities, would be unfairly burdened by negative health or environmental effects. The government would have one year after completing those studies to make a final decision on each export application.

The bill also removes a current regulatory shortcut that allows some LNG export decisions to skip full environmental review under federal law. It would require the Energy Department to write new rules within one year of the bill becoming law, and it would give the public, including people with language barriers or disabilities, a formal chance to weigh in before any export is approved.

The people most directly affected would be energy companies that want to export natural gas, since they would face a more detailed and potentially longer approval process. American consumers could also be affected, because the bill specifically requires the government to study how exports impact home energy bills for low-income households, small businesses, manufacturers, and others. Communities located near LNG terminals or pipelines, often called fence-line communities, would have new legal protections and a stronger voice in the approval process.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: RESEARCHER Act
ai_summary:
This bill targets a specific problem: graduate students and postdoctoral researchers at universities often earn low stipends that make it hard to cover basic living costs. The bill directs the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy to create a set of guidelines, within six months, for federal agencies that fund research. Those guidelines would push agencies to look for ways to raise stipends, tie pay to local cost of living, and improve access to health care, housing, transportation, food assistance, and child care for these researchers. Federal research agencies would then be required to use those guidelines to build their own concrete policies and share them with universities receiving federal research money.

The bill also orders several rounds of fact-finding. The National Science Foundation would fund outside research to collect data on financial hardship among these researchers, broken down by demographics. The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine would conduct a formal study comparing researcher stipends to actual local costs for things like housing, food, and child care. The Government Accountability Office would separately review how well federal agencies actually followed through on the new guidelines. Congress would receive regular reports on all of this.

The people most directly affected are graduate students and postdoctoral researchers working at colleges and universities that get federal research funding. Universities themselves, and the federal agencies that hand out research grants, would also need to adjust their policies. The bill does not guarantee any specific pay raise; it sets up a process to study the problem and create consistent standards across agencies, which could eventually lead to higher pay and better benefits for these researchers.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology.

title: Rosie the Riveter Commemorative Coin Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Treasury to create special commemorative coins in 2028 honoring the American women who worked on the "Home Front" during World War II, often symbolized by the famous "Rosie the Riveter" image. Three types of coins would be made: a gold $5 coin, a silver $1 coin, and a half-dollar coin. These are collector's coins, not meant for everyday spending, and they would only be sold during the year 2028.

When someone buys one of these coins, the price includes the coin's face value, production costs, and an extra fee called a surcharge. Those surcharges go directly to the Rosie the Riveter Trust, a nonprofit organization that supports the Rosie the Riveter WWII Home Front National Historical Park in Richmond, California, as well as related educational programs. The bill is written so that the government does not lose any money on the program. Taxpayers do not fund the coins; buyers do.

This bill mainly affects coin collectors and history enthusiasts who choose to purchase the coins, as well as the Rosie the Riveter Trust, which would receive the extra fees from sales. It has no impact on people who do not buy the coins. The U.S. Mint would handle production, and the coins' designs would be chosen in consultation with the Rosie the Riveter Trust and arts advisory groups.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

title: BOP Release Card ID Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill requires the federal Bureau of Prisons to give every U.S. citizen a photo ID card when they are released from a federal prison. The card must meet federal REAL ID standards and must remain valid for at least 18 months after release. The Bureau of Prisons has 180 days from the bill becoming law to put this system in place.

The ID card would be accepted as official proof of identity for a wide range of federal programs and agencies. That includes Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, food stamps, federal housing programs, veterans benefits, Department of Education programs, and entry into federal buildings. The Bureau of Prisons would also work with individual states to see if those states will accept the card when someone applies for a state-issued ID, like a driver's license. The Attorney General would also issue guidance to help states create similar ID programs for people leaving state prisons.

This bill directly affects people leaving federal prison, who often have no valid ID when they are released, making it harder to access housing, benefits, employment, and government services. It also affects the Bureau of Prisons, which would be responsible for creating and managing the card program, and federal agencies that would be required to accept the card. State governments would be encouraged, but not required, to participate in a similar system for people leaving state prisons.

title: To amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to provide a credit for increasing wages paid to child care providers.
ai_summary:
This bill creates a new federal tax credit for businesses that employ child care workers and raise those workers' wages. If an employer increases the average hourly pay of its child care staff compared to the previous year, it can claim a tax credit worth 5% of the total wages paid to those workers. Employers in rural areas get a slightly higher credit of 7%. The credit only kicks in if wages actually go up year over year, so it is designed to reward pay increases rather than just paying workers at the same rate.

The businesses that would be directly affected are licensed child care facilities that serve at least six children and receive some form of payment, whether from parents, government programs, or grants. These could include day care centers, preschools, and similar operations. The workers who could benefit are the employees at those facilities who directly provide care, education, or supervision to children.

The practical effect on families and the broader public is indirect. By giving employers a financial incentive to raise wages, the bill aims to make child care jobs more attractive, which could help facilities hire and keep more workers and potentially expand the supply of child care slots. Child care workers themselves, who are generally paid low wages, could see higher pay if their employers choose to use the credit. The credit is structured as part of the existing general business credit system, and employers can also receive it as a direct payment from the government in some cases.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: Nigeria Religious Freedom and Accountability Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill requires the U.S. Secretary of State to write a detailed report within 90 days of the law passing, and then every year after that, about what the United States is doing to address religious violence and persecution in Nigeria. The report must cover things like whether Nigeria is punishing the people responsible for attacks, whether U.S. aid money might accidentally be helping those causing harm, how displaced people are being cared for, and whether Nigeria is moving toward repealing laws that allow people to be imprisoned or executed for blasphemy. The reporting requirement continues as long as Nigeria holds a "Country of Particular Concern" designation under U.S. religious freedom law.

The bill also lays out the opinion of Congress, known as a "sense of Congress," on several related matters. It expresses support for considering sanctions, including travel bans and asset freezes, against specific groups and individuals connected to the violence. It calls on the State Department to look at whether certain armed Fulani militias should be formally labeled as foreign terrorist organizations, and it encourages the U.S. to work with Nigeria and other countries to reduce violence and support affected communities.

The people most directly affected by this bill are U.S. foreign policy and State Department officials, who would be required to produce and act on these reports. Indirectly, it concerns Nigerians experiencing religious violence, displaced persons, and organizations currently receiving or potentially receiving U.S. humanitarian aid in Nigeria. It does not create new spending or directly change U.S. law toward American residents, but it could influence how U.S. foreign assistance to Nigeria is shaped going forward.

title: ADAS Functionality and Integrity Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) to create official guidelines about how driver-assistance safety features in cars — things like automatic emergency braking, lane-keeping assist, and blind-spot warnings — should behave after a vehicle has been modified or repaired. Right now, there are no standard rules for how these systems need to be checked or recalibrated when someone, say, lifts their truck, changes their tires, or gets into a collision repair. The bill gives NHTSA two years to publish those guidelines, and it requires a study to be completed within one year to figure out what those guidelines should look like. Starting with 2028 model year vehicles, car makers would also have to share technical information with owners and NHTSA about how their systems handle modifications.

The guidelines would cover things like how much a vehicle's height, wheel size, or sensor position can change before safety features stop working correctly, and what steps mechanics should follow to make sure those features still work after any changes. Independent repair shops and car owners would get clear testing procedures they can use to confirm the safety systems are functioning properly. Car makers who do not meet these guidelines could face financial penalties under existing federal law.

This bill affects a wide range of people. Car owners who customize or modify their vehicles would benefit from clearer information about what changes are safe. Independent auto repair shops would have standardized procedures to follow. Car manufacturers would face new reporting and compliance requirements. And everyday drivers who rely on modern safety features would generally benefit from knowing those systems work correctly even after their car has been serviced or altered.
ai_headline: Federal safety rules would govern driver-assist systems after vehicle repairs
last_action_text: Forwarded by Subcommittee to Full Committee by Voice Vote.

title: FED UP with Bleeding Disorders Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill directs the federal government to take a closer look at bleeding disorders, especially in women, girls, and underserved communities. The Department of Health and Human Services would be required to review existing research, doctor training, and access to treatment for people with conditions like hemophilia and von Willebrand disease. Within two years, they must publish a public report with findings and recommendations, and they must accept public comments during the process. The goal is to figure out where gaps exist and how different federal agencies can better work together on this issue.

The bill also creates a national public education campaign targeting both patients and healthcare providers such as pediatricians, OB-GYNs, and school nurses. The campaign would be designed to reach people in rural and underserved areas and would include materials in different languages and cultural contexts. It would also share information with schools, health departments, and medical facilities. The government would track whether the campaign is actually working and report back to Congress.

The people most directly affected are women and girls with bleeding disorders, particularly those who have gone undiagnosed or who live in areas with limited healthcare access. Doctors and other medical providers would also be targeted, since the bill highlights that many patients wait over 16 years for a correct diagnosis. Up to 50 million dollars over five years is authorized to fund the awareness campaign portion of the bill.
ai_headline: Federal bill targets bleeding disorder gaps for women and underserved groups
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: End Diaper Need Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill does two main things. First, it adds $200 million per year in federal funding from 2026 through 2029, channeled through an existing program called the Social Services Block Grant, specifically to help pay for diapers and related supplies. States would receive this money and pass it along to local organizations, nonprofits, and diaper banks, which would then distribute free diapers and supplies to families who need them. The bill also covers adult incontinence products for low-income adults and people with disabilities who need them. To qualify as a low-income family under this bill, a household must earn no more than twice the federal poverty level.

Second, the bill changes tax rules so that people with Health Savings Accounts (HSAs), Medical Savings Accounts, Health Flexible Spending Accounts, and Health Reimbursement Arrangements can use those pre-tax funds to pay for medically necessary diapers and diapering supplies. This would apply to people of any age who need diapers for medical reasons, such as a diagnosed bladder or bowel condition or a severe skin disorder.

The people most directly affected are low-income families with babies and toddlers, children with complex medical conditions who require diapers past age three, and low-income adults or adults with disabilities who rely on incontinence products. People who have employer-sponsored tax-advantaged health accounts and face medical diapering needs would also benefit from the tax change. The bill requires states to report yearly data on how the money was spent and who received help, and it calls for an independent study to measure the program's health outcomes.
ai_headline: Federal bill would fund free diapers for low-income families and ease HSA rules
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Ways and Means, and in addition to the Committee on the Budget, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

title: Seniors’ Access to Critical Medications Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill creates a temporary exception to an existing Medicare rule called the "Stark Law," which normally prevents doctors from referring patients to health services in which the doctor has a financial interest. Starting January 1, 2026, and running through December 31, 2030, doctors and their medical group practices would be allowed to dispense certain Medicare Part D prescription drugs directly from their own offices and bill Medicare for them. To qualify, the patient must have an ongoing relationship with the doctor, must have had at least one in-person visit with that practice in the past year, and the drugs must be prescribed and dispensed by the same doctor or practice. Patients could pick up the medications in person or receive them by mail or delivery.

This bill primarily affects Medicare beneficiaries, who are mostly Americans aged 65 and older or people with certain disabilities. It could make it easier for some patients to get their medications directly from their doctor's office rather than going to a separate pharmacy. Doctors and medical group practices that choose to dispense medications in-house would also be significantly affected, as they would gain a new way to provide and bill for prescription drugs under Medicare.

The bill also requires the Government Accountability Office, an independent federal watchdog agency, to study and report to Congress within three years on how physician offices are integrating drug dispensing into their practices. This study is meant to monitor whether the new exception leads to unusual prescribing patterns or potential conflicts of interest. The bill also slightly reduces a Medicare improvement fund by $18 million, likely to help offset costs.
ai_headline: Medicare doctors could dispense drugs in-office under five-year Stark Law waiver
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported by the Yeas and Nays: 38 - 7.

title: Fair Competition for Small Business Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes a federal law called the Clayton Act to give state attorneys general a new legal tool. Right now, state attorneys general can sue big companies on behalf of their state's residents when those companies break antitrust rules under the Sherman Act. This bill adds another law to that list — the Robinson-Patman Act — which is the federal rule that bans large suppliers from charging different prices to different buyers in ways that hurt competition. In plain terms, if a big supplier charges a small store much higher prices than it charges a giant retailer for the same product, that could be price discrimination under the Robinson-Patman Act.

With this change, a state attorney general could take a company to court and seek money damages on behalf of residents harmed by that kind of pricing. Before this bill, enforcing the Robinson-Patman Act was mostly left to private lawsuits or the federal government. This bill opens a new door at the state level.

The people most directly affected are small and independent businesses — like local grocery stores, pharmacies, or hardware shops — that compete against large chain retailers. If those small businesses are being priced out because suppliers give massive discounts only to big-box stores, their state's attorney general could now fight back in court on their behalf. Everyday consumers could also be affected, since the idea behind the law is that fairer competition among businesses can lead to more choices and better prices.
ai_headline: State attorneys general gain power to sue over supplier price discrimination
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.what: HR 6830 amends the Clayton Act to add the Robinson-Patman Act to the list of laws that state attorneys general can enforce through lawsuits. The Robinson-Patman Act prohibits large suppliers from charging different prices to different buyers in ways that harm competition. State attorneys general could now seek money damages in court on behalf of residents harmed by such pricing.

This change opens a new avenue for states to act when suppliers offer large discounts exclusively to big-box retailers in ways that disadvantage smaller competitors.

title: College for All Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 3543, the College for All Act of 2025, would create a program where the federal government partners with states to eliminate tuition and required fees at public colleges and universities. Starting in the 2026-2027 school year, the federal government would cover the full cost at first, then gradually shift so states pay 20 percent and the federal government covers 80 percent by 2030. Community colleges would be fully free for all qualifying students, while public four-year universities would be free for students from families earning up to $150,000 for single-parent or single households, or $300,000 for two-parent or married households. Tribal colleges would receive 100 percent federal funding. Private nonprofit Historically Black Colleges and Universities and other minority-serving institutions would also receive grants to eliminate tuition for eligible students.

The bill comes with rules that states must follow to receive the money. States cannot reduce their own higher education spending, must maintain support for need-based financial aid, and cannot use the new federal money to replace existing state funds. Schools would be required to improve transfer credit policies so community college credits count toward four-year degrees, and at least 75 percent of classes must be taught by tenured or tenure-track faculty within five years. The bill also increases Pell Grant support and provides extra funding to schools that serve low-income and first-generation students.

This bill would affect a wide range of people. Students attending public community colleges or four-year universities, particularly those from low- and middle-income families, would potentially pay no tuition. Undocumented students who qualify for in-state tuition under state law would also be eligible. College faculty, especially part-time instructors, could see improved pay and job stability. State governments would need to meet spending requirements to participate. The bill has not yet passed and would need approval from both the House and Senate to become law.
ai_headline: Federal bill would eliminate tuition at public colleges for millions of students
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce, and in addition to the Committees on Ways and Means, and the Budget, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

title: Encouraging States to establish "Veterans Tax Relief Weekends" that coincide with Memorial Day, Independence Day, and Veterans Day, providing a practical way for communities across the country to recognize the service of veterans and members of the Armed Forces by providing financial relief to them.
ai_summary:
This resolution asks states to consider creating special "Veterans Tax Relief Weekends" around Memorial Day, Independence Day, and Veterans Day. During these three-day windows, veterans, active-duty military members, reservists, and National Guard members would be exempt from paying state sales tax on their purchases. Congress is not ordering states to do this — it is simply expressing its opinion that it would be a good idea and encouraging states to act on their own.

Because this is a "sense of Congress" resolution, it does not create any new law, require any state to act, or spend any federal money. It carries no legal force. It is more like an official statement of support, similar to how Congress might pass a resolution honoring a sports team or recognizing a historical event. States already run similar sales tax holidays for things like back-to-school shopping, so the concept is familiar.

The people most directly affected would be the roughly 18 million veterans living in the U.S., along with active-duty service members and their families. If a state chose to follow this suggestion, those groups would simply pay less at the register during those holiday weekends. Everyday shoppers who are not veterans would not receive the tax break. State governments would see a small reduction in sales tax revenue on those days if they chose to participate.
ai_headline: House resolution urges states to offer veterans sales tax breaks on holiday weekends
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: NSF AI Education Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill directs the National Science Foundation (NSF) to create and expand programs that help students, teachers, and workers learn about artificial intelligence (AI). It would allow NSF to give scholarships and fellowships to college and community college students studying AI, covering tuition, fees, and living expenses for up to five years. It also sets up fellowships for K-12 teachers, school counselors, and industry professionals so they can get trained in AI and then bring those skills back to classrooms or workplaces. NSF would also be required to run a nationwide outreach campaign so more people know these opportunities exist, with a special focus on reaching rural schools, tribal colleges, and schools in areas that traditionally get less federal research funding.

The bill also creates up to eight "Centers of AI Excellence" at community colleges and career and technical education schools across different regions of the country. These centers would develop best practices for teaching AI, connect students with internships and apprenticeships, and help identify new types of jobs being created by AI. They would be required to track their results and report back to Congress. Separately, NSF could fund research on how to best teach AI to students from pre-kindergarten through 12th grade, studying which teaching methods actually work and how AI affects student learning.

The people most directly affected are college and community college students interested in AI careers, K-12 teachers and school counselors, industry professionals who want to teach or get retrained, and schools in rural or underserved areas that often miss out on federal programs. Indirectly, it could affect K-12 students nationwide if their teachers receive AI training funded by these programs.

title: Biomanufacturing Excellence Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new National Biopharmaceutical Manufacturing Center of Excellence, run through the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The government would award up to $120 million to one qualifying organization, such as a university, a public-private partnership, or a group of those entities working together. That organization would build and operate a facility focused on improving how the United States makes biopharmaceuticals, which are medicines made using living cells or biological organisms, like certain vaccines, insulin, and cancer treatments. The center would work on making that manufacturing process faster, cheaper, and less dependent on foreign countries for supplies and equipment.

The center would also serve as a hub for research and collaboration, bringing together universities, pharmaceutical companies of all sizes, nonprofits, and government agencies. A key part of its mission is helping new manufacturing ideas move from the laboratory stage to large-scale commercial production, which is currently one of the biggest challenges American biotech companies face. The center would also be required to share its findings and best practices with other parts of the federal government and make progress reports to Congress and the public.

The people most directly affected include workers in the biotechnology and pharmaceutical industries, since the bill includes funding for job training programs to help people learn the skills needed in this field. American drug and biotech companies, especially smaller ones trying to scale up their products, could benefit from access to shared research and facilities. More broadly, the bill is aimed at making the United States more self-sufficient in producing medicines and reducing reliance on foreign manufacturing.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology.

title: Preserving Social Security and Medicare for Citizens Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would change who is allowed to receive Social Security and Medicare benefits. Under current law, some non-citizens in certain immigration categories can qualify for these programs. This bill would limit Social Security benefits to only U.S. citizens, U.S. nationals, and immigrants who have been granted lawful permanent residence (green card holders). It would also apply similar restrictions to Medicare eligibility. These changes would take effect for benefit payments starting after the bill becomes law.

The bill also makes a change to payroll taxes. Right now, certain groups of workers are exempt from paying Social Security and Medicare taxes through their paychecks. The bill would remove those exemptions, meaning more workers would have to pay into these programs through FICA taxes, even if they would not qualify to receive the benefits.

The people most directly affected would be non-citizens who currently receive or expect to receive Social Security or Medicare benefits but are not green card holders or citizens. This could include some visa holders and other immigrants in specific legal categories. Workers who were previously exempt from payroll taxes, such as certain temporary visa workers, would also be affected because they would start having money withheld from their paychecks for Social Security and Medicare. U.S. citizens and green card holders would not see changes to their eligibility under this bill.
ai_headline: Bill would bar most non-citizens from Social Security and Medicare

title: To amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to exempt qualified student loan bonds from the volume cap and the alternative minimum tax.
ai_summary:
This bill changes two tax rules that apply to a specific type of government bond called a "qualified student loan bond." These are bonds that state and local governments issue to raise money, which is then lent out to students to help pay for college. Right now, these bonds face two limits: a cap on how many can be issued in a given state each year, and a tax called the Alternative Minimum Tax that investors may have to pay on the interest they earn from them. This bill would remove both of those restrictions for qualified student loan bonds issued after the law takes effect.

The main practical effect is that state agencies that run student loan programs would find it easier and cheaper to raise money through these bonds. When investors do not owe extra taxes on the interest from a bond, they are usually willing to accept a lower interest rate. That lower rate can mean the agency pays less to borrow money, which could allow it to offer students slightly lower interest rates on their loans. Removing the annual cap also means states would not have to compete as hard with other types of projects for permission to issue these bonds.

This bill most directly affects state and local housing finance and student loan agencies that issue these bonds, as well as investors who buy them. College students who borrow through state-run loan programs could potentially see some benefit if lower borrowing costs are passed on to them, though the bill does not require that to happen. It does not affect federal student loans like those through the Department of Education.
ai_headline: Bill would lift tax and issuance caps on state student loan bonds

ai_sections.tldr: HR 2660 removes the Alternative Minimum Tax and annual issuance caps on qualified student loan bonds issued by state and local governments.

title: No Lifeline for the Dead Act
ai_summary:
The Lifeline program is a federal program that helps low-income Americans pay for phone and internet service. This bill tells the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to tighten up the rules for who can receive that benefit. Specifically, it requires that all applicants be checked through two federal databases that verify identity and prevent duplicate benefits. Right now, some states use their own systems instead of these federal tools. This bill would close that loophole and force everyone to go through the same national process.

The bill also requires anyone who was approved for Lifeline without going through those federal databases to be re-screened within 180 days. If they do not pass that re-screening, they lose the benefit. On top of that, the bill limits eligibility to U.S. citizens and certain legal immigrants, and it requires applicants to provide a Social Security number or a Tribal identifier to qualify.

This bill mainly affects people who currently receive or are applying for Lifeline phone or internet discounts, as well as the telecom companies that provide the service. Some existing recipients could lose their benefits if they fail the re-screening or do not meet the new citizenship and identification requirements. The FCC would have 120 days after the law passes to put the new rules in place.

title: NOPAIN for Veterans Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require the Department of Veterans Affairs to add certain non-opioid pain medications to its approved drug list, called the national formulary. Right now, the VA controls which medications it will provide and pay for. This bill says that when the FDA approves a non-opioid pain drug for use after surgery, and that drug qualifies for special payment status under Medicare rules, the VA must add it to its formulary within one year. The VA would also have to include these drugs on its standardized drug list, which helps make them consistently available across VA facilities.

The main effect is that veterans who need pain management after surgery would have better access to non-opioid options through the VA health system. Currently, a veteran's access to a specific pain medication can depend on which VA facility they use. This bill tries to make that more consistent nationwide by requiring the VA to keep up with newly approved non-opioid pain treatments rather than leaving it up to each facility or the VA's own timeline.

The bill affects veterans who receive medical care through the VA, particularly those recovering from surgery who may benefit from alternatives to opioid pain medications. It also directs the VA Secretary to begin carrying out these changes within 90 days of the bill becoming law. The bill specifically states that money from the Cost of War Toxic Exposures Fund, which is set aside for veterans exposed to burn pits and other hazards, cannot be used to pay for this.

title: Protecting Community Television Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes a small but significant change to a law that governs how cable TV companies operate in local communities. Right now, cable companies pay a "franchise fee" to local governments in exchange for the right to run cables through public streets and spaces. The current law defines what counts as that fee in a loose way. This bill tightens that definition by changing the word "includes" to "means," and by adding the word "monetary" to clarify that only money payments count as the fee. The goal is to prevent cable companies from arguing that non-cash contributions, like free cable channels given to the city, should count toward what they owe.

This matters because many local governments use franchise fee money to fund public, educational, and government access TV channels, often called PEG channels. These are the local channels that broadcast city council meetings, school programs, and community content. If cable companies can count non-cash items as part of their fee, they may pay less actual money to local governments, which could reduce funding for those channels.

This bill mainly affects local governments, cable TV companies, and residents who watch or rely on local public access television. Cities and towns that depend on franchise fee payments to keep community channels running would benefit if the bill passes. Cable companies might be affected because they would have less flexibility in how they meet their franchise fee obligations.
ai_headline: House bill would lock cable franchise fees to cash-only payments
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

The bill targets a specific legal ambiguity in how franchise fees are currently defined.

Cities and towns that fund community channels through franchise fee revenue have a stake in the outcome, as do cable companies whose payment options would be narrowed.

title: HOPE with Fertility Services Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require employer-sponsored group health insurance plans to cover infertility treatments if the plan already covers pregnancy and childbirth services. Coverage would include treatments like in vitro fertilization (IVF), egg freezing, intrauterine insemination, and ovulation-stimulating medications. The bill also covers what it calls "iatrogenic infertility," which means infertility caused by medical treatments like chemotherapy, radiation, or major surgery. In those cases, the plan would also have to pay for fertility preservation services, such as freezing eggs or sperm, before those treatments begin. These new requirements would take effect starting in 2027.

The bill applies to people who get health insurance through their employer. Insurance companies and plan administrators would still be allowed to use standard tools like prior authorization and cost-sharing (copays, deductibles), but those restrictions cannot be stricter for fertility care than they are for other medical and surgical benefits. Insurance companies would be banned from pressuring patients or doctors away from using covered fertility treatments, and doctors must be free to discuss all covered options with their patients.

To make sure insurance companies follow the rules, they would have to submit annual reports to the federal government for the first five years explaining how they manage and limit fertility care benefits. If a company is found to be out of compliance, it faces fines of up to $100 per day per affected person. The government would also publish public reports identifying which plans are not following the law. People covered by these plans must be notified about their fertility coverage rights starting in 2028.

title: To provide for the designation of Burma for temporary protected status.
ai_summary:
This bill would grant Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, to people from Burma (also called Myanmar) who are currently living in the United States. TPS is a legal protection the government can give to people from countries experiencing serious crises, like wars, disasters, or extreme violence. It lets them stay and work in the US legally for a set period of time without being deported. This bill would set that protection period at 18 months, starting November 25, 2025.

To qualify, a person from Burma would need to have been continuously living in the US since the date this bill becomes law, not have certain criminal or immigration violations on their record, and register with the Department of Homeland Security. The bill also allows people with TPS to travel outside the US temporarily in emergency situations, as long as the government approves the trip beforehand.

This bill directly affects Burmese nationals currently living in the United States who do not have permanent legal status. Burma has been experiencing a serious political and humanitarian crisis since a military coup in 2021, which is the background context for this proposal. TPS does not give people a path to permanent residency or citizenship on its own, but it does provide temporary legal protection and work authorization while the situation in their home country remains dangerous.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Election Results Accountability Act
ai_summary:
This bill would set strict time limits on how quickly states must count votes and declare official winners in federal elections, meaning races for Congress and the presidency. States would have to count at least 90 percent of ballots within 72 hours after polls close. They would then have to finish counting all remaining ballots and officially certify the final results within two weeks of Election Day. Both of those results would need to be made public.

The bill does allow some flexibility. States would not be penalized if they miss these deadlines due to natural disasters, public health emergencies, cyberattacks, equipment failures, or if they are conducting a recount. A state could also get a one-time pass the first time it rolls out new election procedures. However, to qualify for any exception, both the federal Election Assistance Commission and the Attorney General would have to agree that the situation was a legitimate reason for the delay.

The main consequence for missing these deadlines without an approved excuse is financial. States that do not comply could lose federal funding that helps pay for running future elections. To get that money back, the state would have to submit a plan to fix the problem and then actually follow through on it. This bill would affect every state, since all 50 states run federal elections, and it would indirectly affect voters who want faster, more uniform election results across the country.
ai_headline: New bill sets 72-hour and two-week deadlines for federal vote counts
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on House Administration.

title: International Human Rights Defense Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would create a permanent, Senate-confirmed government position called the Special Envoy for the Human Rights of LGBTQI+ People inside the U.S. Department of State. The person in this role would be appointed by the President and would serve as the top U.S. diplomat focused on how LGBTQI+ people are treated in other countries. The Special Envoy would coordinate policy across federal agencies, represent the U.S. in international meetings on this topic, and be required to deliver a written global strategy and regular reports to Congress every two years.

The bill also makes two additions to existing law. It would require the State Department's annual human rights reports, which already cover countries around the world, to specifically track and describe laws, violence, and discrimination targeting people based on sexual orientation, gender identity, or sex characteristics in each country. The bill also authorizes the State Department to provide foreign assistance, such as funding programs, building local legal capacity, and training health workers, aimed at reducing violence and discrimination against LGBTQI+ people abroad.

The bill mainly affects how the U.S. federal government is organized and what it does in foreign policy. It does not change any domestic laws or directly affect the rights of people living in the United States. American taxpayers fund the State Department, so this would add a new office and programs to that budget. People outside the U.S., particularly LGBTQI+ individuals in countries with laws criminalizing same-sex relationships, are the intended beneficiaries of the policy goals described in the bill.

title: Guard the Skies Act
ai_summary:
This bill gives the National Guard new authority to defend certain locations from drones. Right now, only a small number of federal agencies have the legal power to detect, track, or disable unmanned aircraft near sensitive sites. The Guard the Skies Act would let state governors request that National Guard units be authorized to do the same thing, with approval from the Secretary of Defense. The Guard members would need to be on official duty orders to use these powers.

The bill also makes sure the Department of Defense gets a seat at the table when rules about drone defense are written or updated, and it allows Guard members to train specifically for this kind of drone-protection mission. It applies mainly to protecting what are called "National Special Security Events," which are high-profile gatherings like presidential inaugurations or major summits that receive extra federal security attention.

The people most directly affected are National Guard members, who would gain new legal authority and training opportunities, and state governors, who would have a new way to request drone defense support without waiting solely on federal agencies. Residents living near or attending major national events could also be indirectly affected, since the bill is aimed at improving security at those locations. Private drone operators flying near protected sites would face the possibility of National Guard intervention in addition to existing federal enforcement.

title: PARTNERS Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill changes who can enforce the rules for Medicare Advantage plans. Right now, only the federal government, specifically the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, has the power to make sure Medicare Advantage insurers follow federal rules. This bill would let individual states also step in and enforce those same federal requirements against Medicare Advantage plans operating within their borders. States could also enter into formal agreements with the federal government to coordinate their enforcement efforts.

Medicare Advantage plans are the private insurance option that about 33 million Americans over 65 use instead of traditional Medicare. The people most directly affected are seniors and disabled individuals enrolled in these plans. If a plan is denying claims improperly, delaying care, or otherwise breaking the rules, this bill would give state attorneys general or state insurance regulators another avenue to take action, rather than patients having to wait solely on federal enforcement.

The bill does not change what the actual Medicare Advantage rules are. It only adds state governments as an additional enforcement partner alongside the federal government. Supporters might say this gives consumers more protection and faster local action. Critics might argue it could create confusion or inconsistent enforcement across different states. The bill was introduced in the House and has been sent to two committees for review.

title: To amend the Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972 to allow importation of polar bear trophies taken in sport hunts in Canada before the date the polar bear was determined to be a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act of 1973.
ai_summary:
This bill makes a narrow change to an existing law called the Marine Mammal Protection Act. Right now, it is illegal to bring polar bear trophies into the United States, even if the hunt happened legally in Canada years ago. This bill would allow the U.S. government to issue import permits for those older trophies under two specific conditions: the polar bear was hunted before February 18, 1997, or it was hunted before May 15, 2008, and came from a Canadian polar bear population that was already approved for trophy imports at that time. Polar bears were listed as a threatened species in the U.S. in May 2008, and that listing is what triggered the import ban. This bill essentially draws a line saying that hunts completed before that protection took effect should be treated differently.

The bill tells the Secretary of the Interior to process and issue these permits quickly, and it waives several normal legal requirements that would otherwise block approval. It does not change any rules about future hunts or future imports. It only applies to trophies from hunts that already happened in the past, specifically before those two cutoff dates.

The people directly affected are American hunters who legally participated in Canadian polar bear hunts years ago and have been unable to bring their trophies home because of the import ban. Canada has its own rules allowing Indigenous communities to sell hunting permits to outside hunters, so those hunts were legal under Canadian law at the time. This bill would not affect polar bears living in the wild going forward, and it would not change any protections currently in place for the species.

last_action_text: Subcommittee Hearings Held

title: Stamp Out Veterans Medical Debt Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a special postage stamp called the "Veterans Medical Debt Relief Stamp." The US Postal Service would sell it each year around Veterans Day. The stamp would cost more than a regular stamp, and the extra money collected from sales would go directly to the Department of Veterans Affairs. That money would then be used to pay down medical debts that veterans owe from unpaid copayments and coinsurance bills related to VA care, including care received through the VA's Community Care Program, which allows veterans to see non-VA doctors.

The funds raised would be distributed to specific VA offices that handle billing and debt, such as the Veterans Health Administration and the VA's Debt Management Center. The bill does not set a cap on how many of these stamps can be sold, meaning the postal service could print and sell as many as the public wants to buy. Participation would be entirely voluntary, relying on members of the public choosing to buy the stamp instead of a regular one.

This bill would directly affect veterans who have outstanding medical debts owed to the VA. It would also affect anyone who buys postage stamps, since they would have the option to purchase this special stamp. The bill does not require any new government spending beyond the cost of producing the stamp, since the program is funded entirely by voluntary public purchases.

ai_summary:
This bill changes a federal rule about Medicaid, the government health insurance program for people with low incomes. Right now, federal law blocks Medicaid from paying for health care for people who are in jail or prison. This bill would create an exception: states would be allowed to use Medicaid to cover medical care for inmates during the last 30 days before they are released. States would not be required to do this, but they would have the option. The bill also requires a government commission to study how healthcare is currently provided in correctional facilities and report back to Congress within 18 months.

The main idea behind the change is to help people connect with healthcare coverage before they walk out the prison door, rather than after. Getting Medicaid set up in advance could make it easier for someone leaving prison to see a doctor, get prescriptions filled, or access mental health and addiction treatment right away instead of facing a gap in care during a vulnerable time.

This bill would most directly affect people who are nearing the end of a jail or prison sentence and who would qualify for Medicaid based on their income. It also affects state governments, which would decide whether to take advantage of the new option and would need to coordinate with their Medicaid programs. Taxpayers would share in the cost through the federal-state Medicaid funding system, though the overall financial impact would depend on how many states choose to participate.
ai_headline: Bill would let states bill Medicaid for inmates' final 30 days
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: MINT Act
ai_summary:
This bill deals with a specific tax rule about government bonds. State and local governments often raise money by selling bonds — basically borrowing money from investors. One benefit of these bonds is that the interest investors earn is usually tax-free. However, a federal rule says that if a bond is "federally guaranteed," it loses that tax-free status. The MINT Act would make it clear that when a Federal Home Loan Bank (a type of government-sponsored bank) backs one of these local bonds with a letter of credit, that does NOT count as a "federal guarantee" — so the bond keeps its tax-exempt status. This was actually allowed before 2010, and this bill would restore and make that treatment permanent going forward.

The practical effect is that state and local governments could more easily use Federal Home Loan Banks to strengthen their bonds, making those bonds more attractive and potentially cheaper to issue. That could make it easier for cities, counties, and states to borrow money at lower cost for things like housing, infrastructure, and community projects.

People most directly affected include state and local governments looking to finance public projects, the Federal Home Loan Banks that issue the letters of credit, and investors who buy tax-exempt municipal bonds. Indirectly, residents in communities that benefit from locally funded projects — such as affordable housing or public improvements — could also be affected.
ai_headline: MINT Act would restore tax-exempt status for bonds backed by federal home loan banks
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7769 would permanently exempt Federal Home Loan Bank letters of credit from the federal guarantee rule that strips municipal bond tax benefits.
ai_sections.what: HR 7769, the MINT Act, would permanently clarify that a Federal Home Loan Bank letter of credit backing a state or local government bond does not constitute a federal guarantee under tax law. Under current rules, a federally guaranteed bond loses its tax-exempt status; this bill would restore an exception that existed before 2010 and make it permanent. The practical result is that state and local bonds backed by Federal Home Loan Bank letters of credit would retain their tax-exempt treatment.
ai_sections.who: State and local governments seeking to finance public projects and the Federal Home Loan Banks that issue letters of credit are directly affected. Investors who purchase tax-exempt municipal bonds, and indirectly the residents of communities served by locally funded projects, are also affected.
ai_sections.why: Retaining tax-exempt status makes municipal bonds more attractive to investors, which could lower borrowing costs for state and local governments. That shift in financing conditions could influence the scale or frequency of publicly funded projects such as housing, infrastructure, and community development.

title: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States to ensure that only citizens are eligible to vote in Federal elections.
ai_summary:
This bill proposes a change to the U.S. Constitution that would officially limit voting in federal elections to U.S. citizens only. Federal elections include races for President, Vice President, U.S. Senate, and U.S. House of Representatives. To become part of the Constitution, the amendment would need approval from two-thirds of both the House and Senate, and then ratification by three-fourths of all 50 states, which is a high bar to clear.

The bill also spells out who controls the rules for enforcing this requirement. Each state legislature would write its own laws to carry it out, but Congress would have the power to step in and change those rules if it chose to. Congress would also handle enforcement for Washington, D.C., since D.C. is not a state with its own legislature.

It is worth knowing that no federal law currently allows noncitizens to vote in federal elections. Some local governments have, on their own, allowed noncitizens to vote in local races like school board or city council elections, but that is separate from federal elections. This amendment would affect noncitizens living in the U.S., state and local governments that set their own election rules, and potentially D.C. residents whose election rules would fall more directly under congressional control.
ai_headline: Proposed amendment would bar noncitizens from voting in federal races
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

To take effect, the amendment must be approved by two-thirds of both the House and Senate, then ratified by three-fourths of all 50 states. Each state legislature would write its own enforcement laws, though Congress could override those rules and would directly govern enforcement for Washington, D.C.

Some local governments have independently allowed noncitizens to vote in local races such as school board or city council elections, and this amendment could create pressure on or constraints around those arrangements at the local level.

title: Vietnam Veteran Commemoration Fund Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill updates and extends a program run by the Department of Defense that honors veterans who served in the Vietnam War. The program was originally created in 2008 to mark the 50th anniversary of the war. The biggest change this bill makes is turning the program from something the military "may" do into something it "shall" do, meaning the government would be required to run it instead of just having the option to.

The program includes activities like ceremonies, outreach efforts, and accepting donations through a special fund to help pay for commemoration events. By making the program mandatory and extending it, the bill ensures these efforts continue and are funded going forward. The changes would take effect on Veterans Day, November 11, 2025.

This bill mainly affects Vietnam War veterans and their families, who would see continued official recognition of their service. It also affects the Department of Defense, which would be legally required to keep the program running. Members of the public who want to donate to Vietnam War commemoration efforts would also be able to contribute through the official fund.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Armed Services.

title: Choices for Increased Mobility Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes how Medicare Part B pays for a specific type of manual wheelchair called an "ultralightweight" wheelchair. Starting January 1, 2026, Medicare would create separate billing codes depending on what material the wheelchair frame is made of — specifically whether it uses titanium or carbon fiber versus other materials. Right now, all ultralightweight wheelchairs are grouped under the same payment rules, which can make it harder for people to get wheelchairs made from lighter, more durable materials.

Under the new rules, Medicare would pay its standard reimbursement amount for titanium or carbon fiber wheelchairs, but suppliers would be allowed to charge the patient the difference between what Medicare pays and what the wheelchair actually costs. So if Medicare pays $1,500 but the wheelchair costs $2,000, the patient could be billed the extra $500 out of pocket. The bill also allows Medicare to require suppliers to give patients a written notice upfront explaining any extra costs they might have to pay before they agree to buy or rent the chair.

This bill mainly affects Medicare beneficiaries — typically people 65 and older, or those with certain disabilities — who need an ultralightweight manual wheelchair, as well as the medical suppliers who provide them. People who want a titanium or carbon fiber frame would have more access to those options through Medicare, but they could face additional out-of-pocket costs depending on the supplier's pricing.
ai_headline: Medicare would split wheelchair payments by frame material starting 2026
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

The bill also allows Medicare to require suppliers to provide patients with written notice of any extra costs before a purchase or rental is finalized.

title: Responsible Cormorant Management and Control Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill tells the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service that it must create regional management plans for double-crested cormorants within 180 days of becoming law. Cormorants are large fishing birds whose populations have grown significantly in recent decades. The plans would spell out who is allowed to kill or remove cormorants, when and how they can do it, and how many birds can be taken while still keeping the overall population at a healthy, sustainable level. The agency would also have to count the cormorant population every five years and update the plans based on those results.

The bill addresses concerns that too many cormorants in one area can hurt fish populations, damage wetland plants, crowd out other birds, affect water quality, and potentially harm threatened or endangered species. The management plans would cover all four major migratory bird regions across the country, including areas within National Wildlife Refuges. States, Native American tribes, licensed hunters, and managers of private lakes and ponds would all be among the groups authorized to carry out cormorant removal under the plans.

This bill most directly affects people who work or depend on freshwater fisheries, such as fish farmers, aquaculture pond operators, lake managers, and recreational anglers who may have seen cormorants competing with them for fish. Wildlife managers, state and tribal agencies, and hunters who might participate in cormorant control programs would also be affected. Everyday residents near large cormorant colonies, who may experience property or environmental impacts, could also see effects depending on how local plans are put into practice.

last_action_text: Subcommittee Hearings Held

title: ENDS Chinese Vapes Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill targets the illegal importation of vapes and e-cigarettes that have not been approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Under existing law, vaping products sold in the U.S. are supposed to go through an FDA review process. This bill creates new financial penalties specifically for anyone who tries to bring unapproved vaping products into the country, whether they do so on purpose or simply through carelessness. Fines range from $500 per device for careless violations up to $5,000 per device for intentional fraud. Those penalties can be multiplied further if the smuggler routed products through another country to hide their origin, or if they have been caught doing this before.

The bill also has a built-in cap, meaning total fines for a single shipment cannot exceed ten times the shipment's estimated U.S. retail value. Companies that are closely connected through shared ownership or leadership are treated as one entity, so they cannot simply create new businesses to avoid repeat-offender penalties. The bill does not replace any existing enforcement tools held by Customs and Border Protection, the FDA, or the Justice Department. Those agencies can still pursue separate civil or criminal actions on top of these new penalties.

The people most directly affected are importers, distributors, and businesses that bring vaping products into the United States without FDA approval. Consumers who vape could indirectly be affected if the law reduces the availability of certain products in the market. Legal vape manufacturers who have gone through the FDA approval process are not affected by this bill.
ai_headline: New fines target smuggled vapes lacking FDA approval
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: Expanding Support for Living Donors Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill makes changes to a federal program that helps pay back people who donate a living organ, like a kidney or part of a liver. Right now, that program has income limits that can block some donors from getting reimbursed for their out-of-pocket costs, such as travel, lodging, and lost wages. This bill would remove those income limits for anyone whose household income is at or below 700 percent of the federal poverty line, which covers the vast majority of Americans. It also sets a clear reimbursement cap of $10,000 per donor starting in 2027, and that cap would automatically adjust each year with inflation. Funding for the program would be extended through 2037.

The bill also adds new transparency rules. Starting in 2027, the government would be required to publish a detailed annual report on how the program is running, including how many donors applied, how much money they received, what organs were donated, and whether the program had enough funding to cover everyone. If the reimbursement cap ever needs to be lowered because of a funding shortage, Congress must be notified at least 30 days in advance, and any donors already approved would not be affected.

People most directly affected are living organ donors across the country, particularly those who were previously shut out of reimbursement because of income-based rules. Recipients of donated organs could also benefit indirectly if more people are willing to donate when the financial burden is reduced. The bill also directs a government watchdog agency, the GAO, to study whether Medicare could help cover some of these same costs in the future.
ai_headline: Living organ donors would get broader reimbursement under HR 7868
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Ways and Means, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

title: Public Lands Workforce Stability Act
ai_summary:
This bill would make it illegal to use federal money to carry out mass layoffs or forced firings at two agencies: the Department of the Interior and the U.S. Forest Service. This protection would last from whenever the bill becomes law through September 30, 2030. There is one exception: individual employees could still be fired for misconduct, poor performance, or other legitimate job-related reasons. Any large-scale workforce cuts would first require approval from the leaders of both the House and Senate Appropriations Committees before moving forward.

The two agencies covered manage a huge portion of the country's public lands, national parks, wildlife refuges, and national forests. The Department of the Interior oversees roughly 500 million acres of land and manages resources like oil, gas, and minerals on federal property. The Forest Service manages about 193 million acres of national forests and grasslands. Together, these agencies employ tens of thousands of workers who handle things like wildfire management, conservation, recreation, and natural resource oversight.

The people most directly affected are the career federal employees who work at these two agencies. If passed, the bill would shield them from large-scale job cuts unless Congress specifically signs off on them. It could also affect Americans who use or depend on public lands, since staffing levels at these agencies influence how well they can manage wildfires, maintain parks and trails, and carry out other public services.

last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Natural Resources, and in addition to the Committee on Agriculture, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

title: Protecting U.S. Farmland and Sensitive Sites From Foreign Adversaries Act
ai_summary:
This bill gives a federal government committee called CFIUS (the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States) stronger power to review and block land purchases made by people or companies connected to six named countries: China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia, and Venezuela. Right now, CFIUS can already review some foreign land deals, but this bill would require it to automatically investigate any purchase near a "sensitive site," which the bill defines broadly to include military bases, airports, seaports, power plants, data centers, NASA facilities, and research labs, among others. Farmland is also included. Under this bill, those kinds of deals would be automatically assumed to be a national security risk and would likely be blocked unless the government can prove otherwise with strong evidence.

The bill also requires the parties involved in one of these flagged land deals to file a formal notice with the government before the transaction goes through. It adds the Secretary of Agriculture as an official voice in the review process when farmland or agricultural technology deals are being examined. The government would also have to consider how foreign purchases of agricultural land could affect the long-term food supply in the United States.

This bill most directly affects foreign buyers connected to those six countries who want to purchase land in the United States, particularly near military or infrastructure sites, or on farmland. It also affects American landowners who might want to sell to such buyers, as those deals could now face mandatory government review and likely rejection. States that already have their own laws restricting foreign land purchases are allowed to keep those rules in place.

title: Special District Fairness and Accessibility Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to issue clear rules telling all federal agencies that special districts count as local governments when deciding who can receive federal money. Special districts are government bodies created by states to handle specific tasks, like a water district, fire protection district, hospital district, or transit authority. Right now, some federal agencies do not consistently recognize these entities as local governments, which can block them from applying for grants and other federal funding.

Under the bill, OMB would have 180 days after the law passes to put out that guidance. Federal agencies would then have one year to update their own rules to match it. Two years after the law takes effect, OMB would report back to Congress on how well agencies are following through.

This bill mainly affects the thousands of special districts that exist across the country, and indirectly the communities those districts serve. If a water district or fire district cannot qualify for federal grants, local residents may end up paying more through local taxes or fees to cover costs that federal funding might otherwise help with. By standardizing how agencies treat special districts, the bill aims to make federal funding opportunities more consistent and accessible for these local government bodies.

title: Recycling Infrastructure and Accessibility Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill creates a federal grant program run by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to help communities build better recycling systems. The EPA would have 18 months to get the program running and could award grants between $500,000 and $15 million to states, local governments, Native American tribes, and public-private partnerships. Up to $30 million per year could be spent on the program from 2025 through 2029. The money can be used to build more transfer stations where recyclables are collected and sorted, expand curbside pickup programs, and create partnerships between government and private companies to lower costs. The grants cannot be used for recycling education campaigns.

The bill focuses especially on underserved communities, meaning places where recycling is hard to access because processing facilities are too far away or too small to handle the local volume of recyclables. At least 70 percent of the grant money each year must go toward these underserved areas. Communities that have no recycling facility within 75 miles get first priority for funding. The federal government would cover up to 90 percent of project costs, though the EPA can waive the local share entirely if a community would face serious financial hardship.

The people most directly affected are residents of rural areas, small towns, and lower-income communities that currently have little or no recycling access. Local governments and tribal nations in those areas could apply for funding to build the infrastructure needed to start or improve recycling programs. Two years after the first grant is awarded, the EPA must report back to Congress on how well the program is working and whether recycling rates improved in the communities it served.

title: Language Access for All Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill requires every federal agency to make its services available to people who have limited ability to read, speak, or understand English. Within one year of the law passing, each agency would have to translate important documents into the most common non-English languages spoken in the United States, provide interpreters by phone or in person, and clearly post notices letting the public know these services exist. Agencies would also need to hire a Language Access Coordinator, a specific staff member whose job is to oversee all of this and train other employees. Each agency must create a written plan explaining how it will meet these requirements, and that plan has to go through a public comment process before it is finalized.

The bill also sets rules around computer-based translation tools. Agencies could use artificial intelligence to help with translation, but they would not be allowed to rely on it completely. A qualified human translator or interpreter would always have to check any AI-generated translation. Every two years, an independent inspector would audit each agency's AI language tools for accuracy and fairness, and the results would be made public.

People who feel they were denied proper language access could file a complaint through a new federal system managed by the Justice Department, which would have to respond within 60 days. If an agency fails to follow the law, it could face the same legal consequences as discrimination under the Civil Rights Act. This bill would most directly affect the roughly 25 million people in the United States who speak English less than very well, as well as the federal agencies and employees who serve them.

title: Julius Rosenwald and Rosenwald Schools National Historical Park Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new unit of the National Park System called the Julius Rosenwald and Rosenwald Schools National Historical Park. The park would be centered at the historic Sears complex in Chicago's North Lawndale neighborhood, where businessman Julius Rosenwald built his fortune, and would also include three restored Rosenwald Schools in Maryland, South Carolina, and Virginia. Between 1912 and 1932, Rosenwald partnered with Booker T. Washington and thousands of Black communities across the South to build about 5,000 schools that educated over 600,000 African American children during the era of segregation. The bill directs the National Park Service to manage these sites, create visitor programs, and develop an educational plan within three years.

The bill also creates something called the Rosenwald Schools National Network, a program inside the National Park Service that would connect surviving Rosenwald School buildings across the country. This network would produce educational materials, conduct research, offer grants, and help share the broader story of these schools with the public. Sites connected to the network could include federal, state, local, and privately owned properties that relate to Rosenwald's life and the schools he helped build.

The people most directly affected would be residents near the park sites in Illinois, Maryland, South Carolina, and Virginia, as well as communities across the South that still have surviving Rosenwald School buildings. More broadly, anyone interested in American history, civil rights history, or education policy could be affected, since the bill would increase public access to this history through new visitor centers, signage, and online resources funded by the federal government.

title: A bill to repeal the sunset provision of the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996.
ai_summary:
The Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 is a law that punishes companies and individuals who invest in Iran's oil industry or help Iran develop weapons. Like many laws, it was written with an expiration date, called a "sunset provision," which requires Congress to periodically renew it or let it expire. This bill would permanently remove that expiration date, meaning the law would stay in force indefinitely without needing future votes to keep it alive.

Right now, the law has to be renewed every few years or it automatically ends. This bill changes that by deleting the section of the original law that sets an end date. If passed, Congress would no longer need to take action to keep the sanctions going — they would simply remain in place unless a future law specifically repealed them.

This bill most directly affects foreign companies and banks that do business with Iran, since they could face U.S. penalties for certain transactions. It also affects U.S. companies that might otherwise seek to invest in Iran's energy sector. American consumers are less directly impacted, though broad sanctions on Iran can influence global oil markets and energy prices. The bill was introduced with support from both Republican and Democratic senators and was sent to the Senate Banking Committee for review.

last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

title: Forced Abortion Prevention and Accountability Act
ai_summary:
This bill would make it a federal crime to give a woman an abortion-inducing drug, such as mifepristone or misoprostol, without her knowledge and consent. If someone does this on purpose, they could face up to 25 years in prison and fines. If the woman is seriously hurt or dies as a result, the person responsible could face an additional 25 years on top of that. The law would apply when the drug involved has traveled across state lines, which covers most situations since these medications are commonly shipped or mailed.

The bill also gives victims the right to sue in civil court. A woman who was given one of these drugs without her consent could seek money damages, including triple the cost of her injuries plus additional punitive damages. The bill also makes it easier to afford a lawsuit by requiring the other side to cover her legal fees if she wins.

This bill would directly affect anyone who prescribes, distributes, or handles abortion-inducing medications, including doctors, pharmacists, and anyone who ships or mails these drugs. It would also affect women who use these medications, since it adds a legal requirement that their consent be clearly documented. Sellers or distributors who do not take reasonable steps to confirm a drug is going to someone who actually wants it could also face criminal charges under the conspiracy provision.
ai_headline: Federal bill would criminalize giving abortion drugs to women without consent
