title: Protecting Sensitive Locations Act
ai_summary:
This bill would make it illegal for immigration agents, including ICE and Border Patrol officers, to conduct arrests, searches, interviews, or surveillance within 1,000 feet of certain locations. These protected places, called "sensitive locations," include schools, hospitals, churches, shelters, polling places, courthouses, libraries, playgrounds, food banks, disaster relief sites, and many others. The only exceptions would be genuine emergencies, such as an immediate threat to someone's life, a hot pursuit of a dangerous person, or a rare pre-approved operation targeting a terrorist or someone posing an extraordinary danger to public safety. Even in those cases, agents must stop the enforcement action as soon as the emergency ends.

If an immigration enforcement action happens at one of these protected locations in violation of the rules, any evidence gathered cannot be used against the person in a deportation case, and that person could ask a judge to immediately end the removal proceedings. Agents who are unsure whether an emergency justifies an exception must stop immediately and get real-time approval from a supervisor before continuing. Immigration agencies would also be required to give officers annual training on these rules and file detailed reports to Congress and internal watchdog offices whenever enforcement does occur near a sensitive location.

This bill primarily affects undocumented immigrants, who would have greater protection from arrest in everyday public spaces. It also affects immigration enforcement agencies, which would face new restrictions, paperwork requirements, and oversight. Americans who use any of the listed locations, such as patients at clinics, students at schools, or people attending religious services, could also be affected since these spaces would see less immigration enforcement activity nearby.

title: Train More Nurses Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires two federal agencies, the Department of Health and Human Services and the Department of Labor, to work together to study all existing government grant programs that support nurses and nursing education. Within one year of becoming law, those agencies must send a written report to Congress with findings and recommendations for how those grant programs could be improved.

The report must focus on three specific goals: getting more people to become nursing instructors, especially in areas that are short on healthcare workers; creating clearer paths for experienced nurses with over 10 years on the job to move into teaching roles at nursing schools; and helping licensed practical nurses (LPNs) advance their education to become registered nurses (RNs).

This bill does not create new programs or spend new money right now. It mainly directs the government to take a closer look at what is already being done and figure out what changes might help grow the nursing workforce. It could affect nursing students, working nurses looking to advance their careers, nursing schools, and communities that struggle to attract enough healthcare workers.

title: Ally’s Act
ai_summary:
Ally's Act would require most private health insurance plans to cover certain hearing devices for people who a doctor or audiologist determines needs them. Specifically, plans would have to cover cochlear implants, bone conduction implants, and their external sound processors. Coverage would also include the surgery to place these devices, hearing assessments, pre- and post-surgery visits, repairs, and rehabilitation services. Every five years, plans would also be required to cover an upgrade or replacement of the devices.

The bill also sets rules about how insurers can treat these benefits. Plans cannot charge patients higher out-of-pocket costs or apply stricter coverage limits for these hearing devices than they do for regular medical or surgical care. Insurers also cannot second-guess or override a doctor's or audiologist's decision that the device is medically necessary. The bill applies to employer-sponsored group health plans, individual market plans, and even older "grandfathered" plans that were in place before the Affordable Care Act.

People who would be most directly affected are those with significant hearing loss who need implantable hearing devices but currently face high costs or coverage denials from their private insurance. Employers who provide health coverage and insurance companies would need to update their plans to meet these new requirements starting with plan years beginning January 1, 2026. The bill does not apply to Medicare or Medicaid, which are separate government programs.

title: Essential Caregivers Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would give nursing home and care facility residents the legal right to have at least one "essential caregiver" visit them in person every day, even during emergencies when regular visiting is shut down, like a pandemic or natural disaster. An essential caregiver is someone the resident chooses, such as a family member or close friend, who agrees to follow the same safety rules the facility's own staff must follow. If a resident has a condition like dementia that prevents them from making that choice, a legal representative can choose on their behalf. Facilities could only block access for up to 7 days at the start of an emergency, or up to 14 days if the state health department approves it, and they must always allow access for residents who are dying or in serious decline.

The bill also sets up a clear system if a facility wrongly blocks a caregiver. The facility must give written warnings before cutting off access, and if access is denied, the caregiver and resident have the right to appeal. A state agency must start looking into the appeal within two business days and decide within 48 hours after that. If the facility is found to have broken the rules, it must immediately restore access and could face fines up to $5,000 for failing to fix the problem.

This bill directly affects the roughly 1.3 million people living in skilled nursing facilities, nursing homes, intermediate care facilities for people with intellectual disabilities, and certain inpatient rehabilitation centers across the country. It also affects the family members and friends who care for those residents, as well as the facilities themselves, which would need to update their policies within two years of the law passing.

last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

title: Bottles and Breastfeeding Equipment Screening Enhancement Act
ai_summary:
This law updates the rules for how TSA officers and private airport security workers must handle breast milk, baby formula, infant water, and juice during airport security screening. The Transportation Security Administration must release new guidelines within 90 days explaining how to screen these items without contaminating them. Those guidelines must be developed with input from maternal health organizations and must meet clean, hygienic standards. The guidelines will be reviewed and updated every five years if needed.

The law also requires that the Department of Homeland Security's Inspector General conduct an audit within one year. That audit will check whether security personnel are actually following the hygiene rules, and it will also look at how different screening technologies, like bottled liquid scanners, affect these items and how often they get blocked from passing through security.

This law mainly affects parents and caregivers traveling through U.S. airports with babies or young children, as well as TSA officers and private security screeners who handle these items at checkpoints. It builds on an earlier 2016 law called the Bottles and Breastfeeding Equipment Screening Act and is meant to give travelers more confidence that their infant food and supplies will not be contaminated during the security process.

title: Ending Passenger Rail Forced Arbitration Act
ai_summary:
This bill would ban Amtrak from putting mandatory arbitration clauses in its passenger contracts. Right now, companies sometimes include fine print in their contracts requiring customers to settle disputes through private arbitration instead of going to court. This bill would make those clauses illegal for Amtrak, and it would also ban any contract language that prevents passengers from joining together in class action lawsuits. A court, not an arbitrator, would decide whether the law applies in any given case.

The bill covers two main types of disputes: consumer disputes, which include things like personal injury claims or problems with service, and civil rights disputes, which involve allegations of discrimination based on race, sex, age, disability, religion, national origin, gender identity, or sexual orientation. Anyone who rides or tries to ride Amtrak would be protected, including minors and people who did not personally pay for their ticket. Amtrak employees are not covered by this bill.

In practical terms, this means that if an Amtrak passenger has a complaint or believes their rights were violated, they would have the right to take Amtrak to court or join with other passengers in a class action lawsuit, even if they signed a contract that said otherwise. The bill would take effect immediately upon being signed into law and would apply to any dispute that comes up after that date.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.

title: CLEAN FTZ Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill directs U.S. Customs and Border Protection to create a public list of all free trade zones operated by foreign countries. Free trade zones are special areas where goods can be stored, manufactured, or traded with reduced taxes and customs rules. Because these zones have looser oversight, they are sometimes used to move illegal goods like drugs, counterfeit products, weapons, or trafficked people. Within two years of passing, the government must publish this list online and update it at least once a year.

After the list is created, the government would rank every country that has one of these zones into four tiers based on how well the zone follows international anti-crime and trade standards. Tier I countries have zones that follow the rules well. Tier II and III countries are trying to improve but are falling short in different ways. Tier IV countries are not following the rules and are not making any real effort to change. The ranking system and the rules used to score each country would also be made public. Countries would be told what tier they are in and could move up or down over time.

For countries ranked Tier II, III, or IV, the U.S. government could offer advice on how to clean up their zones. More importantly, the President could impose serious consequences on foreign individuals or businesses that participate in illegal trade inside these zones, including freezing their U.S.-held assets and banning them from entering the United States. A public phone hotline and website would also be set up so businesses operating in these zones can report illegal activity they witness.
ai_headline: Bill would force U.S. to rank foreign trade zones on anti-crime compliance
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

Every country with such a zone would then be ranked into one of four tiers based on how well the zone meets international anti-crime and trade standards. Countries in Tiers II, III, or IV could face U.S. sanctions, including asset freezes and entry bans on individuals or businesses found participating in illegal trade within those zones.

Ranking countries and enabling sanctions creates pressure on governments to strengthen oversight of these zones or face consequences affecting their access to U.S. markets and financial systems.

title: Chemical Tax Repeal Act
ai_summary:
This bill would eliminate a federal tax that is currently charged on certain chemicals and chemical-based substances. That tax was originally created to fund the Superfund program, which pays for cleaning up heavily polluted sites around the country. The bill would remove the tax and make that removal retroactive, meaning it would be treated as if the tax never applied starting January 1, 2024.

The tax being repealed applies to companies that produce, import, or sell specific industrial chemicals and substances. Removing it would lower costs for those businesses. Supporters of repealing such taxes often argue the savings get passed along to customers, while critics point out that the Superfund program would have less dedicated funding for environmental cleanup.

The people most directly affected are chemical manufacturers, importers, and industries that use large amounts of industrial chemicals, such as plastics, petroleum, and manufacturing companies. Americans who live near Superfund cleanup sites could also be affected, since the program that pays for that cleanup relies in part on this tax revenue. The bill was introduced in January 2025 and has been sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it must advance before any further votes can take place.

title: To amend title 49, United States Code, to except from certain requirements relating to eligibility for essential air service Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill makes a small but specific change to federal law about air travel. Right now, there is a federal program called Essential Air Service (EAS) that helps make sure smaller or more remote communities have access to affordable airline service. The program has certain rules about which communities qualify for that support. Currently, Alaska and Hawaii are treated as special exceptions to some of those rules, because they are far from the mainland and rely heavily on air travel. This bill would add Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands to that same list of exceptions.

In practical terms, this means Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands could more easily qualify for Essential Air Service support without having to meet the same eligibility requirements that apply to communities in the lower 48 states. Like Alaska and Hawaii, these Pacific islands are geographically isolated and depend on air travel in ways that most mainland communities do not. The change recognizes that similar geographic challenges exist in these U.S. territories.

The people most directly affected are residents of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands, which together have a population of roughly 200,000 people. These are U.S. territories in the western Pacific Ocean. Better access to the Essential Air Service program could mean more options for affordable air travel to and from those islands. Airline companies that serve those routes and local governments in the territories would also be affected by this change.

title: Fairness for the Trades Act
ai_summary:
Right now, 529 savings accounts are tax-advantaged accounts that families use to save money for college and other education costs. When you withdraw money from a 529 for an approved expense, you do not pay federal taxes on those earnings. This bill would expand what counts as an approved expense by allowing people to use 529 funds to buy tools and equipment needed to work in a skilled trade, such as construction, plumbing, electrical work, auto repair, logging, or fishing. The equipment must be the kind that can be depreciated over time, meaning physical gear and tools rather than things like buildings.

The trades covered by this bill are defined by specific industry codes and include a wide range of hands-on fields like carpentry, roofing, HVAC, masonry, landscaping, and various repair services. If someone has money saved in a 529 account and goes into one of these fields, they could use that money tax-free to buy the tools their job requires, rather than only being able to use it for tuition or school fees.

This bill would most directly affect people who have 529 savings accounts and are entering or working in a skilled trade profession, as well as parents saving for children who may choose a trade career over a traditional college path. It could also matter to anyone who felt that 529 accounts previously favored college-bound students over those pursuing trade careers.
ai_headline: Bill would let families spend 529 savings tax-free on trade tools
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: Fairness for Servicemembers and their Families Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill deals with two life insurance programs run by the Department of Veterans Affairs. Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance (SGLI) covers active-duty military members, and Veterans' Group Life Insurance (VGLI) covers veterans after they leave service. Right now, the maximum automatic coverage under these programs is $500,000, a number that has not been regularly updated to keep up with inflation. This bill would require the VA Secretary to review that $500,000 maximum every five years, starting January 1, 2026, and compare it to what $500,000 would be worth after adjusting for inflation using the Consumer Price Index.

The review itself does not automatically raise the coverage limit. Instead, the VA Secretary must report the findings to the Veterans' Affairs committees in both the House and Senate. That report can then guide Congress or the VA if they decide to raise the coverage cap to better reflect today's cost of living.

This bill affects active-duty service members enrolled in SGLI and veterans enrolled in VGLI, along with their families who would receive the insurance payout. It also places a new responsibility on the VA to conduct and report these periodic reviews. The bill does not change premiums, eligibility rules, or any other part of the programs right now.
ai_headline: VA ordered to review $500,000 life insurance cap every five years starting 2026
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Veterans' Affairs.

title: FENCE Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change the tax code to make certain nonprofits ineligible for 501(c)(3) status. Right now, 501(c)(3) is the designation that allows charities, churches, food banks, shelters, and other nonprofits to receive tax-deductible donations and avoid paying federal taxes. Under this bill, an organization could lose that status if it knowingly provides financial help, services, benefits, or other material support to people who are in the United States without legal immigration status. The bill says this would apply when the organization "knows or reasonably should know" a person is undocumented.

There are two exceptions written into the bill. It specifically says organizations would not be required to check people's immigration papers or verify their legal status before helping them. It also says religious organizations cannot be forced to act against their religious beliefs.

This bill would affect a wide range of nonprofit organizations, including food pantries, homeless shelters, health clinics, legal aid groups, and other charities that serve low-income communities. If passed, groups that continue providing services to undocumented individuals could lose their tax-exempt status, which would likely reduce their ability to raise money and operate. People who rely on those services could also be affected if organizations change their policies or shut down programs to avoid losing their nonprofit status.
ai_headline: Bill would strip tax-exempt status from nonprofits serving undocumented immigrants
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Department of Energy relating to "Energy Conservation Program for Appliance Standards: Certification Requirements, Labeling Requirements, and Enforcement Provisions for Certain Consumer Products and Commercial Equipment".
ai_summary:
This bill is Congress's way of canceling a rule created by the Department of Energy (DOE) in October 2024. That DOE rule updated how appliance and equipment makers must report their products' energy use, label those products, and face penalties if they don't follow energy conservation standards. Congress is using a law called the Congressional Review Act, which lets lawmakers vote to strike down federal agency rules they disagree with. If this resolution passes both the Senate and House and is signed into law, the DOE rule would be thrown out entirely.

The canceled rule covered both household products and commercial equipment, meaning it touched on things like refrigerators, water heaters, air conditioners, and similar items sold to businesses. The rule had set stricter requirements for how companies certify and label how energy-efficient their products are, and what happens if they don't comply.

This bill most directly affects appliance and equipment manufacturers, who would no longer have to follow the updated certification and labeling requirements if the resolution succeeds. It could also affect businesses and consumers who rely on energy labels to compare products, since those labels might not be updated under the now-voided standards. Energy regulators at the DOE would also lose the enforcement tools the rule had granted them.

title: USA Batteries Act
ai_summary:
This bill would remove three chemicals — lead oxide, antimony, and sulfuric acid — from a list of substances that are taxed under the federal Superfund program. The Superfund excise tax was restored in 2022 to help pay for cleaning up heavily polluted sites around the country. These three chemicals are key ingredients used to make lead-acid batteries, the kind commonly found in cars, trucks, and backup power systems. By removing them from the taxable list, manufacturers would no longer pay this fee when they buy or use these materials in production.

The main argument supporters make is that imported batteries do not face this same tax, which they say puts American battery makers at a disadvantage. Domestic producers pay the tax on the raw chemicals they use, while a finished battery shipped in from another country avoids it entirely. The bill's backers say this creates an uneven playing field and raises costs for U.S. manufacturers.

This bill most directly affects companies that make lead-acid batteries in the United States, as well as the workers employed at those facilities across dozens of states. It could also affect the federal Superfund program, which would collect less money if these chemicals are no longer taxed. Consumers who buy products that use lead-acid batteries, like cars or industrial equipment, could potentially see some indirect effects depending on how manufacturers respond to the change in costs.
ai_headline: Bill would end Superfund tax on three lead-acid battery chemicals
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians Land Transfer Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would transfer roughly 836 acres of land in San Diego County, California, into federal trust status for the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians. When land is held "in trust" by the federal government for a tribe, it becomes part of the tribe's reservation and is treated similarly to other tribal lands. The land in question includes three separate parcels currently administered by or recorded under federal and county records.

The bill includes several conditions on how the land can be used. The public would keep the right to use existing trails and roads on the property for recreation and other purposes, though the tribe could set reasonable rules for that access. Federal agencies like the Bureau of Land Management and Forest Service would still be allowed to enter the land for emergencies such as wildfires or search and rescue operations. The bill also specifically bans casino-style and other regulated gambling on this land, and it does not change any existing water rights or agreements.

The people most directly affected are members of the Barona Band, whose reservation would grow by these parcels. Neighboring landowners and the general public who currently use trails or roads on the property would also be affected, though their access rights are protected under the bill's terms. State and local governments would no longer have normal jurisdiction over the land once it moves into federal trust status, which is standard for reservation land.

title: CHARLIE Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes changes to a federal grant program that pays for American History and Civics education in K-12 schools. Specifically, it would ban the use of those grant funds for teaching content that falls under two categories defined by recent presidential executive orders: "discriminatory equity ideology" and "gender ideology." Those terms, as defined in the executive orders the bill references, generally cover concepts related to systemic racial inequality and the idea that gender identity can differ from biological sex. The bill would also stop the federal government from giving any special preference to schools or organizations when handing out these grants based on race, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, or immigration status.

The people most directly affected are schools, teachers, and educational organizations that apply for these federal civics and history grants. If a school or program includes curriculum or activities that fall under those prohibited categories, it could lose eligibility for the funding. Grant applicants also could no longer receive bonus consideration based on the characteristics listed above.

More broadly, students in schools that receive these grants could see changes in what is taught in history and civics classes, depending on how their school adjusts its curriculum to stay eligible for the money. The bill does not ban any teaching outright in all schools — it only applies to programs that use this specific pot of federal grant funding.

title: REAL AMERICA Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes several changes to federal tax law. First, it would let workers who receive cash tips deduct those tips from their taxable income, meaning they would not owe federal income tax on that money. It also lets workers deduct overtime pay from their taxable income. Both of these deductions are available to everyone, whether or not they itemize on their tax return, but they phase out for individuals earning more than $450,000 per year or couples earning more than $900,000. These changes would start with the 2026 tax year.

Second, the bill would stop taxing Social Security benefits as income, starting in 2026. Currently, many retirees pay federal income tax on part of their Social Security checks depending on their total income. This bill would end that entirely. To make sure the Social Security trust funds do not lose money as a result, the federal government would transfer funds from the general treasury to replace whatever Social Security would have otherwise received.

Third, the bill targets a tax strategy used by some wealthy investment fund managers. Right now, many hedge fund and private equity managers receive a type of payment called "carried interest," which is taxed at the lower capital gains rate rather than the higher ordinary income rate. This bill would close that loophole by requiring that income to be taxed as ordinary income, the same way wages are taxed. It also sets up stricter rules and a higher penalty, up to 40 percent, for anyone who tries to get around these new requirements.
ai_headline: Bill would end taxes on tips, overtime, and Social Security starting in 2026
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

Additionally, it would require that carried interest income earned by hedge fund and private equity managers be taxed as ordinary income rather than at the lower capital gains rate, with penalties up to 40 percent for those who attempt to circumvent the new rules.

title: Truth in Tariffs Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require most businesses to show customers exactly how much of a product's price comes from certain tariffs. Specifically, it covers tariffs that the President put in place on an emergency or discretionary basis starting on or after January 20, 2025. If a product's price went up because of those tariffs, the seller would have to clearly label that added cost as a "tariff surcharge" so shoppers can see it. Businesses would have 30 days after the law passes to start doing this.

Small businesses are exempt from this requirement, so only larger companies would need to follow the rule. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) would be in charge of enforcing the law and could write additional rules to make it work. Companies that don't comply would face the same penalties the FTC uses for other unfair or deceptive business practices.

This bill would affect large retailers, manufacturers, and importers who sell goods to American consumers that are subject to the covered tariffs. Shoppers would see a new line or label on prices showing how much of what they are paying is due to tariffs. It does not change the tariffs themselves or whether they exist — it only requires that their cost be made visible to buyers.
ai_headline: Large retailers would have to label tariff costs on price tags under new bill
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: To oppose the permitting of deep seabed mining and exploration for deep seabed mining, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill tells the U.S. government to actively oppose deep seabed mining at international organizations until stronger rules are in place. Deep seabed mining means pulling up minerals and metals from the ocean floor, sometimes miles underwater. The bill requires the President to instruct U.S. representatives at international bodies to push for a moratorium, meaning a pause or ban, on permits for this kind of mining or even exploration for it. That pause would stay in effect until an international group called the International Seabed Authority creates binding rules backed by solid science, and the President certifies to Congress that those rules truly protect the ocean environment.

The bill is driven by concerns that scientists do not yet fully understand what damage deep seabed mining could cause. It points to risks like destroying rare ocean species, stirring up massive clouds of sediment, creating noise that harms sea life, contaminating fish people eat, and disrupting how the deep ocean stores carbon. Because that scientific understanding is seen as incomplete, the bill argues no mining should move forward yet.

This bill most directly affects U.S. diplomats and how they vote and speak at international forums. It could also affect mining companies hoping to extract minerals like manganese, cobalt, and nickel from the ocean floor, since the U.S. would be working internationally to block permits. Fishing communities, coastal residents, and indigenous peoples who depend on healthy oceans are identified in the bill as groups whose interests the rules are meant to protect.
ai_headline: Bill would direct U.S. to push for deep seabed mining pause abroad
last_action_text: Sponsor introductory remarks on measure. (CR E86-87)

The pause would remain in place until the International Seabed Authority establishes binding rules grounded in solid science and the President certifies to Congress that those rules genuinely protect the ocean environment.

title:
A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, 
United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "California State Motor Vehicle and Engine and Nonroad Engine Pollution Control Standards; The 'Omnibus' Low NOx Regulation; Waiver of Preemption; Notice of Decision".
ai_summary:
This bill uses a federal law called the Congressional Review Act to cancel a specific EPA decision. That decision, made in January 2025, gave California special permission to enforce its own strict rules limiting nitrogen oxide (NOx) pollution from trucks and other diesel engines. California has long had the legal ability to set tougher air quality standards than the rest of the country, but it needs a federal waiver from the EPA to do so. This bill would cancel that waiver and make California's stricter truck emission rules unenforceable.

If the bill passes, California could no longer enforce its "Omnibus Low NOx" regulation, which requires heavy-duty trucks and engines sold or operated in the state to produce significantly less NOx pollution. NOx contributes to smog and respiratory health problems. Other states that had chosen to follow California's stricter standards would also likely be affected, since many states are allowed to adopt California's rules as an alternative to the federal standard.

This bill most directly affects trucking companies, diesel engine manufacturers, and freight operators who do business in California and any states that follow California's emission rules. It also affects California residents and others in those states who would otherwise see air quality benefits from the stricter standards. Consumers could also be affected, since cleaner engine requirements can influence the cost and availability of heavy-duty trucks and goods transported by them.
ai_headline: Senate bill would strip California's authority to enforce tighter truck emission rules
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

Other states that had adopted California's stricter standards in place of the federal standard would also likely be affected.

title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "California State Motor Vehicle and Engine Pollution Control Standards; Advanced Clean Cars II; Waiver of Preemption; Notice of Decision".
ai_summary:
This bill uses a law called the Congressional Review Act to cancel a decision made by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). The EPA decision in question gave California special permission to enforce its own stricter car pollution rules, known as the Advanced Clean Cars II program. California's rules require automakers to sell a growing percentage of zero-emission vehicles in the state each year, eventually banning the sale of new gas-only cars by 2035. If this resolution passes and is signed into law, that EPA permission would be wiped out, and California's stricter rules could not take effect.

The reason California needs EPA permission in the first place is that federal law normally does not allow states to set their own vehicle emission standards. California is the only state with a longstanding legal exception to that rule, and more than a dozen other states have chosen to follow California's standards instead of the federal ones. Canceling the EPA waiver would affect not just California but all those other states as well, since they would lose the ability to follow California's stricter program.

title: No Tariffs on Groceries Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change who has the power to place tariffs on food. Right now, the President can impose tariffs on imported goods, including food, without needing Congress to vote on it first. This bill would require the President to ask Congress for permission before adding any new tariffs on food products. Congress would then have to pass a law specifically approving those tariffs before they could take effect. Existing tariff rules already in place would not be affected.

The bill covers a wide range of food-related goods. "Articles of food" includes anything people or animals eat or drink, ingredients used to make those products, and farm supplies like seeds, fertilizers, and agricultural chemicals. So this would apply not just to finished grocery items, but also to the raw materials and inputs used to grow and produce food.

This bill would most directly affect consumers who buy groceries, farmers and food producers who import ingredients or supplies, and businesses in the food supply chain. It would also shift some authority from the executive branch to Congress when it comes to food-related trade policy. The bill was introduced in the House and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which handles tax and trade legislation. It has not yet been voted on.

title: No Iranian Energy Act
ai_summary:
This bill would expand existing US sanctions on Iran to specifically cover natural gas. Right now, US law already has sanctions on Iran covering many goods and financial dealings, but natural gas has some exceptions. This bill would close those exceptions, making it illegal under US sanctions law to buy, sell, or transfer natural gas to or from Iran. The bill was introduced partly in response to Iraq regularly buying natural gas from Iran to power its electrical grid.

The main target is Iraq's government, which imports Iranian natural gas to keep its lights on. If this bill became law, any country, company, or bank that helps Iran sell its natural gas could face US penalties, such as being cut off from the US financial system or facing trade restrictions. Iraq would have to choose between finding another energy source or risking those penalties.

Ordinary Americans would not be directly affected since the US does not import Iranian gas. However, the bill could indirectly impact energy markets in the Middle East and affect US foreign policy relationships, particularly with Iraq, which is a country the US has close ties with. Energy companies that do business internationally would also need to watch whether any of their deals touch Iranian natural gas.

title: Free Iraq from Iran Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires the U.S. government to create a formal plan within 180 days to reduce Iran's influence over Iraq. The State Department, Treasury Department, and U.S. media agencies would work together on a strategy that includes supporting Iraqi citizens and independent journalists, using intelligence tools to track Iranian-backed militias, and expanding U.S. broadcasting in Iraq to counter what the bill calls Iranian propaganda. The bill also requires the Secretary of State to officially label several specific Iraqi militia groups as foreign terrorist organizations within 90 days of passage.

The bill would cut off all U.S. military and financial aid to the Iraqi government unless Iraq takes concrete steps to remove Iranian-backed militias from its security forces and government. A presidential waiver can lift this ban if Iraq shows real progress. Additionally, the Treasury Department would be required to identify and sanction specific Iraqi political figures, military leaders, judges, and financiers accused of working on Iran's behalf. The bill names several individuals directly, including former Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki and others in current Iraqi government positions.

The bill primarily affects the U.S. government agencies that currently give aid or assistance to Iraq, the Iraqi government itself, and the named militia groups and individuals who could face sanctions. American companies or banks that do any business connected to the listed groups could also be impacted. Iraqi citizens are indirectly affected, since cutting U.S. aid to their government could change how Iraq's security forces operate and what services the government can provide.

title: Stop Fueling Cartel Violence Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires the U.S. Department of Defense to study and write a report on how Mexican drug cartels are stealing and smuggling fuel — things like crude oil, diesel, and gasoline — across the border into the United States. Congress believes this fuel theft has become one of the cartels' biggest sources of money outside of drug trafficking, with smugglers mislabeling stolen oil as "waste oil" to sneak it into the U.S., mainly through parts of Texas. The report must be finished within 180 days of the bill becoming law and sent to congressional defense committees.

The report must cover what the military is already doing to stop this smuggling, and what more could be done. This includes sharing information with other government agencies, working with other countries' security forces, and identifying the key people and networks involved in the smuggling. The bill focuses on non-combat approaches — no military strikes or invasions are called for.

This bill would mainly affect federal agencies like the Defense Department, the Treasury Department, and law enforcement groups such as the DEA and FBI, who would need to coordinate on the issue. It could also affect businesses in Texas's oil industry, since some U.S.-based companies have reportedly been receiving stolen oil shipments. Ordinary Americans could be indirectly affected if the policy eventually disrupts cartel funding, which is tied to fentanyl trafficking as well.

title: Gig Is Up Act
ai_summary:
This bill targets large companies that use a lot of gig or contract workers instead of regular employees. Specifically, it applies to any company that earns at least $100 million per year and uses at least 10,000 independent contractors. For those companies, the bill requires them to withhold payroll taxes from contractor payments, the same way they already do for regular employees. It also doubles the employer's share of Social Security and Medicare taxes for those contractors, meaning the company pays more into those systems on behalf of each contractor.

The bill affects two main groups. First, it affects large gig economy platforms like major rideshare, delivery, or freelance marketplace companies that rely heavily on independent contractors. Those companies would face higher tax costs and new paperwork requirements. Second, it affects the contractors themselves, who would have taxes taken out of their paychecks automatically rather than having to calculate and pay estimated taxes on their own throughout the year. Their payments would also count toward Social Security benefits in a clearer way.

The broader goal of the bill is to close a gap where large companies using gig workers pay less in taxes than companies with traditional employees. Supporters would say it levels the playing field and helps workers build Social Security benefits. Critics might argue it raises costs for companies and could reduce opportunities or earnings for gig workers. The bill was introduced in the House in June 2026 and was sent to the Ways and Means Committee, where tax-related legislation is first reviewed.

title: DC ROADS Act
ai_summary:
This bill would make it illegal for Washington, D.C. to create a congestion pricing program. Congestion pricing is a system where drivers are charged a fee to enter or drive through a busy area, usually to reduce traffic and raise money for transportation. The bill would block D.C.'s city government, both its city council and its mayor, from ever setting up or enforcing that kind of toll on any road, bridge, tunnel, or ramp in or entering the District.

The bill does this by changing D.C.'s Home Rule Act, which is the federal law that spells out what D.C.'s local government is and is not allowed to do. Because D.C. is not a state, Congress has the power to place limits on what D.C.'s government can decide for itself. Adding this restriction to the Home Rule Act means D.C. could not create a congestion toll even if its own elected leaders wanted to.

This bill mainly affects people who drive into or through Washington, D.C., as well as D.C. residents and its local government. Drivers, especially commuters from nearby Virginia and Maryland, would not face new fees for entering the city under this bill. D.C.'s government would lose the ability to use congestion pricing as a tool to manage traffic or raise transportation funding. title: Motor Carrier Safety Screening Modernization Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes changes to how trucking companies check the safety records of their drivers, both when hiring new drivers and when reviewing current employees. Right now, federal law only clearly covers these background checks during the hiring process. This bill expands that to include checks on drivers who are already employed. It also adds new protections so that if a company takes a negative action against a driver based on their safety record data, the driver must be notified and given a fair amount of time to appeal before anything happens to their job.

The bill also addresses problems with the federal safety database system used to track truck driver violations. Within one year of becoming law, the government would be required to clearly label any safety violation in that database as "contested" if a driver is actively challenging it, so that employers can see the dispute is ongoing. It also requires the government to create a formal appeals process where drivers can challenge the outcome of a data review, and that appeal must be decided by someone different from the person who originally issued the violation.

This bill mainly affects commercial truck drivers and the companies that employ them. Drivers benefit from stronger protections against losing their job based on disputed or inaccurate records. Trucking companies are affected because they will have new responsibilities when using safety data to make employment decisions. State transportation agencies that receive federal safety funding will also need to set up the new appeals process.

title: Ensuring Access to General Surgery Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill directs the federal government to study the shortage of general surgeons across the country and figure out a better way to identify which communities do not have enough of them. Right now, the government uses a general system to label areas as having too few health professionals, but this bill says that system may not accurately capture where general surgeons specifically are lacking. The Health Resources and Services Administration would have one year to complete the study and report the findings to Congress. The study would look at things like how long patients wait for care, health outcomes, how far people have to travel to reach a surgeon, and whether hospitals in an area actually have surgical services available.

Based on what the study finds, the Secretary of Health and Human Services would have the option to create an official process for designating "general surgery shortage areas." This would involve analyzing data by ZIP code and hospital service zones, counting active general surgeons, and setting thresholds for what counts as an adequate, inadequate, or critically short supply of surgeons. Those designations would be reviewed every year and updated as needed.

The people most directly affected are residents of rural communities, where the bill notes there are currently only about 69 percent of the general surgeons needed. Hospitals, medical organizations, and patient groups would all be consulted during the process. Doctors completing their training could also be affected down the road, since these shortage designations can influence where new physicians choose or are incentivized to practice.

title: Medical Foods and Formulas Access Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill requires Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and federal employee health plans to cover special medical foods and formulas for people with certain serious digestive and inherited metabolic disorders. These are conditions where a person's body cannot properly break down or absorb regular food, so specially made formulas or low-protein food products become their primary treatment. Right now, coverage for these products is inconsistent, and many patients either pay out of pocket or go without. Under this bill, coverage must include the formulas themselves, related vitamins and amino acids, and any equipment needed to use them, such as feeding tubes when necessary.

The bill covers a specific list of conditions, including rare genetic disorders found through newborn screening, short bowel syndrome, severe food allergies, Crohn's disease, eosinophilic esophagitis, and certain liver and pancreatic diseases. It does not cover everyday diet foods, gluten-free products for general use, or diabetes management foods. Medicare would cover 80 percent of the cost after a fee schedule is set. The bill also says that if any state already has stronger coverage protections in place, those state laws remain in effect and are not overridden.

This bill most directly affects children and adults with rare metabolic disorders, serious gastrointestinal diseases, or severe food-protein allergies who rely on specialized formulas as their main source of nutrition. It also affects their families, who currently often bear high out-of-pocket costs. Federal employees covered through the federal health benefits program would gain coverage as well. The bill does not legally require private insurance companies to provide this coverage, but it expresses Congress's opinion that they should.

title: To require the Secretary of Agriculture to enter into a memoranda of understanding with CFIUS with respect to reports under AFIDA and to update the AFIDA handbook.
ai_summary:
This bill deals with how the U.S. government tracks foreign ownership of American farmland. Right now, a 1978 law called the Agricultural Foreign Investment Disclosure Act (AFIDA) requires foreign buyers to report when they purchase U.S. agricultural land. This bill would require the Department of Agriculture to share that reporting data with CFIUS, which is the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, the federal body that reviews whether foreign purchases of American assets pose national security risks. The two agencies would need to set up a formal agreement to make that sharing happen within one year.

The bill also requires the Department of Agriculture to update its official instruction guide for handling AFIDA reports. That handbook has not been modernized in some time, and a 2024 government watchdog report found problems with how the data is collected, tracked, and shared. Under this bill, the updated handbook would need to reflect those watchdog recommendations and be revised again every ten years going forward.

The people most directly affected are foreign nationals and foreign companies that own or buy U.S. farmland, since their information would now flow to a national security review body. It also affects federal agencies that deal with agricultural land data and foreign investment oversight. American farmers and rural landowners could be indirectly affected if increased scrutiny leads to changes in who can purchase agricultural land near them, though the bill itself does not restrict any purchases.
ai_headline: Farm data on foreign land buyers would go to national security reviewers

title: FIGHT Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill updates an existing federal law called the Animal Welfare Act to specifically ban gambling on animal fighting events. Right now, the law already makes it illegal to organize, participate in, or attend animal fights like cockfighting or dogfighting. This bill adds a new rule making it illegal to place a bet on those fights, whether you are there in person or watching a broadcast of the event.

The bill also updates the official title of that section of law to more clearly list everything that is prohibited, including bringing children under 16 to these events, which was already banned. Adding gambling to the list closes a gap where someone could argue they were only betting on a fight rather than actively taking part in running it.

This affects anyone in the United States who might gamble on animal fights, either at the location of the fight or through some kind of remote viewing or broadcast. People who organize or attend these events were already breaking federal law, and this bill would extend that legal risk to anyone placing a wager on the outcome.

title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Bureau of Land Management relating to "North Dakota Field Office Record of Decision and Approved Resource Management Plan".
ai_summary:
This resolution uses a law called the Congressional Review Act to cancel a land management plan that the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) finalized on January 14, 2025. That plan, called the North Dakota Field Office Resource Management Plan, set the rules for how millions of acres of federal public land in North Dakota would be managed over the coming years. It covered things like oil and gas drilling, grazing, recreation, conservation, and other uses of that land. Congress voted to throw out the plan entirely, meaning it has no legal force.

The Congressional Review Act allows Congress to overturn recent federal agency rules with a simple majority vote in both chambers, followed by the president's signature. That is exactly what happened here. The House passed it in September 2025, the Senate passed it in October 2025, and it was signed into law on December 11, 2025. Once a rule is struck down this way, the agency generally cannot issue a new rule that is substantially the same without new authorization from Congress.

This resolution directly affects people and industries that use or depend on federal public land in western North Dakota, including ranchers with grazing permits, oil and gas companies with drilling interests, hunters, hikers, and conservation groups. With the plan canceled, the BLM must revert to older guidance for managing that land while any future planning process plays out. Local communities whose economies are tied to activities on federal land in that region are also affected by the uncertainty about what rules will govern those lands going forward.

ai_summary:
This bill is Congress's way of canceling a specific decision made by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) in December 2024. That BLM decision effectively stopped an oil and gas leasing program on the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR) in Alaska. Using a law called the Congressional Review Act, Congress can vote to cancel federal agency rules or decisions it disagrees with. If this joint resolution passes both the Senate and the House and is signed by the President, the BLM's decision would be wiped out and have no legal effect.

The practical result would be that the pathway for oil and gas drilling leases on Alaska's Coastal Plain would be reopened. The 2024 BLM decision had blocked that leasing program, so canceling it would put things back toward allowing energy companies to apply for leases to drill in that area. It does not automatically start drilling, but it removes the specific federal decision that was standing in the way.

The people most directly affected are Alaska residents, Alaska Native communities in and around the Arctic region, energy companies interested in drilling there, and federal land managers. More broadly, it touches anyone with an interest in energy production, federal public land use, or wildlife conservation in the Arctic, since the Coastal Plain is considered both an energy resource and a sensitive wildlife habitat.

title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Internal Revenue Service relating to "Gross Proceeds Reporting by Brokers That Regularly Provide Services Effectuating Digital Asset Sales".
ai_summary:
This bill is Congress's way of canceling a rule that the IRS finalized in late 2024. That rule would have required brokers who help people buy and sell digital assets, like cryptocurrency, to report the gross proceeds from those sales to the IRS. Congress has the power to cancel federal agency rules through a process called the Congressional Review Act, and this resolution is an attempt to use that power to block the IRS rule before it takes effect.

If the rule were allowed to stand, brokers operating in the digital asset space would have to send information about customer transactions to the IRS, similar to how traditional stockbrokers already report stock sales. The resolution, if passed by both chambers and signed into law, would wipe out that requirement entirely and prevent the IRS from issuing a similar rule in the future without new direction from Congress.

This primarily affects people and businesses involved in cryptocurrency and other digital assets. That includes crypto exchanges, other platforms that help users trade digital assets, and everyday people who buy or sell crypto. If the rule is canceled, those brokers would not be required to report transaction data to the IRS under this particular regulation. If it stays in place, the IRS would have more information to check whether people are correctly reporting crypto gains on their tax returns.

title: Disaster Related Extension of Deadlines Act
ai_summary:
This bill fixes two specific problems that disaster victims sometimes face with the IRS. First, when the IRS gives people extra time to file their taxes because of a declared disaster, that extra time is supposed to also apply when someone wants to claim a tax refund or credit. Currently, the law has a gap where the disaster extension does not automatically count toward the deadline for requesting a refund, which means some disaster victims lose their right to get money back from the IRS even though they were given more time to file. This bill closes that gap by making the disaster extension count for refund claims too.

Second, the bill addresses collection notices. Right now, the IRS can send demand letters or collection notices based on the original tax deadline, even if a disaster extension has pushed that deadline back. This can create confusion or pressure for people who are supposed to have more time to pay. The bill requires the IRS to factor in any disaster-related deadline extension before sending those collection notices.

The people most affected are taxpayers who live in areas hit by federally declared disasters, significant fires, or terrorist or military actions. This includes homeowners, renters, small business owners, and anyone else who received an IRS disaster filing extension and either wants to claim a refund or is worried about receiving IRS collection notices during their extension period. The bill does not change who qualifies for disaster extensions, only how those extensions are applied in these two situations.

title: Wounded Knee Massacre Memorial and Sacred Site Act
ai_summary:
This bill deals with about 40 acres of land in Wounded Knee, South Dakota, where a massacre of Lakota Sioux people took place on December 29, 1890. The bill would direct the Secretary of the Interior to officially place that land into a special legal status called "restricted fee status," which would be jointly held by two tribes: the Oglala Sioux Tribe and the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe. The tribes already own this land, but this bill would lock in legal protections for it. The government would have one year after the bill becomes law to complete all the necessary paperwork and steps.

Under restricted fee status, the land would become a permanent memorial and sacred site. The tribes would not be able to sell or transfer the land without approval from both Congress and the tribes themselves. The land would not be taxed by state or local governments. The tribes would also have more freedom to use the land without needing constant federal government approval, as long as they follow a 2022 agreement the two tribes made with each other. The bill also specifically bans the land from ever being used for gambling or gaming.

The people most directly affected are members of the Oglala Sioux Tribe and the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe, as well as anyone who visits or has utility or road access rights connected to that land. South Dakota state and local governments would lose any ability to tax that property. More broadly, the bill affects how the federal government handles its legal relationship with these two tribes over this historically significant piece of land.
ai_headline: Senate bill locks Wounded Knee land into permanent tribal memorial status

title: MAPWaters Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill directs several federal agencies to collect, organize, and post information online about public access to federal waterways. Within five years of the law passing, agencies like the National Park Service, Bureau of Land Management, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the Forest Service, and the Bureau of Reclamation would need to create digital maps showing things like which boat ramps are open, where fishing is restricted, speed limits on the water, and what types of watercraft are allowed in different areas. The agencies would also need to agree on shared data standards within two and a half years so their information is compatible and easy to combine. Fishing restriction data would need to be updated in real time, while other access information would be updated at least twice a year.

The bill affects anyone who uses federal waterways for outdoor recreation, including boaters, kayakers, anglers, swimmers, and others. Right now, rules and access information are spread across multiple agencies and can be hard to find. This bill would bring that information together in one place online, making it easier for people to know before they go whether a waterway is open, what the rules are, and where they can launch a boat or fish.

Importantly, the bill does not change any existing rules about who can use the water or open up any new areas to recreation. It only changes how information about current rules is shared with the public. The government would be required to report progress to Congress each year through 2034, and agencies could partner with technology companies, states, tribes, and nonprofits to help get the work done.

title: Temporary Extension of Fentanyl-Related Substances Scheduling Act
ai_summary:
This bill would extend a temporary federal rule that treats fentanyl-related substances as strictly controlled, dangerous drugs. Under current law, these substances are classified as Schedule I drugs, meaning they are illegal to manufacture, sell, or possess without special federal authorization. That classification was set to expire on March 31, 2025. This bill would push that expiration date back by six months, to September 30, 2025, giving Congress more time to decide on a permanent policy.

The rule being extended covers fentanyl analogues, which are chemicals that are similar in structure to fentanyl but slightly different. Drug makers sometimes create these variations to try to get around existing drug laws. By keeping these substances on the controlled list, the government can continue to prosecute people who make, distribute, or possess them illegally.

This bill would affect drug enforcement agencies, courts, and prosecutors who rely on this scheduling to bring criminal cases. It would also affect anyone involved in the manufacture or distribution of these substances, as well as researchers and medical professionals who need special permits to study them. Patients using legitimate fentanyl-based medications prescribed by a doctor are not affected, since those approved drugs are handled under separate rules.

title: Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
ai_summary:
This bill is essentially a government funding law that keeps the entire federal government running through the end of the 2025 fiscal year, which is September 30, 2025. Because Congress did not pass a full set of regular spending bills on time, this law steps in and funds all federal departments and agencies, mostly at the same spending levels used in 2024. It covers everything from the military and border security to schools, hospitals, housing, and foreign aid. The Defense Department receives some adjusted funding levels for military pay, equipment purchases, and shipbuilding, and an extra 8 billion dollars is set aside for military operations in the Middle East and Europe.

The bill also extends a number of health programs that would otherwise have expired. These include funding for community health clinics, diabetes research programs, telehealth services through Medicare, and payments to rural and small hospitals that serve Medicare patients. Medicaid funding to states is also continued, and certain cuts to Medicaid that were previously scheduled are delayed. Teen health education programs and family support centers receive extensions as well.

Beyond the main spending and health sections, the bill includes several smaller but noteworthy items. It extends a federal order that keeps fentanyl-related substances classified as controlled drugs, strengthens rules for protecting certain facilities from drone threats, and continues cybersecurity programs. People most directly affected include federal employees and military service members whose paychecks depend on this funding, as well as seniors on Medicare, low-income families using Medicaid, rural residents relying on community health centers, and anyone who receives federal benefits like Supplemental Security Income or foster care assistance.
ai_headline: Federal government funded through September 2025 under new spending law
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-4.

title: Veteran Fraud Reimbursement Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes the rules for what happens when a fiduciary misuses a veteran's benefits. A fiduciary is a person appointed to manage money on behalf of someone who cannot do so themselves, such as a veteran with a disability. Under this bill, if a fiduciary steals or misuses those benefits, the Department of Veterans Affairs must repay the full amount directly to the veteran or a new fiduciary. Currently, repayment rules are more limited and inconsistent. This bill makes repayment a clear requirement rather than something that depends on certain conditions being met first.

The bill also addresses what happens if the veteran dies before receiving that repayment. In that case, the money would go to the veteran's eligible survivors or estate, following existing rules. Importantly, the fiduciary who committed the fraud cannot receive any of that money. The VA is also required to make a genuine effort to recover the stolen funds from the bad actor, and any money recovered would be paid back to the veteran or their successor.

This bill primarily affects veterans who rely on a fiduciary to manage their VA benefits, along with their families. It also sets rules for VA oversight, requiring the department to develop a process for determining whether its own negligence contributed to fraud, but without using that review as a reason to delay repaying the veteran. Veterans service organizations and VA administrators would also be affected by the new procedures this bill puts in place.

Under current law, repayment rules are limited and depend on certain conditions being met first. ai_summary:

A fiduciary is someone appointed to manage benefit payments on behalf of a veteran who cannot manage their own finances. The VA also has to make a genuine effort to recover that money from the dishonest fiduciary.

Family members or legal representatives of affected veterans may also be impacted if they become successor fiduciaries or survivors entitled to repayment.

title: Youth Prevention and Recovery Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews a federal grant program focused on preventing drug and alcohol misuse among young people and helping those already dealing with substance use problems. The program was originally created in 2018 and was set to expire. This bill would extend it through 2028 and fund it from 2026 through 2030, starting at 10 million dollars per year and growing to 15 million dollars by 2030. It also makes some updates to the program's language, such as replacing the older term "abuse" with "misuse," and broadening eligibility so that groups of school districts can apply together, not just individual ones.

The bill also expands which schools can receive grants. Previously only high schools were mentioned, but the updated language includes all secondary schools, which can mean middle schools as well depending on how a state defines that term. Tribal nations are also specifically included as eligible recipients, and the bill updates the legal definitions used to refer to them. Grant applicants would now also be required to show a plan for how their programs will continue after the federal funding ends.

The people most directly affected are middle and high school students, especially those considered at higher risk for substance misuse. Schools, school districts, community organizations, and tribal nations that apply for these grants would also be affected, as would the staff who run prevention and recovery programs funded through this money. Parents and families of young people in those communities could also feel the impact if their local programs receive funding.

title: A bill to authorize the President to award the Medal of Honor to James Capers, Jr., for acts of valor as a member of the Marine Corps during the Vietnam War
ai_summary:
This bill would allow the President to give the Medal of Honor to James Capers, Jr., a Marine Corps veteran who served during the Vietnam War. Normally, there are strict deadlines for awarding military medals, and decades must not have passed since the acts took place. This bill specifically waives those time limits so Capers can receive the honor despite how much time has gone by.

The Medal of Honor is the highest military award the United States gives out. Capers was previously awarded the Silver Star for his bravery during a four-day period in late March and early April 1967. This bill recognizes that his actions during that time may have deserved an even higher level of recognition than he originally received.

This bill directly affects James Capers, Jr., and his family. More broadly, it is part of a long-standing pattern in Congress of revisiting past military awards to correct cases where veterans, sometimes from minority groups who faced discrimination in the military, may not have received the full recognition they earned. If the bill passes, the President would have the legal authority to present Capers with the Medal of Honor, though the President would not be required to do so.

title: Trafficking Survivors Relief Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill creates a legal process for people who were victims of human trafficking to clear their federal criminal records. If someone was forced or coerced into committing a crime because they were being trafficked, they can ask a federal court to wipe away certain convictions or arrests. For non-violent offenses, a court can completely erase the conviction. For arrests that did not lead to a conviction, the records can also be cleared. People currently in prison for crimes they committed because of trafficking may also ask for a shorter sentence. Filing these requests is free, and all paperwork is kept private to protect the person's identity.

The bill also creates a formal legal defense that trafficking survivors can use if they are currently facing federal charges. If a defendant can show strong evidence they were being trafficked at the time of the crime, the law would treat their actions as likely done under duress, meaning they were forced into it. Even if someone did not use this defense during their original trial, they can still bring it up later when asking for a reduced sentence or other relief.

This bill mainly affects people who were victims of human trafficking and ended up with federal criminal records as a result of crimes they were made to commit. It also affects federal prosecutors, judges, and legal aid organizations. The government will be required to track how the law is used and report back to Congress. Legal aid groups that receive certain federal grants would also be allowed to use that money to help trafficking survivors navigate this process.

title: Miracle on Ice Congressional Gold Medal Act
ai_summary:
This law honors the 20 players and coaching staff of the 1980 U.S. Olympic Men's Ice Hockey Team by awarding them Congressional Gold Medals, which is one of the highest honors Congress can give a civilian or group. The team, made up of amateur college players, famously defeated the heavily favored Soviet Union team during the 1980 Winter Olympics in Lake Placid, New York, in a game that became known as the "Miracle on Ice." They then beat Finland to win the gold medal. Congress is recognizing this achievement as a moment that lifted American spirits during a difficult time in the country's history.

Three physical gold medals will be made and placed on permanent public display, one each at the Lake Placid Olympic Center in New York, the United States Hockey Hall of Fame Museum in Minnesota, and the United States Olympic and Paralympic Museum in Colorado. The U.S. Mint will also be allowed to make and sell bronze copies of the medal to the public at a price that covers the cost of making them. Any money from those sales goes back into the U.S. Mint's operating fund, so there is no net cost to taxpayers from the duplicate medals.

This law directly affects the surviving members of the 1980 team, who receive the honor, and the three museums, which will house the medals. It also gives the general public a chance to purchase bronze versions as collectibles. Anyone interested in American sports history, Cold War history, or ice hockey would likely find this law meaningful, but it does not change taxes, government programs, or everyday rules for ordinary Americans.

title: Filing Relief for Natural Disasters Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes two main changes to how the IRS handles tax deadlines during natural disasters. First, it allows state governors to formally request that the IRS extend tax deadlines for people in their state after a state-declared disaster, not just federally declared ones. Right now, the IRS can only automatically extend deadlines when the federal government officially declares a disaster. Under this bill, a governor could ask the IRS to grant the same kind of relief even if the disaster hasn't reached the federal declaration level.

Second, the bill doubles the minimum automatic extension period from 60 days to 120 days. When a qualifying disaster occurs, affected taxpayers would have at least 120 days of extra time to file returns, make payments, and meet other IRS deadlines, instead of the current 60-day minimum. This applies to disasters in U.S. territories like Puerto Rico, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands as well, not just the 50 states and Washington, D.C.

This bill affects anyone who lives or does business in an area hit by a natural disaster such as a hurricane, tornado, wildfire, flood, earthquake, or similar event. That includes individual taxpayers, small business owners, and others who might struggle to meet IRS deadlines while dealing with disaster recovery. The changes would only apply to disaster declarations made after the bill becomes law.

title: LET’S Protect Workers Act
ai_summary:
This bill raises the fines that businesses can be charged when they break federal laws meant to protect workers. Right now, many of those fines are so low that some employers find it cheaper to break the rules than to follow them. The bill would sharply increase penalties across several areas: child labor violations, minimum wage and overtime rules, workplace safety, farmworker protections, mine safety, and family medical leave. For example, fines for serious or repeated workplace safety violations would jump from a maximum of $70,000 to $800,000, and fines for child labor violations causing death or serious injury could reach $700,000. Employers who violate workers' rights to organize a union could face fines up to $50,000 per violation, and company directors or officers could be held personally responsible in some cases.

The bill also addresses a specific problem with mine operators who refuse to pay fines they owe. If a mine company ignores a final penalty order for more than 180 days, the government could shut down the mine until the debt is paid. Additionally, the bill clarifies that recordkeeping violations are considered ongoing until the employer actually fixes them, which prevents companies from avoiding larger fines by dragging their feet on paperwork corrections.

This bill would affect a wide range of people. Workers in industries like construction, agriculture, mining, and food service would potentially see stronger enforcement of their existing legal protections. Employers, especially those with repeated violations, would face significantly higher financial consequences. Health insurance plan administrators would also face new penalties if they fail to provide equal coverage for mental health and substance use treatment compared to physical health care.

title: REPO Implementation Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill updates an existing law called the REPO for Ukrainians Act, which was passed in 2024 and allows the US government to seize or freeze Russian government money held in the United States because of Russia's war against Ukraine. The new bill makes changes to how that frozen money is managed and sent to Ukraine. Specifically, it requires the Treasury Department to invest the frozen funds in US government bonds to earn interest while the money sits in a special account called the Ukraine Support Fund. It also sets up a schedule requiring at least $250 million to be released from that fund every 90 days for Ukraine's benefit.

The bill also directs the US government to work with other countries, including G7 nations, European Union members, and Australia, to encourage them to do something similar with Russian assets frozen in their own countries. The State Department would be asked to push these countries to redirect at least 5 percent of those assets every quarter toward helping Ukraine. The President would also be required to report to Congress on where Russian sovereign assets are located around the world, how much exists, and whether those assets are frozen or earning interest.

This bill mainly affects the executive branch agencies that manage frozen foreign assets, including the Treasury and State Departments. It indirectly affects Ukraine, which would receive financial assistance from the fund, and Russia, whose government money would be used. Ordinary Americans are not directly affected in their daily lives, though the bill reflects decisions about how the US handles foreign policy and the use of foreign government assets held in this country.

ai_summary:
This bill would create a new team inside the FBI specifically focused on animal cruelty crimes. The group would investigate and enforce existing federal laws that already ban things like dogfighting, cockfighting, and crush videos (illegal videos showing animals being harmed). Animal welfare organizations and federal agencies involved in related work would also be part of the broader effort.
