title: To amend title XVIII of the Social Security Act to provide coverage for wigs as durable medical equipment under the Medicare program, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill would change Medicare rules to cover wigs, referred to in the bill as "cranial prostheses," as a type of medical equipment. Right now, Medicare generally does not pay for wigs, even when a person loses their hair due to a medical condition. If passed, Medicare would cover the cost of a wig when a doctor — specifically a dermatologist, oncologist, or the patient's primary physician — provides a written statement confirming it is medically necessary. The coverage would apply to hair loss caused by health conditions like cancer, chemotherapy, or autoimmune diseases such as alopecia.

This bill would affect Medicare beneficiaries, who are mostly Americans aged 65 and older, as well as younger people on Medicare due to disability. Among those most directly affected would be cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy and people with autoimmune conditions that cause hair loss. Without this bill, those patients must pay for wigs entirely out of pocket, which can cost hundreds to thousands of dollars.

The bill does not give everyone on Medicare automatic wig coverage. A doctor must certify in writing that the wig is medically necessary, and coverage is limited to cases tied to specific health conditions. Medicare would not cover wigs purchased for non-medical reasons. The bill was introduced in the House and has been sent to two committees for review before any further action.

title: RURAL Healthcare Act
ai_summary:
This bill is about temporary healthcare workers called "locum tenens" professionals. These are doctors, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, and certified nurse anesthetists who fill in at hospitals or clinics on a short-term basis, often in rural or underserved areas where finding permanent staff is difficult. The bill would officially classify these temporary workers as independent contractors rather than employees under two major federal laws: the Fair Labor Standards Act, which covers things like minimum wage and overtime, and the National Labor Relations Act, which covers workers' rights to organize and bargain collectively.

In practical terms, this means that healthcare facilities using these temporary workers would not be required to treat them like regular employees under those two laws. The facilities would not be obligated to provide certain employee-related protections or benefits that those laws require. To qualify under this bill, the worker must have a written contract agreeing to contractor status and must work at any single location for no more than one continuous year.

This bill most directly affects temporary healthcare professionals who travel and fill short-term staffing gaps, as well as the hospitals, clinics, and healthcare systems that hire them. It could make it easier and less costly for rural facilities to bring in temporary help, but it also means those workers would have fewer legal protections tied to employee status under these two specific federal laws. Patients in rural or underserved communities could see indirect effects if the change influences how often these workers are available in their area.
ai_headline: Bill would strip employee protections from traveling healthcare temps
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 18 - 15.

title: Portable Ultrasound Reimbursement Equity Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would change how Medicare pays for portable ultrasound services. Right now, Medicare already pays separately for the cost of transporting and setting up portable X-ray machines when a technician brings equipment directly to a patient, such as at a nursing home or the patient's house. This bill would extend that same payment system to portable ultrasound machines, so that the transportation and setup costs for bringing ultrasound equipment to patients would also be covered and paid for separately by Medicare. The change would take effect starting January 1, 2027.

The people most directly affected are Medicare patients who cannot easily travel to a clinic or hospital, such as elderly or disabled individuals living in nursing homes or receiving home health care. Currently, getting a portable ultrasound brought to them may be harder to arrange because providers and suppliers are not reimbursed for that service the same way they are for portable X-rays. This bill aims to close that gap so ultrasound access works the same way.

Suppliers and healthcare providers who offer portable diagnostic imaging services would also be affected. They would become eligible to receive separate Medicare payments for the work of transporting and setting up ultrasound equipment, similar to what they already receive for portable X-ray services. The bill also directs the government to set standards for these suppliers that are similar to existing rules for portable X-ray providers.
ai_headline: Medicare would cover portable ultrasound transport costs starting 2027
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Ways and Means, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.what: HR 2477 would extend Medicare's existing separate payment system for transportation and setup costs to include portable ultrasound equipment, not just portable X-ray machines. Under current law, Medicare reimburses providers separately when they transport and set up portable X-ray equipment at a patient's location, but no equivalent reimbursement exists for ultrasound. The bill would take effect January 1, 2027, and would also direct the government to set supplier standards similar to those already in place for portable X-ray providers.

Suppliers and healthcare providers who offer portable diagnostic imaging services would also be affected, becoming eligible for the new separate payments.
ai_sections.why: Without equivalent reimbursement for portable ultrasound, providers and suppliers currently have less financial incentive to bring ultrasound equipment directly to patients, which can make access harder to arrange. The bill aims to align portable ultrasound reimbursement with the system already in place for portable X-rays.
ai_sections.cost: Medicare would be required to pay separately for the transportation and setup costs of portable ultrasound equipment, mirroring existing separate payments it already makes for portable X-ray services.

title: Temporary Family Visitation Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates a new type of temporary visa specifically for foreign relatives of U.S. citizens and green card holders who want to visit family in the United States. Right now, those relatives typically use a standard tourist or visitor visa, which requires them to prove they do not intend to immigrate. This new "family purpose" visa category would make it easier for close relatives, including spouses, children, parents, grandparents, siblings, aunts, uncles, and cousins, to visit for things like weddings, births, graduations, religious events, or just everyday family time. The visit would be limited to no more than 90 days per calendar year.

To qualify, the U.S.-based family member must sign a financial support declaration taking responsibility for the visitor, and the visiting relative must have health insurance that covers them during their stay. The visitor also must sign a sworn statement saying they understand they are required to leave when their time is up and that there are legal consequences for overstaying. If a U.S. sponsor previously helped bring over a relative who then overstayed their visa, that sponsor would generally lose the ability to petition for future visitors under this program.

This bill would affect U.S. citizens and green card holders who have family members living abroad and want a clearer legal path to host them for visits. It would also affect those foreign relatives themselves. Additionally, people already in line for a permanent immigration visa could still use this temporary visa to visit while they wait, but that temporary visit could not be used as a stepping stone to apply for a green card from inside the United States.
ai_headline: New family visit visa would cap foreign relatives' stays at 90 days
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

Eligible relatives include spouses, children, parents, grandparents, siblings, aunts, uncles, and cousins. Visits are limited to no more than 90 days per calendar year.

However, a visitor could not use the temporary stay as a stepping stone to apply for a green card from inside the United States, and sponsors with a prior overstay on their record would lose eligibility to petition for future visitors under the program.

title: Right to Read Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill aims to strengthen students' access to school libraries and reading materials across the United States. It officially defines what an "effective school library" looks like, including having a certified librarian on staff, up-to-date books and digital resources, and equal access for all students. It also creates a formal "right to read," which means every student should have access to good reading instruction, library resources, materials at home, and the freedom to choose what they read.

The bill makes changes to existing federal education law to require states and school districts to explain in their plans how they will improve school libraries, especially for low-income students, minority students, students with disabilities, and English learners. It would authorize up to $500 million per year for literacy grants and $100 million per year for programs in high-need schools. It also directs the federal government to collect and report data every two years on school libraries nationwide, tracking things like staffing levels, book collections, and how librarians work with teachers.

The bill also includes two legal provisions worth noting. First, it protects teachers, librarians, and other school staff from lawsuits if they follow their school's or state's policies on student reading access. Second, it requires schools receiving federal funds to confirm they will protect students' First Amendment rights in libraries, meaning book selections cannot be driven by partisan or political motivations, and that school boards must make library decisions in a way that is consistent with constitutional free speech protections.
ai_headline: HR 6440 would fund school libraries and establish a federal right to read
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6440 creates a federal right to read, sets library standards, and authorizes up to $600M yearly for literacy and high-need schools.
ai_sections.what: HR 6440 defines what an effective school library must include, establishes a formal right to read for every student, and requires states and districts to address library improvement in their federal education plans. The bill also mandates that schools receiving federal funds protect students' First Amendment rights in libraries, prohibiting book selections driven by partisan or political motivations. Every two years, the federal government would collect and publish national data on school library staffing, collections, and librarian-teacher collaboration.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects students nationwide, with specific attention to low-income students, minority students, students with disabilities, and English learners. Teachers, librarians, and school staff are also addressed through a legal protection shielding them from lawsuits when they follow school or state policies on student reading access.
ai_sections.why: States and districts would be required to revise their education plans to account for library resources and access, creating new compliance obligations. Schools accepting federal funds would face a requirement to formally affirm their commitment to First Amendment protections in library decision-making.
ai_sections.cost: The bill authorizes up to $500 million per year for literacy grants and up to $100 million per year for programs in high-need schools.

title: Data BRIDGE Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to update its National Broadband Map by adding a new layer showing where farmland and agricultural areas are located across the country. The FCC would have 180 days after the law passes to make this change and would need to keep the map updated going forward. To build this layer, the FCC would work with the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which already has data on where farms and agricultural land are located.

The National Broadband Map is a tool that shows where high-speed internet service is and is not available in the United States. By adding a farm and agriculture layer on top of that existing map, policymakers and agencies could more easily see which farming areas lack reliable internet access. This could help guide decisions about where to build out or improve broadband infrastructure in rural and agricultural regions.

This bill would most directly affect farmers and people living in rural agricultural communities, since better data could help direct internet service to areas that currently lack it. It also affects the FCC, which would be responsible for creating and maintaining the new map layer, and the USDA, which would help provide the underlying data. Local and state governments could also use the updated map when planning their own broadband projects.
ai_headline: FCC ordered to add farmland layer to National Broadband Map
last_action_text: Forwarded by Subcommittee to Full Committee by Voice Vote.

The FCC has 180 days after enactment to complete this change and must keep the layer updated going forward. The FCC would use data provided by the U.S. Department of Agriculture to build the layer.

title: First-Time Homebuyer Tax Credit Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would create a tax credit of up to $15,000 for people buying their first home. The credit equals 10% of the home's purchase price, so if you buy a $150,000 home, you could get the full $15,000. To qualify, you must not have owned a home in the past three years, you must be at least 18 years old, and the home must be bought with a federally backed mortgage. The credit is refundable, meaning you can receive it even if it is larger than what you owe in taxes. The $15,000 limit will also adjust over time to keep up with inflation.

Not everyone qualifies for the full amount. The credit phases out if your income is above 150% of the median income for your area, meaning higher earners get a smaller credit or none at all. The credit also shrinks if the home's price is well above the typical price in your local area. Married couples filing separately can each claim up to $7,500. If two unmarried people buy a home together, they split the credit between them.

There is a catch if you sell or move out of the home within four years of buying it. You may have to pay back part of the credit, up to 25% for each remaining year in that four-year window. There are exceptions, such as if you die, lose your home to a natural disaster, move for a new job, or are a military or government employee on official orders. The bill also allows buyers to transfer the credit directly to their mortgage lender at closing, which could lower upfront costs like a down payment right away instead of waiting for tax season.
ai_headline: First-time homebuyers could claim up to $15,000 tax credit under HR 4717
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 4717 offers first-time homebuyers a refundable tax credit up to $15,000, equal to 10% of the purchase price, with income and price limits.

The credit adjusts for inflation over time. Buyers may also transfer the credit directly to their mortgage lender at closing to reduce upfront costs immediately.
ai_sections.who: To qualify, a buyer must not have owned a home in the past three years, must be at least 18 years old, and must purchase the home using a federally backed mortgage. The credit phases out for earners above 150% of their area's median income, and also shrinks if the home's price is well above the typical local price.
ai_sections.why: Because the credit is refundable, buyers can receive the full amount even if it exceeds what they owe in taxes. Buyers who sell or move out within four years of purchase may be required to repay up to 25% of the credit for each remaining year in that window, with exceptions for death, natural disaster, job relocation, or military and government orders.

title: Healthy H2O Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates a federal grant program through the U.S. Department of Agriculture to help certain people in rural areas pay for water filters and other drinking water treatment systems for their homes or facilities. To qualify, applicants must first get their water tested by a certified lab showing that harmful contaminants are present, such as lead, arsenic, PFAS chemicals, or E. coli. The grants can cover the cost of buying, installing, and maintaining approved filtration products. Nonprofit organizations can also receive grants to help connect rural residents with testing and filtration services. The program would be funded at up to $10 million per year from 2025 through 2029.

The program focuses on people who cannot easily access clean water through public systems, especially those who rely on private wells. Grants are limited to households or businesses earning no more than 150 percent of the median rural income for their state, which is roughly a middle- or lower-income threshold. Priority goes to private well users, since they have no public utility overseeing their water quality. Small rental property owners with 25 or fewer units and licensed child care facilities in rural areas are also eligible.

The bill affects rural residents across the country who face drinking water contamination but may not be able to afford filtration equipment on their own. It does not replace larger infrastructure projects like replacing old pipes or upgrading public water systems. Instead, it is meant as a faster, more immediate solution while longer-term fixes are worked on. The USDA would also be required to report to Congress each year on how the program is working and what water quality challenges remain.
ai_headline: USDA rural water filter grants would reach private well users starting 2025
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.

title: ALS Better Care Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change how Medicare pays for care given to people with ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig's disease. ALS is a serious illness that damages the nervous system and gradually takes away a person's ability to move, speak, and breathe. Starting in 2027, Medicare would cover a bundle of services specifically designed for ALS patients, including visits with doctors or nurse practitioners, physical therapy, speech therapy, occupational therapy, nutrition support, respiratory care, and help getting medical equipment. Medicare would pay the provider a flat fee of $800 per visit for this care package, and patients would pay nothing out of pocket for it. The payment amount would be reviewed and adjusted over time to keep up with rising costs.

The bill also addresses telehealth, recognizing that many ALS patients live far from specialized clinics or eventually have trouble traveling as their condition worsens. By including remote care as part of the covered services, the bill aims to make sure patients in rural areas or places with few medical providers can still get the specialized help they need without making long trips.

A separate part of the bill requires the Department of Health and Human Services to submit a report to Congress within 90 days of the bill becoming law. That report would look at the problems facing ALS clinical trials, such as difficulty finding enough staff or funding, and would suggest steps the government could take to fix those problems. The people most directly affected by this bill are Medicare patients diagnosed with ALS, the clinics and healthcare providers who treat them, and researchers working on ALS treatments.

title: BOOST American Business Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates a new group of specialized diplomats called the Commercial Diplomatic Service, housed within the State Department. These officers would be dedicated to helping American businesses sell their products and services overseas, find foreign partners, navigate foreign regulations, and compete for contracts in other countries. The goal is to grow this group to 750 officers by 2028. The bill also creates a new leadership position, a Director General, to oversee both the traditional Foreign Service and this new commercial track.

The bill is largely a response to deep budget cuts proposed for the Commerce Department's Foreign Commercial Service, which currently handles much of this work with about 207 officers at roughly one-third of U.S. diplomatic posts. By moving this function to the State Department, the bill aims to make commercial support available at more posts worldwide and better connect business advocacy with broader foreign policy.

The people most directly affected are American businesses, especially smaller exporters and companies in industries the government considers strategically important, who would gain more on-the-ground help from U.S. diplomats abroad. It also affects current Foreign Service officers, some of whom could transfer into the new service, and job seekers with business backgrounds who could be hired directly under a streamlined process. Taxpayers and government employees at both the State and Commerce Departments would also see changes in how these overlapping functions are organized and funded.

The service would grow to 750 officers by 2028. A new Director General position would oversee both this commercial track and the traditional Foreign Service.

title: MACV–SOG Congressional Gold Medal Act
ai_summary:
This bill would award a Congressional Gold Medal to the members of MACV-SOG, a secret special operations unit that carried out dangerous missions in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia between 1964 and 1972. The unit conducted spy missions, sabotage, and rescue operations deep inside enemy territory. Because their work was classified, these soldiers never received public recognition for their service. About 1,579 Americans were killed or went missing while serving with the group, and more than 50 are still unaccounted for.

The medal itself would be a single gold medal designed by the U.S. Treasury Department and presented by Congress. After the ceremony, the medal would be permanently held at the Smithsonian Institution, where it could be displayed and studied. The government would also be allowed to make and sell bronze copies of the medal to cover the cost of producing them.

This bill mainly affects surviving veterans who served with MACV-SOG and the families of those who did not come home. It has no direct impact on taxes or government spending, since the cost of making the medals is covered by the U.S. Mint's own operating fund and any sales of bronze copies.

title: U.S. Customs and Border Protection Officer Retirement Technical Corrections Act
ai_summary:
This bill fixes a retirement benefit problem for a specific group of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers. In 2008, a law was passed that gave CBP officers better retirement benefits, including higher pension payments and protection from being forced to retire at a certain age. However, some officers got left out because of a timing technicality. These officers received job offers before July 6, 2008, but did not actually start working until on or after that date. Because of that gap, they were treated as if the 2008 law did not apply to them, even though it was meant to cover them.

The bill would fix that by officially counting those officers as if they were already on the job on July 6, 2008. This means they would receive the same higher pension benefits as their colleagues, and they would no longer face mandatory retirement age rules that others in their situation were exempt from. For officers who have already retired, the fix would apply retroactively, meaning they could receive back payments to make up for what they were shortchanged. The Department of Homeland Security and the Office of Personnel Management would handle the process of identifying who qualifies and correcting their benefits within 120 days of the law passing.

The bill directly affects a relatively small group of CBP officers who fell into this specific timing gap during the 2008 hiring process. It also directs the Government Accountability Office to review how CBP handles retirement benefit eligibility more broadly and report its findings to Congress within 18 months. Taxpayers would fund any corrected or back payments owed to eligible officers.

title: Hospice CARE Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill makes major changes to how Medicare oversees and pays for hospice care. Hospice is end-of-life care for people who are terminally ill and choose comfort-focused treatment instead of curative treatment. The bill does two main things: cracks down on fraud and low-quality providers, and updates how hospice services are paid for.

On the oversight side, the bill puts a five-year freeze on new hospice companies joining Medicare, with exceptions for areas that truly lack access. It requires all existing hospice programs to re-verify their enrollment information, and it forces more frequent inspections of newer or suspicious programs. Starting in 2028, hospice companies must give Medicare 90 days advance notice before changing ownership. Doctors who are financially tied to a hospice company can no longer be the ones certifying that a patient is terminally ill. Patients who enroll in hospice will receive a written notice explaining their benefits and who to call if they suspect fraud.

On the payment side, the bill restructures how Medicare pays hospice providers, shifting from a flat daily rate toward a system that also pays per visit for direct care like nursing or therapy. It also allows Medicare to cover certain treatments previously excluded from hospice, such as palliative chemotherapy, radiation, dialysis, or blood transfusions, at higher payment rates. The people most affected are Medicare patients nearing the end of life, their families, hospice companies, and the doctors and nurses who work in hospice care.

title: Future in Logging Careers Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change current child labor laws to allow 16- and 17-year-olds to work in logging and timber harvesting jobs that are currently off-limits to minors. Right now, federal law treats most logging work as too dangerous for anyone under 18. This bill would create an exception, letting teenagers work in a wide range of logging tasks, including operating heavy equipment like feller-bunchers, log loaders, bulldozers, excavators, and other large machinery used to cut, move, and process timber.

There is one important limit in the bill. The Secretary of Labor can still identify specific jobs within logging that are considered especially dangerous, and those particular jobs would remain restricted for 16- and 17-year-olds. However, if the teenager works for a logging business owned or operated by a parent or legal guardian, even those extra hazardous job restrictions would not apply.

This bill would most directly affect teenagers in logging and timber communities who want to work in the family business or enter the industry early, as well as the employers who hire them. It would also affect the Department of Labor, which would be responsible for deciding which specific logging tasks are still too dangerous for minors to perform. States with active timber industries, such as Maine, Pennsylvania, and Idaho, would likely see the most real-world impact.

title: Loggers Economic Assistance and Relief Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a federal relief program specifically for businesses that cut down trees (timber harvesters) and businesses that haul raw timber. If one of these businesses loses at least 10% of its income during any month or quarter because of a federally declared major disaster, such as a hurricane, wildfire, or even a large insect infestation that destroys forests, it can apply for government payments. The payment would equal 10% of what the business normally earned during that same time period in the prior year. The money can only be used for operating expenses, like fuel, equipment upkeep, or employee wages.

The program would be run by the U.S. Department of Agriculture through its Farm Service Agency. Congress would need to approve up to $50 million per year from 2026 through 2029 to fund it. The agency is required to set up the rules quickly, within 30 days of the bill becoming law, and must report to Congress every year on who received payments and how much they got.

The people most directly affected are workers and owners of small and mid-sized logging and timber trucking businesses, particularly in heavily forested states like Maine, Oregon, Washington, and others where the timber industry is a major employer. Indirectly, it could affect rural communities that depend on these businesses for jobs and local economic activity.

title: The Nuclear First-Strike Security Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would place new restrictions on when the United States can use nuclear weapons first, meaning before an enemy has actually launched a nuclear strike. Under the bill, if the President wants to order a first-use nuclear strike, the Secretary of Defense must notify key congressional leaders in writing at least seven days before the strike happens. That notification must confirm that the President's decision is valid and legal. The bill does not ban first-use strikes entirely, but it adds a reporting step to Congress before one can happen.

There are three situations where that seven-day notification requirement would not apply. If Congress has already declared war, if the U.S. or one of its named allies has already been hit by a nuclear weapon, or if early warning systems detect an incoming missile, the President could act without waiting. The allies covered by the bill include NATO member countries, Japan, South Korea, and Australia.

This bill mainly affects the President's military powers and the chain of command around nuclear weapons decisions. It does not directly impact everyday Americans in terms of taxes, benefits, or daily life, but it would change how and when nuclear strikes could legally be ordered. Military officials and congressional leaders would be the most directly involved if this law were ever put into use.
ai_headline: Bill requires 7-day congressional notice before any first-use nuclear strike

title: Endometriosis CARE Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the federal government to take several steps related to endometriosis, a painful condition where tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus. It tells the National Institutes of Health (NIH) to fund more research on the disease, including looking for better treatments and possibly a cure, with up to $50 million per year from 2026 to 2030. It also requires the government to create an online resource where patients and doctors can find information about endometriosis research and treatment options.

The bill requires the Department of Health and Human Services to study why people with endometriosis have trouble getting treatment. This includes looking at things like transportation problems, doctor shortages, insurance coverage gaps, and out-of-pocket costs. The government would review data from Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program, and private insurance plans to understand these barriers. A report on the findings would need to be published within two years and sent to Congress.

The bill also calls for public education campaigns about endometriosis, with specific attention to racial and ethnic minority groups and other underserved communities. It directs the government to share guidance with doctors and health systems about how to better detect and treat the condition. Finally, it asks the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine to study whether certain groups, based on race, geography, income, or other factors, face worse outcomes with endometriosis. The bill primarily affects people living with endometriosis, their doctors, insurance companies, and state health programs.

title: U.S.-Greece Defense Cooperation Advancement Act
ai_summary:
This bill would allow the U.S. government to provide military education and training assistance to Greece. Specifically, it sets aside up to $1.8 million per year from 2027 through 2031, totaling up to $9 million over five years. That money would be used to train Greek military personnel, with a focus on things like leadership, human rights, civilian oversight of the military, and learning to work alongside U.S. forces.

The training program this bill uses already exists for other countries. It is called the International Military Education and Training program, or IMET. This bill simply extends that program to Greece, which is a NATO ally. The goals listed include building a stronger working relationship between U.S. and Greek armed forces and making it easier for the two militaries to operate together if needed.

Most Americans would not be directly affected by this bill in their daily lives. It primarily impacts U.S. defense and foreign policy officials who manage these programs, Greek military personnel who would receive the training, and U.S. taxpayers who fund it. The amounts involved are relatively small compared to the overall federal budget.

title: Secret Service Transfer Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would move the U.S. Secret Service out of the Department of Homeland Security and place it directly inside the Executive Office of the President, which is the part of the federal government that supports the White House and the President personally. Right now, the Secret Service operates as an agency under the Department of Homeland Security, which is led by a Cabinet secretary who reports to the President. Under this bill, the Secret Service would instead report directly to the President with no department in between. The transfer would need to be completed within one year of the bill becoming law.

The bill says all Secret Service employees, equipment, contracts, and responsibilities would move over to the new location without major disruption. Workers would keep their jobs, pay, and working conditions. The current Director would stay in the role but would now be appointed by and answer directly to the President. The Director would also have the ability to reorganize the agency over time, though the structure would stay the same at first.

This change would mainly affect how the Secret Service is overseen and who it ultimately answers to. Currently, there is a layer of oversight through the Department of Homeland Security and Congress monitors that department. Moving the agency into the Executive Office of the President shifts that chain of command closer to the President. This could affect federal workers at the Secret Service, the President and other officials the agency protects, and the broader system of checks on how the agency is supervised. The bill was introduced by two members of Congress and has been sent to committees for review.

title: Robert Lodge Medal of Honor Act
ai_summary:
This bill would allow the President to award the Medal of Honor to Robert Lodge, an Air Force pilot who served during the Vietnam War. Normally, there are strict time limits on when the Medal of Honor can be awarded after an act of valor, but this bill would waive those time limits specifically for Lodge. It recognizes his actions on May 10, 1972, though the bill itself does not describe the details of what he did that day.

Robert Lodge was a highly decorated Air Force officer who shot down multiple enemy aircraft during the Vietnam War and was killed in action on May 10, 1972, the same date referenced in the bill. The Medal of Honor is the highest military honor the United States can give, and bills like this one are sometimes passed by Congress when it is believed a service member's actions were overlooked or not fully recognized at the time.

This bill directly affects Robert Lodge's legacy and his surviving family members, who would receive the medal on his behalf since he died in combat. It also affects the process of military honors more broadly, since Congress must pass a special law to get around the normal time deadline in cases like this. The general public is not directly affected, but taxpayers fund the small administrative costs involved in the award ceremony.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Armed Services.

Lodge shot down multiple enemy aircraft during the Vietnam War and was killed in action on that same date. The Medal of Honor is the United States' highest military decoration.

title: PLAY Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells the Secretary of Health and Human Services to create a new government task force within 180 days of the law passing. The task force would bring together leaders from about a dozen federal agencies, including the departments of Education, Housing, Transportation, and Agriculture, among others. Their job would be to study the problem of children not having enough safe places to play and exercise, find out what is getting in the way, and come up with recommendations for how the government can help fix it. The task force would also look for successful examples of playgrounds and outdoor spaces, including partnerships between government, businesses, and nonprofits, that could be copied in other communities.

The task force does not hand out money or build anything directly. Instead, it produces reports. A preliminary report would go to Congress within 180 days of the task force forming, and a final report with specific recommendations would follow about a year after that. Once the final report is submitted, the task force closes down. The whole process from start to finish would take roughly three years.

This bill mainly affects children under 18, especially those in communities that currently lack safe outdoor play spaces. It also involves a wide range of federal agencies that manage public land, housing, schools, and environmental issues. Local governments, nonprofits, and community organizations could also be affected if the task force's eventual recommendations lead to new programs or policy changes down the road.

title: NO TIME TO Waste Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Department of Agriculture to set up new programs aimed at cutting food waste in half by 2030 compared to 2016 levels. It creates a new Office of Food Loss and Waste inside the USDA to research how much food gets wasted, study new technologies to prevent it, and share that information with the public and Congress. The bill also sets up regional coordinators who would connect farmers, food companies, and food banks to help move surplus food to people who need it instead of letting it go to waste. Grants would be available to state, local, and tribal governments to improve food recovery systems, like better storage facilities and refrigerated transportation.

The bill also changes some existing rules. Companies that hold federal government contracts would now be required, not just encouraged, to donate leftover food and report on their food waste efforts. Federal agencies would have to share those reports with Congress every two years. The bill also pushes for public-private partnerships between local governments, restaurants, grocery stores, hospitals, and nonprofits, all working together with shared goals and measurements to track progress on reducing waste.

Everyday Americans would be affected mainly through a national education campaign the bill requires. That campaign would teach people how to store food properly, understand what date labels like "Best If Used By" actually mean, and learn how to compost food scraps. People living in food-insecure communities would be a priority focus. Food businesses, schools, faith organizations, and local governments would also receive educational materials. The bill authorizes roughly 3.5 million dollars per year for the office and additional millions for grants and the awareness campaign through 2030.

title: Defense Community Infrastructure Program Revisions Act
ai_summary:

The people most directly affected are residents of communities located near Coast Guard bases, since their local governments could now apply for federal infrastructure grants they previously could not access. Coast Guard personnel and their families living near those bases could also benefit if local roads, utilities, or services are improved. title: Keep Our PACT Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require the federal government to fully fund two major education programs that currently receive less money than Congress originally promised. The first is Title I, which sends extra federal dollars to public schools with large numbers of low-income students. The second is the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, or IDEA, which funds special education services for students with disabilities. Right now, both programs are authorized at higher funding levels than what Congress actually appropriates each year. This bill would make up that gap by automatically providing the difference, starting in 2026 and increasing each year through 2035.

For Title I, the bill would gradually increase federal funding from current levels up to about $54 billion by 2035. For special education under IDEA, it would ramp up federal contributions to reach 40 percent of the average cost of educating a student with a disability, a target Congress set in 2004 but has never actually hit. The bill labels this spending as an emergency requirement, which is a budget process tool that allows the spending to bypass some of the usual rules that limit new federal expenditures.

The people most directly affected would be students from low-income families and students with disabilities, along with the public schools that serve them. Schools rely on Title I and IDEA funding to pay for reading specialists, tutors, special education teachers, aides, and other support staff. States and local school districts would likely see more federal dollars flowing in, which could reduce the pressure on local property taxes to cover these costs. Parents, teachers, and school administrators in communities with high poverty rates or large special education populations would feel the biggest impact.

title: Sanctioning Russia Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would set up a system of automatic, sweeping economic penalties against Russia if the President determines that Russia refuses to negotiate a peace deal with Ukraine, breaks any peace agreement, or launches another military invasion. Within 15 days of that determination, the U.S. would freeze the American assets of top Russian government and military officials, ban Russian stocks from U.S. exchanges, block U.S. banks from moving money to or from Russia, stop American companies from investing in Russia's energy sector, ban imports of Russian uranium, and slap a tariff of at least 500 percent on all goods coming from Russia. The bill also targets other countries that buy Russian oil, uranium, or gas, hitting them with the same 500 percent tariff on their exports to the U.S.

The sanctions would apply to a wide range of people and institutions, including named Russian banks like Sberbank and VTB, Russian oligarchs, foreign companies that sell weapons or supplies to the Russian military, and any global financial messaging service that keeps doing business with sanctioned Russian banks. U.S. financial firms, investment funds, and brokerages would all be barred from dealings that benefit the Russian government. The President could lift all the penalties only after certifying to Congress that Russia has genuinely stopped its problematic actions and signed a peace agreement with Ukraine. If Russia later violated that agreement, all penalties would snap back immediately.

Everyday Americans would likely feel the effects mainly through energy and product markets, since the bill could reduce the global supply of oil and uranium and pressure countries that trade with Russia. U.S. investors and financial institutions would face new legal restrictions on any Russia-linked business. The bill carves out exceptions for humanitarian aid to the Russian people, U.S. intelligence operations, and international treaty obligations, so those activities would not be blocked.

Within 15 days of that determination, the U.S. would freeze assets of top Russian officials, ban Russian stocks from U.S. exchanges, block U.S. bank transfers to or from Russia, bar American investment in Russia's energy sector, ban Russian uranium imports, and impose a tariff of at least 500 percent on all Russian goods. Countries that buy Russian oil, uranium, or gas would also face the same 500 percent tariff on their exports to the U.S.
ai_sections.who: The sanctions would apply to named Russian banks including Sberbank and VTB, Russian oligarchs, foreign companies supplying the Russian military, and any financial messaging service that continues doing business with sanctioned Russian banks. U.S. financial firms, investment funds, and brokerages would face new legal restrictions on any Russia-linked dealings.
ai_sections.why: The bill could reduce the global supply of oil and uranium and create economic pressure on countries that trade with Russia. U.S. investors and financial institutions would face new legal constraints, and the tariffs could affect product and energy markets for everyday Americans.

title: To require the Secretary of Homeland Security to notify Congress of any serious injury or death of any individual in the custody of the Department of Homeland Security, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
HR 9113 would require the head of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to formally notify Congress whenever someone in DHS custody is seriously injured or dies. This would apply to people held by any DHS agency, which includes Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP). The bill sets up a reporting requirement so that lawmakers are kept informed about these incidents.

The bill primarily affects people who are detained by DHS, which is most commonly immigrants and asylum seekers held in detention facilities while their cases are being processed. It also affects DHS officials, who would be responsible for sending these notifications, and members of Congress, who would receive them.

Right now, there is no consistent legal requirement for DHS to directly inform Congress when these events occur. This bill would create that formal obligation. Supporters of similar measures often argue it increases government accountability, while critics sometimes raise concerns about the administrative burden or the scope of reporting. The bill does not change how DHS operates its detention facilities or affect immigration policy directly — it solely focuses on the flow of information to Congress.
ai_headline: DHS would have to alert Congress after detainee deaths or injuries
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Border Security and Enforcement.

title: CLIMB Act
ai_summary:
The CLIMB Act would stop federal agencies from punishing banks, insurers, accountants, lawyers, landlords, tech companies, and other businesses simply because they work with a cannabis company that is legal under state law. Right now, even though many states have legalized cannabis, it remains illegal under federal law. That mismatch means companies that serve legal cannabis businesses can face federal penalties, which causes many of them to refuse that business. This bill would remove that federal threat for anyone providing services to a state-licensed cannabis operation.

The bill also changes federal securities law to create a legal "safe harbor" for stock exchanges, brokers, and other financial market participants. Under this change, it would not be a federal violation for a stock exchange like the NYSE or Nasdaq to list shares of a cannabis company that operates legally under state law. Currently, those exchanges largely avoid listing cannabis stocks because doing so could expose them to federal liability under the Controlled Substances Act.

This bill would affect a wide range of people and businesses. State-licensed cannabis companies would have an easier time getting bank accounts, loans, insurance, office space, and access to public stock markets. Banks, accountants, real estate owners, and technology firms that want to serve those cannabis companies would gain legal protection for doing so. Investors could more easily buy and sell shares of cannabis companies on major exchanges. The bill does not legalize cannabis itself and does not change anything for cannabis businesses operating without a valid state license.
ai_headline: Federal bill would shield businesses that serve legal cannabis firms from penalties
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7987 would bar federal agencies from penalizing banks, insurers, and others for serving state-licensed cannabis businesses.

The bill would also create a federal safe harbor in securities law, allowing stock exchanges, brokers, and other financial market participants to list or trade shares of state-licensed cannabis companies without facing liability under the Controlled Substances Act. The bill does not legalize cannabis itself and does not extend any protection to cannabis businesses operating without a valid state license.

Federal agencies currently authorized to penalize businesses that serve cannabis companies would lose that authority under the bill.
ai_sections.why: Because cannabis remains illegal under federal law despite legalization in many states, businesses that serve legal cannabis operations currently face federal penalties, leading many to turn away that business. Removing that federal threat would change the legal calculus for financial institutions, professional service providers, and public markets deciding whether to work with state-licensed cannabis companies.

title: Early Action and Responsiveness Lifts Youth Minds Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how states can use federal mental health block grant money. Currently, those grants focus on people who already have serious mental illness. This bill would let states spend up to 5% of their grant funds on prevention and early intervention programs, meaning services designed to catch mental health problems early or stop them from getting worse, before someone reaches a crisis point. States are not required to do this, but they now have the option.

The bill specifically includes children and teenagers as a target group, even if they have not been diagnosed with a serious mental illness. That is a notable shift, since the existing program has generally focused on adults with more severe conditions. States that choose to offer these early programs would need to use approaches that have scientific evidence behind them.

The bill also requires the federal government to report to Congress every two years on which states used this option, what programs they ran, who was served, and whether those programs actually reduced delays in getting mental health care or reduced how severely conditions developed. This affects state governments that receive these federal grants, families and young people who might gain access to earlier mental health support, and federal health officials who would track and report on the results.
ai_headline: Federal mental health grants could fund early intervention under HR 1735
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: Parity for Tribal Law Enforcement Act
ai_summary:
This bill would give tribal police officers the legal authority to enforce federal law on tribal lands, as long as they meet certain requirements. Right now, tribal officers often have limited power to enforce federal crimes even when those crimes happen in their jurisdiction. Under this bill, tribal officers who complete training equal to Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) officers, pass a background check, and get certified by the federal government would be treated as federal law enforcement officers. That means they would have the same legal protections, retirement benefits, and liability coverage as federal officers while doing their jobs.

The bill also sets up a certification process. The federal government would have two years to create official standards and a credentialing system for tribal officers. Tribal officers could voluntarily opt into the federal benefits system, including retirement, and could get credit for years they already worked. The bill also makes sure officers funded through Department of Justice grants can still participate.

Additionally, the bill directs the U.S. Attorney General to better coordinate the federal government's public safety efforts in tribal communities, improve data collection, and update planning documents for federal prosecutors working in those areas. The people most directly affected are tribal police officers and the Native American communities they serve, particularly on reservations and other tribal lands where law enforcement gaps have historically been a problem.
ai_headline: Tribal police would gain federal law enforcement authority under HR 4712

title: No Rewards for January 6 Rioters Act
ai_summary:
This bill would block the federal government from using taxpayer money to pay or compensate people who were prosecuted for taking part in the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol. That includes money from the Judgment Fund, which is a pool of federal money sometimes used to settle legal claims against the government. The bill also prevents the government from creating any new fund specifically designed to pay these individuals. Importantly, this rule applies even to people who were later pardoned for their January 6 crimes.

The bill also addresses money that was already paid by people who were convicted of January 6-related crimes. If someone paid fines, restitution, or court fees as part of their conviction, this bill would prevent the government from refunding that money to them, even if they were later pardoned. Any money that would have been returned is instead sent to the Architect of the Capitol, the agency responsible for maintaining the Capitol building and grounds.

This bill would directly affect people who were charged with crimes related to January 6 and who might otherwise seek financial compensation from the government, for example by filing a legal claim arguing their prosecution was improper. It would also affect anyone who paid court-ordered fines or fees and expected a refund after receiving a pardon. The bill does not affect people who had no involvement in January 6 events.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

The bill blocks use of the Judgment Fund and bars creation of any new fund for this purpose. title: Medical Device Nonvisual Accessibility Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would require certain home-use medical devices to be accessible to people who are blind or have low vision. Right now, many medical devices like blood pressure monitors, sleep apnea machines, and home chemotherapy equipment use touchscreens and visual menus that someone who cannot see well simply cannot use on their own. The bill would require that these devices work just as well for blind or low-vision users as they do for sighted users, through features like text-to-speech or other non-visual methods. The FDA would have one year to propose rules and two years to finalize them, with devices required to comply one year after the final rules are published.

The bill covers medical devices in FDA risk categories Class II and III that have a screen or app interface and are meant for home use, not just for use by doctors or hospitals. Manufacturers could apply for a waiver if making their device accessible would fundamentally change how it works or create a serious financial burden, particularly for smaller companies. The FDA would also be required to provide training to help manufacturers understand and meet the new standards, and it must consult with people who are blind or have low vision when writing those rules.

This bill most directly affects people who are blind or have low vision and rely on home medical devices, as well as the companies that make those devices. Patients in this group would gain the ability to use their own medical equipment privately and independently. Device manufacturers would need to build accessibility into their products from the design stage, which the bill notes can be done at little or no added cost if planned early.
ai_headline: Bill would require home medical devices to work for blind users
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: Remembering American Hostages Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would require the Hostage and Wrongful Detainee flag to be flown on specific dates and at more government locations than currently required. The flag already exists in law and is sometimes displayed, but this bill adds new required dates: November 4 and January 20 (tied to the 1979 Iranian hostage crisis), August 19 (the day journalist James Foley was killed while held captive in 2014), and October 7 (the date of the 2023 Hamas attack when over 240 people, including Americans, were taken hostage). It also requires the flag to be flown at State Department offices, U.S. embassies and consulates, Justice Department buildings, and every location where Americans can apply for or renew a passport.

The bill also expands which government officials are responsible for making sure the flag is displayed, adding the Attorney General, Secretary of Education, Secretary of Transportation, and Secretary of Commerce to the existing list. It expresses Congress's opinion that state governments, local governments, and airports should also fly the flag on those same dates, and whenever a hostage returns home or is confirmed to have died in captivity.

This bill most directly affects federal agencies and the buildings they operate. Ordinary Americans would mainly notice the flag appearing more often and in more places, such as passport offices. The bill does not create new spending programs, change foreign policy, or require anything from private citizens or businesses.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: PROTECT Immigration Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would end a federal program known as 287(g), which currently allows local and state police departments to sign agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and then act as immigration enforcers. Under those agreements, local officers can question people about their immigration status, arrest them, and hold them for immigration violations. This bill would shut down that program and make it clear in federal law that immigration enforcement is only the job of federal officers, not local or state police.

The bill does carve out a few narrow exceptions that already exist in other laws, such as situations involving terrorism or immigrant smuggling, where some local involvement may still apply. But for routine immigration enforcement, the bill would remove the ability of local departments to participate, even if they wanted to and ICE was willing to partner with them.

This would mainly affect local and state law enforcement agencies that currently have 287(g) agreements with ICE, as well as the communities where those agencies operate. It could also affect undocumented immigrants who currently interact with local police in areas where those agreements are in place. Supporters and critics of this type of local-federal immigration cooperation would both feel the impact of this change, since it would be a significant shift in how immigration enforcement works on the ground across the country.
ai_headline: Bill would strip local police of immigration enforcement authority
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

Federal law would be updated to make immigration enforcement the exclusive responsibility of federal officers. title: Pregnant Women in Custody Act
ai_summary:
This bill sets new rules for how the federal government must treat pregnant women who are held in federal prisons, immigration detention centers, border patrol custody, and refugee shelters. It requires these facilities to provide prenatal care, proper nutrition including prenatal vitamins, mental health screenings, and education about parenting rights. Women must be given a pregnancy test when they enter a facility, and those with high-risk pregnancies must be evaluated and can be transferred to a halfway house closer to their families. The bill also requires facilities to let mothers spend at least 60 minutes bonding with their newborns and to offer programs that allow mothers and babies to stay together after birth.

The bill bans the use of solitary confinement and physical restraints on pregnant women from the time pregnancy is confirmed until at least 12 weeks after delivery. Restraints or isolation can only be used in very limited situations where someone poses an immediate physical danger, and even then, officials must review that decision every single day and document their reasoning in writing. Women in their third trimester cannot be placed in solitary confinement under any circumstances. Facilities must also train staff on these rules within 180 days and twice yearly after that.

The bill affects pregnant women held in any federal custody, including those in Bureau of Prisons facilities, ICE detention, CBP holding, and Office of Refugee Resettlement shelters. It also requires the government to start collecting and publishing detailed data on pregnant women in custody nationwide. Women who believe their rights under this law were violated can sue the responsible federal agency in court to seek money damages or other relief.
ai_headline: Federal bill would ban restraints on pregnant women in U.S. custody
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Oversight, Investigations, and Accountability.

title: Small Business Tax Cut Act
ai_summary:
This bill would increase a tax deduction that self-employed people and small business owners can take on their income. Right now, under a rule called the Section 199A deduction, eligible business owners can deduct 20% of their qualified business income from their taxable income. This bill would raise that percentage to 23%. It would also adjust how the deduction is phased out for higher earners and update the income thresholds for inflation starting from 2025 rather than 2018. These changes would take effect starting in the 2027 tax year.

The bill also expands who qualifies for a similar deduction. Currently, certain dividends from real estate investment trusts (REITs) already qualify for this tax break. This bill would extend the same treatment to interest dividends paid out by Business Development Companies, which are investment firms that lend money to or invest in smaller businesses. That means investors who receive those dividends could also deduct a portion of that income.

The people most directly affected are owners of pass-through businesses, meaning sole proprietors, partners in partnerships, and owners of S-corporations, since these are the business structures that use the Section 199A deduction. Investors who receive dividends from qualifying Business Development Companies would also be affected. Wage employees who receive a regular paycheck from an employer would not be impacted by this change.
ai_headline: Self-employed deduction would rise from 20% to 23% under HR 8415
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8415 raises the Section 199A business income deduction from 20% to 23% for pass-through business owners, effective tax year 2027.

The bill would also adjust phase-out thresholds for higher earners and reset the inflation indexing from 2018 to 2025. Additionally, it would extend the deduction to interest dividends paid by Business Development Companies, a treatment previously limited to REIT dividends.

title: Rental Housing Investment Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes the tax code to give landlords and real estate investors a bigger upfront tax deduction when they build new rental housing. Normally, property owners have to spread out their tax deductions for a building over many years. Under this bill, they could instead deduct up to $150,000 per apartment unit all at once in the first year the building is put into service. If the property qualifies as affordable housing under existing federal rules, that amount goes up to $250,000 per unit. The property must be newly built, have at least two units, and be located in the United States.

There is a catch built into the bill. If the owner stops using the property as rental housing within 10 years of opening it, they have to pay back some of those tax benefits. For affordable housing projects, that payback window extends to 15 years. This is meant to discourage investors from taking the tax break and then quickly converting the property to something else.

This bill mainly affects real estate developers, landlords, and investors who build new multi-unit rental properties. Renters could be indirectly affected if the tax incentive encourages more rental housing to be built, which could influence housing availability in their area. The change does not apply to existing rental properties, only newly constructed ones placed into service more than a year after the bill becomes law.
ai_headline: New tax bill lets landlords deduct up to $250,000 per unit in year one
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

For properties that qualify as affordable housing under existing federal rules, the deduction rises to $250,000 per unit. The property must be newly constructed, contain at least two units, and be located in the United States.

title: EMPSA Act
ai_summary:
This bill targets a specific rule in the Supplemental Security Income (SSI) program. Right now, when two SSI recipients marry each other, their combined benefit is cut — the government treats them as a household and pays them less than they would receive as two single people. This bill would change that rule for adults with intellectual or developmental disabilities (like Down syndrome or autism). Under the new rule, a married person in that group would still receive the same SSI amount they would get as a single individual, and the government would not count their spouse's income or savings against them when deciding how much they qualify for.

SSI is a federal program that provides monthly cash payments to people with low income and limited resources who are elderly, blind, or disabled. The current marriage penalty can discourage people with disabilities from getting married because doing so reduces their financial support. This bill would remove that financial consequence specifically for adults diagnosed with an intellectual or developmental disability, allowing them to marry without losing a portion of their benefits.

The people directly affected are adults aged 18 and older who have an intellectual or developmental disability and currently receive or could qualify for SSI. Their spouses would also be indirectly affected, since the spouse's income and assets would no longer be factored into the disabled person's benefit calculation. The bill does not change SSI rules for other disability groups, seniors, or blind individuals.
ai_headline: Bill would end SSI marriage penalty for adults with intellectual disabilities
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 1757 would let adults with intellectual or developmental disabilities keep full SSI benefits after marrying.
ai_sections.what: HR 1757 would remove a rule that reduces Supplemental Security Income payments when two SSI recipients marry. Under current law, married recipients are treated as a household and receive less than two single individuals would. The bill would allow adults with intellectual or developmental disabilities to receive the same SSI amount after marriage as they would as single individuals, with a spouse's income and assets no longer counted against them.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects adults aged 18 and older who have an intellectual or developmental disability and receive or could qualify for SSI. Spouses of those individuals are also indirectly affected, as their income and assets would no longer factor into the disabled person's benefit calculation.
ai_sections.why: Under current rules, marrying another SSI recipient reduces both partners' payments, creating a financial consequence tied to marriage. The bill would eliminate that consequence specifically for adults with intellectual or developmental disabilities, without changing SSI rules for other disability groups, seniors, or blind individuals.

title: To classify qualified locum tenens professionals and advanced care practitioners as independent contractors for the purposes of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 and the National Labor Relations Act.
ai_summary:
This bill would automatically classify certain temporary healthcare workers as independent contractors under two major federal laws. Specifically, it targets "locum tenens" professionals, which is a term for doctors, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, and certified registered nurse anesthetists who fill in temporarily at hospitals, clinics, or other healthcare facilities, usually for up to one year at a time. For these workers to qualify, they must have a written contract stating they will not be treated as employees.

The two federal laws mentioned are important. The Fair Labor Standards Act sets rules about minimum wage, overtime pay, and other basic protections that apply to employees. The National Labor Relations Act gives employees the right to form unions and bargain collectively. By classifying these temporary healthcare workers as independent contractors rather than employees, the bill would mean those protections no longer apply to them in these temporary assignments.

This bill directly affects temporary healthcare workers who fill staffing gaps at medical facilities, as well as the hospitals, clinics, and staffing agencies that hire them. Workers in this category would lose access to federal wage protections and the right to unionize under these laws in their temporary roles. Healthcare facilities and staffing agencies, on the other hand, would have clearer legal standing to hire these workers without providing employee benefits or recognizing union organizing efforts. Patients could also be indirectly affected, since the rules governing how temporary medical staff are hired and compensated can influence healthcare staffing and availability.
ai_headline: Bill would strip federal wage and union rights from temporary fill-in doctors
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

title: Department of Peacebuilding Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would create a brand-new cabinet-level federal agency called the Department of Peacebuilding, led by a Secretary of Peacebuilding appointed by the President. The department would have several divisions focused on areas like peace education, domestic violence prevention, international conflict resolution, arms control, and human rights. The Secretary of Peacebuilding would also gain a seat on the National Security Council, meaning they would have a formal role in top-level national security discussions alongside officials like the Secretary of Defense and Secretary of State. The bill requires the Secretaries of Defense and State to consult with this new department before and during armed conflicts or situations that could lead to violence.

The department would work on a wide range of domestic issues, including gun violence, school bullying, drug abuse, police-community relations, domestic violence, and racial inequality. It would fund grants for schools and community organizations to develop peace education programs, train conflict resolution specialists, and support restorative justice programs. The bill also calls for creating a Peace Academy similar to military service academies, where graduates would commit to five years of public service in conflict resolution work. At least 85 percent of the department's budget would have to go toward domestic programs.

This bill would affect a broad range of Americans. Students and teachers could see new peace-focused curriculum in schools. Communities could receive grants for local violence prevention programs. Veterans, crime victims, and people leaving prison could access new support services. Internationally, the department would work on issues like nuclear disarmament, human trafficking, and post-conflict rebuilding. The bill does not specify a dollar amount for funding, leaving that for future congressional decisions.
ai_headline: New federal Department of Peacebuilding proposed with cabinet-level authority
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

The department would include divisions focused on peace education, domestic violence prevention, international conflict resolution, arms control, and human rights. title: Alyssa’s Act of 2025
ai_summary:
Alyssa's Act of 2025 expands a federal program called the School Safety Clearinghouse, which is run by the Department of Homeland Security. The bill directs that program to do several new things: educate the public and school staff about preventing and responding to school emergencies, hire school safety experts to advise individual schools, research and test panic alarm technology (wearable devices that can instantly contact police, fire, or other emergency services), and create a national data center to collect and track information about school violence, injuries, deaths, and what safety measures are actually working. The government would also have to file annual reports to Congress summarizing all of this activity.

The bill also sets new rules for emergency response maps used by schools and first responders. If any federal money is spent on these maps, the maps must be digital, work on phones and computers, be updated in real time, be stored only on servers inside the United States, and be shared freely with local police, fire, and emergency agencies that serve that school. Schools would have to walk through their buildings every year to make sure the maps are accurate.

This bill would directly affect K-12 public schools, school administrators, and local law enforcement and emergency responders across the country. It does not force schools to do anything on their own, since the bill specifically states it gives the federal government no power to create new regulations. Instead, it focuses on giving schools and first responders better information, tools, and guidance to help prevent and respond to emergencies.
ai_headline: Alyssa's Act expands school safety tools, panic alarms, and violence data tracking
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Counterterrorism and Intelligence.

title: Transformation to Competitive Integrated Employment Act
ai_summary:
This bill would end a longstanding federal rule that allows certain employers to pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage. That rule, called Section 14(c) of the Fair Labor Standards Act, lets approved employers pay disabled workers based on their productivity compared to non-disabled workers, which often results in wages of just a few dollars or even cents per hour. Under this bill, no new employers could get that kind of approval starting immediately, and existing approved employers would have to gradually raise wages to full minimum wage over four years. After that four-year period, the sub-minimum wage program would be completely shut down.

To help with that change, the bill would create a grant program run by the Department of Labor. States could apply for grants of up to $10 million over five years to help employers in their state shift to regular, integrated workplaces where disabled workers earn at least minimum wage alongside non-disabled coworkers. Individual employers who already use the sub-minimum wage program could also apply for smaller grants, up to $500,000 over three years, to help redesign their business models and find competitive jobs for their workers with disabilities. A separate nonprofit would receive funding to share best practices and offer technical help to employers making this transition.

This bill directly affects people with disabilities who currently work in sheltered workshops or similar programs that use sub-minimum wage certificates, as well as the organizations and employers that run those programs. It also affects state governments, which would need to update their disability services and employment plans. Families of people with disabilities, vocational rehabilitation agencies, and Medicaid programs would all be involved in carrying out the transition. The goal is to move disabled workers into regular jobs that pay standard wages in typical community workplaces.
ai_headline: Bill would phase out sub-minimum wages for disabled workers over four years
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

After that four-year period, the sub-minimum wage program would be completely eliminated.

States would need to update their disability services and employment plans, and multiple agencies and programs would take on new responsibilities during the transition period.
