title: Estate Tax Rate Reduction Act
ai_summary:
This bill would lower the federal estate tax rate from its current top rate of 40 percent down to a flat 20 percent. The estate tax is a tax on the total value of money and property a person leaves behind when they die, before it is passed on to their heirs. The same lower 20 percent rate would also apply to gift taxes, which apply to large sums of money given away while a person is still alive, and to generation-skipping transfer taxes, which apply when wealth is passed directly to grandchildren or later generations instead of children. These changes would apply to deaths and transfers that occurred after December 31, 2024.

This bill would mainly affect people who inherit or receive very large amounts of wealth. Under current law, the estate tax only kicks in when the total value of an estate exceeds about $13.6 million per individual, so most Americans are not affected by this tax at all. The people who would directly benefit from this bill are heirs of very large estates, since the tax owed on those estates would be cut roughly in half compared to current law.

The bill also includes a provision saying that its costs do not need to be counted against federal budget rules that normally require new tax cuts or spending increases to be offset. Independent budget analysts have estimated that reducing the estate tax rate this way would reduce federal tax revenue by a significant amount over time, meaning less money coming into the government. How that might affect federal programs or the national debt would depend on other budget decisions made by Congress.
ai_headline: House bill would cut estate tax rate in half, to 20 percent flat
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Ways and Means, and in addition to the Committee on the Budget, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

title: When Minutes Count for Emergency Medical Patients Act
ai_summary:
This bill does two main things. First, it creates a five-year test program where Medicare pays ambulance agencies extra money to help cover the cost of keeping critical medications and blood products on hand. Right now, Medicare only pays for ambulance services when those services are actually used on a Medicare patient. The new payments would instead cover the cost of stocking and maintaining supplies like epinephrine, albuterol, fentanyl, and blood products so agencies can keep enough on hand even during shortages, regardless of whether a given patient is on Medicare. At least one ambulance agency in each of the country's ten federal regions must be selected, and agencies from different geographic areas like rural, suburban, and urban communities are included. After the program ends, the government must report to Congress on whether it improved care and saved lives.

Second, the bill directs two separate government bodies to study and report on how Medicare pays for emergency medical services more broadly. One advisory group called MedPAC must look at whether current Medicare payments are enough to properly pay EMS doctors who oversee paramedics, whether low Medicare payments are contributing to paramedic shortages, and how to measure the quality of EMS care. The bill also requires federal health officials to issue guidance to hospital emergency rooms about a problem called wall time, which is when paramedics arrive at a hospital but are stuck waiting more than 30 minutes before hospital staff takes over care of the patient.

The people most directly affected are Medicare patients who call 911, paramedics and EMTs, EMS agency directors, and hospital emergency departments. Rural and underserved communities get specific attention because ambulance services in those areas often struggle most with medication shortages and staffing problems. The bill does not change what patients pay or how they access Medicare, but it could affect the quality of emergency care they receive if the program leads to better-stocked ambulances and a more stable EMS workforce.
ai_headline: Medicare pilot would pay ambulance agencies to stock critical drugs
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Ways and Means, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

The bill also directs MedPAC and federal health officials to study Medicare payments for emergency medical services and issue guidance on the problem of extended hospital wait times for paramedics.

Rural and underserved communities receive specific attention because ambulance agencies in those areas face the greatest challenges with medication shortages and staffing.

If the pilot leads to better-stocked ambulances and a more stable EMS workforce, the quality of emergency care could change for patients across coverage types.

title: WATCH Personnel Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill deals with a funding gap for the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), the federal agency that runs airport security checkpoints. Starting February 14, 2026, the TSA lost its normal government funding due to a lapse in appropriations, meaning Congress had not passed a budget to keep it running. This bill would provide temporary emergency money to keep paying TSA workers during that gap, and it would stay in effect until Congress passes a proper budget or until September 30, 2026, whichever comes first.

The bill also makes two changes to TSA worker pay. First, it sets a minimum salary of $40,000 per year for Transportation Security Officers, with automatic increases each year tied to inflation. Second, it gives a one-time $1,000 bonus to every TSA officer who was actively employed on February 14, 2026, the day the funding lapse began. The bonus would not count toward retirement or other benefit calculations.

The people most directly affected are the roughly 60,000 TSA employees, particularly frontline security officers who screen passengers and baggage at airports across the country. Without this bill, those workers could face delayed or missed paychecks during the funding gap. Travelers passing through airport security could also be indirectly affected, since TSA operations and staffing levels depend on this funding remaining in place.

last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Maritime Security.

title: Transportation Security Administration Transfer Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would move the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) from the Department of Homeland Security, where it has been housed since 2003, back to the Department of Transportation. Right now, the TSA is run under the Secretary of Homeland Security. If this bill passed, it would be run under the Secretary of Transportation instead. All of the TSA's existing rules, contracts, employees, and ongoing legal cases would carry over as-is during the move, so day-to-day operations would not suddenly stop or restart.

The TSA is the agency responsible for security screening at airports, including the agents who check passengers and luggage at checkpoints. It also oversees security for other forms of transportation like railroads and pipelines. Moving the agency does not change what the TSA does or give it new powers — it only changes which cabinet department supervises it and who the TSA administrator ultimately reports to.

This bill would mainly affect how the federal government manages transportation security from an administrative standpoint. Travelers going through airport security would likely notice no immediate change. Federal employees who work for the TSA would still have the same jobs. Congress, the White House, and the Office of Management and Budget would need to coordinate the details of the transfer. The bill was introduced by one Democrat and one Republican together, making it a bipartisan proposal.

title: WORK to Save Lives Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Department of Labor's workplace safety agency, OSHA, to take two related actions within 270 days of becoming law. First, OSHA would publish voluntary guidance for private employers on how to stock and maintain opioid overdose reversal medication, like naloxone (often known by the brand name Narcan), at their workplaces. That guidance would also encourage employers to offer optional annual training so workers know how to use the medication if someone overdoses on the job. Importantly, this part is not a requirement for private businesses, just official advice they can choose to follow.

Second, the bill does create a firm requirement for federal government agencies. Every federal agency would be legally required to keep opioid overdose reversal medication on hand. Those agencies would also need to offer voluntary, annual training to their employees on how to use it. This mandatory rule covers federal agencies broadly, including the Veterans Health Administration, but it specifically leaves out the United States Postal Service from the private-employer guidance section.

This bill affects two main groups. Federal government workers across all agencies would have guaranteed access to overdose reversal medication at their workplaces. Private-sector workers and their employers would not face any new legal requirements, but their employers would have clear official guidance available if they choose to act on it. The bill is largely focused on making workplaces better prepared to respond to opioid overdoses, which remain a leading cause of accidental death in the United States.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

title: SAFER Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill says that if someone applies for asylum in the United States, they cannot return to the very country they fled from. Right now, immigration law allows people to seek asylum if they face persecution in their home country. Under this bill, if an asylum seeker goes back to that country while their case is pending, they would automatically be disqualified from getting asylum. The idea behind the bill is that returning to the country you claimed was dangerous suggests the fear of persecution may not be genuine.

The bill also applies to people who have already been granted asylum. If someone with approved asylum status goes back to their home country, the government could cancel their asylum, and they could even face deportation or have their citizenship stripped if they were naturalized. There are two narrow exceptions: if the President certifies the trip is for national security reasons, or if the Secretary of State certifies that the country in question has had a real change in government that makes it safer.

This bill directly affects people who are currently applying for asylum or who already hold asylum status in the United States. It would be enforced by the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice. It does not affect U.S. citizens who were born here, or immigrants in other visa categories. The bill was introduced in the House and has been sent to the Judiciary Committee, so it has not become law yet.
ai_headline: Asylum seekers who return home would lose protected status under HR 8240
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: PEER Support Act
ai_summary:
This bill focuses on peer support specialists, who are people with personal experience recovering from mental health conditions or substance use disorders and who help others going through similar struggles. The bill officially defines this role in federal law, requires the government to add peer support specialist as a recognized job category in its official occupational classification system by early 2026, and creates a new federal office called the Office of Recovery inside the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. That office would be led by someone with direct recovery experience and would work to improve training, certification, career development, and professional standards for peer support specialists across the country.

The bill also directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to produce a report, due within one year, that looks at how criminal background check rules in each state affect who can become a peer support specialist. Because many people in recovery have past criminal records, background check requirements can prevent them from working in this field even if they are otherwise qualified. The report would study what each state currently requires, what barriers those rules create, and offer recommendations on how states could adjust their processes to make it easier for qualified people to enter the profession.

This bill most directly affects people in recovery from mental health or substance use conditions who want to work as peer support specialists, as well as people currently struggling who could benefit from their services. It also affects state agencies that oversee certification, healthcare providers who employ peer support workers, and federal agencies involved in mental health funding and oversight. It does not create a new federal spending program but sets up a formal structure and research process to strengthen and grow this workforce.

title: Rural Microentrepreneur Assistance Program Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill updates a federal program that helps small businesses in rural areas get loans and financial support. The Rural Microentrepreneur Assistance Program works by giving money to nonprofit lenders, who then loan that money to very small rural businesses, typically those with ten or fewer employees. The bill makes three changes: it raises the maximum loan size from $50,000 to $75,000, it allows the program to fully cover loan amounts rather than just 75 percent, and it extends the program's funding authorization from the years 2019 to 2023 forward to 2026 through 2030. Without this extension, the program would have no authorized funding going forward.

The bill also adds a new rule about how loan money can be used. If a business wants to use loan funds for construction, demolition, or other real estate improvements, no more than half the loan can go toward those costs. This is meant to keep the program focused on general business needs rather than large building projects.

The people most directly affected are small business owners in rural communities who need access to loans that traditional banks may not offer them. Nonprofit organizations that serve as middlemen lenders in the program are also affected, since they receive federal grant money to manage and absorb potential losses on these loans. Broadly, rural communities could benefit if more small businesses are able to start up or grow with this financial support.

A new rule limits construction, demolition, and real estate improvement costs to no more than half of any loan.

title: A bill to clarify the use of direct deposit for contributions to ABLE programs.
ai_summary:
ABLE accounts are special savings accounts for people with disabilities. They let eligible individuals save money without losing access to government benefits like Medicaid or Supplemental Security Income. This bill makes it clear that people can use direct deposit to put money into these accounts, removing any legal confusion about whether that payment method is allowed.

Right now, there is some uncertainty in existing law about whether direct deposit can be used to fund ABLE accounts. This bill fixes that by stating plainly that no law should be read as blocking direct deposit as a contribution method. It does not create a brand new program or change who qualifies for an ABLE account. It simply removes a legal gray area.

This bill mainly affects people with disabilities who have ABLE accounts, as well as their families and employers who might want to set up automatic payroll contributions. title: Invest to Protect Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill creates a federal grant program through the Department of Justice to help small, local law enforcement agencies. Only agencies with fewer than 175 officers qualify, including those run by tribal governments. The program would be funded at up to $50 million per year from 2026 through 2030. The application process is designed to be simple enough that a local government could complete it in two hours or less, with help available from dedicated staff at the Justice Department.

Agencies that receive grants can use the money in several specific ways. They can pay for officer training in areas like de-escalation, handling domestic violence calls, active shooter situations, and responding to people with mental health or substance use issues. They can also offer signing bonuses to recruit new officers, retention bonuses of up to 20 percent of salary for officers with at least five years on the job, and stipends of up to $10,000 for officers pursuing graduate degrees in mental health or social work. Grant money can also be used to provide mental health and counseling services for officers themselves.

The bill includes strong accountability rules. The Justice Department's Inspector General would regularly audit grant recipients to check for misuse of funds. Agencies found to have misused money would be barred from receiving future grants for three years and could be required to pay the money back. All signing and retention bonuses must be publicly disclosed. This bill primarily affects residents of smaller communities, local law enforcement officers, and the local governments that employ them.

title: Access to Counsel Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would require U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to give certain travelers the chance to speak with a lawyer or a trusted person when they are pulled aside for extra questioning at airports, border crossings, or other ports of entry. Specifically, that opportunity must be offered within one hour of the extra screening starting. The lawyer or trusted contact would also be allowed to share documents and speak up on the traveler's behalf during the process.

The bill covers a specific group of people, not everyone who crosses the border. It applies to U.S. citizens, green card holders returning from trips abroad, people with valid visas, refugees, asylees, and people who have been approved for parole into the country. There is also a special rule for green card holders: CBP could not ask them to sign away their permanent resident status during that screening unless they first had a chance to talk to a lawyer, or clearly and voluntarily chose in writing to skip that step.

This bill would most directly affect travelers in those categories who get sent to "secondary inspection," which is a more detailed screening that happens after the initial checkpoint. It would also affect CBP officers, who would be required to follow the new procedures. The bill does not give people the right to a government-appointed lawyer at no cost, only the right to contact one they arrange themselves.

title: No Tax Breaks for Outsourcing Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how US tax law treats American companies that operate or are based overseas. Right now, US companies can earn profits through foreign subsidiaries and pay lower tax rates on that income than they would on domestic profits. This bill would close several of those gaps. It would require companies to pay taxes on foreign subsidiary profits year by year, calculated country by country, rather than using a blended global rate that can hide low-tax arrangements. It also removes a special reduced tax rate that currently applies to certain foreign earnings, and eliminates a tax deduction loophole where companies load up their US operations with debt to reduce their American tax bill while keeping profits abroad.

The bill also targets two specific ways companies try to lower their US taxes through their corporate structure. First, it tightens rules on corporate inversions, where a US company legally relocates its headquarters to a foreign country mostly on paper while still operating in the US. Second, it would treat any foreign company as a US company for tax purposes if its top executives and key decision-makers are actually running it from inside the United States, regardless of where the company is officially registered.

This bill mainly affects large multinational corporations, particularly those with significant overseas operations or foreign subsidiaries. It does not directly change tax rules for individuals or small businesses with only US operations. Foreign companies that do substantial business in the US but are managed from American soil would also be affected. The bill was introduced in February 2025 and has been referred to the Senate Finance Committee, meaning it has not yet been voted on.
ai_headline: Senate bill would end key offshore tax breaks for US multinationals

title: Combating Illicit Xylazine Act
ai_summary:
Xylazine is a drug currently approved only for use in animals, such as to sedate livestock. In recent years it has increasingly shown up mixed into illegal drugs like fentanyl, making overdoses harder to treat and causing severe skin wounds in people who use it. This bill would place xylazine on Schedule III of the Controlled Substances Act, putting it in the same legal category as anabolic steroids and some prescription medications. That means it would become a federally controlled substance with rules around how it is tracked, stored, and distributed.

The bill makes clear that legitimate uses of xylazine are still allowed. Veterinarians can still prescribe it, pharmacies can still dispense it, and people or organizations using it legally for animals, wildlife programs, or government animal control would not be treated as criminals. Manufacturers already producing xylazine are given a grace period of up to one year to meet the new labeling and packaging requirements, and 60 days to get registered under the new rules. The FDA and DEA are directed to help manufacturers move through the required paperwork quickly.

The bill also requires the government to track xylazine through its existing drug monitoring system and directs the U.S. Sentencing Commission to review whether criminal penalties for illegally trafficking xylazine are appropriate. Additionally, the DEA and FDA must report to Congress within 18 months on how xylazine is being diverted and where it is coming from, with a follow-up report due in four years. This bill primarily affects veterinarians, pharmacies, drug manufacturers, law enforcement, and people involved in the illegal drug supply chain.

title: Insurance Data Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill would limit the ability of certain federal agencies to collect data directly from insurance companies. Right now, the Federal Insurance Office (part of the Treasury Department) and other financial regulators like the Office of Financial Research can request information straight from insurers. This bill would remove that direct access. Instead, before going to an insurance company for data, federal regulators would first have to check whether the information they need already exists somewhere else, like with a state insurance regulator or a public source. They could only go directly to an insurance company if the data truly cannot be found anywhere else, and even then they would have to follow additional rules about how they collect it.

The bill also adds privacy protections around any insurance data that does get shared with federal regulators. It says that when an insurance company shares private data with a regulator, that does not mean the company gives up any legal protections over that information. The data would still be treated as confidential, and existing privacy agreements would remain in force. Any data shared could be passed along to state insurance regulators only through formal agreements that maintain those confidentiality protections.

This bill primarily affects insurance companies and the federal agencies that oversee financial stability and risk. Insurance is mostly regulated at the state level, and supporters of the bill argue it reinforces that arrangement by keeping federal data collection limited. Everyday consumers are not directly affected by the bill, but it could influence how closely the federal government monitors the insurance industry for potential financial risks.
ai_headline: Federal agencies would lose direct access to insurer data under S 1544
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

title: Criminal History Access Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would give state police oversight agencies official access to federal criminal history records. These agencies, often called POST (Peace Officer Standards and Training) agencies, are the state-level bodies that decide whether someone is qualified to become or remain a law enforcement officer. Right now, federal law does not clearly allow them to look up a person's criminal background through the national FBI database. This bill would change that by adding them to the list of agencies legally authorized to access those records.

The main goal is to make it easier for states to screen law enforcement officers and candidates. If a state agency is deciding whether to certify, license, or remove a police officer, it would be able to check federal criminal records as part of that process. The Attorney General would also be required to update federal regulations within 180 days of the bill becoming law to reflect this change.

This bill affects state POST agencies in all 50 states, Washington D.C., Puerto Rico, and other U.S. territories. It also indirectly affects current and prospective law enforcement officers, since their criminal histories could be reviewed by these oversight bodies more easily. Everyday residents are not directly affected, but they may have an indirect interest since the bill relates to how law enforcement officers are screened and kept accountable.

title: Canyon’s Law
ai_summary:
This bill would ban the use of M-44 devices, also called "cyanide bombs," on federal public lands. These are spring-loaded devices placed in the ground that shoot a burst of cyanide gas into an animal's mouth when triggered. They are currently used by government agencies to kill coyotes, foxes, and wild dogs that prey on livestock. If passed, any M-44 devices already on federal land managed by agencies like the National Park Service, Forest Service, or Bureau of Land Management would have to be removed within 30 days.

The bill is named Canyon's Law, a reference to a family dog killed in Idaho in 2017 when a child accidentally triggered one of these devices and was also exposed to cyanide. The bill's findings point out that M-44s only kill their intended target about half the time and have accidentally harmed or killed people, pet dogs, bald eagles, wolves, bears, and other animals over the years. At least 42 people have been accidentally exposed to cyanide from these devices since 1984.

This bill mainly affects federal land management agencies, which would no longer be allowed to use or authorize this method of predator control on public land. It would also affect ranchers and farmers who rely on government wildlife control programs to protect their livestock from predators, since one tool those programs use would be restricted on federal land. Private land would not be covered by this ban.
ai_headline: Senate bill would remove cyanide traps from all federal public lands
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

The ban would not apply to private land.

title: Marijuana Impact on Medicaid Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill requires the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services to gather data on how much money the Medicaid program spends on hospital and emergency room visits that are connected to marijuana use. Within one year of the bill becoming law, the department would need to send a report to Congress summarizing what it found, and that report would also be made available to the public. The department would also be allowed to include recommendations for any changes to laws or policies based on the findings.

Medicaid is a government health insurance program that covers low-income individuals and families, and it is funded by both the federal government and state governments. This bill focuses specifically on figuring out how much of Medicaid's spending on hospital care can be linked to marijuana use, whether that means inpatient stays, outpatient visits, or emergency room trips.

The bill most directly affects federal health officials who would be responsible for collecting the data and writing the report. It could also be relevant to state governments that share Medicaid costs, as well as lawmakers who might use the findings to shape future policy. Medicaid enrollees themselves are not directly required to do anything under this bill, but the data collected would be about their medical visits.

title: ABLE MATCH (Making Able a Tool to Combat Hardship) Act
ai_summary:
ABLE accounts are special savings accounts for people with disabilities, letting them save money without losing access to government benefits. This bill would create a government match for contributions that low- and moderate-income people make into their own ABLE accounts. For every dollar a qualifying person puts in, up to $2,000 per year, the federal government would match it dollar-for-dollar and deposit that money directly into the account. The match starts phasing out for single filers earning above $28,000 and for married couples filing jointly earning above $56,000, and disappears entirely at $20,000 above those thresholds. The bill takes effect starting with the 2027 tax year.

The people directly affected are Americans with disabilities who have ABLE accounts and fall within those income limits. To get the match, they file a tax return claiming it, and the government sends the money to their ABLE account rather than as a regular tax refund check. People who already claim a related savings credit called the Saver's Credit would have to choose one or the other, not both. The bill also protects the matching funds from being seized to pay off other federal debts, such as student loans or back taxes.

The bill also includes two additional pieces. First, ABLE program administrators would be required to collect and report demographic data about account holders, including race, gender, and disability type, so Congress can better understand who is using these accounts. Second, it sets aside up to $5 million per year from 2027 through 2030 in grants to help states spread the word about ABLE accounts and the new matching benefit.

title: Pesticide Injury Accountability Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would give people the legal right to sue pesticide makers directly in federal court if they believe a pesticide harmed them or damaged their property. Right now, federal pesticide law does not clearly give individuals that ability on its own. Under this bill, someone could seek two types of money damages: compensatory damages to cover actual losses like medical bills or ruined crops, and punitive damages meant to punish the company if a court sees fit. However, the bill does not require the pesticide company to cover the person's lawyer fees or court costs, meaning those expenses would still fall on the person filing the lawsuit. The bill also makes clear that it does not cancel out any existing state laws that already let people sue over pesticide injuries.

The people most directly affected would be anyone who claims they were harmed by a registered pesticide, such as farmworkers, rural residents living near fields, or homeowners who used a pesticide product. On the other side, pesticide manufacturers and companies that hold federal pesticide registrations would face the possibility of new lawsuits they could not previously be sued for under federal law alone.

The bill is still in early stages. It was introduced in the Senate in July 2025 and sent to the Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee, where it would need to be approved before the full Senate could vote on it.

title: Officer John Barnes and Chief Michael Ansbro Public Safety Officers' Benefit Program Expansion Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill makes changes to a federal program that pays benefits to public safety officers and their families when an officer is killed or seriously injured on the job. Right now, families sometimes wait years to find out if their claim was approved. The bill tries to fix that by setting clear deadlines. The government agency handling claims would have 90 days to tell a claimant if anything is missing from their paperwork, and 270 days to make a final decision once a claim is complete. If the agency misses that 270-day deadline, it must send an interim payment to the family while the final decision is still being worked out. The bill also requires the agency to use its legal authority to force other government agencies to hand over documents needed to process a claim, instead of letting those delays stall a family's benefits.

The bill also creates a new category of benefits for officers who are permanently but not totally disabled. Under current law, benefits are mainly available for death or total disability. This bill would allow officers who can no longer work as a public safety officer due to a serious permanent injury, but who are not completely unable to work at all, to receive half the standard benefit amount. If that disability later gets worse and becomes total, the officer can apply for the full benefit.

The bill also makes it easier for claims connected to the September 11th attacks to be approved. If the 9/11 Victim Compensation Fund or the World Trade Center Health Program has already certified that someone's death was related to 9/11, the benefits agency must accept that as strong evidence and approve the claim unless there is clear proof otherwise. This bill affects active and retired public safety officers, including police, firefighters, and emergency responders, as well as their families who file for death or disability benefits.

The bill sets a 90-day deadline for agencies to flag incomplete paperwork and a 270-day deadline to reach a final decision, with an interim payment required if that deadline is missed. It also creates a new partial disability benefit equal to half the standard amount for officers permanently but not totally disabled, and streamlines approval of claims tied to the September 11th attacks.

title: Providing Child Care for Police Officers Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill creates a pilot grant program run by the Department of Health and Human Services. The government would give out grants to state-level child care agencies, which would then pass money along to police departments or groups of departments to help set up or expand child care programs. The goal is to create child care options that fit the unusual schedules police officers work, like overnight shifts, weekends, and holidays, when regular daycare centers are typically closed. The program is set to run from 2026 through 2030, with up to $24 million available each year.

To receive money, police departments or partnerships between departments and local organizations would have to apply and meet certain requirements. They also have to contribute some of their own money over time, starting at 10 percent in the first year and rising to about 33 percent by the third year. At least 20 percent of the total grant money must go to smaller departments with fewer than 200 officers. No single applicant can receive more than $3 million. The money can be used for things like startup costs, training child care workers, helping pay for child care directly, and even building or renovating facilities.

The bill primarily affects law enforcement officers who have children, particularly those working non-traditional hours who struggle to find child care. It also affects police departments, especially smaller ones, which may have trouble recruiting and keeping officers partly because of this challenge. The government will study how well the program works and whether similar first responders, such as firefighters and emergency medical workers, have the same unmet needs.

title: PARITY Act
ai_summary:
The PARITY Act would get rid of a rule called the "90/10 rule" that currently applies to for-profit colleges and universities. Under that existing rule, these schools cannot get more than 90% of their total revenue from federal financial aid programs like Pell Grants and student loans. The idea behind the rule was to make sure for-profit schools have some financial stake in attracting paying students, not just relying almost entirely on government money.

If this bill passes, for-profit schools would no longer have that 90% cap. They could receive as much of their income as they want from federal student aid programs, with no legal limit. Supporters of removing the rule argue it treats for-profit schools unfairly compared to public and nonprofit colleges, which have no such cap. Critics of removing it have argued the rule helps protect taxpayers and students from schools that might enroll students primarily to collect federal aid money.

The people most directly affected are students who attend for-profit colleges and the schools themselves. It could also affect taxpayers, since federal student aid money comes from the federal budget. For-profit colleges enroll millions of students across the country, including many working adults, military veterans, and lower-income students who rely heavily on federal financial aid to pay for school.

title: Support our Firefighters Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes two main changes for federal wildland firefighters who work for the U.S. Forest Service or the Department of the Interior. First, it creates a new paid "rest and recuperation" leave program. After working a long wildfire deployment, a firefighter would get mandatory paid days off to recover. For example, after 14 days on a fire, a firefighter would receive 3 paid rest days, and after 21 days, they would receive 4 paid rest days. This leave must be taken right after returning from a fire assignment and cannot be saved up or cashed out later.

Second, the bill permanently removes the cap on overtime pay for these wildland firefighters. Previously, Congress had to keep renewing a temporary waiver that allowed firefighters to earn overtime beyond normal federal limits. This bill makes that waiver permanent so firefighters are not cut off from overtime earnings in future years. The bill also allows up to $5 million in existing wildfire funding to be moved between the Forest Service and Interior Department to keep firefighter pay programs running without interruption.

This bill affects federal civilian employees who fight wildfires, including both full-time and part-time workers officially classified as wildland firefighters. It does not cover state or local firefighters. People who live in areas at risk of wildfires could be indirectly affected if these changes help agencies recruit and retain experienced federal firefighters.

last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

title: Freedom of Association in Higher Education Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would add a new rule to the Higher Education Act that protects students who join single-sex social organizations, like fraternities and sororities, at colleges and universities. Specifically, it says that any college receiving federal funding cannot punish a student simply because they belong to an organization that limits membership to one gender. Colleges also could not block students from applying to financial aid, scholarships, campus jobs, housing, sports teams, or letters of recommendation just because of that membership.

The bill also protects the organizations themselves. Colleges could not place special recruiting restrictions on fraternities or sororities unless the organization and the school both agree to those rules in writing. However, colleges are still allowed to discipline students for actual misconduct, and they are not required to officially recognize any organization. Professors can still speak freely about these groups, and the organizations themselves keep the right to choose their own members.

This mainly affects college students who are members or potential members of fraternities, sororities, and similar single-sex social clubs, as well as the colleges and universities that receive federal funding. Students at schools that have tried to discourage or penalize participation in these groups would have new federal protections. Schools that already allow these organizations to operate freely would see little practical change.

Colleges could also not impose special recruiting restrictions on these organizations without written agreement from the organization itself.

title: Written Informed Consent Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require the Department of Veterans Affairs to expand an existing rule about patient consent. Right now, VA doctors must get written consent from veterans before starting them on long-term opioid pain treatment. This means the doctor has to explain the risks and benefits in writing, and the veteran has to sign off before receiving the medication. This bill would apply that same written consent requirement to five additional types of medications: antipsychotics, stimulants, antidepressants, anti-anxiety medications, and narcotics.

In practice, this means that before a VA doctor could prescribe any of these medications to a veteran, they would need to walk the veteran through the risks and benefits in writing and get the veteran's signature agreeing to the treatment. The goal is to make sure veterans are fully informed before starting these kinds of drugs, which can have significant side effects or long-term consequences.

This bill directly affects veterans who receive their healthcare through the VA system and the VA doctors and staff who treat them. It does not apply to private doctors or non-VA healthcare settings. Veterans already on these medications would likely need updated consent forms as well, depending on how the VA chooses to implement the new rule.

Veterans already taking any of these medications may also need to complete updated consent forms depending on how the VA implements the rule.

title: Supreme Court Ethics, Recusal, and Transparency Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would require the Supreme Court to create and publish a formal code of ethics within 180 days of the law passing. Right now, Supreme Court justices operate under no legally binding ethics rules, unlike other federal judges. The bill would change that by forcing the Court to write clear conduct standards, post them publicly online, and set up a process for people to file complaints against justices. Complaints would be reviewed by a panel of five randomly selected federal circuit court judges who could investigate, hold hearings, and issue public reports on their findings.

The bill also tightens rules about when a justice must step aside from a case, called recusal. A justice would be required to recuse if a party in the case gave them gifts, income, or travel within the past six years, or if that party spent significant money supporting the justice's confirmation. Justices would have to actively find out about potential conflicts rather than waiting for someone to point them out, and they would have to notify all parties in a case as soon as a conflict comes up. Any recusal decisions would be posted publicly on the Court's website.

The bill affects Supreme Court justices most directly, but also touches other federal judges, lawyers arguing cases before the Court, and outside groups that file amicus briefs, which are documents submitted by people or organizations who are not directly part of a case but want to share their views. Those outside filers would have to disclose who funded them. Ordinary Americans are affected indirectly, since the bill is aimed at increasing public trust and transparency in the nation's highest court.

last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

title: CHOICE Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates a new type of employer health benefit called a "CHOICE arrangement." Instead of offering a traditional group health insurance plan, an employer could give workers a set amount of money each year to help pay for their own individual health insurance. Workers would use that money to buy their own plan on the private market or through a health insurance exchange, and the employer's contribution would be tax-free. The bill also allows workers enrolled in a CHOICE arrangement to use pre-tax dollars through a cafeteria plan to buy exchange coverage, which is currently not allowed.

The bill sets rules to make sure employers use this fairly. Employers must offer the same dollar amount to all workers in a given category, such as full-time or part-time employees, though they can offer somewhat more to older workers or those with dependents. Employers cannot offer this arrangement to some workers while giving others a traditional group plan, with a few limited exceptions. Workers must also be enrolled in their own individual insurance or Medicare for the money to be used. Employers must give workers written notice at least 60 days before the plan year begins explaining how the arrangement works.

The bill also offers a tax credit to smaller employers who are new to offering this kind of benefit. Businesses that are not considered "large employers" under federal law can receive up to $100 per enrolled employee per month during the first year they offer a CHOICE arrangement, and $50 per month in the second year. This bill would affect employers of all sizes who want an alternative to traditional group health coverage, workers who would receive a set benefit to shop for their own insurance, and the individual insurance market where those workers would be buying plans.
ai_headline: Senate bill lets employers fund workers' individual health plans tax-free
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

title: Native American Seeds Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Department of the Interior to work with federally recognized Native American tribes to identify and help protect seeds that hold traditional or cultural importance to those tribes. Within one year of becoming law, the Secretary of the Interior must begin coordinating with tribes to figure out which seeds qualify, and then support tribal efforts to preserve them. That support could include helping fund or maintain Native seed banks and backing traditional farming practices used to grow and harvest these seeds.

An important privacy protection is built into the bill. If a tribe shares information with the federal government as part of this process and labels that information as culturally sensitive, proprietary, or confidential, the government is not allowed to share it publicly or with other parties. This gives tribes control over sensitive knowledge about their seeds and agricultural traditions.

The bill affects federally recognized Native American tribes across the country, as well as the Department of the Interior, which would take on new coordination responsibilities. One notable limitation is that the bill does not set aside any new money to pay for these activities, meaning they can only happen if Congress separately approves funding. If the law is ever challenged in court, judges are instructed to defer to the Secretary of the Interior's reasonable interpretation of any unclear parts of the bill.

title: HELPER Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill creates a special home loan program through the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) for first responders and teachers. Eligible workers include full-time police officers, firefighters, paramedics, emergency medical technicians, and K-12 teachers at public or private schools. Under this program, qualified borrowers could buy a home with zero down payment, meaning they would not need to save up thousands of dollars upfront to purchase a house. Instead of paying monthly mortgage insurance fees, borrowers would pay a one-time upfront insurance premium when the loan closes.

To qualify, a person must be buying their first home, have worked in one of the eligible jobs for at least four of the past five years, be in good standing at their job, and complete a government-approved homebuyer counseling program. The borrower also has to plan to stay in the job for at least one year after closing on the home. The program is set to run for five years once it launches, and each person can only use it once.

This bill affects full-time law enforcement officers, firefighters, paramedics, EMTs, and public and private school teachers across the country who have never owned a home before. It does not apply to part-time workers in those fields. The government would set aside just over one million dollars total to administer the program between 2026 and 2032, though the actual home loans themselves would be backed by the existing FHA insurance fund rather than direct government spending.

title: Lowering Broadband Costs for Consumers Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would change who pays into the Universal Service Fund (USF), a program that helps bring affordable phone and internet service to rural areas, low-income households, schools, libraries, and hospitals. Right now, traditional phone companies pay into this fund, and those costs are often passed on to consumers as fees on their phone bills. The bill would require the FCC to write new rules within 18 months that expand who contributes to the fund, adding large internet companies and big internet service providers to the list of required contributors alongside traditional phone companies.

The bill specifically targets large "edge providers," meaning major tech companies that offer things like streaming, social media, search engines, cloud services, online gaming, app stores, and e-commerce platforms. However, smaller companies are exempt. A company would only need to contribute if it carried at least 3 percent of all broadband data traffic in the United States and earned at least five billion dollars in U.S. revenue in the past year. Very small contributors from any category would also be exempt. The idea is that by making large tech and internet companies share the cost, the fees currently passed on to everyday consumers through their phone bills could go down.

The bill also directs the FCC to create a new support program for internet providers serving high-cost areas, like rural communities, to help cover expenses that cannot be recovered through customer rates alone. Everyday consumers could potentially see lower fees on their phone and internet bills if the fund is spread across more large companies. Large technology companies would face new financial obligations. Rural residents and underserved communities could see more stable or improved broadband service as a result of the updated funding structure.

title: Health Equity and Access under the Law for Immigrant Families Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would expand access to government health insurance programs to more immigrants living in the United States. Right now, many immigrants must wait five years after getting a green card before they can qualify for Medicaid or CHIP, and undocumented immigrants are blocked from buying health insurance through the ACA marketplace even if they pay out of pocket. This bill would remove those waiting periods, require states to cover lawfully present immigrants in Medicaid and CHIP, and allow undocumented immigrants to purchase ACA marketplace plans and receive financial help paying for them. It would also extend Medicare eligibility to lawfully present immigrants who currently do not qualify.

The bill also gives states the option to go further. States could choose to open up Medicaid and CHIP to undocumented immigrants who would otherwise qualify based on income and family situation, treating them the same as U.S. citizens for those programs. States would not be required to do this, but the federal government would share in the cost if they do. People who have been granted deferred action status, such as DACA recipients, would be treated as lawfully present and eligible for these programs as well.

The people most directly affected are immigrants who currently lack health coverage, including green card holders still in waiting periods, people with temporary or deferred immigration status, and undocumented individuals. It would also affect state governments, which would face new coverage requirements and new options. Taxpayers would fund the expanded federal spending, and health care providers who currently treat uninsured immigrant patients could see changes in how that care is paid for.

States could also choose to cover undocumented immigrants in Medicaid and CHIP on the same terms as U.S. citizens, with the federal government sharing those costs.

title: Moms Matter Act
ai_summary:
The Moms Matter Act would create two federal grant programs focused on mental health and substance use problems during and after pregnancy. The first program, funded at up to $25 million per year from 2027 to 2031, would send money to hospitals, community organizations, clinics, tribal organizations, and local health departments. Those groups could use the funds to expand mental health services for pregnant and postpartum women, train doctors and nurses to spot warning signs of depression or addiction, reduce stigma, set up hotlines, and connect mothers to treatment for substance use disorders. Priority would go to organizations working in areas where maternal death rates and health disparities are already highest.

The second part of the bill would spend up to $15 million per year over the same period to help schools and training programs grow the number of mental health providers who specialize in maternal care. Preference would go to programs that actively recruit students from minority backgrounds, train providers to work in underserved areas, and require all students to complete training on bias and discrimination in healthcare.

The people most directly affected are pregnant women and new mothers, especially those in communities with high rates of maternal death or poor birth outcomes. Healthcare workers, training programs, and community organizations that serve these women would also be affected, as they could apply for the grant money. The bill does not guarantee funding; Congress would still need to approve the actual spending each year.

title: Health Care Cybersecurity and Resiliency Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill requires the federal government to strengthen cybersecurity protections across the entire American healthcare system. It directs the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to work together more closely, share information about cyber threats, and create a formal response plan for when cyberattacks hit healthcare organizations. It also sets new required security standards for healthcare entities, including things like multi-factor authentication (a two-step login process) and data encryption to protect patient health information.

The bill updates the public database where healthcare data breaches are reported, requiring more details to be listed, including how many patients were affected and what corrective actions were taken. It also creates a system where healthcare organizations that already follow strong security practices may receive more favorable treatment when fines are being considered after a breach. Special attention is given to rural healthcare providers, who often have fewer resources, with specific guidance and a government study to check how well those smaller organizations are able to keep up with cybersecurity requirements.

The bill affects a wide range of people and organizations. Hospitals, rural health clinics, community health centers, academic medical centers, and Indian Health Service facilities would all face new cybersecurity rules and could apply for federal grants to help pay for upgrades. Healthcare workers would receive more cybersecurity training. Patients nationwide would benefit from stronger protections of their personal medical records. The bill does not yet have a set funding amount beyond authorizing grants through 2030.

title: North Platte Canteen Congressional Gold Medal Act
ai_summary:
This bill would award a Congressional Gold Medal to the thousands of volunteers and community members who ran the North Platte Canteen in North Platte, Nebraska, during World War II. The canteen operated from December 25, 1941, to April 1, 1946, and served free food and hospitality to roughly 6 million U.S. troops passing through on trains. About 55,000 volunteers, mostly women, from communities in Nebraska, Colorado, and Kansas kept it running entirely without government funding.

The medal would be designed and produced by the U.S. Treasury's Mint, then displayed at the Lincoln County Historical Museum in North Platte so the public can see it. The government can also make and sell bronze copies of the medal, with the money from those sales going back into the Mint's operating fund. The cost of making the original gold medal would come from that same Mint fund, so no separate government spending is required.

This bill mainly affects the historical legacy of those specific World War II volunteers and their communities. It does not create new programs, change existing laws, or provide money to any individuals. It is a symbolic honor recognizing a piece of American home-front history, similar to other Congressional Gold Medals awarded to groups or individuals for notable service or contributions to the country.

title: MARKET Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill requires the U.S. Department of Agriculture to publish a report every year looking at how much American farmers depend on selling crops and food products to countries considered adversaries of the United States, such as China. The report would cover major farm exports like soybeans, corn, beef, pork, chicken, dairy, cotton, and tree nuts. It would identify risks to those export markets and suggest ways the U.S. could reduce its reliance on hostile nations as buyers of American farm goods.

The yearly report would also look for new, friendlier countries where American farmers could sell their products if trade with an adversarial country were suddenly cut off due to a conflict or political dispute. Multiple government agencies, including the State Department, Commerce Department, and the U.S. Trade Representative, would work together on the recommendations. The Secretary of Agriculture could also add countries to the adversary list beyond those already defined in existing law if they are seen as a serious threat to U.S. national security.

The bill mainly affects the federal government and how it tracks and reports on farm trade risks. American farmers and agricultural businesses could be asked to share information voluntarily to help build the reports, and their private data would be kept confidential and never publicly identified. The reports would stop being required once the government decides that American farm export markets are spread out enough that no single adversarial country poses a major risk.

title: Pechanga Band of Indians Water Rights Settlement Technical Amendments Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes small technical fixes to an existing federal law called the Pechanga Band of Luiseno Mission Indians Water Rights Settlement Act, which was originally passed in 2016. That law settled a long-running legal dispute over how much water the Pechanga Band, a federally recognized Native American tribe in Southern California, has the right to use. This bill updates two specific parts of that law to correct and clarify language, without changing the overall agreement itself.

The first fix updates the legal definition of the Pechanga Reservation by listing specific historical dates when land was officially added to the reservation, going back to 1882. It also clarifies that certain nearby land held in trust by the federal government, and future land placed into trust within the local Santa Margarita River Watershed, counts as part of the reservation for water rights purposes. The second fix broadens how money in a special water quality fund can be spent. Instead of only being allowed to pay for groundwater desalination in a specific area called the Wolf Valley Basin, the fund can now be used for any activities that address water quality problems in that area.

This bill mainly affects the Pechanga Band of Indians and the federal government, particularly the Department of the Interior, which manages tribal trust lands and must update related agreements to match the new language. It also indirectly affects local water users and agencies in the Santa Margarita River Watershed region of Riverside County, California. The bill explicitly states that no existing water rights held by anyone are changed by these updates.

title: FARM AI Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill tells the U.S. Department of Agriculture to make artificial intelligence a bigger part of its farming programs. It officially adds AI to the list of research priorities the USDA funds, meaning grant money can now go toward projects that use AI for things like managing crops, tracking weather, saving water, and protecting farm computer systems from hackers. It also updates the Cooperative Extension program, which is the network that helps farmers learn new techniques, so that it specifically teaches people how to use AI and data tools on their farms.

The bill also creates a new government position called the Artificial Intelligence Agriculture Advisor. This person, based inside the USDA, would be in charge of promoting AI adoption across all 50 states and U.S. territories. They would coordinate training programs, share best practices with farmers, work with outside partners, and team up with the National Institute of Standards and Technology to set national AI standards for agriculture.

The people most directly affected are farmers, ranchers, and rural communities across the country, especially small and family-run farms that might not otherwise have the money or know-how to try new technology. Agricultural colleges, extension offices, and research institutions would also be affected because they could receive new grant funding tied to AI education and training.

title: Exchange Stabilization Fund Transparency Act
ai_summary:
The Exchange Stabilization Fund (ESF) is a pot of money controlled by the U.S. Treasury Department that can be used to stabilize currency markets or provide financial help to foreign countries. Right now, the Treasury Secretary can use this fund with very little advance notice to Congress. This bill would require the Treasury Secretary to notify specific congressional committees at least 24 hours before committing ESF money to help a foreign government or foreign financial institution. That notice would have to explain what the help is, how much it costs, why it serves U.S. interests, what conditions are attached, and what the repayment plan looks like. Within 7 days of any such action, the Treasury would also have to brief those committees in person.

The bill also looks backward. Within 30 days of becoming law, the Treasury would have to submit a report covering every time the ESF was used to help a foreign country or entity during the previous four years, including copies of any agreements and an assessment of whether more help might be needed soon. If some information is not ready at the time of the initial notice, the Treasury has up to 14 days to fill in the gaps, or must do so once $500 million has been spent, whichever comes first.

This bill mainly affects the Treasury Department and Congress. It does not directly change benefits, taxes, or services for ordinary Americans. Indirectly, it could matter to U.S. taxpayers because the ESF is funded with government money, and the bill is designed to make sure elected representatives know how that money is being used before it goes out the door. The bill was introduced with support from both a Democratic and a Republican senator.

title: To amend the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act to provide for the regulation of fishing in marine national monuments.
ai_summary:
This bill changes who has the power to regulate fishing inside marine national monuments, which are protected ocean areas created by presidential order. Right now, a president can use the Antiquities Act to restrict or ban fishing inside these monuments when they are created or modified. This bill would take that power away from the president and require that fishing in these areas be regulated only through the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act, which is the main federal law governing ocean fishing and is administered through regional fishery management councils and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

The practical effect is that any existing presidential proclamations that currently limit or ban fishing inside marine national monuments would no longer apply to fishing activities. Future presidents also could not use the Antiquities Act to restrict fishing when designating new monuments. Instead, fishing rules inside these protected ocean areas would go through the same standard fishery management process used everywhere else in U.S. federal waters.

The people most directly affected are commercial and recreational fishermen who fish near or inside marine national monuments, particularly those around Hawaii, American Samoa, and the Pacific Islands, where several large monuments exist. Environmental and conservation groups that have supported fishing bans inside these monuments would also be affected, as would federal agencies whose authority over these areas would shift. The bill was introduced by a representative from American Samoa, a territory with significant fishing interests near several monument areas.
ai_headline: Bill strips presidents of power to ban fishing in marine monuments
last_action_text: Subcommittee Hearings Held

Instead, all fishing in these protected ocean areas would be governed exclusively by the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act. title: No Payouts for Political Insiders Act
ai_summary:
This bill is about a specific government fund called the "Anti-Weaponization Fund" and a lawsuit called Trump v. Internal Revenue Service. In that lawsuit, a settlement agreement was reached that could result in the government paying out money to certain people. This bill would block those payments from going to a specific group of people, including the President, the Vice President, members of Congress, and senior executive branch officials, as well as people who work for the President's or Vice President's official campaign committees.

The bill also adds a transparency requirement. Before any payment from this fund is made under that settlement, the government would have to publicly disclose, at least 180 days in advance, the name of the person receiving the money, the amount, a summary of why they are owed it, and who their lawyer is.

This bill would mainly affect high-ranking political figures and their close associates who might otherwise receive a payout from this settlement. For most everyday Americans, the bill has no direct financial impact. However, it could affect public knowledge about how government settlement money is spent, since the disclosure requirement would make that information available to the public.

title: A bill to prioritize the finalization of design requirements for new Ready Reserve Force vessels, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill focuses on a fleet of cargo ships called the Ready Reserve Force, which the U.S. military uses to quickly move tanks, trucks, weapons, and other equipment to other parts of the world during a crisis or war. These ships sit in reserve and can be activated on short notice. The bill tells the Secretary of the Navy and the head of the Maritime Administration to make finishing the design plans for new Ready Reserve Force ships a top priority.

The bill also requires those officials to report back to Congress within 180 days. That report must cover several things: how the design of a new type of cargo ship called a roll-on/roll-off vessel is coming along, what the plan and timeline look like for hiring a construction manager to oversee building new ships, how much money will be needed each year to build up to 10 new ships, and how the new ship program will work alongside an existing program that buys used ships in the meantime.

This bill mainly affects the Navy, the Maritime Administration, and U.S. shipyards that could potentially be chosen to build these vessels. Indirectly, it affects military readiness and the defense industrial base, since the Ready Reserve Force plays an important role in the country's ability to send equipment overseas quickly. Average Americans are not directly affected in their daily lives, but the bill is part of broader efforts to maintain and modernize the country's military shipping capacity.

title: A bill to improve transparency with respect to foreign influence on Department of Defense contractors.
ai_summary:
This bill requires companies that want to do business with the U.S. military to disclose who actually owns them behind the scenes. Right now, a company might have hidden foreign owners who could influence how it operates. Under this bill, any company bidding on a Defense Department contract would have to reveal its "beneficial owners," meaning the real people who ultimately own or control the company, even if their names are not listed on official business documents. The Defense Department would have two years to update its contracting rules to make this a standard requirement.

The bill also lowers the dollar threshold for when the military must investigate foreign ownership risks in its supply chain. Previously, that extra scrutiny kicked in for contracts worth more than $5 million. This bill drops that trigger to $500,000, meaning far more contracts would be reviewed for potential foreign influence before they are awarded.

The people most directly affected are companies that sell goods or services to the U.S. military, including both prime contractors and their subcontractors. Smaller companies that previously fell below the $5 million review threshold would now face additional screening. Taxpayers and military operations could benefit if the rules help block foreign adversaries from quietly influencing U.S. defense suppliers.

title: AGE Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new federal tax credit for people who pay out of pocket to care for elderly relatives or household members. If you spend money on things like medical care, adult day programs, home modifications, assistive devices, personal care, or even caregiver counseling for a qualifying senior, you could get back up to 20 percent of those costs on your federal taxes. The most expenses you can claim is $6,000 per year, so the maximum credit would be $1,200. The credit phases down as your income rises above $120,000 and disappears entirely at higher income levels.

To qualify, the person being cared for must be 65 or older, need help with basic daily activities, and be a parent, stepparent, in-law, grandparent, or someone else who lives in your home. You cannot use this credit for payments made to someone you already claim as a dependent on your taxes, and you must provide the care provider's name, address, and tax ID number when you file. Care facilities used must follow all state and local regulations.

This bill would primarily affect working-age adults who are helping to support aging parents or other elderly family members and paying for that care themselves. It would not directly help the elderly individuals receiving care, but it could reduce the financial burden on the family members and caregivers writing those checks. The bill has been introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee but has not become law yet.

title: Applying Existing Tax Anti-Abuse Rules to Digital Assets Act
ai_summary:
This bill applies two existing tax rules to cryptocurrency and other digital assets. Right now, those rules only cover stocks and bonds. The first rule is called the "wash sale" rule. It stops investors from selling an asset at a loss just to claim a tax deduction, then immediately buying the same asset back. The second rule is called the "constructive sale" rule. It prevents investors from locking in gains on an asset without actually selling it by using financial tricks, like short selling, to avoid owing taxes. The bill would make both rules apply to digital assets like Bitcoin and Ethereum, the same way they already apply to traditional investments.

There are a few exceptions built into the bill. Stablecoins pegged to the U.S. dollar and issued by qualified issuers are generally left out of these rules. Crypto earned through mining or staking, meaning the process of verifying blockchain transactions, is also exempt from the wash sale rule. Brokers are given until 2028 to adjust their reporting systems to track the new requirements.

This bill most directly affects people who actively buy and sell cryptocurrencies, especially those who use losses to reduce their tax bills at year's end. It also affects crypto exchanges and brokers who will need to update how they track and report customer transactions. Miners and stakers are largely unaffected by the wash sale portion but should be aware the constructive sale rules could still apply to them in some situations.
ai_headline: Bill extends wash sale and constructive sale tax rules to cryptocurrency
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: Charitable Deductions for Digital Asset Donations Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes a tax rule about donating cryptocurrency and similar digital assets to charity. Right now, when someone donates property worth more than $5,000 to a charity and wants to claim a tax deduction, they generally must pay for a formal appraisal to prove its value. Stocks that trade on public markets are already exempt from this requirement because their prices are easy to look up. This bill would extend that same exemption to certain widely traded digital assets, like major cryptocurrencies, starting in 2027. To qualify, the digital asset must have been publicly traded for at least a full year, had a market value of over $500 million for most of that year, and the donor cannot own or control more than 10% of the total supply.

The bill also adds official tax code definitions for several terms, including "digital asset," "widely traded digital asset," "stablecoin," and related concepts. This matters because the tax code currently lacks clear definitions for these things. The Treasury Department is given some authority to adjust the rules over time to stop potential abuse or price manipulation and to account for changes in the market.

This bill most directly affects people who own large amounts of widely traded cryptocurrency and want to donate it to a nonprofit or charity. It would make that process simpler and less expensive by removing the need to hire an appraiser. Charities that accept digital asset donations could also see an increase in such gifts. It does not change how digital assets are taxed in other situations, and it does not settle legal questions about whether any particular digital asset is a security or commodity.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
