title: PAR Act
ai_summary:
The PAR Act changes how the federal tax code treats cryptocurrency and other digital assets. Right now, the tax rules for things like stocks and bonds are well established, but similar rules for digital assets are unclear or missing. This bill tries to fix that by applying familiar tax rules to digital assets that are actively traded and meet certain size requirements. For example, it sets up rules for when someone lends out their digital assets, similar to how stock lending already works, so the lender does not trigger a taxable event just by lending.

The bill also lets professional crypto dealers and traders choose a special accounting method called mark-to-market, which means they report gains and losses based on the value of their holdings at the end of each year rather than only when they sell. This is already an option for stock traders and is meant to simplify tax reporting for people who trade digital assets professionally. Additionally, foreign investors who trade digital assets in the United States for their own accounts would be protected from being taxed as if they were running a U.S. business, again following the same rules that already exist for stocks and commodities.

The people most directly affected are professional traders, investment dealers, and businesses that work with cryptocurrency and other digital assets. Everyday investors who buy and hold crypto are less directly impacted, though the bill does clarify some definitions that could affect how all digital asset transactions are eventually reported. The bill does not change whether a digital asset counts as a stock or security under other laws, only how it is taxed.
ai_headline: Tax rules for crypto traders would mirror existing stock market law
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 9176 applies established stock and bond tax rules to digital assets, affecting professional traders, dealers, and foreign investors.
ai_sections.what: HR 9176, the PAR Act, updates the federal tax code to apply existing stock and bond tax rules to actively traded digital assets that meet certain size requirements. It clarifies rules for digital asset lending so lenders do not trigger a taxable event simply by lending out holdings. The bill also allows professional crypto dealers and traders to use mark-to-market accounting, reporting gains and losses based on year-end values rather than only at the point of sale.
ai_sections.who: Professional traders, investment dealers, and businesses working with cryptocurrency and other digital assets are most directly affected. Foreign investors trading digital assets in the United States for their own accounts are also covered under the bill's provisions.
ai_sections.why: Current tax rules for digital assets are unclear or missing, creating uncertainty for those who trade or lend them professionally. Applying familiar stock and commodity rules to digital assets could change how gains, losses, and lending arrangements are reported across the industry.

title: Digital Assets Voluntary Disclosure Program Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a voluntary program run by the IRS that lets people come forward and correct mistakes they made on their taxes related to cryptocurrency and other digital assets like NFTs. If someone failed to report income from buying, selling, or owning digital assets in past years, they could use this program to file corrected tax returns, pay what they owe plus interest, and pay a reduced penalty. The program would need to be set up within one year of the bill becoming law, and participants would have two years after that to file their corrected returns.

The penalties people pay depend on their situation. Taxpayers who can swear under oath that their mistakes were honest and not intentional pay lower penalties, ranging from 0 to 5 percent of the extra taxes owed. Those who cannot make that claim pay higher penalties, between 25 and 40 percent of the unpaid tax. Either way, these penalties are lower than what the IRS could normally charge. People who come forward also get protection from criminal prosecution for the tax violations they disclose, as long as they are not already under a criminal investigation.

This bill mainly affects people who own or have traded digital assets like Bitcoin or Ethereum and did not properly report those transactions on their federal taxes. That could include everyday investors, traders, or anyone who received digital assets as payment and did not report it. It does not affect people who are already under criminal investigation unless the IRS grants them a special waiver to participate.
ai_headline: IRS voluntary program would cut penalties for unreported crypto taxes
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: Tax Clarity for Mining and Staking Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the IRS taxes cryptocurrency that people earn through mining and staking. Right now, the tax rules for these activities are unclear. Under this bill, when someone mines or stakes crypto and receives new digital coins as a reward, those coins would be taxed as ordinary income the moment they receive them, based on the coins' value at that time. However, the bill also creates an option to delay paying that tax. If a miner or staker chooses this option, they can wait until they actually sell or trade their coins to pay taxes, and the profit would be treated as regular income rather than a capital gain at that point.

The bill also sets clear definitions for terms like "mining," "staking," and "digital assets" so the IRS and taxpayers are working from the same rulebook. It includes rules for investment trusts that hold and stake crypto, making sure these trusts are not accidentally treated as businesses, which would change how they are taxed. There are also rules clarifying whether income from these activities counts as U.S. income or foreign income depending on where the taxpayer lives.

This bill mainly affects people and businesses that earn cryptocurrency by validating blockchain transactions, meaning crypto miners, stakers, and the investment funds built around those activities. It also affects tax professionals who advise these clients. Everyday crypto holders who simply buy and sell coins are not directly targeted by this bill. The changes would only apply going forward from the date the bill becomes law, and they do not change how past crypto earnings are treated.
ai_headline: IRS crypto mining and staking tax rules would be set by new bill
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

The bill also creates an optional deferral, allowing miners and stakers to delay paying that tax until they sell or trade the coins, at which point the profit is still treated as ordinary income rather than a capital gain. The bill adds clear legal definitions for mining, staking, and digital assets, and sets rules for investment trusts that hold and stake crypto.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects cryptocurrency miners, stakers, investment funds built around those activities, and tax professionals who advise them. Everyday crypto holders who only buy and sell coins are not targeted by this bill.
ai_sections.why: The bill replaces currently unclear IRS rules with a defined framework, which changes how and when affected taxpayers calculate and report income from blockchain validation activities. The changes apply only going forward from the date the bill becomes law and do not alter how past crypto earnings are treated.

title: Fiscal Year 2025 Veterans Affairs Major Medical Facility Authorization Act
ai_summary:
This bill gives the Department of Veterans Affairs official permission to build a major new medical campus in St. Louis, Missouri. The project includes a new hospital bed tower, expanded clinic space, an administrative building, a warehouse, a utility plant, and parking garages. Congress must formally authorize large construction projects like this before any money can be spent, and this bill takes that step.

The bill also sets a spending limit for the project of up to about $1.76 billion, to be funded during the 2026 federal budget year. Authorizing the money does not automatically release it — a separate appropriations bill would still need to actually provide the funds — but this authorization is a required first step.

The people most directly affected are veterans in the St. Louis area who use VA health care. A larger, more modern facility could mean more beds, more services, and less crowding. Construction workers and local businesses in the St. Louis region could also be affected by a project of this size. title: Small Business Tax Relief Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes four main changes to tax law. First, it lowers the corporate tax rate for smaller companies. Right now, all corporations pay a flat 21 percent tax rate. Under this bill, corporations earning up to 5 million dollars a year would pay 18 percent on their first 400,000 dollars of income, and 21 percent on anything above that. Larger corporations would still pay the full 21 percent on everything they earn.

Second, the bill targets something called the "carried interest" tax break. Right now, certain investment fund managers, such as those running hedge funds or private equity firms, can pay the lower capital gains tax rate on a big portion of their earnings, even though those earnings come from managing other people's money as part of their job. This bill would require that income to be taxed as ordinary income instead, meaning it would be taxed at the same higher rates that most working people pay on their wages. It also adds a stiff 40 percent penalty for anyone who tries to get around these new rules.

Third, the bill helps self-employed workers who earn under 400,000 dollars a year by letting them deduct a larger share of their self-employment taxes. Currently they can deduct half; this bill raises that to three-quarters. Fourth, it raises the excise tax on stock buybacks, when companies repurchase their own shares, from 1 percent to 1.5 percent. Overall, this bill primarily affects small business owners, self-employed individuals earning under 400,000 dollars, and high-earning investment fund managers.
ai_headline: HR 3275 cuts rates for small corporations and self-employed, closes hedge fund loophole
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

Corporations earning up to 5 million dollars a year would pay 18 percent on their first 400,000 dollars of income and 21 percent above that, while larger corporations remain at 21 percent on all earnings. Self-employed workers earning under 400,000 dollars a year could deduct three-quarters of their self-employment taxes, up from one-half.

title: No Tax Breaks for Radical Corporate Activism Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change the federal tax code to remove a tax deduction that businesses currently use when they pay for certain employee benefits. Right now, companies can deduct the cost of employee benefits as normal business expenses. This bill would take away that deduction specifically for two things: when a company pays for an employee's travel to get an abortion, and when a company covers medical costs for gender transition procedures for an employee's minor child (under age 18). The bill does not make these benefits illegal — it just means companies could no longer reduce their taxable income by offering them.

The main people affected are employers who currently offer these benefits as part of their health or wellness packages. Losing the deduction would make these benefits more expensive for companies to provide, since they would no longer get a tax break for doing so. Employees whose companies offer these benefits could also be indirectly affected if employers decide to drop the coverage to avoid the added cost.

The bill was introduced in February 2025 and was sent to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which handles tax legislation. It has not become law. The abortion travel provision applies to employees themselves, while the gender transition provision applies only to procedures for a worker's child who is under 18. Medical treatments for certain conditions present at birth that affect biological sex characteristics are specifically excluded from the gender transition definition.

title: SAFEGUARD Veterans Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill is aimed at protecting veterans from being charged illegal fees by unauthorized people who help them apply for VA benefits. Right now, there is no criminal penalty for someone who charges a veteran money to help file a VA claim unless that person is officially approved by the VA. This bill would bring back criminal penalties, including fines and up to one year in prison, for anyone who charges veterans fees without being authorized to do so. It would also ban repeat offenders from ever working with VA claims for up to 10 years. Only VA-approved agents, attorneys, and veterans service organizations would be allowed to help veterans file claims, and most of those approved helpers are required by law to provide their services for free.

The bill also requires the VA to take several steps to better inform and protect veterans. The VA would have to send notices to veterans who file claims without a representative, letting them know where to find a list of approved helpers. The VA's websites would need to display warnings about potentially predatory fee-charging practices and include a way for veterans to report anyone who charged them illegally. VA claim forms would also have to ask veterans whether someone charged them for help filing, and veterans would be warned not to share their VA or bank account login information with anyone.

The bill affects veterans filing for VA benefits, people who help veterans with those claims (such as lawyers or claim agents), and the VA itself, which would be required to upgrade its accreditation tracking system and improve public-facing websites. It also updates federal communications law to restrict automated phone calls to federal agencies, which could relate to scam operations that target veterans.
ai_headline: Senate bill restores criminal penalties for charging veterans illegal VA claim fees
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Veterans' Affairs.

Repeat offenders could be barred from working with VA claims for up to 10 years. The bill also requires the VA to notify veterans of approved helpers, add warnings and reporting tools to its websites, and update claim forms to ask whether veterans were charged.

Restoring penalties and adding VA disclosure requirements could alter how both legitimate and unauthorized claim helpers operate.

title: Department of Veterans Affairs Claim Sharks Effective Warnings Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill requires the Department of Veterans Affairs to show warning messages on all of its public-facing websites and online tools, not just when a veteran logs in. The warnings are meant to protect veterans from people who might try to take advantage of them while helping file VA benefits claims. The bill also adds a new warning telling veterans not to share their VA account or bank account login information, like usernames and passwords, with anyone.

The bill targets a problem sometimes called "claim sharks," which refers to unlicensed or unaccredited people who charge veterans fees or gain unauthorized access to their accounts while helping them file disability or benefits claims. Current law already required some warnings, but this bill expands where those warnings appear and adds the new message about protecting login credentials. It also puts the Chief Veterans Experience Officer in charge of carrying out these requirements.

This bill mainly affects U.S. military veterans who use VA websites to manage their benefits claims. It could also affect agents and attorneys who help veterans file claims, since the warnings specifically mention that some of those individuals may not be officially recognized by the VA. The changes would take effect 180 days after the bill becomes law.

title: Veterans Benefits Information Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill would make it illegal to use automated calling systems, like robocall machines, to contact federal government phone numbers. Specifically, it targets equipment that can make repeated calls on its own and exchange information automatically, without a real person actively controlling each call. The restriction applies when the automated system is being run by someone other than the person whose information is actually involved in the call.

The bill is named after veterans because a common scam involves third-party companies using robocalls to contact the Department of Veterans Affairs or other federal agencies on behalf of veterans, often to harvest or manipulate their personal benefits information without proper authorization. Under this bill, that kind of automated contact with federal agency phone lines would be prohibited.

This primarily affects companies or individuals who use robocall technology to interact with federal agencies like the VA, Social Security Administration, or others. Veterans and other Americans who deal with federal agencies could be better protected from having their personal information accessed or shared through these automated systems without their direct involvement. The bill would not prevent regular people or businesses from calling government agencies the normal way, with a real person on the line.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: Protecting VA Employees Act
ai_summary:
This bill would roll back a 2017 law that gave the Department of Veterans Affairs special, faster authority to fire, demote, or suspend its employees. Under the 2017 law, VA managers could remove workers more quickly and with fewer protections than most other federal employees have. This bill would repeal those special VA-specific rules and put VA employees back under the same standard federal employment rules that cover other government workers across all agencies.

The bill also restores older grievance and disciplinary procedures that applied specifically to Veterans Health Administration medical staff before 2017. Those procedures gave VHA clinical employees, like doctors and nurses, a particular process for challenging disciplinary actions. This bill would bring those procedures back.

The people most directly affected are VA employees, particularly those working at the Veterans Health Administration. Under current law, they can be fired or disciplined more quickly and with fewer appeal rights than other federal workers. If this bill became law, they would regain stronger job protections and appeal rights. Veterans who receive care at VA facilities could also be indirectly affected, since changes to how VA staff are hired and fired can influence staffing levels and workplace conditions.

title: Stop Illegal Entry Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill makes the punishments harsher for two things that are already illegal under federal law: entering the United States without permission and coming back to the US after being formally removed. Right now, the maximum prison sentence for illegally entering the country is 2 years. This bill would raise that to 5 years. It also adds a new rule: if someone entered illegally and then gets convicted of any crime that could result in more than a year in prison, they would face a minimum of 5 years behind bars and could potentially be imprisoned for life.

The bill also increases penalties for people who return to the US after being officially deported or removed. The basic maximum sentence for illegal reentry would go from 2 years to 10 years. People with more serious histories face even steeper consequences. For example, someone previously removed who had a felony conviction before leaving could face a mandatory minimum of 10 years, with no upper limit on the sentence. Someone removed three or more times who comes back could face up to 15 years.

This bill directly affects non-citizens who enter the US without legal permission or who return after being deported, especially those with prior criminal convictions. It would also affect federal courts and prosecutors, who would be required to apply these higher mandatory minimum sentences in certain cases. The bill was introduced in the House in May 2025 and has been sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where it would need to be approved before moving forward.

last_action_text: Received in the Senate.

title: Southcentral Foundation Land Transfer Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill transfers ownership of a small piece of federal land in Anchorage, Alaska, to the Southcentral Foundation (SCF), a nonprofit Alaska Native health care organization. The property is about 3.4 acres and must be handed over within two years of the bill becoming law. The transfer is free of charge, meaning SCF pays nothing for it, and the federal government gives up all ownership rights with no strings attached. SCF is expected to use the land for health and social services programs.

The bill also spells out who is responsible if environmental problems are found on the property. The federal government stays on the hook for any contamination that happened before the transfer date. SCF would not be held liable for past pollution, but it would be responsible for any contamination that occurs after it takes control of the land. The government must also follow existing federal environmental disclosure rules before handing the property over.

This bill most directly affects the Southcentral Foundation, which serves Alaska Native and American Indian people in the Anchorage area. It also involves the Department of Health and Human Services, which currently holds the property. The broader community served by SCF's health and social programs could benefit if the organization uses the land to expand or improve its services.

title: Archie Cavanaugh Migratory Bird Treaty Amendment Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes a federal wildlife law called the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. That law protects migratory birds and generally makes it illegal to buy, sell, or transport them or their parts. The bill adds a clear exemption specifically for Alaska Native traditional handicrafts. If an item is handmade by a verified Alaska Native using natural materials and traditional techniques, it can legally contain non-edible bird parts, such as feathers, beaks, or talons, and can be bought, sold, traded, or shipped. The exemption does not apply if the bird parts came from birds that were killed illegally or wastefully.

The bill also directs the State Department and the Interior Department to update international agreements and federal regulations within 180 days to match this new rule. The United States has bird protection treaties with Canada, Mexico, Japan, and Russia, and this bill instructs the government to work with those countries to make sure the Alaska Native handicraft exemption is recognized internationally as well.

This bill directly affects Alaska Natives who create and sell traditional artwork that uses bird parts, such as ceremonial clothing, carvings, or beadwork. It also affects buyers, traders, and shippers of those items. Federal wildlife enforcement agencies would need to update how they apply the law. The general public and non-Native artists are not covered by this exemption.

title: Northern Mariana Islands Small Business Access Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes a small but specific change to an existing federal program called the SBA Microloan Program. Right now, that program allows certain U.S. territories like Guam to participate, but the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) is left out. This bill would add the CNMI to the list of places where nonprofits and other lending organizations can receive federal funds to make small loans to local businesses and startups.

The Microloan Program works by giving money to approved nonprofit lenders, who then loan it out in small amounts, usually up to $50,000, to entrepreneurs and small business owners who may have trouble getting traditional bank loans. By including the CNMI, lenders based there would become eligible to receive those federal funds and pass them along to local small business owners on the islands.

The people most directly affected are small business owners and entrepreneurs living in the Northern Mariana Islands, a U.S. territory in the Pacific Ocean. Nonprofit lenders in the CNMI would also be affected, since they could now apply to be part of this federal program. The bill does not change how the program works anywhere else in the country.

title: Affordable HOMES Act
ai_summary:
This bill would stop the federal government from enforcing energy efficiency rules on manufactured homes, which are factory-built homes sometimes called mobile homes. Specifically, it cancels a 2022 rule from the Department of Energy that set standards for how well these homes must be insulated and how efficiently they must use energy. The bill also removes the law from 2007 that gave the government the authority to create those standards in the first place.

The people most directly affected are the roughly 22 million Americans who live in manufactured homes, as well as the companies that build them. Supporters of this kind of bill typically argue that energy efficiency requirements raise the upfront cost of building these homes, making them less affordable for buyers who often have lower incomes. Critics of this kind of bill typically argue that without the standards, residents end up paying higher utility bills over time because their homes use more energy to heat and cool.

Manufactured housing is one of the largest sources of unsubsidized affordable housing in the country, so this bill touches a broad group of people. Builders, retailers, and contractors in the manufactured housing industry would no longer need to meet federal energy rules. State and local governments could still choose to set their own energy standards, but the federal requirement would be gone entirely.
ai_headline: Bill would strip federal energy rules from factory-built homes

title: Combatting International Drug Trafficking and Human Smuggling Partnership Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill expands the authority of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), specifically its Air and Marine Operations division, to work inside other countries. Right now, CBP's ability to operate on foreign soil is limited. This bill would formally allow CBP officers to partner with foreign governments, conduct joint operations, and use aircraft and other tools abroad to track and intercept illegal drugs, smuggled people and goods, and terrorist threats headed toward the United States. These operations would only happen in countries that have signed an agreement with the U.S. government allowing it.

The bill also allows CBP to pay money claims filed by people in foreign countries who feel they were harmed by CBP operations on their soil. Those claims must be filed within two years of an incident, and the government's ability to pay such claims would expire after five years. Within 90 days of that expiration, the Department of Homeland Security would have to report to Congress detailing every payment made, who received it, how much they got, and why.

The people most directly affected are CBP Air and Marine Operations personnel, who would gain new legal authority to work overseas, and residents of foreign countries where these joint operations take place. Americans could be indirectly affected if the operations successfully reduce drug trafficking or smuggling into the U.S. Foreign governments that choose to sign partnership agreements with the U.S. would also take on a significant role, since their cooperation is required before any of this can happen.
ai_headline: Bill would let border agents run joint ops in foreign countries
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Foreign Relations.

title: SHOWER Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the federal government legally defines the word "showerhead." Right now, federal energy law uses its own definition, which has been used to set water flow limits on shower products. This bill would replace that definition with one from a 2024 industry plumbing standard called ASME A112.18.1-2024. Safety showers, like the emergency eyewash stations you see in labs or factories, would be left out of this new definition. The Department of Energy would have 180 days to update its rules to match the new definition.

The practical effect depends on how the industry standard defines a showerhead compared to current federal rules. The current federal definition has been used to regulate multi-head shower systems, meaning a shower with several spray nozzles had to meet the same total water flow limit as a single-head shower. Changing to the industry standard could allow shower systems with multiple heads to use more water overall, since each head might be treated separately under different rules.

This bill would most directly affect manufacturers who make shower products, retailers who sell them, and homeowners or builders who install them. People who prefer high-flow shower systems or multi-head setups could have more options available if the rule change allows those products to be sold more freely. It could also affect water usage in homes, which may matter more in areas where water conservation is a concern.
ai_headline: Federal showerhead definition would shift to 2024 industry standard under HR 4593
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

title: Union Auto Workers Job Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill has two main parts. The first part requires any company that wants to sell vehicles to the federal government to share detailed information about where those vehicles are made. Companies bidding on government contracts would have to disclose things like the factory locations, worker pay ranges, how many temporary workers are employed, and any past violations of labor or workplace safety laws. If a company later wants to move production to a different factory, it would need government approval first and would have to notify any affected unions right away.

The second part focuses specifically on the U.S. Postal Service and its contract with Oshkosh Defense, the company currently building new mail delivery trucks. The bill would block federal money from being spent on those delivery vehicles unless Oshkosh Defense signs a "union neutrality agreement." That means the company would have to agree not to interfere with or oppose workers' efforts to form or join a union. The company would also have to certify this agreement as a condition of getting paid under the contract.

This bill most directly affects companies that manufacture vehicles and sell them to the federal government, as well as the workers at those factories. It also affects federal agencies that buy vehicles, including the Postal Service. Workers at Oshkosh Defense facilities would be particularly impacted, since the bill specifically targets their contract and could affect whether those workers have an easier path to unionize. Taxpayers who fund government vehicle purchases are also affected, since the bill adds new rules to how that money can be spent.
ai_headline: Federal vehicle contractors would face new labor disclosure rules under HR 5338
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

title: Motor Carrier Safety Selection Standard Act of 2024
ai_summary:
This bill creates a national safety checklist that businesses must follow when hiring trucking companies to move goods. Under the bill, a company that hires a trucking carrier is considered to have made a responsible choice if it checks three things within 45 days before the shipment: the carrier is properly registered with the federal government, the carrier has the required insurance, and the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration confirms the carrier meets all safety standards. If a business follows these steps and something goes wrong, it has a legal defense against lawsuits claiming it made a negligent hiring decision.

The bill also directs the Department of Transportation to create a new, clearer system within one year for rating whether a trucking company is safe or unsafe to operate. The FMCSA would publish a simple public statement for each carrier saying either that it is approved to operate or that it fails to meet requirements. Once that new rating system is officially in place, it replaces the checklist described above.

Ordinary people moving their own household belongings are treated differently under this bill. If an individual hires a moving company for a personal move, they automatically meet the reasonable standard just by showing they used a registered carrier, without having to do the full verification checklist. The bill affects businesses that ship goods, freight brokers, moving companies, and trucking carriers across the country, but does not apply to companies that transport passengers or to certain local port trucking operations governed by state law.

last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.

title: Life Month Resolution
ai_summary:
This resolution asks Congress to officially support calling June "Life Month" each year. It does not create any new laws, spend any money, or ban anything. It is a symbolic statement, meaning its only real effect is expressing the opinion of Congress on a topic. Resolutions like this are fairly common and carry no legal enforcement power.

The resolution references the 2022 Supreme Court decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, which removed the federal constitutional right to abortion and let each state set its own abortion laws. The resolution frames that ruling positively and calls on lawmakers to pass laws protecting what it calls "unborn life." It also praises pregnancy resource centers, faith-based groups, and others who support pregnant women in continuing their pregnancies.

This resolution would directly affect no one in a legal or financial sense since it is purely symbolic. However, it signals the priorities of the lawmakers who introduced it. People who could take note include pregnant women, abortion providers, pregnancy resource centers, religious organizations, and state lawmakers who may look to Congress for guidance on future policy. Anyone interested in abortion-related policy in the United States would find this resolution relevant to understanding the current direction of some members of Congress.

title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "Phasedown of Hydrofluorocarbons: Management of Certain Hydrofluorocarbons and Substitutes Under the American Innovation and Manufacturing Act of 2020".
ai_summary:
This bill is Congress's way of canceling a specific EPA rule before it can take effect. The rule in question was created by the EPA in late 2024 and dealt with hydrofluorocarbons, or HFCs, which are chemical gases used in air conditioners, refrigerators, and other cooling equipment. The EPA rule set limits on how these chemicals can be used, bought, sold, and tracked as part of a broader plan to gradually reduce HFC use in the United States. This bill uses a law called the Congressional Review Act, which allows Congress to vote to strike down a federal agency's rule.

If this bill passes, the EPA rule would be completely canceled and could not be enforced. The phasedown of HFCs was originally authorized by a 2020 law called the American Innovation and Manufacturing Act, but the specific regulations the EPA wrote to carry it out would no longer apply.

The people most directly affected would be businesses that make, sell, or use HFC-based equipment, such as heating and cooling companies, refrigeration manufacturers, supermarkets, and chemical suppliers. Consumers who buy air conditioners or refrigerators could also be indirectly affected, since changes in what chemicals manufacturers are allowed to use can influence product availability and pricing. Environmentalists and scientists who study climate change have pointed to HFCs as potent greenhouse gases, so this bill's outcome matters to people concerned about that issue as well.

title: Earn it First Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would make it illegal for a sitting president to name any government building or facility after themselves while they are still in office. It also bars any White House staff or executive branch employees from doing it on the president's behalf. The rule would apply for the entire time that person serves as president.

The buildings covered include federal government buildings managed by agencies like the General Services Administration, as well as any building or facility that receives federal funding. That second category is broad and could include things like federally funded airports, courthouses, or other public infrastructure projects.

This bill affects the executive branch, specifically the president and their staff. It would not stop Congress from naming a building after a sitting president, since that is a separate process. It also would not prevent a building from being named after a former president once they leave office. Ordinary citizens would not be directly affected, though anyone involved in naming or dedicating a federally connected building during a presidential administration would need to follow this rule if it became law.

title: Tipped Worker Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill would get rid of the federal "tipped minimum wage," which currently allows employers to pay tipped workers as little as $2.13 per hour as long as tips bring their total earnings up to the regular federal minimum wage. Under this bill, that two-tier system would be phased out gradually. During the transition, the minimum cash wage for tipped workers would start at $3.60 per hour and go up by $1.50 each year until it reaches the regular federal minimum wage, at which point the tipped wage category would be eliminated entirely and tipped workers would be paid the same minimum wage as everyone else.

The bill also changes the rules around tips themselves. Employers would be required to pass all tips directly to workers and could not keep any portion to cover credit card processing fees or other costs. Managers and supervisors would be banned from taking any share of tips. Workers at a business could vote to set up a tip-pooling system to share tips among non-supervisory employees, but participation would have to be voluntary and free from employer pressure. The bill also requires employers to clearly disclose to customers and employees what any mandatory service charges are for and whether employees actually receive that money.

The people most directly affected are tipped workers such as restaurant servers, bartenders, hotel staff, and delivery workers, along with their employers. Currently about 30 states already require employers to pay tipped workers the full state minimum wage, so the biggest change would be felt in the remaining states that still rely on the lower federal tipped wage. Businesses that rely on tip credits, particularly restaurants, would need to adjust their pay structures over the transition period.
ai_headline: Federal tipped minimum wage would be phased out under HR 5112
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce, and in addition to the Committee on Ways and Means, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

title: Medicare and Social Security Fair Share Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes changes to how Social Security and Medicare are funded by adjusting which income gets taxed and at what rates. Right now, workers and employers only pay Social Security payroll taxes on wages up to a certain cap, which is around $176,100 in 2025. This bill would close a gap by also applying that tax to wages between that cap and $400,000, meaning someone earning $300,000 would pay Social Security taxes on more of their income than they do today. It also adds a new 1.2 percent Medicare tax on wages above $400,000 for single filers and above $500,000 for married couples filing jointly. Self-employed people would face similar changes on their business earnings.

The bill also targets investment income, which is money earned from things like stocks, rental properties, and dividends rather than from a paycheck. Currently there is a 3.8 percent tax on investment income for higher earners. This bill would significantly raise that rate for people above certain income thresholds, adding over 13 additional percentage points in some cases. The extra money collected from these investment income taxes would be divided up and sent directly into the Social Security and Medicare trust funds to help keep those programs financially stable.

The people most affected are higher-income earners, roughly those making above $160,000 to $400,000 or more per year, as well as wealthy investors and business owners with significant investment income. Lower and middle-income workers would not see any change to their current tax rates or take-home pay. The stated goal is to bring more money into Social Security and Medicare, programs that tens of millions of retirees, disabled Americans, and low-income individuals rely on for income and health coverage.

title: Ski Hill Resources for Economic Development Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates a special government bank account called the "Ski Area Fee Retention Account." Right now, when ski resorts operate on National Forest land, they pay rental fees to the federal government, and most of that money goes into the general treasury. This bill would instead keep those fees in a dedicated account so the Forest Service can spend them directly on ski area and recreation-related needs, without waiting for Congress to approve separate funding each year.

The money collected would be split up in a specific way. Eighty percent would stay with the local national forest that collected it, and twenty percent could be used at any national forest across the country. Within that local share, seventy-five percent would go toward running the ski area permit program, processing applications, wildfire planning near recreation sites, and visitor services. The other twenty-five percent would go toward things like repairing trails and roads, parking areas, avalanche education, search and rescue, and law enforcement at recreation sites. The money cannot be used for actually fighting wildfires or buying new land.

This bill mainly affects the U.S. Forest Service, the ski resorts that lease and operate on national forest land, and the communities near those forests. Skiers and outdoor recreation visitors could see more maintained trails, better signage, and improved facilities as a result. There are roughly 120 ski areas operating on national forest land across the country, so the effects would be spread across many states, particularly in the West and Northeast.

title: Flatside Wilderness Additions Act
ai_summary:
This bill would expand the Flatside Wilderness area in the Ouachita National Forest in Arkansas by adding about 2,212 acres of nearby land. The existing protected area would be renamed the Flatside-Bethune Wilderness. Wilderness designation means the land is protected under the federal Wilderness Act, which generally prohibits roads, motorized vehicles, and commercial development in order to keep the area in its natural state.

The bill also makes clear that adding this land to the wilderness does not take away the federal government's ability to manage fires, insect outbreaks, or tree diseases in the area. Those management tools would still be available under existing law.

This mostly affects people who use or live near the Ouachita National Forest in central Arkansas, including hikers, hunters, and outdoor recreation enthusiasts. People who currently use that specific 2,212-acre area with motorized equipment like ATVs would no longer be permitted to do so if the bill becomes law. Federal land managers at the U.S. Forest Service would also need to manage the newly added acres under the stricter rules that apply to designated wilderness.

The expanded area would be protected under the federal Wilderness Act, which prohibits roads, motorized vehicles, and commercial development. The bill preserves existing federal authority to manage wildfires, insect outbreaks, and tree diseases in the area.
ai_sections.who: The bill primarily affects hikers, hunters, and outdoor recreation users of the Ouachita National Forest in central Arkansas. People who currently use the 2,212-acre area with motorized equipment such as ATVs would be prohibited from doing so if the bill becomes law, and U.S. Forest Service managers would be required to apply stricter wilderness rules to the newly added acres.
ai_sections.why: Designating the additional 2,212 acres as wilderness would restrict land use in that area to non-motorized, non-commercial activity under the Wilderness Act. Federal land managers would face new obligations in how they oversee the expanded area, while existing fire and pest management tools would remain available.

title: To prohibit the disclosure of records by the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development of individuals for the purposes of immigration enforcement, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill would stop the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) from sharing people's personal information with immigration enforcement agencies. Right now, HUD holds records on millions of people who apply for or receive federal housing assistance, including names, addresses, and household details. Under this bill, HUD could not hand that information over to agencies like ICE or CBP for the purpose of enforcing immigration law, unless the person whose record it is personally requests it or gives written permission. Local public housing authorities would also be protected, meaning the federal government could not force them to share their records either.

The bill would affect anyone whose personal information is stored in HUD systems, which includes tenants in public housing, people receiving housing vouchers, and others who have applied for federal housing programs. It would also directly affect HUD itself and local public housing agencies, which would no longer be legally required to cooperate with immigration enforcement requests. Within 90 days of becoming law, HUD would have to report to Congress explaining how it plans to follow the new rules, confirm the records are secure, and describe any past sharing of records with immigration authorities.

People who could be most directly affected are immigrants living in or applying for federally assisted housing, since the bill is specifically designed to prevent their housing records from being used against them in immigration proceedings. The bill does not change who is eligible for housing assistance. It only addresses whether HUD can share personal data for immigration enforcement purposes.
ai_headline: HR 5340 would bar HUD from sharing housing records with immigration agents
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Financial Services, and in addition to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 5340 blocks HUD from giving housing applicant records to ICE or CBP without the resident's written consent.
ai_sections.what: HR 5340 would prohibit HUD from sharing personal information stored in its systems with immigration enforcement agencies such as ICE or CBP. Exceptions apply only when the person whose record is involved personally requests or gives written permission for that sharing. Within 90 days of enactment, HUD would be required to report to Congress on its compliance plan, data security, and any past sharing with immigration authorities.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects immigrants living in or applying for federally assisted housing, including public housing tenants and housing voucher recipients. HUD and local public housing authorities would also be affected, as neither could be compelled to cooperate with immigration enforcement data requests.
ai_sections.why: Local public housing agencies would be shielded from federal pressure to turn over resident records to immigration enforcement. The bill does not alter eligibility rules for housing assistance programs; it addresses only the sharing of personal data for immigration enforcement purposes.

title: Cold-blooded Animal Research and Exhibition Act
ai_summary:
This bill would expand an existing law called the Animal Welfare Act to cover cold-blooded animals for the first time. Right now, that law sets rules for how animals must be treated in research labs, zoos, and similar settings, but it only applies to warm-blooded animals. This bill would add reptiles, amphibians, fish, and cephalopods (like octopuses and squids) to the list of animals that receive those same legal protections.

The change means that facilities using or displaying these cold-blooded animals would have to follow federal standards for their care, housing, and treatment. There are some exceptions built in. Fish raised for food or for improving farming practices would not be covered, keeping agricultural operations mostly outside the new rules. Birds, lab rats, and lab mice bred specifically for research are also still excluded, which is a limitation that already existed in the original law.

The people most directly affected would be research laboratories that use reptiles or fish in experiments, aquariums, zoos, and other exhibition facilities that display these animals. Those organizations would likely need to meet new federal oversight and care requirements from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which enforces the Animal Welfare Act. Everyday Americans who visit zoos or aquariums, or who work in animal research, could see indirect effects, but the bill's main impact falls on the institutions that house or study these animals professionally.
ai_headline: Bill extends federal animal welfare law to reptiles, fish, and cephalopods
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 2976 would bring cold-blooded animals under the Animal Welfare Act, requiring labs, zoos, and aquariums to meet federal care standards.
ai_sections.what: HR 2976 would expand the Animal Welfare Act to include reptiles, amphibians, fish, and cephalopods such as octopuses and squids for the first time. Facilities that house or display these animals would be required to follow federal standards for their care, housing, and treatment. Fish raised for food or to improve farming practices are excluded, as are birds, lab rats, and lab mice bred specifically for research.
ai_sections.who: Research laboratories that use reptiles or fish in experiments, along with aquariums, zoos, and other exhibition facilities, would be most directly affected. The U.S. Department of Agriculture, which enforces the Animal Welfare Act, would oversee compliance for these institutions.
ai_sections.why: Facilities currently using cold-blooded animals face no federal welfare standards under existing law, so passage would introduce new oversight and care requirements for those organizations. People who work in animal research or visit zoos and aquariums could see indirect effects, though the primary impact falls on the institutions themselves.

title: K2 Veterans Total Coverage Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill deals with veterans who were stationed at Karshi Khanabad Air Base in Uzbekistan, also known as "K2," after the September 11 attacks. That base was known to have serious environmental hazards, including contaminated soil, water, and air from old Soviet-era dumping sites. The bill would add a legal "presumption of service connection" for a long list of illnesses in veterans who served there. This means that if a K2 veteran develops one of these conditions, the VA would automatically assume their military service caused it, without the veteran having to prove a direct link.

The list of covered conditions is broad and includes all cancers, thyroid disease, bone disease, heart and cardiovascular disease, skin disease, neurological disease, reproductive disease, respiratory disease, endocrine disease, liver disease, kidney disease, blood disorders, immune system disorders, unexplained chronic illness, and cataracts. Right now, many K2 veterans have had to fight the VA to get benefits for these conditions because they must show proof connecting their illness to their service. This bill would remove that burden for the diseases listed.

The people most directly affected are U.S. military veterans who were deployed to K2 in Uzbekistan, primarily between 2001 and 2005 during operations related to the war in Afghanistan. Their families could also be affected, since VA disability benefits can impact survivor benefits. The bill was introduced in the House and referred to the Committee on Veterans' Affairs, so it has not become law yet.
ai_headline: Bill would end VA proof burden for K2 veterans with toxic exposure illnesses
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Disability Assistance and Memorial Affairs.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 3441 would presume service caused illness in K2 vets, covering all cancers and 13 other disease categories.

The base had documented environmental hazards including contaminated soil, water, and air from Soviet-era dumping sites. Covered conditions include all cancers, thyroid, bone, heart, skin, neurological, reproductive, respiratory, endocrine, liver, kidney, blood, immune system, and other diseases, as well as cataracts and unexplained chronic illness.

title: To designate the facility of the United States Postal Service located at 1225 Kempsville Road in Virginia Beach, Virginia, as the "Colonel Edward Shames Post Office Building".
ai_summary:
This bill would officially rename the post office at 1225 Kempsville Road in Virginia Beach, Virginia, after Colonel Edward Shames. The building would be known as the "Colonel Edward Shames Post Office Building." Any official government documents, maps, or records referring to that location would use the new name going forward.

Colonel Edward Shames was a World War II veteran who served with the 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment, part of the famous "Easy Company" of the 101st Airborne Division — the unit made well known by the book and TV series "Band of Brothers." He was one of the last surviving officers from that unit before his death in 2021, and he lived in Virginia Beach.

This bill mainly affects the local Virginia Beach community and any official postal or government records tied to that building. It does not change how the post office operates, affect postal rates, or impact anyone outside the area in a practical way. Bills like this one are common in Congress and are typically a symbolic way to honor veterans and other notable figures in local communities.

title: Trusted Importer and Competitive Manufacturing Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill creates a new federal program called the "Trusted Importer" program, run by the Department of Commerce. Businesses that import goods into the United States could apply to get certified as a Trusted Importer if they follow trade laws, have secure supply chains, are financially stable, and help support American manufacturing. Once certified, those businesses would receive a license allowing them to pay lower or even no tariffs on certain imported goods. The license would last 10 years and could be renewed. The President would have the final say on which goods get the reduced tariffs and by how much.

Not every tariff can be reduced under this program. Tariffs that were put in place before January 1, 2025, tariffs tied to anti-dumping or trade injury investigations, and tariffs already set at the base rate in the U.S. tariff schedule cannot be waived or lowered. Companies linked to foreign governments or entities considered threats to national security would not be allowed to apply. Licenses can also be taken away if a company breaks trade laws, submits false information, or is involved in smuggling or fraud.

This bill mainly affects businesses that import goods into the United States, particularly manufacturers and retailers who rely on foreign-made parts or products. If it becomes law, certified importers could save money on import taxes, which might lower their costs. American manufacturers who compete with cheaper imported goods could be helped or hurt depending on how the program is applied, and the government would be required to report on those effects every two years.
ai_headline: New federal program would let vetted importers pay lower tariffs
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6914 would let certified U.S. importers reduce or eliminate certain tariffs for up to 10 years under a new Commerce Department program.
ai_sections.what: HR 6914 establishes a Trusted Importer program administered by the Department of Commerce. Qualifying businesses could receive a 10-year, renewable license to pay reduced or zero tariffs on certain imported goods. The President would determine which goods qualify for reductions and by how much.

ai_sections.why: Certified importers could face lower import costs, which may affect their pricing or sourcing decisions. American manufacturers competing with imported goods could be helped or hurt depending on how the program is applied, and the government would be required to report on those effects every two years.

title: Main Street Parity Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes a small but specific change to an existing small business loan program run by the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) called the 504 loan program. That program helps small businesses borrow money to buy or build facilities like buildings, equipment, or land. Right now, the law lists several specific conditions a business must meet to qualify for one of these loans. This bill removes two of those conditions, leaving fewer requirements for businesses to navigate when applying.

The practical effect is that it may be easier for some small businesses to qualify for a 504 loan, since there are now fewer boxes to check in that part of the law. The exact conditions being removed involve specific qualifying criteria tied to plant acquisition, construction, conversion, or expansion projects. By cutting those requirements, Congress would be streamlining the rules small businesses and lenders have to follow.

This bill mainly affects small business owners who want to borrow money through the SBA 504 program to build, buy, or improve a physical location, as well as the lenders and certified development companies that process these loans. It does not create a new program or add new spending. It simply trims existing eligibility rules. As of its introduction in October 2025, it has been referred to the House Committee on Small Business and has not yet been voted on.
ai_headline: House bill trims SBA 504 loan eligibility rules for small businesses
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 5763 removes two eligibility conditions from the SBA 504 loan program, potentially making it easier for small businesses to qualify.
ai_sections.what: HR 5763 removes two specific eligibility conditions from the SBA 504 loan program, which helps small businesses borrow money to buy, build, or improve physical facilities. The conditions being removed are tied to qualifying criteria related to plant acquisition, construction, conversion, or expansion projects. No new program is created and no new spending is added.
ai_sections.who: The bill primarily affects small business owners seeking SBA 504 loans to build, buy, or improve a physical location. Lenders and certified development companies that process these loans are also affected.
ai_sections.why: With fewer eligibility conditions to meet, some small businesses that previously did not qualify may now be able to access SBA 504 financing. The change also reduces the rules that lenders and certified development companies must navigate when processing these loans.

title: Raise the Wage Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would gradually raise the federal minimum wage from its current $7.25 per hour up to $17.00 per hour over six years. It starts at $9.50 and goes up by roughly $1.50 each year. After reaching $17.00, the minimum wage would automatically adjust every year based on how median wages across the country are changing, so it would not fall behind over time.

The bill also changes rules for specific groups of workers. Tipped workers, like restaurant servers, currently can be paid as little as $2.13 per hour by employers who count customer tips as part of their wages. This bill would raise that base pay in steps and eventually require tipped workers to receive the same full minimum wage as everyone else. Workers under age 20 who are newly hired currently can be paid just $4.25 per hour during their first 90 days. This bill raises that starting pay and eventually eliminates the lower youth wage entirely. The bill also phases out a rule that allowed employers to pay workers with disabilities below the regular minimum wage, ending that practice within five years.

The people most directly affected are the roughly tens of millions of American workers currently earning at or near the federal minimum wage, including restaurant and service industry workers, young workers, and workers with disabilities. Employers in those industries, particularly small businesses, would also be significantly affected since their labor costs would increase. States and cities that already have minimum wages above $17.00 would not see any change, since this bill only sets a national floor.
ai_headline: Federal minimum wage would rise to $17 an hour over six years
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 2743 raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $17.00 over six years, then ties future increases to median wage growth.
ai_sections.what: HR 2743 would raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 per hour to $17.00 per hour over six years, starting at $9.50 and increasing by roughly $1.50 each year. After reaching $17.00, the wage would adjust automatically each year based on changes in median wages nationwide. The bill also phases out lower wage rules for tipped workers, workers under 20, and workers with disabilities.

Employers in those industries, particularly small businesses, would face higher labor costs.

title: AI for Main Street Act
ai_summary:
This bill adds a new job to Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs), which are federally funded offices that already give free or low-cost advice to small business owners across the country. Under this bill, those centers would be required to help small businesses understand and use artificial intelligence. That includes teaching best practices, explaining how AI can improve things like cybersecurity and customer service, and reaching out to businesses that may not know where to start.

The bill affects small business owners and the roughly 1,000 SBDC locations nationwide that would need to offer this new type of guidance. It does not create a new agency or program. Instead, it expands the list of services existing centers are already expected to provide. The bill also officially defines "artificial intelligence" using a definition already written into federal law.

One important detail is that the bill does not authorize any new funding to pay for these added responsibilities. SBDCs would have to carry out this work within their current budgets. Whether that is realistic depends on how much time and resources each center already has available.
ai_headline: Federal small business centers would take on AI advising under new bill
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship.

The bill also formally adopts an existing federal definition of artificial intelligence.

title: 504 Program Risk Oversight Act
ai_summary:
This bill deals with the SBA 504 loan program, which is a federal program that helps small businesses get long-term loans at lower interest rates to buy things like buildings, land, or major equipment. Right now, there is no requirement for the government to regularly check how risky the overall collection of these loans is. This bill would require the Small Business Administration to do a detailed risk analysis of all 504 loans every year and send a report to Congress by December 1st each year, with the full report posted publicly online within a week.

The report would need to break down risk in several specific ways, such as by industry type, loan size, how old the loan is, and whether the borrower was a brand-new business or an established one. It would also look at riskier categories like loans used for special-purpose properties, such as gas stations or car washes, which can be harder to sell if a borrower defaults. The SBA would also have to report on defaults, money lost, recovered funds, and any enforcement actions taken against lenders in the program.

This bill mainly affects the SBA and the lenders, known as Certified Development Companies, that make 504 loans. Small business owners who use or plan to use 504 loans are indirectly affected, since the oversight could lead to changes in how the program is managed. Taxpayers have a stake as well, since the federal government backs these loans and covers losses when borrowers default.
ai_headline: SBA would face yearly risk audits of its 504 small-business loan portfolio
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship.

The analysis must break down risk by industry, loan size, loan age, borrower type, and special-purpose properties such as gas stations or car washes. A report must reach Congress by December 1 each year and be posted publicly online within one week.

The added oversight could lead to changes in how the program is managed, which may affect how 504 loans are made or approved going forward.

title: AI–WISE Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Small Business Administration (SBA) to create free online educational materials to help small business owners understand and use artificial intelligence tools wisely. The materials must cover topics like how AI works, what its limitations are, how to spot AI-generated content, how to protect customer privacy when using AI, and how to decide whether an AI tool is actually worth adopting. The SBA has 180 days after the bill becomes law to have these resources up and running on an existing SBA online platform.

To keep the information accurate and up to date, the bill requires the SBA to form an advisory working group made up of AI experts from the private sector, universities, and privacy-focused organizations, as well as people with experience helping small businesses. The SBA must also work with its network of local resource partners, like Small Business Development Centers and SCORE chapters, to spread the word and develop localized versions of the training materials. The bill specifically says the materials cannot favor or promote any particular AI company or product over another.

This bill mainly affects small business owners across the country, particularly those who may not have the resources or technical background to evaluate AI tools on their own. It could also affect the SBA staff who build the program and the local organizations that help distribute it. The bill states that no new money is authorized to pay for this, meaning the SBA would need to fund it within its existing budget.
ai_headline: SBA ordered to build free AI literacy tools for small business owners
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship.

title: ESTUARIES Act
ai_summary:
This bill renews a federal program called the National Estuary Program, which was set to expire in 2026. The only change it makes is extending the program's funding deadline from 2026 to 2031, giving it five more years to operate. The National Estuary Program was created to protect and restore estuaries, which are coastal areas where rivers meet the ocean, like bays, harbors, and inlets.

The program works by providing federal money to local and regional groups that manage specific estuaries around the country. These groups develop plans to clean up pollution, protect wildlife habitats, and keep these waterways healthy. There are 28 designated estuaries in the program, spread across coastal and Great Lakes states.

People most directly affected are those who live near estuaries, including fishing communities, coastal residents, swimmers, and boaters who depend on clean and healthy waterways. Local governments, environmental organizations, and businesses tied to coastal tourism or fishing would also be impacted, since the program funds ongoing cleanup and conservation work in their areas.
ai_headline: Federal estuary protection program extended five years to 2031
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

The program funds local and regional groups that manage 28 designated estuaries across coastal and Great Lakes states. These groups use federal money to address pollution, protect wildlife habitats, and maintain healthy waterways.
