title: To require the Secretary of Agriculture to carry out activities to suppress wildfires, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill would require the U.S. Forest Service to aggressively fight wildfires on certain National Forest lands, with a goal of putting out any new fire within 24 hours of it being spotted. It applies specifically to forest areas that are either in severe to extreme drought, at the highest national wildfire alert level, or in zones already identified as being at very high risk of wildfire spread. In those areas, the Forest Service would be required to use all available resources to extinguish fires as quickly as possible.

The bill also sets strict rules around how fire can be used as a land management tool. Controlled burns, called prescribed fires, could still be used, but only if they follow existing laws and stay within planned boundaries. If a prescribed burn gets out of control, it must be put out immediately. Backfires and burnouts, which are fires intentionally set to stop a wildfire from spreading, could only be started by the person in charge of the firefighting operation or to protect the safety of firefighters on the ground.

This bill would most directly affect Forest Service employees, land managers, and firefighters who work on federal forest lands. It could also matter to people who live near national forests, especially in drought-prone states like California, Arizona, and others in the West, where wildfires regularly threaten homes and communities. Critics and supporters may disagree on whether faster suppression is always the best approach, but the bill itself focuses strictly on requiring faster and more aggressive government response to wildfires in high-risk areas.
ai_headline: Forest Service would have 24 hours to suppress fires in high-risk zones
last_action_text: Reported (Amended) by the Committee on Natural Resources. H. Rept. 119-429, Part I.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 178 requires the Forest Service to extinguish new wildfires within 24 hours in drought or high-risk national forest areas.
ai_sections.what: HR 178 would require the U.S. Forest Service to use all available resources to put out wildfires within 24 hours of detection in national forest areas experiencing severe to extreme drought, the highest wildfire alert level, or very high risk of fire spread. Prescribed burns would still be allowed under existing laws but must be extinguished immediately if they escape planned boundaries. Backfires and burnouts could only be authorized by the incident commander or to protect firefighter safety.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects Forest Service employees, land managers, and wildland firefighters working on federal forest lands. People living near national forests, particularly in drought-prone western states such as California and Arizona, would also be affected.
ai_sections.why: Requiring faster suppression in defined high-risk conditions could limit the spread of wildfires that threaten homes and communities near national forests. Some land managers and critics may dispute whether aggressive suppression in all high-risk situations is the most effective long-term approach to forest health.

title: Association Health Plans Act
ai_summary:
This bill would allow businesses to band together through trade groups or other associations to buy health insurance as if they were one large employer. Right now, a small business buying health insurance on its own is subject to rules for the small-group insurance market, which can mean higher prices and fewer options. Under this bill, groups of small employers could pool together, and those pooled groups would be treated under federal law as a single large employer, potentially giving them access to better rates. To qualify, an association would need to have existed for at least two years, cover at least 51 employees combined, and be run by a governing board made up mostly of the member businesses themselves.

The bill also allows self-employed individuals with no employees to join these association health plans, as long as they work at least 10 hours a week in their own business and earn income from it. A group made up entirely of self-employed people would need at least 20 members to pool rates together. In all cases, the bill keeps some consumer protections in place: plans cannot turn someone away or charge them more because of a pre-existing health condition, and they cannot discriminate based on a person's health status.

This bill would mainly affect small business owners, self-employed workers, and their employees who currently struggle to find affordable health coverage on their own. It would not change much for people who get insurance through a large employer or through government programs like Medicare or Medicaid. State insurance rules could still apply in some cases, and the associations running these plans would have to follow existing federal health coverage requirements.
ai_headline: Small businesses could pool health coverage under single large-employer rules
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 357.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 2528 lets small employers and self-employed workers join association health plans treated as a single large employer under federal law.
ai_sections.what: HR 2528 allows small businesses to band together through trade groups or associations to purchase health insurance as a single large employer under federal law. Qualifying associations must have existed at least two years, cover at least 51 employees combined, and be governed mainly by member businesses. Self-employed individuals working at least 10 hours a week and earning income from their business may also join, with groups of self-employed-only members requiring at least 20 participants to pool rates.
ai_sections.who: This bill primarily affects small business owners, self-employed workers, and their employees who currently seek coverage independently. People insured through large employers or government programs like Medicare or Medicaid would largely be unaffected.
ai_sections.why: Small employers buying insurance individually fall under small-group market rules, which can produce higher costs and fewer plan options. Pooling under large-employer rules could change the market conditions those groups face, while state insurance rules may still apply in some cases and existing federal health coverage requirements remain in force.

title: HONDURAS Act
ai_summary:
This bill would allow the U.S. president to cut off all American financial and military assistance to Honduras under a specific condition. That condition is if Honduras refuses to continue hosting U.S. military and civilian personnel at Soto Cano Air Base, a U.S. military installation located in Honduras. The base has been used for decades for military operations, drug interdiction, and disaster relief in the region. If Honduras forces those American personnel to leave, this bill gives the president the authority to stop sending aid.

The bill covers a wide range of assistance, including money and support tied to a military agreement the two countries signed back in 1954, as well as any updates made to that agreement since then. The word "authorize" means the president would have the option to cut funding, but would not be required to do so automatically.

This bill mainly affects the relationship between the U.S. government and the government of Honduras. It could also have an indirect impact on Honduran citizens who benefit from U.S. foreign aid programs, such as development or humanitarian assistance. For Americans, it relates to military presence and national security interests in Central America, a region the U.S. has long considered important for countering drug trafficking and other security concerns.
ai_headline: Bill lets president cut U.S. aid if Honduras expels troops from Soto Cano base
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 525 gives the president optional authority to end U.S. aid to Honduras if American personnel are removed from Soto Cano Air Base.
ai_sections.what: HR 525 would give the U.S. president the option to cut off all American financial and military assistance to Honduras. This authority would apply if Honduras refuses to continue hosting U.S. military and civilian personnel at Soto Cano Air Base. The bill covers assistance tied to a 1954 military agreement between the two countries and any later updates to that agreement.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects the relationship between the U.S. government and the government of Honduras. Honduran citizens who receive U.S. foreign aid, such as development or humanitarian assistance, could be indirectly affected.
ai_sections.why: If the president exercises this authority, U.S. foreign aid programs benefiting Honduran civilians could be reduced or eliminated. The bill also touches on broader U.S. national security interests in Central America, a region long associated with U.S. drug interdiction efforts.
ai_sections.cost: The bill would authorize the president to stop sending financial and military assistance to Honduras, which is tied to a military agreement dating to 1954 and its updates. No specific dollar amounts are stated in the bill summary.
costChips: Financial and military aid at risk

title: Critical Minerals and Manufacturing Support Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes the tax rules for companies that make battery parts in the United States. Right now, there is a tax credit that helps pay for the production of certain battery materials. This bill would raise that credit from 10 percent to 25 percent for a key category of battery ingredients called electrode active materials. It also expands the list of materials that count under the program, adding things like solid-state electrolytes, binders, and several chemical compounds used to make battery components. The changes would take effect starting January 1, 2026.

The bill also adds new rules about where the materials and parts must come from in order to qualify for the tax credit. Starting in 2026, at least 70 percent of the critical minerals in a battery component must come from the United States, a country the U.S. has a free trade agreement with, or be recycled in North America. That threshold rises to 80 percent after 2026. Similarly, a growing share of the actual battery parts must be made in North America, eventually reaching 100 percent by 2029. Companies would need to certify they meet these requirements. Any battery component that used materials processed or made by certain foreign companies considered a security concern would not qualify for the credit at all.

This bill mainly affects companies that manufacture battery components, mine or process minerals like lithium, cobalt, and silicon, and produce electric vehicle or energy storage batteries. Businesses further up the supply chain, such as chemical suppliers and materials processors, are also directly impacted. Consumers are not directly affected by the tax credit itself, but the rules could influence where battery manufacturing happens and how supply chains are structured over time.
ai_headline: Bill would raise battery manufacturing tax credit from 10% to 25%
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 3200 raises the battery materials tax credit to 25% and requires up to 100% North American parts by 2029.
ai_sections.what: HR 3200 would increase the existing tax credit for producing certain battery materials from 10 percent to 25 percent, specifically for electrode active materials. The bill also expands which materials qualify, adding solid-state electrolytes, binders, and several chemical compounds. Changes would take effect January 1, 2026, with domestic content requirements rising through 2029.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects companies that manufacture battery components, mine or process minerals such as lithium, cobalt, and silicon, and produce electric vehicle or energy storage batteries. Chemical suppliers and materials processors further up the supply chain are also directly impacted.
ai_sections.why: The escalating North American content thresholds, reaching 80 percent for critical minerals after 2026 and 100 percent for battery parts by 2029, would pressure companies to restructure their supply chains. Battery components using materials processed by companies deemed a foreign security concern would be disqualified entirely from the credit.

press_names: Critical Minerals and Manufacturing Support Act

title: Advancing Skills-Based Hiring Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill creates a voluntary program at the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) where employers can submit their hiring tests and screening tools for review. The EEOC would look at the evidence an employer provides and decide whether their tests are truly connected to job performance and legally justified. If the EEOC approves the test, the employer receives a "safe harbor," meaning that approval can be used as a legal defense if the employer is ever sued over their hiring process. Employers with more than 100 employees would pay a fee for this review. Importantly, anything an employer voluntarily shares during this process cannot be used against them in court or in a future government enforcement action.

The bill focuses on what it calls "skills-based hiring," which means judging job applicants on their actual abilities rather than on things like college degrees or other credentials. Employers would submit scientific studies showing their tests accurately predict who will do well on the job. The EEOC would also be required to offer guidance and education to employers about how to properly validate these kinds of tests. Even if a test is shown to screen out certain protected groups at higher rates, employers can still submit it for review, as long as they include that information in their submission.

This bill affects employers of all sizes, though larger companies with over 100 employees would face a fee for the review service. It also affects job seekers, since it could influence how companies decide who gets interviewed or hired. The EEOC would take on new responsibilities and workload as a result of running this program. The program is entirely voluntary, so no employer is required to participate.
ai_headline: EEOC would review employer hiring tests and grant legal safe harbors
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 4050 lets employers voluntarily submit hiring tests to the EEOC for approval that can serve as a legal defense in discrimination suits.
ai_sections.what: HR 4050 creates a voluntary program at the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) where employers submit hiring tests and screening tools for agency review. If the EEOC determines a test is connected to job performance and legally justified, the employer receives a safe harbor that can be used as a legal defense in lawsuits. Anything an employer shares during the review process cannot be used against them in court or in a future government enforcement action.

ai_sections.cost: Employers with more than 100 employees would pay a fee to submit their hiring tests for EEOC review, though the specific fee amount is not defined in the summary.
costChips: Fee required for employers over 100 staff

title: Critical Infrastructure Security Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes the rules for a government committee called CFIUS, which stands for the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States. CFIUS reviews deals where foreign companies or individuals try to buy or invest in American businesses or land, especially when that deal could be a security risk. Right now, CFIUS can block or investigate real estate purchases near sensitive U.S. government facilities. This bill expands that list to specifically include intelligence agency buildings, National Laboratories (like the nuclear research labs run by the Department of Energy), and critical infrastructure such as drinking water systems.

The bill also requires CFIUS member agencies to do a formal checkup every year. By January 31 each year, each agency on the committee must review and update its own list of sensitive facilities and properties, and submit a report signed off by a senior official. Those reports go to the CFIUS chairperson. The bill also adds drinking water infrastructure to the types of deals that get extra scrutiny, and requires that completed reviews involving these sensitive properties be included in the committee's annual public report to Congress.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies that sit on CFIUS, foreign investors or buyers looking to purchase real estate or businesses near sensitive U.S. sites, and members of Congress who oversee national security. Everyday Americans are not directly affected, but the bill is intended to add oversight around foreign purchases of land or property near places like water treatment facilities or national labs, which are considered part of the country's critical infrastructure.
ai_headline: Bill expands CFIUS oversight to labs, water systems, and spy agencies
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Financial Services, and in addition to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, and Foreign Affairs, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 5236 expands CFIUS review to cover foreign purchases near intel agencies, National Labs, and drinking water systems.
ai_sections.what: HR 5236 expands the authority of CFIUS to scrutinize foreign real estate and business purchases near intelligence agency buildings, National Laboratories, and drinking water infrastructure. Each CFIUS member agency would be required to review and update its list of sensitive facilities annually, submitting a signed report to the CFIUS chairperson by January 31 each year. Completed reviews involving these sensitive properties must also be included in the committee's annual public report to Congress.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects federal agencies that sit on CFIUS and foreign investors or buyers seeking to purchase real estate or businesses near designated sensitive U.S. sites. Members of Congress who oversee national security are also affected through expanded reporting requirements.
ai_sections.why: Adding intelligence facilities, National Laboratories, and drinking water systems to the list of protected sites increases the range of foreign transactions subject to national security review. The annual agency reporting requirement creates a formal accountability mechanism that did not previously exist under CFIUS rules.

title: Taxpayer Data Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill sets new rules about who is allowed to access the federal government's payment systems, which are run by the Bureau of the Fiscal Service inside the Treasury Department. These are the systems the government uses to send out money, including things like Social Security checks, tax refunds, and payments to federal contractors. Under the bill, only people who meet strict requirements could access these systems or the financial data inside them. Those requirements include having worked for the Treasury Department or held a government contract for at least one year, having a satisfactory job performance record, holding the right security clearance, completing privacy and cybersecurity training, and signing a formal ethics agreement.

The bill also closes a potential legal loophole. Right now, conflict-of-interest laws apply mainly to regular government employees. This bill says that anyone who accesses these payment systems, even if they are not a normal government employee, must follow those same conflict-of-interest rules. It also specifically bars "special Government employees," which is a category that covers short-term advisers and consultants, from accessing these systems at all.

Finally, the bill requires the Treasury Department's Inspector General to investigate and report to Congress within 30 days any time someone accesses these systems without authorization. That report must describe what happened, assess any risks to privacy or national security, and list any payments that were stopped or changed during the unauthorized access. This bill would most directly affect Treasury Department staff, contractors, and any outside individuals who might seek access to government payment data or systems.
ai_headline: Bill would restrict access to federal payment systems to vetted staff only
last_action_text: Sponsor introductory remarks on measure. (CR H625-626)

ai_sections.tldr: HR 1101 bars unqualified and short-term advisers from federal payment systems and requires Inspector General reports within 30 days of any breach.
ai_sections.what: HR 1101 sets strict eligibility requirements for anyone seeking access to federal payment systems operated by the Bureau of the Fiscal Service within the Treasury Department. Qualifying criteria include at least one year of Treasury employment or contracting, a satisfactory performance record, the appropriate security clearance, completed privacy and cybersecurity training, and a signed ethics agreement. The bill also bars a category of short-term advisers and consultants known as special Government employees from accessing these systems entirely.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects Treasury Department staff, contractors, short-term government advisers, and any outside individuals who seek access to federal payment data or systems. Conflict-of-interest rules that previously applied mainly to regular government employees would now extend to all who access these systems, regardless of employment status.
ai_sections.why: Extending conflict-of-interest requirements and access restrictions to non-traditional government workers closes a legal loophole that previously left those systems less regulated for outside personnel. Requiring the Treasury Inspector General to report unauthorized access to Congress within 30 days, including an accounting of any payments stopped or changed, creates a formal oversight mechanism where none currently exists.

title: To define "showerhead" for the purpose of determining the acceptable water pressure for a showerhead, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill is about how the federal government defines the word "showerhead" when it comes to water flow rules. Under current federal law, showerheads cannot use more than 2.5 gallons of water per minute. The question this bill addresses is whether that limit applies to the entire shower unit as a whole, or to each individual spray nozzle separately. A 2020 rule said the limit applies to each nozzle on its own, meaning a multi-nozzle shower system could use much more total water. A 2021 rule reversed that and said the limit applies to the whole shower system combined. This bill would cancel the 2021 rule and bring the 2020 rule back into effect.

In practical terms, this means multi-nozzle or body-spray shower systems would no longer have to stay under 2.5 gallons per minute for the whole unit. Each nozzle could use up to 2.5 gallons per minute on its own, allowing higher total water use for these types of showers.

This bill would most directly affect manufacturers who make high-end or multi-spray showerheads and the consumers who buy them, particularly those who want systems with multiple nozzles running at the same time. It could also affect water utilities and conservation efforts, since more water use per shower would be permitted under this definition. The bill has been sent to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, where it will be reviewed before any further action.
ai_headline: House bill would let each showerhead nozzle use 2.5 gallons per minute
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 5042 would restore a 2020 rule letting each nozzle in a multi-spray shower use up to 2.5 gal/min, not the whole unit.
ai_sections.what: HR 5042 would cancel a 2021 federal rule and restore a 2020 rule that applied the 2.5-gallons-per-minute water flow limit to each individual nozzle of a showerhead, rather than to the entire shower unit combined. This means a multi-nozzle shower system could use more than 2.5 gallons per minute in total, as long as no single nozzle exceeds that amount.
ai_sections.who: The bill most directly affects manufacturers of high-end or multi-spray showerheads and the consumers who purchase them. Water utilities and conservation programs would also be affected, as total water use per shower could increase.
ai_sections.why: Allowing each nozzle to be measured separately rather than the whole unit permits higher total water consumption in showers with multiple spray heads. This change could have consequences for water conservation efforts and the demand placed on water utilities.

title: Small Modular Reactor Commercialization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill focuses on small modular reactors, which are a newer type of nuclear power plant that is smaller and meant to be built more quickly than traditional nuclear plants. The bill does two main things. First, it raises the official size limit for what counts as a "small modular reactor" from 300 megawatts to 500 megawatts of electricity output. This matters because the size definition affects which projects qualify for government funding and certain legal protections. Second, it creates a new government working group made up of officials from multiple federal agencies, including the Departments of Energy, Defense, Commerce, and State. That group would study how to help the U.S. become a global leader in building and manufacturing these reactors, and it would report to Congress each year through 2030.

The bill also makes sure that federal funding programs cannot automatically reject nuclear projects just because a single reactor produces between 50 and 500 megawatts. This removes a barrier that some reactor designs were running into when applying for government grants or support. The working group is also directed to look at job training and workforce needs, manufacturing investment, and ways to bring more of this industry to the United States, including reactors that were first built in other countries.

The people most directly affected are companies and researchers developing small modular reactor technology, workers in nuclear manufacturing and construction, and communities that might eventually host these plants. More broadly, electricity customers and utility companies could be affected in the long term if these reactors become a larger part of the U.S. power supply. The bill does not build any reactors itself or guarantee any specific funding amounts.
ai_headline: House bill raises small modular reactor size limit to 500 megawatts
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 2813 raises the small modular reactor size cap from 300 to 500 MW and creates a federal working group to grow U.S. leadership in the sector.
ai_sections.what: HR 2813 raises the official size limit for small modular reactors from 300 megawatts to 500 megawatts of electricity output. It also bars federal funding programs from automatically rejecting nuclear projects where a single reactor produces between 50 and 500 megawatts. A new multi-agency working group is established to study U.S. global competitiveness in building and manufacturing these reactors, with annual reports to Congress required through 2030.
ai_sections.who: Companies and researchers developing small modular reactor technology, nuclear manufacturing and construction workers, and communities that may host these plants are most directly affected. Electricity customers and utility companies could be affected long term if these reactors grow as a share of U.S. power supply.
ai_sections.why: Expanding the size definition changes which projects qualify for government funding and certain legal protections, removing a barrier some reactor designs faced when applying for support. The working group requirement means federal agencies across energy, defense, commerce, and foreign policy will coordinate on workforce, manufacturing, and industry-reshoring questions through at least 2030.

title: Make Gaza Great Again Act
ai_summary:
This bill would give the President the power to punish Middle Eastern governments that refuse to accept Palestinians from Gaza into their countries. If a foreign government official turns down a U.S. request to let Palestinian refugees in, that official could be added to a sanctions list. Being on that list means the U.S. could freeze any money or property they have in the United States and ban them from entering the country. The bill explicitly does not apply to Israel or Israeli citizens.

The bill also lets the President strip certain countries of their "Major Non-NATO Ally" status and cut off U.S. foreign aid, including military assistance, if those countries refuse to take in Palestinians from Gaza. These penalties could last up to five years, after which the law would expire. The President can make exceptions if national security requires it or if waiving the penalty is in the U.S. national interest.

This bill would mainly affect the governments and officials of Middle Eastern countries, excluding Israel, that the President believes are not cooperating with U.S. efforts to relocate Palestinians from Gaza. It could also affect those countries' relationships with the U.S. military and foreign aid programs. Palestinians from Gaza are the group the bill is centered on, as the stated goal is to pressure other nations to offer them a place to go. The bill was introduced in February 2025 and has been sent to the House Foreign Affairs and Judiciary Committees for review.
ai_headline: Bill would sanction Middle East officials who refuse Palestinian refugees
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Foreign Affairs, and in addition to the Committee on the Judiciary, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 1136 would let the President sanction Middle Eastern officials and cut aid to countries refusing Palestinian refugees from Gaza.
ai_sections.what: HR 1136 would give the President power to sanction foreign government officials in Middle Eastern countries who refuse U.S. requests to accept Palestinian refugees from Gaza. Sanctions could include freezing U.S.-held assets and banning those officials from entering the United States. The President could also revoke a country's Major Non-NATO Ally status and cut off foreign and military aid for up to five years.
ai_sections.who: Middle Eastern governments and their officials, excluding Israel and Israeli citizens, are the primary targets of this legislation. Palestinians from Gaza are the central focus, as the bill aims to pressure other nations to accept them.
ai_sections.why: Countries that decline to cooperate could lose military partnerships and foreign aid that support their relationship with the United States. The bill includes presidential waiver authority for national security or national interest reasons, which limits how automatically the penalties would apply.

title: Improving SBA Engagement on Employee Ownership Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells the Small Business Administration (SBA) to do more to spread the word about employee ownership, which is when workers own a share of the company they work for. Specifically, it requires the SBA to show up to meetings and working groups about employee ownership that are hosted by other federal agencies, as long as the SBA is invited or already has a relationship with the hosting group. It also directs the SBA to use an existing program to provide outreach and assistance on employee ownership within 180 days of the bill becoming law.

The bill also expands who gets certain information about investment companies. Under current law, the SBA already reaches out to small business investment companies about employee ownership. This bill adds investors and limited partners of those companies to the list of people who should receive that outreach.

This bill would mainly affect small business owners who are thinking about transitioning their business to employee ownership, as well as the workers who might become co-owners through that process. It could also affect investors who work with small business investment companies. The bill does not create a new program or spend new money. It focuses on making the SBA more active in conversations and education efforts that are already happening around the topic of employee-owned businesses.
ai_headline: SBA directed to step up employee ownership outreach under HR 5778
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 358.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 5778 requires the SBA to join federal meetings and use existing programs to promote employee ownership, at no new cost.
ai_sections.what: HR 5778 requires the SBA to participate in federal agency meetings and working groups focused on employee ownership when invited or when an existing relationship applies. Within 180 days of enactment, the SBA must use an existing program to provide outreach and assistance on employee ownership. The bill also expands outreach about employee ownership to include investors and limited partners of small business investment companies, not just the companies themselves.
ai_sections.who: The bill primarily affects small business owners considering a transition to employee ownership and the workers who could become co-owners through that process. Investors and limited partners connected to small business investment companies are also newly included in the scope of SBA outreach.
ai_sections.why: By embedding the SBA in existing federal conversations, the bill could increase the visibility and accessibility of employee ownership as a business model. Expanding who receives outreach may lead more investors and small business stakeholders to engage with or consider employee ownership structures.

press_names: Improving SBA Engagement on Employee Ownership Act

title: Haiti Economic Lift Program Extension Act
ai_summary:
This bill extends a trade program that lets certain goods made in Haiti enter the United States without paying import taxes, called tariffs. That program was set to expire, and this bill would keep it running through December 31, 2028. The main goods covered are clothing and apparel items. The bill also restores duty-free status to some products that used to qualify for the program but lost that status due to technical changes in how the government classifies imported goods.

The bill also deals with a gap in coverage. The original program appears to have lapsed around September 30, 2025, before this bill was introduced in December 2025. Any Haitian goods imported during that gap period would normally have had tariffs charged on them. This bill would allow importers to apply for refunds on those tariffs, as long as they file a request with U.S. Customs and Border Protection within 180 days of the bill becoming law.

The people most directly affected are American businesses, especially clothing retailers and manufacturers, that import goods made in Haiti. Haitian workers in the garment industry are also affected, since U.S. demand for duty-free Haitian products supports jobs there. American consumers could indirectly benefit if lower import costs keep prices on certain clothing items from rising. The bill does not create new spending programs or change domestic U.S. tax policy.
ai_headline: Haiti trade program extended to 2028, gap refunds allowed for importers
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6504 extends duty-free status for Haitian apparel through Dec. 31, 2028 and allows tariff refunds for goods imported during a coverage gap.
ai_sections.what: HR 6504 extends a trade program that allows certain Haitian goods, primarily clothing and apparel, to enter the United States without paying import tariffs, keeping it active through December 31, 2028. The bill also restores duty-free status to products that lost eligibility due to changes in how the government classifies imported goods. Importers who paid tariffs on Haitian goods during a lapse in coverage that began around September 30, 2025 may apply for refunds by filing a request with U.S. Customs and Border Protection within 180 days of the bill becoming law.
ai_sections.who: American businesses that import Haitian goods, especially clothing retailers and manufacturers, are directly affected, as are Haitian garment workers whose employment is tied to U.S. demand for duty-free products. American consumers may be indirectly affected if import cost changes influence prices on certain clothing items.
ai_sections.why: Without the extension, Haitian apparel exports to the United States would be subject to tariffs, which could reduce U.S. purchasing of those goods. The refund provision addresses tariffs already collected during the coverage gap, affecting importers who paid those charges before the bill became law.

press_names: Haiti Economic Lift Program Extension Act

title: Chinese Spy Balloon Assessment Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires the Secretary of Defense to write a report within 90 days of the law being passed. The report must cover what harm, if any, the Chinese spy balloon caused to U.S. national security when it flew over the country before being shot down in February 2023. The report must also include details about the technology and materials recovered from the balloon wreckage, including where those parts were made.

The report has to be made available to the public in an unclassified form, meaning ordinary people can read it. However, the law does allow a separate classified section to be added for information too sensitive to share openly. The report goes to the Armed Services Committees in both the Senate and the House of Representatives.

This bill mainly affects the Department of Defense, which has to do the research and write the report. It also matters to members of Congress who oversee military affairs, and to the general public, who would gain access to official findings about what the balloon actually saw or collected during its flight over the United States, including over military bases.
ai_headline: Defense secretary ordered to report on Chinese spy balloon damage
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Armed Services.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 934 requires the Defense Secretary to publicly report within 90 days on national security harm and recovered technology from the 2023 Chinese balloon.
ai_sections.what: HR 934 requires the Secretary of Defense to produce a report within 90 days of enactment on the Chinese spy balloon that flew over the United States before being shot down in February 2023. The report must address any national security harm caused and detail the technology and materials recovered from the wreckage, including where those parts were manufactured. The report must be publicly available in unclassified form, though a separate classified section is permitted for sensitive information.
ai_sections.who: The Department of Defense is responsible for researching and writing the report. The report is delivered to the Armed Services Committees of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, and its unclassified version is available to the general public.
ai_sections.why: The public would gain access to official findings about what the balloon collected or observed during its flight over the United States, including over military bases. Members of Congress who oversee military affairs would receive the same findings in a formal, accountable report.

title: Self-Insurance Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill is about a type of insurance that some employers buy to protect themselves financially. When a company pays for its workers' health care directly out of its own funds instead of buying a traditional insurance plan, it is called "self-insuring." To protect against unexpectedly large medical bills, these employers often buy something called stop-loss insurance, which kicks in when their health care costs go above a certain limit. This bill would officially define that stop-loss insurance as something separate from regular health insurance under federal law.

The bill also deals with a conflict between state and federal rules. Right now, states can regulate stop-loss insurance, and some states have set rules that make it harder for smaller employers to buy it. This bill would prevent states from passing laws that stop a self-insured employer from getting stop-loss coverage, essentially giving federal law the final say on that question.

The people most directly affected are employers, especially small and mid-sized businesses, that self-insure their workers' health benefits. It could also affect the workers at those companies, since easier access to stop-loss insurance might make it more practical for more employers to self-insure. State insurance regulators would have less authority over this area if the bill becomes law. It does not directly change what health benefits employees receive, but it does change how the financial risk behind those benefits is managed and regulated.
ai_headline: Federal bill would shield self-insured employers from state stop-loss rules
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 356.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 2571 would bar states from blocking self-insured employers' access to stop-loss insurance and define it separately from regular health insurance.
ai_sections.what: HR 2571 would formally define stop-loss insurance as distinct from traditional health insurance under federal law. It would also prohibit states from passing laws that prevent self-insured employers from purchasing stop-loss coverage. Stop-loss insurance is a product employers use to cap their financial exposure when they pay workers' health costs directly from their own funds.
ai_sections.who: The bill most directly affects small and mid-sized employers that self-insure their workers' health benefits and the employees at those companies. State insurance regulators would lose authority over this area if the bill is enacted.
ai_sections.why: Some states have set rules that make it harder for smaller employers to purchase stop-loss insurance, and this bill would override those restrictions by making federal law the final authority. Easier access to stop-loss insurance could make self-insuring a more practical option for more employers, which may shift how financial risk behind employee health benefits is managed and regulated.

title: Delaware River Basin Restoration Program Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews a federal program that funds conservation and restoration work in the Delaware River Basin. The program was set to expire in 2023, and this bill extends it through 2032, giving it nine more years to operate. It also officially adds Maryland as a recognized state in the program, expanding the region covered from four states to five. The Delaware River Basin includes parts of Delaware, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, and now Maryland.

The program gives out grants for projects that improve the health of the river and its surrounding watershed. This can include things like cleaning up water, protecting land near rivers and streams, and restoring natural habitats for fish and wildlife. The bill adds a new guideline saying that when choosing which projects to fund, officials can give priority to small towns, rural areas, or communities that have fewer resources.

People most directly affected include residents living near the Delaware River and its tributaries across all five states, especially those in smaller or lower-income communities who may have more to gain from having their water and local environment improved. Local governments, conservation groups, and water utilities that apply for these federal grants would also be affected, since the program gives them funding to carry out restoration projects in the region.

title: SAVE Our Poultry Act
ai_summary:
This bill adds highly pathogenic avian influenza, commonly known as bird flu, to a list of high-priority research topics that the federal government funds through grants. Right now, land-grant universities can receive federal research money for many agricultural topics, and this bill would officially put bird flu on that list. That means universities could apply for grants specifically to study how to fight bird flu in poultry flocks.

The research money would go toward two main goals. First, it would fund work on developing and improving vaccines for chickens, turkeys, and other poultry, including figuring out how well vaccines work across different bird species, improving how the vaccines are made, and looking at how vaccination might affect poultry sales at home and abroad. Second, it would fund research on better biosecurity, meaning the safety practices farmers use to keep disease off their farms, such as improved training, farm-level protections, and new disinfection methods.

The people most directly affected are poultry farmers, especially those raising chickens, turkeys, and eggs, as well as the universities that would conduct the research. Consumers could also be affected over time, since bird flu outbreaks have caused egg and poultry prices to rise sharply in recent years. The bill does not directly provide new funding on its own, but it makes bird flu research eligible for an existing federal grant program.

title: Say No to Indoctrination Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change the rules for how federal education money can be spent in K-12 public schools. Right now, the Elementary and Secondary Education Act already has a list of things schools cannot use that federal funding for. This bill adds one more item to that list: schools could not use federal funds to teach or promote what the bill calls "gender ideology." The bill defines that term by pointing to a January 2025 executive order signed by President Trump, which describes gender ideology as the idea that a person's gender identity can differ from their biological sex.

In practical terms, if this bill became law, public schools that receive federal education funding would need to make sure lessons, materials, and school programs do not include content that falls under that definition. Schools that violate the rule could potentially risk losing access to federal education dollars, which many districts rely on for programs serving low-income students, students with disabilities, and other groups.

This bill would affect public school students, teachers, and administrators across the country, since most public schools receive some form of federal funding under the Elementary and Secondary Education Act. It would also affect parents who have opinions on what is or is not taught in schools. The bill was introduced in the House and sent to the Education and Workforce Committee, meaning it has not become law yet and still has several steps to go through before that could happen.

title: Reserved for the Speaker.

ai_summary:
This bill would block the federal government from carrying out a specific land management plan for Muleshoe National Wildlife Refuge, located in west Texas. This bill would prevent the Secretary of the Interior from putting that plan into action in any way.

The Muleshoe National Wildlife Refuge is the oldest national wildlife refuge in Texas and provides habitat for migratory birds and other wildlife. A Land Protection Plan typically identifies private lands near a refuge that the federal government might want to buy or place conservation agreements on, usually on a voluntary basis with willing landowners. The concern from the bill's sponsor appears to be about the potential for expanded federal land control in the region.

This bill mainly affects landowners near the Muleshoe refuge in west Texas, federal land managers, and potentially conservation groups. Private landowners in the area would no longer face the possibility of the federal government pursuing land acquisitions or agreements under this particular plan. It does not change the refuge itself or any existing federal land ownership.

title: The White Oak Resilience Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Department of the Interior to work together to restore and protect white oak trees across the country. It creates a voluntary coalition of federal, state, tribal, and private groups to coordinate white oak restoration efforts and recommend policy changes. The Forest Service would run five pilot projects in national forests, and the Interior Department would first assess its lands, then run five more pilot projects on land it manages, such as wildlife refuges and former mine sites. A new non-regulatory grant program would funnel money to landowners and partners to support restoration work, managed in cooperation with the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation.

The bill also tackles a shortage of white oak tree seedlings by requiring the USDA to develop a national strategy to boost nursery capacity. It allows research partnerships with universities, including land grant colleges and tribal institutions, to study things like which white oak trees are most resistant to disease, drought, and climate stress, and how to restore white oak on land that was previously mined. Most of these programs are set to expire seven years after the bill becomes law.

The people most directly affected are forest landowners, farmers, and timber producers who rely on white oak, since white oak wood is widely used for furniture, flooring, and barrels for whiskey and wine. Tribal nations, state forestry agencies, and wildlife conservationists would also be involved as partners. Everyday Americans living near national forests or public lands in white oak country, which stretches across much of the eastern United States, could see long-term changes to their local forests as a result.

title: National Earthquake Hazards Reduction Program Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews and updates a federal program that has been working to reduce earthquake dangers in the United States since 1977. It keeps funding flowing to four main agencies: FEMA, the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), the National Science Foundation, and the National Institute of Standards and Technology. Together, these agencies study earthquakes, issue early warnings, help communities prepare, and develop building safety standards. The bill also officially includes Tribal governments as partners in this work, alongside state and local governments, and adds new definitions for terms like "functional recovery," which means getting a building back to normal use after a quake.

The bill makes several practical updates to what these agencies are required to do. USGS would expand the earthquake early warning system to more high-risk areas, issue aftershock forecasts after major quakes, and coordinate with the FCC to broadcast alerts quickly in multiple languages. FEMA would help governments create lists of risky buildings and offer evacuation planning assistance. Agencies would also pay more attention to earthquake-related dangers beyond the shaking itself, such as fires, tsunamis, and landslides made worse by climate change.

The people most directly affected are the nearly half of all Americans who live in earthquake-prone areas, particularly in states like California and Alaska but also in other regions. Local officials, builders, engineers, and Tribal communities would gain access to more federal guidance and technical help. The bill authorizes roughly $176 million per year across all four agencies from 2024 through 2028 to carry out this work.

title: Protect Small Businesses from Excessive Paperwork Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill makes one specific change to an existing law about business reporting. Under a rule that took effect in 2024, many businesses are required to file a report listing their "beneficial owners" — meaning the real people who actually own or control the company. This was designed to help the government track financial crimes like money laundering. The original deadline gave older businesses two years from when the rule took effect to file this report. This bill would change that deadline to a fixed date: January 1, 2026.

The practical effect is straightforward. Businesses that were already up and running before January 1, 2024 would have until January 1, 2026 to file their ownership information with the federal government. This mostly lines up with the original two-year window, but sets a clear, specific calendar date instead of a deadline tied to when regulations were officially published, which created some confusion.

This bill mainly affects small businesses, since larger corporations are generally exempt from this reporting requirement. If you own or co-own a smaller LLC, corporation, or similar business that was registered before 2024, this bill directly applies to you and your filing deadline. It does not eliminate the reporting requirement — it only adjusts when existing businesses must comply with it.

title: Crow Revenue Act
ai_summary:
This bill arranges a land swap involving mineral rights in Montana. The federal government currently holds mineral rights to about 4,530 acres in Musselshell County, known as the Bull Mountains Tracts. A private group called the Hope Family Trust holds mineral rights to about 4,660 acres inside the Crow Reservation in Big Horn County. Under this bill, the Hope Family Trust gives its mineral rights to the Crow Tribe, and in exchange, the federal government gives the Hope Family Trust the Bull Mountains Tracts. The whole swap has to happen within 60 days of the bill becoming law. Before the deal closes, the Crow Tribe and the Hope Family Trust must agree in writing on how to share any future revenue if the swapped lands are ever developed.

The Crow Tribe benefits most directly. Once the mineral rights in the Hope Family Tracts are transferred to the Tribe, those rights are held in trust by the federal government on the Tribe's behalf, meaning the Tribe controls them but they are protected from being taken or sold without federal approval. The state of Montana cannot tax those mineral interests. The bill also makes clear that receiving these benefits cannot be used as a reason to cut or deny the Tribe or its members any other federal services or programs they are already entitled to.

The Hope Family Trust also benefits by gaining new mineral and surface rights in the Bull Mountains area. The existing coal lease on that land must first be relinquished by the current leaseholder before the transfer happens. General members of the public are largely unaffected, though residents of Musselshell and Big Horn Counties in Montana may eventually see effects depending on whether the transferred lands are developed for minerals in the future.

title: National Earthquake Hazards Reduction Program Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews and updates the National Earthquake Hazards Reduction Program, a federal program that has existed since 1977. It keeps the program running through 2030 and authorizes about $83 million per year in funding. At least $30 million of that annual funding must go toward finishing a nationwide network of seismic sensors called the Advanced National Seismic System, which detects earthquakes and helps send out early warnings before shaking arrives.

The bill also makes several updates to how the program operates. It requires the U.S. Geological Survey to work more closely with the FCC to make sure earthquake alerts go out quickly and in the main languages spoken in affected areas. It expands the early warning system to more high-risk areas, adds tsunami hazard mapping, requires aftershock forecasts after major earthquakes, and improves coordination with NOAA and FEMA for ocean earthquakes and tsunamis. It also adds Tribal governments as official partners alongside state and local governments throughout the program.

The people most directly affected are anyone living in earthquake-prone parts of the country, particularly in the western United States, Alaska, and other seismically active regions. Building designers, construction contractors, and local emergency managers would also be affected, since the bill updates safety standards for buildings and critical infrastructure like power and water systems. Tribal communities gain a more formal role in planning and decision-making under this updated version of the law.

title: Direct Hire To Fight Fires
ai_summary:
This bill would make it easier and faster for the federal government to hire wildland firefighters and support staff. Right now, federal agencies like the U.S. Forest Service and the Department of the Interior must follow a lengthy, competitive hiring process before bringing someone on board. This bill would let those agencies skip several of those steps and hire qualified people directly, without going through the usual ranking and selection rules. It applies to a range of positions, including forestry technicians, aircraft operators, equipment specialists, and dispatchers who support firefighting operations.

The bill also requires the agencies to clean up their hiring process within one year. That means cutting down the time it takes to hire someone, removing repeated or unnecessary steps, making it easier to rehire workers who have done the job in previous years, and reducing obstacles for firefighters who want to move between agencies. These changes are aimed at helping the government fill firefighting jobs more quickly, especially during peak wildfire seasons when staffing shortages can be a serious problem.

Starting one year after the bill becomes law, the Forest Service and the Department of the Interior would each have to submit a yearly public report to Congress showing how many firefighters they have, how many they need, where job openings exist, and what is getting in the way of hiring. The people most directly affected by this bill are current and future federal wildland firefighters and support workers, as well as communities in fire-prone areas, particularly in western states, that depend on these agencies to protect land and lives.

Within one year of enactment, agencies must also streamline their hiring processes by cutting timelines, removing redundant steps, easing rehiring of returning seasonal workers, and reducing barriers to moving between agencies.

title: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027
ai_summary:
This bill, HR 6500, is a temporary funding package that keeps the federal government running while lawmakers finish work on full-year budget bills. Its main part is a "continuing resolution" that extends government funding at basically fiscal year 2026 levels through December 11, 2026, covering everything from defense and veterans affairs to housing, transportation, and agriculture programs. It includes special provisions for certain programs—like WIC nutrition assistance, wildfire suppression, disaster relief, shipbuilding cost overruns, and nuclear weapons facility projects—to make sure they can keep operating smoothly instead of getting stuck at reduced funding levels. It also rescinds (cancels) some old unused funds from past laws and redirects similar amounts to related programs, and it includes one-time death benefit payments to family members of two former members of Congress.

Beyond the main funding extension, the bill renews a number of expiring laws and programs: trade preferences for African and Caribbean countries (AGOA and Haiti trade programs), customs and passport fees, cybersecurity information-sharing laws, patent office fee authority, and religious freedom commission funding. It also extends federal highway, transit, and infrastructure programs (the Surface Transportation Extension Act) so states can keep receiving road and transit funding without interruption, and it extends numerous Department of Veterans Affairs programs covering healthcare copays, rural veteran health services, suicide prevention grants, homeless veteran housing assistance, and education benefits.

This bill affects nearly everyone who interacts with federal programs, including veterans, farmers, travelers, taxpayers, government employees, and people relying on federal housing, nutrition, or health services. It's designed to prevent a government shutdown and keep federal agencies, contractors, and beneficiaries operating without disruption while Congress negotiates permanent full-year spending bills.

last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-103.

title: Expediting Federal Broadband Deployment Reviews Act
ai_summary:
Note: The bill number in the title (HR 1681) does not match the actual bill text provided, which is HR 1680, the UPLIFT Act. The summary below is based on the actual text provided.

This bill targets so-called "sanctuary" policies, which are rules in some cities and states that limit how much local police cooperate with federal immigration enforcement. The bill would require all state and local government workers, including police, to share information about a person's immigration status with federal agencies like ICE when asked. It would also forbid states and cities from blocking their employees from helping federal immigration agents or from participating in private immigration detention facilities.

The bill strengthens the legal power of ICE "detainers," which are requests for local jails to hold a person longer so ICE can pick them up. It spells out what counts as enough legal reason to issue one of those holds, and gives local agencies legal protection from lawsuits if they follow them. It also creates a new right for crime victims to sue a city or state in federal court if a person in the country unlawfully was released from local custody against an ICE detainer and then committed a serious crime like murder or rape against them.

This bill would affect local and state governments across the country, especially those with sanctuary policies. It would also affect undocumented immigrants held in local jails, crime victims in those situations, and private companies that run detention facilities.

last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
