It would prohibit states and cities from preventing their employees from cooperating with federal immigration agents or from participating in private immigration detention facilities. The bill also strengthens the legal standing of ICE detainers, clarifying what legally justifies a hold and shielding local agencies from lawsuits when they comply.
ai_sections.who: The bill would directly affect state and local governments that currently operate under sanctuary policies, as well as undocumented immigrants held in local jails and private companies that run detention facilities. Crime victims are also affected, as the bill creates a new federal right to sue a city or state if an undocumented person released against an ICE detainer later committed a serious crime such as murder or rape against them.
ai_sections.why: Localities with sanctuary policies would be required to change how their employees handle immigration information and cooperation with federal agents. Undocumented immigrants in local jails could be held longer under ICE detainers that local agencies would now have stronger legal footing to honor.

title: Accreditation Choice and Innovation Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how colleges and universities get accredited, which is the official seal of approval that allows schools to receive federal student aid money. Right now, accreditation agencies are mostly private nonprofit organizations that review schools and certify they meet quality standards. This bill would allow states to designate their own accreditors, including industry groups, as long as at least one other state also recognizes them. It also makes it easier for new accreditation agencies to get federally approved faster, within two years instead of longer. Accreditors would have to judge schools more heavily on measurable outcomes like graduation rates, loan repayment rates, and how much extra money graduates earn compared to what the program cost.

The bill also changes how accreditors treat religious colleges. It gives religiously affiliated schools a formal complaint process if they believe an accreditor punished them because of their religious mission. During that complaint process, the school keeps its accreditation status. The accreditor would have to prove its decision had nothing to do with the school's religious beliefs, which is a higher bar than current law. Schools that lose accreditation for religious reasons can stay federally certified while they find a new accreditor.

The people most directly affected are students at colleges and universities, especially those using federal financial aid like Pell Grants or student loans. Colleges themselves, accreditation agencies, and state governments would also see significant changes in their roles and responsibilities. Students at religious institutions and programs with weak job or earnings outcomes would likely feel the biggest effects.
ai_headline: Bill rewrites college accreditation rules, adds religious school protections
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 360.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 4054 lets states pick their own college accreditors and requires agencies to weigh graduation and earnings outcomes more heavily.
ai_sections.what: HR 4054 changes how colleges earn accreditation, the approval required to receive federal student aid. States could designate their own accreditors, including industry groups, if at least one other state also recognizes them. New accreditation agencies could receive federal approval within two years, and all accreditors would be required to weigh measurable outcomes such as graduation rates, loan repayment rates, and graduate earnings relative to program cost.
ai_sections.who: Students at colleges and universities who use federal financial aid such as Pell Grants or student loans are most directly affected. Colleges, accreditation agencies, and state governments would also see significant changes in their roles.
ai_sections.why: Programs with weak graduation, loan repayment, or earnings outcomes would face greater scrutiny under the new accreditation standards. Religious schools would gain new procedural rights, including keeping their accreditation status during a complaint process while an accreditor bears the burden of proving its decision was unrelated to the school's religious beliefs.

title: Uplifting First-Time Homebuyers Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would change a tax rule that lets people withdraw money from retirement accounts, like an IRA, to buy their first home. Right now, first-time homebuyers can take out up to $10,000 from a retirement account without paying the usual 10% early withdrawal penalty. This bill would raise that limit to $50,000. The change would apply starting with the 2025 tax year.

It is important to know that you would still owe regular income taxes on the money you withdraw. The bill only removes the penalty, not the tax itself. The current $10,000 limit has been in place since 1997 and has never been updated for inflation, so this would be a significant increase.

This bill would affect people who have never owned a home and have money saved in a qualifying retirement account, such as a traditional IRA. It does not apply to employer-sponsored plans like a 401(k) under this specific rule. Anyone planning to buy a first home and considering using retirement savings to help cover the costs, like a down payment, would be the main group impacted.
ai_headline: Senate bill raises first-home retirement withdrawal limit from $10,000 to $50,000
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

ai_sections.tldr: S 2867 would raise the penalty-free retirement withdrawal limit for first-time homebuyers from $10,000 to $50,000 starting in 2025.
ai_sections.what: S 2867 would raise the penalty-free early withdrawal limit from qualifying retirement accounts, such as a traditional IRA, from $10,000 to $50,000 for first-time homebuyers. The current $10,000 limit has been in place since 1997 and has never been adjusted for inflation. The change would take effect beginning with the 2025 tax year.
ai_sections.who: This bill would affect people who have never owned a home and hold money in a qualifying retirement account such as a traditional IRA. It does not apply to employer-sponsored plans like a 401(k) under this specific rule.
ai_sections.why: Withdrawers would still owe regular income taxes on any amount taken out, since the bill removes only the 10% early withdrawal penalty, not the tax itself. First-time homebuyers using retirement savings toward costs such as a down payment would be the primary group whose financial decisions are affected.

title: Taxpayer Notification and Privacy Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the IRS must notify taxpayers when it contacts outside parties, like banks or employers, to gather information during an audit or investigation. Currently, the IRS is required to give taxpayers advance notice before reaching out to third parties, but the notice does not have to spell out exactly what information is being requested. Under this bill, if the IRS wants information from a third party that it has not already asked the taxpayer for and that the taxpayer could reasonably provide themselves, the IRS must first tell the taxpayer specifically what information it is seeking. The taxpayer would then get at least 45 days to respond and provide that information directly before the IRS contacts the outside party.

The bill also creates exceptions. The new specific-notice rules would not apply when the IRS is collecting an already-established tax debt, or when the IRS Secretary determines that going to the third party is necessary regardless of whether the taxpayer could supply the information. These carve-outs are meant to prevent the rules from interfering with active collection efforts or sensitive investigations.

This bill would affect everyday taxpayers who are being audited or investigated by the IRS, as well as the third parties the IRS contacts, such as financial institutions or business associates. It gives taxpayers a clearer picture of what the IRS is looking for and a real chance to respond before their personal or financial information is sought elsewhere. The changes would take effect one year after the bill becomes law.
ai_headline: IRS must tell taxpayers exactly what it wants before contacting banks or employers
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6495 gives taxpayers 45 days to provide information themselves before the IRS contacts third parties like banks or employers.
ai_sections.what: HR 6495 requires the IRS to specifically tell taxpayers what information it is seeking before contacting outside parties such as banks or employers, but only when that information has not already been requested from the taxpayer and the taxpayer could reasonably provide it themselves. Taxpayers would then have at least 45 days to respond directly before the IRS reaches out to any third party. The rules would take effect one year after the bill becomes law.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects taxpayers who are under IRS audit or investigation, as well as third parties such as financial institutions and business associates who might otherwise be contacted. It does not apply when the IRS is actively collecting an already-established tax debt or when the IRS Secretary determines that contacting the third party is necessary regardless of what the taxpayer could provide.
ai_sections.why: Under current law, the IRS must give advance notice before contacting third parties but is not required to specify what information it is requesting, leaving taxpayers with limited ability to respond. This bill would alter that process, giving taxpayers earlier and more detailed notice and a defined window to act before their financial or personal information is sought from outside sources.

title: Pregnant Students’ Rights Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires colleges and universities that receive federal financial aid to inform students about their rights and available support if they become pregnant while enrolled. Schools would need to share information about on-campus and local resources to help pregnant students continue their education, carry a pregnancy to term, and care for a baby after birth. They would also have to explain what accommodations are available, such as schedule flexibility or medical leave.

Schools would be required to spread this information in several ways, including sending an annual email to all enrolled students, posting it on their public website, including it in student handbooks, covering it at student orientations, and making it available at health and counseling centers. The goal is to make sure students know where to turn and what help exists before they ever need it.

This bill affects all colleges and universities that participate in federal student aid programs, which includes most public and private schools across the country. It directly impacts current and prospective students who are pregnant or could become pregnant during their time in school. It does not create new legal rights beyond what already exists under Title IX, the federal law that prohibits sex discrimination in education, but it does require schools to make sure students know those rights exist.
ai_headline: Colleges must tell pregnant students about their rights and campus resources
last_action_text: Received in the Senate. Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 303.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6359 requires federally funded colleges to notify all students annually about pregnancy rights and available campus support.
ai_sections.what: HR 6359 requires colleges and universities receiving federal financial aid to inform students about their rights and available support if they become pregnant while enrolled. Schools must share information about on-campus and local resources, available accommodations such as schedule flexibility or medical leave, and how to access help. This information must be distributed through annual emails, public websites, student handbooks, orientations, and health and counseling centers.
ai_sections.who: The bill applies to all colleges and universities that participate in federal student aid programs, which includes most public and private schools in the country. It directly affects current and prospective students who are pregnant or could become pregnant during their enrollment.
ai_sections.why: The bill does not create new legal rights beyond those already established under Title IX, the federal law prohibiting sex discrimination in education. It requires schools to ensure students are aware those existing rights and resources exist before they ever need them.

title: Ending Improper Payments to Deceased People Act
ai_summary:
This bill is designed to reduce the number of government payments that accidentally go to people who have already died. Right now, the Social Security Administration collects death records from states and other sources. This bill would require the Social Security Administration to share that death record information with a federal tool called the "Do Not Pay" system, which is used by government agencies to check whether someone should actually receive a payment before sending it out.

The Do Not Pay system is already used to screen out payments to people who are ineligible, such as those who owe certain debts or are on fraud lists. By feeding death records into it, federal agencies across the government would have a better chance of catching and stopping payments before they go out to deceased individuals. The bill sets a start date of December 28, 2026, giving agencies time to set up the necessary data-sharing agreements.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies that send out payments, such as benefit programs, grants, or contracts. It also affects the Social Security Administration, which would take on the responsibility of sharing its death data. For everyday people, the practical effect would be indirect: less taxpayer money wasted on payments to people who have passed away.
ai_headline: Federal death records would feed into payment-screening tool under House bill
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 371.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 2716 requires SSA to share death records with the Do Not Pay system by Dec. 28, 2026, to stop payments to deceased individuals.
ai_sections.what: HR 2716 requires the Social Security Administration to share its death record data with the federal Do Not Pay system, which agencies use to screen recipients before sending payments. The Do Not Pay system already screens for ineligible recipients, and adding death records would allow agencies to catch payments destined for deceased individuals before they go out. The bill sets an implementation date of December 28, 2026.
ai_sections.who: Federal agencies that issue payments, such as benefit programs, grants, or contracts, would use the expanded Do Not Pay system. The Social Security Administration would take on responsibility for sharing its death data with the system.
ai_sections.why: Without this change, federal agencies may continue sending payments to deceased individuals because death record information is not currently routed through the Do Not Pay system. Connecting the two systems is intended to reduce the amount of taxpayer money lost to payments sent to people who have already died.

press_names: Ending Improper Payments to Deceased People Act

title: Supporting Pregnant and Parenting Women and Families Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes a change to how states can spend a federal block grant called TANF, which stands for Temporary Assistance for Needy Families. Right now, states receive TANF money to help low-income families, but the rules are not completely clear about whether that money can go to pregnancy centers. This bill would explicitly allow states to direct TANF funds to organizations that support pregnant women and new parents, such as places that offer free diapers, baby clothing, prenatal education, pregnancy testing, and relationship counseling.

The bill defines a "pregnancy center" as any organization that supports the life of both the mother and the unborn child and provides practical help to mothers, fathers, and families. These are often called pregnancy resource centers or pregnancy help organizations. Under this bill, states would have a clear legal green light to fund them through TANF dollars, removing any ambiguity about whether doing so is allowed.

This bill mainly affects two groups. First, it affects states, giving them a confirmed option to send federal family assistance money to these types of centers if they choose to. Second, it affects pregnant women and new parents who are low-income and might use services at these centers, since more funding could expand what those centers offer. It does not require any state to fund pregnancy centers, it simply clarifies that they are permitted to do so.
ai_headline: Bill would let states fund pregnancy centers with federal TANF dollars
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6945 clarifies that states may direct TANF block grant funds to pregnancy resource centers serving low-income families.
ai_sections.what: HR 6945 amends the rules for the TANF federal block grant to explicitly permit states to fund pregnancy centers using those dollars. Current law is ambiguous on whether TANF money can flow to these organizations. The bill defines a qualifying pregnancy center as one that supports the life of both the mother and unborn child and provides practical assistance to mothers, fathers, and families.
ai_sections.who: States receive the direct policy change, gaining a confirmed legal option to fund pregnancy centers through TANF if they choose. Low-income pregnant women and new parents who use these centers are the end population affected, as expanded funding could change the scope of services available to them.
ai_sections.why: Removing the legal ambiguity could lead some states to direct existing TANF dollars toward pregnancy centers that offer services such as diapers, baby clothing, prenatal education, pregnancy testing, and relationship counseling. No state is required to make that choice, so the practical effect will vary depending on individual state decisions.
ai_sections.cost: TANF is an existing federal block grant already distributed to states; this bill does not create new spending but would determine which organizations are eligible to receive a portion of those existing funds.
costChips: Redirects existing TANF block grant dollars
Eligibility rules for fund recipients change

press_names: Supporting Pregnant and Parenting Women and Families Act

title: To authorize leases of up to 99 years for land held in trust for federally recognized Indian Tribes.
ai_summary:
This bill would allow federally recognized Indian Tribes to sign leases on their trust land for up to 99 years. Right now, a 1955 federal law already permits certain specific tribes to offer these long-term leases, but not all federally recognized tribes have that same authority. This bill would extend the 99-year lease option to every tribe on the official federal list of recognized tribes.

Trust land is land that the federal government holds on behalf of a tribe. Longer leases can make it easier for tribes to attract businesses, housing developers, or other partners who need a long enough time horizon to justify building on or investing in that land. Without the ability to offer a lengthy lease, potential partners may be unwilling to commit resources.

This bill directly affects all federally recognized Indian Tribes that currently cannot offer 99-year leases on their trust land, as well as businesses, developers, or individuals who might want to lease that land. It does not transfer ownership of the land or change who it belongs to. It simply gives tribes more flexibility in how they manage agreements with outside parties.
ai_headline: All federally recognized tribes would gain 99-year trust land lease authority
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Indian Affairs.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 5910 extends 99-year trust land lease authority to all federally recognized tribes, not just those covered by a 1955 law.
ai_sections.what: HR 5910 would allow every federally recognized Indian Tribe to sign leases on their trust land for up to 99 years. A 1955 federal law already grants this authority to certain specific tribes, but not all recognized tribes share it. This bill would extend that same 99-year lease option to every tribe on the official federal list of recognized tribes.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects all federally recognized Indian Tribes that currently cannot offer 99-year leases on their trust land. It also affects businesses, developers, and individuals who might seek to lease that land.
ai_sections.why: Without the ability to offer long-term leases, potential partners may be unwilling to commit resources to trust land. Longer leases can change the calculus for businesses, housing developers, or others who need a sufficient time horizon to justify investment or construction on that land.

title: Clergy Act
ai_summary:
Current law allows clergy members to opt out of Social Security by filing for an exemption. Once they opt out, that decision is permanent and cannot be changed. This bill would create a one-time window where clergy who previously opted out could change their minds and rejoin the Social Security system. To do so, they would need to file paperwork with the IRS by a deadline tied to their 2029 tax return. If they choose to opt back in, they would start paying Social Security taxes going forward and would eventually be able to collect Social Security benefits in retirement.

The bill affects ordained ministers, licensed clergy, members of religious orders, and Christian Science practitioners who previously chose to be exempt from Social Security. These individuals currently have no legal path to undo that choice. If the bill passes, they could opt back in starting with either their 2028 or 2029 tax year. However, the decision would be final in the other direction too — anyone who rejoins cannot apply for the exemption again later.

The bill also requires the IRS and Social Security Administration to create an outreach plan within 90 days of the bill becoming law, so that eligible clergy members are actually informed that this option exists. This affects a relatively small and specific group of religious workers, not the general public. It does not change Social Security rules for anyone else, and it does not force any clergy member to make a change.
ai_headline: Clergy who left Social Security could get a one-time chance to rejoin
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 227 would open a one-time window for exempt clergy to rejoin Social Security, with a filing deadline tied to their 2029 tax return.
ai_sections.what: HR 227 would create a one-time window allowing clergy who previously opted out of Social Security to rejoin the system. To do so, they would need to file paperwork with the IRS by a deadline tied to their 2029 tax return. If they opt back in, they would pay Social Security taxes going forward and could eventually collect retirement benefits.
ai_sections.who: The bill applies to ordained ministers, licensed clergy, members of religious orders, and Christian Science practitioners who previously chose to be exempt from Social Security. It does not change rules for any other workers or the general public.
ai_sections.why: Under current law, clergy who opted out have no legal path to reverse that decision. If this bill passes, rejoining would also be permanent — those who opt back in could not apply for the exemption again later.

title: No Amnesty for Hamas Sympathizers Act
ai_summary:
This bill would end or block nearly every legal pathway that people from Palestinian-controlled territories (the West Bank and Gaza) could use to stay in or enter the United States. Specifically, it cancels a 2024 policy that let certain Palestinians temporarily stay without being deported, and it permanently bars people from those areas from receiving asylum, refugee status, temporary protected status, or humanitarian parole. It also blocks any government money from being used to give Palestinians those protections. Anyone who already holds a Palestinian Authority passport or travel document would be treated the same way, regardless of where they currently live.

The bill also changes federal immigration law directly. It adds Palestinians from those territories to the list of people who are automatically inadmissible, meaning they cannot legally enter the U.S., and to the list of people who are deportable, meaning those already here could be removed. If someone from these territories was previously given permanent resident status and later commits a violent crime, that status would be taken away.

This bill would affect Palestinians living in the West Bank or Gaza who are trying to come to the U.S., as well as Palestinians already inside the U.S. who hold Palestinian Authority travel documents or have applied for legal protections. It was introduced in the House in June 2025 and has been sent to the Judiciary Committee, where it would need to advance before any further votes take place.
ai_headline: House bill would bar Palestinians from nearly all U.S. immigration pathways
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 3724 would permanently block Palestinians from the West Bank and Gaza from asylum, refugee status, TPS, and humanitarian parole in the U.S.
ai_sections.what: HR 3724 would cancel a 2024 policy allowing certain Palestinians to temporarily remain in the U.S. and permanently bar people from the West Bank and Gaza from receiving asylum, refugee status, temporary protected status, or humanitarian parole. The bill also adds Palestinians from those territories to federal lists of people who are automatically inadmissible or deportable. Palestinians already holding permanent resident status who later commit a violent crime would lose that status under the bill.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects Palestinians living in the West Bank or Gaza who are seeking to enter the U.S., as well as Palestinians already in the U.S. who hold Palestinian Authority travel documents or have applied for legal protections. Anyone holding a Palestinian Authority passport or travel document would be covered regardless of where they currently live.
ai_sections.why: Palestinians currently in the U.S. with Palestinian Authority documents or pending legal applications could face deportation or loss of status. Those outside the U.S. seeking protection would have no remaining legal pathway to enter under this bill.
ai_sections.cost: The bill blocks any government money from being used to grant Palestinians the covered immigration protections.

title: Grazing for Wildfire Risk Reduction Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Forest Service to come up with a plan to use livestock grazing as a tool to reduce wildfire risk on federal lands. The idea is that animals like cattle and sheep eat the dry grasses and brush that can fuel wildfires. The bill asks the Forest Service to make it easier for ranchers to graze their animals on federal land specifically to reduce that fire risk, including on land where grazing permits are not currently active.

The bill includes a few specific steps. It would speed up the environmental review process so ranchers can move their animals to unused grazing areas during droughts or natural disasters. It also calls for more use of "targeted grazing," which means directing animals to specific areas where dry vegetation is a fire hazard, and for expanding temporary grazing permits to help clear out invasive grasses that spread wildfires. After a fire has already burned an area, grazing could also be used to help the land recover.

This bill mainly affects ranchers and farmers who hold or want permits to graze livestock on federal land, as well as federal land managers in the Forest Service. It would also indirectly affect people in fire-prone communities, particularly in western states like California, Oregon, Washington, and others where wildfires are a major concern. The bill does not provide new funding but directs the government to use existing legal authorities to expand these grazing opportunities.
ai_headline: Federal grazing bill would put livestock to work fighting wildfires
last_action_text: Reported (Amended) by the Committee on Natural Resources. H. Rept. 119-433, Part I.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 1110 directs USDA and the Forest Service to expand livestock grazing on federal land as a wildfire risk-reduction tool.
ai_sections.what: HR 1110 directs the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Forest Service to develop a plan using livestock grazing to reduce wildfire risk on federal lands. The bill would speed up environmental reviews so ranchers can move animals to unused grazing areas during droughts or natural disasters. It also calls for targeted grazing in high-risk areas, expanded temporary permits to address invasive grasses, and post-fire grazing to aid land recovery.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects ranchers and farmers who hold or seek permits to graze livestock on federal land, as well as Forest Service land managers. People living in fire-prone communities, particularly in western states such as California, Oregon, and Washington, would be indirectly affected.
ai_sections.why: Dry grasses and brush that livestock would consume are among the fuels that drive wildfires, so the bill's approach links grazing activity to fire hazard levels. Expanding access to currently inactive permit areas and accelerating review timelines could change how quickly and broadly federal land managers can respond to fire risk.

press_names: Grazing for Wildfire Risk Reduction Act

title: Taxpayer Due Process Enhancement Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes some rules around what happens when the IRS tries to collect a tax debt that a taxpayer is disputing. Right now, if you challenge an IRS collection action like a lien or levy, there are strict deadlines for filing a refund claim, and those deadlines can run out even while your case is still being fought. This bill pauses those deadlines while your dispute is officially ongoing, so you do not lose your right to claim a refund just because the process dragged on. The pause stops if you give up your legal fight or miss a court deadline.

The bill also stops the IRS from automatically using a tax refund you are owed to pay off a tax debt you are currently disputing, unless you agree to it. So if the IRS owes you money from an overpayment but you are also fighting a separate tax bill, the IRS cannot quietly apply your refund to that disputed amount while the case is still open.

Finally, the bill gives the U.S. Tax Court broader authority to handle these disputes. It allows the court to review not just the IRS collection decision itself, but also the underlying tax amount being disputed, and it lets the court decide whether to extend the 30-day window to file if there is a good reason it was missed. This bill affects any U.S. taxpayer who is currently in or enters a formal dispute with the IRS over a collection action such as a tax lien or levy.
ai_headline: Disputed IRS debts would pause refund deadlines under new bill
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6506 pauses refund claim deadlines and blocks IRS from offsetting refunds while a tax collection dispute is open.
ai_sections.what: HR 6506 pauses the deadline to file a refund claim while a taxpayer is formally disputing an IRS collection action such as a lien or levy, so the right to claim a refund cannot expire during an ongoing case. The pause ends if the taxpayer drops their legal challenge or misses a court deadline. The bill also bars the IRS from automatically applying a refund to a disputed tax debt without the taxpayer's agreement, and it gives the U.S. Tax Court authority to review the underlying disputed tax amount and to extend the 30-day filing window for good cause.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects any U.S. taxpayer who is currently in or enters a formal dispute with the IRS over a collection action such as a tax lien or levy. The U.S. Tax Court gains expanded jurisdiction under the measure.
ai_sections.why: Refund claim deadlines currently continue to run during active disputes, which can cause taxpayers to lose refund rights before their cases are resolved. Allowing the IRS to offset refunds against disputed amounts during open cases creates financial pressure on taxpayers whose liability has not yet been determined.

title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Bureau of Land Management relating to Public Land Order No. 7917 for Withdrawal of Federal Lands; Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties, MN.
ai_summary:
This resolution cancels a rule that the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) put in place in January 2023. That rule had withdrawn certain federal lands in Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties in northeastern Minnesota from mining and mineral leasing activities for 20 years. By passing this resolution, Congress is effectively reversing that decision and making the land available again for potential mining operations, including copper, nickel, and other mineral extraction.

The resolution was passed using the Congressional Review Act, a law that allows Congress to cancel recent federal agency rules it disagrees with. Once Congress passes such a resolution and it is signed into law, the agency rule is treated as if it never existed and the agency cannot issue a substantially similar rule without new permission from Congress. This resolution was signed into law on April 27, 2026.

This affects people in northeastern Minnesota and surrounding areas, including mining companies, Indigenous communities such as the Ojibwe tribes, environmental groups, outdoor recreation businesses, and anyone who relies on the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and nearby waterways. Supporters of the withdrawal had argued the mining ban protected water quality and wilderness; supporters of this resolution argue it opens the region to economic development and domestic mineral production.
ai_headline: Federal mining ban on northeastern Minnesota lands reversed by law
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-85.

ai_sections.tldr: A 20-year federal mining withdrawal covering three Minnesota counties was canceled by Congress and signed into law April 27, 2026.

The cancellation means those lands are now available again for mining activities, including copper, nickel, and other mineral extraction. The rule is treated as if it never existed, and BLM cannot issue a substantially similar rule without new congressional authorization.
ai_sections.who: The resolution affects people and organizations in northeastern Minnesota, including mining companies, Ojibwe tribes and other Indigenous communities, environmental groups, and outdoor recreation businesses. Anyone who relies on the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and nearby waterways is also affected.
ai_sections.why: Supporters of the original withdrawal argued the mining ban protected water quality and wilderness in the region. Supporters of this resolution argue it reopens the area to economic development and domestic mineral production.

title: Accreditation for College Excellence Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would place new rules on the organizations that accredit colleges and universities. Accreditors are private groups that review schools and decide whether they meet quality standards. Schools generally need accreditation to qualify for federal student aid. Under this bill, accreditors would be banned from requiring, encouraging, or pressuring colleges to support a particular political viewpoint, ideology, or position on social and cultural issues. Accreditors also could not judge a school based on its commitment to any specific belief system, or force a school to treat people differently based on race, sex, or other protected categories beyond what federal law already requires.

The bill carves out some exceptions. Religious colleges would still be allowed to require students, staff, and contractors to follow a statement of faith or a code of conduct tied to their religious mission. Schools could also still require people to take an oath to uphold the U.S. Constitution. The bill also limits the Department of Education's ability to add extra requirements on top of what Congress has already spelled out in existing law.

This bill would primarily affect accrediting agencies, colleges and universities, and indirectly the students who attend them. If a school loses accreditation, its students typically lose access to federal financial aid like Pell Grants and student loans, so accreditation rules have a real impact on millions of students. Supporters and critics disagree about whether current accreditation practices include political pressure on schools, but the bill is specifically aimed at preventing that from happening.
ai_headline: Bill would bar college accreditors from pushing political viewpoints on schools
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 380.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 2516 bans accreditors from pressuring colleges on political ideology, with exceptions for religious schools and constitutional oaths.
ai_sections.what: HR 2516 places new restrictions on private accrediting agencies that determine whether colleges meet quality standards. Accreditors would be prohibited from requiring, encouraging, or pressuring schools to support a particular political viewpoint, ideology, or position on social and cultural issues. They also could not judge schools based on specific belief systems or force race- or sex-based treatment beyond what federal law already requires.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects accrediting agencies and the colleges and universities they review. Students are indirectly affected because losing accreditation typically means losing access to federal financial aid such as Pell Grants and student loans.
ai_sections.why: Accreditation determines whether students at a given school can receive federal financial aid, meaning accreditor rules have real consequences for millions of students. The bill also limits the Department of Education's authority to impose requirements beyond what Congress has already established in existing law.

title: Proven Forest Management Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill tells the U.S. Forest Service and other federal land managers to work more closely with local governments, tribes, fire departments, and other groups when making decisions about managing national forests. It requires that forest management activities try to achieve several goals at once, such as reducing wildfire risk, protecting water quality, and keeping nature diverse. However, it includes an exception that lets the agency skip those extra requirements if meeting them would cost too much.

One of the bigger changes in this bill is that it makes it easier and faster to carry out projects aimed at reducing wildfire fuel, such as clearing brush or thinning trees. Right now, many federal projects must go through a detailed environmental review process under a law called the National Environmental Policy Act. This bill would allow fuel-reduction projects of up to 10,000 acres to skip that review process, as long as the project follows the existing forest plan and was developed with input from local officials and community groups.

This bill mainly affects people who live near or rely on national forests, including residents of rural communities in the western United States, local governments, Native American tribes, and anyone who uses public lands for recreation, water supply, or work. It also affects federal land managers, who would have new rules about how they coordinate with outside groups and carry out forest projects. Environmental groups and logging or timber industries could also be affected depending on how the law is put into practice.
ai_headline: Federal wildfire bill lets forest agencies skip environmental review on projects up to 10,000 acres
last_action_text: Reported (Amended) by the Committee on Natural Resources. H. Rept. 119-430, Part I.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 179 lets federal agencies skip NEPA environmental review for wildfire fuel-reduction projects up to 10,000 acres.
ai_sections.what: HR 179 requires the U.S. Forest Service and other federal land managers to coordinate more closely with local governments, tribes, and fire departments when making forest management decisions. The bill allows fuel-reduction projects of up to 10,000 acres to bypass the environmental review process normally required under the National Environmental Policy Act, provided the project follows the existing forest plan and was developed with input from local officials and community groups. A separate provision allows agencies to skip multiple-goal management requirements if meeting them would cost too much.
ai_sections.who: The bill primarily affects rural communities near national forests, local governments, and Native American tribes, as well as federal land managers who would face new coordination requirements. Environmental groups and the logging and timber industries could also be affected depending on how the law is implemented.
ai_sections.why: Skipping environmental review could speed up brush-clearing and tree-thinning projects intended to reduce wildfire risk, but it also removes a layer of oversight that currently applies to federal land management decisions. The cost-based exception to multi-goal management requirements could reduce how consistently agencies balance wildfire risk, water quality, and biodiversity in their planning.
ai_sections.cost: The bill includes an exception that allows agencies to skip certain management requirements if meeting them would cost too much, but the summary does not specify funding levels, spending amounts, or who bears those costs.

title: Unfunded Mandates Accountability and Transparency Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill updates a 1995 law that deals with federal regulations and their costs. Right now, federal agencies have to analyze the costs of new rules that affect state and local governments. This bill expands that requirement by forcing agencies to study the costs and benefits of any major rule before it takes effect. A "major rule" means one that could cost $100 million or more per year, significantly raise prices, or harm jobs, competition, or public health. Agencies would have to publish these cost-benefit analyses, consider alternative approaches, and pick the option that provides the most benefit for the least cost. The bill also extends these requirements to independent regulatory agencies like the FCC and SEC, which were previously exempt.

The bill also strengthens the public input process. Before finalizing a major rule, agencies would have to consult early and often with state and local governments, tribal governments, and private businesses including small businesses. They would need to post a public notice at least 90 days before officially proposing a rule, giving people more time to weigh in. An office called the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs would oversee agency compliance and report to Congress each year on how well agencies are following the rules.

People and businesses harmed by a major rule would gain the right to sue in federal court if they believe an agency skipped or mishandled the required cost-benefit analysis. This bill would affect federal agencies across the government, businesses of all sizes, state and local governments, and anyone subject to federal regulations. It does not apply to Federal Reserve monetary policy decisions.
ai_headline: Federal agencies would face mandatory cost-benefit reviews under HR 580
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 381.

People and businesses harmed by a major rule would gain the right to sue in federal court if an agency skipped or mishandled the required cost-benefit analysis.

title: Employee Profit-Sharing Encouragement Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes the tax rules for larger companies that pay their top executives high salaries. Right now, businesses can deduct executive pay from their taxable income, which lowers what they owe the government. Under this bill, a company would lose that tax deduction for executive compensation unless it also runs a profit-sharing program for its regular employees. To qualify, the profit-sharing plan must pay out at least 5 percent of the company's net income to workers, and part-time employees who have been there at least a year must be included. The payments also have to be spread fairly across the workforce, not just given to higher-paid workers.

The bill applies to companies above a certain size, based on how much money they bring in each year. There is a limited exception if a company can prove to the IRS that paying out profit-sharing money would seriously threaten its ability to stay in business. The IRS would also have the power to step in if a company tries to game the system, for example by quietly cutting workers' regular wages or benefits to offset the new profit-sharing requirement.

This mainly affects larger employers and their highest-paid executives, as well as the rank-and-file employees who work for those companies. Companies that already run qualifying profit-sharing plans would not need to change anything. Companies that do not have such plans would face a choice: either set one up or give up the tax deduction for executive pay. The bill does not force companies to pay executives less or require profit-sharing by law, it simply removes a tax benefit for those that do not share profits with workers.
ai_headline: Bill would strip executive pay deductions from companies without profit-sharing
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6418 removes the executive pay tax deduction for large companies that don't share at least 5% of net income with workers.
ai_sections.what: HR 6418 would eliminate the tax deduction companies currently take for executive compensation unless they operate a qualifying profit-sharing program for regular employees. To qualify, a plan must distribute at least 5 percent of the company's net income to workers, include part-time employees who have been there at least one year, and spread payments fairly across the workforce. The bill applies to companies above a certain revenue threshold and does not legally require profit-sharing or cap executive pay.
ai_sections.who: The bill primarily affects larger employers and their highest-paid executives. Rank-and-file employees at those companies, including part-time workers with at least one year of tenure, are also directly affected.
ai_sections.why: Companies without a qualifying profit-sharing plan would face a choice between establishing one or forgoing the tax deduction for executive compensation. The IRS would gain authority to intervene if a company offsets profit-sharing costs by reducing workers' regular wages or benefits.

title: Amtrak Transparency and Accountability for Passengers and Taxpayers Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require Amtrak's Board of Directors to hold its meetings openly to the public, following the same rules that apply to most other federal government agencies. Right now, Amtrak is not fully required to follow the federal "Government in the Sunshine Act," which is the law that forces government bodies to let the public watch and know about their meetings. This bill would change that, making Amtrak's board meetings open by default.

However, the bill also spells out certain exceptions where Amtrak could still meet privately. Those include situations involving contract negotiations where sharing details publicly could hurt Amtrak's ability to compete, union contract talks with employees, and discussions about hiring, firing, or evaluating specific workers. These closed-door exceptions are similar to the ones other federal agencies already use.

This bill mainly affects Amtrak passengers, taxpayers who fund Amtrak through federal dollars, and Amtrak itself as an organization. Passengers and taxpayers would gain more ability to see how Amtrak's leadership makes decisions, while Amtrak would face new requirements to publicize meeting schedules and keep records. Amtrak employees involved in contract or personnel matters would still have some privacy protections under the exceptions described in the bill.
ai_headline: HR 188 would open Amtrak board meetings to the public
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 113.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 188 would require Amtrak's board to meet publicly by default, with limited exceptions for contracts and personnel matters.

Closed sessions would still be permitted for contract negotiations, union talks, and discussions about specific employees. Amtrak would also be required to publicize meeting schedules and keep records.
ai_sections.who: Amtrak passengers and taxpayers who fund Amtrak through federal dollars would gain greater visibility into how the board makes decisions. Amtrak as an organization and its employees involved in contract or personnel matters are also directly affected.

Amtrak would face new administrative requirements to announce meetings and maintain records, while retaining the ability to close sessions in defined circumstances.

title: A bill to amend the Native American Tourism and Improving Visitor Experience Act to authorize grants to Indian tribes, tribal organizations, and Native Hawaiian organizations, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill updates an existing law called the Native American Tourism and Improving Visitor Experience Act. The change it makes is straightforward: it creates a formal grant program that allows the federal government to give money directly to Native American tribes, tribal organizations, and Native Hawaiian organizations. These grants would be used to support and grow tourism in Native communities, which is what the original law was already trying to encourage. The bill sets aside up to $35 million for these grants, spread across five years from 2025 to 2029.

Several federal agencies would be involved in handing out these grants. The Bureau of Indian Affairs could give grants to tribal groups, the Office of Native Hawaiian Relations could give grants to Native Hawaiian organizations, and other departments like Commerce, Transportation, Agriculture, Health and Human Services, and Labor could also participate. This gives Native communities multiple doors to knock on when applying for funding.

The people most directly affected are members of federally recognized Native American tribes, tribal organizations, and Native Hawaiian groups. If funded, these grants could help those communities develop tourism businesses, cultural programs, and visitor experiences, which could bring jobs and income to those areas. The broader public could also benefit by having more access to Native cultural tourism, but the main focus of the bill is on supporting Indigenous communities themselves.
ai_headline: Federal grant program for Native tourism gets $35M over five years
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

ai_sections.tldr: S 612 creates a $35M federal grant program from 2025–2029 to fund tourism development in Native American and Native Hawaiian communities.
ai_sections.what: S 612 amends the Native American Tourism and Improving Visitor Experience Act to establish a formal grant program for Native tourism development. The federal government could award funds directly to tribes, tribal organizations, and Native Hawaiian organizations. Multiple federal agencies are authorized to distribute the grants, giving applicants several agencies to approach for funding.
ai_sections.who: Federally recognized Native American tribes, tribal organizations, and Native Hawaiian organizations are the eligible recipients. Members of those communities are the primary people affected by the bill.
ai_sections.why: If funded, grants could support the development of tourism businesses, cultural programs, and visitor experiences in Native communities. The bill also expands public access to Native cultural tourism as a secondary effect.

title: Small Entity Update Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to take a fresh look at how it defines a "small entity" — meaning small businesses, organizations, or other groups that are subject to SEC rules. Right now, that definition is outdated and may not reflect how much financial markets have grown over the years. The bill requires the SEC to study the definition within one year of the law passing, and again five years after that, then report its findings to Congress and update its rules based on what it finds.

The practical effect is that more businesses could qualify as "small entities" under SEC rules. That matters because federal law already requires regulators to consider the burden their rules place on small entities and, when possible, make things easier for them. If the definition is expanded, more companies would be entitled to that consideration when the SEC writes new regulations. The bill also requires the SEC to automatically adjust its size thresholds every five years to keep up with inflation, so the definition does not fall out of date again.

This bill most directly affects small and mid-sized businesses that deal with securities laws — such as smaller investment firms, broker-dealers, or companies that raise money from investors. It could also affect investors and the broader public indirectly, since changes to how the SEC regulates smaller financial companies can influence market rules more broadly. The bill does not eliminate any existing regulations; it simply directs the SEC to study whether its current size categories still make sense.
ai_headline: SEC ordered to modernize its outdated small business size rules
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 3382 requires the SEC to review and update its "small entity" definition within one year and every five years after, with inflation adjustments.

The bill also requires automatic adjustments to size thresholds every five years to account for inflation. No existing regulations are eliminated; the bill solely directs the SEC to evaluate whether its current size categories remain appropriate.

ai_sections.why: The current definition of "small entity" is considered outdated and may not reflect the growth of financial markets over time. If more businesses qualify as small entities, they become entitled to regulatory burden considerations that federal law already requires agencies to apply when writing new rules.

title: To amend the Act of August 9, 1955 (commonly known as the “Long-Term Leasing Act”), to authorize leases of up to 99 years for land in the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe Reservation and land held in trust for the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah), and for other purposes
ai_summary:
This bill changes a federal law called the Long-Term Leasing Act to give two Native American tribes in Massachusetts new leasing powers. Right now, that law limits how long certain tribes can lease their land to outside businesses or individuals. This bill would allow the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe and the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah) to sign leases for their tribal lands for up to 99 years, matching a right that several other tribes across the country already have.

Longer leases matter because businesses and developers are generally more willing to invest in building on land when they have a long-term agreement in place. A 99-year lease gives companies or partners enough time to build and use facilities like housing, businesses, or other projects in a way that makes financial sense. Without this authority, the tribes face more difficulty attracting that kind of economic development on their reservation lands.

This bill directly affects the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe, located on Cape Cod, and the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah), located on Martha's Vineyard. It could indirectly affect businesses, developers, or individuals who want to enter into long-term agreements with either tribe. For most other Americans, the practical impact would be minimal, but for tribal members it could influence economic opportunities and self-sufficiency on their lands.
ai_headline: Two Massachusetts tribes would gain 99-year land leasing authority under HR 681
last_action_text: Committee on Indian Affairs. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 681 lets two Massachusetts Wampanoag tribes sign 99-year land leases, a right other U.S. tribes already hold.
ai_sections.what: HR 681 amends the Long-Term Leasing Act to allow the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe and the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah) to lease their tribal lands for up to 99 years. Current federal law restricts how long these tribes can lease their land to outside businesses or individuals. The 99-year limit is already available to several other tribes across the country.

ai_sections.why: Shorter lease terms make tribal lands less attractive to businesses and developers who require long-term agreements before committing to construction or investment. Longer leases could alter the level of economic development activity and degree of financial self-sufficiency on these reservations.

title: Access to Pediatric Technologies Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill addresses a gap in how Medicare pays for certain medical devices designed for children. Right now, if a device is FDA-approved specifically for kids but does not yet have a set payment code in Medicare's billing system, doctors may not get paid properly for using it. Starting January 1, 2026, this bill would require Medicare to create official payment rates for these pediatric devices when a manufacturer formally requests it. The process would follow Medicare's standard annual rulemaking schedule, with a May 1 deadline each year determining whether a device gets its payment rate set that year or the following year.

The bill defines which devices qualify fairly specifically. A device must be FDA-approved, covered by Medicare, currently labeled with a temporary billing code for new technologies, and either used mostly in procedures on children or specifically designed for pediatric patients. Manufacturers asking for a payment rate would need to submit supporting data such as pricing information, claims records, or time-and-motion studies to help Medicare set an appropriate rate.

The people most directly affected are children who need specialized medical devices and the doctors who treat them, even though Medicare primarily covers adults 65 and older and people with certain disabilities. Children can qualify for Medicare in some circumstances, and setting clearer payment rates could encourage doctors to adopt and use pediatric-specific devices more widely. Medical device manufacturers that make FDA-approved pediatric products would also be affected, since they gain a formal path to request Medicare reimbursement rates for their products. The bill does not guarantee coverage of any specific device.
ai_headline: Senate bill would set Medicare pay rates for FDA-approved pediatric devices
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

ai_sections.tldr: Starting Jan. 1, 2026, S 249 would require Medicare to create official payment rates for qualifying pediatric medical devices upon manufacturer request.

The process would follow Medicare's standard annual rulemaking schedule, with a May 1 deadline each year determining whether a device's rate is set that year or the next. To qualify, a device must be FDA-approved, covered by Medicare, currently carrying a temporary billing code for new technologies, and either used mostly in procedures on children or specifically designed for pediatric patients.

Clearer payment rates could influence whether physicians choose to use pediatric-specific devices, though the bill does not guarantee coverage of any particular device.

title: Flood Insurance for Farmers Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill makes two main changes to the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP), which is run by FEMA. First, it allows local governments to grant farmers a waiver from the usual requirement to elevate or floodproof agricultural buildings located in high-risk flood zones. Right now, communities that do not enforce those elevation and floodproofing rules can be kicked out of the federal flood insurance program entirely, which would leave all residents unable to buy NFIP coverage. This bill says communities cannot be penalized just for giving farmers that kind of waiver, as long as certain conditions are met. Farmers receiving the waiver can still buy flood insurance, but their premiums are set as if the building had been properly floodproofed.

There are limits on who qualifies for a waiver. The building cannot sit in a regulated floodway or in an area prone to high waves, and local officials must confirm that elevating or floodproofing is not a realistic option. The structure also cannot have had more than one flood insurance claim over $1,000 in any ten-year stretch before the waiver is granted. Local officials, not the federal government, make the call on each waiver, and they must confirm it will not create extra safety risks or raise flood levels for neighbors.

The second part of the bill lets FEMA offer a single umbrella flood insurance policy covering multiple buildings on the same property, including farms, apartment complexes, and commercial sites. Buying this bundled policy would be optional, not required, and the premium must still reflect the actual flood risk. FEMA would also have to report back to Congress within five years on how the umbrella policy option is working. This bill primarily affects farmers and agricultural landowners, rural and farming communities, local governments in flood-prone areas, and property owners with multiple structures on one lot.
ai_headline: Bill shields farming communities from flood insurance penalties over barn waivers
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

It allows local governments to waive elevation and floodproofing requirements for agricultural buildings in high-risk flood zones without losing NFIP participation. It also lets FEMA offer a single optional umbrella policy covering multiple buildings on one property, with a required congressional report within five years.

Farmers who receive a waiver can still buy flood insurance, but their premiums are calculated as if the building had been properly floodproofed, and eligibility is limited by location, safety, and claims history conditions.

title: No Tax on Overtime for All Workers Act
ai_summary:
This bill would let workers deduct overtime pay from their taxable income, meaning they would not owe federal income tax on the extra money they earn for working more than their normal hours. Under current law, overtime wages are taxed just like regular wages. This bill would change that by creating a tax deduction specifically for overtime earnings, so workers would keep more of what they make when they put in extra hours.

The bill covers two groups of workers. The first group includes employees who are legally required to receive overtime pay under federal labor law, which generally means hourly workers who earn overtime after 40 hours in a week. The second group includes workers who have a formal agreement with their employer, like a union contract, that sets overtime rules even if federal law does not require it. This second group specifically includes railroad and airline workers, whose schedules are governed by a separate federal law.

Anyone who regularly works overtime could benefit from this, particularly hourly workers in industries like manufacturing, retail, healthcare, transportation, and construction. The deduction would apply to tax years starting January 1, 2025. The bill does not eliminate payroll taxes like Social Security and Medicare on overtime, only federal income tax. As with all tax bills, it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and has not yet become law.
ai_headline: Senate bill would let workers deduct overtime pay from federal taxes
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

Under current law, overtime wages are taxed the same as regular wages. The deduction would apply to tax years beginning January 1, 2025.

title: Financial Institution Regulatory Tailoring Enhancement Act
ai_summary:
This bill raises the size threshold that determines when banks and other financial institutions face certain federal rules. Right now, many of these rules kick in once a bank holds $10 billion in assets. This bill would move that line up to $50 billion, meaning a bank would have to be five times larger before those rules apply to it. The specific rules affected include oversight by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), restrictions on risky trading by banks (the Volcker Rule), certain mortgage lending standards, and capital reserve requirements.

In practical terms, banks and credit unions with assets between $10 billion and $50 billion would no longer have to follow these particular regulations. That covers a significant number of mid-sized banks across the country. Supporters would say this reduces unnecessary burden on banks that are not large enough to pose a major risk to the financial system. Critics might say it weakens consumer protections and financial safeguards for a large segment of the banking industry.

The people most directly affected are employees and shareholders of mid-sized banks, and customers who use those banks. Customers at these institutions might see changes in the types of loans offered or how complaints are handled, since CFPB direct supervision would no longer apply. Broader effects on financial stability or consumer protection would depend on how regulators respond to the change.
ai_headline: Bill would lift federal bank oversight threshold from $10B to $50B in assets
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 132.

Rules affected include CFPB oversight, the Volcker Rule restricting risky trading, certain mortgage lending standards, and capital reserve requirements. title: Fix Our Forests Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Fix Our Forests Act, is designed to reduce the risk of wildfires on federal and tribal forest lands across the United States. It would create a new government center called the Fireshed Center, which would use data and technology, including artificial intelligence, to track and predict wildfire risks across the country. The bill identifies the most fire-prone areas, called fireshed management areas, and fast-tracks forest management work in those zones, such as thinning overgrown trees, clearing dead wood, controlled burns, and managing vegetation. It also cuts down on some of the environmental review steps that currently slow down this kind of work, making it easier for agencies to act more quickly in high-risk areas.

The bill also focuses on protecting neighborhoods near forests, often called the wildland-urban interface, where homes and communities sit close to fire-prone land. It would create a program to help those communities reduce their wildfire risk, including support for fire-resistant building practices and grants to help local governments and tribes take protective action. It also addresses the safety of power line corridors through forests, supports reforestation after fires, and includes a program to help the families of wildland firefighters who are killed or injured on the job.

The people most directly affected include residents living near national forests or other public lands in fire-prone states, particularly in the American West. Federally recognized tribes with forested lands would also be significantly involved, as the bill gives them more partnership opportunities in land management. Logging contractors, ranchers with federal grazing permits, and local governments near federal forests would also see changes in how they can work with federal agencies. Environmental groups may be affected by new limits on their ability to go to court to stop or delay forest management projects.
ai_headline: Fix Our Forests Act would speed up wildfire prevention on federal land
last_action_text: Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Subcommittee on Conservation, Forestry, Natural Resources, and Biotechnology. Hearings held. With printed Hearing: S.Hrg. 119-27.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 471 fast-tracks tree thinning, controlled burns, and AI-based fire tracking on federal and tribal forest lands.

The bill designates the most fire-prone federal and tribal lands as fireshed management areas and fast-tracks forest management work there, including thinning trees, clearing dead wood, controlled burns, and vegetation management. It also reduces environmental review steps that currently slow down such work in high-risk zones.

title: America the Beautiful Motorcycle Fairness Act
ai_summary:
The America the Beautiful Pass, sometimes called the National Parks Pass, lets one vehicle and all its passengers enter federal recreation areas for free. Right now, the rules are unclear about how motorcycles are treated. This bill clears that up by officially stating that when a passholder arrives on a motorcycle, the pass covers that motorcycle and its passengers, plus one additional motorcycle traveling with them and its passengers.

The main practical effect is that a motorcycle rider with this annual pass can bring along one buddy on a separate motorcycle, and both bikes get in free together. This puts motorcycle groups on more equal footing with car travelers, since a single car can already carry multiple people under one pass. Without this change, a second motorcycle in the same group would likely have to pay a separate entrance fee.

This bill affects people who own the America the Beautiful Pass and travel to national parks, national forests, Bureau of Land Management sites, and other federal recreation areas by motorcycle. It also affects the federal agencies that manage those lands, since they would need to update their entrance fee guidelines. It does not change anything for people who visit in cars, trucks, or other vehicles.
ai_headline: Motorcycle riders with federal parks pass could bring a second bike in free
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

title: Financial Services and General Government and National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2026
ai_summary:
This bill is a federal spending bill that sets the budget for several government departments and agencies for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2026. It covers two main areas. The first is everyday government operations, including the Treasury Department, the IRS, the White House, federal courts, and independent agencies like the Federal Election Commission and the Small Business Administration. The second is national security and foreign affairs, including the State Department, foreign aid programs, and international organizations. It also provides a $174,000 payment to the widow of the late California Representative Doug LaMalfa, which is a traditional congressional practice for deceased members.

For most Americans, the biggest direct impact comes from the IRS funding included in the bill. The IRS receives about $11 billion total for taxpayer services, tax enforcement, and technology upgrades. The bill also funds programs that help low-income people file taxes for free and provides money for clinics that assist people who cannot afford tax lawyers. Other parts of the bill fund drug enforcement programs, federal courts that handle everyday legal cases, and community development programs that help bring financial services and grocery stores to low-income neighborhoods.

The foreign affairs portion funds the State Department, U.S. embassies around the world, foreign aid, and international organizations. It also requires the government to report to Congress on the newly created Strategic Bitcoin Reserve, explaining how government-held cryptocurrency affects law enforcement funds and crime victim compensation. People who interact with federal agencies, pay taxes, receive foreign assistance, or live in low-income communities are most directly affected by this bill.

title: Chugach Alaska Land Exchange Oil Spill Recovery Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill sets up a land swap between the federal government and Chugach Alaska Corporation, which is an Alaska Native regional corporation. After the 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill, settlement money was used to buy and protect more than 600,000 acres of land in Alaska, including about 241,000 acres in the Chugach region. A problem arose because the government bought the surface rights to that land for conservation, but Chugach Alaska still owned the underground mineral rights beneath it. This created a conflict: the government wanted to protect the land, but Chugach Alaska had legal rights and responsibilities to develop the resources below it for the benefit of its Native shareholders.

To fix this conflict, the bill directs a trade. Chugach Alaska would give up roughly 231,000 acres of its underground mineral rights to the federal government, which would allow the government to fully protect that land without interference. In return, the federal government would give Chugach Alaska about 65,374 acres of land that it fully owns, meaning both the surface and underground rights in most cases. The government has one year after the bill becomes law to complete the exchange if Chugach Alaska agrees to proceed.

The people most directly affected are the Alaska Native shareholders of Chugach Alaska Corporation and the Alaska Native village corporations in the region, including communities like Chenega, English Bay, Eyak, and Tatitlek. The deal also affects federal land managers, since the land being transferred comes from the National Forest System, the Bureau of Land Management, and the National Park Service. Environmental conservation efforts in the Chugach region would also be affected, as the swap is designed to make the government's conservation goals easier to carry out by eliminating the split ownership situation.
ai_headline: Federal land swap would resolve split ownership across 231,000 Alaskan acres
last_action_text: Received in the Senate.

The government has one year after enactment to complete the exchange if Chugach Alaska agrees to proceed.

ai_sections.why: The swap is designed to eliminate a split-ownership conflict that arose after Exxon Valdez oil spill settlement funds were used to purchase surface rights to more than 600,000 acres for conservation, while Chugach Alaska retained the underlying mineral rights. Resolving that conflict would affect how conservation goals in the Chugach region are carried out and how Chugach Alaska meets its legal responsibilities to develop resources for its shareholders.
