title: Retire through Ownership Act
ai_summary:
This bill deals with Employee Stock Ownership Plans, or ESOPs. An ESOP is a type of retirement plan where employees receive shares of the company they work for as part of their benefits. When a company wants to sell stock to its ESOP, the law requires that the price paid be "adequate consideration," meaning the plan cannot overpay for the shares. The tricky part is that many of these companies are privately held, meaning their stock is not traded on a public market, so figuring out a fair price requires a professional appraisal. This bill clarifies exactly what standard an appraiser must use to determine that fair price.

Specifically, the bill says that ESOP managers, called fiduciaries, are legally protected if they hire an independent appraiser who follows a long-standing IRS standard known as Revenue Ruling 59-60. That ruling lays out established methods for valuing a privately held company. Right now, there is some legal uncertainty about whether following that standard is enough to satisfy the law. This bill removes that uncertainty by formally writing the standard into federal retirement law.

This primarily affects employees at privately held companies that have ESOPs, the business owners who want to sell their companies to those plans, and the professional appraisers who value the stock. Supporters would say it makes it easier and less risky to set up ESOPs, which could expand employee ownership. Critics might argue it could make it harder to challenge an appraisal even if employees end up overpaying for company stock.
ai_headline: Bill would anchor ESOP appraisal standard in federal retirement law
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 383.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 5169 writes an IRS appraisal standard into federal law to clarify what counts as a fair stock price for employee ownership plans.
ai_sections.what: HR 5169 addresses how privately held companies must value their stock when selling shares to an Employee Stock Ownership Plan. The bill formally incorporates a long-standing IRS standard, Revenue Ruling 59-60, into federal retirement law. This removes existing legal uncertainty about whether following that standard satisfies the requirement to pay a fair price for shares.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects employees at privately held companies with ESOPs, business owners seeking to sell their companies to those plans, and professional appraisers who determine stock value. ESOP fiduciaries, the managers who oversee these plans, are also directly affected.
ai_sections.why: Codifying the IRS standard could make it easier to establish ESOPs by reducing legal risk for fiduciaries who hire independent appraisers following Revenue Ruling 59-60. At the same time, the change could make it more difficult for employees to challenge an appraisal, even in cases where they may have overpaid for company stock.

title: KAMALA Act
ai_summary:
This bill deals with Community Development Block Grants, which are federal funds the government sends to cities, counties, and states to pay for things like affordable housing, neighborhood improvements, and community services. The bill would make it illegal to use any of that grant money to help people who are not U.S. citizens or legal permanent residents. This would apply starting with money granted in the 2024 fiscal year and beyond.

The bill goes a step further with a broader restriction. It would block an entire city, county, state, or tribal government from receiving any Community Development Block Grant funding if that government runs any housing or community development program that helps undocumented immigrants, even if that program uses separate, local money rather than federal funds. So a city could lose all of its federal block grant money simply for having its own local program that serves undocumented residents.

The people most directly affected would be undocumented immigrants who currently receive services funded through these grants, such as housing assistance or community programs. Local and state governments would also be affected, particularly those in cities or states that have chosen to serve undocumented residents with their own programs, since they could lose significant federal funding. Legal permanent residents and U.S. citizens who rely on these community programs could also be indirectly affected if their local governments lose funding as a result.
ai_headline: Federal housing grants would be cut off for cities that serve undocumented residents
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

Beyond that direct restriction, the bill would deny all block grant funding to any city, county, state, or tribal government that operates its own housing or community development program serving undocumented immigrants, even if that local program uses no federal money.

Local and state governments that have chosen to serve undocumented residents with local funds would also face the loss of significant federal funding, as would the U.S. citizens and legal permanent residents who depend on the same community programs.

The communities those grants support — including affordable housing and neighborhood improvements — could be reduced or eliminated as a result.

title: Dads Matter Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services to launch a national public awareness campaign about the health benefits of fathers being involved during pregnancy, childbirth, and the period after birth. The campaign would share information about how a father's presence and support can improve health outcomes for both mothers and babies, including things like attending prenatal appointments, supporting breastfeeding, recognizing warning signs of complications, and bonding with the newborn through skin-to-skin contact. The department would have two years after the bill becomes law to get this campaign running.

The bill also requires the department to issue guidance to states within one year, helping them encourage hospitals, birth centers, doctors, midwives, and health insurers to train their staff on how to better include and engage fathers in the care process. That guidance would cover topics like how to talk with fathers from different cultural backgrounds, how to screen fathers for depression, and how to give fathers practical information about what to expect before, during, and after birth.

The people most directly affected are expectant and new fathers, pregnant women and new mothers, and the healthcare providers who work with them, including OB-GYNs, pediatricians, and midwives. State health agencies and managed care organizations would also receive new federal guidance under this bill. Six years after passage, the Government Accountability Office would be required to study and report on whether the law actually made a difference.

title: NFIP Extension Act of 2026
ai_summary:
The National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) is a federal program that lets homeowners, renters, and businesses buy flood insurance. Without it, most private companies won't offer flood coverage at all. This bill would extend the program's authorization through September 30, 2026, keeping it legally allowed to operate and sell policies. If the bill passes after the September 30, 2025 deadline has already passed, it would be treated as if it was signed on time, closing any gap in the program.

This kind of bill is called a reauthorization or extension. It does not change how the program works, what it costs, or what it covers. It simply keeps the existing program running for another year rather than letting it expire. Congress has passed many short-term extensions like this one over the years instead of passing a longer-term overhaul.

The people most directly affected are the roughly five million policyholders who currently have NFIP flood insurance, most of whom live in flood-prone areas along coasts, rivers, and low-lying regions. If the program were to lapse, new policies could not be issued and some real estate closings requiring flood insurance could be delayed or blocked. Mortgage lenders, home buyers, and communities in high-risk flood zones all have a stake in whether the program stays active.

title: Vicksburg National Military Park Boundary Modification Act
ai_summary:
This bill would transfer two small pieces of land currently inside Vicksburg National Military Park in Mississippi from the federal government to the state of Mississippi. The first piece is about 3.66 acres, which the state could use to build a welcome center or other public facility. The second piece is about 6.48 acres, intended for an interpretive center, museum, or similar public use. The federal government would hand over this land at no cost to the state. Once the transfer happens, the official boundary of the park would be redrawn to no longer include those parcels.

The bill also requires the Secretary of the Interior to set any conditions on the transfer that seem appropriate, giving the federal government some say in how the land is used going forward. The park itself would continue to exist and operate normally, just with a slightly smaller official boundary.

This bill mainly affects the National Park Service, the state of Mississippi, and visitors or residents in the Vicksburg area. If the state builds a welcome center or museum on the transferred land, local residents and tourists visiting the Civil War battlefield could have new facilities available to them. There is no financial cost to taxpayers for the land transfer itself, though the state would presumably spend its own money to develop the sites.

title: Small Cemetery Conveyance Act
ai_summary:
This bill would allow the U.S. Forest Service to transfer ownership of small cemeteries located on national forest land to certain groups, completely free of charge. Right now, federal land generally cannot be given away without payment, but this bill creates a special exception for burial sites up to 40 acres in size. The land would be transferred to a state or local government, a federally recognized Native American tribe, or a traditional New Mexico community land grant that has a historical connection to that cemetery.

There is an important catch built into the transfer. The new owner can only use the land as a cemetery. If the land ever gets used for anything else, the federal government can take it back. The bill also allows the government to waive the usual paperwork and processing fees if the new owner cannot afford them.

This bill mainly affects communities that have burial grounds sitting on federal forest land but do not legally own or control them. That includes Native American tribes with ancestral burial sites, small towns or counties with old community cemeteries on Forest Service land, and historic Spanish and Mexican land grant communities in New Mexico. Everyday Americans outside those situations would not be directly affected, though the bill does make clear it does not change existing federal law that protects Native American graves and sacred objects.

title: Training and Nutrition Stability
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the government calculates income for people who receive SNAP benefits, which is the federal food assistance program commonly known as food stamps. Right now, if someone on SNAP gets paid through a job training or workforce development program, that money can count as income and potentially reduce or eliminate their food benefits. This bill would change that rule so that money earned through approved job training programs would no longer count against a person's SNAP eligibility or benefit amount.

The bill covers several types of programs, including general workforce training programs, vocational rehabilitation programs for people with disabilities, and refugee employment programs. The idea is that someone trying to build job skills would not have to worry about losing food assistance while they participate in training.

This bill would affect low-income individuals and families who are currently on SNAP and are also enrolled in qualifying job training or employment programs. That includes people with disabilities going through vocational rehab and refugees participating in employment assistance programs. Employers, training organizations, and state agencies that run these programs could also be affected by how they track and report participant earnings.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.

The bill covers general workforce training, vocational rehabilitation programs for people with disabilities, and refugee employment programs. title: American Seabed Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill would ban the U.S. government from issuing any permits or licenses for mining the deep ocean floor or the Outer Continental Shelf, which is the underwater land extending off America's coastlines. The only exception is scientific research, which would still be allowed. The ban applies to exploring for minerals as well as actually extracting them. At the same time, the bill directs the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to work with the National Academies of Sciences to conduct a major study on how ocean floor mining could harm marine ecosystems, ocean life, and the climate.

The study required by the bill would look at a wide range of potential environmental effects, including damage to unique deep-sea species, clouds of sediment stirred up by mining equipment, greenhouse gas emissions, and impacts on fish that people eat. It would also examine whether the minerals found on the ocean floor could be replaced by recycling existing materials or finding alternatives, and would consider impacts on commercial fishing, recreational users, and indigenous communities connected to the ocean.

People most directly affected would be any companies currently seeking permits to mine the ocean floor for minerals like manganese, cobalt, and nickel, which are used in batteries and electronics. Commercial fishermen, indigenous coastal communities, and environmental researchers would also be affected. More broadly, industries that depend on those deep-sea minerals, including electric vehicle and technology manufacturers, could feel indirect effects if ocean floor mining remains off-limits.

Scientific research would remain permitted. title: Ending Chemical Abortions Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would make it a federal crime to prescribe, dispense, distribute, or sell any drug used to end a pregnancy. This mainly targets mifepristone and misoprostol, which are the pills used in medication abortions. Anyone who provides these drugs for the purpose of ending a pregnancy could face up to 25 years in prison and fines. The bill would not punish the woman who takes the medication, only the providers involved in supplying or prescribing it.

There are three exceptions written into the bill. The ban would not apply to contraceptives used before pregnancy is confirmed, to drugs used to treat a miscarriage, or to cases where a physician certifies that the pregnancy puts the woman's life in danger. Ectopic and molar pregnancies are also excluded from the definition of abortion, so treating those conditions would not be covered by the ban.

This bill would affect doctors, pharmacists, and other medical providers who currently prescribe or dispense these medications. It would also affect patients, since medication abortion currently accounts for more than half of all abortions in the United States. The bill has been referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has not yet been voted on.
ai_headline: Bill would make prescribing abortion pills a federal crime
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

The bill includes exceptions for contraceptives used before pregnancy is confirmed, drugs used to treat a miscarriage, cases where a physician certifies the pregnancy endangers the woman's life, and treatment of ectopic or molar pregnancies. The bill has been referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has not yet been voted on.

title: National Food as Medicine Program Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would create a federal grant program allowing states to use Medicaid funding to provide certain patients with medically prescribed food and nutrition support. The Department of Health and Human Services would give grants to states to build or expand these "Food as Medicine" programs, which could include giving eligible Medicaid patients fresh fruits and vegetables, medically tailored meals, and nutrition coaching prescribed by a doctor or dietitian. The food provided must come from local or regional farms using organic or regenerative farming methods when possible. States would be required to report back on the program's results, such as whether participants had fewer hospital visits or needed less medication.

The Department of Agriculture would also have a role, working with universities, food hubs, and regional food business centers to help farmers connect with local healthcare providers so they can supply food for these programs. The bill gives priority to helping beginning farmers and socially disadvantaged farmers participate as suppliers.

The people most directly affected are low-income Americans who receive Medicaid benefits, particularly those with diet-related chronic conditions like diabetes, heart disease, or obesity, as well as people experiencing food insecurity. Small and mid-sized farmers using organic or regenerative practices could also benefit by gaining a new market through healthcare partnerships. Healthcare providers would receive new guidance and training on how to incorporate food-based treatments into patient care.

title: ARMENIA Security Partnership Act
ai_summary:
This bill deals with the relationship between two countries in the South Caucasus region: Armenia and Azerbaijan. It requires the U.S. Secretary of Defense to check, within 180 days and every year after that, whether Azerbaijan has taken real steps toward peace. Those steps include pulling its military out of Armenian territory, releasing Armenian prisoners, stopping attacks on Armenia, and allowing ethnic Armenians who fled the Nagorno-Karabakh region to return home. Nagorno-Karabakh is a disputed territory that Azerbaijan took full control of in 2023, causing most of its ethnic Armenian population to flee.

If the Secretary of Defense cannot confirm that Azerbaijan is making meaningful progress on those points, two things happen automatically. First, the Pentagon must quickly review what military aid and training the U.S. is currently giving Armenia, look for gaps in Armenia's ability to defend itself, and report those findings to Congress. Second, the President loses the ability to use a special legal waiver that normally allows the U.S. to send certain aid to Azerbaijan. That waiver comes from a 2002 law, and blocking it would be a direct consequence of Azerbaijan not meeting the listed conditions.

This bill primarily affects U.S. foreign and defense policy toward Armenia and Azerbaijan. It does not directly change anything for everyday Americans at home, but it could shape how much military support and aid flows to both countries. Members of the Armenian-American community have a strong interest in the outcome, and U.S. defense contractors or agencies involved in foreign military assistance could also be affected depending on how the reviews turn out.
ai_headline: Bill ties U.S. military aid to Azerbaijan's peace steps toward Armenia
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs.

Those steps include withdrawing from Armenian territory, releasing prisoners, halting attacks, and allowing displaced ethnic Armenians from Nagorno-Karabakh to return. If the Secretary cannot confirm progress, two automatic consequences follow: a Pentagon review of Armenia's defense gaps and a block on the presidential waiver that permits certain U.S. aid to Azerbaijan.

ai_sections.why: Blocking the waiver would remove a legal tool the President currently uses to send certain aid to Azerbaijan, a power granted under a 2002 law. The mandatory defense review could reshape the volume and type of military support flowing to both countries.

title: Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation Land Exchange Act
ai_summary:
This bill sets up a land swap between the federal government and the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation, a federally recognized Native American tribe in San Bernardino County, California. The tribe would give the U.S. government about 1,460 acres of land it currently owns, and in return the federal government would hand over about 1,475 acres of San Bernardino National Forest land to the tribe. The exchanged land is in the same general area, and the deal must be completed within 120 days once the tribe formally makes its offer.

The National Forest land given to the tribe would become tribal property, while the land the tribe gives up would be added to the San Bernardino National Forest and managed like the rest of that forest. The federal government keeps the right to use certain existing Forest Service roads that run through the land it transfers to the tribe. The tribe also must agree in writing to protect a well-known local landmark called the Arrowhead, a natural rock formation that is historically and culturally significant.

This bill directly affects the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation and the U.S. Forest Service. It also has some impact on local residents and visitors in the San Bernardino area, since land that was previously part of a national forest would change hands. People who hike or use those Forest Service roads would still have access to them. The general public can view the maps showing exactly which land is being exchanged at Forest Service offices.

title: Arctic Refuge Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill would cancel the oil and gas drilling program that was set up inside the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR) in Alaska. That drilling program was created by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. If this bill passed, all leases, permits, and plans connected to oil and gas development in that area would be wiped off the books.

The bill would also officially label about 1.56 million acres of ANWR's coastal plain as federally protected wilderness. Under the Wilderness Act, that designation would ban roads, buildings, vehicles, and most commercial activity in the area permanently. The land would be managed by the Department of the Interior alongside the wilderness areas already existing within the refuge.

This bill most directly affects energy companies that hold or might seek oil and gas leases in ANWR, as well as the state of Alaska, which would lose potential revenue from drilling activity. Indigenous communities in the region, particularly the Gwich'in and Iñupiat peoples who have different views on drilling there, would also be affected. American energy consumers and the broader oil industry could feel indirect effects depending on how much oil the refuge might have produced. The bill was introduced by House Democrats and referred to the Natural Resources Committee, where it would need to advance before any further votes.
ai_headline: House bill would end ANWR drilling and lock away 1.56 million acres as wilderness
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.

title: INFORM Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would require the federal government to notify the family of an immigration detainee within 24 hours whenever that person is moved to a different detention facility. The notification must include the reason for the transfer and the new facility's name, address, phone number, and a contact person. Right now, there is no federal law requiring this kind of notice, which means families can lose track of a detained loved one when they are moved.

The bill applies to anyone held by the Department of Homeland Security under immigration law. "Immediate family" is defined broadly to include parents, children, siblings, spouses, stepfamily members, foster family members, and partners in civil unions or domestic partnerships.

This bill would most directly affect immigrants currently in detention and their families. It would also create a new requirement for the Department of Homeland Security and the facilities that house detainees. The bill was introduced in the House in August 2025 and has been referred to the House Judiciary Committee, meaning it has not yet been voted on.

title: Pro Codes Act
ai_summary:
This bill deals with technical standards that governments write into law by reference. Many safety codes and technical rules used by federal, state, and local governments are actually written by private organizations, not by the government itself. Instead of copying those standards word for word into a law, governments often just point to them and say "follow this standard." The bill says that when that happens, the private organization that created the standard must make it freely readable online, with a searchable table of contents, so ordinary people can look up the rules that apply to them. In return, the organization keeps its copyright and can still sell copies or subscriptions to people who want to buy them.

The bill sets a clear deal: free public reading access in exchange for keeping copyright protection. The online version has to meet federal accessibility requirements so people with disabilities can use it too. Creating a free account or agreeing to basic terms of service is allowed, but the organization cannot charge money or collect personal data without the user's permission. If someone claims an organization is not living up to these rules, the person making that claim has to prove it in court, not the other way around.

This affects private standards organizations, such as those that write building codes, electrical codes, or safety standards, as well as federal agencies, state and local governments, and everyday people who need to know what rules legally apply to their homes, businesses, or workplaces. Currently, many of these standards cost money to access even though they carry the force of law. The bill would require free online reading access for any standard that has been written into law or regulation.
ai_headline: Bill would require free online access to safety codes written into law
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 4072 requires private standards organizations to post legally binding codes online for free, while retaining their copyright.

The online version must meet federal accessibility requirements so people with disabilities can use it. Organizations may require a free account or basic terms of service agreement, but cannot charge money or collect personal data without user permission.

title: PAR Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes a rule in the tax code that currently blocks certain tax-exempt bonds from being used to fund private or commercial golf courses and country clubs. Right now, when local governments or other entities issue a special type of low-interest bond called a "small issue" or "qualified private activity bond," the money raised cannot go toward golf courses or country clubs. This bill would remove golf courses and country clubs from that restricted list, making them eligible for that type of financing.

The bill also affects two related programs. In federal Empowerment Zones and Opportunity Zones, businesses that qualify for certain tax breaks currently cannot include private golf courses or country clubs. This bill would change that, allowing those businesses to qualify for the same tax incentives available to other businesses in those zones.

This mainly affects developers, investors, and business owners who want to build or improve private or commercial golf courses and country clubs in areas covered by these tax programs. It could also affect local governments that use these types of bonds to attract development. Everyday residents in Empowerment Zones or Opportunity Zones could be indirectly affected if golf-related businesses bring jobs or development to their communities.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: To take certain land into trust for the benefit of the Las Vegas Tribe of Paiute Indians.
ai_summary:
This bill would transfer about 3,156 acres of federal land currently managed by the Bureau of Land Management to the U.S. government to hold "in trust" for the Las Vegas Tribe of Paiute Indians. When land is held in trust this way, it becomes part of the tribe's official reservation and is protected for their long-term use. The federal government acts as a kind of legal guardian over the land on the tribe's behalf. The bill also requires a survey to be done within 180 days to formally mark the boundaries of this new trust land.

There are a few important conditions attached to the land transfer. The tribe must allow a roughly 300-foot strip of the land to be used as a right-of-way for high-voltage electric power lines connected to renewable energy projects. No casino-style gambling of any kind is allowed on this specific land. The bill also makes clear that existing water rights and a 2021 agreement between the tribe and the City of Las Vegas remain unchanged.

The people most directly affected are members of the Las Vegas Tribe of Paiute Indians, who would gain a significantly larger reservation. People living or working near the land in the Las Vegas, Nevada area could also be affected, since the land use and governance of that area would change. The bill also matters to energy companies involved in renewable power transmission in the region, since they are guaranteed access to run power lines across part of the land.

title: Susan E. Lukas 9/11 Servicemember Fairness Act
ai_summary:
This bill focuses on military veterans who were stationed at the Pentagon on or after the September 11, 2001 terrorist attack. When the Pentagon was hit that day, the building burned and collapsed in one section, releasing toxic smoke, jet fuel fumes, and other harmful materials into the air. Service members who worked at the Pentagon in the weeks that followed were potentially exposed to those hazardous substances. The bill covers the period from September 11, 2001 through November 19, 2001.

The core change the bill makes is called a "presumption of service connection." Right now, a veteran who gets sick must prove to the Department of Veterans Affairs that their illness was directly caused by their military service, which can be difficult and time-consuming. This bill would flip that process for covered veterans. If a qualifying veteran develops certain illnesses, the VA would automatically assume the illness is connected to their Pentagon service, without requiring the veteran to produce records proving it.

The illnesses covered are broad and include asthma, emphysema, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, any type of cancer, any cardiovascular disease, any skin disease, and any respiratory disease. Veterans who qualify are those who were actively stationed at the Pentagon Reservation during that roughly ten-week window after 9/11. The bill is named after Susan E. Lukas, though no background on her is provided in the text itself.
ai_headline: Pentagon 9/11 veterans would get automatic VA illness coverage under new bill
last_action_text: Forwarded by Subcommittee to Full Committee by Voice Vote.

That presumption means the VA would automatically treat covered illnesses as linked to Pentagon service, removing the requirement that veterans individually prove the connection. Covered illnesses include asthma, emphysema, COPD, any cancer, any cardiovascular disease, any skin disease, and any respiratory disease.

title: Fit to Serve Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal law to ban the military from treating service members differently based on their gender identity. That includes people whose gender identity does not match the sex they were assigned at birth, as well as anyone diagnosed or potentially diagnosed with gender dysphoria. Specifically, the military could not use gender identity as a reason to set enlistment rules, force someone out of service, deny them healthcare, or block them from joining or re-enlisting.

The bill directly affects transgender and nonbinary people who want to serve in or are already serving in the U.S. Armed Forces. It would also affect military branches and their leadership, since they would be required to follow these new rules in how they recruit, retain, and provide medical care to service members.

This bill has been introduced in the House and sent to the Armed Services Committee, which means it has not become law yet. It is a response to ongoing policy debates about who is eligible to serve in the military. Whether it advances further in Congress is uncertain.

title: BRAVE Act of 2025
ai_summary:
The BRAVE Act of 2025 is a bill focused on improving mental health care for military veterans through the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). It directs the VA to study whether mental health counselors at Vet Centers are being paid fairly compared to similar jobs in the private sector, and to report any staffing problems caused by low pay. The bill also orders reviews of how well Vet Centers are expanding their locations, especially in rural areas, and requires the VA to update its technology systems used to run those centers. Additionally, it calls for better coordination between Vet Centers and VA hospitals to make sure high-risk veterans do not fall through the cracks.

The bill includes specific attention to women veterans. It requires the VA to survey women veterans to find out whether current suicide prevention programs actually work for them, since risks like military sexual trauma and domestic violence are not always reflected in existing tools. The VA would be required to update its REACH VET program, which identifies veterans at risk of mental health crises, to better account for those risks specific to women. The bill also looks at whether retreat-based therapy programs for veterans and their families are meeting demand, including programs for women and veterans with disabilities.

The bill affects U.S. military veterans broadly, especially those using VA mental health services, Vet Centers, or transitioning out of the military. Women veterans, veterans with spinal cord injuries, and those in rural areas would see particular attention under this bill. It also extends and increases funding for an existing suicide prevention grant program and requires the VA and Department of Defense to work together more effectively on mental health care for service members moving back into civilian life.
ai_headline: VA ordered to study pay gaps and expand mental health access for veterans
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Health.

The bill extends and increases funding for an existing suicide prevention grant program.

title: Working Americans’ Tax Cut Act
ai_summary:
This bill has two main parts that work together. The first part caps how much federal income tax lower- and middle-income people have to pay. Specifically, if your income is below about 175% of a set "cost-of-living" amount (roughly $80,500 for a single person, based on the bill's $46,000 baseline), your total federal income tax cannot exceed 25.5% of your income above that baseline cost-of-living amount. The idea is that money needed just to cover basic living expenses would not be taxed. The baseline amount adjusts each year with inflation.

The second part adds a new surcharge on top of regular income taxes for very high earners. Single filers pay an extra 5% on income between $1 million and $2 million, 10% on income between $2 million and $5 million, and 12% on income above $5 million. Married couples filing jointly get higher thresholds before these rates kick in. These dollar amounts also adjust for inflation over time. Both parts of the bill would take effect starting with the 2026 tax year.

Lower- and middle-income workers would potentially see a tax reduction or cap on what they owe, while individuals earning over $1 million annually would face higher tax bills than they do under current law. People in between those income ranges would generally not be directly affected by either provision.
ai_headline: Tax bill caps burdens on lower earners, adds surcharge above $1 million
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7937 caps federal income tax for earners below ~$80,500 baseline and adds up to 12% surcharge on incomes above $5 million, starting 2026.

First, it limits total federal income tax to 25.5% of income above a baseline cost-of-living amount, set at roughly $80,500 for a single person, for those earning below about 175% of that baseline. title: Sunshine Protection Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would make daylight saving time permanent across the United States. Right now, most Americans set their clocks forward one hour in the spring and back one hour in the fall. If this bill becomes law, that clock-changing routine would end, and the country would stay on daylight saving time all year long. Practically speaking, that means mornings would be darker in winter but evenings would stay lighter later.

The bill works by changing the legal definition of standard time in each U.S. time zone, shifting it forward by one hour. States that already opted out of daylight saving time, like Arizona and Hawaii, would have a choice to keep their current time setup or adopt the new permanent daylight saving time. They would not be forced to change.

This bill affects virtually every person living in the United States, since time zones touch daily life in areas like work schedules, school start times, television programming, and travel. Businesses that operate across time zones, airlines, and anyone who coordinates with other countries could also see changes in how they manage scheduling. The bill was introduced in January 2025 and has been sent to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, where it would need to advance before any further votes could happen.

title: Fight Book Bans Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a federal grant program run by the U.S. Department of Education. When a school district decides to keep a book or other teaching material available to students, and someone challenges that decision through a legal or formal appeals process, the school district could apply for federal money to help pay its legal costs. Grants could cover up to $100,000 per case, for things like attorney fees and court costs. The total program would be funded at up to $15 million between 2027 and 2031.

The key detail is what triggers the grant: it only applies when a school district chose to keep a material, not remove it, and then faced a formal challenge to that decision. If a school district decided to remove a book and someone challenged that removal, this grant would not apply. The bill also requires that the government award grants using neutral criteria, meaning the actual content of the book or material in question cannot be a factor in deciding who gets the money.

This bill would most directly affect public school districts that receive federal education funding and face legal challenges after deciding to keep instructional or library materials in use. It could also indirectly affect students, parents, and communities involved in disputes over school books and curriculum materials. School districts, their lawyers, and ultimately local taxpayers could feel the financial effects of whether such grants become available.

title: MATCH Act
ai_summary:
The MATCH Act would tighten US controls on the sale and transfer of chip-making equipment to countries like China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and Cuba. Within 150 days of becoming law, the federal government would be required to block American companies from exporting specialized semiconductor manufacturing machinery to factories in those countries. It would also block foreign-made equipment from reaching those factories if the equipment contains enough American technology or parts to fall under US rules. Notably, the bill targets specific Chinese companies by name, including SMIC, Huawei, and YMTC, treating them as high-priority threats.

The bill also pushes US allies to match these restrictions. The government would immediately begin diplomatic talks with countries like Japan, the Netherlands, and South Korea, which also make this kind of equipment, to get them to adopt the same export bans. If an ally refuses or drags its feet past the 150-day deadline, the US would use its own rules to extend American legal authority over that country's chip equipment exports, essentially forcing compliance by threatening to cut off access to US technology components those allied manufacturers depend on.

The law would last five years before expiring. It mainly affects US and allied companies that make and sell semiconductor manufacturing equipment, chip factories located in the listed countries, and the global semiconductor supply chain more broadly. Everyday American consumers are not directly targeted, though the bill could have ripple effects on technology products and global chip prices over time.

title: To amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to temporarily suspend certain fuel excise taxes for fuel separated during periods in which the national average price of gasoline exceeds $3.99 per gallon, and to prohibit certain credits or deductions for oil and gas companies during such periods.
ai_summary:
This bill creates a two-part system that kicks in automatically whenever the national average price of gasoline goes above $3.99 per gallon. First, it temporarily cuts the federal fuel excise tax that refiners and fuel distributors pay when gasoline or diesel enters the market. The tax reduction is calculated cent-for-cent based on how far above $3.99 the price rises. So if the average price is $4.49, the tax would drop by 50 cents per gallon. The idea is that this tax cut would be passed along the supply chain and eventually lower prices at the pump. Importantly, the bill also requires the federal government to replace the lost tax revenue by transferring money from the general treasury into the Highway Trust Fund and the Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund, so road and infrastructure funding would not be reduced.

The second part of the bill works in the opposite direction for oil and gas companies. During those same high-price periods, it takes away three specific tax benefits that oil and gas producers currently use: a deduction for certain drilling costs, a tax credit for enhanced oil recovery projects, and a tax credit for production from low-output oil and gas wells. The goal appears to be offsetting the cost of the fuel tax cut by reducing tax breaks for producers while prices are high.

This bill would affect several groups. Everyday drivers could potentially see lower gas prices if the tax savings are passed through to retail fuel costs, though that is not guaranteed. Oil and gas companies would lose access to certain tax deductions and credits during high-price periods, which would increase their tax bills. Fuel distributors and refiners would deal with the changed tax calculations. The bill applies starting with tax year 2026 and has no set end date beyond the automatic price trigger.
ai_headline: Bill would cut federal gas tax automatically when prices top $3.99 a gallon
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: CHAMPVA Children’s Care Protection Act of 2025
ai_summary:
CHAMPVA is a federal health insurance program that covers medical costs for certain family members of veterans who are permanently disabled due to a service-connected condition, or who died in the line of duty. Right now, children in this program lose their coverage when they turn 23. This bill would raise that cutoff age to 26, matching the age limit that exists for most private health insurance plans under the Affordable Care Act.

The change would take effect as soon as the bill becomes law, meaning any covered child who is currently between ages 23 and 25 could regain eligibility right away. The bill also makes clear that children with permanent disabilities who are already covered beyond the normal age limit would not be negatively affected by this change.

This bill directly affects the children of eligible veterans, specifically those whose parent is either permanently and totally disabled from a service-related injury or died from a service-connected cause. It would allow those young adults to stay on CHAMPVA coverage through age 25, rather than having to find their own insurance at 23. Veterans themselves are not affected, as they receive care through a separate VA system.

title: United States-Israel Defense Partnership Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill creates several new programs to deepen military cooperation between the United States and Israel. The biggest piece is a new joint program focused on countering drones and other unmanned aircraft, with up to $150 million per year authorized from 2026 through 2030. It also extends and increases funding for two existing programs, one dealing with underground tunnels used by military groups and another already focused on drone defense, and adds $50 million per year for joint research into cutting-edge technologies like artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and robotics. The bill also extends the U.S. military's authority to store weapons and equipment in Israel through 2029 and directs the Pentagon to open a Defense Innovation Unit office in Israel within six months.

Beyond the spending pieces, the bill asks the Defense Department to look into whether Israel could formally join the "national technology and industrial base," a legal category that currently includes the U.S., Canada, Australia, and the United Kingdom, and that allows closer sharing of defense contracts and technology. It also requires the Pentagon to assess how well air and missile defense systems work across the Middle East region, looking at lessons from Iranian missile attacks on Israel in 2024 and identifying what more money or legal changes might be needed to improve regional defense cooperation.

The people most directly affected are U.S. and Israeli military and defense personnel, defense contractors and technology companies in both countries who could compete for the new research and development work, and U.S. taxpayers who would fund the authorized spending. Broader regional effects could reach other Middle Eastern countries that coordinate with the U.S. on missile defense, and indirectly, any groups or nations whose use of drones or tunnels as military tools these programs are designed to counter.

title: Crucial Communism Teaching Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation, a nonprofit organization established by Congress, to create a high school civics curriculum about communism and totalitarianism. The curriculum would cover historical and current communist governments, their human rights records, and how those systems compare to American democratic values. It would also include a collection of personal stories from people who lived under communist rule, called "Portraits in Patriotism." The Foundation would then work with state and local school officials to make these materials available to schools.

The bill does not require any school to actually use the curriculum. It only funds and creates the educational materials and makes them available. The curriculum is designed to fit into existing classes like social studies, history, government, and economics. It would be updated over time to include current events, such as China's treatment of Uyghur Muslims and tensions around Taiwan and Hong Kong.

The people most directly affected would be high school students if their schools choose to adopt these materials, along with teachers and school administrators who would decide whether to use them. The Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation would take on the work of building and distributing the curriculum. There is no funding amount specified in the bill's text, and it has been referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, meaning it has not yet become law.

title: Medical Research for Our Troops Act
ai_summary:
This bill would restore about $1.18 billion in funding to the Defense Health Agency's medical research budget. Earlier in 2025, a government funding law accidentally or intentionally cut that money out. This bill would put it back, as if the cut had never happened.

The restored money would go specifically to something called the Congressionally Directed Medical Research Programs, or CDMRP. These are research programs that Congress has personally approved to study diseases and health conditions. The bill requires the Department of Defense to fund those programs at the same levels and in the same way they were funded under a 2024 spending law, following a specific list of projects outlined on certain pages of that law's documentation.

The people most directly affected are military service members, veterans, and their families, since CDMRP research focuses heavily on health conditions that affect troops, such as cancer, traumatic brain injury, and other illnesses. Scientists, universities, and medical institutions that receive grants through these programs would also be affected, since their funding was at risk of being cut off. The bill does not create any new programs — it simply tries to restore money that was already planned and approved.

title: Buying American Cotton Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill creates a new federal tax credit for businesses that sell finished products made with American-grown cotton. The credit is calculated based on how much U.S. cotton is in the product, its market price, and a percentage that varies depending on where the cotton was processed. Companies get a higher credit rate (24%) if the cotton was processed entirely in the United States or in countries that have a trade agreement with the U.S., and a lower rate (18%) if any processing happened in a country without such an agreement. Businesses that make U.S. cotton into yarn or fabric can receive even larger credits, up to 6.5 times the base amount for fabric. To qualify, companies must track the cotton digitally through the entire supply chain using a government identification number tied to each bale of cotton.

The bill affects businesses across the textile and apparel supply chain, including cotton farmers, textile mills, clothing manufacturers, and retailers. Any company that sells a finished cotton-containing product at the retail level could potentially claim this credit, as long as the cotton was grown in the United States and properly tracked. The credit can only be claimed once per batch of cotton, so companies must notify buyers about whether they plan to use it, preventing double-dipping. Businesses can also transfer the credit to other parties under existing tax law.

Everyday consumers are not directly involved in claiming anything, but the credit is designed to make American cotton more financially attractive to manufacturers. Whether that leads to lower prices, more domestic jobs, or other effects on shoppers would depend on how businesses respond to the incentive.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: Defense Community Infrastructure Program Tribal Eligibility Act of 2026
ai_summary:
The Defense Community Infrastructure Program (DCIP) is an existing federal program that helps pay for improvements to roads, utilities, schools, and other infrastructure in communities located near military bases. The idea is that military installations put a strain on nearby areas, so the program helps those communities handle that extra demand. Right now, the law allows state and local governments to apply for this funding, but tribal governments are not included. This bill would change the law to add federally recognized Indian tribes to the list of eligible applicants.

If passed, tribal governments that are located near military installations would be able to apply for DCIP grants to improve local infrastructure just like a city or county government can. The bill also adds a clear definition of "Indian tribe" by pointing to an existing federal law, the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act, so there is no confusion about who qualifies.

This bill would most directly affect federally recognized Native American tribes whose lands are near U.S. military bases, as well as the people who live in those communities. It would also affect the Department of Defense, which runs the DCIP program and would now be responsible for reviewing and potentially approving tribal applications for funding.

title: Protecting Life from Chemical Abortions Act
ai_summary:
This bill does two main things. First, it blocks the Secretary of Health and Human Services from declaring a public health emergency related to abortion. Some states have used or considered using public health emergency powers to expand access to abortion medications or services, and this bill would prevent that at the federal level and cancel any such declaration already in place. Second, the bill requires that abortion pills, such as mifepristone, can only be given to patients in person at a clinic, medical office, or hospital by a certified provider. During and after the COVID-19 pandemic, federal rules had been loosened to allow these medications to be prescribed online and mailed to patients. This bill would reverse that and bring back the stricter in-person requirement permanently.

The bill also puts conditions on any future loosening of rules around abortion pills. Before federal health officials could reduce any safety requirements, every state would first have to report detailed abortion data to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That data would include information like the patient's age, race, how far along the pregnancy was, the method used, and whether the fetus survived, among other details. Currently, reporting abortion data to the CDC is voluntary for states, and not all states participate.

This bill primarily affects people who are pregnant and seeking medication abortion, particularly those in areas without easy access to a clinic or doctor who provides abortion services. It also affects doctors, pharmacists, and telehealth providers who currently prescribe or dispense abortion pills remotely. States and federal health agencies would also be affected, since their authority to respond to abortion-related health situations using emergency powers would be limited.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: Veterinary Services to Improve Public Health in Rural Communities Act
ai_summary:
This bill would allow the Indian Health Service to provide veterinary and animal health services to Native American tribes and tribal organizations, with a focus on preventing diseases that can spread from animals to people, like rabies. Specifically, it would fund services such as vaccinating animals, spaying and neutering pets, tracking disease outbreaks, and other efforts to reduce health risks in tribal communities. The government could send public health veterinarians into these areas and would need to report to Congress every two years on how the program is working.

The bill also directs the U.S. Department of Agriculture to study whether oral rabies vaccines can be effectively delivered to wild animals in Arctic parts of the United States. This is important because wildlife like foxes and other animals in those remote regions can spread rabies to people, and reaching them with traditional methods is difficult. The study would look at how well those vaccines work and suggest ways to improve delivery.

The people most directly affected are members of Native American tribes living in rural and remote areas, including Alaska, where access to veterinary care is limited and the risk of animal-borne diseases is higher. It also adds the Indian Health Service as a formal participant in the federal government's broader public health emergency planning framework, giving tribal health needs a more official seat at the table.

title: Medicare Audiology Access Improvement Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes how Medicare covers hearing care. Right now, Medicare patients usually need a doctor's referral or order before seeing an audiologist, and coverage is limited mostly to diagnostic tests. Starting January 1, 2027, this bill would allow audiologists to see Medicare patients directly, without a referral or doctor's supervision. It would also expand what services audiologists can provide under Medicare to include both diagnostic and treatment services, as long as those services are legal under the audiologist's state license.

The bill also sets how Medicare would pay for these services. Medicare would cover 80 percent of the approved cost, meaning patients would be responsible for the remaining 20 percent, the same cost-sharing structure used for most other Medicare Part B services. The bill also allows audiologists to work in rural health clinics and federally qualified health centers, which are clinics that serve lower-income and underserved communities.

This bill mainly affects Medicare beneficiaries, who are generally adults 65 and older, as well as younger people on Medicare due to disability. It also affects audiologists, who would gain more independence to treat patients without physician oversight. Doctors and other healthcare providers who currently oversee or refer patients for hearing care could also see their role in that process change.
ai_headline: Medicare patients could see audiologists without a referral starting 2027

title: Veterans Member Business Loan Act
ai_summary:
Current law limits how much money federal credit unions can lend out as "member business loans," capping that total at 12.25% of the credit union's assets. This bill changes the rules by removing loans made to veterans from that category entirely. That means when a credit union gives a business loan to a veteran, it would not count toward the cap.

The practical effect is that credit unions could lend more money to veteran-owned businesses without bumping into the legal limit. Right now, once a credit union gets close to its cap, it has to turn away business loan applicants. By excluding veteran loans from the count, credit unions would have more room to approve those loans.

This bill mainly affects two groups. First, veterans who want to start or grow a business and are members of a federal credit union would have an easier time getting a loan. Second, federal credit unions that serve veterans would have more flexibility in their lending. The change would kick in six months after the bill is signed into law.
ai_headline: Business loans to veterans would no longer count against credit union lending caps
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

title: Fraud Accountability and Recovery Act
ai_summary:
This bill would cut off U.S. foreign aid to any country that refuses to hand over people convicted of defrauding the U.S. government, or that refuses to help return stolen federal money. If a foreign country shelters a convicted fraudster or won't help freeze and return stolen funds, the President would be required to stop sending that country assistance money. The President can make an exception only by telling Congress in writing that cutting off aid would hurt national security, and must do so at least 15 days before the waiver takes effect.

The bill was partly inspired by a real case in Minnesota, where a nonprofit called Feeding Our Future stole over $250 million meant to feed children during the COVID-19 pandemic. Some of that money was sent overseas, including to Kenya, putting it out of reach of U.S. authorities. The bill would require the State Department to publish a yearly report naming countries that are not cooperating with fraud recovery efforts and estimating how much stolen money remains unrecovered because of their inaction.

This bill mainly affects the executive branch, which manages foreign aid, and foreign governments that receive U.S. assistance. It could also affect Americans and organizations involved in federal programs, since it aims to make it harder for fraudsters to hide stolen money abroad. Ordinary U.S. taxpayers are the broader group the bill is designed to protect, since the fraud losses it references come from federal programs funded by tax dollars.
ai_headline: Bill would cut U.S. aid to countries shielding federal fraud convicts
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs.

title: Kidney Care Access Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes several changes to how Medicare pays for kidney dialysis care. First, it extends special temporary payments for new dialysis drugs and medical devices from two years to at least three years. After that temporary period ends, dialysis centers would receive a permanent extra payment equal to 65 percent of what those new drugs actually cost, updated each year for inflation. The bill also makes sure that Medicare Advantage plans, which are private versions of Medicare, pay dialysis centers the same way regular Medicare does for these newer treatments. Separately, it adjusts how Medicare updates its dialysis payment rates each year to better account for actual price changes, fixing errors in past payment estimates going back to 2021 and 2022.

The bill also expands two Medicare benefits related to kidney health. Starting in 2026, Medicare's free annual wellness visit would include screening for chronic kidney disease. Currently, education sessions to help patients understand their kidney disease and treatment options are only available to people with stage IV kidney disease, but this bill would add people with stage V as well. It also allows dialysis centers and nurse practitioners and physician assistants, not just doctors, to provide and bill for those education sessions.

The people most directly affected are the roughly 800,000 Americans on Medicare who have end-stage renal disease and rely on dialysis, as well as the clinics that treat them. Patients could gain access to newer drugs and devices more quickly because dialysis centers would have stronger financial reasons to offer them. Older Medicare enrollees who have not yet reached end-stage kidney disease could also be affected, since the expanded wellness screenings might catch kidney problems earlier.
ai_headline: Medicare dialysis payment rules would shift under HR 6214
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Ways and Means, and in addition to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

Separately, it corrects errors in how Medicare calculated annual dialysis payment rate updates going back to 2021 and 2022.

title: Honoring our K9 Heroes Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates a grant program through the Department of Homeland Security to help pay for medical care for retired federal working dogs. These are dogs that served with federal law enforcement or military agencies and have officially been given retirement status by their agency. To qualify for the grants, the dog must also be living with its former handler. The program would be authorized to spend up to $1 million per year from 2026 through 2030.

The grants would not go directly to individual dog owners. Instead, the money would go to nonprofit organizations that already have at least two years of experience helping cover medical costs for retired federal law enforcement and military dogs. These organizations would apply to the government and then use the funds to help cover a portion of veterinary and medical expenses for qualifying retired dogs.

The people most directly affected are the former handlers who adopted their working dogs after retirement, since the program could reduce the out-of-pocket costs of caring for animals that may have health issues from years of service. Nonprofit groups that support retired working animals would also be affected, as they would have access to a new source of federal funding to expand their work.

title: Leveling the Playing Field 2.0 Act
ai_summary:
This bill updates the rules the US government uses to protect American businesses from unfair foreign competition. Right now, US law allows the government to place extra taxes called antidumping and countervailing duties on imported goods when foreign companies sell products in the US at unfairly low prices or when foreign governments subsidize their companies. This bill strengthens and tightens those rules in several ways. For example, it makes it harder for foreign companies to dodge existing tariffs by slightly changing their products or routing them through a third country. It also allows the government to treat a foreign country's currency manipulation as an illegal subsidy, potentially triggering extra import taxes.

The bill also targets situations where foreign governments distort the true cost of making goods, such as by controlling the price of raw materials or ignoring labor and environmental laws. It gives US trade investigators more tools and clearer legal authority to account for those distortions when calculating fair prices. It also creates stricter rules for foreign-based importers, requiring them to hold enough US assets to cover any duties they might owe, so they cannot simply disappear and avoid paying.

American manufacturers, factory workers, and domestic industries that compete with foreign imports would be the most directly affected, as the bill is designed to give them stronger legal protection. Importers, especially foreign-based ones, would face tougher requirements and potential penalties. American consumers could see some effect as well, since stronger tariff enforcement may result in higher prices on certain imported goods. The bill also applies to goods coming from Canada and Mexico under the existing US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement.
ai_headline: Bill tightens US tariff rules to close foreign trade loopholes
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 1548 strengthens antidumping and trade duty rules to block foreign companies from dodging US import taxes.

The bill closes loopholes that let foreign companies avoid tariffs by slightly altering products or rerouting shipments through third countries. It also allows investigators to treat foreign currency manipulation as an illegal subsidy and gives them clearer authority to account for distorted production costs caused by government price controls or ignored labor and environmental laws.

ai_sections.why: Stronger tariff enforcement may result in higher prices on certain imported goods for American consumers. The bill also extends its rules to goods arriving from Canada and Mexico under the existing US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement.

title: Biotechnology for All High School Students Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the National Science Foundation to create a grant program that gives money to high schools, school districts, colleges, and nonprofits to build or expand biotechnology education. Schools could use the funding to train teachers, buy lab equipment, develop course materials, and set up credentials students can carry into college or the workforce. The grants would be competitive, meaning schools apply and the strongest proposals win funding, with priority going to schools that currently have little access to these kinds of resources.

The bill also requires the creation of a National Biotechnology Education Consortium within six months of the law passing. This group, made up of at least six members from government agencies, schools, and the biotech industry, would advise the NSF on how to run the program effectively. The consortium would automatically shut down after five years.

The people most directly affected are high school students, especially those in schools with fewer science resources, along with their teachers and school administrators. Schools in underserved communities are specifically mentioned as a priority for funding. Colleges, nonprofits, and private biotech companies could also be involved as partners in these programs.

title: Protect Elections from Deceptive AI Act
ai_summary:
This bill would make it illegal to knowingly share AI-generated images, audio, or video that falsely depicts a federal candidate — such as a fake video showing a candidate saying something they never said — if the goal is to influence an election or raise money. The fake content has to be convincing enough that a reasonable person would be misled about what the candidate actually said or did. The ban applies to individuals, political campaigns, and outside groups.

There are some important exceptions. News organizations can show this kind of content if they clearly disclose that it may not be authentic. Satire and parody are also allowed, so political comedy that is obviously not real would not be covered.

If someone breaks this rule, the candidate shown in the fake content can sue for damages and ask a court to stop the content from spreading further. The person bringing the lawsuit has to prove the violation with a high level of evidence. Any violation would also automatically count as defamation under the law. This bill primarily affects political campaigns, outside groups that run election ads, and anyone who creates or shares AI-generated election content online.
ai_headline: Bill would ban deceptive AI fakes of federal candidates before elections
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on House Administration.

The fake content must be realistic enough to mislead a reasonable person. Satire, parody, and news disclosures are exempt from the ban.

title: Amending title 36, United States Code, to direct the President to issue an annual proclamation establishing Democracy Day.
ai_summary:
This bill would require the President to officially declare one day each year as "Democracy Day." The President would issue a formal proclamation naming the day and call on state and local governments, schools, and citizens to mark it with events and activities. The bill was introduced on January 6, 2026, and its text strongly suggests that date is the intended day, given its references to the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack. However, the bill's actual legal language leaves the specific date up to the President each year.

The bill would not create a federal holiday, meaning workers would not get a day off and there would be no change to the official federal calendar. It would simply add a new entry to the part of U.S. law that covers patriotic observances and celebrations, similar to existing proclamations for Flag Day or Constitution Day. States, cities, and schools would be encouraged but not required to hold programs or activities.

This bill affects the President, who would be legally directed to issue the proclamation annually, as well as state and local governments and schools, which would be encouraged to participate. Everyday Americans might see school programs or public events tied to the observance, but nothing in the bill forces anyone to take part.

title: To amend titles XVIII and XIX of the Social Security Act to require coverage of certain food and nutrition services under the Medicare and Medicaid programs.

The bill affects two large groups of people. Medicare covers roughly 65 million Americans, mostly adults 65 and older along with certain people with disabilities. The bill also affects healthcare providers who offer nutrition-related services, since they would now have a clearer path to getting reimbursed through these programs. States that run Medicaid would be required to include this as a mandatory benefit rather than having the option to leave it out. Both the Medicare and Medicaid changes would take effect 180 days after the bill is signed into law.

title: Timber Harvesters, Haulers, and Landowners Market Disruptions Relief Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a federal relief program for businesses that harvest timber, haul forest products, or own timberland when those businesses get hit hard by a major disruption in the wood products market. A "market disruption" could mean things like a sawmill or pulp mill shutting down in a region, a big drop in timber prices, a foreign country blocking U.S. wood exports, or some other serious threat to the industry. A state governor or the head of the U.S. Forest Service would have to formally request that the Secretary of Agriculture declare a disruption before any money flows.

Once a disruption is declared, qualifying businesses can apply for financial assistance. An initial payment of up to $20,000 can be issued quickly, with a possible follow-up payment later based on how much revenue the business actually lost that year. If market conditions stay bad, payments can continue for up to five more years. The money can only be used for real business costs like payroll, fuel, equipment repairs, debt payments, or finding new markets within the forest products industry. The funding source is specific: it would come from tariffs the U.S. already collects on softwood lumber imported from Canada.

The people most directly affected are small to mid-sized timber harvesting and hauling companies, and large private timber landowners, particularly those who depend heavily on forest products for their income. To qualify, a business must earn at least $35,000 a year from the industry and get at least 75 percent of its revenue from harvesting or hauling. Landowners must also meet minimum timber sales thresholds over recent years. Rural communities where forestry is a major employer would likely feel the broader economic impact of this program.

last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Forestry and Horticulture.

title: 287(g) Cooperation Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new requirement for local and state police departments to sign a cooperation agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) if they want to receive federal COPS grants. COPS grants are federal funds that help local police departments hire officers, buy equipment, and run community policing programs. The agreement, called a 287(g) memorandum, allows local officers to perform certain immigration enforcement duties that are normally handled by federal agents. Departments would have 180 days after the law passes to sign one of these agreements or lose access to the grant money.

The bill affects state and local law enforcement agencies across the country, particularly smaller or mid-sized departments that rely on COPS grant funding to cover basic operating costs. If a department chooses not to sign a 287(g) agreement with ICE, it would no longer be eligible to apply for or receive COPS grants starting in fiscal year 2027. The Attorney General and the Secretary of Homeland Security would work together to verify which departments have signed agreements before approving any grant awards.

In short, the bill uses federal grant money as leverage to encourage local police departments to formally partner with ICE on immigration enforcement. Departments that want the funding would need to participate in the 287(g) program. Those that prefer not to take on immigration enforcement responsibilities would have to give up access to that federal funding source.
ai_headline: Bill ties federal COPS grants to ICE partnership agreements
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Marriage Equality for Disabled Adults Act
ai_summary:
This bill addresses a current rule in Social Security law that cuts off certain disability benefits when a disabled adult gets married. Right now, adults who receive Social Security benefits as a "Disabled Adult Child" — meaning they became disabled before age 22 and receive benefits based on a parent's work record — lose those benefits if they marry. This bill would remove that marriage restriction, allowing them to marry without losing their Social Security disability payments.

The bill also protects other benefits connected to that income. Under current rules, getting married can reduce or eliminate a person's Supplemental Security Income (SSI) because a spouse's income and assets get counted toward the disabled person's eligibility. This bill would block that from happening for this specific group. It also includes protections to make sure marriage does not cause these individuals to lose their Medicaid health coverage, which often comes along with SSI.

The people most directly affected are adults with disabilities who became disabled before age 22 and currently receive benefits tied to a parent's Social Security record. Their potential spouses are also affected, since the spouse's finances would no longer be counted against the disabled person's benefit eligibility. Families of disabled adults who have avoided marriage specifically to protect benefits would also see a change. The bill does not affect people who receive disability benefits through their own work history rather than through a parent's record.
ai_headline: Bill would let disabled adults keep Social Security if they marry
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Ways and Means, and in addition to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

The bill would also block a spouse's income and assets from being counted against the disabled person's SSI eligibility. It includes protections to prevent marriage from triggering a loss of Medicaid coverage tied to SSI.

title: Tribal Regulatory Reform Implementation Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill makes a change to a law from the year 2000 that was meant to help Native American tribes cut through government red tape and grow their businesses. Specifically, it moves certain administrative duties from whoever currently holds them to the Secretary of the Interior. The Secretary of the Interior already oversees most federal programs related to Native American tribes, so this shift would put those responsibilities under one roof.

In practical terms, this is a housekeeping or reorganization move inside the federal government. It does not create new programs, cut funding, or change the goals of the original 2000 law. It just decides which cabinet official is in charge of carrying out certain paperwork and oversight tasks tied to that law.

The people most directly affected are Native American tribal governments and the federal officials who work with them. Tribal leaders and businesses that interact with this program would now deal with the Department of the Interior instead of whichever office previously handled these duties. For most everyday Americans who are not part of a tribe or do not work in federal Indian affairs, this bill would have little to no direct impact.
