title: To direct the Secretary of the Interior to carry out a feasibility study on a selective water withdrawal system at Glen Canyon Dam, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill tells the U.S. Department of the Interior to study whether a special water release system could be built at Glen Canyon Dam in Arizona. The dam sits on the Colorado River and holds back Lake Powell. Right now, water released from the dam comes from a fixed depth, which means the temperature and quality of that water cannot be controlled. A "selective water withdrawal system" would allow operators to pull water from different depths of the reservoir, giving them more control over what gets released downstream.

The study would look at two main goals. First, it would explore whether releasing water from the right depth could improve electricity generation at the dam. Second, it would examine whether better-controlled releases could help stop invasive species, like quagga mussels, from spreading further into the river system. The government has 18 months to finish the study after the bill becomes law. If the study finds the system is worth building and power companies that use the dam agree, construction could move forward.

This bill most directly affects people and communities that depend on the Colorado River, including water users, electric utility customers, and fishing and recreation industries across seven Western states: Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming. It also matters to environmental groups and tribal nations with interests in the river's health. The study itself is paid for with federal taxpayer money, and the bill specifies that money spent on it does not have to be paid back.
ai_headline: Interior Department ordered to study depth-control system at Glen Canyon Dam
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.

Such a system would let operators draw water from different depths of Lake Powell, giving them control over the temperature and quality of water released downstream. The study has two focus areas: whether the system could improve electricity generation and whether it could help stop invasive species like quagga mussels from spreading.

title: Access to Genetic Counselor Services Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would allow Medicare to directly pay genetic counselors for their services, starting January 1, 2027. Right now, Medicare only covers genetic counseling when it is billed through a doctor. This bill changes that by recognizing genetic counselors as their own type of provider under Medicare Part B, meaning patients could see a genetic counselor and have Medicare pay for the visit directly. Medicare would cover 80 percent of the cost, similar to how it covers other outpatient services.

The bill also sets rules for who counts as a genetic counselor under Medicare. A person must either be licensed by their state or, if their state does not license genetic counselors, be certified by the American Board of Genetic Counseling. The bill also includes a "balance billing" protection, which limits how much a genetic counselor can charge a patient beyond what Medicare pays.

This bill primarily affects Medicare beneficiaries, who are mostly people 65 and older, along with certain people with disabilities. It also affects genetic counselors who currently cannot bill Medicare on their own. Genetic counselors help people understand their risk for inherited conditions like cancer or heart disease, so easier access to these services could matter for patients dealing with those health concerns. Doctors and other providers can still bill Medicare for genetic counseling as they do today.
ai_headline: Medicare would pay genetic counselors directly starting in 2027

title: Scratch Cooked Meals for Students Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a pilot grant program run by the U.S. Department of Agriculture to encourage schools to prepare meals from scratch — meaning using whole or minimally processed ingredients — rather than relying heavily on pre-made or heavily processed foods. The government would award competitive grants to school districts, and each grant would last two school years. Schools could use the money for things like staff training, buying kitchen equipment, upgrading cafeteria facilities, paying workers for the extra time scratch cooking requires, and educating students about food through taste tests and cooking activities. Up to $20 million per year could be funded from 2027 through 2031.

Not every school district that applies would receive a grant. The bill prioritizes districts where the highest share of students qualify for free or reduced-price lunch, meaning lower-income communities would be first in line. The program also favors districts that run their own food service operations rather than contracting it out to private companies, and districts whose food service workers have or are working toward a union contract or similar agreement.

Schools that receive grants would work with a nonprofit technical assistance center to assess their needs and create a plan. After the grant period ends, they must report back to the federal government on how much their menus shifted toward scratch-cooked meals. This bill directly affects school cafeteria staff, school administrators who manage food programs, and the millions of students who eat school lunches and breakfasts every day.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

Grants would last two school years and could fund staff training, kitchen equipment, facility upgrades, additional labor costs, and student food education activities. Districts that receive grants must report afterward on how much their menus shifted toward scratch-cooked meals.

title: To provide for the leasing of certain deposits of minerals located within the City of Carlsbad, New Mexico.
ai_summary:
This bill would change a rule that currently blocks the federal government from leasing mineral rights inside incorporated cities and towns. Right now, federal law does not allow the government to offer mineral leases on federal land that sits within city limits. This bill would create an exception specifically for Carlsbad, New Mexico, allowing the U.S. Department of the Interior to lease minerals found on federal land located inside that city.

The bill has one important safeguard built in: the city of Carlsbad itself must give written permission before any leasing can happen. So the federal government cannot move forward unless local officials agree. If the city consents, the leasing would follow the same rules that normally apply to federal mineral leases on land outside of cities.

The people most directly affected are residents and officials of Carlsbad, New Mexico, as well as any mining or energy companies interested in extracting minerals from that area. Carlsbad sits in an area known for potash and other valuable minerals. The federal government would also collect lease revenue from any deals made under this new authority. People living near any future mining activity could see economic and environmental effects, depending on what minerals are extracted and how operations are carried out.

title: High-Quality Charter Schools Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates a new federal tax credit for people who donate money to certain charter schools or charter school management organizations. If you donate to a qualifying charter school group, you can get back 75 cents in tax savings for every dollar you give. The credit is capped at either 10 percent of your yearly income or $5,000, whichever is larger. There is also a nationwide limit of $5 billion in total credits available each year, handed out on a first-come, first-served basis. The credit would start applying to donations made after December 31, 2025.

Not just any charter school qualifies. To be eligible, an organization must either have received a federal grant for expanding high-quality charter schools, or be ranked in the top 10 percent for student performance in its state. Qualifying organizations must keep donation money in a separate account, spend it on creating or expanding charter schools within a set timeframe, and pass annual independent financial audits. If an organization fails to spend the money as required, future donations to it no longer qualify for the credit.

This bill would primarily affect individual taxpayers who itemize or plan their taxes carefully and who want to support charter school growth, as well as the charter school organizations themselves. It could also affect students and families in areas where new or expanded charter schools might open as a result of increased private funding. Public school systems could see indirect effects if students shift to charter schools that grow due to this new funding stream.

title: A bill to establish the Grand Village of the Natchez Indians and Jefferson College as affiliated areas of the National Park System, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill would officially connect two historic sites in Natchez, Mississippi to the National Park System as "affiliated areas." The two sites are the Grand Village of the Natchez Indians, an important archaeological site tied to the history of the Natchez people, and Historic Jefferson College, one of Mississippi's oldest educational institutions. Being an affiliated area means they are formally recognized by the National Park Service but are not fully owned or operated by the federal government.

The day-to-day management of both sites would stay with the Mississippi Department of Archives and History, not the federal government. The federal government could offer technical help and some financial assistance for things like marketing, signage, and preservation, but the bill specifically says the federal government cannot buy property there or take over the costs of running the sites.

The people most directly affected are visitors and local residents in and around Natchez, Mississippi, as well as historians and members of the Natchez Indian community. The affiliated area status could bring more national attention, tourism, and potential preservation resources to both sites. Taxpayers could see some federal dollars go toward support and cooperation with the state, though the bill limits how much direct financial responsibility the federal government takes on.

title: A bill to amend title 18, United States Code, to include rioting in the definition of racketeering activity.
ai_summary:
This bill would add rioting to the list of crimes that count as "racketeering activity" under federal law. Racketeering laws, commonly known as RICO laws, were originally created to fight organized crime like the mafia. They allow prosecutors to charge people not just for a single crime, but for being part of a larger criminal organization or pattern of illegal activity. Adding rioting to this list means that if someone is involved in a riot, they could potentially face these more serious organized crime charges in addition to, or instead of, standard rioting charges.

Under current federal law, rioting is already its own crime, covering actions like traveling across state lines to start or participate in a riot. This bill would not change the definition of rioting itself. What it changes is how rioting can be prosecuted. If rioting becomes a racketeering offense, prosecutors could use RICO tools, such as charging multiple people together as part of a criminal enterprise, seeking higher penalties, and making it easier to connect individuals to a broader group accused of organizing or funding riots.

This bill would most directly affect people charged with participating in riots, as well as anyone accused of organizing, funding, or encouraging riot activity. It could also affect protest organizers and groups, since RICO laws can be used to target organizations, not just individuals. Civil liberties advocates and law enforcement would likely see significant changes in how riot-related cases are investigated and prosecuted. The bill was introduced in the Senate and has been sent to the Judiciary Committee, where it would need approval before moving forward.

title: MERICA Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes the rules for mining certain minerals on federal lands that the government has purchased or otherwise acquired. Right now, a law called the Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands covers things like oil, gas, and coal on those lands, meaning companies must get a lease from the federal government to extract them. This bill would add "hardrock minerals" to that same system. Hardrock minerals include metals like gold, silver, copper, and other base and precious metals, as well as gemstones. Currently, hardrock mining on acquired federal lands operates under a different, older set of rules.

In practical terms, this means that anyone who wants to mine hardrock minerals on these specific federal lands would need to go through the federal leasing process, just like they already do for oil and gas. That process involves applying for a lease, paying fees or royalties to the government, and following the terms the federal government sets. The bill does not apply to coal, oil, natural gas, or a few other specific minerals, which stay under their existing rules.

The people most directly affected are mining companies and individuals who currently mine or want to mine metals and gemstones on federally acquired lands. It could also affect local communities near those lands, state governments that share in federal mineral revenues, and industries that rely on these minerals for manufacturing products like electronics and batteries. Federal land managers, particularly within the Department of the Interior, would also take on a larger role in overseeing these mining activities.
ai_headline: Federal leasing rules would extend to hardrock minerals on acquired lands
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

Anyone seeking to mine those minerals on covered lands would need to apply for a federal lease, pay fees or royalties, and follow terms set by the federal government. Coal, oil, natural gas, and certain other minerals remain under their existing rules and are not affected by this bill.

title: Hydropower Licensing Transparency Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires a federal agency called the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, or FERC, to send Congress a yearly report on hydropower dams that are going through the process of renewing their operating licenses. Hydropower dams need a federal license to operate, and those licenses expire over time. The renewal process can take many years, and right now there is no regular, public accounting of where each dam stands in that process. Starting within 180 days of the bill becoming law, FERC would have to track and report on every dam whose owner started the renewal process at least three years ago but still has not received a new license.

Each yearly report would have to include specific details for every dam caught in this backlog, such as when the renewal process began, what the case number is, whether a formal application has been filed, when FERC expects to finish reviewing it, what meetings or hearings are coming up, and what steps still need to be completed by the dam owner or by government agencies like fish and wildlife offices.

This bill primarily affects companies and utilities that own hydropower dams with licenses currently under review, as well as the federal and state agencies involved in that review. It could also matter to people who live near dams, use the electricity they generate, or care about river ecosystems, since those groups often have a stake in whether and how a dam keeps operating. The bill does not change the rules for approving or denying a license, it only requires better public tracking of how long the process is taking.

title: Wabeno Economic Development Act
ai_summary:

Second, the bill requires the Department of the Interior to study how the federal government currently issues permits for mining stone, sand, and gravel on federal lands. Within 180 days of the bill becoming law, the department must submit a report to Congress explaining how the permitting process works, where it may be slow or redundant, and what could be done to make it faster. The report must also look at the economic effects of current permitting timelines on the stone, sand, and gravel industries.

title: Snow Water Supply Forecasting Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews and updates a federal program that measures how much water is stored in snowpack across the American West. Snowpack — the layers of snow that build up in mountains over winter — is a major source of drinking water, irrigation water, and river flow for millions of people. The program uses advanced technology like airborne lasers and imaging tools to measure that snow and predict how much water will be available when it melts in spring and summer. The bill extends the program's funding through 2031 and shifts its focus toward technologies that combine real-time measurements with computer modeling to give water managers faster and more accurate forecasts.

The bill also removes a requirement for the program to produce a specific report before moving forward with expanding its work. Instead of waiting on that report, the program can now focus directly on deploying better measurement tools and building forecasting systems that respond more quickly to changing weather and watershed conditions. It also puts new emphasis on river basins that cross state lines, so that neighboring states sharing the same water sources can make better-coordinated decisions together.

This bill most directly affects water managers, farmers, and local governments in western states like Colorado, California, Utah, and others that depend heavily on snowmelt for their water supply. It also matters to residents in those regions who rely on that water for daily use. Federal agencies involved in water management, as well as researchers and technology companies working in this field, would also be affected by the updated program priorities.

title: A bill to amend the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States to provide a uniform 8-digit subheading number for all whiskies.
ai_summary:
This bill changes how all types of whiskey are classified in the United States tariff code, which is the official list the government uses to track and tax imported goods. Right now, different whiskies have different classification numbers, which can create confusion or inconsistent treatment at the border. This bill would give all whiskies a single, unified classification number while still keeping separate tracking codes underneath it for statistical purposes, so the government can still count how much of each type, like Scotch, bourbon, or rye, is coming into the country.

The actual tax rate on imported whiskey does not change. The bill keeps the existing duty, which is either free or $2.04 per proof liter depending on the trade agreement in place. The only thing changing is the organizational structure of how whiskies are listed in the tariff schedule, not how much importers pay.

This mainly affects importers who bring foreign whiskey into the United States, customs brokers who file paperwork at the border, and government agencies that track trade data. Domestic whiskey producers and everyday consumers are unlikely to notice any direct impact, since this is a technical bookkeeping change rather than a shift in taxes or trade policy.

title: Secure Trade Act
ai_summary:
This bill does two main things. First, it adds a new 10 percent tax on all goods imported into the United States from any country, on top of whatever taxes already exist. For goods coming from China specifically, the taxes would be much higher — at least 35 percent for most products, and at least 100 percent for items considered strategically important, like computer chips, steel, and other goods tied to national security. These China-specific increases would be phased in gradually over several years. The President would have some ability to adjust the rates but could not eliminate them entirely. The bill also changes how Chinese goods are valued for tax purposes, using the U.S. retail price rather than the price China charges, which would generally result in higher taxes being collected.

Second, the bill tightens rules around foreign investment in the United States. Right now, a government agency called CFIUS reviews foreign purchases of American companies for national security risks. This bill expands that review to cover situations where a foreign government from a country of concern — including China — buys or leases land in the U.S. and builds a new factory or facility on it. Those deals would now require a mandatory government review, even if no existing American company is being purchased.

This bill would affect a wide range of people. American consumers could see higher prices on imported goods, since businesses often pass tariff costs along to shoppers. U.S. companies that rely on imported parts or materials would face higher costs. Businesses that export to or import from China would be significantly impacted. Foreign companies — especially Chinese ones — looking to build facilities in the United States would face new government scrutiny and possible rejection of their plans.
ai_headline: New bill would add 10% tariff on all imports, hit China with up to 100%

title: PROTECT Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill requires a government security review process for a specific type of foreign investment that currently does not have to go through that process. Right now, a government body called the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, or CFIUS, reviews deals where foreign companies try to buy or take control of existing American businesses. This bill expands that oversight to also cover situations where a foreign investor buys or leases land in the United States and then builds a brand-new factory or facility on it. That type of investment is called a "greenfield" investment, and it has largely been outside CFIUS's reach until now.

The bill specifically targets investments connected to "foreign countries of concern," a category defined in existing law that generally includes nations considered adversaries or security risks, such as China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea. If a company or individual linked to one of those governments wants to build a new facility on American soil, they would now be required to file a formal notice with CFIUS before moving forward. CFIUS could then investigate whether the project poses a national security risk and potentially block it.

This bill mainly affects foreign investors from those designated countries who want to build new operations in the United States, as well as American landowners or businesses that might partner with them. It could also indirectly affect communities that might otherwise receive foreign-funded factories or jobs. title: Wildfire Prevention Act of 2025
ai_summary:
S. 140, the Wildfire Prevention Act of 2025, is a Senate bill that aims to reduce wildfire risk on federal lands managed by the U.S. Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management. The bill sets required targets for how many acres of federal forest land must be thinned or treated with controlled burns each year. Starting in 2025, agencies must at least match their average treatment levels from 2019 to 2023, then increase that work by 20 percent in 2027 and 2028, and by 40 percent starting in 2029. The bill also requires the agencies to publicly report their progress each year, use standardized methods to track and measure their work, and test new technologies like drones, AI, and remote sensors to help prevent and detect wildfires.

The bill also makes several changes to how federal land is managed. It expands the zone around power lines where hazardous trees can be cleared, raising it from 10 feet to 50 feet. It creates a faster approval process for removing dangerous trees near roads, trails, and recreation areas on national forest land. It raises the dollar threshold for smaller timber sales that qualify for a simplified process. It also directs agencies to study how livestock grazing could be used as a tool to reduce the amount of dry vegetation that fuels wildfires.

This bill primarily affects federal land management agencies, timber and logging industries, electric utility companies with power lines crossing federal land, local governments and tribal nations near federal forests, and people who live in or near forested areas at risk from wildfires. Communities in western states with large amounts of national forest land would likely feel the most direct impact. The bill does not create new spending on its own but sets requirements for how existing agency resources and authorities must be used.

title: Wildland Firefighters Congressional Gold Medal Act
ai_summary:
This bill would award the Congressional Gold Medal to wildland firefighters as a group, honoring their service protecting forests, grasslands, and communities across the United States. The Congressional Gold Medal is one of the highest honors Congress can give to civilians. A single gold medal would be designed by the U.S. Treasury Department, working with the National Interagency Fire Center, and then displayed at that center where the public could view it.

The bill also allows the U.S. Mint to make and sell bronze copies of the medal to the public at a price that covers production costs. Any money made from those sales would go back into the U.S. Mint's operating fund. The cost of making the original gold medal would come from that same fund, so no separate taxpayer appropriation is required.

This bill affects wildland firefighters employed by federal agencies like the Forest Service, Bureau of Land Management, and National Park Service, as well as state, local, and volunteer wildland firefighters. It is purely a recognition measure and does not change pay, benefits, hiring, or any other policy related to wildland firefighters. Any member of the public interested in the medal could potentially purchase a bronze duplicate from the U.S. Mint.

title: Finger Lakes National Heritage Area Act
ai_summary:
This bill would officially designate the Finger Lakes region of New York as a National Heritage Area. That is a federal recognition given to places with special historical, cultural, or natural significance. The area covered would include 14 counties in central and western New York, such as Tompkins, Monroe, Onondaga, and Seneca counties. The Finger Lakes Tourism Alliance, a local nonprofit organization, would be put in charge of coordinating the area and would need to submit a management plan to the U.S. Department of the Interior within three years.

Being named a National Heritage Area does not create a national park or put land under federal ownership. Instead, it allows the area to receive federal support, guidance, and some funding to help preserve and promote its history and culture. That federal support would last for up to 15 years under this bill.

The people most directly affected are residents, local governments, businesses, and tourism organizations in those 14 New York counties. The designation could bring increased tourism, federal resources for preservation projects, and greater national attention to the region's history, which includes Indigenous heritage, early American settlement, the women's rights movement, and the wine and agricultural industries. Private landowners in the area would not be forced to change how they use their property.

title: Ensuring Patient Access to Critical Breakthrough Products Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would require Medicare to automatically cover certain high-tech medical devices during a temporary period while the government decides whether to provide long-term, permanent coverage. These devices are ones that already received a special "breakthrough" designation from the FDA, meaning the FDA considered them particularly promising and put them on a faster approval track. Under the bill, once a device gets this Medicare breakthrough label, it would be covered by Medicare for up to four years while officials complete a full review of whether it should be permanently covered. The only exceptions are if the device is being used in a way that goes against its FDA-approved instructions, or if the government determines it poses too much risk to patients.

The bill also sets deadlines to make sure the government does not drag its feet. If a manufacturer asks Medicare to make a formal, permanent coverage decision, the government must finish that review before the four-year temporary period runs out. It also gives the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services 10 million dollars per year from 2026 through 2031 to carry out these new responsibilities.

This bill mainly affects Medicare patients, which are largely adults 65 and older as well as some younger people with disabilities. It also directly affects companies that make advanced medical devices, since it creates a pathway for faster Medicare payment for their newest products. Without this bill, there can be a significant gap between when the FDA approves a new device and when Medicare agrees to pay for it, meaning some patients may currently wait years before their insurance covers the latest technology.

title: Critical Minerals Security Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill requires the U.S. government to keep close track of critical minerals and rare earth elements around the world. These are materials like neodymium, lithium, and cobalt that are used in things like electric vehicles, smartphones, military equipment, and other advanced technology. The Secretary of the Interior would need to produce a detailed report every two years showing where these minerals are located, who controls them, how much is being mined, and whether hostile foreign governments or companies have influence over those supplies.

The bill also sets up a process to help American companies that want to sell their ownership stakes in foreign mines. If a U.S. company needs to sell, the government would try to help them find a buyer that is not connected to a foreign adversary. On top of that, the bill directs the government to create a strategy for working with allied countries to develop better technology for mining, refining, and recycling these minerals, and to figure out how to share that technology with those allies.

The people most directly affected are government officials who would have to produce these reports, U.S. companies involved in mining or mineral processing abroad, and policymakers who rely on this kind of information to make decisions. More broadly, the bill is aimed at reducing American dependence on countries considered adversaries for materials that the U.S. economy and military depend on heavily.

title: Food Security and Farm Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill would stop states and cities from making their own rules about how farm products are grown in other states. For example, if California passes a law saying that pork sold in California must come from pigs raised with a certain amount of space, this bill would make that law unenforceable for farms located outside California. Under this bill, a farm in Iowa would only have to follow Iowa's rules and federal rules, not California's rules, even if they want to sell their products in California.

The bill also creates a new legal tool that lets a wide range of people sue to block those kinds of state or local rules. Farmers, truckers, distributors, consumers, trade groups, and even other governments could take a state to court and ask for money damages. Importantly, the bill makes it easier to get a temporary court order that immediately stops the state rule from being enforced while the lawsuit plays out, unless the state can prove it will clearly win the case.

This bill would most directly affect states that have passed animal welfare, environmental, or food safety laws that reach outside their borders, and the farmers, businesses, and consumers connected to that food supply. States like California, Massachusetts, and others that have enacted stricter farm production standards would find those laws harder to enforce. Farmers in other states who currently must meet those standards to sell in those markets could see fewer requirements placed on them.

title: Holocaust Education and Antisemitism Lessons Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum to conduct a nationwide study on how public elementary and secondary schools currently teach about the Holocaust. title: Dismantle DEI Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would eliminate diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programs across the federal government. It would shut down DEI offices in all federal agencies within 90 days, lay off employees whose jobs are tied to those offices, and ban the use of federal money on DEI-related training, positions, or programs. It would also cancel several executive orders from the Biden administration that directed federal agencies to promote equity and inclusion. Federal employees could not be required to take DEI training or sign statements about race, gender, or other group identities as a condition of keeping or advancing in their jobs.

The bill also reaches beyond the federal government itself. Companies that have federal contracts or receive federal grants would be prohibited from using that federal money for DEI offices or training. College accrediting organizations could not require schools to have DEI programs as part of getting or keeping accreditation. Financial regulators, the Department of Defense, the Department of Homeland Security, and intelligence agencies would all have their DEI-related programs and reporting requirements removed. Existing civil rights offices and offices that enforce disability law would stay in place.

Anyone who believes the law has been violated could sue in federal court and collect at least $1,000 per day per violation, plus attorney fees and other damages. The bill affects federal workers, federal job applicants, government contractors, grant recipients such as universities and nonprofits, financial institutions regulated by the federal government, and military personnel.

title: Stop Sextortion Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes it a federal crime to threaten to share child sexual abuse material, even if the person making the threat does not actually have any such images. Right now, federal law mainly covers people who actually possess or distribute this material. The Stop Sextortion Act closes a loophole by also criminalizing the threat itself, whether or not the images exist. Using these threats to intimidate, pressure, or extort someone would become a federal offense.

The bill also increases prison sentences for people who use child sexual abuse material as a tool of extortion or coercion. Under the new rules, the maximum prison term for related crimes could be increased by up to 10 additional years if a person knowingly uses such material to harm, control, or manipulate a victim. This applies across several existing federal laws that deal with child exploitation.

This bill primarily affects two groups of people. First, it targets predators and criminals who use real or fake threats involving child sexual abuse material to control or blackmail victims, often minors. Second, it affects victims of this type of abuse, who are frequently children and teenagers targeted online. Law enforcement agencies would also gain clearer legal tools to prosecute these cases at the federal level.

title: Hydropower Licensing Transparency Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires a federal agency called the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, or FERC, to send Congress a yearly report about hydropower dam licenses that are currently being processed. Hydropower dams need government permission, called a license, to operate and generate electricity from water. Getting or renewing one of these licenses can take many years, and this bill is designed to make sure Congress can track how those processes are going.

The report would cover any dam project where someone filed a notice of intent to apply for a license at least three years ago but still has not received one. For each of those cases, the report must include key details like when the process started, what the current status is, when a decision is expected, any upcoming meetings or hearings, and what actions have already been taken by the dam operator, government agencies, and others involved.

The people most directly affected are companies, local governments, tribes, and individuals who own or want to build hydropower facilities and are waiting on FERC to approve their licenses. Indirectly, it affects communities near dams and anyone who gets electricity from hydropower. The bill does not change how licenses are approved or how long the process takes. It only requires better reporting so that Congress, and by extension the public, can see where things stand and identify cases that may be taking longer than expected.

title: Western South Dakota Water Supply Project Feasibility Study Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells the U.S. Department of the Interior to study whether it is practical and affordable to build a pipeline system that would carry water from the Missouri River to communities in western South Dakota. The study would look at costs, engineering challenges, and whether the project makes sense to actually build. After finishing the study, the federal government would write a report with a recommendation on whether to move forward and how costs should be split between the federal government and local partners. Congress would receive that report, and it would also be made available to the public.

The federal government would pay up to half the cost of the study itself, with a local nonprofit called the Western Dakota Regional Water System covering the other half. If the project were eventually built, the local side would be required to pay at least 25 percent of construction costs. Up to $10 million in federal money is authorized to fund the study, and the government's authority to act on this bill expires in 10 years if nothing has been done by then.

This bill mainly affects people living in western South Dakota, including residents of towns, farms, and businesses that depend on local water supplies in that region. It could also matter to Native American tribes and state and local governments in the area, since they would be consulted during the study process. At this stage, no water system is being built and no construction money is being spent. The bill only funds research to figure out if such a project is worth doing.

title: FLOWS Act
ai_summary:
The FLOWS Act makes two main changes to how the federal government oversees hydropower. First, it reduces paperwork for companies that already hold licenses to operate dams and water-based power projects. Right now, those operators must get federal approval even for small, routine tasks like fixing equipment or making minor upgrades. This bill says operators no longer need that approval for routine maintenance, small repairs, or minor changes to their facilities. It also lets them make temporary adjustments to how they run their projects when unexpected situations arise, like a flood or drought, without first getting sign-off from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC). Safety oversight and enforcement by FERC are not removed by this change.

Second, the bill creates a new, faster licensing path for small "micro hydrokinetic" energy projects, which are devices that generate electricity from the natural movement of water, such as river currents, ocean tides, or waves, without building a dam. These projects must produce no more than 5 megawatts of power, which is enough for a few thousand homes. Under the new process, FERC would have one year to approve or deny an application, which is faster than the current process. The bill also directs FERC to use simplified environmental reviews for small, low-impact projects.

The bill most directly affects companies and individuals who operate existing hydropower facilities, as well as developers interested in building small water-current or tidal energy systems. It could also affect communities near rivers, coastlines, or waterways where these projects might be built. FERC is required to report back to Congress within five years on how the new small-project licenses affect the environment, local economies, and electricity costs.

title: Snow Water Supply Forecasting Program Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews a federal program that tracks how much water is stored in snowpack across the American West and uses that information to predict future water supplies. The program collects data from mountain snowfields and uses technology like satellites, sensors, and computer models to estimate how much water will flow into rivers and reservoirs when snow melts. The bill keeps the program running through 2031 and sets its funding at $6.5 million per year, replacing the old funding structure.

The bill also updates what technologies the program can use. It adds machine learning, imaging spectroscopy, and advanced computer modeling to the list of approved tools. The goal is to make water supply forecasts more accurate and faster, especially as weather patterns become less predictable. It also removes a requirement for a specific written report that the program was previously required to produce.

The people most directly affected are water managers, farmers, cities, and states in the West that depend on snowmelt for their water supply. The program helps these groups plan ahead for dry spells or floods by giving them better estimates of how much water is coming. Federal agencies including the Department of Agriculture and NOAA are also involved as partners in collecting and sharing data.

title: SAFE Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells the U.S. Sentencing Commission, the federal agency that sets recommended prison terms for federal crimes, to update its rules for how judges sentence people convicted of crimes involving child sexual abuse material. Right now, many of those sentencing rules were written years ago and do not fully account for how the internet and technology have changed how these crimes are committed. The bill says the new rules must better reflect the real harm to victims, the wide range of how serious different offenses are, and how dangerous different offenders actually are.

The bill lists specific things the updated rules must take into account. These include whether the offender also physically abused a child, whether they used technology to hide their identity, how many victims or images were involved, whether they shared material widely online, how graphic the material was, and whether a victim died by suicide as a direct result of the offense. The bill also removes several older laws that had previously locked in certain sentencing rules, giving the Sentencing Commission more flexibility to build a cleaner, updated system. One key limit stays in place though: the new rules cannot lower the minimum starting point for sentences that already exists in current guidelines.

This bill most directly affects people convicted of federal crimes related to child sexual abuse material, as well as federal judges and prosecutors who rely on sentencing guidelines when handling these cases. Indirectly, it affects child victims whose cases may be prosecuted under federal law. It does not change what counts as a crime, only how prison sentences for those crimes are calculated.

title: ABC-ED Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the ABC-ED Act of 2025, focuses on a common problem in hospital emergency rooms called "boarding." Boarding happens when patients who need to be admitted to the hospital end up stuck waiting in the emergency department because no regular hospital beds are available. This creates long waits, overcrowded ERs, and ties up ambulance crews who cannot leave until they hand off their patients. The bill would allow existing federal grant money, already set aside for updating public health data systems, to also be used to build real-time tracking systems that show how many hospital beds are available and how that shortage is affecting emergency rooms. It would also require a public website where people can see that information, with personal details removed to protect privacy.

The bill also directs a federal program run through Medicare and Medicaid to test new approaches to emergency care for two specific groups: older adults and people experiencing a mental health crisis. For older adults, the pilot programs could include things like better-trained staff, redesigned ER spaces, and improved communication between ERs and nursing homes or assisted living facilities. For people in psychiatric crisis, it could mean creating separate dedicated units in ERs and speeding up transfers to psychiatric care facilities.

Finally, the bill asks the Government Accountability Office, which is Congress's independent watchdog agency, to study what methods work best for tracking hospital capacity across states and regions, and to report back to Congress within one year. This bill would most directly affect hospitals, emergency medical services workers, and patients who use emergency rooms, particularly elderly patients and those seeking mental health care.

title: Urban Canal Modernization Act
ai_summary:
This bill focuses on aging water canals that run through cities and towns. Right now, federal law allows the government to help pay for major repairs on certain water infrastructure, but urban canals have not been clearly included in that program. This bill adds a new category called "urban canal of concern," which covers canal segments where a failure or collapse could put more than 100 people at risk. Once a canal is labeled this way, the federal government gets clearer legal authority to fund and carry out major repair work on it.

When it comes to paying for repairs, the bill sets up a cost-sharing arrangement. The federal government would cover 35 percent of the repair costs with no expectation of being paid back. The rest of the money would be loaned by the federal government and repaid over time by whoever operates that canal locally. The bill also includes a provision that makes those repayable federal funds count as non-federal money for the purpose of other federal grant programs, which can help local operators qualify for additional funding sources.

The people most affected are residents who live near urban water canals managed under old federal reclamation projects, mainly in western states like Idaho and Oregon, which is where the two senators who introduced the bill are from. Local water districts and canal operators would also be directly affected, since they would be responsible for repaying part of the costs. The broader goal is to reduce the safety risk to communities living near canals that have not been updated in many years.

title: ECCHO Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates a new federal crime targeting adults who pressure, manipulate, or threaten children into hurting themselves or others. Specifically, it would be illegal to coerce a minor into attempting suicide, killing someone, harming a person or animal, committing arson, or carrying out online attacks like doxxing or swatting. Doxxing means posting someone's personal information online to harass them, and swatting means making a fake emergency call to send a police SWAT team to someone's home. The coercion can happen through threats, blackmail, fraud, humiliation, or manipulation, and it counts even if the adult uses another person as a go-between.

The penalties are serious. If someone coerces a child to attempt suicide or kill another person, the offender could face life in prison. For the other offenses on the list, the maximum sentence is 30 years. The bill also updates existing laws about reporting online child exploitation so that this new crime is included alongside child sexual abuse offenses in the systems that technology companies and law enforcement already use to track and report those crimes.

This bill would most directly affect children who are targeted online by adults trying to manipulate them into dangerous or violent actions. It also affects parents, schools, and law enforcement, who would have new legal tools to pursue adults behind this kind of online manipulation. Tech companies that are already required to report child exploitation material would have expanded reporting duties under this bill as well.

title: IGNITE HBCU Excellence Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates a federal grant program to help Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs) improve their physical campuses. Schools can apply to the Department of Education for competitive grants and use the money for things like repairing or replacing old buildings, upgrading heating and air systems, installing high-speed internet, buying research equipment, improving campus security, and building workforce training facilities. Schools can also apply for more than one grant. Up to 5 percent of grant money can be used for administrative costs and planning. The bill covers fiscal years 2027 through 2032, though it does not set a specific dollar amount, leaving that to future appropriations decisions by Congress.

The grants are not handed out equally. Priority goes to schools with the oldest or most run-down facilities, limited ability to raise their own money, high numbers of low-income students receiving Pell Grants, and public schools that have seen cuts in state funding. The bill also cancels certain older federal loans that were made to HBCUs under a separate program before 2021, if those loan funds had not yet been paid out to the schools.

The people most directly affected are students, faculty, and staff at HBCUs across the country, particularly those attending schools with aging infrastructure and fewer financial resources. The bill requires the Department of Education to report to Congress regularly on how the money is being used, and it directs the Government Accountability Office to study whether the program is working and whether more funding is needed.

title: Dakota Mainstem Water Supply Project Feasibility Study Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells the U.S. Department of the Interior to look into whether it makes sense to build a large water supply system for communities across parts of South Dakota, Iowa, Nebraska, and Minnesota. The area would be served by a nonprofit organization called the Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System. The study would examine whether such a project is practical and affordable before any construction decisions are made.

The federal government would pay for no more than half the cost of the study, with the other half coming from non-federal sources. Congress would authorize up to $10 million for the study. If the study is not completed within 10 years of the bill becoming law, the government's authority to carry it out expires.

The people most directly affected are residents of rural towns, farms, and businesses in the four-state region who may currently have limited or aging water supply infrastructure. The study itself does not approve or fund any construction — it only determines whether building such a water system would be feasible. If the study is completed and shows the project is practical, separate legislation or approvals would be needed before anything gets built.

title: Ensuring Seniors’ Access to Quality Care Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes two main changes to federal rules about nursing homes. First, it updates the process for deciding when a nursing home can run its own training programs for nurse aides. Under current law, nursing homes that have been fined or cited for poor care are automatically banned from running these in-house training programs. This bill replaces that automatic ban with a more flexible system. If a nursing home is fined at least $10,697 for providing poor care and has not fixed the problems, the government can block that facility from running its own nurse aide training for up to two years. Once the facility proves it has corrected the problems, has had a clean record for two years, and did not put patients in immediate danger through abuse or neglect, the ban can be lifted. Some nursing homes that are currently banned under the old rules would also get a fresh review under this new system.

Second, the bill expands who is allowed to search the National Practitioner Data Bank, which is a federal database that tracks healthcare workers who have faced disciplinary actions, malpractice payments, or other red flags. Right now, mainly hospitals can use this database for background checks. This bill would allow a broader range of Medicare and Medicaid providers and suppliers, including nursing homes and other care facilities, to search the database when hiring employees.

The people most directly affected are residents of nursing homes and other long-term care facilities, especially seniors on Medicare or Medicaid. Nursing home operators and their employees are also affected, since the bill changes how training programs are approved and how background checks can be conducted. State governments and the federal Department of Health and Human Services would take on updated responsibilities for carrying out these new rules.
ai_headline: Senate bill eases nursing home training bans, expands background check access
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

Facilities that demonstrate two years of clean records and no patient abuse or neglect can have the ban lifted. The bill also lets a broader set of Medicare and Medicaid providers, including nursing homes, search the National Practitioner Data Bank when hiring staff.

title: Water Project Navigators Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates a program called the Water Project Navigators Program, run by the Department of the Interior. The program would provide grants to states, tribes, local governments, water districts, and nonprofit groups to hire or support "navigators," which are basically dedicated staff members who help communities plan and carry out water projects. These projects must serve more than one purpose, such as improving water supply, reducing drought risk, cleaning up water quality, protecting wildlife habitat, or helping communities deal with the effects of climate change on their water systems. The government would cover up to 75 percent of the cost, with the local group paying the rest, though that requirement can be reduced or waived for tribes and lower-income communities facing financial hardship. Up to 15 million dollars per year is authorized for this program from 2027 through 2032.

The people most directly affected are communities that struggle to develop water projects on their own because they lack staff, money, or technical know-how. The bill specifically prioritizes Native American tribes, rural communities, and lower-income communities when deciding who gets funding first. The navigators hired through this program would help these groups with tasks like writing grant applications, managing projects, and doing early engineering or environmental reviews that are often too complex or expensive for smaller organizations to handle alone.

The bill applies only to states and territories that fall under existing federal water law, which generally means the western United States, along with Alaska, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico. It does not apply to the eastern states. Within five years of passing, the federal government would be required to report to Congress on how well the program is working and what concrete benefits it has produced.
ai_headline: Federal navigators program targets water planning gaps in western states
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported with an amendment favorably.

title: Dakota Water Resources Act Amendments of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill updates a decades-old federal water law to authorize new federal funding for water supply projects in North Dakota. It sets aside specific dollar amounts for things like water treatment plants, pump stations, pipeline upgrades, and distribution system expansions in several regions of the state. The money is meant to finish projects that were already planned but never fully funded. The amounts are also designed to adjust over time with construction cost changes, so inflation does not leave projects underfunded.

A large portion of the new funding, about $743 million, is directed specifically toward completing rural water systems on four Native American reservations in North Dakota: Fort Totten (Spirit Lake), Fort Berthold (Three Affiliated Tribes), Standing Rock, and Turtle Mountain. There is also a smaller amount set aside for a feasibility study and possible construction of a water system on the Lake Traverse Reservation. These tribal water systems would provide clean drinking water to reservation communities that currently have incomplete or aging infrastructure.

The rest of the funding, roughly $637 million, targets non-tribal rural areas and cities in North Dakota, including projects in the northwest, central, eastern, and southwest parts of the state. People who would be most directly affected are rural North Dakota residents, farmers, small-town households, and tribal members who rely on these water systems for safe drinking water. The bill does not guarantee the money will be spent; it only authorizes Congress to appropriate it in future budget bills.

title: To amend the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008 to modify the definition of food.
ai_summary:
This bill makes one specific change to the federal food stamp program, known as SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program). Right now, SNAP benefits generally cannot be used to buy hot, ready-to-eat foods. This bill would create an exception by allowing SNAP recipients to use their benefits to purchase hot rotisserie chicken at grocery stores and other authorized retailers.

The change is small but targeted. Rotisserie chicken is already sold in many grocery stores where SNAP is accepted, but because it is served hot and ready to eat, it currently falls outside what SNAP covers. This bill would add it to the list of approved food items by name, making it the first hot prepared food explicitly allowed under the program.

This affects the roughly 42 million Americans who currently receive SNAP benefits, as well as grocery stores and retailers that sell rotisserie chicken. Shoppers who rely on SNAP would gain the option to buy this item without paying out of pocket, which could be helpful for people who lack time or equipment to cook. Retailers could also see more SNAP dollars spent on their prepared food sections.
ai_headline: SNAP would cover hot rotisserie chicken under new House bill
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.

title: Veterans Flight Training Responsibility Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill sets a cap on how much money the federal government will pay for flight training under the Post-9/11 GI Bill. Right now, there is no specific dollar limit on flight training costs at public colleges and universities, meaning the VA can pay the full cost no matter how high it goes. Under this bill, the VA would pay a maximum of $100,000 total for a veteran's flight training at a public college or university. That cap would automatically go up each year based on inflation, using the Consumer Price Index as the measuring stick.

The change would apply to veterans who start a flight training program on or after August 1, 2026. Veterans who are already enrolled in flight training before that date would not be affected by the new limit.

This bill directly affects veterans and eligible servicemembers who plan to use Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits to pay for pilot training through a public college or university. If flight training costs more than $100,000, those students would need to find another way to cover the difference. The bill does not appear to change rules for flight training at private schools or for other types of GI Bill programs.
ai_headline: GI Bill flight training payments capped at $100,000 for public schools
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by Voice Vote.

title: End the Cyprus Embargo Act
ai_summary:
For decades, the United States has had a policy of denying arms sales and military equipment transfers to Cyprus, a small island nation in the eastern Mediterranean. This bill would end that embargo and allow the U.S. government to sell or transfer weapons and defense equipment to Cyprus, as long as the Cypriot government is the buyer and end user. There is one exception: if there are credible human rights concerns tied to a specific request, the denial policy can still be applied. The president can also temporarily pause the policy change for one year if national security requires it.

The bill includes conditions meant to keep Cyprus accountable. If Cyprus stops cooperating with U.S. efforts on anti-money laundering rules or starts allowing Russian military ships to use its ports again, the president can suspend the arms access. Congress would need to be notified before that happens. The bill also expresses support for Cyprus eventually joining NATO's Partnership for Peace program and for ongoing peace efforts related to the island's long-standing political division between its Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities.

This bill mainly affects U.S. defense contractors and the Cypriot government, since it opens a new market for American military equipment. It also has broader implications for U.S. strategy in Europe and the eastern Mediterranean, particularly regarding limiting Russian military influence in the region. For everyday Americans, the direct impact is limited, though it could affect foreign policy relationships with countries like Turkey, which has historically opposed arms sales to Cyprus.
ai_headline: U.S. moves to lift decades-old arms embargo on Cyprus
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported by the Yeas and Nays: 47 - 2.

Sales would be allowed when the Cypriot government is the buyer and end user, with an exception for requests linked to credible human rights concerns. title: Tax Fairness for Survivors Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change the tax code so that money received from lawsuits or settlements related to sexual assault or sexual harassment would not be counted as taxable income. Right now, depending on the type of claim, some of that money can be taxed by the federal government. Under this bill, the full amount a person receives, whether it comes all at once or in payments over time, would be tax-free. That includes things like back pay, punitive damages, and money to cover attorney's fees.

The bill also makes sure those settlement payments would not be subject to Social Security taxes, Medicare taxes, unemployment taxes, or wage withholding. In other words, it closes off multiple ways the federal government could take a cut of what someone receives after making a sexual assault or harassment claim.

This would affect people who win a court judgment or reach a settlement in a sexual assault or sexual harassment case. It could also affect employers or defendants who pay those settlements, since they would no longer need to withhold taxes from those payments. The change would apply starting with the tax year after the bill is signed into law, if it passes.
ai_headline: Sexual assault settlement money would be fully tax-free under HR 1306
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

The exemption covers lump-sum and structured payments alike, including back pay, punitive damages, and attorney's fees. It would also block Social Security, Medicare, unemployment, and wage withholding taxes from applying to those payments.

title: Agent Raul Gonzalez Officer Safety Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes it a federal crime to intentionally drive away from a Border Patrol agent or any law enforcement officer working with Border Patrol within 100 miles of the US border. The basic penalty is up to 2 years in prison and fines. If someone is seriously injured during the chase, the penalty jumps to 5 to 20 years. If someone dies, the person fleeing could face 10 years to life in prison.

The bill also adds immigration consequences. Non-citizens convicted of this offense can be denied entry into the United States, deported, or made ineligible for asylum and other immigration protections. This applies even if a person admits to the conduct without a formal conviction in some cases.

The bill primarily affects people driving near the US border, which covers large portions of states like Texas, California, Arizona, and New Mexico, among others. Non-citizens face additional consequences beyond the criminal penalties. The bill also requires the Justice Department to report to Congress each year on how many people were charged, caught, or convicted under this law. The bill is named after Border Patrol Agent Raul Gonzalez, who was killed during a vehicle pursuit.

title: Improving SCRA Benefit Utilization Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes changes to how the military teaches service members about their financial rights, and how banks and lenders must treat military debt. Right now, a federal law called the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (SCRA) limits the interest rate on debts that service members took on before joining the military to 6% while they are on active duty. This bill adds lessons about that interest rate protection to the financial training that military members already receive. It also requires that reservists be notified of their SCRA rights when they first join a reserve unit and again whenever they are called up to active duty for more than 30 days.

The bill also changes what banks and lenders are required to do. Currently, when a service member notifies a lender and asks for the 6% interest rate cap, it only applies to the specific debt they mention. Under this bill, once a lender is notified, they would have to apply that same interest rate cap to all debts that service member has with them, even debts the service member did not specifically list. Lenders would also be required to let service members submit the necessary paperwork online, by mail, or by fax, giving them flexible options.

This bill primarily affects active duty military members, National Guard and Reserve members called to active duty, and their families. It also affects banks, credit card companies, and any other lenders who hold debts that service members took on before entering military service. The goal is to make sure more service members actually use protections that already exist under the law.
ai_headline: Military debt interest cap would expand automatically under House bill
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by Voice Vote.

Once a lender receives notice from a service member, the cap would automatically apply to all debts that service member holds with that lender, not only debts specifically listed. The bill also adds SCRA financial rights training to existing military education and requires reservists to be notified of their rights at enlistment and again before any active duty period exceeding 30 days.

title: Wildfire Risk Evaluation Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires three federal departments — Agriculture, Interior, and Homeland Security — to work together to review the state of wildfire risk in the United States every four years. The first report would be due within one year of the bill becoming law, and the reviews would continue for 20 years. Each review must look at how changes to land and communities have affected wildfire danger, and must also examine how wildfires impact public health, with input from the EPA and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Each report must include a summary of wildfire challenges expected over the next 20 years, an assessment of progress toward existing national wildfire management goals, and recommendations for new laws or government actions to better handle wildfires. The reviews are meant to help the government plan ahead rather than just react when fires break out. The reports go to several congressional committees in both the House and Senate.

This bill primarily affects federal agencies and how they plan and coordinate wildfire policy. It does not directly change funding levels or create new programs on its own. People who could be most affected in practical terms include residents in wildfire-prone areas, particularly in Western states, as well as firefighters, emergency managers, and local and tribal governments who rely on federal planning and resources when wildfires strike.

last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute (Amended) by Unanimous Consent.

title: To reauthorize the Fort Peck Reservation Rural Water System Act of 2000.
ai_summary:
This bill extends the life of a federal program that helps build and maintain a rural water system on the Fort Peck Indian Reservation in northeastern Montana. The original program was passed in 2000 and has been updated several times since then. Right now, federal funding and authorization for the program are set to expire in 2026. This bill would push that deadline to 2028, giving the program two more years to continue its work.

The Fort Peck Reservation Rural Water System is a infrastructure project designed to bring clean, reliable drinking water to homes and communities on the reservation. Without this reauthorization, federal support for the project would end, which could slow down or stop construction and maintenance of water lines and related facilities.

This bill most directly affects the residents of the Fort Peck Indian Reservation, which is home to members of the Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes. It also affects federal agencies and contractors involved in managing and building the water system. For anyone living in that area who depends on this system for safe drinking water, the bill is essentially asking Congress to keep the funding and legal authority in place for two more years.

last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

title: Justice for Breonna Taylor Act
ai_summary:
This bill would ban "no-knock" warrants, which are search warrants that allow police to enter a home or building without first announcing who they are and why they are there. Under this bill, any federal law enforcement officer would be required to identify themselves and explain their purpose before forcing their way into a property. The bill is named after Breonna Taylor, who was killed in 2020 during a no-knock police raid in Louisville, Kentucky.

The bill also applies pressure on state and local police departments. Any state or local law enforcement agency that receives funding from the Department of Justice would have to follow the same rule — officers must announce themselves before entering a property by force. Agencies that use no-knock warrants could risk losing that federal funding.

This bill would most directly affect law enforcement agencies at the federal, state, and local levels, since it changes how search warrants can be carried out. It would also affect ordinary residents, since people in their homes would be guaranteed to hear a warning before police force entry. Currently, no-knock warrant policies vary widely from state to state, so the impact would be felt differently depending on where someone lives.
ai_headline: Federal bill would require police to announce themselves before forced entry
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

States and local agencies that receive Department of Justice funding would face the same requirement. Agencies that continue using no-knock warrants could lose that federal funding.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies that carry out search warrants or receive DOJ funding. Residents in their homes would also be affected, as they would be guaranteed a verbal announcement before police force entry.
ai_sections.why: No-knock warrant policies currently vary widely from state to state, meaning the practical impact of this bill would differ depending on where someone lives. The bill was named after Breonna Taylor, who was killed during a no-knock police raid in Louisville, Kentucky in 2020.

title: Optimizing Postpartum Outcomes Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill focuses on pelvic health care for women after giving birth. It tells the federal Department of Health and Human Services to release guidance within one year explaining how state Medicaid and CHIP programs can cover two specific services: pelvic floor exams and pelvic health physical therapy during and after pregnancy. The guidance would help states understand their payment options, share best practices from other states, and clarify the medical codes used to identify pelvic floor problems. At the same time, the Government Accountability Office would study where gaps in coverage currently exist for postpartum women on Medicaid.

The bill also directs the CDC, working with other federal health agencies, to create a public education program. That program would train health care providers on pelvic floor exams and physical therapy, and it would inform new mothers about why these services matter, how to get them, and what to expect. Up to $2 million per year from 2027 through 2031 could be authorized to fund this education effort.

The people most directly affected are women who are enrolled in Medicaid or CHIP during or after pregnancy, along with the health care providers who treat them and the state agencies that run those programs. Women dealing with common post-childbirth issues like bladder leakage, bowel problems, pelvic pain, or muscle weakness could potentially gain better access to specialized physical therapy and exams if their states act on the federal guidance. The bill does not guarantee coverage on its own but pushes states toward making these services available.
ai_headline: Senate bill pushes Medicaid coverage of postpartum pelvic care

title: Don’t Penalize Victims Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes a small but significant change to federal disaster relief law. Right now, if someone receives money from any other source after a disaster, such as an insurance payout or a charity donation, the federal government subtracts that amount from the disaster assistance it provides through FEMA. This bill would remove the words "or any other source" from that rule, which would limit when the government can reduce a person's federal disaster aid based on money they received elsewhere.

In practical terms, this could mean that disaster victims would not have their FEMA assistance reduced just because they also received help from a private insurance company, a nonprofit, or another outside source. The existing law was designed to prevent people from getting paid twice for the same loss, but critics argue it ends up penalizing victims who were responsible enough to carry insurance or who received charitable help.

This bill would most directly affect homeowners, renters, and business owners in areas that have been declared federal disaster zones, particularly those who also have insurance or who receive donations after a disaster. It would not change the overall disaster relief program itself, just this one rule about how outside money affects a person's eligibility for federal aid.
ai_headline: Bill would stop FEMA from cutting aid when disaster victims have insurance
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Economic Development, Public Buildings, and Emergency Management.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 2254 would remove a rule that lets FEMA reduce disaster aid when victims receive money from insurance or charities.

Under current law, payments from insurance companies, nonprofits, or other outside sources can trigger a reduction in federal disaster aid. This bill would change that one rule without altering the broader disaster relief program.
