title: Honor Our Living Donors Act
ai_summary:
This bill deals with how living organ donors are reimbursed for their out-of-pocket costs, like travel, lost wages, or other expenses they face when donating an organ such as a kidney. Right now, some reimbursement programs look at how much money the organ recipient earns when deciding whether to help cover a donor's costs. This bill would ban that practice, meaning a donor's eligibility for reimbursement could no longer be affected by whether the person receiving their organ is rich or poor.

The bill also removes a rule that allowed programs to expect organ recipients to pay back some of those donor costs. Going forward, recipients would not be on the hook for reimbursing donors through these grant programs. Additionally, the bill requires the federal government to publish a yearly report showing whether donors are being fully covered, how many were not reimbursed completely, and how much money would be needed to cover everyone.

The people most directly affected are living organ donors, meaning people who voluntarily give an organ while still alive, and to a lesser extent the people who receive those organs. Donors who give organs to lower-income recipients may have been disadvantaged under the old rules, and this bill aims to fix that. Program administrators and the Department of Health and Human Services would also be affected, since they would need to change how they run these grant programs and produce the new annual reports.
ai_headline: Bill bars organ donor reimbursement from hinging on recipient's income
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 628 stops reimbursement programs from using organ recipients' income to decide whether living donors get covered for out-of-pocket costs.
ai_sections.what: HR 628 prohibits reimbursement programs from considering the organ recipient's income when determining a living donor's eligibility for cost reimbursement. The bill also eliminates a rule that allowed programs to require recipients to repay donor costs. A new annual federal report would be required, tracking whether donors are fully covered, how many were not fully reimbursed, and how much funding would be needed to cover all donors.
ai_sections.who: Living organ donors are most directly affected, particularly those who donated to lower-income recipients and may have received less reimbursement under prior rules. Program administrators and the Department of Health and Human Services are also affected, as they must revise grant program operations and produce the new yearly reports.
ai_sections.why: Under the previous rules, a donor's access to reimbursement could vary depending on the financial situation of the person receiving the organ, creating unequal outcomes among donors. The annual reporting requirement would make gaps in donor reimbursement visible at the federal level each year.
ai_sections.cost: The bill requires the federal government to publish a yearly report on donor reimbursement coverage and the funding that would be needed to cover all donors fully, but the summary does not specify an appropriated dollar amount.

title: Medicare and Medicaid Fraud Prevention Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires state Medicaid programs to regularly check a federal database called the Death Master File to make sure that doctors, clinics, and other medical providers enrolled in Medicaid are still alive. Starting January 1, 2027, states would need to run this check when a provider first signs up or renews their enrollment, and then at least once every three months after that. The Death Master File is a Social Security Administration database that tracks when people die.

The goal is to stop a known type of fraud where someone uses the identity of a deceased doctor or medical provider to bill Medicaid for services that were never actually provided. By catching these cases faster and more regularly, the federal government and states could avoid paying out fraudulent claims.

This bill mainly affects state Medicaid agencies, which would need to build these checks into their enrollment systems. It could also affect the roughly 80 million low-income Americans who rely on Medicaid, since reducing fraud can help protect funding for the program. Legitimate healthcare providers who participate in Medicaid would not face any new burdens beyond the routine enrollment process they already go through.
ai_headline: Bill would require quarterly Medicaid checks against federal death records
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 2309 requires states to check Medicaid providers against a federal death database at enrollment and every 90 days starting Jan. 1, 2027.
ai_sections.what: HR 2309 requires state Medicaid programs to check enrolled providers against the Social Security Administration's Death Master File when providers sign up or renew, and at least once every three months after that. These checks would begin January 1, 2027. The goal is to detect cases where someone uses a deceased provider's identity to submit fraudulent Medicaid billing.
ai_sections.who: State Medicaid agencies would need to build these checks into their enrollment systems. The roughly 80 million low-income Americans enrolled in Medicaid could be indirectly affected, as could legitimate healthcare providers who participate in the program.
ai_sections.why: Without regular checks against death records, fraudulent claims submitted under deceased providers' identities can go undetected and result in improper Medicaid payments. More frequent verification would allow states and the federal government to identify and stop this type of fraud sooner.

title: Lifespan Respite Care Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews a federal program that helps people who take care of family members with disabilities, chronic illnesses, or other special needs. The program funds "respite care," which means temporary relief for caregivers — things like having a trained helper come in for a few hours so a caregiver can rest, run errands, or take a break. Without this kind of support, caregiving can become overwhelming. The bill keeps this program running through 2029 by continuing its federal funding.

The bill also makes a small but meaningful change to who counts as a "family caregiver" under the law. Previously, only unpaid adults could qualify. The new wording changes that to "unpaid individuals," which could open the door for younger caregivers, like teenagers who help care for a parent or sibling, to be recognized and potentially supported under the program.

This affects family caregivers across the country — people who look after children or adults with disabilities, elderly relatives, or loved ones with serious health conditions, all without being paid to do so. It also affects the states and organizations that receive federal grants to run respite care services locally. If passed, it simply keeps an existing program alive for another five years rather than letting it expire.
ai_headline: Federal respite care program for family caregivers renewed through 2029
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 2560 extends federal respite care funding through 2029 and may let teen caregivers qualify for support.
ai_sections.what: HR 2560 reauthorizes an existing federal program that funds temporary relief services for unpaid family caregivers, commonly called respite care. This includes services like trained helpers covering caregiving duties so a caregiver can rest or handle personal needs. The bill also broadens the legal definition of a family caregiver from "unpaid adults" to "unpaid individuals," potentially including younger caregivers such as teenagers.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects unpaid family caregivers across the country who care for relatives with disabilities, chronic illnesses, serious health conditions, or age-related needs. It also affects the states and local organizations that receive federal grants to operate respite care programs.

title: Care for Military Kids Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill deals with Medicaid coverage for military families who move to a new state because of military orders. Right now, when a service member gets relocated, their family members with disabilities or special health needs can lose their Medicaid coverage or lose their place on waiting lists for home and community-based services, like personal care aides or therapy. Starting January 1, 2028, this bill would require every state's Medicaid program to automatically treat these relocated family members as residents of the new state, so their coverage can continue without a gap.

The bill also protects waiting list spots. Some Medicaid services, like in-home care for people with disabilities, have long waiting lists because states limit how many people can receive them. If a military family member was already on one of those waiting lists before the move, this bill would require the new state to keep that person on a similar waiting list rather than starting them over from scratch. They would stay on the list until the new state evaluates them for eligibility or until they choose to be removed.

The people most directly affected are military service members on active duty, recently retired veterans within the last year, and their dependents, especially children or family members with disabilities who rely on Medicaid-funded home and community-based care. State Medicaid programs across the country would also need to update their rules to comply. The federal government would provide one million dollars per year from 2026 through 2030 to help states carry out those changes.
ai_headline: Military families would keep Medicaid coverage after relocations under HR 3399
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

ai_sections.what: Starting January 1, 2028, HR 3399 would require every state Medicaid program to automatically recognize relocated military family members as state residents, preventing coverage gaps. The bill also requires new states to carry over waiting list positions for home and community-based services rather than restarting the process, until the new state evaluates eligibility or the individual opts out.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects active-duty service members, veterans who retired within the last year, and their dependents, particularly family members with disabilities who rely on Medicaid-funded home and community-based care. State Medicaid programs nationwide would also be required to update their rules to comply.
ai_sections.why: Without this requirement, military family members with disabilities or special health needs can lose Medicaid coverage or their place on long waiting lists each time a relocation order moves them to a new state. States currently have no uniform obligation to recognize prior coverage or waiting list status from another state.
ai_sections.cost: The federal government would provide one million dollars per year from 2026 through 2030 to help states implement the required changes.

title: INFANT Act of 2025
ai_summary:
The WIC program (Women, Infants, and Children) provides food assistance to low-income pregnant women and young children, including free infant formula. Right now, each state picks just one formula company through a bidding process, and that single company supplies all the WIC formula in that state. This bill would change the rules so that states pick two companies instead of one — a primary supplier and a secondary supplier — both chosen based on who offers the lowest price through sealed bids.

The main reason this matters goes back to the 2022 infant formula shortage, when a single factory shutdown caused a nationwide crisis because so many states depended entirely on one manufacturer. By requiring states to contract with two companies at once, the bill aims to build a backup into the system so that if one supplier has problems, there is already another approved and ready to go.

This bill mainly affects low-income families with infants who rely on WIC benefits, as well as the infant formula companies that compete for these government contracts. States that run WIC programs would also need to update how they handle their bidding processes. The bill does not change who qualifies for WIC or how much formula families can receive — it only changes how states choose which companies provide that formula.
ai_headline: WIC formula contracts would require two suppliers per state under House bill
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 5759 requires states to contract with two infant formula suppliers for WIC instead of one, creating a backup if a supplier fails.
ai_sections.what: HR 5759 would change how states select infant formula suppliers for the WIC program, requiring them to contract with both a primary and a secondary supplier chosen through sealed-bid lowest-price competition. Currently each state contracts with only one company. The bill does not change eligibility rules or the amount of formula families can receive.
ai_sections.who: Low-income families with infants who rely on WIC benefits are directly affected, as are infant formula companies that compete for these government contracts. State agencies that administer WIC programs would also need to update their bidding processes.
ai_sections.why: The 2022 infant formula shortage demonstrated that relying on a single supplier per state created nationwide supply risk when one factory shut down. Requiring a secondary contract means a pre-approved backup supplier would already be in place if the primary supplier encounters problems.

title: Care for Military Kids Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes it easier for military families to keep their Medicaid benefits when they move to a new state because of a military relocation order. Right now, when a service member is transferred to a new state, their family members who rely on Medicaid, including children or dependents with disabilities who need special home health services, can lose coverage or lose their place on waiting lists. Starting January 1, 2028, this bill would require every state to automatically treat these relocated military families as residents for Medicaid purposes, so their coverage continues without interruption. The family can choose to opt out of this if they want, but the default would be that coverage keeps going.

The bill also protects the spot that a military family member holds on a waiting list for home and community-based services, which are things like in-home nursing care or support for people with disabilities. These waiting lists can be very long, sometimes years. Under this bill, if a family is forced to move due to military orders, they keep their place on that waiting list in the new state until a slot opens up and the state decides if they qualify. The bill covers active-duty service members, those who recently left active duty within the past 12 months, and their dependents who move with them.

This bill affects military families across the country, particularly those with members who have disabilities or ongoing medical needs and depend on Medicaid. It also affects state Medicaid programs, which would need to update their rules to follow these new requirements. The federal government sets aside one million dollars per year from 2026 through 2030 to help states make those changes.
ai_headline: Bill shields military families from losing Medicaid when they relocate

title: Telehealth Modernization Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes several telehealth rules that were set to expire in 2025 permanent through at least 2027 for Medicare patients. Specifically, it keeps rules in place that let patients get telehealth care from their homes instead of requiring them to travel to a clinic, allows a wider range of healthcare providers to offer telehealth visits, and lets patients use phone-only calls instead of video when needed. It also delays until 2027 a rule that would have required Medicare mental health patients to have an in-person visit before continuing to receive therapy online.

The bill also extends two other programs. First, it extends through 2030 a program that allows certain hospital patients to receive care at home instead of staying in a hospital building, and it requires the government to study whether that home-based hospital care is safe and effective. Second, it lets online-only providers join the Medicare Diabetes Prevention Program through 2030, meaning people at risk for diabetes can take prevention classes entirely over the internet.

The bill affects Medicare recipients, meaning mostly Americans 65 and older, as well as people with disabilities who qualify for Medicare. It also affects doctors, nurses, therapists, community health centers, rural health clinics, and hospice providers who treat Medicare patients. Additionally, the bill adds new anti-fraud rules for medical equipment and lab test billing, and directs the government to issue guidance on how to better serve telehealth patients who have limited English proficiency.

last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Ways and Means, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

title: Telehealth Modernization Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes several temporary telehealth rules that were set to expire in September 2025 last through September 2027 for Medicare patients. Under current law, Medicare had loosened telehealth rules during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, but those looser rules were about to end. This bill keeps them going for two more years. Specifically, it lets Medicare patients receive telehealth care from their homes rather than requiring them to travel to a clinic, allows more types of health care providers to offer telehealth visits, permits phone-only appointments for people who cannot use video, and lets patients receive mental health care via telehealth without first having an in-person visit. It also extends a program that lets some hospital patients recover at home instead of staying in a hospital bed, and it expands the Medicare Diabetes Prevention Program so people can take it fully online.

The bill also adds some new requirements aimed at stopping fraud. Starting in 2028, Medicare will take a closer look at claims for medical equipment and devices when the doctor who ordered that equipment has no previous history of treating that patient. The bill also asks a federal watchdog agency to study which lab tests are most at risk for fraudulent billing and report back to Congress.

People most affected are Medicare enrollees, meaning mostly Americans 65 and older or those with certain disabilities. This includes people in rural areas who may live far from doctors, people who speak limited English (the bill requires new guidance to help them use telehealth), people with heart or lung conditions who might qualify for at-home rehabilitation, and people at risk for type 2 diabetes who can now join prevention programs entirely online. Health care providers who deliver services remotely, community health clinics, and hospice programs are also directly affected.
ai_headline: Medicare telehealth flexibilities extended two more years under Senate bill
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

The bill also extends a program letting some hospital patients recover at home and expands the Medicare Diabetes Prevention Program to allow fully online participation.

title: Save Our Safety-Net Hospitals Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes how much money certain hospitals can receive through a Medicaid program called Disproportionate Share Hospital, or DSH, payments. DSH payments are extra funds the federal government sends to hospitals that treat a large share of low-income and uninsured patients. Right now, there is a cap on how much any single hospital can receive, and the bill changes how that cap is calculated. Specifically, it would allow Medicare payments and payments from other insurance plans to count when figuring out how much a hospital has already been paid, which can affect how much additional DSH money they qualify for. It also removes a special rule that previously treated certain hospitals differently under that cap.

The bill also gives states more flexibility with unspent DSH funds going back to October 2021. If a state did not use its full federal DSH allotment in a given year, it could go back and distribute that leftover money to qualifying hospitals, as long as the payments follow the updated rules. States would not be forced to take back payments already made to hospitals under the old rules, and they would have a limited window of time to make these retroactive adjustments.

The hospitals most affected are often called safety-net hospitals, meaning facilities in urban and rural areas that serve high numbers of Medicaid patients, uninsured patients, and people who cannot fully pay their bills. States that run Medicaid programs would also be affected because they would gain new options for how to distribute federal DSH funds. Patients who rely on these hospitals for care could be indirectly affected if the additional funding helps those hospitals stay open or maintain services.
ai_headline: Senate bill rewrites Medicaid safety-net hospital payment caps
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

It removes a special rule that previously treated certain hospitals differently under that cap. States may also redistribute unspent DSH funds from federal allotments going back to October 2021, within a limited time window and under updated rules.

State Medicaid programs gain new flexibility in how they distribute federal DSH funds, and patients who depend on safety-net hospitals could be indirectly affected.
ai_sections.why: Changing how the cap is calculated alters which hospitals qualify for additional DSH payments and how much they can receive. Allowing retroactive redistribution of unspent funds gives states new options but also requires them to operate within updated federal rules going back several years.
ai_sections.cost: The bill affects the distribution of existing federal DSH allotments, including unspent funds going back to October 2021. No new spending totals or cost figures are specified in the summary.

title: Dennis John Benigno Traumatic Brain Injury Program Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill keeps alive a set of federal programs focused on traumatic brain injury, or TBI, which is any injury that damages the brain from an outside force or internal cause like lack of oxygen. The funding authorization for these programs had expired, and this bill extends it through 2030. It also expands what the programs track, adding a focus on how common TBIs are in the population, what causes them, and which groups of people face higher risks, including people in certain jobs and victims of domestic violence or sexual assault. The CDC would be required to make this data publicly available on its website.

The bill also updates federal grant programs that give money to states and tribal communities to help people living with TBIs. States receiving these grants would now need to keep spending their own money at roughly the same level they did the year before receiving federal funds, to make sure federal dollars are adding to efforts rather than replacing them. However, the federal government can waive up to half of that requirement if a state or tribe genuinely cannot afford it. The bill also clarifies the legal definition of traumatic brain injury to include injuries from causes like oxygen loss due to trauma, infection, surgery, or vascular problems, while excluding conditions present at birth or caused by aging.

The bill directs the Department of Health and Human Services to produce two reports within two years. The first would look specifically at higher-risk populations like domestic violence survivors and public safety officers, examining gaps in data collection and outreach efforts. The second would study long-term health problems that can follow a TBI, including possible connections to conditions like dementia and mental health disorders. People most directly affected by this bill include TBI survivors and their caregivers, people in high-risk occupations such as first responders and athletes, domestic violence survivors, and state and tribal health programs that receive federal funding for TBI services.

title: Mikaela Naylon Give Kids a Chance Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill makes two main changes to federal law related to drugs for children with cancer. First, it requires drug companies that are seeking FDA approval for a new adult cancer drug to also study whether that drug could work against childhood cancers, specifically cancers driven by the same genetic or molecular targets. These required pediatric studies must produce real, usable data on safe dosing and early signs of effectiveness for children of different ages. This requirement kicks in three years after the bill becomes law, and the FDA must release guidance explaining how it all works within about two years.

Second, the bill extends a program called the Rare Pediatric Disease Priority Review Voucher program through September 2030. Under this program, a drug company that gets FDA approval for a treatment targeting a rare childhood disease earns a voucher. That voucher can be used, or sold to another company, to make the FDA review a different drug application faster. The idea is to give companies a financial reason to develop medicines for rare childhood diseases that might not otherwise be profitable enough to pursue.

The bill mainly affects pharmaceutical and biotech companies developing cancer drugs, the FDA, and children with cancer or rare pediatric diseases. Families of kids with these conditions could eventually benefit if more treatments get developed or tested as a result. Government watchdog agencies are required to study and report back to Congress on whether these rules are actually working, so lawmakers can see if children are truly getting more treatment options over time.

title: Bipartisan Health Care Act
ai_summary:
This bill is a large package of health care changes that extends or updates dozens of existing federal health programs while adding some new ones. The biggest pieces deal with Medicare and Medicaid. On the Medicaid side, it makes it easier for doctors in one state to serve Medicaid patients in another state, requires states to check their enrollee lists against death records to remove deceased people, and lets working adults with disabilities keep Medicaid coverage past age 65. On the Medicare side, it extends extra payments to rural and small hospitals that might otherwise close, keeps telehealth rules in place that were put in place during the pandemic, adds Medicare coverage for multi-cancer screening tests and certain home infusion treatments, and cracks down on how pharmacy benefit managers operate. It also requires more transparency about how pharmacies are paid under both programs.

The bill also reauthorizes and funds several public health programs. It continues funding for community health centers, rural health clinics, and programs that fight the opioid crisis, including treatment grants, recovery centers, and first responder training. It extends special programs for diabetes research, the 9/11 first responder health program, and maternal health studies. There is also a large section updating the country's pandemic preparedness systems, including the Strategic National Stockpile, disease surveillance, and emergency volunteer networks.

The people most directly affected are the roughly 90 million Americans enrolled in Medicare and Medicaid, people in recovery from opioid addiction, military families who move between states and need to keep their health coverage, residents in rural areas who depend on small hospitals and community health centers, and health care workers who receive loan repayment or training support through the programs being renewed. Because many of these provisions simply keep existing programs running rather than creating entirely new ones, the practical effect for most people would be that services they already rely on continue without interruption.

title: Prove It Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires federal agencies to be more transparent and thorough when making regulations that could affect small businesses. Right now, agencies can simply certify that a new rule will not significantly impact small businesses without doing a full analysis. The Prove It Act would force agencies to also consider indirect costs, meaning businesses that do not deal with an agency directly but still feel the effects of a rule, such as a supplier or customer of a regulated company. It also creates a formal process where small businesses can challenge an agency's claim that a rule won't hurt them, by filing a petition with the Small Business Administration's Office of Advocacy for an independent review.

The bill also requires agencies to publicly post guidance documents related to rules that affect small businesses and allow those businesses to comment on them. Additionally, federal agencies are already supposed to review their existing rules every ten years to see if they still make sense. This bill adds teeth to that requirement by saying that if an agency misses that ten-year review deadline, the rule automatically stops being in effect until the agency goes through a process to bring it back.

The people most directly affected are small business owners across all industries, since the bill gives them a new formal way to push back on federal rules they believe were incorrectly assessed. Federal agencies that write regulations would also face new procedural requirements and stricter deadlines. The bill does not provide any new funding to carry out these changes, meaning agencies would need to handle the added responsibilities within their current budgets.

Agencies would also be required to publicly post guidance documents related to these rules and accept comments from small businesses on them.

title: Prove It Act of 2025
ai_summary:

The bill creates a new process where small businesses can challenge an agency's claim that a rule will not hurt them. A small business or group representing small businesses could file a petition with the Small Business Administration's Office of Advocacy. That office would review the challenge, hold a meeting with the agency, and publish its findings within 30 days. If the office agrees the rule does affect small businesses significantly, the agency has to do a full impact study. If an agency refuses to cooperate with that review, the rule simply cannot apply to small businesses at all.

The bill also addresses what happens when agencies do not keep up with required check-ins on existing rules. Federal law already requires agencies to review rules every 10 years to see if they still make sense for small businesses. This bill says that if an agency misses that deadline, the rule automatically stops being effective until the agency justifies bringing it back. Anyone who might be affected includes small business owners across many industries, federal regulatory agencies, and the Small Business Administration, which would take on a larger oversight role under this bill.

title: BUILD America 250 Act
ai_summary:
This bill is a major transportation funding law that would authorize hundreds of billions of dollars for roads, bridges, public transit, rail, and highway safety programs from 2027 through 2031. It replaces the current federal transportation funding law, which is set to expire. The name references America's 250th birthday in 2026. It covers almost every form of ground transportation in the country, including highways, city buses, Amtrak trains, freight trucks, and even ferries and wildlife crossings. The bill would also speed up the environmental review process for new projects, meaning construction could begin faster than it does today.

The bill affects a very wide range of Americans. Drivers would see funding for road repairs, bridge replacements, and safety improvements at dangerous intersections. People who ride buses, subways, or commuter trains would see continued federal support for those systems. Truckers and freight companies face new rules around drug testing, leasing agreements, and self-driving trucks. Rural communities, tribal nations, and U.S. territories like Puerto Rico also receive dedicated funding. The bill includes rules meant to give small businesses owned by socially and economically disadvantaged people a fair shot at winning federal transportation contracts.

The bill also addresses newer topics like self-driving vehicles, per-mile road usage fees being studied as a possible replacement for the gas tax, cybersecurity of transportation systems, and safer transport of hazardous materials like lithium-ion batteries. Amtrak would face stricter transparency and accountability requirements. Rail safety rules would be updated following recent concerns about train derailments and hazardous cargo. Overall, if passed, this bill would shape how the federal government funds and regulates nearly all forms of ground transportation for the next five years.

title: Moms Matter Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Moms Matter Act, would create two main federal grant programs focused on mental health and substance use treatment for pregnant women and new mothers. The first program would give out up to $25 million per year to local health organizations, clinics, nonprofits, tribal groups, and government agencies. These groups could use the money to add mental health services to prenatal care, start or grow support programs for postpartum depression and anxiety, train doctors and nurses to spot warning signs, connect patients to addiction treatment, and work to reduce the stigma around seeking help. Priority would go to organizations working in areas that already have high rates of maternal death or poor birth outcomes.

The second part of the bill would provide up to $15 million per year to schools and training programs to grow the number of mental health professionals who specialize in caring for pregnant and postpartum patients. Schools that make an effort to recruit students from minority and underserved communities, and that train students to work in areas with doctor shortages, would be given preference for funding. The bill also requires that all programs funded through these grants include training on bias and racism in healthcare.

The people most directly affected are pregnant women and new mothers, especially those in communities with higher rates of maternal death or limited access to healthcare. Healthcare workers, training programs, community clinics, and local health departments would also be affected, as they would be the ones applying for and using these grants. The bill covers the period from 2027 through 2031 and requires regular public reporting on how the money is being used.

title: Save our Safety-Net Hospitals Act of 2025
ai_summary:
Medicaid has a program that gives extra money to "safety-net hospitals," which are hospitals that treat large numbers of low-income and uninsured patients. These extra payments are called Disproportionate Share Hospital, or DSH, payments. Current law limits how much extra money each hospital can receive, and those limits are based partly on how much the hospital loses caring for Medicaid and uninsured patients. This bill changes how those loss limits are calculated by also counting money the hospital receives from Medicare and certain other insurance plans, which could allow some hospitals to qualify for higher DSH payments than they can get under the current rules.

The bill also addresses past years going back to October 2021. If a state did not use all of its available DSH money in a given year, the bill would let that state go back and distribute that leftover money to hospitals, as long as the payments follow the new rules. States would be allowed to make small adjustments to their Medicaid plans retroactively to do this, though there is a deadline tied to when the state must submit its annual audit for that year.

This bill most directly affects safety-net hospitals, particularly those in states where hospitals treat a high mix of Medicaid and Medicare patients together. Hospital administrators and state Medicaid officials would need to recalculate payment limits under the new rules. Patients at these hospitals are not directly paid or billed differently, but the financial health of the hospitals that serve low-income communities could be impacted depending on whether their state takes advantage of the new options.

The bill also allows states to retroactively distribute unused DSH funds from years going back to October 2021, subject to new rules and an audit-linked deadline.

title: PETSAFE Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes two main changes to existing federal disaster law. First, it raises the amount of federal money that can cover pet-related emergency preparedness from 50 percent to 90 percent of costs. That means state, local, and tribal governments would only need to come up with 10 cents for every dollar spent on pet-related disaster supplies, instead of the usual 50 cents. The bill also creates a specific list of things that grant money can be spent on, including animal crates, pet food and supplies, veterinary equipment, rescue gear, animal shelter equipment, and training for animal response teams.

Second, the bill requires that emergency preparedness plans — the official documents governments must submit to receive federal disaster funding — now include a plan for animal shelters. Specifically, those plans must address the needs of shelters that house stray, lost, or abandoned animals before, during, and after a disaster.

This bill affects state and local governments that apply for federal emergency preparedness grants, as well as the animal shelters and emergency responders in those communities. Pet owners could indirectly benefit if their area has better resources to care for animals during disasters. The bill does not directly give money to individuals or require anyone to evacuate with their pets, but it makes it easier and cheaper for governments to build the infrastructure to handle animals in emergencies.

title: CBP SPACE Act
ai_summary:
This bill is about how U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) pays for buildings and equipment at sea ports of entry, which are the ports where ships bring goods and passengers into the country. Right now, CBP collects fees on imported goods, called merchandise processing fees, to cover its operating costs. This bill would expand what those fees can be used for, specifically allowing the money to also cover "capital costs," meaning things like construction, facility improvements, and equipment upgrades at seaports. The bill also calls on the Treasury Department and CBP to work together to set fee levels high enough to actually fund those needs.

The bill also adds two other rules. First, it says CBP cannot require seaports to provide or pay for office space, training rooms, or break rooms for CBP staff. That responsibility would no longer fall on the ports themselves. Second, it requires CBP to submit a yearly report to Congress explaining how much fee money was collected, how much went toward seaport facilities, and what construction or equipment needs still exist.

This bill mostly affects businesses that import goods into the United States, since they are the ones who pay the merchandise processing fees. It also affects the operators of sea ports of entry, who would no longer be on the hook for providing certain facilities to CBP. American consumers could be indirectly affected if changes in fees influence the cost of imported products, though the bill does not set a specific new fee amount.

title: To amend title 38, United States Code, to require the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to transmit a veteran's history of opioid prescriptions to a Community Care health care provider.
ai_summary:
This bill requires the Department of Veterans Affairs to share a veteran's opioid prescription history with outside doctors when that veteran receives care through the VA's Community Care program. Community Care is when the VA pays for a veteran to see a doctor outside the VA system, such as a private or local doctor, instead of at a VA facility. Right now, those outside doctors may not automatically receive the veteran's full prescription records from the VA.

Under this bill, when a veteran goes to a non-VA doctor through Community Care, the VA must send that doctor the veteran's history of opioid prescriptions. This information would be passed along through a third-party administrator, which is a company the VA already uses to help manage and coordinate outside care.

This bill affects veterans who use the VA's Community Care program to see doctors outside the VA system, as well as the outside doctors who treat them. The goal is to make sure those doctors know what opioids a veteran has already been prescribed before providing new treatment, which could help avoid dangerous drug interactions or duplicate prescriptions.

title: PLAN for Broadband Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs a top Commerce Department official to create a coordinated national plan for all federal broadband programs. Right now, more than a dozen federal agencies each run their own separate broadband programs, which can lead to wasted money, duplicate projects, and confusion. The bill requires the government to map out all those programs, identify where they overlap or conflict, and write a clear strategy to get them working together. An independent watchdog, the Government Accountability Office, would later review whether the plan is actually working.

The bill also addresses some specific problems. It requires federal agencies to track how long they take to process applications for installing broadband equipment on government-owned property, and to fix delays. It also makes large broadband construction projects on federal land go through a faster permitting review process if the project costs more than five million dollars. Agencies must publicly report how they are spending broadband money and how many locations are actually getting connected.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies, state and local governments, Tribal nations, and broadband internet providers who apply for federal funding or permits. Indirectly, it could affect any American who currently lacks reliable, affordable internet access, since the goal is to make federal spending on broadband less wasteful and more effective. The bill specifically calls out Tribal lands as an area needing extra attention. It does not give the government new power to regulate broadband service itself.

last_action_text: By Senator Cruz from Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation filed written report. Report No. 119-123. Minority views filed.

title: PART Act
ai_summary:
The PART Act is a bill designed to cut down on catalytic converter theft, which has surged in recent years because these car parts contain valuable metals. The bill requires the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to create new rules within 180 days that would make car manufacturers stamp or mark catalytic converters with identification numbers, similar to how vehicle identification numbers (VINs) already work for car bodies. It also sets up a $7 million grant program so that law enforcement agencies, car dealers, repair shops, and nonprofits can stamp existing catalytic converters with ID numbers at no cost to car owners, focusing first on areas where theft is most common.

The bill also changes how catalytic converters can be legally bought and sold. Sellers of these parts would have to provide their name, address, a copy of their ID, and proof of where the part came from. All sales would have to be paid for using traceable methods like checks or wire transfers, and paying with cash or cryptocurrency would become illegal. Selling or buying a converter with its markings removed would also be against the law. These rules apply to businesses in the salvage, recycling, and repair industries.

On the criminal side, the bill creates new federal crimes specifically for stealing catalytic converters or knowingly trafficking stolen ones, with penalties of up to five years in prison and fines. It also expands the legal definition of a chop shop to include places that extract precious metals from stolen car parts. This bill affects car owners broadly, as well as scrap metal dealers, auto recyclers, law enforcement, and anyone involved in buying or selling used car parts.
ai_headline: New federal bill targets catalytic converter theft with ID rules and prison time
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

The bill also bans cash and cryptocurrency payments for these parts, requires sellers to provide identification and proof of origin, and makes it illegal to sell or buy a converter with its markings removed. New federal crimes for stealing or trafficking stolen catalytic converters carry penalties of up to five years in prison and fines.

title: Preventing Child Labor Exploitation in Federal Contracting Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires companies that want to do business with the federal government to disclose whether they have been found guilty of violating child labor laws in the past three years. That includes the company itself, as well as any subcontractors it plans to use. If a company has a violation on record, it can still potentially win a government contract, but only if it works with the Department of Labor to fix the problem. Companies that refuse to address violations or lie about their record can be banned from receiving federal contracts for at least four years. The bill also raises the fines for child labor violations significantly, going from a maximum of $11,000 per violation up to $100,000, and from $50,000 to $500,000 for the most serious cases involving child injury or death.

This bill affects any private company, contractor, or subcontractor that does business with the federal government. It also directs the Department of Labor to train employees across multiple agencies, including Health and Human Services and Homeland Security, to better spot and report child labor violations. The Government Accountability Office would also be required to study how common these violations actually are among federal contractors and report back to Congress.

Everyday Americans are not directly required to do anything under this bill. Its main impact is on the business community that profits from government contracts, and it is intended to make sure taxpayer money does not go to companies that illegally employ children. The Department of Labor would publish annual reports on how the law is working, making that information available to the public.
ai_headline: Federal contractors would have to disclose child labor violations
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

Companies with violations on record can still compete for contracts if they work with the Department of Labor to correct the problem. title: TPS Reform Act of 2025
ai_summary:
Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, is a program that lets people from certain dangerous or disaster-hit countries stay and work in the United States temporarily. Right now, the executive branch, specifically the Secretary of Homeland Security, decides which countries qualify, for how long, and when to end or extend that protection. This bill would change that process so that only Congress can make those decisions, through a formal vote and a new law each time a country is added, extended, or removed from the program.

Under this bill, a country could only receive TPS designation if Congress passes a law stating that one of the usual qualifying conditions exists, such as an ongoing armed conflict, a major natural disaster, or other extraordinary temporary dangers. Any designation would last no more than 18 months to start, and extensions could only be granted in 12-month increments, again requiring a new act of Congress each time. The bill also adds a new rule that people who lack any lawful immigration status at all would be disqualified from receiving TPS, which is not an automatic bar under current law.

This bill would most directly affect the roughly 700,000 or more people currently holding TPS, as well as future applicants from countries that might face crises. It would also shift significant decision-making power from the executive branch to Congress, meaning the process for granting or ending TPS protections would become slower and subject to full legislative debate and votes. Employers who hire TPS holders, immigration courts, and federal agencies would also be affected by any changes to who qualifies and how long protections last.
ai_headline: Bill moves TPS decisions from executive branch to Congress
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 4201 would require an act of Congress to grant, extend, or end TPS, affecting 700,000+ current holders.

Initial designations would be capped at 18 months, with extensions granted only in 12-month increments through separate acts of Congress. The bill also adds a new disqualification barring people with no lawful immigration status from receiving TPS, a restriction not present under current law.

Employers who hire TPS holders, immigration courts, and federal agencies would also be affected by changes to eligibility and duration.
ai_sections.why: Shifting decisions to Congress would make the process for granting or ending TPS protections slower and subject to full legislative debate and votes. The added disqualification for people with no lawful immigration status would reduce the pool of people eligible to apply under existing conditions.

title: IRS Whistleblower Program Improvement Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes several changes to the IRS whistleblower program, which pays rewards to people who report others for cheating on their taxes. Right now, if someone tips off the IRS about tax fraud and later disputes the reward amount they receive, a court reviews the case but is limited in what it can consider. This bill would allow the court to take a fresh, thorough look at the case, including new evidence that wasn't available before. It also protects whistleblowers from having their identity revealed in court unless a judge decides there is a strong public reason to do so.

The bill also adds financial protections for whistleblowers. If the IRS takes more than 12 months after collecting money from a tax case to notify the whistleblower about their reward, the government must pay interest on top of the award amount. Additionally, whistleblower awards would be protected from automatic federal budget cuts known as sequestration, which have in the past reduced these payments. The bill also fixes a tax rule so that whistleblowers can deduct attorneys fees on their taxes regardless of which part of the law their award falls under, not just one specific section.

The people most directly affected are individuals who report tax law violations to the IRS and are waiting for their reward payments. It also affects taxpayers who are reported and investigated, as well as tax attorneys who work these cases. More broadly, the bill is intended to encourage more people to come forward with information about tax fraud by making the process fairer and safer for those who do.
ai_headline: Senate bill would strengthen IRS whistleblower rewards and protections
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

ai_sections.tldr: S 4639 expands court review, adds interest penalties, and shields IRS whistleblower awards from federal budget sequestration cuts.
ai_sections.what: S 4639 changes how courts review IRS whistleblower reward disputes, allowing judges to consider new evidence and conduct a full fresh review of each case. The bill shields whistleblower identities in court unless a judge finds a strong public reason to reveal them. It also fixes a tax deduction rule so whistleblowers can deduct attorneys fees regardless of which legal provision their award falls under.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects individuals who report tax law violations to the IRS and are awaiting reward payments, as well as tax attorneys who handle these cases. Taxpayers who are reported and investigated by the IRS are also affected.
ai_sections.why: The changes are intended to make the whistleblower process fairer and safer, which proponents say could encourage more people to report tax fraud. Past sequestration cuts have reduced whistleblower payments, and reward notification delays have gone uncompensated under current law.
ai_sections.cost: If the IRS takes more than 12 months after collecting money from a tax case to notify a whistleblower, the government must pay interest on top of the award. Whistleblower awards would also be shielded from automatic federal budget cuts known as sequestration.

title: IRS Whistleblower Program Improvement Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes several changes to improve how the IRS handles people who report tax cheating, known as whistleblowers. Right now, when someone tips off the IRS about a person or company hiding income or avoiding taxes, the IRS can pay that person a reward. This bill strengthens the rules around those rewards. Specifically, it lets whistleblowers get a fresh, thorough review from a federal tax court if they disagree with their reward amount, rather than a more limited review. It also requires the IRS to pay interest on rewards if the agency takes too long to notify a whistleblower about their payment, starting if no notice is given within 12 months after the tax money is collected.

The bill also adds privacy protections, allowing whistleblowers to stay anonymous in Tax Court unless the court decides there is a strong public reason to reveal their identity that outweighs the risk of harm to them. Additionally, it requires the IRS's annual whistleblower report to include descriptions of up to 10 of the biggest tax avoidance schemes that whistleblowers exposed that year. It also fixes a tax rule so that whistleblowers can deduct their attorney's fees on their taxes regardless of which part of the whistleblower law their award came under.

This bill primarily affects people who report tax fraud or large-scale tax avoidance to the IRS and are waiting for a financial reward. It also affects the IRS itself, which would face new requirements around timely payments, reporting, and court proceedings. Ordinary taxpayers are not directly affected, though the program in general is meant to help the government collect taxes that might otherwise go unpaid.
ai_headline: IRS whistleblower rewards would get stronger court oversight and privacy rules
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7959 strengthens IRS whistleblower rewards with full court review, interest penalties, anonymity, and attorney fee deductions.

The bill also requires the IRS to pay interest on rewards if it fails to notify a whistleblower within 12 months of collecting the reported tax money.

The IRS is also directly affected, facing new requirements around court proceedings, timely payment notices, annual reporting, and anonymity rules.

The IRS would face additional procedural obligations, including publishing descriptions of up to 10 major tax avoidance schemes exposed by whistleblowers each year.

title: Housing Temperature Safety Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would create a three-year test program run by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). The government would give grants to landlords and public housing agencies so they can install internet-connected temperature sensors in federally subsidized rental apartments. The sensors would track indoor temperatures to help make sure homes stay within required temperature ranges. Landlords would need to get written permission from a tenant before putting a sensor in their unit, and any personal information collected would be protected under rules HUD must set up within six months.

The program would track temperature-related complaints and violations before and after sensors are installed to see if the devices actually help. HUD would publish a progress report after one year and a final report after the program ends, comparing different sensor types by cost, features, and how well they worked in different climates. The bill does not set a specific dollar amount but authorizes Congress to fund the grants, program administration, and technical help for participating landlords.

This bill mainly affects people living in federally assisted housing, including public housing, Section 8 project-based housing, and supportive housing programs for elderly people and people with disabilities. It also affects the landlords and public housing agencies that manage those properties. Private market renters who do not receive federal housing assistance would not be covered by this program.
ai_headline: HUD would run three-year sensor test in federally subsidized rentals
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 638 would fund a 3-year HUD pilot installing temperature sensors in federally subsidized apartments, with tenant consent required.
ai_sections.what: HR 638 would create a three-year pilot program in which HUD gives grants to landlords and public housing agencies to install internet-connected temperature sensors in federally subsidized rental units. The sensors would monitor indoor temperatures to verify homes stay within required ranges. HUD would publish a one-year progress report and a final report comparing sensor types by cost, features, and performance across different climates.
ai_sections.who: The program would directly affect residents of federally assisted housing, including public housing, Section 8 project-based housing, and supportive housing for elderly people and people with disabilities, as well as the landlords and public housing agencies managing those properties. Private market renters without federal housing assistance would not be covered.
ai_sections.why: Tracking temperature complaints and violations before and after sensor installation would allow HUD to measure whether the devices produce measurable improvements in compliance. The results could inform future policy decisions about temperature monitoring in federally assisted housing.
ai_sections.cost: No specific dollar amount is set in the bill. Congress is authorized to fund grants, program administration, and technical assistance for participating landlords.

title: VA Home Loan Awareness Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill makes one small but specific change to the standard home loan application form used across the country. When someone applying for a mortgage checks "yes" to the question asking about military service, a new notice would appear directly on that form saying they may qualify for a VA Home Loan and should ask their lender about it. The goal is to make sure veterans and servicemembers do not miss out on this benefit simply because they did not know it existed.

The bill also requires a government watchdog agency, the Government Accountability Office, to check in 18 months and report to Congress on whether lenders are actually including this notice on the form. If fewer than 80 percent of lenders are doing so, Congress would be informed and could decide whether further action is needed.

This mainly affects military veterans, active-duty servicemembers, and surviving spouses who apply for a home mortgage, since those are the people who could qualify for VA home loans. It also affects mortgage lenders and the two government-backed companies, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, that oversee the standard loan application form, since they would be required to update it within six months of the law passing.
ai_headline: Veterans could see VA loan alert added to standard mortgage form
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 2362 adds a VA loan notice to mortgage applications when applicants indicate military service, reaching veterans who may not know the benefit exists.

Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, which oversee the form, would have six months after enactment to make the update. The Government Accountability Office would report to Congress within 18 months on whether lenders are complying, with a compliance threshold set at 80 percent.

ai_sections.why: If the notice requirement works as intended, fewer eligible applicants would bypass VA loan benefits due to lack of awareness. The GAO reporting mechanism gives Congress a defined trigger point for deciding whether additional enforcement is needed.

title: Streamlining Rural Housing Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill tells two federal agencies, the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the Department of Agriculture (USDA), to work together more closely on housing projects they both fund. Right now, when a housing project receives money from both agencies, developers often have to go through separate review processes for each one, including separate environmental reviews and property inspections. The bill requires both agencies to sign a formal agreement within 180 days to coordinate those processes, reduce duplication, and agree on which agency takes the lead on a given project.

The bill also creates an advisory working group made up of people from across the housing world, including nonprofit builders, property managers, state housing agencies, and actual residents of assisted housing. This group helps guide how the agreement gets put into practice. Within one year, both agencies must send Congress a report recommending ways to make government-funded housing projects run more efficiently, with a specific requirement that any changes not reduce resident safety, raise long-term costs for residents, or weaken environmental protections.

The people most directly affected are those who live in or are trying to build affordable housing in rural areas, since USDA's housing programs focus heavily on rural communities. Housing developers, nonprofit organizations, and local housing agencies that work with both HUD and USDA funding would also be affected, as they currently deal with the overlapping paperwork and reviews this bill aims to simplify.
ai_headline: HUD and USDA must coordinate housing reviews under new bill
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 4989 requires HUD and USDA to sign a coordination agreement within 180 days to reduce duplicated reviews on jointly funded housing projects.
ai_sections.what: HR 4989 requires the Department of Housing and Urban Development and the Department of Agriculture to sign a formal agreement within 180 days to coordinate their review processes, including environmental reviews and property inspections, on projects both agencies fund. The bill also establishes an advisory working group drawn from nonprofit builders, property managers, state housing agencies, and residents of assisted housing. Within one year, both agencies must submit a report to Congress recommending efficiency improvements, with a condition that changes must not reduce resident safety, raise long-term costs for residents, or weaken environmental protections.

Housing developers, nonprofit organizations, and local housing agencies that currently navigate overlapping paperwork from both HUD and USDA would also be affected.

This bill aims to designate a lead agency per project and reduce that overlap, though the required safeguards indicate concerns that streamlining could otherwise affect resident welfare or environmental standards.

title: HUD Accountability Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would require the head of the Department of Housing and Urban Development, known as the HUD Secretary, to appear before Congress once a year to answer questions and give a report. Right now, there is no law forcing the HUD Secretary to do this on a regular schedule. The bill would make it a legal requirement, not just an option.

During these annual hearings, the Secretary would have to cover specific topics. These include how HUD's programs are running, the condition of public housing, the financial health of the FHA mortgage insurance program, efforts to prevent waste and fraud among groups that receive HUD money, progress on affordable housing and homelessness, and whether the department has what it needs to do its job.

This bill mostly affects government officials and how Congress oversees HUD. Indirectly, it could matter to anyone who rents public housing, receives housing assistance, or has an FHA-backed mortgage, since regular congressional hearings could lead to more scrutiny of how those programs are managed. The bill was introduced by members of both parties and has been sent to the House Committee on Financial Services for review.
ai_headline: HUD Secretary would face mandatory annual testimony under HR 3774
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 3774 would legally require the HUD Secretary to testify before Congress once a year on housing programs and department operations.
ai_sections.what: HR 3774 would make it a legal requirement for the HUD Secretary to appear before Congress once a year, replacing what is currently an optional practice. The Secretary would be required to report on specific topics including public housing conditions, FHA mortgage insurance finances, affordable housing progress, homelessness, fraud prevention, and departmental resources.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects the HUD Secretary and congressional oversight. Indirectly, it could affect renters in public housing, recipients of housing assistance, and homeowners with FHA-backed mortgages.
ai_sections.why: Regular mandatory hearings would increase congressional scrutiny of HUD programs and how they are managed. This added oversight could affect how housing assistance and mortgage programs are administered for people who rely on them.

title: Legislative Accountability Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require Congress to publicly identify which lawmakers are responsible for specific parts of legislation. When a committee approves a bill, the committee chair would have to report the names of any members who added amendments to it. For major spending and tax bills from key committees like Appropriations, Ways and Means, and Finance, chairs would also have to name who is responsible for each individual provision included in the bill. These names would then appear as footnotes in the official published versions of the legislation, including the final enacted law.

The goal is to create a paper trail showing exactly who added what to a piece of legislation. Right now, it can be difficult for the public to know which lawmaker slipped a specific provision or spending item into a bill. Under this bill, that information would be attached directly to the text of the law itself, making it easier to look up.

This primarily affects members of Congress and how they do their work, but the broader audience is everyday Americans, journalists, watchdog groups, and voters who want to know more about how laws get made. It does not change what lawmakers can put into bills, only whether their names are attached to what they add.
ai_headline: Bill would put lawmakers' names directly in the text of laws they shaped
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Rules, and in addition to the Committee on House Administration, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 3507 would require lawmakers' names to appear as footnotes in legislation showing who added each provision.
ai_sections.what: HR 3507 would require committee chairs to publicly identify which members added amendments or specific provisions to a bill. For major spending and tax bills from committees such as Appropriations, Ways and Means, and Finance, chairs would also have to name who is responsible for each individual provision. Those names would appear as footnotes in the official published text of the legislation, including in the final enacted law.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects members of Congress and how they handle legislation. The broader audience includes everyday Americans, journalists, watchdog groups, and voters who want to understand how laws are made.
ai_sections.why: Currently, it can be difficult for the public to identify which lawmaker added a specific provision or spending item to a bill. Attaching names directly to the text of the law would create a searchable paper trail tied to the final enacted legislation.

title: HUD-USDA-VA Interagency Coordination Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells three federal agencies, the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), the Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), to start working more closely together on housing programs. First, it requires the three agencies to sign a formal agreement to share housing research and data with each other. Second, within 180 days of becoming law, the agencies must write a joint report identifying ways they can team up to run their housing programs more efficiently and submit it to Congress.

Before that report goes to Congress, it must be published publicly for 30 days so that ordinary people can read it and submit comments. This is a study and coordination bill, meaning it does not directly change any housing rules or create new programs right now. It is mainly designed to get agencies talking to each other and to gather ideas for future improvements.

This bill could affect a wide range of people who use federal housing assistance. That includes low-income renters and homebuyers who use HUD programs, rural residents who rely on USDA home loans and rental assistance, and military veterans who use VA home loan benefits. If the agencies find better ways to coordinate, those programs could potentially become easier to access and less wasteful over time, though the bill itself does not guarantee any specific changes.
ai_headline: Federal housing agencies ordered to coordinate and share data under HR 5429
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 5429 requires HUD, USDA, and VA to share housing data and file a joint efficiency report to Congress within 180 days.
ai_sections.what: HR 5429 requires HUD, USDA, and the VA to sign a formal data-sharing agreement and produce a joint report identifying ways to run their housing programs more efficiently. The report must be submitted to Congress within 180 days of the bill becoming law. Before reaching Congress, the report must be posted publicly for 30 days to allow comment from the general public.

If the agencies identify efficiencies, those programs could potentially become easier to access and less wasteful over time, though no specific changes are guaranteed by this bill.

title: Housing Unhoused Disabled Veterans Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the government counts income when deciding if a disabled veteran qualifies for a specific federal housing program called HUD-VASH. HUD-VASH provides housing vouchers to homeless veterans. Right now, disability payments that veterans receive from the Department of Veterans Affairs count as income when the government checks if someone qualifies. This bill would stop those VA disability payments from being counted as income during that eligibility check. That means more disabled veterans could qualify for the program, even if their VA disability checks bring their total income above the current limit.

The bill also applies this same rule to future housing programs built on VA-owned property and run by the Department of Housing and Urban Development. So if new veterans housing programs are created down the road, VA disability benefits would be excluded from income calculations there too. One important detail: the exclusion only applies to figuring out who is eligible, not to calculating how much rent a person pays once they are in the program. Rent amounts can still take that income into account.

The people most directly affected are homeless or at-risk veterans who receive VA disability compensation or pension benefits. Veterans who currently earn too much to qualify for HUD-VASH housing vouchers because of those disability payments could become eligible under this new rule. Housing administrators and local public housing agencies that run the HUD-VASH program would also need to update how they process applications.
ai_headline: VA disability pay would stop counting against veterans in federal housing program
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 965 would exclude VA disability payments from income calculations when disabled veterans apply for HUD-VASH housing vouchers.
ai_sections.what: HR 965 changes how income is calculated for disabled veterans applying to HUD-VASH, a federal program that gives housing vouchers to homeless veterans. Under the bill, VA disability compensation and pension payments would not count as income when determining eligibility. The same exclusion would apply to future HUD-run housing programs built on VA-owned property.
ai_sections.who: Homeless or at-risk veterans who receive VA disability compensation or pension benefits are the primary people affected. Local public housing agencies and administrators who process HUD-VASH applications would also need to update how they review eligibility.
ai_sections.why: Veterans whose VA disability payments currently push their total income above the program limit could become eligible for housing vouchers under this change. The exclusion applies only to eligibility determinations, not to rent calculations, so rent amounts could still reflect those disability payments once a veteran is enrolled.

title: Helping More Families Save Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates a test program to help low-income families who receive federal housing assistance build savings. Up to 25 housing agencies or private landlords that participate in federal housing programs would be selected to run the program, serving up to 5,000 families total. Here is how it works: when a participating family earns more money and their rent goes up as a result, the extra rent amount gets deposited into a savings account in the family's name instead of simply being paid out. That money grows with interest over time, and the family can withdraw it after five years, or earlier if they leave the housing program or want to use the funds for an approved goal like education or starting a business.

The program includes a few important protections for families. Any extra income a family earns while in the program cannot be counted against them when calculating eligibility for other government benefits. Families can also update their income information more than once a year so their rent adjusts more quickly. Participation is completely voluntary, families can opt out at any time, and choosing not to join cannot affect their housing assistance in any way. Families cannot be in this program and the existing Family Self-Sufficiency program at the same time.

The people most directly affected are low-income renters who use Section 8 housing vouchers or live in public housing and whose household income is below 80 percent of the median income in their area. The program runs for ten years, costs up to $5 million for startup and evaluation, and requires a government report on whether it actually helped families become more financially independent.
ai_headline: Pilot program would let low-income renters build savings as income rises
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 4385 lets up to 5,000 assisted-housing families save the rent increases tied to higher earnings instead of paying them out.
ai_sections.what: HR 4385 establishes a ten-year pilot program in which up to 25 housing agencies or private landlords run savings accounts for participating families. When a family earns more money and their rent rises as a result, the added rent amount is deposited into a savings account in the family's name rather than collected as rent. Families can withdraw the funds after five years, or earlier if they leave the housing program or use the money for an approved purpose such as education or starting a business.
ai_sections.who: The program targets low-income renters who use Section 8 housing vouchers or live in public housing and whose household income is below 80 percent of the area median income. Participation is voluntary, capped at 5,000 families across all selected agencies and landlords.

A government report on whether the program improved financial independence is required, and families already enrolled in the Family Self-Sufficiency program cannot participate at the same time.
