title: Community Investment and Prosperity Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes a simple change to existing banking law. Right now, national banks and certain state banks are allowed to invest a portion of their money into projects that benefit the public good — things like affordable housing, community development, or economic programs in low-income areas. The current law caps how much a bank can put into these kinds of investments at 15% of the bank's capital and surplus funds. This bill would raise that cap to 20%.

The change gives banking regulators — specifically the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Reserve — more flexibility to allow banks to invest more in these community-focused projects if they choose to do so. It does not require banks to invest more, it just raises the ceiling on how much they are permitted to invest in this category.

The people most directly affected are national banks, state member banks, and the communities where these public welfare investments typically go. That often includes lower-income neighborhoods that benefit from things like affordable housing construction or small business lending programs. Bank regulators would also have broader authority to approve larger investments in this area than they currently can.
ai_headline: Banking bill raises community investment cap from 15% to 20%
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 5913 raises the cap on bank public welfare investments from 15% to 20% of capital and surplus, giving regulators broader approval authority.
ai_sections.what: HR 5913 raises the maximum share of capital and surplus that national banks and certain state banks may invest in public welfare projects from 15% to 20%. This applies to investments in areas such as affordable housing, community development, and economic programs in low-income areas. The bill does not require banks to invest more — it only raises the permitted ceiling.

The Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Reserve would also gain broader authority to approve larger investments in this category.

Communities in low-income areas could see larger or more frequent investments in things like affordable housing and small business lending programs, depending on whether individual banks choose to invest more.

title: BUILD Housing Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how environmental reviews are handled for certain housing projects funded by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). Right now, when HUD gives money for housing, the federal government handles the environmental review process, which checks whether a project could harm the surrounding environment. This bill would allow HUD to shift that responsibility to state and local governments for a broader range of housing assistance programs, similar to a process that already exists for some HUD-funded projects.

The bill also expands who can take on that environmental review responsibility. Currently, only states and local governments can take over these reviews. This bill adds federally recognized Native American tribes to that list, giving tribal governments the same ability to conduct and be accountable for environmental reviews on housing projects in their communities.

The people most directly affected are state, local, and tribal government officials who manage HUD-funded housing programs, as well as the developers and organizations building those homes. Indirectly, it could affect anyone living in or near communities where HUD-funded housing is being built, since the entity overseeing environmental protections would change. Supporters of this kind of change generally argue it speeds up housing development by reducing federal red tape, while critics sometimes raise concerns about whether local oversight provides the same level of environmental protection as federal review.
ai_headline: HUD environmental review authority would extend to tribal governments under HR 4810
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

It also adds federally recognized Native American tribes to the list of entities eligible to conduct and be accountable for those reviews. Currently only states and local governments hold that option, and only for a narrower range of programs.

ai_sections.why: Shifting review authority to more local levels of government changes which entity is accountable for ensuring environmental protections are met on housing projects. title: WEAR IT Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change tax rules to let people use money from Health Savings Accounts (HSAs), Flexible Spending Accounts (FSAs), and similar tax-free health accounts to pay for certain wearable health devices. Right now, these accounts can only be used for items that qualify as medical expenses under the tax code. The WEAR IT Act would add wearable devices to that list, as long as the device collects health data or helps diagnose or treat a medical condition. Examples could include smartwatches or fitness trackers that monitor heart rate, blood oxygen, or other health signals. There is a cap of $375 per year that can be spent this way. The change would take effect starting January 1, 2026.

The bill defines a qualifying wearable device as something worn on the body, or software connected to such a device, that tracks physical health data for medical purposes or helps with diagnosis or treatment of a health condition. Not every fitness gadget would qualify automatically. The device or its software would need to meet the medical-purpose requirement described in the bill.

This bill affects anyone who has an HSA, FSA, Health Reimbursement Arrangement, or Archer Medical Savings Account. That covers tens of millions of Americans, particularly those with employer-sponsored health plans or high-deductible health insurance. It could also affect makers and sellers of wearable health technology, since qualifying products could become more affordable for consumers using pre-tax dollars.
ai_headline: Tax-free health accounts could cover wearable devices under new bill
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

A device qualifies if it is worn on the body, tracks physical health data for medical purposes, or helps diagnose or treat a health condition. Spending through this provision is capped at $375 per year, and the change would take effect January 1, 2026.

Not all fitness or wearable gadgets would automatically qualify, so the distinction between qualifying and non-qualifying devices would carry financial consequences for both consumers and manufacturers.

title: Rural Health Clinic Location Modernization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the government decides whether a medical clinic qualifies as a "Rural Health Clinic" under Medicare. Right now, a clinic cannot get that designation if it is located in an area the Census Bureau calls "urbanized," which currently means any area with 50,000 or more people. The Census Bureau recently updated its definitions, which caused some clinics that had long been considered rural to suddenly lose their rural status. This bill locks in the 50,000-person population threshold in federal law so that clinics in areas under that size can still qualify as rural, regardless of how the Census Bureau updates its terminology going forward. The change would take effect on January 1, 2027.

Rural Health Clinics get a higher Medicare reimbursement rate than regular doctor's offices, which helps them stay financially stable in areas where patients may be spread out and harder to serve. By keeping the 50,000-person cutoff in place, the bill is designed to prevent clinics in smaller communities from losing that higher payment rate simply because the Census Bureau changed how it labels geographic areas, not because the communities themselves actually became more urban.

The people most affected are patients who rely on clinics in smaller towns and communities near the 50,000-population boundary, as well as the clinics themselves and the healthcare workers employed there. If clinics lost their Rural Health Clinic status, they could receive less money from Medicare, which might force them to cut services or close. This bill aims to protect access to care in those areas by keeping the existing standard in law.
ai_headline: Bill locks in 50,000-person threshold for rural clinic Medicare status
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Ways and Means, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

The change prevents Census Bureau terminology updates from stripping rural status from clinics in communities that have not actually grown more urban. The law would take effect on January 1, 2027.

Reduced payments could lead some clinics to cut services or close, affecting patient access to care in those communities.

title: RESIDE Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates a five-year test program, running from 2027 to 2031, where the federal government would award grants to local governments and housing authorities to turn run-down, empty buildings into housing. The buildings targeted are places like old warehouses, factories, malls, strip malls, and hotels that have been left vacant and are unsafe or legally abandoned. The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) would hand out grants between $1 million and $10 million each on a competitive basis, but only if the existing federal HOME housing program is already funded above a certain level. The money could be used for buying properties, tearing down unsafe structures, cleaning up health hazards, and constructing or renovating the buildings into homes.

The housing created must be affordable or attainable, meaning it is priced for people earning at or below the local median income, with most units reserved for lower-income households. Priority goes to communities facing economic hardship, designated opportunity zones, and local governments that have already cut red tape to make these kinds of conversions easier. The program does not replace existing housing funds that communities already receive — it would be extra money on top of that.

This program would most directly affect local governments that apply for the grants, developers who partner with them, and residents in communities with vacant or blighted properties. People who could benefit from the resulting housing include lower- and middle-income renters and buyers, as well as elderly people, people with disabilities, and veterans, who are specifically called out in a required follow-up report HUD must send to Congress after the program ends.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

Eligible buildings include warehouses, factories, malls, strip malls, and hotels that are unsafe or legally abandoned. Grant funds may be used for acquiring properties, demolishing unsafe structures, cleaning up health hazards, and constructing or renovating homes.

title: Choice in Affordable Housing Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill tries to get more landlords to accept Section 8 housing vouchers. Section 8, officially called the Housing Choice Voucher program, helps low-income families, elderly people, and people with disabilities pay for housing by giving them vouchers they can use at private rentals. The problem is that many landlords refuse to accept these vouchers, and thousands of landlords have been leaving the program every year. This bill creates several financial incentives to bring more landlords in, especially in neighborhoods with lower poverty rates and better access to schools and jobs. It would set up a fund of up to $100 million per year from 2025 to 2029 to pay for these efforts.

The main tools the bill uses are a one-time bonus payment to landlords who are new to the program, government-backed security deposits so tenants can more easily move in, and bonus payments to housing agencies that hire staff dedicated to recruiting and helping landlords. The bill also makes it easier for landlords to get their units approved by allowing inspections already done through other federal housing programs to count, so landlords do not have to go through the process twice. It also expands the use of zip-code-level rent calculations so vouchers can more accurately match real rents in different neighborhoods.

The people most affected are low-income renters who already have vouchers but struggle to find landlords who will accept them, as well as private landlords who might now join the program because of the new financial incentives. Local housing agencies would also be affected since they would receive new funding and face new requirements to track and report results. The bill does not change who qualifies for vouchers or how much assistance families receive.
ai_headline: New bill offers landlords cash bonuses to accept Section 8 vouchers
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

The bill offers one-time bonus payments to new landlords, government-backed security deposits, and bonuses to housing agencies that hire staff dedicated to landlord recruitment. It also allows inspections completed through other federal housing programs to count toward Section 8 approval, and expands zip-code-level rent calculations so vouchers more closely match actual rents in different neighborhoods.

ai_sections.why: Thousands of landlords have been leaving the Section 8 program each year, reducing the number of units available to voucher holders. Expanding landlord participation could change where low-income families are able to rent, particularly in lower-poverty neighborhoods with greater access to schools and jobs, though outcomes would depend on how many landlords respond to the incentives.
ai_sections.cost: The bill establishes a fund of up to $100 million per year from 2025 through 2029 to pay for the incentives and agency support described in the bill.

title: HOME Investment Partnerships Reauthorization and Improvement Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews and updates the HOME Investment Partnerships Program, a long-running federal program that gives money to states, cities, and counties to build, buy, or fix up affordable housing for low- and moderate-income people. The bill would authorize about $5 billion in federal funding for 2025, growing to about $6 billion by 2029. It also creates a new loan guarantee program, meaning the federal government would back up to $2 billion in loans to help local governments finance affordable housing projects when they cannot get that financing on their own.

The bill makes several practical changes to how the program works. It removes a deadline that previously required local governments to commit their funds within a certain time period, gives local governments more flexibility on setting resale prices for homes bought with program money, and adds new rules to protect tenants in small rental properties of four units or fewer. It also strengthens penalties when local governments misuse or mismanage program funds, and requires that property inspections be reported publicly so residents can see how well housing is being maintained.

The people most directly affected are low- and moderate-income renters and homebuyers who rely on affordable housing, as well as the state and local governments and nonprofit organizations that manage these housing programs. Community land trusts, which are nonprofits that keep homes permanently affordable, receive clearer rules and more flexibility under the bill. Military members who are deployed or receive new orders are given special protections so they are not penalized for leaving a home purchased through the program.
ai_headline: Federal affordable housing program renewed with $5B in new funding
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

The bill removes a prior deadline requiring local governments to commit funds within a set period and adds new tenant protections for renters in properties of four units or fewer. It also strengthens penalties for misuse of program funds and requires public reporting of property inspections.

title: HOME Reform Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill updates the HOME Investment Partnerships Program, which is a long-running federal program that gives money to states and local governments to build, repair, and help people afford housing. The bill makes several changes to how that money can be used. It expands who qualifies for help, raising the income limit from "low-income" to anyone earning up to 100 percent of the median income in their area, which means more middle-income families could receive assistance. It also lets smaller housing projects skip some environmental reviews, raises the size threshold before federal labor rules kick in from 12 units to 24 units, and allows federal housing funds to pay for basic infrastructure like water lines and roads near affordable housing in smaller communities.

The bill also makes it easier to count certain units as "affordable" if tenants are already using Housing Choice Vouchers, sometimes called Section 8. For homeownership, it raises a price cap from 95 percent to 110 percent of an area's median home value, adds community land trusts and shared equity models as approved ways to keep homes affordable long-term, and creates exceptions for military members who are deployed or reassigned and for heirs who inherit a HOME-assisted home as their primary residence.

People most directly affected include renters and homebuyers with low to moderate incomes, nonprofit housing developers, and local governments that receive HOME funding. Smaller cities and towns that do not receive other federal community development grants could also benefit from the new option to use HOME funds for nearby infrastructure. The bill also removes some rules from the "Buy American" requirements and certain local hiring mandates for smaller projects, which could affect contractors and workers involved in federally assisted housing construction.

title: Identifying Regulatory Barriers to Housing Supply Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires cities, counties, and other local governments that receive federal Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) money to submit a report to the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) at least once every five years. In that report, they must describe their local land use and zoning rules across a list of about 22 specific topics — things like whether they allow duplexes in single-family neighborhoods, accessory dwelling units, office-to-apartment conversions, or reduced parking requirements. They have to say whether they have already adopted each policy, whether they plan to, and how it might help housing in their area. The bill gives HUD one year after passage to set up the standardized form communities would use.

Importantly, the bill does not force any local government to actually change its zoning laws. Submitting the report does not commit a community to doing anything, and HUD cannot use the information to punish or take enforcement action against a community. It is essentially a data-collection and transparency measure — the federal government learns what local rules exist across the country that may be limiting the construction of new homes.

The people most directly affected are local governments that receive CDBG funding, which includes many cities and counties of varying sizes across the country. Renters and homebuyers could be indirectly affected over time if the collected information leads to broader policy discussions about housing costs and availability. Builders, developers, and housing advocates who follow zoning reform would also watch the data this bill generates.

title: HOME Reform Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill updates the HOME Investment Partnerships Program, a long-running federal program that gives money to states and local governments to build and repair affordable housing. The main changes would make it easier and faster for communities to use those funds. Small construction projects of 15 units or fewer, infill housing built on empty lots inside cities, property purchases for affordable housing, and basic rehabilitation projects would no longer need to go through a full federal environmental review. If a project already went through one environmental review, it would not have to repeat the process just because funding sources changed. The bill also removes a rule that caused unspent housing funds to expire, and it loosens limits on how much a home can cost and still qualify for the program, raising the price ceiling from 95 percent to 110 percent of the area median.

The bill also expands who qualifies for HOME Program assistance. Right now the program mainly targets low-income families. This bill would raise the income limit so that families earning up to 100 percent of the local median income could be eligible, which in many areas means middle-income working families would now qualify. Renters who already use a Housing Choice Voucher (Section 8) would more easily count toward a project's affordability requirements. The bill also adds flexibility for military members who get deployed and for heirs who inherit a home that was purchased with HOME funds, so those families do not lose their housing benefits due to circumstances outside their control.

Smaller cities and rural communities that do not receive separate federal block grant money would gain a new option to use HOME funds for nearby infrastructure like water lines, sidewalks, and roads, as long as those improvements directly support affordable housing projects. Nonprofit community housing organizations would have more time and flexibility to spend reserved funds before the money gets redirected. This bill would affect local governments, housing developers, nonprofit housing organizations, renters using vouchers, moderate- and low-income homebuyers, and military families across the country.

It also removes the rule that causes unspent HOME funds to expire and raises the qualifying home price ceiling from 95 percent to 110 percent of the area median.

Smaller cities and rural communities without separate federal block grant funding would also gain new options under the bill.

title: Housing Supply Frameworks Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to create a set of guidelines and best practices for how states and cities can change their zoning laws to allow more homes to be built. Zoning laws are local rules that control what can be built where, and right now many of those rules make it harder to build new housing. HUD would have three years to publish these guidelines, and along the way it must take public comments and consult a task force made up of planners, builders, housing advocates, community members, researchers, and local officials. The guidelines are not binding — states and cities don't have to follow them — but they give local governments a menu of options to consider.

The specific recommendations the guidelines must cover include things like reducing required parking spaces, allowing smaller lot sizes, permitting more types of homes (like duplexes, triplexes, and backyard accessory units), speeding up the permit approval process, building more housing near public transit, and protecting lower-income residents from being pushed out of their neighborhoods. The bill also shuts down an older, similar federal program called the Regulatory Barriers Clearinghouse and replaces it with this new approach. HUD would get up to $3 million per year from 2026 through 2030 to fund the work, and would report back to Congress five years after the guidelines are published on which states and cities actually used them.

This bill mainly affects state and local governments that make zoning and land use decisions, as well as housing developers, builders, and renters or homebuyers who are struggling with high housing costs. It does not force any community to change its laws, but it could influence future federal grant decisions and give local officials a clearer roadmap if they want to allow more housing to be built in their area.
ai_headline: HUD would publish voluntary zoning guidelines to spur homebuilding under new bill
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

The guidelines are nonbinding, so no community is required to change its laws, though the bill notes the guidelines could influence future federal grant decisions.

title: Disabled Veterans Housing Support Act
ai_summary:
This law changes how the government calculates income when disabled veterans apply for certain housing assistance programs. Specifically, any disability compensation a veteran receives from the Department of Veterans Affairs because of a service-connected injury or illness will no longer be counted as income. This applies to housing programs funded under the Housing and Community Development Act of 1974, which includes community development block grants used by states, cities, and tribal governments to support affordable housing.

Before this change, that disability pay could push a veteran's counted income high enough to disqualify them from low- or moderate-income housing help, even if the money is meant to cover costs related to their disability. Now, states, local governments, and tribal governments must leave that compensation out of the income calculation when deciding who qualifies for those programs.

The law also requires the Government Accountability Office to submit a report to Congress within one year. That report must look at how VA disability compensation is treated across all HUD programs, flag any programs that still count it as income, and suggest fixes. The people most directly affected are veterans who receive VA disability compensation and are seeking affordable housing assistance through federally supported local programs.
ai_headline: VA disability pay excluded from income rules for veteran housing aid
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-70.

title: PERMIT Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes the legal definition of "navigable waters" under the Clean Water Act, which is the main federal law that controls water pollution and regulates what can be discharged into U.S. waterways. Right now, there is ongoing debate about exactly which bodies of water the federal government has the authority to protect and regulate. This bill writes specific exclusions directly into the law, meaning certain types of water would no longer fall under federal Clean Water Act protections. Those excluded categories include wastewater treatment ponds, streams that only flow after it rains (called ephemeral streams), farmland that was converted from wetlands before 1985, and groundwater. It also gives the EPA Administrator and the Army Corps of Engineers the power to exclude additional water features in the future.

The people most directly affected are farmers, landowners, and developers. If a body of water on or near their property no longer counts as a "navigable water," they would not need a federal permit to discharge into it or fill it in. That could make it faster and cheaper to build on land, farm, or develop property near certain wetlands or seasonal streams. Environmental regulators and state governments would also be affected, since states would need to decide whether to fill any gaps in protection through their own laws.

Ordinary residents who live near streams, wetlands, or rural water sources could see impacts too, since federal oversight of those specific water types would be reduced. People who rely on well water or downstream drinking water sources may be affected depending on how groundwater and seasonal streams connect to larger water supplies in their area. The bill does not eliminate the Clean Water Act overall, but it does narrow which waters receive federal protection under it.

title: To require approval from the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development for any Federal manufactured home and safety standards, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill changes who has the final say over safety and construction rules for manufactured homes, which are factory-built homes sometimes called mobile homes. Right now, multiple federal agencies can create their own standards for how these homes must be built. Under this bill, the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) would become the lead authority, and any other federal agency that wants to create a new rule for manufactured homes would first have to get HUD's approval before that rule could take effect.

The bill gives HUD the power to reject another agency's proposed standard for several reasons, including if HUD believes the rule would significantly raise the cost of producing manufactured homes, if it conflicts with rules HUD already has in place, or for any other reason HUD decides is appropriate. It also adds "energy efficiency" to the list of topics that manufactured home standards can cover.

This bill most directly affects the roughly 22 million Americans who live in manufactured homes, as well as the companies that build and sell them. It could also affect other federal agencies, like the Department of Energy, that currently have or might want to create their own rules for manufactured home construction. Whether the bill leads to stronger or weaker safety and efficiency standards would depend on how HUD uses its new approval authority.
ai_headline: HUD would gain veto power over federal manufactured home rules
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

title: Unlocking Housing Supply Through Streamlined and Modernized Reviews Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the Department of Housing and Urban Development handles environmental reviews under a law called the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA. Right now, many housing projects that receive federal funding must go through environmental review, which can take months or years. This bill tells HUD to reclassify a wide range of housing activities into faster-track review categories, or exempt them from review entirely, based on how much environmental impact they are likely to cause. Activities like rental assistance, down payment help, and emergency home repairs would be fully exempt. Smaller projects like fixing up a 1-to-4 unit home or converting an office building into apartments would go through a lighter review process.

The bill targets what it calls "infill projects," meaning housing built on small, already-disturbed lots inside city limits that are vacant or underused. These projects, along with small-scale new construction of up to 15 units, would qualify for streamlined review. Larger scattered-site projects, flood-zone buyouts, and office-to-residential conversions would also move to a faster track, though they would still have some environmental checks. None of these changes would apply to projects that significantly change environmental conditions or go well beyond their original scope.

The people most directly affected are housing developers, nonprofit housing organizations, and local governments that receive federal housing funding and currently must navigate lengthy review processes. Renters and homebuyers in areas with tight housing supply could also be affected if the streamlining leads to more homes being built faster. Starting two years after the law passes, HUD would be required to report annually to Congress for five years on whether review times and costs actually went down, with a focus on affordable housing outcomes.

title: To amend the Housing and Urban Development Act of 1968 to provide reforms to housing counseling and financial literacy programs.
ai_summary:
This bill updates federal rules for housing counseling programs run through the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). Right now, HUD funds nonprofit agencies that give free or low-cost advice to people buying homes or struggling to make mortgage payments. The bill adds new accountability measures for those agencies, including regular performance reviews and the ability to check whether a counselor's clients are more likely to default on their loans compared to similar borrowers in the same area. If a counselor consistently underperforms, HUD could require extra training, retesting, or in repeated cases, permanently remove that person's certification. Agencies that fail program requirements could lose their HUD funding, but they must get at least 60 days' notice and have the right to an informal meeting to explain any circumstances outside their control.

The bill also creates a new protection for homeowners who fall behind on certain government-backed mortgages. If a borrower is 30 or more days late on an FHA, VA, USDA, or Native American guaranteed loan, the lender must give them a chance to receive foreclosure prevention counseling. For FHA loans specifically, the cost of that counseling would be covered by the Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund, meaning the borrower would not have to pay out of pocket.

The people most directly affected are homeowners with government-backed mortgages who are at risk of foreclosure, first-time homebuyers who use HUD-approved counseling services, and the nonprofit agencies and individual counselors who provide those services. The bill also adjusts how HUD distributes funding to make sure both urban and rural areas are served, rather than focusing on areas with high foreclosure rates as the current rule requires.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

title: Stop Insider Trading Act
ai_summary:
This bill would ban members of Congress from buying individual stocks while they are in office. It also covers their spouses and dependent children. They would still be allowed to own diversified funds like index funds, keep small business investments, and hold stocks in certain kinds of trusts where they have no control over investment decisions. The only stock purchases that would still be allowed are reinvesting dividends from stocks they already own.

The bill also puts new rules on selling stocks. Before selling, a member of Congress must publicly announce the planned sale between 7 and 14 days in advance. The notice has to include the date of the planned sale, a description of it, and the number of shares. This notice would be posted online for the public to see. Spouses or dependents who work in finance and trade stocks as part of their job would be exempt from this requirement.

Anyone who breaks these rules faces a financial penalty of either $2,000 or 10 percent of the transaction value, whichever is larger, plus any profits made from the illegal trade. Members cannot use their official office budgets or campaign funds to pay these fines. The ethics office overseeing the member could also refer the case to the Justice Department if the member leaves office without paying. This bill affects all sitting members of Congress and their immediate family members who live with them or are financially dependent on them.

title: Point-Access Housing Guidelines Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill tells the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to create guidelines for a specific type of apartment building called a "point-access block" building. These are apartment buildings up to five stories tall where all residents use a single shared staircase to reach their units, instead of the multiple stairwells required by most current U.S. building codes. HUD would have 18 months to publish model rules, best practices, and technical advice that states, cities, tribes, and territories could voluntarily choose to follow. The bill also directs HUD to work with the International Code Council, the organization that writes the widely used building codes that many local governments adopt.

The guidelines would have to address fire safety issues like sprinklers, smoke detectors, and emergency exits, as well as construction costs and how this building type might help create more housing in expensive areas. HUD could also offer grants to local governments, developers, researchers, nonprofits, and other groups to run pilot projects testing whether these buildings are safe, practical, and affordable. The bill specifically says it does not override any existing state or local building codes, meaning no government is required to change their rules.

This bill would most directly affect apartment developers, architects, city planners, and local building departments who make decisions about what kinds of housing can be built. It could also affect renters and homebuyers in high-cost cities, since supporters of single-staircase buildings argue they can be built more cheaply and could increase the number of available housing units. No one is forced to change anything under this bill; it only creates optional guidance for those who want to use it.

title: Affordable Housing Through Common-Sense Standards Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Government Accountability Office (GAO), which is the research and watchdog arm of Congress, to study whether the United States should create a single, nationwide set of rules for building homes. Right now, building codes vary widely from state to state and even city to city. The GAO would have one year to complete its research and send a report to Congress.

The study would look at three main questions: whether a national building code could speed up the local approval process for new home construction, whether it could lower the cost of building homes, and whether it could improve the quality and availability of affordable housing. Importantly, this bill does not create any new rules itself. It only asks for research and a report.

This bill could affect a wide range of people. Homebuilders and contractors who currently have to follow different rules in different places might see changes to how they operate if a national standard were ever adopted based on this study. Local and state governments, which currently control their own building codes, could potentially lose some of that authority in the future. Everyday Americans looking for affordable housing could also be affected, since the study is aimed at understanding whether national standards might help bring housing costs down.

title: To require Federal monitors and receivers of public housing agencies to testify before the Committee on Financial Services of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs of the Senate.
ai_summary:
This bill would require certain federal officials called "monitors" and "receivers" to testify before Congress every year. These are people the federal government appoints to take over or closely supervise a local public housing agency when that agency is found to be mismanaged or failing. Right now, these officials can operate with limited direct accountability to Congress. This bill would change that by making them appear before two specific congressional committees and explain what they have been doing.

The affected committees are the House Committee on Financial Services and the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, both of which oversee housing policy. Any monitor or receiver who was involved in overseeing a public housing agency during the past year would have to show up and testify by October 1 of the following year. The goal is to give Congress a regular, formal way to check on how these officials are managing housing agencies that have been placed under federal control.

The people most directly affected are the federal monitors and receivers themselves, along with the public housing agencies they oversee. Indirectly, this could matter to the residents who live in those housing developments, since better congressional oversight might lead to more scrutiny of how troubled housing agencies are being managed and whether improvements are actually happening.

title: CAT Act
ai_summary:
The CAT Act requires public housing agencies across the country to post detailed information about their contracts on their own websites. This includes what goods or services were purchased, who the vendor is, when bids were requested, what bids or price quotes came in, and which official was in charge of the process. The Department of Housing and Urban Development would have one year after the law passes to put this requirement in place.

Public housing agencies are the local and state organizations that manage government-subsidized housing for low-income residents. Right now, there is no consistent federal rule requiring these agencies to make their contracting details easy for the public to find. This bill would change that by making the information available directly on each agency's website.

The people most affected are the roughly 3,000 public housing agencies operating across the United States, as well as the millions of residents who live in or rely on public housing. Taxpayers who fund these programs would also gain easier access to information about how that money is being spent. Vendors who bid on contracts with these agencies would see their bids and quotes made public as well.

title: SAW Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the SAW Act (Snowmobiles Aren't Weapons Act), would make it a federal crime to intentionally use any motor vehicle to hunt, chase, harm, trap, or kill mammalian predators on federal land. That includes vehicles like snowmobiles, ATVs, trucks, or even aircraft. Someone who breaks this law could face a fine of up to $10,000, up to five years in prison, or both. The only exception is if a person used a vehicle against a predator to protect themselves or someone else from serious injury or death.

The bill covers federal lands such as national forests, national parks, and Bureau of Land Management land. It does not apply to land held in trust for Native American tribes. The Secretary of the Interior would be responsible for deciding exactly which animals count as "mammalian predators" and would oversee investigations into possible violations, with the ability to call on the FBI, other federal agencies, and state and local law enforcement for help.

This bill mainly affects hunters, outdoor recreation users, and anyone who accesses federal lands with motor vehicles. It would not change rules for hunting predators on foot or using other legal methods. People who live near or recreate on federal lands, particularly in western states where snowmobiling and off-road vehicle use are common, would be most directly impacted by this change.

title: Disapproving the action of the District of Columbia Council in approving the D.C. Income and Franchise Tax Conformity and Revision Temporary Amendment Act of 2025.
ai_summary:
This bill is Congress using its authority to block a tax law that Washington, D.C.'s local government had passed. The D.C. Council approved a temporary change to how the city calculates income and business taxes in December 2025. Under a special federal law called the D.C. Home Rule Act, Congress has the power to review and reject D.C. local laws before they take effect, and that is exactly what this resolution does. By passing this joint resolution, Congress officially canceled the D.C. tax law.

The canceled D.C. law was about "conformity," which is a process where a city or state lines up its own tax rules to match federal tax rules. When Congress changes the federal tax code, states and cities often update their own codes to stay in sync. The D.C. Council's temporary act was meant to make those kinds of adjustments to local income and business taxes. Congress's disapproval means those D.C. tax changes cannot go into effect.

This directly affects people who live and work in Washington, D.C., as well as businesses that operate there and pay D.C. income or franchise taxes. Because Congress blocked the local law, D.C. tax rules will not reflect the changes the D.C. Council intended to make. D.C. residents and businesses may need to follow older tax rules instead of the updated ones the local government had approved. It is a reminder that, unlike U.S. states, D.C.'s local laws are subject to congressional review and can be overturned.

title: Housing Our Communities Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new federal grant program run by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). State and local governments, counties, and regional planning agencies could apply for these grants. The money would be awarded through a competitive process, meaning applicants would have to make a case for why they should receive funding. Grants could be used for things like updating local zoning laws, building new affordable homes, improving housing inspection programs, and developing community plans to increase the supply of affordable housing.

The bill spells out two main ways the money can be spent, depending on who receives it. Regional planning agencies would focus on creating and improving housing and community development plans. States, cities, and counties would focus more on actually putting those plans into action, such as changing zoning rules, funding housing construction, and improving access to public transportation near housing. No more than 10 percent of any grant can go toward administrative costs, meaning most of the money has to go toward actual programs and projects.

This bill would primarily affect local and state governments, regional planning organizations, and the communities where they operate. Everyday residents could feel its effects if their local government uses the funding to build more affordable homes, make it easier to rent or buy housing, or improve public transit options near where people live. The bill was introduced in December 2025 and has been sent to the House Committee on Financial Services, where it would need to be approved before moving forward.

title: Housing Affordability Act
ai_summary:
This bill updates the maximum dollar amounts that the federal government will insure on loans used to build or renovate apartment buildings. The Federal Housing Administration (FHA) insures these loans, which means the government backs them if a borrower defaults. The current dollar limits in the law are decades old and far below what it actually costs to build housing today. This bill raises those limits dramatically, roughly four times higher than the old figures, to better match current construction costs. Starting in 2026, the limits would also automatically adjust each year based on a construction cost index published by the Census Bureau, so they would not fall behind inflation again.

The bill affects apartment developers, builders, and property owners who use FHA-backed loans to finance multifamily housing projects, meaning buildings with five or more units. With higher loan limits, these borrowers could get federal backing on larger loans, which may make it easier and less expensive to finance the construction or rehabilitation of apartment buildings. It also affects renters indirectly, since the availability of financing can influence how many new rental units get built.

The bill does not directly control rents or give money to renters or landlords. It is a technical change to federal lending rules. Whether higher loan limits actually lead to more housing being built depends on many other factors, including local zoning, land costs, and interest rates.
ai_headline: FHA loan limits for apartment construction set to roughly quadruple under House bill
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6132 raises FHA multifamily loan limits roughly fourfold and ties them to a Census construction index starting in 2026.

The new limits are roughly four times higher than the figures currently written into law, which are decades old and far below current construction costs. Beginning in 2026, the limits would adjust automatically each year using a construction cost index published by the Census Bureau.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects apartment developers, builders, and property owners who use FHA-backed loans to finance multifamily housing projects. Renters are indirectly affected, since available financing can influence how many new rental units are built.
ai_sections.why: Higher loan limits would allow borrowers to obtain federal backing on larger loans, which may change the cost and feasibility of financing apartment construction or rehabilitation. Whether more housing actually gets built depends on other factors, including local zoning, land costs, and interest rates.

title: Critical Mineral Dominance Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Critical Mineral Dominance Act, aims to boost domestic mining of hardrock minerals, which include things like rare earth elements, gold, copper, and other metals used in electronics, defense equipment, and clean energy technology. Right now, the U.S. imports many of these minerals from other countries. The bill directs the Secretary of the Interior to speed up the approval process for mining projects on federal land, identify which federal lands might hold valuable mineral deposits, and report to Congress on how much the country's reliance on imported minerals actually costs the economy.

The bill also requires a review of existing rules and regulations to find ones that slow down or block mining projects. Federal agencies would have to gather feedback directly from the mining industry about what is getting in the way, and then take steps to reduce or remove those barriers. Additionally, the government would need to map out underground mineral deposits across the country more thoroughly so better decisions can be made about where mining could happen.

This bill mainly affects mining companies, workers in the mining industry, and communities near federal lands where mining could expand. It also has implications for federal agencies like the Department of the Interior and the U.S. Geological Survey, which would take on new reporting and mapping responsibilities. Environmental groups and communities near public lands may also have a stake in how the bill is carried out, since it prioritizes faster permitting for projects on federally managed land.
ai_headline: Bill would speed federal permits and expand mapping for domestic hardrock mining
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

ai_sections.tldr: The Critical Mineral Dominance Act would fast-track mining permits on federal land and require new mapping and reporting on U.S. mineral reliance.
ai_sections.what: The Critical Mineral Dominance Act directs the Secretary of the Interior to speed up approval of mining projects on federal land and identify which federal lands may hold valuable mineral deposits. The bill also requires a review of rules that slow or block mining, direct industry feedback to federal agencies, and more thorough mapping of underground mineral deposits nationwide. Agencies would also report to Congress on the economic cost of U.S. dependence on imported hardrock minerals such as rare earth elements, gold, and copper.
ai_sections.who: Mining companies, mining industry workers, and communities near federal lands where mining could expand are directly affected. Federal agencies including the Department of the Interior and the U.S. Geological Survey would take on new reporting and mapping responsibilities, and environmental groups may also have a stake in how the bill is implemented.
ai_sections.why: The U.S. currently imports many hardrock minerals used in electronics, defense equipment, and clean energy technology from other countries. Faster permitting and expanded mapping on federal lands could change where and how quickly new domestic mining projects move forward.

title: Digital Literacy and Equity Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new federal group called the Digital Literacy and Equity Commission. Its main job would be to study how well Americans can use technology and find reliable information online, especially in lower-income and disadvantaged communities. The commission would also look at what other countries are doing in this area and identify strategies that work best. Within two years, it would send a report to Congress with findings and recommendations.

The commission would be made up of leaders from several federal agencies, including the Departments of Education, Health and Human Services, and Housing and Urban Development, along with the Federal Communications Commission. A few outside experts from schools, nonprofits, and state or local governments would also serve on it. All meetings would be open to the public.

The bill would mainly affect people who lack strong digital skills, particularly those living in lower-income areas, since the study focuses on closing gaps in access to digital education and resources. It could also affect schools, libraries, and community organizations that provide technology training, as the final report would recommend ways the federal government could better support and measure digital literacy across the country. The bill does not directly create new programs or spend money on its own, but its recommendations could shape future policy decisions.
ai_headline: New federal commission would study digital literacy gaps in low-income communities
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

The commission would focus on lower-income and disadvantaged communities, examine approaches used by other countries, and identify effective strategies. Within two years of its formation, it would deliver a report of findings and recommendations to Congress.

title: Bank-Fintech Partnership Enhancement Act
ai_summary:
This bill tells three federal banking regulators, the Federal Reserve, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and the FDIC, to study the relationship between traditional banks and fintech companies. Fintechs are tech-based financial companies like apps or online platforms that offer financial services. The regulators must complete their study and send a report to Congress within six months of the bill becoming law.

The study focuses on two main questions. First, can working with fintechs help start new banks and keep smaller community banks healthy? This includes looking at whether these partnerships help banks offer products faster, cut down on paperwork and legal costs, bring in more customers, improve technology, and find new sources of money. Second, the study asks whether any current federal banking laws or regulations should be changed to make these kinds of partnerships work better.

This bill mainly affects bank regulators, community banks, and fintech companies. It does not directly change any laws or create new rules right now. It only requires a study and a report. Everyday bank customers could eventually be affected if the study leads to future policy changes that shape how banks and tech companies work together, but no immediate changes to banking services or consumer protections are made by this bill itself.
ai_headline: Federal regulators ordered to study bank-fintech partnerships within six months
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 456.

The study must examine whether fintech partnerships support new bank formation and community bank health, and whether existing federal laws or regulations should be changed to improve such partnerships. A report must be delivered to Congress within six months of the bill becoming law.

ai_sections.why: The bill does not change any existing laws or create new rules on its own. Its findings could inform future legislation or regulatory changes affecting community banks, fintechs, and potentially the customers they serve.

title: Databases of Publicly Owned Land Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require cities and counties that receive a certain type of federal grant money to create and maintain a public, searchable online database listing all undeveloped land they own. The grant program involved is called the Community Development Block Grant, or CDBG, which the federal government uses to help communities with housing and local development projects. The database would need to be available on a publicly accessible website so anyone could look up what vacant or undeveloped land the local government holds. This requirement would kick in starting October 1, 2026.

The main idea is to make it easier for the public to see what land their local government owns but is not currently using or developing. Right now, that information can be scattered across different offices and hard to find. A single searchable database would put it all in one place.

This bill affects local governments, specifically cities, counties, and other communities that receive CDBG funding. There are hundreds of these grantees across the country. It could also affect everyday residents, housing developers, nonprofit organizations, and researchers who might want to know where publicly owned vacant land is located, perhaps to propose new housing, parks, or other community uses for it.
ai_headline: Federal bill would require cities to post vacant land lists online
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6773 requires CDBG-funded cities and counties to publish searchable online databases of publicly owned undeveloped land by October 1, 2026.
ai_sections.what: HR 6773 would require cities, counties, and other local governments that receive Community Development Block Grant funding to create and maintain a publicly searchable online database of all undeveloped land they own. The database must be available on a public website so anyone can look up vacant government-held land. This requirement would take effect on October 1, 2026.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects local governments across the country that receive CDBG funding. Residents, housing developers, nonprofit organizations, and researchers who want to find or propose uses for publicly owned vacant land would also be affected.
ai_sections.why: Information about government-owned undeveloped land is currently spread across different offices and difficult to locate. A single searchable database would consolidate that information into one publicly accessible place.

title: Housing Crisis Response Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Housing Crisis Response Act of 2025, would direct a very large amount of federal money toward building, repairing, and preserving affordable housing across the country. It was introduced in December 2025 and covers many different programs at once. The biggest pieces include roughly $63 billion to fix up and replace public housing, nearly $25 billion for programs that help states and cities build affordable homes, and $22 billion for rental vouchers that help low-income families pay rent. It also sets aside money for housing specifically designed for elderly people and people with disabilities, housing in rural areas, and housing in Native American and Native Hawaiian communities. A separate fund would help make affordable housing buildings more energy-efficient and better able to handle floods and other climate risks.

The bill would also make it easier for first-generation homebuyers, meaning people whose parents never owned a home, to get down payment help. It expands community development block grants, which are funds cities and counties can use for local housing and infrastructure projects. There is also money aimed at communities known as colonias, which are low-income, often unincorporated communities near the U.S.-Mexico border. A new rule in the bill would require that a larger share of units in any new multifamily building, like an apartment complex, be physically accessible to people who use wheelchairs or have vision or hearing impairments. Single-family homes built with federal money would also need to meet basic accessibility standards.

The people most directly affected are low-income renters, people experiencing or at risk of homelessness, survivors of domestic violence, elderly Americans, people with disabilities, rural residents, and members of Native American tribes. First-time homebuyers with low to moderate incomes could also benefit. Landlords, housing developers, public housing agencies, and local governments would all play a role in carrying out the programs and receiving the funding.
ai_headline: Federal bill would send over $100 billion to affordable housing programs
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Appropriations, and in addition to the Committee on Financial Services, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

The bill also addresses energy efficiency, climate resilience, accessibility standards, down payment assistance for first-generation homebuyers, and housing in rural, border, and Native American communities.

Landlords, housing developers, public housing agencies, and local governments would carry out the programs and receive the funding.
ai_sections.why: If enacted, the bill would significantly expand the federal role in housing production and preservation, reshaping how states, cities, and housing agencies access and deploy affordable housing funds. Changes to accessibility requirements and down payment rules would affect construction standards and eligibility criteria for federally funded housing projects going forward.

title: FHA Small-Dollar Mortgages Act
ai_summary:
This bill would let the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) create a test program to make it easier for people to get small home loans. Specifically, a "small-dollar mortgage" means a home loan of $100,000 or less on a property where the borrower actually lives. The program could pay lenders a bonus to encourage them to offer these smaller loans, reduce some FHA fees tied to them, and give buyers direct grants to help cover down payments, closing costs, appraisals, and title insurance. The program would run for up to four years and must be launched within three years of the bill becoming law.

The problem the bill is trying to address is that lenders often avoid small home loans because the fees and work involved are about the same as a large loan, but the profit is much smaller. This makes it hard for buyers in lower-cost housing markets to get financing, since many mainstream lenders simply don't find it worth their time. HUD would also be required to study the issue and report to Congress each year, tracking how many small loans were made, who got them, and whether the program put any strain on the federal mortgage insurance fund.

The people most affected would be buyers looking at lower-priced homes, which are more common in rural areas, smaller cities, and lower-income neighborhoods. First-time buyers and people with modest incomes who might not need a large loan could benefit if lenders start offering more of these mortgages. Lenders who work with FHA loans would also be directly affected, since the program could change the fees and incentives tied to these smaller loans.
ai_headline: HUD small-loan pilot would pay lenders to offer mortgages under $100,000
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6774 lets HUD run a 4-year pilot paying bonuses to lenders and grants to buyers to expand home loans of $100,000 or less.
ai_sections.what: HR 6774 would authorize HUD to run a test program, lasting up to four years, aimed at expanding access to home loans of $100,000 or less on owner-occupied properties. The program could offer lenders bonus payments, reduce certain FHA fees on small loans, and provide buyers direct grants to cover down payments, closing costs, appraisals, and title insurance. HUD must launch the program within three years of the bill becoming law and report to Congress annually on loan volume, borrower demographics, and any impact on the federal mortgage insurance fund.
ai_sections.who: Buyers seeking lower-priced homes, particularly in rural areas, smaller cities, and lower-income neighborhoods, are the primary population the bill targets, including first-time and modest-income buyers. Lenders that participate in FHA loan programs would also be directly affected through changed fee structures and new financial incentives.
ai_sections.why: Lenders currently tend to avoid small home loans because the administrative work and fees are similar to those of larger loans while the profit is significantly smaller, leaving many buyers in lower-cost markets without financing options. If the program does not generate sufficient lender participation or strains the federal mortgage insurance fund, HUD's annual reports to Congress would be required to document those outcomes.
ai_sections.cost: The bill would direct HUD to pay bonuses to lenders and issue direct grants to buyers for costs such as down payments, closing costs, appraisals, and title insurance, though no specific dollar amounts are stated in the summary. The program would also reduce some FHA fees tied to small-dollar mortgages, which could affect revenue flowing into the federal mortgage insurance fund.

title: Housing Supply Expansion Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes the legal definition of a "manufactured home" under federal law. Right now, a home must be built on a permanent steel chassis (a fixed metal frame) to officially count as a manufactured home. This bill removes that requirement, so factory-built homes without a permanent chassis would also qualify. The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) would be required to create new safety and construction standards for these chassis-free homes and give them their own labels and paperwork to tell them apart from traditional manufactured homes.

States would need to update their own laws to treat these chassis-free homes the same as traditional manufactured homes when it comes to financing, insurance, taxes, permits, and sales. States have one year to certify they've done this, or two years if their legislature only meets every other year. After that, states must re-certify every year. If a state fails to certify on time, it would be blocked from allowing the manufacture, sale, or installation of these newer chassis-free homes within its borders.

This bill primarily affects people who build, sell, or buy factory-built housing, as well as state housing agencies, lenders, and insurers who deal with manufactured homes. Supporters say it could make it easier and cheaper to build more homes by allowing new construction methods, which could expand housing options. People currently living in or shopping for affordable housing could also be affected if the change leads to more available units on the market.
ai_headline: Federal bill drops steel chassis rule for factory-built homes
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6293 removes the steel chassis requirement for manufactured homes and gives states one year to update their laws or lose manufacturing rights.
ai_sections.what: HR 6293 removes the requirement that a manufactured home must be built on a permanent steel chassis to qualify under federal law. Chassis-free factory-built homes would gain official status, and HUD would be required to write new safety and construction standards for them, along with distinct labels and paperwork to tell them apart from traditional manufactured homes.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects home builders, sellers, buyers, state housing agencies, lenders, and insurers who work with manufactured homes. States face direct regulatory obligations and potential penalties under the new framework.
ai_sections.why: Removing the chassis requirement could allow new construction methods to enter the manufactured housing market, which may affect the supply of factory-built units available for sale. States that do not certify compliance on time would be blocked from allowing the manufacture, sale, or installation of chassis-free homes within their borders.

title: Rural Housing Regulatory Relief Act
ai_summary:
This bill removes a specific federal review requirement for certain rural housing projects. Right now, when the U.S. Department of Agriculture provides loans or grants to build or repair homes in rural areas, those projects often have to go through an environmental review process required by the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA. That process can take time and cost money. This bill would skip that review for projects built on "infill sites," meaning land that already has basic infrastructure like water lines, sewer lines, and roads in place. It would not apply to undeveloped land like farms or forests, and it would not apply to sites in high-risk flood or wildfire zones.

The people most directly affected are low- and moderate-income rural residents who apply for USDA housing assistance, as well as the developers, nonprofits, and local organizations that build or renovate affordable homes in rural communities. By cutting out the NEPA review step for these specific projects, supporters say it could speed up approvals and lower costs. Critics of similar exemptions have raised concerns about reducing environmental oversight, though the bill does keep all other environmental laws in place.

The bill also requires the Secretary of Agriculture to report back to Congress within five years on whether the change actually sped up approvals, saved money, and affected rural affordable housing overall. That report would also include recommendations about whether similar exemptions should be expanded or adjusted in the future.
ai_headline: Rural housing bill would waive federal environmental reviews on already-developed land
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Financial Services, and in addition to the Committee on Natural Resources, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.why: Removing the NEPA review step for these projects could reduce the time and cost required to approve certain rural housing developments. Critics of similar exemptions have raised concerns about reduced environmental oversight, even when other environmental laws remain in place.

title: To authorize the President to award the Medal of Honor to Doris Miller posthumously for acts of valor while a member of the Navy during World War II.
ai_summary:
This bill would give Congress's approval for the President to award the Medal of Honor to Doris Miller, a Black Navy sailor who showed remarkable bravery during the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. Miller helped move his mortally wounded captain to safety and then manned a machine gun to fire at enemy aircraft, even though he had never been formally trained on that weapon. He was later killed in action in 1943. Because he has been dead for decades, a special law is needed to get around normal time limits that restrict when medals can be awarded.

The bill points out that Miller previously received the Navy Cross, which is a high honor, but not the highest. It also notes that 15 other sailors received the Medal of Honor for similar actions at Pearl Harbor, and none of them were African American. The bill argues that racial barriers of that era kept Miller from being fully recognized at the time, and that awarding the Medal of Honor now would correct that.

This bill directly affects Doris Miller's surviving family members and descendants, who would receive the medal on his behalf. More broadly, it affects how the U.S. military officially records and honors his service. It does not create new spending, change military policies, or directly impact the general public's daily life.
ai_headline: Bill seeks Medal of Honor for Black Pearl Harbor hero passed over in 1941
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Armed Services.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 2335 would authorize the Medal of Honor for Navy sailor Doris Miller, whose 1941 bravery at Pearl Harbor was never fully recognized due to racial barriers.

Miller helped carry his mortally wounded captain to safety and fired a machine gun at enemy aircraft despite having no formal training on the weapon. Because Miller died in 1943 and decades have passed, a special law is required to bypass standard time limits on medal awards.

Awarding the medal now would change the official military record to reflect that corrected recognition.

title: Stop Sexually Violent Predators Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Stop Sexually Violent Predators Act, changes federal law to increase tracking and consequences for people convicted of serious sex offenses who are legally classified as "sexually dangerous persons." It requires states to send the U.S. Attorney General an annual list of people convicted of sexually dangerous offenses. The Attorney General would then review that list to decide whether any of those individuals should also face federal criminal charges, in addition to whatever state charges they already faced.

The bill also affects health coverage for this specific group. People who have been convicted of a sexually violent offense and officially determined to be "sexually dangerous persons" would generally lose access to Medicaid and Medicare benefits. There is an exception: if the person is currently a patient in a hospital or nursing home and is receiving mandatory (involuntary) treatment there, they can still receive coverage. Finally, the bill adds a new requirement to the national sex offender registration system (SORNA), requiring that information about relevant court cases be included in offender registry records.

This bill would primarily affect convicted sex offenders who meet the legal definition of "sexually dangerous," state and federal law enforcement and prosecutors who handle these cases, and health agencies that administer Medicaid and Medicare. It could also indirectly affect taxpayers and healthcare systems, since removing coverage for some individuals may shift costs elsewhere, such as to hospitals providing required emergency or involuntary care.
ai_headline: Bill would strip Medicaid, Medicare from "sexually dangerous" offenders
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, and in addition to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.tldr: People convicted of serious sex offenses and deemed "sexually dangerous" would generally lose Medicaid and Medicare coverage.
ai_sections.what: This bill requires states to send the Attorney General an annual list of people convicted of sexually dangerous offenses so federal charges can be considered alongside state charges. It also removes Medicaid and Medicare eligibility for people convicted of a sexually violent offense who are deemed "sexually dangerous," except while they receive mandatory treatment as inpatients. It adds a requirement that sex offender registry records include information about relevant court cases.
ai_sections.who: It affects convicted sex offenders classified as "sexually dangerous," state and federal law enforcement and prosecutors, and Medicaid/Medicare administering agencies.
ai_sections.why: Losing health coverage could shift care costs elsewhere, such as to hospitals providing required emergency or involuntary treatment, and expands the reach of federal prosecution into cases already handled by states.

title: Marsh-Billings-Rockefeller National Historical Park Establishment Act Amendments Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill updates the law that created Marsh-Billings-Rockefeller National Historical Park in Vermont, expanding the park's official boundaries to match a 2023 revised map. The new boundaries would organize the park into a "historic zone" (including the Marsh-Billings-Rockefeller Mansion, surrounding buildings, and part of Mt. Tom), a "protection zone" (including the Billings Farm and Museum), and the King Farm property, which would be split between the two zones as the Secretary of the Interior decides is appropriate.

The bill also changes how the National Park Service can acquire land within the new boundaries, allowing donations, purchases from willing sellers, transfers from other federal agencies, or land exchanges. For the King Farm specifically, it guarantees access rights between the farm and the rest of the park, and specifies the land can continue to be used for farming, forestry, conservation, and education once acquired—preserving its working-farm character rather than converting it entirely to a typical park setting. Additionally, the bill formally establishes a "National Park Service Stewardship Institute" at the park, which would run workshops and programs to share best practices in conservation and land stewardship across the National Park Service.

This bill mainly affects people connected to the park: nearby landowners (including King Farm's current owners, if they choose to sell or donate), Vermont residents near Woodstock where the park is located, farmers and educators using the site, and National Park Service staff who manage it. It does not have broad effects on the general public outside of visitors to the park and those interested in historic preservation or conservation education programs.
ai_headline: Bill would expand Vermont's Marsh-Billings-Rockefeller park boundaries
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
