title: Trump’s Birthday and Flag Day Holiday Establishment Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal law to make June 14 an official legal public holiday, combining "Trump's Birthday" with the existing observance of Flag Day, which already falls on that date. June 14 is both President Donald Trump's birthday and the day the United States adopted its flag in 1777. The bill would add this holiday to the list found in federal law that already includes holidays like Memorial Day, Independence Day, and Thanksgiving.

If passed, this change would affect federal employees, since legal public holidays typically mean a paid day off for government workers and can also affect bank schedules, mail delivery, and other federally regulated operations. It would not automatically require private employers, state governments, or schools to close, though many businesses often choose to align with federal holiday schedules. The bill was introduced by Representative Claudia Tenney and referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, where it would need to be reviewed before any further action, such as a vote, could happen.
ai_headline: Bill would rename Flag Day to include Trump's birthday as federal holiday
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 1395 would make June 14 an official federal holiday combining Flag Day with "Trump's Birthday."
ai_sections.what: HR 1395 would add June 14 to the federal list of legal public holidays, combining the existing Flag Day observance with a new designation marking President Trump's birthday. June 14 also marks the 1777 adoption of the U.S. flag. This joins other listed federal holidays like Memorial Day, Independence Day, and Thanksgiving.
ai_sections.who: The change would primarily affect federal employees, who typically get a paid day off for legal public holidays, and federally regulated operations like banks and mail delivery. Private employers, state governments, and schools would not be automatically required to close.

title: Merchant Marine Allies Partnership Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Merchant Marine Allies Partnership Act, would loosen the "Jones Act" rules that normally require ships carrying goods between U.S. ports to be American-built, American-owned, and American-crewed. Under this bill, the Secretary of Transportation could allow ships built in, owned by, or crewed by people from allied foreign countries to carry cargo between U.S. ports for up to five years at a time, with the possibility of renewal. To decide which countries qualify, the Secretary of State would keep an official "Foreign Ally Shipping Registry," which would automatically include all NATO member countries. A country could be removed from this list if it's no longer considered an ally, and removal would happen immediately if Congress declares war on that country. Ships would lose their trade privileges if their home country is taken off the list.

The bill also removes the usual citizenship and licensing requirements for crew members from allied countries working on these approved ships, and it exempts ship repairs done in shipyards in these allied countries from certain import duties that would normally apply.

This bill would primarily affect the U.S. shipping and maritime industry, including American shipbuilders, shipping companies, and merchant mariners, who currently benefit from protections against foreign competition in domestic waterborne trade. It could also affect workers and shipyards in allied countries (especially NATO members) who might gain new business opportunities. Consumers and businesses that ship goods domestically by water could potentially see changes in shipping costs or options, depending on how the new rules are used.
ai_headline: Bill would let allied nations' ships haul cargo between US ports
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill lets NATO and other allied countries' ships carry cargo between U.S. ports for up to five years, easing Jones Act rules.

The bill also drops citizenship/licensing rules for allied crew members and exempts allied shipyard repairs from certain import duties.

title: Veterans Earned Education Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change the rules for transferring GI Bill education benefits (known as Post-9/11 educational assistance) to family members. Currently, service members generally must commit to a specific service agreement, such as serving at least six more years, to qualify for transferring these benefits to a spouse or child. This bill adds new ways to qualify: a service member who has already completed at least 17 years of service, or who is medically retired from the Armed Forces under the military's disability retirement process, would also become eligible to transfer their unused education benefits to a dependent.

In practical terms, this expands the pool of veterans and service members who can share their earned education benefits with family. It would particularly help long-serving troops nearing retirement and those forced to retire early due to a service-related medical condition, groups who may not currently meet the existing transfer requirements. The bill affects active-duty and retired military personnel, their spouses, and their children who might use these benefits for college or other approved education and training programs. It does not change how much benefit is available, only who can qualify to pass it on to a dependent.
ai_headline: Bill adds new ways to qualify for transferring GI Bill benefits
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill lets troops with 17+ years of service or medical retirees transfer unused GI Bill benefits to family.

It adds two new qualifying paths: completing at least 17 years of service, or being medically retired under the military's disability retirement process. title: Understanding the True Cost of College Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill requires the U.S. Department of Education to create a single, standardized "Financial Aid Offer" form that every college and university must use when telling students what financial aid they're getting. Right now, colleges use different formats and terms, which makes it hard for students and families to compare offers or understand the true cost of attending different schools. The new form would clearly list total costs (tuition, fees, housing, food, books, transportation), then separately show grants and scholarships that don't need to be repaid, followed by the "net price" a student would actually owe. Loans would have to be clearly labeled as loans (not confused with grants), with information on interest rates and repayment options.

The bill also requires disclosures about work-study opportunities, private loans versus federal loans, veteran and military education benefits, and deadlines for accepting or declining aid. The Department of Education must consult with students, families, schools, financial aid experts, and consumer groups to design the form, test it with a small group of colleges, and then finalize it based on feedback. Once finalized, all colleges that receive federal funding would be legally required to use this exact form and standardized terminology in their financial aid communications.

This bill mainly affects prospective and current college students, their families, and financial aid offices at colleges and universities nationwide. It's designed to help students make more informed decisions about borrowing and choosing schools by making aid offers easier to understand and compare, reducing confusion caused by inconsistent terminology across institutions.
ai_headline: Bill would require one standard financial aid offer form for colleges
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

ai_sections.tldr: This bill would create one standardized financial aid offer form all federally funded colleges must use.

The form must clearly separate total costs, grants and scholarships, net price, and loans, and disclose work-study, private versus federal loans, veteran benefits, and aid acceptance deadlines. It would be tested with a small group of colleges before being finalized and required nationwide.

title: Keeping Gun Dealers Honest Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would increase government oversight of licensed gun dealers, importers, and manufacturers. It allows the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) to conduct up to three compliance inspections per year instead of just one, and lets ATF hire at least 80 additional staff to carry out this expanded inspection work. It also raises criminal penalties for dealers who falsify records or fail to keep required paperwork, increasing the maximum prison sentence from one year to five years, and up to ten years if the recordkeeping violation is linked to illegal gun trafficking or sales to prohibited buyers. Additionally, it makes it easier for the Attorney General to suspend or revoke a dealer's license or issue fines up to $10,000 per violation, and removes the current legal requirement that a violation be "willful" before penalties can apply, meaning dealers could face consequences even for unintentional violations.

The bill also gives the Attorney General more power to deny a dealer's license application if issuing it would threaten public safety or if the applicant seems unlikely to follow the law, and requires dealers to conduct a physical inventory of their guns if they've been convicted of illegal transfers or if ten or more guns sold by them are traced to crimes. It shortens the window during which someone under felony indictment can keep operating as a licensed dealer. Finally, it requires ATF to report to Congress every two years on how these changes are working. This bill mainly affects federally licensed gun dealers, manufacturers, and importers, along with the ATF itself, which would gain more inspection authority, enforcement tools, and staff. Gun buyers and the general public would be affected indirectly, through stricter oversight intended to reduce illegal gun sales and trafficking.
ai_headline: Bill would triple ATF inspections and toughen penalties for gun dealers
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill boosts ATF inspections and staff and raises penalties for gun dealers who falsify or skip required records.

It raises maximum prison sentences for falsified or missing dealer records from one year to five, or up to ten years if tied to trafficking or sales to prohibited buyers. It also makes it easier to suspend, revoke, or fine dealer licenses (up to $10,000 per violation) without needing to prove the violation was "willful," and lets the Attorney General deny license applications on public safety grounds, require inventory checks after certain violations, and shortens how long felony indictees can keep dealing.

title: Rural Depositories Revitalization Study Act
ai_summary:
HR 6536, called the Rural Depositories Revitalization Study Act, would require the main federal banking regulators—the Federal Reserve, the Comptroller of the Currency, and the FDIC—to work together on a study about banks and credit-related institutions that primarily serve rural communities. The study would look for ways to help these rural banks grow, stay financially stable, and remain profitable. It would also identify any existing federal laws or regulations that make it harder for rural banks to grow or that discourage the creation of brand-new banks (called "de novo" institutions) in rural areas.

The bill doesn't change any banking rules itself. Instead, it directs these agencies to produce a report with their findings and send it to Congress within six months of the law being enacted. Congress could then use that report to decide whether new legislation is needed to support rural banking.

This bill would primarily affect federal banking regulators, who would be responsible for conducting the study and writing the report. It could also eventually affect rural communities, small banks, and credit unions that operate in less populated areas, since any future policy changes based on the study's findings might make it easier to start or expand rural financial institutions. For now, though, the bill's direct impact is limited to research and reporting, not to actual banking rules or funding.
ai_headline: Bill would order federal study on boosting rural bank growth
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 404.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6536 requires federal regulators to study how to help rural banks grow and report findings to Congress within six months.

The study would identify ways to help rural banks grow, stay stable, and remain profitable, plus any federal laws or rules that hinder rural bank growth or discourage new "de novo" rural banks. Agencies must send Congress a report within six months of enactment.

title: Sustainable Cardiopulmonary Rehabilitation Services in the Home Act
ai_summary:
This bill would make permanent certain rules for cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation programs delivered through telehealth that were temporarily allowed during the COVID-19 pandemic. Cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation are supervised exercise and education programs for people recovering from heart or lung conditions, normally done in person at a hospital or clinic. During the pandemic, Medicare allowed patients to receive some of these services from home using video technology, and this bill would keep that option available permanently starting January 1, 2026, instead of letting it expire.

Specifically, the bill changes Medicare law so that a patient's home can count as an approved location for these rehab programs, and doctors or other providers can supervise sessions virtually through live video rather than being physically present. It also removes certain geographic restrictions that normally limit where patients must be located to qualify for telehealth reimbursement, at least for these particular rehab programs. The Department of Health and Human Services would be required to set up standards for treating a patient's home as an official extension of a hospital for billing purposes, similar to rules used during the pandemic emergency.

This bill mainly affects Medicare beneficiaries recovering from heart attacks, heart surgery, heart failure, or chronic lung disease who participate in rehab programs, as well as hospitals, doctors, and other health providers who deliver these services. It could make it easier for patients—especially those in rural areas or with mobility challenges—to complete rehab from home rather than traveling to a facility, while also affecting how Medicare pays providers for offering these virtual services long-term.
ai_headline: Bill would make home-based cardiac rehab via telehealth permanent
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

ai_sections.tldr: S 248 would permanently allow Medicare patients to do cardiac and pulmonary rehab from home via video starting January 1, 2026.

It would let a patient's home count as an approved rehab location, allow virtual supervision by providers, and remove certain geographic restrictions for telehealth reimbursement in these programs. HHS would need to set standards for treating a patient's home as an extension of a hospital for billing.

ai_sections.why: The change would affect how and where patients can access rehab and how Medicare pays providers for virtual services on an ongoing basis, particularly for rural or mobility-limited patients.

title: Physician and Patient Safety Act
ai_summary:
HR 3413, the Physician and Patient Safety Act, would require the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services to create official rules protecting doctors' rights when hospitals try to fire them, restrict their work, or take away their staff privileges. Under these rules, doctors would be guaranteed a fair hearing and a chance to appeal before any such action takes place, using the hospital's own internal medical staff process.

The bill sets specific ground rules for these protections. Hospitals could not get around the hearing requirement by outsourcing decisions to a third-party company, and they could not force doctors to give up their right to a hearing as a condition of getting or keeping a job. It also says that the hearing process and its results generally must stay confidential and not be reported to outside entities, including the National Practitioner Data Bank (a national database that tracks disciplinary actions against doctors) or future employers—unless there's an ongoing risk to patient safety or reporting is already legally required.

This bill mainly affects physicians who hold hospital staff privileges, giving them stronger job protections and more control over how disputes with hospitals are handled. It also affects hospitals and hospital administrators, who would need to follow new federal standards when making decisions about a doctor's privileges or workload. Indirectly, it could affect patients, since supporters argue that protecting doctors from unfair termination helps ensure medical decisions are based on patient care rather than administrative or financial pressures. HHS would have 18 months after the bill becomes law to write and finalize these regulations.
ai_headline: Bill would require hearings before hospitals fire or restrict doctors
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 3413 would require HHS to guarantee doctors a hearing and appeal before hospitals fire or restrict them.
ai_sections.what: HR 3413 would require HHS to create rules guaranteeing doctors a fair hearing and appeal through the hospital's internal medical staff process before they can be fired, restricted, or lose staff privileges. Hospitals could not outsource these decisions to third parties or force doctors to waive hearing rights as a job condition. Hearing details would generally stay confidential and not be reported to the National Practitioner Data Bank or employers unless patient safety is at risk or reporting is already required by law.

ai_sections.why: The change would shift how hospitals handle disputes with doctors, requiring formal internal review before adverse action and limiting outside reporting of those disputes.

title: Innovate Less Lethal to De-Escalate Tax Modernization Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change how the federal government taxes and regulates certain "less-than-lethal" weapons, like devices designed to stun or subdue someone without causing death or serious injury. Right now, some of these devices can get caught up in the same tax rules and strict regulations that apply to firearms, including a special manufacturing tax and the National Firearms Act (a law that heavily regulates things like machine guns and short-barreled rifles). This bill creates a clear legal definition for "less-than-lethal projectile devices" and exempts them, along with their ammunition, from that firearms tax and from the National Firearms Act's stricter rules.

To qualify, a device would need to meet specific criteria: it can't fire regular gun ammunition, its projectiles generally can't exceed 500 feet per second, it must be designed to avoid causing death or serious injury, and it can't use magazines typically found on semiautomatic firearms. The bill also sets up a process where manufacturers can ask the Treasury Department to officially classify their product as "less-than-lethal," with a decision required within 90 days. The government would keep a public, annually updated list of approved devices, plus a separate list of similar devices that don't qualify only because their speed exceeds 500 feet per second, with details reported to Congress each year.

This bill mainly affects companies that make less-lethal weapons (such as those used by police, security companies, or for personal self-defense), as well as retailers and buyers of these products. By removing extra taxes and NFA restrictions, it could make these devices cheaper and easier to produce, sell, and legally obtain. It would also affect the Treasury Department, which would take on new responsibilities for reviewing and classifying these devices and reporting to Congress.
ai_headline: Bill would exempt less-lethal stun devices from firearms tax and NFA rules
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 407.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 4242 would exempt qualifying "less-than-lethal" stun devices from the firearms manufacturing tax and National Firearms Act rules.

Treasury would review manufacturer requests within 90 days and maintain public lists of approved and near-qualifying devices, reporting annually to Congress.

title: Let’s Get to Work Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Let's Get to Work Act of 2025," would change the work requirements for people receiving SNAP benefits (formerly known as food stamps) and extend similar rules to certain housing assistance programs.

Currently, SNAP has work requirements for able-bodied adults without dependents, generally limiting benefits to 3 months within a 3-year period unless they work or participate in job training a certain number of hours per week. This bill changes several details of those rules. It lowers the age exemption for older adults from 55 to over 60, meaning people between 55 and 60 who are not currently required to work would now have to meet work requirements. It narrows the exemption for parents of dependent children so that only parents of children under 6 years old are automatically exempt (rather than any dependent child, which often meant under 18). However, the bill adds a new 6-month exemption period for parents or caregivers with a dependent child, and it creates an exemption for someone caring for a dependent individual (such as an elderly or disabled family member) if their spouse is already meeting the work requirements. The bill also removes an existing exemption category from the law.

Beyond SNAP, the bill extends these same work requirements to people living in public housing and to people receiving housing vouchers (tenant-based rental assistance) through the Department of Housing and Urban Development. This means individuals in these housing programs who are not otherwise exempt would need to meet work or job-training requirements similar to those in SNAP. Overall, this bill would affect low-income individuals and families who rely on SNAP, public housing, or rental assistance vouchers, particularly working-age adults without young children, older adults aged 55-60, and caregivers of dependents.
ai_headline: Bill would tighten work rules for SNAP and extend them to housing aid
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Nutrition and Foreign Agriculture.

It also removes an existing exemption category and extends similar work requirements to people in public housing and those receiving HUD rental vouchers.

ai_sections.why: The changes would require more people to work or participate in job training to keep receiving benefits, narrowing who automatically qualifies for exemptions.

title: LAUNCH Act
ai_summary:
HR 5602, called the LAUNCH Act, aims to make it easier and faster for private companies to get government approval for rocket launches, spacecraft reentries, and satellite imaging operations. The bill directs the Department of Transportation to review how current launch/reentry safety rules (known as "Part 450") are working, identify what's causing delays, and report back to Congress with fixes that don't just involve hiring more staff. It also creates an industry advisory committee to suggest rule changes, requires the government to assign a dedicated staff person to help each company through the licensing process, and requires officials to accept reasonable safety proposals from companies rather than only their own preferred methods.

The bill also requires the government to build an online system so companies can track the status of their license applications in real time, similar to tracking a package. It sets up a new Commercial Space Transportation Administration inside the Department of Transportation to handle this licensing work, allows faster hiring of staff for this office, and requires annual public reports on how long approvals are taking. Separately, it changes rules for satellite imaging ("remote sensing") licenses, clarifying that cameras used just for a spacecraft's own safety checks (not for taking pictures of Earth) don't need this type of license, and requires similar dedicated staff support and transparency for those applicants.

This bill mainly affects companies in the commercial spaceflight and satellite imaging industries, such as rocket launch providers and satellite operators, by aiming to speed up and simplify the federal approval process. It also affects the Department of Transportation, the Department of Commerce, and federal agencies like NASA and the Department of Defense, which may need to coordinate more closely on safety reviews. Everyday taxpayers are affected indirectly, since government funding ($5 million) would go toward building the new digital tracking system, and the reforms could influence how quickly and competitively the U.S. space industry grows compared to other countries.
ai_headline: Bill seeks faster federal approvals for rocket launches and satellite imaging
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology.

ai_sections.tldr: The LAUNCH Act would speed up federal licensing for rocket launches, reentries, and satellite imaging operations.

It also establishes a Commercial Space Transportation Administration, allows faster hiring, requires annual public reports on approval times, and clarifies that safety-check cameras on spacecraft don't need remote sensing licenses.

title: Protecting Taxpayers from Student Loan Bailouts Act
ai_summary:
This bill would limit the power of the U.S. Secretary of Education to create new rules or take executive actions related to federal student loan programs. Specifically, if a proposed regulation or executive action is considered "economically significant" (meaning it would affect the economy by $100 million or more, or have a major impact on jobs, communities, or public health), and if that regulation would increase the cost of loan subsidies to the government, the Secretary would be blocked from moving forward with it. This applies at every stage: draft, proposed, and final versions of a rule.

In practice, this bill targets the kind of large-scale student loan forgiveness or repayment-relief programs that have cost the government significant money, such as broad loan cancellation plans. The stated goal, based on the bill's title, is to prevent the Department of Education from issuing sweeping debt relief measures without going through Congress, on the reasoning that such actions shift costs to taxpayers. This would affect current and future student loan borrowers, since it could prevent the Department of Education from creating new relief programs, adjusting repayment plans, or forgiving debt if those actions are judged too costly. It would also affect how the Department of Education operates going forward, since it adds a new legal check on its rulemaking process specifically for student loan policy.
ai_headline: Bill would block costly student loan rules without Congress approval
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

title: United States Leadership in Immersive Technology Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would create a federal advisory panel and a designated advisor within the Department of Commerce focused on "immersive technology," which includes virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality. Congress states in the bill that this technology is expected to become the next major computing platform and that the United States should maintain leadership in the field, particularly as other countries like China invest heavily in it. The Secretary of Commerce would appoint a principal advisor to coordinate policy on immersive technology across federal agencies and would establish an advisory panel made up of officials from agencies like Defense, Energy, Education, Labor, and Veterans Affairs, along with outside experts from universities, think tanks, private companies, and consumer advocacy groups.

The advisory panel's job would be to study how immersive technology affects the economy and national security, and to make recommendations on things like technical standards, cybersecurity, data privacy protections, and how the government and private companies can work together. Within two years, the panel must complete a detailed study looking at how this technology affects industries such as healthcare, manufacturing, education, agriculture, and entertainment, and how it could impact jobs and small businesses. The Secretary of Commerce would then submit a public report to Congress summarizing the findings and recommending any further action.

This bill mainly affects the federal government's internal structure and planning rather than creating new rules or requirements for the public. It would primarily involve government officials, agency staff, and outside experts who serve on the panel. Indirectly, it could affect technology companies, workers in fields that might adopt VR/AR tools, and consumers, since the panel's recommendations could eventually shape future laws or regulations on privacy, safety standards, or industry investment—though this bill itself does not create any binding rules yet.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: Tribal Labor Sovereignty Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Tribal Labor Sovereignty Act of 2025, would change the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA), which is the main federal law governing how workers can unionize and how labor disputes are handled. Currently, the National Labor Relations Board has taken the position that tribal governments and tribal-owned businesses on tribal lands count as "employers" under this law, meaning their employees can unionize and file complaints the same way employees at private companies do. This bill would officially add Indian tribes and tribally-owned enterprises located on Indian lands to the list of entities exempted from the definition of "employer," similar to how federal, state, and local governments are already exempted.

In practice, this means businesses and government operations owned and run by tribes on their own lands—such as casinos, hotels, or other tribal enterprises—would no longer be required to follow federal labor law rules about union organizing and collective bargaining enforced by the National Labor Relations Board. The bill also adds clear legal definitions for terms like "Indian tribe," "Indian," and "Indian lands," including specific language covering former reservation lands in Oklahoma.

This bill mainly affects tribal governments, tribal-owned businesses, and the employees who work for them. Supporters argue it respects tribal sovereignty by treating tribal governments like other sovereign governments (federal, state, local) that are already exempt from this law. Critics argue it could reduce legal protections and unionization rights for employees working at tribal enterprises. It does not affect private, non-tribal businesses operating on or off tribal land.
ai_headline: Bill would exempt tribal enterprises from federal labor board oversight
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 393.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill would exempt tribal governments and tribal-owned businesses from the National Labor Relations Act's union rules.

title: College Financial Aid Clarity Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill requires colleges and universities to use a standard, easy-to-understand format for financial aid offer letters, the documents schools send to admitted students explaining grants, scholarships, and loans they qualify for. Currently, schools design these letters however they want, using different terms and layouts, which makes it hard for students and families to compare offers between colleges. This bill would require the Department of Education to develop consistent formatting rules, test them with students, families, counselors, and other groups, and then require all colleges receiving federal financial aid funding to follow these rules starting July 1, 2029.

Specifically, financial aid offers would need to clearly separate grants and scholarships (money that doesn't need to be repaid) from loans (money that must be repaid), use the word "loan" explicitly, distinguish between subsidized and unsubsidized loans, and include information like total cost of attendance, net price after aid, work-study opportunities, and deadlines for accepting or declining aid. Schools would also need to provide links to government websites like the College Scorecard and a net price calculator, and disclose things like how loan interest rates affect long-term costs and whether aid amounts might change in future years.

This bill mainly affects colleges and universities that participate in federal student aid programs, requiring them to redesign their award letters. It also affects prospective and current college students and their families, who would receive clearer, more standardized information to help them compare financial aid packages across different schools and understand exactly what they're being offered before deciding where to enroll.
ai_headline: Bill would standardize college financial aid letters by 2029
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 394.

title: AMERICANS Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the AMERICANS Act, deals with military service members who were discharged or punished for refusing the COVID-19 vaccine when it was required by the Department of Defense. That vaccine requirement was already lifted by Congress in 2022, but this bill goes further by creating specific remedies for those affected and by making sure a similar mandate cannot be reinstated in the future without new congressional approval.

Specifically, the bill requires the Secretary of Defense to change discharge records to "honorable discharge" for anyone kicked out solely for refusing the vaccine, as long as their record was otherwise clean. It also allows affected service members to apply for reinstatement at their previous rank, with back pay and benefits restored, and requires that any negative marks related to vaccine refusal be erased from their files. Time spent out of service due to the mandate would count toward retirement pay calculations. Additionally, anyone who had to repay enlistment or reenlistment bonuses after being discharged would no longer owe that money, and those who already repaid it would get reimbursed.

The bill also directs the military to actively try to retain unvaccinated service members, giving them equal opportunities for promotion and career development. Vaccination status could only factor into deployment decisions if a foreign country legally requires vaccination for entry and the service member's presence there is necessary. The bill affects current and former U.S. military members who faced discharge, demotion, or other penalties over COVID-19 vaccine refusal, as well as Department of Defense leadership, who would have new legal obligations to correct records and provide compensation.

title: To require the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to extend the time period during which licensees are required to commence construction of certain hydropower projects.
ai_summary:
This bill would give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) more flexibility to extend deadlines for building certain hydropower projects. Under current law, companies that receive a federal license to build a hydropower dam or facility normally have up to 8 years to start construction, with FERC able to grant extensions within that limit. This bill applies to projects licensed before March 13, 2020, and allows FERC to grant additional extensions of up to 6 more years beyond that original 8-year limit, broken into up to three 2-year increments, if the license holder shows good cause and gives proper notice.

The bill also addresses a specific problem: some licenses may have already expired between the end of 2023 and whenever this bill becomes law, because companies ran out of time to start construction. In those cases, FERC would be allowed to reinstate the expired license as if it had never lapsed, and then apply the new extension period to it.

This bill mainly affects companies that hold FERC licenses to build hydropower projects (dams and similar facilities that generate electricity from moving water), giving them more time to secure financing, complete permitting, or resolve construction delays before losing their license. It could also affect communities near these project sites, environmental groups monitoring river and land use, and utility customers who may eventually receive power from these projects, since it extends the timeline before construction must begin or the license is lost.
ai_headline: Bill would give hydropower projects up to 6 more years to start building
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 408.

title: State Public Option Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the State Public Option Act, would let states create a "public option" health insurance plan by allowing anyone to buy into their state's Medicaid program, starting in 2026. Currently, Medicaid is generally limited to people who meet certain income or disability requirements, but under this bill, any state resident who isn't already covered by other insurance could choose to purchase this Medicaid coverage instead of a private insurance plan. States could charge premiums and cost-sharing fees based on income, and people who qualify could use the same tax credits and subsidies currently available under the Affordable Care Act to help pay for this coverage. The plan would be sold through each state's health insurance marketplace (Exchange), alongside private insurance options.

The bill also makes several related changes to Medicaid. It permanently increases payment rates for primary care doctors (and expands which providers, like nurse practitioners and physician assistants, qualify for higher pay) to make sure enough providers accept Medicaid patients. It also permanently extends a higher federal funding match for states that expanded Medicaid under the ACA, directs the Department of Health and Human Services to update quality-of-care measurement standards for this new population by 2030, and requires state Medicaid programs to cover "comprehensive sexual and reproductive health care services," including abortion and abortion-related services, as a condition of receiving federal Medicaid funding.

This bill would primarily affect people currently uninsured or buying individual health insurance, especially those in areas with limited insurance company competition, by giving them a new lower-cost coverage choice. It would also affect state governments (which would administer the program and receive federal funding to help cover administrative costs), health care providers (who would see changed payment rates), and insurance markets more broadly, since a public Medicaid option could compete with private insurance plans sold on state exchanges.
ai_headline: States could let anyone buy into Medicaid starting in 2026

title: District of Columbia Attorney General Appointment Reform Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would change how Washington, D.C.'s Attorney General is chosen. Currently, D.C. residents elect their own Attorney General, similar to how many states let voters choose their state's top legal officer. Under this bill, the President of the United States would instead appoint the D.C. Attorney General, without needing approval from the Senate. The Attorney General would serve only as long as the President wants them to, and their term would end whenever the President's term ends.

The bill would also immediately end the term of whoever is serving as D.C.'s Attorney General when this law is enacted, replacing the current elected official right away. Employees who work in the Attorney General's office would not automatically become federal employees because of this change, unless another law specifically says so.

This bill mainly affects the roughly 700,000 residents of Washington, D.C., who would lose their ability to vote for this position and instead have it filled by presidential appointment. It also affects the office of the D.C. Attorney General itself, which handles local legal matters like consumer protection, civil rights enforcement, and prosecuting certain local crimes. Supporters and critics of D.C. self-governance (sometimes called "home rule") would likely view this bill very differently, since it shifts power over a locally elected position to the federal government.

last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 270.

title: Children and Teens’ Online Privacy Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill updates the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), which was originally written in 1998 and only covered kids under 13. The biggest change is extending many privacy protections to teenagers ages 13 through 16 for the first time. Under this bill, websites, apps, and online services would be banned from collecting personal information from teens for targeted advertising purposes, and companies would need consent from either a parent (for children under 13) or the teen themselves (for those 13-16) before gathering personal data. It also expands what counts as "personal information" to include things like voiceprints, facial scans, DNA data, and location information, and it requires companies to delete a child's or teen's data upon request, correct inaccurate information, and avoid keeping data longer than necessary.

The bill also broadens the definition of "operator" to clearly include mobile apps and connected devices (like smart speakers or tablets), not just websites, reflecting how kids and teens use technology today. It sets rules for how schools can allow ed-tech companies to use student data for educational purposes without needing separate parental consent each time. Companies would be required to use reasonable security practices to protect this data and could not kick a child or teen off a service just because their parent or the teen asked the company to delete their information.

This bill would primarily affect tech companies, app developers, advertisers, and online platforms that reach children and teen audiences, since they would face new compliance requirements and potential enforcement actions from the FTC and state attorneys general. It would also affect parents, teens, and children, who would gain more control over how their personal data is collected, used, and shared, as well as new rights to review, correct, or delete that data. Additionally, the bill directs the FTC and Government Accountability Office to study and report on enforcement efforts and on privacy risks teens face when using financial apps, meaning more oversight and public reporting on how well these protections are working.
ai_headline: Bill would extend online privacy protections to teens ages 13 to 16

title: District of Columbia Cash Bail Reform Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would change how the court system in Washington, D.C. handles bail and detention decisions for people accused or convicted of crimes. It requires judges to automatically hold anyone charged with a "crime of violence" or "dangerous crime" in jail before trial, without the option of release, and it also requires mandatory detention after conviction for these same offenses. It narrows the legal definitions of "burglary" and "robbery" so that only more serious versions (like first-degree burglary or robbery involving a weapon) count as automatically detainable offenses.

The bill also creates a new category called "public safety or order crimes," which includes things like fleeing from police, rioting, stalking, obstruction of justice, and lower-level burglary or robbery. For these offenses, instead of being released without paying anything (as sometimes happens now), the accused person would be required to pay cash bail or post a secured bond—meaning they'd have to put up money or property that they'd lose if they don't show up for court. If someone violates the terms of release, a bail bondsman (surety) would be allowed to arrest them and bring them before a judge.

This bill would primarily affect people arrested in Washington, D.C.—since D.C. is not a state, Congress has authority to directly set its criminal justice rules. It would affect defendants, judges, prosecutors, bail bond companies, and D.C. residents generally, as it shifts the district away from some current no-cash-bail practices toward a system with more mandatory detention and required cash bail for certain crimes. It would take effect 30 days after becoming law and apply to future criminal charges.

title: Strong Sentences for Safer D.C. Streets Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 5172, called the "Strong Sentences for Safer D.C. Streets Act of 2025," would change criminal sentencing laws specifically for Washington, D.C. Because D.C. is not a state, Congress has the power to directly rewrite its local criminal code, which is what this bill does. It increases the mandatory minimum prison sentences for several serious crimes committed in the District, including first-degree murder, second-degree murder, rape, first-degree sexual abuse, kidnapping, carjacking, and first-degree burglary. For example, first-degree murder would carry a mandatory sentence of life in prison without release, rape would require at least 25 years (30 years for repeat violent offenders), and burglary's minimum sentence would double from 5 to 10 years.

The bill also removes some existing legal provisions that currently give judges flexibility, such as special rules for reducing sentences or requiring extra proof of "aggravating circumstances" before imposing longer prison terms. This means judges in D.C. would have less discretion in these cases and would generally have to impose harsher minimum sentences than current law allows.

This bill would primarily affect people who are charged with these crimes in Washington, D.C. after the law takes effect—it would not apply retroactively to people already convicted. It would also affect D.C.'s criminal justice system more broadly, including judges, prosecutors, defense attorneys, and the D.C. Council, since it overrides local D.C. sentencing law with federal legislation. Residents of D.C. and visitors to the city could be affected if involved in the criminal justice system, and the debate around such bills often centers on the balance between local self-governance for D.C. and Congress's authority over the city's laws.

title: Clean and Managed Public Spaces Act
ai_summary:
This bill, H.R. 5163, would make it illegal to camp outdoors on public property anywhere in the District of Columbia. "Camping" is defined broadly as using any materials to set up or maintain a temporary place to live, which could include tents, tarps, sleeping bags, or similar setups used as makeshift shelter. Anyone who violates this rule could be fined up to $500, jailed for up to 30 days, or both.

This bill would mainly affect people experiencing homelessness in Washington, D.C., since outdoor camping on public land, such as parks, sidewalks, or other government-owned spaces, is often used as a form of shelter by people without stable housing. It could also affect protesters, activists, or others who set up temporary encampments on public property for demonstrations or other purposes. Local officials, police, and social services in D.C. would be responsible for enforcing the law, and the bill does not include funding or requirements for alternative housing or shelter options for those displaced by the ban.

Because the District of Columbia is not a state, Congress has the authority to pass laws directly affecting it, which is why this bill applies specifically to D.C. and not to other cities. Supporters and critics of similar measures nationwide often disagree about whether such bans effectively address homelessness or simply criminalize it, but this summary does not take a position on those debates.

title: Common-Sense Law Enforcement and Accountability Now in DC Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 5107, called the "CLEAN DC Act," is a bill that would cancel a Washington, D.C. law called the Comprehensive Policing and Justice Reform Amendment Act of 2022. That D.C. law was passed by the city's own council and included various changes to how police officers are regulated and held accountable, such as rules about the use of force, disciplinary procedures, and public access to police disciplinary records. If Congress repeals it, all the older rules and laws that were in place before 2022 would come back into effect, as though the reform law had never been passed.

This bill matters because Congress has special authority over Washington, D.C.'s laws, even though D.C. has its own local government and city council. Normally, D.C. residents and their elected council make local laws like this one, but Congress can override or cancel them since D.C. is not a state. If passed, this bill would directly affect D.C. residents, police officers, and city officials by changing the rules governing police conduct and accountability back to what they were before the 2022 reforms. It would not affect policing laws in any U.S. state, since Congress's power to repeal local laws this way applies only to the District of Columbia.

The bill was introduced by a group of Republican lawmakers and has been sent to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform for further consideration. As of this text, it has not been voted on or passed into law.

title: Payment Choice Act of 2025
ai_summary:
The Payment Choice Act of 2025 would require most physical, in-person retail businesses to accept cash as payment for purchases up to $500, and it would ban businesses from charging cash-paying customers more than customers who pay by card or other methods. The bill includes some exceptions: stores temporarily unable to process cash due to system failures or lack of change, and businesses that offer free, no-minimum-deposit cash-to-prepaid-card machines that don't collect personal information. For the first five years, businesses also would not be required to accept $50 or $100 bills, though after that period, regulators would set rules on which bills must be accepted, with $1, $5, $10, and $20 bills always required.

This bill would primarily affect brick-and-mortar retailers and their customers, especially people who rely on cash rather than credit cards, debit cards, or mobile payment apps—often lower-income individuals, older adults, or those without bank accounts. Businesses that have gone "cashless" would need to change their policies or qualify for an exception. The bill also sets up a legal process for customers to challenge violations, including required notice to the business, potential lawsuits, financial penalties, and possible damages. Additionally, it would require banks and credit unions to report annually on the locations of their ATMs, giving regulators more insight into cash access across different communities.

title: Improving Law Enforcement Officer Safety and Wellness Through Data Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Attorney General, working with the FBI and the National Institute of Justice, to produce three separate reports to Congress within 270 days of the law passing. The reports would study violence against police officers from different angles: how often officers are deliberately targeted or ambushed, how well current federal and local responses and training programs address these attacks, and whether equipment programs like bulletproof vest grants are reaching officers who need them. The bill does not create new crimes, funding, or programs itself—it only requires studying the issue and gathering data.

The second report would examine whether a new category should be added to national crime databases to track aggressive or traumatic incidents against officers that are currently too minor or too common to be formally logged as crimes, such as threats or minor assaults. The third report focuses on officer mental health, looking at how stress and trauma affect police, what support programs already exist (especially peer counseling), how often officers use them, and whether mental health screening should be expanded.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies like the Department of Justice and FBI, which would have to do the research and writing, as well as state and local police departments, who may be asked to share data or participate in surveys. Indirectly, it affects police officers and their families, since the goal is to eventually improve safety training, equipment distribution, and mental health resources. Ordinary citizens aren't directly affected, though the resulting reports could shape future laws or funding related to policing and officer wellness.

title: District of Columbia Home Rule Improvement Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would change how Congress oversees laws passed by the District of Columbia's local government. Currently, D.C. operates under "home rule," meaning its elected Council and Mayor pass their own local laws, but Congress has always kept a review period during which it can block those laws. This bill would extend that review period from 30 days to 60 days for most laws, remove a shorter alternative review period that currently applies to certain criminal-law changes, and close a loophole that let the Council avoid review by declaring a law an "emergency" and then re-passing it repeatedly. It also lets Congress disapprove just part of a D.C. law instead of the whole thing, and for the first time gives Congress the power to review and block the Mayor's executive orders and regulations, not just laws passed by the Council.

The bill also adds new restrictions: the Council could not withdraw a law from congressional review once submitted, and if Congress blocks a law, the Council could not simply pass a nearly identical law later without special permission. Finally, it would require the D.C. Council Chair and Mayor to testify before House and Senate committees once a year to report on the "state of the District."

This bill mainly affects District of Columbia residents and their local government, since it expands federal control over locally passed laws, executive actions, and regulations. It would also affect members of Congress, particularly those on the relevant House and Senate committees, who would gain more oversight authority and additional review responsibilities. Supporters would say this strengthens accountability over D.C.'s government, while critics would say it reduces D.C.'s self-governance; this summary does not take a position on those arguments.

title: Public Safety Officer Concussion and Traumatic Brain Injury Health Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services, working through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), to gather and share information about concussions and traumatic brain injuries (TBIs) affecting public safety officers, such as police officers and firefighters. This includes research on best practices, recommendations for protective equipment, and medical guidance on diagnosing and treating these injuries, as well as ways to reduce how often they happen on the job.

The bill requires the CDC to update its website with this information and find other ways to share it with several groups: doctors and public health workers, employers and unions representing public safety officers, mental health professionals studying links between brain injuries and issues like depression or suicidal thoughts, patients and their families, and researchers at universities. The CDC must also consult with these groups to make sure the information is useful and relevant. Additionally, the Secretary is allowed to support outside efforts, including through grants or contracts, to develop model guidelines and treatment practices for these injuries.

This bill mainly affects public safety officers—police, firefighters, and similar workers—who face risks of head injuries on the job, along with their families, employers, and the medical professionals who treat them. It does not create new funding programs or mandates beyond directing HHS and the CDC to collect and distribute information, so its main impact would be improving awareness, research, and treatment practices rather than changing laws or benefits directly.

title: Improving Access to Nutrition Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Improving Access to Nutrition Act of 2025, would remove a specific rule from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as SNAP or food stamps. That rule currently limits food assistance to three months within a three-year period for "able-bodied adults without dependents" between certain ages, unless they meet work or job-training requirements for a set number of hours per week. The bill would eliminate this time limit and work requirement entirely, along with making several technical changes to related sections of federal law that reference it, including provisions in the tax code and workforce training laws.

If passed, this would primarily affect adults without children or other dependents who currently must prove they are working, training, or volunteering a minimum number of hours to keep receiving SNAP benefits beyond three months. Removing this requirement means these individuals could continue receiving food assistance regardless of employment status. The bill's supporters argue, through the findings listed in the text, that work requirements don't reduce poverty, create administrative burdens that cause eligible people to lose benefits, and disproportionately affect Black Americans, Native Americans, and people facing homelessness or health problems that make steady work difficult.

The change would take effect 180 days after the bill becomes law, giving states time to adjust their SNAP administration systems. This bill would need to pass both the Senate and House and be signed by the President to become law; it has currently only been introduced and referred to committee.

title: To repeal the Second Chance Amendment Act of 2022 and the Incarceration Reduction Amendment Act of 2016.
ai_summary:
This bill would cancel two Washington, D.C. criminal justice laws by using Congress's authority over the District of Columbia. The first, the Second Chance Amendment Act of 2022, allowed people who committed crimes before age 25 to ask a judge to reduce their sentence after serving a significant amount of time in prison, if they could show they had been rehabilitated. The second, the Incarceration Reduction Amendment Act of 2016, gave similar resentencing opportunities to people who committed crimes as minors (under 18). Both laws were part of D.C.'s effort to give long-serving prisoners, especially those who were young at the time of their offense, a chance to have their cases reviewed by a judge.

If this bill passes, both laws would be treated as if they never existed, meaning the legal provisions they changed would go back to how they were before these acts were passed. This would end the ability of eligible D.C. prisoners to petition for sentence reductions under these specific programs going forward. It would primarily affect incarcerated individuals in the D.C. prison system who were convicted of crimes committed when they were young, as well as the D.C. courts and corrections system that have been implementing these resentencing procedures. Because Congress has authority to review and overturn D.C. laws, this bill reflects an ongoing debate between federal lawmakers and D.C.'s local government over how much control Congress should exercise over the District's own criminal justice policies.

title: ABC Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Alleviating Barriers for Caregivers Act (ABC Act), directs two federal agencies — the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and the Social Security Administration (SSA) — to review how family caregivers interact with Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and Social Security programs. The goal is to find ways to make paperwork, applications, and communication simpler for people who help family members apply for and use these benefits. This could include reducing repeated paperwork, cutting phone wait times, improving websites, offering translation and disability-accessible services, and better training staff to help caregivers.

After completing this review, the agencies must take steps to fix the problems they find and report their findings to Congress within two years, with a follow-up report two years after that. These reports must be made public and include cost estimates and any recommended legal changes. The bill also asks CMS to send guidance to state Medicaid and CHIP directors encouraging similar reviews at the state level.

This bill would mainly affect family caregivers — people who help aging parents, disabled family members, or children get and keep health coverage or Social Security benefits — as well as the federal and state employees who manage these programs. It does not create new benefits or change eligibility rules; it focuses on making the existing process easier to navigate and less bureaucratic.

title: Fighting Foreign Illegal Seafood Harvests Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, the FISH Act of 2025, aims to crack down on illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing by foreign vessels and companies, especially fishing tied to forced labor. Its main tool is a public "blacklist" of foreign fishing vessels, fleets, and their owners found to be involved in illegal fishing or forced labor. Vessels on this list would be banned from U.S. ports, barred from receiving fuel, supplies, or services from U.S. vessels, and prohibited from importing their seafood into the United States. The bill also allows the Treasury Department to impose sanctions—such as freezing assets and denying visas—on people or companies connected to illegal fishing or trafficking of endangered fish species.

Beyond the blacklist and sanctions, the bill directs several federal agencies (NOAA, the Coast Guard, Customs and Border Protection, the State Department, and others) to strengthen coordination, share data, and work with international organizations to fight illegal fishing worldwide. It calls for new studies on the scale and economic cost of illegal fishing, the role of new technologies (like drones and satellite tracking) in monitoring fishing activity, and the relationship between Russian and Chinese fishing industries and their effects on U.S. seafood markets. It also encourages U.S. support for other countries' fisheries management and enforcement capacity, particularly in regions where illegal fishing is common.

This bill would primarily affect foreign fishing companies, vessel owners, and countries involved in illegal or forced-labor fishing, who could face U.S. trade bans and financial sanctions. It would also affect U.S. seafood importers and processors, who may see new import restrictions or reporting requirements aimed at keeping illegally caught seafood out of U.S. markets. Ordinary consumers could benefit indirectly through more transparency about where their seafood comes from, while government agencies like NOAA, the Coast Guard, and Customs and Border Protection would gain new responsibilities and funding to enforce these rules.

last_action_text: Held at the desk.

title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "Greenhouse Gas Emissions Standards for Heavy-Duty Vehicles-Phase 3".
ai_summary:
This bill would cancel a federal regulation issued by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) called "Greenhouse Gas Emissions Standards for Heavy-Duty Vehicles—Phase 3," which was published in April 2024. The bill uses a special power Congress has under the Congressional Review Act, which allows lawmakers to vote down recently issued federal agency rules with a simple majority vote instead of the normal lawmaking process. If passed by both the House and Senate and signed by the President (or if a presidential veto is overridden), the EPA rule would be treated as if it never took effect.

The rule in question set stricter limits on greenhouse gas emissions from heavy-duty vehicles, like large trucks and buses, starting with certain future model years. The goal of the original EPA rule was to reduce pollution linked to climate change by pushing truck and bus manufacturers toward cleaner engines, including more electric and low-emission vehicles. If this bill becomes law, those stricter emissions standards would be blocked, meaning manufacturers would not be required to meet them.

This bill mainly affects truck and bus manufacturers, trucking companies, and fleet operators, who would no longer face the new emissions requirements. It also affects the environment and public health more broadly, since supporters of the original rule argued it would cut pollution and improve air quality, while opponents argue it could raise costs for manufacturers and reduce their flexibility. Additionally, because of how the Congressional Review Act works, if this resolution passes, the EPA would be blocked from creating a very similar rule in the future without new authorization from Congress.

title: Least Cost Exception Act
ai_summary:
**HR 6547 — Least Cost Exception Act** would change how the FDIC handles the failure of a bank. Normally, when a bank fails, the FDIC is required by law to resolve it (sell it, merge it, or liquidate it) in whatever way costs the Deposit Insurance Fund the least amount of money—this is called the "least-cost" requirement. This bill would let the FDIC choose a more expensive option instead, specifically to avoid selling a failed bank to one of the very largest banks in the world (called "global systemically important banks," or G-SIBs, which include institutions like JPMorgan Chase or Bank of America).

To use this exception, the FDIC and the Federal Reserve would have to agree, after talking with the Treasury Department, that avoiding further concentration of the banking industry among these mega-banks is worth the extra cost. The FDIC would also have to set a cap on how much extra cost it can take on, and if it picks a pricier option, it must report the details to Congress within 30 days. If the alternative involves another company buying the failed bank's assets, that buyer would have to pay back the difference in cost to the Deposit Insurance Fund over at least five years.

This bill would mainly affect how bank failures are handled going forward, particularly larger or mid-sized bank failures that might otherwise be sold to a giant bank. It's aimed at preventing the biggest banks from getting even bigger by scooping up failed competitors, even if doing so costs the FDIC's insurance fund more money in the short term. Bank regulators, large financial institutions, and taxpayers (who indirectly back the deposit insurance system) would all be affected by this change.
ai_headline: Bill would let FDIC pick pricier option to block mega-bank takeovers
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 405.

title: Federal Broadband Deployment Tracking Act
ai_summary:
HR 1343, the Federal Broadband Deployment Tracking Act, deals with a government form called "Form 299," which companies use to get permission to build communications equipment, like cell towers or broadband lines, on federal land. This land can be managed by agencies such as the Bureau of Land Management, National Park Service, Fish and Wildlife Service, Bureau of Reclamation, or the National Forest System. The bill requires a federal official, the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information, to create and submit a plan to Congress within 180 days explaining how the government will track these applications from start to finish and give companies better updates on where their applications stand.

In practical terms, this bill doesn't change any rules about who can build broadband infrastructure or where. Instead, it's focused on improving transparency and efficiency in the government's internal process for handling these applications. The plan must also identify any obstacles that might make it hard to set up this tracking system.

This bill mainly affects telecommunications and broadband companies that apply for permits to install equipment on federal land, since they would benefit from clearer information about their application status. It could also indirectly benefit everyday Americans, especially in rural or underserved areas, if faster and more transparent permitting leads to quicker broadband expansion. The bill does not provide funding or set deadlines for approving individual permits—it simply asks for a plan to improve how the process is tracked and communicated.

title: District of Columbia Electronic Transmittal of Legislation Act
ai_summary:
This bill would update the process by which Washington, D.C. sends its passed laws to Congress for review. Under current rules, Congress must review D.C. laws before they can take effect, and that transmission has traditionally been done on paper. This bill would allow the Chairman of the D.C. Council to send those laws, as well as amendments to the city's charter, to Congress electronically instead of only in physical paper form.

The bill also specifies that both the House of Representatives and the Senate must treat electronically transmitted D.C. laws the same way they treat paper submissions for all official purposes, such as counting the required review period. This means an electronic submission would carry the same legal weight as a paper one, avoiding any confusion or delay caused by outdated transmission methods.

This change mainly affects the D.C. city government and Congress's internal procedures for reviewing local D.C. legislation. It does not change what powers D.C. has or what laws it can pass—it simply modernizes the paperwork process. Residents of Washington, D.C. could benefit indirectly from faster, more efficient handling of their local laws, since electronic transmission could speed up the process compared to mailing physical documents. It does not affect other states or the general public outside of D.C.'s legislative process.

title: Preserving Integrity in Immigration Benefits Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Preserving Integrity in Immigration Benefits Act, would require U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to review immigration benefit applications that were approved between January 20, 2021, and whenever this bill becomes law. Specifically, it targets cases connected to Presidential Proclamation 10998, a December 2025 order restricting entry of certain foreign nationals for security reasons. The goal of the review is to check whether these earlier approvals followed proper procedures and met the correct legal standards at the time they were granted.

The bill sets a deadline of September 15, 2026, for USCIS to complete two things: give an in-person briefing to the Judiciary Committees in both the House and Senate explaining what the review found, and publish a public report online with the same results. The bill itself does not cancel or change anyone's immigration status directly, but it could set the stage for future action if the review finds problems with how certain cases were handled.

This bill would mainly affect USCIS staff, who would have to carry out the review and reporting work, and members of Congress, who would receive the briefing. It could also affect immigrants whose applications were approved during that time period and fall under the proclamation's scope, since their cases would be reexamined. Depending on what the review uncovers, this could lead to increased scrutiny or future policy changes affecting people who received immigration benefits during those years, though the bill itself only calls for review and reporting, not immediate changes to anyone's status.

title: Stop the Cartels Act
ai_summary:
The Stop the Cartels Act is a wide-ranging bill focused on drug cartels, immigration enforcement, and border security. It requires U.S. intelligence agencies to produce detailed reports on drug trafficking organizations and human smuggling operations in Mexico and 18 other countries in Latin America, and to review whether U.S. intelligence resources are being properly focused on these threats. It also lets the Secretary of State formally designate cartels like the Sinaloa Cartel and Jalisco New Generation Cartel as "Special Transnational Criminal Organizations," which would make it a federal crime to provide them material support and would allow the government to freeze their financial assets. The bill also blocks certain funding to Mexico's government until it removes barriers to law enforcement cooperation with the U.S.

On immigration, the bill makes major changes to how migrant families and asylum seekers are handled at the border. It would let the Department of Homeland Security detain migrant children and families together for longer periods, override a long-standing court settlement (the "Flores agreement") that currently limits how migrant children can be detained, and remove state licensing requirements for family detention facilities. It tightens the standards for claiming asylum, making it harder to pass a "credible fear" screening, and permanently bars people with felony convictions or prior removals from applying for asylum. It also creates new refugee processing centers in Mexico and Central America where people could apply for U.S. refugee status without traveling to the border, and it cuts off federal grant funding to state and local governments that limit cooperation with immigration enforcement (so-called "sanctuary" jurisdictions).

Finally, the bill shifts federal drug-treatment funding. It increases funding for one large substance-abuse block grant program but pays for this by eliminating several other federal programs, including certain substance abuse treatment grants, the Drug-Free Communities program, community mental health block grants, jail diversion grants, and Project AWARE. This bill would affect immigrants and asylum seekers, border communities, state and local governments that receive federal grants, mental health and addiction treatment providers, and U.S. relations with Mexico and other Latin American countries.

last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Border Security and Enforcement.

title: Eviction Helpline Act
ai_summary:
The Eviction Helpline Act would require the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to set up a national hotline within one year of the bill becoming law. This hotline would give tenants information and assistance related to evictions. Congress would provide funding for this hotline starting in fiscal year 2026 and continuing in future years, though the exact amount isn't specified in the bill.

The hotline would only be available to tenants living in certain types of housing that receive federal assistance. This includes public housing, Section 8 rental assistance, HOME Investment Partnerships properties, homes for elderly or disabled residents supported by federal programs, housing tied to AIDS assistance programs, Native American and Native Hawaiian housing programs, and properties with government-backed mortgages. In short, this covers many forms of subsidized or federally connected rental housing, but not all private rentals.

This bill would primarily affect renters living in federally subsidized housing who may be facing eviction, giving them a new resource to get information and help. It would also affect HUD, which would be responsible for creating and running the hotline, and it could involve federal spending, since taxpayer money would fund the program each year going forward.

title: To authorize the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development to award grants to eligible entities to select pre-reviewed designs of covered structures of mixed-income housing for use in the jurisdiction of the eligible entity, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Accelerating Home Building Act, would let the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) give grants to local governments, tribal governments, and organizations that represent cities and towns. The money would be used to help these groups pick "pre-reviewed" building designs, sometimes called pattern books, for small to mid-sized housing buildings like duplexes, triplexes, townhouses, and accessory dwelling units. These are pre-approved blueprints that already meet local building codes, so builders can get permits faster instead of waiting through lengthy design reviews. Importantly, the grant money could only be used to select and approve these designs, not to actually build, renovate, or repair housing.

When deciding who gets grants, HUD would consider factors like local affordable housing needs, whether the area is a "high opportunity area" (a place with good access to jobs, schools, and services), and how well the local government coordinates with state agencies and transportation planners. At least 10% of the funding each year would be set aside for rural communities. Governments that receive grants would have to report back on how many housing permits and units resulted from using these designs, and if they don't actually adopt the designs within five years, they may have to return the grant money.

This bill would mainly affect local and tribal governments, housing developers, and communities looking to build more affordable, mixed-income housing more quickly. Everyday residents could be affected indirectly if their city or town uses these grants to speed up housing construction, potentially increasing the supply of moderate-cost homes in their area. The bill does not guarantee new housing will be built—it only funds the planning and design-approval stage, not actual construction.
ai_headline: HUD grants would fund pre-approved housing designs to speed permits
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
