title: Strengthening Housing Supply Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would change the rules for a federal program called the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) program, which gives cities and states money for local development projects. Right now, that money can be used to fix up or rehabilitate existing housing, but it generally cannot be used to build brand-new affordable housing. This bill would add "new construction of affordable housing" as an approved use of these federal grant dollars, using the definition of affordable housing already established in an existing housing law.

In practical terms, this means local governments that receive CDBG funding could choose to spend some of that money on building new affordable housing units, not just repairing older ones. The bill also updates related rules about serving low- and moderate-income residents to include new construction alongside existing rehabilitation activities. These changes would only apply to money appropriated after the law takes effect, so it wouldn't retroactively change how past grants were used.

This would primarily affect local and state governments that manage CDBG funds, housing developers who partner with them, and lower-income renters or homebuyers who might benefit from new affordable housing supply. It could also affect how Congress and HUD (Department of Housing and Urban Development) allocate and oversee these grant funds going forward.
ai_headline: Bill would let CDBG grants fund new affordable housing, not just repairs
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

The changes would apply only to funds appropriated after the law takes effect, not past grants.

title: Ending Homelessness Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 4872, the Ending Homelessness Act of 2025, is a large bill aimed at significantly expanding federal housing assistance to reduce and eventually end homelessness in the United States. The biggest change is a major expansion of the Housing Choice Voucher program (commonly known as Section 8), which helps low-income renters afford housing. The bill would add millions of new vouchers over several years and, starting in 2029, turn housing vouchers into an "entitlement," meaning any eligible low-income family who applies would be guaranteed assistance, similar to how programs like SNAP (food stamps) work today. It also removes certain rules that currently make some people ineligible for public housing, such as past criminal records, and requires that rent assistance be based on more accurate local rental costs (using ZIP-code level data instead of broader regional averages).

The bill also creates new protections and funding streams. It amends the Fair Housing Act to ban housing discrimination based on a person's "source of income," meaning landlords could not refuse tenants simply because they use vouchers, Social Security, disability payments, or child support to pay rent. It funds new emergency grants to help communities with the highest homelessness needs, more money for the national Housing Trust Fund (which supports affordable housing construction), and funding to help state and local governments coordinate health care and housing services for homeless individuals. It also permanently authorizes funding for existing homelessness assistance programs and keeps the U.S. Interagency Council on Homelessness operating indefinitely.

This bill would affect renters, particularly low-income individuals and families, people experiencing or at risk of homelessness, and landlords/property owners who would face new anti-discrimination rules. It would also affect state and local governments and public housing agencies, which would receive more federal funding but also more responsibilities and reporting requirements. Nonprofit and faith-based organizations that provide housing services would become eligible for expanded federal grants. Because the bill significantly increases federal spending and government involvement in housing policy, it would also have major budgetary implications for the federal government.
ai_headline: Bill would expand housing vouchers and guarantee them by 2029
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Financial Services, and in addition to the Committee on the Judiciary, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

title: A bill to amend the Digital Coast Act to improve the acquisition, integration, and accessibility of data of the Digital Coast program and to extend the program.
ai_summary:
This bill makes changes to the Digital Coast Act, a law that supports a federal program called Digital Coast, which is run through NOAA (the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration). Digital Coast collects and shares data about coastal areas, such as maps, flooding information, and land-use data, so that local governments, businesses, and researchers can make informed decisions about coastal development, hazard planning, and conservation.

The bill makes three specific updates. First, it strengthens the requirement that the data collected through Digital Coast be not just "readily accessible" but also "fully and freely available," meaning the public should be able to get this information without unnecessary restrictions or costs. Second, it expands the type of information covered by the program to include data about underground infrastructure and subsurface utilities, such as pipes, cables, and other buried systems, which is useful for planning construction and understanding what lies beneath coastal areas. Third, it extends the program's authorization from 2025 to 2030, meaning Congress is allowing the program to keep operating and receiving funding for five more years.

This bill would primarily affect coastal communities, local governments, urban planners, engineers, and businesses that rely on accurate coastal and underground infrastructure data for construction, disaster preparedness, and environmental planning. It could also benefit everyday residents in coastal areas by improving the quality and availability of information used to plan for flooding, storms, and infrastructure projects in their communities.
ai_headline: Bill extends NOAA's Digital Coast program through 2030, adds underground data
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill renews NOAA's Digital Coast program through 2030 and expands it to cover underground infrastructure data.
ai_sections.what: The bill updates the Digital Coast Act by requiring that coastal data be "fully and freely available," not just accessible. It expands the program to include data on underground infrastructure like pipes and cables, and extends its authorization from 2025 to 2030.
ai_sections.who: The changes affect coastal communities, local governments, urban planners, engineers, and businesses that use coastal and underground infrastructure data. Everyday residents in coastal areas could also be affected through improved planning information.
ai_sections.why: The changes could increase public access to coastal data and add new categories of information available for construction and infrastructure planning. Continuing the program's authorization allows it to keep operating and receiving funding for five more years.

title: Energy Choice Act
ai_summary:
The Energy Choice Act would stop state and local governments from passing laws, building codes, or policies that ban or restrict certain types of energy hookups based on what kind of energy source is being used. This means a city or state could not, for example, require new homes to be all-electric and ban natural gas lines, or otherwise favor one energy type over another when it comes to connecting, installing, or expanding energy service to homes and businesses. The bill lists the energy types covered, including natural gas, hydrogen, propane, electricity, biodiesel, and other fuels.

In practical terms, this bill targets a growing trend in some cities and states that have passed "natural gas bans" or similar rules requiring new construction to use electric-only appliances and utilities as a way to reduce fossil fuel use and address climate change. If passed, those kinds of local rules would no longer be allowed, since local governments couldn't limit energy hookups based on the type of fuel involved.

This would primarily affect city councils, state legislatures, and local utility regulators, who would lose the ability to write these kinds of energy-source restrictions into building codes or ordinances. It would also affect homebuilders, utility companies, and energy producers (like natural gas and propane suppliers), who would be guaranteed continued market access regardless of local climate or energy policies. Homeowners and renters could be affected indirectly, since it would preserve their ability to choose gas, electric, or other energy hookups in new construction, rather than being limited by local government decisions.
ai_headline: Bill would bar local bans on natural gas hookups in new construction
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 412.

This directly targets "natural gas ban" ordinances that require new construction to be all-electric.

ai_sections.why: Local governments would no longer be able to use building codes to favor one energy source over another for climate or policy reasons. This would preserve market access for gas, propane, and other fuel suppliers regardless of local goals.

title: Student Financial Clarity Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Student Financial Clarity Act of 2025, aims to make it easier for students and families to understand exactly what college will cost before they enroll. It requires the Department of Education to overhaul the existing College Scorecard website so it shows detailed, program-specific information for each college and each degree or certificate program—things like acceptance rates, average time to finish, typical debt loads, loan repayment outcomes, and graduates' earnings. Importantly, this information would be broken down by student characteristics such as income level, race, sex, disability status, in-state versus out-of-state status, and type of financial aid received, so people can compare costs and outcomes for students similar to themselves rather than relying on vague school-wide averages.

The bill also creates a new "Universal Net Price Calculator," a single government tool that lets students plug in their personal and financial details and get a customized estimate of what they would actually pay—after grants and scholarships—at specific colleges and specific programs, not just the school overall. Colleges would eventually be required to link to this tool or offer their own calculator with the same level of detail. The bill also formally defines what counts as a "program of study" (tying it to specific degree types and fields) so that cost and outcome data can be compared consistently across schools, and it retires an older, separate cost-estimator tool and renames "College Navigator" as "College Scorecard" throughout federal law.

This mainly affects prospective and current college students, their families, and colleges and universities that participate in federal financial aid programs, since those schools will face new reporting and disclosure requirements. The Department of Education would also have added responsibilities to build and maintain these tools. The changes would not take effect until the 2027–2028 school year, giving schools and the government time to prepare.
ai_headline: Bill would overhaul College Scorecard with program-level cost data
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 395.

title: Baby Hygiene Tax Relief Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Baby Hygiene Tax Relief Act, would stop the President from using a specific emergency law (the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, often used to justify tariffs during trade disputes or national emergencies) to place import taxes, called duties or tariffs, on certain baby care products. If tariffs on these items are already in place under that law when the bill becomes law, they would have to be ended. The bill also blocks the President from using any other legal authority to impose similar tariffs on these same products, meaning the government couldn't simply switch to a different legal justification to keep the tariffs going.

The specific products covered include diapers, diaper liners, diaper cream, diaper bags, changing tables, baby wipes, baby soap, baby shampoo, baby bathtubs, and baby towels. The bill would primarily affect parents and caregivers of infants by potentially keeping prices lower on these essential items, since tariffs on imported goods are often passed on to consumers through higher retail prices. It would also affect companies that import or sell baby hygiene products, as well as government agencies responsible for setting and collecting tariffs. The bill does not eliminate all possible tariffs on these goods, only those imposed under the specific emergency powers law mentioned, or substantially similar tariffs under other authorities.
ai_headline: Bill would bar emergency tariffs on diapers and other baby care items
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Ways and Means, and in addition to the Committee on Foreign Affairs, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

title: Combating Organized Retail Crime Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill aims to crack down on organized theft rings that steal large amounts of retail goods and cargo to resell for profit, a problem Congress says has grown sharply in recent years alongside violence against store workers and security guards. It updates federal criminal law to make it easier to prosecute these groups by allowing prosecutors to add up the value of multiple thefts committed over a 12-month period, even if individual thefts were small, to reach the dollar thresholds needed for federal charges. It also expands the definition of "stolen goods" crimes to cover things like gift cards and prepaid cards, and allows the government to seize money and property connected to these crimes, similar to how it handles other theft and fraud cases.

The bill also creates a new "Organized Retail and Supply Chain Crime Coordination Center" within the Department of Homeland Security. This center would bring together various federal agencies (like the FBI, Secret Service, and Customs and Border Protection), along with state, local, and tribal law enforcement, to share information, coordinate investigations, and work with retail and shipping companies to track and stop these crime rings. The center would also study trends, publish annual reports, and evaluate whether existing grant and training programs adequately help local police fight this type of crime. It would operate for seven years unless renewed.

This bill would primarily affect retailers, shipping and logistics companies, and their employees and customers, who have been dealing with rising theft and related violence. It also affects law enforcement agencies at all levels, who would gain new legal tools and a central hub for cooperation. Consumers could benefit indirectly if reduced theft helps stabilize prices and product availability, particularly for items like medicine and baby formula that have been targeted by theft rings.
ai_headline: Bill targets organized retail theft rings with new federal tools
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 2853 lets prosecutors combine theft values over 12 months and creates a federal crime coordination center.

title: Digital Coast Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews and slightly updates the Digital Coast Act, a federal program run through the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) that provides coastal mapping data, tools, and training to communities dealing with coastal issues like flooding, erosion, and development planning. The original law was set to expire, so this bill extends its funding authorization from 2025 through 2030, allowing the program to keep operating.

The bill also makes a few small but meaningful changes to how the program works. It requires that coastal data be not just "readily accessible" but "fully and freely available," meaning the public, researchers, and local governments should be able to get this information without cost or unnecessary barriers. It also expands the type of data covered to specifically include information about underground infrastructure and subsurface utilities, such as pipes, cables, and other underground systems near coastlines, which can be important for construction planning and disaster response.

This bill mainly affects coastal state and local governments, urban planners, emergency management agencies, and researchers who rely on NOAA's coastal data for decisions about flooding, storm preparedness, and development. It could also indirectly affect everyday residents in coastal areas, since better data can lead to improved planning for flood risks and infrastructure projects. The bill does not create new regulations for individuals or businesses; it simply continues and slightly broadens an existing federal data-sharing program.

last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 310.

It also requires coastal data to be "fully and freely available" rather than just "readily accessible," and expands covered data to include underground infrastructure like pipes and cables near coastlines.

title: To require the name of military installation under jurisdiction of Secretary of the Army located in Fayetteville, North Carolina, to be known and designated as Fort Bragg, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill would legally require the Army base in Fayetteville, North Carolina, to officially be named "Fort Bragg." Once passed, any government law, map, document, or record referring to this military installation would automatically be treated as referring to "Fort Bragg." This is relevant because the base's name has changed before: it was originally called Fort Bragg, then renamed Fort Liberty in 2023 as part of a broader effort to remove Confederate names from military bases, and more recently the Army renamed it Fort Bragg again in 2025, but under a different naming rationale honoring a different individual with the same surname rather than the original Confederate namesake. This bill would make that "Fort Bragg" name permanent and legally required, rather than leaving it subject to change through Department of Defense policy alone.

This mainly affects how the base is officially referred to in government paperwork, signage, and legal references, and it affects service members, their families, and civilians connected to the base in Fayetteville. It does not change how the base operates, its funding, staffing, or mission—it only addresses the legal name. The bill also relies on an existing legal definition of "military installation" found in federal law to make clear exactly which facility is covered.
ai_headline: Bill would permanently lock in "Fort Bragg" name by law
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Armed Services.

title: Weatherization Enhancement and Readiness Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill updates a federal program that helps low-income households make their homes more energy-efficient, called the Weatherization Assistance Program. It raises the average amount of money that can be spent per home on weatherization work from $6,500 to $12,000, allowing for more substantial improvements like better insulation, sealing, and heating or cooling upgrades. It also removes some restrictions that previously limited homes from getting help if they had already received certain other types of federal or non-federal assistance, and it extends the program's funding authorization through 2030.

The bill also creates a new "weatherization readiness program." This addresses a common problem where homes are too run-down to safely receive weatherization work—for example, homes with roofing, plumbing, electrical, or structural problems must currently be turned away or "deferred." Under this new program, the Department of Energy would give grants to states and tribal organizations to fix these underlying issues first, so more low-income homes can qualify for energy upgrades. The program would receive $50 million per year from 2026 through 2030, with limits on how much of that money can go toward administrative costs.

This bill mainly affects low-income homeowners and renters who rely on weatherization assistance to lower energy bills and improve home safety, as well as state agencies, tribal organizations, and contractors who carry out these programs. By expanding funding limits and adding a readiness program, more households—especially those with older or damaged homes—could become eligible for help that was previously out of reach.
ai_headline: Home weatherization aid nearly doubles to $12,000 per household
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 410.

title: Territories Health Equity Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would change how Medicare and Medicaid work in U.S. territories—Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, and American Samoa—to bring their funding closer to how states are treated. Currently, federal Medicaid funding for territories is capped at a set dollar amount each year, and the federal government's matching share of costs is limited to a fixed percentage, unlike states, which get open-ended funding based on need. This bill would eliminate those funding caps and percentage limits starting in 2026, and would let territories qualify for extra Medicaid payments (called "DSH" payments) that help hospitals serving many low-income patients. It also adjusts how Medicare pays hospitals in the territories, removes certain late-enrollment penalties for Medicare Part B in Puerto Rico, adjusts Medicare Advantage payment rates for Puerto Rico, and automatically qualifies more low-income territorial residents for Medicare prescription drug cost help.

The bill also requires the government to publish more information about Medicaid and CHIP spending in the territories so people can see how funds are used, and to study how territories have been left out of the ACA's health insurance exchanges (the online marketplaces where people buy insurance in states). Finally, it creates a new system letting residents in territories without any exchange plans available buy insurance through the Washington, D.C. exchange, with the same tax credits and subsidies available to members of Congress, while protecting D.C. residents from bearing extra costs.

This bill mainly affects residents of U.S. territories, especially low-income individuals, Medicare enrollees, and hospitals that serve many uninsured or low-income patients. It would likely increase federal health spending directed to these territories and give residents there benefits closer to what people in the 50 states receive.
ai_headline: Bill would end Medicaid funding caps for US territories starting 2026

title: Federal Mechanical Insulation Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Federal Mechanical Insulation Act, updates a federal energy law to officially recognize insulation on mechanical systems—like pipes, ducts, and heating or cooling equipment—as a legitimate energy or water efficiency upgrade for federal buildings. Currently, the law lists various improvements that count toward energy efficiency goals, but it doesn't clearly mention this type of insulation. This bill adds a specific definition so that insulation materials meeting industry standards (set by the American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers) and that reduce energy loss are formally counted as an approved efficiency measure.

The bill also requires that when federal agencies conduct their regular energy and water evaluations of buildings, they must specifically look at whether installing this kind of insulation could help save energy or water. This means building inspectors and facility managers will need to consider insulation upgrades as one of the options when assessing government buildings.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies that own or manage government buildings, as well as contractors and companies that make or install mechanical insulation products. It doesn't directly affect private citizens, but it could lead to more federal buildings getting upgraded insulation, which may reduce energy waste and lower costs for taxpayers who fund government operations over time.
ai_headline: Bill would count pipe and duct insulation as federal energy upgrade
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 411.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill formally defines mechanical insulation as an approved energy or water efficiency upgrade for federal buildings.
ai_sections.what: The bill amends federal energy law to officially recognize insulation on mechanical systems, such as pipes, ducts, and heating or cooling equipment, as an approved energy or water efficiency measure. It adds a definition requiring the insulation to meet industry standards set by ASHRAE and to reduce energy loss. It also requires federal agencies to specifically evaluate this insulation as an option during their regular building energy and water assessments.

title: ASCEND Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the ASCEND Act, directs NASA to formally establish a program that buys satellite images and data about Earth from private companies. NASA already does this on a smaller scale through a pilot program started in 2019, which officials say has been successful. This bill would make that effort permanent and expand it, requiring NASA to acquire commercial satellite data to support scientific research, agency operations, and educational programs.

The bill sets several rules for how this program must work. NASA must try to buy this data from U.S.-based companies whenever practical. It also requires that licensing agreements with vendors not block scientists from publishing research based on the purchased data or images. Additionally, NASA must set license terms that allow the data to be used as widely as possible, not just by NASA-funded researchers. NASA would also be required to submit an annual report to Congress listing which companies are providing data, describing the licensing terms, and explaining how the data supports scientific priorities.

This bill mainly affects NASA, commercial satellite and remote-sensing companies (particularly U.S. firms), and scientific researchers who rely on satellite imagery for things like climate studies, disaster response, and environmental monitoring. It could benefit American satellite companies by increasing government business, and it could help researchers and other federal agencies gain broader access to useful Earth-observation data. Everyday residents would likely see indirect effects, such as improved weather forecasting, environmental tracking, or disaster response tools that rely on this data.
ai_headline: Bill would make NASA's commercial satellite data program permanent

title: To reauthorize the Integrated Coastal and Ocean Observation System Act of 2009.
ai_summary:
**HR 2294** renews and updates a law from 2009 that supports the U.S. system for monitoring America's coasts and oceans, called the Integrated Coastal and Ocean Observation System. This system collects data on things like water temperature, currents, weather, and sea conditions, which is used for weather forecasting, fishing, shipping safety, disaster preparedness, and environmental research. The bill continues funding for this program, setting the budget at $56 million per year from 2026 through 2030.

The bill also makes some organizational changes, such as renaming a coordinating body from the "National Ocean Research Leadership Council" to the "Ocean Policy Committee," and updating references throughout the law to match. It adds new requirements for federal agencies involved in ocean observation to work more closely with regional coastal monitoring programs, making sure data is shared effectively at the local and regional level. It also clarifies that the program should support actual ocean measurement activities, not just research planning.

This bill mainly affects government agencies like NOAA that run ocean and coastal monitoring programs, along with the scientists, regional organizations, and local governments that rely on this data. Indirectly, it affects everyday people who benefit from accurate weather forecasts, hurricane tracking, water safety information, and fisheries management, since this data collection system feeds into many of those public services.

title: Home School Graduation Recognition Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Home School Graduation Recognition Act, would change federal education law to officially count homeschool students as "high school graduates" once they finish their secondary education. Specifically, it amends the Higher Education Act of 1965, which governs rules for federal student aid and college admissions eligibility. Under current law, students who don't have a traditional diploma sometimes have to go through extra steps, like taking an "ability to benefit" test, to prove they're qualified for federal financial aid. This bill would clarify that homeschool graduates don't need to jump through those extra hoops, as long as their homeschooling was conducted in a way that's recognized as a home school or private school under their state's laws.

In practical terms, this affects families who educate their children at home and students who plan to apply for federal student aid, such as Pell Grants or student loans, after finishing homeschool. It would make the process more straightforward for them, treating their homeschool completion the same way a traditional high school diploma is treated for financial aid eligibility purposes. It would also affect colleges and universities, which rely on these federal definitions when determining whether an applicant meets basic eligibility requirements for aid programs. States would still control how homeschooling is defined and regulated, since the bill relies on each state's existing legal definition of homeschooling or private schooling.
ai_headline: Bill would count homeschool completion as diploma for federal aid rules

title: EBSA Investigations Transparency Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require the Employee Benefit Security Administration (EBSA), the federal agency that oversees employer-sponsored retirement and health benefit plans, to send Congress a yearly report on its investigations. EBSA enforces rules under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA), the main law protecting workers' pensions and benefit plans. Under this bill, the agency would have to disclose details about each investigation it opens, such as which regional office handled it, when it started, when the agency first asked the target for documents, and whether the case was wrapped up within three years of that document request. If an investigation drags on longer than three years, EBSA would have to explain why and give an estimated finish date.

The bill also protects privacy by requiring that the report not name any individual companies, plan sponsors, employees, or other parties under investigation. It clarifies that if the focus of an investigation shifts over time, that's still considered one continuing case rather than several separate ones, so the timeline tracking stays accurate.

This bill mainly affects how EBSA operates and reports its work to Congress, rather than changing any rules for workers or employers directly. It would primarily impact the agency's internal recordkeeping and reporting duties. Businesses, retirement plan administrators, and employee benefit plan sponsors who are sometimes investigated by EBSA could see more public accountability and transparency about how long investigations take, without their specific identities being revealed. Everyday workers and retirees who rely on pension or health benefit plans wouldn't experience direct changes, but they could benefit indirectly if increased transparency leads to faster, more efficient enforcement of the laws that protect their benefits.
ai_headline: Bill would require yearly reports on benefit plan investigations
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 418.

title: ASCEND Act
ai_summary:

The bill requires that any commercial data NASA buys can still be published and shared for scientific purposes, meaning companies can't use contract terms to block researchers from releasing findings based on that data. It also says NASA should, whenever practical, buy this satellite data from U.S.-based companies rather than foreign vendors, and should try to make the data available not just to NASA-funded researchers but to other users as well. Finally, NASA would have to report to Congress every year on which companies it's working with, what the licensing terms are, and how the data is being used for research.

This mainly affects NASA, commercial satellite and remote-sensing companies (who could gain new government contracts), and scientific researchers, universities, and other federal agencies that rely on Earth-observation data for things like climate research, weather forecasting, disaster response, and environmental monitoring. Everyday Americans could see indirect benefits through improved scientific research, environmental tracking, and potentially business opportunities for U.S. satellite companies.

title: ACERO Act
ai_summary:
HR 390, called the ACERO Act, directs NASA to continue and expand a research program aimed at improving how firefighting aircraft and drones respond to wildfires. NASA would work on better technology for managing airspace during wildfire responses, sharing real-time data among response teams, creating a shared system so agencies can track aerial firefighting equipment, and building a coordinated plan involving federal, state, and local agencies so different groups can work together smoothly during a fire.

The bill also says NASA generally cannot buy drones made by certain foreign companies (specifically those flagged as national security concerns under existing law) for this program, though the NASA Administrator can approve exceptions if it's in the national interest and needed specifically to fight wildfires, as long as Congress is notified. NASA would have to report to Congress every year through 2030 on how the program is going, including whether it's actually helping prevent injuries, save lives, protect property, and reduce damage from wildfires. The bill authorizes $15 million for this work in fiscal year 2026.

This bill mainly affects NASA, federal wildfire response agencies, and state and local firefighting organizations that coordinate aerial operations during wildfires. Indirectly, it could affect people living in wildfire-prone areas, since the goal is to make aerial firefighting faster, safer, and better coordinated. It does not create new firefighting agencies or change how wildfires are fought on the ground; it focuses on research, technology, and coordination for aircraft and drones used in wildfire response.

title: Small Business Artificial Intelligence Advancement Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to create helpful materials for small businesses about using artificial intelligence. These resources could include technical standards, best practices, guides, and real-world case studies showing how businesses of different sizes and types have used AI successfully. The goal is to help small business owners better understand AI, figure out good ways to use it, and adopt it if they choose to.

The bill sets rules for how these resources should be designed: they must be usable by many different kinds of small businesses, avoid favoring specific technology brands, align with existing international standards, and connect to other federal resources like cybersecurity education programs. NIST would need to review and update these materials at least every two years to keep them current as AI technology changes. NIST would also work with the Small Business Administration to actually get these materials out to small business owners through SBA's existing network of support offices.

This bill mainly affects small business owners, who would gain access to free government guidance on AI, and NIST, which would take on new responsibilities to create and maintain this material. Use of the resources is completely voluntary—no business would be required to follow them. After four years, NIST must report back to Congress on how the program is going, including feedback from businesses that used the resources and suggestions for further action.

title: PIPES Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 5301, the PIPES Act of 2025, updates the federal law that governs pipeline safety. It reauthorizes funding for the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA), the federal agency that inspects and regulates oil, gas, and hazardous liquid pipelines, setting specific budget levels through 2029 for inspections, state safety grants, emergency response, and a new grant program to help publicly-owned natural gas utilities (cities, counties, and tribal governments) repair or replace old, leak-prone pipelines. It also expands PHMSA's authority to cover carbon dioxide pipelines, which are increasingly used for carbon capture projects, applying similar safety rules to them as apply to oil and gas pipelines.

The bill makes many procedural changes aimed at speeding up and improving how pipeline regulations are written and enforced. It requires PHMSA to report regularly on overdue safety rules, update industry safety standards more consistently, publish clearer inspection priorities, and create an "Office of Public Engagement" to communicate with communities near pipelines. It also directs new government studies on topics like using composite materials for hydrogen pipelines, blending hydrogen into natural gas systems, geological hazards (like landslides or floods) affecting pipelines, and the effectiveness of current safety programs. Excavation/damage-prevention rules are strengthened, requiring states to adopt "best practices" for utility locating services (like calling 811 before digging) to reduce accidental pipeline damage.

Finally, the bill increases penalties for people who intentionally damage pipeline equipment or tamper with valves, raises the maximum civil fine for safety violations, and creates working groups to better coordinate oversight of liquefied natural gas (LNG) facilities between different federal agencies. Overall, this bill affects pipeline operators (energy companies), state regulators, local governments and utilities that own gas systems, construction and excavation companies, and indirectly, everyday consumers who rely on safe delivery of natural gas, oil, and emerging carbon-capture pipelines. It does not ban or promote any particular energy source but focuses on modernizing safety oversight, funding, and enforcement across the pipeline industry.

title: Reorganizing Government Act of 2025
ai_summary:
**H.R. 1295 — Reorganizing Government Act of 2025**

This bill brings back a power the President used to have but lost decades ago: the authority to submit "reorganization plans" to Congress that restructure federal agencies. Under this authority, the President could propose merging, eliminating, or restructuring parts of the executive branch, including cutting the number of federal employees, eliminating rules and regulations seen as burdensome, and shutting down government programs or offices deemed unnecessary. These plans would take effect unless Congress votes to block them, which is a faster process than passing new laws through normal legislative steps. The bill also updates the deadline for using this authority to the end of 2026 and broadens the definition of what counts as an "executive department" covered by these powers, while excluding the Government Accountability Office.

Notably, the bill removes an old restriction that prevented the President from abolishing agencies' enforcement functions or statutory programs through this process, but it also adds a new limit: any reorganization plan cannot result in a net increase in federal employees or spending, meaning plans must shrink or keep government the same size, not grow it.

This bill would primarily affect federal employees, whose jobs and agencies could be reorganized, merged, or eliminated, as well as the general public, who interact with federal agencies for services, regulations, and enforcement (such as environmental rules, consumer protections, or program benefits). It also shifts power between the President and Congress, giving the executive branch more direct ability to restructure government operations with reduced congressional pushback, since lawmakers would only be able to block plans rather than needing to actively approve new legislation for each change.
ai_headline: Bill would restore presidential power to reorganize federal agencies
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 397.

title: Tipped Employee Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change how the federal Fair Labor Standards Act defines a "tipped employee," which affects how workers like servers, bartenders, and other tip-earning employees are paid. Under current law, someone counts as a "tipped employee" if their job is the type where they customarily and regularly earn more than $30 a month in tips. This bill removes that focus on job duties and instead says a worker qualifies as tipped if their tips plus the required cash wage from their employer add up to at least the federal minimum wage, measured over a time period the employer chooses (a day, a week, two weeks, a pay period, or a month).

In practice, this means employers could classify more employees as "tipped," including people whose main job duties aren't traditionally tip-based, as long as their combined tips and wages meet minimum wage over the chosen period. It also gives employers flexibility in choosing shorter or longer tracking periods to determine whether workers are earning enough through tips to qualify for the lower "tipped" cash wage rate, rather than the standard minimum wage.

This bill would primarily affect workers in industries where tipping is common—restaurants, bars, salons, and similar service jobs—as well as the business owners who employ them. Workers' pay calculations and employer payroll practices could change depending on how employers choose to apply the new rules, and how tips are tracked and averaged could affect whether a worker earns at least minimum wage overall.
ai_headline: Bill would redefine "tipped employee" based on pay, not job type

title: Home Appliance Protection and Affordability Act
ai_summary:
This bill, nicknamed the "Don't Mess With My Home Appliances Act," would change how the Department of Energy sets energy efficiency rules for home appliances like refrigerators, water heaters, and washing machines. It adds stricter requirements the Secretary of Energy must meet before creating or updating any efficiency standard: the standard must be technologically feasible, must not raise net costs for consumers, must achieve meaningful energy or water savings (specific minimum thresholds are set), must not hurt product performance or market competition, and cannot be justified using estimates of climate-related costs or benefits. It also requires the Department to publicly disclose meetings with certain groups tied to foreign entities like China when developing these rules.

The bill also makes it easier for outside parties to petition the government to weaken or cancel existing efficiency standards, and requires the Department to review new standards within two years to check if they still meet these tougher criteria—if not, the standard would stop being enforced. Separately, it permanently bans the Department from creating any new or updated efficiency standards for "distribution transformers" (equipment used in the electric grid to change voltage levels), though existing rules for other equipment would remain in place.

This bill would primarily affect appliance manufacturers, utility companies, and the Department of Energy's regulatory process. Consumers could be affected indirectly: supporters might argue it prevents rules that raise appliance prices, while critics might argue it could slow future improvements in energy and water efficiency. The changes would also affect environmental advocacy groups and industry groups that engage in the rulemaking process, since new disclosure and petition rules change how those rules get made and challenged.
ai_headline: Bill would tighten rules for setting home appliance efficiency standards
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

title: La Paz County Solar Energy and Job Creation Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Secretary of the Interior to transfer about 3,400 acres of federal land in La Paz County, Arizona, currently managed by the Bureau of Land Management, over to the county government. The transfer would happen after the county formally requests it, and the goal is to open up the land for uses like solar energy development, which supporters expect could create local jobs. The land would be shown on a specific BLM map, and any small errors in that map's boundaries or acreage could later be corrected by mutual agreement between the county and the Secretary.

The bill includes several conditions on the transfer. The county must pay the full fair market value of the land, based on a professional appraisal, plus all costs associated with the transfer such as surveys and administrative fees. Any land containing important cultural, environmental, wildlife, or recreational resources would be excluded from the deal. The land would also be off-limits to mining and mineral leasing. To protect Native American heritage, the county and any future landowners must make good-faith efforts to avoid disturbing tribal artifacts, work with the Colorado River Indian Tribes' historic preservation office, and allow tribal representatives to rebury any artifacts that are uncovered.

This bill mainly affects residents and officials of La Paz County, Arizona, who would gain control over this land for local development purposes, potentially including solar energy projects. It also affects the Bureau of Land Management, which currently oversees the land, and the Colorado River Indian Tribes, who have a formal role in protecting cultural sites during any future development. More broadly, it could interest people following federal land-use policy, renewable energy development, and tribal cultural preservation issues, since the money from the sale would go into a federal fund used for other land management purposes rather than general government spending.

title: Protecting Prudent Investment of Retirement Savings Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal rules that govern how 401(k) plans and other employer-sponsored retirement plans are managed, specifically the responsibilities of the "fiduciaries" who oversee these plans. The most significant part requires that investment decisions be based mainly on financial factors like risk and return, not on other considerations (such as environmental, social, or governance goals), unless a fiduciary can show that purely financial factors weren't enough to distinguish between investment choices, and documents why the non-financial factor was used. It also bars retirement plans from choosing investment managers, advisors, or service providers based on race, sex, religion, or similar characteristics, requiring those decisions to be based on qualifications and cost instead.

The bill also addresses how plan managers vote on shareholder matters (called "proxy voting") for stocks held in retirement accounts. It says these votes must be based on what's financially best for retirement savers, and it creates "safe harbor" rules letting fiduciaries skip voting on certain proposals without it being seen as neglecting their duties, especially when the plan's investment in that company is small. Finally, the bill requires extra warnings for people who use "brokerage windows"—optional features in some retirement plans that let individuals pick their own investments beyond the standard menu. Before using these accounts, savers would have to see a notice explaining that these investments aren't vetted by the plan's professional overseers and could carry more risk, along with a chart showing how different investment returns could affect their retirement savings by age 67.

This bill would primarily affect people who have 401(k)-style retirement plans through their employers, the companies that manage those plans, and financial advisors or investment firms that help make investment decisions for them. Supporters and critics have different views on how these changes would affect investment options and retirement outcomes, but the bill itself is focused on setting clearer legal standards for how retirement plan managers must operate.

title: Rural Housing Service Reform Act of 2025
ai_summary:
S. 1260, the Rural Housing Service Reform Act of 2025, updates and expands programs run by the U.S. Department of Agriculture that help people in rural areas buy, keep, or improve their homes. It makes several technical fixes, such as applying standard foreclosure rules to USDA-held multifamily properties while protecting rental assistance for tenants during foreclosure, funding IT and staffing upgrades, and requiring studies and reports on loan performance and outdated agency technology. It also makes permanent a program that lets the USDA restructure loans on aging rural apartment buildings (through reduced interest, deferred payments, or debt adjustments) so they can stay affordable, and requires landlords and tenants to get advance notice when a property's loan is about to mature so residents aren't caught off guard.

The bill also creates a new lending program that sets aside federal mortgage funds for Native-owned Community Development Financial Institutions, aiming to boost homeownership in Tribal and Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian communities. It raises the loan/grant limit for minor home repairs under the Section 504 program from $7,500 to $15,000, reserves more of that money for very low-income applicants, and creates a new "Rural Community Development Initiative" grant program to help nonprofits and Tribes build local housing and community development capacity. It extends allowable rural home loan terms to up to 40 years, makes it easier to transfer a loan when a home is sold, allows accessory dwelling units (like small in-law units) to count toward loan eligibility, and removes restrictions that discourage licensed home-based child care businesses from getting rural housing loans.

Overall, this bill mainly affects rural homeowners, renters, landlords of USDA-financed apartment buildings, nonprofit housing organizations, Native American communities, and the USDA's Rural Housing Service itself. It does not create major new entitlements but rather updates existing rural housing finance rules, adds consumer protections (like notice requirements and housing vouchers for displaced tenants), and directs more oversight and reporting to Congress on how well these programs are working.
ai_headline: Bill overhauls USDA rural housing loans, aid for tribes and repairs

title: Empowering Employer Child and Elder Care Solutions Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change how overtime pay is calculated under the Fair Labor Standards Act, the main federal law governing minimum wage and overtime rules. Currently, when an employer's regular rate of pay is calculated for overtime purposes, certain benefits must be included in that calculation. This bill would allow employers to exclude the value of child care and dependent care services or payments they provide to employees from that overtime rate calculation. In other words, if an employer offers benefits like on-site child care, daycare subsidies, or help paying for elder care, the value of those benefits would not count toward figuring out an employee's overtime pay rate.

The practical effect is that employers could offer these caregiving benefits without it increasing the overtime rate they owe workers who work more than 40 hours a week. Supporters would argue this removes a disincentive for businesses to offer child and elder care assistance, since currently doing so can raise their overtime costs. Critics might see it as reducing the amount some hourly workers receive in overtime pay, since caregiving benefits would no longer factor into the base rate used for those calculations.

This bill mainly affects hourly and non-exempt workers who work overtime and whose employers provide child care or dependent (elder) care benefits, as well as businesses deciding whether to offer such benefits. It would take effect for workweeks starting after the bill becomes law, if passed.
ai_headline: Bill would exclude child care benefits from overtime pay formula

title: National STEM Week Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates an official "National STEM Week," a yearly designated week meant to draw attention to science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) education across the country. A federal government body called CoSTEM, which coordinates STEM policy across agencies, would pick the specific week each year and work with schools, families, and businesses to organize activities. The goal is to highlight STEM career paths, encourage families to do STEM activities at home, and connect students with mentors and real-world experiences through partnerships with companies and industry leaders.

The bill does not create new funding programs or require schools to participate—it mainly encourages voluntary involvement from schools, students, families, and businesses. Schools (elementary, secondary, and colleges), STEM-related industries, and communities—especially those in rural, urban, and underserved areas—are the main groups affected, since the bill emphasizes closing gaps in STEM access and opportunity. CoSTEM would also be required to report to Congress each year on how National STEM Week is going and whether it's helping improve STEM education and reduce disparities.

Overall, this is a largely symbolic and coordinating measure rather than one that changes laws, provides new money, or imposes mandates. Its main effect would be to formally recognize a national week for promoting STEM awareness and encouraging cooperation between schools, families, and industry.
ai_headline: Bill would establish annual National STEM Week to boost awareness

title: Mining Regulatory Clarity Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes federal mining law to clarify how companies can use nearby public land to support their mining operations. Under current law, mining companies that hold a mining claim (called a "lode" or "placer" claim) can also claim a small separate piece of land, called a "mill site," to use for things like storing waste rock or processing ore. This bill allows companies to claim multiple mill sites—not just one—as long as they are reasonably needed for the approved mining operation. Each mill site is capped at 5 acres, and claiming a mill site does not give the company any mineral rights or ownership of minerals on that land, and it cannot be turned into private property through a "patent" process. The bill also makes clear that these changes do not override existing environmental and land-protection laws, such as the Endangered Species Act, the Wilderness Act, and historic preservation laws.

The bill also creates a new government fund called the "Abandoned Hardrock Mine Fund." Money that mining companies already pay as required annual fees to maintain these new mill site claims would go into this fund. That money would then be used to help clean up and reclaim old, abandoned hardrock mines (like abandoned gold, silver, or copper mines) under an existing federal cleanup program, without needing Congress to approve new spending each time.

This bill mainly affects mining companies, particularly those operating hardrock mines (metals and minerals, not coal or oil) on federal public lands, especially in Western states like Nevada. It also affects federal land management agencies, such as the Department of the Interior and the Forest Service, which oversee these mining claims. Indirectly, it affects communities near abandoned mine sites, since more funding could become available for environmental cleanup of hazardous abandoned mines.
ai_headline: Bill would let mining firms claim multiple 5-acre mill sites for waste and ore
last_action_text: Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 357.

It also creates an "Abandoned Hardrock Mine Fund" funded by companies' required annual fees for these claims, to be used for cleanup of old abandoned mines without new congressional approval each time.

title: To amend the Grand Ronde Reservation Act to address the hunting, fishing, trapping, and animal gathering rights of the Confederated Tribes of the Grand Ronde Community, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
HR 1499 updates a 1988 law called the Grand Ronde Reservation Act, which governs the hunting, fishing, trapping, and gathering rights of the Confederated Tribes of the Grand Ronde Community, a Native American tribe in Oregon. The bill keeps in place a 1986 agreement between the tribe, the state of Oregon, and the federal government that spells out these rights, and says that agreement stays valid unless the tribe and the state jointly agree to replace or change it. Any future updates would have to be agreed to by both the tribe and the state.

The bill also sets rules for what those future agreements can and cannot do. They cannot be used to expand, limit, or otherwise affect the tribe's (or any other tribe's) broader treaty or legal rights, and they cannot stop Oregon from making separate deals with other tribes. It clarifies that any hunting and fishing rights created under a new agreement would come from Oregon state authority, not from tribal treaty rights. Additionally, it directs a federal court in Oregon, if asked to review or change a related 1987 legal decree, to consider the case on its actual facts rather than automatically dismissing it based on prior rulings.

This bill mainly affects the Confederated Tribes of the Grand Ronde Community, the state of Oregon, and federal courts handling related disputes. It does not create new rights but instead clarifies and preserves the legal framework already in place, while making sure any future changes go through a formal agreement process and don't get tangled up with other tribes' separate legal claims.
ai_headline: Bill preserves Grand Ronde tribe's 1986 hunting and fishing rights deal
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.

title: Solid American Hardwood Tax Credit Act
ai_summary:
**S. 1964 — Solid American Hardwood Tax Credit Act**

This bill would change an existing federal tax credit that homeowners can currently claim for energy-efficient home improvements (like insulation, windows, or efficient furnaces). It would add a new category to that credit for what it calls "natural carbon sinks" — specifically, hardwood flooring, paneling, cabinetry, window frames, and similar wood products made from deciduous trees (like oak or maple) that are grown and processed in the United States. Homeowners installing these American hardwood products in their primary residence could claim a tax credit, similar to how they currently get credits for things like energy-efficient windows. The bill would also extend this overall home improvement tax credit program, which is currently set to expire in 2032, out to 2035.

This mainly affects homeowners who make qualifying home improvements using domestic hardwood products, potentially lowering their tax bills, and it likely benefits the U.S. hardwood lumber industry by encouraging demand for American-grown wood. Separately, the bill ends a different, unrelated tax benefit: an increased tax credit for companies that build carbon capture equipment (technology that traps carbon dioxide from industrial sources) after the bill becomes law. This would affect energy and industrial companies that had been planning to use that stronger incentive, effectively making it less profitable to build new carbon capture projects going forward.
ai_headline: Tax credit bill would reward American hardwood use in homes through 2035
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

Separately, it ends an increased tax credit for companies building carbon capture equipment after enactment.

title: DO NOT Call Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the DO NOT Call Act, would toughen the penalties for people and companies that make illegal robocalls or robotexts under existing federal telephone consumer protection law. Currently, violations of this law are mostly handled through civil fines. This bill would add criminal penalties: someone who willfully and knowingly breaks the robocall rules could face up to 1 year in prison, a fine, or both. If the violation is especially serious—such as making huge volumes of calls (over 100,000 in a day, 1 million in a month, or 10 million in a year), using the calls to help commit a felony, causing at least $5,000 in losses to victims, or having a prior conviction for the same offense—the penalty could increase to up to 3 years in prison.

The bill also raises the fines for "spoofing," which is when someone fakes or falsifies caller ID information to trick people into answering or trusting a call. The maximum fine for this would double, from $10,000 to $20,000 per violation.

This bill would primarily affect telemarketers, scam callers, and companies that use automated dialing systems or prerecorded messages to contact people without permission. Everyday phone and text message users would benefit indirectly, since the stronger penalties are meant to discourage illegal robocalls, robotexts, and caller ID spoofing scams that many people receive regularly. Legitimate businesses that follow existing consumer consent rules would not be affected, but those that knowingly break the rules could face more serious legal consequences than before.
ai_headline: Bill would add prison time for illegal robocalls and caller ID spoofing
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

It also doubles the maximum spoofing fine from $10,000 to $20,000 per violation.

title: Homeowner Energy Freedom Act
ai_summary:
HR 4758, the "Homeowner Energy Freedom Act," would cancel several federal programs created by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act (Public Law 117-169) that help homeowners pay for energy-efficient home upgrades. Specifically, it would eliminate the High-Efficiency Electric Home Rebate Program, which gave rebates to households buying electric appliances like heat pumps, electric stoves, or upgraded electrical panels. It would also end grants that helped states train contractors to install energy-efficient equipment, and grants that helped states and local governments adopt updated, more energy-efficient building codes. Any money set aside for these programs that hasn't already been spent would be taken back and no longer available.

This bill would primarily affect homeowners who might have used these rebates to lower the cost of switching to electric appliances or making energy-efficient home improvements, as well as contractors and state agencies that received training or planning funds tied to these programs. Supporters of repealing these programs generally argue that the government shouldn't subsidize private home upgrades and that homeowners should make their own energy choices without federal involvement. Those who support keeping the programs argue they help reduce household energy costs, cut pollution, and support jobs in the clean energy and construction industries. The bill has been introduced and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, meaning it would need committee approval, a full House vote, Senate approval, and the President's signature before becoming law.
ai_headline: Bill would end federal rebates for energy-efficient home upgrades
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

title: Department of the Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, H.R. 4754, sets the federal budget for the Department of the Interior and several related agencies for the fiscal year starting October 2025. It provides funding for a wide range of government activities, including managing public lands (through the Bureau of Land Management), protecting wildlife and endangered species (Fish and Wildlife Service), running national parks (National Park Service), conducting scientific research on water, geology, and natural resources (U.S. Geological Survey), and overseeing offshore oil and gas drilling safety (Bureau of Ocean Energy Management and Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement). It also funds coal mine cleanup programs, historic preservation grants, and wildfire prevention and firefighting efforts across federal lands.

A large portion of the bill funds programs for Native American communities, including the Bureau of Indian Affairs and Bureau of Indian Education, covering schools, housing, road maintenance, law enforcement, and trust fund management for tribal lands and resources. It also includes money for U.S. territories like Guam, American Samoa, and the U.S. Virgin Islands, as well as support for Pacific Island nations connected to the U.S. through the Compact of Free Association.

This bill affects a broad range of people: park visitors, hunters and anglers who benefit from wildlife programs, communities near coal mines or oil rigs, Native American tribes and students in tribal schools, residents of U.S. territories, historic preservation groups, and federal employees in these agencies. It also indirectly affects anyone concerned about public lands, environmental protection, wildfire response, or natural resource management, since it determines how much money these programs receive and how they can be used for the coming year.

title: SAFE Sunscreen Standards Act
ai_summary:
HR 3686, the SAFE Sunscreen Standards Act, aims to change how the FDA reviews and approves new sunscreen ingredients. Currently, no new sunscreen active ingredients have been approved in the U.S. since 1999, even though other countries use ingredients that American regulators haven't cleared. This bill directs the FDA to create updated standards for judging whether sunscreen ingredients are safe and effective. Notably, it allows the agency to accept "real-world evidence," observational studies, and other scientific approaches instead of relying only on traditional clinical trials. It also pushes the FDA to consider non-animal testing methods, such as lab-based or computer modeling techniques, as alternatives to animal testing, and requires the agency to issue guidance on this within 180 days of the law passing.

The bill also addresses a pending FDA order about sunscreen ingredients that has been stalled for years, requiring the agency to factor in historical safety data for ingredients already used in sunscreens sold in the U.S., and to acknowledge that sunscreen helps prevent skin cancer. Finally, it requires HHS to report annually to Congress on how these new evidence standards are being applied and on progress toward reducing animal testing, with those reports made public on the FDA's website.

This bill would primarily affect sunscreen manufacturers, who may find it easier to get new ingredients approved, and consumers, who could eventually have access to more sunscreen products already sold in Europe, Asia, or elsewhere. It could also affect animal testing practices and how quickly new sun-protection technology reaches store shelves. The bill's supporters cite rising skin cancer rates and an outdated approval process as reasons for the changes, though it does not itself approve any specific new ingredient—it changes the process by which future decisions get made.
ai_headline: Bill would ease FDA rules for approving new sunscreen ingredients
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: RIDE Act
ai_summary:
The RIDE Act would create a brand-new type of temporary work visa, called P-4, specifically for people who work in traveling entertainment businesses like carnivals and circuses. This would cover workers who set up, run, take down, and maintain rides, games, and food or drink booths at fairs, festivals, and similar traveling events. Employers would only be allowed to hire these foreign workers after the Department of Labor certifies that there aren't enough available U.S. workers to fill the jobs and that hiring foreign workers won't hurt the pay or working conditions of American employees doing similar work.

The bill also allows spouses and children of these visa holders to come to the U.S. along with them. After the bill becomes law, the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Labor would have 180 days to propose official rules for how this new visa program works, and one year to finalize those rules.

This bill mainly affects owners and operators of traveling carnivals, circuses, and fair-related food or game concession businesses, who often struggle to find enough seasonal workers. It would also affect foreign workers seeking short-term U.S. jobs in this industry, and indirectly it could affect U.S. workers in the same field, since the law requires protections to ensure American workers aren't undercut on wages or job availability.

title: Skin Substitute Access and Payment Reform Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how Medicare pays doctors and hospitals for "skin substitute products," which are special materials (made from human tissue, animal tissue, or synthetic materials) placed on wounds to help them heal, often used for diabetic ulcers, burns, or other hard-to-heal injuries. Currently, these products are paid for in a way that has led to huge price differences and, according to critics, has invited overbilling. Starting in 2026, the bill would set a single, standardized payment rate based on an average of 2023 prices, which would then increase each year based on inflation. It also creates one billing code for all these products instead of the many different codes currently used, and requires patients to pay their normal 20% share based on this new standard rate.

The bill also tries to crack down on potential fraud or abuse. Starting in 2025, Medicare would identify the top 3% of providers who bill the most for these products and refer them to government investigators. These "outlier" providers would face extra scrutiny, such as having their claims reviewed before payment or needing prior approval before using these products, unless they show a strong track record of legitimate, approved claims. If a provider's prior-approval requests are denied more than 75% of the time for six months or more, Medicare would treat that as a sign of abuse and could refer the provider for removal from federal health programs. At the same time, the bill protects legitimate use of these products in 2026 by preventing Medicare from denying coverage for a specific product based only on a review of clinical research, unless there's evidence the product is unsafe.

This bill mainly affects Medicare patients with chronic wounds, the doctors and wound-care clinics that use skin substitute products, and the manufacturers who make them. Patients could see changes in out-of-pocket costs, providers will face new billing rules and possible audits, and companies selling these products will operate under a new standardized payment system instead of the current system, which has allowed wide price variation.

title: Rural Hospital Closure Relief Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would make it easier for certain struggling rural hospitals to qualify for special Medicare status as "critical access hospitals," which comes with better payment rates from Medicare. Normally, hospitals must be located more than 35 miles from another hospital to qualify. This bill lets states waive that distance rule for hospitals that meet other criteria, such as being in a high-poverty area, a health-shortage area, or serving a large share of Medicare patients, and that have lost money for two years in a row. To qualify, a hospital would also have to submit a financial recovery plan and commit to adding or expanding a needed service, like maternity care or mental health care.

The program would be capped at 120 hospitals nationwide, with no more than 5 per state, and it would expire after 9 years. Hospitals that get this special status would have to report on their progress and could lose the designation if they don't. The bill also directs government watchdogs (GAO and MedPAC) to study how well this is working and to eventually recommend better long-term payment systems for rural hospitals. Separately, it adjusts bed-limit rules for hospitals in Guam, American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands, and the U.S. Virgin Islands, giving them more flexibility than the standard 25-bed limit.

This mainly affects rural communities at risk of losing their local hospital, since it gives those hospitals a financial lifeline through higher Medicare payments. It also affects Medicare, since expanding the number of critical access hospitals could increase program spending, which is why the bill requires studies on the cost and effectiveness of the change.

title: Unlock American Energy and Jobs Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Unlock American Energy and Jobs Act of 2026, changes several federal laws to speed up approval of energy projects like pipelines, power lines, LNG (liquefied natural gas) terminals, and nuclear power plants. It rewrites the water pollution permitting process (Clean Water Act Sections 401 and 404) so that states must review and decide on permits within strict deadlines—generally no more than one year—and if they miss the deadline, the permit is automatically considered approved or the certification requirement is waived. It also limits what states can consider when denying permits, requires "clear and convincing evidence" for denials, extends how long general permits last (from 5 to 10 years), and makes it harder to legally challenge these decisions by setting short filing deadlines and requiring courts to rule quickly.

The bill also changes rules for natural gas and nuclear projects. For LNG export terminals, it removes the ability of regulators to consider environmental impacts under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) when deciding if a project serves the "public interest." For nuclear power, it extends reactor license terms from the current limits up to 60 years, makes site permits last indefinitely, and allows building new reactors at existing nuclear sites without a full environmental review. Separately, it rewrites the NEPA legal review process nationwide: courts can no longer cancel or block a project over environmental-review flaws (only send it back to the agency to fix within 180 days), lawsuits must be filed quickly and by people directly affected, and cases must be resolved faster.

This bill would primarily affect energy companies seeking permits for pipelines, power plants, LNG terminals, and nuclear facilities, making it easier and faster for them to get approvals. It would also affect state environmental agencies, which would face tighter deadlines and less discretion in reviewing projects. Environmental groups, tribes, and communities near these projects would have fewer opportunities and less time to challenge permits in court, while companies and workers in the energy sector could benefit from faster project approvals and reduced legal delays.

title: Equitable Access to School Facilities Act
ai_summary:
S. 1723, called the Equitable Access to School Facilities Act, is a bill focused on helping charter schools get better and more affordable buildings to operate in. It updates an existing federal education law (the Elementary and Secondary Education Act) to change how federal grant money is distributed to states for charter school facilities. It creates a competitive grant program where states can apply for federal funds to build or improve programs that help charter schools buy, lease, renovate, or maintain school buildings. States that make it easier for charter schools to access public buildings, get tax breaks, or buy surplus government property would get priority for this funding. The bill authorizes $100 million per year from 2026 through 2030 for this purpose.

The bill also adjusts existing rules about how charter school grant money can be used. It allows states to set aside up to 10% of certain funds to create loan programs that help new charter schools cover start-up costs or fix up their buildings. It reduces the required percentage of funds states must pass through to individual charter schools from 90% to 80%, giving states more flexibility to use money on broader support activities, like helping schools navigate local building codes or connecting them with facilities. It also expands the kind of technical assistance the federal government can provide, including help with charter school oversight, identifying best practices for schools in rural areas or serving students with disabilities, and supporting states that have recently passed pro-charter-school laws.

This bill would primarily affect charter schools (public schools run independently of traditional school districts), state education agencies that manage these federal grants, and by extension, students and families who attend or are considering charter schools, especially in low-income and rural areas. Traditional public school districts could also be affected if their state's policies increase charter schools' access to public buildings or surplus properties, since these are resources that districts may currently use themselves.
ai_headline: Bill offers $100 million a year to help charter schools secure buildings
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
