title: Jamie Reed Protecting Our Kids from Child Abuse Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Jamie Reed Protecting Our Kids from Child Abuse Act, would create a new federal legal pathway for people to sue over gender-transition medical care they received as minors. Specifically, it would let someone who received puberty blockers, hormone treatments, or gender-related surgery before turning 18 sue the clinic, hospital, university, or medical provider involved, if that care caused them physical or mental harm. People could file these lawsuits up to 30 years after turning 18, and could seek compensatory damages, punitive damages, and attorney's fees. Clinics or doctors could avoid liability only if they genuinely didn't know and had no reason to know the patient was a minor. The bill also cuts off federal funding to any clinic that provides these treatments to minors, and to any hospital or university connected to such a clinic.

The bill excludes certain situations from this liability, such as treatments for individuals with differences in sex development (sometimes called intersex traits), treatment of medical complications from a prior procedure, or emergency procedures needed to prevent death or serious bodily harm. Notably, the law would apply retroactively, meaning it could cover procedures performed even before the bill becomes law. This bill would primarily affect transgender minors and their families, pediatric gender clinics, doctors and other medical practitioners who provide this care, and hospitals or universities affiliated with such clinics. It does not change criminal law but creates a civil lawsuit option and a funding restriction, and it would need to pass the Senate, House, and be signed by the President to become law.
ai_headline: Bill would let patients sue over youth gender-transition care for decades
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

title: GLRI Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would extend funding for the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative (GLRI), a federal program that pays for projects to clean up pollution, restore wildlife habitats, and fight invasive species in the Great Lakes region. The GLRI has existed for years as part of the Clean Water Act, and Congress periodically needs to renew, or "reauthorize," its funding so the program can keep operating. This bill sets the funding level at $500 million per year for fiscal years 2027 through 2031, continuing support for the program beyond its current funding period.

In practical terms, the bill directs money toward efforts like reducing harmful algae blooms, cleaning up contaminated sites, restoring wetlands and fish populations, and controlling invasive species such as zebra mussels and Asian carp in and around the Great Lakes. These projects are carried out by federal agencies like the EPA, working alongside state governments, local communities, and tribes in the eight Great Lakes states: Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and New York.

This bill mainly affects residents of the Great Lakes region, including people who rely on the lakes for drinking water, fishing, tourism, and recreation. It also affects environmental agencies and organizations that receive federal grants for restoration work. Because the bill only reauthorizes and sets funding levels for an existing program, it does not create new regulations or agencies; it simply ensures the initiative can continue operating with a set budget for five more years, pending actual appropriations from Congress.

last_action_text: Committee on Environment and Public Works. Hearings held.

title: Ski Hill Resources for Economic Development Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the government handles fees collected from ski resorts that operate on National Forest land. Currently, ski areas pay rental fees to the U.S. Forest Service for using public land, and this bill sets up a special "Ski Area Fee Retention Account" so that money can be kept and reused by the Forest Service instead of simply going into the general federal treasury. Under the bill, 80% of fees collected at a specific ski area's national forest unit would stay there to fund things like permit processing, staff training, visitor services, wildfire risk reduction, trail and facility repairs, parking improvements, avalanche safety programs, and search-and-rescue operations. The remaining 20% would be distributed to other national forest units across the country for similar purposes.

The bill includes some safeguards. If a local forest unit doesn't need all its allotted money, the Forest Service can reduce the local share (but not below 60%) and send the extra funds elsewhere in the National Forest System. The money cannot be used for actually fighting wildfires or for buying new land. It's also meant to add to, not replace, the regular funding Congress already provides for these areas.

This bill would mainly affect ski resorts operating on national forest land, the U.S. Forest Service, and communities near ski areas that rely on nearby forest recreation infrastructure. Skiers and other forest visitors could benefit indirectly through better-maintained trails, roads, safety programs, and faster permit processing. Taxpayers would be affected in that these fees would stay within the Forest Service system rather than going to the general treasury, though the bill states this is meant to supplement, not replace, normal funding.
ai_headline: Bill would let ski resorts' forest fees stay with local Forest Service units

title: Mining Regulatory Clarity Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Mining Regulatory Clarity Act, changes federal mining law to clarify how companies that mine for hardrock minerals (like gold, silver, or copper) on public lands can use nearby land for waste disposal and other support activities. Under current law, mining companies can claim small parcels of land called "mill sites" to store waste rock, tailings, or other mining byproducts. This bill confirms that companies can claim multiple mill sites, not just one, as long as they are reasonably needed for the mining operation described in their approved plan of operations. Each mill site is capped at 5 acres, and claiming a mill site does not give the company any mineral rights or allow them to eventually gain full ownership (patent) of that land.

The bill includes several protections and clarifications: mill site claims cannot override existing environmental laws, wilderness protections, endangered species protections, or historic preservation rules, and they cannot restore mining rights on land that was previously closed off to mining. This is meant to settle legal uncertainty after a federal court ruling questioned whether companies could hold more than one mill site per mining claim.

The bill also creates a new government account called the Abandoned Hardrock Mine Fund. Money collected from required annual fees that companies pay to maintain these mill site claims will go into this fund, which will be used to help clean up and reclaim abandoned hardrock mines around the country, using rules already set up in a 2021 infrastructure law.

This bill mainly affects mining companies operating on federal public lands, particularly in Western states with significant hardrock mining activity like Nevada, Idaho, and Alaska. It also affects federal land management agencies (the Department of the Interior and the Forest Service), environmental and conservation groups concerned about mining's impact on public lands, and communities near abandoned mine sites that could benefit from cleanup funding. The bill's sponsors include senators from both parties representing mining-heavy states.

title: Maritime Fuel Tax Parity Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Maritime Fuel Tax Parity Act, would change federal tax law regarding fuel used by certain boats and ships. Currently, the tax code exempts some vessels from paying excise taxes on alternative motorboat fuels when that fuel is purchased as "supplies" for their vessel. However, this exemption has only applied to vessels traveling between different coasts (for example, from an Atlantic port to a Pacific port). The bill would expand this tax break to also cover vessels that only operate along a single coast, such as ships that only travel between different Atlantic ports or only between different Pacific ports, without crossing between the two coasts.

In practical terms, this means commercial vessel operators who run routes exclusively along one coastline (rather than coast-to-coast) would no longer have to pay this federal fuel excise tax, putting them on equal footing with vessels that travel between coasts. The bill would apply retroactively, covering fuel sales made after December 31, 2023, meaning affected companies could potentially seek refunds or credits for taxes already paid during that period. The people most affected would be businesses in the maritime shipping and boating industries, particularly those operating vessels along a single coast, as well as the federal government, which would collect less excise tax revenue as a result of this expanded exemption.
ai_headline: Fuel tax break would extend to single-coast ships, not just coast-to-coast
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

Currently only vessels traveling coast-to-coast qualify; this bill adds vessels operating solely along one coast, such as only between Atlantic ports or only between Pacific ports. title: National STEM Week Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a "National STEM Week," an annual designated week meant to highlight science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) education across the country. A federal science education committee (called CoSTEM) would be responsible for choosing the week each year and organizing activities around it. The goal is to raise awareness about STEM education, encourage schools to participate, get families involved in STEM activities at home, and build partnerships between schools and businesses so students can get mentorships, site visits, and guest lectures from industry professionals.

The bill doesn't create new funding programs or requirements for schools—it mainly encourages participation rather than mandating it. Schools, families, and businesses would be invited to take part voluntarily. States and local communities would also be encouraged to design their own STEM Week events suited to their needs, including in rural, urban, and underserved areas where access to STEM education can be more limited.

This would affect students and teachers at elementary schools, high schools, and colleges nationwide, as well as families and businesses that choose to participate. Each year, CoSTEM would report to Congress on how many schools and communities took part, whether the effort is helping close gaps in STEM education, and suggestions for improving future STEM Weeks. Overall, this bill is a promotional and organizational effort rather than one that changes funding, curriculum requirements, or school policy.

title: To repeal the Impoundment Control Act of 1974.
ai_summary:
This bill would completely eliminate the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, a law that currently governs how the president can handle money that Congress has approved for spending. Right now, if a president wants to delay or cancel spending that Congress has authorized (called "impoundment"), the law requires the president to formally notify Congress and get its approval before doing so. This system was created after disputes in the 1970s when President Nixon refused to spend money Congress had approved for certain programs, and Congress wanted to make sure it kept control over federal spending decisions.

If this bill became law, the president would no longer be required to ask Congress for permission before withholding or canceling approved federal funds. This would shift significant power over spending decisions from Congress to the executive branch. Supporters of repealing the law generally argue it would give the president more flexibility to manage the budget and cut what they see as wasteful spending. Critics generally argue it would weaken Congress's constitutional authority over the "power of the purse" and give the president too much unchecked control over how taxpayer money is actually spent.

This bill would affect anyone who relies on federal programs and funding, since it changes who ultimately decides whether approved money actually gets spent. It would also affect the balance of power between Congress and the president, a topic of ongoing debate regardless of which party controls the White House or Congress.
ai_headline: Bill would repeal 1974 law limiting president's spending power

title: Critical Mineral Consistency Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Critical Mineral Consistency Act of 2025, would change how the federal government defines "critical minerals" under an existing law, the Energy Act of 2020. Right now, two different federal agencies use somewhat different lists and definitions for materials considered essential to the economy and national security: the U.S. Geological Survey maintains a "critical minerals" list, while the Department of Energy maintains a separate "critical materials" list. This bill would fold the Department of Energy's "critical materials" into the official definition of "critical minerals," so the two lists become more consistent with each other.

Specifically, the bill requires that whenever the Secretary of Energy officially determines something to be a "critical material," that item must automatically be added to the broader critical minerals list within 45 days. This is meant to reduce confusion and duplication between agencies that currently classify materials differently for regulatory and funding purposes.

This bill mainly affects government agencies, mining and manufacturing companies, and businesses involved in supply chains for materials like rare earth elements, lithium, cobalt, and other substances used in electronics, batteries, defense equipment, and clean energy technology. By aligning definitions, companies may find it easier to know which materials qualify for federal support programs, permitting benefits, or supply chain initiatives tied to "critical mineral" status. It does not create new spending or programs itself, but it could expand which materials qualify for existing critical minerals policies and incentives.

last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 335.

It requires that whenever the Secretary of Energy designates something a "critical material," that item must automatically be added to the broader critical minerals list within 45 days, aligning the Department of Energy's list with the U.S. Geological Survey's separate list.

title: Territorial Student Access to Higher Education Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require certain U.S. public colleges and universities to charge students from Guam, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, American Samoa, and the U.S. Virgin Islands the same tuition rate they charge in-state residents, rather than the higher out-of-state or international rate. This would apply to any public school that receives federal funding under the Higher Education Act, which includes nearly all public colleges. To qualify, a student would need to be a resident of one of these territories and a U.S. national.

In practice, this means students from these Pacific and Caribbean territories could attend public universities anywhere in the United States and pay the lower, in-state tuition price instead of the much higher out-of-state price that non-residents typically face. Colleges that accept federal student aid money would be required to follow this rule as part of their standard participation agreements with the Department of Education.

This bill mainly affects residents of Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, American Samoa, and the U.S. Virgin Islands who want to pursue higher education at public universities on the U.S. mainland or in other states/territories, since many of these residents currently have limited local college options and would otherwise pay significantly more to study elsewhere. It would also affect public universities, which would need to adjust their tuition policies and billing systems to accommodate this new tuition category, and it could have a modest financial effect on state institutions if it changes how much tuition revenue they collect from these students.
ai_headline: Bill would give territory students in-state tuition nationwide

title: Wintergreen Emergency Egress Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Wintergreen Emergency Egress Act, would require the Secretary of the Interior to grant permission for a new emergency exit road to be built across National Park Service land along the Blue Ridge Parkway in Virginia, near the Wintergreen community. Currently, the law only says the Secretary "may" allow such a right-of-way, meaning it's optional. This bill would change that to "shall," making it mandatory once certain conditions are met.

Before the right-of-way could be issued, the Secretary would have to certify three things: that officials studied other possible escape routes that wouldn't cross federal land (including whether existing trails could be turned into roads), that they analyzed how wildfires might behave in that area, and that all required environmental and historic preservation reviews have been completed under existing federal laws.

This bill mainly affects residents of the Wintergreen area in Virginia, who have raised concerns about having only one main road in or out of their community, which could be dangerous during a wildfire or other emergency. It also affects the National Park Service, which manages the Blue Ridge Parkway land involved, and would need to follow the new process for evaluating and approving this specific emergency exit route near milepost 9.6.
ai_headline: Bill would require park service to approve Wintergreen escape road
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

It changes existing law from "may" allow the right-of-way to "shall," making approval mandatory once conditions are met. Before granting it, the Secretary must certify that alternative routes were studied, wildfire behavior was analyzed, and environmental and historic preservation reviews were completed.

title: Open RAN Outreach Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Open RAN Outreach Act, directs a federal official at the Department of Commerce, the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information, to help small phone and internet companies learn about a newer technology called Open RAN. Open RAN stands for "Open Radio Access Network," which is a way of building wireless networks using equipment from different manufacturers that can work together, instead of being locked into one company's proprietary system. The idea is that this approach can lower costs and increase flexibility for network providers.

Specifically, the bill requires this official, working through an office called the Office of Internet Connectivity and Growth, to do two things: educate small communications providers about the benefits and challenges of Open RAN and similar open-standard networks, and help these small providers understand how to apply for an existing federal grant program called the Wireless Supply Chain Innovation Grant Program, which was created by a 2021 defense law to support the development of alternative wireless network equipment.

This bill mainly affects small telecommunications and internet service providers, particularly those in rural or underserved areas that may lack the resources or technical knowledge to explore newer network technologies on their own. It does not create new funding or grants itself, but instead focuses on outreach, education, and helping smaller companies access support and programs that already exist. Larger telecom companies and consumers are not directly targeted, though improved competition and technology among small providers could eventually affect network options available to the public.
ai_headline: Bill directs Commerce Dept to help small carriers learn Open RAN tech
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

title: Dual Hatting Limitation Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Dual Hatting Limitation Act of 2026, would stop certain top federal officials from holding two important government jobs at the same time, a practice sometimes called "dual hatting." Specifically, it targets the heads of a few key agencies: the Office of Personnel Management (which manages federal employees), the Office of Special Counsel (which investigates federal whistleblower complaints and misconduct), the Office of Government Ethics (which oversees ethics rules for federal employees), and the National Archives. Under this bill, the person leading any of these agencies—whether permanently appointed or just temporarily filling in as "acting" head—could not also perform the duties of any other federal position at the same time.

The bill also changes the rules for filling vacant government positions more broadly. It says the President could not appoint someone to temporarily fill a vacant office if that person is already acting as the temporary head of a different office. Additionally, it applies this same one-job-at-a-time rule to all officials holding the very top-level government positions (known as "Level I" of the Executive Schedule, which includes cabinet secretaries and similar high-ranking roles).

This bill would primarily affect senior federal officials and the presidential administration's ability to manage staffing during leadership transitions or vacancies. It would limit the President's flexibility to have one trusted official temporarily oversee multiple agencies at once, a practice that has become more common in recent years when Senate confirmation of new appointees is delayed. Everyday citizens would not interact with this law directly, but it could affect how quickly government agencies get new permanent leaders and how federal agencies are run during leadership gaps.
ai_headline: Bill would bar top officials from holding two federal posts at once
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

title: American Music Tourism Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 617, the American Music Tourism Act of 2025, updates an existing law called the Visit America Act, which guides how the federal government promotes travel and tourism to and within the United States. The bill adds "music tourism" as an official focus area. This means the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Travel and Tourism, a government official who oversees national tourism promotion efforts, would now be specifically responsible for identifying music-related locations and events, such as historic music sites, museums, studios, concert venues, and festivals, and promoting travel to them for both domestic travelers (people traveling within the U.S.) and international visitors coming from other countries.

The bill also requires the Assistant Secretary to submit a report to Congress every two years describing progress made toward these tourism goals, including music tourism efforts. Additionally, it formally defines "music tourism" in federal law, covering both visiting music-related landmarks and attending live music events like concerts and festivals.

This bill mainly affects the federal tourism promotion office, state and local tourism boards, and businesses connected to the music and travel industries, such as venues, festivals, hotels, and local attractions tied to music history. Everyday travelers could see more organized federal promotion of music-related destinations, and communities with strong music heritage, such as cities known for jazz, country, blues, or rock history, could benefit from increased visibility and visitor interest. The bill does not create new funding programs; it mainly changes the responsibilities and reporting duties of an existing federal tourism office.
ai_headline: Bill would add music tourism to federal travel promotion duties
last_action_text: Received in the Senate. Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 59.

title: Advancing the Mentor-Protégé Program for Small Financial Institutions Act
ai_summary:
This bill, H.R. 3709, would create a new "Financial Agent Mentor-Protégé Program" run by the U.S. Department of the Treasury. Under this program, large financial institutions (banks or credit unions with $50 billion or more in assets) or existing "financial agents" of the government (national banks designated to act on the Treasury's behalf) could serve as mentors to small financial institutions. The goal is to help these smaller institutions build the skills and capacity needed to eventually serve as financial agents themselves, or to simply improve the services they offer their own customers.

The bill defines "small financial institutions" broadly to include banks or credit unions with $2 billion or less in assets, minority-owned depository institutions, and rural banks with less than $10 billion in assets located in rural areas. The Treasury Secretary would be required to hold outreach events at least once a year to encourage banks to participate, and would need to create rules for excluding participants who don't meet program standards. The Treasury's Office of Minority and Women Inclusion would also have to report yearly to Congress on how many institutions are participating and how many outreach events were held.

This bill mainly affects banks and credit unions, particularly smaller, minority-owned, or rural institutions that might benefit from mentorship and support from larger banks. It does not directly affect individual consumers, though it could indirectly help by strengthening smaller banks that serve rural or underserved communities. The changes would take effect 90 days after the bill becomes law.
ai_headline: Treasury program would pair large banks with small ones as mentors
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

title: To allow certain Federal minerals to be mined consistent with the Bull Mountains Mining Plan Modification, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill would require the Department of the Interior to approve a specific coal mining plan in Montana without any changes or delays. The plan, called the Bull Mountains Mining Plan Modification, involves about 800 acres of federal land in Musselshell County, Montana, where a company holds a federal coal lease (Lease MTM 97988) for the Bull Mountains Mine No. 1. This plan had already received preliminary approval from a Interior Department official in 2020, but this bill would force final, official government approval within 30 days of the law taking effect, regardless of any other reviews, objections, or environmental concerns that might normally be considered.

In practical terms, this bill affects the coal mining company operating the Bull Mountains Mine, allowing it to continue or expand mining federal coal reserves in that specific area without going through the usual regulatory review process. It could also affect nearby landowners, local communities, and environmental groups who might otherwise have a chance to weigh in on or challenge the mining plan through standard government procedures. Supporters of such mining plans often cite jobs and energy production as benefits, while critics may raise concerns about environmental impact or bypassing standard review steps. The bill does not address other coal leases or mining plans elsewhere—it applies specifically to this one lease and this one plan modification in Montana.
ai_headline: Bill would force fast approval of Montana coal mining plan

title: Meat and Poultry Special Investigator Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new office inside the U.S. Department of Agriculture called the Office of the Special Investigator for Competition Matters. This office would be part of the Packers and Stockyards Division, which is the part of the government that oversees fair competition in the meat and poultry industry. The office would be led by a "Special Investigator" appointed by the Secretary of Agriculture, whose job would be to investigate and take legal action against companies that violate fair competition laws related to livestock, meat, and poultry markets.

The Special Investigator would have significant powers, including the ability to issue subpoenas (legal orders demanding information or testimony), bring civil or administrative legal cases, and hire a staff of lawyers and other experts to support investigations. This person would also work closely with other federal agencies, including the Department of Justice, the Federal Trade Commission, and the Department of Homeland Security, to address competition problems and security concerns in the food and agriculture supply chain.

This bill would mainly affect large meat and poultry companies, farmers, and ranchers, since it targets unfair business practices such as price-fixing or market manipulation in that industry. It could also affect consumers indirectly, since more oversight of competition in the meat and poultry industry could influence food prices and market fairness. Government agencies involved in food safety, antitrust enforcement, and agricultural policy would also see new coordination responsibilities under this law.
ai_headline: Bill would create new USDA office to police meat market competition
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry.

title: Defending Domestic Orange Juice Production Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would change the federal rule that defines what counts as "pasteurized orange juice" for sale in the United States. Currently, federal regulations require orange juice to contain at least 11.8 percent orange juice soluble solids (the natural sugars, acids, and other dissolved material from the fruit) to be labeled as pasteurized orange juice. This bill would lower that minimum requirement to 10.0 percent.

The change is significant because Florida's orange crop has been hit hard in recent years by citrus greening disease, hurricanes, and other problems, making it harder for growers to produce oranges that meet the older, higher solids standard. By lowering the required threshold, more domestically grown Florida oranges could be used to make juice that still qualifies as "pasteurized orange juice" under federal rules, rather than being rejected or classified differently. Supporters argue this would help struggling Florida citrus growers and juice producers stay competitive, particularly against imported orange juice that may already meet the lower standard.

This bill would primarily affect orange growers, juice processors, and grocery retailers, especially in Florida, where several of the bill's sponsors are from. It could also affect consumers, since it changes what nutritional content can be legally labeled as orange juice, though the practical difference in taste or nutrition for most shoppers would likely be minor. The bill does not eliminate the federal government's ability to further adjust these standards in the future; it simply sets a new minimum now while leaving the Department of Health and Human Services able to revise the rule later if needed.
ai_headline: Bill would lower federal solids standard for pasteurized orange juice
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

The Department of Health and Human Services would retain authority to revise the standard again in the future.

title: FAIR ACT
ai_summary:
This bill, called the FAIR Act, would create a fast-track approval system at the FDA for drugs that treat life-threatening diseases if those drugs have already been approved by certain trusted foreign regulators. Under the bill, a drug company could ask the FDA to approve a medicine within 30 days if it's already legally sold in the European Union, United Kingdom, or Canada (or another country the Secretary of Health and Human Services later approves), and if the FDA hasn't previously pulled it from the market for safety reasons. The FDA could later withdraw this "reciprocal approval" if new evidence shows the drug is unsafe or if the foreign regulator withdraws its own approval. The bill also lets drug companies use foreign authorization to more quickly get permission to run clinical trials in the United States, again with a 30-day decision window from the FDA.

The goal is to help patients with serious, life-threatening conditions get access to new treatments faster, especially medicines already proven safe and effective abroad, and to keep more clinical trials happening in the U.S. rather than overseas. This would primarily affect patients with rare or life-threatening diseases who are waiting for new treatment options, pharmaceutical and biotech companies developing these drugs, and the FDA, which would need to build new review processes and report to Congress after five years on how well the program is working. It could mean faster access to cutting-edge medicines for patients, but it also raises questions about whether relying on foreign regulatory decisions could affect the FDA's usual safety review standards.
ai_headline: FDA could fast-track drugs already approved abroad under new bill
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

The FDA would have 30 days to decide, but could later withdraw approval if new safety evidence emerges or the foreign regulator withdraws its own approval. It also speeds up permission to start U.S. clinical trials using foreign authorization, with the same 30-day window.

title: Direct Seller and Real Estate Agent Harmonization Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal labor law to make clear that direct sellers (like people who sell products for companies such as door-to-door or party-plan sales businesses) and qualified real estate agents are not considered "employees" under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA). The FLSA is the main federal law that sets rules for minimum wage, overtime pay, and other worker protections. The bill borrows definitions already used in the tax code to decide who counts as a "direct seller" or "qualified real estate agent."

In practical terms, this means these workers would continue to be treated as independent contractors rather than employees for purposes of federal wage and hour law. That matters because employees are entitled to protections like minimum wage and overtime pay, while independent contractors generally are not. Real estate agents and direct sellers already tend to be treated as independent contractors under tax law, and this bill would align labor law with that same tax classification.

This bill would primarily affect real estate agents, direct sales workers (such as those in multi-level marketing or commission-based sales), and the companies or brokerages that work with them. Supporters might see it as providing clarity and consistency across federal laws, while critics might raise concerns about whether it could limit certain workplace protections for people in these industries. The bill does not change how these workers are taxed; it only affects how they are classified under federal labor law.
ai_headline: Bill would exclude direct sellers, real estate agents from FLSA employee status
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 420.

title: Critical Mineral Consistency Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 755, the Critical Mineral Consistency Act of 2025, changes how the government decides which minerals count as "critical minerals." Under current law, the Department of the Interior keeps an official list of critical minerals, while the Department of Energy separately identifies "critical materials" needed for energy technology. These two lists don't always match, even though the materials often overlap. This bill would require that anything the Department of Energy labels a "critical material" automatically also be added to Interior's official critical minerals list within 45 days.

In practical terms, the bill amends the Energy Act of 2020 to make the definitions and lists used by these two agencies consistent with each other, rather than having separate, potentially conflicting classifications. This matters because being labeled a "critical mineral" can affect federal permitting rules, funding priorities, supply chain policies, and incentives for mining or manufacturing companies.

This bill mainly affects mining companies, manufacturers who rely on specialized materials (like those used in batteries, electronics, or clean energy technology), and federal agencies that manage mineral policy and permitting. It could also indirectly affect industries tied to national security and energy production, since many critical minerals are used in defense equipment, semiconductors, and renewable energy systems. Everyday consumers would likely see effects only indirectly, through changes in mining regulations or supply chains for products that use these materials.

title: Enhancing Administrative Reviews for Broadband Deployment Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Enhancing Administrative Reviews for Broadband Deployment Act, directs two federal agencies, the Department of the Interior and the Department of Agriculture, to look into why it takes so long to approve permits for communications equipment, like cell towers or broadband lines, on public lands and national forests. Companies that want to build this kind of infrastructure on federal land need government approval first, and this bill assumes that process can be slow or inefficient.

Specifically, the bill requires the two departments to study whether there are administrative or procedural obstacles slowing down these approvals, whether current rules could be updated to make the process faster, and whether there's a way to prioritize certain requests. Within one year, they must submit a joint report to relevant congressional committees explaining what they found and presenting a staffing plan to ensure these reviews happen in a timely manner going forward.

This bill mainly affects telecommunications and internet companies that want to expand broadband or cell service using federal land, as well as the federal agencies and local offices (like Bureau of Land Management and Forest Service offices) that handle these permit requests. Indirectly, it could also affect everyday Americans, especially in rural areas, who are waiting for improved internet or cell coverage, since faster government approvals could speed up when new infrastructure gets built. The bill itself doesn't change any rules yet; it just requires research and a plan to be created first.

last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

The agencies must study procedural obstacles, possible rule updates, and ways to prioritize certain requests, then submit a joint report within one year that includes a staffing plan for timely reviews.

title: Unemployment Integrity Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Unemployment Integrity Act of 2025, would change the rules states must follow when running their unemployment benefit programs. It would require people receiving unemployment checks to respond to requests related to available jobs, schedule and attend interviews, take part in reemployment services, and comply with "reasonable requests" from the state, which could include drug testing or skill assessments. Employers who are trying to hire someone collecting unemployment benefits would also be given a way to voluntarily report to the state if that person fails to follow these requirements, such as skipping a job interview.

The bill also directs the Secretary of Labor to study whether increasing random audits of unemployment claims (through an existing program called Benefit Accuracy Measurement) would improve how states manage their programs. If the study shows audits would help, the Secretary would be required to increase them. Additionally, the bill says that federal extended or emergency unemployment funds cannot be sent to a state unless that state has adopted these new interview and reporting requirements in its own laws.

This bill mainly affects people who receive unemployment benefits, requiring them to actively engage in job-search-related activities or risk losing eligibility. It also affects state governments, which would need to update their unemployment laws to keep receiving certain federal funds, and employers, who would gain a formal way to report noncompliant job candidates. The changes would take effect one year after the bill becomes law, with extra time given to states whose legislatures don't meet every year.
ai_headline: Bill would tie jobless benefits to new job-search compliance rules
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: LIVE Beneficiaries Act
ai_summary:
HR 1403, called the LIVE Beneficiaries Act, changes how state Medicaid programs check whether people enrolled in the program are still alive. Starting January 1, 2027, every state and the District of Columbia would be required to check a federal database called the "Death Master File" at least once every three months to see if any Medicaid enrollees have died. This database, maintained by the Social Security Administration, contains death records for people across the country.

If a state finds that someone in this database has died, it must remove that person from Medicaid and stop making payments on their behalf, except for medical care they received before they died. The bill also includes a safeguard: if a state mistakenly identifies someone as deceased and removes them from Medicaid by error, the state must immediately reinstate their coverage and make it retroactive, so there's no gap in their benefits. States are also allowed to use other data sources to catch deceased enrollees faster, as long as they still meet these new requirements.

This bill mainly affects state Medicaid agencies, which would need to update their systems and procedures to perform these quarterly checks. It could also affect Medicaid beneficiaries, particularly if errors occur in matching records, since someone could be temporarily and mistakenly removed from coverage before being reinstated. The stated goal is to prevent Medicaid payments from continuing on behalf of people who have died, which supporters describe as a way to reduce improper payments in the program.
ai_headline: States would face quarterly death checks for Medicaid enrollees starting 2027
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: FAIR Act
ai_summary:
The FAIR Act (H.R. 5315) would require federal agencies to only buy or use large language models (AI chatbots and similar tools) that meet certain standards for being truthful, accurate, and politically neutral. Specifically, the AI tools would need to prioritize factual accuracy, acknowledge uncertainty when information is incomplete, and avoid favoring ideological viewpoints, including specifically naming "diversity, equity, and inclusion" as an example of ideology that should not be built into the AI's responses. Developers would also be barred from secretly programming political or ideological bias into the AI's answers unless that bias is something users specifically ask for or can easily see.

This bill would affect federal agencies, which would have to verify that any AI language models they purchase meet these standards before buying them. It would also affect companies that develop AI systems and want to sell them to the federal government, since they would need to design their products to comply with these rules to qualify for government contracts. The bill would not apply to the Government Accountability Office. Everyday citizens would not be directly regulated by this law, but the AI tools used by government agencies they interact with could be shaped by these requirements, and companies may adjust their broader products to meet federal standards if the government is a major customer.
ai_headline: Bill would require federal AI tools to be accurate and politically neutral
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

title: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States prohibiting the United States Government from increasing its debt except for a specific purpose by law adopted by three-fourths of the membership of each House of Congress.
ai_summary:
This bill proposes an amendment to the U.S. Constitution that would make it much harder for the federal government to borrow money. Currently, Congress can increase the national debt through normal lawmaking, which requires a simple majority vote in the House and Senate. Under this proposed amendment, the government could only increase the debt if three-fourths of all members in both the House and Senate agree, and only for a specific, named purpose. This is a much higher bar than the usual majority vote needed to pass most laws.

Like any constitutional amendment, this would need to pass Congress with a two-thirds vote in both chambers, and then be ratified by three-fourths of state legislatures within seven years. If all that happened, the amendment itself says it wouldn't actually take effect until ten years after ratification, giving the government a long transition period to adjust its finances.

This bill would affect essentially everyone in the country, since it deals with how the federal government pays for programs like Social Security, Medicare, defense, infrastructure, and emergency responses. Supporters of this kind of measure generally argue it would force more fiscal discipline and limit growing national debt. Critics generally worry that requiring such a large supermajority could make it difficult to respond to emergencies, recessions, wars, or other situations where quick borrowing might be needed. As of now, this is only a proposal introduced in the House and has not been passed or sent to the states.
ai_headline: Proposed amendment would require 75% vote in Congress to raise debt
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Protection of Women in Olympic and Amateur Sports Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, H.R. 1028, would change federal law governing the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee and national sports governing bodies (like USA Swimming, USA Track and Field, and similar organizations that oversee amateur and Olympic sports in the United States). It adds specific legal definitions of "male," "female," and "sex" based on reproductive biology, and it requires these sports organizations to bar anyone whose sex is defined as male from competing in athletic competitions designated for females, women, or girls.

In practical terms, the bill targets participation policies in Olympic-track and amateur sports organizations recognized under the Ted Stevens Olympic and Amateur Sports Act. These organizations would be required to adopt eligibility rules based on the bill's biological definitions rather than gender identity when determining who can compete in women's and girls' categories. This would primarily affect transgender women and girls, as well as intersex athletes, who wish to compete in female divisions of amateur and Olympic sports overseen by these national governing bodies.

The bill would not apply to school sports generally, professional sports leagues, or activities outside the scope of organizations chartered under this federal sports law. Its effects would be limited to competitions and organizations covered by that specific statute, such as those preparing athletes for the Olympics, Paralympics, and related amateur competitions.

title: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States to provide for balanced budgets for the Government.
ai_summary:
This bill proposes an amendment to the U.S. Constitution that would require the federal government to balance its budget each year, meaning the government generally could not spend more money than it collects in revenue. To spend more than it takes in, Congress would need a two-thirds vote in both the House and Senate through a recorded vote. The President would also be required to submit a balanced budget proposal to Congress each year before the fiscal year begins.

The amendment includes exceptions that would allow deficit spending without a two-thirds vote in specific situations: during a declared war, during a declared national emergency, or during a declared natural disaster, as long as Congress approves these declarations through a joint resolution passed by a simple majority in both chambers. Congress would also be given authority to pass laws to enforce and carry out the balanced budget requirement, using estimates of spending and revenue as needed.

Because this is a proposed constitutional amendment, it would not take effect immediately even if Congress passed it. It would first need approval by two-thirds of both the House and Senate, then ratification by three-fourths of state legislatures (38 states). If ratified, the requirement would not start until the fifth fiscal year after ratification, giving the government time to adjust. This bill would affect all Americans indirectly, since it could significantly change how federal spending on programs like Social Security, Medicare, defense, and other services is decided, especially during economic downturns when governments often spend more than they collect.
ai_headline: Proposed amendment would require federal government to balance its budget
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Household Goods Shipping Consumer Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Household Goods Shipping Consumer Protection Act, aims to strengthen oversight of companies that move people's household belongings, such as moving companies and brokers who arrange moves. It gives the Secretary of Transportation clearer authority to directly issue civil fines against moving companies and brokers that break federal shipping rules, rather than relying solely on a separate review board. It also allows states to use existing federal grant money to enforce these household goods shipping rules (this would be optional, not required) and lets states keep any fines they collect from enforcement actions instead of sending that money elsewhere.

The bill also tightens registration requirements for moving companies, brokers, and freight forwarders. These businesses would need to designate an actual physical "principal place of business" where management works and records are kept, rather than just a P.O. box or vague address. Companies applying for registration would also have to disclose if they have ownership, management, or family ties to other moving companies or brokers within the past three years — a measure aimed at preventing shady operators from shutting down one company and quietly reopening under a new name to dodge complaints or penalties. The Secretary of Transportation would gain explicit power to suspend or revoke a company's registration if it fails to maintain a legitimate business address.

This bill primarily affects moving companies, brokers, and freight forwarders in the household goods shipping industry, as well as everyday consumers who hire movers when relocating. By making it harder for problem companies to hide behind fake addresses or shell companies, and by strengthening enforcement tools for both federal and state regulators, the bill is intended to reduce common consumer complaints in the moving industry, such as hostage loads, hidden fees, and fraudulent operators.

last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.

title: Proposing a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution of the United States.
ai_summary:
This bill proposes an amendment to the U.S. Constitution that would require the federal government to balance its budget each year, meaning it could not spend more money than it collects, unless two-thirds of both the House and Senate specifically vote to allow spending beyond income for that year. Because this is a constitutional amendment, it needs approval by two-thirds of both chambers of Congress and then must be ratified by three-fourths of state legislatures within seven years to actually become part of the Constitution. This is a high bar that most proposed amendments never clear.

The amendment would require the President to submit a balanced budget proposal to Congress each year before the fiscal year starts. It defines "receipts" as all government income except money from borrowing, and "outlays" as all spending except payments toward existing debt. Congress would be responsible for passing laws to carry out and enforce this rule, and could use estimates rather than exact figures when determining whether the budget is balanced. If ratified, the requirement would not start immediately—it would take effect five fiscal years after ratification, giving the government time to adjust.

If this amendment became law, it would affect nearly every American, since it could significantly change how the federal government funds programs like Social Security, Medicare, defense, education, and infrastructure. Supporters argue it would control national debt growth, while critics worry it could force spending cuts or tax increases during economic downturns, when deficit spending is sometimes used to stabilize the economy. As a joint resolution proposing a constitutional amendment, it does not require the President's signature and instead goes through the separate constitutional amendment process.

title: Appraisal Industry Improvement Act
ai_summary:
HR 6025, the "Appraisal Industry Improvement Act," makes several changes to how home appraisals work, especially for homes bought with FHA-insured mortgages (loans backed by the Federal Housing Administration, often used by first-time or lower-income buyers). The bill allows any appraiser who is properly licensed or certified by their state to perform appraisals on FHA-backed homes, as long as they also meet existing national competency standards and complete specific training on FHA appraisal rules. It also lets federal employees who do appraisals only need one state license to work nationwide. HUD would have to issue clear guidance within about 8 months explaining exactly what appraisers need to do to qualify, and appraisers already approved before the new rules take effect would be given a way to show they already meet the requirements.

The bill also updates rules for "appraisal management companies" (firms that connect lenders with appraisers), allowing their registration fees to be adjusted to help fund oversight. It creates a formal recognition of "state credentialed trainee appraisers"—people training to become licensed appraisers—and allows certified appraisers to use trainees to help with appraisals, though the certified appraiser remains responsible for the final report. States would need to report trainee licensing information to a national registry, though they aren't required to create trainee programs if they don't already have one.

Finally, the bill sets up grant funding to help train new appraisers and address worker shortages in the field, and it adds the Department of Veterans Affairs, USDA's Rural Housing Service, and HUD to the Appraisal Subcommittee, the federal body that oversees appraiser standards. Overall, this bill mainly affects real estate appraisers, appraisal companies, state licensing agencies, and home buyers or sellers using FHA, VA, USDA, or HUD-related mortgages, aiming to expand the pool of qualified appraisers and modernize training and oversight rules.
ai_headline: Bill would let state-licensed appraisers handle more FHA home loans

title: Veterinary Education Equity Act
ai_summary:
HR 8505, called the Veterinary Education Equity Act, would change a federal grant program that helps support veterinary services, particularly in rural or underserved areas. The bill amends a 1977 agricultural law to officially add "1890 Institutions" as eligible applicants for these veterinary services grants. 1890 Institutions are historically Black land-grant colleges and universities, originally established under the Second Morrill Act of 1890, which created land-grant schools for Black students during a time when many other universities excluded them.

In addition to making these schools eligible to apply, the bill directs the Secretary of Agriculture to give higher priority to funding proposals from 1890 Institutions when deciding which projects receive grant money under this program. In practical terms, this means that when the government reviews applications for veterinary services grants, projects coming from these historically Black colleges and universities would be considered more favorably compared to other applicants.

This bill would primarily affect 1890 Institutions themselves, giving them a new funding opportunity and an advantage in the grant selection process. It could also affect other colleges, universities, and organizations that currently apply for these same veterinary services grants, since increased competition or priority given to one group may change the distribution of limited federal funding. More broadly, communities that rely on veterinary services supported by these grants—especially in rural or underserved areas—could also be affected depending on how funding patterns shift.
ai_headline: Bill would give historically Black colleges edge in vet grant funding
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.

title: Parris Island Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Parris Island Protection Act, would block the federal government from using any money to close or reorganize the Marine Corps Recruit Depot at Parris Island, South Carolina. It also prevents federal funds from being used even to plan or study a possible closure or realignment of the base. Parris Island has been a Marine Corps training site since 1891 and is one of the two locations where Marine recruits go through basic training.

The bill includes a list of reasons why lawmakers believe Parris Island should be protected, citing its long history, its role in training Marines for major U.S. conflicts, and its importance to the Marine Corps' Eastern Recruiting Region. The actual legal change is contained in one short section: it simply forbids federal spending on closing, downsizing, or reorganizing the base.

This bill would primarily affect the Department of Defense and Marine Corps, limiting their flexibility in making future decisions about military base structure, staffing, or budget priorities involving Parris Island. It would also affect the local community in Beaufort County, South Carolina, where the base is a significant source of jobs and economic activity, as well as military families and recruits connected to the depot. More broadly, it reflects a recurring pattern in Congress where members introduce legislation to protect military installations in their home states from potential future base closure or realignment decisions, which are normally handled through a separate defense review process.
ai_headline: Bill would bar federal funds from closing Parris Island base
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Armed Services.

title: Establishing the ratification of the Equal Rights Amendment.
ai_summary:
This resolution declares that the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA), which was first passed by Congress in 1972, should now be officially recognized as part of the U.S. Constitution. The ERA would guarantee that equal rights under the law cannot be denied or limited based on a person's sex. Back in 1972, Congress set a deadline for enough states to approve (ratify) the amendment, but that deadline passed before three-fourths of the states had done so. However, in 2020, Virginia became the 38th state to ratify it, which supporters argue met the three-fourths requirement, just later than the original deadline allowed.

This bill does not create a new amendment or change its wording. Instead, it argues that the original time limit set by Congress doesn't prevent the ERA from being valid now, since the required number of states eventually ratified it. If passed, it would declare the ERA officially part of the Constitution, without needing further state approval.

This measure would affect all U.S. residents, since it deals with constitutional protections against sex-based discrimination. It could impact laws and legal cases involving gender equality, workplace discrimination, and civil rights protections. However, there is ongoing legal and political disagreement about whether Congress can bypass the original ratification deadline this way, meaning the resolution's approach may face court challenges even if passed by Congress.
ai_headline: Resolution seeks to declare Equal Rights Amendment part of the Constitution
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Department of Energy relating to "Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Commercial Water Heating Equipment".
ai_summary:
This bill would cancel a federal regulation issued by the Department of Energy that set new energy efficiency standards for commercial water heating equipment, such as the large water heaters used in businesses, apartment buildings, hotels, and other commercial settings. The rule, published in October 2023, would have required newer commercial water heaters to meet stricter energy-saving requirements. Using a special power called the Congressional Review Act, lawmakers can vote to undo recently issued federal regulations, and if this resolution passes both the House and Senate and is signed by the President (or Congress overrides a veto), the water heater efficiency rule would be completely canceled and treated as if it never took effect.

This would affect manufacturers of commercial water heating equipment, who would no longer need to meet the new efficiency standards, as well as businesses and building owners who purchase this equipment. Supporters of blocking the rule often argue it would have raised equipment costs or limited product choices, while supporters of the original rule generally argue it would have lowered long-term energy use and utility costs. If the rule is overturned, older, less efficient water heater standards would remain in place, and the Department of Energy would also be restricted from issuing a similar new rule in the future without specific new authorization from Congress.

title: Return to Sender Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Return to Sender Act," would cancel unspent money that was set aside under two specific sections of the Inflation Reduction Act, a major 2022 law. Specifically, it targets sections 70002 and 70003 of that law, which provided funding related to environmental and climate justice programs, including grants aimed at reducing pollution and its effects in communities. If any of that money hasn't yet been officially committed or spent by the time this bill becomes law, it would be taken back and those sections of the law would be repealed entirely, meaning no future funding could be distributed under them.

In practical terms, this bill affects government agencies, community organizations, and local governments that were expecting to apply for or receive grants under these programs. Groups involved in environmental justice work, such as efforts to reduce pollution in low-income or minority communities, would likely be most affected, since they were the intended recipients of this funding. Taxpayers could also be indirectly affected, since the bill would reduce future federal spending tied to these programs.

This bill is still in an early stage of the legislative process. It has been introduced and referred to a committee, but it has not been voted on or passed by the House or Senate. Whether it becomes law depends on further committee action, floor votes in both chambers, and the President's signature.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

title: Proposing a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution of the United States.
ai_summary:
This is a proposed amendment to the U.S. Constitution that would require the federal government to balance its budget each year, meaning it couldn't spend more money than it collects, unless a large majority of Congress specifically votes to allow it. Because it's a constitutional amendment, it would need to pass both the House and Senate with two-thirds support and then be approved by three-fourths of state legislatures before becoming law—a very high bar that most proposed amendments don't clear.

The bill sets several rules: Congress could only spend more than it takes in if three-fifths of both the House and Senate agreed through a recorded vote, and the same three-fifths threshold would apply to raising the national debt limit. The President would have to submit a balanced budget proposal each year. Any bill to raise taxes would need majority approval in both chambers with a recorded vote. These rules could be temporarily waived during a declared war or a serious military conflict, but only through a formal process, and only to cover costs directly tied to that conflict. The amendment would not take effect until five years after states ratify it, giving the government time to adjust.

This would affect virtually everyone in the country, since it could reshape how the federal government funds programs like Social Security, Medicare, defense, and other services during economic downturns or emergencies. Supporters argue it would force fiscal discipline and reduce long-term debt, while critics worry it could limit the government's ability to respond quickly to recessions, natural disasters, or other crises that require flexible spending.
ai_headline: Proposed amendment would require federal budget to balance each year
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

Rules could be waived during a declared war or serious military conflict, and the amendment wouldn't take effect until five years after state ratification.

title: Strengthening Supply Chains Through Truck Driver Incentives Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new tax credit for commercial truck drivers, worth up to $7,500 per year for experienced drivers and up to $10,000 for people who are new to truck driving. To qualify, a person would need to hold a Class A commercial driver's license, drive a large tractor-trailer (Group A vehicle), and put in a substantial number of hours on the job—generally at least 1,900 hours a year, or an average of 40 hours a week if they're new to the field. People training through registered truck-driving apprenticeship programs could also count their training hours toward this requirement, even before getting their license.

The credit would only be available to drivers whose income falls below certain limits: $90,000 for single filers, $112,500 for heads of household, and $135,000 for married couples filing jointly. Drivers who work fewer hours (down to 1,420) would get a partial credit based on how much they worked. The credit amounts would also rise slightly each year to keep pace with inflation. Because it's a "refundable" credit, drivers could get money back even if they owe little or no federal income tax.

This bill would mainly affect commercial truck drivers, especially newer drivers and apprentices entering the trucking industry, by giving them a financial incentive tied to how much they work. It could also affect trucking companies and the broader supply chain, since the bill's supporters aim to address driver shortages. The tax credit would only last for two years, applying to taxable years 2025 and 2026, unless Congress renews it.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: Working Families Flexibility Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would let private-sector employers offer "comp time" (paid time off) instead of cash overtime pay to hourly employees who work more than 40 hours a week. Currently, federal law requires most private employers to pay time-and-a-half in wages for overtime hours; this bill would let employees choose to bank that overtime as paid time off instead, at the same rate (1.5 hours off for every overtime hour worked). This option would only be available if the employee agrees to it voluntarily, in writing, and has worked at least 1,000 hours for that employer in the past year. Employees could still choose regular overtime pay if they prefer, and unions would negotiate this benefit separately for unionized workplaces.

The bill sets rules to protect workers: employees could accumulate up to 160 hours of comp time, employers would have to cash out unused time above certain limits or by year's end, and workers could request cash payment for their banked time at any point. If someone quits or is fired, any unused comp time must be paid out in cash. Employers would be barred from pressuring workers to choose comp time over pay, and violations could lead to financial penalties. The Department of Labor would need to update its official notices explaining these rights, and the Government Accountability Office would monitor and report on how the program is used over time.

This mainly affects hourly, non-government workers eligible for overtime pay, as well as private employers who choose to offer this option. It would not apply to public-sector employees, who already have similar comp-time options under existing law. The changes would automatically expire five years after the bill becomes law unless Congress renews them.

title: Flight Education Access Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Flight Education Access Act, would let college students studying to become commercial pilots borrow more money through federal student loans than is normally allowed. Currently, federal loan limits are the same for all undergraduates regardless of major, and these limits often don't cover the high cost of flight training, which can involve expensive flight hours and equipment on top of regular tuition. This bill creates special, higher loan limits specifically for students enrolled in accredited flight training programs that lead to a commercial pilot certificate, with the amounts increasing each year as the student progresses through the program.

To qualify for these higher limits, a school's flight program must eventually maintain a 70% completion rate (tracked over time, with new programs given a 3-year grace period to build up data). The bill also requires schools to give students clearer information about their loans before the money is disbursed, including estimated monthly payments and total repayment costs, so students understand what they're signing up for. The Department of Education would have to collect data on student enrollment, completion rates, and demographics, and report to Congress periodically on how the program is working.

This mainly affects college students pursuing pilot careers, the colleges and universities that run accredited flight training programs, and the federal student loan system generally. It could help address a national pilot shortage by making flight training more financially accessible, but it also means eligible students could take on significantly more debt than typical borrowers. The bill authorizes $3 million per year through 2035 to help the Department of Education administer these changes, and requires a government watchdog report after two years to evaluate how well the program is working.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

title: Proposing a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution of the United States.
ai_summary:
This bill proposes an amendment to the U.S. Constitution that would require the federal government to balance its budget, meaning spending should generally match income over time rather than every single year. Under this proposal, spending would not include payments made to pay off existing debt, and income would not include money borrowed. Congress would have ten years after the amendment is ratified to actually achieve this balance. There is also an emergency exception: if two-thirds of both the House and Senate agree, the government could spend more than the balanced-budget rules would normally allow for a limited time, but any debt created this way would need to be paid off as soon as reasonably possible.

Because this is a proposed constitutional amendment, it faces a very high bar before it could take effect. It would need approval from two-thirds of both the House and Senate, and then it would need to be ratified by three-fourths of state legislatures (38 of 50 states) within seven years. This is a much harder process than passing a regular law, which only requires majority votes in Congress and the president's signature.

If ratified, this amendment would affect how the federal government manages spending on programs like Social Security, Medicare, defense, education, and other services, potentially requiring cuts, tax increases, or both to meet balanced-budget requirements. It would affect all Americans who rely on federal programs, receive government benefits, or are affected by federal economic policy, since it would place a permanent, enforceable limit on how the government can spend and borrow money going forward.
ai_headline: Proposed amendment would force federal budget to balance over time
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Lung Cancer Screening and Prevention Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would let Medicare cover new types of lung cancer screening tests beyond the one type it currently pays for. Right now, Medicare only covers a specific screening method (low-dose CT scans) for lung cancer under a rule set years ago. This bill would give the Secretary of Health and Human Services the authority to approve additional screening tests for lung cancer, as long as those tests have been cleared or approved by the FDA. The Secretary would decide how often these tests could be used and how much Medicare would pay for them, after consulting with relevant medical organizations.

The bill also simplifies the approval process a bit by removing one specific procedural requirement that normally applies when Medicare decides whether to cover new preventive services, though it keeps the standard national coverage determination review process in place. The Secretary could still consider advice from expert medical groups, including those focused on preventive care research, when making these decisions.

This bill mainly affects Medicare beneficiaries, particularly older adults and people at risk for lung cancer who rely on Medicare for their health coverage. It could also affect doctors and hospitals that provide lung cancer screenings, as well as companies that make new screening technologies, since it opens the door for newer tests (such as blood tests or other emerging screening methods) to eventually be covered by Medicare if approved by the FDA and accepted through the coverage review process.

title: To acknowledge the courage and sacrifice of veterans of the Vietnam war and formally apologize for the treatment they received upon returning home.
ai_summary:
This bill is a resolution—not a law that spends money or changes regulations—expressing Congress's formal recognition of Vietnam War veterans and apologizing for how they were treated when they returned home. It lays out historical background about the war, including the number of troops who served, the more than 58,000 who died, the hundreds of thousands wounded, and the harm caused by exposure to Agent Orange. It also describes the divisive atmosphere in the country during the war, including protests that sometimes targeted military recruiting stations and training facilities.

The resolution itself takes four specific actions: it officially recognizes and thanks Vietnam veterans for their service; it calls on the President to acknowledge the mistreatment these veterans faced; it issues a formal apology on behalf of the American people to veterans and their families for how they were treated during and after the war; and it expresses support for improving how schools teach about the Vietnam War and veterans' experiences.

This bill mainly affects Vietnam War veterans and their families in a symbolic way—it does not create new veterans' benefits, healthcare programs, or funding. It could indirectly affect public education if schools or state curricula respond to the resolution's call for better historical education about the war and its veterans. Because it's a joint resolution focused on commemoration rather than policy change, its primary impact is symbolic recognition rather than a concrete change in law or spending.

title: Enhancing Detection of Human Trafficking Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Enhancing Detection of Human Trafficking Act, would require the Secretary of Labor to create a training program for certain Department of Labor employees to help them recognize signs of human trafficking while doing their regular jobs. Within 180 days of the bill becoming law, the Department would need to set up this training, which could be done in person or online. The training would cover current trends in trafficking, how to identify possible victims and suspects, and clear steps for reporting suspected cases to the Department of Justice and other authorities, while working with victim advocacy groups and local officials.

The bill specifically asks the Secretary to pay attention to employees in the Wage and Hour Division, especially those working in states that have seen a notable rise in illegal child labor, since these workers may be more likely to encounter trafficking situations. After completing the training, employees would give feedback on how useful it was, which the Department would use to improve the program over time.

This bill mainly affects Department of Labor employees, who would receive new training as part of their jobs, and indirectly benefits the general public by potentially improving early detection of human trafficking cases, including child labor exploitation. The Secretary of Labor would also need to report annually to Congress on how the training is going, how many people completed it, and how many trafficking cases were referred to law enforcement. There is no direct cost or requirement placed on private citizens or businesses; the bill focuses on training and internal Department of Labor procedures.
