title: National Emergency Medical Services Memorial Extension Act
ai_summary:
This bill extends the deadline for a group called the National Emergency Medical Services Memorial Foundation to build a memorial in Washington, D.C. honoring EMS workers. Congress previously gave the foundation legal permission to build this memorial, but there's a standard rule that says groups only have seven years to complete a commemorative work before their approval expires. This bill changes that deadline, allowing the foundation until November 3, 2032, to finish the project.

This is a routine, procedural type of bill that Congress passes fairly often when memorial projects take longer than expected to plan, fund, and build. It doesn't create the memorial itself or spend taxpayer money directly; it simply keeps the foundation's legal authority active so their existing plans don't expire before construction is complete.

The bill mainly affects the National Emergency Medical Services Memorial Foundation, which organizes fundraising and planning for the memorial, and indirectly affects EMS workers and their families, who are the ones being honored. It has little to no direct impact on the general public, other than eventually adding a new monument to the D.C. area once completed.

title: Protecting Private Job Creators Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Protecting Private Job Creators Act," deals with a technical rule from the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) called Rule 15c2-11. That rule requires brokers who quote prices for certain securities (like stocks or bonds) to first confirm that basic financial information about the company is publicly available, so investors aren't trading blind. The rule was originally designed for stock markets, but the SEC later signaled it would also apply this rule to fixed-income securities, such as bonds, notes, and certificates of deposit. This bill would permanently stop that rule from applying to fixed-income securities at all.

In plain terms, the bill says brokers who quote prices on bonds and similar debt securities won't have to follow Rule 15c2-11's disclosure-checking requirements. Supporters of this approach argue that bond markets work differently than stock markets, and that applying stock-market rules to bonds could make it harder or more expensive for companies to raise money by issuing debt. The bill notes that the SEC itself has already granted temporary exemptions for some fixed-income securities, and this legislation would make that exemption permanent and broader through an act of Congress rather than leaving it to SEC discretion.

This bill would primarily affect companies that raise money by issuing bonds or similar debt instruments, the brokers and dealers who trade those securities, and investors who buy them. Businesses that rely on bond markets for financing could see fewer regulatory hurdles, while investor advocates might raise questions about whether reduced disclosure requirements could affect the information available to people buying these securities.

title: SCORE Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the SCORE Act, sets up national rules for how college athletes can earn money from their name, image, and likeness (NIL), replacing the current patchwork of state laws with one federal standard. It confirms that athletes have the right to sign NIL deals and hire agents, while banning "prohibited compensation" — payments disguised as NIL deals that are really just pay-for-play or recruiting inducements, or payments that exceed spending limits set by a national college sports association like the NCAA. It also lets colleges, conferences, and national athletic associations create and enforce their own rules on things like NIL disclosure, agent registration, transfer eligibility, and season length, and protects those rules from antitrust lawsuits. Athletes would still not be classified as employees of their schools.

The bill also requires larger athletic programs (those with a coach earning over $250,000 a year) to provide expanded support to athletes, including medical care for a few years after they leave school, mental health and career counseling, protection of scholarships regardless of injury or performance, and degree-completion assistance for athletes who don't finish their studies. Schools with at least $50 million in annual media rights revenue would be barred from using student fees to fund athletics, and all schools would have to publicly report how student athletic fees are spent. Finally, the bill would override (preempt) state laws on athlete compensation, employment status, and NIL rights, meaning states could no longer set their own rules in these areas.

This bill mainly affects college athletes, universities and their athletic departments, conferences, national governing bodies like the NCAA, sports agents, and state lawmakers who have previously passed their own NIL laws. Everyday taxpayers and students could be indirectly affected through athletic fee transparency rules and how universities fund their sports programs.

The resolution provides for consideration of H.R. 4312, H.R. 1005, H.R. 1049, H.R. 1069, H.R. 2965, and H.R. 4305 under a closed rule with one hour of general debate and one motion to recommit on each bill.

title: SBA Fraud Enforcement Extension Act
ai_summary:
This bill would give the government more time to prosecute fraud connected to two COVID-19 pandemic relief programs run by the Small Business Administration: the Shuttered Venue Operators Grant program, which helped live event venues and theaters that were closed during the pandemic, and the Restaurant Revitalization Fund, which gave grants to restaurants hurt by pandemic shutdowns. Under the bill, prosecutors and government agencies would have up to 10 years after a fraud-related crime occurred to file criminal charges or civil enforcement actions, rather than being limited by the shorter deadlines that would normally apply under existing law.

The bill specifically covers a list of federal crimes often used in fraud cases, such as false statements, identity theft, wire and mail fraud, money laundering, and making false claims against the government. This mainly affects people or businesses that received these pandemic grants and may have committed fraud, such as lying on applications or misusing the money. It gives the Department of Justice, the SBA's oversight offices, and other investigators a longer window to detect fraud, build cases, and pursue legal action, even years after the original grants were issued.

For everyday Americans, this bill doesn't create new taxes, benefits, or direct requirements. Its main effect is on accountability and law enforcement: it makes it harder for people who committed fraud in these two specific pandemic programs to avoid consequences simply because too much time has passed. Business owners who received these grants legitimately would not be affected, since the extended deadline only applies to actual fraud or conspiracy to commit fraud.

title: Department of Homeland Security Appropriations Act, 2026
ai_summary:
This bill provides funding for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for the fiscal year running through September 2026. It sets specific dollar amounts for every major part of DHS, including Customs and Border Protection, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), the Coast Guard, the Secret Service, FEMA, and cybersecurity operations. Beyond just setting budget numbers, it includes detailed rules about how the money can and cannot be used—for example, funding body cameras for immigration enforcement agents, restricting certain surveillance technology purchases, limiting fees at border crossings, and requiring various agencies to report regularly to Congress on spending, staffing, and major projects.

The bill affects a wide range of people. Travelers will notice funding for airport security staff and equipment through TSA. People living near the border, in immigration detention, or involved in immigration enforcement are affected by funding levels for ICE and Border Patrol, plus new oversight rules such as cutting off funding for detention contractors with poor performance records, and requirements to protect pregnant women in CBP custody. Coast Guard funding affects maritime safety and drug/human trafficking enforcement. FEMA grant money flows to states, cities, tribes, nonprofits, fire departments, and transit systems for emergency preparedness and security. The bill also affects government oversight—it requires DHS's Inspector General to audit spending, monitor detention facilities, and report on how money tied to a related law (Public Law 119-21) is being used.

The bill also contains many specific restrictions and conditions, such as banning funds for certain intelligence activities, prohibiting the reduction of ICE's international law enforcement presence without justification, exempting Congress members and top officials from any special treatment in airport security screening, and blocking funds for weaponized long-range drones. It requires numerous reports, briefings, and spending plans to Congress so lawmakers can track how DHS is using taxpayer money throughout the year.

title: Flexibility for Workers Education Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change the Fair Labor Standards Act, the federal law that sets rules for minimum wage and overtime pay. Currently, employers must generally count as "hours worked" any time employees spend in training or educational activities, especially if those activities are connected to the job. This bill says that if an employee attends lectures, training programs, or similar educational activities outside of their normal work hours, that time does not have to count as "hours worked" for pay purposes — as long as three conditions are met: the employee isn't required to attend, their job or working conditions won't suffer if they skip it, and they don't do any actual work for the employer while participating.

In practical terms, this means employers would not be required to pay employees, including overtime pay, for voluntary training, classes, or educational programs that happen outside regular work hours, even if the employer offers or organizes those programs. This affects hourly workers covered by wage-and-hour law, particularly those who take advantage of job-related training, certification courses, or continuing education offered by their employer. Supporters might see this as encouraging more employers to offer educational opportunities without added labor costs, while critics might worry it could reduce pay for time employees spend improving their skills, especially if "voluntary" is hard to define in practice. The bill would apply to hours worked starting on the date it becomes law.
ai_headline: Bill would exempt voluntary off-hours job training from overtime pay rules
last_action_text: Motion to reconsider laid on the table Agreed to without objection.

title: Modernizing Access to Our Public Oceans Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Secretary of Commerce to create a single, easy-to-use online map system showing information that recreational boaters, anglers, and divers need to safely and legally use federal ocean waters. Within about four years, the government would have to publish data showing where fishing restrictions apply, which areas are open or closed to boating and diving (including closures for safety reasons like harmful algae), speed or motor restrictions, protected areas like national marine sanctuaries, and basic navigation information such as water depths and charts. This data would need to be updated regularly, with certain sensitive information—like the location of archaeological sites or private commercial fishing data—kept confidential.

In practice, this bill mainly affects people who use federal ocean waters for recreation, such as boaters, fishers, and divers, by making it easier to find accurate, up-to-date information about where they can go and what rules apply. It could also help state governments, tribes, nonprofit groups, and private companies that manage or study ocean areas, since the bill encourages the Commerce Department to work with these outside groups when building the system. The bill does not change any existing laws about who controls U.S. waters or how fisheries are managed—it only requires better organization and public access to existing information. It also specifically protects tribal fishing rights and waters, stating that the new rules do not apply to tribal fishing areas and do not replace any required consultations with tribes.

last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 438.

title: MAWS Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, known as the MAWS Act of 2025 (H.R. 4294), directs the Secretary of Commerce to create a three-year pilot program aimed at controlling the population of blue catfish, an invasive species, in the Chesapeake Bay Watershed. Blue catfish are not native to the area and have been harming local ecosystems by eating native fish and other species. The program would provide funding to companies that make pet food, animal feed, or aquaculture feed so they can buy blue catfish from local fishermen ("watermen") and seafood processors, encouraging more of these fish to be caught and removed from the bay. The government would set a minimum price per pound to make sure fishermen are fairly paid, and companies could use a small portion of the funding to cover transportation costs.

The program would run from January 2027 through December 2029, with $2 million per year authorized for it. At the end, the Secretary would report to Congress on how well the program worked, including its effects on the blue catfish population, the environment, and the incomes of participating watermen, plus recommendations on whether to continue or expand the idea to other regions, such as using similar methods to fight invasive carp in the Mississippi River area.

This bill mainly affects commercial fishermen and seafood processors in the Chesapeake Bay region (parts of Delaware, Maryland, New York, Pennsylvania, Virginia, West Virginia, and Washington, D.C.), as well as companies that produce pet food, animal feed, or aquaculture feed. It could also indirectly benefit the environment and other wildlife in the bay by reducing the number of invasive blue catfish, and it may offer a model for handling similar invasive species problems in other parts of the country.
ai_headline: Pilot program would pay watermen to catch invasive Chesapeake blue catfish

title: Put America on Commission Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Put America on Commission Act of 2026," creates a new whistleblower reward program aimed at catching fraud related to COVID-19 small business loans. It sets up an "Office of Whistleblower Awards" inside the Small Business Administration (SBA). If someone reports original, previously unknown information about fraud or financial misconduct involving pandemic-era loans (such as PPP or EIDL loans), and that tip leads to a criminal conviction or a settlement/plea deal, the whistleblower can receive a cash reward. The reward would be 10% of the money collected if the wrongdoer is a U.S. person or company, or 15% if the wrongdoer is foreign. The bill also creates a new fund at the Treasury Department to hold and pay out these rewards, financed partly by a new civil penalty equal to 30% of the fraudulent loan amount, charged to anyone convicted or who settles related to COVID loan fraud.

The bill includes several protections and rules: whistleblowers who helped plan the fraud themselves can have their reward reduced or denied, and those convicted of related crimes must repay any award they received. It also protects whistleblowers from retaliation by employers, sets a one-year deadline for paying out awards, and allows whistleblowers to appeal decisions in federal court. The SBA must issue detailed rules for the program and report annually to Congress on how many tips were received and how much money was paid out. The program would eventually end once all COVID-related loan fraud cases are fully resolved.

This bill mainly affects people who have inside knowledge of COVID-era small business loan fraud (potential whistleblowers), businesses or individuals who received pandemic loans and may be investigated, the SBA and its Inspector General (who must build and run this new system), and taxpayers, since it creates new government spending and enforcement authority meant to recover fraudulently obtained COVID loan funds.

title: Save Local Business Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Save Local Business Act, would change how the law decides when two separate businesses count as "joint employers" of the same workers. Under current rules, businesses can sometimes be treated as joint employers if one has indirect or potential influence over another company's workers, even without directly managing them day to day. This bill would tighten that definition so that a company can only be considered a joint employer if it directly, actually, and immediately controls key parts of a worker's job, such as hiring, firing, pay, benefits, scheduling, daily supervision, or discipline. This change would apply to both the National Labor Relations Act, which covers union organizing and collective bargaining, and the Fair Labor Standards Act, which covers minimum wage and overtime protections.

This matters most for businesses that operate through franchises, staffing agencies, or contractors, such as fast food chains, hotel chains, and companies that hire temp workers. Under the stricter definition, a parent company or franchisor would be less likely to be held legally responsible for labor violations, unpaid wages, or unfair labor practices committed by a franchisee or staffing agency, since it would need to show direct, hands-on control to be considered a joint employer. Supporters argue this protects local franchise owners and small businesses from being lumped in with large corporations in legal disputes. Critics argue it could make it harder for workers to hold the larger company accountable when their actual employer, like a franchisee, cannot pay damages or fix labor violations, or when workers want to organize a union that includes decisions made by the larger company.
ai_headline: Bill would narrow definition of "joint employer" in labor law
last_action_text: Rule H. Res. 988 passed House.

This change would apply to both the National Labor Relations Act and the Fair Labor Standards Act.

title: Water Power Research and Development Reauthorization Act
ai_summary:
This bill updates and renews federal funding for research into water-based energy, including hydropower (energy from dams and rivers) and marine energy (energy from ocean waves, tides, and currents). It extends and expands a program originally created in 2007, setting new funding levels of $300 million per year from 2026 through 2030, up from the previous $186.6 million per year. Of that amount, $200 million a year would go to marine energy research and $100 million a year to hydropower research.

The bill makes several changes to how this research money can be used. It adds new priorities like building domestic manufacturing for marine energy equipment (including advanced materials and 3D-printed parts), improving hydropower licensing processes, addressing cybersecurity risks for dams and power systems, and developing technology for extreme conditions like icy or high-tide environments. It also emphasizes workforce training, including partnerships with universities, tribal colleges, and maritime academies to train future workers in these fields. Additionally, it expands the criteria for choosing "National Marine Energy Centers" (research hubs) to include sites with strong natural advantages like powerful currents or cold water, and it requires the Department of Energy to brief Congress every two years, instead of annually, on research progress.

This bill mainly affects the Department of Energy, national research labs, universities, and companies involved in renewable energy research and manufacturing. It could also affect coastal and river communities, tribal nations, and workers in energy-related fields, since it supports local partnerships, job training programs, and infrastructure projects tied to hydropower and ocean energy development.

last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by Voice Vote.

title: Modern Worker Security Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Modern Worker Security Act, addresses a specific question that matters for gig workers and independent contractors: whether a company can offer certain benefits without that being used as evidence the worker is actually an employee rather than a contractor. Under current law, companies often worry that offering things like health insurance, retirement savings, paid leave, or job training to independent contractors could make it look like those workers should legally be classified as employees, with all the added costs and legal protections that come with that status.

This bill says that when the government decides whether someone is an "employee" under federal law, it cannot count the fact that a company provided "portable benefits" as a factor in that decision. Portable benefits are defined as work-related benefits that stay with the worker even if they stop working for that particular company, similar to how a 401(k) retirement account can move with a person from job to job. This could include things like workers' compensation, health coverage, disability protection, or savings contributions.

The bill mainly affects gig economy companies (like rideshare or delivery platforms), independent contractors, and freelance workers. Supporters of this type of policy argue it would let companies offer more benefits to contractors without fear of legal consequences, potentially improving worker security. Critics of such policies generally worry it could make it easier for companies to avoid classifying workers as employees, which affects wages, protections, and benefits workers are legally guaranteed. The bill does not create any new benefit programs itself; it only changes how the law treats the provision of such benefits when determining worker classification.
ai_headline: Bill would shield gig firms offering benefits from employee status claims
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 432.

Portable benefits are defined as benefits that stay with a worker across jobs, similar to a 401(k). The bill does not create any new benefit programs; it only changes how offering benefits affects worker classification decisions.

title: Balance the Scales Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Balance the Scales Act, changes how the U.S. Department of Labor's Employee Benefit Security Administration (EBSA) can help workers who want to sue their employer, pension plan, or plan managers over retirement or benefit plan violations. Under current law, EBSA sometimes shares information or assistance with workers or their attorneys when investigating possible violations of pension and benefit laws. This bill requires that before EBSA gives this kind of help—called "adverse assistance"—to someone considering a lawsuit, it must sign a written agreement spelling out exactly what help it's providing, and give a copy of that agreement to the employer or plan manager who might be sued. It also requires EBSA to file a detailed annual report to Congress listing every such agreement, including logs of meetings, phone calls, and what information was shared, though the report must hide details that could identify the employer or company involved.

The bill mainly affects three groups: government regulators at EBSA, who would face new paperwork and reporting duties; employers and pension plan administrators, who would get more visibility into when the government is helping build a case against them; and employees or their lawyers, who might find it harder or slower to get government assistance if extra procedural steps are required first. The bill also adds language to federal retirement law stating that Congress wants to encourage employers to voluntarily offer pension plans, framing the changes as supporting the broader goal of keeping employer-sponsored retirement plans available and stable.
ai_headline: Labor department would face new limits on helping workers sue employers
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 430.

title: Modern Worker Empowerment Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Modern Worker Empowerment Act, would change how the federal government decides whether a worker counts as an "employee" or an "independent contractor." This distinction matters a lot because employees are protected by laws covering minimum wage, overtime pay, and the right to unionize, while independent contractors are not.

Under this bill, a worker would be classified as an independent contractor if the company doesn't control the specific details of how the work gets done (even if it controls the final result), and if the worker has some freedom to use business judgment or take on entrepreneurial risk. The bill also says certain common business practices can't be used as evidence that someone is an employee—for example, requiring workers to follow safety rules, carry insurance, meet deadlines, or comply with legal requirements. This standard would apply both to the Fair Labor Standards Act (which governs wages and hours) and the National Labor Relations Act (which governs unionizing rights).

This bill would primarily affect gig workers, freelancers, delivery drivers, rideshare drivers, and other workers whose employment status has been legally disputed in recent years. Businesses that rely on independent contractors, such as app-based platforms and staffing companies, would likely find it easier to classify workers as contractors rather than employees. Supporters argue this gives workers more flexibility and clarity, while critics worry it could make it easier for companies to avoid providing minimum wage, overtime, and union protections to workers who might otherwise qualify as employees.
ai_headline: Bill would make it easier to classify workers as contractors, not employees
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 431.

A worker could be classified as a contractor if the company doesn't control the specific details of the work and the worker has some business judgment or entrepreneurial risk. Common requirements like safety rules, insurance, deadlines, or legal compliance could not be used as evidence of employee status.

title: To amend the Federal Water Pollution Control Act to make certain technology investments eligible for additional subsidization, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill would update the Federal Water Pollution Control Act (commonly known as the Clean Water Act) to expand what types of projects can qualify for extra financial help, called additional subsidization, through the Clean Water State Revolving Fund program. This fund gives states money to make low-interest loans to communities for water infrastructure projects. The bill specifically adds new categories of eligible technology investments, including software used for managing infrastructure assets, software for analyzing how systems are operating, and advanced digital tools used in construction management.

In practical terms, this means local governments and water utilities that use modern software and digital technology to run their water systems more efficiently could get additional financial benefits when applying for these loans. The bill emphasizes projects that improve water efficiency, energy efficiency, reduce stormwater runoff, or are otherwise cost-effective and sustainably designed. By officially listing these digital tools as eligible, the bill makes it easier and clearer for communities to justify using loan funds on modern technology, not just physical construction like pipes or treatment plants.

This bill would mainly affect local governments, water utilities, and engineering or technology companies that build or supply water infrastructure software and digital systems. Taxpayers and water customers could see indirect effects too, since more efficient systems built with better technology may lower long-term costs or improve water and wastewater services in their communities. The change is relatively narrow and technical, focused on updating a single provision of existing law rather than creating a large new program.
ai_headline: Bill adds digital tools to eligible costs in water loan fund
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment.

title: Honor Our Commitment Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Honor Our Commitment Act of 2026, would stop the U.S. government from detaining or deporting certain Vietnamese nationals who have final orders of removal. To qualify for this protection, a person must be a citizen of Vietnam, must have entered the United States on or before July 12, 1995, and must have lived in the country continuously since then. There are exceptions: the protection would not apply if the Department of Homeland Security determines the person is a genuine security threat, or if the person is wanted for extradition to face charges elsewhere.

The bill also requires Homeland Security to notify eligible individuals within 60 days of the law passing, explaining their rights and how to file paperwork to reopen their old immigration cases. Additionally, it allows these individuals to legally work in the United States by giving them official work permits. Finally, the bill allows people harmed by violations of this law to sue in federal court, including through class action lawsuits.

This bill mainly affects long-term Vietnamese immigrants who came to the U.S. decades ago, often as refugees after the Vietnam War, but who later received deportation orders for various legal reasons. It would give many of them a way to stay in the country, work legally, and challenge their removal, unless they are considered dangerous or wanted for extradition.
ai_headline: Bill would shield long-term Vietnamese immigrants from deportation
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: American FIRST Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, known as the American FIRST Act of 2025, requires U.S. banking regulators to give Congress much more detailed yearly reports about their involvement with international financial organizations. The agencies affected are the Federal Reserve Board, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC). These are the agencies that oversee and regulate banks in the United States, and they often work with global groups like the Bank for International Settlements, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, and the Financial Stability Board to coordinate international banking rules.

Under this bill, each agency would have to report who funds these international groups, what positions U.S. regulators took at meetings, what new rules or standards were discussed or adopted, and how those changes might affect U.S. banks and the economy. The agencies would also need to explain how any new international agreements might require changes to U.S. laws or regulations, and justify whether the benefits of following international standards outweigh the costs. Additionally, Federal Reserve officials would have to testify to Congress twice a year specifically about these international interactions, on top of their existing testimony requirements.

The bill mainly affects how transparent and accountable U.S. bank regulators are to Congress, rather than changing how banks themselves operate. Its main effect would be giving lawmakers and the public more visibility into how international financial rule-making influences U.S. banking policy, and it does not directly change any banking rules, fees, or requirements for consumers or financial institutions.

title: Pay FEMA Personnel Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Pay FEMA Personnel Act of 2026, is designed to keep the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) running and its employees paid even if the federal government shuts down due to Congress failing to pass a budget. It sets aside money automatically so FEMA staff can keep receiving their regular pay, benefits, and allowances during a shutdown, whether they work on disaster relief programs or on other grants and contracts the agency manages. It also ensures FEMA can continue awarding and distributing grant money to communities even without normal funding in place.

The funding would start from February 14, 2026, and last until either Congress passes a real budget, passes a temporary funding measure, or until September 30, 2026, whichever comes first. Money spent under this law would later be counted against whatever official budget is eventually approved, so it's essentially a bridge measure, not new extra spending. The bill also applies retroactively to February 13, 2026, meaning it would cover any gap starting from that date.

This bill mainly affects FEMA employees, who would be protected from missing paychecks during a shutdown, and it affects communities and organizations that rely on FEMA disaster aid and grants, since those programs could keep operating without interruption. It does not address funding for other federal agencies—only FEMA.

title: Shivwits Band of Paiutes Jurisdictional Clarity Act
ai_summary:
This bill would give the State of Utah authority to hear civil lawsuits that involve the Shivwits Band of Paiutes, a federally recognized Native American tribe, when those lawsuits arise on the tribe's trust or restricted lands. Currently, legal jurisdiction over such matters can be unclear or split between tribal, state, and federal authorities, which can create confusion for businesses, contractors, or individuals dealing with the tribe. This bill aims to clarify that Utah state courts can handle these civil cases.

The bill also addresses federal court jurisdiction by stating that contracts or agreements involving the tribe's lands count as "commerce" under federal arbitration law, and that lawsuits arising from those contracts can be treated as federal cases under U.S. law. This makes it easier for disputes—such as those involving business deals, leases, or contracts on tribal land—to be resolved in federal court if needed. Importantly, the bill specifies that it does not take away the tribe's sovereign immunity, meaning the tribe still cannot be sued without its consent unless it chooses to waive that protection.

Finally, the bill updates a 1955 federal leasing law to specifically include land held in trust for the Shivwits Band of Paiutes, giving the tribe clearer authority to lease its trust lands, similar to rules already in place for other tribes. This bill mainly affects the Shivwits Band of Paiutes, Utah's court system, and anyone doing business, signing contracts, or engaging in legal disputes involving the tribe's lands.
ai_headline: Bill would let Utah courts hear civil suits on Shivwits Paiute land

title: Enhancing Bank Resolution Participation Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require two federal banking regulators, the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), to jointly study special tools used when a bank fails. The first tool, called a "shelf charter," lets investors get preliminary approval to start a new bank before they actually need it, so it's ready to quickly take over a failing bank's operations. The second tool, the "modified bidder qualification process," allows companies that don't already own a bank to bid on buying up a failed bank's assets and deposits. The study would look at how these tools have been used since 2008 and specifically examine whether they were considered during the 2023 bank failures (such as Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank).

The regulators would have 270 days to report their findings to Congress, including whether wider use of these tools could have attracted more bidders, increased competition, protected the FDIC's insurance fund, or reduced the need for emergency government interventions during a bank collapse. They would also need to identify any legal or regulatory obstacles preventing wider use of these tools and recommend changes, while consulting with the Federal Reserve on related legal questions.

This bill doesn't change any current banking rules or authorize any bank takeovers itself. It mainly affects federal banking regulators, who would have to spend time and resources conducting this study. Indirectly, it could affect banks, potential bank investors, and the broader financial system if Congress later acts on the report's recommendations to make it easier for a wider range of buyers to step in when a bank fails.

title: New Opportunities for Business Ownership and Self-Sufficiency Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes the rules for state "self-employment assistance" programs, which let unemployed workers use their unemployment benefits to start a business instead of job-hunting for an employer. Currently, federal law says someone can only join these programs if they're likely to run out of regular unemployment benefits soon. This bill removes that requirement, meaning more unemployed workers could qualify to try starting a business while collecting benefits, regardless of how much benefit time they have left.

The bill also updates what counts as an approved activity for participants—now including entrepreneurial training, business counseling, technical assistance, or working from an approved business plan and market feasibility study. Additionally, participants would need to check in weekly with a state-designated agency to report their progress. The cap on how many people nationwide can be enrolled in these programs is doubled, from 5% to 10% of the unemployment insurance system's participants.

This bill would mainly affect unemployed workers who want to start their own business instead of returning to traditional employment, as well as state unemployment agencies that run these programs. The changes wouldn't take effect until two years after the bill becomes law, though states could update their own laws sooner. Overall, the bill aims to make it easier and more common for unemployed Americans to use benefits toward launching a business rather than restricting the option to only those about to lose their unemployment payments.
ai_headline: Bill would expand access to self-employment programs for jobless workers

title: Securities Research Modernization Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal securities law to allow more companies to benefit from a rule about research reports. Under current law, when a brokerage firm or bank publishes research reports (analysis and opinions about a company's stock) while that company is preparing to sell securities to the public, there's a special exception that allows this for "emerging growth companies" (generally smaller, newer public companies) specifically regarding their common stock. This bill would expand that exception to cover any company issuing any type of security, not just emerging growth companies and not just common stock.

In practical terms, the bill removes limits on which companies can receive this treatment and what kinds of securities are covered. Currently, publishing research about a company during certain periods around a securities offering could be considered an improper "offer" under securities law unless the emerging-growth-company exception applies. By broadening this exception to all issuers and all security types (such as bonds or preferred stock, not just common stock), the bill would let banks and brokerages publish research reports more freely around a wider range of public securities offerings.

This change would primarily affect investment banks, brokerage firms, and financial analysts who produce research reports, as well as companies of all sizes planning to offer securities to the public. Investors could also be affected, since they may have access to more analyst research during the offering process. Supporters of this type of change typically argue it increases available information for investors, while critics may raise concerns about analysts issuing overly favorable research to help firms sell securities they're underwriting. The bill does not change other securities disclosure rules, only this specific research report exception.

title: BARCODE Efficiency Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the BARCODE Efficiency Act, aims to speed up how the IRS processes paper tax documents. If someone prepares their tax return using tax software but then prints it out and mails it in instead of e-filing, the printed form would have to include a scannable code (like a barcode or QR code) that contains all the return's data. The IRS would then be required to scan that code instead of manually typing the information into its computer systems, which should reduce errors and processing delays.

For paper returns that weren't prepared electronically, or in cases where the scannable code can't be read properly, the IRS would instead have to use optical character recognition (OCR) technology—software that can "read" printed text and convert it into digital data. This same OCR requirement would apply to other paper correspondence the IRS receives, such as letters or paper forms. The IRS could skip these tech requirements only if it determines the technology is actually slower or less reliable than current methods, but it would have to report that decision to Congress within 30 days.

This bill mainly affects the IRS's internal operations and, indirectly, taxpayers who file paper returns rather than e-filing. The changes would roll out gradually: about 6 months after the bill becomes law for individual income tax returns, about 12 months for most other returns and correspondence, and about 24 months for estate and gift tax returns. The goal is faster, more accurate processing of paper tax documents, which could mean quicker refunds and fewer errors for people who don't file electronically.

title: Excess Urban Heat Mitigation Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, the Excess Urban Heat Mitigation Act of 2025, directs the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to create a grant program that helps cities and towns deal with extreme heat. Congress notes that heat kills hundreds of Americans each year and that low-income areas and communities of color often have fewer trees and hotter temperatures than wealthier, whiter neighborhoods. The grants would fund projects like planting trees, installing cool or green roofs, building shaded bus stops, creating cooling centers, starting community gardens, and developing city-wide tree canopy plans. States, cities, tribal governments, and nonprofits (working with local governments) could apply for the money.

The bill requires that at least 75% of grant funding go to high-poverty census tracts, including historically "redlined" neighborhoods that were unfairly denied investment decades ago. Applicants generally have to cover 20% of project costs themselves, though HUD can waive this for communities facing economic hardship. A portion of the funding is set aside for technical assistance to help communities apply for and carry out projects, and a small oversight board—including representatives from the EPA, HHS, Energy Department, USDA, nonprofits, and academic experts—would help select grant winners and track their progress. HUD would report yearly to Congress on who received funding and where.

This would primarily affect city and local governments, tribal governments, nonprofit organizations, and residents of hotter, lower-income urban neighborhoods, who could benefit from cooler streets, more shade, and reduced heat-related health and energy costs. The program would be funded at $30 million per year from 2026 through 2033, and would need to be established within a year of the bill becoming law.

title: Addressing Hostile and Antisemitic Conduct by the Republic of South Africa Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, introduced in the House in June 2025, would place new restrictions on U.S. dealings with the South African government in response to actions Congress views as hostile toward Israel and Jewish communities, including South Africa's legal case against Israel at the International Court of Justice. The bill would cut off most direct U.S. government assistance to South Africa unless the Secretary of State certifies that the country has stopped supporting legal actions seen as unfairly targeting Israel or Jewish people, made progress fighting government corruption, and cooperated with U.S. diplomats on these issues. Humanitarian aid and public health programs run by nongovernmental organizations would be exempt from this cutoff.

The bill also directs the President to impose targeted sanctions (travel bans and financial restrictions) on any South African official, past or present, who promotes antisemitic policies, uses their office to target Israel or Jewish individuals in international venues, or engages in serious corruption involving public funds or foreign aid. The State Department would have to report to Congress within 90 days on South Africa's actions toward Israel and Jewish institutions over the past five years, plus a summary of U.S. assistance provided, with annual updates for three years. These restrictions would end once the President certifies South Africa has changed course on these fronts.

This bill primarily affects the South African government, its officials, and U.S. agencies that administer foreign aid. It would not affect private charitable giving, general diplomatic contact, or trade and tariff policies unrelated to these specific issues. American taxpayers would be affected indirectly, since it would limit how U.S. foreign aid dollars can be spent regarding South Africa.

title: Promoting Free and Fair Elections Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Promoting Free and Fair Elections Act of 2025, would limit how federal government agencies can be involved in voter registration efforts. It specifically targets Executive Order 14019, a 2021 order that directed federal agencies to take steps to make voting easier and encourage voter participation. The bill says that order would no longer apply where it conflicts with existing federal voter registration law, and it would stop agencies from using taxpayer money to pursue the order's goals until they first report to Congress on what plans they had already made under it.

The bill also stops federal agencies from partnering with outside nonprofit or advocacy organizations to register voters or hand out voting materials (like absentee ballot applications or voting instructions) on government property or government websites. Additionally, it changes federal work-study rules so that college students working federally funded jobs could no longer be assigned to register or mobilize voters as part of that work, whether on or off campus. Agencies would also be required to file reports with Congress within 30 days describing any voter-related activities they had already carried out under the executive order.

This bill would primarily affect federal agencies and their employees, nonprofit organizations that partner with government agencies on voter outreach, and college students in work-study programs who might have been involved in voter registration drives. It would not change state or local election laws, but it would restrict the federal government's own role in encouraging voter registration and turnout.

title: Downpayment Toward Equity Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Downpayment Toward Equity Act of 2025, would create a federal program giving money to first-generation homebuyers to help them purchase a home. The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) would distribute grant money to states and certain organizations (like community development banks, nonprofits, and local governments), which would then give assistance directly to qualifying buyers. This money could cover down payments, closing costs, interest rate reductions, or modifications needed for buyers with disabilities. Grants would be capped at $20,000 or 10% of the home's price, though HUD could allow more in expensive housing markets or for disadvantaged buyers. The bill authorizes $100 billion for this program.

To qualify, a buyer must have income at or below 120% (or 140% in high-cost areas) of their area's median income, be a first-time homebuyer, and be a "first-generation" buyer—meaning their parents never owned a home, or they grew up in foster care. Buyers would self-report this eligibility without needing extra paperwork, and lenders wouldn't be penalized if a buyer's self-reported information turns out to be inaccurate. Recipients generally must live in the home for five years or gradually repay the assistance if they move out or sell early, though hardship exceptions apply. Buyers must also complete a homeownership counseling course.

This bill would primarily affect lower- and middle-income Americans trying to buy their first home, especially those from families with no prior homeownership history. It's designed with an explicit goal of narrowing the racial homeownership gap, and includes provisions requiring HUD to track demographic data, ensure fair housing compliance, and reallocate funds if a state isn't distributing aid equitably across racial groups. State housing agencies, nonprofits, community banks, and local governments would take on new administrative responsibilities to run these programs, and HUD would gain expanded authority to set rules and monitor outcomes.

title: Reserved for the Speaker.
ai_summary:
This bill number, HR 10, does not contain any actual legislative text. It is labeled "Reserved for the Speaker," which is a common practice in Congress where certain low bill numbers, like HR 1, HR 2, HR 10, and similar numbers, are set aside for the use of House leadership, particularly the Speaker of the House.

These reserved numbers are often used later for priority legislation that leadership wants to highlight, but until that happens, the bill number exists without any actual content, policy proposals, or effects. Because there is no substantive text, this placeholder does not do anything and does not affect any individuals, businesses, or government programs at this time.

If the Speaker later assigns real legislative content to HR 10, a new explanation would need to be based on that actual text once it is introduced.

title: RED TAPE Act
ai_summary:
The RED TAPE Act would change how federal agencies analyze the costs and benefits of new regulations. Currently, when agencies write rules (like environmental protections, workplace safety standards, or consumer regulations), they often consider factors that are hard to put a dollar value on, such as fairness, community impact, or long-term environmental health, alongside factors that can be measured in dollars. This bill would ban agencies from considering any factor in their official analysis that cannot be assigned a specific monetary value. It would also stop the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), which oversees agency rulemaking, from allowing or considering such non-monetized factors.

The bill requires agencies to publicly publish detailed cost-benefit analyses and methodology for every proposed rule, and gives OMB 90 days to issue new guidance ensuring compliance. Importantly, it also creates a new legal tool: any person or business affected by a federal rule could sue in court if they believe an agency improperly relied on non-monetized factors, and if a judge agrees, the rule would be automatically thrown out. This provision would apply retroactively to rules issued since November 2023.

This bill would primarily affect federal agencies that write regulations—such as the EPA, Labor Department, FDA, and others—by limiting the kinds of justifications they can use to support new rules. It would also affect businesses, advocacy groups, and individuals who might use the new lawsuit provision to challenge regulations they oppose. Supporters argue this would make regulations more predictable and focused on measurable economic effects, while critics may argue it could make it harder to justify rules addressing harder-to-quantify concerns like environmental justice, public health risks, or safety.
ai_headline: Bill would bar agencies from citing non-dollar factors in rules
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, and in addition to the Committee on Small Business, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

title: SOAR Permanent Authorization Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes changes to the SOAR Act, which runs the D.C. Opportunity Scholarship Program—a federally funded program that gives lower-income Washington, D.C. families vouchers to help pay private school tuition. The bill would allow grants to the organizations running the program to be renewed for up to 5 more years without requiring a new competitive application process, and it increases the total money authorized for the program from $60 million to $75 million per year starting in fiscal year 2027. It also expands who can serve on the boards of participating organizations, allowing members to live anywhere in the broader Washington metro area (including nearby Maryland and Virginia counties) rather than only in D.C. itself.

The bill also updates several operational details: schools can now count accreditation from a wider range of recognized bodies, scholarship money can be used for pre-kindergarten (not just kindergarten and up), organizations can set lower maximum scholarship amounts if they choose, and scholarship funds can now also pay for tutoring services for students needing extra academic help. It changes how often the program must be formally evaluated (from more frequent reviews to reports every 7 years, with the next one due by January 1, 2028) and adjusts what those evaluations must measure, including comparing academic progress, graduation rates, college enrollment, and school safety between scholarship students and public school students.

This bill mainly affects D.C. families who use or might use these scholarships, the private schools that accept them, and the nonprofit organizations that administer the program. It also affects federal agencies like the Department of Education, which oversees evaluations and reporting. It does not appear to change eligibility rules for individual students or families directly, but it does adjust funding levels, oversight requirements, and administrative flexibility for the program going forward.

title: REVIEW Act of 2025
ai_summary:
**HR 6544 — REVIEW Act of 2025** would change how often and how thoroughly federal banking and financial regulators check whether their rules are working well or creating unnecessary burdens. Currently, a 1996 law requires these agencies to review their regulations once every 10 years and ask the public for feedback. This bill shortens that cycle to once every 5 years, meaning reviews happen twice as often.

The bill also expands who is covered—broadening the review requirement from just "banking agencies" to the wider group of "financial institutions regulatory agencies"—and adds a new requirement for each agency to conduct its own internal review, separate from public comments. This internal review must look at how regulations affect consumers' access to financial products, how they affect availability of credit and financial services for businesses, how they impact market liquidity, and whether the benefits of the rules outweigh their costs. Agencies would also need to estimate the economic costs of their regulations where possible and recommend ways to simplify, streamline, or eliminate rules that are outdated, duplicative, or overly burdensome. A summary of these internal findings would then be included in reports sent to Congress.

This bill primarily affects federal agencies that regulate banks and other financial institutions, such as the Federal Reserve, FDIC, and similar bodies. Indirectly, it affects everyday consumers and businesses that use financial products and services, since the goal is to identify and potentially reduce regulations that make banking, lending, or financial services more costly or harder to access. Banks and financial companies dealing with regulatory compliance would also be affected by any changes that result from these more frequent reviews.
ai_headline: Bill would double frequency of bank regulation reviews to every 5 years
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 452.

It also expands coverage from "banking agencies" to the broader "financial institutions regulatory agencies" and adds a new internal review requirement covering consumer access, credit availability, market liquidity, and cost-benefit analysis, with findings summarized for Congress.

title: Digital Commodity Intermediaries Act
ai_summary:
S 3755, the Digital Commodity Intermediaries Act, sets up a new system for the federal government to regulate cryptocurrencies and similar digital assets, mainly through the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). Right now, most crypto is traded without clear federal oversight rules for the exchanges, brokers, and dealers that handle it. This bill creates legal definitions for terms like "digital commodity," "digital asset," "blockchain," and "decentralized finance," and requires companies that operate crypto exchanges or act as brokers/dealers in digital commodities to register with the CFTC, similar to how stock brokers register with the SEC. It also requires customer crypto funds to be held by "qualified digital asset custodians" (regulated entities like banks or trust companies) rather than just kept by the trading company itself, which is meant to protect customers if a company fails or misuses funds.

The bill affects several groups. Crypto exchanges, trading platforms, and brokers/dealers will need to register with the CFTC and follow new rules on custody, conflicts of interest, recordkeeping, and disclosures, with penalties for operating unregistered after certain deadlines. It also coordinates with the SEC to sort out which digital assets count as "commodities" (CFTC's job) versus "securities" (SEC's job), and creates rules for "mixed" transactions involving both. Software developers, decentralized finance protocols, and certain "decentralized governance systems" get some protections or exclusions from being treated as regulated intermediaries, as long as they don't control user funds. Everyday crypto investors and users are affected indirectly: the goal is more consumer protection (like required disclosures and safer custody of funds), but the bill also creates a formal, regulated marketplace, which could change how crypto companies operate, what coins they can offer, and how disputes or fraud are handled. Full implementation would take about 18 months after the bill becomes law, with various CFTC and SEC rulemakings needed to fill in the details.
ai_headline: New bill would set federal rules for crypto exchanges and brokers
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 312.

Full implementation would take about 18 months, with CFTC and SEC rulemakings needed to fill in details.

title: 123 GO Act
ai_summary:
**H.R. 4263 — "123 GO Act"** aims to help U.S. nuclear power companies compete for business in other countries. The bill's main focus is on "123 agreements," which are formal deals the U.S. signs with other nations under the Atomic Energy Act that allow peaceful nuclear cooperation, such as sharing technology or selling nuclear fuel and equipment. The bill directs the Secretary of State to negotiate at least 20 new agreements like this by January 2029, and to renew or update existing agreements that are set to expire within the next 10 years.

The bill also requires the State Department, working with the Commerce and Energy Departments and White House science and economic advisors, to create a program that makes it easier for American nuclear companies, investors, and lenders to win contracts overseas. This includes speeding up government-to-government agreements on nuclear fuel supply, encouraging more countries to join an international treaty on compensating victims of nuclear accidents, identifying U.S. rules or laws that make it harder to export nuclear technology, and generally encouraging foreign governments to choose U.S. nuclear products and services over competitors from other countries like Russia or China.

This bill mainly affects the nuclear energy industry, including companies that build reactors or supply nuclear fuel, as well as U.S. government agencies involved in diplomacy, trade, and energy policy. It does not directly affect individual consumers, but it could influence U.S. foreign relations, trade policy, and the global nuclear energy market. It also references an executive order on advanced nuclear reactor technology, expressing Congress's support for that policy direction.
ai_headline: Bill directs push for 20 new U.S. nuclear trade pacts by 2029
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Foreign Affairs, and in addition to the Committees on Armed Services, Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, and Science, Space, and Technology, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

It also requires State, Commerce, and Energy departments, plus White House advisors, to create a program helping U.S. nuclear companies win overseas contracts, speed fuel-supply agreements, and promote a treaty on nuclear accident compensation.

title: STAR Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the STAR Act of 2025, would expand an existing tax credit for semiconductor (computer chip) manufacturing to also cover chip design work. Currently, companies can get a 25% tax credit for building or investing in chip manufacturing facilities in the United States. This bill adds a new 25% tax credit for money companies spend on designing semiconductors in the United States, including employee wages for design work, supplies used in design, computer resources used for design, and payments to outside contractors who do design work.

The bill carefully defines what counts as "qualified" design work, generally meaning research and development aimed at creating new or improved chip functions, performance, or reliability. It excludes things like cosmetic design choices, routine testing, market research, or copying an existing chip design. It also includes rules to prevent companies from claiming this new credit and a separate research tax credit for the same expenses. The credit would apply to money spent after the bill becomes law and would expire for expenses or construction after December 31, 2036.

This bill mainly affects semiconductor companies, from large chip manufacturers to smaller design firms and startups, by making it cheaper for them to do chip design work in the U.S. rather than overseas. It could indirectly affect American workers in the tech and engineering fields, since it encourages companies to hire chip designers domestically. Taxpayers broadly are affected because the credit reduces tax revenue collected from these companies, similar to other business tax incentives.
ai_headline: Bill would add 25% tax credit for US chip design work
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: The STAR Act of 2025 would give a 25% tax credit for semiconductor design expenses in the U.S., through 2036.

It defines qualifying design work and bars companies from claiming both this credit and a separate research credit for the same expenses. The credit applies to spending after enactment and expires for expenses or construction after December 31, 2036.

ai_sections.why: By lowering the cost of U.S.-based chip design, the bill could shift design work away from overseas locations. The tax credit also reduces the amount of tax revenue collected from affected companies.

title: Respect State Housing Laws Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change a rule left over from the 2020 CARES Act, the law Congress passed early in the COVID-19 pandemic. That law included a section requiring landlords of certain federally backed rental properties to give tenants at least 30 days' notice before requiring them to move out for not paying rent. This bill would remove that 30-day notice requirement entirely by striking it from the law.

In practical terms, this means landlords covered by that section of the CARES Act would no longer be bound by a federal notice period and would instead follow whatever eviction notice rules exist under their state or local laws. Some states require shorter notice periods, others require longer ones, so the effect would vary depending on where a tenant lives. The bill's name reflects its stated purpose: supporters argue that housing and eviction procedures should be governed by state law rather than a federal mandate that was originally tied to a temporary pandemic emergency.

This bill would primarily affect renters and landlords in properties with federally backed mortgages, such as those insured or backed by agencies like Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, or HUD programs. Tenants in these properties could see their eviction notice timelines shortened or lengthened depending on their state's laws, while landlords would have more flexibility to follow state procedures instead of the specific federal standard set in 2020.
ai_headline: Bill would end CARES Act's 30-day eviction notice rule
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 446.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 1078 would strike the CARES Act's 30-day eviction notice requirement, leaving notice periods to state and local law.
ai_sections.what: This bill would remove the CARES Act provision requiring landlords of certain federally backed rental properties to give tenants at least 30 days' notice before eviction for nonpayment of rent. Landlords would instead follow whatever state or local eviction notice rules apply.

ai_sections.why: Eviction notice timelines for affected tenants could get shorter or longer depending on state law, since the federal 30-day floor would no longer apply.

title: One Citizen, One Seat Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "One Citizen, One Seat Act," would require the U.S. Census Bureau to redo the population counts from the 2020 census so that only U.S. citizens are counted, leaving out non-citizens (such as green card holders, visa holders, or people living in the country illegally). The Secretary of Commerce, who oversees the Census Bureau, would have to send each state this revised, citizens-only population number within 60 days of the bill becoming law.

The bill would also require states to actually use these new citizen-only numbers for anything they previously used the regular census numbers for. This matters because census population counts are used for many important purposes, including drawing congressional districts, deciding how many seats in the House of Representatives each state gets, and distributing federal money for programs like schools, roads, and healthcare. To enforce this, the bill says that starting 60 days after a state receives the new numbers, that state cannot receive federal grant money unless it switches entirely to using the citizens-only counts.

This bill would affect all 50 states, since it changes how population is measured nationwide. States with large populations of non-citizens would likely see bigger changes to their official population totals, which could affect their political representation in Congress and the amount of federal funding they receive. State and local governments, agencies that rely on federal grants, and residents in areas with significant non-citizen populations could all be impacted by this change.
ai_headline: Bill would redo 2020 census to count only U.S. citizens
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

ai_sections.what: The bill requires the Census Bureau to redo 2020 census population counts excluding non-citizens, and gives each state this revised number within 60 days of enactment. States would then have to use these citizens-only numbers for all purposes that previously relied on regular census data, including redistricting and House seat allocation.
ai_sections.who: All 50 states are affected, with states that have large non-citizen populations likely seeing bigger changes. State and local governments, federal grant recipients, and residents of areas with significant non-citizen populations would feel the impact.

title: Gateway Partnership Act
ai_summary:
This bill would let the Secretary of the Interior make a formal agreement with the Gateway Arch Park Foundation, a nonprofit partner group, to host private events inside buildings at Gateway Arch National Park in St. Louis, such as the Arch Visitor Center and the Old Courthouse. The agreement would set rules for how many events can happen each week, require proper National Park Service staffing, and require the Foundation to carry enough liability insurance to protect the federal government from being sued over injuries or damages connected to these events.

The bill also requires that any private events fit with the park's purpose and not damage its appearance or historical value, and that they not block public access to the park or its buildings during normal use times. The Secretary must charge fees to cover wear and tear on the buildings and can also recover other costs, like staff time, related to hosting these events. The National Park Service would still be free to hold its own events or grant permits to other groups separately.

This bill mainly affects visitors to Gateway Arch National Park, the National Park Service, and the Gateway Arch Park Foundation. It could open the door to private events (such as weddings, receptions, or fundraisers) being held in park buildings, while aiming to make sure taxpayers aren't stuck with any costs or legal risks from those events, and that public access to the park isn't reduced.
ai_headline: Bill would allow private events inside Gateway Arch buildings
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

The agreement would limit weekly event numbers, require National Park Service staffing, and require the Foundation to carry liability insurance. title: Regulation A+ Improvement Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 6541, the "Regulation A+ Improvement Act of 2025," changes the rules for how small companies can raise money from investors without going through the full, expensive process of registering with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Currently, companies using this simplified fundraising method (known as Regulation A+) can raise up to $50 million per year. This bill raises that limit to $150 million, and requires the SEC to adjust that number every two years to keep up with inflation, based on the Consumer Price Index.

In plain terms, this makes it easier for small and mid-sized businesses to raise larger amounts of money from everyday investors without the heavy paperwork and legal costs required for a traditional public stock offering. It mainly affects small businesses looking to grow, startup founders, and investors (including regular individuals, not just wealthy or institutional investors) who might buy shares in these companies. It could also affect the SEC, which oversees these rules and would need to periodically update the dollar limits.

This bill does not change other investor protections or disclosure requirements tied to Regulation A+; it specifically focuses on raising the dollar cap on how much money can be raised under this simplified process and ensuring that cap rises with inflation over time.
ai_headline: Bill would triple cap on Regulation A+ small business fundraising
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 451.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6541 would raise the annual Regulation A+ fundraising cap from $50 million to $150 million, adjusted for inflation.
ai_sections.what: HR 6541 raises the annual limit small companies can raise under Regulation A+, a simplified SEC fundraising method, from $50 million to $150 million. It also requires the SEC to adjust this cap every two years based on the Consumer Price Index. Other investor protections and disclosure rules under Regulation A+ remain unchanged.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects small and mid-sized businesses, startup founders, and everyday individual investors who buy shares through Regulation A+ offerings. It also affects the SEC, which must periodically update the dollar cap.

This shifts regulatory responsibility onto the SEC to maintain updated inflation-adjusted limits.

title: Gun Owner Registration Information Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Gun Owner Registration Information Protection Act, would stop federal agencies from giving money or other support to states that want to create or maintain databases listing gun owners or the firearms they legally own. In other words, if a state wanted to build a system tracking who owns guns, the federal government could not help pay for it or otherwise support it. This applies to all states, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories like Puerto Rico and Guam.

There is one exception: federal agencies could still support state databases that track firearms or owners who have reported their guns as lost or stolen. This carve-out means law enforcement could still get federal help maintaining records related to stolen or missing weapons, but not general registries of legal gun owners.

This bill would mainly affect state governments that rely on federal funding or technical support for record-keeping systems, as well as federal agencies that currently provide such support. It would not directly change any laws about who can own a gun or how background checks work; it specifically targets federal financial or logistical involvement in building databases that list lawful gun owners. Gun owners themselves would be affected indirectly, since it aims to limit the creation of government databases containing their personal ownership information.
ai_headline: Bill would bar federal aid to states building gun owner databases
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill would block federal money or support for state databases listing legal gun owners, except stolen-firearm records.
ai_sections.what: The Gun Owner Registration Information Protection Act would stop federal agencies from funding or supporting state efforts to build or maintain databases of gun owners or their legally owned firearms. It applies to all states, DC, and U.S. territories. An exception allows federal support for databases tracking guns or owners reported as lost or stolen.
ai_sections.who: State governments that depend on federal funding or technical help for record-keeping systems, and federal agencies currently providing that support. Gun owners are indirectly affected since the bill limits databases containing their ownership information.

title: Respect State Housing Laws Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change a rule that was originally created during the COVID-19 pandemic as part of the CARES Act. That law included a provision requiring landlords of certain federally backed rental properties to give tenants at least 30 days' notice before requiring them to move out for not paying rent. This bill would remove that 30-day notice requirement entirely from federal law.

In practical terms, this means landlords covered by that section of the CARES Act would no longer be bound by a federal rule dictating how much notice they must give tenants before starting eviction proceedings. Instead, the amount of notice required would be left entirely up to whatever rules each state or local government has in place, since many states already have their own notice-period laws for evictions. The bill's name, "Respect State Housing Laws Act," reflects its stated purpose of letting state and local housing laws govern this issue instead of a federal mandate left over from the pandemic emergency.

This would primarily affect tenants living in properties with federally backed mortgages (such as those insured by the FHA or backed by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac) and the landlords who own those properties. Depending on the state, some tenants might see shorter or different notice periods before eviction proceedings could begin, while landlords would have more flexibility to follow only state and local timelines rather than an additional federal requirement.

last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

title: North Rim Restoration Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the North Rim Restoration Act of 2025, gives the National Park Service faster and more flexible tools to hire contractors to repair damage at Grand Canyon National Park caused by the Dragon Bravo Fire. Normally, government contracting involves a lengthy approval process, but this bill lets the Secretary of the Interior (through the National Park Service) use emergency contracting rules to quickly approve companies to clear debris, rebuild structures, manage forest recovery, and make improvements in the fire-damaged area. This authority only applies to work directly related to fire recovery, not to unrelated park projects.

To make sure this speeded-up process is used responsibly, the bill requires regular reports to Congress every 180 days. These reports must detail how much money is being spent, which contractors are doing the work, whether there are any conflicts of interest, and whether there are signs of waste, fraud, or abuse. The reports must also estimate when the recovery work will be finished. If another wildfire breaks out and disrupts the recovery efforts, the agency can ask Congress for a 12-month extension. Otherwise, this special authority automatically ends after five years or once recovery work is complete, whichever happens first.

This bill mainly affects the National Park Service, government contractors bidding on recovery work, and people who use or care about Grand Canyon National Park, including nearby communities and visitors who want the North Rim facilities rebuilt and reopened faster. It does not change contracting rules anywhere else or for any other type of project.
ai_headline: Bill would fast-track contracting to rebuild fire-damaged Grand Canyon North Rim
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

The authority ends after five years or when recovery is complete, whichever comes first, though a new wildfire disruption could trigger a 12-month extension request.
