title: To amend the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 to repeal certain disclosure requirements related to conflict minerals, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill would remove a rule that currently requires certain publicly traded companies to check and report whether the minerals they use in their products come from conflict zones, particularly the Democratic Republic of Congo and neighboring countries. This rule, known as the "conflict minerals" provision, was created as part of the 2010 Dodd-Frank financial reform law. It targets four minerals often called "3TG" — tin, tantalum, tungsten, and gold — because profits from mining these minerals have historically been used to fund armed groups involved in violence in central Africa.

The bill would eliminate this requirement entirely by repealing the relevant section of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and removing Section 1502 from the Dodd-Frank Act. In practice, this means companies that manufacture electronics, jewelry, cars, and other products using these minerals would no longer have to investigate their supply chains or file public reports with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) disclosing whether their materials are linked to conflict financing.

This change would primarily affect large publicly traded manufacturers, which have argued that the reporting requirements are costly and burdensome, especially since supply chains can be complex and hard to trace. It would also affect human rights organizations and advocacy groups, who have used these disclosures to pressure companies toward more ethical sourcing practices. Consumers would likely see no direct or immediate effects, but they would lose access to public information about whether products they buy contain minerals connected to conflict in central Africa.
ai_headline: Bill would repeal Dodd-Frank's conflict minerals disclosure rule
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 481.

title: Daylight Act of 2026
ai_summary:
HR 7378, the "Daylight Act of 2026," would permanently change how U.S. time zones are set and end the twice-yearly practice of switching clocks for daylight saving time. Instead of eliminating daylight saving time by keeping standard time (as some past proposals have suggested), this bill takes a different approach: it shifts every U.S. time zone's official offset from Greenwich Mean Time by half an hour, effectively locking in something close to permanent daylight saving time without requiring clocks to change twice a year. For example, zones currently offset by 5 hours would become 4.5 hours, and so on across all the listed time zones.

In practical terms, this means Americans would stop the biannual ritual of "springing forward" and "falling back" each year. Instead, the country would settle into one fixed time year-round that is closer to what most areas currently experience during daylight saving time (meaning later sunsets, especially in the summer, and correspondingly later sunrises in the winter). The change would take effect 90 days after the bill becomes law, if passed.

This bill would affect nearly everyone in the United States, since it changes how clocks are set nationwide. Industries that rely on precise scheduling across time zones, such as airlines, broadcasting, shipping, and international business, would need to adjust their systems accordingly. It would also affect people's daily routines, including school start times, sunrise-dependent work like farming, and general daylight patterns throughout the year. This bill is currently just introduced and referred to committee, meaning it would need further approval from Congress and the President before becoming law.
ai_headline: Bill would shift all US time zones by 30 minutes, ending clock changes
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: School Resource Officer Reform Act
ai_summary:
HR 4248, called the "School Resource Officer Reform Act," would change federal tax rules and death benefit rules for certain school resource officers—the police officers who work at schools to help with safety.

The bill has two main parts. First, it would let retired law enforcement officers who come back to work as armed school resource officers exclude their pay from federal income taxes. This means that money wouldn't count as taxable income, and it also wouldn't be subject to Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes or federal income tax withholding. This benefit would only apply to retired officers who left their previous law enforcement job "in good standing" and are now working as armed officers at a public elementary or secondary school. Second, the bill would add "school resource officer" to the list of jobs covered under the federal Public Safety Officers' Benefits program. This program provides a payment to the families of police officers, firefighters, and similar public safety workers who are killed or seriously injured in the line of duty. By adding school resource officers to this list, their families would become eligible for these federal death and disability benefits if something happened to them while working.

This bill would mainly affect retired police officers who take jobs as armed school resource officers, giving them a tax break on that income, as well as their families, who would gain access to federal benefits in case of death or injury on the job. It could also affect school districts that employ these officers, since the tax change might make these positions more attractive to retired law enforcement officers looking for post-retirement work.

title: AID Youth Employment Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the AID Youth Employment Act, would create a new federal grant program to help states, local governments, Native American tribes, and community organizations pay for summer and year-round jobs for young people ages 14 to 24. The Department of Labor would award competitive grants for both planning (designing a program) and implementation (actually running it). Up to $1.8 billion could go toward summer jobs programs and up to $2.4 billion toward year-round jobs programs, with money authorized from 2026 through 2030. At least 20% of summer job funds would go to rural areas and at least 5% to tribal areas, and funding would be split evenly between programs serving students still in school and those who have left school.

To qualify, applicants would need to team up with several partners, such as school districts, workforce agencies, juvenile justice or child welfare agencies, and employers. Programs would be required to pay at least minimum wage, limit weekly work hours depending on the participant's age and school status, and offer support like mentoring, counseling, transportation help, and connections to future job or education opportunities. Extra attention would go toward "marginalized" youth, including those who are homeless, in foster care, involved in the justice system, or living in communities affected by poverty or violence.

This bill mainly affects young people looking for work experience, especially those facing economic or social hardship, as well as the schools, tribal governments, nonprofits, and local agencies that would apply for and run these employment programs. Employers who hire youth through subsidized positions would also benefit, since part of the wage costs would be covered by grant funds. The Department of Labor would oversee the program, track outcomes like job placement and education credentials, and report results to Congress each year.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

title: To take certain land in the State of California into trust for the benefit of the Pechanga Band of Indians, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill would transfer about 1,261 acres of federal land in Riverside County, California, from the U.S. Bureau of Land Management into trust status for the Pechanga Band of Indians, a Native American tribe. When land is "taken into trust," it legally becomes part of the tribe's reservation and is managed under the same rules that apply to other tribal trust lands, rather than being treated as ordinary federal public land.

The bill places specific limits on how this land can be used. It must remain as open space and can only be used for purposes that protect and preserve archaeological sites, cultural resources, and wildlife on the property. Construction of utilities or structures is allowed only if it supports those same preservation goals. Gambling operations, including both class II and class III gaming under federal Indian gaming law, are explicitly banned on this land. Existing legal rights—such as water rights, road access agreements, leases, and easements—must stay in place and are not changed by this transfer.

This bill mainly affects the Pechanga Band of Indians, who would gain trust status over this land, as well as nearby residents, land users, and government agencies connected to existing agreements on the property, including a memorandum of understanding tied to the Santa Margarita Ecological Reserve. The tribe is required to notify Congress and federal officials if that agreement ends or is violated. Overall, the bill is a fairly narrow, location-specific land transfer rather than a broad policy change affecting people outside this particular area.

title: North Dakota Trust Lands Completion Act of 2026
ai_summary:
**H.R. 2252 — North Dakota Trust Lands Completion Act of 2026**

This bill sets up a land-swap system in North Dakota to fix a long-standing problem: when the state became a state, it received certain "school land" parcels to generate money for schools and universities, but some of those parcels ended up located inside Indian reservations. This creates conflicts over jurisdiction and management. Under this bill, North Dakota could voluntarily give up its ownership of these state land parcels that sit within reservation boundaries. In exchange, the federal government would let the state pick other, roughly equal-value federal land elsewhere in North Dakota (land managed by the Bureau of Land Management) to replace what it gave up. The land given up by the state would then be transferred to the federal government, and if the affected Tribe requests it, that land would be placed into trust for the Tribe and become officially part of the reservation.

The bill lays out detailed rules for how this trade would work: land values must be appraised and roughly balanced (with limited cash payments or "ledger accounts" allowed to settle small differences), certain sensitive federal lands (like conservation areas, military land, or land within reservations) can't be selected as replacements, and existing leases, grazing permits, and mineral rights would generally carry over to whoever ends up owning the land. Tribes must be consulted before any relinquished land inside their reservation is transferred. The bill also makes clear that it doesn't change any existing treaty rights, doesn't affect land already held in trust for Tribes, and doesn't interfere with any ongoing lawsuits over land or mineral ownership in the state.

This mainly affects North Dakota's state government (specifically the agency that manages school trust lands), Indian Tribes with reservations in North Dakota, and the federal Bureau of Land Management. It could also indirectly affect ranchers with grazing leases, energy companies with mineral leases, and residents near affected lands, since ownership and management of certain parcels would shift as a result of these exchanges.
ai_headline: North Dakota could swap reservation school lands for federal land elsewhere

title: Chiricahua National Park Act
ai_summary:
This bill would upgrade Chiricahua National Monument in southeastern Arizona to full "National Park" status, renaming it "Chiricahua National Park." The boundaries would stay exactly the same as they are now, and any money already set aside for the monument would automatically carry over to the newly named park. All existing rules, laws, and presidential proclamations that currently govern the monument would continue to apply, along with the general laws that apply to all national parks.

The bill also includes specific protections for Native American cultural and religious sites within the park. The Secretary of the Interior would be required to protect these sites and consult with Indian Tribes about them. Tribal members would be guaranteed access to these sites for traditional and customary purposes, and tribes could request that the Secretary temporarily close small parts of the park to the general public in order to protect ongoing cultural or religious activities. Any such closure would have to be as small and short as possible.

This bill mainly affects visitors to and the management of Chiricahua National Monument, which is a scenic area known for unusual rock formations. A name change to "National Park" often increases public recognition and tourism, since "National Park" is viewed as a more prestigious designation than "National Monument," potentially boosting visitor numbers and local tourism economies. Native American tribes with historical or cultural ties to the area would gain formal, legally protected access rights to sacred or culturally important sites within the park, which is the most substantive policy change beyond the name and status upgrade.
ai_headline: Chiricahua National Monument would become a national park

title: Senior Savings Protection Act
ai_summary:
HR 6210, called the "Senior Savings Protection Act," continues funding for programs that help older Americans and low-income people understand and access benefits like Medicare and other assistance programs. It extends money for four types of programs through fiscal years 2026 to 2030: State Health Insurance Assistance Programs (which offer free, one-on-one Medicare counseling), Area Agencies on Aging (which coordinate local services for seniors), Aging and Disability Resource Centers (which help people find services for aging or disability needs), and efforts to inform older Americans about benefits they may qualify for under federal and state programs.

Specifically, the bill sets aside $15 million per year for State Health Insurance Assistance Programs, $15 million per year for Area Agencies on Aging, $5 million per year for Aging and Disability Resource Centers, and $15 million per year for benefit outreach coordination efforts, each for five years (2026 through 2030). This is essentially a renewal of existing funding authority that would otherwise expire, rather than the creation of a brand-new program.

This bill mainly affects senior citizens, people with disabilities, and low-income individuals who rely on these programs for help navigating Medicare, Medicaid, and other government benefits. It also affects the local and state organizations, such as area aging agencies and counseling services, that receive federal funding to run these outreach and assistance efforts. Indirectly, it affects taxpayers, since it continues a specific stream of federal spending for these purposes.

title: Closing the Bump Stock Loophole Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would ban devices that make semiautomatic guns fire faster, like bump stocks and similar attachments or modifications. Specifically, it would make it illegal to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess devices that attach to a semiautomatic firearm and either significantly increase its rate of fire or make it act like a fully automatic machine gun. It would also ban firearms that have been modified in ways that produce these same effects, even without an added device. This closes what lawmakers call a "loophole" left after a 2024 Supreme Court ruling that said the ATF could not regulate bump stocks under existing law, since the agency's ban was struck down for exceeding its authority.

The bill also updates legal definitions in federal gun law to clearly define what counts as a "semiautomatic firearm" and adds these rate-of-fire-increasing modifications to the legal category of regulated weapons under the National Firearms Act, similar to how machine guns are treated. People who already legally own a firearm that has been modified in this way before the law takes effect would not have to give it up, but they would be required to register it with the government within 120 days, similar to how other heavily regulated weapons are registered.

This bill would primarily affect gun owners, sellers, and manufacturers, particularly those who own or deal in bump stocks or similar rate-increasing devices or modified semiautomatic weapons. Law enforcement agencies, the military, and government entities would be exempt from the ban. Gun rights groups and gun control advocates are likely to view this differently, since it touches on ongoing debates over gun regulation, but the bill itself is a technical legal fix aimed at restoring a federal ban on bump-stock-type devices after the earlier ban was invalidated in court.
ai_headline: Bill would restore federal ban on bump stocks after court ruling

title: Restoring the Secondary Trading Market Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Restoring the Secondary Trading Market Act, would change federal securities law to limit the power of individual states to regulate certain stock trading. Specifically, it deals with "off-exchange secondary trading," which means buying and selling securities (like stocks) that happens outside of major stock exchanges such as the New York Stock Exchange. Under this bill, if a company makes certain current, publicly available financial information available—following existing SEC disclosure rules—then states would no longer be allowed to place restrictions, conditions, or limits on the resale of that company's securities in these off-exchange markets.

In practical terms, the bill would shift more regulatory authority from state securities regulators to federal rules already set by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Supporters of this kind of change generally argue it would make it easier and less costly for companies and investors to trade securities across state lines without having to comply with a patchwork of different state laws. Critics of similar proposals often worry that reducing state oversight could weaken investor protections, especially for smaller or newer companies whose stock isn't traded on major exchanges.

This bill would mainly affect companies whose stocks trade informally or over-the-counter (not on major exchanges), investors who buy and sell those securities, state securities regulators, and brokers or dealers involved in these transactions. It would not change the SEC's own disclosure requirements, but it would limit what states can additionally require once a company meets those federal information standards.
ai_headline: Bill would limit state power over off-exchange stock trading rules

title: Benton MacKaye National Scenic Trail Feasibility Study Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture to study whether the Benton MacKaye Trail should be officially designated as a national scenic trail. The trail is a 287-mile hiking path that runs through Georgia, Tennessee, and North Carolina, passing through wilderness areas, national forests, and the Great Smoky Mountains National Park. The bill itself does not create the designation—it only requires a formal feasibility study to be completed and submitted to Congress within one year, which would look at whether the trail meets the standards for this special status.

The bill lists reasons Congress believes the trail is a strong candidate, including its scenic beauty, biodiversity, accessibility for hikers of different skill levels, and its economic benefits to nearby rural communities that rely on visitor spending. It also notes that the trail is already well-maintained by a volunteer organization, the Benton MacKaye Trail Association, and that most of the land (95%) is federally owned, meaning the trail could gain official status without high additional costs.

This bill would mainly affect people who use or live near the trail, including hikers, nearby rural communities that benefit from tourism, and land management agencies like the U.S. Forest Service. If the trail is eventually designated as a national scenic trail (through a future, separate action), it could lead to increased funding, federal protections, and visibility, potentially boosting tourism but also increasing oversight and maintenance requirements. For now, though, this bill only sets up the study—it does not change the trail's legal status.

title: Star-Spangled Summit Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would require the U.S. Forest Service to allow a flagpole flying the American flag to be put up and kept at Kyhv Peak Lookout Point, a mountain overlook in the Uinta National Forest near Utah Valley, Utah. The Secretary of Agriculture, who oversees the Forest Service, would have 180 days after the bill becomes law to issue a 10-year permit for this purpose. The permit would first be offered to a specific named individual, Robert S. Collins of Provo, Utah. If he turns it down, the permit would go to another qualified person or group from Utah County with experience maintaining flagpoles.

The bill lays out rules for how future permits would work after the first 10-year period ends. Priority would go first to whoever held the previous permit, then to someone that person recommends, and finally to other applicants the Forest Service considers suitable. The Forest Service could set conditions to make sure the flagpole is properly maintained, and could cancel the permit early if those conditions aren't met. Notably, the bill waives the usual land-use fees the Forest Service would normally charge, and it exempts this project from environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act, meaning the standard environmental impact studies wouldn't be required before the flagpole goes up.

This bill mainly affects the Forest Service, which would have new legal obligations to grant and manage this specific permit, and residents or organizations in Utah County who might apply to maintain the flagpole in the future. It also affects the general public in that it sets a precedent for Congress directly mandating a specific land-use permit and waiving standard environmental review for a symbolic, local project rather than leaving that decision to normal agency processes.

title: Unrecognized Southeast Alaska Native Communities Recognition and Compensation Act
ai_summary:
This bill would grant official federal recognition to Native communities in five Southeast Alaska towns—Haines, Ketchikan, Petersburg, Tenakee, and Wrangell—that were left out of the original 1971 Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA). That law resolved Alaska Native land claims by creating regional and village Native corporations and giving them land and money, but these five communities were excluded at the time, even though Alaska Natives from those areas were enrolled as members of the regional corporation for Southeast Alaska. This bill lets Native residents of these five communities form their own "Urban Corporations," similar to what other Alaska Native villages already have.

Practically, the bill would let eligible Alaska Natives in these towns become shareholders in their new local corporations, receiving 100 shares each, while still keeping their existing benefits from the regional corporation. Each new Urban Corporation would receive about 23,040 acres of federal land (the surface rights), while the regional corporation would keep the rights to any minerals underground. The bill sets rules for how that land gets transferred, protects existing rights like hunting, fishing, and recreational access to the land, addresses road and easement usage, and allows the new corporations to set up trusts to fund community health, education, and cultural programs.

This bill mainly affects Alaska Native individuals and families connected to these five communities who missed out on the original ANCSA benefits, as well as federal and state agencies managing Alaska land, and existing regional/village Native corporations whose land and financial arrangements could be affected. It does not change the overall funding formulas among Native corporations but creates a mechanism to correct a historical gap in recognition and compensation.

title: Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act, directs the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to update its rules so that civilian aircraft can legally fly faster than the speed of sound over the United States without needing special government permission. Currently, federal rules generally ban civilian supersonic flight over land because of the loud "sonic booms" these flights create, which can be disruptive or even damaging to buildings below. The bill requires the FAA to act within one year of the law being passed.

The key condition is that supersonic flights would only be allowed if they're conducted in a way that prevents the sonic boom from actually reaching the ground. This reflects newer aircraft designs and flight techniques that aim to reduce or eliminate the noise impact of breaking the sound barrier, sometimes called "boomless" or low-boom supersonic travel. In other words, the bill doesn't remove all restrictions—it shifts the rule from banning supersonic flight outright to allowing it as long as people on the ground don't hear or feel the boom.

This bill would primarily affect the aviation industry, especially companies developing next-generation supersonic passenger jets, as well as the FAA, which would need to write new technical regulations. Airline passengers could eventually benefit from faster flight times if such planes become commercially available. People living under flight paths could also be affected, since the rule change centers on managing noise impacts from supersonic travel rather than banning it entirely.
ai_headline: Bill would let supersonic jets fly over US if sonic booms don't reach ground
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

title: Smart Space Act of 2026
ai_summary:
The Smart Space Act of 2026 directs the General Services Administration (GSA), the federal agency that manages government buildings, to find new ways to pay for constructing or renovating federal buildings without relying solely on direct government spending. Within 90 days of becoming law, the GSA administrator would have to hold public meetings with experts from private real estate, federal real estate, and state governments to discuss options like public-private partnerships, where private companies might design, build, finance, or operate government facilities in exchange for arrangements such as long-term leases.

Within 120 days, the GSA would have to send the President a report recommending which financing methods and projects make sense, focusing on buildings that serve essential government functions, that could allow agencies to consolidate or move out of underused, costly space, and that meet at least 60 percent building utilization. This report would also go to relevant congressional committees and be posted publicly online, and any delays would have to be reported to Congress and the President. The President could then direct GSA to move forward with specific projects, though actual construction would still depend on Congress approving the funding.

This bill mainly affects how the federal government manages its real estate portfolio, potentially benefiting taxpayers if it reduces long-term costs, and affecting federal agencies that may be relocated or consolidated. It could also create opportunities for private real estate developers and companies to partner with the government on building projects. The bill does not create new legal powers for GSA beyond what it already has; it primarily sets up a process for study, consultation, and reporting.
ai_headline: Bill pushes GSA to explore private financing for federal buildings

title: Federal Building Threat Notification Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Federal Building Threat Notification Act, directs two federal agencies—the General Services Administration (GSA) and the Federal Protective Service (FPS)—to create official guidance for handling emergency communications in federal buildings. This guidance would apply during "life safety events," which means situations like fires, natural disasters, or security threats that require police, firefighters, or emergency rescue teams to respond. The agencies would have one year after the bill becomes law to develop and share this guidance with the security committees responsible for each federal building.

The guidance itself must cover two main things: standard procedures for warning people working in or visiting a federal building that there's a threat, and instructions on what safety steps people should take when a threat or danger level increases. Each federal building's designated security official would be in charge of putting these new procedures into practice at their specific location. Additionally, within 18 months of the bill passing, the GSA would need to send Congress a report describing the best practices and protocols that were actually put in place.

This bill mainly affects people who work in or visit federal buildings owned by the GSA and protected by the FPS, as well as the security officials and committees responsible for managing safety at those buildings. The goal is to make sure there are clear, consistent rules across federal buildings for warning occupants about danger and telling them how to stay safe, rather than leaving each building to figure out its own approach without standardized guidance.

title: American Water Stewardship Act
ai_summary:
This bill renews funding authority for several EPA programs that clean up and protect major bodies of water around the country, including the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative, Long Island Sound, the Columbia River Basin, San Francisco Bay, and the National Estuary Program (which covers coastal bays and estuaries nationwide, including a newly added site, Mississippi Sound). Most of these programs had funding authorizations that were expiring or already expired; this bill extends them through 2031, allowing Congress to keep providing money for water quality monitoring, pollution cleanup, and habitat restoration in these areas.

The bill also makes some program changes. It updates how the San Francisco Bay program can distribute money, allowing grants to a wider range of recipients (including federal agencies and private groups) while requiring at least 25% local matching funds. It expands the beach water-quality monitoring program to test more areas, like river mouths and shallow coastal waters, and directs the EPA to use updated testing technology. It blocks any of this funding from going to organizations tied to "foreign countries of concern" (such as certain adversarial nations). Finally, it requires a government watchdog report within two years evaluating how well these EPA regional water programs are managed and whether they're achieving their goals.

This bill mainly affects coastal and Great Lakes states, local governments, environmental agencies, and nonprofit organizations that rely on federal grants for water pollution cleanup and beach safety monitoring. Everyday residents who live near these waters, use public beaches, or depend on these water sources for drinking water, fishing, or recreation would benefit from continued funding, though the bill mostly deals with reauthorizing existing programs rather than creating major new policies.

title: ACPAC Modernization Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the ACPAC Modernization Act, makes changes to the Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee (ACPAC), a group originally set up to give the government advice on airline passenger issues like fees, delays, and customer service. The committee was created under a 2012 law and includes representatives from different parts of the aviation industry, such as airlines, airports, and travelers' groups.

The main change in this bill is adding "ticket agents" to the list of groups represented on the committee. Ticket agents are businesses or platforms that sell airline tickets to the public, including travel agencies and online booking services. By including them, the bill aims to make sure the committee gets input from all major players involved in the ticket-buying process, not just airlines and airports.

This bill would mainly affect the aviation industry and the way consumer protection policy is shaped for air travel. Everyday airline passengers could be indirectly affected because a more complete committee membership might lead to policy recommendations that better address problems people experience when buying tickets, such as fees, cancellations, or refund issues. Ticket agents themselves would be directly affected, since they would gain an official role in advising the government on these issues.
ai_headline: Bill would add ticket agents to airline consumer advisory panel
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

Currently the committee includes representatives from airlines, airports, and travelers' groups.
ai_sections.who: Ticket agents would gain a formal advisory role. Airlines, airports, travelers' groups, and everyday airline passengers are also connected to the committee's work.

title: Aviation Supply Chain Safety and Security Digitization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Government Accountability Office (GAO), led by the Comptroller General, to study why the aviation industry has been slow to switch from paper records to digital documentation when tracking airplane parts. The goal is to make it easier to spot counterfeit or falsified parts, which can pose serious safety risks. The study would look at challenges faced by manufacturers, repair stations, airlines, aircraft leasing companies, and parts brokers in adopting digital forms, such as the FAA's Form 8130-3 (a certificate showing a part meets safety standards). It would also examine why the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) itself still relies on paper records and physical signatures instead of digital ones.

Within one year of the bill becoming law, the Comptroller General must submit a report to two congressional committees with findings and recommendations. These recommendations would cover how to encourage aviation businesses of all sizes to use digital documentation and verification tools, and how the FAA can speed up its own shift to digital records. The Secretary of Transportation would then have 120 days to respond to any recommendations aimed at the Department of Transportation.

This bill mainly affects people and businesses involved in the aviation supply chain—part manufacturers, repair shops, airlines, aircraft brokers, and government agencies like the FAA. Indirectly, it could benefit airline passengers and the general public by helping reduce the risk of counterfeit or unsafe aircraft parts entering the system. The bill does not create new regulations itself; it only requires a study and a report, leaving any future action up to Congress or the Department of Transportation based on what the study finds.
ai_headline: GAO study to probe slow shift to digital aircraft parts records
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

title: Wildfire Aerial Response Safety Act
ai_summary:
HR 6618, the Wildfire Aerial Response Safety Act, directs the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to study how privately owned drones interfere with firefighting efforts during wildfires. When a wildfire breaks out, the FAA often issues temporary flight restrictions to keep the airspace clear so firefighting aircraft, like helicopters and air tankers, can operate safely. Sometimes hobbyist or other private drones fly into these restricted zones anyway, forcing firefighting aircraft to be grounded or delayed. This bill asks the FAA to formally research how often that happens and what impact it has.

Specifically, the FAA, working with the Department of the Interior and the U.S. Forest Service, would need to look at the past five years of data on drone incursions on federal lands. They would examine how these incidents affected the time it took to put out fires, delayed the deployment of aircraft, and increased government costs. The study would also evaluate possible solutions, such as using radio towers to detect or block drones, using force to disable them, physically capturing them with nets, or simply educating the public about the dangers of flying drones near wildfires.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies involved in wildfire response, including the FAA, Interior Department, and Forest Service, as well as firefighting agencies operating aircraft over public lands. It does not create new rules or penalties for drone operators; instead, it requires a report—due within 18 months—to Congress with findings and recommendations. Everyday drone hobbyists, firefighters, and communities near wildfire-prone areas could be indirectly affected if the study leads to future legislation restricting drone use near fires.
ai_headline: Bill orders FAA study on drones disrupting wildfire aircraft operations
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

It requires review of five years of federal land data, examining effects on fire suppression time, aircraft delays, and government costs, plus possible solutions like drone detection, disabling, netting, or public education. A report to Congress is due within 18 months.

title: Recreational Drone Empowerment Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Recreational Drone Empowerment Act, would make a small but technical change to federal aviation law regarding where hobbyist drone operators can fly without needing special air traffic control permission. Current law lets recreational drone pilots fly in "uncontrolled" airspace, known as Class G airspace, near airports without prior authorization from air traffic control. This bill would expand that exception to also include certain areas of Class E airspace—specifically the Class E airspace that sits above Class G airspace, as well as Class E airspace that extends around Class B, C, D, or E surface areas (which are typically zones around busier airports).

In plain terms, this means hobbyist drone flyers would have more legal room to fly without jumping through extra bureaucratic hoops, since some airspace that currently requires special permission would now be treated more like the simpler, uncontrolled zones. This mainly affects recreational drone hobbyists, who would gain more flexibility in choosing where to fly. It could also matter to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which oversees drone rules, and to pilots of manned aircraft who share that airspace, since the change involves loosening some of the coordination requirements between drone operators and air traffic control in these specific airspace types.
ai_headline: Bill would let hobbyist drone pilots fly in more airspace without prior OK
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

title: Made in America Jobs Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Made in America Jobs Act of 2026, would change an existing law called the Public Works and Economic Development Act of 1965. That older law allows the federal government to give grants to communities for things like public works projects, economic development planning, job training, and business assistance. This bill adds new approved purposes for those grants: projects that help bring jobs back to the United States from other countries (sometimes called "reshoring") and projects that help grow the manufacturing industry.

In practical terms, the bill doesn't create a brand-new grant program. Instead, it expands the list of activities that already-existing federal grants can be used for. Local governments, economic development groups, and regions applying for these grants could now use the money specifically to attract companies to move factories or other employers from overseas back to the U.S., or to support the growth of manufacturing businesses more generally. This applies to several types of grants under the law, including those for public works construction, planning studies, training and technical assistance, and general economic adjustment support.

The people most affected would be local and regional economic development agencies, city and county governments, and manufacturing businesses that might benefit from these grants. Workers in manufacturing communities could also be affected if these grants lead to new factories or expanded production facilities in their area. The bill does not create new taxes or spending levels on its own; it simply broadens how existing federal grant money can be used.
ai_headline: Bill would let existing federal grants fund factory reshoring efforts
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill expands existing federal economic development grants to cover reshoring jobs and growing manufacturing.

It does not create a new grant program, but broadens how current grants for public works, planning, training, and economic adjustment can be spent.

title: Airport Regulatory Relief Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Airport Regulatory Relief Act of 2025, would change federal rules about how small airports build and repair their runways and taxiways. Currently, airports that receive federal funding generally must follow specific federal design standards for pavement. This bill would let smaller, "nonprimary" airports (those that don't handle major commercial traffic) use their state's highway construction standards instead, but only for airports that serve smaller aircraft weighing 60,000 pounds or less.

For this option to apply, two conditions must be met: the state must formally notify the federal government that its smaller airports plan to use highway standards instead of the usual federal airport standards, and the Secretary of Transportation must confirm that doing so won't create safety problems. This would apply to money already available through certain federal airport grant programs.

This bill mainly affects state transportation departments, local airport authorities, and construction contractors who build or repair runways at smaller regional and community airports. It could make it easier and potentially cheaper for these airports to get pavement work done, since state highway specifications and materials may be more readily available or familiar to local contractors than specialized federal airport standards. Everyday travelers who use small regional airports could see faster or more frequent pavement improvements, though the practical effects would depend on how individual states and the Federal Aviation Administration implement the change.
ai_headline: Small airports could use state highway standards for runway work
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

ai_sections.tldr: Small "nonprimary" airports serving planes under 60,000 pounds could use state highway standards instead of federal pavement rules.

title: Local Water Protection Act
ai_summary:
HR 7376, the Local Water Protection Act, updates a section of the federal Clean Water Act that deals with "nonpoint source pollution." This is pollution that doesn't come from a single identifiable source like a factory pipe, but instead washes into rivers, lakes, and streams from things like farm runoff, city streets, construction sites, and lawns. The law provides federal grant money to states and local governments to help them reduce this kind of pollution.

What this bill actually does is simple: it extends the funding authorization for these programs. The current law authorized money to be spent through fiscal year 2027, and this bill pushes that authorization out further, covering fiscal years 2027 through 2031. It does not create new programs, change how the money can be used, or alter the rules states must follow. It essentially keeps an existing federal grant program alive for several more years by renewing Congress's permission for it to continue receiving funding.

This bill mainly affects state and local governments that rely on these federal grants to fund water quality projects, such as reducing agricultural runoff or managing stormwater. It also indirectly affects everyday residents who benefit from cleaner rivers, lakes, and drinking water sources, as well as farmers, developers, and municipalities that participate in pollution-reduction efforts. Because the bill only reauthorizes funding rather than guaranteeing it, actual funding levels would still depend on future appropriations decisions made by Congress.
ai_headline: Bill would extend Clean Water Act runoff grants through 2031
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 487.

title: Defending American Property Abroad Act of 2026
ai_summary:
HR 7084, the "Defending American Property Abroad Act of 2026," changes U.S. port law to add penalties for foreign governments that seize American-owned property in ports overseas. Currently, U.S. law already restricts certain vessels from entering U.S. ports, waters, or transferring cargo at U.S. facilities under specific circumstances. This bill adds a new category: ships that have used a port, harbor, or marine terminal in a Western Hemisphere country (one that has a free trade agreement with the U.S.) would be barred from U.S. ports if that foreign facility was accessible only through land owned or controlled by an American person or company, and if the foreign government has nationalized or expropriated (taken over) that property.

The President would have the power to officially "designate" such a foreign port as off-limits once a government seizes American-owned property tied to it, effectively blocking ships that use that seized port from entering U.S. waters. The President could later remove that designation if the property is returned, if the U.S. owner is fairly compensated, or if the dispute is otherwise resolved. There are exceptions for emergencies (like a ship in distress) and for cases where the American property owner specifically authorizes a ship to use the facility.

This bill would primarily affect shipping companies, foreign governments in the Western Hemisphere, and U.S. businesses with port or terminal investments abroad. It's designed to give the U.S. government a tool to pressure foreign countries against seizing American-owned infrastructure by threatening to cut off access to U.S. ports for vessels connected to that seized property. Everyday consumers would likely only feel indirect effects, mainly if trade or shipping routes were disrupted in response to such a dispute.
ai_headline: Bill would bar ships from US ports if allies seize American property abroad
last_action_text: Received in the Senate.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill lets the President block U.S. port access to ships using foreign ports built on seized American-owned land.

Exceptions exist for emergencies and cases where the American owner authorizes use of the facility.

title: Keeping Violent Offenders Off Our Streets Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal law that deals with fraud in the insurance and bail bond business. It amends a section of the U.S. Code (Title 18, Section 1033) that already makes it a crime to commit fraud affecting interstate commerce in the business of insurance. The bill adds specific language clarifying that this fraud law also covers the posting of monetary bail, criminal bail bonds, and federal immigration bail bonds. In other words, it makes clear that fraud committed in connection with bail bonds—including immigration-related bail bonds—can be prosecuted under this same federal fraud statute.

In practical terms, this would affect bail bond companies, agents, and anyone involved in posting bail for criminal defendants or immigration detainees. If someone commits fraud while arranging or posting bail—such as lying about finances, forging documents, or misusing funds meant for bail—they could be charged under this federal law, which carries its own penalties. The bill is aimed at closing a potential gap in the law by explicitly naming bail bonds as covered activity, rather than leaving it ambiguous whether existing insurance fraud rules apply to bail transactions.

This bill mainly affects people and businesses in the bail bond industry, including those who handle bail for people facing state or federal criminal charges and those who post bonds for immigration detainees. It does not change bail amounts, who qualifies for bail, or sentencing for other crimes—it specifically targets fraud committed during the bail-posting process.
ai_headline: Bill would extend federal fraud law to cover bail bond transactions
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Sharri Briley and Eric Edmundson Veterans Benefits Expansion Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would increase certain veterans' benefits and change some VA home loan fee rules. First, it gives an extra $833.33 per month to veterans who already qualify for a special "aid and attendance" allowance—this typically applies to severely disabled veterans who need help with daily living or are housebound. This increase would start December 1, 2026.

Second, it changes how survivor benefits called Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (DIC) are calculated. These are payments made to spouses, children, or parents of veterans who died from service-related causes. Currently these payments increase along with Social Security's annual cost-of-living adjustment. Under this bill, DIC payments would increase by that same Social Security percentage, plus an extra 1%, for five consecutive increases starting December 1, 2026. This means survivors would see slightly bigger raises than under current law, but only for a limited time (five adjustments).

Third, the bill changes rules about fees charged for VA-backed home loans. Currently, veterans with a disability rating are often exempt from paying these loan fees. This bill would allow the VA to charge the fee on a second or later loan to veterans whose disability rating is 70% or below, starting August 1, 2026, and lasting through September 2035. This mainly affects veterans using their VA home loan benefit more than once who have moderate (not severe) disability ratings—they would now have to pay a fee they might have previously avoided. Overall, the bill affects disabled veterans, survivors of deceased veterans, and veterans using VA home loans multiple times.
ai_headline: Bill raises disabled veterans' benefits, trims some home loan fee exemptions
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Veterans' Affairs.

title: To amend the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 to extend the authorities of title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 through October 20, 2027, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
HR 8035 is a short bill that extends a key part of U.S. surveillance law rather than making major policy changes. Specifically, it pushes back the expiration date for Title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), which contains the legal authority the government uses to collect foreign intelligence, including the widely discussed Section 702 program. Instead of expiring on its current schedule, these authorities would now continue until October 20, 2027. The bill also updates related "transition" rules so that any procedures for winding down surveillance activities if the law ever does lapse remain consistent with the new deadline.

In plain terms, this bill keeps the government's existing tools for monitoring foreign threats — such as terrorism suspects or foreign spies communicating with people in the U.S. — active for about two more years, rather than letting them expire or forcing Congress to renegotiate the underlying rules right now. It does not create new surveillance powers or change how the programs operate; it simply extends the deadline before lawmakers must revisit the issue.

This bill mainly affects national security and intelligence agencies (like the NSA and FBI), which rely on these authorities to gather foreign intelligence, and indirectly affects the general public because Section 702 surveillance can sometimes incidentally include communications involving Americans. People interested in privacy rights, civil liberties, and national security policy would be the main groups tracking this legislation, since it maintains the status quo on a program that has been the subject of ongoing debate about oversight and privacy protections.
ai_headline: Bill would extend foreign surveillance law to October 2027
last_action_text: Rule H. Res. 1175 failed passage of House.

title: To amend the Catawba Indian Tribe of South Carolina Land Claims Settlement Act of 1993.
ai_summary:
This bill would change a federal law from 1993 that settled a land claims dispute involving the Catawba Indian Tribe of South Carolina. Specifically, it removes a requirement in that law about who can become a tribal member in the future. Currently, the law says a person can only join the tribe if they are a direct descendant of someone listed on the tribe's original "base membership roll" (a historical list of members) and have kept up an ongoing political relationship with the tribe. This bill would delete that requirement entirely.

In practical terms, this means the Catawba Indian Tribe would have more freedom to decide its own membership rules going forward, without being bound by the specific descendancy and political-relationship test written into federal law. The tribe could potentially set its own criteria for who qualifies as a member, rather than being restricted by this older federal standard.

This bill mainly affects the Catawba Indian Tribe itself and its governance over membership decisions. It could also affect individuals who want to join the tribe in the future but don't meet the current lineal descendant requirement. Since tribal membership can affect access to certain federal benefits, services, and legal rights tied to tribal citizenship, this change could have implications for how the tribe grows and who is officially recognized as a member going forward.
ai_headline: Bill would let Catawba Tribe set its own membership rules
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Indian Affairs.

title: HEATS Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the HEATS Act, changes the rules for companies that want to drill for geothermal energy (heat from underground used to produce power). Right now, even on private land, companies sometimes need a federal drilling permit if the U.S. government owns part of the underground mineral rights. This bill says that if the federal government owns less than 50% of the underground geothermal resource, and the company already has a permit from the state, the company will not need a separate federal permit. Companies could start work just 30 days after giving the state permit to the federal government.

The bill also reduces the number of federal environmental and historical reviews that would normally apply. It says these geothermal projects won't count as "major federal actions," so they would be exempt from certain requirements under the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act. Historic preservation reviews would only apply if the state doesn't already have its own law protecting historic sites. The federal government would still collect royalty payments from energy production and could still inspect sites to make sure companies are reporting and paying correctly. However, none of these changes would apply to land owned by or held in trust for Native American tribes.

This bill mainly affects geothermal energy companies, state governments, and federal land and environmental agencies like the Department of the Interior. Supporters would likely say it speeds up clean energy development by cutting red tape, while critics might be concerned about reduced environmental and historical review. Everyday residents could be affected if they live near geothermal project sites, depend on protected wildlife habitats, or care about environmental oversight in their state.
ai_headline: Bill would cut federal permits for geothermal drilling on private land
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources Subcommittee on Public Lands, Forests, and Mining. Hearings held.

ai_sections.tldr: The HEATS Act would let geothermal companies skip federal permits if the U.S. owns under 50% of underground rights and a state permit exists.
ai_sections.what: The bill lets geothermal energy companies bypass a separate federal drilling permit if the federal government owns less than 50% of the underground geothermal resource and the company already holds a state permit. Companies could begin work 30 days after submitting the state permit to federal authorities. The bill also exempts these projects from being classified as "major federal actions," reducing reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and Endangered Species Act, and limits historic preservation reviews to cases where states lack their own protections.

title: EQUALS Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the EQUALS Act of 2025, would change how long new federal employees must work before their jobs become permanent. Currently, most new federal workers (in the "competitive service," the standard hiring track) serve a one-year probationary period before their position is finalized. This bill would double that to two years for most new hires, though veterans who qualify as "preference eligible" would keep the shorter one-year period. During this probationary period, agencies would have to actively certify that keeping the employee serves the public interest, or else the employee would automatically be terminated. The bill also creates a similar two-year "trial period" for employees hired into the "excepted service" (positions filled outside the normal competitive hiring process), which currently has no standard trial period at all.

The bill also extends related deadlines elsewhere in federal personnel law. For example, rules about when employees gain certain job protections against being fired for poor performance or conduct would now kick in after two years of service instead of one (again, with a one-year exception for veterans). It also applies these new rules to the FAA and TSA, agencies that have their own separate personnel systems. Agencies would be required to give employees and their supervisors clear notice of probationary deadlines and requirements along the way.

This bill mainly affects people newly hired into federal government jobs, as well as federal agency managers who oversee hiring and firing decisions. It does not affect current employees who already completed their probationary period, and it carves out exceptions for the U.S. Postal Service, Postal Regulatory Commission, and Congress. Supporters and critics may view this differently: some may see it as a way to help agencies more carefully evaluate new hires, while others may see it as making federal jobs less stable for new employees, including veterans in some categories. The changes would take effect one year after the bill becomes law, and the Office of Personnel Management would have 180 days to write implementing regulations.
ai_headline: Bill would double federal job probation to two years for most new hires
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 524.

title: SEED Act
ai_summary:
The SEED Act of 2025 would change the federal tax code to let early childhood educators claim the same tax deduction that K-12 teachers already receive for money they spend on classroom supplies. Currently, teachers can deduct a limited amount (up to a few hundred dollars) each year for things like school supplies, books, and classroom materials they buy out of their own pocket, but this deduction only applies to teachers from kindergarten through 12th grade. This bill would expand that definition to include early childhood educators, meaning those who work with children before they reach kindergarten, such as preschool and pre-K teachers.

If passed, this change would apply starting with expenses from the 2025 tax year onward. The people most directly affected would be early childhood educators, who often spend their own money on supplies for young children but haven't been eligible for this particular tax break. This would give them a small tax benefit similar to what elementary and secondary teachers already get, potentially easing some of the financial burden of buying classroom materials.

The bill does not change the deduction amount itself or create any new spending program; it simply broadens who qualifies for the existing deduction. It affects the federal tax code only and does not involve state licensing, funding for schools, or other education policy areas.
ai_headline: Bill would extend teacher supply tax deduction to preschool educators
last_action_text: Message on Senate action sent to the House.

The deduction, previously limited to K-12 teachers, would apply to early childhood educator expenses starting in the 2025 tax year. The bill does not change the deduction amount or create a new spending program.

title: Housing not Handcuffs Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 4182, called the Housing Not Handcuffs Act of 2025, would stop federal agencies from punishing homeless people for doing basic things needed to survive on federal public land, such as sitting, sleeping, eating, resting, or protecting themselves from weather. This applies to land owned by the federal government, including parks, sidewalks, public buildings, parking lots, and similar spaces. The bill also protects people's rights to move freely in public places, ask for or give out food and money, keep and store their belongings without unreasonable searches, pray or practice religion, and live in a parked car or RV. If someone's vehicle is going to be towed, they'd get a chance to move it first, retrieve belongings, and get it back at a reduced cost if they can't afford the full fee.

There's an exception: if the government offers "adequate alternative indoor space," these protections wouldn't apply to sleeping or camping outdoors. The bill defines this very strictly, requiring things like locking doors, climate control, bathrooms, no cost, no time limits, and room for pets, partners, and belongings. People accused of breaking laws against these life-sustaining activities could also use a legal defense in court, arguing they had no adequate indoor space available, and courts would generally assume that's true unless proven otherwise.

The bill affects homeless individuals on federal property, federal agencies and officials who enforce anti-camping or loitering rules, and courts handling related cases. It creates new ways to sue: the U.S. Attorney General or any harmed individual could take legal action against officials who violate these rules, and winning plaintiffs would have their legal costs covered. Supporters and critics disagree on how this would affect local enforcement of homelessness-related laws, but the bill itself only applies to federal land and federal agencies, not state or city property.
ai_headline: Bill would bar federal agencies from punishing homeless people on public land
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and in addition to the Committees on Oversight and Government Reform, Natural Resources, and the Judiciary, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 4182 would stop federal agencies from punishing homeless people for surviving on federal land, with limited exceptions.

Protections don't apply to outdoor sleeping if "adequate alternative indoor space" is offered, a term defined with strict requirements.

It applies only to federal land, not state or city property, leaving disagreement over its effect on local enforcement.

title: STOP China Act
ai_summary:
The STOP China Act would expand existing federal rules that block the use of federal transportation money to buy buses, trains, or other vehicles made by companies connected to China (or other countries identified as national security concerns). It builds on a current law covering federal transit funding and adds a new, broader rule covering nearly all other Department of Transportation funding as well. Under the bill, agencies could not use covered federal funds to purchase vehicles from a "covered entity" — meaning a company based in, controlled by, or closely tied to China or another flagged nation — or to buy vehicles that use electric power trains made by such companies. Money also could not be used to build or maintain charging or fueling stations for buses that fall under this ban.

The bill directs the U.S. Trade Representative, working with the Attorney General and the Secretary of Transportation, to create and regularly update a public list of these restricted companies. There are some exceptions, such as allowing vehicles to be bought for safety testing, inspections, or research purposes. Existing contracts that were already in progress before the law passed could still be completed.

This bill would mainly affect public transit agencies, state and local governments, and companies that build buses, trains, or vehicle components, especially those with supply chains linked to Chinese manufacturers. Supporters frame it as a national security and economic protection measure, while it could also affect vehicle costs or availability for transit systems that rely on parts or vehicles from restricted companies. Taxpayers could be indirectly affected through changes in how federal transportation dollars are spent.
ai_headline: Bill would widen ban on federal transit funds for Chinese-linked vehicles
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.

ai_sections.tldr: The STOP China Act would block nearly all DOT funds from buying vehicles or parts tied to China or flagged countries.

It adds a broader rule covering nearly all other Department of Transportation funding, banning purchases of vehicles, electric power trains, or related charging/fueling infrastructure from these "covered entities." Exceptions apply for safety testing, inspections, research, and contracts already underway.

ai_sections.why: The change could limit vehicle or parts options for transit systems and possibly affect costs or availability where supply chains rely on restricted companies.

title: ESA Amendments Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill makes major changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA), the 1973 law that protects plants and animals at risk of extinction. Overall, it shifts the law toward giving more flexibility to private landowners, states, and federal agencies, while adding new deadlines, cost disclosures, and limits on lawsuits and regulations. It sets a formal process (a "national listing work plan") for deciding which species get reviewed for protection and when, ranking them by priority so agencies focus first on the most at-risk species. It also locks in several Trump-era regulatory definitions (like "foreseeable future" and "habitat") as permanent law, and narrows what counts as critical habitat, excluding land only occasionally visited by a species and land already under private conservation plans.

The bill creates new incentives for private landowners, companies, and states to voluntarily help conserve species before they're officially listed as endangered, offering legal protections ("assurances") that they won't face new restrictions later if the species does get listed. It also exempts certain permits from environmental review requirements under a separate law (NEPA) and limits when federal agencies can require extra habitat protections or mitigation measures. Other sections require more public disclosure of the scientific data and cost information behind listing decisions and lawsuits, restrict when courts can review certain agency decisions, and change rules for importing/exporting foreign species and awarding legal fees in ESA lawsuits.

This bill would affect landowners, ranchers, farmers, and developers whose property may contain endangered species habitat, since it eases some restrictions and creates new voluntary agreement options. It also affects federal wildlife agencies (Fish and Wildlife Service, NOAA Fisheries), state and tribal governments, environmental and conservation groups, and industries like energy, mining, and construction that need permits near protected species habitat. Supporters generally frame these changes as reducing red tape and encouraging conservation partnerships, while critics may see them as weakening protections for endangered species — but this summary does not take a position on those debates.
ai_headline: Bill would ease Endangered Species Act rules for landowners and states
last_action_text: Rules Committee Resolution H. Res. 1189 Reported to House. Rule provides for consideration of H.R. 4690, H. Res. 1182, H.R. 1897 and H.R. 5587. The resolution provides for one motion to recommit on H.R. 4690, H.R. 1897, and H.R. 5587.

ai_sections.what: HR 1897 revises the Endangered Species Act by creating a prioritized "national listing work plan," locking in Trump-era regulatory definitions, and narrowing what counts as critical habitat. It also offers legal protections to landowners and states who voluntarily conserve species before listing, exempts some permits from NEPA review, and restricts lawsuits and court review of agency decisions.
ai_sections.who: Landowners, ranchers, farmers, and developers with potential endangered species habitat are directly affected, along with federal wildlife agencies like Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries. State and tribal governments, conservation groups, and energy, mining, and construction industries needing permits are also affected.
ai_sections.why: The changes would reduce regulatory requirements and legal exposure for landowners and industries while narrowing habitat protections and limiting court challenges to agency decisions on species listings.

title: Preventing Hospital Overbilling of Medicare Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Preventing Hospital Overbilling of Medicare Act, aims to stop hospitals from charging more for the same services just because they're delivered at an off-campus outpatient location instead of the main hospital building. Currently, some hospitals own outpatient clinics or emergency rooms located away from the main campus, but they bill Medicare as if the visit happened at the hospital itself, which often results in higher charges. This bill closes that loophole by changing the legal definition of "off-campus outpatient department" and removing special billing exceptions, particularly for emergency departments, starting January 1, 2026.

To make billing more transparent, the bill requires that each off-campus location get its own unique identification number (separate from the main hospital's number) and that this number be used whenever bills are submitted to Medicare or private insurance. This means hospitals could no longer disguise where care was actually provided. The bill also directs the Department of Health and Human Services to work with the National Association of Insurance Commissioners to create model rules allowing insurance companies to reject claims that don't follow these new billing identification rules, based on a similar law already in place in Colorado.

This bill would primarily affect hospitals that operate outpatient facilities away from their main campus, insurance companies, and Medicare. Patients could benefit through more accurate billing and potentially lower costs, since hospitals would no longer be able to charge hospital-level rates for services performed at smaller, off-site clinics. Health care providers and insurers would need to update their billing systems and identifiers to comply with the new requirements by 2026.
ai_headline: Bill would end higher Medicare fees at off-campus hospital clinics
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Ways and Means, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.tldr: Starting in 2026, hospitals could no longer bill Medicare at higher hospital rates for care given at off-campus outpatient locations.
ai_sections.what: This bill stops hospitals from billing Medicare at hospital-level rates for services delivered at off-campus outpatient locations, including emergency departments, starting January 1, 2026. It redefines "off-campus outpatient department" and removes special billing exceptions, and requires each off-campus site to have its own unique billing identification number used on all Medicare and private insurance claims. HHS must also work with the National Association of Insurance Commissioners to develop model rules letting insurers reject claims that don't follow the new identification requirements.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects hospitals that operate off-campus outpatient facilities, insurance companies, and Medicare; patients receiving outpatient care are also affected.
ai_sections.why: Hospitals and insurers would need to update billing systems and identifiers to comply, and hospitals would lose the ability to bill hospital-level rates for care provided at smaller, off-site clinics.

title: Cashless Bail Reporting Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Cashless Bail Reporting Act, would require the U.S. Attorney General to create and publish a public list identifying every state and local government that allows "cashless bail" practices. Specifically, this means places that let people accused of crimes be released before trial without paying money, either by simply promising to return for court dates (personal recognizance) or by signing an agreement to pay a bond only if they fail to appear (unsecured appearance bond). The Attorney General would have 30 days after the bill becomes law to publish this list and would need to update it every three months.

The bill itself does not ban cashless bail or force any state or city to change its bail policies. It only creates a transparency and reporting requirement at the federal level, making information about which jurisdictions use these practices easily accessible to the public.

This bill would primarily affect the Department of Justice, which would take on the administrative task of tracking and publishing this information. It would also indirectly affect state and local governments, since their bail policies would be publicly listed and potentially scrutinized. Everyday residents wouldn't experience direct personal impact from this bill, but it could increase public awareness and debate about local bail systems, since the published list could become a reference point for policymakers, advocacy groups, and the media discussing criminal justice practices in different areas.
ai_headline: Bill would require public list of places allowing cashless bail
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Emergency Reporting Act
ai_summary:
The Emergency Reporting Act directs the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to be more transparent and thorough when major disasters knock out phone and internet service. The FCC has a tool called the Disaster Information Reporting System, which communications companies use to report outages during hurricanes, wildfires, and other emergencies. Under this bill, whenever that system is activated for a week or more because of a specific disaster, the FCC must hold at least one public hearing about it each year and then issue a report within 120 days. These reports would detail how many people lost internet, phone, or mobile service, how long outages lasted, and whether 911 call centers were affected. The FCC is also encouraged to invite local officials, tribal leaders, affected residents, first responders, utility companies, and telecom providers to participate in these hearings.

The bill also requires the FCC to study ways to improve how outages are reported to 911 centers, including whether adding visual information (like maps or graphics) about outages would help emergency dispatchers understand what's happening. It would also examine whether some 911 service outages are currently going unreported because they don't meet existing reporting thresholds, and whether new rules are needed.

This bill mainly affects the FCC, telecommunications and internet providers, and state/local/tribal emergency response agencies, requiring them to share more information and coordinate more closely after disasters. Everyday residents would benefit indirectly through better public information about service outages during emergencies and potentially more reliable 911 systems, though the bill does not create new regulations on internet providers beyond the reporting and study requirements specified.
ai_headline: Bill would force FCC to report publicly on disaster-related outages
last_action_text: Received in the Senate. Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 375.

ai_sections.tldr: The Emergency Reporting Act requires FCC hearings and reports on phone, internet, and 911 outages after major disasters.
