These reports must detail how many people lost service, how long outages lasted, and whether 911 centers were affected. The FCC must also study ways to improve outage reporting to 911 centers, including using visual information and addressing possible reporting gaps.
ai_sections.who: The bill mainly affects the FCC, telecommunications and internet providers, and state, local, and tribal emergency response agencies. Residents would be indirectly affected through improved public information and potentially more reliable 911 systems.
ai_sections.why: The bill increases reporting and coordination requirements on the FCC and telecom providers after disasters, without creating new regulations on internet providers beyond these reporting and study requirements.

title: USDA Loan Modernization Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the USDA Loan Modernization Act, changes the rules for who can qualify for certain farm loans backed by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Currently, farmers applying for USDA farm ownership, operating, or emergency loans generally must own a "majority" (more than 50%) stake in the farm business to qualify. This bill lowers that bar slightly, allowing people or business entities that own "at least 50 percent" to qualify instead, making it a bit easier for co-owners or partners with exactly half ownership to access these loans.

The bill also updates the rules for more complicated farm business structures, such as farms owned through layered companies or partnerships (sometimes called "embedded entities"). It creates clearer standards for when someone who only operates a farm, but doesn't own the land, can still qualify for a loan, and it clarifies that entities are eligible if at least 75% of their ownership ultimately traces back to qualified farm operators. The USDA Secretary would have authority to define exactly what counts as a "qualified operator" and adjust certain ownership percentage thresholds.

This bill mainly affects farmers, ranchers, and agricultural businesses that use USDA-backed loans to buy land, cover operating costs, or recover from emergencies like natural disasters. It could particularly help farm families, partnerships, or multi-generational farm businesses with shared or split ownership structures that previously didn't meet strict "majority owner" requirements. The changes are technical and administrative, aiming to modernize eligibility rules rather than create new loan programs or spending.
ai_headline: Bill would ease ownership rule for USDA farm loan eligibility
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill lowers the USDA farm loan ownership threshold from "majority" to "at least 50 percent."
ai_sections.what: This bill changes eligibility rules for USDA farm ownership, operating, and emergency loans, lowering the required ownership stake from more than 50% to at least 50%. It also sets clearer standards for layered or "embedded" farm business structures, including a rule that entities qualify if at least 75% of ownership traces back to qualified farm operators, and gives the USDA Secretary authority to define "qualified operator" and adjust ownership thresholds.

title: CRACKDOWN Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the CRACKDOWN Act of 2026, would change the rules for how states manage federal child care funding through the Child Care and Development Block Grant program. This program helps low-income families pay for child care so parents can work or go to school. The bill focuses specifically on "overpayments," meaning money that was sent out incorrectly, such as payments made in the wrong amount or to someone who wasn't actually eligible.

Under this bill, if a state's overpayment rate goes above 5 percent of the total money it distributed in a given year, that state would be required to create and submit a corrective action plan to the federal government explaining how it will fix the problem and get the rate back under 5 percent. The state would also have to send regular reports proving it's following through on that plan. If a state's overpayment rate stays above 5 percent for two years in a row, the state could lose its eligibility to receive this federal child care funding entirely, unless it can show the government that it will bring the rate down soon or is making real progress on its corrective plan.

This bill would mainly affect state government agencies that run child care assistance programs, since they would face new paperwork requirements and potential funding risks. Indirectly, it could also affect low-income families who rely on this assistance, since if a state loses funding or has to tighten its payment processes, it could become harder or slower for some families to access child care subsidies while states work to reduce errors.
ai_headline: States with high child care overpayment rates would face funding risk
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 507.

ai_sections.tldr: States with child care overpayment rates above 5 percent for two straight years could lose federal funding.

States that stay above 5 percent for two consecutive years could lose eligibility for federal child care funding unless they show progress or a near-term fix.
ai_sections.who: State government agencies that administer the Child Care and Development Block Grant program would face new reporting requirements and funding risk. Low-income families who rely on child care subsidies could be indirectly affected.
ai_sections.why: States may need to tighten payment processes to avoid losing federal funding, which could slow or complicate access to child care subsidies for some families.

title: First Responder Network Authority Reauthorization Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill renews and updates the law governing FirstNet, the First Responder Network Authority, which runs the nationwide wireless broadband network used by police, firefighters, paramedics, and other emergency responders. The bill extends FirstNet's authorization to continue operating through September 30, 2037, instead of letting it expire after its original 15-year period. It also gives the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), the federal agency that oversees FirstNet, more direct control by requiring NTIA approval for FirstNet's major actions, rather than letting FirstNet operate as a fully independent authority.

The bill makes several organizational changes: it requires FirstNet's governing board to include at least five members with public safety backgrounds, adjusts how board members' terms are staggered, and creates a new "Associate Administrator" position to manage day-to-day operations under NTIA's oversight. It also expands what counts as part of the public safety network, allowing it to include a broader range of technologies and spectrum, not just the initial set defined in 2012.

Other provisions focus on accountability and transparency. FirstNet's private contractor (the company that builds and runs the network) will now be required to submit disaster recovery plans, report network outages within 30 minutes, and provide agencies with real-time outage information. NTIA must also submit annual reports to Congress on cybersecurity issues and network adoption rates, and give Congress briefings each year. Finally, Congress can request and must receive copies of FirstNet's contracts with its network operator within seven days. Overall, this bill mainly affects government agencies, emergency responders, and the company that operates the FirstNet network—not the general public directly—though it aims to make emergency communications more reliable and better overseen by Congress.
ai_headline: Bill would extend FirstNet emergency network authority through 2037
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7386 extends FirstNet's authorization through 2037 and gives NTIA more direct oversight of its operations.

It gives NTIA approval power over FirstNet's major actions, restructures its governing board, adds an Associate Administrator role, and expands what technologies count as part of the public safety network. It also adds new transparency requirements, including faster outage reporting and congressional access to contracts.

title: CLEAR (Committee Leadership and Enhanced Accountability for Resilience) Defense Production Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill updates the Defense Production Act of 1950, a law that gives the federal government special powers to direct industries and businesses to prioritize production of goods needed for national defense (this was used, for example, during COVID-19 to boost supplies like ventilators and vaccines). The bill focuses on improving how the government organizes and tracks its use of these powers, rather than changing the powers themselves.

First, it strengthens the committee that coordinates these defense production activities across federal agencies. It creates a formal "Chairperson" position for this committee, a senior full-time government official who reports directly to the Secretary of Commerce, and requires each involved federal agency to designate a senior staff member to work with this chairperson. The bill also requires a government watchdog, the Comptroller General, to review how well this committee is doing its job and report back to Congress within two years.

Second, the bill creates a new public "DPA Registry," a secure online database tracking how and why federal agencies have used these special defense production powers. Agencies would have to log their actions, update the database quarterly, and the registry would be designed so that the public can see much of this information, while sensitive national security details could be restricted. This mainly affects federal agencies that use these emergency powers, government oversight bodies, and members of the public or businesses interested in transparency about how the government uses its authority to direct private industry during national emergencies.
ai_headline: Bill adds chairperson and public registry to defense production law
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 3542 adds a formal chairperson and a public tracking registry to oversee defense production powers.

It also establishes a public "DPA Registry," a secure online database where agencies log and quarterly update how they use defense production powers, with sensitive national security details restricted.
ai_sections.who: Federal agencies that use these emergency production powers, the Secretary of Commerce, the Comptroller General, and members of the public or businesses seeking transparency.
ai_sections.why: The changes aim to improve coordination and tracking of government authority over private industry during national emergencies, without altering the underlying powers themselves.

title: Safeguarding Taxpayer Dollars in Child Care Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Safeguarding Taxpayer Dollars in Child Care Act," aims to crack down on fraud in two federal programs that help pay for child care: the Child Care and Development Block Grant program and the Child and Adult Care Food Program. Both programs provide government funding to child care providers, with the block grant helping cover child care costs for families and the food program helping cover meal costs for children in care.

The bill requires the government to investigate fraud claims and permanently ban any child care provider found guilty of fraud from receiving money through either program. Fraud is defined clearly and includes things like lying on paperwork to get funding, falsely claiming children are enrolled or attending when they aren't, operating without proper state licensing, misusing program funds, or any other fraudulent activity related to the money. Importantly, the bill also links the two programs together: if a provider is banned from one program for fraud, they automatically get banned from the other program too.

This bill mainly affects child care providers and day care operators who receive federal funding through these programs, as well as the government agencies that oversee them. Families who rely on these programs for child care assistance could be affected indirectly, since providers found committing fraud would be removed from the system, potentially requiring families to find new care options. The bill does not change funding levels or benefits for honest providers or families—it specifically targets those who defraud the system, with the goal of protecting taxpayer money and ensuring the programs serve children and families as intended.
ai_headline: Bill would permanently ban child care providers caught defrauding federal programs
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 509.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill permanently bans child care providers found guilty of fraud from two federal child care funding programs.
ai_sections.what: The bill requires investigation of fraud claims against child care providers and imposes a permanent ban from the Child Care and Development Block Grant program and the Child and Adult Care Food Program for anyone found guilty. Fraud includes lying on paperwork, falsely claiming children's enrollment or attendance, operating without proper licensing, or misusing funds. A ban from one program automatically triggers a ban from the other.

title: Closing the Provider Fraud Gap Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Closing the Provider Fraud Gap Act, would require the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a federal watchdog agency, to study how well fraud prevention works in certain government programs that help pay for early childhood education, child care, and children's nutrition. Specifically, the study would look at Head Start and Early Head Start, the Child and Adult Care Food Program, and the Child Care and Development Block Grant program. The GAO would examine whether the government is collecting enough data to catch fraud committed by service providers, whether that data is actually being used effectively, and how well states are managing program integrity when they hand off responsibilities to counties or local governments.

Within two years of the bill becoming law, the GAO would have to send a report to relevant committees in the House and Senate. This report would summarize what they found and suggest possible changes to laws or regulations to reduce fraud in these programs.

This bill doesn't change any existing program rules, funding levels, or requirements for providers or families right now—it simply orders a government study and report. The people most directly affected would be federal agencies, state governments, and organizations that administer these child care and nutrition programs, since they would likely need to provide data and information for the study. Families who rely on these programs and the providers who deliver services aren't directly impacted by this bill itself, though future legislation based on the study's findings could eventually lead to changes in how these programs are run or monitored.

title: Child Care for Working Families Act
ai_summary:
HR 4418, the Child Care for Working Families Act, is a large federal bill aimed at making child care more affordable, higher quality, and more widely available for families with children from birth through age five. It would create a new federal-state program in which states that submit approved plans receive federal money to help cover child care costs for eligible children, especially those from lower-income families, and would guarantee assistance to any qualifying family starting in October 2026. Families earning up to 85% of their state's median income would pay nothing out of pocket, while higher-income families would pay child care costs on a sliding scale based on income, capped at 7%. The bill also sets rules requiring states to pay child care providers enough to cover fair wages and operating costs, and it ties funding levels to quality standards, such as staff training and safety requirements.

Beyond direct payments to families, the bill funds efforts to increase the supply of child care providers, including grants for starting new child care businesses, renovating or building facilities, training workers, and helping unlicensed providers become licensed. It also directs money toward improving quality through a tiered rating system, banning harmful practices like suspending or expelling young children from care, and supporting children with disabilities, kids experiencing homelessness, and other vulnerable groups. States that don't participate would still see federal money flow to local governments and Head Start programs in their area instead.

This bill would primarily affect parents of young children who need child care to work, study, or job search; child care providers and workers, who could see higher pay and more support to meet licensing and quality standards; and state governments, which would take on new administrative responsibilities to run these programs. It would also affect federal spending, since it creates guaranteed, ongoing funding (an "entitlement") for child care assistance from 2026 through 2031, rather than funding that must be renewed and capped each year through regular budget decisions.
ai_headline: Bill would guarantee child care help for families starting in 2026
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

title: Doug LaMalfa Federal Disaster Tax Relief Certainty Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes federal tax rules to make it easier for people who suffer losses from major disasters or wildfires to get tax relief, and it makes some temporary rules from past legislation more permanent going forward.

The first part deals with "casualty losses," meaning property damage or loss from disasters like hurricanes, floods, or fires. Normally, claiming these losses on taxes involves complicated rules and limits based on income. This bill makes it easier for people in federally declared disaster areas to deduct these losses, even if they don't itemize their taxes (meaning they can still claim the loss even while taking the standard deduction). It also removes some of the stricter income-based limits that would otherwise reduce how much people can deduct. This applies to disasters declared between July 2025 and the end of 2026, and the rules would apply starting with the 2025 tax year.

The second part deals specifically with wildfire victims. Currently, money that people receive to compensate them for wildfire-related losses—like living expenses, lost wages, injuries, or emotional distress—can sometimes count as taxable income. This bill says that such wildfire relief payments won't be taxed as income, as long as insurance or other sources haven't already covered those costs. This tax break would apply to payments received from 2026 through 2030. Overall, this bill mainly affects individuals and families who live in areas hit by federally declared disasters, especially wildfires, by reducing their tax burden and simplifying how they can claim losses.
ai_headline: Bill would ease tax relief for disaster and wildfire victims
last_action_text: Presented to President.

title: Impacts and Outcomes for Health Career Training Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Impacts and Outcomes for Health Career Training Act, changes how the federal government studies "health profession opportunity grants." These grants fund programs that help train people, often those with lower incomes, for jobs in healthcare fields like nursing or medical assisting. The bill requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to formally study how well these training programs work, looking at short-term, medium-term, and long-term results, including whether participants actually get jobs and how much they earn afterward.

To make sure this research actually happens, the bill requires that at least 4 percent of the total money set aside each year for these grant programs be used specifically for studying and evaluating them, including hiring staff to do this work. This means less of the total grant money would go directly to running training programs and more would go toward tracking whether those programs are effective.

This bill mainly affects the federal agency that oversees these grants, the organizations that receive the grants to run job training programs, and indirectly the people enrolled in those programs, since the money spent on evaluation is money not spent on direct training services. It would take effect starting October 1, 2025, and does not create new grants or eliminate old ones — it only changes how existing grant money must be used for research and oversight.

title: Child Care Integrity Monitoring Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would change how the federal government oversees state child care assistance programs funded through the Child Care and Development Block Grant, which helps low-income families pay for child care. Under current law, states already have to submit audits and reports, but this bill would require the Secretary of Health and Human Services to conduct a full, in-depth review of each state's performance every three years, rather than relying only on the existing reporting system.

Based on these reviews, the Secretary would be required to label a state as "high risk" if it has a pattern of problems, such as repeated unresolved audit issues, failure to fix problems identified in past corrective action plans, or repeated violations of its approved state child care plan. States labeled high risk would then face extra monitoring and oversight from the federal government to make sure problems are being fixed.

This bill mainly affects state governments that run child care assistance programs, since it adds new reporting and oversight requirements they must meet. Indirectly, it could also affect families who rely on subsidized child care and child care providers, since increased federal scrutiny is intended to catch mismanagement or compliance problems that could affect how reliably the program is run. The bill does not change eligibility rules or benefits for families directly; it focuses on strengthening federal monitoring of how well states are administering the program.

title: Kari's Law Reporting Act
ai_summary:
HR 5201, called the Kari's Law Reporting Act, directs the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to publish a report reviewing how well the country is following Kari's Law, a 2017 law named after a woman who died after her daughter tried to call 911 from a hotel room phone but couldn't get an outside line without dialing an extra number first. Kari's Law requires multi-line telephone systems, the kind of phone setups used in hotels, offices, schools, and similar buildings, to let people dial 911 directly without needing a prefix like "9" to get an outside line.

Under this new bill, the FCC would have 180 days after the law passes to post a public report on its website. That report must explain how well phone system manufacturers and vendors are complying with Kari's Law, identify any problems or obstacles companies are facing in following the rule, suggest ways the FCC could improve its enforcement, and offer recommendations to Congress if new legislation is needed to fix ongoing issues.

This bill mainly affects businesses that install or manage multi-line phone systems, such as hotels, hospitals, schools, and office buildings, since it puts pressure on regulators to check whether they're meeting 911 access requirements. Everyday residents benefit indirectly, since the report could lead to better enforcement and fewer emergency-calling failures in buildings that use these shared phone systems.
ai_headline: FCC would have to report on compliance with 911 dialing law Kari's Law
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

title: Stop Child Care Fraud Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Stop Child Care Fraud Act of 2026, would change the rules for how states apply for federal child care funding through the Child Care and Development Block Grant program. This program helps low-income families pay for child care. Under the bill, states would be required to include new information in their official plans explaining how they prevent and catch fraud in the program.

Specifically, states would need to describe their internal controls for making sure money is spent properly, explain how they investigate and recover payments that were fraudulently obtained, describe how they punish parents or child care providers who commit fraud, and outline the steps they use to check that families are actually eligible for assistance. States would also need to explain how they share information with other state and local agencies that oversee child care providers, so that fraud can be caught more easily by comparing records across different government offices.

This bill mainly affects state governments that run child care assistance programs, since they would have new paperwork and reporting requirements. It could also indirectly affect families who receive child care assistance and child care providers who accept these payments, since states may create stricter verification or monitoring processes as a result. The bill does not change who is eligible for child care assistance or how much funding is available; it focuses on requiring states to be more transparent about their fraud-prevention efforts.

States would need to describe internal controls, fraud investigation and recovery methods, penalties for fraud, eligibility verification steps, and information-sharing with other agencies.

title: Child Care Payment Integrity and Fraud Accountability Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would change how states handle child care funding they receive from the federal government through the Child Care and Development Block Grant program, which helps low-income families pay for child care. Specifically, it updates the law so that when states are required to track and report overpayments, they must now clearly include fraudulent payments as part of that accounting, rather than treating fraud separately or leaving it out.

The bill also requires each state to submit an annual report to the Secretary of Health and Human Services detailing improper payments in specific, standardized categories. States would need to break down the numbers and percentages into groups such as suspected fraud, verified fraud, non-fraudulent overpayments, underpayments, and errors caused by technical or system problems. This is meant to give the federal government clearer, more consistent data about where child care funding is being misused or mishandled.

This bill mainly affects state agencies that administer child care subsidy programs, since they would face new reporting requirements and administrative work. It could indirectly affect families who rely on child care assistance, as increased oversight and fraud tracking may lead to stricter monitoring of how payments are issued and verified. Child care providers who receive these subsidy payments could also see more scrutiny of billing and payment accuracy.

title: No Waivers for Fraud Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "No Waivers for Fraud Act of 2026," would change how the federal government handles states that break the rules of the Child Care and Development Block Grant program. This program provides federal funding to help states offer child care assistance to low-income families. Under current law, if a state is found to be noncompliant with program rules, the federal government can impose sanctions, but it also has the authority to waive or excuse those sanctions under certain circumstances. This bill would remove that waiver authority specifically for sanctions, meaning once a state is penalized for violating program requirements, that penalty could no longer be forgiven or lifted early.

In practical terms, this bill makes penalties more permanent and less flexible when states misuse or mismanage this federal child care funding. It does not change what counts as a violation or how sanctions are decided in the first place; it only removes the option for federal officials to later waive those sanctions once imposed. The bill still allows waivers in other parts of the law unrelated to sanctions, such as certain reporting or procedural requirements, since it targets only specific references to "sanctions" in the statute.

This bill would primarily affect state governments that administer child care assistance programs, particularly those found to have committed fraud, mismanagement, or other compliance failures. Indirectly, it could affect low-income families who rely on subsidized child care, since stricter and less forgiving sanctions might lead to funding disruptions if a state loses access to certain federal dollars. Federal agencies overseeing the program, such as the Department of Health and Human Services, would also see their discretion reduced when deciding how to respond to state violations.

title: DPA Modernization Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill updates and reorganizes the Defense Production Act of 1950 (DPA), a law that lets the federal government direct private industry to prioritize production of goods needed for national defense, respond to emergencies, and support critical supply chains. The bill renumbers and reorganizes many sections of the law, but it also makes real policy changes. It limits how long the government can control distribution of civilian goods (generally one year, with possible extensions), raises several dollar thresholds for penalties and loan/investment limits (for example, raising minimum loan guarantee thresholds from $50 million to $100 million), and shifts some decision-making power from the President directly to a new "Fund manager" and an interagency "Defense Production Act Committee," which would include officials like the OMB Director. It also creates new programs, such as a "Critical Minerals Resilience Initiative" to help build supply chains for critical minerals outside the control of countries like China, and requires agencies to plan for shortages of medical supplies, critical minerals, and shipbuilding materials.

The bill also adds new safeguards and reporting requirements. It bans discrimination based on energy source when providing financial assistance, prohibits senior government officials (the President, Vice President, committee members) and their close family from personally benefiting from DPA assistance through business ownership, and requires new fraud-prevention procedures. It creates a public "one-stop shop" website so businesses can find information about DPA contracts and opportunities, and it requires new government studies and reports, including a GAO study on stockpiling critical supplies. This bill mainly affects federal agencies that manage national security and emergency supply chains, defense contractors and manufacturers, mining and critical mineral companies, and businesses that might seek federal loans, grants, or purchase agreements. Ordinary consumers could be affected indirectly, especially during future national emergencies, health crises, or natural disasters, since the law governs how the government can direct production and allocate scarce resources during such events.

last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 529.

title: REMITTANCE Act
ai_summary:
This bill would raise the federal excise tax on "remittance transfers" — money sent by people in the United States to family or others in other countries — from 1 percent to 25 percent. It also removes existing limits and exceptions that currently reduce or eliminate this tax for certain types of transfers, meaning the higher tax rate would apply more broadly than before. The money collected from this tax would be set aside specifically to help reduce the national debt, rather than being used for other government spending.

The bill also creates a new tax credit for U.S. citizens who pay this excise tax on transfers made for business or travel purposes. If a U.S. citizen pays this tax while sending money abroad for a business trip or personal travel, they could claim that amount back as a credit on their federal income taxes. This effectively means U.S. citizens sending money for those specific purposes could avoid the financial impact of the higher tax, while other senders — including non-citizens, such as immigrants (including those living in the U.S. legally) sending money to family in their home countries — would not qualify for this credit and would pay the full 25 percent tax.

This bill would primarily affect immigrants and foreign workers in the U.S. who regularly send money to relatives abroad, since remittance transfers are commonly used for that purpose. Businesses that process these transfers, such as money transfer companies and some banks, would also be affected, as they may need to collect and report the tax. Additionally, this could indirectly affect people and economies in other countries who rely on money sent from relatives working in the United States.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: DPA Specialized Staffing Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "DPA Specialized Staffing Act," would create a faster hiring process for certain government agencies that work on national defense production issues. Specifically, it applies to agencies that sit on the Defense Production Act Committee, a group involved in deciding which projects or companies receive federal financial support to boost production of goods considered important for national security or emergency needs.

Normally, federal agencies have to follow standard civil service hiring rules, which include specific competitive examination and hiring procedures found in federal law. This bill would let those agencies skip those standard steps when hiring "subject matter experts"—people with specialized knowledge or experience—so they can hire them more quickly and directly. However, this special hiring power could only be used for one purpose: bringing in experts to help identify, review, and approve projects or activities that might receive financial assistance under the Defense Production Act.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies involved in defense-related production decisions and the experts they might hire, rather than the general public directly. In practice, it could speed up the government's ability to bring in outside specialists—such as people with industry, technical, or financial expertise—to help evaluate which companies or projects qualify for government funding tied to national defense production needs. Everyday Americans could be indirectly affected if this leads to faster, more informed decisions about which industries or companies get federal support during supply chain or national security emergencies.

title: DPA Emerging Technology Act of 2026
ai_summary:
HR 8053, the DPA Emerging Technology Act of 2026, updates the Defense Production Act of 1950, a law that lets the federal government direct industries and resources to support national defense needs. The bill requires the Defense Production Act Committee, a group of federal officials who oversee how this law is used, to meet at least twice a year and gives its chairperson authority to create new subcommittees when needed to better coordinate government agencies working on defense-related production issues.

The main change is the creation of a new Subcommittee on Emerging Technology. This subcommittee would study how new technologies—such as artificial intelligence, robotics, biotechnology, quantum computing, advanced materials, semiconductors, and space technology—could affect national defense needs and how they might be used to improve efficiency, spark innovation, and fix gaps in supply chains. The subcommittee would also have to come up with its own official definition of what counts as "emerging technology" for these purposes.

The bill also directs this new subcommittee to study, within 18 months, whether the government should create a strategic reserve of biological manufacturing materials (similar to stockpiles of oil or medical supplies) that could be important for national defense. Finally, it fixes a small wording error in the original 1950 law's title. Overall, this bill mainly affects federal agencies involved in defense and industrial policy, and indirectly affects industries in fields like tech, biotech, and manufacturing that might work with the government on defense-related production in the future. It does not directly affect the general public's daily life.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

title: Baby Changing on Board Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Baby Changing on Board Act, would require Amtrak to install baby changing tables in bathrooms on its passenger trains. Specifically, it applies to new train cars that Amtrak orders after this law takes effect—it does not require Amtrak to retrofit trains it already owns or operates, and it does not apply to trains Amtrak operates but doesn't own (such as certain commuter rail services).

Under the bill, every new train car would need to have a baby changing table in at least one bathroom, including in bathrooms that meet accessibility standards under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). title: DPA Transparency Act of 2026
ai_summary:

First, it blocks certain companies from receiving government assistance under this law if the President, Vice President, or a member of the Defense Production Act Committee (or their spouse, child, or in-laws) owns 20% or more of that company. This is meant to stop top officials or their family members from personally benefiting from government contracts or aid handed out under this program. Second, it raises the maximum financial penalties for violations of the law from $10,000 to $100,000, making punishments for misuse much steeper. Third, it requires the committee overseeing the program to set up formal procedures to detect and prevent fraud, train staff on those procedures, and appoint a specific person responsible for handling fraud issues.

It also affects federal agencies that administer this law, since they'll have new fraud-prevention duties and reporting requirements. Everyday citizens would be affected indirectly, through added safeguards intended to ensure that emergency production programs are run fairly and are less vulnerable to insider dealing or fraud.

title: A bill to amend title 31, United States Code, to require only foreign entities to report beneficial ownership information, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill would change the federal Corporate Transparency Act, which currently requires many companies to report information about their "beneficial owners" (the real people who own or control them) to the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN). This reporting system was set up to help law enforcement fight money laundering, tax evasion, and other financial crimes by making it harder for people to hide behind anonymous shell companies.

Under this bill, only companies formed in foreign countries that register to do business in the United States would have to report their ownership information. American individuals and U.S.-formed companies would be completely exempt from these reporting requirements. The bill also requires FinCEN to delete, within 90 days, any beneficial ownership information it has already collected about U.S. persons, while allowing it to keep information about foreign owners.

This bill would primarily affect U.S. business owners, particularly people who own small businesses, LLCs, and corporations, by removing a federal paperwork requirement and reporting obligation that was scheduled to apply to millions of American companies. It would also affect foreign companies operating in the U.S., who would still need to comply with reporting rules. Additionally, it affects law enforcement and financial regulators, who use this ownership database to investigate financial crimes, since the pool of available ownership information would shrink significantly once U.S. persons' data is removed.

title: ISLET Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the ISLET Act, changes how the federal government classifies human "islets" taken from deceased donors for transplant into patients, typically people with severe type 1 diabetes. Islets are clusters of cells in the pancreas that produce insulin, and transplanting them from a donor can help some patients control their blood sugar without daily insulin shots. Currently, these islets can be treated similarly to drugs or biological products under federal law, which subjects them to certain regulatory pathways. This bill would instead classify human cadaveric islets the same way whole organs like kidneys or the pancreas itself are classified, meaning they would be regulated as organs for transplantation rather than as drugs, biological products, or human tissue products.

The bill specifically directs that islets from deceased donors should not be considered a "drug," a "biological product," or "human cells, tissues, or cellular or tissue-based products" under existing federal definitions. It requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to update relevant regulations within one year of the bill becoming law, and to report to Congress on that progress within six months.

This bill would mainly affect patients who need islet transplants, doctors and hospitals that perform these transplants, organ procurement organizations, and pharmaceutical or biotech companies involved in processing islets. Supporters of this type of reclassification generally argue that treating islets as organs rather than drugs could simplify the regulatory process and potentially make transplants more available, since organ transplant rules differ from the more complex approval processes required for drugs and biological products.

title: Protecting Our Democracy Act
ai_summary:
HR 8831, the "Protecting Our Democracy Act," is a large package of reforms aimed at limiting presidential power and increasing government accountability and transparency. It covers pardons, self-dealing, foreign influence, and oversight of the executive branch. On pardons, it requires the Attorney General to share investigation records with Congress within 30 days of certain pardons involving the President, family members, or political appointees; it makes bribery in exchange for a pardon a crime; and it declares that a president cannot pardon himself or herself. It also removes the statute of limitations "clock" so that federal crimes committed by a president or vice president (before or during their term) can still be prosecuted after they leave office, and it cuts off a former president's pension and benefits if convicted of a felony related to their time in office.

The bill also strengthens rules against foreign and domestic payments to officials ("emoluments"). It bans the President, Vice President, and other senior officials from accepting money, gifts, or business deals from foreign governments without Congress's approval, requires new financial disclosures, and lets Congress or private citizens sue to enforce these rules. It sets stricter limits and disclosure requirements on inaugural committee donations, restricts legal defense funds for officials from accepting money from lobbyists or foreign agents, and blocks a president from personally profiting from federal or state government funds. Other sections strengthen enforcement of congressional subpoenas, restrict a president's ability to withhold funds Congress has approved (impoundment), improve whistleblower protections, expand Hatch Act enforcement against political use of government resources, require presidential/VP tax return disclosure, and create new oversight offices, including an inspector general for the White House itself.

Finally, the bill addresses foreign interference in elections by requiring campaigns to report contacts from foreign governments, banning foreign money in ballot initiatives, and extending online political ad transparency rules (the "Honest Ads" provisions) to social media platforms. It also limits political favoritism in federal hiring, restricts corporate executives with conflicts of interest from serving in government, and clarifies what counts as an "official act" for legal purposes. Overall, this bill would primarily affect the President, Vice President, senior political appointees, federal agencies, Congress's oversight powers, campaign committees, and online platforms that run political ads — with the stated goal of limiting abuses of executive power and increasing transparency and accountability across the federal government.

title: United States Foreign Service Commemorative Coin Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Treasury to create special commemorative coins honoring the U.S. Foreign Service, the branch of government responsible for American diplomacy overseas, on the 100th anniversary of its founding. The Treasury would produce up to three types of coins: a $5 gold coin, a $1 silver coin, and a half-dollar coin made of standard coin metal. These coins would be legal tender but are mainly intended for collectors, not everyday cash use. The designs would honor the history and role of American diplomats, and they could only be sold during 2029.

The coins would be sold at a price covering their face value, production costs, and an extra "surcharge" added to each sale. That surcharge money—up to $35 per gold coin, $10 per silver coin, and $5 per half-dollar coin—would go to the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training, a nonprofit that preserves the history of American diplomacy through oral histories, books, and educational materials. The bill requires that the Treasury not lose money on this program; all production costs must be recovered before any surcharge funds are distributed to the nonprofit.

This bill mainly affects coin collectors, the U.S. Mint, and the nonprofit organization set to receive proceeds. It does not affect taxes, regular currency, or the general public directly, since these are optional collectible coins rather than something added to everyday circulation. Congress members who support it view it as a way to celebrate the history and contributions of American diplomats while raising money for historical preservation efforts, without cost to taxpayers.

title: Veteran Education Assistance Adjustment Act
ai_summary:
This bill would increase the money that veterans receive under the Post-9/11 GI Bill to help pay for books, supplies, and other school-related expenses. Currently, the maximum yearly stipend for these costs is $1,000. The bill would raise that amount to $1,400. It would apply to veterans using the full benefit as well as those using it at a reduced percentage rate, since both parts of the law dealing with this stipend would be updated.

The bill also sets up a system so this amount doesn't stay stuck at $1,400 forever. Starting in fiscal year 2026, the Department of Veterans Affairs would be required to automatically adjust the stipend every year based on inflation, using the Consumer Price Index (a common measure of how prices change over time). This means the stipend would rise or stay level along with the general cost of living, rather than requiring Congress to pass a new law every time prices go up.

This bill mainly affects veterans and service members who are using or plan to use the Post-9/11 GI Bill for college, trade school, or other approved education programs. It would give them more money each year to cover the cost of books and supplies, which have often become more expensive than the current stipend allows. It does not change other GI Bill benefits, such as tuition payments or housing allowances, and it does not affect people who are not using this specific education benefit.
ai_headline: Bill would raise GI Bill supply stipend from $1,000 to $1,400
last_action_text: Forwarded by Subcommittee to Full Committee by Voice Vote.

title: Alpha-gal Allergen Inclusion Act
ai_summary:
This bill would officially add alpha-gal, a sugar molecule found in most mammal products, to the U.S. government's list of "major food allergens" that food makers must clearly disclose on product labels. Alpha-gal allergy is a condition, often triggered by certain tick bites, that causes people to have allergic reactions to red meat and other products made from mammals like beef, pork, or lamb. Right now, alpha-gal is not on the official major allergen list, which currently includes things like peanuts, milk, eggs, and shellfish, meaning companies aren't legally required to flag it on packaging the way they must for those other allergens.

Under this bill, the definition would cover ingredients that come from non-human mammals as well as a specific type of red algae that can also contain trace amounts of alpha-gal. It would exclude ingredients from special "alpha-gal-knockout" animals that have been genetically modified so their products don't contain the allergen above a detectable level, since those products wouldn't pose a risk. If passed, the change would take effect 18 months after the bill becomes law, giving food manufacturers time to update their labels and processes.

This bill mainly affects people diagnosed with alpha-gal syndrome, an allergy that has become more common due to tick bites (especially from the lone star tick), by making it easier for them to identify and avoid unsafe foods. It also affects food and supplement manufacturers, who would need to test for and disclose alpha-gal content on labels, similar to current rules for allergens like tree nuts or soy.
ai_headline: Bill would add tick-linked meat allergy to required food label warnings
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

The change would take effect 18 months after enactment.

title: Farmer to Farmer Education Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Farmer to Farmer Education Act of 2026, would change federal law to formally support "farmer-to-farmer networks," which are groups of farmers who share knowledge, advice, and support with each other about farming practices. The U.S. Department of Agriculture, through its Secretary, would be allowed to sign agreements with organizations like nonprofits, universities, tribal governments, local governments, states, and farmer groups themselves. These organizations would receive support to help set up mentor programs, host training events, connect farmers with each other, and build networks that help farmers learn practical, science-based methods for improving conservation on their land, such as protecting soil, water, or forests.

The bill directs the USDA to prioritize helping farmers who are historically underserved, have limited resources, or work in high-poverty areas. Organizations that receive funding would need to do things like match farmers with mentors, coordinate training, and, if needed, provide help in a farmer's native language. They could also pass along smaller grants ("subawards") to other groups or even individuals to run local events, and those participants would need to be paid fairly for their time. Organizations receiving funds must report yearly on their work, and the USDA must report to Congress within four years on how the program is going and what it accomplished.

This bill would mainly affect farmers, ranchers, and forest landowners, especially smaller-scale or underserved producers, as well as agricultural nonprofits, universities, tribal organizations, and local governments that might apply for these federal grants. It does not create a new tax or mandate; it simply expands and formalizes an existing USDA conservation program to encourage more farmer-to-farmer learning and mentorship.
ai_headline: New bill would fund farmer-to-farmer mentoring for conservation practices
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.

These networks would teach farmers science-based conservation methods for soil, water, and forests, with priority given to historically underserved, limited-resource, or high-poverty producers.

title: No Taxes on Utility Bills Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "No Taxes on Utility Bills Act," would change federal tax law to let people deduct certain costs from their taxable income. Specifically, it would allow taxpayers to deduct any taxes and state-required surcharges that appear on their gas or electric utility bills. Right now, taxpayers generally cannot deduct these small add-on charges that utility companies collect on behalf of state or local governments; this bill would change that by adding them to the list of deductible taxes under the federal tax code.

In practice, this means that when people file their federal income taxes, they could potentially reduce their taxable income by the amount of taxes and surcharges they paid as part of their gas and electric bills throughout the year. This would primarily benefit taxpayers who itemize their deductions rather than taking the standard deduction, since this new deduction would be added to the existing list of deductible taxes (like state and local income or property taxes). Homeowners and renters who pay utility bills directly, especially in states with higher utility taxes or surcharges, would see the most benefit. The change would apply starting the first tax year after the bill becomes law, if passed.

This bill affects everyday utility customers, tax preparers, and the federal government's tax revenue. Utility companies themselves are not directly affected, since the bill deals with how customers report these charges on their personal tax returns, not with how utilities bill or collect the charges in the first place.
ai_headline: Bill would let taxpayers deduct taxes and fees on gas, electric bills
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: The "No Taxes on Utility Bills Act" would let taxpayers deduct taxes and surcharges on gas and electric bills.

The change would take effect starting the first tax year after the bill becomes law.

title: Armed Forces Carry Rights Protection Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Armed Forces Carry Rights Protection Act of 2026, would change the rules about whether service members can carry their personal firearms on military bases when they are off duty. Currently, military installations have a process for deciding whether to let members carry personal weapons, but the decision is largely up to base commanders' discretion. This bill would tilt that process so that approval becomes the default expectation, meaning a service member's request would generally be granted unless there's a specific reason to deny it.

The bill does this by amending a 2016 defense law to add a "rebuttable presumption" in favor of letting members carry their own firearms while on base, as long as they aren't currently performing official duties. In practical terms, this shifts the burden of proof: instead of a service member having to justify why they should be allowed to carry, the base would have to justify why they should not be allowed to.

The bill also requires that if a request is denied, the denial must be given in writing and must include a clear, specific, and individual reason — not a vague or blanket policy explanation. This affects active-duty military personnel stationed on U.S. bases, as well as base commanders and military leadership, who would have less flexibility to broadly restrict personal firearms and would need to document specific justifications for any denials.
ai_headline: Bill would make base commanders default to allowing personal firearms
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Armed Services.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill would presume approval for off-duty service members to carry personal firearms on base unless a specific reason justifies denial.

Denials would have to be in writing with a specific, individual reason rather than a vague or blanket policy explanation.

title: Azerbaijan Sanctions Review Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Azerbaijan Sanctions Review Act of 2025, would require the President to review whether specific Azerbaijani officials should face U.S. sanctions for human rights abuses. It does not impose sanctions itself. Instead, within 180 days of becoming law, the President would have to send Congress a formal report explaining whether each of the 53 named individuals meets the legal criteria for sanctions under two existing U.S. laws: the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act and a related State Department appropriations law. Those laws allow the U.S. to penalize foreign officials connected to serious human rights violations or corruption.

The named individuals include Azerbaijani military commanders, prosecutors, judges, prison officials, and border security officers. The bill's introduction includes a long list of accusations against Azerbaijan, including claims of war crimes, torture, and mistreatment of Armenian prisoners of war during and after the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh conflict and the 2023 military action that led to the displacement of ethnic Armenians from the region. It also cites concerns about Azerbaijan's treatment of journalists, activists, and political opponents domestically.

If passed, this bill would mainly affect U.S. foreign policy processes and the named Azerbaijani officials, who could potentially face asset freezes or entry bans into the U.S. if the administration later decides to impose sanctions based on the review's findings. It would not directly affect everyday Americans, though it reflects ongoing congressional interest in U.S. relations with Azerbaijan and could influence broader U.S.-Azerbaijan diplomatic and economic relations, including issues related to the Armenia-Azerbaijan peace process.
ai_headline: Bill would order review of sanctions on 53 Azerbaijani officials
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Foreign Affairs, and in addition to the Committee on the Judiciary, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

title: Modernizing Agricultural and Manufacturing Bonds Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes federal tax rules for certain types of bonds that state and local governments issue to help finance private businesses, specifically small manufacturers and first-time farmers. These "private activity bonds" let businesses borrow money at lower interest rates because the interest paid to bondholders is tax-exempt, similar to municipal bonds.

For manufacturing, the bill broadens what counts as a "manufacturing facility" to include places that create certain intangible property (like patents or designs) and related support facilities, not just places making physical products. It also significantly raises the dollar limits on these bonds: the cap on a single bond issue goes from $10 million to $30 million, and the total amount a business can have outstanding in these bonds rises from $40 million to $120 million. These limits would also increase automatically over time to keep pace with inflation. These changes would apply to bonds issued after the law takes effect, mainly benefiting small and mid-sized manufacturers looking to expand or upgrade facilities using this cheaper financing option.

For farmers, the bill increases the amount of debt a first-time farmer can finance through these tax-exempt bonds, raising the limit from $450,000 to $1,000,000, and eliminates a separate, lower limit that applied specifically to used farm equipment. It also changes how "substantial farmland" is measured, switching from the median farm size in a county to the average farm size, which could make more land purchases eligible for this financing. These farm-related changes would apply to bonds issued after December 31, 2025. Overall, the bill mainly affects small manufacturing businesses, new farmers trying to buy land or equipment, and the state and local agencies that issue these bonds on their behalf.
ai_headline: Bill raises tax-exempt bond limits for small manufacturers and new farmers
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services relating to "Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Marketplace Integrity and Affordability".
ai_summary:
This bill would cancel a federal regulation issued by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) called "Marketplace Integrity and Affordability," which was published in June 2025. It uses a special process under the Congressional Review Act that allows Congress to reverse recently issued federal agency rules with a simple resolution. If passed, the rule would be treated as if it never took effect.

The underlying CMS rule made changes to how the Affordable Care Act's health insurance marketplaces operate, affecting things like enrollment procedures, eligibility verification, or plan requirements (the specific details are in the original regulation, not fully included here). Rules with this title typically involve efforts to tighten enrollment rules, reduce improper sign-ups, or adjust subsidy and verification requirements for people buying insurance through healthcare.gov or state marketplaces.

This bill would primarily affect people who buy individual health insurance through ACA marketplaces, insurance companies that sell marketplace plans, and state and federal agencies that run the exchanges. If Congress disapproves the rule, the older marketplace rules would remain in place instead of the new CMS changes, and CMS would be blocked from issuing a substantially similar rule in the future unless authorized by a new law.
ai_headline: Resolution would undo CMS rule on ACA marketplace enrollment

title: Armenian Genocide Education Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Armenian Genocide Education Act, would direct the Librarian of Congress to create and run a national program to help schools teach students about the Armenian Genocide, the mass killing and displacement of Armenians, Greeks, Assyrians, and other Christian groups by the Ottoman Empire between 1915 and 1923. The program would develop teaching materials (both digital and print), create best practices for teachers, offer training workshops, and support a fellowship program to help educators become leaders in teaching this history. The Library of Congress would also maintain a public website section with resources on the topic.

The bill allows the Librarian to partner with schools, school districts, and organizations that work with them, giving priority to those that don't currently offer any Armenian Genocide education programs. These partner organizations could receive support and guidance to build their own teaching programs. The Librarian would also be allowed to accept private donations specifically for this purpose, which would go into a dedicated account separate from other Library of Congress funds.

This bill mainly affects public and independent K-12 schools, teachers, and students, particularly those who may choose to participate in the new program, as well as the Library of Congress, which would gain new responsibilities and be required to report annually to Congress on its progress. The bill authorizes $2 million per year in federal funding for five years (2026–2030) to pay for these activities. It does not mandate that any school teach this material; participation would be voluntary.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on House Administration.

title: Health ACCESS Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Health ACCESS Act, would change federal anti-kickback rules to allow doctors, hospitals, and other healthcare providers to pay online scheduling and directory services (like websites or apps that let patients search for and book appointments with doctors) without that payment being treated as an illegal kickback under Medicare and Medicaid fraud laws. Normally, paying someone to refer or connect patients to your medical practice can violate federal anti-kickback laws, but this bill creates a specific exception for these online booking platforms, as long as they follow strict rules.

Those rules include: the platform can't rank or promote providers based on who pays more, can't share a patient's contact information with providers other than the one the patient picked, can't offer perks like free rides, and can't do targeted marketing calls or texts to people who haven't used the service before. The payment amount also has to be reasonable, agreed to in writing in advance, and not based on how much a provider bills federal health programs. The platform must also clearly disclose its financial relationships with providers and use fair, consistent criteria for which providers can join.

This bill mainly affects healthcare providers, insurers, and companies that run online doctor-finder or appointment-booking websites, as well as patients who use those websites, especially people on Medicare or Medicaid. The goal is to make it easier for these scheduling platforms to operate and partner with healthcare providers without running afoul of fraud laws, while including safeguards meant to prevent patients from being steered toward providers simply because they paid more money to the platform.
ai_headline: Bill would exempt doctor-booking platforms from anti-kickback law
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Ways and Means, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

title: Veterans’ ACCESS Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 740, the Veterans' ACCESS Act of 2025, makes a series of changes to how the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) handles outside medical care for veterans, known as the Veterans Community Care Program. This program lets veterans see private doctors when the VA can't provide timely care. The bill sets clear rules for how far and how long veterans should have to travel and wait before qualifying for outside care (for example, 20 days or 30 minutes drive for primary/mental health care), requires the VA to notify veterans quickly about their eligibility, tell them why a request was denied and how to appeal, discuss telehealth options, and consider veterans' personal preferences and need for caregivers. It also gives outside health providers more time (one year instead of 180 days) to submit bills for payment.

The bill also focuses heavily on mental health and substance abuse treatment. It requires the VA to create a standardized, fast screening process (within 48 hours) to determine which veterans need priority admission to residential mental health or substance abuse programs, and to admit priority cases quickly. If the VA can't meet these timelines, veterans must be offered care at approved outside facilities. The bill adds requirements for tracking wait times, training staff, coordinating care during transitions, creating discharge care plans, and allowing veterans or providers to appeal admission delays or denials.

Finally, the bill directs the VA to develop an online tool for veterans to schedule appointments, track referrals, and appeal decisions, and updates rules for the VA's internal innovation office that tests new care and payment models. It also requires a new three-year pilot program letting veterans access outpatient mental health and substance abuse care without needing prior referral or approval, prioritizing areas with high veteran suicide or overdose rates. Various government reports to Congress are required throughout to track how well these changes are working. Overall, this bill primarily affects veterans who use VA health care, the VA itself, and outside/private health providers who partner with the VA to deliver care.
ai_headline: Bill sets wait-time rules and mental health fast-track for VA outside care
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by Voice Vote.

It also creates a 48-hour screening process for priority mental health and substance abuse admissions, an online scheduling and appeals tool, and a three-year pilot letting some veterans access mental health care without prior referral.

title: Empty Lots to Housing Act
ai_summary:
H.R. 3459, the "Empty Lots to Housing Act," changes federal highway law to make it easier to turn unused government-owned land into housing near transit. Currently, when state or local agencies acquire property using federal highway funds but later no longer need that land, there are restrictions on what can be done with it. This bill allows the U.S. Secretary of Transportation to let recipients of that federal funding transfer the leftover land to local governments, nonprofits, or in some cases private developers, specifically so housing can be built there, without the usual requirement to repay or account for the federal money originally used to buy the land.

If the land goes to a private company instead of a government or nonprofit, the Secretary must first confirm that no local government or nonprofit is able to take it, that the public benefits outweigh simply selling the land for its market value, and that the private developer has a solid track record building or running affordable housing. Any transfer also comes with a 30-year affordability requirement: at least 40% of the housing units built must be reserved for lower-income families (earning 60% or less of the area's median income) at capped rents, and within that group, at least 20% of units must go to very low-income families (30% or less of area median income).

This bill would primarily affect state transportation departments, local governments, nonprofit and for-profit housing developers, and residents in need of affordable housing near public transit. It could create new opportunities to build affordable housing on leftover highway-related land, while giving federal officials oversight to ensure the land is used for its intended public benefit rather than simply sold off.
ai_headline: Bill would let surplus highway land be turned into affordable housing
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill lets leftover federal highway land transfer for housing, with 30 years of affordability rules attached.

Any transfer requires 40% of units reserved for lower-income families for 30 years, with 20% of those going to very low-income families.

title: Fair Treatment of Religious Organizations Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Fair Treatment of Religious Organizations Act of 2026, makes two main changes. First, it changes federal tax law so that the IRS cannot deny an organization "tax-exempt" status just because of its religious beliefs or practices about marriage, sexuality, or gender identity—even if those beliefs conflict with other laws or general public policy. It also says a belief still counts as "religious" even if it isn't a core or required part of that religion's teachings. In practice, this means churches, religious schools, and similar groups couldn't lose their nonprofit tax status solely because of their positions on these topics.

Second, the bill says federal agencies cannot penalize religious organizations—like religious corporations, schools, or associations—that receive federal grants, loans, or contracts because those organizations hire based on shared religious beliefs. It reinforces existing legal exemptions that already let religious employers give preference to people of their own faith when making hiring decisions, even while receiving federal funding.

This bill would primarily affect religious nonprofits, churches, religious schools, and faith-based charities, especially those that hold traditional views on marriage, sexuality, or gender identity. It would also affect the IRS and other federal agencies that oversee tax-exempt status and distribute federal grants or contracts, by limiting their ability to factor in these religious positions when making funding or tax-status decisions. title: CRP Improvement and Flexibility Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would update the Conservation Reserve Program (CRP), a federal program that pays farmers and landowners to take environmentally sensitive farmland out of crop production and instead plant grasses or other cover to protect soil, water, and wildlife habitat. The bill makes several technical changes to how the program operates, including adding a wildlife habitat category to a continuous enrollment option, adjusting rules for emergency haying and grazing (cutting or grazing the protected land during droughts, floods, wildfires, or other emergencies), and adding new protections to prevent that emergency use from causing long-term damage to habitat that supports wildlife like ground-nesting birds.

The bill also expands what the government will help pay for on enrolled land. It allows cost-sharing funds to cover grazing infrastructure such as fencing and water systems, not just water systems as before, when grazing is part of the conservation plan. It also makes clear that land with this new grazing infrastructure can be replanted and re-enrolled in CRP after a contract ends. Additionally, it changes how "management" payments work for activities other than haying or grazing, and raises the yearly cap on rental payments a landowner can receive under the program from $50,000 to $125,000.

This bill mainly affects farmers, ranchers, and landowners who participate in CRP, as well as USDA officials who administer the program. Raising the payment cap could make it more attractive for larger landowners to participate, while the infrastructure funding could help those who want to combine conservation with limited grazing. Wildlife conservation groups and rural communities dealing with drought or natural disasters may also be affected by the emergency-use and habitat-protection provisions.

last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Conservation, Research, and Biotechnology.

title: Healthy Foods for Native Seniors Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Healthy Foods for Native Seniors Act, directs the U.S. Department of Agriculture to create a test program allowing Native American tribal governments and organizations to buy their own food supplies for a federal nutrition program called the Commodity Supplemental Food Program. This program normally provides food packages to low-income seniors, and currently the USDA decides what foods are included. Under this new pilot project, selected tribes would be allowed to purchase their own agricultural products instead of simply receiving whatever the government supplies, as long as those foods are grown in the U.S., meet similar nutrition standards, and don't significantly increase the overall amount of food provided. Foods with cultural or traditional significance to a tribe could also be included.

To take part, a tribal entity would need to already be successfully running the food program and show it has the ability to handle purchasing responsibilities. The USDA would consult with tribes to figure out how the selection process works and would report to Congress each year on how the project is going. The bill sets aside up to $5 million for the program itself and about $1.2 million per year from 2026 through 2029 to hire staff to manage these special contracts with tribes.

This bill mainly affects Native American tribes, tribal organizations, and Indian reservations that participate in the senior food assistance program, as well as the USDA staff who administer it. Indirectly, it could affect elderly Native Americans who receive food assistance, since the foods available to them might better reflect their tribe's dietary preferences or traditions if their tribe joins the program.
ai_headline: Bill would let tribes buy their own foods for senior nutrition program
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Nutrition and Foreign Agriculture.

Participating tribes must already be running the program successfully and show they can handle purchasing duties.

title: Universal Savings Account Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new type of tax-advantaged savings account called a "Universal Savings Account" (USA), which any individual could open at a bank or other qualified financial institution. People could contribute up to $10,000 per year in cash (with the limit rising slightly each year and adjusting for inflation, capped at $25,000), and the money in the account would grow completely tax-free. Unlike retirement accounts such as IRAs or 401(k)s, there would be no restrictions on when or why money could be withdrawn—account holders could take money out at any time, for any reason, without paying taxes or penalties on withdrawals.

The accounts would work somewhat like Roth IRAs but with far more flexibility, since there's no requirement to use the money for retirement, education, or any specific purpose. If the account holder dies, a surviving spouse could take over the account and keep its tax benefits; otherwise, the account would be treated as fully distributed and closed. The bill also sets rules for how these accounts must be managed, requires financial institutions to report account activity to the IRS, and creates penalties for excess contributions or improper use of the accounts, similar to existing rules for IRAs.

This bill would affect any American who wants an additional way to save money tax-free, particularly people looking for more flexible savings options than retirement or education-specific accounts. It would also affect banks and financial institutions, which would need to offer and administer these new accounts, and the IRS, which would oversee compliance and collect reports on contributions and withdrawals. The change would apply starting with the 2025 tax year.
ai_headline: New bill would let anyone open a tax-free "Universal Savings Account"
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
