title: Melanie's Law
ai_summary:
HR 8733, called Melanie's Law, creates a new federal grant program to help states strengthen protective orders (sometimes called restraining orders) related to domestic violence. It specifically encourages states to make sure their courts can issue protective orders that cover not just romantic partners, but also family members connected to people in intimate relationships. For example, if someone is in a relationship where domestic violence occurs, this law would push states to give courts the authority to also protect that person's or their partner's relatives, such as parents, children, or in-laws, who might be threatened or harmed as a result of the relationship.

To qualify for the federal funding, a state must show that its laws already give courts this expanded authority. States can then use the grant money for things like training police and prosecutors, improving how protective orders are delivered and tracked across different jurisdictions, funding specialized domestic violence units, and providing victim services such as legal help, emergency shelter, counseling, transportation, and hotlines. Up to 75% of funds would be distributed to states based on population, up to 22% through competitive grants, and a small portion for federal administrative costs.

This bill would primarily affect state court systems, law enforcement agencies, and domestic violence victim service organizations, since they would be eligible to receive and use this funding. It would also affect victims of domestic violence and their extended family members, who could gain broader legal protections. The program would run from 2026 through 2036, with $200 million authorized each year, though actual funding would still depend on future congressional appropriations.
ai_headline: Melanie's Law offers grants to widen domestic violence protective orders
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Protecting Our Second Amendment Data Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change the rules for certain federal grant programs that help state and local police departments, called Byrne Justice Assistance Grants and COPS grants. Under this bill, before a state, city, tribal government, or private organization could receive these federal grants, they would have to certify (officially promise) that they had not leaked or shared personal information about people who registered a firearm, applied for a concealed or open carry permit, or went through a background check to buy a gun. This would apply whether the leak was done on purpose, by accident, or in any other way.

The personal information covered includes things like a person's name, Social Security number, birth date, fingerprints or other biometric data, phone numbers, and medical or financial details. If a government agency or organization applying for these grants had exposed this kind of information about gun owners or applicants in the previous year, they would not be able to certify compliance, which could affect their eligibility for the funding.

This bill mainly affects state and local law enforcement agencies, police departments, and organizations that apply for these federal justice grants, since it adds a new paperwork requirement they must meet. Indirectly, it also affects people who own guns or have applied for gun permits or background checks, since the goal is to encourage agencies to better protect their personal information from being disclosed.
ai_headline: Bill ties police grant funding to protecting gun owners' personal data
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: VICTIM Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the VICTIM Act of 2026, would create a new federal grant program to help police departments solve more homicides and gun-related violent crimes. The Attorney General would be required to set up this program within 180 days, and state, local, and tribal law enforcement agencies could apply for funding. Grant money could be used for things like hiring and training detectives and forensic staff, buying new investigative or forensic technology, improving communication between police units, analyzing crime trends, and supporting officers dealing with job-related stress or trauma.

A significant part of the bill also focuses on crime victims and their families. Agencies could use grant funds to help victims access emergency food, housing, transportation, counseling, legal advice, and financial compensation, as well as to train staff in trauma-informed interview techniques and language or disability accommodations. The bill requires agencies that receive grants to report detailed data each year, including clearance rates, victim and suspect demographics, and how the money was spent, and it sets up audits to prevent misuse of funds. It also requires the Justice Department to study which practices work best for solving these crimes and to report results to Congress.

This bill would mainly affect local, state, and tribal police departments (especially in rural and small communities, which are guaranteed a minimum share of funding), crime victims and their families who could receive better support services, and taxpayers, since it authorizes $60 million per year from 2027 through 2031 to fund the program. It does not change criminal laws or penalties directly—it focuses on funding, training, technology, and accountability measures aimed at improving how violent crimes are investigated and how victims are treated.

title: Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities for All Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the federal government hands out money to states, tribes, and communities to prepare for disasters before they happen, such as building flood barriers, strengthening buildings, or improving drainage systems. Currently, some of this "predisaster hazard mitigation" funding is awarded competitively, with the President choosing which local governments get funding based on recommendations from governors. This bill would replace that competitive process with a fixed formula: one-third of the money would be split equally among all eligible states, one-third would be distributed based on each state's population, and one-third would go to states with the most vulnerable critical infrastructure (like power plants, water systems, or bridges). It also guarantees that Native American tribal governments receive at least $75 million total.

The bill also changes the approval process so that states, not the President directly, choose which local projects get funded, though the President can still approve outside projects in unusual circumstances. States would be required to pass along at least half of their funding to local governments for specific recommended projects, with the rest going toward broader mitigation planning activities. Additionally, the bill clarifies that receiving money under this predisaster program won't disqualify a project from also receiving separate federal disaster recovery funding after an actual disaster occurs, and vice versa.

This bill would primarily affect state and local governments, emergency management agencies, and tribal governments that apply for federal disaster-preparedness funding. Indirectly, it affects everyday residents in disaster-prone areas, since it changes which communities are more likely to receive funding to protect against floods, storms, wildfires, and other hazards before they strike.
ai_headline: Bill would replace competitive disaster-prep grants with fixed formula
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Economic Development, Public Buildings, and Emergency Management.

title: GATE CRASHERS Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the GATE CRASHERS Act, would create a new federal crime for entering Department of Defense property without permission when that property is clearly marked as closed or restricted. This could include military bases, testing sites, or other facilities controlled by the military.

Under the bill, penalties would increase for repeat offenders. A first offense could result in a fine and up to 180 days in jail. A second offense would carry a penalty of up to 3 years in prison, and a third or later offense could lead to up to 10 years in prison, along with fines in either case.

This bill would primarily affect people who trespass onto military property, including protesters, curious trespassers, or anyone who crosses into restricted areas without authorization. It gives federal prosecutors a specific law to charge repeat trespassers more severely than they might be charged under existing general trespassing laws, aiming to deter people from repeatedly entering restricted military sites.

title: CRP Improvement and Flexibility Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would make several changes to the Conservation Reserve Program (CRP), a federal program that pays farmers and landowners to take environmentally sensitive land out of crop production and plant grasses or other vegetation to protect soil and wildlife habitat. The bill adds a wildlife habitat option to the list of activities eligible for continuous (rather than competitive) enrollment, meaning landowners could sign up for this specific conservation practice at any time rather than only during limited enrollment periods.

The bill also changes rules around emergency haying and grazing on CRP land during droughts, floods, wildfires, or other disasters. It creates clearer conditions for when farmers can cut hay or graze livestock on their CRP land during emergencies, based on drought severity ratings or crop loss percentages, while adding a safeguard to prevent this activity from causing long-term damage to wildlife habitat. Additionally, it expands cost-sharing payments so the government can help pay for grazing infrastructure like fencing and water systems on CRP land, and allows land with this infrastructure to be re-enrolled in the program after a contract ends. Finally, it raises the cap on rental payments a landowner can receive under CRP contracts from $50,000 to $125,000 per year.

This bill primarily affects farmers, ranchers, and rural landowners who participate in or are considering joining CRP, as well as USDA officials who administer the program. It could make the program more flexible and financially attractive for larger landowners, while also aiming to balance emergency farming needs with wildlife conservation goals during natural disasters.

title: Humanitarian Theft Enforcement Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Humanitarian Theft Enforcement Act, would allow the U.S. government to hold foreign individuals or organizations financially responsible if they steal, misuse, or destroy American-funded humanitarian aid. This includes aid that the U.S. pays for but that is actually distributed through international organizations like the United Nations. If the Secretary of State determines that a foreign person or group diverted supplies (like food, medicine, or other relief items) away from their intended use, or destroyed them without authorization, that person or group would owe the U.S. government money equal to the value of what was lost.

The bill directs the Secretary of State to try to recover that money from the responsible parties. Any funds actually collected would go into a U.S. government account and could be used again for related purposes, rather than being sent back to the general treasury. If the aid had originally been funded by a different federal agency, the money recovered could be transferred to that agency instead of being kept by the State Department.

The bill also gives the Secretary of State the power to waive this liability entirely if doing so is judged to be in the "national interest," meaning the government wouldn't have to pursue payment in every case. This bill would primarily affect foreign governments, organizations, militias, or individuals accused of stealing or destroying U.S.-funded aid supplies abroad. It would also affect how the State Department and other federal agencies track, investigate, and financially respond to aid theft or destruction in conflict zones or disaster areas where U.S. humanitarian assistance is distributed.
ai_headline: Bill would make foreign actors pay for stolen U.S. aid supplies
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 45 - 1.

title: WELLS Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the WELLS Act, would require hospitals that accept Medicare patients to create a special discharge plan for pregnant patients who show up with signs of labor but are sent home before actually delivering. Starting in 2027, if a doctor decides a pregnant patient in labor should be discharged rather than admitted, the hospital would have to document why, check how far the patient lives from the hospital and whether they have reliable transportation, identify a backup hospital for delivery, have the plan reviewed by a nurse or social worker, and go over all this information with the patient in their own language before they leave. This applies to all hospitals, critical access hospitals, and rural emergency hospitals that participate in Medicare, even for patients who aren't on Medicare themselves.

The bill also expands an existing rural maternal health training grant program by requiring grant recipients to meet performance goals, such as training a certain percentage of their staff, in order to keep receiving funding. It requires more detailed annual public reports on how these grants are used, including which organizations get them, how training is delivered, and whether it improves patient outcomes and reduces racial disparities. Finally, it directs federal health agencies to create a research initiative comparing different training methods for maternal health providers and to build a public online dashboard tracking maternal health outcomes nationally.

Overall, this bill mainly affects hospitals (especially rural ones), pregnant patients experiencing labor symptoms, and federal health agencies involved in maternal health training and research. Supporters would frame it as addressing patient safety concerns in maternity care, particularly in rural areas, though implementation would create new administrative and documentation requirements for hospitals.

title: Bereaved Parents Rights Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Bereaved Parents Rights Act, would change Medicare law to require hospitals and freestanding birth centers to tell parents about their rights when a miscarriage or stillbirth happens and the facility ends up with custody of the fetus. Specifically, within 6 hours of the miscarriage or stillbirth (or before the parent is discharged, whichever comes first), the facility would have to give the parent or parents a government-created form explaining that they have the right to choose a private or shared burial, cremation, or having the hospital dispose of the fetus. If a parent decides in writing within 72 hours that they want to arrange a burial or cremation, the facility must follow the same rules that their state already has in place for handling fetal deaths.

This would affect parents who experience a miscarriage or stillbirth at a hospital or birth center, giving them a formal, guaranteed choice in what happens to the fetus rather than leaving it entirely up to hospital policy. It would also affect hospitals and birth centers, which would need to create new procedures, forms, and staff training to comply, since facilities that don't follow these rules could face lawsuits from people harmed by a violation. Because the bill amends Medicare law, it would likely apply broadly, since nearly all hospitals participate in Medicare and must follow its conditions of participation.

title: Risk-based Oversight for Integrity Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change how the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) oversees and inspects organic farms and food businesses under the National Organic Program. Right now, certified organic farms and handling operations (companies that process, package, or store organic products) generally must undergo annual on-site inspections. This bill would keep that requirement for farms and operations located outside the U.S., but for domestic operations, it would allow on-site inspections once every three years, with the in-between years' inspections done either on-site or virtually, depending on how much risk that farm or business poses to "organic integrity" — meaning the risk that a product labeled organic isn't actually meeting organic standards. Businesses that only buy and sell organic products without physically handling them could be inspected using virtual methods instead of in-person visits.

The bill also directs USDA to study whether it should overhaul its oversight system to be based more heavily on risk levels. Within a year, USDA would have to research options like tiered certification systems, standardized organic farming plans, and clearer guidance for certifiers and farmers, taking into account each operation's size, complexity, location, and compliance history. USDA would need to consult with organic industry groups, certifiers, farmers, and consumers, then report its findings to Congress within 18 months. Based on that report, USDA could issue new regulations adjusting oversight rules, potentially easing requirements for lower-risk operations while focusing more resources on higher-risk ones.

This bill would primarily affect certified organic farmers, food processors and handlers, and the certifying agents who inspect them, potentially reducing inspection burdens for smaller or well-established domestic operations. Consumers who buy organic products could also be affected if oversight changes affect how strictly organic standards are enforced, though the bill states current enforcement authority to protect organic integrity would not be limited.
ai_headline: Bill would ease annual inspections for domestic organic farms
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Nutrition and Foreign Agriculture.

title: Promoting Access to Local Agriculture Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture to make it easier for farmers and ranchers who sell directly to customers—such as at farmers markets or through community-supported agriculture programs—to participate in federal nutrition assistance programs. Currently, farmers who want to accept SNAP (food stamps), WIC farmers' market benefits, senior nutrition program benefits, and incentive programs like the Gus Schumacher Nutrition Incentive Program often have to fill out separate applications for each program, which can be time-consuming and discourage participation. The bill requires the USDA to create either one combined application for all these programs or a system where getting approved for one program automatically qualifies the farmer for the others.

The bill also requires the USDA to simplify how these farmers process benefit payments, encouraging the use of standardized technology like a single piece of equipment or a mobile app, rather than juggling multiple systems for different programs. Additionally, it updates existing law to require that when states provide equipment for processing SNAP benefits, that equipment must be appropriate for the situation—specifically calling for wireless or mobile technology suited to farmers markets and other direct-sales settings, where traditional wired card readers may not work well.

This bill mainly affects small and local farmers who sell directly to consumers, making it simpler for them to accept government nutrition benefits and potentially reach more customers. It could also benefit low-income shoppers, seniors, and WIC recipients by increasing the number of farmers markets and local food vendors that accept their benefits. The USDA would be required to report back to Congress within a year on its progress implementing these changes.
ai_headline: Bill would streamline farmer sign-up for SNAP and other food aid programs
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

title: Increasing Access to Lung Cancer Screening Act
ai_summary:
This bill aims to make it easier for people to get lung cancer screenings and help with quitting smoking or vaping, without extra costs or red tape. For Medicaid, it would require states to cover annual lung cancer screenings at no cost to patients, as long as those screenings match current medical guidelines from the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (a panel of medical experts). It also removes the requirement for prior authorization, meaning patients wouldn't need special pre-approval from insurance before getting screened. Additionally, it expands Medicaid coverage of tobacco-cessation counseling and medication—currently only guaranteed for pregnant women—to all Medicaid enrollees, including coverage for quitting e-cigarettes and vape pens.

The bill also changes rules for Medicare and private/employer health insurance, blocking insurers from requiring prior authorization before covering annual lung cancer screenings for people who qualify under medical guidelines. This means eligible patients could get scheduled for scans without waiting on insurance approval first. Separately, the bill sets aside $10 million per year (2028–2032) for a public education campaign to raise awareness about lung cancer screening, particularly targeting high-risk groups.

Finally, the bill directs a government watchdog agency (the Government Accountability Office) to study who is currently getting diagnosed with lung cancer versus who is eligible for screening under current rules. This includes looking at groups who may be missed by existing guidelines, such as firefighters, veterans, and younger women. Overall, the bill primarily affects Medicaid enrollees, Medicare beneficiaries, and people with private health insurance, especially current or former smokers and those at high risk for lung cancer, as well as state Medicaid programs and health insurers who must adjust their coverage rules starting in 2028.

last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance. (text: CR S2377-2379)

title: Legalizing Premium Health Care Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Legalizing Premium Health Care Act of 2026, would change how doctors and other health providers can charge Medicare patients. Currently, doctors who don't fully participate in Medicare face restrictions on what they can charge beneficiaries beyond Medicare's approved rates. Under this bill, doctors and Medicare patients could sign private contracts allowing the doctor to charge whatever price they agree on for a service, while the patient could still submit a claim to Medicare and get reimbursed at the normal Medicare rate. Importantly, the doctor wouldn't lose their Medicare participation status just because they made this kind of arrangement with a particular patient.

The bill includes some consumer protections: the contract must be in writing, signed in advance, and cannot be made during a medical emergency or urgent situation. It must clearly explain that the patient is responsible for payment and that normal Medicare payment limits don't apply to the agreed charges. People who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid (dual-eligible individuals) would not be allowed to use these contracts. The bill also would stop states from enforcing their own laws that limit how much these providers can charge for Medicare-covered services, overriding any state price caps.

This bill would primarily affect Medicare beneficiaries (mostly people 65 and older, plus some people with disabilities) and the doctors and other licensed professionals who treat them. Supporters generally argue it gives patients and doctors more flexibility and choice in arranging care and payment. Critics generally worry it could lead to higher out-of-pocket costs for patients, since providers could charge more than Medicare's standard rates. The bill does not change what services Medicare covers, only how payment can be arranged for those services.
ai_headline: Bill would let doctors and Medicare patients sign private pay contracts
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

Contracts must be written, signed in advance, and can't be made during emergencies. title: EPSTEIN Act
ai_summary:
HR 7814, called the EPSTEIN Act, would create a new independent commission within Congress to oversee how the Department of Justice handles the so-called "Epstein files"—records related to Jeffrey Epstein's crimes and his associates. This commission would have eight members split evenly between appointments from Senate and House leaders of both parties, and none of them could be current members of Congress or DOJ employees. The commission would pick its own chair and vice-chair, who must be from different political parties, to help keep the group balanced.

The commission's job would be to investigate Epstein's crimes and any associates, review unredacted files, and push for transparency in how the DOJ enforces human trafficking laws. It would have real legal power: it could request documents from federal agencies, issue subpoenas to compel testimony or evidence, and refer potential criminal cases to prosecutors or state attorneys general. If someone refuses to comply with a subpoena, the commission could ask a federal court or U.S. attorney to enforce it, similar to how congressional investigations work. The commission would issue quarterly progress reports and, within 18 months, a comprehensive public report with findings and recommendations, though it could withhold sensitive material like victims' personal information or child abuse imagery.

This bill would mainly affect the Department of Justice, FBI, and U.S. Attorneys' offices, which would be required to share records with the commission. It would also affect anyone connected to the Epstein investigation who might be called to testify or face referral for prosecution. For everyday Americans, the bill's main effect would be increased public oversight and transparency regarding a high-profile case, potentially leading to new prosecutions or public reports about how the government handled the investigation.
ai_headline: New bill would create congressional commission to oversee Epstein files
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Ending Predator Access to Union Power Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Ending Predator Access to Union Power Act," would change federal labor law to bar people convicted of sex offenses against minors from holding certain positions of power within labor unions. It amends a section of the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act of 1959, a law that already prevents people convicted of certain serious crimes (like murder or crimes involving significant bodily harm) from serving as union officers, employees, or in other key roles for a set period of time after their conviction. This bill adds "sex offense against a minor" to that existing list of disqualifying crimes.

In practical terms, this means someone convicted of a sex crime against a child would be legally barred from serving as a union officer, consultant, or in other specified union leadership positions, similar to how people convicted of other serious violent crimes are already barred. The bill also makes a small technical fix to the law's punctuation. If passed, the change would take effect 30 days after becoming law.

This bill would primarily affect labor unions and their members, since it governs who can hold leadership or trust-based positions within these organizations. It would also affect individuals with past convictions for sex offenses against minors who might otherwise seek such positions, as they would now be explicitly prohibited from doing so under federal law.
ai_headline: Bill would bar child sex offenders from union leadership roles
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 33 - 0.

title: Dry-Redwater Regional Water Authorization Act
ai_summary:
This bill authorizes the federal government to help build a large water supply system called the Dry-Redwater Regional Water Authority System, which would serve rural communities in five Montana counties (Dawson, Garfield, McCone, Prairie, and Richland) and one North Dakota county (McKenzie). The goal is to give these communities reliable access to clean water for homes, farms, ranches, and businesses. The U.S. Secretary of the Interior would enter into an agreement with the local water authority to help plan, design, and build the system, including pipelines, pumping stations, treatment facilities, and related infrastructure. The federal government would pay up to 75% of the costs, with the rest covered locally, and Congress would authorize $602 million for construction between 2027 and 2037, an amount that could be adjusted for inflation or unexpected cost increases.

The bill also addresses electric power needed to run the water system. Because two of the counties (McCone and Garfield) were previously affected by the construction of the Fort Peck Dam and were promised certain benefits under a older federal power program (the Pick-Sloan Program), this bill directs the Western Area Power Administration to supply the electricity needed to operate the water system at standard "firm power" rates. The local water authority would be responsible for paying for that power and for any necessary electrical transmission upgrades.

This bill mainly affects residents, farmers, ranchers, and industries in the specified rural Montana and North Dakota counties, who would gain improved water infrastructure. It also affects the federal agencies involved (Department of the Interior and Western Area Power Administration) and local governments who would share construction costs. The bill specifies that it does not change any state water rights laws, meaning Montana and North Dakota would keep control over how their water resources are managed.
ai_headline: Bill authorizes $602 million for rural Montana-North Dakota water system
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

title: Dry-Redwater Regional Water Authorization Act

title: Containing Effects of Mineral Extraction Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Containing Effects of Mineral Extraction Act of 2026, adds new rules for large mining operations that dig up materials like gravel, sand, and stone (called "mineral materials") on federal land. It applies specifically to big projects—those producing more than 1 million tons per year—that are located within 25 miles of a city or near ecologically sensitive areas, and that haven't started operating yet. Before the federal government can approve a contract or permit for one of these projects, the company must submit several studies: an assessment of how truck traffic will affect local roads and safety, a plan to manage truck trips and control dust and noise, a water conservation plan to offset the water the project will use, and an analysis of whether rail transport could be used instead of trucks. The company must also show it has proper water rights and environmental permits already in place, and it must work with local and state governments, who can request changes if needed.

Once a project is approved, the company must file annual reports on water use, truck trips, and whether it's following through on its commitments. This information stays confidential, but the government will publish a general summary each year and review overall trends every five years. The Secretary of the Interior can suspend or cancel a permit if a company doesn't follow the rules. This bill mainly affects large mining companies operating near cities, along with the state, local, and tribal governments and nearby residents who deal with the traffic, noise, dust, and water impacts of these projects. It does not replace existing environmental laws like NEPA or state permitting rules—it adds extra requirements on top of them.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.

Companies must also prove they have water rights and environmental permits, and coordinate with local and state governments.

title: Officer Wellness and Peer Support Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Officer Wellness and Peer Support Act of 2026, would require the U.S. Attorney General to write a report about how to help law enforcement officers deal with mental health issues. The report would look at effective ways to reduce the shame or embarrassment ("stigma") that often keeps officers from seeking help, and would suggest methods to encourage officers to use mental health screenings, peer counseling, and other support services. It would also address how to keep these mental health services private and confidential.

To create this report, the Attorney General would need to work with other officials, including leaders from the FBI, the Office of Community Oriented Policing Services, and the National Institute of Justice. They would also have to consult with police agencies at all levels of government, labor unions, academic experts, and mental health or suicide prevention organizations. The report would be due to Congress within 270 days after the bill becomes law.

This bill mainly affects law enforcement officers broadly defined to include police, corrections officers, probation and parole officers, and judicial officers. It does not create new programs or funding directly; instead, it directs government agencies to study the issue and recommend future actions. Everyday residents would be affected indirectly, since improving officer mental health support could influence police workforce well-being and, potentially, community policing outcomes.

title: Title VIII Nursing Workforce Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews and updates federal funding programs that help train and support nurses across the country. These programs, known as "Title VIII" programs, have existed for years and provide grants to nursing schools, hospitals, and clinics to train nurse practitioners, nurse-midwives, nurse anesthetists, clinical nurse specialists, and nursing faculty. The bill extends funding authorization through 2030 and increases the funding levels: one funding category rises from about $137.8 million to about $184.3 million per year, and another rises from about $117.1 million to about $121.1 million per year.

Beyond just renewing funding, the bill also updates what the money can be used for. It allows grants to cover costs for clinical training supervisors ("preceptors"), modern teaching tools like simulation labs, virtual reality, and telehealth technology, and efforts to recruit more nursing faculty and students to address nursing shortages. It also expands support for training related to survivors of sexual assault, in addition to survivors of domestic violence, and encourages partnerships between nursing schools and hospitals, community health centers, or clinics to expand hands-on training opportunities for nursing students.

This bill mainly affects nursing schools, nursing students, hospitals and clinics that train nurses, and ultimately patients who depend on a well-staffed nursing workforce. Because the country has faced ongoing nursing shortages, especially in rural and underserved areas, supporters generally frame this bill as a way to help train more nurses and keep nursing education programs adequately funded. It does not change nursing licensing rules or patient care requirements directly; it primarily deals with federal grant funding and how that funding can be used.

title: ABLE Employment Flexibility Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the ABLE Employment Flexibility Act, changes federal tax law to give workers with disabilities more flexibility in how their employer's retirement contributions are used. ABLE accounts are special tax-advantaged savings accounts that people with disabilities can use without losing eligibility for programs like Medicaid or Supplemental Security Income (SSI), which normally have strict limits on how much money a person can have saved. Currently, if an employer automatically contributes to a worker's 401(k) or similar retirement plan, that money could complicate a disabled worker's benefit eligibility, since retirement funds work differently than ABLE accounts.

Under this bill, employers could let eligible employees choose to redirect what would normally be a retirement plan contribution into their ABLE account instead. This option would have to be offered equally to all eligible employees, not just some. The bill also clarifies that employers can make direct contributions or matching contributions to a worker's ABLE account, and that these employer contributions count as if the employee made them personally (which matters for annual contribution limits). Additionally, it directs the Treasury Department to update tax rules so these employer contributions are treated as a normal business expense (deductible compensation), and to inform employers that they should tell workers who opt out of automatic retirement enrollment about the option to contribute to an ABLE account instead.

This bill primarily affects working adults with disabilities who have ABLE accounts, along with their employers. It gives these workers more control over retirement-related benefits without risking their eligibility for disability assistance programs, and it gives employers clearer legal guidance on how to offer this option.
ai_headline: Bill would let workers redirect 401(k) contributions into ABLE accounts
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

It also clarifies that employers can make direct or matching contributions to ABLE accounts, counted as if the employee made them, and directs Treasury to treat these as deductible business expenses and to require employers to notify opted-out workers of this option.

title: ADAPT Act
ai_summary:
The ADAPT Act aims to increase access to mental health care by allowing trainee psychologists to provide services that get reimbursed through Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP (the Children's Health Insurance Program). Currently, Medicare generally only pays for psychological services performed by fully licensed clinical psychologists. This bill would change that by allowing "advanced psychology trainees"—meaning doctoral students completing required supervised internships or recent graduates completing post-degree supervised training before licensure—to provide services that Medicare will pay for, as long as a licensed psychologist supervises their work generally (meaning overseeing their training without necessarily being present for every session). The supervising psychologist would bill for the service, and Medicare would create a special billing code ("GC modifier") to track these trainee-provided services.

The bill also directs the Department of Health and Human Services to help state governments figure out how to cover similar trainee-provided services under Medicaid and CHIP, which serve lower-income individuals and children. This includes providing guidance on legal strategies, billing codes, and real-world examples from states that have already found ways to cover these services.

This bill would primarily affect Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP beneficiaries seeking mental health care, especially in areas where licensed psychologists are in short supply. It would also affect psychology graduate students and postdoctoral trainees, who could gain more opportunities to provide supervised care that insurance will cover, as well as supervising psychologists and training programs, which could see expanded roles and reimbursement opportunities. Supporters generally frame it as a way to address mental health provider shortages, since trainees already provide care in many settings but face reimbursement obstacles under current rules.

title: Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill requires the Department of Commerce to create new safety rules for companies that make or sell synthetic DNA and RNA, as well as companies that sell the machines used to create these genetic materials. Companies would have to screen orders against a government-maintained list of "sequences of concern" (genetic codes that could be used to create dangerous pathogens), verify that customers are legitimate, and report suspicious split orders that might be an attempt to evade detection. The government would audit companies for compliance, and those that fail could lose their certification or face lawsuits with significant fines. Businesses and researchers receiving federal funding would only be allowed to buy synthesis products from companies that follow these new rules.

The bill also creates a "biotechnology governance sandbox," a safe testing space where companies, researchers, and government agencies can experiment with new biosecurity tools and oversight methods without the same regulatory risk. Additionally, it directs the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy to study how biosecurity responsibilities are currently spread across different federal agencies and to propose a plan to streamline and consolidate that oversight, potentially recommending new authorities or even a new government body.

This bill would primarily affect companies that synthesize DNA/RNA or sell gene-synthesis equipment, research institutions and universities that order genetic materials (especially those using federal grants), and federal agencies involved in biosecurity oversight. The broader public could be affected indirectly, as the bill aims to reduce the risk that dangerous biological agents could be created and misused, whether by accident, negligence, or malicious intent, while also trying to avoid slowing down legitimate scientific and medical research.

title: Clergy Act
ai_summary:
The Clergy Act would give ministers, members of religious orders, and Christian Science practitioners a new opportunity to opt back into Social Security if they had previously chosen to be exempt from it. Under current law, clergy members can request an exemption from paying Social Security self-employment taxes based on religious objections, but that decision is normally permanent. This bill creates a limited window for those who already have that exemption to reverse it and start paying into Social Security again, meaning they would become eligible for Social Security benefits later in life.

To use this option, an eligible person would need to file an application by the tax filing deadline (including extensions) for their second tax year after 2027. Once revoked, the exemption could not be requested again, so the decision would be final. If someone applies late for a given tax year, they would also need to pay the back Social Security taxes they would have owed for that year, calculated as if they had never been exempt.

This bill mainly affects clergy and religious workers who once opted out of Social Security, often earlier in their careers, and who may now want retirement, disability, or survivor benefits they currently lack. It does not affect the general public or change Social Security rules for anyone outside this specific group. The bill also requires the IRS and Social Security Administration to develop a plan to inform eligible clergy about this option, ensuring they know the window exists and understand how to apply.
ai_headline: Clergy would get one-time chance to rejoin Social Security

title: Promoting Access to Diabetic Shoes Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change Medicare rules about therapeutic shoes for people with diabetes. Currently, Medicare covers special diabetic shoes and shoe inserts, but a doctor must certify that the patient needs them and document the medical necessity. This bill would allow nurse practitioners and physician assistants to also complete this required documentation, not just physicians.

In practical terms, this means patients with diabetes who need these specialized shoes could get the required paperwork done by a nurse practitioner or physician assistant instead of having to see a physician specifically for that purpose. Diabetic shoes and inserts help prevent foot injuries and complications like ulcers, which can be serious for people with diabetes, so timely access to this documentation matters for patient care.

This change would primarily affect Medicare beneficiaries with diabetes, especially those who receive most of their regular care from nurse practitioners or physician assistants rather than physicians, which is common in rural areas or places with doctor shortages. It would also affect healthcare providers, since nurse practitioners and physician assistants would gain new authority to complete this specific Medicare documentation, potentially making the process faster and more convenient for patients.

title: FIGHT Act of 2025
ai_summary:
S. 1454, the FIGHT Act of 2025, is a bill that would strengthen federal laws against animal fighting, with a particular focus on cockfighting (rooster fighting). It amends the existing Animal Welfare Act to add a formal legal definition of "rooster" and makes it explicitly illegal to gamble on any animal fighting event, whether attending in person or watching a broadcast. It also closes a loophole by making it illegal to use the mail or other interstate shipping services to transport roosters, since these methods have reportedly been used to move birds for illegal fights, especially in places like Puerto Rico and Guam where cockfighting was legal until recently.

The bill also creates new enforcement tools. It allows private citizens, not just government officials, to file civil lawsuits against people they believe are violating animal fighting laws, with fines up to $5,000 per violation. To prevent misuse, people must first notify authorities and wait 60 days before suing, and they can't sue if the government is already pursuing the same case. Additionally, the bill allows the government to seize real estate and property connected to organizing or hosting animal fighting events, similar to asset forfeiture rules used in other criminal cases.

This bill would primarily affect people involved in organizing, attending, or gambling on animal fighting events, as well as breeders or shippers of roosters used for fighting. It would give federal and state authorities, along with private citizens, stronger legal tools to identify, penalize, and shut down illegal animal fighting operations. Everyday citizens who have no connection to animal fighting would not be directly affected by this bill.
ai_headline: Bill would let citizens sue over cockfighting and seize related property
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

title: Find It Early Act
ai_summary:
The Find It Early Act would require most health insurance plans, including private employer and marketplace plans, Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, and the VA health system, to fully cover additional breast imaging tests for people at higher risk of breast cancer, without charging copays, deductibles, or other out-of-pocket costs. This includes people identified as high-risk under established medical guidelines, those with dense breast tissue (which can make cancer harder to detect on a standard mammogram), and anyone else a doctor determines needs extra screening due to factors like age, race, ethnicity, or family history. Covered tests would include 2D and 3D mammograms, breast ultrasounds, MRIs, molecular breast imaging, and similar technologies, with no limits on how often these tests can be done if medically needed.

Currently, many insurance plans only fully cover a basic annual mammogram, and people who need follow-up or supplemental imaging because of dense breasts or elevated risk often face significant out-of-pocket costs, which can discourage them from getting further testing. This bill aims to remove that financial barrier so cancer can be caught earlier. It would affect nearly everyone with health coverage in the U.S., including workers with job-based insurance, people buying individual marketplace plans, Medicare beneficiaries, Medicaid enrollees, military families using TRICARE, and veterans using VA health care. The changes would take effect starting January 1, 2026, though states needing to pass their own legislation to comply with the Medicaid provisions would be given additional time.

title: Pay Paraprofessionals and Support Staff Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Pay Paraprofessionals and Support Staff Act, aims to raise pay for school support workers like teacher's aides, classroom assistants, and other education support staff. It would set a minimum annual salary of $45,000 for full-time support staff and a minimum wage of $30 an hour for part-time support staff, starting in 2026 through 2030. After that, these minimums would increase every five years based on inflation or at least 2%, whichever is higher. States would set their own specific pay levels above these floors and would need pay to increase with employee experience.

To help pay for this, the federal government would provide $25 billion in the first year, with the amount adjusted for inflation in future years. States would apply for grants and create a plan showing how they'll reach the new pay minimums within four years. States must then pass at least 98% of this money down to individual school districts, with extra help prioritized for districts serving many low-income students. Districts could use the money not just for support staff, but also to raise pay for teachers, principals, bus drivers, and other school employees, and to fund training or certification programs.

This bill would primarily affect public school paraprofessionals and support staff (such as teacher's aides and classroom assistants), school districts, and state education agencies, who would all face new pay requirements and reporting duties. Students, especially those in low-income districts, could also benefit if better pay helps schools recruit and retain support staff. The bill does not override existing union contracts but requires that any new agreements comply with the new minimum pay rules.
ai_headline: Bill sets $45,000 pay floor for school support staff starting 2026
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

title: Native ELDER Act
ai_summary:
S 870, the Native ELDER Act, updates the Older Americans Act of 1965 to better support elderly Native Americans, Alaska Natives, and Native Hawaiians. Its main feature is creating an 11-member "Older Americans Tribal Advisory Committee" made up of tribal and Native Hawaiian representatives, appointed jointly by federal officials and congressional leaders. This committee would advise federal aging programs, help identify problems facing Native elders, propose policy fixes, and report yearly to Congress. Members would be paid for their work, and at least one member must be Alaska Native and one must be Native Hawaiian.

The bill also makes smaller technical changes: it allows funding for in-home services to cover home modifications (like ramps or grab bars) that help older adults stay safely in their homes, updates outdated funding-year references in the law, and improves training programs for tribal grant recipients so they can better manage federal aging-services grants.

Finally, the bill requires two federal reports. One, from the Assistant Secretary for Aging, must study whether a Native American caregiver support program modeled on a veterans' caregiver program would work, assess unmet needs for home modifications among Native elders, and identify barriers tribes face in accessing federal aging funds. The other, from the Secretary of Labor, must report on how job-training programs for older Americans are serving Native American communities. Overall, this bill mainly affects tribal governments, Native aging-services organizations, federal aging agencies, and elderly Native American, Alaska Native, and Native Hawaiian individuals who rely on these programs.
ai_headline: Bill creates tribal advisory panel to guide Native elder aging programs
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

title: Highway Funding Transferability Improvement Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change a federal rule about how states can move around highway funding they receive from the federal government. Currently, under a section of federal transportation law, states are allowed to transfer up to 50 percent of the highway funds allocated to them from one federal highway program category to another. This bill would raise that limit to 75 percent, giving states more flexibility to shift money between different types of highway-related programs.

In practical terms, this means state transportation departments would have more freedom to direct federal highway dollars toward whatever projects they consider most urgent, rather than being restricted to how the money was originally categorized. For example, if a state receives more funding than it needs for one type of road program but needs more for another, it could move a larger share of that money between the two.

This bill mainly affects state governments and their transportation departments, since it changes their flexibility in managing federal highway funds. It could indirectly affect everyday drivers and communities, since it may influence which road, bridge, or safety projects get funded and how quickly. It does not change the total amount of federal highway funding available—only how much of it states can shift between program categories.
ai_headline: Bill would let states shift 75 percent of highway funds between programs
last_action_text: Committee on Environment and Public Works Senate Subcommittee on Transportation and Infrastructure. Hearings held.

title: To amend the Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972 to allow the transport, purchase, and sale of pelts of, and handicrafts, garments, and art produced from, Southcentral and Southeast Alaska northern sea otters that are taken for subsistence purposes.
ai_summary:
**HR 8401 – Sea Otter Pelt and Product Sales**

This bill would change the Marine Mammal Protection Act, a federal law that generally bans killing, selling, or trading marine mammals like sea otters. Alaska Native communities are already allowed to hunt northern sea otters for subsistence purposes (for food, clothing, and traditional use) under existing law. This bill would go a step further by allowing the pelts from these legally hunted otters—specifically otters from the Southcentral and Southeast Alaska populations—to be transported, bought, and sold. It would also allow handicrafts, garments, and art made from those pelts to be transported, bought, sold, or even exported, whether the items are traditional or modern in style, and whether the pelt was altered a little or a lot.

The bill mainly affects Alaska Native hunters and artisans who currently take sea otters for subsistence but face restrictions on selling raw pelts or certain finished products made from them. It would give them new economic opportunities to sell items like fur garments, crafts, and artwork, including to buyers outside Alaska or overseas. It could also affect people who buy or deal in these goods, such as art dealers, tourists, and fur traders. Wildlife conservation groups and federal agencies that manage marine mammal populations would likely be interested in the bill as well, since it touches on how sea otter products are tracked and regulated, even though it does not change hunting limits themselves.
ai_headline: Bill would let Alaska Natives sell sea otter pelts and crafts
last_action_text: Subcommittee Hearings Held

title: To permanently extend the exemption from the engine compartment portion of the pre-trip vehicle inspection skills testing requirement for school bus drivers, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill deals with how school bus drivers get their commercial driver's license (CDL). Normally, drivers who want a CDL must pass a skills test that includes checking under the hood of the vehicle to identify engine components and demonstrate knowledge of the engine compartment. In late 2024, the Department of Transportation granted a temporary exemption allowing certain school bus driver applicants to skip this specific under-the-hood portion of the test, while still requiring them to pass the rest of the pre-trip inspection test. This bill would make that exemption permanent instead of temporary, along with the specific terms and conditions that came with the original exemption.

The bill also requires states that use this exemption to report each year, for six years, on how many drivers obtained their commercial driver's license this way. This reporting requirement helps the federal government track how widely the exemption is being used.

This bill mainly affects people applying to become school bus drivers, especially in areas facing driver shortages, since skipping this part of testing could make it somewhat quicker or easier to get licensed. It could also affect state transportation and licensing agencies, which would need to track and report data on drivers using the exemption. Indirectly, it affects school districts that rely on bus drivers, as well as parents and students who depend on school bus transportation, since the change is intended to help address ongoing shortages of qualified school bus drivers in many parts of the country.
ai_headline: Bill would permanently waive engine test for school bus CDL applicants
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.

title: Natural GAS Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Natural GAS Act of 2025, changes how the U.S. Department of Energy is allowed to set energy efficiency rules for gas-powered water heaters, furnaces, boilers, and kitchen cooktops, ranges, and ovens. Currently, the Department of Energy periodically updates efficiency standards for home appliances, and some past proposals have made it harder for gas appliances to meet new requirements, effectively pushing consumers toward electric models. This bill would require the Department to conduct a "full fuel cycle analysis," which looks at the total energy used to produce and deliver fuel (not just how efficiently the appliance uses it at home). Before finalizing any new rule, the Department would have to certify that the rule is not likely to cause a major shift from gas to electric appliances.

The bill also requires that the results of this fuel-cycle analysis be clearly displayed on labels shown to consumers at the point of sale, so buyers can see this information when shopping. Small appliance manufacturers would be exempted from any new rules created under this law. For gas cooktops, ranges, and ovens specifically, the bill also protects certain features—like quick boil times, burner sizes, and grate designs—from being restricted by future efficiency regulations.

This bill would primarily affect appliance manufacturers, the Department of Energy's rulemaking process, and consumers who buy gas-powered home appliances. Supporters of stricter efficiency rules and advocates for gas appliance manufacturers would be the main groups with interest in how this bill changes the regulatory process, since it could influence whether future rules make gas appliances harder or easier to sell compared with electric alternatives.
ai_headline: Bill would require full fuel-cycle review before new gas appliance rules
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: To amend title 49, United States Code, to grant the United States Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico eligibility to issue commercial driver's licenses, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal law so that the U.S. Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico are officially recognized as places that can issue commercial driver's licenses (CDLs), the special licenses needed to legally drive trucks, buses, and other large commercial vehicles. Currently, these territories are not included in the legal definition of a "state" for this particular part of federal transportation law, which has limited their ability to issue CDLs under the same national system used by the 50 states.

The bill directs the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (the federal agency overseeing truck and bus safety rules) to work directly with the Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico to help them meet all the federal safety and licensing standards required to issue these commercial licenses properly. It also sets up a five-year grace period during which the territories won't lose federal highway funding even if they haven't yet fully met all the licensing compliance rules — giving them time to build up their systems without being penalized right away. Additionally, it clarifies how federal funding penalties would apply to the Virgin Islands if compliance issues arise after that period.

This bill mainly affects residents of Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, especially truck drivers, bus operators, and others who need commercial licenses to work in transportation, construction, or delivery jobs. It could make it easier for people in these territories to get properly recognized CDLs without having to rely solely on mainland U.S. systems, potentially expanding job opportunities and improving the territories' transportation and shipping industries.

last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.

title: Next-Generation Geothermal Research and Development Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Department of Energy to expand federal support for advanced geothermal energy technologies, including so-called "next-generation" systems like enhanced geothermal, closed-loop geothermal, and supercritical geothermal (which taps into extremely hot underground rock). It updates definitions in existing energy law, creates a formal research and development program within the Department's Geothermal Technologies Office, and directs at least one existing geothermal test site (a "FORGE" site) to gain the ability to test these newer technologies. The bill also calls for better data-sharing between agencies, a public database of geothermal information, studies on water use and site selection for supercritical geothermal, and a new "center of excellence" to coordinate research, workforce training, and technical assistance.

The bill also updates a separate law requiring the U.S. Geological Survey to reassess the nation's geothermal energy potential every four years, including U.S. territories like Puerto Rico and Guam, with special attention to supercritical geothermal resources. It authorizes $150 million per year from 2027 through 2031 for these efforts, drawn from money already allocated to a different DOE office. Additionally, it sets up "commercial-readiness" grants to help private companies test and deploy new geothermal drilling and monitoring technologies, with the federal government covering up to 80% of project costs.

This bill would primarily affect the Department of Energy, national laboratories, universities, and private companies involved in geothermal energy research and development. It could also affect states, tribal governments, and territories with geothermal potential, as well as workers in the emerging geothermal industry through new workforce training programs. Everyday consumers would likely see effects only indirectly, over the longer term, if the research leads to new, more reliable sources of clean electricity.

title: Carnivals are Real Entertainment Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Carnivals are Real Entertainment Act," would create a new visa category for foreign workers who travel with carnivals and circuses in the United States. Currently, immigration law has a "P" visa category for certain entertainers and athletes, but this bill would add a new type specifically for workers who perform jobs essential to running mobile entertainment operations, such as setting up and taking down rides, operating games, running food and beverage stands, and maintaining equipment.

Under the bill, these workers would have to follow similar rules as those in the existing H-2B visa program, which is commonly used for temporary, seasonal foreign workers in industries like landscaping or hospitality. The Department of Labor already has regulations governing that program, and mobile entertainment providers would need to meet those same standards. The bill defines "mobile entertainment provider" broadly to include traveling carnivals and circuses, as well as related businesses like food or game concessions that travel to state and local fairs, festivals, or charity fundraising events.

This bill would mainly affect carnival and circus companies that rely on seasonal foreign labor, the foreign workers themselves who travel with these shows, and U.S. agencies like the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Labor, which would need to write new rules within a year to implement the program. It could also indirectly affect local fairs, festivals, and nonprofit fundraising events that depend on traveling carnivals for entertainment and revenue.
ai_headline: New visa category proposed for traveling carnival and circus workers
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 2729 would create a new visa for foreign workers who set up, run, and maintain traveling carnivals and circuses.

These workers would follow rules similar to the H-2B visa program, which the Department of Labor already regulates.

Local fairs, festivals, and charity fundraising events that depend on traveling carnivals could also be affected.
ai_sections.why: The change would formalize immigration status for a category of traveling entertainment workers who previously may not have fit clearly into existing visa rules, requiring new federal regulations within a year.

title: Apostle Islands National Park and Preserve Act
ai_summary:
This bill would rename the Apostle Islands National Lakeshore, located in Lake Superior off the coast of Wisconsin, as "Apostle Islands National Park and Preserve." The area would be split into two parts: a national park section and a national preserve section, each with its own boundaries shown on an official map created for this purpose. Both sections would still be managed together by the National Park Service as one unit, following the same general rules that apply to other national parks.

The main practical difference involves hunting and trapping rules. In the new national park section, hunting and trapping would generally be banned, except where allowed under existing treaties with Native American tribes. In the national preserve section, hunting and trapping would continue to be allowed just as they were before this change. Fishing rules would stay the same across the entire area, matching how fishing was managed before the redesignation. The bill also protects existing tribal treaty rights, meaning Ojibwe tribes and others would keep any rights they already have to hunt, fish, gather, or trap in the area.

This bill mainly affects people who visit, hunt, fish, or have historical ties to the Apostle Islands region, including local tribes, hunters, anglers, and tourists. It also requires the Park Service to add educational displays at visitor centers explaining the area's history, including Ojibwe heritage, early settlers, fur trading, logging, quarrying, lighthouses, and commercial fishing. Overall, the bill is largely about elevating the site's status and name recognition (similar to other "national parks") while making a modest legal distinction between areas where hunting is allowed and where it is not.
ai_headline: Apostle Islands lakeshore would become a national park and preserve
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 20 - 17.

title: Highway Funding Transferability Improvement Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal highway funding rules to give states more flexibility in how they use money the federal government gives them for road and transportation projects. Under current law, states can transfer up to 50 percent of the funds allocated to certain highway programs into other approved transportation programs. This bill would raise that limit to 75 percent, meaning states could shift a larger share of their federal highway dollars between different program categories rather than being locked into spending them only on the specific program they were originally assigned to.

In practical terms, this affects state transportation departments, which would gain more control over budgeting decisions for highways, bridges, transit, and related infrastructure projects. It could allow states to respond more easily to local priorities, such as directing more money toward a program with urgent needs while pulling back from one with less demand in a given year. Ordinary residents would be affected indirectly, through how quickly and where road repairs, safety improvements, or transit projects get funded in their state, though the total amount of federal highway money each state receives would not change.
ai_headline: Bill would let states shift 75 percent of highway funds between programs
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.

States would gain more flexibility to shift federal highway dollars between program categories rather than spending strictly within original allocations.

title: Driving Forward Act
ai_summary:
S. 1284, called the Driving Forward Act, deals with how school bus drivers get their commercial driver's license (CDL). Normally, people applying for a CDL that includes a special "passenger" or "school bus" endorsement must pass a skills test that includes inspecting the engine compartment (the "under-the-hood" part of a vehicle inspection). In late 2024, federal regulators had already granted a temporary exemption allowing certain school bus driver applicants to skip that engine-compartment portion of the test, recognizing that many school bus drivers don't need to perform that specific mechanical inspection as part of their daily job. This bill would make that exemption permanent instead of temporary.

In practical terms, this makes it somewhat easier and faster for people to become licensed school bus drivers, since they won't need to learn and demonstrate engine-compartment inspection skills to get certified. Supporters of this kind of change generally argue it helps address school bus driver shortages by simplifying the licensing process. The bill also requires states that use this exemption to report every year, for six years, on how many drivers got their CDL under this rule, so the federal government can track how the exemption is being used.

This bill mainly affects school bus drivers and applicants, state agencies that issue CDLs, school districts that employ bus drivers, and indirectly, families with children who ride school buses. It does not change safety rules for actually operating the bus—only the testing requirement related to inspecting the engine compartment during the CDL skills test.
ai_headline: Bill would permanently drop engine check from school bus driver testing
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

ai_sections.tldr: The Driving Forward Act would permanently exempt school bus CDL applicants from the engine-compartment inspection test.

It does not change any rules for actually operating a school bus. States using the exemption must report annually for six years on how many drivers were licensed under it.

ai_sections.why: Removing this testing requirement could make it faster to become a licensed school bus driver, potentially easing driver shortages, while reducing the mechanical knowledge applicants must demonstrate before licensing.

title: Law Enforcement Officer and Firefighter Recreation Pass Act
ai_summary:
This bill would give free annual passes for national parks and other federal recreational lands to law enforcement officers and firefighters, similar to a benefit already available to members of the military and their families. Currently, federal law allows active-duty military members and their dependents to get this "America the Beautiful" style pass at no cost, and this bill would expand that same free-pass program to include police officers and firefighters as well.

The bill defines "law enforcement officer" broadly to include federal, state, local, and tribal officers or employees who prevent, detect, or investigate crimes, or who supervise convicted offenders (such as parole or probation officers). It defines "firefighter" as any federal, state, local, or tribal employee whose job involves suppressing fires, including wildfires. To get the free pass, these workers would need to show proof that they qualify, based on rules the Secretary of the Interior would set.

This bill mainly affects working law enforcement officers and firefighters across the country, who would gain a new financial benefit in the form of free access to national parks, forests, and other federal recreation sites that normally charge entrance or day-use fees. It would not change fees for the general public, but it could slightly reduce fee revenue collected by federal land management agencies, since more visitors would be entering for free.

last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources Subcommittee on National Parks. Hearings held.

Qualifying workers would need to show proof of eligibility under rules set by the Secretary of the Interior.

title: Economic Relief for Specialty Crops Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Economic Relief for Specialty Crops Act, would provide $5 billion in federal funding for fiscal year 2027 to help farmers who grow "specialty crops." Specialty crops generally include fruits, vegetables, tree nuts, dried fruits, and nursery or greenhouse crops, as opposed to major commodity crops like corn, wheat, or soybeans. The money would go to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), which would distribute it to eligible farmers through an existing assistance program (or a similar future program) run under the Commodity Credit Corporation, a government entity that funds various farm support efforts.

The bill directs the USDA to make these payments using the same rules and guidelines already laid out in a program the department announced in February 2026, as well as terms described in a related federal notice from January 2025. In practical terms, this means the bill isn't creating a brand-new program from scratch—it's providing the money needed to fund an assistance effort the USDA had already planned or started, ensuring farmers can actually receive payments under it.

The people most directly affected are specialty crop farmers and producers across the country, who may be dealing with financial pressures such as low prices, high production costs, weather-related losses, or trade disruptions. Consumers could see indirect effects if the funding helps stabilize the supply of fruits, vegetables, and other specialty crops. Taxpayers are also affected, since the bill authorizes a significant new federal expenditure.
ai_headline: Bill would send $5 billion to specialty crop farmers in 2027
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

USDA would distribute the money through an existing (or similar future) Commodity Credit Corporation assistance program, using rules from a February 2026 USDA program announcement and a January 2025 federal notice. It funds an already-planned effort rather than creating a new program.

title: Defective Firearms Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Defective Firearms Protection Act, would change federal law so that guns and ammunition are treated as "consumer products" under the Consumer Product Safety Act. Currently, firearms and ammunition are specifically excluded from this law, which means the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC), the federal agency that regulates the safety of everyday products like appliances, toys, and furniture, has no authority over them. By removing this exclusion, the bill would allow the CPSC to apply the same kinds of safety oversight to firearms that it applies to other consumer products.

In practical terms, this could give the CPSC the power to set safety standards for guns, investigate reports of defects or malfunctions, and potentially recall firearms found to have safety problems, similar to how car seats or space heaters can be recalled. It would also remove a specific limit on the agency's rulemaking authority related to firearms that currently exists in law.

This bill would primarily affect firearm manufacturers, sellers, and the CPSC itself, since they would now operate under a new regulatory relationship. Gun owners and buyers could also be affected, since new safety rules or recall processes might apply to firearms they already own or plan to purchase. Supporters and opponents of firearm regulation may view this change very differently, but the bill itself is limited to changing which federal agency has authority to review firearm safety issues; it does not address other aspects of gun ownership, sales, or use.
ai_headline: Bill would let safety agency regulate guns like other consumer products
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill would remove firearms' exemption from Consumer Product Safety Act oversight, letting the CPSC regulate them.

This could give the CPSC power to set safety standards, investigate defects or malfunctions, and potentially recall firearms, similar to its authority over other products. It also removes a specific legal limit on the agency's firearm-related rulemaking authority.
