ai_sections.why: The change shifts authority over firearm safety issues to a federal consumer safety agency, without altering other laws on gun ownership, sales, or use.

title: Election Security Partnership Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Election Security Partnership Act, would set aside an extra $20 million in federal funding for states that help run elections. However, states could only get this money if they agree to share their complete list of registered voters with the Department of Homeland Security at least four times a year. DHS would then check that list against a database called SAVE (Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements) to look for people on the voter rolls who are not U.S. citizens.

The amount of extra money a state could receive depends on how much it already got through the existing 2026 election security grant program—states could get up to an additional 10% of that amount. To qualify, a state must have already received funding under that 2026 program and must sign a written agreement with DHS to share voter registration data going forward.

This bill would affect state election officials, who would decide whether to participate, and state governments, which would receive the funding if they meet the requirements. It could also affect registered voters, since their personal registration information would be shared with a federal agency for citizenship verification purposes. States that choose not to share this data with DHS would not receive the additional grant money, though they could still receive funding under the regular 2026 program.
ai_headline: States could get extra election funds for sharing voter rolls with DHS
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration.

A state's extra funding would be capped at 10% of what it already received under the existing 2026 election security grant program.

title: SAVE America Through REAL ID Act
ai_summary:
HR 9141, called the "SAVE America Through REAL ID Act," would create a federal grant program run by the Department of Homeland Security to help states cover the costs of issuing REAL ID-compliant driver's licenses and identification cards to low-income residents at no charge. REAL IDs are the federally standardized identification cards that will eventually be required for things like boarding domestic flights or entering certain federal buildings. Under this bill, states could apply for federal money to waive application fees, cover administrative costs, run public awareness campaigns, offer mobile or remote services in underserved areas, and help people gather the documents needed to apply.

To qualify as "low-income," a person would need to have household income at or below 200% of the federal poverty level, or already be enrolled in another means-tested assistance program, with states determining eligibility. States that want to participate would need to submit an application explaining how they'd identify eligible residents, eliminate fees, conduct outreach, and protect applicants' privacy and data security. Funding would be distributed using a formula based on each state's low-income population and demonstrated need, with every participating state guaranteed a minimum amount.

This bill would primarily affect low-income individuals who currently face cost barriers to obtaining a REAL ID, as well as state motor vehicle agencies that issue these IDs and would receive federal funding to support the effort. It would also affect federal taxpayers, since the bill authorizes $50 million per year from 2027 through 2031 (a total of $250 million) to fund the program. States would be required to report annually on how many IDs they issued for free, their outreach efforts, and how they spent the money, and the program would be subject to federal audits and annual reporting to Congress.
ai_headline: New bill would fund free REAL ID cards for low-income Americans
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

title: ROBINHOOD Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the ROBINHOOD Act of 2026, targets a strategy sometimes used by extremely wealthy people to avoid paying income taxes: borrowing large sums of money using stocks or other assets as collateral instead of selling those assets. Normally, if you sell stock that has gone up in value, you owe capital gains tax on the profit. But if you simply borrow against that stock, no sale happens, so no tax is owed — even though the person gets cash to spend. This bill says that for certain very wealthy taxpayers, taking out a large loan will be treated as if they sold enough of their investments to cover the loan amount, triggering capital gains tax on those "phantom sales." Long-term leases lasting more than five years are treated similarly.

The rule only applies to "applicable taxpayers" — people with more than $100 million in yearly income, or more than $1 billion in assets (half those amounts for married people filing separately), sustained over three years. It also applies to certain large trusts, estates, and people who have renounced U.S. citizenship to avoid taxes. Everyday retirement accounts, health savings accounts, education savings plans, and similar ordinary savings vehicles are excluded from being counted as taxable assets. Special rules address partnerships and business entities to prevent wealthy owners from using a company to take out the loan instead of themselves personally, and other rules address foreigners with U.S. business income and Americans living abroad.

In short, this bill would affect only a very small number of extremely wealthy Americans — likely a few thousand billionaires and near-billionaires — by closing a tax loophole that lets them access wealth through loans without ever paying income tax on the underlying investment gains. It would not affect the vast majority of Americans, including most business owners, retirees, or even most millionaires, since the income and asset thresholds are set extremely high. If enacted, it would take effect for tax years starting after December 31, 2026.
ai_headline: Bill would tax loans that ultra-wealthy use to avoid selling stock
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

ai_sections.tldr: The ROBINHOOD Act would tax large loans backed by stock as if the assets were sold, hitting only the ultra-wealthy.
ai_sections.what: This bill would treat large loans taken out against stocks or other assets by very wealthy people as if enough of those assets were sold to cover the loan, triggering capital gains tax. Long-term leases over five years would be treated the same way, closing a loophole where borrowing against assets avoids taxes that selling them would trigger.
ai_sections.who: It applies only to "applicable taxpayers": people with over $100 million in yearly income or over $1 billion in assets sustained over three years, plus certain large trusts, estates, and people who renounced citizenship to avoid taxes. Ordinary Americans, most millionaires, retirees, and typical business owners are not affected.
ai_sections.why: The change would eliminate a strategy allowing the extremely wealthy to access cash from investment gains without ever paying income tax on those gains. It would not change tax treatment for the vast majority of taxpayers, whose income and assets fall far below the thresholds.

title: TDIU Reform Act of 2026
ai_summary:
HR 9135, the TDIU Reform Act of 2026, would take an existing VA policy called "Total Disability based on Individual Unemployability" (TDIU) and write it directly into federal law. Currently, TDIU is handled through VA regulations rather than a formal statute. This program lets veterans who can't hold a steady, well-paying job because of service-connected disabilities receive compensation at the same rate as if they were rated 100% disabled, even if their official disability rating is lower. The bill spells out who qualifies: generally, veterans with one disability rated 60% or higher, or multiple disabilities combining to 70% or higher with at least one rated 40% or higher. It also describes how the VA should evaluate veterans who don't meet those thresholds but still can't work due to their service-connected conditions.

A significant change in this bill is a new age limit: veterans who first start receiving TDIU benefits on or after December 31, 2026, would no longer be eligible for these payments once they turn 67. This is a notable shift, since TDIU currently has no such age cutoff. The bill also formally defines "marginal employment" (such as low-income or sheltered work situations) so that it doesn't count as real, substantial employment, meaning veterans in those situations could still qualify.

This bill would primarily affect disabled military veterans who rely on TDIU payments, especially those who become eligible after the law's effective date and are nearing or past age 67. It could also affect VA staff who process these claims, since the criteria and procedures would now be defined in law rather than agency policy. Veterans already receiving TDIU before the cutoff date would not be subject to the new age restriction.
ai_headline: Bill would write veterans' unemployability benefit into law, add age 67 cutoff
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs.

ai_sections.tldr: New veterans on TDIU benefits after Dec. 31, 2026 would lose them at age 67, unlike current recipients.
ai_sections.what: HR 9135 would move the VA's TDIU program, which pays veterans at the 100%-disabled rate if service-connected disabilities prevent steady, well-paying work, from regulation into federal statute. It sets eligibility thresholds (one disability at 60%+, or combined disabilities at 70%+ with one at 40%+), defines "marginal employment" as not disqualifying, and adds a new rule ending benefits at age 67 for veterans first receiving TDIU on or after December 31, 2026.
ai_sections.who: Disabled veterans who receive or apply for TDIU, particularly those newly eligible after the effective date and nearing or past 67, plus VA staff who process these claims.
ai_sections.why: The change would create a benefits cutoff based on age that does not currently exist, altering long-term financial expectations for future TDIU recipients while leaving current recipients unaffected.

title: Manufacturing Jobs for Veterans Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Manufacturing Jobs for Veterans Act of 2026, would create a small pilot program run by the Secretary of Labor to help veterans get jobs in manufacturing. Under the program, the government would award competitive grants to three states, which would then use that money to help pay manufacturing companies and labor organizations for training costs. This training could include apprenticeships, on-the-job training, or programs that lead to a recognized certification, as long as it teaches skills specific to manufacturing work.

To qualify for a grant, a state would need to show it has enough veterans and a strong manufacturing industry to make the program work. States would then pass grant money to manufacturing employers, who must report information like how much they pay veteran trainees compared to other workers in similar jobs. Money could only be used to train veterans, not other employees, and unused funds would have to be returned to the government. States and employers would also have to submit regular reports so the Secretary of Labor can track how the program is working, and the Secretary would report results and recommendations to Congress each year.

This bill mainly affects veterans looking for manufacturing jobs, manufacturing companies and labor groups that want to train them, and the three states chosen to run the pilot programs. It authorizes $10 million per year from 2027 through 2031 to pay for the effort. Because it's a small-scale pilot program limited to three states, its immediate effects would be limited, though the results could shape future decisions about expanding similar veteran employment programs nationwide.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

title: To amend title 38, United States Code, to increase the authorization of appropriations for comprehensive service programs for homeless veterans.
ai_summary:
This bill changes how much money the federal government is allowed to spend on programs that help homeless veterans. It updates a section of federal law that sets spending limits for these programs year by year, extending the previous limit through 2024, then setting a new spending cap of $350 million for 2025. For 2026 and every year after that, it allows "such sums as may be necessary," meaning Congress could approve whatever amount is needed without being locked into a fixed number.

In practical terms, this bill doesn't create a new program—it adjusts the funding authorization for an existing one called the comprehensive service program for homeless veterans, run through the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). These programs provide services like housing assistance, job training, health care coordination, and other support to veterans who are homeless or at risk of becoming homeless. Raising the authorized funding level doesn't guarantee the money will actually be spent; it just raises the ceiling on what Congress could allocate in future budget bills.

This bill mainly affects veterans experiencing homelessness or at risk of homelessness, who could benefit from expanded services if Congress follows through with actual funding. It also affects the VA, which administers these programs, and the nonprofit and community organizations that partner with the VA to deliver housing and support services. Taxpayers are indirectly affected, since this bill sets the stage for potentially higher federal spending, though actual appropriations would still need to be approved separately through the regular budget process.
ai_headline: Bill raises funding cap for homeless veterans programs through 2025
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity.

title: COLAs Don’t Count Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would change how the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP, formerly known as food stamps) counts certain income when deciding how much benefit a household receives. Specifically, it deals with cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) that people receive from Social Security or Supplemental Security Income (SSI). Right now, when these benefits go up each year due to COLA increases, SNAP has a rule about when that extra income starts counting against a household's SNAP eligibility. This bill moves that "counting start date" from July 1 to January 1, which would give households more time before the COLA increase affects their food assistance benefits.

The bill also adds a new type of income to the list of things SNAP does not count at all: state supplementary payments made alongside SSI (extra state-provided cash assistance for elderly, blind, or disabled individuals with low incomes). By excluding these payments from income calculations, more of a household's resources would be protected, potentially allowing them to keep receiving higher SNAP benefits.

This bill mainly affects low-income seniors, people with disabilities, and others receiving Social Security or SSI benefits who also rely on SNAP for food assistance. If passed, it would take effect on October 1, 2027, and would likely mean somewhat higher or more stable SNAP benefits for affected households, since less of their income would be counted against them. It was introduced by Senator Welch along with several co-sponsors and has been referred to the Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee for further consideration.
ai_headline: Bill would delay when Social Security COLAs count against SNAP benefits
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

It would also exclude state supplementary payments made alongside SSI from SNAP income calculations entirely. If passed, the changes would take effect October 1, 2027.

title: Affordable Housing Supply Chain Clarity Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to study how a federal law called the Build America, Buy America Act is being applied to the HOME Investment Partnerships Program. The HOME program provides federal money to states and local governments to build, buy, or fix up affordable housing for low-income residents. The Build America, Buy America Act generally requires that materials used in federally funded infrastructure projects be made in the United States. The bill's sponsors want to make sure this "Buy American" rule is being applied clearly and consistently when it comes to affordable housing construction.

Specifically, the bill requires HUD to complete a review within 180 days of the law passing, then issue updated guidance within 90 days after that review clarifying how the Buy America rules should apply to HOME-funded housing projects. Finally, HUD must send a report to relevant congressional committees within 270 days summarizing what the review found and what guidance was issued.

This bill mainly affects state and local housing agencies, nonprofit housing developers, and contractors who use HOME program funds to build or renovate affordable housing, since they must currently navigate potentially confusing rules about which materials qualify as "American-made." It could also indirectly affect low-income renters and homebuyers who rely on HOME-funded housing, since clearer rules might speed up or simplify construction projects. The bill does not change funding levels or housing policy itself—it simply requires HUD to study and clarify existing rules.
ai_headline: HUD must clarify Buy American rules for affordable housing program
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

title: Stop Secret Spending Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Stop Secret Spending Act of 2025, aims to make federal government spending more visible to the public, especially a type of contract called an "other transaction agreement" (OTA). OTAs are special deals federal agencies use, often for research or technology projects, that let them skip some of the usual contracting rules. Right now, this spending doesn't always show up on USAspending.gov, the government's public website for tracking how tax dollars are spent. The bill requires the Treasury Department to update the website so OTA spending is automatically included and easy to find in one place, within three years.

The bill also requires new accountability steps. Agencies would have to publish yearly reports explaining any federal spending that isn't showing up on the website, including reasons like national security secrecy or contracts handled by Congress or the courts. It requires inspectors general (internal government watchdogs) to regularly check and report on how well agencies are complying with these transparency rules. It also directs the Treasury and the White House budget office to determine which agencies must report spending data, publish that list publicly, and set standards to make sure the data posted is accurate and consistent.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies, government contractors, and inspectors general, who would face new reporting and disclosure duties. For everyday Americans, taxpayer advocates, journalists, and researchers, it would mean better access to information about how the government spends money, particularly on contracts that have previously been harder to track. It does not create new spending or cut any programs; it focuses only on increasing transparency and oversight of existing federal spending.
ai_headline: Bill would force disclosure of secretive federal contracts online
last_action_text: Presented to President.

title: ARTIST Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the ARTIST Act, would change federal law to strengthen protections for Alaska Native people who make and sell traditional handicrafts, clothing, and artwork using materials from marine mammals, such as walrus or whale ivory, bone, and baleen. It updates the Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972 to more clearly define what counts as an "authentic Alaska Native article," spelling out that these items must be made using traditional methods like carving, sewing, weaving, or beading, without machines like pantographs or mass-production tools. It also confirms that Alaska Natives living on the coasts of the North Pacific or Arctic Ocean can hunt marine mammals for subsistence or to make and sell these traditional items, as long as it's not done wastefully.

The bill adds new rules to protect this practice. It says states cannot ban the sale, trade, or possession of marine mammal ivory, bone, or baleen if it's part of an authentic Alaska Native handicraft — meaning states couldn't pass their own laws blocking these sales, even if they restrict ivory sales generally. It also sets stricter requirements for the federal government if it wants to limit hunting due to concerns about a species' population, requiring solid evidence, public hearings, and written justification, including consideration of Indigenous knowledge.

This bill mainly affects Alaska Native artisans, hunters, and their communities, who rely on these traditional practices for cultural and economic reasons. It could also affect state governments that currently restrict ivory sales, as well as federal wildlife regulators who oversee marine mammal protections, since the bill limits how and when new hunting restrictions can be imposed.
ai_headline: Bill would shield Alaska Native ivory crafts from state sales bans
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 588.

It bars states from banning sale, trade, or possession of marine mammal ivory, bone, or baleen used in such handicrafts, and sets stricter evidence, hearing, and justification requirements before federal officials can restrict subsistence hunting.

title: Advancing Automation Research and Development in Agriculture Act
ai_summary:
This bill renews and expands a federal program that funds research on "specialty crops," which include fruits, vegetables, nuts, and nursery plants (as opposed to crops like corn, wheat, or soybeans). It extends the existing Specialty Crop Research Initiative through 2031 and creates a new grant program specifically focused on mechanization and automation for these crops. The goal is to help farmers develop and adopt machines, robotics, and other technology that can reduce the amount of manual labor needed to grow, harvest, process, and package specialty crops, while also improving safety and working conditions for farmworkers.

Under the bill, the U.S. Department of Agriculture would award competitive grants to universities, research organizations, and other eligible groups for projects like building prototypes, testing new equipment in real fields, and helping the industry adopt new technology faster. Priority would go to projects that train farmworkers to use, repair, or program this new equipment and that share their results publicly. The bill sets aside at least $30 million per year from 2026 through 2031 specifically for this new automation program, while continuing funding for the broader specialty crop research initiative.

This bill mainly affects farmers and businesses that grow fruits, vegetables, and other specialty crops, as well as farmworkers whose jobs may change as automation increases. It also affects agricultural researchers, universities, and technology developers who could receive grant funding, and it involves the USDA, which will run the program and decide how the money is distributed. The rest of the bill makes technical corrections to existing law so that references to renumbered sections stay accurate.

last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

title: FRESH Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the FRESH Act, would create a new grant program to help schools buy and install equipment for storing and serving milk. The U.S. Department of Agriculture would give out competitive grants to schools, school districts, tribal organizations, or groups of these entities so they can purchase things like refrigeration units or bulk milk dispensers—machines that keep milk cold and let students pour it directly into a cup instead of relying only on individual cartons. The federal government would cover up to 75 percent of the cost of each project, with the applicant covering the rest. The bill sets aside $4 million per year from 2027 through 2031 to fund these grants.

The bill mainly affects public schools (elementary and secondary), school food service programs, and tribal organizations that run school meal programs. By helping schools upgrade their milk storage equipment, the program is intended to make it easier for schools to serve fresh, cold milk to students and potentially reduce food waste from unused or spoiled milk cartons. Students who eat school meals could benefit indirectly through improved access to properly chilled milk, while school administrators would be the ones applying for and managing these grants.

title: Firearm Safety Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal law so that firearms and ammunition are no longer excluded from the definition of "consumer product" under the Consumer Product Safety Act. Currently, guns and ammunition are specifically carved out from that law, meaning the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) has no authority to regulate them for safety purposes the way it does with things like toys, appliances, or car seats. By removing this exclusion, the bill would give the CPSC the legal ability to create and enforce safety standards for firearms, similar to how it oversees other consumer goods.

In practical terms, this means the CPSC could potentially require safety features on guns, investigate firearm-related injuries as product safety issues, or recall firearms found to have dangerous defects, though the bill itself does not create specific new rules. It simply removes the legal barrier that currently prevents the agency from acting in this area. This would primarily affect firearm manufacturers and sellers, who could face new federal oversight and potential safety requirements, as well as gun owners and buyers, who might see changes in how firearms are designed, labeled, or sold if the CPSC later issues new standards.

The bill is sponsored by Senator Booker and several Democratic co-sponsors and has been referred to the Senate Commerce Committee. As with any newly introduced bill, it would need to pass committee review, both chambers of Congress, and be signed by the President before becoming law.
ai_headline: Bill would let CPSC regulate guns as consumer products for safety
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

title: Extinction Prevention Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill sets up four separate grant funds inside the U.S. Treasury, each aimed at protecting a different group of struggling wildlife species: butterflies across North America, plants in the Pacific Islands (Hawaii, Guam, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands), freshwater mussels across the United States, and desert fish in Southwestern states like Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico, and California. For each group, the Secretary of the Interior would be authorized to hand out competitive grants—including multi-year grants—to states, tribes, universities, nonprofits, and other qualified groups to fund habitat protection, research, population monitoring, law enforcement, and public education projects. Federal agencies themselves couldn't lead or directly receive this funding, though they could partner on projects.

Each fund would be allowed to accept private donations in addition to money Congress appropriates, and unspent money could be invested in interest-earning government bonds to grow over time. The bill authorizes $5 million per year for each of the four funds (a total of $20 million per year) from 2027 through 2032, meaning $120 million total if fully funded over six years. The Secretary would have to prioritize projects protecting species already listed as threatened or endangered, and would be required to report to Congress every year on how the money was spent and how the species are doing.

This bill mainly affects wildlife conservation agencies, tribal governments, research institutions, and environmental nonprofits that could apply for these grants, as well as taxpayers, since it would authorize new federal spending. It could also affect landowners, farmers, or developers in areas where these species live, since conservation projects sometimes involve land-use planning or habitat restrictions. It does not itself change any endangered species regulations—it primarily creates new funding mechanisms to support existing conservation law.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.

title: Jocelyn Nungaray National Wildlife Refuge Act
ai_summary:
This law officially renames the Anahuac National Wildlife Refuge in Texas to the "Jocelyn Nungaray National Wildlife Refuge." The refuge itself doesn't change in any physical way—its land, wildlife protections, and management remain the same. The only thing that changes is its official name, which will now be used on all government maps, documents, laws, and records referring to this location.

The renaming honors Jocelyn Nungaray, a 12-year-old girl from Houston who was murdered in June 2024. According to the bill, two people who were in the country illegally and allegedly connected to a gang called Tren de Aragua were charged with her murder. Congress noted her love of animals and her hometown's closeness to the refuge as reasons for choosing this location as a tribute. This action follows an earlier executive order from President Trump in March 2025 that had already proposed the same name change.

This bill mainly affects how the refuge is referred to in official contexts—park signage, federal paperwork, maps, and legal references will be updated accordingly. It does not change public access, environmental protections, funding, or the day-to-day operations of the refuge. Visitors, nearby residents, and wildlife groups will see no practical difference beyond the new name.

last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-30.

title: Accountability for Government Censorship Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Accountability for Government Censorship Act," would require federal agencies to report on their past communications with social media platforms and other online services about removing or restricting content. Specifically, each agency would have to look back five years and document any time an employee contacted a platform to request that lawful speech be taken down, labeled with a warning, or that a user's access be restricted. Agencies would need to provide details like which office was involved, who made the request, what legal authority (if any) justified it, which platform was contacted, why the request was made, and what happened as a result. If an agency had no such communications, it would simply certify that fact.

After collecting this information, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) would compile it into a report for two congressional committees—one in the Senate and one in the House. Most of this report would have to be public, though some sensitive details could be kept in a classified section. Each agency's independent watchdog (Inspector General) would then review whether the agency followed the law correctly, and any agency found to be non-compliant would have to brief Congress directly about the problem.

This bill would affect federal agencies and their employees, particularly those who interact with tech companies and social media platforms as part of their jobs—for example, agencies dealing with public health, national security, or election information. It would also affect congressional oversight committees, which would receive new reporting power, and indirectly affect the public, since it aims to create more transparency about how the government has interacted with online platforms regarding content moderation.
ai_headline: Bill would force agencies to disclose past content takedown requests
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

title: Promoting Police Leadership Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Promoting Police Leadership Act, updates the federal COPS program (which supports local police departments) to focus on training police supervisors and mid-level leaders, such as officers who oversee operations in a specific precinct or district. It directs the U.S. Attorney General to create or identify training programs covering topics like leadership skills, handling major incidents, risk management, officer mental health and wellness, using data to guide policing decisions, and building trust with communities. These training programs would mostly involve in-person instruction, include a hands-on project where officers solve a real problem in their department, and use tests before and after training to measure what participants learned.

The bill also sets up a certification system so the Attorney General can approve specific training courses that meet these standards, and can remove that approval if a course stops meeting them. Training providers would need to partner with universities or educational institutions to keep improving their courses. The Attorney General must publish a public list showing which police departments have officers who completed this training, and must report to Congress periodically on how the program is going. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) would also review the program's implementation after three years.

This bill mainly affects state, local, and tribal police departments and their command-level officers (like sergeants, lieutenants, and captains) who could receive new leadership training opportunities funded or coordinated through federal grants. It does not force any state or local agency to participate, and it explicitly does not override state or local authority to set their own police training and certification requirements.

last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: COLAs Don’t Count Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "COLAs Don't Count Act of 2026," would change how the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP, also known as food stamps) counts certain income when deciding who qualifies for benefits and how much they receive. Specifically, it would exclude annual cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) to Social Security retirement and disability benefits, Supplemental Security Income (SSI), Railroad Retirement benefits, and certain veterans' benefits from being counted as income for a period each year (through September 30). It would also exclude certain supplementary state payments tied to SSI from being counted as income at all.

In plain terms, this matters because many people who receive SNAP also receive Social Security, SSI, veterans' benefits, or railroad retirement. Each year, these programs typically give recipients a small raise (a COLA) to keep pace with inflation. Currently, that raise can count as new income, which sometimes pushes a household's income just high enough to reduce their SNAP benefits or make them lose eligibility entirely, even though the COLA was only meant to offset rising prices, not to make people better off. This bill would prevent that "COLA penalty" by allowing the extra income from a COLA to be temporarily ignored when SNAP eligibility and benefit amounts are calculated.

The people most affected would be older adults, people with disabilities, veterans, and railroad retirees who rely on both SNAP and one of these federal benefit programs. If passed, it would take effect on October 1, 2027, and could help these households keep more consistent SNAP benefits despite annual increases in their other federal payments.
ai_headline: Bill would stop Social Security COLAs from cutting SNAP benefits
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Nutrition and Foreign Agriculture.

title: Supporting Urban and Innovative Farming Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill updates and strengthens the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Office of Urban Agriculture and Innovative Production, which supports farming in cities and other non-traditional settings, such as rooftop gardens, hydroponic systems, and vertical farms. It expands the office's duties to include helping farmers navigate local zoning laws, business registration, and land-management paperwork, as well as promoting conservation practices suited to urban environments, like managing stormwater runoff on city land. It also extends key deadlines and programs from 2023 to 2030, turning what had been temporary "pilot" programs into ongoing, permanent efforts. Additionally, it opens up eligibility for grants and partnerships to more groups, including Tribal organizations, state and territorial governments, agricultural cooperatives, and K-12 schools.

The bill also increases funding. It guarantees at least $15 million per year starting in fiscal year 2026 for urban agriculture programs, and it authorizes Congress to approve up to $50 million per year through 2030 if lawmakers choose to fund it at that level. Separately, it directs USDA research grant programs to specifically include funding for controlled-environment farming technologies like hydroponics and aquaponics, and it boosts funding for the USDA's data collection efforts on urban and small-scale farms, raising the budget from $14 million (over three years) to $18 million per year through 2030.

This bill mainly affects urban farmers, community garden organizers, schools running farming programs, nonprofit organizations, Tribal governments, and local officials involved in food access and land-use policy. It could also matter to everyday consumers, since better support for urban farming may improve access to fresh, local food in cities and underserved neighborhoods where grocery options are limited.

last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

title: RESTORE Act
ai_summary:
**HR 3589, the RESTORE Act**, focuses on a specific approach to fertility care called "restorative reproductive medicine" — treatments that try to diagnose and fix the underlying causes of infertility (like endometriosis, PCOS, or blocked fallopian tubes) rather than bypassing them with technologies like IVF. The bill directs federal health agencies (HHS, CDC, NIH) to study these conditions more, add related questions to national health surveys, fund training programs for doctors, and update medical billing codes so doctors can be properly paid for diagnosing and surgically treating these conditions. It also opens up Title X family planning grant money and Teen Pregnancy Prevention program funds to clinics and educators that specialize in this type of care and in "fertility awareness-based methods" (natural cycle-tracking methods).

The bill also includes a notable protection: it says the federal government, and any state, local government, or organization that gets federal funding, cannot punish or discriminate against a health care provider who refuses — for religious or moral reasons — to participate in assisted reproductive technology (things like IVF, artificial insemination, or egg/embryo donation). This means hospitals or clinics that decline to offer these services couldn't lose federal funding or face other penalties for that choice.

This bill would primarily affect patients dealing with infertility or reproductive health conditions, doctors and clinics that provide fertility-related care, and federally funded health programs. Supporters frame it as expanding research and treatment options and protecting conscience rights for providers. Critics may see it as favoring one particular philosophy of fertility treatment over others (like IVF) and potentially limiting access to certain reproductive services in federally funded settings. The bill does not ban any treatments outright — it focuses on research, training, funding access, billing codes, and provider protections.
ai_headline: Bill pushes root-cause fertility care and shields providers who refuse IVF
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: Grasslands Grazing Act of 2025
ai_summary:
The Grasslands Grazing Act of 2025 makes a small but meaningful change to how federal law treats ranchers who graze livestock on national grasslands. Currently, a section of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act refers to "lands within National Forests" when describing rules for grazing leases and permits. This bill rewords that section so it instead refers to the "National Forest System" as a whole, a legal term that includes national grasslands, not just national forests. The goal is to make sure ranchers with grazing agreements on national grasslands are treated the same way, under the same legal standards, as ranchers who graze livestock on other types of federal land like national forests.

In practical terms, this is meant to close a gap or inconsistency in how grazing permits are administered depending on which specific federal land category a rancher's permit falls under. National grasslands, which are managed by the U.S. Forest Service and located mostly in the Great Plains and parts of the West, have sometimes been treated differently from national forest lands for permitting purposes. The bill clarifies that grasslands should get the same treatment.

The people most directly affected are ranchers and livestock producers who lease grazing rights on national grasslands, since they would gain the same legal protections and permitting rules that apply to grazing on national forest land. The bill also specifies that this change does not alter other existing laws related to farm tenancy or rangeland improvement, meaning its effect is narrowly focused on this one area of grazing permit consistency rather than a broad overhaul of land management law.
ai_headline: Bill would align grazing rules for national grasslands with forests

title: Army Organic Industrial Base Mineral Partnerships Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would let the Army partner with private companies to extract valuable minerals—like rare earth elements, lithium, titanium, and nickel—from land, waste materials, and byproducts at Army-run industrial facilities such as arsenals and depots. Instead of these minerals going unused or being treated as waste, private businesses could recover and process them under contracts with the Army, similar to how the government sometimes partners with companies to make use of government property.

The bill sets rules for these partnerships. Private companies doing the mineral extraction would have to follow environmental laws, clean up any pollution they cause, and financially protect the government if something goes wrong, such as through insurance or bonds. In exchange, the Army would receive payment, which could be cash, equipment, materials, or other useful support, and this compensation could be used to maintain, modernize, or clean up Army facilities without needing separate congressional approval. The bill also exempts these arrangements from certain existing rules about surplus property sales and mineral leasing on federal land, giving the Army more flexibility in structuring these deals. Importantly, Army personnel themselves would not be allowed to perform the actual mining or drilling—only private companies would do that work under contract.

This bill mainly affects the Department of the Army, private mining and materials companies, and communities near Army industrial facilities. It could create new business opportunities for companies specializing in mineral recovery and processing, while giving the Army new funding sources for facility upgrades. The public would be affected indirectly through potential benefits to national defense supply chains for critical minerals, as well as through environmental oversight of these mining activities near military sites. The Army would be required to report annually to Congress on how many such partnerships exist and what minerals are involved.

title: To amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to allow a deduction for loan interest payments made with respect to certain vehicles.
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal tax law to let more people deduct the interest they pay on vehicle loans. Currently, the tax code allows a deduction for loan interest on certain "qualified passenger vehicles," but this bill expands that definition to clearly include recreational vehicles (RVs), campers, and trailers designed for temporary living, camping, or seasonal use—whether they are motorized or meant to be towed behind another vehicle. It also keeps standard passenger vehicles like cars, minivans, SUVs, pickup trucks, and motorcycles eligible, as long as they weigh less than 14,000 pounds and count as motor vehicles under the Clean Air Act.

In plain terms, this means that if someone takes out a loan to buy an RV, camper, or similar recreational vehicle after December 31, 2025, they may be able to deduct the interest paid on that loan from their federal taxes, similar to how people can currently deduct interest on some vehicle and mortgage-related loans. This would primarily benefit people who purchase RVs or campers using financing, potentially lowering their tax bills. It would also affect the federal government's tax revenue, since expanding deductions generally reduces the total amount of taxes collected. RV dealers, manufacturers, and lenders in that industry could also see effects, since the tax break might make financing an RV more financially attractive to consumers.
ai_headline: Bill would let buyers deduct loan interest on RVs and campers
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: Veteran Scam Victims Foundation Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new nonprofit organization called the Veteran Scam Victims Foundation. Even though it's set up through a change to federal veterans' law, the Foundation would not actually be a government agency. Its main job would be to accept private donations and use that money to help protect veterans and their family members from scams, including educating them about common scams and supporting people who have already been victimized. Importantly, the Foundation would not pay veterans back for money they lost to scammers—its role is prevention and education, not reimbursement.

The Foundation would be run by a governing board chaired by the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, along with representatives appointed by agencies like the Department of Defense, the FTC, the IRS, and the Social Security Administration, plus additional citizen members chosen by the VA Secretary. Board members would serve without pay, though their travel expenses could be covered. The Foundation could accept gifts of money or property, invest and manage those funds, use some VA services and facilities, and would be exempt from federal, state, and local taxes, similar to other charitable organizations. It would have to file an annual report with Congress detailing its finances and activities. The federal government would not be financially responsible for any debts or legal problems the Foundation runs into.

This bill mainly affects veterans and their beneficiaries, who are the intended audience for the scam-prevention and support efforts. It would also affect the VA, which would help oversee and coordinate with the new Foundation, and the federal officials and agencies responsible for appointing board members.

title: Newborn Screening Saves Lives Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews and updates federal programs that help states screen newborn babies for rare genetic and metabolic disorders, many of which can cause serious health problems or death if not caught early. It extends funding authorization through 2030 and increases the money Congress can provide, raising one funding stream from about $11.9 million to $20.9 million and another from $8 million to $22.25 million per year. The bill also updates the "Advisory Committee on Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children," a group of experts that recommends which conditions should be included in the standard newborn screening panel, requiring it to publish clearer public information about how new tests get added to that list and how doctors should use genetic testing for children already diagnosed with certain conditions.

The bill also improves how health agencies track newborns after an initial positive screening, pushing for better data-sharing between state health departments, birth defect registries, and disability programs so families can be connected to follow-up care and long-term support services. It strengthens laboratory quality efforts, such as developing new screening tests and improving how lab results are interpreted and shared. Additionally, it makes the "Hunter Kelly Research Program," which funds research into rare newborn conditions, a required (rather than optional) program and updates rules for ethical research review involving newborn blood samples used for public health research.

This bill mainly affects state public health departments, hospitals, medical laboratories, parents of newborns, and researchers working on rare genetic diseases. Because it reauthorizes and expands existing programs rather than creating new ones, its main real-world effect would be more consistent funding and improved coordination for newborn screening and follow-up care nationwide.

last_action_text: Forwarded by Subcommittee to Full Committee by Voice Vote.

title: Medical Laboratory Personnel Shortage Relief Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill aims to address a nationwide shortage of workers who perform medical lab testing, such as phlebotomists (people who draw blood), lab technicians, histotechnologists, and genetic counselors. It does this by officially adding "medical laboratory personnel" to several existing federal health workforce programs. Specifically, it expands the National Health Service Corps—a program that places health workers in underserved areas in exchange for scholarships or loan repayment—so that lab workers can now qualify for these benefits and be assigned to areas identified as having a shortage of lab services, similar to how the program already works for doctors, dentists, and mental health providers.

The bill also creates a new grant program allowing the Department of Health and Human Services to fund hospitals, allied health schools, and nonprofit training programs that educate medical lab workers. These grants, each lasting three years, would help schools develop degree or certificate programs, train instructors, and use innovative teaching methods. Priority would go to programs that train students from rural or disadvantaged backgrounds or that teach teamwork and cultural competency skills. Congress would authorize $25 million for the first year, with continued funding in later years as needed.

This bill mainly affects people training for or working in medical laboratory jobs, students considering this career path, and communities facing shortages of lab testing services (which affects timely diagnosis and treatment of diseases). It could also benefit healthcare institutions and training programs by giving them new sources of funding and government-supported staffing options.

title: Student Protection and Success Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Student Protection and Success Act, changes how colleges are held responsible for their students' ability to repay federal student loans. Starting in 2028, colleges where 15% or fewer of borrowers are able to make at least a $1 payment toward their loan balance within two years of entering repayment would lose access to federal student loan programs, Pell Grants, and other federal financial aid programs for three years. Schools could appeal this decision, but if they keep receiving federal loan money during the appeal and then lose the appeal, they must repay the government for those loans. The bill also creates a "College Opportunity Bonus Program" that rewards colleges with strong repayment rates (above 25%) and many low-income students, giving them grants to expand financial aid, student support services, and faster degree programs.

The bill also introduces a "risk-sharing" system, where colleges participating in federal student loan programs must pay the government a penalty based on how many of their borrowers fail to pay down their loans over time, adjusted for national unemployment rates. This is meant to create a financial incentive for schools to help students succeed and repay their debts rather than leaving them with unaffordable loans. Additionally, the Department of Education would be required to study and report on best practices for improving repayment rates, especially at schools serving many low-income students, and to collect more detailed data on how colleges spend money on student services versus recruitment and marketing.

This bill would mainly affect colleges and universities that participate in federal financial aid programs, especially those with poor student loan repayment outcomes, such as certain for-profit or under-resourced institutions. Students attending these schools could be affected if their school loses eligibility for federal loans or grants, while schools with strong outcomes for low-income students could benefit from additional funding. It does not directly change loan terms or repayment obligations for individual borrowers, but instead targets institutions to encourage better student outcomes.

title: A joint resolution requesting the Secretary of the Interior to authorize unique and one-time arrangements for displays on the National Mall and the Washington Monument during the period beginning on December 31, 2025, and ending on January 5, 2026.

If approved, it would affect visitors to Washington, D.C., during the New Year's period, potentially drawing large crowds similar to past national celebrations, and it would involve coordination between the Interior Department and the U.S. Semiquincentennial Commission, the group already tasked with planning events for the 250th anniversary. Ordinary Americans would mainly be affected as potential visitors or viewers of the event, either in person or through media coverage, rather than through any change in law, taxes, or regulation.

title: VICTIM Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the VICTIM Act of 2026, directs the U.S. Attorney General to create a new federal grant program to help police departments solve more homicides and gun-related violent crimes. Right now, many such cases go unsolved, and this bill aims to change that by giving state, local, and tribal law enforcement agencies money to hire more investigators, train staff, buy or upgrade forensic and investigative technology, and develop better strategies for cracking cases. Agencies could also use the funds to support crime victims and their families, such as helping them access emergency housing, counseling, legal advice, and trauma-informed support during investigations.

To receive funding, police agencies would need to apply and show specific plans for improving their "clearance rates" — the percentage of crimes that end in an arrest or an identified suspect. The bill requires at least 5% of funds to go to tribal agencies and another 5% to rural agencies, ensuring smaller and less-resourced departments aren't left out. Agencies receiving grants would have to report back yearly on how the money was used, including data on victims and suspects, and undergo audits to prevent misuse of funds. There are also rules requiring background checks on newly hired officers to screen for prior misconduct records.

This bill would primarily affect local, state, and tribal police departments, especially those investigating violent crimes, as well as crime victims and their families who might benefit from expanded support services. It would also affect Justice Department offices responsible for managing grants, conducting audits, and reporting to Congress. The program would run with $60 million per year in federal funding from 2027 through 2031, and its effectiveness would be studied and reported on every two years by the National Institute of Justice.

title: Extending WIC for New Moms Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change the rules for the WIC program, which stands for the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children. WIC provides food assistance, nutrition education, and other support to low-income pregnant women, new mothers, and young children. Under current law, women who have recently given birth can generally stay eligible for WIC benefits for six months after childbirth, and mothers who are breastfeeding can stay eligible for up to one year. This bill would extend both of those time periods to 24 months, meaning new mothers could receive WIC support for up to two years after having a baby, whether or not they are breastfeeding.

The bill would mainly affect low-income mothers and families who rely on WIC for baby formula, healthy food, and nutrition counseling. By allowing mothers to stay in the program longer, supporters intend to give new parents more consistent access to food assistance during a financially and physically demanding stretch of early parenthood, rather than losing benefits after just six months or a year. It could also affect state and local agencies that run WIC programs, since they would need to serve people for a longer eligibility window.

The bill also requires the U.S. Department of Agriculture to study the effects of these changes within two years of the law taking effect. That report would look at how the extended eligibility affects maternal and infant health, breastfeeding rates, racial and ethnic health disparities, and how families experience the program overall. This bill has been introduced in the Senate and referred to committee; it would need to pass both chambers of Congress and be signed by the President before becoming law.

title: A bill to require the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to extend the time period during which licensees are required to commence construction of certain hydropower projects.
ai_summary:
This law gives hydropower companies more time to start building projects that have already received a license from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC). Normally, under existing law, a company that gets a federal license to build a hydropower project has up to 8 years to begin construction, or the license can expire. This bill allows FERC to grant additional time beyond that 8-year limit, up to 6 more years, broken into three 2-year extensions, for projects that were licensed before March 13, 2020. Companies must request the extension and show good cause for needing it.

The bill also addresses a specific problem: some project licenses may have already expired between the end of 2023 and when this law was signed, before companies had a chance to use this new extension option. For those cases, FERC is allowed to reinstate the expired license as if it had never lapsed, and then apply the new extension period to it.

This mainly affects companies developing hydropower (water-based electricity) projects, giving them more breathing room to secure financing, complete permits, and begin construction without losing their federal license. It could also matter to communities near these project sites, environmental groups, and electric utilities, since it affects how quickly, or slowly, these energy projects move forward. The law does not create new hydropower projects or approve new sites; it simply adjusts deadlines for projects that already have licenses.
ai_headline: FERC gains power to extend deadlines for licensed hydropower projects
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-90.

title: District of Columbia Transportation Funding Equality Act
ai_summary:
HR 6950, the District of Columbia Transportation Funding Equality Act, would change federal law so that Washington, D.C. is treated the same as a state when it comes to certain federal transportation grant programs. Currently, some of these programs list D.C. separately from states, which can affect how funding is calculated or whether D.C. qualifies on equal footing. This bill adjusts the legal language in a few specific programs so D.C. is included alongside states rather than treated as a separate category.

Specifically, the bill affects four programs: formula grants used to fund buses and bus facilities, an apportionment formula based on population growth and density, a grant program for replacing and repairing culverts (drainage structures under roads), and the Safe Streets and Roads for All program, which funds local projects aimed at reducing traffic deaths and injuries. By classifying D.C. as a state in these specific sections of transportation law, the bill could change how much funding D.C. receives or how it applies for these grants.

This bill mainly affects officials who manage D.C.'s transportation infrastructure, such as road, bus, and public safety agencies, as well as D.C. residents who rely on public transit, roads, and culvert systems. It would not change how any other state receives funding; it only adjusts D.C.'s treatment within these particular federal programs.
ai_headline: Bill would treat DC as a state in four federal transportation grants
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 6950 would classify D.C. as a state in four federal transportation grant programs instead of listing it separately.

The change could affect how much funding D.C. qualifies for or how it applies.

title: Let Experienced Pilots Fly Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would raise the mandatory retirement age for airline pilots from 65 to 67 years old. Currently, federal law requires pilots flying for commercial airlines (under what's called "Part 121" operations, which covers most scheduled passenger and cargo flights) to stop flying once they turn 65. This bill would allow them to keep flying for two more years, until age 67. It also allows pilots who already turned 65 and were forced to retire to come back to work, as long as they haven't yet turned 67.

The bill includes some additional details to make the change work smoothly. It protects airlines and others from being sued over decisions made in following the old or new rules. It requires that any changes to union contracts or pilot benefit plans resulting from this law be worked out through agreement between the airline and the pilots' union, rather than imposed unilaterally. It also sets stricter medical certification rules for pilots over 60, requiring them to renew their top-level medical certification every six months. Finally, it requires the Federal Aviation Administration to study and report back to Congress within six months on whether the retirement age should be raised even further in the future.

This bill would primarily affect commercial airline pilots nearing retirement age, giving them the option to keep working longer, as well as airlines, pilot unions, and the FAA, which would need to update its regulations and medical certification processes. It could also indirectly affect airline staffing levels and pilot hiring pipelines, since keeping experienced pilots in the workforce longer may change how many new pilots airlines need to hire in the near term. Passengers could be affected as well, depending on how the change influences pilot experience levels and airline staffing decisions industry-wide.
ai_headline: Bill would raise airline pilot retirement age from 65 to 67
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill raises the mandatory retirement age for commercial airline pilots from 65 to 67.
ai_sections.what: This bill would raise the mandatory retirement age for commercial airline pilots from 65 to 67, letting them fly two more years. Pilots already forced to retire at 65 could return to work until age 67. It also sets stricter medical checks for pilots over 60 and requires an FAA study on whether to raise the age further.

It also shifts legal and contractual arrangements, requiring union agreement for related changes and shielding airlines from lawsuits over retirement-age decisions.

title: DEFENSE Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the DEFENSE Act, would let the Secretary of Homeland Security or the U.S. Attorney General give special authority to state or local police officers so they can help protect certain large public events from drones. This includes places like major sporting events, big public gatherings, or other sites where the government has put up a "temporary flight restriction" (a no-fly zone for aircraft, including drones). Currently, this kind of drone-detection and countermeasure authority mostly rests with federal agencies; this bill would extend it to trained local and state officers working alongside them.

To use this authority, local or state officers would first have to complete specific training approved by federal officials, and their actions would be overseen by federal agencies, including the Department of Transportation and the FAA. The equipment they use to detect, track, or stop unauthorized drones would also have to come from an approved list, developed jointly by Homeland Security, the Justice Department, the FAA, the FCC, and the National Telecommunications and Information Administration.

This bill would primarily affect law enforcement agencies, event organizers, and security planners for large public gatherings such as major sports games, concerts, or public celebrations. It could also affect drone operators, since new rules would empower more officers to detect and possibly disable drones flying in restricted areas. The general public attending these events could benefit from tighter security, though the bill does not change everyday drone use outside of designated high-security event areas.
ai_headline: Bill would let local police help federal agents counter drones at big events
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation.

ai_sections.tldr: The DEFENSE Act would let trained state and local police help federal agencies detect and stop drones at major public events.

title: Farm Credit Adjustment Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change how often the Farm Credit Administration (FCA) is required to inspect certain lenders in the Farm Credit System, which is a network of banks and associations that provide loans to farmers, ranchers, and rural communities across the country. Currently, the law sets a maximum time period between required examinations of these institutions. This bill would give the FCA the option, at its own discretion, to extend that gap to as long as 24 months, but only for institutions the agency itself has determined to be "low-risk."

In practical terms, this means the FCA would have more flexibility in deciding how often to closely review the financial health of lenders it considers to be operating safely and soundly. Institutions the agency views as higher-risk would presumably continue to be examined on whatever shorter schedule already applies. This change would primarily affect the Farm Credit System institutions themselves (by potentially reducing the frequency of regulatory exams and related compliance work) and the FCA's own oversight workload. Farmers and other borrowers who rely on these institutions for loans would be affected indirectly, since the change concerns how closely their lenders are monitored by federal regulators, not the loan terms or services borrowers receive directly. If passed, the change would take effect on October 1, 2026.
ai_headline: Bill would let FCA inspect low-risk farm lenders less often
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

Higher-risk institutions would presumably keep their current, shorter examination schedule. The change would take effect October 1, 2026, if passed.

title: To require the Secretary of Agriculture to make cost-share grants for retrofitting agricultural tractors with rollover protection structures, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill would create a federal grant program to help farmers and agricultural schools pay for adding rollover protection structures (ROPS) to older tractors that don't already have them. Rollover accidents are one of the leading causes of death and injury on farms, and many older tractors were built before these safety cages or frames were required equipment. The bill directs the Secretary of Agriculture to hire an outside organization, chosen through competitive bidding, to run the program: identifying which safety structures and tractors qualify, managing applications, and operating a website and phone hotline to help people apply.

Under the program, eligible farmers and qualifying schools (vocational schools, colleges, or high schools that teach agriculture) could apply for grants covering 70% of the cost to buy, transport, and install an approved rollover protection structure, including a seatbelt. If those costs go above $500, the government would cover an even higher percentage, at the Secretary's discretion. The structures must meet recognized safety standards set by engineering organizations.

The bill authorizes $725,000 per year from 2027 through 2031 to fund this effort. Of that, $500,000 each year would go directly to grants for farmers and schools, while the remaining $225,000 would pay the outside administrator to run the website, hotline, and outreach. This primarily affects farmers and ranchers who operate older, unprotected tractors, as well as agricultural training programs, giving them financial help to make equipment safer and potentially prevent serious injuries or deaths from tractor rollovers.
ai_headline: Bill would fund grants for rollover safety bars on older tractors
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.

The Secretary of Agriculture would hire an outside organization to run the program, including approving equipment, managing applications, and operating a website and hotline.

title: Increasing Insurance Access for Specialty Crops Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Increasing Insurance Access for Specialty Crops Act, aims to make federal crop insurance work better for farmers who grow "specialty crops" — things like fruits, vegetables, nuts, and other non-commodity crops that often have different risks and needs than crops like corn or soybeans. It would create a new Specialty Crop Advisory Committee within the Federal Crop Insurance Corporation, made up of at least five producers (up to ten total members) representing different regions of the country (West, Midwest, South, and Northeast). This committee would advise federal officials on how to design, improve, and review insurance policies specifically suited to specialty crop growers, and would meet at least twice a year.

The bill also updates the job duties of the existing "Specialty Crops Coordinator," a federal position responsible for representing these farmers' interests. Under the bill, this coordinator would work closely with the new advisory committee and act as a bridge between specialty crop producers and the insurance agency. Additionally, whenever the Corporation reviews potential new crop insurance policies each year, it would now be required to consult with the new committee before moving forward.

Overall, this bill mainly affects specialty crop farmers, insurance program administrators, and USDA officials who manage crop insurance. It does not create new insurance programs itself, but it sets up a structure meant to ensure these farmers have a stronger voice in shaping insurance policies that better reflect their unique risks, such as weather damage, trade issues, or supply chain problems.
ai_headline: New advisory panel would give specialty crop farmers a voice on insurance
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

The committee would have five to ten producer members representing the West, Midwest, South, and Northeast, meeting at least twice a year. It also updates the Specialty Crops Coordinator's duties to work with the committee, and requires consultation with the committee whenever new crop insurance policies are reviewed annually.

title: Save Our Sequoias Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Save Our Sequoias Act, aims to protect giant sequoia trees in California from threats like wildfires, insects, and drought. It sets up a partnership between federal agencies (the Forest Service, National Park Service, and Bureau of Land Management), the State of California, and the Tule River Indian Tribe to jointly manage sequoia groves. It also creates a "Giant Sequoia Lands Coalition" made up of the various agencies, tribal government, and other landholders that already care for sequoia lands, and requires this group to produce a detailed scientific assessment of which groves are healthy, damaged, or at risk, along with a public website tracking this information.

The bill declares an "emergency" for sequoia groves for the next 7 years, which lets land managers skip some of the usual lengthy environmental review processes so they can more quickly do things like clear dead trees, thin overcrowded forests, and conduct controlled burns to reduce wildfire risk. It creates "Strike Teams" of federal employees, contractors, and volunteers to carry out this work, sets up a grant program to fund related projects (like markets for wood waste and tree nurseries), and expands "stewardship contracting," a method of hiring outside partners to do forest work. It also establishes a system for monitoring tree-killing insects and creates a new charitable fund, run through existing park and forest nonprofit foundations, so private donors can contribute money specifically for sequoia protection, with at least 15% of funds set aside to support tribal conservation efforts.

This bill mainly affects federal land management agencies, the State of California, the Tule River Tribe, and communities near the affected forests and parks (including Sequoia, Kings Canyon, and Yosemite National Parks, and several national forests). It could also affect nearby small businesses, loggers, and researchers involved in forest restoration work, as well as members of the public who may see faster tree-clearing projects with less opportunity for standard environmental review and public comment.
ai_headline: Save Our Sequoias Act speeds tree-clearing to fight wildfire threats
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. (Sponsor introductory remarks on measure: CR S1056)

title: BRUSH Fires Act
ai_summary:
The BRUSH Fires Act directs the Secretary of Agriculture, through the U.S. Forest Service, to study how well current wildfire prevention methods work in shrubland areas like chaparral, coastal sage scrub, and sagebrush. These are dry, brush-covered landscapes common in states like California that are especially prone to fast-moving wildfires. The study must look at things like fuel breaks, controlling invasive plants, helping native shrubs regrow after fires, preventing sparks from power lines and human activity, and how weather and terrain affect fire risk. It also requires examining what obstacles firefighters and land managers face in actually using these prevention methods, and how well the Forest Service works with local governments and private groups to protect homes and roads near these fire-prone areas.

Within one year of the bill becoming law, the study must be completed, and within 90 days after that, a public report must be sent to relevant congressional committees. This report would summarize findings, recommend best practices, point out where more research is needed, and suggest ways to improve teamwork between federal and local partners.

This bill mainly affects communities living near shrubland ecosystems, particularly in wildfire-prone Western states, along with the Forest Service and other agencies involved in wildfire management. It does not create new regulations or spending programs on its own; it simply requires research and reporting, laying groundwork for future policy decisions on wildfire prevention.
ai_headline: Bill orders Forest Service study on wildfire prevention in shrubland areas
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by Unanimous Consent.

title: Checkoff Transparency Act
ai_summary:
**HR 7851 — Checkoff Transparency Act** deals with "commodity checkoff programs," which are USDA-run promotion programs funded by fees that farmers and producers pay on things like beef, dairy, cotton, and eggs. These fees pay for advertising campaigns (like "Got Milk?" or "Beef: It's What's for Dinner") and research meant to boost demand for these products. Each commodity has a board that manages this money, and those boards are already required to submit audits and evaluations to the USDA.

This bill would require the Secretary of Agriculture to actually make that information public by posting it on the USDA's website. Specifically, it would require publishing yearly audit reports, the budgets and activities each board has approved, and the results of independent evaluations of these programs. The USDA would have to post five years of past records within 180 days of the bill becoming law, and then keep posting new information each year within 365 days of the fiscal year ending.

This mainly affects farmers, ranchers, and other producers who pay into these checkoff programs, since it would give them (and the general public) easier access to see how their money is being spent and whether the programs are being run effectively. It doesn't change how the checkoff programs work or how much people pay into them — it only adds a requirement that the USDA make existing records more publicly visible and accessible.
ai_headline: Bill would force USDA to post checkoff program spending records online
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.
