title: A bill to require the Secretary of Agriculture to make cost-share grants for retrofitting agricultural tractors with rollover protection structures, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill would create a federal program to help farmers and agricultural schools pay for adding rollover protection to older tractors that don't already have it. Tractor rollovers are one of the leading causes of death and injury on farms, and many older tractors were never equipped with the protective frames and seatbelts that newer models include. Under this bill, the Department of Agriculture would hire an outside organization to run the program, identify approved safety equipment and eligible tractors, manage applications, and operate a website and phone hotline to help people apply.

Farmers and eligible schools (vocational schools, colleges, and high schools that teach agriculture) could apply for grants covering 70% of the cost to buy, ship, and install approved rollover protection structures on their tractors. If the cost is more than $500, the government could cover an even higher percentage. This means it would be cheaper for farms and schools to retrofit older, unprotected tractors with modern safety equipment, potentially preventing injuries and deaths.

The bill sets aside $725,000 per year from 2027 through 2031: $500,000 each year for the actual grants, and the rest for running the program's website and hotline. Because funding is limited, only a certain number of tractors could be retrofitted each year, and eligible entities would need to apply and prove their costs to receive help. The bill mainly affects farmers, ranchers, agricultural schools, and students who work with tractors as part of their training.

title: Over-the-Counter Monograph Drug User Fee Amendments
ai_summary:
This bill renews and updates a program that allows the FDA to collect fees from companies that make over-the-counter (OTC) drugs, like pain relievers, cold medicines, and allergy pills sold without a prescription. These fees help fund the FDA's work reviewing the safety and effectiveness of OTC drug ingredients and the facilities that produce them. The current version of this fee program was set to expire, so this bill extends it through 2030 and adjusts how the fees are calculated and collected.

Specifically, the bill updates the schedule for when companies must pay facility fees, adjusts formulas used to account for inflation and FDA operating costs, and sets specific dollar amounts for additional funding in certain years. It also adds a new category allowing the FDA to recognize modern, voluntary industry testing standards for drug quality without requiring a lengthy formal process. Additionally, it extends FDA reporting requirements to Congress about how the fee money is used, and pushes back key deadlines and expiration dates to align with the new 2026–2030 timeframe.

This bill mainly affects pharmaceutical and consumer health companies that manufacture OTC drugs, since they pay these user fees. Indirectly, it affects everyday consumers who buy OTC medicines, because the fees fund the FDA's ability to monitor drug safety, review new ingredients, and keep manufacturing facilities up to safety standards. There is no direct cost or requirement placed on individual consumers; the bill is focused on industry fees and FDA administrative processes.

title: Aaron Salter, Jr., Responsible Body Armor Possession Act
ai_summary:
This bill, named after a security guard killed in the 2022 Buffalo, New York mass shooting, would make it illegal for most civilians to buy, own, or possess "enhanced body armor" — protective gear like vests, helmets, or shields that meet or exceed a high ballistic protection standard (called RF1) set by the National Institute of Justice. This refers to heavy-duty armor capable of stopping rifle rounds, not the lighter vests commonly used for personal protection against handguns.

The law includes several exceptions. It would still be legal for federal, state, tribal, and local government agencies to purchase and use this armor, as well as for active and retired law enforcement officers (including corrections officers) who qualify under existing federal rules. People who already legally own this type of armor before the law takes effect would be allowed to keep it. Anyone who violates the ban after it takes effect could face up to 5 years in prison and fines.

This bill would primarily affect civilians who currently own or might want to purchase high-level protective armor, including collectors, security contractors, and private citizens seeking maximum personal protection. title: Aaron Salter, Jr., Responsible Body Armor Possession Act
ai_summary:

title: Energy Cost Fairness and Reliability Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Energy Cost Fairness and Reliability Act of 2026," addresses concerns that data centers, especially those supporting artificial intelligence, are putting strain on the nation's electric grid and driving up electricity costs for regular households. It directs the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to create new rules for how very large electricity users, defined as facilities using more than 50 megawatts of power, connect to the transmission grid. Under the bill, these large users would have to pay the full cost of any studies and infrastructure upgrades needed to connect them to the grid, rather than spreading those costs to everyday ratepayers. They would also need to prove they can reduce or shift their power use when the grid is stressed, and in many cases would need to arrange for their own new power generation to match their energy needs.

The bill also creates incentives for large facilities to prioritize projects that use battery backup power, pay prevailing union-level wages, use apprentice labor, or sign labor peace agreements with unions, moving those projects faster through the approval process. It sets rules to prevent existing power plants from diverting electricity to serve a new large customer if doing so would hurt reliability for existing customers. Additionally, it requires the Department of Energy to collect data on data centers' energy and water use, protect that data from public disclosure, and build a research "testbed" to study more energy-efficient AI computing methods.

This bill would primarily affect large technology and data center companies, electric utilities, grid operators, and state energy regulators, since it changes how new mega-scale power users get connected to the grid and who pays for it. Indirectly, it could affect everyday electricity customers, since the goal is to prevent the costs of powering data centers and AI systems from being passed on to regular households in the form of higher electric bills. It does not change state authority over retail electricity rates, meaning individual states still control the prices consumers ultimately pay.
ai_headline: Bill would make big data centers pay their own grid connection costs
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

title: Whole Milk for Healthy Kids Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This law changes federal rules about the milk schools can serve in the National School Lunch Program. Previously, schools could only offer low-fat or fat-free milk options. Under this new law, schools are now allowed to also offer whole milk and reduced-fat milk, in both flavored and unflavored varieties, along with organic options. It also expands who can request special dairy substitutions for a student — previously only a physician could authorize this, but now a parent or legal guardian can as well. Additionally, the fat in whole milk served in schools won't count against the meal's overall saturated fat limit, making it easier for schools to include whole milk while still meeting nutrition standards.

The law also allows schools to offer nondairy beverages (like fortified soy milk) as long as they meet nutritional standards similar to cow's milk, including required levels of calcium, protein, and vitamins A and D. This mainly affects school nutrition programs, food service directors, and families with children in public schools, giving them more milk options at lunch. Separately, the bill adds a requirement that school food service staff receive training on food allergies — including how to prevent, recognize, and respond to allergic reactions — as part of existing required training programs. This portion affects school cafeteria workers and, indirectly, students with food allergies, by aiming to make school meal service safer.

title: TREES Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the TREES Act of 2025, would create a new grant program run by the Department of Energy to help pay for planting trees around homes in ways that lower energy use. The idea is that trees planted in the right spots can shade homes in the summer and block wind in the winter, which reduces how much energy people need for heating and cooling. The Secretary of Energy would work with the U.S. Forest Service to set up the program within 90 days of the bill becoming law.

Local governments, state governments, Native American tribes, nonprofit organizations, and power companies could apply for these grants. When deciding who gets funding, the government would favor projects that help lower-income neighborhoods, areas with few trees already, communities with many children or seniors, and places where people spend a large share of their income on energy bills. Projects that hire local workers, especially those who are unemployed or underemployed, and that involve the community in planning would also get priority. The federal government would cover 90% of project costs, and the goal is to plant at least 300,000 trees per year, with $50 million per year set aside from 2026 through 2030.

This bill would mainly affect homeowners and renters in eligible neighborhoods, who might see new trees planted near their homes and potentially lower energy bills over time. It would also affect local governments, tribes, nonprofits, and utility companies, who could apply for funding to run these tree-planting projects, as well as local workers who might be hired to plant and maintain the trees.

title: Protecting Consumers from Deceptive AI Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Protecting Consumers from Deceptive AI Act, aims to make it easier to tell when images, videos, audio, or text have been created or altered by artificial intelligence, especially "deepfakes" that can look or sound completely real. It directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to set up task forces with experts from government, tech companies, academia, media, privacy groups, and others to develop technical standards for labeling AI-generated content. These standards would include things like watermarks, digital fingerprints, and metadata tags that identify content as AI-made, and the task forces would report their progress to Congress over several years.

Beyond just research, the bill also creates actual legal requirements. Companies that make AI tools capable of generating images, video, or audio would have to embed a machine-readable disclosure marking that content as AI-generated, and take steps to prevent that label from being stripped out or tampered with. Large online platforms (those with at least $50 million in annual revenue or 25 million monthly users) would be required to display this AI-origin information to users and would be banned from removing it. The Federal Trade Commission would write detailed rules to implement all this and would enforce violations as deceptive business practices, similar to how it polices false advertising. Companies could also follow FTC-approved industry self-regulation guidelines instead of the government's exact rules, as long as those guidelines meet the same goals.

This bill would primarily affect AI companies (like those making image, video, or voice-generation tools), large social media and search platforms, and businesses that advertise using AI-generated content. Everyday consumers would be affected mainly by seeing more disclosure labels when they encounter AI-generated media online, which supporters say is meant to reduce scams, fake celebrity endorsements, election misinformation, and confusion caused by realistic deepfakes.

title: TAKE IT DOWN Act
ai_summary:
The TAKE IT DOWN Act makes it a federal crime to knowingly publish intimate or sexually explicit images or videos of a real person without their consent, including "deepfakes" created or altered using artificial intelligence. This applies to images of adults published in ways intended to cause harm or that actually cause psychological, financial, or reputational harm, and to any such images of minors published to abuse, harass, or sexually exploit them. Penalties include up to 2 years in prison for offenses involving adults and up to 3 years for offenses involving minors, plus penalties for threatening to publish such content. The law includes exceptions for law enforcement, legal proceedings, medical or educational purposes, and people sharing images of themselves.

The law also requires websites, apps, and online platforms that host user-generated content (like social media sites) to set up a system letting victims request removal of these nonconsensual images. Platforms must clearly explain this process to users and must remove reported content, along with any known copies, within 48 hours of a valid request. Platforms that act in good faith to remove reported content are protected from lawsuits over those takedowns. The Federal Trade Commission is responsible for enforcing these platform requirements, treating violations as unfair or deceptive business practices.

This law affects everyday internet users, particularly people who could be victims of "revenge porn" or AI-generated fake explicit images, by giving them a faster legal path to get such content removed and by criminalizing its distribution. It also affects social media companies, websites, and apps that host user content, since they now have legal obligations to respond quickly to takedown requests or face FTC enforcement action. Small email providers and services with only preselected (non-user-generated) content are generally not covered by the platform rules.

last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-12.

title: Northwest Straits Marine Conservation Initiative Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews and updates a federal program that supports marine conservation efforts in the Northwest Straits, a region of Puget Sound in Washington State that includes the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Originally created in 1998, the Northwest Straits Marine Conservation Initiative funds a citizen-led commission that works to protect water quality, marine wildlife, and habitats in the area, which have been damaged over the decades by pollution, habitat loss, and now climate change effects like rising seas and ocean acidification. The bill reauthorizes this program, updates its structure, and provides funding of $10 million per year from 2026 through 2031, with funding continuing afterward at whatever levels Congress decides are needed.

The bill spells out how a 14-member advisory commission is formed, with representatives from seven Washington counties, two members representing Tribal governments, one representing a state environmental partnership, and four general members appointed by the governor. It also updates the commission's goals and duties, such as collecting scientific data, building partnerships with Tribal governments and other agencies, running education programs, and issuing annual public reports on progress. The commission cannot create or enforce federal regulations—its role is advisory and coordinating, not regulatory.

This bill mainly affects residents of the seven named Washington counties, Tribal governments in the region, and organizations involved in marine conservation, fishing, tourism, and coastal management in Puget Sound. It also affects federal agencies like NOAA, which will continue partnering with and funding the commission. For most Americans outside this region, the bill has little direct effect, though it reflects continued federal investment in protecting a nationally significant marine ecosystem.

title: SMART Community Policing Act
ai_summary:
HR 8886, called the SMART Community Policing Act, would change an existing federal grant program (the COPS program, run through the Department of Justice) to allow local police departments and communities to use that federal money for new types of mental health-related responses. Right now, COPS funding can be used for things like hiring police officers and crime prevention programs. This bill would add new approved uses, including creating or expanding "mobile crisis teams" that send mental health professionals and paramedics—sometimes alongside police—to respond to 911 calls or community requests involving people in a mental health or emotional crisis, rather than relying solely on armed officers.

The bill also allows funding for "co-responder programs," where a police officer is paired directly with a mental health clinician or paramedic to jointly respond to crisis calls, and for "case management and outreach teams" that follow up with people after a crisis to connect them with ongoing mental health care, housing help, or substance abuse treatment, and to reduce repeat 911 calls involving the same individuals. Departments could also use the money to train officers to work alongside these mental health professionals.

This bill would primarily affect local police departments and city/county governments that apply for COPS grants, mental health workers and paramedics who might be hired under these new programs, and everyday residents—especially people experiencing homelessness, poverty, mental illness, or substance use crises—who interact with emergency responders. It does not mandate that any city adopt these programs; it simply expands what federal grant money is allowed to pay for, giving communities more flexibility if they choose to apply for and use these funds this way.

title: January 6th Law Enforcement Heroes Compensation Fund Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a federal fund to compensate law enforcement officers who defended the U.S. Capitol during the events of January 6, 2021. It sets up a claims process, run by a "Special Master" appointed by the Attorney General, where officers (or, if an officer died, their family representative) could file for payment covering injuries, lost wages, medical costs, and emotional or psychological harm like PTSD, including deaths reasonably linked to their service that day, such as suicide. Claims would need to be filed within three years of the program's rules being finalized, and each officer could only file one claim.

The bill sets a minimum payment of about $5 million for any claim involving a death connected to January 6. It also creates a separate, additional payment to every eligible officer, regardless of whether they were personally injured, calculated by dividing a set amount (plus money tied to any settlements the government has paid to people convicted of January 6-related crimes) among all the claimants. The Special Master's decisions on claims would be final and not reviewable in court, though claimants would have rights to legal representation and to present evidence. Payments would not require separate future budget approval, since the bill itself authorizes the spending.

This bill mainly affects law enforcement officers (such as Capitol Police and Metropolitan Police officers) who worked to defend the Capitol on January 6, 2021, and their families in cases of death. It would also involve the Department of Justice, which would administer the program, and taxpayers, since the compensation would be funded through federal spending authorized directly by this law.

title: End Prison Gerrymandering Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the End Prison Gerrymandering Act, changes how incarcerated people are counted in the U.S. Census. Currently, people in prison are counted as living at the facility where they are incarcerated, even though many prisons are located far from the neighborhoods where inmates actually lived before being locked up. Starting with the 2030 Census, this bill would require the Census Bureau to instead count incarcerated individuals as residents of their last usual home address before they went to prison, not the location of the prison itself.

The bill also affects how states draw congressional districts. It requires states to use each incarcerated person's pre-incarceration address, rather than the prison's address, when redrawing district lines after the census. This matters because census numbers are used to decide how many representatives each state gets in Congress and how district boundaries are drawn within states. When large prisons are counted as having thousands of "residents," it can artificially boost the population—and therefore the political representation—of the district containing the prison, even though those incarcerated individuals cannot vote there and have no real ties to that community.

This bill would primarily affect states and counties with large prison populations, particularly rural areas where prisons are often built. It would shift population counts (and potentially some political representation) away from those areas and back toward the urban or other communities that incarcerated individuals originally came from. It would also affect the Census Bureau, which would need to collect and verify pre-incarceration address information, and lawmakers involved in redistricting after each census.

title: Safe Check-Ins for Immigrants Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Safe Check-Ins for Immigrants Act, would change immigration law to let certain immigrants check in remotely instead of in person while their deportation cases are being decided. Right now, immigrants who have been released from detention while their case moves through the system are often required to periodically report in person to an immigration officer or a case manager as a condition of their release. This bill would require the Department of Homeland Security to give these individuals the option to complete those check-ins by video call instead of showing up in person.

The bill applies specifically to immigrants who have been released from custody under existing law while awaiting a decision on whether they will be removed (deported) from the United States, and who are required to check in periodically as part of the terms of their release. This could include people enrolled in "alternatives to detention" programs, which are supervision programs used instead of holding someone in a detention facility.

This change would primarily affect immigrants going through removal proceedings, the case managers and officers who supervise them, and the immigration enforcement system more broadly. Supporters of such measures generally argue that virtual check-ins reduce travel burdens, missed work, and logistical difficulties for immigrants, while the Department of Homeland Security would be responsible for setting up and managing the video teleconference option to carry out the requirement.

title: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States to require that the Supreme Court of the United States be composed of nine justices.
ai_summary:
This bill proposes an amendment to the U.S. Constitution that would permanently fix the number of Supreme Court justices at nine. Currently, the number of justices on the Supreme Court is not set by the Constitution itself but by federal law, which Congress can change with a simple majority vote. This amendment would lock the number nine into the Constitution, meaning that changing it in the future would require another constitutional amendment rather than just a new law.

To become part of the Constitution, this proposal would need to pass both the House and Senate with a two-thirds majority vote, and then be approved by three-fourths of state legislatures (38 out of 50 states) within seven years. This is a much higher bar than passing regular legislation, which only needs a simple majority in Congress and the president's signature.

This bill affects the entire country, since it deals with the structure of the highest court in the federal judicial system. It comes amid ongoing national debates about whether Congress should have the power to increase or decrease the number of justices, a practice sometimes called "court packing." Supporters of fixing the number at nine argue it would protect the Court's stability and independence from political pressure, while those who might oppose it could argue that removing Congress's flexibility to adjust the Court's size limits future options for addressing perceived problems with the judiciary. As a constitutional amendment, this would apply permanently unless later repealed by another amendment.
ai_headline: Proposed amendment would lock Supreme Court at nine justices
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: A proposed constitutional amendment would permanently set the Supreme Court's size at nine justices.

Currently that number is set by federal law, which Congress can change with a simple majority; the amendment would require another constitutional amendment to change it in the future.

Passing it requires a two-thirds vote in both chambers and ratification by 38 of 50 states within seven years, a far higher bar than regular legislation.

title: SPEED and Reliability Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the SPEED and Reliability Act of 2025, changes federal rules about how new high-voltage power lines get approved. Currently, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) can only approve certain transmission line projects in specially designated "national interest" corridors. This bill removes that requirement, allowing FERC to approve necessary transmission projects anywhere in the country as long as they meet certain standards, such as reducing power congestion, improving electric grid reliability, and making good use of existing towers and rights-of-way. It also sets clearer rules for how landowners, states, and tribes must be consulted, and how costs for new power lines get divided among the utility customers who benefit from them.

The bill also streamlines the federal permitting process by naming a single "lead agency" (usually FERC, or the Department of the Interior for offshore projects) to coordinate approvals, aiming to cut down on delays caused by multiple agencies reviewing the same project. It sets stricter deadlines for permitting decisions and clarifies that FERC cannot override a state's own authority to decide whether a transmission line can be built within that state's borders. Texas's power grid (ERCOT), which operates largely independently from the rest of the country, is specifically excluded from these rules.

This bill would primarily affect electric utility companies, landowners near proposed transmission routes (including farmers and ranchers), state governments, and energy regulators. Supporters of these kinds of changes generally argue faster permitting helps meet rising electricity demand and improves grid reliability, while critics of similar proposals in the past have raised concerns about reduced state or local control and the impact on landowners. The bill does not address electricity rates for consumers directly or expand FERC's authority over retail electricity sales.
ai_headline: Bill would let FERC approve power lines outside special corridors
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

ai_sections.tldr: The SPEED and Reliability Act would let FERC approve needed transmission lines anywhere, not just in designated corridors.
ai_sections.what: This bill removes the current requirement that FERC only approve transmission lines within specially designated "national interest" corridors, letting it approve projects anywhere that meet standards like reducing congestion and improving grid reliability. It also names a single lead agency to coordinate permitting, sets stricter decision deadlines, and clarifies rules for consulting landowners, states, and tribes and dividing costs among utility customers.
ai_sections.who: Electric utility companies, landowners near proposed routes (including farmers and ranchers), state governments, and energy regulators would be affected. Texas's ERCOT grid is specifically excluded.
ai_sections.why: Faster permitting could speed up transmission projects nationwide, but the changes could also reduce the role of specially designated corridors and raise questions about state and local control over projects, even though the bill preserves states' authority to decide whether lines can be built within their borders.

title: Constitutional Accountability Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Constitutional Accountability Act, would change federal law to make it easier to sue government agencies when police officers or other law enforcement officials violate a person's constitutional rights. Currently, under a law known as Section 1983, individuals can sue officers for civil rights violations, but suing the city, state, or federal government that employs those officers is much harder. Courts have generally required proof that the violation resulted from an official government policy, and states have often been protected entirely from such lawsuits due to legal immunity rules. This bill would remove those barriers by making the United States, states, local governments, and their agencies directly liable whenever one of their law enforcement employees or contractors violates someone's constitutional rights, regardless of whether there was an official policy involved.

Specifically, the bill redefines "person" under Section 1983 to include the federal government, state and local governments, and government agencies, meaning they can now be sued directly. It also removes state governments' ability to claim "sovereign immunity" (a legal protection that normally shields states from certain lawsuits) in these cases, and it has the federal government waive its own immunity as well. Additionally, liability would apply even if the individual officer involved would normally be protected by legal defenses like qualified immunity.

This bill would primarily affect people who believe their constitutional rights were violated by police or other law enforcement officers, giving them a clearer path to seek financial compensation directly from government bodies. It would also affect federal, state, and local governments and taxpayers, since these entities could face increased legal exposure and potential costs from lawsuits. Law enforcement agencies might also be affected indirectly, as increased liability could push them to strengthen officer training, hiring practices, and oversight to reduce legal risk.
ai_headline: Bill would let governments be sued directly for officer rights violations
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
policy_area: Civil Rights and Liberties, Minority Issues

ai_sections.tldr: The bill lets people sue federal, state, and local governments directly when law enforcement violates constitutional rights.
ai_sections.what: The Constitutional Accountability Act would redefine "person" under Section 1983 to include the federal government, states, local governments, and their agencies, making them directly liable when law enforcement violates constitutional rights. It removes states' sovereign immunity and waives federal immunity in these cases, and liability applies even if the officer would be shielded by qualified immunity.

title: Medicare Dental, Vision, and Hearing Benefit Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would add dental, vision, and hearing benefits to traditional Medicare, which currently does not cover most of these services. Starting in 2026, Medicare would pay 100% of the cost for preventive dental care like cleanings and exams (limited to twice a year), and would gradually begin covering other dental work such as fillings, root canals, crowns, and extractions, with Medicare's share rising from 30% in 2027 to 80% by 2029. Dentures would also be covered starting in 2027 at 80%, limited to one set every five years. Lower-income beneficiaries who qualify for certain subsidies would get full coverage for preventive dental services and 80% coverage for other dental work starting immediately in 2026, without waiting for the phase-in.

The bill also adds vision coverage, including yearly eye exams, and 80% payment toward eyeglasses, contact lenses, and low-vision devices, subject to dollar limits that adjust for inflation over time. Similarly, it adds hearing coverage, including hearing exams and hearing aids, with Medicare paying 80% of the cost, limited to one hearing aid per ear every four years. The Health and Human Services Secretary would have authority to set additional rules, limits, or prior authorization requirements for these new benefits. The bill also requires that the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, which issues health screening recommendations, include at least one oral health expert.

This bill would primarily affect the roughly 65 million Americans enrolled in Medicare, especially those in traditional Medicare (as opposed to private Medicare Advantage plans, many of which already offer limited dental/vision/hearing benefits). It would also affect dentists, optometrists, audiologists, and other health providers who bill Medicare, as well as federal spending on the Medicare program, since these new benefits would represent a significant new cost.
ai_headline: Bill would add dental, vision, and hearing coverage to traditional Medicare
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Ways and Means, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.tldr: Starting in 2026, traditional Medicare would phase in coverage for dental, vision, and hearing care.
ai_sections.what: The bill adds dental, vision, and hearing benefits to traditional Medicare, which mostly lacks this coverage now. Preventive dental care starts at 100% coverage in 2026, with other dental work phased in from 30% (2027) to 80% (2029), dentures at 80% starting 2027, vision and hearing services at 80% coverage, and full/faster coverage for lower-income beneficiaries starting in 2026.
ai_sections.who: This affects roughly 65 million Medicare enrollees, particularly those in traditional Medicare rather than Medicare Advantage. It also affects dentists, optometrists, audiologists, and other providers who bill Medicare.
ai_sections.why: The changes would gradually expand what Medicare pays for, shifting costs and coverage rules over several years while giving HHS authority to set limits and prior authorization requirements.
ai_sections.cost: The new benefits would represent a significant new cost to federal spending on the Medicare program.

title: Delivering for Rural Seniors Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 1538, the "Delivering for Rural Seniors Act of 2025," would create a new pilot grant program to help deliver food directly to the homes of low-income elderly people who participate in the Commodity Supplemental Food Program (CSFP). This existing federal program provides monthly food packages to low-income seniors, but many recipients—especially those in rural areas—struggle to pick up food boxes due to distance, lack of transportation, or health limitations. This bill aims to fix that by paying for home delivery instead.

Under the bill, state agencies could apply for competitive grants (up to $4 million each, based on a formula tied to their CSFP caseload) from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. States would then pass this grant money to local organizations to cover costs like transportation, delivery staff, and outreach to let eligible seniors know home delivery is available. Priority would be given to organizations serving seniors in rural areas. States receiving grants would have to report back on how many people were served, how many deliveries were made, and how cost-effective the program was.

This bill mainly affects low-income seniors enrolled in CSFP, particularly those living in rural or hard-to-reach areas, as well as the state and local agencies that run the program. It would authorize $10 million per year in federal funding for fiscal years 2026 through 2028 to test this delivery approach nationwide.
ai_headline: Bill would fund home food delivery for rural seniors on federal aid
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Nutrition and Foreign Agriculture.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 1538 would create a pilot grant program funding home food delivery for low-income seniors in CSFP who struggle to pick up food boxes.
ai_sections.what: HR 1538 would establish a pilot grant program letting state agencies apply for competitive USDA grants of up to $4 million each to fund home delivery of food to CSFP participants. States would pass funds to local organizations for transportation, delivery staff, and outreach, with priority given to rural-serving organizations. Grantees would report on people served, deliveries made, and cost-effectiveness.

title: Under Pressure Act
ai_summary:
HR 7011, called the "Under Pressure Act," directs the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) to study why pressure relief devices on rail tank cars sometimes fail during train derailments. These devices are safety valves designed to release pressure from tank cars carrying hazardous materials, helping prevent explosions or worse damage in accidents. Within 18 months of the bill becoming law, the FRA administrator would have to deliver a detailed report to Congress covering how often these failures happen, what causes them, and specific details about each incident, such as how many tank cars were involved, whether fire was present, how hot and long any fire burned, and how the safety device was positioned on the tank car.

The report would also need to include recommendations for preventing these failures in the future and update Congress on whether railroads have properly responded to safety recommendations previously issued by the National Transportation Safety Board. To gather accurate information, the FRA would be required to consult with several groups: the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration, railroad companies, unions representing rail workers, and the companies that build, ship with, or own tank cars.

This bill mainly affects the freight rail industry, including railroad companies, tank car manufacturers, and rail workers, as well as communities located along rail lines where hazardous materials are transported. It does not create new regulations or safety requirements itself; instead, it focuses on gathering information and data that could be used later to write stronger safety rules. This type of legislation often follows high-profile train derailments involving hazardous materials, such as the 2023 East Palestine, Ohio incident, where concerns were raised about whether existing safety equipment functioned properly.
ai_headline: FRA must study why rail tank car safety valves fail in derailments
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials.

ai_sections.tldr: The "Under Pressure Act" requires FRA to report to Congress within 18 months on why tank car pressure relief devices fail during derailments.

The report must detail failure frequency, causes, incident specifics (number of tank cars, fire presence, heat and duration, device positioning), prevention recommendations, and railroad responses to prior NTSB safety recommendations.

title: Buy Now, Pay Later Protection Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Buy Now, Pay Later Protection Act of 2025, would extend federal consumer protection rules to "buy now, pay later" loans—the short-term payment plans offered by companies like Klarna, Afterpay, and Affirm that let shoppers split a purchase into a few interest-free installments. Currently, these loans aren't fully covered by the Truth in Lending Act, the main federal law that regulates credit cards and other consumer loans. The bill officially defines a "buy now, pay later loan" as a purchase loan repaid in four or fewer interest-free payments, and then changes several sections of the law so those protections also apply to this type of loan.

Specifically, the bill would give buy now, pay later customers similar rights to credit card holders, including the ability to dispute charges and withhold payment if there's a problem with a purchase (similar to disputing a credit card charge), and other billing-related protections. It also requires the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) to write formal rules within a year to put these changes into effect. Additionally, it gives the CFPB authority to supervise and examine companies that offer these loans, similar to how it currently oversees banks, credit card companies, and other large financial institutions.

This bill would mainly affect consumers who use buy now, pay later services for online and retail purchases, giving them stronger legal protections if there's a billing dispute or problem with a purchase. It would also affect companies that offer these loans, such as fintech firms and payment apps, since they would face new federal oversight and compliance requirements similar to those already faced by credit card issuers and other lenders.
ai_headline: Bill would apply credit card-style rules to buy now, pay later loans
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill would extend Truth in Lending Act protections and CFPB oversight to buy now, pay later loans.

It gives buy now, pay later users rights similar to credit card holders, such as disputing charges and withholding payment over purchase problems, and requires the CFPB to write implementing rules within a year and gain supervisory authority over these lenders.

title: Marine Mammal Climate Change Protection Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would update the Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972 to specifically address threats from climate change. It directs the Secretary of Commerce, working with the Marine Mammal Commission, to identify whales, seals, dolphins, and other marine mammal species or populations that are likely to decline because of climate change effects like warming oceans, habitat loss, or shifts in food supply. For each species on this list, officials would have to create a detailed "climate impact management plan" laying out steps to protect the animals, such as reducing conflicts with fishing operations, protecting habitat, and managing prey populations. These plans would need regular public review, updates every five years, and reports to Congress on progress.

The bill also sets up a new monitoring program within NOAA to track how climate change is affecting marine mammal populations, improve scientific models predicting future changes, and study how these animals contribute to ocean health, including carbon storage. It requires new regulations for deciding which species qualify for climate-related protections, and states that a lack of complete scientific data cannot be used as an excuse to avoid listing a species. Other federal agencies would be required to make sure their own actions don't conflict with these conservation plans. The bill also calls for reviewing and updating international agreements with other countries on shared marine mammal populations affected by climate change.

This bill would primarily affect federal wildlife agencies (NOAA, the Department of Interior, and the Marine Mammal Commission), which would receive new funding and responsibilities, as well as fishing industries and coastal communities whose activities might be adjusted to reduce harm to protected marine mammals. Conservation groups, scientists studying ocean ecosystems, and countries that share responsibility for migratory marine mammal species would also be affected. The bill authorizes about $16 million per year from 2027 through 2031 to carry out these new requirements.
ai_headline: Bill would add climate change protections for whales and other marine mammals
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.

It also creates a NOAA monitoring program and requires new listing regulations, barring incomplete data as an excuse to avoid protections.

title: Destroy Zombie Guns Act
ai_summary:
HR 7134, called the "Destroy Zombie Guns Act," aims to close a loophole related to how firearms are destroyed. Currently, when guns are turned in or ordered destroyed (for example, guns seized by police or surrendered voluntarily), businesses that handle the destruction don't always have to destroy every part. This means some components, like the metal receiver or frame, which legally counts as the actual "firearm," could survive intact and later be reassembled into a working gun using replacement parts—essentially creating a "zombie gun" that comes back to life. This bill would make it illegal for anyone in the business of destroying firearms to leave any component undestroyed when the firearm has crossed state lines or international borders at some point.

The bill also defines what it means to be "engaged in the business" of destroying firearms, clarifying that this applies to people or companies who do this work regularly and mainly to earn a profit, not as a one-time favor or hobby. This ensures the law targets commercial destruction operations rather than casual or personal disposal.

For penalties, anyone who violates this rule could face fines and up to two years in prison, on top of any other penalties they might already face under existing gun laws. Additionally, if the violator holds a federal license to deal in firearms, the Attorney General could suspend that license for a first offense and must revoke it for repeat violations. This bill would primarily affect licensed firearm dealers, destruction companies, and businesses that contract with police departments or other entities to destroy confiscated or surrendered weapons. Everyday gun owners would not be directly affected unless they operate such a destruction business.
ai_headline: Bill would require full destruction of guns, closing "zombie gun" loophole
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: The Destroy Zombie Guns Act would require firearm destruction businesses to destroy every part, not just some components.
ai_sections.what: HR 7134 would make it illegal for businesses that destroy firearms to leave any component intact when the firearm has crossed state or international lines. This closes a loophole where parts like the metal receiver or frame, legally considered the "firearm," could survive and be rebuilt into a working gun. The bill also defines "engaged in the business" to mean regular, profit-driven destruction work, not casual or one-time disposal.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects licensed firearm dealers, commercial destruction companies, and businesses contracted by police or other entities to destroy confiscated or surrendered weapons. Everyday gun owners are not affected unless they operate such a destruction business.
ai_sections.why: Without this change, incompletely destroyed firearm parts could be reassembled into working guns using replacement components. The bill adds criminal penalties and licensing consequences to deter incomplete destruction by commercial operators.

title: No Tax on Restored Benefits Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "No Tax on Restored Benefits Act," would change federal tax law so that certain Social Security benefit increases are not counted as taxable income. It specifically applies to extra benefits people started receiving because of the Social Security Fairness Act of 2023, an earlier law that eliminated rules (known as the Windfall Elimination Provision and Government Pension Offset) that had previously reduced Social Security payments for people who also received pensions from jobs not covered by Social Security, such as many teachers, firefighters, and police officers.

Under this bill, the portion of monthly Social Security payments that increased because of that 2023 law—specifically for the period from January 2025 through December 2025—would be excluded from a person's gross income for federal tax purposes. In simple terms, this means retirees who got a bump in their Social Security checks due to the Fairness Act would not have to pay federal income tax on that extra amount, at least for benefits covering that one-year window.

This bill would mainly affect retired public sector workers, such as teachers, police officers, and government employees, who saw their Social Security benefits increase after the 2023 law took effect. It would not change taxes on regular Social Security benefits people were already receiving before that law—only the additional amount tied specifically to the Fairness Act adjustments during the specified time period. The bill has been introduced in the House and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, meaning it still needs further review and votes before it could become law.
ai_headline: Bill would exempt 2025 Social Security Fairness Act increases from taxes
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: Bill would exclude from federal taxes the 2025 Social Security benefit increases tied to the 2023 Fairness Act.
ai_sections.what: This bill would exempt from federal income tax the portion of Social Security benefits that increased due to the Social Security Fairness Act of 2023, covering January through December 2025. It would not affect taxes on regular Social Security benefits people already received before that law.

title: SROS Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the SROS Act, would change federal tax law so that retired military members and retired law enforcement officers who go on to work as school resource officers do not have to pay federal income tax on their retirement pensions while working in that job. Currently, retirement income like military or police pensions is generally taxable, even if the retiree takes on a new job. This bill would exclude that pension income from taxable income specifically for the years someone works as a school resource officer.

The bill also includes a bonus for long-serving school resource officers: if someone works in that role for at least 10 years, their retirement income becomes permanently tax-exempt for the rest of their life, even after they stop working as a school resource officer. To qualify, the person must have passed required background checks and be following the training and certification rules set by their state's law enforcement standards agency. Police departments and other agencies that employ these officers would be required to report to the IRS when someone starts and stops working in this role, and there are penalties for failing to file that paperwork.

This bill would primarily affect retired service members and retired police officers who choose to work as school resource officers, potentially giving them a financial incentive to take these jobs by increasing their after-tax income. It could also affect school districts trying to recruit experienced, retired officers for these positions, and it would have a modest effect on federal tax revenue, since less income would be taxed for those in this situation.
ai_headline: Bill would exempt school resource officers' pensions from federal tax
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

ai_sections.tldr: The SROS Act would make retired military and police pensions tax-free while working as school resource officers.

title: the Military PFAS Transparency Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 4192, the Military PFAS Transparency Act of 2025, requires the Department of Defense to be more open about how it is cleaning up PFAS contamination ("forever chemicals") at military sites. PFAS are man-made chemicals linked to health problems, often found in firefighting foam used on military bases, which has contaminated soil and groundwater at many installations around the country. This bill doesn't create new cleanup rules directly, but it forces the Pentagon to track and report on its progress more closely.

Specifically, the bill requires the Secretary of Defense to submit an annual report to Congress detailing funding, spending, and the status of cleanup projects at each contaminated site. This includes information like whether design work, contracts, or construction are on schedule, explanations for delays longer than a year, and any obstacles slowing the work down. The bill also requires DoD to create a strategy within 180 days for speeding up cleanup, including ranking sites by health and environmental risk and expanding lab capacity to test for PFAS. Finally, it requires a public online dashboard, updated twice a year, showing site-by-site funding, progress, timelines, and contacts for local communities.

This bill mainly affects the Department of Defense, Congress, and communities near military bases dealing with PFAS contamination. Residents living near affected installations, environmental advocates, and local officials would benefit from easier access to information about cleanup progress and funding. It does not change environmental cleanup laws directly but increases oversight and public accountability for how quickly and effectively the military addresses PFAS pollution.
ai_headline: Bill would force Pentagon to report yearly on PFAS cleanup progress
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Armed Services.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 4192 requires DoD to report annually to Congress and post a public dashboard on PFAS cleanup at military sites.

title: Investing in the American Dream Act
ai_summary:
HR 8563, the "Investing in the American Dream Act," would clarify who counts as eligible to own a small business that receives certain federal loans and financial help from the Small Business Administration (SBA). This includes standard SBA-guaranteed loans, microloans, certain investment loans, and surety bond guarantees. The bill states that a business qualifies as long as it is located in the United States and at least 51 percent owned and controlled by U.S. citizens or nationals, or by other "eligible individuals" who are lawfully present in the country and authorized to work here.

The bill specifically lists categories of people who would count as "eligible individuals" if they meet these lawful presence and work authorization requirements. This includes people granted asylum, refugees, certain nonimmigrant visa holders whose stay hasn't expired, lawful permanent residents (including conditional green card holders), and people granted deferred action under the 2012 DACA (Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals) policy. The bill also states that a business cannot be denied one of these loans simply because it is owned by such eligible individuals, as long as the ownership and residency rules are met.

This bill would primarily affect small business owners who are immigrants with legal status in the U.S., including DACA recipients, refugees, asylees, and certain visa holders, by clarifying their ability to qualify for SBA loans and related financial programs. It could also affect banks and lenders that work with the SBA, since it defines more specifically who counts as an eligible borrower. The bill notes that it does not give the SBA authority to change the required ownership percentage, meaning the 51 percent ownership rule would remain fixed.
ai_headline: Bill would clarify which immigrants qualify for SBA small business loans
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Small Business.

title: TECH Act
ai_summary:
The TECH Act is a bill that would let vocational and technical schools apply for certain federal education and job training grants on the same footing as traditional two-year and four-year colleges. Right now, some federal grant programs are only open to colleges and universities, even though technical schools often teach the hands-on skills needed for jobs in areas like healthcare, manufacturing, transportation, and infrastructure. This bill would change that by requiring federal agencies to update their rules so qualifying technical schools can compete for the same grants.

Specifically, the bill covers grant programs run by the Department of Education (like the Strengthening Institutions Program, TRIO, and a child care assistance program for student parents) and a Department of Labor grant program aimed at community colleges. To qualify, a technical school would need to offer approved "career pathway" or short-term "job training" programs—generally lasting 8 to 15 weeks—that lead to industry-recognized credentials in fields facing worker shortages, such as skilled trades, healthcare, or public safety. Federal agencies would have 180 days after the bill becomes law to update their eligibility rules and issue guidance on how to fairly divide grant money between colleges and technical schools.

This bill would primarily affect technical and vocational schools, which could gain new access to federal funding streams previously reserved for traditional colleges. It could also affect students at those schools, who might benefit from expanded resources, and traditional colleges, which would now share these particular grant pools with more institutions. Federal agencies like the Departments of Education and Labor would be responsible for implementing the changes and deciding how to balance funding across school types.
ai_headline: Bill would open federal college grants to technical schools
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

title: Bivens Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Bivens Act of 2025, would make it easier for people to sue federal government officials in court when those officials violate their constitutional rights. Currently, a law known as Section 1983 allows people to sue state and local government officials (like police officers) for civil rights violations, but it does not clearly cover federal officials in the same way. Lawsuits against federal officials have instead relied on a 1971 Supreme Court decision called "Bivens," which the courts have limited significantly over the years, making it very hard for people to actually win such cases or even get them heard.

The bill changes the wording of the existing civil rights law (42 U.S.C. 1983) to explicitly include officials acting under the authority of the United States government, not just state governments. In practical terms, this means someone whose rights were violated by a federal agent, officer, or employee acting in their official capacity could sue for damages in federal court using the same legal process currently used to sue state officials, rather than relying on the more restrictive Bivens legal doctrine.

This bill would primarily affect individuals who believe their constitutional rights—such as protection against unreasonable searches, excessive force, or unlawful arrest—have been violated by federal employees, including agents from agencies like the FBI, ICE, DEA, or Border Patrol. It would also affect federal employees and agencies themselves, since it could expose them to more lawsuits and potential financial liability. Courts would play a key role in interpreting and applying this expanded legal remedy once the law goes into effect.

title: To prohibit the Department of Homeland Security from entering into, modifying, extending, or renewing, any contract or intergovernmental service agreement to establish or operate any new immigration detention model, including the use of warehouses, modular facilities, soft-sided structures, tent systems, and processing centers.
ai_summary:
This bill, introduced in the House, would stop the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) from creating new types of immigration detention facilities. This includes converting warehouses, industrial buildings, tents, "soft-sided structures," modular units, or similar spaces into places where immigrants are held or processed. The bill would block DHS from signing, changing, extending, or renewing any contracts to build or run these kinds of facilities, whether operated directly by the government or by outside contractors.

The bill also cuts off funding for these efforts. It says no federal money, whether already allocated or from any other source, can be used to build, expand, renovate, or run these new-style detention facilities. Agencies also could not shift or "reprogram" money from other budgets to pay for them. Any funds that had been set aside for these facilities would instead be redirected to things like affordable healthcare and housing programs. The bill's authors cite concerns about detainee treatment, deaths in detention, health and safety conditions, and impacts on local communities (such as strain on water, electricity, and infrastructure) as reasons for the ban.

This bill would primarily affect DHS and ICE operations, government contractors who build or manage detention facilities, and immigrants held in civil immigration detention. It could also affect local communities near proposed detention sites, since the bill aims to prevent new facilities from being built in their areas. As of this text, the bill has only been introduced and referred to committees; it has not been voted into law.

title: SAFE Act of 2025
ai_summary:
**HR 1661 — SAFE Act of 2025** would expand an existing federal law that currently bans slaughtering dogs and cats for human food, adding horses, mules, donkeys, and other equines to that same prohibition. The bill amends a section of the 2018 farm bill so that it becomes illegal to slaughter horses and other equines for people to eat, just as it's already illegal to do so with dogs and cats.

Currently, there are no horse slaughterhouses operating in the United States, but horses are sometimes transported to Canada or Mexico to be slaughtered there for meat that is exported and consumed abroad (horse meat is not commonly eaten in the U.S.). This bill wouldn't necessarily stop that export practice directly, since it targets slaughter for human consumption under U.S. law, but it would close any legal loophole that might allow a domestic horse slaughter industry for food purposes to restart in the future.

This bill mainly affects horse owners, breeders, ranchers, animal welfare organizations, and companies involved in transporting or processing livestock. Supporters argue it protects horses, which many Americans view differently from typical livestock animals, from being killed for meat. The bill has a large, bipartisan group of cosponsors from both parties, suggesting broad interest in the issue, though as with any livestock-related legislation, agricultural groups and rural communities may have varying views on its practical impact.

title: First Rhode Island Regiment Congressional Gold Medal Act
ai_summary:
This bill would award a Congressional Gold Medal, one of the highest civilian honors Congress can give, to the First Rhode Island Regiment. This was a Revolutionary War military unit notable for recruiting free Black, enslaved, and Indigenous men to serve, with enslaved recruits promised freedom in exchange for military service. The regiment fought in several battles, including the Battle of Rhode Island in 1778, and served through the end of the war in 1783. The bill lays out historical background explaining why Congress believes this recognition is deserved, including details about how the regiment was formed and the hardships some soldiers faced afterward, such as fighting against re-enslavement.

Practically, the bill directs the Treasury Department to design and produce a single gold medal honoring the regiment collectively. That medal would then be given to the Rhode Island State Library for public display and research access, with Congress expressing a preference that it also be shown at other historically relevant sites. The Treasury would also be allowed to sell bronze duplicate copies of the medal to the public to cover production costs, with proceeds going back into the U.S. Mint's operating fund.

This bill mainly affects historical recognition rather than everyday policy or spending in a major way—it does not create new laws affecting the public directly. It would matter most to historians, descendants of regiment members, Rhode Island residents, and people interested in Revolutionary War history or the history of Black and Indigenous military service in early America. The costs involved are for medal production, funded through an existing Mint account, not new taxpayer appropriations.

title: No Deductions for Marijuana Businesses Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal tax law to make sure marijuana businesses cannot deduct normal business expenses on their federal taxes, even in states where marijuana is legal. Currently, a tax code section called 280E already blocks businesses that sell illegal drugs from taking standard tax deductions (like rent, wages, and utilities) that most other businesses can claim. There has been debate about whether this rule still applies to marijuana businesses operating legally under state law, especially since federal agencies have discussed reclassifying marijuana under drug scheduling rules. This bill would close that door by rewriting the law to clearly state that marijuana businesses are still covered by this deduction ban, regardless of any changes in how marijuana is classified as a controlled substance.

In practical terms, this affects marijuana growers, processors, and retailers operating in states that have legalized marijuana for medical or recreational use. Because they could not deduct typical business costs, these businesses would generally pay higher effective federal taxes than businesses in other industries, since they'd be taxed on revenue rather than profit after expenses. This could impact the profitability of state-legal marijuana businesses and potentially affect prices, business growth, or investment in that industry. It would not change whether marijuana is legal under state or federal law; it only affects how these businesses are taxed.
ai_headline: Bill would keep marijuana businesses barred from federal tax deductions
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.

title: Roadside Pollinator Program Amendments Act
ai_summary:
This bill updates and extends a federal program that encourages planting flowers and habitat for pollinators (like bees and butterflies) along highways and roadsides. It changes the list of groups allowed to apply for program funding, adding nonprofit organizations that qualify as tax-exempt charities under IRS rules, alongside the state transportation departments, federal land agencies, and Indian tribes already eligible. It also updates how tribal consultation works during planning, requiring agencies to consult with tribes whose land is within 50 miles of a proposed project, and requires the Federal Highway Administration to consult with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service when setting certain program guidelines.

On the money side, the bill raises the cap on individual grants from $150,000 to $500,000, meaning larger projects could get more federal support. It also increases and extends the program's overall funding, from $2 million per year (which was set to run through 2026) to $5 million per year, covering fiscal years 2026 through 2031.

This bill mainly affects state transportation agencies, federal land management agencies, Indian tribes, and now nonprofit conservation or environmental organizations that want to create pollinator habitat along highways. Indirectly, it could affect everyday drivers and nearby communities by supporting more roadside wildflower plantings and habitat restoration, which supporters say help bee and butterfly populations important for agriculture and ecosystems.

title: Humane Cosmetics Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 1657, the Humane Cosmetics Act of 2025, would make it illegal, starting one year after the law is passed, to test cosmetics on animals in the United States or to sell/ship cosmetics across state lines if they were developed using new animal testing. It also limits when companies can use animal-testing data to prove a cosmetic ingredient is safe, generally only allowing it if there's no available non-animal testing method and other strict conditions are met. There are some exceptions, such as testing done to comply with foreign country requirements, testing specifically ordered by the U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary after a public review process, testing for drugs regulated separately, or testing done for reasons unrelated to cosmetics.

The bill affects cosmetics companies and manufacturers, who would need to stop animal testing for cosmetic products and switch to alternative safety-testing methods, such as lab-grown tissue models or computer simulations. It also affects the FDA, which would gain authority to grant exemptions, request company records, and issue fines (up to $10,000 per violation) for companies that break the rules. Consumers would be affected indirectly, since cosmetic products sold in the U.S. would need to meet these new testing standards. The bill also blocks states from passing their own, different animal-testing rules for cosmetics, meaning there would be one uniform national standard instead of a patchwork of state laws.
ai_headline: Bill would ban animal testing for cosmetics sold in the US
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: Pacific Northwest Gray Wolves Relief Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, known as the Pacific Northwest Gray Wolves Relief Act of 2025, would require the Secretary of the Interior to bring back a specific federal rule about gray wolves within 60 days of the bill becoming law. That rule, originally issued in 2020, had removed gray wolves from the federal endangered species list. The bill would apply this rule specifically to gray wolf populations in Oregon and Washington state.

In practical terms, this means gray wolves in those two states would lose federal Endangered Species Act protections and would instead be managed under state wildlife laws, similar to how many other animal populations are handled. This could affect ranchers, farmers, and landowners who deal with wolf-livestock conflicts, since state management often allows more flexibility in controlling wolf populations, including hunting or trapping in some cases. It would also affect wildlife conservation groups and government agencies involved in wolf recovery efforts, as well as residents in rural areas of Oregon and Washington where wolf populations have been expanding. The bill does not change wolf protections in other states.

title: Expanding Market Access Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Expanding Market Access Act, updates federal programs that help American farmers sell their crops overseas. It amends the Agricultural Trade Act of 1978, which funds programs helping U.S. agricultural producers promote and export their products to other countries.

The bill makes several changes. First, it lets the U.S. Department of Agriculture pay for technical assistance to improve infrastructure in foreign countries—like better cold storage and port facilities—so that American farm products don't spoil or get damaged before reaching customers, with spending capped at $1.5 million in 2027 and $5 million per year after that. Second, it requires the Secretary of Agriculture to produce a more detailed report every two years on how competitive U.S. "specialty crops" (like fruits, vegetables, and nuts) are internationally, including analysis of foreign tariffs, trade barriers, food safety rules, and what the government is doing to address unfair practices. This report must be made public in an easy-to-use digital format. Third, the bill significantly increases and extends funding for these trade promotion programs through 2031, raising amounts from about $255 million in 2026 up to $533 million per year by 2028-2031, with specific funding guaranteed for various sub-programs. Finally, it repeals a couple of older, outdated legal provisions related to this funding.

This bill mainly affects American farmers, ranchers, and agricultural exporters, particularly those in the fruit, vegetable, and specialty crop industries, by giving them more government support to compete in foreign markets. It also affects trade organizations and nonprofit groups that help facilitate agricultural exports, as well as congressional committees that oversee agriculture and trade policy, who will receive more detailed reporting on international trade barriers affecting U.S. farm exports.

last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

This bill would close that loophole by making the underlying act of slaughtering equines for food illegal under federal law, not just restricting funding for inspections. Animal welfare advocates, horse owners, and rescue organizations would be the groups most directly affected, along with anyone involved in the transport or export of horses for slaughter purposes.

title: New Producer Economic Security Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new federal program, called the New Producer Economic Security Program, run by the Farm Service Agency within the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Its goal is to help beginning, small-scale, low-income, or otherwise disadvantaged farmers, ranchers, and forest owners get better access to farmland, money, and markets. Instead of giving money directly to individual farmers, the USDA would award grants, loans, or cooperative agreements to organizations like state or tribal governments, nonprofits, community development banks, universities, and cooperatives. Those organizations would then use the funding to directly help qualifying farmers with things like buying land, covering closing costs, getting better mortgage terms, clearing land title issues, improving soil and water, building infrastructure, and getting technical training on business planning, taxes, and succession planning.

The bill defines who counts as a "qualified beneficiary" — generally people who are new to farming, rent their land, have low incomes, or are otherwise economically disadvantaged, including those working through certain small family-run or worker-based business entities. It also lays out priorities for which projects get funded first, favoring those that give direct financial help to farmers, protect farmland from being resold for non-farm use, support Tribal land rights, help farmworkers, or promote conservation practices. A stakeholder committee would help USDA design and evaluate the program.

This bill mainly affects farmers and ranchers just starting out or facing financial hardship, along with the organizations that support them, such as nonprofits, tribal governments, and community lenders. It does not set a specific funding amount — it simply authorizes Congress to provide "such sums as necessary" in future budgets, meaning actual funding levels and impact would depend on later appropriations decisions.

title: Credit for Caring Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new federal tax credit for people who work while also caring for a family member with significant health or disability needs. Under the plan, caregivers could claim a credit equal to 30% of their qualifying caregiving expenses above $2,000 each year, up to a maximum credit of $5,000 (this cap would rise over time to keep pace with medical cost increases). To qualify, the caregiver must have earned at least $7,500 in income for the year, and the person receiving care must be a spouse or close relative who a licensed health professional certifies as needing substantial help with daily activities—such as eating, bathing, or moving around—for at least 180 days.

The credit could cover a wide range of expenses, including hiring in-home aides, home modifications, transportation, medical equipment, respite care, counseling, and even wages lost from taking unpaid time off work to provide care. However, expenses already covered by other tax benefits (like dependent care credits or health savings accounts) couldn't be double-counted. The credit amount would gradually shrink for higher earners, phasing out for individuals with income above $75,000 (or $150,000 for married couples filing jointly), with these thresholds also adjusted upward over time for inflation.

This bill would mainly affect working adults—often middle-aged—who are caring for aging parents, spouses, or other relatives with disabilities or chronic illnesses while holding a job. It would not create a new direct payment or benefit program; instead, it would reduce the amount of federal income tax caregivers owe, provided they keep proper documentation and meet the certification requirements. If passed, the changes would apply starting with the 2025 tax year.

last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
