ai_sections.why: Because this works through the tax system rather than direct payments, caregivers would need to meet certification and income requirements and keep documentation to reduce what they owe in federal income tax.

title: Mental Health in Aviation Act of 2025
ai_summary:
The Mental Health in Aviation Act of 2025 aims to make it easier and less stigmatizing for pilots and air traffic controllers to seek help for mental health concerns without automatically losing their ability to work. Currently, many aviation workers avoid disclosing mental health struggles because doing so can trigger lengthy reviews or jeopardize their medical certification. This bill directs the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to update its regulations within two years to encourage people to seek treatment and be honest about their mental health, rather than hiding conditions out of fear of losing their job.

The bill also requires the FAA to review and act on past recommendations from a special committee that studied mental health rules for pilots, and to consult with groups like pilot unions, air traffic controller unions, and aviation schools when making changes. It sets up an annual review of the "special issuance" process (the system used to approve pilots or controllers who have disclosed a mental health condition), looking at things like whether more medications could be safely allowed and whether examiners need better training. Funding is included—up to $15 million a year through 2029 to hire and train more aviation medical examiners (including psychiatrists) and clear backlogged cases, plus up to $1.5 million a year for a public information campaign to reduce stigma and share mental health resources with pilots, controllers, and aviation students.

This bill mainly affects commercial and private pilots, air traffic controllers, aviation medical examiners, flight schools, airlines, and airports, since it changes how the FAA handles medical certification related to mental health. Indirectly, it could affect airline passengers and aviation safety overall, since supporters argue that encouraging early treatment rather than concealment may improve safety in the long run. The bill does not change any specific medical conditions or list new rules itself—it requires the FAA to study, consult, and revise policies over the next few years.
ai_headline: FAA must ease mental health rules for pilots and air traffic controllers
last_action_text: Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

title: Puerto Rico Nutrition Assistance Fairness Act
ai_summary:
This bill would move Puerto Rico off its current food assistance system, called the Nutrition Assistance Block Grant, and into the regular Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) that operates in the 50 states, Guam, and the Virgin Islands. Currently, Puerto Rico receives a fixed amount of federal money each year for food assistance, regardless of need, and residents there have historically not been eligible for SNAP the way other Americans are. Under this bill, Puerto Rico would submit a transition plan to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, receive federal technical help preparing it, and once approved, be certified to join SNAP as if it were a state. The switch would happen gradually, with the block grant system continuing for up to five years during the transition, and the actual legal changes taking effect 10 years after the bill becomes law.

This change would primarily affect low-income residents of Puerto Rico, who would gain access to SNAP’s standard eligibility rules and benefit levels, which are generally more generous and flexible than the block grant amount. Because SNAP benefits automatically adjust based on need and cost of living, funding could increase over time rather than staying fixed. The bill also adjusts related provisions affecting American Samoa, which would continue receiving block grant funding after Puerto Rico transitions out. Congress would need to approve ongoing funding, and the Secretary of Agriculture would be required to report annually on the transition’s progress and costs.
ai_headline: Bill would move Puerto Rico into regular SNAP over 10 years
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

title: Faster Labor Contracts Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Faster Labor Contracts Act, changes federal labor law to speed up the process of getting a first contract after workers vote to unionize. Currently, after employees vote to form a union, it can take well over a year (an average of 465 days, according to one study cited in the bill) for the company and the new union to agree on a contract. Congress found that these delays often work in favor of employers who oppose the union, since dragging things out can wear down worker support.

To fix this, the bill sets firm deadlines. Once a union is officially certified, the employer must start bargaining within 10 days. If the two sides can't reach a deal within 90 days, either side can ask a federal mediation agency to help. If mediation doesn't work within another 30 days, the dispute goes to a three-person arbitration panel—one person picked by the union, one by the employer, and a neutral third member—who will decide the terms of the contract. That decision would be binding for two years, based on factors like the company's finances, cost of living, and what similar employers pay their workers. The bill also requires the government's watchdog agency (GAO) to study, after one year, how these changes affect the actual time it takes to reach first contracts.

This bill mainly affects private-sector employers and newly unionized workers covered by the National Labor Relations Act. Supporters argue it would help workers actually benefit from unionizing more quickly, while employers may see it as limiting their flexibility in contract negotiations by imposing strict timelines and potential binding arbitration.
ai_headline: Bill would set deadlines forcing faster union contract deals
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

If no deal is reached in 90 days, either side can request federal mediation, and after 30 more days without success, a three-person arbitration panel decides binding contract terms for two years.

title: AI Accountability and Personal Data Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new federal law allowing people to sue companies or individuals who use their personal data without getting clear, upfront permission first. This applies broadly to any personal information—names, location data, browsing habits, biometric data, and more—and specifically covers situations where companies use someone's data to train artificial intelligence systems, or where AI generates content that imitates or is based on a real person's data or copyrighted material. If someone's data is used without proper consent, they could sue in court and potentially collect money damages (actual losses, triple any profits the company made, or at least $1,000), punitive damages, and have their legal fees covered.

The bill sets strict rules for what counts as valid consent: it must be a clear, specific, upfront "yes" from the person, not something buried in fine print or a general privacy policy, and it can't be forced as a condition of using a product unless truly necessary. If a company plans to share data with other third parties, it has to specifically name those parties and get clear acknowledgment, not just a vague reference. Companies also could not force people into arbitration or block them from joining class-action lawsuits over these data violations—those clauses would be void, though existing labor union arbitration agreements are mostly unaffected.

This would primarily affect tech companies, AI developers, data brokers, and any business that collects or uses consumer data, potentially exposing them to significant lawsuits and financial penalties. It would benefit everyday consumers by giving them a direct legal tool to fight back against misuse of their personal information, including when AI systems are trained on their data or generate content based on it. The bill would not override any stronger state privacy laws already in place, meaning states could still enforce additional protections beyond this federal minimum.
ai_headline: Bill would let people sue over data used without clear consent
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

title: SOAR Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the SOAR Act of 2025, changes how Medicare pays for home oxygen equipment and related supplies and services for people with breathing conditions. Currently, oxygen equipment is included in a "competitive bidding" program that sets prices through supplier bidding. This bill removes oxygen from that program starting in 2026 and replaces it with a new payment formula, including special, higher payment rates for liquid oxygen (which is more expensive to provide) and extra payments for patients who need high oxygen flow rates. It also requires Medicare to regularly review whether these payment amounts are still adequate.

The bill spells out exactly what services suppliers must provide to patients in exchange for payment—things like proper equipment setup, patient education, 24-hour emergency support, safety checks, and help finding a new supplier if a patient moves or travels. It also allows Medicare to pay for services provided by respiratory therapists directly, which it doesn't clearly do now. To fight fraud while still protecting patients, the bill creates a standardized electronic form doctors use to justify why a patient needs oxygen, and it tells Medicare auditors to use reasonable clinical judgment (not overly rigid rules) when reviewing these claims, similar to how audits worked before 2009.

Finally, the bill creates a formal list of patient rights, such as the right to choose or switch suppliers, get clear information about costs and coverage timelines, receive properly maintained equipment, get advance notice before being dropped by a supplier, and file complaints without fear of retaliation. Overall, this bill mainly affects Medicare beneficiaries who use home oxygen therapy, the medical equipment suppliers who provide it, and respiratory therapists, aiming to improve access, payment fairness, and patient protections in this specific corner of Medicare.
ai_headline: Bill would overhaul Medicare payment rules for home oxygen therapy
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

title: Business Owners Protection Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Business Owners Protection Act of 2025, would eliminate certain powers that Congress gave the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) back in 2010 through the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act. Dodd-Frank was a major law passed after the 2008 financial crisis that gave regulators like the SEC new tools to oversee financial companies. Over time, the SEC has used some of these tools to write rules, but others have never been acted on. This bill targets that second group: any Dodd-Frank power that let the SEC choose whether to create a new rule for private companies, but where the SEC never actually started the formal rulemaking process or issued guidance before January 1, 2025. Those unused powers would automatically end once this bill becomes law.

The bill also requires the SEC to publish a public list, within 180 days, spelling out exactly which authorities were eliminated. This is meant to create transparency about what powers the agency lost.

In practice, this affects businesses and industries regulated by the SEC, particularly publicly traded companies, financial firms, and investment-related businesses, since it removes the possibility that the SEC could later use these dormant Dodd-Frank powers to impose new requirements on them. Supporters of this type of bill generally argue it reduces uncertainty for businesses by clearing away regulatory powers that were authorized but never used. It does not affect SEC rules that are already in effect or the powers the agency has already used to issue guidance or start rulemaking. Ordinary consumers and investors are affected indirectly, since the change limits which financial rules the SEC could create in the future using this specific set of Dodd-Frank authorities.
ai_headline: Bill would end unused SEC rulemaking powers from Dodd-Frank
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

The SEC would then have 180 days to publish a public list of exactly which authorities were eliminated. Rules already in effect and powers already used are not affected.

title: LABEL Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the LABEL Act, changes the rules for how fish sold in the United States must be labeled. Under current law, grocery stores and other sellers are already required to tell shoppers where fish comes from (its country of origin) and whether it was farm-raised or caught in the wild. This bill strengthens that requirement by saying the label must be easy to see and read, and specifically that the country-of-origin and production method information cannot be printed in smaller text than the words describing whether the fish is "farm-raised" or "wild-caught." In other words, sellers couldn't make the origin information tiny or hard to notice while making other marketing text large and eye-catching.

The bill applies to fish sold as a "covered commodity" under the existing Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946, which generally covers retail food sellers. It affects grocery stores, seafood markets, and other retailers that sell fish directly to consumers, as well as suppliers and producers who package fish for sale. Consumers would benefit by being able to more easily see where their fish came from and how it was produced, which supporters might argue helps people make informed choices, such as favoring domestic or wild-caught seafood.

If passed, the law would take effect 180 days after being signed, giving businesses time to adjust their labeling practices. The bill does not create new categories of information that must be disclosed; it only changes how prominently existing required information must be displayed.
ai_headline: Bill would require fish origin labels as large as "wild-caught" text
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

It does not add new disclosure categories, only changes how prominently existing required information must appear. The law would take effect 180 days after being signed.

title: Safe Step Act
ai_summary:
The Safe Step Act would change how employer-sponsored health insurance plans handle "step therapy," a common practice where insurers require patients to try cheaper or preferred medications first before covering a more expensive or different drug their doctor originally recommended. This bill doesn't ban step therapy, but it requires health plans to create a clear, timely process for patients or their doctors to request an exception to that requirement, and to actually approve those exceptions when certain medical situations apply.

Under the bill, exceptions would be required if the standard treatment already failed, would likely cause harm, would delay care in a way that could seriously worsen the patient's condition, would prevent someone from doing daily activities or their job, or if the patient is already stable on the drug their doctor prescribed. Plans would have to respond to exception requests quickly—generally within 72 hours, or 24 hours in urgent cases—and if an exception is granted, coverage must last at least a year. Plans would also need to publish clear information about this process and report data to the government each year on how many requests they receive and approve or deny.

This bill would primarily affect people with employer-based health insurance (regulated under the federal ERISA law), especially patients with chronic illnesses, complex conditions, or those needing specialized medications, since they are most likely to run into step therapy rules. It would also affect insurance companies and employers who sponsor health plans, who would need to build new appeals processes and reporting systems, as well as doctors, who would have a more defined path for requesting exceptions on behalf of patients.
ai_headline: Bill would require insurers to offer exceptions to step therapy rules
last_action_text: Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. Hearings held.

Plans would also have to publish information on the process and report annual data on requests and approvals.

title: HARPOON Act
ai_summary:
The HARPOON Act is a bill that would let the U.S. military help other countries fight illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing, often called IUU fishing. This type of fishing hurts fish populations, harms honest fishermen, and is linked to other crimes like smuggling and human trafficking. The bill adds "countering illegal fishing" to the list of things the Secretary of Defense is already allowed to help train and support foreign military and security forces on, alongside things like counterterrorism.

The bill also directs the Secretary of the Navy and the Commandant of the Coast Guard to work with foreign governments to set up joint patrols aimed at stopping illegal fishing, fighting related crimes, and improving security in ocean regions. Each year, they would have to send Congress a report explaining which countries want to cooperate, what's holding back stronger partnerships, how well current efforts are working, and ideas for improvement.

This bill mainly affects U.S. military and Coast Guard operations abroad, foreign countries dealing with illegal fishing in their waters, and international fishing industries. It could also matter to American fishermen and seafood consumers, since illegal fishing affects global fish supplies and market fairness, and to U.S. foreign policy in regions like the Pacific Islands or West Africa where illegal fishing is a major problem.
ai_headline: Bill would let US military train allies to fight illegal fishing
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Foreign Relations.

title: Fair Wages for Home Care Workers Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal labor law so that home care workers—such as home health aides and personal care aides who help elderly or disabled people with daily activities—are guaranteed minimum wage and overtime pay under the Fair Labor Standards Act. Currently, these workers can be exempted from those protections under a rule originally meant for casual babysitters and companions. This bill narrows that exemption so it applies only to actual babysitting of infants and children on an occasional basis, not to professional in-home caregiving work.

Specifically, the bill rewrites the legal definitions of "babysitting services" and "casual basis" so they clearly exclude trained caregiving professionals like nurses, home health aides, and personal care aides. It also removes a separate section of the law that currently allows companionship service workers to be exempt from minimum wage and overtime rules. The effect is that home care agencies and individual employers would be legally required to pay these workers at least the federal minimum wage and time-and-a-half for overtime hours, just like most other employees.

This bill mainly affects home care workers, who are often paid low wages and work long hours caring for aging or disabled clients, as well as the agencies and families who employ them. Supporters would likely see it as improving pay and working conditions for a workforce that has historically been excluded from basic labor protections, while employers and home care agencies would need to adjust budgets and staffing to comply with new wage and overtime requirements.
ai_headline: Bill would guarantee home care workers minimum wage and overtime pay
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

title: Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians Water Rights Settlement Act
ai_summary:
# Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians Water Rights Settlement Act (S. 4368)

This bill would approve and put into law a water rights settlement agreement between the Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians (a Native American tribe in the Palm Springs, California area) and two local water agencies, the Coachella Valley Water District and the Desert Water Agency. It resolves a long-running legal dispute over how much groundwater the tribe has the right to use. Under the deal, the tribe's right to use up to 20,000 acre-feet of groundwater per year is officially confirmed, with a priority date going back to the 1870s, meaning its claim outranks competing claims by the water districts. In exchange, the tribe and the federal government agree to drop related lawsuits and claims against the water districts and the United States.

The bill also sets up a trust fund with $500 million in federal money for the tribe, split into accounts for water infrastructure projects, groundwater replenishment, water system management, and maintenance costs. It gives the tribe authority to charge its own fees on water use and delivery on the reservation instead of paying certain existing local charges, and it lets the tribe collect a replacement property-type tax on land leased to non-tribal members (instead of Riverside County collecting that tax), while still passing through money to local governments and school districts that would have received a share. The bill also allows some federal land to be transferred into trust for the tribe and some federal land to be sold to the water district.

This mainly affects residents and businesses on or near the Agua Caliente reservation in the Palm Springs/Coachella Valley area, including people who lease tribal land, customers of the two water agencies, Riverside County and local taxing agencies (schools, fire districts, etc.) that currently receive property tax revenue, and tribal members and individual Allottees (tribe members with individually held trust land) whose water rights are affected. It does not have direct effects on people outside this region, other than U.S. taxpayers funding the settlement.
ai_headline: Bill confirms Agua Caliente tribe's water rights, sets up $500M trust fund
last_action_text: Committee on Indian Affairs. Hearings held.

title: Blocking CCP Spy Tech Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Blocking CCP Spy Tech Act of 2026," requires U.S. national security agencies to review whether certain Chinese technology companies pose a security risk to the United States. The companies named include DeepSeek (an artificial intelligence company), Unitree Robotics and DEEP Robotics (robotics makers), BrainCo, Manycore Tech, and Game Science Interactive. The review would also cover any subsidiaries, business partners, or companies licensed by these firms. Agencies would have one year to decide whether these companies' products or services are risky, and if they don't act in time, the products would automatically be added to a federal "covered list" of banned communications equipment.

If a company's technology is found to be a national security risk, it gets added to this covered list, which generally restricts its use in U.S. government systems and networks. If found not to be a risk, other agencies still have to double-check that conclusion. All findings must be reported to Congress, though sensitive details can be kept classified. The bill also directs the Secretary of Defense to consider labeling any of these companies as a "Chinese military company," a designation that can trigger additional restrictions.

This bill would primarily affect the named Chinese tech companies and any U.S. businesses, government agencies, or consumers who use their products, such as AI tools, robots, or related software. It could also affect U.S. companies that partner with or resell these companies' technology, since restrictions on the "covered list" typically limit federal purchasing and network use of listed equipment.

last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Select Committee on Intelligence.

title: Terrorism Risk Insurance Program Reauthorization Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill extends the federal Terrorism Risk Insurance Program for another seven years, pushing its expiration date from 2027 to 2034. This program was created after the September 11, 2001 attacks to help stabilize the insurance market for terrorism-related losses. Under the program, the federal government agrees to share the cost of claims with insurance companies if a certified act of terrorism causes damages above a certain threshold, which helps ensure that businesses and property owners can still buy affordable terrorism insurance coverage.

The bill also adjusts the timeline for how the government recoups money it spends under the program. If federal funds are used to help cover terrorism-related insurance losses, the law requires that money to eventually be paid back through small surcharges on insurance policies. This bill shifts those repayment deadlines further into the future, generally by about seven years, to match the extended program timeline.

This bill mainly affects insurance companies, businesses that carry commercial property and casualty insurance, and policyholders in general, since terrorism insurance costs and availability depend on this federal backstop. Without reauthorization, insurers might have raised prices or reduced terrorism coverage due to uncertainty. The bill does not change how claims are paid out or who is eligible—it simply keeps the existing program running longer and updates related financial deadlines.

title: Medicare Advantage Improvement Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would change how Medicare Advantage (MA) plans—the private insurance alternative to traditional Medicare—handle approvals for medical care, aiming to speed up decisions and reduce paperwork burdens on patients and doctors. Starting in 2028, MA plans would have to respond to most prior authorization requests within 72 hours (24 hours for urgent cases), and certain routine, low-risk, or frequently-approved services would require instant, automated approval through electronic health record systems. Plans would also be barred from demanding new authorizations for minor adjustments to already-approved care, and appeals of denied claims would have to move through a faster, more structured review process with outside reviewers.

The bill also cracks down on practices that critics say let insurers deny or claw back payment after care has already been given. Once a service is authorized and delivered, the plan generally couldn't later deny it for "not being medically necessary" or downgrade the billing code to pay less, except in cases of fraud. It requires MA plans to pay claims for authorized services just as promptly as traditional Medicare does, and it limits insurers' use of third-party companies that review claims — especially companies paid based on how often they deny or approve requests. Additionally, MA plans must use the same medical necessity standards as traditional Medicare (rather than stricter internal rules) and must publicly post their coverage criteria.

Finally, the bill creates a new government scoring system that grades MA insurance companies on compliance with these rules — including timely decisions, fair payment, and honest marketing — and cuts their Medicare payments if they score poorly. This scoring would also factor into the public "star ratings" system consumers use to compare plans. Overall, this bill mainly affects the roughly 30+ million Americans enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans, along with the doctors, hospitals, and other providers who treat them, and the insurance companies that run these plans, by aiming to speed up care approvals, reduce surprise denials, and increase transparency and accountability for MA insurers.
ai_headline: Bill would force faster care approvals from Medicare Advantage plans
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

title: Coast Guard Personnel Equipment Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes federal law so that the Coast Guard has to follow the same "Buy American" type rules that already apply to the Department of Defense and other military branches. The rule in question, found in Section 4862 of title 10 of the U.S. Code, requires certain items—like clothing, tents, and other personnel equipment—to be purchased from American manufacturers rather than foreign suppliers. Currently, this requirement applies mainly to the Department of Defense, and the Coast Guard, which operates under the Department of Homeland Security during peacetime, is not fully covered by it.

The bill updates the wording of the law so that "any branch of the Armed Forces," including the Coast Guard, is included in this domestic-sourcing requirement. It also adjusts who is responsible for enforcing and overseeing the rule: instead of only the Secretary of Defense handling certain decisions, the Secretary of Homeland Security would share that authority when it comes to the Coast Guard (since the Coast Guard falls under Homeland Security except when it's operating as part of the Navy, such as during wartime).

This bill mainly affects Coast Guard purchasing practices, requiring the service to prioritize buying gear and equipment from American companies, similar to other military branches. It could affect U.S. manufacturers who supply military and personnel equipment, potentially increasing demand for domestically produced goods. It may also have modest effects on Coast Guard procurement costs or supplier options, depending on availability of American-made alternatives.
ai_headline: Coast Guard would face same Buy American rules as military branches
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill extends Buy American purchasing rules for gear like clothing and tents to the Coast Guard.

It also gives the Secretary of Homeland Security shared authority with the Secretary of Defense over enforcement decisions affecting the Coast Guard.
ai_sections.who: Affects the Coast Guard, the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Defense, and U.S. manufacturers of military and personnel equipment.
ai_sections.why: The change requires the Coast Guard to prioritize domestic suppliers, which could affect its procurement costs and supplier options depending on availability of American-made alternatives.

title: Mobile Workforce State Income Tax Simplification Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Mobile Workforce State Income Tax Simplification Act of 2025, sets a national rule for when states can tax the wages of employees who travel to work in more than one state. Under the bill, a state could only tax an employee's income if that person lives there or if the person physically works in that state for more than 30 days during the year. This means employers would generally not have to withhold income tax for states where an employee only briefly travels for work, such as attending a short meeting or conference.

The bill also sets rules for how employers track where employees work. Employers could rely on an employee's own good-faith estimate of where they'll work during the year, unless the employer already uses a daily time-tracking system, in which case that system's data would apply instead. This is meant to reduce paperwork and confusion for businesses that send employees to multiple states, and to prevent workers from owing income taxes in many different states for just a few days of work each.

Certain groups are excluded from these protections, including professional athletes, professional entertainers, certain film/TV production workers, and prominent public figures who are paid for one-time appearances like speeches. These groups would continue to be taxed under existing state rules. The bill would mainly affect employees who travel for work across state lines, employers who manage payroll and tax withholding for traveling staff, and state governments, which could see changes in how much income tax revenue they collect from nonresident workers. If passed, the law would take effect at the start of the second calendar year after it is signed, and would not apply to taxes owed before that date.
ai_headline: Bill would limit states to taxing traveling workers after 30 days
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance. (text: CR S2566-2567)

ai_sections.tldr: A new bill would let states tax nonresident workers' wages only after they work there more than 30 days a year.

States could see shifts in tax revenue depending on how often nonresident employees currently exceed or fall short of the 30-day threshold.

title: Preserving Patient Access to Accountable Care Act
ai_summary:
This bill would extend a Medicare bonus program for doctors and other health providers who participate in "alternative payment models," which are payment systems designed to reward quality care and cost savings rather than just paying for each individual service performed. Under current law, this bonus program is set to expire, and the bill pushes back several key deadlines by one year, adding 2027 as an additional year in which qualifying providers can receive these incentive payments.

Specifically, the bill adds a 3.53 percent bonus payment for providers who participate in these alternative payment models in 2027, similar to the 1.88 percent bonus that applied in earlier years. It also adjusts related technical deadlines in Medicare law, such as the timeline for updating provider payment rates, to keep everything consistent with the one-year extension.

This bill mainly affects doctors, hospitals, and other healthcare providers who participate in Medicare's value-based care programs, such as Accountable Care Organizations. It also indirectly affects Medicare patients, since these payment models are intended to encourage more coordinated, efficient care. Without this extension, the bonus payments would have ended, potentially reducing financial incentives for healthcare providers to participate in these cost-saving, quality-focused programs.
ai_headline: Bill would extend Medicare bonus for value-based care into 2027
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance. (text: CR S2567)

It adds 2027 as a new qualifying year, offering a 3.53 percent bonus payment, and adjusts related technical deadlines in Medicare law to match the extension.

title: Gerald E. Connolly Esophageal Cancer Awareness Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, named after the late Congressman Gerald E. Connolly, directs a government watchdog agency to study esophageal cancer's impact on federal employees' health insurance. Specifically, it requires the Comptroller General (who leads the Government Accountability Office) to submit a report to Congress within one year of the bill becoming law. That report must look at two things: how much money is being spent on esophageal cancer care under the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and how often people covered by that program who are considered high-risk for the disease actually get screened for it, based on medical guidelines.

The bill also includes a section laying out facts about esophageal cancer, noting it is one of the fastest-growing and deadliest cancers in the country, with survival rates that improve significantly when caught early. It highlights that certain groups—such as older men, smokers, people with chronic acid reflux, obesity, or a family history of the disease—are at higher risk and could benefit from earlier screening.

This bill mainly affects federal employees, retirees, and their families who get health insurance through the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, since it focuses on studying their care and screening rates. It does not create new insurance benefits or require new screenings itself; rather, it sets up a study meant to give Congress information that could support future action, such as improving cancer screening policies or raising awareness among federal workers and the general public.
ai_headline: Bill named for Rep. Connolly orders federal study on esophageal cancer care
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

title: Protecting Children with Food Allergies Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would update federal training requirements for school food service workers to include specific education about food allergies. It amends the Child Nutrition Act of 1966, which already requires training programs for local food service personnel who prepare and serve meals in schools. The bill adds a new requirement that these training programs cover food allergies specifically, including best practices for preventing allergic reactions, recognizing the signs when a reaction is happening, and responding appropriately if a student has one.

The bill also updates the certification rules to make sure this new food allergy training component is properly included when training programs are reviewed or approved. In practical terms, this means cafeteria workers, food service staff, and others involved in preparing and serving school meals would receive standardized instruction on handling food allergies as part of their existing required training, rather than this being left up to individual schools or districts to address on their own.

This bill mainly affects public school food service workers, who would receive additional training content, and by extension, students with food allergies and their families, who may benefit from better-prepared staff in school cafeterias. It does not create a brand-new training program; it adds a required topic to training modules that already exist under current law. School districts and state agencies that administer school meal programs would also be involved in implementing the updated training standards.
ai_headline: Bill would add food allergy training for school cafeteria workers
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry. (text: CR S2568)

title: Ensuring Disaster Recovery and Resilience for Specialty Crops Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Ensuring Disaster Recovery and Resilience for Specialty Crops Act, would create a permanent system for the federal government to help farmers who grow "specialty crops" when disasters or major market problems hurt their businesses. Specialty crops include things like fruits, vegetables, nuts, nursery plants, and similar products—basically farm goods that aren't the large-scale commodity crops like corn, wheat, or soybeans, which already have long-standing federal disaster and insurance programs.

Under the bill, the Secretary of Agriculture would set up a formula to calculate payments to affected farmers based on their past sales of specialty crops, adjusted by a factor meant to account for losses. The Secretary would also have to consider that specialty crops often cost more to grow and are worth more per acre than traditional commodity crops, and that specialty crop farms are organized in many different business structures. The bill sets limits on how much money any one person or company could receive, similar to limits already used in other farm programs, though farmers who earn most of their income from farming could qualify for higher payments (at least $500,000) if the Secretary decides that's appropriate.

This bill would mainly affect specialty crop farmers and growers, especially in states like California, which grows a large share of the nation's fruits, vegetables, and nuts. It could also affect USDA operations, since the agency would need to create and administer this new permanent disaster-assistance program, and it may have budget implications since it would establish ongoing federal payments rather than one-time disaster relief.
ai_headline: Bill would create permanent disaster aid program for specialty crop farmers
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill sets up a permanent federal payment system for specialty crop farmers hit by disasters or market losses.

The Secretary of Agriculture would set a formula based on past sales, adjusted for losses, and account for the higher costs and varied business structures of specialty crop farms. Payment limits would apply per person or company, though full-time farmers could get higher payments of at least $500,000 if the Secretary approves.

title: HUD Payment Integrity and Accountability Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill requires the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to check its rental assistance programs for improper payments—meaning money sent to the wrong people, in the wrong amounts, or without proper verification. By December 1, 2027, HUD must complete an official assessment of improper payments in two major programs: Tenant-Based Rental Assistance (like Section 8 vouchers, which help renters pay landlords directly) and Project-Based Rental Assistance (which subsidizes specific housing developments). HUD must also create a clear plan and timeline for testing and reporting these payment errors going forward.

The bill also sets up a fraud-detection system. If housing assistance payments or the number of landlords/agencies receiving funds in a specific ZIP code jumps by more than 100% in a single year, HUD must tell its own Inspector General (an internal watchdog) within 60 days. The same rule applies to community development and disaster recovery grants. If any program or area grows by 400% or more over five years, the Inspector General must audit it for fraud and compliance problems. Additionally, the Inspector General must independently verify HUD's methods are sound, and conduct a separate deep-dive fraud risk assessment of the roughly $50 billion spent annually on rental assistance, including checking why HUD hasn't been using the Treasury Department's "Do Not Pay" fraud-prevention database.

This bill mainly affects HUD's internal operations and oversight process, not tenants or landlords directly. It's aimed at government accountability—making sure taxpayer money for housing assistance is tracked accurately and that unusual spending spikes get investigated. Landlords, public housing agencies, and grant recipients could face more scrutiny or audits if their funding patterns look unusual, but the bill doesn't change eligibility rules or benefit amounts for renters.
ai_headline: HUD must audit rental aid programs for improper payments by 2027
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

title: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions and Other Matters Act, 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, S. 2882, is a "continuing resolution" that keeps the federal government funded and operating past September 30, 2025, when the current budget year ends. Rather than passing all 12 individual spending bills for fiscal year 2026, Congress uses this stopgap measure to keep most agencies running at roughly the same funding levels as fiscal year 2025, generally through October 31, 2025, giving lawmakers more time to negotiate full-year budget bills. It blocks agencies from starting new programs or increasing production of things like weapons systems beyond current levels, and it includes special provisions protecting certain programs from funding cuts, such as WIC (food assistance for women, infants, and children), community health centers, and Indian health facilities.

The bill also contains numerous unrelated add-ons. It provides extra money for court and judicial security, Capitol Police, and congressional member security following recent threats against officials. It funds death benefit payments to families of three members of Congress who died in office. It extends various expiring health programs, including Medicare telehealth flexibilities, hospital payment rules for small and rural hospitals, and diabetes research funding. It also includes provisions on NASA missions, nuclear weapons programs, Hanford nuclear waste cleanup, public broadcasting funding, and a capital increase for the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.

This bill affects nearly everyone in the US, since it determines whether federal agencies keep operating normally or face disruptions. Federal employees, government contractors, Medicare and Medicaid patients, WIC recipients, veterans, rural hospital patients, telehealth users, and people relying on federal courts, security services, or disaster relief would all be affected by whether and how this funding continues. Members of Congress, congressional staff, and federal judges are also directly affected by the security funding provisions.
ai_headline: Stopgap bill would fund government through October 31, avoiding shutdown
last_action_text: Motion by Senator Schumer to reconsider, under the order of 10/9/2025, not having voted on the prevailing side, the vote by which the third cloture motion on the motion to proceed to S. 2882 was not invoked (Record Vote No. 557) entered in Senate.

It also adds unrelated provisions on security funding, health program extensions, NASA, nuclear programs, and public broadcasting.

title: Every Kid Outdoors Reauthorization Act
ai_summary:
HR 5541, the Every Kid Outdoors Reauthorization Act, updates and makes permanent a federal program that gives fourth and fifth graders (and homeschooled children ages 10 or 11) free annual passes to national parks, forests, and other federal lands and waters. The current program, created under a 2019 law, allowed only fourth graders and 10-year-old homeschoolers to get the pass. This bill expands eligibility to include fifth graders and homeschooled kids who are either 10 or 11 years old, giving more families a chance to use the free pass.

The bill also sets a permanent funding level of $25 million per year for the program, instead of relying on funding that could expire or need periodic renewal. That money would go toward running the program, promoting it to schools and families, providing transportation help for schools and youth groups with the greatest financial need, and reaching out specifically to underserved communities and children with disabilities.

This bill mainly affects families with children in elementary school, especially those who might not otherwise be able to afford park entrance fees or transportation to visit public lands. It also affects schools, youth organizations, and federal agencies like the National Park Service, which help operate and promote the program. Because the bill permanently authorizes funding and expands who qualifies, it could increase the number of children with access to outdoor educational experiences on public lands each year.
ai_headline: Bill would expand free national park pass to fifth graders permanently
last_action_text: Referred to the Subcommittee on Forestry and Horticulture.

title: Making appropriations for the Legislative Branch for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2027, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
HR 9010 is the annual funding bill that pays for the day-to-day operation of Congress and its support agencies for the fiscal year starting October 2026. It covers salaries and office budgets for the House of Representatives (including leadership offices, committees, and each member's staff allowance), the Capitol Police, the Architect of the Capitol (who maintains the Capitol building, grounds, and power plant), the Library of Congress and Copyright Office, the Congressional Research Service, the Government Publishing Office, and the Government Accountability Office. It also includes smaller items like a one-time death benefit payment to the widow of a deceased House member and funding for the Capitol Visitor Center and Botanic Garden.

Beyond just setting dollar amounts, the bill includes various policy rules. It bans House offices from buying computers or IT equipment from companies linked to the Chinese military or blacklisted by the U.S. government, and bars purchasing surveillance equipment or drones from certain Chinese manufacturers. It requires members under active House Ethics Committee investigation to complete workplace conduct training in person rather than online. It blocks a cost-of-living pay raise for members of Congress in 2027, caps vehicle lease payments from member office budgets, and requires leftover member office funds to eventually go toward reducing the federal deficit or debt. It also changes how the Librarian of Congress and the Director of the Government Publishing Office are appointed and removed, shifting that power to a bipartisan commission of congressional leaders rather than the President alone.

This bill mainly affects how Congress itself is run and funded—it does not directly provide services to the general public. However, it indirectly affects the public through things like Capitol tours, Library of Congress services, government publishing (including public access to federal documents), and Capitol Police security. Congressional staff, interns, committee employees, and various legislative support agencies would see their budgets and rules set by this bill for the coming fiscal year.

title: A bill to designate the facility of the United States Postal Service located at 201 West Oklahoma Avenue in Guthrie, Oklahoma, as the "Oscar J. Upham Post Office".

title: Uniformed Services Leave Parity Act
ai_summary:
This bill would give commissioned officers of the U.S. Public Health Service (PHS) the same leave benefits that Army officers receive under existing military law. The Public Health Service is one of the eight uniformed services of the United States, and its officers include doctors, nurses, scientists, and other health professionals who serve in agencies like the CDC, FDA, and Indian Health Service. Currently, PHS officers operate under a separate set of leave rules, and this bill would instead tie their leave entitlements directly to the leave chapter of the law that governs Army officers, ensuring consistency between the two services.

Specifically, the bill amends the Public Health Service Act so that "Chapter 40, Leave" of title 10 of the U.S. Code—the section of federal law covering military leave—applies to PHS officers as well. It also repeals a separate, older section of the Public Health Service Act that currently addresses leave for these officers, since that section would become redundant once the Army's leave rules apply directly.

The people most affected are PHS commissioned officers and their families, who would gain "parity," or equal treatment, with Army officers when it comes to how much leave they can earn, carry over, or use, including for things like illness, family needs, or emergencies. This is largely a technical, administrative fix intended to align benefits across uniformed services rather than a broad policy change affecting the general public.

title: Retire through Ownership Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Retire through Ownership Act, changes a federal law that governs employee retirement plans (ERISA) to clarify how the value of certain company stock should be determined. Specifically, it deals with Employee Stock Ownership Plans (ESOPs), which are retirement plans that give workers ownership shares in the company they work for. When a company isn't publicly traded on the stock market (called "closely held" stock), figuring out what that stock is actually worth can be tricky, since there's no public stock price to reference.

The bill says that the people responsible for managing these ESOPs (called fiduciaries) can rely in good faith on an existing set of guidelines from the IRS, known as Revenue Ruling 59-60, when they calculate the fair market value of this stock. This ruling has long been used for tax valuation purposes, and the bill essentially extends its use as an accepted method for retirement plan purposes too. The goal appears to be giving plan managers clearer legal footing and more certainty when valuing stock, potentially reducing lawsuits or disputes over whether they paid a fair price for shares on behalf of employees.

This bill would mainly affect employees who participate in ESOPs at privately held companies, as well as the business owners, plan administrators, and fiduciaries who manage these retirement plans. It could also matter to attorneys and financial professionals who advise on ESOP transactions, since it may reduce uncertainty and legal risk around stock valuation decisions. The change would apply to valuations made after the law is enacted, if passed.
ai_headline: Bill would let ESOP managers rely on IRS rule to value private stock
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

ai_sections.tldr: The Retire through Ownership Act lets ESOP fiduciaries rely on IRS Revenue Ruling 59-60 to value privately held company stock.

It allows them to rely in good faith on IRS Revenue Ruling 59-60, an existing tax valuation standard, when determining fair market value. The change would apply to valuations made after enactment.

title: A bill to authorize additional funding for the San Joaquin River Restoration Settlement Act.
ai_summary:
S. 1413 would increase the amount of money the federal government is allowed to spend on the San Joaquin River Restoration project in California. This project was created by a 2009 law to restore fish populations and river flows on the San Joaquin River after decades of water being diverted for farming, while also protecting water supplies for farmers and communities who rely on the river. The original law capped funding at $250 million from federal sources and $250 million from non-federal sources; this bill raises both of those caps to $750 million. It also increases funding allowed for improvements to the Friant Division, a system of canals and facilities that delivers irrigation water to Central Valley farms, from $50 million to $75 million.

This bill doesn't create new spending by itself—it just raises the ceiling on how much Congress could approve in future budget bills. Actual money would still need to be appropriated separately. The people most affected would be Central Valley farmers who depend on water from the Friant-Kern Canal system, environmental and fishery interests working to restore salmon runs on the river, and local communities along the San Joaquin River in California. Taxpayers nationally could also be affected if more federal dollars are eventually directed to this project instead of other priorities.
ai_headline: Bill would triple funding cap for San Joaquin River restoration project
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

title: Housing Unhoused Disabled Veterans Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Housing Unhoused Disabled Veterans Act, changes how the government counts veterans' disability benefits when deciding if they qualify for certain housing assistance programs. Currently, VA disability payments can count as income, which sometimes pushes a veteran's total income too high to qualify for programs like HUD-VASH (a supported housing program that combines rental vouchers with VA support services). This bill would exclude those disability benefits from the income calculation used to determine eligibility for that program, making it easier for veterans receiving disability compensation to qualify for housing assistance.

The bill also applies this same rule to veterans applying to live in housing built on VA property, ensuring their disability benefits don't count against them when HUD determines eligibility for those units. However, the exclusion would not apply when calculating "adjusted income," which is used for other purposes like determining how much rent a person actually pays.

This bill mainly affects veterans, especially those who are homeless or at risk of homelessness and rely on disability benefits as a significant part of their income. It would make more of these veterans eligible for supported housing programs, potentially helping more disabled veterans get off the streets or out of unstable housing situations. It does not affect non-veterans or other federal housing programs beyond the specific ones mentioned.
ai_headline: Bill would exclude VA disability pay from housing aid eligibility count
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs. (Sponsor introductory remarks on measure: CR S2565-2566)

title: West Coast Ocean Protection Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the West Coast Ocean Protection Act of 2025, would permanently ban new oil and gas drilling in federal waters off the coasts of California, Oregon, and Washington. It works by changing an existing law, the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, to say that the government can no longer issue leases or permits for oil and gas exploration, development, or production in four specific ocean zones identified by federal ocean management maps: the Washington/Oregon area, Northern California, Central California, and Southern California planning areas.

In practical terms, this means energy companies would be blocked from seeking new offshore drilling rights in these areas indefinitely, regardless of future political or economic conditions, unless Congress later changes the law again. This mainly affects oil and gas companies looking to expand offshore drilling on the West Coast, coastal communities and fishing industries concerned about oil spills or environmental damage, and environmental groups who have long pushed for permanent protections in this region. It would not affect existing approved leases already in place, but it would prevent any new ones from being issued in these zones.

The bill was introduced by Senator Padilla along with several co-sponsors, all Democrats, and has been referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources for further review. At this stage, it is only a proposal and would need to pass through committee review, the full Senate, the House of Representatives, and be signed by the President before becoming law.
ai_headline: Bill would permanently ban new offshore drilling off West Coast
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. (Sponsor introductory remarks on measure: CR S2566)

Existing approved leases would remain unaffected, but no new ones could be issued in these zones.

title: Homebuyers Privacy Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Homebuyers Privacy Protection Act, changes federal credit reporting rules to limit a practice known as "trigger leads." Currently, when someone applies for a mortgage, the lender checks their credit, and credit reporting agencies often sell that information to other lenders, who then bombard the homebuyer with unsolicited calls, texts, and mail offering competing loans. This bill would stop credit reporting agencies from sharing that information so widely, except in specific situations.

Under the bill, a credit agency could only pass along a consumer's information to another company if that company already has the consumer's permission, or if the company already has an existing relationship with the consumer, such as being the lender that originated their current mortgage, the company currently servicing their mortgage, or a bank or credit union where the consumer already holds an account. Any offer made using this information would also have to be a genuine, firm offer of credit or insurance, not just a marketing pitch.

This change mainly affects everyday people applying for a home mortgage, who would likely see far fewer unwanted solicitation calls and letters during the homebuying process. It also affects mortgage lenders, banks, credit unions, and credit reporting agencies like Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion, who would need to change how they use and sell mortgage-related credit inquiry data. The new rules would take effect 180 days after the bill becomes law.

title: Housing for All Act of 2025
ai_summary:
The Housing for All Act of 2025 is a large-scale proposal aimed at reducing homelessness and expanding affordable housing across the country. It would pump tens of billions of dollars into existing federal housing programs, including the Housing Trust Fund, HOME Investment Partnerships, and supportive housing programs for elderly people and people with disabilities. It also expands the Housing Choice Voucher program significantly, adding millions of new vouchers over several years, and eventually would make rental assistance an entitlement, meaning that any eligible low-income family could receive help rather than being placed on a waiting list. Other funding increases target emergency shelters, homelessness prevention programs, and permanent supportive housing.

Beyond funding boosts, the bill creates new programs and studies. These include grants for "safe parking" programs where homeless individuals can sleep safely in their vehicles, funding to convert hotels, motels, and vacant commercial buildings into housing, grants for free legal help to tenants facing eviction, and funding for mobile crisis response teams as an alternative to police responses for people in mental health or addiction crises. It also funds library-based homelessness assistance pilot programs, studies on eviction patterns and racial disparities in housing, and coordination efforts between health care and homelessness services, particularly for people with substance use or mental health issues. A new Commission on Racial Equity in Housing would be created to study and report on racial disparities in housing and homelessness.

This bill would primarily affect low-income renters, people experiencing or at risk of homelessness, seniors, people with disabilities, veterans, and other groups shown to face higher rates of housing instability. It would also affect state and local housing agencies, nonprofit housing and legal aid organizations, landlords participating in federal rental assistance programs, and federal agencies like HUD, which would receive significantly expanded responsibilities and funding to administer these programs.
ai_headline: Bill would pour billions into housing programs, expand rental vouchers
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs. (Sponsor introductory remarks on measure: CR S2568)

title: AVERT Future Violence Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the AVERT Future Violence Act of 2026, directs the U.S. Attorney General to study the connection between animal cruelty and future violence against people. Within three years, the Department of Justice's National Institute of Justice would research what causes people to abuse animals, whether certain types of animal cruelty (like torture, neglect, or animal fighting) predict later violence toward humans, and what kinds of human violence are most linked to these behaviors. The study excludes normal practices like farming, hunting, veterinary care, and food-animal slaughter. After completing the research, the Justice Department must send Congress specific policy recommendations for preventing animal cruelty and helping offenders avoid committing future violent acts.

The bill also creates a grant program allowing the Attorney General to fund states, local governments, tribes, courts, and nonprofit organizations (such as animal shelters, domestic violence services, and mental health providers) to improve how communities detect and respond to animal cruelty. Grant money could pay for training police officers, judges, and prosecutors; building specialized units to handle animal cruelty cases; creating early intervention programs; and improving data systems that track arrests and prosecutions related to animal cruelty.

This bill mainly affects law enforcement agencies, courts, animal welfare organizations, domestic violence and child abuse service providers, and mental health professionals who may receive funding or training under the new grant program. It could also affect people convicted of animal cruelty offenses, who may be directed toward intervention or rehabilitation programs. The bill authorizes $2 million for the study and $2 million for the grant program, meaning actual funding still depends on future budget decisions. It does not create new crimes or penalties—it focuses on research and support programs.
ai_headline: Bill orders study linking animal cruelty to future human violence

title: Recruiting Families Using Data Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Recruiting Families Using Data Act of 2025, changes how states find and keep foster and adoptive families for children in the foster care system. It requires every state to create a "family partnership plan" as part of its existing federal child welfare plan. This plan must explain how the state will identify and involve relatives as potential caregivers, create recruitment plans tailored to each individual child needing a home, involve youth in recruitment efforts, and use data to track progress. States would also need to set up foster family advisory boards to help improve recruitment and retention efforts.

The bill also requires states to regularly collect and report detailed data, including how many licensed foster and adoptive families they have, how many aren't being used and why, how many children are in group homes ("congregate care") instead of family settings, and feedback from foster/adoptive parents about why they stop fostering or why placements fail. States must also study and report on barriers to recruiting foster and adoptive families whose racial and ethnic backgrounds match the children in the system, and describe efforts to fix those gaps.

Finally, the bill updates an existing annual report that states send to Congress on child welfare outcomes, requiring it to include this new state-by-state data on foster and adoptive family recruitment, retention challenges, and diversity-related barriers. This primarily affects state child welfare agencies, which will have new planning and reporting duties, as well as foster and adoptive families, birth and kinship families, and children in foster care, who may benefit from more organized, data-driven efforts to find suitable homes. States get some flexibility on timing if they need to pass their own legislation to comply, with the changes generally taking effect starting October 2026.

title: Mental Health for Latinos Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Mental Health for Latinos Act of 2025, would direct a federal health official (the Assistant Secretary for Mental Health and Substance Use, within the Department of Health and Human Services) to create and carry out a national outreach and education program focused on mental health in Hispanic and Latino communities. The goal is to reduce the stigma often associated with mental illness and substance abuse in these communities and to make sure people have access to information and treatment options that fit their culture, language, age, and other personal factors like gender or sexual orientation.

To do this, the government would work with advocacy groups and mental health organizations that already serve Hispanic and Latino populations. The program would aim to raise awareness about common mental health symptoms, share information about effective and culturally appropriate treatments, and involve community members directly in creating outreach materials. The Secretary would also be required to report to Congress each year on how well the program is working and make that report public.

This bill mainly affects Hispanic and Latino individuals and families, as well as health organizations and advocacy groups that serve these communities, since they would be involved in shaping and delivering the outreach efforts. It could also affect federal health agencies, which would take on new responsibilities for running the program. The bill sets aside $1,000,000 for fiscal year 2026 to fund these activities.

title: Domestic Terrorism Prevention Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would create dedicated offices inside the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Justice, and the FBI whose specific job is to track, investigate, and help prosecute domestic terrorism. It requires these agencies to report every six months to Congress on domestic terrorism trends, including detailed statistics on investigations, arrests, prosecutions, and convictions, with special attention to white supremacist and neo-Nazi activity. Most of this reporting would be made public online, though sensitive information could be kept in a classified section. The offices and reporting requirements would automatically end after 10 years unless renewed.

The bill also sets up a committee to coordinate between federal, state, and local law enforcement, and to hold community forums aimed at building trust between police and communities affected by domestic terrorism. It requires training for law enforcement and prosecutors on recognizing and handling domestic terrorism cases, including training to detect extremist infiltration of police, corrections agencies, and the military. A new interagency task force involving the Justice Department, FBI, Homeland Security, and the Defense Department would specifically study whether white supremacist or neo-Nazi groups have infiltrated the armed forces or federal law enforcement, reporting findings to Congress. Additionally, the FBI would be required to have a hate-crimes liaison in every field office to handle cases connected to domestic terrorism.

This bill mainly affects federal law enforcement and national security agencies, their staff, and the members of Congress who oversee them, rather than the general public directly. It could also affect state, local, and tribal police departments that receive federal anti-terrorism training and resources. The bill includes a clause stating it cannot be used to violate First Amendment rights or other legal protections, and it does not create new crimes—it focuses on organizing government resources, oversight, and reporting rather than expanding what conduct is illegal.

title: Women and Lung Cancer Research and Preventive Services Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Women and Lung Cancer Research and Preventive Services Act of 2025, directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to work with the Department of Defense and the Department of Veterans Affairs to study how lung cancer research and prevention efforts are currently addressing women and other underserved groups. The goal is to figure out what research has already been done, where the gaps are, and how the government can improve efforts related to screening, prevention, and education around lung cancer.

Specifically, the review would look at things like environmental and genetic factors that may cause lung cancer in women, ways to improve imaging and early detection technology, and how to create a national strategy to expand access to lung cancer screenings—especially for women and underserved populations who qualify under current screening guidelines. It would also explore creating a public awareness campaign to help people understand lung cancer risks and the importance of catching it early.

This bill mainly affects public health policy and research planning rather than creating any new programs immediately. It would require HHS to report back to Congress within two years with findings and recommendations. The people most affected would be women, underserved communities (such as those with limited healthcare access), researchers studying lung cancer, and government health agencies that may later use this report to shape future screening and education programs.

title: A joint resolution terminating the national emergency declared with respect to energy.
ai_summary:
This bill would end the national emergency on energy that the President declared on January 20, 2025, through Executive Order 14156. That order had declared that the availability and affordability of energy in the United States was in a state of emergency, which can give the executive branch special powers or allow it to bypass certain normal rules and procedures to speed up energy-related actions, such as permitting for energy production or infrastructure projects. If passed, this resolution would cancel that declaration and remove the special authorities tied to it.

Under the National Emergencies Act, Congress has the power to vote to end a national emergency declared by the President, and this resolution is an exercise of that power. It affects federal agencies that may have been using emergency powers to fast-track energy projects, permits, or regulations, as well as businesses, states, and communities involved in energy production and distribution who might be operating under emergency provisions. Everyday residents could be affected indirectly if the emergency declaration had been used to speed up or change energy policies, such as oil, gas, or electricity production and infrastructure permitting, since ending it would return those processes to standard, non-emergency procedures.

This bill was introduced in the Senate by Senator Kaine, along with Senator Heinrich, and has been referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources for further consideration. As of the information given, it has not yet been voted on or passed into law.
ai_headline: Senate resolution seeks to end Trump's 2025 energy emergency declaration
last_action_text: Failed of passage in Senate by Yea-Nay Vote. 47 - 51. Record Vote Number: 554.

title: Fire Ready Nation Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Fire Ready Nation Act of 2025, directs the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to build a more organized, better-funded system for predicting wildfires, fire-related weather, and wildfire smoke. It would create a formal "fire weather services program" that coordinates NOAA's existing offices, improves computer models and satellite/drone data collection, and speeds up getting new research tools into real-world use through a "fire weather testbed." It also sets up a permanent Incident Meteorologist Service, whose forecasters deploy directly to fire scenes to help emergency responders make decisions, and requires NOAA to upgrade weather-monitoring equipment like automated weather stations and rain gauges used to track flooding after fires.

The bill also addresses workforce issues. It temporarily lifts federal pay caps in 2025 so wildland firefighters, incident meteorologists, and related emergency personnel can be paid overtime without hitting salary limits, and it requires agencies to create a longer-term staffing plan by 2026. It calls for annual public reports on fire season outlooks, workforce needs, and mental health support for responders, plus independent Government Accountability Office reviews of how well these programs are working and whether various federal wildfire-related committees overlap or waste resources.

This bill mainly affects NOAA, the National Weather Service, and other federal land-management agencies (like the Forest Service and Department of the Interior), along with their employees who work on wildfire response. Indirectly, it affects anyone living in wildfire-prone areas—especially rural, remote, and tribal communities—by aiming to provide more accurate fire forecasts, smoke and air-quality alerts, and emergency coordination. title: STOP GAMES Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the STOP GAMES Act of 2026, changes how the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) handles certain petitions that people or companies file to challenge generic drugs or biosimilar products before they can be approved. Under current law, companies (often brand-name drug makers) can file "citizen petitions" asking the FDA to investigate or delay approval of a competing generic or biosimilar drug. Critics have long argued that some companies misuse this process just to keep cheaper competitors off the market longer, even when the petitions don't raise real scientific concerns. This bill gives the FDA clearer authority to quickly deny petitions that appear to be filed mainly to cause delay, and it lists specific warning signs the FDA can use to spot these delay tactics, such as filing petitions right before a patent expires, raising issues that could have been raised earlier, or repeating complaints the FDA already addressed.

The bill also requires the FDA to shorten the petition deadline (petitions must be filed within 60 days of learning about an issue, rather than anytime), refer suspected bad-faith petitioners to the Federal Trade Commission, and requires more detailed public reporting on how petitions affect drug approval timelines. Additionally, it tightens court rules so that people challenging FDA drug decisions in lawsuits must first go through the FDA's petition process and follow strict deadlines, or their lawsuits get dismissed.

This bill mainly affects pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies, especially brand-name drug manufacturers that file these petitions and generic or biosimilar drug makers seeking approval. Indirectly, it could affect everyday consumers and patients, since faster approval of generic and biosimilar drugs generally leads to lower-cost medication options becoming available sooner.
ai_headline: Bill targets petitions used to delay generic and biosimilar drugs
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

It lists warning signs of delay tactics, shortens the petition filing deadline to 60 days, requires referrals of suspected bad-faith filers to the FTC, and tightens court rules requiring people to first go through the FDA's petition process before suing.
