title: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States to require that certain individuals are natural born citizens.
ai_summary:
This bill proposes an amendment to the U.S. Constitution that would require certain federal officials to be "natural born citizens"—meaning people born U.S. citizens, rather than immigrants who became citizens later through naturalization. Currently, the Constitution only requires the President and Vice President to be natural born citizens; members of Congress, federal judges, and Senate-confirmed officials only need to be U.S. citizens (natural born or naturalized), often with a minimum number of years as a citizen.

If passed, this amendment would extend the natural-born-citizen requirement to Representatives, Senators, federal judges (including Supreme Court justices), and any officer requiring Senate confirmation, such as ambassadors, cabinet secretaries, and other high-level appointees. Naturalized citizens—people born in another country who later became U.S. citizens—would be permanently barred from holding these positions, even if they've lived in the U.S. for decades and gone through the full citizenship process.

This would affect naturalized citizens currently serving in Congress, on the federal bench, or in Senate-confirmed roles, as well as future naturalized citizens who might want to run for these offices. Existing officeholders would be affected once their current terms end, based on the effective dates in each section. Because this is a constitutional amendment, it requires two-thirds approval in both the House and Senate, plus ratification by three-fourths of state legislatures within seven years, making it a difficult and lengthy process rather than a simple law change.
ai_headline: Amendment would bar naturalized citizens from Congress, courts, top posts
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Empower Charter School Educators to Lead Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes changes to an existing federal grant program that helps states support charter schools. It updates a law called the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, specifically the part that gives money to states to help open and improve charter schools.

The bill adds a new type of grant called a "pre-charter planning subgrant," worth up to $100,000, for people who want to start a new charter school but need help planning it first. To qualify, these charter school founders must be educators with at least 54 months (about four and a half years) of hands-on school experience, such as teaching or running after-school or summer programs, and must show they're good leaders who get results with students. They also need to already have a basic plan showing what their community needs and how their proposed school would meet those needs. The bill also directs states to give technical help and training to the agencies that approve and oversee charter schools, including help with financial audits, loans, and finding school buildings.

To pay for these new activities, the bill adjusts how grant money already given to states must be divided up. It reduces the share that must go directly to charter schools (from 90% to 80%), while increasing the amount states can keep for oversight and administration, and setting aside up to 5% specifically for the new pre-charter planning grants. This bill mainly affects state education agencies, charter school authorizers, and people or groups planning to open new charter schools; it does not directly change rules for traditional public schools.

title: FLEX Act
ai_summary:
The FLEX Act would update the federal Charter Schools Program, which is the main source of federal grant money that helps states and organizations start, grow, or improve charter schools. The bill changes how that federal money gets divided up, increasing the guaranteed minimum shares that go toward state-level grant programs (from 12.5% to at least 15%) and to charter management organizations (from 22.5% to at least 25%), while reserving at least 30% for other purposes like facilities help and national research. It also gives the Department of Education more flexibility in deciding how to spend any money left over after these minimum allocations.

The bill expands what the grant money can be used for. Charter schools could now use funds not just to open new schools or replicate successful ones, but also to add or expand programs at existing high-quality charter schools, such as new curricula or personalized learning approaches. It also allows funds to cover things like teacher hiring, academic subscriptions, building repairs, and facility operating costs — expenses that were previously restricted or excluded. Additionally, it streamlines paperwork requirements, limits the Secretary of Education's ability to impose extra regulations beyond what's legally required, and requires more direct consultation with charter school operators before new rules are proposed.

This bill mainly affects charter schools, state education agencies that distribute these federal grants, and charter management organizations that oversee multiple charter schools. It could also affect students and families at charter schools, since the changes are meant to make it easier for existing high-quality charter schools to expand their offerings and enroll more students, and to address practical needs like student transportation and facility upkeep. Organizations that already have grants when this law passes can choose to continue under the old rules or switch to the new ones for the rest of their grant period.

last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 566.

title: Maritime Cybersecurity Act
ai_summary:
The Maritime Cybersecurity Act would strengthen cybersecurity rules for certain U.S. port and maritime facilities that are already required to have security plans under existing law. The Coast Guard, working with the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, would have to check these facilities every year for weaknesses in the software and hardware they use, including cranes and other equipment, especially items made by or connected to foreign countries or companies considered national security risks (such as China). The Coast Guard would be allowed to do these checks even if a contract or software license would normally prevent it, and without needing permission from the equipment's owner.

Port and facility operators would also have new paperwork duties: each year they'd need to report what foreign-made or risky software/hardware they use, disclose any cybersecurity incidents, and certify that their systems meet federal cybersecurity standards. If they can't certify that certain equipment meets these standards, they generally would not be allowed to use it—though the Coast Guard could grant a waiver if the security risk is low and the equipment benefits commerce. This information would stay confidential and not be released to the public, though it could be shared with other government agencies for security purposes.

This bill mainly affects operators of regulated port and maritime facilities (like shipping terminals and cargo facilities), equipment manufacturers whose products are used there, and federal agencies overseeing maritime security. Indirectly, it could affect the broader shipping and supply chain industry, since it may require replacing or upgrading certain foreign-made equipment, potentially raising costs or requiring compliance work for port operators. Everyday consumers could see indirect effects if these changes affect the speed or cost of goods moving through U.S. ports.
ai_headline: Bill would mandate yearly cybersecurity checks at US ports
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

title: A joint resolution to direct the removal of United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against the Islamic Republic of Iran that have not been authorized by Congress.
ai_summary:
This resolution, introduced by Senator Warnock, seeks to force an end to U.S. military involvement in hostilities with Iran unless Congress has formally authorized that involvement through a declaration of war or a specific law. The bill points to a military campaign called "Operation Epic Fury," which began on February 28, 2026, and led to American casualties, a shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz by Iranian forces, and a worldwide economic disruption. Although a ceasefire took effect on April 8, 2026, the U.S. then announced a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, which the resolution's sponsor argues continues to involve U.S. forces in hostilities without Congress ever having voted to approve the conflict.

The core argument is constitutional: only Congress has the power to declare war, and the President is required to consult Congress before or during military engagements. Since lawmakers never voted on this operation, the resolution invokes the War Powers Resolution and related laws to compel the President to withdraw forces from combat operations against Iran. It does include exceptions, allowing the military to still defend U.S. troops and facilities from attack, share intelligence with allies like Israel, help partner nations defend themselves from Iranian retaliation, and evacuate American citizens from the region.

This bill would primarily affect U.S. military personnel currently deployed in or around Iran, the executive branch's authority to conduct the operation, and broader U.S. foreign policy toward Iran. It could also matter to Americans concerned about troop safety, gas and shipping prices affected by Strait of Hormuz disruptions, and the balance of war-making power between Congress and the President. As a joint resolution, if passed by both chambers and signed by the President (or passed over a veto), it would carry the force of law.
ai_headline: Senator seeks vote to end unauthorized U.S. combat role against Iran
last_action_text: Motion to discharge Senate Committee on Foreign Relations rejected by Yea-Nay Vote. 47 - 48. Record Vote Number: 174.

title: Equitable Community Access to Pharmacist Services Act
ai_summary:
This bill would allow Medicare Part B to pay pharmacists directly for certain healthcare services they provide, something Medicare generally does not do now. Specifically, pharmacists could be paid for testing and treating patients for COVID-19, flu, RSV (a common respiratory virus), and strep throat, as well as for services needed during declared public health emergencies. Pharmacists would need to follow their state's rules, which may require them to work under a doctor's supervision or in collaboration with a physician, depending on where they practice.

Under the bill, Medicare would pay pharmacists 80% of either their actual charge or 85% of the standard Medicare physician payment rate for these services (100% during public health emergencies). Pharmacists would also be barred from "balance billing," meaning they couldn't charge patients extra beyond what Medicare and the patient's normal share already cover. This change would start on January 1, 2026.

This bill mainly affects Medicare patients (typically people 65 and older or those with certain disabilities), who may find it easier and cheaper to get tested or treated for common illnesses at a local pharmacy instead of a doctor's office. It also affects pharmacists, who could be formally reimbursed by Medicare for services they already have the training and state authorization to provide, and physicians, who may work collaboratively with pharmacists under new payment arrangements. Supporters generally argue this could improve access to care, especially in areas with doctor shortages, since pharmacies are often more accessible than clinics.

title: Access to Prescription Digital Therapeutics Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would require Medicare and Medicaid to cover "prescription digital therapeutics" — software-based products, apps, or devices that are cleared by the FDA to prevent, manage, or treat a medical condition, and that work primarily through software rather than physical hardware. Examples might include apps prescribed by a doctor to help treat conditions like substance use disorder, insomnia, or certain mental health conditions. Starting January 1, 2026, these products would become a covered benefit under Medicare, similar to other medical services, and Medicaid would be required to cover them as well.

The bill also sets up a system for how these products get paid for. Within a year of the bill becoming law, Medicare would need to create a payment method for manufacturers, considering things like the product's list price and what private insurers already pay for it. Within two years, Medicare would create specific billing codes for each product, using temporary codes in the meantime. Manufacturers would be required to report pricing and usage data annually, including how much private insurers pay and how many people use the product. Manufacturers that fail to report this information accurately could face fines of up to $10,000 per day.

This bill mainly affects Medicare and Medicaid patients who could gain access to app-based or software-based treatments prescribed by their doctors, as well as the companies that make these digital therapeutics, who would gain a clearer path to getting paid by government health programs. Doctors and health systems could also be affected, since this creates a formal, billable category of treatment they could prescribe alongside traditional drugs and devices.

title: Medicare Audiology Access Improvement Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would change how Medicare covers hearing and balance care provided by audiologists. Starting January 1, 2027, Medicare patients would be able to see an audiologist directly for both testing and treatment services without first getting a referral from a doctor or being under a physician's supervision, as long as the audiologist is licensed to provide those services under their state's laws. Currently, Medicare mainly covers audiologists for diagnostic testing, and patients often need a physician's order to access these services.

The bill also updates how audiologists get paid. Medicare would pay 80% of the approved fee schedule amount for these services, similar to how other Medicare providers are paid, and audiologists would be added to the list of providers who bill Medicare on an "assignment" basis (meaning they agree to accept Medicare's approved payment amount as full payment). Additionally, audiologists could work as recognized practitioners at Rural Health Clinics and Federally Qualified Health Centers, which serve rural and low-income communities. The bill specifically states it does not expand the types of services audiologists can bill Medicare for beyond what was allowed as of the end of 2026 — it mainly removes the referral and supervision requirements.

This bill mainly affects Medicare beneficiaries (mostly people 65 and older) who need hearing or balance care, and it affects audiologists as healthcare providers. Older adults, especially those in rural areas or without easy access to physicians, could benefit from more direct and potentially faster access to hearing care. Audiologists would gain more independence in treating patients and greater ability to bill Medicare directly for their services.

title: Expanding Seniors Access to Mental Health Services Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how Medicare pays for mental health services provided by clinical social workers, especially for people living in nursing homes. Currently, when someone is a resident in a skilled nursing facility, the facility is paid a flat daily rate meant to cover most services, and clinical social worker services get bundled into that rate. This bill removes clinical social worker services from that bundled payment system, meaning Medicare would pay for these services separately. The goal is to make it easier and more financially practical for nursing homes to actually provide mental health counseling and support to residents, since providers would be paid directly for that specific care rather than relying on the facility to cover it out of a fixed payment.

The bill also expands what counts as covered "clinical social worker services" under Medicare. It adds coverage for health and behavior assessment and intervention services, not just traditional diagnosis and treatment of mental illness. These are services that help patients manage the emotional, behavioral, and psychological sides of physical health conditions, like helping someone cope with chronic illness or follow medical treatment plans.

This mainly affects seniors and people with disabilities who are enrolled in Medicare, particularly those living in nursing homes, by potentially increasing their access to mental health and behavioral health support. It would also affect clinical social workers, who could be paid more directly for a wider range of services, and nursing facilities, which would no longer need to absorb the cost of this care within their standard Medicare payments. The changes would take effect for services provided starting January 1, 2026.

title: World War II Women's Memorial Location Act
ai_summary:
S 1088, the World War II Women's Memorial Location Act, would allow a planned memorial honoring women who worked on the home front during World War II to be built on or near the National Mall in Washington, D.C. Congress had already approved the creation of this memorial back in 2022 through the World War II Women's Memorial Foundation, but normal federal rules restrict new memorials from being placed in certain highly protected areas of the National Mall, known as "the Reserve," because space there is limited and reserved for only the most significant national memorials. This bill would create an exception to that rule specifically for this memorial.

In practical terms, the bill doesn't create funding or design the memorial itself—it simply changes where the memorial is legally allowed to be located, making it possible to place it in a more prominent, symbolically important area near other national monuments. The main people affected are the women veterans and home-front workers being honored (and their families), visitors to Washington, D.C., and officials who oversee National Mall planning, such as the National Park Service and the National Capital Memorial Advisory Commission, who help decide how the physical space on the Mall is used.

This bill is sponsored by senators from both parties, reflecting bipartisan support for honoring the estimated 18 million women who contributed to the war effort through jobs like building aircraft, munitions, and military equipment during World War II.

title: TREATS Act
ai_summary:
The TREATS Act would change federal drug law to make it easier for doctors to prescribe certain addiction treatment medications through telehealth appointments instead of requiring an in-person visit. Currently, the Controlled Substances Act generally requires patients to have at least one face-to-face medical evaluation before a doctor can prescribe certain controlled substances. This bill would add an exception: for medications in schedules III, IV, or V that the FDA has approved specifically to treat substance use disorders (such as buprenorphine, commonly used to treat opioid addiction), a telehealth evaluation—done by phone or video call—could count instead of an in-person visit.

The bill defines "telehealth evaluation" as a medical evaluation conducted using real-time, two-way audio or audio-video technology, following existing state and federal telehealth rules. This means patients could potentially start addiction treatment medication after only a remote consultation, without needing to travel to a clinic first.

This bill would primarily affect people seeking treatment for substance use disorders, especially those in rural areas or places with limited access to addiction specialists, as well as doctors and healthcare providers who prescribe these medications. It could also affect telehealth companies and addiction treatment programs that rely on remote care. The change would make permanent a flexibility that was temporarily allowed during the COVID-19 pandemic, when in-person requirements were relaxed to expand access to care during lockdowns.

It would make permanent a flexibility that was temporarily allowed during the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: SAT Streamlining Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the SAT Streamlining Act, aims to speed up how the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) handles applications from companies that want to launch satellites or operate ground stations that communicate with them. Right now, these approvals can take a long time. The bill sets specific deadlines: generally one year to approve or deny satellite and ground station license applications, 90 days for minor technical modifications, 30 days for straightforward equipment replacements, and 180 days for renewals. If the FCC misses these deadlines and the applicant notifies them in writing, the application is automatically considered approved. The bill does allow the FCC to extend deadlines in limited situations, such as national security concerns or emergencies.

The bill also creates a 15-year limit on "market access" grants (permission for foreign-licensed satellites to operate in the U.S.), requires closer coordination between the FCC and the Commerce Department, limits how much paperwork companies must submit, requires reviews of national security risks for companies with significant foreign ownership, and prevents state and local governments from regulating the rates satellite companies charge customers. It also requires the FCC to report yearly on its backlog of unprocessed applications.

This bill mainly affects satellite companies (like those building broadband, communications, or imaging satellites), ground station operators, and the FCC itself, which would face new legal deadlines and reporting requirements. Indirectly, it could affect consumers and businesses who rely on satellite internet or communication services, since faster approvals could mean quicker deployment of new satellite systems. It does not apply to amateur radio operators or experimental radio services.

title: DLARA
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Disaster Loan Accountability and Reform Act (DLARA), aims to tighten oversight of the Small Business Administration's (SBA) disaster loan program, which provides loans to businesses and homeowners after disasters. It requires the SBA to give Congress more detailed monthly reports on loan spending, including warnings about when funding will run low, and penalizes the SBA Administrator (by blocking official travel funds) if these reports are late. It also requires more detailed budget requests that compare disaster loan costs to 10-year averages, and it restricts the SBA from forgiving loans or writing off debts unless Congress specifically approves it, instead requiring unpaid debts to be sent to the Treasury Department for collection.

The bill also limits how the SBA handles loans when funding is running low, requiring faster notice to Congress and restricting large loans that don't require collateral during shortages. It removes the SBA's ability to raise the loan amount that doesn't require collateral during major disasters. Additionally, it blocks the SBA from issuing new rules that would increase program costs, and it orders independent reviews: the Government Accountability Office (GAO) must study the effects of recent SBA rule changes on loan costs, and the SBA's Inspector General must investigate a 2024 funding shortfall in the disaster loan program to find out what went wrong and how to prevent it in the future.

Overall, this bill mainly affects how the SBA manages and reports on its disaster loan program. It would most directly impact SBA administrators and staff, who would face new reporting and rule-making restrictions, and members of Congress, who would receive more detailed financial information. Indirectly, it could affect small businesses and individuals who rely on SBA disaster loans, since stricter rules on collateral and loan forgiveness could make some loans harder to get or repay.
ai_headline: Bill seeks tighter oversight of SBA's disaster loan program
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 22.

title: Critical Minerals Supply Chain Resiliency Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill deals with critical minerals, which are materials like lithium, cobalt, and rare earth elements used in electronics, batteries, defense equipment, and other important products. In 2022, a presidential order allowed the Department of Defense to invest in projects that boost domestic production of these materials, such as mining operations, processing facilities, and efforts to recycle mining waste into usable products. This bill would automatically classify those Defense Department-backed projects as "covered projects" under an existing federal permitting law, and list them on the government's official Permitting Dashboard, a public website that tracks major infrastructure and energy projects moving through the federal approval process.

In practical terms, this status change is meant to speed up and simplify the permitting process for these mineral projects by giving them the same tracking and coordination benefits other major infrastructure projects get, such as a lead agency to help review the project and clearer timelines. Companies would still have the choice to opt out if they don't want their project listed this way. This mainly affects companies involved in mining, mineral processing, and related industries, as well as federal agencies responsible for environmental and permitting reviews, and communities near proposed mining or processing sites who may see faster movement on these projects.

The bill does not change environmental laws or reduce required reviews; it mainly changes how these projects are tracked and coordinated administratively. Its overall goal is to help the United States rely less on foreign countries, particularly for materials important to national defense and manufacturing, by making it easier to expand domestic mineral production.
ai_headline: Bill would fast-track permitting for Defense-backed mineral projects
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 602.

title: State Department Recurring Reports Repeal and Sunset Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, H.R. 8668, is aimed at reducing the amount of paperwork the State Department has to produce for Congress. Over the years, Congress has passed many laws requiring the State Department to submit regular reports on topics like foreign sanctions, human rights, arms sales, nuclear cooperation, and international treaties. Some of these reports are required every 90 days, every 180 days, or on other frequent schedules. This bill either eliminates certain reports entirely, reduces how often others must be submitted (for example, changing a report from every six months to just once a year), or sets an end date after which the reporting requirement will expire, such as December 31, 2030, or 2038.

In practical terms, the bill does not change U.S. foreign policy positions on sanctions, human rights, or international agreements. Instead, it changes how often the State Department must formally update Congress on these issues in writing. Supporters of this type of legislation generally argue it reduces bureaucratic busywork and lets State Department staff spend more time on actual diplomatic work rather than compiling repetitive reports. Critics of reducing reporting requirements might argue that regular reports help Congress and the public keep track of sensitive issues like sanctions enforcement, trafficking, or nuclear security.

The people most directly affected are State Department employees, who will have fewer recurring reports to prepare, and members of Congress and congressional staff, who will receive less frequent formal updates on these many foreign policy topics. The general public would mainly be affected indirectly, through potentially less frequent public reporting on issues such as sanctions against countries like Iran, North Korea, and Russia, human trafficking, religious freedom abroad, and arms control treaties.
ai_headline: Bill would cut how often State Department must report to Congress
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by Voice Vote.

title: Ohkay Owingeh Rio Chama Water Rights Settlement Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill approves a legal settlement over water rights between Ohkay Owingeh, a Native American pueblo in New Mexico, and other parties who use water from the Rio Chama river system. For many years, there has been a court case sorting out who has rights to use water from this river. This bill confirms an agreement reached in 2023 that officially recognizes the pueblo's water rights, protects those rights from ever being lost due to non-use, and sets up rules for how the pueblo can use, share, or lease its water both on and off its own land, with leases limited to 99 years.

To make the settlement work, the bill creates a trust fund and directs the federal government to put in about $745 million, which will be used for things like water infrastructure, environmental restoration of the "bosque" (a forested area along the river), and building irrigation systems. New Mexico state government and the local government of the City of Espanola also agree to contribute money for irrigation ditch improvements and water system upgrades. In exchange for receiving these rights and funds, the pueblo and the federal government agree to drop related lawsuits and claims connected to past water disputes in this river system.

This bill mainly affects people and communities along the Rio Chama in New Mexico: the Ohkay Owingeh tribal members, nearby farmers who rely on traditional irrigation ditches called acequias, the City of Espanola, and the state government. It does not affect other tribes' water rights, and it does not change any general water laws outside this specific river system. If the settlement process is not fully completed and certified by a certain deadline (2038), the agreement and its legal waivers would expire, and any unused federal money would have to be returned.

last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 428.

title: Tribal Trust Land Homeownership Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Tribal Trust Land Homeownership Act of 2025, aims to speed up how the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) handles mortgage paperwork for homes and businesses built on Indian trust land. Currently, getting a mortgage approved on tribal land can take a long time because the BIA must review and verify land titles and lease documents, and there have been complaints about slow processing. This bill sets strict deadlines: the BIA must acknowledge receipt of mortgage paperwork quickly, complete an initial document check within 10 days, and approve or deny leasehold mortgages within 20 days, and right-of-way or land mortgages within 30 days. It also requires the BIA to complete required title status reports within set timeframes and to notify lenders if deadlines are missed.

The bill also improves communication and transparency. Lenders and tribes would get updates electronically or by mail, and federal agencies like the USDA, HUD, and VA would gain read-only access to a BIA computer system called TAAMS, which tracks land records. The BIA would have to publish an annual report showing how well each office is meeting these deadlines, and the Government Accountability Office would study whether digitizing tribal land records could make the process faster. Finally, the bill creates a new position, a "Realty Ombudsman," who would monitor the BIA's compliance with these rules and act as a go-between for tribes, lenders, and federal agencies when problems arise.

This bill mainly affects Native American individuals and tribes who want to build homes or businesses on trust land, lenders who issue loans for those projects, and the BIA staff who process the paperwork. Its overall goal is to make homeownership and business development easier and faster for people living on tribal trust lands by reducing bureaucratic delays.
ai_headline: Bill sets deadlines for BIA to speed up tribal land mortgage approvals
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 439.

ai_sections.why: Faster, more transparent processing could reduce bureaucratic delays that have historically slowed homeownership and business development on tribal land, though it also adds new compliance and reporting requirements for the BIA.

title: A bill to amend the Passport Act of June 4, 1920, to authorize certain public libraries to collect and retain a fee for the execution of a passport application.
ai_summary:
This bill changes the rules about who can accept passport applications and keep the fee for doing so. Right now, when someone applies for a passport in person, a government office or the U.S. Postal Service usually collects a small "execution fee" for processing the paperwork. This bill would let certain public libraries — specifically ones set up as nonprofit or charitable organizations, or trusts, rather than direct government agencies — also serve as official passport acceptance locations and keep that fee for themselves, as long as they follow the State Department's rules for handling passport applications.

The bill also requires the State Department to quickly (within 30 days) re-authorize any public libraries that were already accepting passport applications before this law passed, as long as they were following the rules. The State Department would have to report to Congress confirming it did this, or explain why it didn't.

This mainly affects public libraries that offer passport services as a convenience to their communities, giving them a new way to earn revenue instead of that fee going only to government agencies or the Postal Service. It also affects everyday people applying for passports, since it could mean more local locations, including libraries, are available to process passport applications, potentially making it more convenient in some communities. It does not change passport prices or requirements for applicants themselves.
ai_headline: Bill would let nonprofit public libraries keep passport fees
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 503.

title: A bill to repeal certain Acts that impose sanctions upon Syria.
ai_summary:
This bill would cancel two U.S. laws that impose sanctions and restrictions on Syria: the Syria Accountability and Lebanese Sovereignty Restoration Act of 2003 and the Syria Human Rights Accountability Act of 2012. These laws were originally passed to punish the Syrian government for actions such as supporting terrorism, interfering in Lebanon, developing weapons programs, and committing human rights abuses during its civil war. Repealing them would remove the legal basis for many of these specific sanctions and reporting requirements related to Syria.

In practical terms, this bill is part of a broader effort to update U.S. policy toward Syria, especially after major political changes in the country in recent years, including the fall of the former government. Supporters of repealing these older sanctions laws generally argue that conditions in Syria have changed enough that the original justifications no longer apply, and that continuing the restrictions could hinder diplomatic relations, economic recovery, or humanitarian assistance. It's worth noting that repealing these specific acts would not necessarily remove all U.S. sanctions on Syria, since other sanctions authorities and executive orders may still apply separately.

This bill would primarily affect U.S. foreign policy and diplomatic relations with Syria, as well as American businesses, banks, and humanitarian organizations that currently must navigate sanctions rules when dealing with Syrian individuals, entities, or the government. It could also affect Syrian individuals and companies who have been restricted from certain financial or trade dealings with the United States. Members of Congress, the State Department, and Treasury officials who oversee sanctions policy would be involved in implementing any changes if the bill becomes law.
ai_headline: Bill would repeal two long-standing US sanctions laws on Syria
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 501.

title: A bill to permit visiting dignitaries and service members from Taiwan to display the flag of the Republic of China.
ai_summary:
This bill would require the U.S. Secretary of State and Secretary of Defense to allow Taiwanese government officials, military members, and representatives from Taiwan's unofficial embassy (TECRO) to publicly display symbols of Taiwan's sovereignty—most notably the flag of the Republic of China (Taiwan)—while conducting official business in the United States. This would apply to situations like wearing official military uniforms with Taiwanese insignia, hosting or attending government ceremonies, and appearing in official social media posts from the State Department or Defense Department that highlight U.S.-Taiwan relations.

Currently, U.S. policy on displaying Taiwan's flag has often been restricted or handled cautiously because the United States does not officially recognize Taiwan as an independent country, maintaining a "One China" policy that recognizes Beijing's government. This bill would formally change that practice for specific official contexts, making it easier for Taiwanese officials and service members to visibly represent their government's symbols during visits or joint events with U.S. counterparts.

This bill primarily affects U.S. government agencies (State and Defense Departments), Taiwanese officials and military personnel visiting or working with the U.S., and the broader diplomatic relationship between the U.S., Taiwan, and China. It could also have foreign policy implications, since China considers Taiwan a part of its territory and has historically objected to actions that appear to boost Taiwan's international standing or symbols of sovereignty.
ai_headline: Bill would let Taiwan officials display flag at US events
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 499.

title: Veteran Caregiver Reeducation, Reemployment, and Retirement Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Veteran Caregiver Reeducation, Reemployment, and Retirement Act, aims to help family members who serve as full-time caregivers for veterans through the VA's caregiver program, especially when their role as a caregiver ends. Currently, when someone stops being an official caregiver, they can lose access to VA benefits fairly quickly. This bill extends their health care coverage for 180 days after they leave the program, unless they were removed for fraud or abuse. It also blocks people from getting this extra coverage if they already have Medicare during that period.

The bill also creates new job-related help for former caregivers, such as covering up to $1,000 over their lifetime for licensing or certification fees, giving them free access to VA training courses, and connecting them with job-placement help through Military OneSource, the Department of Labor, and VA programs. Caregivers would also get support transitioning out of caregiving, help finding new jobs, and bereavement counseling if the veteran they cared for passes away. The VA would need to study whether a "returnship" program (helping former caregivers re-enter the workforce) and hiring former caregivers directly into VA jobs are practical ideas.

Finally, the bill requires several government studies and reports: one on how well the VA is helping caregivers transition out of caregiving, and another on whether the government should help these caregivers save for retirement, since many spend years out of the regular workforce and may lack retirement savings. Overall, this bill mainly affects military veterans' family caregivers enrolled in the VA's Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers, aiming to ease their move back into jobs, education, or retirement planning after their caregiving duties end.
ai_headline: Bill would extend health coverage for former veteran caregivers 180 days
last_action_text: Committee on Veterans' Affairs. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

title: Uyghur Policy Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Uyghur Policy Act of 2025, is a US response to human rights abuses against Uyghurs and other minority groups in China's Xinjiang region. It states Congress's position that China should stop detaining people in "political reeducation" camps, allow journalists and international observers into the region, release specific named prisoners, and stop harassing Uyghurs and their families who live outside China. These statements don't force China to do anything, but they officially put the US government's opinion on record.

The bill also directs US agencies to take concrete actions. The Secretary of State would be required to prioritize Uyghur human rights issues, maintain contact with Uyghur community leaders, support independent journalism like Radio Free Asia, and create a system for people to report incidents of Chinese government harassment happening inside the United States. It also calls for expanding Uyghur language training for US diplomats, ensuring at least one Uyghur speaker is stationed at each US diplomatic post in China, and pushing at the United Nations for greater attention to the situation, including appointing a special investigator. A small amount of existing State Department funding ($250,000 per year for three years) would be set aside to support human rights advocates speaking at international forums, especially in Muslim-majority countries.

This bill mainly affects US foreign policy operations and diplomatic staff, rather than creating new laws for ordinary Americans. It would matter most to Uyghur Americans and Uyghur communities living in exile, who may benefit from new protections against harassment and increased US government attention to family members still in China. It could also affect US-China diplomatic relations, since the bill takes a critical stance toward Chinese government policies. The bill notably doesn't authorize any new government spending beyond redirecting existing funds, and most of its requirements would expire five years after becoming law.
ai_headline: Senate bill directs US agencies to press China on Uyghur rights abuses
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 496.

title: Unlocking Native Lands and Opportunities for Commerce and Key Economic Developments Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes federal rules about how Native American tribes can lease their land and grant rights-of-way (permission for things like roads, pipelines, or power lines to cross tribal land). It expands the list of tribes covered by the existing 1955 leasing law and removes some outdated limits on how long certain leases can last. These changes are meant to make it easier and faster for tribes to enter into long-term land deals for housing, business, or development projects without as much federal red tape.

The bigger change is in how rights-of-way are approved. Currently, the Secretary of the Interior must approve most rights-of-way across tribal trust land. Under this bill, a tribe could instead create its own regulations for approving rights-of-way, and if the Secretary approves those tribal rules, the tribe could grant rights-of-way on its own—without needing case-by-case federal sign-off. The tribe's rules would still need to include an environmental review and public comment process, though the bill exempts the Secretary from having to separately apply certain major federal environmental laws (like NEPA and the Endangered Species Act) when approving these tribal regulations. The federal government would still have some oversight, including the ability to step in, enforce, or cancel a right-of-way if tribal rules are violated, following a notice-and-hearing process.

This bill primarily affects Native American tribes, especially those seeking more control over economic development on their own land, as well as companies or governments seeking to build infrastructure (roads, utilities, pipelines) across tribal land. It could speed up development and give tribes more self-governance over land-use decisions, while somewhat reducing the federal government's direct role in approving individual projects.
ai_headline: Bill would let tribes approve their own land rights-of-way
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 459.

ai_sections.tldr: Tribes could gain authority to approve land rights-of-way and long-term leases without case-by-case federal sign-off.

It also lets tribes write their own rules for approving rights-of-way across tribal trust land, which the Secretary of the Interior could approve, ending case-by-case federal review.

title: PAID OFF Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the PAID OFF Act of 2025, changes rules under the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA), a law requiring people and companies working on behalf of foreign governments or organizations to register with the U.S. government and disclose their activities. Currently, certain groups get exemptions from these registration requirements, including exemptions for commercial activities and some legal or public relations work. This bill removes those exemptions for any foreign agent that is owned or controlled by a government on the U.S. State Department's list of "countries of concern" — a list that currently includes countries like China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea. In practice, this means companies or organizations controlled by those governments would face stricter disclosure requirements and could no longer use certain loopholes to avoid registering as foreign agents.

The bill also creates a formal process for updating which countries count as "countries of concern." The Secretary of State, working with the Attorney General, could propose adding or removing countries from this list, but the change would only take effect if Congress passes a joint resolution approving it. This gives Congress direct oversight over any changes to the list rather than letting the executive branch change it alone.

This bill would primarily affect businesses, lobbyists, consultants, and organizations that work in the U.S. on behalf of foreign governments, particularly those linked to countries the U.S. considers strategic rivals or threats. It could also affect people who hire or work with such entities, since transparency requirements would become stricter. The changes are not permanent — they are set to expire five years after the bill becomes law unless Congress acts again. Ordinary Americans wouldn't be directly regulated by this bill, but it could increase public transparency about foreign influence in U.S. politics, media, and business.

title: Medication Affordability and Patent Integrity Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires drug companies to keep the information they give to two different government agencies consistent with each other. When a company applies to sell a drug, it deals with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which decides if the drug is safe and effective, and separately with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO), which decides if the company can hold a patent on the drug. Under this bill, companies would have to certify that what they tell the FDA about a drug's makeup, testing data, and manufacturing matches what they tell the Patent Office when seeking patent protection, and vice versa. They would also have to share relevant technical information between the two agencies rather than potentially presenting different facts to each one.

The goal is to stop companies from using inconsistent or misleading information to obtain multiple patents that extend their control over a drug longer than intended, a practice sometimes called "patent thicketing" that critics say delays cheaper generic or biosimilar competition. If a company fails to make these required disclosures or certifications, it could face FDA enforcement penalties. Additionally, if a patent holder didn't properly disclose information as required, a generic or biosimilar company being sued for patent infringement could use that failure as a legal defense in court.

This bill would primarily affect pharmaceutical and biotech companies that develop brand-name drugs and biologics, as well as their legal and regulatory teams who interact with both the FDA and USPTO. Indirectly, it could affect consumers and patients, since supporters argue that reducing improper patent extensions could speed up generic drug competition and potentially lower medication prices, though the bill itself does not directly regulate drug pricing.

title: Saving Lives and Taxpayer Dollars Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Saving Lives and Taxpayer Dollars Act," aims to stop the U.S. government from destroying foreign aid supplies like food, medicine, and vaccines before they can be given to the people who need them. It requires that items such as food aid, HIV medications, vaccines, and family planning supplies be delivered to their intended recipients—such as refugees, disaster survivors, or people in developing countries—before they expire or spoil, rather than being thrown away. The bill also requires government agencies to quickly release any funding needed to get these supplies delivered on time, and it says items can only be destroyed as a last resort, after every reasonable effort has been made to sell or donate them.

The bill also creates a reporting requirement: if any aid supplies do end up expiring, spoiling, or being destroyed, the Secretary of State, USAID, and the Department of Agriculture must report to Congress each year explaining why, what efforts were made to prevent it, who the supplies were meant for, and how much money was lost.

This bill would primarily affect federal agencies involved in foreign aid (the State Department, USAID, and the Department of Agriculture), organizations that partner with the government to distribute aid overseas, and people in other countries who rely on U.S. assistance, including refugees, disaster survivors, and low-income communities. It could also indirectly affect U.S. taxpayers and farmers, since the bill's supporters argue that wasted aid represents lost tax dollars and lost opportunities for U.S. agricultural exports used in food assistance programs.

title: American Decade of Sports Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the American Decade of Sports Act, directs the U.S. State Department to create an official strategy for using major sporting events happening in the U.S. between 2024 and 2034 as tools for diplomacy and international relations. These events include the 2026 FIFA World Cup, the 2028 Summer Olympics, the 2034 Winter Olympics, and several other international competitions. The idea is that hosting these events gives the U.S. a chance to build relationships with other countries, showcase American culture, and boost its global image—often called "soft power."

Specifically, the bill requires the Secretary of State to write two five-year strategy documents (one soon after the bill passes, another five years later) explaining how the government will partner with host cities, local communities, athletes, businesses, and human rights groups during these events. The strategy must also address making visa processing faster and more secure for athletes, staff, and international visitors, and must be shared publicly online. The bill renames an existing State Department office as the "Office of Sports Diplomacy," gives it specific responsibilities for coordinating this work, and requires at least three additional staff be assigned to it through 2034.

This bill mainly affects the State Department's operations and budget, not everyday laws or taxes. It could indirectly affect people involved in hosting these sporting events—host cities, athletes, sports organizations, diaspora communities, and international visitors—by potentially speeding up visa processing and creating more coordinated cultural programming around the events. Regular citizens would mostly notice this through public reports the government releases and possibly smoother visa experiences for international guests attending these competitions.

title: Strengthening the Rule of Law in the Brazilian Amazon Act
ai_summary:
This bill aims to help the United States work with Brazil to fight crimes that are destroying the Amazon rainforest, such as illegal logging, illegal mining, and illegal fishing and wildlife trade, along with related corruption and violence. It encourages the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation to look for legitimate business investment opportunities in the Brazilian Amazon and report back to Congress on what it finds and what obstacles exist. It also directs the State Department and USAID to help Brazil build up its law enforcement capabilities, trace illegal money, support criminal investigations, and fund programs that promote legal jobs, protect Indigenous peoples' rights, and manage protected lands. The bill authorizes up to $10 million per year from 2025 to 2028 for these efforts.

The bill also requires several government reports, including one examining how U.S. consumer demand for products like farm goods, timber, minerals, and wildlife may be contributing to Amazon destruction, and another looking at China's role in illegal resource extraction there. Finally, it directs U.S. representatives at international financial institutions like the World Bank and IMF to push those organizations to support sustainable development in the Amazon and oppose loans that would worsen deforestation. This bill mainly affects U.S. government agencies (State Department, USAID, Treasury, and others) that would carry out these new responsibilities, American businesses considering investment in Brazil, and indirectly, Brazilian communities, Indigenous peoples, and environmental conditions in the Amazon region.

title: Energy Security Pacts Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Energy Security Pacts Act, would let the U.S. Secretary of State create special multi-year agreements, called "Energy Security Pacts," with other countries. The goal is to help the U.S. and its partner countries get more reliable access to energy and critical minerals (like lithium or cobalt used in batteries and electronics), reduce dependence on countries like China, and support American businesses competing overseas. To do this, the bill sets up a new Office of Energy Security Pacts within the State Department, led by a new "Director for Energy Security Pacts," along with an interagency council made up of officials from agencies like the Department of Energy, Treasury, Defense, and Commerce, plus organizations like the Export-Import Bank and the Development Finance Corporation. These groups would work together to negotiate deals, fund projects, and track progress.

The bill allows money to be moved between various federal accounts to pay for these pacts, but it includes safeguards: funds can't be used for military assistance, can't be used for projects that would hurt American jobs, can't create environmental or safety hazards, and can't benefit government officials or their family members financially. Countries must meet certain eligibility rules to participate, such as not being classified as a "country of concern" (a category that generally includes nations like China). Congress must be notified before pacts are signed or expanded, and the Government Accountability Office must review the program's effectiveness every year. Pacts can last up to 10 years, and the authority to create new ones would expire 15 years after the bill becomes law.

This bill mainly affects the State Department, other federal agencies involved in trade and development finance, and foreign countries that could become "partner countries" for energy and mineral cooperation. Indirectly, it could affect American companies in the energy and mining sectors, U.S. taxpayers (through funding decisions), and consumers who rely on supply chains for materials used in electronics, batteries, and clean energy technology.

title: United States Commission on International Religious Freedom Reauthorization Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill extends the life of the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), a government body that monitors and reports on religious freedom conditions in other countries. Without this bill, the commission's funding and legal authority would expire in September 2026. The bill pushes that expiration date to September 30, 2028, and updates the years for which Congress can provide funding to cover 2026 through 2028.

In practical terms, this bill keeps an existing agency running rather than creating anything new or changing what it does. USCIRF investigates religious persecution around the world, publishes an annual report, and recommends actions the U.S. government can take, such as sanctions or diplomatic pressure, against countries that severely violate religious freedom. This kind of reauthorization is a routine administrative action that Congress does periodically to keep agencies like this operating.

This bill mainly affects the commission itself and its staff, whose jobs and funding depend on continued authorization. It also indirectly affects U.S. foreign policy work related to religious freedom, since the commission's reports and recommendations feed into decisions made by the State Department and Congress. Everyday Americans are not directly affected by this bill, though those interested in international human rights and religious freedom issues may follow the commission's ongoing work.

title: BANNED in Latin America Act
ai_summary:
This bill, known as the BANNED in Latin America Act, would require the U.S. Secretary of State to create and submit a detailed strategy to Congress within 180 days of the bill becoming law. The strategy would focus on countering what the bill describes as influence operations by Iran and the group Hezbollah in Latin American countries, including propaganda efforts, cultural outreach programs, and networks that the bill's sponsors believe are used for radicalization or supporting terrorism.

The required strategy would need to cover several specific areas: ways to limit Iranian cultural centers operating in Latin America, restrictions on travel for Iranian diplomats and officials linked to these activities, stronger U.S. intelligence efforts to track and disrupt these networks (including any ties to universities or nonprofit organizations), plans to restrict Spanish-language media outlets linked to Iran (HispanTV) and Hezbollah (Al Mayadeen Espanol), and consideration of formally labeling an Iranian religious education network, Al Mustafa International University, as a terrorist organization. The strategy must be shared publicly, though sensitive details could be included in a separate classified section.

This bill would primarily affect U.S. government agencies, particularly the State Department and intelligence community, by creating new reporting and planning requirements. It would not directly regulate ordinary Americans, but it could affect U.S. foreign policy, diplomatic relations with Latin American countries, and organizations or media outlets identified as linked to Iran or Hezbollah, potentially through sanctions or travel restrictions. It reflects broader U.S. concerns about foreign influence and national security in the Western Hemisphere.

title: Iran Human Rights, Internet Freedom, and Accountability Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Iran Human Rights, Internet Freedom, and Accountability Act of 2026, aims to help ordinary Iranians communicate freely and document human rights abuses despite their government's efforts to censor the internet and suppress protests. It puts the Secretary of State in charge of coordinating U.S. efforts to expand internet access in Iran, including studying new technologies like satellite-based cell phone service and mesh networks that could help people get online even during government-imposed internet blackouts. It also increases funding (to at least $20 million per year through 2030) for internet freedom grants, sets up a working group with the Defense Department and other agencies to develop and deploy censorship-beating technology, and directs agencies to provide cybersecurity training, VPNs, and encrypted messaging tools to journalists and activists in Iran.

The bill also focuses on accountability and information-sharing. It requires the President to investigate and report on foreign individuals or companies that help Iran's government censor the internet or violate human rights, so Congress can push for sanctions against them. It calls for a strategy to strengthen U.S.-backed broadcasting into Iran (like Voice of America's Persian service) and support independent journalists, along with a government audit of how past funding for democracy programs in the Middle East was spent. Regular reports to Congress are required to track progress.

This bill mainly affects U.S. government agencies (State Department, Defense Department, USAGM, Treasury, Commerce) that would take on new coordination and reporting duties, as well as companies and organizations that develop internet and communications technology, since some could receive grants or contracts to build circumvention tools. Iranian citizens, journalists, and activists are the intended beneficiaries, as the bill's goal is to help them access uncensored information and organize safely. It explicitly does not authorize any military action.

title: Reassessing the United States-Tanzania Bilateral Relationship Act
ai_summary:
This bill responds to a disputed October 2025 election in Tanzania, where Congress says the government engaged in vote-rigging, violence against protesters, disappearances of opposition figures, religious persecution, and an internet shutdown that killed hundreds of citizens and disrupted the economy. The bill directs the U.S. State Department, working with other agencies, to conduct a full review of the U.S.-Tanzania relationship, including Tanzania's ties to China, and report back to Congress within 90 days on democratic conditions, security cooperation, and impacts on American businesses.

The bill also requires the State Department to identify specific Tanzanian government, military, police, and ruling-party officials responsible for human rights abuses, such as abductions, censorship, religious persecution, and violence against journalists or opposition members. Once identified, the President would have authority (not a requirement) to sanction these individuals by freezing their U.S. assets and barring or revoking their visas. The bill exempts humanitarian aid, medicine, and food from these sanctions.

Additionally, the bill would cut off most U.S. security assistance, development financing, and Millennium Challenge Corporation funding to Tanzania until the government certifies it has made reforms—such as holding fair elections, releasing political prisoners, and ending censorship. Humanitarian, health, and democracy-support aid would continue regardless. This bill mainly affects U.S. foreign policy officials, Tanzanian government and security officials who could face sanctions, and organizations involved in U.S.-Tanzania trade, aid, and investment. It does not directly affect ordinary American citizens, though it could affect U.S. businesses operating in Tanzania and Americans traveling there.

title: Expanded Consular Fellows Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Expanded Consular Fellows Act of 2026, changes how long certain State Department employees can serve in temporary positions handling consular work. Consular services include things like processing visa applications, helping Americans traveling or living abroad, and supporting international adoptions. Currently, these temporary, non-career appointments are generally limited to five years. This bill would allow appointments specifically for consular service workers to last up to eight years, with the possibility of an additional two-year extension if the Foreign Service needs it, bringing the maximum to ten years.

The bill explains its reasoning: consular offices process millions of visa applications yearly, tourism is a major part of the U.S. economy, and the U.S. is about to host a series of major international events (like the World Cup and Olympics) between 2024 and 2034 that will increase demand for visas and travel-related consular services. Congress argues that extending these appointment limits will help the State Department keep experienced staff longer, reduce the cost and delay of constantly hiring and training new workers, and better handle the expected surge in demand.

This bill mainly affects State Department employees working in the Consular Fellows Program and similar consular roles, as well as the broader system of U.S. visa and passport processing. Indirectly, it could affect anyone applying for a U.S. visa, Americans traveling abroad, families pursuing international adoptions, and the travel and tourism industry, since more experienced consular staff could mean faster or more consistent processing of applications.

title: No Paydays for Hostage-Takers Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "No Paydays for Hostage-Takers Act," focuses on Iran's history of taking American citizens hostage or wrongfully detaining them. It doesn't create new criminal penalties itself, but instead requires the President and State Department to regularly report to Congress on several Iran-related issues over the next several years. These include tracking $6 billion in Iranian funds that were transferred to Qatar (originally meant for humanitarian purposes), reviewing whether sanctions are being properly applied to people involved in hostage-taking, and reporting on frozen Iranian assets worldwide.

The bill also pushes for tighter travel restrictions on Iranian diplomats visiting the U.S. for United Nations business, especially those already sanctioned for terrorism or weapons proliferation. It expresses Congress's opinion that the Secretary of State should consider declaring U.S. passports invalid for travel to Iran, similar to what was done for North Korea after the death of Otto Warmbier. Finally, it requires the President to create and submit a formal government strategy for deterring hostage-taking by hostile countries, including clear rules against paying ransoms.

This bill mainly affects government agencies (the President, State Department, Treasury, and Justice Department), requiring them to produce detailed reports and reviews for Congress. It could also affect Iranian diplomats seeking visas to the U.S., and indirectly affects American citizens by shaping policy meant to protect U.S. nationals traveling abroad from being taken hostage or wrongfully detained, particularly in Iran.

title: Cape Fox Land Entitlement Finalization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill settles a long-standing land claim involving Cape Fox Village Corporation, the Alaska Native corporation for the Village of Saxman near Ketchikan, Alaska. Under the 1971 Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, Alaska Native village corporations were entitled to select certain amounts of federal land near their communities. Cape Fox has not yet received all the land it was originally promised. This bill finalizes that process by excusing Cape Fox from having to select about 185 acres near Saxman that it would normally have been required to take, and instead allows it to select about 180 acres of land elsewhere within the Tongass National Forest, based on a specific map created for this purpose.

Once Cape Fox formally notifies the Secretary of the Interior that it wants this replacement land, the government must transfer the surface rights to Cape Fox within a set timeframe (aiming for 180 days). At the same time, the underground mineral rights (subsurface estate) for that same land will go to Sealaska Corporation, the regional Alaska Native corporation for southeast Alaska, since regional corporations typically hold subsurface rights under village lands. This transfer would count as fully satisfying both companies' remaining land entitlements under the original 1971 law. The bill also requires that a public access route be preserved through the transferred land so people can still reach nearby national forest land further inland.

This bill mainly affects Cape Fox Village Corporation, Sealaska Corporation, and residents of Saxman, Alaska, by resolving decades-old land ownership questions. It could also matter to the U.S. Forest Service, which manages the Tongass National Forest, and to the public, since it guarantees continued access to forest land even after the property changes hands.

title: Zuni Indian Tribe Water Rights Settlement Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill approves a legal settlement that resolves a long-running dispute over water rights for the Zuni Indian Tribe in the Zuni River area of New Mexico. It confirms the Tribe's rights to use a certain amount of water from the Zuni River Stream System, protects those rights from being lost through non-use, and sets up a trust fund of about $685 million (paid by the federal government, with a small contribution from the state of New Mexico) to help the Tribe build and maintain water systems, such as wells, irrigation, and pipelines. In exchange, the Tribe and the federal government agree to drop related legal claims against each other and other parties involved in the settlement, once certain conditions—like court approval and full funding—are met.

The bill also protects the Zuni Salt Lake, a site of deep cultural and religious importance to the Tribe, by withdrawing about 92,000 acres of federal land around it from mining, drilling, and new development. It limits activities like new water wells, grazing increases, and road-building in that area to preserve the lake and its water supply. Additionally, it directs the federal government to transfer certain federal lands into trust for the Tribe, effectively expanding Zuni-owned land holdings.

This bill mainly affects the Zuni Tribe, the U.S. Department of the Interior, the State of New Mexico, and other water users in the Zuni River basin, including individual landowners (called “Allottees”) who hold separate water rights on allotted lands. It does not affect other tribes’ water rights or land claims. The practical effect for most everyday Americans is limited, though taxpayers would help fund the settlement, and residents of the region—especially those relying on the same river system—could see changes in water management and land use rules.

title: Safe Access to Cash Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Safe Access to Cash Act of 2026, creates new federal crimes for robbing or damaging ATMs (cash machines). Currently, federal bank robbery laws mainly cover crimes at bank buildings themselves. This bill closes a gap by making it a specific federal crime to rob, threaten, or use violence against people using or servicing an ATM—even if that machine is standing alone in a store, gas station, or parking lot rather than inside a bank. It also makes it a crime to break into, damage, or steal from an ATM itself, with penalties depending on how much money was involved (up to 10 years if over $1,000 was taken, up to 1 year if not). Assaulting someone during these crimes can bring up to 25 years, and killing someone or forcing them to come along against their will carries at least 10 years up to life in prison. The bill also covers people who knowingly receive or sell stolen ATM cash or property, and it applies to armored car workers who transport cash to and from ATMs.

The bill also slightly updates the existing federal bank robbery law by adding "conspires to take" money, meaning that planning or agreeing to rob a bank could itself be prosecuted, not just the actual robbery.

This bill mainly affects people who commit or attempt ATM-related crimes, who would now face clearer and potentially tougher federal charges. It also affects ATM owners and operators (banks, credit unions, savings institutions, and independent ATM companies), armored car and cash-delivery employees, and ordinary people using ATMs, all of whom would gain stronger legal protections under federal law. Law enforcement and prosecutors would gain a clearer legal tool to charge ATM crimes at the federal level, regardless of whether the machine is physically located at a bank.
ai_headline: New federal bill would make robbing or damaging ATMs a specific crime
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 350.

It also updates existing bank robbery law to cover conspiring to rob a bank.

title: Laken Riley Act
ai_summary:
This law, known as the Laken Riley Act, changes federal immigration rules about who must be detained and how states can challenge federal immigration enforcement decisions. It requires the Department of Homeland Security to take into custody any non-citizen who is in the country illegally or otherwise not lawfully admitted, and who has been charged with, arrested for, convicted of, or admits to committing crimes like theft, shoplifting, burglary, larceny, assaulting a police officer, or any crime causing death or serious injury. Importantly, detention can be triggered even if the person is only charged or arrested, not necessarily convicted. Previously, mandatory detention under this part of immigration law generally applied to more serious or specific criminal categories; this law expands it to cover theft-related and assault-on-officer offenses as well.

The law also gives state attorneys general new power to sue the federal government. If a state believes it or its residents were harmed—including financial harm of more than $100—by the federal government failing to detain or deport someone as required, or by decisions to release, parole, or grant bond to certain non-citizens, the state can go to federal court to force compliance through injunctions (court orders). This applies to several areas of immigration law, including detention of people applying for entry, parole decisions, and enforcement of deportation orders. Courts are directed to fast-track these lawsuits.

This law mainly affects non-citizens facing criminal charges (even without conviction), federal immigration agencies like DHS and the Department of Justice, and state governments, which gain a new legal tool to challenge federal immigration enforcement decisions in court. Supporters and critics disagree on its effects, but factually, it broadens mandatory detention categories and expands state governments' ability to influence federal immigration enforcement through litigation.
ai_headline: Laken Riley Act expands mandatory detention, lets states sue over enforcement
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-1.

title: Tribal Trust Land Homeownership Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This law, called the Tribal Trust Land Homeownership Act of 2025, sets strict deadlines for the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) to review and approve mortgage paperwork for homes and businesses built on Indian trust land. Because tribal land is held in trust by the federal government, anyone wanting a mortgage on that land needs BIA approval before a loan can go through. In the past, this process could take a very long time, making it hard for Native Americans to buy homes, build businesses, or get loans backed by agencies like HUD, the VA, or the USDA. The bill requires the BIA to acknowledge receipt of paperwork quickly, check within 10 days that all documents are included, and approve or deny completed mortgage applications within 20 to 30 days depending on the type. It also sets deadlines for producing "title status reports," which confirm who owns the land and whether there are any liens against it.

The law also requires the BIA to notify lenders and applicants if a deadline is missed and to respond to status inquiries within two days. It gives relevant federal agencies and tribes read-only access to the BIA's land records database (TAAMS) so they can track progress themselves. To keep the BIA accountable, the bill creates a new position called a "Realty Ombudsman," who will monitor whether deadlines are being met, help resolve complaints from tribes, tribal members, and lenders, and act as a go-between with other federal agencies. The BIA must also report yearly to Congress on how well it's meeting these deadlines, and the Government Accountability Office must study whether digitizing tribal land records would help speed things up further.

This bill mainly affects Native American individuals and tribes who want to get mortgages or business loans using trust land as collateral, as well as lenders and federal housing agencies involved in those loans. Its goal is to reduce bureaucratic delays that have historically made it harder for Native Americans to access home and business financing compared to people living on non-trust land.
ai_headline: New law sets deadlines for BIA to approve tribal land mortgages
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-88.
