title: ARTIST Act
ai_summary:
This law, called the ARTIST Act, updates the Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972 to clarify and expand rules about Alaska Native handicrafts made from marine mammal parts, including ivory from walrus tusks and whale teeth. It confirms that Alaska Natives living on the coast of the North Pacific or Arctic Ocean can legally hunt marine mammals for food (subsistence) or to make traditional handicrafts and clothing, as long as the hunting isn't wasteful. These handicrafts must be made by hand, using traditional methods like carving, weaving, sewing, or beading, without machines that mass-produce copies.

The law also sets rules for selling these items. Genuine Alaska Native handicrafts can be sold across state lines, and states are not allowed to ban the sale, trade, or possession of marine mammal ivory, bone, or baleen when it's part of an authentic Alaska Native product. Edible parts of animals taken for handicraft-making can be sold for food within Alaska Native communities. If wildlife officials determine that a species is being over-hunted or is at risk, they can create temporary regulations limiting the practice, but they must publicly show clear evidence—including Indigenous knowledge—to justify those rules, and remove them once no longer needed.

This bill mainly affects Alaska Native artisans, hunters, and communities involved in traditional handicraft production, as well as state governments and federal wildlife regulators who oversee marine mammal protections. It aims to protect cultural traditions and income sources for Alaska Native communities while maintaining some federal oversight to prevent overharvesting of marine mammal populations.
ai_headline: New law expands protections for Alaska Native ivory handicrafts
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-99.

ai_sections.tldr: The ARTIST Act protects Alaska Native handicrafts from marine mammal parts and limits states' power to ban their sale.

title: Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act
ai_summary:
This law extends and updates two federal programs, called SBIR and STTR, that give research grants to small businesses working on new technology, often for government agencies like the Defense Department or NASA. These programs were set to expire, and this bill keeps them running through September 30, 2031. It also adds new rules aimed at national security, requiring agencies to check whether a small business applying for a grant has risky ties to foreign governments or companies, especially those linked to China, before giving out money. If a business is denied funding because of a security concern, agencies now must (when possible) tell the business why, and make clear that being denied once doesn't block them from applying again later.

The bill also creates a new type of larger grant called a "strategic breakthrough award," letting agencies give up to $30 million to a small business that has already succeeded in an earlier round of funding and can show it's attracting private investment or other government contracts. This is meant to help promising technologies move from research into real-world use, particularly for defense needs. Other changes reduce paperwork by placing caps on how many grant proposals one company can submit per year, improve training for government contract officers so they better understand these programs, and require better tracking of how grant money is used and whether it leads to bigger contracts later on.

Overall, this bill mainly affects small businesses and startups that rely on federal research grants, especially in technology, defense, and science fields. It also affects federal agencies that run these grant programs, requiring them to do more security screening, report more data to Congress, and follow new procedures. Everyday taxpayers are affected indirectly, since the bill shapes how billions of dollars in federal research funding are given out and monitored, with an added focus on protecting against foreign security risks.
ai_headline: Small business research grant programs extended through 2031 with security checks
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-83.

title: University of Utah Research Park Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the University of Utah Research Park Act, deals with a piece of land in Salt Lake City that the federal government originally gave to the University of Utah back in 1968. The land, about 593 acres, was transferred under a law called the Recreation and Public Purposes Act, which requires that such land be used for public benefit, like parks, schools, or research facilities. The university has used this land for decades as a research park, following a plan approved by the Department of the Interior in 1970.

The bill officially confirms that the university's use of this land as a research park, along with any updates to that plan approved over the years, counts as a valid "public purpose" under the original 1926 law. It also confirms that other related uses, such as building student housing or a transit hub on the land, would also count as valid public purposes going forward. Essentially, this removes any legal uncertainty about whether the university is complying with the terms of the original land grant, even as it expands or changes how the land is used.

This bill mainly affects the University of Utah, Salt Lake City residents near the research park, and businesses or organizations operating within it. It does not change ownership of the land or transfer new federal land; instead, it provides legal clarity so the university can continue operating and developing the research park, including newer projects like housing and transportation infrastructure, without worrying about violating federal land-use rules.
ai_headline: Bill confirms University of Utah research park meets 1968 land grant rules
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 337.

title: A bill to make technical corrections to the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026.
ai_summary:
This bill makes small technical fixes to the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, a large law that was already passed to fund and set policy for the military. It does not create major new policy; it corrects wording problems that were noticed after the original law was enacted.

The first fix changes the rules for military lawyers, known as judge advocates, who serve in the armed forces. The original law said these lawyers must maintain their law license in good standing, and this bill clarifies that they need to maintain a license status that makes them eligible to practice law. This is a minor legal wording adjustment affecting military attorneys and the standards they must meet.

The second fix relates to an award for Isaac "Ike" Camacho, a veteran being honored with the Distinguished Service Cross for bravery during the Vietnam War. The original law referred to this as a posthumous award, meaning it would be given after his death. This bill removes the word "posthumous" from the title of that section, which suggests the award may now be given to him while he is alive rather than after his death. This change mainly affects Camacho, his family, and the formal record of how the honor is described in law.
ai_headline: Bill corrects wording in 2026 defense law on lawyers and Camacho honor

title: Protecting Domestic Mining Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Protecting Domestic Mining Act of 2025, changes how mining projects are treated under a federal law called the FAST Act. The FAST Act set up a system to speed up government approval for major infrastructure projects, like highways, pipelines, and energy facilities, by having a special council coordinate the permitting process across different agencies. This bill adds "mining" specifically to the list of industries whose projects can qualify for this faster, more coordinated permitting process, known as "covered project" status.

The bill also blocks a specific rule change that federal regulators had proposed in 2023. That proposed rule would have narrowed which mining projects could qualify for this expedited permitting treatment, likely by excluding certain types of mining activities. This bill prevents that proposed rule from ever being finalized or enforced, essentially locking in a broader definition of mining projects that can benefit from faster permitting.

This bill mainly affects mining companies, particularly those involved in extracting minerals used in things like batteries, electronics, and construction materials. It could speed up approval timelines for new mines or mining-related infrastructure. It may also affect federal agencies involved in environmental review and permitting, communities near proposed mining sites, and environmental groups, since faster permitting processes are sometimes associated with less time for public input or environmental review compared to standard procedures.
ai_headline: Bill adds mining to fast-track federal permitting system under FAST Act
last_action_text: Motion to reconsider laid on the table Agreed to without objection.

title: Promoting Police Leadership Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Promoting Police Leadership Act, directs the U.S. Attorney General to create or identify training programs specifically for "command-level" police personnel—officers who supervise or manage operations in a specific area, like precinct commanders or district supervisors. The training would cover topics such as leadership, handling major incidents, risk management, officer wellness, using data to guide policing decisions, and building trust with communities. The programs must mostly involve in-person instruction, include a hands-on project where officers develop and present solutions to real problems in their department, and use before-and-after tests to measure what participants learned.

The bill also sets up a certification system so the Justice Department can approve (or later revoke approval from) specific training courses that meet these standards, and requires partnerships with universities to keep improving the coursework. The Attorney General must publish a public list showing which police departments have officers who completed this training, and must report to Congress periodically on how the program is going. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) would also review the effort a few years after the law passes to check its effectiveness.

This bill mainly affects state, local, and tribal police departments and their supervisory officers, since it creates new federally supported leadership training options for them. It does not force any department to participate, and it explicitly does not override state or local authority over police certification and training standards—it simply adds a federal training resource through the existing COPS program, which supports community policing efforts nationwide.

title: Carla Walker Act
ai_summary:
This bill, named after Carla Walker, sets up federal grant programs to help police, prosecutors, medical examiners, and coroners use advanced DNA testing technology to solve difficult criminal cases and identify unknown human remains. Specifically, it creates two grant programs administered by the U.S. Attorney General: one that pays for actually running advanced DNA tests (called "forensic genetic genealogy") when standard DNA database searches have failed to identify a suspect or victim, and another that helps forensic labs purchase the equipment and supplies needed to perform this kind of testing. This technology examines far more genetic markers than routine DNA testing and can be cross-checked against genealogy databases (like those used for ancestry research) to generate new leads in cold cases or unsolved crimes.

The bill directs $5 million per year for both grant programs, for fiscal years 2025 through 2029 (about $10 million per year total). It requires grant recipients to follow existing Justice Department guidelines on this technology, keep detailed records, and report back on how the money was used, how many cases were tested, and whether the testing led to identifications or arrests. It also requires the Attorney General to send Congress a report after two years evaluating how well the programs are working and what additional funding or rules might be needed.

This bill mainly affects state, local, and tribal law enforcement agencies, prosecutors' offices, medical examiners, and coroners who investigate unsolved crimes or unidentified remains—giving them new federal funding options. It could also affect crime victims' families and communities with cold cases, since the goal is to help solve previously unsolvable investigations using newer DNA technology.

last_action_text: Held at the desk.

title: Cross-Boundary Wildfire Solutions Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Government Accountability Office (GAO), led by the Comptroller General, to study how well current federal programs and rules support wildfire prevention work that crosses property lines between federal and non-federal land. Wildfires don't stop at property boundaries, but government programs, funding rules, and agency authorities often are organized around specific land ownership types, which can make coordinated fire prevention efforts difficult. The study would look at what's working, what's getting in the way, and whether federal agencies, states, local governments, and tribal governments have enough access to funding and authority to do this cross-boundary work effectively.

The bill specifically asks GAO to examine a provision from the 2003 Healthy Forests Restoration Act to see if it has actually helped agencies and states get more funding for wildfire mitigation, and how it could be improved. Within two years of the bill becoming law, GAO would have to deliver a report to relevant House and Senate committees with its findings and recommendations for simplifying cross-boundary wildfire prevention efforts.

This bill would primarily affect federal land management agencies (like the Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management), the Department of Agriculture, FEMA, state and local governments, and tribal governments involved in wildfire prevention. It does not create new programs or funding itself; it simply requires a study and recommendations. People living in wildfire-prone areas near federal lands could eventually benefit if the study leads to policy changes that make coordinated wildfire prevention easier and more effective, but this bill alone doesn't change any existing laws or funding.

title: Theodore Roosevelt National Park Wild Horses Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires the National Park Service to keep a herd of at least 150 wild horses in the South Unit of Theodore Roosevelt National Park in North Dakota. It changes federal law so the Secretary of the Interior must maintain a genetically diverse population of horses there rather than potentially removing them, as had been previously proposed by park managers who were considering eliminating the herd due to concerns about their environmental impact and their status as a non-native species in the park.

The bill also requires the Interior Department to create a management plan within 120 days that keeps costs reasonable while protecting the park's natural resources, and to publish yearly public reports on the horses' population size, health, and overall herd makeup. Horses could only be removed from the park if doing so was part of an approved plan to maintain genetic diversity, or in emergencies or situations affecting public health and safety.

This bill mainly affects the National Park Service, which would be legally required to keep the herd rather than reduce or remove it. It also affects visitors to Theodore Roosevelt National Park, wildlife and conservation groups interested in the horses, nearby communities that benefit from tourism tied to the horses, and Native American tribes and historians who view the horses as culturally and historically significant to the region.

title: Fix Our Forests Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Fix Our Forests Act, is designed to help federal agencies reduce wildfire risks by making it easier and faster to manage forests on national forest land, land run by the Bureau of Land Management, and tribal land. It sets up a system for identifying the highest-risk wildfire zones (called "firesheds"), creates a new "Wildfire Intelligence Center" to combine data and science for predicting and responding to fires, and streamlines environmental reviews so that thinning trees, clearing brush, and conducting controlled burns can happen more quickly in these high-priority areas. It also expands partnerships between the federal government, states, tribes, and local communities to plan and pay for these projects, and it updates rules for logging contracts, grazing programs used to reduce fuel buildup, and reforestation efforts after fires.

Other parts of the bill focus on protecting communities near forests (the "wildland-urban interface") by funding local wildfire defense grants, supporting vegetation clearing near power lines to prevent fires caused by utilities, and improving tree nurseries and seed programs for replanting after fires. It also includes provisions to reduce lawsuits that can delay forest management projects, expand legal protections for people who conduct prescribed burns, and create a new assistance program for the families of firefighters killed or injured in the line of duty.

Overall, this bill would affect federal land management agencies (U.S. Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management), state and tribal governments, firefighters, timber and logging companies, ranchers who graze livestock on public land, environmental and conservation groups, electric utility companies, and residents living in or near fire-prone forested areas. Supporters argue it would reduce catastrophic wildfires and speed up forest restoration, while critics may raise concerns about reduced environmental review and potential impacts on wildlife habitat—though this summary does not take a position on those debates.

title: No Fentanyl on Social Media Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the No Fentanyl on Social Media Act, would require the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to study and report on how minors are able to access fentanyl through social media platforms. The FTC would work with the Food and Drug Administration and the Drug Enforcement Administration to research how drug dealers use social media to market and sell fentanyl, including fake prescription pills, to young people. The report, due within one year of the bill becoming law, would look at how common this problem is, the health and safety risks to minors, the tactics dealers use, how app design features may make this easier, what social media companies are already doing to stop it, and what more Congress could do to address the issue.

Before finishing the report, the FTC would need to consult with parents, social media companies, law enforcement, medical professionals, and other experts. Some sensitive details about law enforcement methods could be left out of the public version if disclosing them might interfere with active investigations or strategies. This bill does not create new criminal penalties, regulations, or requirements for social media companies—it simply requires research and a public report to give Congress information it could use to write future laws. It would primarily affect federal agencies, who would need to do the research, and indirectly affect social media companies, parents, and health and law enforcement officials who may be asked to provide input.

title: Pacific POWER Act
ai_summary:
The Pacific POWER Act is a bill focused on using geothermal energy (power generated from heat inside the earth) as a tool of U.S. foreign policy in the Indo-Pacific region. The bill notes that many U.S. allies and partners, especially Taiwan, depend heavily on energy imports, making them vulnerable to pressure or blockade from China. Since geothermal energy is reliable and many Pacific countries sit on strong geothermal resources, Congress wants the State Department to help allied nations develop this energy source as a way to strengthen their energy independence and, in turn, U.S. national security relationships in the region.

The bill directs the Secretary of State, working with the Department of Energy and other agencies, to study global geothermal potential, identify countries where U.S.-backed geothermal projects would most help American interests, and formally select at least five "geothermal partner" countries (with at least three in the Indo-Pacific, such as Taiwan, the Philippines, Japan, Australia, Indonesia, India, New Zealand, or Papua New Guinea). It then creates an "International Geothermal Program" to pursue agreements with these countries, covering things like technology sharing, workforce training, financing tools, regulatory advice, and supply chain support. U.S. agencies like the Export-Import Bank and the Development Finance Corporation would help fund these projects, and American geothermal companies would be encouraged to pursue business opportunities in partner countries.

This bill mainly affects U.S. foreign policy agencies (State Department, Energy Department, and related financial agencies), American geothermal companies looking to expand overseas, and the partner countries chosen for cooperation. It doesn't create new domestic geothermal regulations or directly affect most Americans' daily lives, but it could expand export markets for U.S. energy companies and deepen diplomatic and economic ties with Pacific allies. Congress would need to approve funding for the program from 2027 through 2031 for it to be carried out.

title: Non-Domiciled CDL Integrity Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change the federal rules for how states issue commercial driver's licenses (CDLs) to people who are not permanently domiciled in the United States, such as foreign workers driving trucks or buses. Under current law, states can issue these "non-domiciled" CDLs to people living in foreign countries under certain conditions. This bill tightens those conditions by requiring that applicants have lawful immigration status, hold a visa specifically connected to a legitimate job that requires a CDL, and pass a status check by the state before getting, renewing, transferring, or upgrading the license. It also limits how long these licenses can last—no more than one year, or until the person's authorized stay in the U.S. ends, whichever comes first. States would also have to keep records on these licenses for at least two years and hand them over to federal officials within 48 hours if asked.

The bill separately addresses applicants from U.S. territories like Puerto Rico, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands. For these individuals, it would require proof of U.S. citizenship or lawful permanent resident status before a state could issue them a CDL, along with the same recordkeeping and reporting rules.

This bill mainly affects commercial truck and bus drivers who are foreign nationals working in the U.S. trucking industry, as well as state motor vehicle agencies that issue CDLs and trucking companies that employ these drivers. It could also affect residents of U.S. territories applying for commercial licenses, since they would now need to specifically prove citizenship or permanent resident status. Supporters and critics may view the bill's tighter verification and shorter license terms differently, but the practical effect is more paperwork, stricter eligibility checks, and shorter license validity periods for the affected groups.

title: National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2027
ai_summary:
# What This Bill Does

HR 8595 is an annual funding bill that pays for the State Department, U.S. diplomacy efforts, foreign aid programs, and international security assistance for the budget year starting October 2026. It sets specific dollar amounts for things like operating U.S. embassies overseas, protecting diplomats and embassy buildings, processing passports and visas, and funding cultural exchange programs like the Fulbright Program. It also pays U.S. dues to international organizations such as the United Nations, funds peacekeeping missions (with rules requiring Congress be notified before new missions start), and supports institutions like the International Boundary and Water Commission with Mexico.

Beyond running the State Department itself, the bill funds foreign aid: global health programs (fighting HIV/AIDS, malaria, and other diseases), humanitarian and refugee assistance, economic development aid, and democracy-promotion programs like the National Endowment for Democracy. It also funds military and security assistance to foreign countries, including foreign military financing (grants so allied countries can buy U.S. weapons), anti-terrorism and landmine-clearing programs, and training for foreign militaries. Additionally, it provides money for U.S. contributions to international development banks (like the World Bank and African Development Bank) and funds independent agencies including the Peace Corps, Millennium Challenge Corporation, Export-Import Bank, and the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation.

The bill includes many conditions attached to the money—for example, restrictions on funding abortion-related activities abroad, requirements that the Secretary of State notify Congress before major policy changes, human rights vetting for UN peacekeepers, and rules ensuring Israel isn't excluded from nuclear-related international programs. It also funds oversight offices, like Inspectors General, to monitor how this money is spent and prevent waste or fraud.

This bill mainly affects the day-to-day operations of U.S. foreign policy and diplomacy. It matters most directly to federal employees at the State Department and related agencies, foreign countries receiving U.S. aid or military assistance, American businesses involved in defense exports or overseas development contracts, U.S. citizens applying for passports or visas, and organizations that run exchange or humanitarian programs abroad. Everyday Americans are affected indirectly, since this spending shapes U.S. relationships abroad, national security partnerships, and America's role in responding to global health crises, refugee situations, and international conflicts.

title: Take Care of America’s Veterans Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Take Care of America's Veterans Act, is a large package of changes affecting veterans' pay, health care, education benefits, and how the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) is run. One major piece ends a longstanding rule that reduced retirement pay for service members who were medically retired due to combat-related disabilities, meaning they could soon receive both full military retirement pay and VA disability compensation at the same time. It also changes rules for survivor benefits, allowing surviving spouses who remarry to keep certain VA and military survivor payments they previously would have lost, and expands compensation increases for spouses of veterans who died from ALS (Lou Gehrig's disease) or need extra in-home care.

The bill also tries to speed up and improve the VA's claims and appeals process. It bars the VA from denying a claim just because a veteran missed a medical exam appointment, requires new tracking and reporting on how long claims and appeals take, and gives the Board of Veterans' Appeals new tools to group similar cases together and issue guidance that can apply to future similar claims. Other sections address health care access (like expanding community care options, telehealth, rural hospital partnerships, and mental health and suicide-prevention programs), education benefits (like housing stipends and job training payments), staffing and hiring at VA facilities, and infrastructure projects such as a possible new VA hospital and improvements to burial and memorial benefits.

Overall, this bill would primarily affect veterans, their spouses and survivors, and people employed by or doing business with the VA, including VA doctors, contractors, and administrative staff. Retired disabled veterans and military survivors stand to see increased or restored payments, while veterans who use VA health care and disability claims systems could see faster processing and more service options. It does not target any specific political group—it is a broad administrative and benefits bill focused on the VA and veteran support systems.

title: Write the Laws Act
ai_summary:
**S. 60 — Write the Laws Act**

This bill aims to stop Congress from letting federal agencies write rules that carry the force of law unless Congress itself spells out the details in an actual statute. Right now, Congress often passes broad laws and leaves agencies like the EPA, FDA, or Labor Department to fill in the specifics through regulations. The bill's supporters argue this violates the Constitution, which gives lawmaking power only to Congress. Starting 90 days after the law takes effect, any new federal rule, regulation, or presidential directive that isn't fully spelled out in a law passed by Congress would have no legal force. It also requires the Comptroller General (a government watchdog official) to report to Congress on how many existing laws improperly hand off lawmaking power to agencies, so those could eventually be phased out.

The bill would let people sue the federal government if they're harmed by a rule that doesn't meet this new standard, and courts would review such cases fresh, without deferring to the agency's judgment. This would affect nearly every federal agency that issues regulations affecting businesses and individuals, including environmental rules, workplace safety standards, financial regulations, and health guidelines, since many of these are currently based on general laws that let agencies work out the technical details.

In practice, this would be a major shift in how the federal government operates. Supporters say it would force Congress to take more direct responsibility for laws instead of letting unelected officials make key decisions. Critics might argue it could make government slower and less able to respond to new problems, since Congress would have to pass detailed legislation for situations agencies currently handle through rulemaking. The bill affects everyday Americans indirectly, through changes to how quickly and specifically rules on things like pollution limits, product safety, or workplace protections could be created or updated.

last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

title: D.C. Taxing Authority Review Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the D.C. Taxing Authority Review Act, would change how laws passed by the District of Columbia's local government are reviewed by Congress. Under current law, most D.C. laws automatically take effect after Congress has a period of time to review them, unless Congress actively votes to block them. This bill would flip that process specifically for D.C. tax and fee laws: any new D.C. law that creates or raises a tax or fee, or that falls under the section of D.C. law dealing with taxation (title 47), would not take effect unless Congress specifically passes a resolution approving it within 60 days. If Congress does nothing or fails to approve it in that window, the D.C. law would not go into effect.

The bill also sets rules for how quickly Congress must handle these approval votes, limiting debate on the resolution to just one hour, split evenly between supporters and opponents, to speed up the process. These changes would only apply to D.C. tax and fee laws passed after this bill becomes law.

This would primarily affect the D.C. city government and its ability to independently set local tax policy, such as income taxes, sales taxes, property taxes, or various fees charged within the city. It would also affect D.C. residents and businesses, since any new or increased local taxes would depend on approval from the U.S. Congress rather than being decided solely by D.C.'s locally elected officials. Additionally, it affects members of Congress, who would gain a new, more direct role in approving or rejecting D.C.'s tax decisions within a set timeframe.

title: Main Street Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Main Street Act, makes a wide range of changes to how banks (especially smaller and community banks) are regulated by federal agencies like the FDIC, Federal Reserve, and Comptroller of the Currency. It gives new banks a three-year phase-in period to meet capital requirements, sets faster deadlines for regulators to approve or deny bank applications and mergers (with automatic approval if they miss deadlines), and requires regulators to publish data on how quickly they process bank charter applications. It also raises several dollar thresholds that determine which banks face the toughest "too big to fail" style regulations, meaning some banks that previously qualified as large, closely-watched institutions would face lighter oversight. Other provisions target rural banks specifically, allowing them to use a simpler capital calculation and expanding what kinds of agricultural loans savings associations can make.

The bill also changes how bank examinations work. It creates rules requiring regulators to complete exams within set timeframes, give banks written explanations of findings, and respond to bank questions faster. It sets up a new independent office where banks can formally appeal or challenge a regulator's negative findings, aiming to make the examination process feel less arbitrary. It also revises the CAMELS rating system (the main tool regulators use to grade a bank's financial health) to make grading more objective and less dependent on individual examiners' subjective judgment, particularly the "management" component.

This bill mainly affects banks themselves — especially small, community, and rural banks, and people trying to start new banks — by reducing regulatory burdens and speeding up government decisions. It could also affect bank customers indirectly: supporters would argue it helps banks lend more freely to local businesses and farmers, while critics might worry that loosening oversight and raising the asset thresholds for strict regulation could reduce financial safety checks on larger banks. Everyday depositors, farmers, small business owners seeking loans, and communities served by smaller local banks are the groups most likely to feel the effects.

It gives new banks a three-year phase-in for capital requirements, sets faster approval deadlines with automatic approval if missed, raises asset thresholds for strict oversight, and creates new rules for faster, more standardized bank examinations plus an appeals office for disputed findings.

ai_sections.why: Raising the thresholds for strict "too big to fail" oversight means some previously closely-watched banks would face lighter regulation, and faster, more automatic approval deadlines could reduce the time regulators have to scrutinize applications and mergers.

title: Restoring Executive Branch Authorities to Oversee Offices of the United States Attorneys Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would change how U.S. Attorneys are appointed when there's a temporary vacancy in that office. U.S. Attorneys are the top federal prosecutors in each judicial district, normally nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate. When a vacancy occurs, current law allows the Attorney General to appoint someone to temporarily fill the role, but if that temporary appointment lasts more than 120 days without a permanent replacement being confirmed, the district court judges get the power to appoint someone to fill the position until a permanent U.S. Attorney is confirmed.

This bill would eliminate that court authority by removing subsection (d) from the relevant law. In practice, this means federal judges would no longer be able to step in and appoint an interim U.S. Attorney if the executive branch's temporary appointment expires. The bill also makes a small clarifying edit to the language about when someone is appointed. The stated purpose is to keep the power to fill these law enforcement positions within the executive branch (the president and Attorney General) rather than allowing judges, who are part of a separate branch of government, to make such appointments.

This change would primarily affect the process for filling vacant U.S. Attorney positions during transitions or when Senate confirmation is delayed. It matters to anyone concerned with how federal prosecutors are chosen, since U.S. Attorneys oversee prosecution of federal crimes in their districts, and it touches on broader questions about the separation of powers between the executive and judicial branches of government.
ai_headline: Bill would end judges' power to name interim U.S. Attorneys
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 12 - 11.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill removes federal judges' authority to appoint interim U.S. Attorneys when temporary vacancies exceed 120 days.
ai_sections.what: This bill removes subsection (d) from current law, eliminating district court judges' power to appoint an interim U.S. Attorney if the Attorney General's temporary appointee serves more than 120 days without Senate confirmation of a permanent replacement. It also makes a small clarifying edit to the appointment language.
ai_sections.who: This affects U.S. Attorneys, the top federal prosecutors in each judicial district, along with the Attorney General, federal district court judges, and the Senate confirmation process.
ai_sections.why: The change keeps appointment power for these law enforcement positions within the executive branch, removing judicial branch involvement and raising separation-of-powers considerations.

title: PBM Kickback Prohibition Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the PBM Kickback Prohibition Act, would change federal retirement and benefits law to stop a specific type of payment arrangement in the health insurance world. Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are companies that manage prescription drug benefits for employer health plans, deciding which drugs are covered and negotiating prices with drug manufacturers and pharmacies. The bill would make it illegal for a PBM to pay money, directly or indirectly, to brokers, consultants, or advisors as a reward for steering an employer's health plan business toward that PBM. In other words, if a company hires a benefits consultant to help pick a PBM, that consultant could no longer receive a secret payment or kickback from the PBM in exchange for recommending them.

This matters because many employers rely on outside brokers and consultants to help choose which PBM will manage their employees' drug benefits. Critics of the current system argue that when PBMs pay these advisors under the table, the advice employers receive may be biased toward whichever PBM pays the most, rather than whichever PBM offers the best deal for employees. By banning these payments, the bill aims to make sure that consultants are giving employers honest, unbiased recommendations based on cost and quality, not hidden financial incentives.

The people most affected would be employers who sponsor health plans for their workers, the benefits brokers and consultants who advise them, and the PBM companies themselves. Employees who get prescription drug coverage through employer-sponsored health plans could also be indirectly affected, since more transparent PBM selection could potentially lead to better drug pricing or coverage decisions. The rule would apply starting with health plan years that begin after the law is enacted, if passed.
ai_headline: Bill would ban PBM kickbacks to health plan brokers and consultants
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 634.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill would ban PBMs from paying brokers or consultants to steer employer health plans toward them.
ai_sections.what: The bill would amend federal retirement and benefits law to make it illegal for pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) to pay brokers, consultants, or advisors, directly or indirectly, as a reward for steering an employer's health plan business toward that PBM. It would apply starting with health plan years beginning after enactment.
ai_sections.who: Employers who sponsor health plans, benefits brokers and consultants, and PBM companies would be directly affected; employees with employer-sponsored drug coverage could be indirectly affected.
ai_sections.why: Critics argue current hidden payments can bias consultant recommendations toward whichever PBM pays the most rather than the best deal for employees, so banning them changes how PBM selection advice is generated.

title: FAFSA Verification Efficiency Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change how the government checks Social Security numbers for people applying for federal student financial aid, like FAFSA. Currently, the Higher Education Act allows the Secretary of Education to verify Social Security numbers under certain conditions. This bill would make that verification mandatory rather than optional, requiring the Secretary of Education to work with the Social Security Administration to confirm both the Social Security number and citizenship status of anyone applying for federal student aid.

In practical terms, this means the verification process would become a required step rather than a discretionary one, and it would explicitly apply to citizenship status as well as Social Security numbers. The phrase "notwithstanding any other provision of law" suggests this requirement would take priority over other conflicting rules that might otherwise apply.

This bill would primarily affect college students and their families who fill out the FAFSA form to apply for federal financial aid such as grants, loans, and work-study programs. It would also affect the Department of Education and the Social Security Administration, since these two agencies would need to coordinate more closely to confirm applicant information. Colleges and universities that process financial aid could also see changes in how quickly or smoothly student aid applications are verified, depending on how the new mandatory checks are carried out.
ai_headline: Bill would require SSN and citizenship checks for federal student aid applicants
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 635.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill would make Social Security number and citizenship verification mandatory for federal student aid applicants like those filing the FAFSA.
ai_sections.what: This bill would change Social Security number verification for federal student aid applicants from optional to mandatory under the Higher Education Act. It would require the Secretary of Education to work with the Social Security Administration to confirm both Social Security numbers and citizenship status for anyone applying for aid, and this requirement would override conflicting laws.
ai_sections.who: College students and families who complete the FAFSA for federal grants, loans, or work-study would be affected. The Department of Education, the Social Security Administration, and colleges that process financial aid would also be affected.
ai_sections.why: The change could affect how quickly or smoothly student aid applications are processed, depending on how the mandatory checks are implemented. It shifts verification from a discretionary agency practice to a legal requirement, adding a citizenship-status check that wasn't explicitly required before.

title: Shadow Wolves Improvement Act
ai_summary:
This bill, S. 572, aims to strengthen the Shadow Wolves Program, a specialized Native American law enforcement unit within U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) that patrols tribal lands, particularly the Tohono O'odham Nation, for drug and human trafficking. The bill requires ICE's director to work with tribal governments to clearly define the program's mission and goals, determine how many agents are needed nationally, and identify the skills those agents should have. It also requires ICE to update its existing strategy with specific timelines and measurable goals for recruiting and retaining officers, and to create a succession plan to fill positions left by retiring agents.

The bill also addresses job classification issues within the program. Current Shadow Wolves officers would receive clear written information to help them decide whether to reclassify from "tactical officers" to "special agents," including how the change would affect their pay, retirement benefits, and training requirements. Additionally, after three years of service, Shadow Wolves members could be automatically moved into permanent career government positions without having to compete again for their jobs, making their employment more stable. The bill requires ICE to plan for expanding the program to additional tribal lands, considering funding needs and proximity to law enforcement training facilities.

This bill mainly affects members of the Shadow Wolves unit, ICE leadership, and tribal governments like the Tohono O'odham Nation who partner with the program. It could also indirectly affect other tribes located near federal law enforcement training centers if the program expands to their lands. Congress would receive a progress report within a year to track how these changes are being implemented.
ai_headline: Bill seeks clearer mission and job security for Shadow Wolves unit
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 251.

ai_sections.tldr: S. 572 would strengthen ICE's Shadow Wolves tribal law enforcement program and stabilize its officers' job classifications.

It also mandates an updated recruitment and retention strategy with timelines, a succession plan for retiring agents, clearer information for officers considering reclassification, automatic conversion to permanent positions after three years, and planning for expansion to other tribal lands.

title: Modernizing Government Technology Reform Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes changes to the Technology Modernization Fund (TMF), a government fund that helps federal agencies pay to upgrade outdated computer systems. The fund works like a loan program: agencies get money to modernize their technology, then pay that money back over time so the fund can keep helping other agencies. This bill tightens the rules around how that money is used and repaid, making sure agencies stick closer to the fund's original purpose—replacing old IT systems, improving cybersecurity, and boosting agency efficiency. It also adds a rule that if an agency lies or provides misleading information to get funding, the government can cut off or stop that funding.

The bill also creates a new tracking system. Each federal agency's technology officer would have to make a list of their oldest, riskiest computer systems every year and send it to the government's top technology official. That official would then combine these lists into a government-wide inventory and pick the 10 riskiest systems across the entire federal government, reporting this to Congress and government watchdogs annually. The goal is to give lawmakers a clearer picture of which outdated systems pose the biggest security or operational risks.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies and their technology staff, not everyday citizens directly. However, since many government services—taxes, benefits, healthcare records, and more—rely on these computer systems, improvements or failures in this modernization effort can eventually affect how well government services work for the public. The bill also pushes the fund's expiration date to after December 31, 2032, giving it more time to operate under these updated rules.
ai_headline: Bill tightens rules on federal tech upgrade fund, extends it to 2032
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 42 - 0.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill tightens repayment and use rules for a federal tech upgrade fund and extends it past December 31, 2032.
ai_sections.what: This bill tightens rules on how the Technology Modernization Fund is used and repaid, requiring agencies to focus on replacing old IT systems, improving cybersecurity, and boosting efficiency. It lets the government cut off funding if an agency lied or gave misleading information to get it. It also creates an annual tracking system where agencies list their riskiest old computer systems, which are combined into a government-wide inventory highlighting the 10 riskiest systems for Congress and watchdogs.

title: SPUR Act
ai_summary:
HR 818, called the SPUR Act, would change how the federal government tracks and grades agencies on their efforts to hire small businesses for government contracts. Currently, the government uses a "scorecard" system to rate each federal agency on how well it meets goals for awarding contracts to small businesses, including ones owned by veterans, women, and people in economically disadvantaged situations. This bill adds a new requirement: agencies would also have to report how many "new" small businesses—meaning companies that have never before won a federal contract—were awarded contracts that year, broken down by industry category. Agencies would also have to compare that number to the previous year, so lawmakers and the public can see whether new businesses are actually breaking into government contracting or whether the same established companies keep winning the work.

The bill defines exactly what counts as a "new small business entrant" and clarifies what a "scorecard" officially means under the law. It does not create any new programs or spending; a section of the bill specifically states that no additional federal money is authorized to carry out these changes.

This bill would mainly affect federal agencies, which would have new reporting requirements, and small business owners, especially those trying to win their first government contract, since better tracking could increase attention on whether opportunities are actually reaching new companies. It could also matter to policymakers and watchdog groups interested in ensuring that small business contracting goals are being met fairly rather than concentrated among the same repeat contractors.
ai_headline: Bill would track how many new small firms win federal contracts
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship.

ai_sections.tldr: The SPUR Act would require agencies to report how many first-time small businesses won federal contracts each year.
ai_sections.what: HR 818, the SPUR Act, would add a new requirement to the existing agency "scorecard" system for small business contracting. Agencies would have to report how many new small businesses—those that never before won a federal contract—received contracts, broken down by industry, and compare that number to the prior year. The bill also formally defines "new small business entrant" and "scorecard" under the law.
ai_sections.who: Federal agencies would face new reporting duties, and small business owners seeking their first government contract would be directly affected. Policymakers and watchdog groups tracking fairness in small business contracting would also have a stake in the data.
ai_sections.why: The added reporting could reveal whether new companies are actually gaining access to federal contracts or whether the same established firms continue to dominate the work.

title: Small County PILT Parity Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change how the federal government calculates Payments in Lieu of Taxes, known as PILT, for counties and other local governments that have a lot of federally owned land within their borders. PILT payments help make up for the property tax revenue that local governments lose out on because the federal government doesn't pay property taxes on land it owns, such as national forests or public land managed by federal agencies. Currently, the payment formula has a starting population tier that begins at 5,000 people. This bill lowers that starting point to 1,000 people and adds a more detailed payment scale for places with populations between 1,000 and 50,000, replacing the old table with a new one that specifies exact dollar amounts per person at each population level.

The main effect is that very small counties and towns, those with fewer than 5,000 residents, would now be eligible for a more tailored PILT calculation instead of being lumped into the old formula's starting tier. Supporters of this kind of change typically argue it gives small, rural communities a fairer or more accurate share of these payments, since a county with only 1,500 residents has very different needs and resources than one with close to 5,000. This bill would primarily affect rural counties, particularly in Western states with large amounts of federal land, such as national parks, forests, and Bureau of Land Management territory, since those are the places that rely most heavily on PILT funding to help pay for local services like schools, roads, and emergency responders.
ai_headline: Bill would extend PILT payments to counties as small as 1,000 people
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 474.

ai_sections.tldr: S 1175 would lower the PILT payment formula's starting population tier from 5,000 to 1,000 residents.
ai_sections.what: S 1175 would change how the federal government calculates Payments in Lieu of Taxes (PILT) for local governments with significant federal land. It lowers the formula's starting population tier from 5,000 to 1,000 people and adds a detailed payment scale with exact dollar amounts per person for populations between 1,000 and 50,000, replacing the old table.
ai_sections.who: This affects small rural counties and towns with fewer than 5,000 residents that contain federally owned land, particularly in Western states with national forests, parks, and Bureau of Land Management territory.
ai_sections.why: Small communities with populations between 1,000 and 5,000 would move from being grouped into the old formula's lowest tier to a more tailored calculation based on their specific population size.

title: Alaska Native Landless Equity Act
ai_summary:
This bill would let people from five southeastern Alaska communities—Haines, Ketchikan, Petersburg, Tenakee, and Wrangell—form their own Native "Urban Corporations" and receive land and shares under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA), a 1971 law that gave Alaska Native people land and corporate shares in exchange for giving up other land claims. These five communities were originally left out of that law because they already had reservations or other designations at the time, and this bill is meant to fix that "landless" gap decades later.

Specifically, the bill lets Alaska Natives enrolled in these five communities set up corporations, get 100 shares of stock each (with special rules for people who inherited shares), and receive about 23,040 acres of federal land per community (roughly 115,000 acres total) from national forest land. The land would still allow public hunting, fishing, and recreational access, and existing roads, trails, and agreements with the Forest Service and State of Alaska would generally continue. The bill also sets up processes for phased land transfers (including special conditions in Haines involving mining claims), easements, and a mutual use agreement for shared roads. It authorizes $12.5 million in federal grants to help the new corporations get started.

The people most affected are Alaska Native residents and descendants from these five communities, who would gain corporate ownership, land, and financial benefits similar to what other Alaska Native groups already received. It could also affect the U.S. Forest Service, the State of Alaska, mining and outfitting businesses operating on the affected land, and members of the public who use the land for recreation, since ownership and management would shift from federal to Native corporate control while keeping public access rights largely intact.
ai_headline: Bill would give five Alaska towns Native corporations and federal land
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: S 2554 would let five southeast Alaska communities form Native corporations and receive about 115,000 acres of federal land.

Each corporation would get 100 shares of stock and about 23,040 acres of national forest land, totaling roughly 115,000 acres, with public hunting, fishing, and recreational access largely preserved.

title: Crystal Reservoir Conveyance Act
ai_summary:
This bill would transfer ownership of Crystal Reservoir and about 45 acres of surrounding land in Ouray County, Colorado, from the U.S. Forest Service to the City of Ouray. The transfer includes the reservoir itself, Full Moon Dam, a spillway, an outlet, an irrigation ditch, and the water rights tied to these features. The land would be given to the city for free, though the city would have to pay for any land surveys needed to complete the transfer, and the federal government would cover other transfer costs.

In exchange for receiving the land, the city would have to follow several rules. It must keep the area open to the public forever for recreation like fishing, without charging any access fees. It cannot build commercial development on the land, aside from what's needed to maintain the dam and reservoir. The city also takes on full responsibility for maintaining and repairing the dam and related infrastructure going forward, and must grant the Forest Service continued access rights for any existing trails or roads crossing the property. If the city ever stops following these conditions, the federal government could take the land back.

This bill mainly affects the City of Ouray, Colorado, and its residents, who would gain local control over a water source used for irrigation and other purposes, along with the responsibility of maintaining it. It could also affect recreational users of the area, such as anglers and hikers, since public access must be preserved permanently. More broadly, this is a local land-transfer bill and would have little to no effect on people outside this specific area of Colorado.
ai_headline: Bill would transfer Crystal Reservoir land to City of Ouray for free
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

The Forest Service can take the land back if the city violates these conditions.

title: Lewis & Clark Regional Water System Expansion Feasibility Study Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Secretary of the Interior to study whether it would be feasible to expand the Lewis & Clark Regional Water System, a rural water supply network that provides drinking and industrial water to communities in Iowa, Minnesota, and South Dakota. The study would look at increasing both the capacity and the geographic reach of the system so it could serve more towns, rural areas, and businesses. After the study is finished, the Secretary must write a report recommending whether the expansion project should be approved for construction and how much of the cost local users versus the federal government should each pay, with local sources covering at least 25% of construction costs.

The bill sets up a cost-sharing arrangement for the study itself: the federal government would pay up to half the study's cost, while the Lewis & Clark Regional Water System organization would cover the rest. Congress would authorize $10 million for this study, and the Secretary's authority to carry it out would expire 10 years after the law passes. The report would be shared with relevant congressional committees and made available to the public.

This bill mainly affects residents, farmers, and businesses in the three-state region served by the water system, since an eventual expansion could bring reliable water access to more communities. It also affects federal and state agencies, Tribal governments, and local authorities who would be consulted during the study, as well taxpayers, since federal money would fund part of the study and potentially part of any future construction.
ai_headline: Study ordered on expanding Lewis & Clark rural water system
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

title: SAFEGUARDS Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the SAFEGUARDS Act of 2025, deals with the "9/11 Security Fee" that airline passengers pay on their tickets. That fee was originally created to help pay for aviation security, but over the years some of that money has been redirected to other government spending instead of being used specifically for security improvements. This bill says Congress believes that practice should stop by 2027, and that all the fee money should go toward actual aviation security purposes, like screening equipment and staffing.

To make this happen, the bill changes how the fee money is divided into two specific funds. First, it increases the amount that must go into the existing Aviation Security Capital Fund, from $250 million per year up to $500 million per year starting in fiscal year 2026. Second, it creates a brand-new fund called the Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund, which would receive an additional $250 million per year. This new fund is specifically meant to pay for buying, installing, and maintaining security screening technology at airport checkpoints and exit lanes, such as upgraded scanners and detection equipment. The bill even allows the TSA to reimburse some technology projects going back to January 2023.

This bill mainly affects airline passengers (who pay the fee), the Transportation Security Administration (which manages the funds and equipment), and airports (which may receive upgraded security technology). Indirectly, it could affect general government spending decisions, since less fee revenue would be available for non-security purposes if the diversion of funds is phased out as described.
ai_headline: Bill would redirect 9/11 security fee fully to airport screening
last_action_text: Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: The SAFEGUARDS Act would stop diverting the 9/11 airline fee and boost security funding to $750 million a year by 2026.

It also creates a new Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund that would get an additional $250 million per year for screening equipment, and it states Congress's intent to end other diversion of the 9/11 fee by 2027.
ai_sections.who: Airline passengers who pay the 9/11 Security Fee, the Transportation Security Administration, and airports that may receive upgraded screening technology.
ai_sections.why: Redirecting fee revenue toward security purposes would reduce the amount available for other government spending that has relied on this money in the past.
ai_sections.cost: The bill raises the Aviation Security Capital Fund to $500 million per year and adds a new $250 million-per-year fund for checkpoint technology, with some reimbursements allowed back to January 2023.

title: Providing congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "California State Motor Vehicle and Engine Pollution Control Standards; Heavy-Duty Vehicle and Engine Emission Warranty and Maintenance Provisions; Advanced Clean Trucks; Zero Emission Airport Shuttle; Zero-Emission Power Train Certification; Waiver of Preemption; Notice of Decision".
ai_summary:
This bill cancels a federal approval that had allowed California to enforce its own stricter pollution rules for heavy-duty trucks and buses. Under the Clean Air Act, California can ask the EPA for a "waiver" to set vehicle emission standards tougher than federal ones, and other states can choose to follow California's rules instead of the national standard. In 2023, the EPA granted California this waiver for its "Advanced Clean Trucks" program, which included requirements like phasing in zero-emission trucks, rules for zero-emission airport shuttles, and warranty/maintenance standards for heavy-duty engines. This bill uses a special process called the Congressional Review Act to formally reject that EPA approval, meaning the waiver no longer has legal effect.

In practical terms, this stops California (and the states that had adopted California's stricter truck rules) from requiring truck makers and fleet operators to follow those specific zero-emission and clean-truck standards under this waiver. It mainly affects truck and engine manufacturers, trucking companies, airport shuttle operators, and states that follow California's vehicle emissions rules rather than the federal standard. Supporters of blocking the rule argued it eases regulatory burden and cost on businesses, while supporters of the original EPA rule argued it helped reduce air pollution and push cleaner vehicle technology; this resolution does not take a position itself, but simply eliminates the waiver.

This bill passed the House on April 30, 2025, passed the Senate on May 22, 2025, and was signed into law on June 12, 2025, becoming Public Law 119-15.
ai_headline: Congress revokes California's EPA waiver for clean truck rules
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-15.

ai_sections.tldr: This law cancels EPA's 2023 approval letting California enforce stricter zero-emission truck rules.

title: Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, HR 5167, is the annual funding authorization for U.S. intelligence agencies for fiscal year 2026. It covers organizations like the CIA, NSA, and other agencies that make up the intelligence community, giving them legal permission to spend money on their operations. Most of the actual dollar amounts are kept in a classified section attached to the bill, which is not public, so specific budget figures for spy satellites, data collection, personnel, and other intelligence programs are not disclosed to the general public, though they are shared with congressional committees and the President.

The bill does specify a few public numbers: $642 million for the Intelligence Community Management Account (which funds the office of the Director of National Intelligence, the official who oversees and coordinates all intelligence agencies) and $514 million for the CIA's retirement and disability fund, which supports pensions and disability payments for CIA employees. The bill also includes standard legal safeguards, clarifying that this funding does not authorize any intelligence activity that isn't already allowed under the Constitution or existing law, and it allows for pay and benefit increases for intelligence community employees if those increases are separately authorized by other laws.

This bill mainly affects federal intelligence agencies, their employees, and retirees, since it determines their budgets and operating authority for the year. Indirectly, it affects all Americans, since intelligence agencies are responsible for national security, counterterrorism, and foreign intelligence gathering. However, because most spending details are classified, the general public and even most lawmakers outside the intelligence committees won't see exactly how the money is used.
ai_headline: Bill sets 2026 intelligence budget, keeps most spending figures classified
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 339.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 5167 authorizes fiscal year 2026 funding for U.S. intelligence agencies, but most dollar figures remain classified.

title: Love Lives On Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Love Lives On Act of 2025, changes federal rules about benefits for surviving spouses of military veterans and service members when those spouses remarry. Under current law, remarrying can cause a surviving spouse to lose certain benefits they received because their husband or wife died while serving in or having served in the military. This bill removes some of those penalties.

Specifically, the bill allows surviving spouses who remarry to keep receiving Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (a benefit for families of veterans who died from service-related causes) and certain other related payments, regardless of remarriage. It also changes the Survivor Benefit Plan, a military pension program, so that spouses of service members who died while on active duty won't lose their monthly annuity payments just because they remarried. Some spouses who remarried before turning 55, and lost these payments in the past, would have their payments restarted. Additionally, the bill expands TRICARE, the military's health insurance program, so that a widow or widower who remarried and whose new marriage later ended through death, divorce, or annulment can qualify as a dependent again and regain health coverage.

This bill mainly affects surviving spouses of veterans and military service members, especially those who chose to remarry after their spouse's death and lost financial or health benefits as a result. It does not affect the general public, but it could restore or extend income and health coverage for thousands of military widows and widowers nationwide.
ai_headline: Bill would let military widows and widowers remarry without losing benefits
last_action_text: Committee on Veterans' Affairs. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: The Love Lives On Act of 2025 would let surviving military spouses remarry without losing survivor benefits and health coverage.

It lets them keep receiving Dependency and Indemnity Compensation and Survivor Benefit Plan annuities regardless of remarriage, restarts payments for some who lost them after remarrying before age 55, and lets remarried spouses regain TRICARE coverage if their new marriage ends through death, divorce, or annulment.
ai_sections.who: Surviving spouses of veterans and service members who died from service-related causes, particularly those who remarried after their spouse's death, are affected.

title: Providing congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "California State Motor Vehicle and Engine and Nonroad Engine Pollution Control Standards; The "Omnibus" Low NOX Regulation; Waiver of Preemption; Notice of Decision".
ai_summary:
This bill cancels a federal approval that had allowed California to enforce its own stricter pollution rules for heavy-duty trucks and engines, known as the "Omnibus" Low NOx Regulation. Under the Clean Air Act, California is normally allowed to set tougher vehicle emissions standards than the rest of the country, but it needs a special waiver from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to do so. The EPA had granted that waiver in January 2025, which would have let California require truck and engine manufacturers to sharply cut nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions, a major contributor to smog and respiratory problems. This resolution uses a special power Congress has, called the Congressional Review Act, to overturn that EPA decision, meaning the waiver—and California's stricter rule—no longer has any legal effect.

This mainly affects truck and engine manufacturers, trucking companies, and residents of California and other states that often adopt California's vehicle emissions standards. Without the waiver, California cannot enforce these tougher NOx limits, so manufacturers won't be required to meet the stricter standards there. This could mean lower compliance costs for truck makers and fleet operators, but it may also mean higher levels of air pollution in areas that were expecting the cleaner-engine requirements to take effect. The bill was passed by the House and Senate and signed into law, officially ending the waiver.
ai_headline: Congress cancels EPA waiver for California truck pollution rule
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-17.

title: Gerald E. Connolly Esophageal Cancer Awareness Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, named after former Congressman Gerald E. Connolly, directs a federal watchdog agency to study esophageal cancer's impact on federal employees and retirees. It does not create new programs, funding, or screening requirements. Instead, it requires the Government Accountability Office (GAO) to produce a report within one year that looks at two things: how much money is being spent on esophageal cancer treatment for people covered by the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program (FEHBP), and how often high-risk individuals in that program are actually getting screened for the disease according to current medical guidelines.

The bill includes a series of findings explaining why lawmakers consider this issue urgent. It notes that esophageal cancer is one of the fastest-growing and deadliest cancers in the country, with low survival rates mainly because it's usually caught too late. It also references medical guidance suggesting that people with certain risk factors—such as being male, over age 50, a smoker, obese, having chronic acid reflux, or having a family history of the disease—should get screened earlier through endoscopy, since early detection dramatically improves survival odds.

This law mainly affects federal employees and retirees, since the report focuses specifically on health data from the FEHBP. It doesn't change insurance coverage or require screenings for the general public. Its practical effect is informational: the GAO's findings could be used later by Congress to consider whether new policies, screening requirements, or funding are needed to catch esophageal cancer earlier among federal workers and retirees.

title: Medicare Advantage MLR Transparency Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Medicare Advantage MLR Transparency Act, would require Medicare Advantage insurance companies to publicly share more detailed financial information about their plans. Medicare Advantage plans are private insurance plans that people can choose instead of traditional government-run Medicare. Starting in 2029, insurance companies offering these plans would have to post information on their websites showing how much money each plan brings in, how much is spent on actual medical claims versus overhead and administrative costs, and what percentage of revenue goes to each category. This is often called the "medical loss ratio," which measures how much of the money collected in premiums actually goes toward patient care versus company profits and expenses.

The bill also requires that when insurers provide plan benefit information electronically, it must be presented in a standardized, easy-to-compare format similar to the format already used by other health insurance plans under existing law. This is meant to make it easier for people to compare different Medicare Advantage plans side by side.

This bill mainly affects people age 65 and older, or people with certain disabilities, who are enrolled in or considering enrolling in Medicare Advantage plans. It also affects the insurance companies that offer these plans, since they would face new reporting and disclosure requirements. The goal is to give consumers clearer information to help them make informed choices, and to give regulators and the public more insight into how insurance companies are spending the money they receive from Medicare.
ai_headline: Medicare Advantage insurers would face new spending disclosure rules by 2029
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 42 - 0.

title: Shandra Eisenga Human Cell and Tissue Product Safety Act
ai_summary:
This bill, named after a patient advocate, aims to improve safety and oversight for human cell and tissue products—things like donated skin, bone, tendons, and other tissue-based products used in medical procedures (not organs for transplant in the traditional sense, though related education applies there too). It requires the Department of Health and Human Services to run a public education campaign teaching healthcare providers and patients about the risks and benefits of these products, how to talk to patients and families about donation, and what screening tests are available to check donor tissue safety.

The bill also creates real financial consequences for companies or individuals who violate federal safety rules for these products, allowing fines up to $20,000 per violation (with extra daily penalties for ongoing violations), plus repayment of the product's value, capped at $10 million per case. This is meant to hold tissue processors and distributors accountable if they cut corners on safety requirements.

Finally, the bill pushes the FDA to be more transparent and organized about how it regulates this industry. It requires the FDA to publish information online about inspections, registered tissue facilities, and how quickly it responds to companies seeking guidance through its "Tissue Reference Group." It also sets up a public comment process and requires a report to Congress by September 2026 with recommendations on modernizing these regulations. Overall, this bill affects patients receiving tissue-based treatments, healthcare providers, tissue banks and processing companies, and FDA regulatory operations—aiming to make the system safer, more transparent, and better understood by both the public and industry.
ai_headline: Bill sets fines up to $20,000 for tissue product safety violations
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
