title: Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026
ai_summary:
This bill is a large government funding package that provides money to run major parts of the federal government through September 30, 2026 (the end of the fiscal year). Instead of passing separate bills for each agency, Congress bundled several spending bills together into one "consolidated" law. It covers the Department of Defense, the Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education, the Department of Transportation and Housing and Urban Development, financial services and general government agencies (including the Treasury and the courts), the State Department and foreign aid programs, and includes extra provisions extending certain expiring programs and making technical fixes to earlier laws.

The Defense portion, which is the largest section shown, sets exact dollar amounts for paying and equipping soldiers, sailors, airmen, Marines, and Space Force members, including active-duty personnel, National Guard, and reserves. It also funds military operations and maintenance, new weapons and equipment purchases (like ships, aircraft, and ammunition), research and development of new military technology, health care for service members through the Defense Health Program, cleanup of environmental contamination at military sites, and counter-drug and counterterrorism programs. It sets rules on how the Pentagon can shift money between accounts, requires regular reports to Congress on how funds are used, and places some restrictions, such as banning ship construction in foreign shipyards and prohibiting the purchase of certain weapons systems in some cases.

This bill affects nearly everyone in some way: military service members and their families who depend on personnel and health care funding, defense contractors and workers who build ships, aircraft, and weapons, government employees at agencies like Labor, HHS, Education, Transportation, HUD, Treasury, and the courts whose operations depend on this money, and Americans who rely on federal programs in health, education, housing, and transportation. It also includes a special one-time payment to the widow of a deceased member of Congress, a routine practice in these funding bills. Because the text is very long and detailed, the portions covering non-defense agencies (like Health and Human Services, Transportation, and State Department programs) are not fully shown here, but they follow the same pattern of setting specific funding levels and rules for how that money can be spent.
ai_headline: Massive spending package would fund defense and civilian agencies through 2026
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-75.

The largest section funds military personnel, operations, equipment, research, health care, and environmental cleanup, with rules on transferring funds and restrictions like banning foreign shipyard construction.

title: Commerce, Justice, Science; Energy and Water Development; and Interior and Environment Appropriations Act, 2026
ai_summary:
This bill is a large government funding law that keeps several federal agencies operating through September 2026. It combines three separate funding packages: one for the Commerce Department, Justice Department, and science agencies; one for the Army Corps of Engineers, Department of Energy, and water projects; and one for the Interior Department and Environmental Protection Agency. Rather than creating new policy, its main purpose is to set specific dollar amounts that each agency, office, and program can spend for the fiscal year, along with rules about how that money can be used, moved between accounts, or carried over into future years.

Within the Commerce section, money is directed to things like patent and trademark processing, export controls, weather and ocean research (NOAA), the Census Bureau, and manufacturing support programs. The Justice Department portion funds the FBI, DEA, ATF, U.S. Marshals, federal prosecutors, immigration courts, and the federal prison system, including specific amounts for prisoner detention, witness protection, and drug enforcement task forces. The bill also includes detailed conditions, such as requiring agencies to notify Congress before shifting funds between programs, limiting how much can be transferred without approval, and setting aside money for specific local "congressionally directed" projects.

This bill affects nearly everyone indirectly, since it funds core government functions like law enforcement, patent processing, weather forecasting, economic data collection, and federal prisons. It directly affects federal employees and contractors in these agencies, businesses that rely on patent and trade services, fishing communities affected by NOAA programs, immigrants going through immigration courts, and communities near federal prisons or research facilities. Because it's a routine annual appropriations bill, it does not change major policies but determines the practical funding level and operating rules for these agencies for the year.

title: VA Budget Shortfall Accountability Act
ai_summary:
This law, called the VA Budget Shortfall Accountability Act, requires government investigators to figure out why the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) ran short on money. Specifically, it directs the Comptroller General, who leads the Government Accountability Office (GAO), to study why the Veterans Benefits Administration ran out of funding in 2024 and why the Veterans Health Administration was expected to face a similar shortfall in 2025. The review must look at how the VA spent its money compared to its official spending plan, whether money was moved between accounts, why any major spending changes happened, and whether the VA's budget estimates were accurate. The GAO must also suggest ways the VA can improve its financial planning and avoid running short on funds in the future.

After finishing this first review, the GAO must send a written report to the VA Secretary, who then has 30 days to share it with Congress's veterans' affairs and appropriations committees. The law doesn't stop there: it requires the GAO to repeat this same kind of review every year for five more years, each time examining the VA's most recent full budget year. This creates an ongoing system of financial oversight and public accountability for VA spending.

This bill mainly affects how the VA manages and reports on its budget, rather than directly changing veterans' benefits or services. However, veterans could be indirectly affected if these reviews lead to changes in how the VA plans and manages money for health care and benefits programs. It also affects VA leadership, who must respond to and report on these financial reviews, and members of Congress, who will receive regular updates to help them monitor whether the VA is using taxpayer money effectively and avoiding future funding gaps.
ai_headline: GAO ordered to probe VA's 2024 funding shortfall and repeat reviews yearly
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-71.

title: Health Care Price Certainty for All Americans Act
ai_summary:
This bill, the Health Care Price Certainty for All Americans Act, expands federal rules requiring hospitals, ambulatory surgical centers, medical laboratories, and imaging providers to publicly post their prices. Starting between 2027 and 2028, these facilities would have to publish their full list of standard charges, negotiated rates with insurance companies, and cash prices for at least 300 common "shoppable" services (like MRIs, blood tests, or scheduled procedures) in formats regular people can actually read and compare, not just complicated spreadsheets. Facilities would also need to post signed statements certifying the information is accurate, and Medicare officials would regularly check compliance. Hospitals, labs, and surgical centers that don't follow the rules could face escalating fines, with harsher penalties for repeat or willful violations, though there are exceptions for rural or struggling facilities facing hardship.

The bill also updates requirements for employer health insurance plans. Starting in 2029, group health plans would have to give members real-time tools to check what they'd personally owe (copays, deductibles, prior authorization rules, etc.) before getting care, and must publicly post negotiated rates with providers and pharmacies, including drug pricing information. This is meant to replace an earlier, more limited price-comparison-tool requirement.

This bill mainly affects hospitals, surgical centers, labs, imaging centers, health insurance companies, and employer health plans, who would face new administrative and legal obligations along with potential fines for noncompliance. Patients and consumers would be the intended beneficiaries, gaining easier access to price information so they can compare costs before receiving care. The Department of Health and Human Services (through the Secretary) would be responsible for writing detailed rules, setting formats, monitoring compliance, and enforcing penalties.
ai_headline: Bill would force hospitals and insurers to post real prices by 2027
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 25 - 15.

title: Essential Caregivers Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Essential Caregivers Act of 2026, would guarantee nursing home residents, hospital patients in long-term care settings, and people in certain rehabilitation or intellectual disability facilities the right to designate up to two "essential caregivers" who can visit them in person, even during situations where a facility has otherwise shut down regular visitation, such as during a disease outbreak or pandemic. Residents could choose these caregivers themselves, or a family member or representative could choose for them if the resident isn't mentally able to decide. Facilities could briefly restrict in-person visits for the first seven days of a shutdown, but only if they offer video calls instead, and they could deny access to a caregiver who is sick with a contagious illness or who won't follow the same safety rules as staff. However, residents receiving end-of-life care could not be denied caregiver visits under any circumstances.

The bill applies to nursing homes, skilled nursing facilities, long-term care hospitals, inpatient rehabilitation facilities, and intermediate care facilities for people with intellectual disabilities that participate in Medicare or Medicaid. It also speeds up how complaints about denied caregiver access are handled, requiring investigations to be prioritized and resolved within three days. Importantly, the bill would prevent the government from waiving these caregiver-visit rules even during a declared public health emergency, which was a major complaint from families during COVID-19 lockdowns when many nursing home residents were cut off from loved ones for extended periods. If passed, the Department of Health and Human Services would have 18 months to write detailed rules, and the requirements would take effect one year after the bill becomes law. This mainly affects elderly and disabled residents of care facilities, their families and caregivers, and the facilities themselves, which would need to update their policies and staff training to comply.
ai_headline: Bill would guarantee nursing home visits even during outbreak lockdowns
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 38 - 0.

Facilities can briefly limit visits for seven days if video calls are offered, and can deny sick or rule-breaking caregivers, but end-of-life patients can never be denied visits.

ai_sections.why: Facilities would need to update policies, training, and complaint-handling procedures, and the government could no longer waive these visitation rights during public health emergencies.

title: Medicare Access to Rural Anesthesiology Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how Medicare pays for anesthesiologist services at certain small rural hospitals. Right now, hospital costs (Part A) and doctor services (Part B) are usually billed separately under Medicare. This bill would let small rural hospitals and "critical access hospitals" bill Medicare for their anesthesiologist's services as part of the hospital's overall costs (Part A), using a "reasonable cost" reimbursement method, instead of having the anesthesiologist bill Medicare separately under Part B.

To qualify, a hospital would need to meet specific conditions: it must have employed or contracted with no more than one full-time anesthesiologist as of the bill's enactment, have had 800 or fewer surgical procedures requiring anesthesia in 2026 (or a higher number set by Medicare officials), and the anesthesiologist must agree not to bill Medicare Part B separately for that work. Hospitals would need to keep meeting the procedure-volume limit each year to continue qualifying.

This mainly affects small, low-volume rural hospitals that struggle to keep anesthesiologists on staff, since separate Part B billing may not generate enough income to justify employing one. By allowing cost-based Part A reimbursement instead, the bill aims to make it financially easier for these hospitals to retain anesthesia services, which supporters argue helps preserve surgical and emergency care access in rural communities. Patients in these areas could benefit from continued access to procedures requiring anesthesia, while Medicare's payment method for these specific services would shift from physician billing to hospital cost reporting.
ai_headline: Bill lets small rural hospitals bill Medicare differently for anesthesia
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 41 - 0.

title: Less Bureaucracy, Better International Education Oversight Act
ai_summary:
This bill would move responsibility for certain international education programs from the Department of Education to the Department of State. Specifically, it transfers oversight of Title VI programs (which fund foreign language study, area studies centers, and international research at universities) and the Fulbright-Hays program (which provides grants and fellowships for Americans to study or do research abroad) to the State Department. It also eliminates a specific program called the Institute for International Public Policy, which currently helps prepare students from historically Black colleges and other minority-serving institutions for careers in international affairs.

The bill spells out the mechanics of this kind of government reorganization: transferring staff, budgets, contracts, and records from Education to State; making sure existing grants, permits, and legal agreements stay valid; continuing any ongoing lawsuits or applications without interruption; and giving the Office of Management and Budget authority to sort out details, while ensuring the move doesn't increase the total number of federal employees. The changes would take effect six months after the bill becomes law, though the transfer could begin sooner.

This bill would mainly affect universities and colleges that receive Title VI grants for language and international studies programs, students and scholars who apply for Fulbright-Hays fellowships, and federal employees who currently administer these programs at the Department of Education, who would instead work under the Department of State. It could also affect minority-serving institutions that benefit from the Institute for International Public Policy, since that program would be eliminated entirely.

title: Less Bureaucracy, Better International Foreign Gift Transparency Act
ai_summary:
This bill moves responsibility for tracking foreign gifts and contracts given to U.S. colleges and universities from the Department of Education to the Department of State. Under current law (Section 117 of the Higher Education Act), colleges must report large gifts or contracts they receive from foreign sources, and the Department of Education currently collects and manages that information. title: Clarity for Compensation Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Clarity for Compensation Act, changes federal securities law to make clear that certain personal business entities set up by stockbrokers or financial advisers do not have to register as brokers themselves. Many financial advisers set up a personal company (often for tax or business purposes) to receive their pay from the brokerage firm they work for, rather than having the firm pay them directly as an individual. Under current rules, it can be unclear whether that personal company counts as a "broker" under the law, which would trigger extra registration and regulatory requirements. This bill creates a specific exemption for these personal service entities, as long as certain conditions are met.

To qualify for the exemption, the brokerage firm must control the amount and timing of payments to the personal entity and keep records of them, the personal entity cannot advertise itself as a broker or do any actual brokerage business, the firm must properly supervise the adviser, there must be a written agreement between the firm and the entity, and the entity can only be owned by the adviser or their immediate family members (or companies fully owned by them). The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) can also add more requirements. The personal entity must keep records available for review by the SEC and relevant industry regulators to prove it continues to qualify.

This bill mainly affects financial advisers and stockbrokers who use personal companies to manage their compensation, the brokerage firms that employ them, and regulators like the SEC. It's a technical fix intended to reduce legal uncertainty and paperwork burdens for these common business arrangements, without changing how customers are protected, since the brokerage firm remains responsible for supervision and compliance. The change would take effect 180 days after the bill becomes law.

title: ALERT Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the ALERT Act, is a response to aviation safety concerns, especially around near-miss incidents and mid-air collision risks involving helicopters and airplanes, such as those seen near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. It requires the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to study and eventually require aircraft to be equipped with better collision-avoidance technology, including upgraded systems for both airplanes (ACAS-Xa) and helicopters (ACAS-Xr), plus broader "collision mitigation technology" for smaller aircraft that don't currently have such systems. It sets deadlines for the FAA to study these technologies, form expert committees involving airlines, pilots, controllers, and manufacturers, propose rules, and finalize regulations over the next several years.

The bill also targets air traffic control operations directly. title: Emergency Conservation Program Improvement Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes how farmers, ranchers, and forest landowners can get government help paying for emergency repairs after disasters like floods, storms, or wildfires. Currently, under USDA's Emergency Conservation Program, producers often have to pay for repairs to fencing, farmland, or conservation structures out of their own pocket first, then get reimbursed later. This bill lets them instead request money upfront: up to 75% of the estimated cost before rebuilding or replacing damaged property, and up to 50% before doing repairs. This is meant to help farmers who don't have enough cash on hand to cover repairs immediately after a disaster.

The bill also expands what counts as a "wildfire" eligible for this aid. It clarifies that fires which spread due to natural causes can still qualify for payments even if the fire wasn't started naturally—including fires started by the federal government (such as a prescribed burn that got out of control)—as long as the spread of damage was due to natural conditions like wind or drought.

Finally, the bill makes a similar change to the Emergency Forest Restoration Program, which helps owners of private, non-industrial forest land recover from disasters. It allows those landowners to receive up to 75% of estimated costs upfront before doing the restoration work. If they don't use that money within 180 days, they must return it. Overall, this bill mainly affects farmers, ranchers, and private forest landowners who experience disaster damage, making it easier for them to afford repairs without needing to front all the costs themselves.
ai_headline: Bill would let farmers get disaster repair aid upfront, not just after
last_action_text: Received in the Senate.

title: American Broadband Deployment Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the American Broadband Deployment Act of 2025 (also referred to in the text as the Proportional Reviews for Broadband Deployment Act), changes the rules for how quickly cell phone companies and other wireless providers can upgrade or modify existing wireless equipment, like cell towers and antennas. Under current law, companies making certain changes to existing wireless facilities—known as "eligible facilities requests"—already benefit from a streamlined approval process. This bill goes further by saying that these projects no longer have to go through federal environmental reviews (required by the National Environmental Policy Act) or historical preservation reviews (required by the National Historic Preservation Act) before getting approved.

In practical terms, this means that when a company wants to add equipment to an existing cell tower, replace outdated wireless infrastructure, or make similar upgrades, federal agencies would not need to study the environmental impact or check whether the changes might affect historic sites. Supporters of this type of change generally argue it would speed up the rollout of better broadband and wireless service, especially in areas that need upgraded infrastructure. Critics of these kinds of exemptions generally worry that skipping environmental and historical reviews could lead to problems that would otherwise have been caught, such as harm to protected land, wildlife, or historic landmarks.

This bill would primarily affect telecommunications companies, federal agencies that currently conduct these reviews (such as the Federal Communications Commission and agencies involved in environmental or historical protection), and communities located near wireless infrastructure sites. Everyday residents could be affected if they live near existing cell towers slated for upgrades, own property near historic sites, or care about environmental protections in their area.
ai_headline: Bill would exempt cell tower upgrades from environmental, historic reviews
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 532.

Companies could add equipment or replace outdated infrastructure without these federal checks.

title: Combatting Money Laundering in Cyber Crime Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, known as the Combatting Money Laundering in Cyber Crime Act of 2025, expands the U.S. Secret Service's legal authority to investigate crimes involving digital assets like cryptocurrency and international cybercrime networks. It specifically allows Secret Service agents to investigate cases involving unlicensed money transmitting businesses, money laundering, and structured transactions (a tactic used to avoid bank reporting requirements). It also removes a limitation that previously restricted certain fraud investigations to only "federally insured" financial institutions, broadening the definition to match a wider legal standard used elsewhere in federal law.

The bill also extends the lifespan of two government programs. FinCEN Exchange, a partnership between the Treasury Department's financial crimes unit and private banks/law enforcement to share information on financial crime, would have its authorization extended from 5 to 10 years. Similarly, a program related to monitoring international financial institutions for compliance with North Korea sanctions would have its authorization extended from 6 to 10 years. Finally, the bill requires the Government Accountability Office (a nonpartisan government watchdog) to study how well a 2020 anti-money laundering law has been working, specifically looking at whether law enforcement can effectively detect and stop money laundering tied to cybercrime.

This bill would mainly affect federal law enforcement agencies (especially the Secret Service), financial institutions, cryptocurrency and money transmitting businesses, and government agencies involved in financial crime enforcement and sanctions monitoring. Everyday consumers would likely see indirect effects, such as potentially stronger protections against financial fraud and cybercrime, but the bill does not create new obligations for average citizens.

last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 530.

title: Withhold Member Pay During Shutdowns Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Withhold Member Pay During Shutdowns Act, would cut the pay of members of Congress for every day the federal government is shut down due to a lapse in funding. If a shutdown happens on any day during a pay period, the Senate and House payroll offices would subtract one day's worth of salary for each day the shutdown lasts.

Because the 27th Amendment to the Constitution prevents changes to congressional pay from taking effect until after the next election, the bill includes a temporary workaround. Until after the November 2026 general election, any withheld pay would not simply disappear—it would be placed in an escrow account (a holding account) rather than paid out immediately. Once the pay reduction rules officially take effect after that election, any money left in escrow would be released back to the members. After that point, however, pay lost to a shutdown would be withheld permanently, not just delayed.

This bill would affect members of the U.S. House and Senate directly, tying their compensation to whether the government is funded and operating. It would not change pay or benefits for federal employees, contractors, or the general public, but it is designed to create a financial incentive for lawmakers to avoid government shutdowns by ensuring their own paychecks are affected when funding lapses.
ai_headline: Bill would dock lawmakers' pay for every day of a shutdown
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 10 - 0.

After that election, any escrowed funds would be released, and future shutdown pay cuts would become permanent.

title: FENCES Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the FENCES Act, changes how the Clean Air Act treats air pollution that drifts into the United States from other countries. Under current law, if a state can show that it would meet national air quality standards except for pollution coming from outside the U.S., it gets some relief from federal penalties. This bill clarifies that this protection applies whether the foreign pollution comes from human activities (like factories or vehicles) or from natural sources (like wildfires or dust storms). It also says that areas cannot be labeled "nonattainment" (meaning they fail to meet air quality standards) if the only reason they fail is because of pollution blowing in from outside the country.

The bill also adds a new provision protecting states from certain penalties and fees related to failing to meet ozone or particulate matter (soot/dust) pollution standards. States would be excused from these penalties if they can prove the failure was due to pollution from outside their area, unusual events like wildfires, or vehicle emissions they cannot realistically control—as long as they are already doing everything within their power to reduce vehicle pollution. States would need to renew this proof every five years, and even if they get this penalty relief, they would still have to keep working toward meeting clean air standards overall.

This bill mainly affects state environmental agencies, industries operating in areas with air quality problems (especially in the West and Southwest, where wildfire smoke and dust from Mexico or Canada can be significant), and residents in regions bordering other countries or prone to wildfires. It could reduce federal pressure and financial penalties on states dealing with pollution sources beyond their control, but it does not change requirements for pollution caused within U.S. borders by human activity.
ai_headline: Bill would shield states from penalties over foreign air pollution
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

ai_sections.tldr: The FENCES Act would excuse states from federal air quality penalties caused by pollution drifting in from other countries.

Areas cannot be labeled "nonattainment" if foreign pollution is the sole cause of failure. States must also prove every five years that they are already limiting vehicle emissions as much as possible to qualify for this relief, and must keep working toward overall clean air goals.

title: To require the Secretary of Homeland Security to designate Haiti for temporary protected status.
ai_summary:
This bill would require the Secretary of Homeland Security to officially designate Haiti for Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for 18 months, starting August 3, 2025. TPS is a program that allows people from countries facing serious problems—like natural disasters, war, or political instability—to legally stay and work in the United States temporarily, without fear of being deported back to a dangerous situation. Haiti has faced ongoing gang violence, political turmoil, and humanitarian crises in recent years, which is the likely reason lawmakers are pushing for this protection.

Unlike the normal process, where the Secretary of Homeland Security has discretion over whether to grant TPS to a country, this bill would make the designation mandatory by law. This removes any uncertainty about whether Haiti's TPS status will continue or be renewed, since the decision would already be set in law rather than left to an executive branch official's judgment.

This bill mainly affects Haitian nationals already living in the United States who may qualify for TPS, allowing them to continue living and working here legally during the designated period. It could also affect U.S. employers who hire Haitian TPS holders, as well as immigration officials and agencies responsible for processing and managing TPS applications. The bill was introduced by a bipartisan group of representatives and referred to the House Judiciary Committee for further consideration.

title: RED Tape Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the RED Tape Act, would change a section of the Clean Air Act that currently requires the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to review and publicly comment on certain federal government actions. Right now, the EPA is required to review proposed legislation, new federally funded construction projects, major federal agency actions that affect the environment, and proposed regulations from other federal departments or agencies. This bill would narrow that requirement so the EPA would only be required to review and comment on proposed legislation, removing its duty to review federal construction projects, major agency actions, and regulations proposed by other agencies.

In practical terms, this means the EPA would have less oversight authority over other federal agencies' projects and regulations. Currently, the EPA acts as a kind of environmental watchdog, checking whether other agencies' plans and rules might harm the environment. If this bill passes, that check would be significantly reduced, and the EPA's formal review role would be limited mainly to reviewing bills being considered by Congress.

This change would primarily affect federal agencies that build infrastructure (like transportation or energy projects) or issue their own regulations, since they would no longer need EPA environmental review and comment before moving forward. It could also affect communities and environmental groups that rely on EPA reviews to flag potential environmental problems in federal projects early in the process. Supporters might argue this reduces duplicate bureaucratic reviews, while critics might worry it removes a layer of environmental oversight.
ai_headline: Bill would narrow EPA's authority to review other agencies' projects
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

Currently the EPA must review proposed legislation, federally funded construction projects, major federal agency actions affecting the environment, and other agencies' proposed regulations; under this bill, EPA would only be required to review proposed legislation.

title: FIRM Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the FIRM Act, would stop federal banking regulators from using "reputational risk" as a factor when they examine and supervise banks and credit unions. Reputational risk refers to the idea that a bank's business with certain customers or industries could create bad publicity or public backlash, which regulators have sometimes used as a reason to discourage banks from serving those customers. The bill points to "Operation Choke Point," a past government effort where regulators reportedly pressured banks to cut ties with certain legal but controversial businesses, as an example of this practice being misused.

The bill would require agencies like the FDIC, Federal Reserve, OCC, National Credit Union Administration, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to remove any mention of reputational risk from their rules, guidance, and examination materials. It would also ban these agencies from creating new rules based on reputational risk, conducting examinations related to it, issuing findings or ratings based on it, or taking enforcement actions tied to it. Within 180 days of becoming law, each agency would have to report back to Congress confirming they made these changes.

This bill would primarily affect banks, credit unions, and the federal agencies that oversee them. Supporters argue it would protect legal businesses and individuals—regardless of their industry or political views—from losing access to banking services simply because regulators worried about public perception. It would not change other reasons regulators can still examine banks, such as financial safety, fraud, or legal compliance issues unrelated to reputational concerns.
ai_headline: Bill would bar bank regulators from citing "reputational risk"
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 131.

ai_sections.tldr: The FIRM Act would ban federal banking regulators from using reputational risk in bank exams or enforcement.

Agencies would have to strip references to reputational risk from rules, guidance, and exam materials, and could not issue findings, ratings, or enforcement actions based on it. Each agency must report to Congress within 180 days confirming compliance.

title: Small Bank Holding Company Relief Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require the Federal Reserve to change the rules that decide which bank and savings and loan holding companies count as "small" for regulatory purposes. Currently, the Federal Reserve's policy statement sets a lower asset limit to define a small bank holding company. This bill would direct the Fed to raise that limit to $25 billion in consolidated assets within 180 days of the bill becoming law.

Being classified as a "small bank holding company" matters because it comes with lighter regulatory requirements, particularly around capital rules that apply to larger, more complex banking institutions. By raising the threshold to $25 billion, more mid-sized bank and savings and loan holding companies would qualify for this simpler regulatory treatment, potentially reducing their compliance costs and paperwork.

This bill would primarily affect banks and savings institutions that fall under this new, higher threshold, along with their holding companies, allowing more of them to operate under lighter regulatory oversight. It could also indirectly affect bank customers and communities served by these institutions, since reduced regulatory burden may influence how banks manage capital, lending, and growth. Consumer advocates and regulators sometimes debate whether raising such thresholds appropriately balances easing burdens on smaller banks against ensuring adequate oversight of the financial system.

title: Bank Failure Prevention Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the Federal Reserve reviews applications from bank holding companies and savings and loan holding companies that want to acquire or merge with other financial institutions. Currently, the clock for the Fed's 90-day decision deadline doesn't start until the Fed considers the application "complete," which can allow the review process to drag on if the Fed keeps requesting more information. This bill sets firm deadlines: the Fed must tell an applicant within 30 days (or 60 days for complex cases) whether their application is complete or what's missing. If the applicant responds to a request for more information, the application is automatically considered complete unless the Fed says otherwise within 30 days. Most importantly, the Fed must approve or deny the application within 90 days of the original submission date no matter what, and if it fails to act in time, the application is automatically approved by default.

The bill also limits what the Fed can consider when deciding if an application is complete, restricting review to information from the applicant only, not information from outside third parties like community groups or competitors who might raise concerns.

This primarily affects banks and savings institutions seeking to merge or be acquired, giving them more certainty and speed in the approval process. It also affects the Federal Reserve, which will have less flexibility to extend reviews for complicated deals, and indirectly affects consumers and communities, since faster, more limited reviews could mean less opportunity for outside input on bank mergers that affect local banking access, competition, or financial stability.

title: Merchant Banking Modernization Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change a rule about how long certain financial companies can hold onto private business investments. Under current banking law, financial holding companies (large banking organizations that qualify for expanded powers) are allowed to make "merchant banking investments," meaning they can buy ownership stakes in non-financial companies, similar to how a private equity firm invests in businesses. However, regulators limit how long these banking organizations can hold onto such investments before they must sell them. This bill would require that regulators generally allow these investments to be held for at least 15 years, which is longer than current typical holding periods. It would also apply this new 15-year minimum retroactively to investments that were already made before the bill becomes law.

In practical terms, this bill mainly affects large bank holding companies and financial holding companies that engage in merchant banking, along with the businesses they invest in. By extending the allowed holding period, the bill would give these banking organizations more flexibility and time to manage, grow, and eventually sell their investments, rather than being pressured to sell within a shorter timeframe. Supporters of such changes often argue it allows investments to mature and generate better returns, while critics of extended bank involvement in commercial businesses sometimes raise concerns about banks holding long-term stakes in non-financial companies. Everyday consumers would not be directly affected by this bill, but it could influence how banks structure their investment activities and interact with businesses they help fund.

title: FDIC Board Accountability Act
ai_summary:
HR 3446, the "FDIC Board Accountability Act," would change how the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) board of directors is structured. The FDIC is the federal agency that insures money in bank accounts and helps oversee the banking system. Currently, its board includes several presidentially appointed members, along with the head of another banking regulator and the director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) as a voting member. This bill would remove the CFPB director's voting power, making that person a non-voting observer instead. It also changes the makeup of the four Senate-confirmed board members, requiring at least one to have state banking supervisory experience and another to have experience working in or overseeing smaller banks (those with less than $10 billion in assets).

The bill also adds term limits: no one could be appointed to the FDIC board for more than two terms, and no one could serve on the board for more than twelve years total, regardless of how their service is structured.

This bill mainly affects how the FDIC is governed rather than everyday banking customers directly. It would matter most to bank regulators, the CFPB, community and regional banks, and policymakers interested in how much influence consumer protection officials have over bank regulation decisions. Supporters of changes like this often argue they ensure more diverse regulatory expertise and prevent any one appointee from serving indefinitely, while critics of removing the CFPB director's vote may see it as reducing consumer protection input in FDIC decisions. The bill does not change deposit insurance coverage or affect individual bank accounts.

title: SAFE Guidance Act
ai_summary:
HR 4460, called the "SAFE Guidance Act," would require certain financial regulatory agencies to add a clear disclaimer statement to any guidance documents they issue. The agencies covered include the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Treasury Department, Federal Reserve, FDIC, SEC, and several other banking and housing regulators. Whenever these agencies release guidance—meaning informal advice or interpretations about how to follow laws and regulations, as opposed to official rules that go through the formal rulemaking process—they would have to prominently state on the first page that the guidance is not legally binding, does not create any rights or obligations, and that failing to follow it doesn't automatically mean someone broke the law.

The bill is meant to draw a clear line between formal regulations, which go through public notice-and-comment procedures and carry legal force, and informal guidance, which agencies sometimes use to signal expectations without going through that formal process. Supporters of this kind of measure generally argue that agencies sometimes use guidance as a way to enforce rules without the accountability of formal rulemaking, and this bill would force agencies to be upfront that such documents aren't legally enforceable in the same way.

This bill would primarily affect banks, credit unions, mortgage lenders, investment firms, and other financial companies that are regulated by these agencies, since they are the ones who read and rely on this guidance to understand what regulators expect. It could also affect consumers indirectly, since guidance often shapes how financial institutions handle things like lending practices, fair housing rules, or consumer protections. The bill does not eliminate agencies' ability to issue guidance—it simply requires them to label it clearly so people understand its legal weight.

title: Bringing the Discount Window into the 21st Century Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Bringing the Discount Window into the 21st Century Act," requires the Federal Reserve to review and modernize its "discount window" system. The discount window is a program that lets banks borrow money directly from the Federal Reserve, usually to help them handle short-term cash shortages or financial emergencies. The bill requires the Federal Reserve to study whether this system is working well, especially whether its technology, communication methods, cybersecurity protections, and operating hours are keeping up with modern banking needs, including newer systems like FedNow, which allows instant payments.

Under the bill, the Federal Reserve would have to start this review within 60 days of the law passing and finish it within 240 days. The public would get a chance to comment on how well the discount window works and suggest improvements. After the review, the Fed would need to create a written plan to fix any problems found, with clear timelines and goals. It would also have to report its findings and improvement plan to Congress within a year, and the Fed Chair would need to testify about it. After that, the Fed and its Inspector General would submit yearly updates to Congress on how the improvements are going. Sensitive information, like cybersecurity weaknesses, could be kept confidential in a separate report.

This bill mainly affects the Federal Reserve System and the banks that use the discount window to borrow money, especially during financial stress. Indirectly, it could affect everyday consumers and the broader economy, since a more modern, reliable discount window could help prevent banking crises or reduce their impact. It does not change interest rates or lending rules directly—it focuses on oversight, technology, and reporting to make sure the system operates efficiently and safely.

title: Community Bank LIFT Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Community Bank LIFT Act, would change the rules for how small banks measure their financial safety cushion, known as the Community Bank Leverage Ratio (CBLR). Currently, banks with less than $10 billion in assets can qualify for this simplified system, and they must hold capital equal to somewhere between 8 and 10 percent of their assets. The bill would raise the size limit to $15 billion, letting more banks qualify, and would lower the required capital range to between 6 and 8 percent, meaning qualifying banks could operate with a smaller financial cushion than before.

The bill also requires federal banking regulators—the Federal Reserve, the Comptroller of the Currency, and the FDIC—to study the current system and report back to Congress within 150 days. This report must include recommendations on how to make the leverage ratio easier for smaller banks to use, including changes to how it's calculated, which banks qualify, and how banks can switch in and out of the simplified system. After reviewing that report, regulators would have up to a year to write and finalize official rules implementing the changes.

This bill mainly affects community banks—smaller, often local or regional banks—by potentially reducing the amount of regulatory paperwork and capital requirements they face. Supporters of this type of change generally argue it reduces unnecessary burdens on small banks so they can lend more to local businesses and communities. Critics of lowering capital requirements generally worry it could reduce the financial safety cushion banks have to absorb losses. Bank customers, small businesses, and local economies that rely on community banks could all be indirectly affected by how these rules are ultimately implemented.

title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027
ai_summary:
This bill, known as the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027, sets funding levels and policy guidelines for the U.S. military for the government's 2027 fiscal year. It's part of an annual process Congress goes through to authorize spending for the Department of Defense. The version shown here covers major categories like procurement (buying equipment and weapons systems), research and development (creating and testing new technology), and operation and maintenance (day-to-day running costs like training, fuel, repairs, and base operations). The actual dollar amounts are listed in separate funding tables referenced in the bill but not included in this excerpt.

In practice, this bill affects a wide range of people and organizations. Active-duty military members and their families are affected because the bill typically sets troop levels and can include pay and benefit provisions. Defense contractors and companies that build military equipment are affected because procurement and R&D funding determines what projects get financed. Communities near military bases are affected through operation and maintenance spending, which supports local jobs and infrastructure. Taxpayers are affected broadly since this authorizes how much money the government can spend on defense, though a separate appropriations bill is usually needed to actually release the funds.

This is an early version of the bill, introduced in the House and referred to the Armed Services Committee. It will likely be revised and expanded significantly, as NDAA bills typically include many more sections covering personnel policy, military construction, cybersecurity, and other defense-related matters before final passage.

title: TIER Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the TIER Act of 2025, changes the dollar amounts used to decide which banks count as "large" enough to face stricter federal oversight. After the 2008 financial crisis, laws like the Dodd-Frank Act set specific dollar thresholds (such as $250 billion in assets) to determine which banks and financial companies get extra scrutiny from regulators like the Federal Reserve. Those numbers were set years ago and haven't been updated, even though the overall economy has grown significantly since then. This bill raises those thresholds now—for example, changing $250 billion to $370 billion—to reflect that growth, and also raises related numbers in the Federal Reserve Act and other banking laws.

The bill also sets up a system for automatically updating these thresholds every five years going forward, based on how much the U.S. economy (measured by GDP) has grown. Starting in 2031, the Federal Reserve would recalculate the thresholds using economic growth data and publish the new numbers. It also requires regulators to periodically review other bank-related rules that use similar dollar cutoffs (even ones not written into law directly) and adjust them in a similar way, then report those changes to Congress.

This bill mainly affects large banks and financial companies, along with the regulators that oversee them—the Federal Reserve, the Comptroller of the Currency, and the FDIC. By raising the asset thresholds, fewer banks would fall into the "large bank" category that faces stricter rules, at least in the short term, until banks grow past the new limits. Everyday bank customers wouldn't see direct changes to their accounts, but the bill could affect how closely regulators watch the banking system for risks that could affect the broader economy.

title: FAIR Exams Act
ai_summary:
HR 940, the "FAIR Exams Act," changes how banks and credit unions are examined by federal regulators like the FDIC, Federal Reserve, and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. It sets firm deadlines: regulators must complete an exit interview within 9 months of starting an exam and deliver a final written report within 60 days after that interview. Banks can also request a full list of the evidence regulators used to reach their conclusions, giving institutions more insight into how decisions about them were made.

The bill also creates a new, independent Office of Examination Review inside the regulatory system, led by a Senate-confirmed director. This office would field complaints from banks about how exams were conducted, check whether regulators are following their own rules consistently, and run a formal appeals process for banks that disagree with a regulator's findings. Banks could request a hearing before an administrative judge, and the reviewing officials would be required to judge the case independently rather than simply defer to the examiner's original opinion. The bill also prohibits regulators from punishing banks for filing appeals, such as by slow-walking unrelated approvals.

This bill mainly affects banks, credit unions, and the federal agencies that supervise them (adding the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to that list for these new rules). It does not change the rules consumers deal with directly, but it could affect how quickly and predictably financial institutions are supervised, which can indirectly affect lending decisions, compliance costs, and how disputes between banks and regulators get resolved.

title: Promoting New Bank Formation Act
ai_summary:
This bill aims to make it easier for new banks, especially in rural areas, to get started and grow. Starting a bank normally requires meeting strict federal capital requirements right away, which can be difficult for brand-new institutions still building their customer base. This bill would require federal banking regulators to create a three-year phase-in period, giving new banks time to gradually meet these capital rules instead of complying immediately. It also allows new banks to request changes to their approved business plans during their first three years, with regulators required to respond within 30 days or the request is automatically approved.

The bill includes special provisions for rural community banks, allowing them to meet a specific capital measurement (the Community Bank Leverage Ratio) at a gradually increasing rate over three years rather than all at once. It also changes the law to allow federal savings associations (a type of savings bank) to make agricultural loans without those loans counting against limits on other types of commercial lending, which could help farmers and rural businesses access credit. Finally, the bill requires regulators to study why so few new banks have been created over the past decade and to report to Congress on ways to encourage more new banks, particularly in communities that currently lack adequate banking services.

This bill would primarily affect people starting new banks (called "de novo" banks), rural communities and farmers seeking loans, and existing rural community banks. It could also indirectly benefit residents in underserved areas if it leads to more local banking options. Banking regulators, including the FDIC and Federal Reserve, would be responsible for writing the specific rules and conducting the required study.

title: TAILOR Act of 2025
ai_summary:
The TAILOR Act of 2025 would require federal banking regulators—the OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC, National Credit Union Administration, and Consumer Financial Protection Bureau—to consider each institution's size, risk level, and business model before applying new regulations. Instead of using a one-size-fits-all approach, regulators would have to tailor rules so smaller or lower-risk institutions face less burden, cost, and paperwork than larger or riskier ones. Agencies would need to explain this tailoring process publicly when proposing and finalizing rules, and report annually to Congress on how they've done so. The bill also requires regulators to look back at rules issued over the past 15 years and revise them, within three years, to meet these same tailoring standards.

The bill also includes provisions specifically for community banks. It directs regulators to create a simplified, shorter version of the required quarterly financial reports ("call reports") for small banks that qualify for the Community Bank Leverage Ratio, a simplified capital standard already available to smaller banks. Additionally, regulators must submit a report to Congress within 18 months examining how bank supervision could be modernized, covering topics like changing business models, examiner training, use of technology, and communication between regulators and banks.

Overall, this bill mainly affects banks, credit unions, and the agencies that regulate them—particularly community banks and credit unions, which often say that current regulations are too costly or complex given their smaller size and lower risk compared to large national banks. Consumers could be indirectly affected if reduced regulatory burdens change the cost, availability, or risk oversight of banking services in their communities.

title: Systemic Risk Authority Transparency Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes what happens after regulators use a special emergency power called the "systemic risk exception." That power lets the government protect all deposits at a failed bank—even amounts above the normal $250,000 insurance limit—if letting the bank fail normally would seriously threaten the financial system. This tool was used, for example, during the 2023 collapses of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank.

The bill requires more detailed public reporting whenever this emergency power is used. The Government Accountability Office would have to review each use of the exception twice (at 60 and 180 days) and report to Congress on why it was used, whether bank executives mismanaged the institution, whether regulators failed to catch problems, and what other factors contributed to the failure. Separately, the bank's primary federal regulator (such as the Federal Reserve, FDIC, or OCC) would have to release its own detailed report, including past examination records and supervisory warnings, within 90 days and again at 210 days. Agencies could redact sensitive personal or business information, claim limited exceptions for withholding material, and get short extensions during ongoing crises, but they would generally have to explain any withheld information to congressional committees.

This mainly affects federal banking regulators, who would face new reporting deadlines and disclosure duties, and large banks that might fail in the future, since executives' decisions and any mismanagement would be more thoroughly documented and made public. It also affects Congress and the public, who would get more transparency into why a bank failed and how regulators and lawmakers responded, aiming to hold both bank leadership and regulators more accountable after a major bank failure.

title: Bank Competition Modernization Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how bank mergers are reviewed by federal regulators. Right now, when two banks want to merge, agencies like the Federal Reserve and FDIC have to check whether the deal would hurt competition or create a monopoly. This bill says that when regulators do that check, they must also look at competition from a wider range of financial companies, not just other banks. This includes credit unions, farm credit lenders, industrial loan companies, and other nonbank financial firms. The idea is that banks today compete with many types of financial businesses, not just other traditional banks, so mergers should be judged with that bigger picture in mind.

The bill also creates an automatic approval rule for smaller mergers. If a merger would result in a combined bank holding less than $10 billion in assets, regulators would be required to determine that the deal does not create a monopoly and does not hurt competition, without needing further competitive analysis. This would apply to reviews under the Federal Deposit Insurance Act, the Bank Holding Company Act, and the Home Owners' Loan Act, which cover banks, bank holding companies, and savings associations (like some thrifts and credit-focused institutions).

This bill would primarily affect banks and savings institutions looking to merge or be acquired, especially smaller and mid-sized banks, since deals resulting in under $10 billion in combined assets would face a much easier and faster approval process. It could make it simpler for smaller banks to combine or be bought, potentially leading to more mergers in that size range. Bank regulators (the Federal Reserve, FDIC, and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency) would have to change how they analyze merger applications. Everyday bank customers could be indirectly affected if increased merger activity changes the number of local banking options, though the practical effects would depend on how the changes are implemented.

title: HUMPS Act of 2025
ai_summary:
**HR 3379, the HUMPS Act of 2025**, deals with how bank regulators grade the health of banks. Regulators currently use a system called CAMELS, which rates banks on six factors: capital, asset quality, management, earnings, liquidity, and sensitivity to market risk. These ratings affect important decisions like whether a bank can merge with another bank and how much it pays for deposit insurance. Congress says this system relies too much on examiners' personal judgment, which can lead to inconsistent grades for similar banks.

The bill requires the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council, which coordinates bank regulators, to recommend changes that make the CAMELS grading criteria clearer and more objective, adjust how much weight each factor gets in the overall score, and either remove the "management" category entirely or narrow it down to objective measures of how well a bank's risk controls are run. After those recommendations are made, banking regulators would have 12 months to write official rules putting them into effect, including a public comment period of at least 60 days so banks, industry groups, and others can weigh in before the rules are finalized.

This bill mainly affects banks, credit unions, and other financial institutions that are examined by federal regulators, as well as the regulatory agencies themselves (like the FDIC, Federal Reserve, and OCC). It could also indirectly affect consumers and communities, since changes to how banks are rated may influence bank mergers, lending practices, and deposit insurance costs. The bill does not eliminate regulators' power to take enforcement action against unsafe banking practices — it only changes how the underlying rating system works.
ai_headline: Bill would overhaul how regulators grade bank health under CAMELS system

title: Merger Process Review Act
ai_summary:
**H.R. 6546 — Merger Process Review Act**

This bill requires the internal watchdogs (Inspectors General) at the main banking and credit union regulators—the Federal Reserve, the Comptroller of the Currency, the FDIC, and the National Credit Union Administration—to regularly check how well those agencies handle applications for bank and credit union mergers. Starting one year after the bill becomes law, and every three years after that, each Inspector General must study how long these merger applications take to process, look for bottlenecks or delays, and recommend ways to make the process faster and more efficient. The findings must be reported to Congress, and the regulator involved must respond in writing with a plan for acting on the recommendations.

The bill doesn't change the actual rules banks and credit unions must follow to merge, and it doesn't give regulators new power to approve or reject mergers. Instead, it's focused on oversight and transparency—making sure the process itself runs smoothly and isn't unnecessarily slow. This would mainly affect the regulatory agencies themselves, who would face new reporting requirements, as well as banks and credit unions seeking to merge, who might benefit from clearer, more predictable review timelines. Everyday consumers could see indirect effects if faster or more efficient merger reviews change how quickly banking mergers move forward in their communities.

title: Mystic Alerts Act
ai_summary:
The Mystic Alerts Act is a bill about how emergency alerts get sent to cell phones. Right now, wireless companies can choose to send emergency alerts (like weather warnings or Amber Alerts) to their customers' phones through cell towers. This bill would let those same companies also choose to send those alerts by satellite, which could help people receive emergency warnings even in areas with no cell tower signal, such as rural areas, mountains, or after a disaster knocks out local networks.

Under the bill, wireless companies would have to tell the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) whether they plan to send alerts by satellite. If a company decides to offer satellite alerts, it must follow technical rules set by the FCC and must let customers opt out of receiving these alerts if they choose. If a company decides not to offer satellite alerts, it has to clearly notify its customers of that decision. The FCC would also be required to create official technical standards for satellite alerts within a year, working with the Department of Homeland Security and FEMA.

This bill mainly affects wireless phone carriers, the FCC, and everyday cell phone users. It doesn't force any company to offer satellite alerts, but it sets up rules so that if they do, the system works consistently and customers are informed and given control over whether they receive these alerts. The goal is to improve the reliability of emergency alerts, especially in places where normal cell service might fail.

title: To amend the Public Health Service Act to reauthorize the telehealth network and telehealth resource centers grant programs.
ai_summary:
This bill continues federal funding for programs that support telehealth services, which let patients connect with doctors and other health providers remotely using phones, video calls, or other technology. Specifically, it extends money for two grant programs under the Public Health Service Act: the telehealth network grant program and the telehealth resource centers program. These programs help hospitals, clinics, and other health organizations set up and improve telehealth systems, especially in rural or underserved areas where it can be hard to access in-person care.

The bill sets the funding level at $42,050,000 per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030. This is a reauthorization, meaning the programs already exist, but their funding approval was set to expire, and this bill would keep the money flowing for five more years. It does not create new programs or change how the money can be used; it simply continues the existing funding structure.

This bill would primarily affect healthcare providers, especially those in rural or low-income areas, who rely on these grants to build or maintain telehealth technology. It would also indirectly affect patients in those areas, who depend on telehealth services to see doctors, specialists, or mental health providers without having to travel long distances. Organizations that run telehealth resource centers, which offer training and technical help to providers, would also continue receiving support.

title: Improving Care in Rural America Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews federal funding for three grant programs that help rural communities get better access to health care. These programs currently expire in 2025, and the bill extends them through 2030, allowing them to continue operating without interruption.

The bill covers three specific programs under the Public Health Service Act: Rural Health Care Services Outreach grants, Rural Health Network Development grants, and Small Health Care Provider Quality Improvement grants. These programs give money to rural clinics, hospitals, and health organizations to help them provide services, build partnerships between local health providers, and improve the quality of care in areas that often lack enough doctors, specialists, or medical facilities. In addition to extending the funding period, the bill adds new requirements: organizations that receive these grants must specifically use the money to meet the health needs of underserved rural populations, and they must involve local residents in planning and running the funded projects, not just deciding on their behalf.

This bill mainly affects people living in rural areas, who often face longer travel distances to see a doctor and fewer local health care options compared to city residents. It also affects rural hospitals, clinics, and health networks that rely on these federal grants to fund outreach efforts, staff, and community health initiatives. Because the bill focuses on reauthorizing and slightly refining existing programs rather than creating new ones, its main practical effect is ensuring these rural health support programs keep operating for another five years, with a stronger requirement that rural communities have a direct say in how the funds are used.

title: Protecting Americans’ Retirement Savings From Politics Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change several rules for how public companies, investment advisers, and "proxy advisory firms" (companies that research corporate shareholder votes and tell big investors how to vote) operate. It says companies only have to disclose information that is "material," meaning something that would actually change an average investor's decision to buy or sell stock — a change meant to limit disclosures about environmental, social, and political issues that some see as unrelated to financial performance. It also creates a new SEC advisory committee made up mostly of corporate executives to weigh in on rules affecting public companies, and orders government studies on European sustainability-reporting laws and on how proxy advisory firms operate.

The bill would require proxy advisory firms to register with the SEC, disclose their methods and conflicts of interest, let companies review and respond to draft recommendations before they're published, and face lawsuits if they push proposals that turn out to violate the law. It would also require large investment managers (like mutual fund companies and pension funds) to report how often they follow proxy advisors' recommendations and to prove their votes serve shareholders' "best economic interest" — defined strictly in terms of financial returns, not social or environmental goals. It bans "robovoting" (automatically following an advisor's recommendation without independent review) and lets passive index funds default to following a company's own board recommendations or investor instructions instead of voting independently.

This bill mainly affects people with retirement accounts, 401(k)s, or mutual fund investments, since it changes how the fund managers who vote on their behalf must operate. It also affects public companies, who could face fewer disclosure requirements and more say over shareholder votes, and proxy advisory firms like ISS and Glass Lewis, who would face new registration, transparency, and liability rules. Supporters say it protects retirement savers from investment decisions driven by political or social causes rather than financial performance; critics may see it as reducing corporate transparency and shareholder influence.

last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 618.

title: China Exchange Rate Accountability Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the China Exchange Rate Accountability Act of 2026 (also referred to in the text as the Exchange Rate Accountability Act of 2026), directs the U.S. government to use its influence at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to oppose giving more voting power, called a "quota increase," to certain large member countries if those countries engage in questionable currency practices. It specifically applies to any of the IMF's 10 biggest member countries. Before the IMF considers boosting one of these countries' quotas, the U.S. Treasury Secretary would have to check whether that country is being transparent about its exchange rate policies, publishing honest economic data, and not manipulating its currency to gain unfair trade advantages. If the country fails these checks, the U.S. representative at the IMF would be required to vote against increasing its quota.

The bill does include some flexibility: the President could waive this requirement if doing so is judged important for U.S. national interests, as long as Congress is notified with an explanation. The rule would automatically expire seven years after the law takes effect.

This bill mainly affects U.S. foreign economic policy and its dealings with the IMF, rather than directly affecting everyday Americans' daily lives. However, it could have broader effects on international trade and currency relations, particularly with countries like China, which has often been accused of managing its currency for trade advantages. By tying U.S. support at the IMF to these transparency and fairness standards, the bill aims to pressure major economies into adopting fairer currency practices, which could influence global trade balances and, indirectly, U.S. businesses and consumers who trade with or compete against those countries.

last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 611.

title: Women and Lung Cancer Research and Preventive Services Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 2319, the "Women and Lung Cancer Research and Preventive Services Act of 2025," directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to work with the Department of Defense and the Department of Veterans Affairs to conduct a review of lung cancer research as it relates to women and underserved populations. The review would look at what research has already been done, identify gaps in knowledge, and find opportunities for new studies, including looking at environmental and genetic factors that might cause lung cancer in women and improving imaging technology for diagnosis and treatment.

The bill also asks HHS to explore creating a national strategy for lung cancer screening, with a focus on expanding access for women and underserved communities, and to consider launching a public awareness campaign about lung cancer risks and the importance of catching it early. This is not a bill that creates new programs or spends money directly on treatment—it simply requires a study and a report. Within two years of the bill becoming law, HHS would need to submit its findings and recommendations to Congress.

This bill would primarily affect government health agencies and researchers, who would be tasked with conducting the review. Indirectly, it could affect women, veterans, and underserved populations (such as low-income or rural communities) who face lung cancer risks, since the findings could eventually lead to new screening guidelines, research funding, or public health campaigns aimed at improving early detection and prevention.

title: Rural Obstetrics Readiness Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Rural Obstetrics Readiness Act, aims to help rural hospitals and clinics handle pregnancy and childbirth emergencies, even when they don't have a dedicated maternity unit. Many small-town hospitals have closed their maternity wards in recent years, so this bill sets up federal grant programs to train doctors, nurses, and other health workers who aren't obstetric specialists to recognize and respond to emergencies like severe bleeding, high blood pressure, heart problems, infections, or mental health crises during pregnancy and after birth. It also funds training on how to safely stabilize and transfer patients to larger hospitals when needed.

The bill also provides money for rural hospitals to buy medical equipment, hire staff, and create formal partnerships with other hospitals for patient transfers. Another section funds a telehealth pilot program, allowing rural providers to call or video-conference with maternal health specialists in real time for urgent guidance during emergencies. Finally, it requires the Department of Health and Human Services to study where maternity wards have closed across the country and how patients are being transported for care, then report the findings to Congress within three years.

This bill mainly affects people living in rural areas, particularly pregnant women and new mothers who may not have easy access to a hospital with a maternity unit. It also affects rural health care workers, hospital administrators, and state health agencies that could apply for these new federal grants. The funding involved is relatively modest—tens of millions of dollars spread over several years—and would need to be approved through the separate congressional budget process before any money is actually spent.

title: SAFE Drugs Act of 2026
ai_summary:
**What the bill does:** This bill tightens federal rules for compounding pharmacies (businesses that mix custom medications for specific patients) and outsourcing facilities (larger operations that produce compounded drugs in bulk). It limits how often a pharmacy can make a "copy" of a drug that's already commercially available—capping it at 20 times per month—unless there's a meaningful medical reason a specific patient needs a customized version instead of the standard product. It also requires pharmacies, facilities, or doctors that compound large quantities of drugs for out-of-state patients to file yearly reports with federal regulators detailing what they're making and how often, though hospital pharmacies are exempt from this reporting rule. Additionally, it creates a new category called "large-scale outsourcing facilities" (those compounding a drug more than 100 times a year), which will face mandatory inspections before making a new product and at least every two years afterward. Finally, it changes how the FDA calculates a yearly registration fee these facilities pay, letting the FDA set the amount based on what's needed to fund safety oversight, rather than a fixed $15,000.

**Who it affects:** This primarily affects compounding pharmacies, outsourcing facilities, and physicians who create customized medications, especially those operating at high volume or shipping across state lines. Patients who rely on compounded drugs—such as people needing medication in special forms (liquid instead of pill, allergen-free versions, or unique dosages)—could be affected if their provider has to change practices to comply with new limits and reporting rules. The bill is aimed at increasing oversight and safety standards, particularly targeting large operations that make copies of existing commercial drugs rather than truly personalized treatments, following past incidents of contamination or fraud involving compounded medications.
