title: CLEAR LABELS Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the CLEAR LABELS Act, would change federal drug labeling rules so that medicine packaging and paperwork must reveal where the drug and its ingredients actually came from. Currently, labels mainly list the name and business address of whoever packages or distributes a drug, which is not always the company that actually manufactured it. Under this bill, labels for active pharmaceutical ingredients (the raw chemical compounds used to make medicine) and finished drug products would need to identify the "original manufacturer" — meaning the last facility that did substantial manufacturing before the product entered interstate commerce — along with a unique facility identifier. This information could be listed directly on the label or made accessible through a barcode, QR code, or online portal, and companies would also have to provide it in a package insert or on paper if someone asks.

The bill also updates customs law so that finished drug products meeting these new FDA labeling rules would be exempt from the separate "country of origin" marking requirements that customs officials normally enforce on imported goods. The FDA would be required to write detailed regulations to implement these changes, with the rules taking effect no sooner than one year after being finalized, applying only to drugs made after that date.

This bill would primarily affect drug manufacturers, packagers, and distributors, who would face new labeling and reporting requirements, especially companies that rely on ingredients or manufacturing done overseas. It would also affect pharmacists, doctors, and consumers, who could gain more visibility into where their medications and ingredients originate. Supporters of this type of measure often frame it as a response to concerns about drug supply chains and reliance on foreign manufacturing, particularly from countries like China and India, though the bill itself is limited to labeling and disclosure requirements rather than restricting imports.

title: SAVE America Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the SAVE America Act, would change federal voter registration and voting rules in two main ways. First, it would require anyone registering to vote in federal elections to show documentary proof of U.S. citizenship, such as a REAL ID-compliant license marked as citizen, a U.S. passport, a birth certificate combined with a government photo ID, military ID with proof of U.S. birth, naturalization papers, or similar documents. States would have to check citizenship status using systems like the Department of Homeland Security's SAVE database or Social Security records, remove noncitizens from voter rolls when discovered, and set up a backup process for people who can't produce these documents right away. It also creates new criminal penalties for registering someone who hasn't shown proof of citizenship or for government employees who help noncitizens register or vote.

Second, the bill would require everyone voting in a federal election—whether in person or by absentee ballot—to show a physical (non-digital) photo ID that indicates U.S. citizenship, issued by a government authority like a state DMV, election office, tribal government, or federal agency. There are some exceptions for people in states that already verify citizenship electronically through SAVE on a regular basis. States that don't currently require voter registration would need to set up their own citizenship-verification system instead.

This bill would primarily affect election officials, who would need to update registration systems, verify documents, and coordinate with federal agencies; voters, who would need to gather and present specific documents to register and vote; and people without easy access to these documents, such as those who lack passports, birth certificates, or updated IDs, who might face extra steps to prove eligibility. States would also bear new administrative and technology costs to comply with the verification and record-keeping requirements.

title: Aviation Medication Transparency Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Aviation Medication Transparency Act of 2025, would require the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to publicly post a list of medications that are approved for pilots and air traffic controllers to use while still being allowed to work. Currently, this information is not always easy for pilots, air traffic controllers, or their doctors to find, which can create confusion about which medications are safe to take without risking a suspended medical certification. The FAA would have one year to create this list and would need to update it every year after that.

The list would have to be written in plain, easy-to-understand language and given to people the first time they apply for medical certification, whether they are current pilots, air traffic controllers, or students training for those jobs. It would cover both prescription and over-the-counter drugs, note which medications are outright banned ("Do Not Issue"), and explain how long someone might need to pause work duties after starting a new medication. The FAA would also have to set up a way for doctors to ask questions about the list. In developing it, the FAA must consult with aviation universities, unions representing pilots and air traffic controllers, and a special working group already created by prior aviation law.

This bill mainly affects airline and private pilots, air traffic controllers, people training for those careers, and the doctors who evaluate them for medical certification. It could also indirectly benefit airline passengers and the public, since clearer medication guidelines may help ensure aviation workers get needed treatment without unnecessary work interruptions, while maintaining safety standards.
ai_headline: FAA would have to publish clear list of pilot-safe medications
last_action_text: Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: The FAA would be required to post and annually update a plain-language list of medications approved for pilots and air traffic controllers.
ai_sections.what: This bill would require the FAA to publicly post a list of medications approved for pilots and air traffic controllers to use while still working. The FAA would have one year to create the list, update it annually, cover prescription and over-the-counter drugs, flag banned "Do Not Issue" medications, and explain wait times after starting new medications.
ai_sections.who: Airline and private pilots, air traffic controllers, aviation students, and the doctors who evaluate them for medical certification are directly affected. Airline passengers and the public could be indirectly affected.
ai_sections.why: Currently, medication safety information is not always easy to find, creating confusion about which drugs risk a suspended medical certification. Clearer FAA guidance could reduce that confusion while maintaining existing safety standards.

title: EMPOWER for Health Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the EMPOWER for Health Act, renews funding for a group of federal health workforce training programs that were set to expire. These programs, created under Title VII of the Public Health Service Act, help train doctors, nurses, dentists, and other health professionals, especially in underserved communities. The bill extends the funding authorization from the 2021-2025 period to 2026-2030 and increases the dollar amounts allowed for several of these programs, covering things like health career training centers, workforce diversity programs, faculty development, and geriatric education.

The bill also makes changes to a specific program that helps place pediatric health specialists (like child surgeons or mental health providers) in areas that need them. It broadens eligibility so professionals can qualify by serving underserved children generally, not just in areas officially designated as having a shortage of their specific specialty. It also updates rules about what counts as "full-time service" for these professionals, allowing for research, teaching, and other duties tied to their fields, and adjusts residency and fellowship program timelines.

Finally, the bill updates the Area Health Education Centers program, which helps train health workers in local communities, by expanding outreach efforts from just high school students to "pre-collegiate" students more broadly, and it changes how program funding cycles are measured (from a fixed number of years to "award cycles"). Overall, this bill mainly affects medical schools, teaching hospitals, pediatric specialists, health students, and residents of medically underserved areas, particularly rural and low-income communities that rely on these training pipelines to have enough doctors and nurses.
ai_headline: Bill would renew health workforce training funds through 2030
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 529.

ai_sections.tldr: The EMPOWER for Health Act extends and expands federal health workforce training funding from 2026 through 2030.
ai_sections.what: The EMPOWER for Health Act renews and increases funding authorization for Title VII health workforce training programs, extending it from the 2021-2025 period to 2026-2030. It also revises eligibility and service rules for a pediatric specialist placement program and updates outreach and funding-cycle rules for the Area Health Education Centers program.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects medical schools, teaching hospitals, pediatric specialists, health students and residents, and communities—especially rural and low-income areas—that depend on these training pipelines.
ai_sections.why: The changes could affect how many health professionals train in and serve underserved communities, and how program funding is structured and measured going forward.
ai_sections.cost: The bill increases the authorized dollar amounts for several Title VII programs and extends funding authorization through 2030, though the summary does not specify exact figures.
costChips: Raises authorized amounts for several programs

title: Patients Deserve Price Tags Act
ai_summary:
S 2355, the "Patients Deserve Price Tags Act," is a health care price transparency bill that expands and strengthens existing rules requiring hospitals, and now other health providers, to publicly post their prices. Currently hospitals must disclose standard charges, but this bill tightens those rules with clearer formatting requirements, requires a hospital executive to personally attest the pricing information is accurate, and creates a stronger enforcement system with daily fines that increase based on hospital size and get much larger for repeat violators (potentially millions of dollars). The bill also extends similar price-posting requirements, for the first time, to medical laboratories (like blood tests), imaging centers (X-rays, MRIs, etc.), and hospital-affiliated outpatient surgery centers, all of which would have to post their gross prices, cash discount prices, and negotiated insurance rates online in standardized, machine-readable formats starting in 2026 and 2027.

The bill also targets health insurance companies. It requires insurers to give patients an easy-to-use online tool showing real-time cost estimates, including deductibles already met and any pre-approval requirements, before they get care. Separately, insurers would have to publish detailed files showing the rates they've negotiated with every doctor and hospital in their network, as well as drug prices, so researchers, employers, and the public can compare costs. Finally, the bill gives employers who sponsor health plans for their workers a legal right to access their own claims data and audit information from insurers and pharmacy benefit managers, preventing those companies from hiding fees or blocking oversight.

This bill mainly affects hospitals, labs, imaging centers, surgery centers, health insurers, and employers who provide employee health coverage, all of whom would face new disclosure duties and potential penalties for noncompliance. Patients and employers are the intended beneficiaries, gaining more information to compare health care costs in advance and potentially negotiate or shop for cheaper care.
ai_headline: Bill would force labs, imaging centers to post prices like hospitals
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 522.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill expands price-posting rules to labs, imaging centers, and insurers, with fines reaching millions for repeat violators.
ai_sections.what: The bill tightens hospital price-disclosure rules by adding formatting requirements, executive attestation of accuracy, and stronger fines. It extends similar price-posting rules to medical labs, imaging centers, and hospital-affiliated surgery centers starting in 2026 and 2027, and requires insurers to offer real-time cost tools and publish negotiated rates.
ai_sections.who: Hospitals, labs, imaging centers, surgery centers, health insurers, and employers offering employee health coverage face new disclosure duties. Patients and employers are meant to benefit from clearer cost information.
ai_sections.why: Noncompliant providers and insurers face daily fines that scale with size and repeat violations, adding legal and financial exposure. Employers gain new audit rights over insurers and pharmacy benefit managers, increasing oversight demands on those companies.
ai_sections.cost: Daily fines for noncompliance increase based on hospital size and grow much larger for repeat violators, potentially reaching millions of dollars.

title: Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act, would direct the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to update its rules so that civilian aircraft can legally fly faster than the speed of sound (supersonic speeds) over the United States without needing special government permission, as long as the flight doesn't create a sonic boom that reaches the ground. Currently, federal aviation rules generally ban civilian supersonic flight over land within the U.S. because of concerns about the loud, disruptive booms these flights can cause. The FAA would have one year after the bill becomes law to write or revise the necessary regulations.

The bill reflects recent advances in aircraft design, where some companies are developing supersonic planes engineered to reduce or eliminate the sonic boom's impact at ground level, sometimes called "boomless" or low-boom technology. By focusing on whether a boom actually reaches the ground rather than banning supersonic speeds outright, the bill would let manufacturers and airlines operate such technology domestically if it meets that noise standard.

This would primarily affect aerospace companies developing supersonic passenger jets, airlines that might eventually offer faster domestic flights, and the FAA, which would need to create new technical standards and testing procedures. Everyday air travelers could eventually benefit from shorter flight times if these aircraft become commercially available, while communities near flight paths could be affected depending on how effectively the "no boom reaches the ground" requirement is enforced.
ai_headline: Bill would let boomless supersonic jets fly over US without special approval
last_action_text: Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill would let civilian planes fly supersonic over the U.S. if no sonic boom reaches the ground, with FAA rules due in one year.
ai_sections.what: The Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act would direct the FAA to update rules allowing civilian supersonic flight over the U.S. without special permission, as long as the flight causes no sonic boom at ground level. The FAA would have one year after enactment to write or revise the needed regulations.
ai_sections.who: Aerospace companies developing supersonic jets, airlines considering faster domestic flights, and the FAA, which must create new standards, would be affected. Air travelers and communities near flight paths could also feel the effects.
ai_sections.why: Current rules generally ban civilian supersonic flight over U.S. land due to sonic boom disruption; this bill shifts the standard to whether a boom reaches the ground, potentially expanding where such flights can legally occur. How well the FAA enforces the "no boom" requirement would determine impacts on nearby communities.

title: Expedited Access to Biosimilars Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change how the FDA reviews "biosimilar" drugs before they can be sold. Biosimilars are medicines that are highly similar to existing biologic drugs (complex medicines made from living cells, like some treatments for arthritis, cancer, or diabetes) but are typically cheaper, similar to how generic drugs work for regular pills. Currently, companies seeking approval for a biosimilar may need to run clinical studies that check things like immunogenicity (whether the drug triggers an unwanted immune reaction), pharmacodynamics (how the drug affects the body), and comparative clinical efficacy (whether it works as well as the original drug in patients).

Under this bill, the FDA would no longer automatically require those three types of studies. Instead, companies would only need to run studies showing the drug is safe and works as expected in at least one approved use, based on simpler pharmacokinetic testing (how the body processes the drug). The FDA could still require the additional immunogenicity, pharmacodynamics, or efficacy studies in specific cases, but only if it notifies the company early, before the application is filed, and provides a written explanation for why the extra testing is needed.

This change would primarily affect pharmaceutical companies that develop biosimilar drugs, potentially reducing the time and cost needed to bring these products to market. It could also affect patients and doctors, since faster approval might mean quicker access to lower-cost biosimilar medicines, though some may have questions about whether reduced testing requirements affect confidence in these drugs' safety or effectiveness. The bill would apply to biosimilar applications submitted after it becomes law.
ai_headline: Bill would ease FDA testing rules for cheaper biosimilar drugs
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 520.

ai_sections.tldr: S 1414 would let biosimilar makers skip certain clinical studies unless the FDA specifically requires them in advance.
ai_sections.what: The bill would end the automatic requirement for immunogenicity, pharmacodynamics, and comparative efficacy studies for biosimilar drug approval. Companies would instead only need to show safety and expected results in one approved use through simpler pharmacokinetic testing. The FDA could still require the extra studies case by case, but only with early written notice explaining why.
ai_sections.who: This mainly affects pharmaceutical companies developing biosimilar drugs, which are cheaper alternatives to complex biologic medicines used for conditions like arthritis, cancer, or diabetes. Patients and doctors could also be affected through changes in access to and confidence in these drugs.
ai_sections.why: Fewer required studies could shorten approval timelines and lower development costs for biosimilar makers, while raising questions for some about whether reduced testing affects confidence in drug safety or effectiveness. The change would apply only to applications submitted after the law takes effect.

title: Aviation Innovation and Global Competitiveness Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to make its process for approving new aircraft designs faster, clearer, and more predictable, especially for new technologies like air taxis and other "advanced air mobility" vehicles (such as powered-lift aircraft that take off and land vertically). Currently, when a company wants FAA approval for a new aircraft, engine, or aircraft part, the agency uses a system of "issue papers" to work through unresolved safety or design questions. Companies have complained this process can be slow, inconsistent, and unpredictable. The bill requires the FAA to publish a public plan for improving this process, set standard timelines for key steps, create clearer rules for when an issue paper is actually needed, and update guidance on when the agency can delegate certification tasks to qualified outside experts rather than doing everything in-house.

The bill affects aircraft manufacturers, airlines, engineers, aviation safety inspectors, and companies developing new technologies like electric air taxis and drones-based passenger vehicles. It requires the FAA to consult with industry groups, airport and "vertiport" operators, and labor unions representing FAA safety staff when making these changes. The FAA must also report to Congress each year on how well it's meeting its own timelines. Importantly, the bill states that these new timelines don't create any new legal rights, meaning companies can't sue the FAA just because it misses a deadline.

This bill mainly affects the aviation industry and the FAA's internal procedures rather than the general public directly, though it could indirectly affect airline passengers and communities near airports if new technologies like air taxis become more common as a result of a faster approval process. It also reflects broader concerns about the U.S. staying competitive globally in developing new aviation technology.
ai_headline: Bill seeks faster, clearer FAA approval process for new aircraft designs
last_action_text: Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill requires the FAA to set clearer, faster, more predictable rules for approving new aircraft designs, including air taxis.
ai_sections.what: The bill directs the FAA to publish a public plan for speeding up and clarifying its aircraft design approval process, including standard timelines, clearer rules on when "issue papers" are needed, and updated guidance on delegating certification tasks to outside experts. It focuses especially on new technologies like air taxis and powered-lift aircraft that take off and land vertically.
ai_sections.who: Aircraft manufacturers, airlines, engineers, safety inspectors, and companies developing electric air taxis or drone-based passenger vehicles are affected. The FAA must also consult industry groups, airport and vertiport operators, and labor unions representing its safety staff.
ai_sections.why: A faster, more predictable approval process could speed development of new aviation technologies, potentially affecting airline passengers and communities near airports as air taxis become more common. The bill specifies that missed timelines create no new legal rights, so companies cannot sue the FAA over delays.

press_names: Aviation Innovation and Global Competitiveness Act

title: Accelerating Broadband Permits Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Accelerating Broadband Permits Act of 2026, aims to speed up the rollout of high-speed internet infrastructure by improving government tracking and permitting processes. It requires the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information to create a public online dashboard showing how states and other grant recipients are spending money from the Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) Program, a federal effort to expand internet access nationwide. This dashboard would show how much grant money has been spent and how many homes or businesses actually got internet service as a result. The bill also requires a new tool to help grant recipients figure out which federal permits their contractors need and track their progress toward getting those permits.

The bill further addresses delays in approving applications to install communications equipment on federal land or structures. Federal agencies already have a 270-day deadline to process these applications, but the bill requires better data collection to track how long approvals actually take, ongoing analysis of what causes delays, yearly reports to Congress, and a warning system to flag applications at risk of missing the deadline. Finally, the bill lowers the cost threshold for broadband projects subject to certain environmental review requirements under NEPA (the National Environmental Policy Act), meaning more broadband construction projects over $5 million would go through this environmental review process labeled as a defined "major" action.

This bill mainly affects state and local governments, internet service providers, and companies receiving federal broadband grants, since they would face new tracking requirements but potentially benefit from faster permit processing. Federal agencies handling permits and environmental reviews would also have new reporting duties. Everyday residents, especially those in rural or underserved areas awaiting broadband expansion, could benefit indirectly if the bill succeeds in reducing bureaucratic delays and getting internet service built faster.
ai_headline: Bill seeks faster broadband permits and public BEAD spending tracker
last_action_text: Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill creates a public dashboard tracking BEAD broadband funds and speeds up federal permit approvals.
ai_sections.what: The Accelerating Broadband Permits Act of 2026 requires a public online dashboard tracking BEAD Program spending and results, plus a tool helping grant recipients identify and track needed federal permits. It also mandates better data collection, delay analysis, yearly reports, and a warning system for permits at risk of missing the existing 270-day deadline, and lowers the cost threshold triggering NEPA environmental review for broadband projects.
ai_sections.who: State and local governments, internet service providers, and companies receiving federal broadband grants face new tracking requirements. Federal agencies handling permits and environmental reviews gain new reporting duties, while rural residents awaiting broadband could be indirectly affected.
ai_sections.why: The changes could reduce bureaucratic delays in broadband deployment, though more projects over $5 million would now undergo formal environmental review, potentially adding steps for some projects.

title: Hurricane Hunter Aircraft Recapitalization Act
ai_summary:
This bill updates the rules for how the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) buys and operates its "Hurricane Hunter" aircraft—the planes that fly into hurricanes and tropical storms to gather weather data used for forecasting and warnings. It expands NOAA's fleet requirement from "up to 6" aircraft to a range of "6 to 9" manned aircraft, and requires NOAA to maintain backup aircraft capability so there's no single point of failure if planes are being replaced or upgraded. It also requires NOAA to keep collecting and sharing real-time weather data, maintain advanced radar systems (like Tail Doppler Radar) for tracking storms, and keep trained NOAA Corps pilots qualified to fly these missions.

The bill also gives NOAA more flexibility in how it pays for these planes. It allows multiyear contracts for buying and maintaining aircraft without the usual time limits that normally apply to government contracts, as long as safeguards are in place. Funding for aircraft acquisition would rise significantly, authorizing $2.5 billion for fiscal years 2027 through 2031 (up from $800 million previously authorized), plus $45 million per year for related aviation operations. Finally, it reorganizes where these rules live in federal law, moving them from the Coast Guard Authorization Act into the Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Act, which is more of a technical/legal cleanup.

This bill mainly affects NOAA, the aircraft manufacturers and maintenance contractors it works with, and the NOAA Corps pilots who fly these missions. Indirectly, it affects everyday Americans—especially those living in hurricane-prone coastal areas—since better and more reliable Hurricane Hunter aircraft improve the accuracy of hurricane forecasts and warnings, which can affect evacuation decisions and public safety.
ai_headline: Bill would expand NOAA's hurricane hunter fleet to 6-9 aircraft
last_action_text: Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: S 4802 expands NOAA's Hurricane Hunter fleet requirement and raises aircraft funding to $2.5 billion through 2031.
ai_sections.what: This bill expands NOAA's Hurricane Hunter aircraft fleet requirement from "up to 6" to "6 to 9" manned aircraft and requires backup aircraft so there's no single point of failure. It also mandates continued real-time weather data sharing, advanced radar systems, and qualified NOAA Corps pilots, while allowing more flexible multiyear purchasing contracts.
ai_sections.who: This mainly affects NOAA, its aircraft manufacturers and maintenance contractors, and NOAA Corps pilots. It indirectly affects people in hurricane-prone coastal areas who rely on storm forecasts and warnings.
ai_sections.why: The changes are meant to prevent gaps in hurricane data collection during aircraft replacement or upgrades, which affects the timeliness and accuracy of storm forecasts used for evacuation decisions.

costChips: plus $45 million per year for operations

title: Disaster Communications Coordination and Preparedness Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to improve how it shares information with state, local, tribal, and territorial officials during disasters and emergencies. It focuses on the Disaster Information Reporting System (DIRS), which phone and internet companies use to report on their network status when disasters hit, and the Mandatory Disaster Response Initiative, which requires certain communications providers to help restore service during emergencies. The bill requires the FCC to review how it notifies people when DIRS is turned on or off, study whether it should create a clearer point of contact for local officials seeking updates during emergencies, and create plain-language guides explaining how these systems work and how officials can use them.

In practical terms, this bill is mostly about improving communication and coordination rather than creating new rules for phone and internet companies. It would affect emergency managers and public safety officials at the state and local level, who often struggle to get clear, timely information about communications outages during hurricanes, wildfires, or other disasters. It would also affect the FCC, which must complete reviews, evaluations, and public materials within set deadlines (180 days to 1 year, depending on the section). Communications companies could be consulted during this process, but the bill specifically states it does not create new reporting requirements or mandates for them.

Overall, this bill aims to make existing disaster communication tools easier to understand and use, without changing the underlying rules or adding new burdens on businesses. It is designed to help local governments better communicate with federal agencies and phone/internet providers when disasters strike, potentially leading to faster, clearer information sharing during emergencies.
ai_headline: FCC bill seeks clearer disaster alerts for local officials
last_action_text: Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill directs the FCC to make disaster network-status tools easier for local officials to understand and use.
ai_sections.what: The bill directs the FCC to review how it notifies people when its Disaster Information Reporting System (DIRS) is activated or deactivated, study creating a clearer contact point for local officials, and produce plain-language guides on DIRS and the Mandatory Disaster Response Initiative. These systems track phone and internet company network status and emergency service restoration during disasters. The FCC must complete these tasks within deadlines ranging from 180 days to one year.
ai_sections.who: State, local, tribal, and territorial emergency managers and public safety officials are the main intended beneficiaries, along with the FCC, which must carry out the reviews and materials. Communications companies may be consulted but face no new requirements.
ai_sections.why: Local officials often struggle to get clear, timely information about communications outages during disasters like hurricanes and wildfires, and this bill addresses that coordination gap without changing existing rules.

title: Making America's Food Safer Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Making America's Food Safer Act, would update federal food safety laws to strengthen the FDA's oversight tools, particularly around imported food. It expands a program that allows outside, accredited auditors to certify that food facilities (both foreign and domestic) meet safety standards. Currently these certifications are used mainly to clear specific food shipments for import, but the bill would broaden their use so the FDA can also rely on them to help decide which facilities qualify for a "trusted importer" program and to help the agency prioritize inspections based on risk. This mainly affects food producers, importers, and the private auditing companies that inspect them.

The bill also makes it easier for the FDA to share detailed food safety information—like outbreak data, lab test results, inspection findings, recall lists, and consumer complaints—with state, local, tribal, and territorial health authorities. This is meant to help these agencies respond faster to contamination problems or outbreaks, though those authorities would generally have to keep the information confidential unless disclosure is needed to handle an outbreak or enforcement action. This change affects public health agencies at all levels of government and, indirectly, consumers who benefit from faster outbreak responses.

Finally, the bill gives the FDA new authority to order the destruction of imported food or products that have been refused entry into the U.S. because they pose a significant public health risk, rather than allowing the importer to simply re-export the goods elsewhere. Importers would get a chance to appeal before destruction happens, but if the order stands, they would have 90 days to destroy the product and would have to pay for it themselves. This primarily affects companies that import food products into the United States.
ai_headline: Bill would let FDA order destruction of unsafe imported food
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 530.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill expands FDA's use of outside food safety audits and lets it order destruction of rejected imports instead of re-export.
ai_sections.what: The bill broadens how the FDA can use accredited third-party audits, letting it apply them to a "trusted importer" program and risk-based inspection priorities, not just import clearance. It also eases FDA sharing of food safety data with state, local, tribal, and territorial health agencies, and gives FDA authority to order destruction of imported food refused entry for posing a significant public health risk.
ai_sections.who: Food producers and importers, both foreign and domestic, along with private auditing companies are directly affected. Public health agencies at all government levels, and indirectly consumers, are also affected.
ai_sections.why: Broader use of audits and faster data sharing could speed up risk targeting and outbreak response. Importers facing destruction orders would lose the option to re-export rejected goods and must cover destruction costs themselves.
ai_sections.cost: Importers whose refused food faces a destruction order would have to pay for the destruction themselves, within 90 days if the order is upheld after appeal.

title: To make technical amendments to update statutory references to certain provisions which were formerly classified to chapters 14 and 19 of title 25, United States Code, and to correct related technical errors.
ai_summary:
This bill makes purely technical corrections to federal law. Years ago, Congress reorganized how Indian affairs laws are numbered in the United States Code, moving many provisions from old sections (like "25 U.S.C. 450") to new section numbers (like "25 U.S.C. 5304"). However, hundreds of other laws across many different topics—agriculture, education, health care, banking, homeland security, criminal law, and more—still contain outdated cross-references pointing to the old, no-longer-used section numbers. This bill goes through those laws one by one and updates the citations so they correctly point to where the provisions actually live now in the law books.

Importantly, this bill does not change any actual rules, benefits, requirements, or eligibility standards. It does not add new programs or take away existing ones. It simply fixes citation errors so that lawyers, judges, government agencies, and everyday citizens looking up these laws can find the correct legal text instead of being sent to a section number that no longer exists or means something different. Think of it like updating outdated page numbers in a table of contents after a book has been reprinted with different pagination.

The people most affected are those who work with these laws professionally—government agency staff, tribal governments and organizations, lawyers, and researchers who rely on accurate citations when interpreting programs related to Native American affairs, health care, education, agriculture, and related fields. For the average person, this bill has no direct practical effect on their rights or benefits; it is routine "housekeeping" legislation to keep the U.S. Code accurate and easier to navigate.
ai_headline: Bill would fix outdated Indian law citations scattered across US Code
last_action_text: Motion to reconsider laid on the table Agreed to without objection.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 4584 updates outdated cross-references to Indian affairs law sections without changing any actual rules or benefits.
ai_sections.what: This bill corrects outdated legal citations in federal law that still point to old, no-longer-used section numbers for Indian affairs statutes. It updates hundreds of cross-references across topics like agriculture, education, health care, and banking to match current U.S. Code section numbers.
ai_sections.who: Government agency staff, tribal governments and organizations, lawyers, and researchers who rely on accurate legal citations are most affected.
ai_sections.why: The bill does not change any rules, benefits, requirements, or eligibility standards; it only ensures citations point to where the law actually resides now. This makes it easier for professionals to locate correct legal text instead of being sent to obsolete section numbers.

title: Modernizing Access to Our Public Oceans Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Secretary of Commerce, who oversees the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), to create a single, standardized, public website showing where and when people can boat, fish, dive, or fly low-elevation aircraft in federally managed waters. Currently, this kind of information—like fishing closures, no-wake zones, speed limits, restrictions on certain boat types, or seasonal fishing bans—is scattered across different agencies and hard for the public to find in one place. The bill requires NOAA to standardize how this data is collected, publish it in a searchable and easy-to-use online format, and update it regularly (twice a year for most information, and in real time for fishing restrictions). It also requires the website to include navigation charts and water depth information, and to let the public submit comments or questions about the data.

This mainly affects boaters, anglers, divers, and pilots who use federal waterways for recreation, as well as businesses like fishing charters, marinas, and outdoor recreation companies that rely on knowing current rules. NOAA is given up to four years to fully build out this system and must work with other agencies, such as the Coast Guard, Army Corps of Engineers, and the Department of the Interior, along with state, tribal, and private-sector partners, to make sure the data is consistent and compatible across different government systems. The bill does not change any existing fishing or environmental regulations—it only aims to make existing rules easier for the public to find and understand. It also protects sensitive information about historical, archaeological, or cultural sites from being revealed through this new public data system.
ai_headline: NOAA to build one website for federal water and airspace rules
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

ai_sections.tldr: NOAA must build a single public website mapping boating, fishing, diving, and low-flight rules in federal waters within four years.

It requires regular updates, navigation charts, water depth data, and a way for the public to submit comments.

title: Protecting American Taxpayers Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Protecting American Taxpayers Act, is a large package aimed at reducing fraud, waste, and improper payments across many federal programs. It requires states and agencies to better track and verify payments in programs like Medicare, Medicaid, child care subsidies, and welfare (TANF), including checking attendance records for child care providers, flagging unusual spikes in payments or provider numbers for investigation, and requiring recovery of improperly paid funds. It also bans people convicted of loan or grant fraud (such as PPP or COVID relief fraud) from getting future Small Business Administration assistance, extends the legal time limit for prosecuting COVID-era fraud, and creates new fraud-alert and data-verification systems, including protections against scams targeting veterans and expanded whistleblower protections for contractors who report wrongdoing.

The bill also rescinds unspent COVID-19 relief funds from several past laws (like the CARES Act and American Rescue Plan) and directs that money toward reducing the federal deficit, unless the President specifically requests to keep funds for national security reasons. It creates a bonus system for federal employees who identify wasteful agency spending, while barring top agency officials from receiving these bonuses themselves. Separately, it restricts U.S. financial assistance from going to entities controlled by agents of certain foreign governments (including Russia, China, North Korea, and Iran), and includes multiple measures aimed at preventing U.S. aid from indirectly benefiting the Taliban in Afghanistan, along with new reporting requirements on foreign assistance programs there.

Finally, the bill increases government spending transparency by requiring more federal contract and grant data (including certain "other transaction agreements" often used for emergency or specialized contracts) to be published online, and requires agencies to report on improper payments in the President's annual budget. Overall, this bill affects federal agencies, state governments running federally funded programs, small businesses and nonprofits receiving federal money, government contractors, veterans, low-income Americans in assistance programs, and organizations involved in foreign aid, particularly related to Afghanistan.
ai_headline: Bill targets fraud and improper payments across federal programs
last_action_text: Read the second time. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 401.

ai_sections.tldr: The Protecting American Taxpayers Act cracks down on fraud in federal programs and rescinds unspent COVID relief funds.

title: Childhood Diabetes Reduction Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Childhood Diabetes Reduction Act of 2026, would require new warning labels on many packaged foods and drinks. Sugary drinks would need a label warning about obesity, diabetes, and tooth decay. Foods or drinks with artificial or high-intensity sweeteners (like stevia, aspartame, or sucralose) would need a label saying they're "not recommended for children." Ultra-processed foods would need a warning about weight gain risks. And any food high in added sugar, saturated fat, or sodium would need a "High in [nutrient]" label. These warnings would need to take up at least 5% of the package's front and appear in a bold, bordered box, similar to warning labels used in some other countries.

The bill also restricts advertising. Companies could not market these labeled "junk foods" to children using things like cartoon characters, celebrity endorsements, toys, contests, or online influencers. Any ad for these foods would also have to include the same warning label used on the packaging. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce these advertising rules and would regain broader authority to write rules about advertising aimed at children—power it had lost in an earlier law. Separately, the bill funds new nutrition research at the National Institutes of Health, requires public meetings on nutrition science every five years, and funds a public education campaign by the CDC about reading these new labels and living healthier lifestyles.

This bill would primarily affect food and beverage manufacturers, retailers, and advertisers, who would face new labeling and marketing requirements enforced by the FDA and FTC. Consumers, especially parents and children, would see new warning labels on many grocery store products and fewer child-targeted ads for sugary or processed foods. Supporters intend it to reduce childhood obesity and diabetes; the food and advertising industries would likely be most affected by compliance costs and marketing restrictions.
ai_headline: New bill would put warning labels on sugary and ultra-processed foods
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 531.

title: Protecting American Taxpayers Act
ai_summary:
S 4952, the Protecting American Taxpayers Act, is a broad package aimed at reducing fraud and improper payments in federal programs. It requires child care providers to be paid based on actual attendance rather than enrollment, and it directs Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and ACA marketplace plans to flag sudden spikes in payments or provider numbers in a given area for investigation by the HHS Inspector General. It bars small businesses and their owners from getting SBA assistance if they've been convicted of loan or grant fraud, cancels unspent COVID-relief funds from several earlier laws (unless the President specifically requests to keep some for national security reasons), and creates a program letting federal employees earn bonuses for identifying wasteful agency spending. It also adds new transparency requirements, like including improper-payment data in the President's annual budget and extending the legal deadline (statute of limitations) to 10 years for prosecuting fraud connected to COVID-era programs like PPP, Shuttered Venue grants, and Restaurant Revitalization grants.

Beyond fraud prevention, the bill touches welfare and foreign policy. It tightens oversight of state Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) programs, requiring better tracking of improper payments and barring states from using federal TANF funds to replace their own spending. It restricts U.S. financial assistance from going to organizations controlled by agents of certain foreign governments (including China, Russia, North Korea, and Iran, among others), and it creates new reporting and strategy requirements related to opposing international support for the Taliban in Afghanistan, including a review of the Afghan Fund and cash assistance programs there. Separately, it also rescinds unspent Afghanistan reconstruction funds and directs that money toward reducing the federal deficit.

Overall, this bill would affect a wide range of people: recipients and providers of Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and child care subsidies would face more monitoring; small businesses seeking SBA loans would face stricter fraud-related eligibility rules; state agencies running welfare programs would have new reporting duties; federal employees could earn bonuses for finding wasteful spending; and organizations receiving federal funds tied to certain foreign countries or the Taliban could lose eligibility for assistance. It also affects taxpayers broadly, since its stated purpose is to recover misspent federal money and reduce the deficit through rescinded and recovered funds.
ai_headline: Bill targets fraud in Medicare, Medicaid, child care, and COVID relief programs
last_action_text: Read the second time. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 452.

title: Value Over Cost Act of 2026
ai_summary:
HR 1118, the "Value Over Cost Act," changes how the federal government is allowed to buy goods and services through what's called the "multiple award schedule" program, run by the General Services Administration (GSA). This program is essentially a pre-approved shopping list that lets federal agencies purchase supplies and services from vendors without going through a lengthy bidding process every time. Currently, the law requires that purchases made this way result in the "lowest overall cost." This bill would change that rule so agencies can instead choose the option that provides the "best value," even if it isn't the cheapest, as long as the GSA Administrator determines that doing so serves the government's best interests.

In practical terms, this gives federal purchasing officers more flexibility. Instead of being locked into picking the lowest-priced option, they could choose a product or service that costs more but offers better quality, reliability, or long-term savings. The bill makes this change in two places: one for general federal purchasing law (title 41) and a matching change for the Department of Defense's purchasing law (title 10), so the same rule applies to military purchases as well.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies, government contractors, and taxpayers. Contractors who offer higher-quality but more expensive products could become more competitive for government contracts, rather than always losing out to the lowest bidder. Supporters of this kind of change typically argue it can improve the quality of goods and services the government buys, while critics might worry it could reduce cost controls or create more subjective decision-making in awarding contracts. The bill does not affect private consumers directly; its impact is limited to how the federal government spends money on procurement.
ai_headline: Bill would let agencies pick "best value" over lowest-cost bids
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

title: Making continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2027, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill is a "continuing resolution," a temporary funding measure that keeps the federal government running when Congress hasn't finished passing its regular annual spending bills. It would keep almost all federal agencies and programs funded at roughly the same levels as fiscal year 2026, using the same rules that applied then, through December 4, 2026, or until new full-year spending laws are enacted, whichever comes first. This avoids a government shutdown while lawmakers continue negotiating final budgets for defense, homeland security, health and human services, transportation, and other departments.

The bill includes several specific provisions beyond just extending old funding levels. It restricts the Defense Department from starting new weapons production or expanding programs beyond 2026 levels. It ensures continued funding for programs like SNAP food assistance, WIC nutrition benefits for women and children, Indian Health Service facilities, wildfire suppression, disaster relief through FEMA, and Small Business Administration loan programs, so these services don't lapse or run out of money. It also extends certain expiring authorities, such as flood insurance programs and livestock market reporting rules, and allows Washington, D.C. to keep spending its local (non-federal) budget as planned.

This affects nearly everyone who relies on federal services, government employees, federal contractors, farmers, small business owners, veterans, Native American communities served by Indian Health Service, and people receiving nutrition assistance. It also includes routine, unrelated items such as death benefit payments to family members of two late members of Congress and a freeze on lawmakers' own cost-of-living pay raises during this period. Essentially, this bill buys more time for Congress to finish its budget work without disrupting government operations or public services.

last_action_text: Received in the Senate.

title: Charlotte Woodward Organ Transplant Discrimination Prevention Act
ai_summary:
This bill, named after Charlotte Woodward, a woman with Down syndrome, aims to stop hospitals and other health care providers from denying organ transplants to people simply because they have a mental or physical disability. Under the bill, providers cannot refuse to evaluate someone, refuse to put them on a transplant waiting list, or deny them a transplant or related care solely because of their disability. There is an exception: doctors can still consider a disability if, after an individual medical evaluation, it is found to genuinely affect whether the transplant would work or be appropriate for that specific patient. The bill also requires providers to make reasonable adjustments, such as involving a patient's support network (family, friends, or caregivers) or using communication aids, to help patients meet post-transplant care requirements, unless doing so would be an undue burden or change the basic nature of the treatment.

This would affect patients with disabilities—such as intellectual disabilities, autism, mental illness, or physical impairments—who need organ transplants, along with the hospitals, doctors, and transplant centers that provide these services. It also affects the national organ transplant oversight board, which would be barred from creating policies that block disabled patients' access to transplants. If a person believes they were discriminated against, they could file a complaint with the Department of Health and Human Services' Office for Civil Rights, in addition to existing legal protections under laws like the Americans with Disabilities Act. The bill does not reduce any stronger protections that states may already have in place.
ai_headline: Bill would bar organ transplant denials based on disability alone

title: No Censors on our Shores Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "No Censors on our Shores Act of 2025," would change U.S. immigration law to bar foreign government officials from entering the United States—or allow them to be deported if already here—if they took actions against a U.S. citizen that would count as violating free speech rights under the First Amendment, had those actions been done by a U.S. official. In simple terms, it targets foreign officials who censor or restrict the speech of Americans, treating that conduct similarly to other reasons someone can be denied entry or removed from the country, such as criminal or security-related grounds.

The bill would amend two parts of the Immigration and Nationality Act: one dealing with who can be denied a visa or entry (inadmissibility) and another dealing with who can be deported after already being in the U.S. It doesn't specify exactly what counts as "censorship"—it uses the standard of whether the action would violate the First Amendment if a U.S. official did it. This means enforcement would likely depend on interpretation by immigration officials, the State Department, or courts.

The people most affected would be foreign government officials—diplomats, regulators, or other representatives of other countries—who are found to have pressured, punished, or restricted American citizens' speech, for example by pushing to remove online content or punishing critics. U.S. citizens are not directly regulated by this bill, but the law could affect diplomatic relations, travel, and how the U.S. handles cases involving foreign governments accused of influencing American speech, including on social media or in other public communications.
ai_headline: Bill would bar foreign officials who censor Americans' speech
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 523.

title: Air Permitting Improvements to Protect National Security Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would change part of the Clean Air Act to make it easier for certain factories to get air pollution permits. Right now, when a new or expanded factory is built in an area with unhealthy air quality, it usually has to "offset" its added pollution by reducing pollution somewhere else, so overall air quality doesn't get worse. This bill would let the President waive that offset requirement entirely for "advanced manufacturing facilities" (mainly semiconductor/computer chip plants) and "critical mineral facilities" (places that mine, process, or refine minerals considered important for national security, like those used in batteries or electronics), if the President decides doing so serves U.S. national security interests. This power could not be handed off to another official.

The bill also sets up a backup option for these same facilities even without a presidential waiver. If a company can show it tried hard to find pollution offsets but couldn't get enough, state permitting agencies would have to allow alternative arrangements—either a different pollution-reduction plan approved by the state, or a fee paid to the state (capped at 1.5 times the recent average cost of pollution controls in that area). States would be required to use that fee money to reduce pollution in the affected area.

This bill would primarily affect companies building semiconductor plants or critical mineral mining/processing facilities, especially in regions with poor air quality where offset requirements are hardest to meet. It could also affect nearby residents, since it loosens a safeguard designed to prevent local air pollution from worsening. Supporters would likely frame this as boosting domestic manufacturing and reducing reliance on foreign supply chains for chips and minerals, while critics might raise concerns about weakened air quality protections for communities near these facilities.
ai_headline: Bill would let president waive pollution offsets for chip plants
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 544.

title: 988 Lifeline Location Improvement Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill sets up a temporary advisory committee to study a specific problem with the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline: when people call or text 988 for help, the system often cannot tell exactly where they are located, unlike the 911 system, which increasingly can pinpoint a caller's precise location. This matters because crisis counselors sometimes need to send emergency help to someone in danger, but without accurate location information, they may not be able to do so quickly or at all.

The 15-member committee would include representatives from phone companies, cell phone manufacturers, 911 call centers, state and local governments, the 988 Lifeline itself, the Veterans Crisis Line, mental health organizations, and advocates for people who are deaf or hard of hearing. Half the members would be appointed by the Federal Communications Commission and half by the Department of Health and Human Services. The committee would study privacy concerns, legal issues, technical challenges, and funding needs related to adding location tracking to 988 calls, then deliver a report with recommendations to Congress and the FCC within one year. After submitting the report, the committee would shut down.

This bill would mainly affect people who use the 988 Lifeline during a mental health crisis, as well as the organizations and companies that operate or support that system. It does not immediately change how 988 works or require any new technology; it only creates a group to study the issue and suggest possible future legislation. The bill also specifies that no new federal money is authorized, meaning the work must be paid for using existing funds.
ai_headline: New panel would study adding location tracking to 988 crisis line
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

title: CLEAR Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the CLEAR Act, would change several parts of the Clean Air Act, the main federal law that regulates air pollution. It stretches the review cycle for national air quality standards from every 5 years to every 10 years, and lets the EPA consider whether a standard is realistically achievable when setting pollution limits, not just health protection. It also gives states more time (up to a year) to fix problems with their pollution-reduction plans before the federal government steps in with its own plan, and it removes certain extra pollution-control requirements for the most polluted "extreme" ozone areas. Additionally, it allows factors like economic feasibility, not just technology, to be considered when setting pollution-reduction requirements in ozone and particulate-matter problem areas.

The bill also changes how "exceptional events" like wildfires are handled. It updates rules for excluding pollution data caused by wildfires or controlled burns from official air quality measurements, sets up a system for states to coordinate when a wildfire affects multiple states, and requires a public website tracking these requests. A new section would protect states from federal penalties or fees if they can show that failing to meet air quality standards was due to pollution from outside their control, such as pollution drifting in from another area, wildfires, or vehicle emissions they can't fully regulate. Finally, it expands the scientific committee that advises the EPA on air quality standards, adding more state representatives from different regions and requiring the committee to weigh in on the economic and social effects of proposed pollution rules.

This bill would primarily affect state environmental agencies, industries and businesses subject to air pollution rules (such as power plants, factories, and vehicle-related industries), and communities living in areas with air quality problems, especially wildfire-prone regions and cities with ozone or particulate matter pollution. Supporters frame it as giving states more flexibility and realistic timelines; critics may see it as weakening pollution enforcement. The bill has been introduced and referred to committee, meaning it has not yet become law.
ai_headline: Bill would loosen Clean Air Act reviews and boost state flexibility
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported by the Yeas and Nays: 27 - 23.

title: Equal Representation Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Equal Representation Act, would make two main changes to how the U.S. government counts people and divides up seats in Congress. First, it would require the Census Bureau to add a citizenship question to the 2030 census and all future censuses. Every person filling out the census would have to say whether they are a U.S. citizen, a U.S. national, a legal immigrant, or an immigrant living in the country without legal permission. The Census Bureau would then have to publicly release state-by-state numbers broken down by these four categories within 120 days of finishing the count.

Second, and more significantly, the bill would change how congressional seats are divided among the states. Currently, the number of U.S. House seats each state gets is based on its total population, including everyone living there regardless of citizenship status. Under this bill, starting with the 2030 census, only U.S. citizens would be counted when determining how many representatives each state gets. This would also affect the Electoral College, since electoral votes are tied to each state's number of representatives.

This bill would primarily affect states with large populations of non-citizens, including both legal immigrants and those living in the country illegally. States like California, Texas, New York, and Florida could potentially lose congressional seats and electoral votes, while states with smaller immigrant populations could gain relative influence. The bill includes a clause saying that if any part of it is later found unconstitutional by courts, the rest of the law would still remain in effect.
ai_headline: Bill would count only citizens for dividing up House seats
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 536.

The Census Bureau would release state-by-state breakdowns within 120 days. title: Ensuring Children Receive Support Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Ensuring Children Receive Support Act," would change how the government handles passports for people who owe significant back child support. Under current law, the State Department has the option to deny, restrict, or revoke passports for people who owe more than $2,500 in child support. This bill would make revocation mandatory instead of optional whenever the Department of Health and Human Services certifies that someone owes more than $2,500. The State Department would also be required to notify the person before taking this action.

The bill does include one exception: if someone is already outside the United States and has an emergency need to return home, the State Department can issue a temporary, limited-use passport just to get them back into the country.

This bill would primarily affect parents who are behind on child support payments by more than $2,500. Instead of leaving it up to officials' discretion, it would require automatic passport revocation once the debt is certified, potentially limiting these individuals' ability to travel internationally, including for work, family, or personal reasons, until their child support debt is resolved. Families owed back child support could benefit from stronger enforcement tools, while people who fall behind on payments—whether due to financial hardship or other reasons—could face significant restrictions on international travel.
ai_headline: Bill would make passport revocation mandatory for unpaid child support
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

title: No Federal Funds for Cashless Bail Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Keep Violent Criminals Off Our Streets Act," would change federal law to withhold certain criminal justice grants from states or local governments that limit the use of cash bail. Specifically, it targets the Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant program, a major source of federal funding that helps state and local police departments, courts, and other criminal justice agencies pay for equipment, programs, and personnel.

Under this bill, if a state or city has a law or policy that significantly restricts judges from requiring cash bail for people charged with certain serious crimes—including violent or sexual offenses like murder, rape, robbery, and assault, as well as offenses like rioting, looting, vandalism, or fleeing from police—that state or local government would become ineligible to receive these federal grants. The restriction would start the first fiscal year after the bill becomes law and continue every year after that.

This would primarily affect states and cities that have adopted bail reform policies, which some jurisdictions have implemented in recent years to reduce or eliminate cash bail requirements, often aiming to avoid keeping people in jail simply because they cannot afford bail while awaiting trial. Local governments and states relying on Byrne grant funding would need to weigh the loss of that funding against keeping their current bail policies. Police departments, court systems, and other agencies that depend on this federal money for training, equipment, and programs could see funding cuts if their jurisdiction's bail laws don't meet the bill's requirements.
ai_headline: Bill would cut federal grants to states that limit cash bail
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 554.

title: Fisher House Availability Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Fisher House Availability Act of 2026, would change federal law to let more people use temporary lodging facilities run by the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), including Fisher Houses. Fisher Houses are homes located near VA medical centers where patients and their families can stay for free while receiving treatment, similar to a "home away from home" during medical care. Currently, this housing is mainly available to veterans and their families. This bill would expand access, on a space-available basis, to certain TRICARE beneficiaries—meaning active-duty military members, retirees, and their families who get healthcare through the military's TRICARE insurance program—when they must travel a significant distance to get medical care at a non-VA facility.

The bill also allows family members or other caregivers who travel with these TRICARE beneficiaries to stay in the lodging as well, as long as space is available. It directs the VA Secretary to set specific rules for deciding who qualifies and how priority is given, since veterans and existing users would still come first. The bill also clarifies and updates some of the legal definitions and cross-references in the relevant part of federal law (Title 38) to make the eligibility rules clearer.

In short, this bill would allow eligible military families using TRICARE—not just VA patients—to stay in VA-supported lodging like Fisher Houses when they have to travel far for medical treatment and there's room available. It aims to make housing support more accessible to more military-connected families, without taking away priority access from veterans.
ai_headline: Bill would open Fisher Houses to TRICARE families with space available
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Veterans' Affairs.

It also lets accompanying family members or caregivers stay, and directs the VA Secretary to set eligibility and priority rules, plus updates related legal definitions in Title 38.

title: Making appropriations for military construction, the Department of Veterans Affairs, and related agencies for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2027, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill provides funding for two main areas: military construction projects and the Department of Veterans Affairs, covering the budget year that runs from October 2026 through September 2027 (with some funds available further into the future). The military construction portion pays for building, renovating, and maintaining bases, housing, and facilities for the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Air Force, National Guard, and Reserves, both in the U.S. and overseas, including America's share of NATO facility costs. It also funds military family housing programs, base closure costs, and includes various rules limiting how the money can be spent, such as requiring Congress to be notified before certain projects begin, favoring U.S. steel and contractors, and blocking any move to close the Guantanamo Bay naval base.

The veterans' portion funds the core services the VA provides, including disability compensation and pension payments, GI Bill and job training benefits, life insurance programs, home loan guarantees, and support for veterans with disabilities. It also funds VA hospitals and clinics, mental health and medical research, community-based care for veterans who can't easily reach a VA facility, the national veterans' cemetery system, and technology upgrades including the ongoing rollout of a new electronic health records system. A large, separate pool of money is set aside specifically for treating illnesses linked to toxic exposures (such as burn pits) faced by veterans during their service.

This bill mainly affects active-duty military families living on base, defense contractors and construction firms, National Guard and Reserve units, and the roughly 9 million veterans who rely on VA healthcare, disability payments, and benefits. It also affects VA employees, hospital staff, and Congressional oversight committees who monitor how this money is spent, since the bill includes detailed reporting and approval requirements before agencies can shift funds between programs.
ai_headline: Bill funds military bases and VA benefits for 2027 budget year
last_action_text: Read the second time. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 455.

title: New Source Review Permitting Improvement Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the Clean Air Act decides when a change at a factory, power plant, or other industrial facility counts as a "modification" that triggers stricter pollution permitting rules. Currently, under the "New Source Review" program, facilities that make physical changes or alter how they operate can be required to install new pollution control equipment if the change increases emissions. This bill would redefine "increase" to mean a higher maximum hourly emission rate compared to any hour in the past 10 years, rather than looking at overall annual emissions increases in some cases. It also says that projects designed to reduce pollution per unit of production, or to improve safety and reliability, would generally not count as a "modification" requiring new permits—unless the EPA determines the change would actually harm human health or the environment.

The bill affects the definitions used across three parts of the Clean Air Act: general new source performance standards, the "Prevention of Significant Deterioration" program (which limits pollution increases in areas with already-clean air), and rules for "nonattainment areas" (places that don't meet air quality standards). In practice, this means industrial facilities—like power plants, refineries, and manufacturing sites—could make certain upgrades, efficiency improvements, or safety-related changes without triggering the more burdensome permitting and pollution-control requirements that currently apply. Supporters of this type of change argue it would make it easier and cheaper for companies to maintain and improve aging equipment. Critics of this type of change argue it could allow some facilities to increase actual pollution output without the environmental review that current law requires. The bill also states it doesn't apply retroactively—it won't reclassify any past changes that weren't previously considered "modifications."
ai_headline: Bill would ease pollution permit rules for factory and plant upgrades
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 542.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 161 redefines "modification" under the Clean Air Act, making it easier for facilities to upgrade without new pollution permits.
ai_sections.what: HR 161 changes how the Clean Air Act determines when a facility change counts as a "modification" triggering stricter pollution permits. It redefines "increase" as a higher maximum hourly emission rate compared to any hour in the past 10 years, rather than annual totals, and generally exempts efficiency or safety upgrades from permitting unless EPA finds they would harm health or the environment.
ai_sections.who: Affects industrial facilities like power plants, refineries, and manufacturing sites, along with the EPA, which enforces Clean Air Act permitting programs.
ai_sections.why: Supporters say it would make upgrading aging equipment cheaper and easier; critics warn it could let facilities increase actual pollution without required environmental review.

title: Monitor Accountability Act
ai_summary:
**HR 8365 — Monitor Accountability Act**

This bill sets new rules for court-appointed "monitors" — people or firms that federal courts assign to oversee state or local governments when a judge orders changes, such as after a lawsuit over policing practices, prison conditions, or civil rights violations. Within 90 days of the law taking effect, the federal courts' administrative office would have to create rules limiting how much monitors can charge, capping their appointment at five years with no reappointment to the same case, and barring them from overseeing more than one monitorship at a time. It also requires public notice and comment before someone is appointed as a monitor, mandates a public hearing before any monitoring requirements can be changed, and requires monitors to file yearly public reports on their fees and services.

The bill also affects monitorships already underway: if one has lasted six years or more, a new monitor must be appointed within 180 days, and the case must be reassigned to a different judge within a year. Going forward, any monitorship still active after six years automatically moves to a new judge.

This bill would primarily affect state and local governments under federal court oversight (for example, police departments, jails, or agencies operating under consent decrees), the attorneys and consultants who serve as monitors, and the federal judges who appoint and supervise them. Supporters would frame it as increasing transparency and limiting costs; critics might see it as adding new procedural hurdles to court oversight. The bill itself is written in neutral, procedural terms without stating a political goal.
ai_headline: New bill would cap court monitors' fees, terms, and reappointments
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill caps court-appointed monitors at five years, limits fees, and shifts long-running cases to new judges.

It also requires public notice before appointment, a public hearing before changing monitoring requirements, and yearly public fee reports. Monitorships lasting six years or more would get a new monitor within 180 days and be reassigned to a different judge within a year, with future cases past six years automatically moving to a new judge.
