title: Clean Air and Building Infrastructure Improvement Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) rolls out new air quality standards under the Clean Air Act, focusing on permits businesses need before building or modifying facilities that release air pollution.

Under current law, when the EPA sets or updates a national air quality standard, companies seeking "preconstruction permits" (approval to build or expand a facility) must show their project complies with that new standard. This bill requires the EPA to simultaneously release clear guidance explaining how to apply for and evaluate permits under any new standard. If the EPA fails to provide that guidance at the same time as the new standard, the new standard would not apply to permit applications until the guidance is actually published. This means companies could get permits based on older, less strict standards if the EPA is slow to issue instructions. The bill also states that companies would still have to use the best available pollution-control technology, and that state, local, or tribal governments could still set stricter rules if they choose.

The bill also directly addresses a specific 2024 EPA rule that tightened standards for fine particulate matter pollution (soot), a pollutant linked to health problems like asthma and heart disease. It says that rule won't apply to certain permit applications that were already complete, or where a preliminary decision was already published, before the area's official pollution designation was finalized. This mainly affects companies applying for permits to build or expand factories, power plants, and other facilities that emit air pollution, as well as state and local permitting agencies. Supporters frame it as reducing delays and uncertainty in the permitting process; critics may see it as potentially slowing enforcement of stricter pollution standards. The bill does not eliminate any state or local authority to set tougher rules.
ai_headline: Bill would delay new EPA air standards without matching permit guidance
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 543.

ai_sections.tldr: New EPA air quality standards wouldn't apply to permits until the agency issues matching guidance.
ai_sections.what: This bill requires the EPA to release permit guidance at the same time it sets a new air quality standard. If the guidance is delayed, the new standard can't be used for permit applications until the guidance is published, meaning older standards would apply in the meantime. Companies would still need best available pollution-control technology, and states, localities, or tribes could still impose stricter rules.

title: Review Every Veterans Claim Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 2137, called the Review Every Veterans Claim Act of 2025, changes how the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) handles claims when a veteran misses a required medical exam. Under current rules, if a veteran doesn't show up for a VA medical examination related to their disability or benefits claim, the VA can sometimes deny the claim simply because the veteran missed that appointment. This bill would stop that practice by requiring the VA to actually review the merits of a veteran's claim rather than reject it outright just because the exam was missed.

The bill makes a technical change to a section of veterans' benefits law, updating language so the rule applies broadly to all types of VA benefit claims, not just compensation claims. It adds a new provision stating clearly that a missed medical exam alone cannot be the sole reason for denying a claim. This means the VA would still be able to consider a missed exam as one factor, but would have to look at other available evidence, like medical records, service history, or previous exams, before deciding whether to approve or deny the claim.

This bill primarily affects military veterans who are applying for benefits such as disability compensation, pension, or other VA-administered programs. Veterans sometimes miss scheduled exams due to transportation issues, health problems, scheduling conflicts, homelessness, or communication breakdowns with the VA. Supporters of this kind of change argue it would prevent veterans from losing benefits due to circumstances beyond their control. The bill would also affect VA staff and adjudicators, who would need to follow updated procedures when evaluating claims where an exam was missed.
ai_headline: Bill would bar VA from denying claims solely over missed exams
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 549.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill stops the VA from denying veterans' benefit claims based only on a missed medical exam.
ai_sections.what: HR 2137, the Review Every Veterans Claim Act of 2025, requires the VA to review the merits of a veteran's claim rather than deny it solely because a required medical exam was missed. It expands an existing rule to cover all VA benefit claims, not just compensation claims, and directs the VA to weigh other evidence like medical records and service history.

title: VA Mental Health Outreach and Engagement Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the VA Mental Health Outreach and Engagement Act, would require the Department of Veterans Affairs to offer yearly mental health check-ins to veterans who receive disability compensation for a service-connected mental health condition. Currently, the VA offers an initial mental health consultation to certain veterans, but this bill adds a requirement for ongoing, annual follow-ups. During these yearly consultations, the VA would assess the veteran's current mental health needs and discuss available treatment options. The bill also requires the VA to actively reach out to these veterans to make sure they know these consultations and other mental health services exist.

The bill includes a safeguard clarifying that going through these consultations cannot be used as a reason to reevaluate or reduce a veteran's disability compensation, which addresses a common fear that seeking mental health care could jeopardize benefits. Additionally, the bill requires the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a federal watchdog agency, to study how well this new system is working within two years of the law passing. That report would look at how many veterans received consultations and outreach, and whether veterans faced any barriers to getting this care.

This bill primarily affects veterans who already receive VA disability payments for mental health conditions such as PTSD, depression, or anxiety. It would not change benefits amounts or eligibility, but it aims to increase regular contact between these veterans and VA mental health services, with the goal of catching problems early and connecting veterans with additional care if needed.
ai_headline: VA would owe annual mental health check-ins to disabled veterans
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 550.

During these check-ins, the VA assesses current mental health needs and discusses treatment options, and must actively reach out so veterans know these services exist. title: Student Aid Fraud Oversight and Accountability Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would change how the U.S. Department of Education decides which colleges and universities get closer scrutiny for how they handle federal financial aid. Specifically, it targets schools that give out federal student aid to students whose financial aid applications (FAFSA) show signs of possible identity fraud. If a school hands out aid to such a student without first verifying that student's identity in person or through a live video call, that school would be flagged and moved to the top of the list for program reviews and audits by the Department of Education.

Schools can avoid this flagging if they properly check a suspicious student's identity before releasing the aid money, using in-person verification or live video verification, and keep records showing they did so. The bill makes clear that simply being flagged doesn't automatically mean a school broke any rules—it just means the school will be reviewed more closely.

This bill mainly affects colleges, universities, and other institutions that participate in federal student aid programs, as well as the Department of Education's oversight processes. It's aimed at reducing fraud in the student aid system, where scammers sometimes use stolen identities to apply for and collect financial aid money meant for real students. Students themselves aren't directly penalized by this bill, but it could lead to schools adopting stricter identity-verification steps when processing financial aid applications.
ai_headline: Bill targets colleges that skip ID checks on suspect student aid
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 582.

title: Geothermal Cost-Recovery Authority Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would let the Department of the Interior charge companies fees to cover the government's costs of processing geothermal energy leases and permits, and inspecting geothermal drilling and facility projects. Geothermal energy uses heat from underground to produce power, and companies must currently apply for federal leases and permits to drill on public lands. Under this bill, from when it becomes law until September 30, 2032, the Interior Department could require these companies to pay back the government's administrative expenses for reviewing applications, issuing permits, and monitoring drilling, well operations, and site construction or cleanup.

The bill includes some flexibility: officials would consider whether a company already has a cost-sharing agreement with the government, and they could reduce fees if full payment would cause financial hardship or would discourage the use of geothermal energy. Money collected would go back into the Interior Department's budget specifically to fund this same leasing and inspection work, rather than going into the general treasury.

This bill mainly affects companies that develop geothermal energy projects on federal lands, as they could face new fees for the permitting and inspection process. It could also affect the Bureau of Land Management, which manages this program, by giving it more funding tied directly to industry activity rather than relying solely on congressional appropriations. Five years after enactment, Interior would have to report to Congress on how this fee system affected the geothermal program and recommend whether to continue or change it, gathering input from industry and other interested parties in the process.

last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 569.

The authority runs from enactment until September 30, 2032. Officials could reduce fees for financial hardship or existing cost-sharing agreements, and money collected would fund this same leasing and inspection work.

title: STEAM Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the STEAM Act, aims to make it faster and easier to explore for and develop geothermal energy (energy created from heat inside the earth) in areas where drilling or environmental studies have already taken place. Geothermal energy is often used to generate electricity or heat buildings, and companies need government approval before drilling new wells or expanding projects.

Specifically, the bill changes a section of the Energy Policy Act of 2005 that currently allows oil and gas projects to skip certain lengthy environmental reviews (required under the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA) if the area has already been reviewed or developed before. This bill extends that same shortcut to geothermal projects. In practice, this means geothermal companies could avoid repeating time-consuming environmental studies in locations that have already been analyzed or drilled, as long as the new work falls under specific existing categories in the law.

This bill mainly affects geothermal energy companies, federal land management agencies (like the Bureau of Land Management), and communities located near geothermal development sites, particularly in Western states like Nevada and Utah where geothermal resources are common. Supporters generally argue it would speed up clean energy development and reduce bureaucratic delays, while critics of similar streamlining measures often raise concerns about reduced environmental oversight. The bill itself does not take a position—it simply changes the review process for future geothermal projects.
ai_headline: Bill would let geothermal projects skip some environmental reviews
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 570.

Geothermal developers could skip certain environmental studies in areas that have already been reviewed or drilled, if the work fits existing legal categories.

title: MAP for Broadband Funding Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the MAP for Broadband Funding Act, aims to improve a federal tool called the Broadband Funding Map, which tracks where government money is being spent to expand internet access across the country. The goal of this map is to prevent different federal programs from wastefully funding internet infrastructure in the same locations, ensuring taxpayer money is used efficiently. The bill directs the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), working with the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), to collect better and more timely data from federal agencies for this map, and to formally study how the map's usefulness, accuracy, and public transparency could be improved.

Specifically, the FCC would have to open a public review process within 270 days of the bill becoming law, examining whether the map's data is complete, up-to-date, and easy for people to use, and whether it should be combined with other FCC mapping tools. Separately, the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a nonpartisan government watchdog agency, would have 180 days to study how well various federal agencies are contributing data to the map and whether the FCC has enough authority to collect that information properly.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies involved in broadband funding, such as the Department of Agriculture, Housing and Urban Development, Health and Human Services, and others, requiring them to better coordinate and share data. Indirectly, it could benefit the general public, especially people in rural or underserved areas waiting for internet expansion, by helping ensure federal broadband dollars are spent more effectively and are not wasted on duplicate projects.
ai_headline: Bill orders review of federal map tracking broadband funding sites
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

The FCC must open a public review within 270 days to assess the map's completeness, accuracy, and usability, and the GAO must study within 180 days how well agencies contribute data and whether the FCC has sufficient authority to collect it.

title: Recover COVID Unemployment Fraud in Banks Act
ai_summary:
This bill aims to recover leftover COVID-19 unemployment benefits that were improperly paid out and are now sitting unused in bank accounts or with state unclaimed property offices. During the pandemic, many unemployment payments were loaded onto prepaid debit cards, and some of that money was never claimed or was tied to fraudulent claims. The bill creates a "National Recovery Coordinator" and a task force made up of officials from the Labor Department, Treasury, Justice Department, FDIC, and Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. This task force would work with states to identify this leftover money, create standard procedures for banks and states to review and return improper payments, and issue guidance on how to handle cases involving identity theft or fraud. The federal government would also reimburse states for costs they incur helping with this effort.

The bill also extends the deadline for prosecuting people who committed fraud to get pandemic unemployment benefits. Currently, criminal and civil cases must be filed within a standard time limit, but this bill extends that window to 10 years from when the fraud occurred, giving investigators more time to build cases and pursue wrongdoers. This change would not revive cases where the old deadline had already passed before this law takes effect.

This bill mainly affects banks and financial institutions that processed pandemic unemployment payments, state unemployment agencies, and people who received (or fraudulently claimed) pandemic unemployment benefits. It does not create new benefits or directly affect people who properly received unemployment assistance; instead, it focuses on recovering misplaced or fraudulently obtained funds and giving law enforcement more time to pursue fraud cases.

last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

title: No Aid for Ghost Students Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "No Aid for Ghost Students Act of 2026," aims to stop fraud in the federal financial aid system by requiring the Department of Education to screen every FAFSA application (the form students fill out to get federal financial aid for college) using an identity fraud detection system. This responds to concerns about fake or "ghost" students—often created using stolen identities—who enroll in classes just to collect financial aid money without actually attending school.

Starting October 1, 2026, if the system flags an application as suspicious, the Department of Education must notify both the applicant and the college or university the student listed on their form. The student would then have to go through extra identity checks—either in person or through a live video call—before their school could release any federal financial aid money to them. Colleges would be required to confirm the person's identity, tell the government it's been verified, and keep records of that verification.

This bill mainly affects college students applying for federal financial aid, especially those whose applications get flagged for review, as well as colleges and universities that must handle the added verification steps. It also affects the Department of Education, which must build the fraud detection system, issue guidelines to schools, and report to Congress each year on how well the system is working. The goal is to prevent taxpayer money from going to fraudulent applicants while trying to minimize inconvenience for legitimate students.
ai_headline: New bill requires fraud screening for every federal financial aid application
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

Starting October 1, 2026, flagged applications trigger notifications to both the applicant and their listed school, and the student must complete identity verification—in person or via live video—before aid is released.

title: Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agency Appropriations Act, 2027
ai_summary:
# H.R. 8646 — Agriculture, Rural Development, FDA Appropriations Act, 2027

This bill decides how much federal money will be spent during the 2027 budget year on the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), rural development programs, and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), along with related agencies. It works by setting specific dollar amounts for dozens of individual offices and programs—everything from the Secretary of Agriculture's office to food safety inspections, farm loans, crop insurance, agricultural research, rural housing, and rural business development. Rather than making new policy from scratch, it mostly continues and adjusts funding for programs that already exist, while attaching various conditions on how the money can be used (for example, requiring agencies to notify Congress before making certain changes, capping construction costs for buildings, or setting minimum funding levels for specific programs like historically Black land-grant colleges or tribal programs).

In practical terms, this bill affects farmers and ranchers (through crop insurance, farm loans, and disaster programs), rural residents (through housing loans, rental assistance, and community facility grants for things like rural hospitals and water systems), consumers (through food safety inspections of meat, poultry, and eggs), and researchers and universities (through agricultural research and extension funding). It also funds the day-to-day operations of USDA's many internal offices, such as civil rights, inspector general oversight, and technology systems. Because the FDA is included in this same funding bill, portions also cover the government's food and drug safety oversight work, though the excerpt provided focuses mostly on USDA and rural development spending.

This is considered a "must-pass" type of bill because without it, or a temporary funding measure, these agencies would lack the money to keep operating past the end of the current fiscal year. The specific dollar figures and rules in the bill determine staffing levels, loan availability, research grants, and support services that farmers, rural communities, and food safety systems rely on nationwide.

title: Stop Child Care Scams Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Stop Child Care Scams Act of 2026 (also referred to in the text as the "No Funds for Repeat Child Care Violations Act"), makes a small but meaningful change to federal law governing child care funding. It amends the Child Care and Development Block Grant Act of 1990, which sends federal money to states to help pay for child care programs, particularly for low-income families.

Specifically, the bill changes one word in the law: it replaces "may" with "shall" in the section dealing with withholding funds from states that don't comply with program rules. Under current law, the Secretary of Health and Human Services has discretion to withhold funding from a state that repeatedly violates the rules of the child care grant program, such as failing to prevent fraud. This bill would remove that discretion and require the Secretary to withhold funds in those situations.

This change mainly affects state governments that administer child care assistance programs funded by this federal grant. If a state is found to be repeatedly noncompliant, particularly regarding fraud prevention, the federal government would now be legally required to cut off funding rather than simply having the option to do so. Indirectly, this could affect families relying on state-run child care assistance and child care providers who receive subsidies, since funding cuts to noncompliant states could disrupt program operations if states don't fix the underlying problems.

title: Transportation, Housing and Urban Development, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2027
ai_summary:
This bill sets spending levels for the Department of Transportation, the Department of Housing and Urban Development, and related agencies for the fiscal year starting October 2027. It funds things like the FAA's air traffic control operations, airport construction grants, highway programs, essential air service to small/rural communities, Amtrak and rail programs, and various transportation research and safety initiatives. It also includes a $100 million provision tied to an executive order about "making DC safe and beautiful," directing money toward Metro transit security and repairs at Washington's Union Station. Money is organized into specific accounts, with detailed rules on how much can be shifted between programs and what Congress must be told before changes happen.

Beyond dollar amounts, the bill includes policy conditions attached to the funding. Examples include blocking the FAA from privatizing air traffic control functions, protecting aircraft owners' ability to keep their flight-tracking data private, limiting political appointees at the FAA, protecting certain airport tower programs from closure, and restricting new aviation user fees. It also addresses specific situations, like reimbursing airports and aviation businesses financially harmed by temporary flight restrictions related to presidential travel, and setting rules for a rural infrastructure technical assistance program and grants for polluted-site cleanup ("PFAS") at airports.

This bill mainly affects people and organizations connected to transportation: airline passengers (through FAA and airport funding), residents of rural areas relying on subsidized flights or road/bridge projects, airport operators, transit riders in the Washington D.C. area, universities receiving earmarked research grants, and federal employees within these agencies. State and local governments, Native American tribes, and companies that build or maintain infrastructure would also be affected, since the bill determines how federal grant and construction money flows to specific projects and regions across the country.

ai_summary:

title: Energy Emergency Leadership Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Energy Emergency Leadership Act, would change how the U.S. Department of Energy is organized by officially assigning "energy emergency and energy security" duties to one of its Assistant Secretaries. Right now, the law that created the Department of Energy lists various responsibilities for its Assistant Secretaries, but it doesn't clearly spell out who handles energy emergencies, infrastructure security, cyberattacks, supply disruptions, or disaster response and recovery. This bill fixes that by adding a specific new duty covering all of these areas, including planning ahead for emergencies and coordinating the government's response when something goes wrong.

The bill also allows state, local, and tribal governments, as well private energy companies, to request technical help from the Department of Energy if they're dealing with threats to their energy systems, such as cyberattacks or infrastructure damage. The Department would be required to work with other federal agencies when providing this support, ensuring a coordinated national response rather than a patchwork of separate efforts.

In practical terms, this bill mainly affects how the federal government is internally organized and staffed, rather than creating new programs or spending money. It could matter to state and local officials, utility companies, and energy infrastructure operators (like power grid or pipeline operators) who might seek federal help during emergencies such as cyberattacks, natural disasters, or fuel shortages. Everyday residents would likely feel the effects only indirectly, through potentially faster or better-coordinated federal responses to energy-related emergencies that could affect electricity, fuel, or other energy services.

title: Secure America Act
ai_summary:
The Secure America Act is a budget bill that provides tens of billions of dollars in extra funding for U.S. border security and immigration enforcement agencies for fiscal year 2026, with the money available through September 2029. It gives roughly $9.5 billion to Customs and Border Protection (CBP) for hiring and equipping Border Patrol agents for non-immigration duties, $7.45 billion to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for its Homeland Security Investigations division (including funding to fight child exploitation), and $3.45 billion for border technology like surveillance systems, inspection equipment, and biometric screening. It also adds $2.5 billion in general Department of Homeland Security funding, all under the "Homeland Security" committee's portion of the bill.

A second part of the bill, overseen by the Judiciary Committee, provides even larger sums specifically for immigration enforcement: about $13 billion to CBP and $31 billion to ICE. The ICE money covers hiring more agents and attorneys, expanding detention and deportation operations, maintaining vehicles and facilities, and supporting local police partnerships known as "287(g) agreements." A notable provision sets aside $350 million specifically for arresting and detaining certain unlawful immigrants with criminal records who are released in places that don't fully cooperate with federal immigration authorities, though Native American tribal lands are excluded from being treated as uncooperative.

This bill mainly affects federal immigration and border agencies (CBP, ICE, and DHS), their employees, and the communities near U.S. borders. It also affects immigrants without legal status, particularly those with criminal charges or convictions, since it funds expanded efforts to detain and deport them. Local and state governments may be affected as well, depending on whether they participate in cooperation agreements with federal immigration authorities, which can influence how much enforcement funding or attention their area receives.

title: COVID Fraud Transparency Act of 2026
ai_summary:
HR 826, the COVID Fraud Transparency Act of 2026, requires the Inspector General of the Small Business Administration (SBA) to regularly report on fraud connected to certain COVID-19 relief loans. Specifically, within 60 days of the bill becoming law, and every three months after that, the Inspector General must send a report to Congress's Small Business Committees covering how many of these loans were issued and their total dollar value, how many new fraud or suspected fraud cases came up, how many fraud cases were resolved, and what types of fraud were involved.

The loans covered by this bill include Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loans and Economic Injury Disaster Loans (EIDL), which were created to help small businesses survive during the pandemic. This reporting requirement would automatically end two years after the bill is enacted, and the bill does not authorize any new government spending to carry it out.

This bill mainly affects government oversight processes rather than everyday citizens directly. It would primarily impact the SBA's Inspector General office, which would take on additional reporting duties, and members of Congress, who would receive more regular updates on fraud tied to pandemic-era small business loans. Indirectly, it could affect small business owners who received these loans, since increased fraud reporting could lead to more scrutiny or investigations related to how the loans were used.

title: Main Street Competes Act
ai_summary:
The Main Street Competes Act would update a 1980 law about small business policy to specifically address how antitrust enforcement affects small companies. It adds language stating that the government should promote competitive markets, protect consumer choice, and support business ownership by enforcing federal antitrust laws against anticompetitive behavior and illegal mergers that harm small businesses.

The bill's main practical effect is creating a new reporting system. Every two years, the Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission (the two federal agencies responsible for enforcing antitrust laws) would have to submit detailed reports tracking their antitrust work as it relates to small businesses. These reports would include how many complaints small businesses filed alleging antitrust violations, how many investigations or enforcement actions resulted from those complaints, and how many additional antitrust actions the agencies took on their own initiative. This information would go to the Small Business Administration's Office of Advocacy, which would then analyze the data and send a summary report to Congress's small business committees, including recommendations for further administrative or legislative action.

This bill would primarily affect small business owners, who might benefit from increased federal attention to whether large companies or mergers are squeezing them out of markets unfairly. It would also create new work requirements for the DOJ and FTC, and give Congress more regular information to evaluate whether antitrust enforcement is adequately protecting small businesses. It does not change antitrust law itself or give agencies new enforcement powers—it mainly increases transparency and data collection about how existing laws are being used.

title: Small Business Cybersecurity Assistance Evaluation Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Government Accountability Office (GAO), led by the Comptroller General, to study how well federal programs help small businesses deal with cybersecurity threats. The study would look at the most common cyberattacks hitting small businesses, catalog existing federal programs and tools meant to help, and assess whether small business owners actually know about and use these resources. It would also evaluate how well different federal programs work together, identify any gaps in basic cybersecurity coverage, and produce recommendations for improving these programs. The GAO would then report its findings to the House and Senate Small Business Committees.

This bill does not create any new cybersecurity programs, funding, or requirements for small businesses themselves. It's purely a review and reporting exercise aimed at figuring out whether current government efforts to help small businesses protect against hacking, scams, and fraud are actually effective and easy to access. The bill also specifies that no new government spending is authorized to carry out this study, meaning it must be done within existing GAO budgets.

The people most affected would be small business owners, who might eventually benefit if the study leads to better-designed or better-publicized cybersecurity assistance programs down the road. Federal agencies that run cybersecurity assistance programs (such as the Small Business Administration and possibly the Department of Homeland Security) would also be affected, since they would likely need to provide information to the GAO for this evaluation. In the near term, though, this bill has no direct effect on the public and simply sets up a study and report for lawmakers to review.

title: Oversight and Transparency for Small Business Certifications Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Oversight and Transparency for Small Business Certifications Act of 2026, would require the Small Business Administration (SBA) to give Congress a detailed yearly report on how small businesses apply for and receive certification to participate in certain federal contracting programs. These programs help small businesses—including those owned by service-disabled veterans, women, and businesses located in economically struggling areas known as HUBZones—get access to government contracts set aside specifically for them.

The report would have to include specific numbers, such as how many businesses applied, how many were certified or denied, how long the certification process took, and how many applications are still waiting for a decision. It would also track whether businesses applied through the SBA's single online application system or through other means, and whether they applied for multiple certification programs at once. For programs specific to veterans and women-owned businesses, the report would break down average processing times separately for first-time applicants versus those renewing their certification.

This bill mainly affects the SBA, which would have new reporting duties, and small business owners who rely on these certification programs to qualify for federal contracts. It does not create new programs or change who is eligible for certification; instead, it aims to give Congress and the public better information about how efficiently the SBA processes these applications, which could help identify delays or problems in the system.

title: Small Business Technological Advancement Act
ai_summary:
HR 915, called the Small Business Technological Act of 2025, would change federal law to make it clearer that small businesses can use Small Business Administration (SBA) loans to pay for modern business software and technology. This includes things like cloud computing services, payroll processing tools, human resources software, sales and billing systems, accounting and inventory tracking programs, and even tools that use artificial intelligence. The bill adds this as a specifically approved use under the SBA's main loan program, known as the 7(a) loan program.

In practical terms, this bill is mainly about clarifying and confirming what SBA loans can be used for, rather than creating a brand-new loan program. It also notes that businesses that already used SBA loans for these kinds of technology purchases before this law passes were not doing anything wrong, since those uses were already allowed. The bill specifically states that loans still cannot be used for research and development, and it does not change any other existing rules about what counts as "working capital" for small businesses.

This bill would primarily affect small business owners who want to modernize their operations with software and technology but need financing to do so. It could also affect banks and lenders that issue SBA-backed loans, since it gives them clearer guidance on approving loans for these technology-related expenses. Overall, the bill is intended to make it easier and less ambiguous for small businesses to get financial support for adopting modern digital tools.

title: Export Controls Enforcement Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Export Controls Enforcement Act, aims to strengthen how the U.S. government monitors and enforces rules about exporting sensitive American technology and goods overseas. Currently, the Bureau of Industry and Security (an agency within the Department of Commerce) only has 11 "export control officers" stationed abroad to check whether exported items are being used properly and not illegally diverted to unauthorized users, such as hostile governments or criminal groups. With only 11 officers covering dozens of countries, Congress found that many regions have no coverage at all, even though the Bureau processes tens of thousands of export license applications worth hundreds of billions of dollars each year.

To fix this gap, the bill requires the Secretary of Commerce to create a five-year program stationing at least 20 export control officers at U.S. embassies and consulates around the world, roughly doubling the current number. A program director would be appointed to oversee hiring and work with the State Department to make sure officers are spread out strategically to cover every world region. These officers would conduct on-the-ground inspections, advise diplomatic staff, work with foreign governments and businesses on compliance, and help identify high-risk situations where illegal diversion of controlled technology might occur.

This bill mainly affects the Department of Commerce and State Department's operations abroad, along with U.S. companies that export controlled technology, such as advanced electronics, weapons components, or dual-use industrial equipment. It could also affect foreign businesses and governments that receive U.S. exports, since they may face more oversight and inspections. Everyday Americans wouldn't interact with this directly, but the bill is meant to reduce risks that sensitive U.S. technology ends up in the hands of adversaries or is used for unauthorized purposes, which relates to national security and foreign policy.

title: Cross-Boundary Wildfire Solutions Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Cross-Boundary Wildfire Solutions Act, asks a government watchdog agency, the Government Accountability Office (led by the Comptroller General), to study how wildfire prevention efforts work when land is owned by different groups, such as the federal government, states, tribes, and private landowners. Wildfires don't stop at property lines, but different rules and funding programs can make it hard for agencies to coordinate fire prevention work across those boundaries. The study would look at which current programs and rules help or get in the way of this kind of teamwork.

Specifically, the study would examine federal agencies that manage land, the Department of Agriculture, FEMA, and the U.S. Fire Administration, along with state, local, and tribal governments, to see if any of them need more funding or authority to do wildfire mitigation work that crosses ownership lines. It would also review a specific existing law (from the Healthy Forests Restoration Act) to see if it has actually helped agencies get more funding for wildfire prevention. Within two years, the results and recommendations would be reported to relevant congressional committees.

This bill does not create new programs or spend money on wildfire prevention itself. Instead, it affects government agencies and lawmakers by requiring research and a report that could inform future legislation. Indirectly, it could benefit communities in wildfire-prone areas, including those living near forests or wildland areas, if the findings lead to better-coordinated wildfire prevention efforts down the road.

title: Department of Homeland Security Appropriations Act, 2027
ai_summary:
# H.R. 9310 — Department of Homeland Security Appropriations Act, 2027

This bill funds the entire Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for the fiscal year starting October 2026, totaling well over $100 billion. It sets specific dollar amounts for every major DHS agency, including Customs and Border Protection (CBP), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), the Coast Guard, the Secret Service, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). Money is designated for things like border vehicles and technology, detention facilities, airport screening staff and equipment, Coast Guard ships and aircraft, Secret Service protective operations, disaster relief funding, and grants to state and local governments for emergency preparedness, firefighting, port security, and cybersecurity.

Beyond just dollar amounts, the bill includes dozens of specific rules and conditions. Examples include: requiring body cameras for immigration enforcement officers, blocking new fees for crossing the northern or southern border, prohibiting funds for non-accredited schools admitting international students, requiring ICE detention facilities to meet minimum performance standards, protecting pregnant detainees' medical care standards, barring gender-transition medical procedures for people in ICE custody, restricting abortion funding except in cases of rape, incest, or life endangerment, and requiring frequent reports to Congress on spending, staffing, detention capacity, and acquisition programs. It also blocks Congress members, cabinet officials, and other senior government leaders from skipping standard airport security screening.

This bill affects nearly everyone in the U.S. in some way: travelers going through airport security, immigrants and asylum seekers interacting with CBP or ICE, communities relying on FEMA disaster aid or firefighter grants, cities receiving federal counterterrorism and cybersecurity grants, and federal employees in these agencies. It also affects people in Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and the Northern Mariana Islands due to specific provisions covering those territories, and businesses or contractors that work with DHS agencies on detention, security equipment, or technology.

title: Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2027
ai_summary:
This bill, H.R. 9260, is the annual funding bill for the Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education for the fiscal year starting October 2027. Rather than creating new policy from scratch, it sets specific dollar amounts that federal agencies can spend on hundreds of existing programs, ranging from job training and unemployment insurance to workplace safety enforcement, veterans' employment services, and pension protections. The excerpt covers mainly the Labor Department portion, funding things like the Job Corps program (job training for young people), state unemployment insurance systems, apprenticeship grants, OSHA and mine safety enforcement, and support for disabled coal miners and injured federal workers.

The bill affects a wide range of everyday people: workers seeking job training or unemployment benefits, veterans transitioning to civilian careers, coal miners with health claims, apprentices in registered training programs, and people with disabilities seeking employment support. It also includes specific policy riders—for example, blocking funds for a proposed heat-safety workplace rule, restricting new wage rules for certain temporary foreign worker visa programs (H-2A and H-2B), limiting high salaries for Job Corps administrators, and barring companies convicted of human trafficking from hiring foreign workers through certain visa programs. Some provisions also rescind (cancel) previously approved but unspent funds and give agencies flexibility to shift limited amounts of money between programs.

Because this is an appropriations bill, its practical effect is mostly on federal agencies and the organizations, states, and contractors that receive federal grants to run these programs—not direct payments to individuals in most cases. However, changes in funding levels can influence how many people are served, how quickly claims are processed, and whether certain regulations move forward, indirectly affecting workers, job seekers, veterans, and businesses that rely on these federal programs.

title: Protect America’s Innovation and Economic Security from CCP Act
ai_summary:
This bill, HR 1468, would create a new program inside the Department of Justice called the "CCP Initiative," housed in the department's National Security Division. Its purpose would be to counter espionage and economic threats linked to the Chinese Communist Party, including spying on U.S. intellectual property and academic institutions. The initiative would focus on identifying researchers, universities, and defense-industry contacts being used to improperly transfer technology; enforcing existing foreign investment review laws; investigating Chinese companies that may violate anti-bribery laws or compete unfairly with U.S. businesses; prosecuting trade secret theft and hacking; protecting critical infrastructure from foreign investment risks; and looking into investments by Chinese companies already flagged on U.S. government watchlists.

The bill requires this initiative to operate as a standalone unit within the Justice Department, with its own dedicated staff and funding that cannot be merged with other programs, even other efforts targeting foreign threats. The Attorney General would have to submit a detailed annual report to relevant House and Senate committees describing the initiative's progress, funding levels, coordination with the FBI and other agencies, and estimates of economic harm caused by Chinese hacking and trade secret theft. The law would automatically expire six years after it takes effect unless renewed.

This bill would primarily affect the Department of Justice, the FBI, and other federal agencies involved in national security and trade enforcement, as well as universities, research labs, and businesses that may be investigated for ties to foreign technology transfer. It could also affect Chinese companies and their U.S.-based subsidiaries. It does not create new crimes or directly affect the general public's daily life, but it could increase government scrutiny of academic and business research partnerships with China-linked entities.

title: SBA Artificial Intelligence Utilization Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the SBA Artificial Intelligence Utilization Act of 2026, would require the Small Business Administration (SBA) to regularly report to Congress on how it uses artificial intelligence and machine learning technology. Within 90 days of the law passing, and then every year after that, the SBA Administrator would have to send a detailed report to the House and Senate small business committees explaining how the agency is using these technologies, what benefits and risks they create, and how the agency plans to manage those risks responsibly. The Administrator would also have to brief Congress in person within 30 days of each report.

The reports would need to cover specific concerns, such as making sure humans stay involved in important decisions rather than letting AI decide things alone, figuring out which tasks AI can actually handle well versus where it might fail, and evaluating whether specific AI tools are worth adopting for the agency's needs. This is meant to help ensure the SBA uses AI carefully and transparently rather than rushing to adopt new technology without oversight.

This bill mainly affects how the SBA itself operates internally—it does not directly change any programs, loans, or services that small business owners receive. However, it could indirectly affect small business owners and entrepreneurs who interact with the SBA, since the agency uses AI in areas like processing loan applications, fraud detection, and customer service. By requiring more oversight and transparency, the bill aims to make sure AI tools used by the SBA are reliable and don't create unfair problems for the people and businesses the agency serves. It would also give Congress more visibility into how a federal agency is adopting AI technology, which could serve as a model for similar oversight at other agencies.

title: Securing Semiconductor Supply Chains Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Securing Semiconductor Supply Chains Act, directs a federal program called SelectUSA to work more closely with state economic development offices to attract foreign investment in semiconductor manufacturing in the United States. Semiconductors are computer chips used in everything from cars to smartphones to military equipment, and the bill notes that supply shortages in recent years have hurt the economy and raised national security concerns. SelectUSA, which is part of the Department of Commerce, already works to bring foreign business investment into the country, and this bill would have it focus specifically on the chip industry.

Under the bill, SelectUSA would have 180 days to gather input from state-level economic development organizations on how to attract more foreign investment in chip-making, packaging, and related materials and equipment. It would also need to identify barriers to that investment and develop recommendations for working with allied countries, while making sure that "foreign adversaries" (a term already defined in existing telecommunications security law, generally referring to countries like China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea) don't benefit from these efforts. Within two years, SelectUSA would have to submit a report to Congress summarizing what it learned and what strategies it plans to use.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies, state economic development offices, and the semiconductor industry, rather than individual citizens directly. It does not authorize any new government spending; the work would be done using SelectUSA's existing budget. Indirectly, workers in manufacturing and technology industries, as well as consumers who rely on products containing semiconductors, could benefit if the effort succeeds in strengthening the domestic supply chain.
ai_headline: Bill directs SelectUSA to boost foreign investment in chip manufacturing
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027
ai_summary:
This bill, the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for Fiscal Year 2027, sets policy and spending limits for the U.S. military and related national security programs for the coming year. It doesn't actually provide the money itself—that happens through separate appropriations bills—but it authorizes how much can be spent and on what, and it sets rules for how the Department of Defense operates. The bill covers an enormous range of topics: buying weapons, ships, aircraft, and equipment; funding research on things like artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and hypersonic weapons; setting the number of active-duty and reserve troops; and determining pay raises and benefits for service members and their families.

Beyond the big-ticket military hardware, the bill also touches everyday concerns for military families and personnel, such as TRICARE health coverage, child care programs, housing conditions on bases, education benefits, and protections for whistleblowers or victims of domestic violence. It includes numerous policy provisions on hot-button issues like diversity and inclusion rules, restrictions on transgender or "male" participation in women's athletics at service academies, and various administrative reforms to modernize the Pentagon's bureaucracy, cybersecurity, and acquisition process. It also proposes renaming the Department of Defense as the "Department of War" and reorganizing several military commands.

This bill mainly affects active-duty service members, military retirees, veterans, and their families, along with defense contractors, civilian employees of the Department of Defense, and communities near military bases. It also has ripple effects for U.S. relationships with allied countries (like Israel, Ukraine, Taiwan, and NATO members) through provisions on foreign military assistance and cooperation. Because it's such a large, wide-ranging bill, it effectively shapes military readiness, national security strategy, and quality-of-life issues for millions of people connected to the armed forces, while also influencing defense industry jobs and international security partnerships.

title: Legislative Branch Agencies Clarification Act
ai_summary:
This bill, HR 6028, changes how several top jobs in Congress's support agencies are filled and overseen. Currently, the Librarian of Congress and the Director of the Government Publishing Office (GPO) are appointed by the President with Senate approval. Under this bill, both positions would instead be selected by a "commission" made up of top House and Senate leaders, based on recommendations from the relevant oversight committees. These officials could also be removed by a majority vote of that same leadership group, rather than through the current process. The bill also sets up clearer rules for appointing Deputy Librarians and Deputy Directors, including deadlines and backup plans if those jobs stay empty too long, and clarifies that these officials aren't "political appointees" for certain pay-related purposes.

The bill makes a bigger change to the Copyright Office, which is currently part of the Library of Congress. It shifts many powers currently held by the Librarian of Congress—like approving certain licensing decisions and copyright rules—directly to the Register of Copyrights, making the Copyright Office more independent. It also sets a 10-year term (with possible 5-year renewals) for the Register of Copyrights, requires the Register to have copyright law experience, creates a separate Inspector General for the Copyright Office, and ratifies actions taken by copyright officials since May 2025 (a period during which there was reportedly a leadership dispute at the Copyright Office).

Finally, the bill updates GPO's personnel rules, extending federal workplace protections (like the Congressional Accountability Act) to GPO employees and requiring GPO to set up a formal merit-based human resources system. It also modernizes the law describing what printing and publishing services GPO can provide to federal agencies. Overall, this bill mainly affects the internal operations, leadership selection, and independence of a few congressional support agencies—the Library of Congress, GPO, and the Copyright Office—rather than the general public. It could still matter to everyday people indirectly, since the Copyright Office handles copyright registration and rules that affect authors, musicians, businesses, and technology users.
ai_headline: Bill would let Congress leaders, not President, pick Librarian and GPO chief
last_action_text: Received in the Senate.

title: Protecting Privacy in Purchases Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Protecting Privacy in Purchases Act, would stop credit card companies, payment networks, and other financial businesses from using a special code that identifies gun stores separately from regular retail or sporting goods stores. These codes, called merchant category codes, are used to classify what kind of business a store is, mainly so credit card companies can track spending patterns. In 2022, a specific code for firearms retailers was created, and some banks began using it to flag purchases at gun stores. This bill would ban that practice, treating gun shops the same as any general retail or sporting goods store for coding purposes.

The bill puts the Attorney General in charge of enforcing this rule. If someone believes a payment company or bank violated the law, they could file a complaint, and the Attorney General would investigate. Companies found in violation would get 30 days to fix the problem before the government could sue them in federal court. Regular people or businesses could not sue on their own. The bill would also cancel out any state or local laws that require or regulate the use of these special gun-store codes.

This bill mainly affects payment processors, banks, credit card networks, gun retailers, and lawmakers in states that have passed their own rules requiring the tracking of firearm purchases through these codes. Supporters of this kind of bill generally argue it protects gun buyers' privacy and prevents unnecessary tracking of legal purchases, while such coding was originally pushed by some advocates as a tool to help detect suspicious bulk firearm or ammunition purchases. The bill does not affect background checks or other existing gun purchase laws—it only deals with how these transactions are coded in the payment system.

title: Energy and Water Development and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2027
ai_summary:
This bill, H.R. 9022, sets the federal government's spending plan for the 2027 budget year for agencies that manage water resources, energy programs, and nuclear security. It funds the Army Corps of Engineers' civil works (like flood control, harbor maintenance, and dam projects), the Department of the Interior's water programs (including the Bureau of Reclamation, which manages dams and irrigation water in the western U.S.), and the Department of Energy (covering everything from nuclear weapons maintenance and cleanup of old nuclear sites to scientific research, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and electric grid programs). It also funds the four regional Power Marketing Administrations that sell electricity from federal dams, and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, which oversees energy markets.

In practical terms, the bill directs specific dollar amounts to hundreds of programs—for example, money for dredging harbors, repairing levees along the Mississippi River, building water infrastructure in the West, researching nuclear power and clean energy technology, maintaining the nuclear weapons stockpile, and cleaning up old nuclear waste sites. It includes rules limiting how agencies can shift money between programs without notifying Congress first, and it requires agencies to keep lawmakers informed about spending plans and project statuses. There's also a provision protecting people's right to carry firearms at Corps of Engineers recreational sites if they're following state law.

This bill affects a wide range of people: communities near rivers, harbors, and dams that rely on flood protection and water infrastructure; farmers and cities in western states dependent on Bureau of Reclamation water projects; Native American tribes with water rights or energy programs; workers and communities near national laboratories and nuclear defense sites; and taxpayers generally, since it determines how tens of billions of dollars in federal money are spent. Utility customers may also be indirectly affected through funding for power administrations and energy regulatory work.

title: DLARA
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Disaster Loan Accountability and Reform Act (DLARA), aims to improve oversight of the Small Business Administration's (SBA) disaster loan program, which provides direct loans to homeowners and businesses after disasters. The bill requires the SBA to give Congress more detailed monthly reports on loan spending, including clearer warnings about when loan funding is running low. It also requires the President's annual budget to include specific comparisons between requested funding and 10-year average costs for disaster loans, including COVID-era loans (COVID-EIDL loans).

The bill also sets new rules for what happens when disaster loan funding gets critically low. If available money drops below 10% of the historical average, the SBA must notify Congress within 24 hours and can temporarily limit loan payouts to only the amount backed by collateral (like property) until Congress provides more funding. Once new funding arrives, the SBA must finish paying out any delayed loan amounts within 14 days. This emergency rule would expire after four years unless renewed. The bill requires several government watchdog reports: the Government Accountability Office (GAO) must study SBA's loan disbursement patterns and the financial effects of recent rule changes to loan limits and terms, and the SBA's Inspector General must investigate a 2024 funding shortfall, including whether SBA properly notified Congress and how internal management or reorganization contributed to the problem.

This bill mainly affects the SBA and its disaster loan program, along with congressional oversight committees. Indirectly, it affects small businesses and homeowners who rely on SBA disaster loans after hurricanes, floods, or other disasters, since the bill could lead to loan payment delays during funding shortages, but also aims to prevent unexpected shortfalls through earlier warnings and better budget planning.

title: USMMA Athletics Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, the USMMA Athletics Act, allows the Secretary of Transportation to set up a nonprofit corporation to support the athletic programs at the United States Merchant Marine Academy (USMMA), a federal service academy that trains merchant marine officers. The corporation would be owned by the U.S. government but run somewhat independently, with a board of directors that mostly consists of private citizens (no more than one-third can be Department of Transportation employees), all serving without pay except for travel expenses.

The bill gives this new corporation and the Secretary broad tools to fund and manage the academy's sports programs: entering contracts (including sole-source deals without normal competitive bidding requirements), leasing academy property for up to five years, accepting money from sources like the NCAA, athletic conferences, ticket sales, and licensing fees, and transferring existing athletic-related funds and equipment to the new corporation. It also updates federal law to let the Secretary license the academy's trademarks (like its name and logos) and keep the resulting fees to pay for licensing costs and student recruiting, rather than sending that money back to the general federal treasury.

This bill mainly affects the USMMA itself, its student-athletes, coaches, and staff, and the Department of Transportation (which oversees the academy). It could also affect businesses or organizations that might partner with the academy for sponsorships, media rights, or merchandise licensing. The general public isn't directly affected, though the bill does involve some spending flexibility and reduced oversight (like allowing sole-source contracts) that lawmakers may want to monitor for accountability.
ai_headline: Bill would let merchant marine academy set up nonprofit for athletics
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

The corporation could sign contracts including sole-source deals, lease academy property for up to five years, accept outside funding like NCAA and ticket revenue, and manage licensing of academy trademarks.

title: Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act
ai_summary:
This bill renews and updates the Social Security Administration's authority to run test programs, called "demonstration projects," related to the Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) program. This testing authority had expired at the end of 2022, and this bill would allow it to continue through the end of 2031. These demonstration projects let the government experiment with different rules for people receiving disability benefits, especially ways to help them try working without immediately losing their benefits, to see what policies actually help people return to the workforce.

The bill makes several technical changes to how these test programs operate. It extends the deadline for starting new projects and for the whole program to run. It gives the government more time (120 days instead of 90) to notify Congress before waiving certain benefit rules for a test project, and requires that any notice include information about how the project's success will be measured. It also clarifies that money for running these projects comes from Social Security's regular administrative budget, while actual benefit payments come from the trust funds, and it adds a protection ensuring that a person's total income cannot go down simply because they chose to participate in one of these test programs.

This bill mainly affects people who receive SSDI benefits and might want to try working again, since it governs the pilot programs designed to help them do so without financial risk. It also affects the Social Security Administration, which runs these projects, and researchers or policymakers who use the results to shape future disability policy. It does not change basic eligibility rules or benefit amounts for the broader SSDI program.
ai_headline: Bill would extend SSDI return-to-work test programs through 2031
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

title: Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2027
ai_summary:
This bill is the yearly funding bill for the U.S. Department of Defense for fiscal year 2027 (October 2026 through September 2027). It doesn't create new military policy so much as decide how much taxpayer money goes to different parts of the military. It covers paying troops (active duty, reserves, and National Guard across the Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps, and Space Force), keeping bases and equipment running, buying weapons and vehicles like ships, aircraft, missiles, and ammunition, funding research on new military technology, paying for military health care through TRICARE, and supporting related agencies like the CIA retirement fund and intelligence programs. It also sets aside money for specific programs like counter-ISIS operations, drug interdiction, environmental cleanup at military sites, and a new missile-defense effort called "Golden Dome for America."

In plain terms, this bill affects millions of people connected to the military: active-duty service members and their families who depend on steady pay and benefits, veterans and retirees tied to military retirement funds, defense contractors and workers who build ships, jets, and weapons, and communities near military bases whose local economies depend on defense spending. It also affects ordinary taxpayers, since this bill authorizes hundreds of billions of dollars in government spending, and it affects U.S. relationships abroad through funding for foreign military training and counterterrorism partnerships.

The bill also includes numerous administrative rules ("general provisions") that control how the Pentagon can move money between programs, limit spending on foreign nationals' pay increases, require reports to Congress, and restrict certain uses of funds. These provisions are mostly about oversight and accountability, ensuring Congress keeps some control over how the military spends money throughout the year, rather than giving the Defense Department a blank check.
ai_headline: Annual defense funding bill sets 2027 military budget and spending rules
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 621.

title: Measuring Illicit Fentanyl Trafficking Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Measuring Illicit Fentanyl Trafficking Act, directs the Secretary of Homeland Security to improve how the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) tracks its efforts to stop fentanyl trafficking. Within one year of becoming law, the Secretary would need to make sure that the different parts of DHS involved in detecting, deterring, and seizing fentanyl actually share relevant information and data with each other, and identify anything that is currently blocking that information-sharing. The bill also requires DHS to create specific performance metrics—measurable standards—for how well the department and its individual components are doing at detecting, deterring, and seizing fentanyl.

In practical terms, this bill does not create new criminal penalties, change law enforcement powers, or provide new funding. Instead, it's focused on improving government management and accountability by making DHS measure its own performance and coordinate better internally. It affects DHS agencies such as Customs and Border Protection, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and other components involved in anti-fentanyl efforts, requiring them to communicate more effectively and report on progress using standardized benchmarks.

This bill mainly affects how DHS operates internally rather than the general public directly. However, everyday Americans could see indirect benefits if better coordination and clearer performance tracking lead to more effective efforts to stop fentanyl from entering the country, which has been linked to overdose deaths nationwide. Members of Congress and oversight committees would also benefit, since standardized metrics would make it easier to evaluate whether DHS's anti-fentanyl programs are working and where improvements are needed.
ai_headline: Bill would require DHS to track and measure anti-fentanyl efforts
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

title: Homeland Security Capabilities Preservation Reporting Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would change how often the federal government has to report on what happens to cities and regions that stop qualifying for a specific homeland security grant program. The program in question, the Urban Area Security Initiative (UASI), gives money to high-risk urban areas to help them prepare for and respond to terrorism and other major security threats. When an area no longer meets the requirements to receive this funding, there are concerns about whether it can keep up the emergency response and security capabilities it built using that money.

A previous law, passed in 2023, already required the Department of Homeland Security to submit one report, 18 months after that law took effect, looking at how areas losing UASI funding manage the transition. This new bill would add a requirement for that same kind of report to be produced again every three years going forward, instead of just the one time. This means Congress and the public would get regular, updated information on how former grant recipients are handling the loss of funding and whether their security capabilities are being maintained.

This bill mainly affects government reporting requirements rather than directly affecting individual citizens. It would matter most to city and county governments that have received UASI funding in the past, emergency management officials, and the Department of Homeland Security, which would be responsible for preparing these recurring reports. Indirectly, it could affect residents of those urban areas by helping ensure that decision-makers have ongoing information about whether local security and emergency preparedness capabilities are being sustained after federal funding ends.
ai_headline: Bill would require recurring reports on cities losing security grant funds
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

title: Weatherizing Infrastructure in the North and Terrorism Emergency Readiness Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would require the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to run a training exercise that simulates a terrorist attack happening at the same time as an extreme cold weather event, like a polar vortex. The exercise would test how well government agencies, private companies, and community groups could work together to protect critical infrastructure—things like power grids, water systems, and communication networks—when both a security threat and severe winter weather are straining these systems at once. The goal is to find weaknesses in emergency response plans before a real crisis happens.

Specifically, the exercise must examine how cold weather could worsen the damage from an attack, how emergency managers and officials at all levels of government could reduce that damage, and how affected communities could become more resilient. It also requires coordination between federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial agencies, as well as private sector partners like utility companies. After the exercise, DHS would have 60 days to send Congress a report detailing what was learned, any changes planned for future DHS operations, and any new laws that might be needed based on the results.

This bill mainly affects DHS operations and planning rather than the general public directly. However, it could indirectly benefit anyone living in areas prone to extreme cold, since improved coordination and infrastructure planning could lead to better emergency responses during future winter storms or grid failures. State and local governments, utility companies, and emergency management agencies would also be affected, as they would likely participate in or be consulted during the exercise.
ai_headline: DHS bill would test response to attack during extreme cold snap
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

title: Expressing support for law enforcement officers.
ai_summary:
This resolution is a formal statement by Congress expressing appreciation and support for police officers and other law enforcement personnel across the country. It does not create any new laws, funding programs, or legal requirements. Instead, it is a symbolic measure meant to publicly recognize the work that officers do, including fighting crime, responding to emergencies, and engaging in community activities like mentoring youth or checking on elderly residents.

The bill also includes language criticizing certain policies, such as efforts to "defund" police departments and "sanctuary city" policies that limit local police cooperation with federal immigration authorities. It credits recent government policies with declines in homicide rates, drug overdose deaths, and violent crime. Because these statements reflect specific political viewpoints, the resolution touches on debates about criminal justice, immigration enforcement, and policing policy.

If passed, this resolution would not change any laws or provide any money to police departments. Its main effect would be as an official expression of Congress's opinion, which could be cited in political debates or used to signal where lawmakers stand on issues related to policing, immigration enforcement, and crime policy. It primarily affects public discourse rather than any specific group directly, though law enforcement officers are the ones being honored, and advocates on different sides of the sanctuary city and police funding debates may view the resolution's language differently.

title: SAVE America Act
ai_summary:
This bill, known as the SAVE America Act, would change federal voter registration rules to require proof of U.S. citizenship before someone can register to vote in federal elections. Instead of just checking a box or signing a statement saying they're a citizen, people would need to show specific documents like a passport, REAL ID, birth certificate, naturalization papers, or military ID with proof of U.S. birth. States would have to verify this documentation, set up backup processes for people who can't immediately provide it, and regularly check registration lists against federal databases (like DHS or Social Security records) to identify and remove noncitizens. States would also gain expanded authority to purge voters believed to be noncitizens, and new criminal penalties would apply to election officials who register someone without proper proof, or government employees who help noncitizens register or vote.

The bill also creates a nationwide photo ID requirement for voting in federal elections, whether in person or by mail. The ID would need to include a photo and an indication of U.S. citizenship, plus an ID number or partial Social Security number. States that already verify citizenship through a federal database (SAVE) on a regular basis could exempt already-registered voters from the citizenship-indicator requirement. This would affect everyday voters, who would need to gather and present specific documents to register and vote; election officials, who would have new duties, potential liability, and coordination requirements with federal agencies; and states, which would need to update systems, forms, and voter list maintenance procedures, likely at some cost and administrative effort. People who lack easy access to documents like birth certificates or passports (due to cost, name changes, or storage issues) could face extra hurdles in registering or voting.
ai_headline: Bill would require citizenship documents and photo ID to vote in federal races
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on House Administration.
