title: Destruction of Hazardous Imports Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Destruction of Hazardous Imports Act, changes the rules for what happens when the FDA refuses to allow a shipment of goods into the United States. Currently, federal law lets the FDA destroy certain refused imports, but mainly limited to specific low-value items like drugs and medical devices. This bill expands that destruction power so the FDA can order the destruction of any refused import—not just drugs and devices—if the agency decides that item poses a "significant public health concern." It also updates related legal language so this broader destruction authority applies consistently.

The bill also makes it illegal to move, ship, or export an item after the FDA has decided it should be destroyed. In other words, once the FDA flags something as a health risk and orders it destroyed, companies or individuals can't try to reroute it, sell it elsewhere, or send it out of the country instead. Violating this would count as a "prohibited act" under federal food and drug law, which can carry legal penalties.

This mainly affects importers, manufacturers, and shipping companies that bring goods into the U.S. that fall under FDA oversight—such as food, cosmetics, drugs, medical devices, and similar products. It could also affect foreign companies exporting goods to the U.S., since it closes a loophole where risky products, once blocked from entering the country, might otherwise be diverted rather than destroyed. The FDA would have 90 days after the law passes to write updated regulations, and the new rules would take effect 180 days after enactment. Everyday consumers are affected indirectly, since the goal is to keep unsafe imported products from reaching the market through alternate routes.
ai_headline: FDA would gain broader power to destroy risky blocked imports
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill lets the FDA destroy any refused import deemed a significant public health risk, not just drugs and devices.

title: FDA Modernization Act 3.0
ai_summary:
HR 2821, the "FDA Modernization Act 3.0," directs the FDA to update its official regulations to catch up with a change Congress already made back in 2022. That earlier law allowed drug companies to use alternatives to animal testing—like lab-grown tissue models, organ-on-a-chip technology, or computer simulations—when developing new drugs, instead of requiring traditional animal studies. However, the FDA's actual regulations (the detailed rules agencies follow) still use outdated language that specifically says "animal" testing, which creates confusion about whether the new alternative methods are truly allowed. This bill requires the FDA to formally rewrite those specific regulations within one year, replacing references to "animal" testing with the broader term "nonclinical testing," so the rules match what the law already permits.

The bill also lets the FDA skip some of the usual lengthy public-comment procedures when issuing this update, allowing the new rule to take effect immediately once published. Additionally, it fixes a minor drafting error in prior law where two different sections had accidentally been given the same label ("subsection (z)"), renaming one of them to avoid confusion.

This bill mainly affects pharmaceutical and biotech companies developing new drugs, as well as researchers and scientists working on alternative testing methods, by giving them clearer legal certainty that non-animal testing methods are officially recognized. It could also indirectly affect patients, since faster or more flexible drug-testing options may influence how quickly new treatments move through development, and it may reduce the number of animals used in laboratory research.
ai_headline: FDA must rewrite rules to formally allow non-animal drug testing methods
last_action_text: Received in the Senate.

title: To amend the Public Health Service Act to reauthorize the school-based health centers grant program.
ai_summary:
This bill would extend federal funding for school-based health centers, which are medical clinics located on or near school grounds that provide health services to students. The current law authorizing this grant program is set to expire after 2026, and this bill would renew it for five more years, covering 2027 through 2031.

The bill also changes how the funding is described. Right now, the law simply allows "such sums as may be necessary," meaning Congress decides the amount each year without a set cap. This bill would replace that with a specific figure of $55 million per year for each of the five years. This creates a clear funding target for lawmakers to work with when deciding future budgets, rather than an open-ended amount.

This mainly affects schools, students, and families who rely on school-based health centers for services like checkups, vaccinations, mental health counseling, and treatment for minor illnesses or injuries. These centers often serve lower-income communities or areas where families may have limited access to nearby doctors or clinics. Health care providers, school districts, and state health agencies that run or support these centers would also be affected, since continued federal funding helps determine whether these programs can keep operating and how much money they can count on in the coming years.
ai_headline: Bill would extend school health center funding through 2031
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 631.

title: To reauthorize and make improvements to Federal programs relating to the prevention, detection, and treatment of traumatic brain injuries, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill renews and updates federal programs that track and respond to traumatic brain injuries (TBIs), such as concussions. These programs were set to expire, and this bill extends their funding through 2030. It renames one of the core surveillance programs the "Bill Pascrell, Jr. National Program for Traumatic Brain Injury Surveillance and Registries" in honor of the late congressman. The bill directs the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to improve how it collects data on brain injuries, including identifying groups at higher risk—such as people in certain occupations, survivors of domestic violence or sexual assault, and public safety officers like police and firefighters. It also requires the CDC to make this information publicly available online, including prevention strategies tailored to at-risk groups.

The bill also updates state grant programs that help fund brain injury services, outreach, and advocacy. States and Native American tribal consortiums receiving these grants would need to maintain their existing funding levels (not cut back just because they got federal money), though the Secretary of Health and Human Services could waive part of the required state matching funds if a state genuinely couldn't afford it. Additionally, it slightly broadens the legal definition of "traumatic brain injury" and gives the Secretary flexibility to update that definition later in consultation with states and experts.

Finally, the bill requires two new reports to Congress within two years: one on outreach efforts and gaps in reaching high-risk populations, and another studying the long-term health effects of brain injuries, including possible links to dementia and mental health conditions. This bill mainly affects public health agencies, state health departments, tribal health programs, brain injury survivors, and advocacy organizations that rely on these federal programs and grants.
ai_headline: Bill extends federal brain injury tracking programs through 2030
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

title: Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill extends a law called the Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Act, which was originally passed to speed up research and treatment development for ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, also known as Lou Gehrig's disease). The original law was set to expire in 2026, and this bill pushes that expiration date to 2031, allowing grant programs for ALS research to keep running for five more years. It also adds some new requirements: when a company applies to renew a research grant for an experimental ALS drug, the FDA must now check how the drug's clinical trial is progressing, including asking drug manufacturers to share interim trial data. The bill also clarifies what counts as a "phase 3" clinical trial, expanding it to include combined phase 2/3 trials and planned phase 3 trials that haven't started enrolling patients yet.

Additionally, the bill requires the FDA to publish an updated action plan within a year, explaining what steps it will take over the next five years to support ALS and related rare neurodegenerative disease research, and to report on how well a similar 2022 action plan was actually carried out. Finally, it requires the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a federal watchdog agency, to submit a report to Congress within four years reviewing how the overall program has been working.

This bill mainly affects ALS patients and their families, pharmaceutical and biotech companies developing ALS treatments, and researchers relying on federal grants for this work. It also affects the FDA, which will have added reporting and oversight duties. Because ALS is a rare and fatal disease with limited treatment options, supporters of programs like this generally aim to encourage faster drug development, though this bill itself is procedural, focused on extending funding authority and improving oversight rather than creating new treatments directly.
ai_headline: Bill would extend ALS research grant law through 2031
last_action_text: Received in the Senate. Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 466.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8205 extends ALS research grant funding authority from 2026 to 2031 and adds FDA oversight steps.

It also requires an updated FDA action plan within a year and a GAO review within four years.

title: Duplication Scoring Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Duplication Scoring Act of 2026, would require the Government Accountability Office (GAO) to check whether new bills moving through Congress create government programs, offices, or initiatives that duplicate ones that already exist. The GAO already publishes an annual report identifying wasteful overlap in federal programs. This bill would connect that report to the lawmaking process by having the GAO review bills approved by committees and flag any new program that seems to repeat something already on that overlap list.

When GAO finds a potential duplication, it would report the details, including the new program's name and the relevant section of the bill, to the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) and the committee that approved the bill. This information would also be posted publicly on GAO's website. The CBO could then choose to include this duplication information alongside its regular cost estimates for the bill, giving lawmakers an extra piece of information when deciding whether to pass it.

This bill mainly affects how Congress operates internally—it does not create new programs or spend money itself. It would affect GAO and CBO staff, who would have added review duties, and it could affect any future legislation that creates new federal programs, since those bills would now get extra scrutiny for overlap. Everyday residents wouldn't be directly affected, but supporters argue it could help reduce government waste and make spending more efficient over time by catching duplicate programs before they're created.
ai_headline: Bill would flag new programs that duplicate existing federal efforts
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 39 - 1.

title: SAVE Act
ai_summary:
The SAVE Act would change federal voter registration rules so that anyone registering to vote in a federal election must show documented proof of U.S. citizenship, rather than simply checking a box or signing a statement under penalty of perjury as current law allows. Acceptable proof would include a REAL ID-compliant license marked as showing citizenship, a U.S. passport, military ID paired with service records showing U.S. birthplace, a certified birth certificate, naturalization papers, or similar documents. States would have to verify this documentation in person for mail-in and driver's license-based registrations, though people who register at a polling place could show proof there. States would also need to create backup processes for applicants who lack these documents, such as allowing other evidence with an official's sworn confirmation.

The bill also directs states to actively check voter rolls against citizenship databases (like DHS and Social Security records), remove noncitizens they find, and requires federal agencies to share relevant data with election officials within 24 hours upon request. It creates new criminal penalties for registering someone without proper proof, and for government employees who help noncitizens register or vote. It also allows private lawsuits against election officials who register someone without the required documentation.

This would affect anyone registering to vote for the first time or updating their registration, including through DMVs or mail-in forms, since it requires physically producing documents rather than attesting to citizenship. Supporters say it strengthens election security, while critics worry about access barriers for citizens who lack ready documentation (such as those without a passport or with name changes from marriage). States would need to set up new verification systems, and the Election Assistance Commission and Department of Homeland Security would take on added coordination duties.
ai_headline: Bill would require documented proof of citizenship to register to vote
last_action_text: Received in the Senate.

States must verify documents in person for mail-in and DMV registrations, though polling-place registrants could show proof there, and states must create backup verification processes for those lacking documents.

title: Directing the President pursuant to section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution to remove United States Armed Forces from unauthorized hostilities in the Islamic Republic of Iran.
ai_summary:
This resolution invokes the War Powers Resolution, a 1973 law that lets Congress order the President to withdraw U.S. troops from combat situations that Congress never formally approved. The bill states that Congress alone has the constitutional power to declare war, and that no such declaration or specific authorization has been made for military action against Iran. It directs the President to stop using U.S. Armed Forces in hostilities against Iran unless Congress specifically authorizes it through a war declaration or similar legal approval. The resolution does include an exception allowing the military to respond if the U.S. faces an imminent attack, meaning it doesn't prevent basic self-defense actions.

The bill also makes clear that it does not interfere with ongoing intelligence-gathering, analysis, or intelligence-sharing with allied countries regarding threats from Iran, and that the President still has discretion over sharing intelligence with coalition partners when it serves national security interests. Additionally, it clarifies that passing this resolution should not be interpreted as giving the President new permission to use military force against Iran—it's meant only to limit unauthorized action, not expand it.

This bill would primarily affect the President's authority to direct military operations involving Iran, members of the U.S. Armed Forces who could be deployed there, and Congress's role in overseeing military engagements abroad. It reflects a broader, recurring debate between the legislative and executive branches over who controls decisions to use military force, particularly during periods of tension with Iran. As a concurrent resolution, it would need to pass both the House and Senate, but it does not require the President's signature and does not carry the force of law in the same way a bill would.
ai_headline: Resolution would order troop withdrawal from unauthorized Iran conflict
last_action_text: Motion to reconsider laid on the table Agreed to without objection.

title: Ensuring Federal Purchasing Efficiency Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change how often the federal government updates certain dollar limits used in its purchasing rules. Currently, federal law requires these acquisition-related thresholds—the dollar amounts that determine things like when stricter contracting rules kick in or when simplified purchasing procedures can be used—to be adjusted for inflation every five years, on years divisible by 5 (such as 2025, 2030, and so on). This bill would change that schedule so the adjustments happen in 2028 and then every three years after that, instead of every five years.

In practical terms, this means the dollar thresholds that federal agencies use when buying goods and services would be recalculated more often to keep pace with inflation. These thresholds affect things like the minimum contract size that requires competitive bidding, or the maximum amount that can be spent under simplified acquisition procedures. By updating them more frequently, the bill aims to keep purchasing rules better aligned with current prices, rather than letting them become outdated over a longer five-year gap.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies that purchase goods and services, as well as businesses and contractors that sell to the government. More frequent adjustments could make it easier for smaller or mid-sized businesses to qualify for simplified contracting processes as inflation rises, and could reduce sudden, larger jumps in thresholds that occur when adjustments are made only every five years. Everyday taxpayers are affected indirectly, since these rules influence how efficiently and competitively the government spends public money.
ai_headline: Bill would update federal purchasing thresholds every three years, not five
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill moves federal contracting threshold updates to 2028, then every three years instead of every five.

title: FIT Procurement Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the FIT Procurement Act, aims to modernize how the federal government buys technology and works with contractors, especially small businesses. It requires agencies to improve training for government employees who handle technology purchases, including hands-on learning and education about newer tools like cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and cybersecurity. It also directs officials to teach faster, simpler buying methods so agencies can get technology more efficiently instead of relying only on slow, traditional processes.

The bill also raises certain dollar limits that determine when agencies can use simpler, faster purchasing procedures rather than full formal contracting steps. It increases the "simplified acquisition threshold" from $250,000 to $500,000 and the "micro-purchase threshold" from $10,000 to $25,000, meaning more purchases could be made with less paperwork. It allows agencies to pay in advance for things like cloud computing subscriptions, similar to how they already pay for other services in advance.

Additionally, the bill focuses on helping small businesses compete for federal contracts by asking agencies to reduce unnecessary red tape, accept a broader range of past work experience as qualification, and study ways to remove barriers small companies face. It requires government watchdog reports on how well small businesses are doing in federal technology contracting and asks for updated rules to prevent conflicts of interest among government employees who manage these contracts. Importantly, the bill states that no new funding will be provided to carry out these changes—agencies must implement them using existing resources. This bill mainly affects federal agencies, their employees who manage contracts, and businesses (particularly small businesses) that sell technology or services to the government.
ai_headline: Bill would raise thresholds for simpler federal tech purchasing rules
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

It raises the simplified acquisition threshold from $250,000 to $500,000 and the micro-purchase threshold from $10,000 to $25,000, and allows advance payment for things like cloud subscriptions.

title: Federal Relocation Payment Improvement Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change how the federal government pays employees who have to move for work-related reasons, such as being transferred to a different city or state. Currently, relocation expenses are typically reimbursed piece by piece, covering specific costs like moving trucks, temporary housing, or travel. This bill would allow agency leaders to instead offer employees a single lump-sum payment that covers relocation costs all at once, instead of requiring detailed reimbursement for each expense.

The bill directs the General Services Administration (GSA) to write detailed rules for how this would work in practice. These rules would cover when agencies can choose the lump-sum option instead of the traditional reimbursement process, how the lump-sum amount should be calculated, and what steps an employee can take if they disagree with the amount they were offered, including the right to appeal to the Civilian Board of Contract Appeals, a federal board that handles certain government contract and expense disputes.

This bill primarily affects federal employees who are relocated for their jobs, giving agencies more flexibility in how they compensate them for moving costs. It could simplify the process for both workers and agency staff who currently manage detailed expense reports, though the actual impact would depend on the specific regulations GSA eventually creates.
ai_headline: Bill would let agencies pay relocating federal workers a lump sum
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

title: Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Billion Dollar Boondoggle Act of 2025," would require the federal government to keep closer track of major projects that are seriously over budget or delayed. Specifically, it targets government-funded projects—like construction, procurement, cleanup efforts, or military acquisitions—that are either more than five years behind their original schedule or have cost at least $1 billion more than originally estimated. These are informally known as "boondoggles," a term for wasteful or poorly managed government spending projects.

Under the bill, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), a White House agency that oversees federal spending, would be required to issue guidance within a year telling other federal agencies to report detailed information about these problem projects every year. That information would include what the project is, where it's happening, when it started, who the contractors are, how much it originally cost versus what it costs now, why it's delayed or over budget, and whether any bonuses were paid to contractors despite the problems. The OMB would then compile this information into a public annual report submitted to Congress and posted online.

This bill would mainly affect federal agencies and government contractors, who would face new reporting requirements and increased public scrutiny over troubled projects. It would also affect taxpayers and the general public by making it easier to see which government projects are wasting money or falling behind, and it would give Congress more information to use when deciding how to oversee or fund these projects in the future. The bill does not cancel any projects or cut funding directly—it focuses on transparency and reporting.

last_action_text: Received in the Senate. Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 467.

title: Expanding Whistleblower Protections for Contractors Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill strengthens legal protections for whistleblowers who work on federal contracts and grants, making sure they can't be punished for speaking up about problems. It updates existing laws covering both defense-related contractors (working with the Department of Defense or NASA) and non-defense federal contractors more broadly. The bill expands who counts as a protected person, adding subcontractors, grantees, subgrantees, state and local government employees working on federal contracts, tribal governments, and people doing personal services work for the government. It also protects people who refuse to follow orders that would require them to break laws or regulations related to a contract or grant.

The bill also closes a specific loophole: it makes clear that no federal official has the authority to order or request that someone retaliate against a whistleblower, and it allows disciplinary action to be proposed against any federal official who does so anyway. Additionally, it guarantees that these whistleblower rights and legal remedies cannot be signed away through employment contracts, workplace policies, or arbitration agreements made before a dispute arises.

This bill mainly affects people who work for companies, state/local governments, tribes, or organizations that receive federal contracts or grants, especially through the Defense Department, NASA, or other federal agencies. It's relevant to employees, contractors, and government officials involved in federal contracting, aiming to make it safer for them to report waste, fraud, abuse, or danger to public health and safety without fear of losing their jobs or facing other retaliation.
ai_headline: Bill widens whistleblower protections for federal contractors and grantees
last_action_text: Received in the Senate. Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 465.

title: To amend the Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act to support nucleic acid screening, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Nucleic Acid Standards for Biosecurity Act," updates an existing law to strengthen safety checks on synthetic DNA and RNA production. Companies and labs can order custom-made genetic material (nucleic acids) for research, medicine, and biotechnology, but this technology could potentially be misused to create dangerous biological agents. The bill directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to research and develop better tools, guidelines, and technical standards to screen these orders and catch potentially dangerous sequences before they're made.

Specifically, the bill has NIST create testing methods to make screening more accurate and reliable, establish best practices for securing databases that track concerning genetic sequences, and develop guidance for companies to implement these safety checks properly. It also adds a new requirement for NIST to address risks from artificial intelligence being used in biological engineering and manufacturing. NIST must bring together a group of industry representatives, universities, nonprofits, and customers to agree on shared priorities and best practices, then report back to Congress within 18 months of that group's first meeting.

This bill mainly affects companies that synthesize DNA/RNA for customers, research institutions, biotechnology firms, and federal agencies involved in biosecurity. It authorizes $5 million per year from 2026 through 2030 for this work. Everyday Americans are affected indirectly, as this is meant to reduce the risk that genetic engineering technology could be exploited to create bioweapons or other biological threats, while still supporting legitimate scientific and medical research.

last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

title: Establishing the congressional budget for the United States Government for fiscal year 2027 and setting forth the appropriate budgetary levels for fiscal years 2028 through 2036.
ai_summary:
This resolution sets up Congress's overall budget plan for the federal government for the 2027 fiscal year, along with spending and revenue targets stretching out through 2036. It's not a law that spends actual money — instead, it's a planning document that sets ceilings and targets for how much the government should take in through taxes and other revenue, how much it can spend, and how large the national debt and yearly deficits are expected to be. It breaks spending down into categories like defense, health, Medicare, Social Security, education, veterans' benefits, and interest on the debt, showing planned amounts for each area every year through 2036. Under this plan, annual deficits (spending exceeding revenue) are projected to stay above $1.3 trillion every year, and the national debt is expected to keep growing substantially.

The bill also kicks off a "reconciliation" process, instructing four House committees (Agriculture, Armed Services, Intelligence, and House Administration) to draft specific legislative changes within their areas that would affect spending, following the dollar limits set for each committee. This reconciliation process is a special procedural tool that can let certain follow-up legislation pass the Senate with a simple majority instead of needing 60 votes, so it often becomes the vehicle for major tax or spending law changes later. The bill also includes technical rules for how House Budget Committee leadership can adjust these numbers over time, such as accounting for emergencies, disasters, wildfire costs, or updated economic projections.

This bill mainly affects how Congress conducts its internal budget process rather than directly changing any taxes, benefits, or programs for individuals right away. However, it matters to ordinary people because it sets the stage for future legislation — the spending caps and reconciliation instructions will shape debates over programs like Medicare, Social Security, veterans' services, and taxes in the coming months. Federal agencies, government contractors, and anyone relying on federal programs could eventually be affected once actual appropriations and reconciliation bills are written based on these targets. As a concurrent resolution, it does not go to the President for signature and does not carry the force of law by itself.

title: Directing the President, pursuant to section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution, to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran.
ai_summary:
This resolution, introduced under the War Powers Resolution, would direct the President to stop using U.S. military forces in hostilities against Iran unless Congress has specifically authorized such action through a declaration of war or another formal authorization. The War Powers Resolution is a law from 1973 that lets Congress force the President to withdraw troops from a conflict if Congress hasn't approved that military action. This bill uses that law to say Congress has not approved combat with Iran, including sending ground troops for fighting or occupation.

The resolution includes some important exceptions. It would not stop the U.S. military from defending itself, its diplomats, or allies if they face an imminent attack. It also would not require removing troops who are stationed in the region but aren't actually fighting Iran, and it wouldn't interfere with intelligence-sharing or information-gathering activities related to threats from Iran. Essentially, it targets active combat operations specifically, not a general U.S. presence in the Middle East.

This bill would primarily affect the President's authority to direct military action against Iran and would reaffirm Congress's role in deciding when the U.S. goes to war. It matters to U.S. service members who might be deployed to the region, to government officials managing foreign policy and national security, and broadly to the public, since it touches on whether the country could become more deeply involved in a military conflict with Iran without a formal congressional vote. As a concurrent resolution, it would need to pass both the House and Senate, but it does not require the President's signature and does not carry the force of law in the same way a bill does.
ai_headline: Resolution would require congressional approval for combat with Iran
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and referred to the Committee on Foreign Relations.

title: SAFE Drugs Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the SAFE Drugs Act of 2025, changes federal rules for pharmacies and facilities that make custom-mixed medications, known as "compounded drugs." Compounding is normally allowed when a patient needs a version of a medicine that isn't available as a standard commercial product, such as a different dosage or an ingredient a patient is allergic to. The bill tightens the definition of what counts as an illegal "copy" of an existing commercial drug, limiting pharmacies to making such near-copies no more than 20 times per month unless there's a documented, meaningful difference for a specific patient.

The bill also adds new reporting requirements: pharmacies, facilities, or doctors that compound the same commercial-ingredient drug more than 20 times a month for out-of-state patients must report those totals to the federal Food and Drug Administration (FDA) each year, though hospital pharmacies treating their own patients are exempt. Additionally, large "outsourcing facilities" — bigger operations that compound drugs in bulk (more than 100 times a year) — would face mandatory inspections before they start making a new drug and at least once every two years afterward. It also removes an exemption that let some outsourcing facilities avoid registering with the FDA, and it changes how the FDA sets a base registration fee for these facilities, letting the agency decide the amount instead of a fixed $15,000.

Overall, this bill affects compounding pharmacies, large-scale drug outsourcing facilities, and prescribing physicians, aiming to give the FDA more oversight and data about who is making large quantities of drugs that resemble existing commercial medications. Patients who rely on customized medications could be indirectly affected if these rules change how available certain compounded drugs are, and drugmakers/pharmacies may face new inspection, reporting, and fee requirements.
ai_headline: Bill would tighten FDA rules on compounded drug copies and inspections
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

title: Restoring Integrity and Efficiency to Inspector General Oversight Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would eliminate the Council of the Inspectors General on Integrity and Efficiency (CIGIE), a coordinating body made up of the inspectors general from various federal agencies. Inspectors general are internal watchdogs who audit and investigate their agencies for waste, fraud, and abuse. CIGIE currently helps these inspectors general work together, share training resources, set common standards, coordinate investigations that cross agency lines, and support whistleblower protections. Under this bill, CIGIE would be abolished one year after the law passes, and its responsibilities would be split up and handed to other existing offices, mainly the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), the Government Accountability Office (led by the Comptroller General), and the Federal Law Enforcement Training Centers.

Specifically, OMB would take over developing workforce training policies, coordinating governmentwide anti-fraud efforts, and mediating disputes between different inspectors general offices. The Comptroller General would set standards for inspections. The Federal Law Enforcement Training Centers would run training academies for investigators and auditors and would receive CIGIE's remaining funds. Inspectors general themselves would take on more direct responsibility for coordinating whistleblower protections. The bill also makes numerous technical changes to other laws that currently reference CIGIE, replacing those references with the new responsible offices.

This bill would primarily affect federal employees who work in offices of inspectors general across dozens of agencies, since their oversight coordination structure would change significantly. It could also affect how efficiently fraud and misconduct that spans multiple agencies gets investigated, since a single dedicated coordinating council would no longer exist. Members of the public who rely on whistleblower protections or who care about how effectively government waste and fraud are policed would be indirectly affected, since the change could alter how consistently these oversight functions are carried out across the government.
ai_headline: Bill would abolish council coordinating federal inspectors general

title: Stopping Foreign Influence in Elections Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Stopping Foreign Influence in Elections Act of 2026," would create new financial penalties for tax-exempt organizations (like nonprofits and advocacy groups) that give money to political committees or certain political nonprofits after having accepted donations from foreign nationals. The goal is to stop foreign money from indirectly influencing U.S. elections by passing through American nonprofit groups.

Under the bill, if a larger tax-exempt organization (generally those with at least $200,000 in yearly income or $500,000 in assets) accepts a donation from a foreign national, and then within a two-year window makes a contribution to a political committee or a politically active 501(c)(4) group, that contribution would be considered "disqualified." The organization would have to pay a penalty equal to twice the amount of that contribution. Separately, the organization could also face escalating taxes on repeated violations—100% of the contribution for a first offense, 200% for a second, and for a third or later offense, 200% plus loss of its tax-exempt status for two years. Organizations could avoid punishment if they reasonably relied on a donor's statement about their citizenship, unless they knew or should have known it was false.

This bill would primarily affect nonprofit organizations involved in political spending, especially those that solicit donations from a wide range of sources, including internationally. It does not directly regulate political campaigns or foreign donors themselves, but instead uses tax penalties to discourage nonprofits from mixing foreign money with political contributions. The changes would take effect for contributions made starting one year after the law is enacted.

title: Fair Treatment of Religious Organizations Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would change part of the federal tax law that governs how the IRS decides whether an organization qualifies as tax-exempt, particularly for religious groups. It says the IRS cannot treat a religious belief or practice about marriage, sexuality, or gender identity as being against the law or public policy when deciding whether a group qualifies for tax-exempt status. It also says a belief still counts as "religious" even if it isn't a required or central teaching of an organized religion. In short, the bill limits the government's ability to use certain views on these social topics as a reason to deny or revoke a group's nonprofit tax status.

This matters because current IRS rules sometimes require tax-exempt organizations—like charities or religious nonprofits—to show that their purpose and activities aren't against established public policy. In the past, this kind of standard was used in cases involving racial discrimination. This bill would specifically prevent that same reasoning from being applied to religious viewpoints on marriage, sexuality, or gender identity, meaning churches, religious schools, or faith-based charities that hold traditional or conservative views on these issues couldn't lose their tax-exempt status for that reason alone.

The bill would primarily affect religious organizations, faith-based charities, and religious schools that rely on tax-exempt status, as well as the IRS's authority to evaluate such groups. It could also affect people who interact with these organizations, such as students, employees, or clients, since the law would make it harder to challenge an organization's tax status based on its religious teachings about these subjects. The change would apply starting with tax years after December 31, 2025.

title: Foreign Funding Transparency Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Foreign Funding Transparency Act, would require certain tax-exempt organizations—like nonprofits and charities—to report more details about money they receive from foreign donors. Specifically, organizations would need to disclose the total amount of contributions they received from foreign nationals each year, and break out separately how much came from countries officially designated as "foreign countries of concern" (a category tied to national security and competitiveness laws).

This requirement would apply to tax-exempt organizations under section 501(c) of the tax code that had gross receipts of $200,000 or more, or assets of $500,000 or more, in the prior year. That means many mid-sized and larger nonprofits, advocacy groups, and similar organizations would be affected, while smaller nonprofits would likely be exempt. Organizations could generally trust a donor's stated nationality unless they had reason to believe it was false, and the IRS would be allowed to set rules for how organizations collect this citizenship information from donors.

The change would take effect for tax years beginning more than one year after the bill becomes law, giving organizations time to prepare. In practice, this bill mainly affects nonprofit organizations' reporting obligations to the IRS, and indirectly affects foreign individuals or entities who donate to U.S. tax-exempt groups, since more information about their contributions would become part of official tax filings.

title: Permanent Trump Secure Border Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Permanent Trump Secure Border Act," would rewrite large parts of U.S. immigration law to make it significantly harder to gain asylum or enter the country without authorization. It requires people to seek protection in other countries they pass through before reaching the U.S. border, tightens the "credible fear" screening that determines whether someone can pursue an asylum case, and adds many new categories of crimes and past actions that would disqualify someone from asylum. It narrows how "particular social group" and "political opinion" (key legal terms for asylum claims) can be defined, limits when gang violence, generalized crime, or domestic disputes count as persecution, and restricts asylum seekers from getting work permits until at least 180 days after applying. It also creates harsher penalties for people who overstay visas or enter illegally, expands the government's ability to detain families and children together (including undocumented children who arrive with parents), and changes rules for reuniting unaccompanied migrant children with their parents. Additionally, it narrows the president's/DHS's ability to grant "parole" (temporary permission to stay) to only a few specific listed circumstances, ending broader parole programs.

The bill would primarily affect people seeking asylum at the U.S. border, migrant families and children in immigration custody, people who have overstayed visas, and immigration attorneys and judges who handle these cases. Supporters frame it as strengthening border security and closing loopholes in asylum law; critics would likely see it as making legal protection much harder to obtain for people fleeing violence or persecution. It also affects U.S. taxpayers and government agencies (DHS, ICE, HHS, immigration courts), since it changes detention requirements, funding needs, and procedures those agencies must follow. If passed, it would represent one of the most sweeping rewrites of asylum and border-related law in decades, though as an introduced bill referred to committee, it would still need to pass the House, Senate, and be signed by the President before becoming law.
ai_headline: Bill would rewrite asylum law, limit parole and expand family detention

title: Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill extends and updates the Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Act, a law originally passed to speed up research and treatment options for people with ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, also known as Lou Gehrig's disease). The original law is set to expire in 2026, and this bill pushes that deadline to 2031, allowing the government to continue funding grants for ALS research and related programs for five more years.

The bill also makes some technical improvements. It requires the FDA to check on the progress of clinical trials—including how many patients have enrolled—before renewing research grants tied to experimental ALS drugs, and it asks drug manufacturers to share interim trial data to help with that review. It also clarifies that "phase 3" clinical trials include certain combined phase 2/3 trials and trials that are planned but haven't started enrolling patients yet, which affects which research projects qualify for grants.

Finally, the bill requires the FDA to publish a public report within a year reviewing how well its 2022 action plan for ALS and other rare neurodegenerative diseases has worked, and to lay out an updated 5-year plan going forward, including how it will better coordinate with communities affected by other rare neurodegenerative diseases beyond ALS. It also updates the timeline for a required Government Accountability Office (GAO) report on the program's overall effectiveness. This bill mainly affects ALS patients and their families, medical researchers, pharmaceutical companies developing ALS treatments, and the FDA, which oversees the research grants and drug approval process.

title: Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027
ai_summary:
This bill, the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027, gives official congressional approval for the government to spend money on U.S. intelligence agencies and activities for the 2027 budget year. Everyday Americans are affected indirectly, since this funding supports national security and intelligence-gathering operations, but the bill does not create new public programs, taxes, or rules that directly touch most people's daily lives.

title: Fiscal Sponsorship Transparency Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Fiscal Sponsorship Transparency Act of 2026, changes federal tax law to add new reporting and penalty rules for "fiscal sponsorship" arrangements. Fiscal sponsorship is when a charity that has tax-exempt status agrees to receive and manage money on behalf of another group or project that doesn't have its own tax-exempt status. This is a common practice that lets new or small organizations operate under an established charity's legal and tax status while they get started. Under this bill, charities that engage in these arrangements would have to report detailed information to the IRS every year, including who they're partnering with, how much money changed hands, what the money was used for, and who at the charity is in charge of overseeing the arrangement.

The bill also creates penalties for what it calls "improper conduit arrangements," which happen when a charity solicits donations for another organization but doesn't actually keep meaningful control over how the money is used—essentially acting as a pass-through rather than genuinely overseeing the project. Donations made under such improper arrangements would no longer count as tax-deductible charitable contributions. Additionally, the charity itself could face a tax penalty of 20% of the misused funds, rising to 100% if the problem isn't fixed in time. Individual charity managers who knowingly approved such arrangements could also personally face fines, up to certain dollar limits.

This bill would primarily affect nonprofit organizations that sponsor other groups or projects, including many small nonprofits, community organizations, and startup charities that rely on fiscal sponsors to operate legally before they get their own tax-exempt status. It would also affect donors, since contributions to improperly run arrangements would lose their tax deductibility. The changes would take effect for tax years beginning after December 31, 2027, giving organizations time to adjust their practices and recordkeeping before the rules apply.

title: Comment Integrity and Management Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how federal agencies handle public comments submitted during the regulatory process, such as on Regulations.gov, when agencies propose new rules. When people or organizations submit comments electronically, agencies would be required to try to verify whether a comment was submitted by an actual human being, rather than generated automatically by a computer program or bot. Agencies would also need to identify "mass comments," meaning large batches of identical or nearly identical comments often submitted through organized campaigns, and label them clearly so the public can see they're part of a larger group of similar submissions.

Instead of posting every single copy of a mass comment campaign, agencies could post just one representative sample or one version of the standardized text, along with a count of how many similar comments were received. The Office of Management and Budget would issue government-wide guidance on how to implement these verification and labeling procedures, and agencies would have to create their own written policies following that guidance. Agencies would also need to update their websites and comment systems, including Regulations.gov, to support these changes. The Government Accountability Office would study how common computer-generated comments (including those created using artificial intelligence) are and report back with recommendations.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies that manage public comment periods for proposed regulations, as well as the General Services Administration, which runs the shared federal rulemaking website. It also affects everyday citizens, advocacy groups, and businesses who participate in rulemaking by submitting comments, since their submissions may now be checked for authenticity and labeled if they're part of a mass campaign. The bill explicitly states that mass comments are still a valid and important part of the process, and that this labeling should not reduce how much agencies consider them.

title: Transparency in Billing Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, the Transparency in Billing Act of 2026, would require hospitals to use special identification codes when billing for services provided at off-campus outpatient locations, such as clinics or facilities that are not physically located on the main hospital campus. Under the bill, hospitals would need to obtain a unique health identifier for each off-campus outpatient department and include that identifier on any bill submitted to a health plan or insurance company. If a hospital doesn't include this identifier, it would not be allowed to bill the insurance plan or charge the patient for those services.

The goal is to make medical billing more transparent by clearly showing where care was actually provided, since off-campus facilities sometimes charge differently than on-campus ones, which has caused confusion and disputes over medical bills. The bill would apply to employer-sponsored group health plans and insurance coverage, starting with plan years on or after January 1, 2027. It also sets up a system for people to report suspected violations and allows the Department of Labor to fine hospitals that don't comply—up to $300 per day for small hospitals (30 beds or fewer) and up to $5,500 per day for larger hospitals.

This bill would primarily affect hospitals, insurance companies, and employers who offer group health insurance, as well as patients who receive care at hospital-owned outpatient clinics. Patients could benefit from clearer billing information, while hospitals would face new administrative requirements and potential penalties for noncompliance. The Department of Labor would be responsible for writing detailed rules to carry out the law.

title: Strengthening America’s Turning Point Act

The park sits on the site of the Battles of Saratoga, a major turning point in the Revolutionary War where American forces defeated the British in 1777, a victory historians often credit with convincing France to formally support the American cause. The bill's short title, "Strengthening America's Turning Point Act," refers to this historical significance.

Beyond the name change, the bill requires that any existing law, map, government document, or official record referring to the park under its old name automatically be treated as referring to the new name instead. This avoids the need to individually update every federal reference to the site.

This bill would primarily affect the National Park Service, which manages the site and would need to update signage, materials, and administrative records to reflect the new name. It could also affect local tourism materials, maps, and educational resources in the Saratoga, New York area. For everyday Americans, the practical impact is minimal, this is largely a symbolic or branding change rather than one that affects funding, park operations, public access, or visitor services. The bill was introduced by New York Representative Elise Stefanik along with Representative Paul Tonko, whose districts include the area.

title: Carson City Public Land Correction Act
ai_summary:
This bill makes several adjustments to federal land in and around Carson City, Nevada, building on an earlier 2009 law that already governed land transfers in the area. It directs federal agencies (the Bureau of Land Management and the Forest Service) to transfer about 1,288 acres of federal land to Carson City for free, to be used for public purposes like parks, recreation, and flood control. It also transfers a small strip of land (less than half an acre) to the city so it can widen a road, with a requirement that the city build a crosswalk for safe pedestrian access to a nearby Forest Service office. The city must cover the administrative costs of these transfers, such as surveys and appraisals.

The bill also arranges for about 360 acres of federal land to be sold to private buyers, with the city keeping certain utility and drainage easements on that land. Separately, if Carson City offers to give the federal government about 20 acres it owns, the federal government must accept it and then resell that land too, with the city retaining some access rights for a water well and a public road. Money made from all these land sales would go into a special account already used for local conservation, wildfire prevention, wildlife habitat projects (including sage-grouse protection), land purchases, and educational purposes in Carson City. Finally, the bill updates the 2009 law to let the city sell or lease certain land to private parties (as long as it's for fair market value) and sets a one-year deadline for federal officials to sell certain land once a qualified buyer is found.

This bill mainly affects Carson City's local government, federal land management agencies, and residents or businesses involved in local development, conservation, and infrastructure projects. It does not have direct effects on people outside that area, since it deals specifically with land boundaries and property transfers in one Nevada community.

title: Reversionary Interest Conveyance Act
ai_summary:
This bill deals with a small, specific piece of land in Sacramento, California—about 8.43 acres—where the federal government currently holds something called a "reversionary interest." This is a leftover legal claim dating back to an 1862 law, originally tied to railroad land grants. Essentially, even though someone else owns and uses this land today, the U.S. government still holds a legal right that could let it reclaim the land under certain old conditions. This bill would allow the government to sell off that leftover claim to the current landowners, clearing up the title.

Under the bill, if a landowner within this area asks the Bureau of Land Management (part of the Department of the Interior) to remove the government's reversionary interest, the government must do so within two years, but only after the landowner pays the fair market value (determined through an official appraisal) plus any related costs like surveys and administrative fees. The money collected goes into a federal land account used for other land-management purposes. The bill also makes clear that this process doesn't affect any existing railroad right-of-way still in place, and it doesn't grant anyone new property rights based on old possession or abandonment claims.

This bill mainly affects property owners in that specific part of Sacramento who want full, unclouded ownership of their land free from old federal claims. It would not affect people outside that defined area, and it does not change broader national land or property law—it's a narrow, local fix designed to clean up a legal technicality tied to historic railroad land grants.

title: Dolores River National Conservation Area and Special Management Area Act
ai_summary:
This bill, sponsored by Colorado Senators Bennet and Hickenlooper, would create two new protected areas along the Dolores River in southwestern Colorado. The Dolores River National Conservation Area would cover about 52,872 acres of Bureau of Land Management land, while the Dolores River Special Management Area would cover about 15,452 acres within the San Juan National Forest. Both areas would be managed to protect scenic, recreational, wildlife, and cultural resources—things like whitewater boating, fishing, hunting, and native fish habitat—while limiting new road construction and restricting motorized vehicles to designated routes. A citizen advisory council of 14 members, including local officials, landowners, tribal representatives, and various interest groups, would help guide management plans for the area.

The bill pays special attention to water rights and existing uses. It explicitly protects existing water rights, the operation of the Dolores Project and McPhee Reservoir (which supplies water for irrigation and other uses), grazing permits, and existing leases, including uranium leases from the Department of Energy. It also guarantees private landowners access to their property through the protected areas and states that no new buffer zones or extra restrictions will be placed on neighboring private land. Tribal treaty rights and traditional uses, such as ceremonies and gathering plants, are also protected.

This bill would primarily affect people living in or near Dolores, San Miguel, and Montezuma counties in Colorado, including ranchers, farmers, private landowners, recreational users like rafters and hunters, and members of the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe. It would also affect federal land managers (the Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management), local water districts, and energy companies with uranium leases in the area, by setting new rules for how this land can be used and developed going forward.

title: Making National Parks Safer Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Making National Parks Safer Act," directs the National Park Service to modernize the 911 emergency call systems used across national parks. Many parks currently rely on older emergency communication systems that may not support newer technology like sharing caller location data, texting to 911, or exchanging information easily with outside emergency responders. This bill aims to upgrade those systems to "Next Generation 911" technology, which is the more advanced, digital standard many cities and counties have already adopted.

Specifically, the bill requires the Secretary of the Interior (through the National Park Service) to first study all existing emergency call centers in national parks within one year, figuring out which ones still need upgrades and how much it would cost to install and maintain the new systems. After that report is finished, the agency has another year to create a detailed plan for actually installing the upgraded systems, in consultation with state and local emergency officials, park stakeholders, and relevant federal agencies like the FCC and Department of Transportation. Parks that already have adequate modern systems would not need to be included in the upgrade plan.

This bill mainly affects visitors and employees of national parks, who would benefit from faster, more reliable emergency response if someone is injured, lost, or in danger while in a park. It also affects National Park Service staff and local/state emergency responders, who would need to coordinate on technology and jurisdiction issues. The bill does not immediately fund or mandate installation of new systems—it sets up a process of assessment and planning as a first step toward improving emergency response capabilities in parks.

title: Strategic Grazing to Reduce Risk of Wildfire Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Department of Agriculture (which oversees national forests) and the Department of the Interior (which oversees other public lands) to create a formal strategy for using livestock grazing as a tool to reduce wildfire risk. Within 18 months of the bill becoming law, these agencies must work with ranchers who hold grazing permits, along with states, tribes, local governments, utility companies, firefighting agencies, and conservation groups, to develop a plan. The strategy would explore ideas like using empty grazing areas during droughts or disasters, targeting grazing in high-risk zones near communities, using temporary permits to let animals graze longer or in new areas specifically to reduce invasive grasses like cheatgrass (which burn easily), using grazing after wildfires to help land recover, and using modern technology like virtual fencing to control where livestock roam without physical fences.

The bill mainly affects ranchers and farmers who lease federal land for grazing, federal land management agencies, and communities located near wildfire-prone public lands or national forests. It could lead to expanded or more flexible grazing arrangements in some areas, particularly in the western United States where wildfire risk and public land grazing overlap significantly. The bill also calls for training federal workers to manage these grazing programs and new technologies effectively.

Importantly, the bill does not change or interfere with any grazing programs already in place. It simply requires agencies to study and plan how grazing could be better used going forward, rather than immediately changing rules or land access. It does not allocate new funding directly in this text, and any actual changes to grazing permits or practices would depend on how agencies choose to implement the resulting strategy.

title: Ukraine Support Act
ai_summary:
HR 2913, the Ukraine Support Act, is a broad bill that combines statements of support for Ukraine with concrete government programs and economic penalties against Russia. It formally reaffirms US backing for Ukraine's sovereignty, condemns Russia's invasion and its abduction of Ukrainian children, and reaffirms commitment to NATO. It creates or extends several programs: war-risk insurance for ships carrying Ukrainian cargo, a "Special Coordinator for Ukrainian Reconstruction" position at the State Department, funding for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty and anti-disinformation efforts, a new "Ukraine Reconstruction Trust Fund" financed by certain tax revenues, and a strategy for US-European cooperation on nuclear energy to reduce reliance on Russian nuclear technology.

On the military and financial side, the bill extends "lend-lease" authority allowing the US to loan or lease defense equipment to Ukraine through 2028, authorizes up to $8 billion in direct loans and military financing for Ukraine and NATO allies, funds security assistance for Baltic countries, and extends the existing Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative with new funding. It also requires regular reports to Congress on allied military contributions and US intelligence cooperation with Ukraine.

The bill's third major section sets up an extensive sanctions regime against Russia. It requires the President to periodically determine whether Russia is still waging war or violating any peace deal, and if so, to impose sanctions on major Russian banks, oil/gas/mining companies, government and military officials, entities involved in Crimea infrastructure projects, the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant occupation, Russia's nuclear agency (Rosatom), vessels violating oil price caps, and parties involved in Russia-North Korea military cooperation. It also would restrict Russian access to SWIFT financial messaging and block trading in new Russian government debt. These provisions mainly affect the executive branch's foreign policy authority, defense and financial agencies, US companies dealing with Russia or Ukraine, shipping and insurance industries, and foreign banks or firms doing business with sanctioned Russian entities. Ordinary Americans would mostly be affected indirectly, through government spending, energy markets, and foreign policy rather than through direct personal obligations.

title: Brian Head Town Land Conveyance Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Department of Agriculture, through the Forest Service, to transfer about 24 acres of national forest land near Brian Head, Utah, to the local town government. The land is currently part of the Dixie National Forest. The transfer would happen at no cost to the town, meaning the town wouldn't have to pay the federal government for the property. Once the transfer is complete, the Forest Service would officially redraw the boundaries of the national forest to remove this parcel from federal ownership.

The town plans to use the land for a public works facility, such as a maintenance yard, storage site, or similar municipal infrastructure, though the bill also allows the town to use it for other purposes it decides are necessary. The Secretary of Agriculture can attach reasonable conditions to the transfer, but the core requirement is that the land must be conveyed to the town.

This bill mainly affects residents of Brian Head, a small town in southern Utah, by giving local officials control over land they likely need for community services and growth. It could also interest people who use the Dixie National Forest for recreation, since the forest's boundaries would shrink slightly. More broadly, it reflects a common type of legislation in which Congress approves small, specific land transfers from federal agencies to local governments to support community projects.

title: Continental Divide National Scenic Trail Completion Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management to prioritize finishing the Continental Divide National Scenic Trail, a long hiking route that runs along the Rocky Mountains from Mexico to Canada through New Mexico, Colorado, Wyoming, Idaho, and Montana. Currently the trail has gaps where it isn't fully connected. The bill sets a goal of completing the trail as one continuous route within 10 years, though this depends on Congress actually providing funding.

To make this happen, the bill requires the two agencies to create a joint "Trail Completion Team" within a year of the law passing. This team would work with state, tribal, and local governments, landowners, and other interested groups—including holders of historic New Mexico land grants and traditional irrigation associations called acequias—to figure out how to finish and improve the trail. Within three years of forming, the team must produce a detailed plan that identifies where the trail still has gaps, looks for opportunities to use land easements from willing sellers (not forced sales), and outlines specific development plans and cost estimates. The agencies are also encouraged to partner with volunteer and nonprofit groups to help build and maintain the trail.

This bill mainly affects people who use or live near the Continental Divide Trail, including hikers, outdoor recreation groups, and landowners in the trail's path. Importantly, the bill does not give the government any new power to seize land, including through eminent domain—it only allows land purchases from willing sellers. It also doesn't guarantee that trail completion will be funded ahead of other government land projects, meaning actual progress will still depend on future budget decisions.

title: A bill to provide for the transfer of administrative jurisdiction over certain Federal land in the State of California, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill deals with a small land swap between two federal agencies in Tuolumne County, California, near Yosemite National Park. It transfers about 160 acres currently managed by the U.S. Forest Service (as part of Stanislaus National Forest) over to the National Park Service, so it becomes part of Yosemite National Park. In exchange, about 170 acres currently managed by the National Park Service (as part of Yosemite) would be transferred to the Forest Service, becoming part of Stanislaus National Forest. This swap is tied to an area known as Ackerson Meadow, based on a map from February 2022.

The bill also spells out the practical details of making this kind of switch. The two agencies can make small boundary corrections later if needed, as long as they publish notice of the change. Each agency stays responsible for cleaning up any hazardous materials found on the land it previously managed, even after the transfer. Existing rights, leases, permits, or easements on the land won't be canceled by this transfer, but going forward, whichever agency takes over the land will be in charge of managing those agreements.

This bill mainly affects federal land management in one specific part of California—it doesn't change land ownership for private citizens or affect other states. The people most directly affected are Forest Service and Park Service staff who manage these areas, plus anyone who uses permits, easements, or rights-of-way on that specific 330 acres of land, such as utility companies, recreational users, or researchers. The general public may notice minor differences in which federal agency oversees trails, rules, or resources in that area, but day-to-day public access is unlikely to change much.

title: A bill to amend the National Trails System Act to direct the Secretary of the Interior to conduct a study on the feasibility of designating the Bonneville Shoreline Trail.
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Secretary of the Interior to study whether the Bonneville Shoreline Trail should be officially designated as a National Scenic Trail or similar recognized trail under the National Trails System Act. The trail in question is a roughly 280-mile network of trails and potential trail routes running along the Bonneville bench, a geological feature in Utah formed by the ancient Lake Bonneville. The route would stretch from the Utah-Idaho border down to Nephi, Utah.

The bill itself does not create the trail or grant it official status. Instead, it adds the Bonneville Shoreline Trail to the list of potential trails that the federal government will formally study for feasibility, meaning experts will examine factors like land ownership, environmental impact, construction costs, and public benefit before deciding whether it deserves official national trail status.

This mainly affects residents of Utah, particularly those living along the Wasatch Front, where the trail already exists in parts as a popular recreational route for hiking, biking, and horseback riding. Local governments, outdoor recreation groups, and land management agencies like the Bureau of Land Management and U.S. Forest Service would likely be involved in or affected by the study process. If the trail is eventually designated after the study, it could lead to increased federal involvement, funding, and protections for the trail, potentially benefiting outdoor recreation and tourism in the region while also raising questions for property owners near the trail route.

title: Cahokia Mounds Mississippian Culture Study Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Secretary of the Interior to conduct an official study of three ancient Native American mound sites in Illinois: Cahokia Mounds, Emerald Mounds, and Pulcher Mounds. These sites are remnants of the Mississippian culture, a major Native American civilization that built a large city near present-day St. Louis between roughly A.D. 700 and 1400. At its height, Cahokia was home to thousands of people and was one of the largest urban centers in the world at the time, larger than London during that era. The bill lays out historical background explaining why Congress considers these sites significant.

The study itself would examine whether these mound sites are nationally significant and whether they should become an official unit of the National Park System, similar to a national park or monument. The Interior Department would also be required to look at other options for protecting and preserving the sites, such as involving state governments, local governments, or private and nonprofit groups, and to estimate the costs of different preservation approaches. Interior officials would need to consult with relevant government agencies, organizations, and interested members of the public during the study. Within three years of receiving funding, the Secretary must submit a report to Congress with the findings and recommendations.

This bill would primarily affect residents near the study sites in St. Clair and Monroe Counties, Illinois, including local governments, tribal nations connected to the Mississippian culture's descendants, and organizations involved in historic preservation or tourism. It does not immediately create a national park or change how the sites are managed; it only authorizes a study to determine whether further federal action, such as national park designation, might be appropriate in the future.

title: Ralph David Abernathy, Sr., National Historic Site Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new National Historic Site in Georgia to honor Reverend Dr. Ralph David Abernathy, Sr., a key leader of the civil rights movement who worked closely with Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. The site would center on the historic West Hunter Street Baptist Church, where Abernathy served as pastor, and would be managed by the National Park Service as part of the national park system. The goal is to preserve the church and tell the story of Abernathy's role in the civil rights movement for future generations to learn from.

The bill doesn't create the site immediately. Instead, it directs the Secretary of the Interior to first make sure enough land has been acquired to properly run the site before officially establishing it. Land can only be obtained through donation, purchase from willing sellers, or land exchanges — the government cannot force anyone to sell property. If land is owned by the state of Georgia or a local government, it can only be added to the site if that government agrees to donate it. Once established, the Park Service would have three years to create a management plan and could partner with the state or other organizations to provide tours, educational programs, signage, and other visitor services.

This bill mainly affects residents near the historic church site in Georgia, potential property owners whose land falls within the proposed boundary, and visitors or students interested in civil rights history. It would also involve the National Park Service, which would take on responsibility for managing and funding the new site, and Georgia state and local governments, who may be asked to donate land or partner on the project.

title: A bill to require the Secretary of Agriculture to convey the Pleasant Valley Ranger District Administrative Site to Gila County, Arizona.
ai_summary:
This bill would require the U.S. Department of Agriculture, through the Forest Service, to transfer ownership of a piece of land known as the Pleasant Valley Ranger District Administrative Site to Gila County, Arizona. The property is about 232.9 acres located within the Tonto National Forest and currently used as a Forest Service administrative site. If the county formally requests the land within 180 days after the bill becomes law, the federal government must hand over the property at no cost, using a quitclaim deed, which transfers whatever interest the government has without guaranteeing clear title.

The county would be responsible for covering all costs related to the transfer, including any required land surveys, environmental reviews, and historic preservation checks. The federal government would not be required to guarantee the environmental condition of the land, meaning the county would take it largely as-is. Importantly, the bill specifies that the land can only be used to serve and support military veterans; if Gila County ever uses the property for something else, ownership could revert back to the federal government.

This bill mainly affects Gila County, Arizona, its local government, and veterans in that area who might benefit from services or facilities built on the land. It could also matter to the Forest Service, which currently manages the site, and to nearby residents interested in how public lands are used. The broader public would likely see little direct impact, since this is a localized land-transfer bill rather than a nationwide policy change.
