title: New Mexico Land Grant-Mercedes Historical or Traditional Use Cooperation and Coordination Act
ai_summary:
This bill deals with "land grant-mercedes" in New Mexico—communities that trace their land rights back to grants made under Spanish or Mexican rule before the U.S. took over the territory. Many of these communities have long used nearby federal land (managed by the Forest Service or Bureau of Land Management) for things like gathering firewood or herbs, grazing livestock, hunting and fishing for personal use, maintaining shrines or cemeteries, and using water. The bill sets up a formal process for the federal government to work with these communities on continuing those traditional activities.

Specifically, it requires the Secretary of Agriculture or the Secretary of the Interior (whichever oversees the relevant land) to sign a formal agreement, called a memorandum of understanding, with the New Mexico Land Grant Council within two years. This agreement would spell out what kinds of traditional activities are allowed, what permits are needed, what fees might apply (and when those fees could be reduced or waived based on a community's financial situation), and how routine maintenance or larger construction projects—like repairing a water well or building a fence—would be approved. It also requires federal land-use plans to consider how other decisions might affect these traditional uses, and it requires consultation with Native American tribes when their interests could be affected.

This bill mainly affects residents of New Mexico who are heirs to these historic land grants, federal land management agencies operating in the state, and Native American tribes whose interests might overlap with these traditional land uses. The bill explicitly states it does not create new legal rights to use federal land, does not override tribal treaty rights, and does not change the state's authority over water or wildlife management—it simply creates a clearer process for cooperation and permitting.
ai_headline: New Mexico land grant communities to get formal federal use process
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 476.

title: A bill to provide for an extension of the legislative authority of the National Emergency Medical Services Memorial Foundation to establish a commemorative work in the District of Columbia and its environs.
ai_summary:
This bill gives more time for a group called the National Emergency Medical Services Memorial Foundation to build a memorial in Washington, D.C., honoring EMS workers. Congress had already approved this memorial years ago through a previous law, but building a monument in the nation's capital is a long process involving fundraising, design approval, and construction, and there are strict time limits set by federal law for getting it done. Normally, once Congress authorizes a memorial, the organizers have seven years to complete it before that authorization expires.

This bill simply extends that deadline, pushing back the expiration date to November 3, 2032, so the foundation has more time to finish raising money and building the memorial without having to start the approval process over from scratch. It does not create new funding from taxpayers, change the design or purpose of the memorial, or affect anyone outside of the organizations involved in planning and building this specific project. The people most affected are the members of the National Emergency Medical Services Memorial Foundation, EMS workers and their families who the memorial honors, and federal agencies like the National Park Service that oversee monument construction in D.C.

last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 484.

title: Disclosing Foreign Influence in Lobbying Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Disclosing Foreign Influence in Lobbying Act, would update the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995 to require more transparency about foreign involvement in lobbying activities in Washington. Specifically, it would require lobbyists who register with the government to disclose the name and address of any foreign government or foreign political party that helps direct, plan, supervise, or control their lobbying work, even if that foreign government or party is not officially their paying client.

Currently, lobbyists must disclose their clients, but this bill closes a potential gap by making sure that if a foreign government or political party is secretly guiding or influencing lobbying efforts behind the scenes, that involvement must be reported too. This mainly affects professional lobbyists and lobbying firms operating in the United States, particularly those who work on behalf of foreign interests. It also affects government watchdog agencies and the public, since it would give citizens, journalists, and regulators clearer information about when foreign governments or political parties are influencing lobbying campaigns aimed at U.S. lawmakers or policies.

The bill is a narrow, technical change rather than a broad overhaul, focused specifically on strengthening existing disclosure rules rather than creating a whole new regulatory system.

title: Lobbying Disclosure Improvement Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change the rules for people or companies that lobby the U.S. government on behalf of others. Lobbyists already have to register and file regular reports under a law called the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995. This bill would add one more piece of information to those reports: lobbyists would have to say whether they are claiming an exemption from a separate law, the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA), which requires people working on behalf of foreign governments or foreign political interests to register and disclose that relationship.

The idea behind this change is to close a potential gap where someone might be doing work that could count as being a "foreign agent" but instead registers only as a regular lobbyist, without making clear whether they believe they qualify for the FARA exemption. By requiring lobbyists to state their exemption status directly on their lobbying disclosure forms, the bill aims to give the public, watchdog groups, and government regulators clearer, more consistent information about who might be representing foreign interests in Washington.

This bill mainly affects registered lobbyists and lobbying firms, who would have a new box to fill out on their disclosure paperwork. It could also affect government agencies that track lobbying and foreign influence, as well as journalists, researchers, and watchdog organizations that rely on these disclosures to understand who is influencing U.S. policy. It does not create new penalties or change who must register as a lobbyist or foreign agent; it simply adds a disclosure requirement to existing paperwork.
ai_headline: Lobbyist disclosure forms would add new foreign agent exemption question

title: Fog Observations and Geographic Forecasting Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Fog Observations and Geographic Forecasting Act, directs a top official at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) to run a project aimed at improving weather forecasts for coastal marine fog. Marine fog can make it dangerous and costly for ships and boats to travel along the coast, so the goal is to make forecasts more accurate and helpful so people on the water can make safer decisions.

To do this, NOAA would expand the tools used to observe fog and ocean conditions, including buoys, weather stations, ships, drones, satellites, and computer algorithms that help detect and track fog early. The agency would also work on improving its computer models to cover more locations with better detail and accuracy, and would work on communicating fog warnings more clearly to the public so people understand the risks and can act on them. NOAA would be required to talk with outside groups, businesses, and Native American tribes while planning this work, and within one year it must create a detailed plan explaining what research and technology upgrades are needed, along with timelines and costs.

This bill would mainly affect coastal communities, commercial and recreational boaters, shipping companies, fishing industries, and coastal Native American tribes who rely on accurate weather information for safety and economic activity. It would also affect NOAA itself, since the agency would be responsible for carrying out the new fog-forecasting project and reporting on its progress.

last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 197.

title: Strengthening America’s Turning Point Act
ai_summary:

Saratoga is the site of a major Revolutionary War battle, often called a turning point in the war for American independence, and the bill's short title, "Strengthening America's Turning Point Act," reflects that historical significance. The bill also directs that any existing laws, maps, government documents, or official records that mention the park under its old name should automatically be treated as referring to the new name, so no further legal updates would be needed elsewhere.

This is a narrow, administrative bill rather than one with broad policy impact. It mainly affects the National Park Service, which manages the site, and would require updates to signage, official websites, publications, and other materials to reflect the new name. Visitors, local businesses, and historians who reference the park would see the name change, but the bill does not alter the park's boundaries, funding, operations, or preservation status. It is essentially a symbolic and branding change meant to emphasize the battlefield's historical importance rather than a change affecting park management or the general public's daily lives.

title: UNLOCK AUKUS Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change a technical rule in the Arms Export Control Act that affects how the United States shares military technology with Australia and the United Kingdom under AUKUS, a defense partnership focused on things like nuclear-powered submarines and advanced military technology. Specifically, it modifies a legal limitation that currently restricts certain export license exemptions, by excluding three specific subclauses from that restriction. In practical terms, this likely makes it easier or faster for U.S. defense companies and government agencies to share certain military technologies and services with Australia and the UK without going through some of the usual licensing hurdles.

The bill doesn't rewrite the whole AUKUS framework; it makes a narrow, technical adjustment to existing law. The three countries have been working to streamline defense trade rules since AUKUS was announced, arguing that current export control laws sometimes slow down cooperation on submarines, cyber capabilities, artificial intelligence, and other advanced defense projects. Supporters of these kinds of changes typically say faster technology sharing strengthens the partnership and speeds up joint military projects; critics of loosening export controls generally worry about oversight, technology security, or unintended consequences of easing restrictions.

This bill primarily affects U.S. defense contractors, exporters, and companies working on AUKUS-related projects, as well as government agencies like the State Department that manage arms export licensing. It would also affect the U.S. government's relationship with Australia and the United Kingdom on defense cooperation. Everyday Americans wouldn't feel direct effects, though the bill could influence national security policy, defense industry jobs, and U.S. military technology partnerships over time.

title: End Sanctuary Cities Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "End Sanctuary Cities Act of 2026," would create a new federal crime targeting state and local officials who block cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. Specifically, it would make it illegal for the top official responsible for a law or policy in a state or local government to knowingly stop their agencies from giving the Department of Homeland Security advance notice before releasing an immigrant who has been charged with or convicted of a crime. Officials would generally need to give at least 48 hours' notice before releasing such a person from custody, unless that's not possible.

The penalties would depend on how serious the underlying crime was. If blocking this notice leads to the release of someone charged with or convicted of murder, rape, or a sex offense against a minor, the responsible official could face 10 to 25 years in prison. If the crime was a "serious violent felony," the penalty would be 5 to 10 years. For any other criminal offense, the penalty would be 30 days to 6 months in prison, along with possible fines in all cases.

This bill would primarily affect governors, mayors, police chiefs, sheriffs, and other senior officials in "sanctuary" jurisdictions—places with policies limiting cooperation with federal immigration authorities. It would not directly target individual immigrants but rather the government officials who set or enforce policies restricting communication with immigration agencies. Supporters and critics of sanctuary policies would likely view this bill very differently, since it directly affects the balance of power between federal immigration enforcement and local governments' authority to set their own law enforcement priorities.
ai_headline: Bill would jail officials who block immigration release notices
last_action_text: Read the second time. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 318.

title: Water Resources Development Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Water Resources Development Act of 2026, is part of a series of laws Congress passes every couple of years to fund and manage the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' work on rivers, harbors, dams, levees, and flood protection, as well as the nation's drinking water and wastewater systems. It authorizes new studies and construction projects across dozens of states, sets rules for how the Corps works with local governments and reports to Congress, and updates or cancels older projects that are outdated or no longer needed. It also includes a second section focused on drinking water and sewer infrastructure, covering things like reducing lead in water pipes, helping small and rural communities upgrade water systems, funding for tribal water programs, and restoration efforts for major water bodies like the Great Lakes and Lake Champlain.

In practical terms, this bill affects local communities near rivers, coastlines, harbors, and lakes where the Corps of Engineers operates, since it directs specific flood control, dredging, and shoreline protection projects in many named locations (from Alaska to Rhode Island to Alabama). It also affects taxpayers generally, since it authorizes federal spending and sets policies for how the Corps prioritizes and reports on its work. Additionally, it impacts people relying on public water systems, particularly in small, rural, tribal, or low-income communities, by funding programs to improve drinking water safety and wastewater treatment. Local governments and utilities that partner with the federal government on these projects will see changes in application processes, funding-sharing rules, and reporting requirements.

title: A joint resolution to direct the removal of United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against the Islamic Republic of Iran that have not been authorized by Congress.
ai_summary:
This resolution, introduced by Senator Van Hollen, responds to a hypothetical ongoing military conflict between the United States and Iran that reportedly began on February 28, 2026, under an operation called "Operation Epic Fury." The bill states that Congress never declared war on Iran or passed a law specifically authorizing military action there, meaning the President committed U.S. forces to combat without the congressional approval required by the Constitution. It cites reported casualties (13 troops killed, 380 wounded) and inflammatory statements attributed to the President about destroying Iranian infrastructure and civilization as reasons for concern.

The core action of the bill is simple: it would formally direct the President to withdraw U.S. Armed Forces from combat operations in or against Iran unless Congress specifically authorizes the war through a declaration of war or separate authorization law. It relies on special "fast-track" procedures under existing law (the War Powers Resolution framework) that allow Congress to force a vote on removing troops without it being blocked or delayed by normal legislative hurdles.

The bill includes exceptions so that, even if passed, the U.S. military could still defend itself and American personnel from attack, share intelligence with allied nations under Iranian attack, help partner countries intercept Iranian retaliatory strikes, and evacuate American citizens from the region. This bill primarily affects the President's war-making authority, active-duty military members involved in the conflict, and U.S. relations with Iran and allied nations in the region. It would not affect ordinary citizens directly, except insofar as it relates to decisions about war, military deployments, and foreign policy carried out in their name.

last_action_text: Motion to discharge Senate Committee on Foreign Relations rejected by Yea-Nay Vote. 47 - 49. Record Vote Number: 207.

title: AI Flaw Reporting and Security Enhancement Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to create a voluntary program for reporting and tracking flaws in artificial intelligence systems. "Flaws" in this case is a broad term covering things like security vulnerabilities, safety hazards, malfunctions, and other unintended problems with AI systems, regardless of whether anyone intended harm. NIST would work with industry, universities, nonprofits, and other government agencies to agree on common definitions for these problems, create standards for how to report and categorize them, and develop ways to detect and monitor AI issues faster.

A key part of the bill is building a national database (or updating an existing one) where these AI flaws can be voluntarily reported and tracked, similar to how cybersecurity vulnerabilities are already documented in existing systems. NIST would either build this database itself or partner with universities and research institutions to do so. The bill also asks NIST to figure out best practices for when problems should be publicly disclosed versus kept private, and to report back to Congress within three years on how all of this is going.

This bill mainly affects AI companies, researchers, and developers, who could choose to participate in reporting flaws they discover, as well as government agencies involved in AI oversight, like NIST and the Department of Homeland Security's cybersecurity division. Because reporting is voluntary rather than mandatory, it doesn't impose new legal requirements on businesses, but it aims to create shared infrastructure that could make AI systems safer and more secure over time. Everyday consumers could benefit indirectly if this leads to AI products with fewer safety or security problems, but the bill doesn't directly regulate how AI is built or used.

last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 35 - 0.

title: Unleashing AI Innovation in Financial Services Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Unleashing AI Innovation in Financial Services Act, would require federal financial regulators—such as the Federal Reserve, FDIC, Securities and Exchange Commission, Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, National Credit Union Administration, and Federal Housing Finance Agency—to set up "AI Innovation Labs." These labs would let banks, credit unions, investment firms, and other regulated financial companies test new products or services that rely heavily on artificial intelligence, even if those products don't fully comply with existing regulations. Companies would apply for approval, explain their AI project and how they'd manage risks, and propose alternative ways to follow the spirit of the rules. If approved, the regulator generally could not take enforcement action against the company for that specific regulation during the test period, which would last at least one year.

The bill lays out detailed rules for how companies apply, how agencies must review applications (generally within 120 days, extendable once), and what happens if an application is denied or if multiple regulators are involved. Regulators would still be allowed to sue to stop a test project immediately if it posed serious risks—like danger to consumers, the financial system, national security, or money-laundering violations—and companies could still be punished for fraud. Agencies would also have to write public regulations spelling out procedures for these labs and issue annual public reports (without confidential details) summarizing what was learned.

This bill would mainly affect financial companies interested in using AI—like banks, investment firms, and fintech companies—by giving them a legal safe harbor to experiment with new AI-driven products without fear of routine enforcement. It would also affect the regulatory agencies themselves, who would need to create new offices, review procedures, and reporting systems. Indirectly, it could affect consumers and investors who use financial products, since new AI-based services might reach the market during testing periods with more flexible oversight than usual.

title: Taxpayer Advocate Participation Act
ai_summary:
This bill would give the National Taxpayer Advocate, an official within the IRS whose job is to help taxpayers resolve problems and represent their interests, a new power to formally weigh in on federal court cases involving tax law. Specifically, it would let the Taxpayer Advocate file "amicus curiae" briefs, meaning "friend of the court" statements, in cases where the outcome could broadly affect taxpayer rights. Courts would be required to allow the Taxpayer Advocate to participate when this happens, rather than deciding case-by-case whether to permit it.

In practice, this means the Taxpayer Advocate could offer the court information or arguments about how a case might impact ordinary taxpayers, even without being a direct party to the lawsuit. This could affect taxpayers generally, since court rulings on tax law can set precedents that apply to many people. It could also affect the IRS, tax attorneys, and judges handling tax disputes, since the Taxpayer Advocate's involvement adds another voice to these proceedings, one focused specifically on protecting taxpayer interests rather than defending IRS policy.

title: CLEAR Path Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the CLEAR Path Act, aims to prevent former high-level government officials from using their government connections to help foreign countries that the U.S. considers "countries of concern" (a list that includes nations like China, Russia, North Korea, and Iran). It would extend existing "revolving door" ethics rules that already restrict what former officials can do after leaving government service.

Specifically, the bill targets people who serve as agency heads, deputy heads, or in other positions requiring Senate confirmation. Under this law, after these officials leave their government jobs, they would be permanently banned from representing, aiding, or advising a foreign government entity from a "country of concern" if they're trying to influence U.S. government decisions. This wouldn't apply to licensed attorneys giving legal advice. Officials would be notified of these restrictions both when they start and when they leave their jobs. The rule would only apply to people appointed after this law takes effect, and the restrictions themselves would expire after 5 years unless renewed.

The bill also sets up a formal process for the Secretary of State to update the list of "countries of concern" over time, working with the Attorney General, but any changes to that list would need Congress to approve them through a specific voting procedure. This bill mainly affects senior government officials who go through Senate confirmation (like cabinet secretaries and agency heads) and limits their future career options regarding foreign government work. It does not affect average government employees or private citizens.
ai_headline: Bill would bar ex-officials from aiding "countries of concern" for life
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

It exempts licensed attorneys giving legal advice, and only applies to officials appointed after the law takes effect. The restrictions expire after 5 years unless renewed, and the Secretary of State, with the Attorney General, can update the country list subject to congressional approval.

title: American Music Tourism Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the American Music Tourism Act of 2025, updates an existing law called the Visit America Act to add music-related travel as an official focus area for the federal government's tourism promotion efforts. It directs the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Travel and Tourism to identify places and events across the country that are important to music history and culture—such as museums, recording studios, concert venues, and music festivals—and to actively promote travel to these locations for both domestic and international visitors.

The bill also formally defines "music tourism" in law, describing it as travel to visit music-related historic or modern sites, or travel to attend concerts, festivals, or other live musical events. Additionally, it requires the Assistant Secretary to report to Congress every two years on progress made toward these tourism goals, including achievements and any weaknesses in the effort.

This bill mainly affects how the federal government promotes tourism, rather than creating new taxes, regulations, or direct payments to individuals. It could benefit local economies, especially in cities and regions known for music history (like Nashville, Memphis, or New Orleans), as well as businesses in the tourism, hospitality, and entertainment industries. Everyday travelers might notice more federally promoted marketing around music destinations and events, but the bill does not create new spending programs, taxes, or requirements for individuals.

title: FASD Respect Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the FASD Respect Act, renews and updates a federal program that deals with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD), a group of conditions that can occur in children whose mothers drank alcohol during pregnancy. The bill continues funding for programs run by the Department of Health and Human Services that work to prevent FASD, help diagnose it, and support people who have it and their families. It expands the program's focus to include not just prevention but also public awareness, early identification, and better coordination between federal, state, and tribal agencies. It also updates outdated language in the law, replacing older terms like "Fetal Alcohol Syndrome" with the broader, more current term "FASD."

The bill creates a system of "FASD Centers of Excellence," which are organizations that receive grants to research FASD, train medical and social service workers, raise public awareness, and act as information hubs for best practices and available services. States, tribal organizations, and nonprofit groups can apply for these grants, and they may be asked to appoint coordinators and create advisory committees to guide their efforts. The bill also requires HHS to report to Congress within four years on how well these programs are working. Funding is authorized through fiscal year 2029.

This bill mainly affects public health agencies, medical and mental health professionals, and nonprofit organizations that work on substance use and child development issues. It could also benefit pregnant women, families raising children with FASD, and healthcare and social service workers who rely on federal guidance and training related to the condition. It does not involve new taxes or major controversial policy changes—it primarily renews and modernizes an existing federal health program.

title: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States to provide that no person shall be elected to the office of the President more than three times.
ai_summary:
This bill proposes an amendment to the U.S. Constitution that would change the current limit on how many times someone can be elected President. Right now, the 22nd Amendment says a person can be elected President only twice, period. This proposal would instead allow a person to be elected up to three times, but with a restriction: they cannot be elected to an additional term right after already winning two elections in a row. In other words, someone could serve two consecutive terms, then would need a break before potentially winning a third term later.

The bill also keeps a version of the existing rule about partial terms. If someone becomes President without being elected (for example, a Vice President who takes over) and serves more than two years of another person's term, that person could only be elected twice on their own, not three times. This mirrors similar language from the current 22nd Amendment but adjusts the numbers to fit the new three-election limit.

Because this is a constitutional amendment, it would need approval from two-thirds of both the House and Senate, and then ratification by three-fourths of state legislatures within seven years. This affects every U.S. voter, since it changes the rules about how many times a President can be elected, potentially allowing certain former Presidents to run again after sitting out an election. It does not name any specific individual, but it would apply to any future President under these new rules.
ai_headline: Proposed amendment would let presidents win a third term after a break
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.

It keeps a similar rule for those who took office without election, limiting them to two elections if they served over two years of another's term.

title: Safe Stay Act
ai_summary:
The Safe Stay Act updates federal fire safety law to require carbon monoxide alarms in places like hotels, motels, and other public lodging facilities. It changes the existing federal guidelines, which currently reference fire alarm and sprinkler standards, to also require that a working carbon monoxide alarm be installed in every sleeping or living unit within these establishments. The bill defines what counts as a "compliant" alarm by referencing established safety codes from organizations like the National Fire Protection Association and the International Code Council, and it directs FEMA to make sure states update their official compliance lists to reflect this new requirement.

The bill also requires hotel and lodging operators to give guests written notice at check-in confirming that the property has working carbon monoxide alarms as required. If a business fails to provide this notice or lies about compliance, it would be treated as a deceptive business practice, and the Federal Trade Commission would have the power to investigate and penalize violators, similar to how it handles other false advertising or consumer protection cases. This notice requirement wouldn't start until one year after the law is enacted, giving businesses time to prepare.

This bill would primarily affect owners and operators of hotels, motels, inns, and similar lodging businesses, who would need to install carbon monoxide detectors if they don't already have them and create a system for notifying guests. Travelers and guests would benefit from increased safety and clearer information about carbon monoxide protections during their stay. State fire safety agencies and FEMA would also be involved in updating official compliance records to reflect the new federal standard.

title: Rural Broadband Protection Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This law changes how the federal government hands out money to companies that promise to bring internet service to rural areas. The money comes from a program called the "high-cost universal service fund," which is meant to help pay for broadband internet in places that are expensive or hard to reach, like remote rural communities. Under this new law, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) must create a screening process to check companies before giving them this funding, rather than just accepting applications at face value.

Specifically, companies applying for this money will now have to prove they actually have the technical skills, financial resources, and a solid business plan to build the internet network they're promising. The FCC will also look at whether the company has a good track record of following through on past government broadband projects. This is meant to prevent situations where a company wins funding, takes government money, but then fails to deliver the promised internet service. The law also sets stiff penalties—at least $9,000 per violation, and potentially 30% or more of the total funding awarded—if a company backs out or defaults before it's even fully approved.

This mainly affects internet and telecom companies that want to receive government subsidies to expand rural broadband, requiring them to meet stricter standards upfront. Indirectly, it affects rural residents and communities waiting for better internet access, since the goal is to make sure the companies awarded funding are actually capable of finishing the job, rather than wasting taxpayer money on projects that never get completed.

title: BIS Licensing Efficiency Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the BIS Licensing Efficiency Act of 2026, aims to speed up and add transparency to how the government reviews export license applications. These licenses are required when U.S. companies want to sell certain controlled products, technologies, or software to other countries, particularly items that could have military or national security implications. The bill amends existing export control law to set clearer expectations: the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), part of the Department of Commerce, should generally issue a decision within 90 days, and if a decision isn't made within 120 days, the agency must notify the applicant, explain the delay, and request any missing information needed to complete the review.

The bill also requires BIS to use licensing officers with relevant subject-matter expertise when reviewing applications, and it creates a new quarterly reporting requirement. These reports must be sent to Congress and include detailed statistics, such as how many applications were submitted, approved, denied, or delayed, how long reviews are taking on average, and breakdowns by country, product type, and which other agencies (like the State Department or Department of Defense) were involved in reviewing certain applications. Additionally, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) must audit BIS's licensing process within 90 days of the bill becoming law and report its findings, including any bottlenecks, within a year.

This bill mainly affects U.S. businesses that export controlled goods and technology, such as manufacturers, tech companies, and defense-related suppliers, by aiming to reduce delays and unpredictability in getting export approvals. It also affects the Department of Commerce and other federal agencies involved in the licensing process, who would face new reporting and oversight requirements, and it affects Congress and the public, who would gain more visibility into how efficiently the export licensing system is functioning.

title: OATH Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the OATH Act of 2025, is designed to help veterans who took part in secret government programs where they were required to sign non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) that threatened them with criminal punishment or court-martial if they revealed any information. A well-known example is the Edgewood Arsenal program at Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland, where soldiers were used in chemical and biological testing between 1948 and 1975. Because these veterans could not talk about their service, many never knew they were eligible for VA disability benefits or never applied for them.

The bill requires the Department of Veterans Affairs to identify veterans who participated in these "secrecy oath programs," notify them of any benefits they may qualify for, and do so within 90 days of the program ending or of the VA discovering their involvement. It specifically requires this outreach for Edgewood Arsenal veterans. The bill also changes how far back disability payments can be backdated: instead of starting from when a veteran applies, benefits would start from the day after the veteran was discharged or released from service, potentially resulting in significant back pay.

This primarily affects veterans who served in classified programs involving secrecy oaths, especially older veterans connected to Edgewood Arsenal, as well as their families who may be entitled to benefits. It also affects the VA, which would take on new responsibilities to track down these veterans and inform them of their rights, and it could increase federal spending on veterans' benefits due to the earlier effective dates for compensation.

last_action_text: Committee on Veterans' Affairs. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

title: Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, H.R. 4121, sets the government's spending plan for fiscal year 2026 for the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), its rural development programs, and the Food and Drug Administration. Rather than creating new policies, it mainly decides how much taxpayer money goes to dozens of existing programs and offices — things like farm loans, crop insurance, food safety inspections, agricultural research, and rural housing and business support. It also includes specific rules attached to the money, such as requiring the USDA to notify Congress before making certain changes, protecting rural county offices from being closed, and setting minimum staffing levels for humane slaughter inspections.

In practical terms, the bill affects farmers and ranchers (through loan programs, crop insurance, and disaster assistance), rural communities (through housing loans, rental assistance, community facility grants, and business development funds), and consumers (through food safety inspections of meat, poultry, and eggs, and support for agricultural research and market data). It also funds USDA's internal operations — legal, civil rights, IT, inspector general oversight — and continues support for institutions like tribal colleges, minority-serving universities, and 1890/1994 land-grant schools through research and extension grants.

Overall, the bill doesn't change major farm or food policy laws; it funds the agencies that carry them out for one year, while adding specific conditions on how that money can be spent, reported on, and monitored by Congress. This funding is significant for rural residents, farm operators, USDA employees, and anyone relying on federally inspected food or rural housing and infrastructure programs, since a lapse or major cut in this funding could disrupt services like farm loan processing, food inspections, or rural housing assistance.

title: Legislative Branch Appropriations Act, 2026
ai_summary:
This bill provides the funding for the "legislative branch" of the federal government for the fiscal year starting October 2025, covering the House of Representatives, the Capitol Police, the Library of Congress, the Government Accountability Office, the Congressional Budget Office, and related offices. In total it sets spending levels for things like member and staff salaries, committee operations, Capitol building maintenance, and security. It includes about $1.98 billion for House operations, $850 million for member office budgets, over $890 million combined for Capitol Police salaries and equipment, and hundreds of millions more for the Library of Congress, Government Publishing Office, and other support agencies. It also includes small death-benefit payments to family members of three House members who died in office (Sylvester Turner, Raul Grijalva, and Gerald Connolly).

Beyond the dollar amounts, the bill contains various policy provisions. It bans House offices from buying computer equipment from companies linked to the Chinese military or on certain U.S. government blacklists, and separately bans acquiring vehicles made by Chinese-government-linked automakers like BYD. It restricts Capitol Police leadership changes, requires unused member office funds to go toward deficit reduction, blocks funding for diversity/equity/inclusion training seen as promoting "divisive concepts," and protects people who act on religious or moral beliefs about marriage from facing federal penalties. It also freezes the annual cost-of-living pay raise for members of Congress in 2026, sets rules for pornography-blocking on congressional networks, and includes several technical legal fixes affecting Capitol Police management, the Architect of the Capitol's leasing authority, and copyright office operations.

This bill mainly affects people who work for or with Congress—lawmakers, staff, Capitol Police officers, Library of Congress and GAO employees—and indirectly affects the public through things like Capitol tours, congressional research services, copyright registration, and library programs for blind and print-disabled readers. It does not affect other federal agencies' budgets, Social Security, defense spending, or general taxpayer programs outside of Congress's own operations.

title: Continuing Appropriations, Agriculture, Legislative Branch, Military Construction and Veterans Affairs, and Extensions Act, 2026
ai_summary:
HR 5371 is a large "must-pass" government funding package that does several things at once. Its main purpose is to keep federal agencies operating past the start of the 2026 fiscal year through a "continuing resolution," meaning most departments continue spending at roughly their 2025 funding levels until January 30, 2026, or until Congress passes regular full-year budget bills. Alongside that stopgap measure, it includes full-year, permanent funding bills for a few specific areas: the Department of Agriculture and food/drug programs, Congress's own operations (the Legislative Branch), and military construction and Veterans Affairs programs. It also extends various expiring health, agriculture, and veterans-related programs so they don't lapse, and renews several unrelated legal authorities (like cybersecurity information-sharing rules, disaster relief funding rules, and court fee provisions) that were set to expire.

In practical terms, this bill affects almost everyone who interacts with the federal government. Farmers and rural communities benefit from continued USDA programs, agricultural research funding, and rural development support. Federal employees are protected from layoffs (reductions in force) during the funding gap, and any such layoffs attempted between October 2025 and the bill's enactment are reversed with back pay. Veterans and military families are affected through continued funding for VA health care, benefits, and military construction projects, including support for specific programs like the E-7 Wedgetail aircraft and Navy shipbuilding. It also includes smaller, specific provisions—such as death benefit payments to families of deceased members of Congress, funding increases for U.S. Marshals protective operations, Supreme Court security funding, and support for U.S. territories and Native American communities—that address narrow but important needs across the government.

Overall, this is a routine but complex "keep the government running" bill combined with a few full-year spending bills and various policy add-ons. It doesn't set new major policy directions so much as ensure that federal agencies, programs, and payments continue without interruption while Congress works out final full-year budgets for the rest of the government.
ai_headline: Funding bill would keep agencies open through January 30, 2026
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-37.

title: TAKE IT DOWN Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the TAKE IT DOWN Act, makes it a federal crime to knowingly publish intimate images of someone without their consent, including AI-generated fake images (often called "deepfakes") that look real. This covers both real photos or videos shared without permission and computer-generated images that convincingly show someone in a way that never actually happened. Violations involving adults could lead to fines and up to 2 years in prison, while violations involving minors carry penalties of up to 3 years. The bill also makes it illegal to threaten to publish such images to intimidate, harass, or extort someone. There are exceptions for law enforcement activities, legal proceedings, medical or educational purposes, and situations where someone is reporting abuse or seeking help.

The bill also requires websites, apps, and online platforms that host user-generated content to set up a system letting victims report nonconsensual intimate images and request their removal. Once a valid request is submitted, the platform must remove the image within 48 hours and make reasonable efforts to find and delete duplicate copies. Platforms must clearly explain this process to users in plain language. Companies that don't comply can be penalized by the Federal Trade Commission, which will treat noncompliance as an unfair business practice. Certain services, like email providers and internet access providers, are exempted from these platform requirements.

This bill mainly affects individuals who might become victims of nonconsensual intimate images or deepfakes, giving them legal protections and a faster way to get harmful content removed. It also affects social media companies, websites, and apps that host user content, since they will need to build new reporting and removal systems and could face government enforcement if they fail to act quickly. People who create or share such images without consent face new criminal penalties under the law.
ai_headline: New federal law criminalizes sharing nonconsensual intimate images, including deepfakes
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 59.

title: To rename the Anahuac National Wildlife Refuge located in the State of Texas as the "Jocelyn Nungaray National Wildlife Refuge".
ai_summary:
This bill would officially rename the Anahuac National Wildlife Refuge in Texas as the "Jocelyn Nungaray National Wildlife Refuge." The refuge is a protected natural area near Houston that provides habitat for birds and other wildlife. The bill states that all official references to the refuge in laws, maps, and government documents would be updated to use the new name.

The bill is named after Jocelyn Nungaray, a 12-year-old girl who was killed in Houston in June 2024. According to the bill, two people who had entered the country illegally and were allegedly connected to a gang were charged with her murder. The bill notes that President Trump had already issued an executive order in March 2025 renaming the refuge in her honor, and this legislation would make that name change permanent through an act of Congress rather than just an executive action.

This bill mainly affects how the refuge is officially identified on government records, signage, and maps. It would not change how the land is managed, who can visit it, or what activities are allowed there. The people most directly affected would be government agencies that maintain official records referencing the refuge, as well as the local community and visitors who would see the new name in place. The bill was introduced by Representative Babin along with several other Texas representatives and has been referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources for consideration.

last_action_text: Placed on the House Calendar, Calendar No. 36.

title: Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This law updates the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016, which lets families and heirs sue to recover artwork stolen by Nazis during World War II. Since 2016, some courts have thrown out these lawsuits by using legal technicalities unrelated to the actual facts of the case, such as arguing too much time had passed (laches), that the current owner had held the item long enough to claim ownership (adverse possession), or that courts shouldn't get involved in matters tied to another country's government actions (act of state doctrine). This new law directly blocks courts from using those excuses to dismiss Nazi-looted art claims, requiring judges instead to decide these cases based on the actual merits and evidence.

The law also clarifies that victims can bring claims regardless of their nationality at the time their property was seized, closing a loophole created by a 2021 Supreme Court decision that had limited such claims when the victim and the government that stole the property shared the same nationality. Additionally, it makes it easier to serve legal papers on defendants anywhere in the country, rather than being restricted to a specific court district.

This mainly affects families and heirs seeking the return of art stolen during the Holocaust, as well as museums, galleries, auction houses, and private collectors who currently possess such artwork and may now face fewer legal defenses against these claims. It applies to lawsuits already in progress, including those on appeal, as well as any new cases filed going forward.
ai_headline: Law closes loopholes that let courts dismiss Nazi-looted art claims
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-82.

title: Save Our Seas 2.0 Amendments Act
ai_summary:
This law makes changes to two related programs that deal with ocean trash and pollution: the federal Marine Debris Program run by NOAA (the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) and the Marine Debris Foundation, a nonprofit group created to help fund and support that work. Essentially, it reorganizes and updates the laws governing these programs, which were originally set up under the Marine Debris Act and the Save Our Seas 2.0 Act, by combining them into one unified law with clearer sections and updated rules.

Among the practical changes, the bill lets NOAA make in-kind contributions (providing resources or services instead of just money) to debris cleanup projects. It updates how the Marine Debris Foundation's board of directors is appointed, requiring Secretary of Commerce approval for certain board decisions, and sets six-year terms for board members. It also requires the Foundation to have a CEO who can hire and manage staff, and requires the Foundation's main office to be located either in the Washington, D.C. area or in a coastal community. Additionally, it expands who can partner with or receive grants from these programs to include Indian Tribes, tribal organizations, regional organizations, and foreign governments, and it directs the Foundation to create better outreach practices for working with Native American tribes.

This bill mainly affects government agencies, nonprofit organizations, and tribal governments involved in ocean cleanup and anti-pollution work, rather than average citizens directly. However, everyday Americans benefit indirectly through cleaner oceans, coastlines, and Great Lakes, since the law is designed to make these debris-reduction programs run more efficiently and extend their partnerships to more communities, including coastal and tribal areas most affected by marine litter.
ai_headline: Bill updates federal ocean debris program and its nonprofit partner
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-65.

title: Veterans’ Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This law increases the monthly payments that veterans receive for service-connected disabilities, as well as payments given to surviving spouses and children of veterans who died from service-related conditions. These increases take effect on December 1, 2025. Rather than picking a specific number, Congress tied the increase to the same percentage used for Social Security's annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA), which is based on inflation. This means if Social Security benefits go up by a certain percent that year, veterans' disability payments and survivor benefits go up by that same percent.

The law affects several specific types of payments: basic disability compensation for wartime veterans, extra payments for veterans with dependents, clothing allowances for certain disabled veterans, and dependency and indemnity compensation (financial support for surviving spouses and children of veterans who died from service-connected causes). The Department of Veterans Affairs is required to calculate the new dollar amounts and publish them in the Federal Register by a specific deadline, so veterans and families can see exactly how much their payments will increase.

This type of bill is passed almost every year to make sure veterans' benefits keep pace with the rising cost of living, similar to how Social Security payments are adjusted annually. It does not change eligibility rules or who qualifies for these benefits—it only adjusts the dollar amounts paid to those already receiving them.
ai_headline: Veterans disability and survivor benefits to rise with Social Security COLA
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-42.

title: Bottles and Breastfeeding Equipment Screening Enhancement Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Bottles and Breastfeeding Equipment Screening Enhancement Act, updates an existing law about how airport security handles breast milk, baby formula, and related items when traveling with children. It requires the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) to create official guidance, within 90 days of the law passing, on how to hygienically handle breast milk, baby formula, purified water for infants, juice, and the ice packs or cooling accessories used to keep them fresh. This guidance must be developed with input from recognized maternal health organizations and must apply to both TSA employees and private security company workers who screen passengers at airports. The guidance would also need to be reviewed and updated every five years.

The bill also requires an independent check on how well these rules are being followed. Within one year, the Inspector General of the Department of Homeland Security must submit a report to Congress reviewing whether TSA and security screeners are complying with the hygiene requirements. This report must also look at how different scanning technologies, like bottled liquid scanners, affect the screening process and how often these baby-related items get rejected from being brought into secure airport areas.

This bill mainly affects parents and caregivers traveling by air with infants, as well as TSA staff and private airport security personnel. Its goal is to make sure that when breast milk, formula, or related supplies are screened or retested at security checkpoints, they are handled in a clean, safe way that doesn't risk contamination, while also holding security agencies accountable for following these standards.

title: Ending Improper Payments to Deceased People Act
ai_summary:
This law aims to reduce the government sending payments, like Social Security benefits, to people who have died. It does this by improving how the Social Security Administration shares death record information with the "Do Not Pay" system, a federal database that agencies check before sending out payments to catch errors like fraud or mistaken payments to deceased individuals. The law sets up an agreement between the Social Security Administration and the agency running the Do Not Pay system to share this death data and split the costs of getting accurate state death records.

The law also adds a safeguard: Social Security cannot mark someone as deceased in its records unless there is "clear and convincing evidence" supporting that decision. This matters because sometimes living people are mistakenly recorded as dead, which can cut off their benefits and cause major financial and bureaucratic headaches. If such an error happens, the law now requires Social Security to notify any other agency that received the incorrect death information, so those agencies can correct their own records too.

This mainly affects people who receive federal benefits, such as Social Security recipients, and government agencies that rely on death records to avoid improper payments. The goal is to save taxpayer money by stopping payments to deceased people while also protecting living people from being wrongly flagged as dead. The changes take effect on December 27, 2026.

last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-77.

title: Congressional Award Program Reauthorization Act
ai_summary:
This bill extends the Congressional Award Program, a private, nonpartisan initiative sponsored by Congress that encourages young Americans to set and achieve goals in areas like volunteer service, personal development, physical fitness, and exploration. Participants who complete certain milestones earn bronze, silver, or gold Congressional Award medals or certificates. The program was set to expire, and this law pushes its authorization deadline from October 1, 2023, to October 1, 2028, and treats that extension as if it had been in effect since 2023 (so there's no gap in the program's legal authority).

The bill also makes small technical changes to the law governing how the award medals are made. Previously, the law specified that medals had to be made of gold-plate over bronze, rhodium over bronze, or plain bronze. This requirement is removed, giving the organization that runs the program more flexibility in deciding what materials to use for the medals going forward.

This bill mainly affects young people (typically teens) who participate in the Congressional Award Program, as well as the nonprofit organization that administers it. It does not create new government spending programs or regulations affecting the general public; it simply keeps an existing recognition program running for five more years and updates minor administrative details about medal production.

title: Great Lakes Fishery Research Reauthorization Act
ai_summary:
This law extends federal funding authorization for scientific research and monitoring work in the Great Lakes Basin. Specifically, it changes a single date in an earlier law—the Further Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2020—pushing the expiration of funding authority from 2025 to 2030. This means the government can continue to allocate money for these programs for five more years without needing to pass a brand-new authorization law right away.

The underlying program supports efforts to monitor, assess, and study the health of the Great Lakes ecosystem, particularly fish populations and habitat conditions. This work is typically carried out by agencies like the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and other federal or regional partners, often in cooperation with state governments, tribal nations, and research institutions around the Great Lakes region.

This bill mainly affects scientists, government agencies, and organizations involved in Great Lakes conservation and fisheries management, as well as the communities and industries that depend on healthy lake ecosystems—such as commercial and recreational fishing, tourism, and drinking water systems. Everyday residents in the eight Great Lakes states (Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and New York) are indirectly affected, since continued research helps track invasive species, water quality, and fish stocks that support local economies and environmental health. The bill does not create new programs or change how the money is spent—it simply keeps existing funding authority alive for a longer period.

title: HALT Fentanyl Act
ai_summary:
This law, called the HALT Fentanyl Act, permanently places entire classes of fentanyl-related chemicals into Schedule I, the most restrictive category of controlled substances under federal drug law. Rather than requiring the government to ban each new fentanyl variant one at a time as drug traffickers create them, the law defines broad categories of chemically similar substances and automatically treats them all as illegal Schedule I drugs, unless a specific substance is later moved to a different schedule by official action. This closes a gap that had allowed manufacturers to slightly alter fentanyl's chemical structure to create technically legal substances. It also updates criminal penalty laws so that trafficking or importing these fentanyl-related substances carries the same penalties as trafficking fentanyl itself.

The bill also changes rules for scientists who want to study Schedule I substances, including fentanyl-related ones, for legitimate research purposes. It creates a faster registration process for researchers, allows one lab to cover multiple staff or nearby research sites without separate approvals, lets registered researchers keep working when a new substance is added to Schedule I while their paperwork is processed, and reduces some duplicate inspections. It also requires the DEA to be transparent when it applies special rules to research on certain substances, and orders a government watchdog report on fentanyl research within a year.

This mainly affects law enforcement, prosecutors, and people involved in manufacturing, distributing, or trafficking fentanyl-like drugs, who now face clearer and broader criminal liability. It also affects medical and scientific researchers studying these substances, who get a somewhat easier registration process. Everyday citizens are affected indirectly, through the government's broader tools to combat the illegal fentanyl supply chain, which has been linked to a large share of U.S. overdose deaths, while research into fentanyl-related treatments may become easier to conduct.

last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-26.

title: HALT Fentanyl Act
ai_summary:

This makes permanent a policy that had previously been temporary and repeatedly extended by Congress. It defines fentanyl-related substances broadly, based on chemical similarities to fentanyl, so that new variations created by drug manufacturers to get around existing laws would automatically be covered, rather than requiring lawmakers to pass new legislation each time a new variant appears.

The bill also changes rules for scientists who want to research these substances. It creates a faster, simpler registration process for researchers studying Schedule I drugs, allows institutions to share one registration among multiple researchers, reduces duplicate inspections, and lets approved researchers continue studying a substance even after it gets newly scheduled, while their updated paperwork is processed. It also increases transparency by requiring the Drug Enforcement Administration to publicly post information when it applies special rules to specific substances.

Additionally, the bill updates federal criminal penalty laws so that trafficking or importing/exporting fentanyl-related substances carries the same penalties as trafficking fentanyl itself. This affects people in the medical and scientific research community who study these chemicals, as well as law enforcement, prosecutors, and individuals involved in manufacturing, distributing, or trafficking fentanyl analogues, since it affects sentencing and prosecution. Supporters say it closes loopholes drug traffickers use to create new fentanyl variants; critics have raised concerns in the past about how broad scheduling could affect research access and sentencing fairness. This summary presents the bill's provisions neutrally without taking a position on those debates.

title: Secure Rural Schools Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This law renews and extends the Secure Rural Schools and Community Self-Determination Act of 2000, a program that sends federal payments to rural counties that contain national forests or other public lands. Because these counties can't collect normal property taxes on federal land, the program helps make up the difference so local governments can still fund schools, roads, and emergency services. The new law pushes the program's expiration date forward to 2026, and extends related authority for special land-management projects and county spending programs out to 2028 or 2029.

The bill also fixes a gap: payments for fiscal years 2024 and 2025 hadn't been fully sorted out, so it sets rules for how those payments should be calculated and requires the Treasury Department to send out any owed money within 45 days of the law taking effect. It keeps counties' previous funding-distribution choices (like how they split money between schools and other local projects) in place for those same years, rather than making them reapply or re-elect options. Additionally, it extends a pilot program for "Resource Advisory Committees," which are local groups that help decide how federal land-management money gets used, and makes a few small technical and wording corrections to the underlying law.

This mainly affects rural counties and school districts located near national forests and other federal lands, especially in states like Oregon, California, Idaho, and others with large amounts of federally owned land. It also affects the U.S. Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management, which administer these programs, and local governments that rely on these payments to fund basic public services.
ai_headline: Rural schools funding law extended through 2026, some parts to 2029
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-58.

It also involves the U.S. Forest Service, Bureau of Land Management, and the Treasury Department.
ai_sections.why: Because these counties cannot tax federal land like private property, the payments replace lost revenue used for schools, roads, and emergency services. Without renewal, this funding source would have expired, disrupting local budgets in affected counties.

title: PRO Veterans Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This law, signed in August 2025, makes several changes aimed at increasing oversight and transparency at the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), which provides health care, benefits, and services to military veterans.

First, it requires the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to give Congress in-person briefings every three months, for three years, about the VA's budget and any funding shortfalls. If the VA doesn't have enough money to cover its legally required obligations, the Secretary must explain during these briefings how the department plans to fix the problem. This is meant to prevent budget surprises and keep lawmakers informed earlier, rather than after problems have already caused disruptions to veterans' services.

Second, the law limits how VA can give special "critical skill" pay incentives to senior executives (top-level managers) working at its central headquarters, while allowing more flexibility for senior staff working at other VA facilities, subject to approval from specific top officials. The VA must also report yearly to Congress on who receives these incentives. Third, the law creates a new "Veterans Experience Office" inside the VA, led by a Chief Veterans Experience Officer, to track veteran satisfaction with services, identify why some veterans don't use benefits they're eligible for, and report this data to Congress annually. This office is required to protect veterans' private information and is set to expire in 2028 unless renewed. The Government Accountability Office must also review how well the VA is using veteran feedback to improve services. Overall, this law mainly affects VA employees, agency management practices, and indirectly benefits veterans through improved oversight and service tracking, rather than changing veterans' direct benefits.
ai_headline: New law adds quarterly VA budget briefings and veteran feedback office
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-33.

title: Laken Riley Act
ai_summary:
This bill, known as the Laken Riley Act, changes federal immigration law to require the Department of Homeland Security to detain undocumented immigrants who are charged with, arrested for, convicted of, or admit to committing theft-related crimes, including burglary, larceny, and shoplifting. Under current law, mandatory detention generally applies to more serious crimes; this bill expands that requirement to cover theft offenses as well, even relatively minor ones like shoplifting. It also requires DHS to issue a detainer (a request to hold the person) and take them into custody if they aren't already being held by other authorities.

The bill also gives state attorneys general new power to sue the federal government in court if they believe federal officials are failing to properly detain, deny entry to, or remove immigrants as required by law, or if they improperly grant parole or bond. States could sue if they or their residents suffer harm, including financial harm of more than $100, which is a very low bar. Courts would be required to fast-track these lawsuits. This significantly increases states' ability to challenge federal immigration enforcement decisions in court.

This bill primarily affects undocumented immigrants who are accused of theft-related offenses, who would face mandatory detention rather than possible release while their cases proceed. It also affects federal immigration agencies, which would have new detention obligations and could face more lawsuits from states. State governments would gain new legal tools to influence federal immigration enforcement, potentially shifting some power over immigration policy from the federal government toward individual states.
ai_headline: Bill would mandate detention for immigrants accused of theft crimes
last_action_text: Read the second time. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 10.

ai_sections.tldr: Undocumented immigrants charged with theft crimes like shoplifting would face mandatory federal detention.

DHS must issue a detainer and take the person into custody if not already held. The bill also lets state attorneys general sue the federal government over immigration enforcement decisions, including cases of harm over $100, with courts required to fast-track these suits.
ai_sections.who: Undocumented immigrants accused of theft-related offenses, federal immigration agencies, and state governments are directly affected.
ai_sections.why: Immigrants accused of even minor theft offenses would face mandatory detention instead of possible release while cases proceed, and states would gain new legal power to challenge federal immigration decisions, potentially shifting enforcement authority toward states.

title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management relating to "Protection of Marine Archaeological Resources".
ai_summary:
This bill cancels a federal regulation that had been put in place by the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM), a government agency that oversees activities like offshore drilling and energy development on the ocean floor. The regulation, called "Protection of Marine Archaeological Resources," was finalized in September 2024 and was meant to set rules for identifying and protecting historically or culturally significant underwater sites, such as shipwrecks or ancient artifacts, from damage caused by offshore energy projects. By passing this resolution, Congress used a special power under a law called the Congressional Review Act, which allows lawmakers to overturn recent federal agency rules with a simple majority vote. Once approved, the rule is treated as if it never took effect.

This action mainly affects companies involved in offshore energy development, such as oil, gas, and wind energy companies, since they would have been required to follow the canceled rule's procedures for protecting archaeological sites during their projects. It also affects historians, archaeologists, and preservation groups who were counting on the rule to safeguard underwater cultural resources. Because the rule is now void, BOEM cannot enforce those specific protections, and the agency is generally barred from creating a substantially similar rule in the future unless Congress passes a new law allowing it.

This resolution passed both the Senate and House in early 2025 and was signed into law on March 14, 2025, officially eliminating the rule.
ai_headline: Congressional resolution voids rule protecting underwater archaeological sites
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-3.

title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency of the Department of the Treasury relating to the review of applications under the Bank Merger Act.
ai_summary:
This bill cancels a rule that a federal banking regulator, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), had put in place in September 2024. That rule changed how the OCC reviews and approves bank mergers under a law called the Bank Merger Act, generally adding more scrutiny and clearer standards for evaluating whether a proposed merger between banks should be allowed. By passing this resolution, Congress used a special power called the Congressional Review Act to formally reject that rule, meaning the rule is now treated as if it never took effect.

In practical terms, this bill does not create new rules itself. Instead, it removes the specific merger-review process the OCC had adopted, so bank mergers will go back to being evaluated under the older procedures and standards that existed before that rule was issued. This mainly affects banks that are considering merging or being acquired, since it changes the process and requirements they must follow to get government approval for such deals. It also affects the OCC itself, since the agency is now blocked from reissuing a substantially similar rule in the future unless Congress specifically allows it.

The bill does not directly affect everyday consumers in an immediate way, but changes to bank merger rules can influence how many mergers happen, how competitive the banking industry is, and how carefully deals are reviewed for risks like reduced competition or financial instability. Because of this, everyday bank customers could see indirect effects over time, such as changes in the number of local banking options or the pace of bank consolidation, depending on how future mergers are reviewed without this rule in place.
ai_headline: Senate resolution scraps OCC's 2024 bank merger review rule
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-19.

title: A joint resolution disapproving the rule submitted by the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection relating to "Overdraft Lending: Very Large Financial Institutions".
ai_summary:
This law cancels a regulation that the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) had created about overdraft fees at very large banks. The original CFPB rule, finalized in December 2024, would have limited how much big financial institutions (generally banks with more than $10 billion in assets) could charge customers when they overdraw their checking accounts. It aimed to cap overdraft fees or require banks to treat overdraft loans more like other forms of credit, making the costs clearer and often cheaper for consumers.

By passing this joint resolution, Congress used its authority under the Congressional Review Act to formally reject the CFPB's rule. This means the overdraft fee limits never took effect and have no legal force. Banks covered by the original rule are not required to follow its restrictions, so they can continue setting overdraft fees the way they did before the rule was finalized.

This mainly affects customers of very large banks who overdraw their checking accounts, since those banks retain more flexibility in how much they charge for overdraft services. It also affects the CFPB itself, since the Congressional Review Act generally prevents the agency from issuing a substantially similar rule in the future unless Congress specifically authorizes it.
ai_headline: Congress overturns CFPB cap on big bank overdraft fees
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-10.

title: Disapproving the rule submitted by the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection relating to "Overdraft Lending: Very Large Financial Institutions".
ai_summary:
This bill would cancel a federal rule that regulated how large banks handle overdraft fees. The rule, issued by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) in December 2024, applied to "very large financial institutions" (generally banks with more than $10 billion in assets) and was designed to change how those banks charge customers for overdrafts, when someone spends more money than they have in their checking account. Under the previous rule, banks would have faced new limits or requirements on overdraft lending, such as treating certain overdraft fees more like loans subject to consumer lending protections, or capping fees at a set amount.

This resolution uses a process under the Congressional Review Act, which allows Congress to reject recently issued federal regulations with a simple majority vote in both chambers and the president's signature. If passed, it would completely undo the CFPB's overdraft rule, meaning it would have no legal effect, and would also prevent the CFPB from issuing a substantially similar rule in the future without new authorization from Congress.

This mainly affects customers of large banks who overdraw their checking accounts, since the rule was meant to reduce or restructure the fees they pay. It also affects large banks themselves, which would avoid the new compliance requirements and fee limits that the rule would have imposed. Smaller banks and credit unions, which were not covered by the rule, would not be directly affected either way.
ai_headline: Resolution would scrap CFPB rule limiting big bank overdraft fees
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 16.
