title: A joint resolution disapproving the rule submitted by the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection relating to "Defining Larger Participants of a Market for General-Use Digital Consumer Payment Applications".
ai_summary:
This law cancels a rule that had been created by the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection (CFPB), the federal agency that oversees banks, lenders, and other financial companies to protect consumers. The rule being cancelled was designed to let the CFPB treat large companies that operate popular digital payment apps (things like mobile wallets or peer-to-peer payment services used for everyday purchases) similarly to how it already treats big banks and credit unions. This would have allowed the CFPB to supervise and examine these large tech-driven payment companies more closely, checking that they follow consumer protection laws.

By passing this joint resolution, Congress used its power under the Congressional Review Act to formally reject the rule. As a result, the rule has no legal effect, and the CFPB cannot enforce it. The agency is also blocked from creating a substantially similar rule in the future unless Congress specifically authorizes it.

This mainly affects large companies that run digital payment apps, since they will not face the extra federal oversight the rule would have created. It also affects everyday consumers who use these apps for shopping, sending money, or paying bills, because the CFPB will have less direct authority to supervise these companies' compliance with consumer protection rules. Banks and credit unions, which are already regulated in similar ways, are not directly affected by this change.
ai_headline: Congressional measure blocks CFPB oversight rule for digital payment apps
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-11.

title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "Review of Final Rule Reclassification of Major Sources as Area Sources Under Section 112 of the Clean Air Act".
ai_summary:
This resolution cancels a specific environmental regulation that had been put in place by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). The rule in question dealt with how certain industrial facilities are classified under the Clean Air Act. Previously, the EPA had made it easier for large industrial polluters, known as "major sources," to be reclassified as smaller "area sources" once they reduced their pollution below a certain threshold. This reclassification matters because major sources face stricter pollution control requirements, while area sources have more relaxed rules. By officially disapproving this rule, Congress has completely eliminated it, meaning it no longer has any legal effect.

This bill was passed using a special process under the Congressional Review Act, which allows Congress to overturn recent federal agency regulations with a simple majority vote, bypassing the usual filibuster rules in the Senate. It passed the Senate in late April/early May 2025 and the House in May 2025, then was signed into law on June 20, 2025.

The practical effect is that industrial facilities, such as chemical plants, refineries, or manufacturing sites, that had been able to reduce their emissions and qualify for reclassification as smaller sources will likely be held to the original, stricter pollution control standards for major sources instead. This affects businesses in heavy industries that emit hazardous air pollutants, as well as communities living near these facilities, since the level of required pollution control can impact local air quality. Environmental regulators, industry groups, and nearby residents are the parties most directly affected by this change.
ai_headline: Congress reverses EPA rule easing polluter reclassification under Clean Air Act
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-20.

title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Bureau of Land Management relating to "National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska Integrated Activity Plan Record of Decision".
ai_summary:
This bill cancels a federal rule that limited oil and gas drilling in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska. That rule, called the Integrated Activity Plan Record of Decision, was put in place by the Bureau of Land Management in 2022 and set aside about half of the reserve's roughly 23 million acres as protected areas where drilling and other industrial activity would be restricted, in order to safeguard wildlife habitats, waterways, and lands important to Alaska Native communities. Congress used a special law called the Congressional Review Act, which allows lawmakers to reverse certain federal agency rules with a simple resolution, to strike down this plan. Once the President signs it, the rule officially has no legal effect, meaning the protections it created no longer apply.

The practical effect is that the more restrictive land-use plan is undone, which generally reopens more of the reserve to potential oil and gas leasing and development, similar to earlier, less restrictive management plans. This mainly affects Alaska, particularly Indigenous communities living in and around the reserve, energy companies interested in drilling there, and environmental groups concerned about wildlife such as caribou herds and migratory birds. It also affects federal land-management policy more broadly, since the Congressional Review Act not only cancels the rule but also normally prevents agencies from creating a substantially similar rule in the future without new authorization from Congress.
ai_headline: Resolution repeals Alaska drilling limits in petroleum reserve
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-47.

title: Salem Maritime National Historical Park Redesignation and Boundary Study Act
ai_summary:
This law changes the official name of the Salem Maritime National Historic Site in Massachusetts to the "Salem Maritime National Historical Park." Any time the old name appears in federal laws, maps, documents, or records, it will now automatically be understood to mean the new name. This is largely a formal change in title and does not, by itself, alter how the site is managed day to day.

The law also directs the Secretary of the Interior to study whether nearby sites in Salem and the surrounding area should be added to the park. The study will look at places connected to maritime history, coastal defense, and military history, including the Salem Armory Visitor Center and Salem Armory Park. Within three years of receiving funding for the study, the Secretary must report the findings and any recommendations to relevant committees in the House and Senate.

This mainly affects the National Park Service, which manages the site, and residents of Salem and nearby communities, since the study could eventually lead to an expanded park boundary. Visitors and historians may also notice references to the site's history and mission expand slightly to reflect the "historical park" designation, which is often used for park units with broader thematic or educational scope. No immediate changes to public access, land ownership, or funding levels are required by this law alone.
ai_headline: Salem Maritime site renamed a national historical park, expansion study ordered
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-25.

title: Shenandoah Mountain Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates the Shenandoah Mountain National Scenic Area, covering about 92,562 acres in Virginia's George Washington and Jefferson National Forests. The goal is to protect the area's scenery, water quality, wildlife habitat (including a rare salamander species), and forests that could grow into old-growth condition, while still allowing recreation like hiking and other non-motorized trail use. Within this larger area, the bill also designates five new or expanded wilderness areas (Skidmore Fork, Ramseys Draft Addition, Lynn Hollow, Little River, and Beech Lick Knob), totaling roughly 33,800 acres, which receive the strongest federal protections under the existing Wilderness Act, meaning no roads, logging, or motorized vehicles.

The bill spells out detailed rules for managing the land: existing roads stay open and no new roads can be built; new trailhead parking is allowed only along existing forest roads; timber harvesting is generally banned except for safety, fire control, or disease management purposes; and the land is off-limits to mining, oil and gas leasing, and new wind or solar energy projects. The Forest Service must also create a trail plan and an overall management plan within two years, with public input, and specifically plan a new trail connecting two popular recreation areas. Private landowners within the boundaries keep their right to access their property, and the state of Virginia keeps authority to maintain the existing access road to the mountain's crest.

This bill mainly affects people who use or manage this part of Virginia's national forest: hikers, campers, hunters, and other recreational users; nearby residents and private landowners; loggers and energy companies (who would lose access to timber, mining, and renewable energy development there); and government agencies like the U.S. Forest Service, which would take on new planning and management duties. It was introduced by Virginia's two U.S. senators and is currently under committee review, so it is not yet law.

last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 214.

title: Health Records Enhancement Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Health Records Enhancement Act, would let certain people add information to the health records of veterans who have died. Within one year of the bill becoming law, the Department of Defense and the Department of Veterans Affairs would have to set up a system allowing a person chosen by the veteran before death, or if no one was chosen, a close family member like a spouse, parent, sibling, or adult child, to add health-related observations or information to that veteran's records. Importantly, this added information could only supplement the existing records, not change or delete anything already there.

This would affect veterans who were enrolled in VA health care or eligible for TRICARE (the military's health program) at the time of their death, as well as their families. The idea seems to be that family members often notice health conditions or symptoms that never made it into official medical records, and this bill would create a formal way to preserve that information after the veteran has died. This could matter for historical accuracy, research, or helping future family members understand hereditary health risks. The bill does not give the Secretaries discretion to refuse the requirement, but it does leave the specific details of how the designation process and record updates would work up to the two departments to figure out jointly.
ai_headline: Bill would let families add notes to deceased veterans' health records
last_action_text: Committee on Veterans' Affairs. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

This added information can only supplement existing records, not change or delete anything already there. The system must be established within one year of enactment.

title: Chloe Cole Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Chloe Cole Act of 2026, would let minors (and their parents or guardians) sue doctors, hospitals, or clinics that provided certain gender-transition treatments to them as children. The treatments covered include puberty blockers, hormone therapy, and surgeries intended to change a child's physical appearance or body away from their biological sex. It does not apply to treatments for verifiable medical conditions like intersex traits, treatments needed to fix injuries or complications from a prior transition-related procedure, or care for unrelated medical emergencies or birth defects.

Under the bill, healthcare providers who perform these procedures on children could be held "strictly liable," meaning the patient wouldn't need to prove negligence, just that the procedure happened. Providers could be sued for financial losses, emotional suffering, and in some cases punitive damages if their actions are shown to be intentional or reckless. The law would apply retroactively, meaning people could sue over treatments that happened even before this law was passed, and lawsuits could be filed up to 25 years after the person turns 18, or within 4 years of paying for "detransition" treatment, whichever is later. The bill also limits doctors' ability to defend themselves by citing existing medical guidelines if those guidelines are shown to have been scientifically disputed at the time.

This bill would primarily affect transgender minors who received or are receiving gender-related medical treatment, their families, and the doctors, hospitals, and clinics that provide such care. It would create new legal risks for medical providers involved in youth gender-transition treatment and give affected individuals and parents a direct way to seek financial compensation through the federal courts.

title: United States Commission on International Religious Freedom Reauthorization Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill keeps the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) running for two more years. USCIRF is a small independent government body that monitors how other countries treat religious freedom and reports its findings and recommendations to Congress, the President, and the State Department. Without this bill, the commission's funding authorization and legal authority to operate would expire on September 30, 2026.

Specifically, the bill changes the law so that Congress can approve funding for the commission for fiscal years 2027 and 2028, instead of just 2025 and 2026. It also pushes back the date when the commission's authority automatically ends, from September 30, 2026, to September 30, 2028. This is a routine reauthorization, meaning it doesn't create new programs or change what the commission does—it simply allows an existing agency to keep functioning and receiving money for a couple more years.

This bill mainly affects the commission itself and its staff, who study religious persecution and discrimination worldwide, particularly against religious minorities. It could also indirectly affect foreign governments and groups that are named in USCIRF reports, since those reports can influence U.S. foreign policy decisions, sanctions, or diplomatic pressure. Everyday U.S. residents aren't directly affected, though the bill supports ongoing U.S. efforts to track and respond to religious freedom violations abroad.

title: Nuclear REFUEL Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes how federal law classifies certain nuclear fuel recycling equipment. Under current law, the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 defines a "production facility" broadly enough that equipment used to reprocess spent nuclear fuel can fall under strict regulatory categories, similar to facilities that enrich uranium or separate weapons-usable plutonium. This bill would carve out an exception: equipment that reprocesses spent nuclear fuel using methods that do NOT separate pure plutonium from other similar heavy elements (called transuranic elements) would no longer count as a "production facility" under the law.

In practical terms, this means certain newer nuclear recycling technologies—ones designed to keep plutonium mixed with other elements rather than isolating it in pure form—would face a lighter regulatory path and likely faster licensing from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. This matters because separating pure plutonium raises nuclear weapons proliferation concerns, so processes that avoid that step are seen as safer from a security standpoint, even though they still reprocess used nuclear fuel.

This bill mainly affects nuclear industry companies developing advanced fuel recycling technology, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and Department of Energy (which oversee licensing and classification), and national security policymakers concerned with nuclear nonproliferation. Indirectly, it could affect utility companies and communities near nuclear plants if it speeds up development of new fuel recycling facilities, potentially reducing nuclear waste stockpiles or enabling reuse of nuclear materials. Everyday consumers wouldn't see immediate effects, but over time this could influence nuclear energy costs, waste management practices, and the pace at which new nuclear fuel technologies reach the market.
ai_headline: Bill would ease rules for nuclear recycling that avoids pure plutonium
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 224.

title: Eliminate PRC Organized Crime Act
ai_summary:
**S. 4723 — Eliminate PRC Organized Crime Act**

This bill would create a U.S. State Department program to help police and law enforcement agencies in Latin American and Caribbean countries fight organized crime groups linked to China. These groups are described as being involved in activities like drug trafficking, money laundering, illegal finance schemes, and efforts by the Chinese government to intimidate people or interfere in other countries' affairs. The assistance could include training on financial investigations and asset seizures, technical help like digital forensics and intelligence-sharing, and support to make sure foreign police forces receiving U.S. help haven't themselves been compromised by these criminal networks. The State Department would work with the Attorney General and, when needed, the Director of National Intelligence to run this program.

The bill also allows the Secretary of State to give this assistance to a country even if that country has otherwise been found to have failed to meet its international drug-control obligations, as long as the Secretary decides it's in the national interest and notifies Congress 15 days in advance. Within a year, intelligence officials would have to report to Congress on which countries received help, what Chinese criminal activity looks like in the region, whether China itself has been helping or hindering these local police efforts, and the status of any legal assistance requests between countries.

This bill mainly affects U.S. foreign policy and diplomatic/law-enforcement cooperation efforts rather than everyday domestic life. It would most directly affect State Department operations, U.S. relations with Latin American and Caribbean governments, and could indirectly affect Americans by aiming to reduce drug trafficking and financial crimes that reach into the United States. It does not create new domestic laws or directly regulate U.S. citizens or businesses.

title: Arctic Security and Diplomacy Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Arctic Security and Diplomacy Act, responds to concerns that Russia and China are increasing military, scientific, and intelligence-gathering activity in the Arctic in ways that could threaten U.S. security. Congress lists several examples, including Russia's military buildup in the region, China's use of research stations and scientific partnerships as cover for espionage, and reports of spying activity affecting Denmark, Greenland, Iceland, and Canada. Based on these concerns, the bill sets a formal U.S. policy of limiting foreign spying and influence operations in the Arctic, sharing information about these threats with allied countries, and using diplomatic tools (like sanctions or removing countries from Arctic organizations) to respond to violations.

The bill's main practical requirement is that foreign scientists and vessels—especially those from countries labeled "foreign adversaries" (North Korea, Iran, China, and Russia)—must get U.S. government approval before conducting ocean research in U.S. waters, including the coastal zone extending 200 nautical miles offshore. Vessels connected to these adversary countries generally would be blocked from getting approval, though the Secretary of State could grant a waiver if it's judged to be in the national interest, with Congress notified of any such waiver. The bill also requires the State Department, intelligence agencies, and Homeland Security to create a strategy for countering Arctic espionage and to submit reports to Congress on foreign spying activities and violations of the research-approval rules.

This bill would primarily affect federal agencies (State Department, intelligence agencies, Homeland Security), foreign governments and research institutions seeking to conduct ocean science in U.S. Arctic waters, and U.S. partnerships or programs involving foreign scientists. Everyday Americans would mostly be affected indirectly, through changes in U.S. foreign policy, national security posture, and diplomatic relationships in the Arctic region, rather than through any direct new rules on individuals or businesses.

title: PEACE in Sudan Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the PEACE in Sudan Act, is aimed at helping end the ongoing civil war in Sudan between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces, which has caused a major humanitarian crisis. It requires the U.S. State Department and intelligence agencies to regularly report to Congress on which foreign countries, militias, and businesses are fueling the conflict by supplying weapons, money, fighters, or other support. It also requires reports on human rights abuses like the use of child soldiers, sexual violence, and attacks on civilians and aid workers. The bill directs the administration to create a formal strategy for reaching a ceasefire and lasting peace, and to study whether armed groups involved in the war should be labeled as terrorist organizations.

The bill also gives the President new authority to impose sanctions—such as freezing assets, restricting financial transactions, and denying visas—on foreign individuals or entities found to be fueling the conflict, committing atrocities, or blocking peace efforts. It restricts most U.S. assistance and international financial institution loans to Sudan's government during the conflict, though it allows exceptions for humanitarian aid and gives the President the ability to waive these restrictions if it's in the national security interest. It extends the term of the U.S. Special Envoy for Sudan and asks for updates to business advisories warning American companies about risks tied to Sudanese gold and gum arabic trade linked to the conflict.

This bill mainly affects U.S. foreign policy operations, diplomats, and agencies like the State Department and Treasury, rather than everyday Americans directly. However, it could affect U.S. companies doing business with Sudan-linked industries, and it may influence humanitarian aid groups working in the region. It does not authorize any U.S. military action—it focuses solely on diplomatic, financial, and reporting tools to try to pressure the warring parties toward peace and hold human rights violators accountable.

title: U.S. Tech PATH Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the U.S. Tech PATH Act, aims to help foreign governments buy computer and technology equipment from trusted American companies instead of turning to countries like China. Lawmakers are concerned that when foreign governments buy cheap technology from "countries of concern," it creates security risks, such as foreign governments being able to access data or spy through that equipment. To address this, the bill sets up a new program at the State Department that would help other countries navigate the process of purchasing U.S.-made technology, including software, computer hardware, cybersecurity tools, telecommunications equipment, and artificial intelligence systems. The program would offer guidance, technical assistance, and help finding financing to make these purchases easier and more affordable.

The bill creates a new office within the State Department to run this program, with a director and staff, and allows for special hiring rules to bring in experts quickly. It also expands a related program that places technology experts at U.S. embassies overseas. Before any country can participate, the State Department must check whether that government has a history of human rights abuses, corruption, or misusing technology to spy on journalists, shut down the internet, or suppress political opponents; countries with such records would be disqualified. The bill also makes clear that the government should not use this program to unfairly interfere with private companies competing for these contracts, though it allows extra help for U.S. small businesses trying to compete internationally.

This bill mainly affects foreign governments and international organizations seeking modern technology, U.S. technology companies (especially those hoping to export products abroad), and U.S. State Department staff who would run the new program. It authorizes $500 million over six years for the technology purchasing program and $2 million for the new office, with the program set to expire after eight years unless renewed. Congress would also receive regular reports and independent government reviews to track how the program is working and ensure taxpayer money is being used effectively and safely.

title: Falun Gong and Victims of Forced Organ Harvesting Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Falun Gong and Victims of Forced Organ Harvesting Protection Act, targets people and organizations involved in forced organ harvesting in China. Forced organ harvesting means taking organs from someone through coercion, deception, or abuse of power, rather than voluntary donation. This practice has long been reported as affecting prisoners of conscience in China, including practitioners of Falun Gong, a spiritual movement banned by the Chinese government.

The bill requires the President to identify foreign individuals and companies known to be directly involved in this practice and to impose sanctions on them. These sanctions include freezing any property or financial assets they have in the United States, and barring them from receiving U.S. visas or entering the country, even canceling visas they already hold. There are some exceptions, such as for humanitarian aid, food and medicine sales, national security or intelligence activities, and U.S. obligations to the United Nations. The President can also waive sanctions in specific cases if it serves U.S. national security interests, but must report on how often that waiver is used. These sanction powers would expire five years after the law is enacted unless renewed.

The bill also directs the State Department, working with health agencies, to produce a detailed report within a year on China's organ transplant practices. This report would estimate how many transplants occur, how many organs come from voluntary donors, how quickly organs are obtained (which may indicate whether they come from forced sources), and whether any U.S. grants have funded related research in China. It would also assess whether this practice counts as an "atrocity" under U.S. law. Overall, this bill mainly affects foreign individuals and entities linked to organ harvesting abuses, Chinese officials or institutions involved in transplants, and U.S. government agencies tasked with monitoring and reporting on the issue. Everyday Americans would not be directly affected, except through U.S. foreign policy and possible diplomatic tensions with China.

title: Biosimilar Red Tape Elimination Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the government approves "biosimilar" drugs, which are medicines that are highly similar to expensive brand-name biologic drugs (biologics are medicines made from living organisms, like many cancer or arthritis treatments). Currently, a biosimilar can be approved as simply "similar" to the original drug, but it needs to go through extra testing and get a separate, harder-to-earn label called "interchangeable" before pharmacists can automatically substitute it for the brand-name drug, similar to how generic pills work. This bill eliminates that extra "interchangeable" category and step. Instead, once a biosimilar is approved as biosimilar, it would automatically be treated as interchangeable, removing the extra testing requirement.

The bill sets a 60-day transition period after it becomes law, and lays out rules for how existing biosimilars and their manufacturers move into the new system, including protecting some companies that already have exclusive rights tied to being the first "interchangeable" version of a drug. It also requires the FDA to update its official guidance documents within 18 months to match the new rules.

This bill mainly affects drug manufacturers (especially companies that make biosimilars), the FDA, pharmacists, insurance companies, and patients who use biologic medications. Supporters argue it will speed up access to cheaper biosimilar drugs by cutting duplicate regulatory steps. Critics might worry about removing an extra layer of testing that was designed to ensure these drugs work exactly the same way when swapped for brand-name biologics. Patients could see more biosimilar options available for automatic substitution at the pharmacy, potentially lowering drug costs.

title: Blue Skies for Taiwan Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, the Blue Skies for Taiwan Act of 2026, aims to help the United States and Taiwan work together on drone technology, specifically to reduce reliance on Chinese-made drone parts. Many commercial drones today contain components made in China, which raises security concerns for both military and government use. The bill would create a "Blue UAS Working Group," run by the State Department and Defense Department, to study Taiwan's ability to design, test, and manufacture drone components, and to find ways to include Taiwanese companies in the Pentagon's existing "Blue UAS" program, which certifies drones as secure and free of Chinese parts.

The bill also directs the government to build a broader partnership with Taiwan and other allied countries in the Indo-Pacific region to create supply chains for drones that don't depend on China, and to make it easier and faster for allied nations to buy Taiwan-made drone parts instead of Chinese ones. It calls for a "fast-track" certification and export-approval process so Taiwanese manufacturers can more quickly meet U.S. security standards. The bill authorizes unspecified funding to carry out these efforts and requires regular reports to Congress on progress.

This bill mainly affects U.S. defense agencies, drone manufacturers, and Taiwan's technology and defense industry. It could benefit American and Taiwanese companies involved in drone production by opening new business and partnership opportunities, while also serving broader U.S. national security goals related to reducing dependence on Chinese technology. It does not change the official U.S. political stance on Taiwan's international status, and everyday consumers would not be directly affected, though the policy could influence U.S.-China relations and defense industry trends over time.

title: Halting Ownership and Non-Ethical Stock Transactions (HONEST) Act
ai_summary:
This bill, formally called the HONEST Act but internally titled the PELOSI Act, would stop members of Congress and their spouses from buying, selling, or holding individual stocks and similar investments while in office. Covered investments include stocks, security futures, commodities, and related financial products like options or derivatives. It would not apply to diversified mutual funds, diversified exchange-traded funds (ETFs), U.S. Treasury bonds, or income a spouse earns from their own separate job or career.

Current members would have 180 days after the law passes to sell off any banned investments, and new members would get 180 days after starting their term. Anyone who breaks the rule would have to give up any profits made and could face escalating fines equal to 10% of the value of the investment they failed to sell, charged every 30 days until they comply. Members would have to certify each year that they're following the rules, and this information would be posted publicly online. The House and Senate ethics committees would enforce the law, though members could appeal fines through a floor vote. The Government Accountability Office would also audit compliance two years after the law takes effect.

This bill would primarily affect sitting members of Congress and their spouses, changing how they can manage personal investments while serving in office. It would not directly affect the general public, though it aims to increase transparency and reduce potential conflicts of interest between lawmakers' financial holdings and their official duties.

title: National Programmable Cloud Laboratories Network Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would create a national network of up to six "programmable cloud laboratories" — high-tech labs equipped with robotics, research instruments, and artificial intelligence that scientists can operate remotely over the internet. The National Science Foundation would run a competitive application process to select universities, nonprofits, private companies, or partnerships to host these labs, called "nodes." Applicants would need to show they have suitable existing infrastructure, plans to become financially self-sufficient over time, and some non-federal funding or investment already lined up. The goal is to make scientific research faster, cheaper, and more collaborative, while keeping the U.S. competitive in fields like materials science, biotechnology, and chemistry, and helping move government-funded research into commercial products.

The bill also requires the selected labs to work together on shared technical standards, cybersecurity protocols, and data-sharing practices, with help from the National Institute of Standards and Technology. After the labs are chosen, the government would study other labs across the country that weren't selected, to see if they could still be connected to the network somehow. Congress would receive yearly briefings on how well the network is meeting its goals, including whether the labs are becoming financially sustainable rather than depending indefinitely on federal money.

This bill mainly affects universities, research institutions, national labs, and private companies involved in scientific research and lab automation, as well as federal science agencies like the NSF and NIST that would manage the program. It could also indirectly affect students and workers training for jobs in automated science and robotics, since the bill emphasizes workforce development. The entire program, including its funding and authority, would automatically end on September 30, 2031, unless Congress acts again to extend it.

title: SHARE Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 2332, called the SHARE Act of 2025, deals with how states can use FBI criminal background check information when licensing workers in certain professions. Many professions, like nursing, counseling, or teaching, participate in "interstate compacts," which are agreements between states that let a professional licensed in one state more easily get recognized in another state. This bill allows the FBI to share criminal history information with state licensing boards specifically so they can process these multi-state license applications through such compacts.

The bill also sets rules for how that sensitive information can be used once a state receives it. A state licensing board can only use the criminal history details to decide whether to approve someone's license or work privilege in another state. It cannot pass along the actual criminal record details to the compact's governing commission, other state agencies, or the public. However, the state is allowed to tell the compact commission simply whether the applicant passed or failed the background check, without revealing the specific record.

This bill mainly affects people who work in licensed professions that use interstate compacts to practice across state lines, as well as the state agencies and boards that issue those licenses. title: RPM Access Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the RPM Access Act, changes how Medicare pays for remote patient monitoring (RPM), which is technology that lets doctors track a patient's health data, like blood pressure or heart rate, from home instead of requiring in-person visits. Currently, Medicare payments are adjusted based on regional cost differences, and some formulas can push payments in certain areas, especially rural ones, below a certain level. This bill sets a minimum "floor" for those regional payment calculations starting in 2026, ensuring rural and other lower-reimbursement areas aren't paid less just because of where they're located, since the actual costs of providing RPM don't vary much by region.

The bill also adds new quality requirements for RPM services. Starting in 2026, Medicare would only pay for RPM if a doctor, nurse practitioner, or similar provider is available in real time to respond to health warning signs detected by the monitoring system, the technology can share data in a format compatible with electronic health records, and providers report certain data to help the government measure cost savings, unless doing so would create unreasonable hardship. Additionally, the Department of Health and Human Services must report back to Congress within five years on how much money RPM has saved Medicare through earlier medical interventions, fewer hospital stays, and better medication adherence.

This bill primarily affects Medicare patients, especially those in rural areas with limited access to healthcare, by potentially expanding access to remote monitoring services and improving their quality and safety. It also affects healthcare providers and companies that offer RPM technology and services, since they would need to meet new standards to receive Medicare payment, and payment rates in some areas may increase.
ai_headline: Bill sets Medicare payment floor for remote patient monitoring starting 2026
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 39 - 0.

title: Emergency Conservation Program Improvement Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes two USDA programs that help farmers, ranchers, and forest landowners recover after disasters like floods, wildfires, and storms: the Emergency Conservation Program and the Emergency Forest Restoration Program. Currently, these programs typically reimburse people after they've already paid to repair damaged farmland, fences, or forest land, which can be a financial burden for producers who don't have extra cash on hand. The bill allows the government to pay farmers and forest landowners in advance—75% of the cost upfront for replacing damaged property (like fences) and 50% upfront for repairs or restoration—before the work is even done. It also extends the deadline for spending these emergency funds from 60 days to 180 days, giving people more time to complete the work.

The bill also clarifies what counts as a "wildfire" for these programs. It specifies that wildfires started by human activity (not just natural causes like lightning) can still qualify for aid, as long as the fire's spread was driven by natural conditions. It also explicitly states that wildfires caused by the federal government itself (such as during a government-managed prescribed burn that gets out of control) count as eligible disasters.

This bill mainly affects farmers, ranchers, and owners of private forest land who experience damage from natural disasters and rely on these USDA emergency programs for financial help. By allowing advance payments and giving more time to use the funds, it aims to reduce the financial strain on producers during recovery, letting them start repairs sooner rather than waiting to be reimbursed after paying out of pocket.
ai_headline: Bill would let USDA pay disaster aid to farmers before repairs are done
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-102.

title: Sloan Canyon Conservation and Lateral Pipeline Act
ai_summary:
This bill expands the Sloan Canyon National Conservation Area, a protected area of public land near Las Vegas, Nevada. It grows the conservation area from about 48,438 acres to 57,728 acres by updating the official boundary map used in the original law. This means more land in the area gets protected status, limiting certain development activities within the new boundaries.

The bill also requires the Bureau of Land Management to grant the Southern Nevada Water Authority the right to build and operate a water pipeline, along with related power lines, facilities, and access roads, in and around the conservation area. This must happen within one year of the law taking effect, and the water authority won't have to pay rent or fees for this right-of-way. The authority is also allowed to dig up and use or dispose of sand, gravel, and other materials removed during pipeline tunneling, with the government and authority working out details on where that material can be dumped on federal land. The pipeline cannot pass through any area officially designated as wilderness, and construction cannot permanently damage the conservation area's surface resources.

This bill mainly affects residents of the Las Vegas, Nevada area, particularly those who rely on the Southern Nevada Water Authority for water service, since it helps clear the way for new water infrastructure. It also affects people who use or care about the Sloan Canyon Conservation Area, such as hikers, conservationists, and nearby landowners, since more land becomes protected while also allowing specific pipeline construction. Existing utility and power line rights in the area are preserved and unaffected by the boundary changes.
ai_headline: Sloan Canyon conservation area near Las Vegas would grow by 9,290 acres
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-91.

title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services of the Department of Health and Human Services relating to "Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, HHS Notice of Benefit and Payment Parameters for 2027; and Basic Health Program".
ai_summary:
This bill would cancel a federal regulation issued by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), the agency that oversees health insurance programs under the Affordable Care Act (ACA). The regulation in question, called the "Notice of Benefit and Payment Parameters for 2027," sets the yearly rules for how ACA marketplace insurance plans operate—things like cost-sharing limits, enrollment procedures, and standards insurers must follow. It also covers the Basic Health Program, an option some states use to provide low-cost coverage to people with modest incomes who don't qualify for Medicaid but still need affordable insurance. Using a law called the Congressional Review Act, lawmakers can vote to formally reject recently issued federal regulations, and this resolution is that kind of disapproval action.

If passed, this resolution would block the 2027 rule from taking effect, meaning the specific insurance market policies and payment guidelines it laid out would not apply. This could affect insurance companies that sell ACA marketplace plans, since they would need to follow different or older rules instead. It could also affect everyday people who buy health insurance through the ACA marketplace or through a state's Basic Health Program, since changes to enrollment procedures, cost-sharing rules, or plan requirements might not take effect as planned.

This resolution was introduced by a group of senators and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee. For it to actually take effect, it would need to pass both the House and Senate and either be signed by the President or have a presidential veto overridden by Congress.

title: Pregnant Students’ Rights Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Pregnant Students' Rights Act, would require colleges and universities that participate in federal student aid programs to regularly share information with students about their rights and available support if they are pregnant or become pregnant while enrolled. Specifically, schools would have to tell students about campus and community resources for carrying a pregnancy to term and caring for a baby afterward, what accommodations are available to help them continue their education while pregnant or parenting, and how to file a complaint with the school or the U.S. Department of Education if they believe they've faced discrimination under Title IX because of their decision to continue a pregnancy.

To make sure students actually see this information, the bill requires schools to send an email to all enrolled students at least once a year, and to include the information in student handbooks, at student orientations, at health or counseling centers, and on the school's public website. The bill also clarifies that it doesn't give the Department of Education authority to demand additional information beyond what's listed, or to create new rights beyond what's specified in the bill.

This would affect nearly all colleges and universities in the country, since most participate in federal financial aid programs covered by the Higher Education Act. It would directly affect pregnant and parenting students by increasing awareness of their existing rights and resources, and it would create new administrative responsibilities for college staff who handle student communications, health services, and Title IX compliance.

title: Export Control Enforcement and Enhancement Act
ai_summary:
HR 8169 changes how the U.S. government decides which foreign companies, organizations, or people get placed on the "Entity List" — a government list of parties that are restricted from receiving certain U.S. exports because they're considered risks to national security or foreign policy. The list is managed by an interagency group called the End-User Review Committee, made up of representatives from agencies like Commerce, State, Defense, and Energy. This bill sets up a faster, more structured process for that committee to add entities to the list, remove them, or change their status, requiring a vote within 30 days of any member proposing a change (with a possible 15-day extension if more information is needed).

The bill also creates a default rule: once an entity is added to the list, license applications for exporting sensitive goods or technology to that entity should generally be denied, unless the committee members who voted to add them agree to allow a different policy. It clarifies that each committee member gets one equal vote and that the committee chairperson cannot overrule the group's decisions, though the chair can pause the voting timeline if everyone on the committee agrees to delay.

This bill mainly affects U.S. companies and exporters that deal with international trade in sensitive technology, equipment, or materials, since it could speed up or change how quickly certain foreign buyers get blocked from receiving U.S. exports. It also affects federal agencies involved in export control decisions, as it standardizes and speeds up their internal decision-making process. Ordinary consumers wouldn't be directly affected, but businesses in industries like defense, semiconductors, aerospace, and technology may see faster and more predictable rulings on who they can and cannot legally trade with.

last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 44 - 0.

title: Joe Fiandra Access to Home Infusion Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, named after a person called Joe Fiandra, would change how Medicare covers certain medical equipment and drugs used for home infusion therapy. Infusion therapy involves getting medications delivered directly into the body, often through an IV, using an external pump. Currently, Medicare only covers this equipment at home if it meets certain rules about being "appropriate for home use." This bill says that even if a drug requires a health care professional to give it or supervise it, Medicare can still cover the pump and drug at home as long as a qualified home infusion therapy provider handles it safely, and the drug needs to be infused at least 12 times a year through an IV, under the skin, or at a rate requiring a pump.

In plain terms, this would let more patients receive infusion treatments at home instead of having to go to a hospital or clinic, even for drugs that need a nurse or other professional to administer them. This mainly affects Medicare beneficiaries who need regular infusion treatments, such as people with chronic illnesses, immune disorders, or infections requiring long-term IV medication. It also affects home infusion therapy companies and health care professionals who provide these services, since more patients could qualify for coverage.

The bill also requires the Department of Health and Human Services to make sure patients are told about the cost differences between getting infusion therapy at home versus in other settings, like a hospital or outpatient clinic, so they can make informed decisions about their care.
ai_headline: Bill would expand Medicare coverage for at-home infusion therapy

title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, known as the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, is the annual law that sets policy and spending limits for the U.S. military and related national security agencies. It doesn't actually hand out money itself—that happens in separate appropriations bills—but it authorizes how much can be spent on things like buying ships, aircraft, and weapons; military research and technology; troop levels; base construction; and service member pay and benefits. This year's version covers Army, Navy, Air Force, and Space Force equipment programs (like new submarines, fighter jets, and drones), funds for military housing and construction projects, and support for the Department of Energy's nuclear weapons programs. It also includes separate sections authorizing the State Department, U.S. intelligence agencies, and the Coast Guard.

Beyond equipment and spending, the bill touches many parts of military life: it sets troop numbers, adjusts pay and allowances, expands parental leave, addresses child care and schools for military families, and updates health care and TRICARE insurance rules. It includes personnel policy changes such as rules on promotions, military justice procedures, recruiting, and training programs. There are also provisions dealing with contamination cleanup near bases (from chemicals like PFAS), environmental and energy programs, and workplace protections for civilian defense employees.

The bill affects active-duty service members, military retirees, National Guard and Reserve members, military families, veterans transitioning to civilian life, and civilian employees of the Department of Defense. It also affects defense contractors and companies in the weapons and technology supply chain, since it sets rules about sourcing materials, competition, and prohibited countries of origin. More broadly, it shapes U.S. military relationships with allies like Israel, Taiwan, Ukraine, and NATO countries, and addresses national security matters such as cybersecurity, space operations, nuclear weapons policy, and missile defense (including a new "Golden Dome" missile defense initiative). Because of its wide scope, the bill indirectly affects nearly every American through its impact on national defense policy, government spending, and military communities across the country.

title: Congressional Oversight and Agency Access Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Congressional Oversight and Agency Access Act, would give members of Congress and their staff guaranteed access to federal buildings so they can carry out oversight of government agencies. Members would need to show congressional identification to enter, while staff would need to be accompanied by the lawmaker they work for and show a valid staff badge. If access outside normal business hours is requested, it must be granted within 24 hours, and access during public meetings must be immediate. The bill also covers buildings run by contractors or through agreements with local governments, not just ones directly owned by the federal government.

The bill also addresses tougher situations. Even during a declared national emergency or public health emergency, members of Congress and their staff would still be allowed in, even if the general public is restricted. For areas requiring security clearance, access would generally be granted within 24 hours if the member sits on a committee overseeing that agency, or with permission from that committee's chair or ranking member if they do not. Additionally, agencies would be barred from making temporary changes to a building to limit what a visiting member of Congress can observe.

This bill would primarily affect federal agencies and the buildings they operate or contract out, as they would need to accommodate these access requirements. It would also affect members of Congress and their staffs, giving them clearer legal authority to inspect federal facilities as part of government oversight. Everyday citizens would not be directly affected, though the bill could influence how transparently federal agencies operate and how quickly oversight issues are identified and addressed.

title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Department of Health and Human Services relating to "Restoring Flexibility in the Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF)".
ai_summary:
This bill uses a special legislative process, called the Congressional Review Act, to cancel a regulation issued by the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). The regulation in question, titled "Restoring Flexibility in the Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF)," was published in May 2026 and dealt with how states manage federal child care funding that helps low-income families pay for child care. If this resolution passes, that HHS rule would be officially overturned and would no longer be in effect, as if it had never been issued.

The Child Care and Development Fund is a program that gives money to states to subsidize child care costs for working parents with lower incomes. The HHS rule being targeted apparently changed how much flexibility states have in running this program, such as rules around eligibility, provider payments, or administrative requirements. Because the bill's text is short, it doesn't spell out exactly what the original rule changed, only that Congress wants to reverse it.

This resolution primarily affects state agencies that administer child care subsidies, child care providers who accept those subsidies, and families who rely on CCDF assistance to afford child care. If passed, states would likely have to revert to the child care rules that existed before this HHS regulation, potentially changing how they manage funding, eligibility, or provider standards. Like all Congressional Review Act resolutions, this would need to pass both the House and Senate and either be signed by the President or survive a veto override to take effect.

title: Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027
ai_summary:
This bill is the annual funding authorization for U.S. intelligence agencies, covering the CIA, NSA, FBI's intelligence functions, and other agencies for fiscal year 2027. Most of the actual dollar amounts are kept secret in a classified section, though the bill does set specific public funding levels, including $568 million for intelligence community management and $514 million for CIA retirement benefits. Beyond funding, the bill makes numerous organizational and policy changes: it restructures leadership positions at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, eliminates several offices and councils considered redundant (like the National Intelligence Management Council and Joint Intelligence Community Council), transfers the National Intelligence University to the National Defense University, and clarifies that the national intelligence chief cannot have police or law enforcement powers.

The bill also addresses several current policy debates. It limits how the National Counterterrorism Center and the Department of Homeland Security's intelligence office can collect information domestically about Americans, aiming to keep their focus on foreign threats rather than domestic surveillance. It creates new rules for "unmasking" - the process by which officials can learn the identity of Americans whose communications were incidentally collected in intelligence reports - with extra safeguards during presidential transitions. New sections address artificial intelligence use in intelligence work, including labeling AI-generated content used for military targeting and reviewing AI security risks. It also restricts intelligence agencies from partnering with think tanks that receive funding from adversarial governments like China, Russia, or Iran.

This bill primarily affects federal intelligence employees, contractors, and agency structures rather than the general public directly. However, ordinary Americans are affected indirectly through provisions protecting citizens' privacy from unwarranted government surveillance, rules limiting domestic data collection by intelligence agencies, and oversight measures like congressional notification requirements when classified information is declassified. It also touches everyday life through related sections on espionage law, trade secret protections, and rules for federal employees, including a new parental bereavement leave benefit.

last_action_text: By Senator Cotton from Select Committee on Intelligence filed written report. Report No. 119-133. Additional and Minority views filed.

title: Fit Future Act
ai_summary:
HR 9723, called the Fit Future Act, would create a new group called the President's Council on Sports, Fitness, and Nutrition. This council would replace or update a similar existing body and would be made up of up to 30 people appointed by the President, serving two-year terms. Its main job would be to advise the President and the Secretary of Health and Human Services on ways to improve physical fitness, sports participation, and nutrition among Americans, especially young people.

Specifically, the council would recommend bringing back an updated version of the Presidential Fitness Test for schools, promoting fitness challenges and awards, setting ambitious health goals for youth, running national campaigns celebrating sports and fitness, and building partnerships with athletes, sports organizations, and community groups. It would also study how rising childhood obesity and inactive lifestyles could weaken future military readiness and workforce health, treating this as a national security concern.

The bill affects everyday Americans mainly through schools and public health programs, since the council's recommendations could influence P.E. classes, fitness testing, and youth sports initiatives nationwide. It also creates a small new government body with an executive director and staff support, funded through Health and Human Services and a related nonprofit foundation. The council would continue operating until the President decides to end it, and members would serve without pay, though they could be reimbursed for travel expenses.

title: GENIUS Act
ai_summary:
# What This Bill Does

The GENIUS Act creates the first comprehensive federal rules for "stablecoins" — digital currencies (like USDC or similar tokens) designed to hold a stable value, usually pegged to the U.S. dollar. Currently, companies can issue these coins with little federal oversight. This law changes that by requiring anyone who issues a stablecoin in the U.S. to be a licensed "permitted payment stablecoin issuer" — either a bank subsidiary, a company approved by the federal Comptroller of the Currency, or a company approved under a state system that meets federal standards. Unlicensed stablecoins would become illegal to offer for sale in the U.S. after a three-year transition period, with fines and possible prison time for violations.

The law requires issuers to back every stablecoin dollar-for-dollar with safe assets like cash, short-term Treasury bonds, or insured bank deposits — not risky investments. Issuers must publicly disclose their reserves monthly, get them audited, and clearly explain how customers can redeem their coins for cash. The bill bans paying interest to stablecoin holders, prohibits misleading marketing (like implying a coin is government-backed or federally insured when it isn't), and requires issuers to comply with anti-money-laundering and sanctions laws just like banks do. Large tech or retail companies that aren't primarily financial businesses face extra hurdles and privacy restrictions if they want to issue stablecoins.

# Who It Affects

This mainly affects cryptocurrency companies, banks, and financial technology firms that create or want to create stablecoins, along with the federal and state regulators (like the Comptroller, Federal Reserve, FDIC, and state banking agencies) who will oversee them. Everyday consumers who use stablecoins for payments, savings, or crypto trading would gain new protections, such as assurance that coins are backed by real reserves and clearer rules for redeeming them for cash. Businesses that accept or use stablecoins in payment systems, as well as investors and crypto exchanges, will also need to adjust to the new licensing and compliance requirements.

last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-27.

It mandates full dollar-for-dollar reserve backing with safe assets, monthly audited disclosures, and bans on interest payments and misleading marketing. Unlicensed stablecoins become illegal to sell in the U.S. after a three-year transition, with fines and possible prison time for violations.

title: Affordable Prescriptions for Patients Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Affordable Prescriptions for Patients Act, changes patent rules for biologic drugs—complex medications made from living organisms, such as many treatments for cancer, arthritis, and other serious conditions. Brand-name biologic drug makers often hold dozens or even hundreds of patents on a single drug, covering not just the drug itself but also its manufacturing process and various uses. Companies seeking to make cheaper copycat versions, called biosimilars, say this "patent thicket" makes it too costly and time-consuming to bring competing products to market, keeping prices high.

The bill limits how many patents a brand-name biologic manufacturer can use to sue a biosimilar maker for patent infringement, generally capping it at 20 patents, with no more than 10 of those being patents issued after a certain point in the approval process. Courts can allow more patents to be included if there's a good reason, such as the biosimilar company changing its product significantly or withholding information. The limit does not apply to patents covering new medical uses of the drug, like new treatment indications.

This bill mainly affects pharmaceutical companies: those that make original biologic drugs and those that want to make cheaper biosimilar versions. Indirectly, it could affect patients and insurers, since supporters argue that reducing legal barriers for biosimilars could speed up competition and lower drug prices, while brand-name manufacturers may see this as limiting their ability to protect their inventions. The changes would apply to new biosimilar applications filed after the law takes effect.
ai_headline: Bill would cap patents biologic makers use against biosimilar rivals

title: Taiwan Assurance Implementation Act
ai_summary:
This law updates the Taiwan Assurance Act of 2020, which deals with how the U.S. State Department manages its official relationship with Taiwan. The State Department keeps internal guidance, known as the "Guidelines on Relations with Taiwan," that instructs U.S. government agencies on how to interact with Taiwan given the sensitive diplomatic situation involving China. This bill requires the State Department to formally review those guidelines at least once every five years and reissue updated versions to other federal agencies, rather than leaving them unchanged indefinitely.

The law also requires the Secretary of State to report to Congress within 90 days after each review is completed. These reports must go to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and must explain what information the guidelines contain and how the updated version supports the broader goals of U.S. policy toward Taiwan. The law also broadens what counts as "guidance" to include any future or related documents, not just the original memorandum, so the reporting requirement can't be avoided simply by renaming or replacing the document.

This bill mainly affects the State Department, federal agencies that deal with Taiwan-related matters, and members of Congress who oversee foreign policy. It does not change U.S. policy toward Taiwan itself; instead, it creates a recurring check-in process to ensure Congress stays informed about how that policy is being implemented and updated over time.

title: Strengthening Export Controls Compliance Act
ai_summary:
This bill updates the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 to strengthen how the U.S. government helps American businesses follow export control rules—laws that regulate the sale or transfer of sensitive goods, technology, and information to other countries for national security reasons. It requires the President to submit a plan to Congress every two years detailing how the Department of Commerce will assist U.S. companies, especially small and medium-sized businesses, with export licensing and compliance. This includes offering counseling, training sessions, seminars, and one-on-one consultations to help businesses understand what items are controlled and how to properly file the required paperwork.

The bill also requires the Bureau of Industry and Security (the Commerce Department agency that oversees export controls) to host an annual public conference on export control policies and to reach out to businesses and the public before issuing major new export control rules, so companies can understand and prepare for upcoming changes. Additionally, it expands the information that must be included in the agency's annual report to Congress, adding details about how many compliance requests businesses submit, how long they take to process, and how many official guidance documents are made public.

This bill mainly affects U.S. companies that export goods or technology abroad, particularly smaller businesses that may lack large legal or compliance teams. It also affects the Department of Commerce, which would have new responsibilities for outreach, training, and reporting. The goal is to make export rules clearer and easier to follow, reducing the chances of accidental violations while helping protect national security and U.S. technological competitiveness.

title: Ensuring Community Access to Pharmacist Services Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Ensuring Community Access to Pharmacist Services Act, would change Medicare rules so that pharmacists can get paid directly for certain health services they provide. Right now, Medicare Part B typically pays doctors and certain other medical practitioners for patient care, but pharmacists are generally not included in this system even though many pharmacists already test for and help treat common illnesses. Under this bill, Medicare would begin covering "pharmacist services" for evaluating and managing patients being tested or treated for COVID-19, the flu, RSV, and strep throat, as well as services related to any officially declared public health emergency.

The bill sets rules for how much pharmacists would be paid—generally a percentage of what doctors would receive for similar services—and requires that pharmacists follow any state laws requiring them to work under a doctor's supervision or in collaboration with one. It also prevents pharmacists from charging patients extra beyond what Medicare approves, similar to protections that apply to doctors, so patients wouldn't face surprise extra costs.

This bill would mainly affect Medicare patients (mostly people 65 and older, or those with certain disabilities), by potentially making it easier and cheaper to get quick testing or treatment for common illnesses at a local pharmacy instead of needing a doctor's visit. It would also affect pharmacists, since it opens up a new way for them to be paid by Medicare for services they already have the training to provide, and could affect doctors and clinics if some patients choose pharmacy visits instead of traditional medical appointments. The changes would take effect for services provided starting January 1, 2026, if passed.

title: Protecting Small Business Competitions Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Protecting Small Business Competitions Act of 2026, would change federal law to make it a firm requirement that certain government contracts be set aside specifically for small businesses. This concept, known as the "Rule of Two," already exists as agency guidance, but this bill would write it directly into the Small Business Act, making it a binding legal rule rather than just a policy practice.

Specifically, the bill says that whenever a federal contract, task order, or delivery order is worth more than the "simplified acquisition threshold" (a dollar amount set by law, generally around $250,000, though it can vary), the contracting officer must reserve that contract for small businesses if they reasonably expect at least two qualified small businesses will bid and that the contract can still be awarded at a fair market price. In other words, if two or more small businesses are likely able to do the job competitively, the government would be required to limit that contract opportunity to small businesses only.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies that purchase goods and services, small business owners who compete for government contracts, and larger companies that currently bid on those same contracts. Small businesses could benefit from more guaranteed opportunities to win federal work, while larger firms might see fewer chances to compete for certain contracts. Government contracting officers would also face new legal obligations, since the rule would no longer be optional guidance but a required part of the law.

title: Ensuring Patient Access to Critical Breakthrough Products Act
ai_summary:
This bill deals with how quickly Medicare covers "breakthrough devices" — medical devices that the FDA has fast-tracked for review because they show promise for treating serious conditions. Right now, even after the FDA approves a breakthrough device, Medicare can take a long time to decide whether it will pay for it, which can delay patients' access to new treatments. This bill sets up a process to speed that up.

Specifically, the bill creates a new "transitional coverage period" of four years, during which Medicare would automatically cover a device once it's officially designated as a "breakthrough device," as long as it's used the way the FDA approved it and doesn't pose safety risks that outweigh its benefits. Manufacturers would apply for this special designation, and Medicare (through the Department of Health and Human Services) would have to decide within 6 months whether a device qualifies, explaining its reasoning if it says no. Medicare would also be required to finish any related national coverage decision before the four-year transitional period ends, so patients aren't left in limbo. The bill includes $10 million per year from 2025-2030 to help Medicare carry out these changes, and it allows Medicare to review billing patterns to watch for potential misuse.

This bill mainly affects Medicare patients (mostly seniors and people with disabilities), medical device manufacturers, hospitals and doctors who use these devices, and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), which runs the program. Patients could gain faster access to cutting-edge devices for serious illnesses, device makers would get a clearer and quicker path to Medicare reimbursement, and CMS would take on new responsibilities and funding to manage this expedited review process.
ai_headline: Bill would give breakthrough medical devices four years of automatic Medicare coverage
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 37 - 3.

title: Provider Reimbursement Stability Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would change how Medicare calculates payments to doctors and other health care providers under the physician fee schedule, a system that determines how much Medicare pays for medical services. Currently, when Medicare adds or changes covered services, it must adjust overall payment rates to keep total spending "budget neutral," and there's a longstanding $20 million threshold that triggers those adjustments. The bill would raise that threshold significantly (to about $54 million in 2027) and adjust it periodically for inflation going forward, meaning smaller changes to Medicare spending would no longer automatically trigger payment adjustments across the board.

The bill also creates a process to double-check estimates: when Medicare predicts how often a new service will be used and bases payment changes on that estimate, this bill requires checking those predictions against actual usage a couple years later and correcting the payment formula if the estimate was significantly off. Additionally, it requires Medicare to update the cost data (like staff wages, equipment prices, and medical supply costs) used to calculate practice expense payments at least every five years, updating all categories together rather than piecemeal, and consulting with medical specialty groups. Finally, it limits how much the payment "conversion factor" (a key number used to calculate all Medicare physician payments) can swing from one year to the next, capping it at 2.5%.

This bill primarily affects doctors, medical practices, and other health care providers who bill Medicare, aiming to make their payments more predictable and stable year to year. It could also indirectly affect Medicare beneficiaries (mostly people 65 and older, plus some people with disabilities) if these changes influence which providers accept Medicare patients or how services are priced. The bill does not change patient benefits or eligibility directly; it's focused on the technical formulas used to pay providers.
ai_headline: Bill would raise threshold for Medicare doctor payment adjustments
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 44 - 0.

title: Protecting American Competition Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Protecting American Competition Act of 2026, changes how the government reviews requests from U.S. companies that want permission to export certain sensitive technology to foreign buyers. Currently, when the government approves the first company's request to sell a controlled item to a specific foreign customer, other American companies that want to sell the same or similar product to that same customer can face delays or difficulties getting their own applications approved. This bill directs the Under Secretary for Industry and Security, a Commerce Department official who oversees export licensing, to recognize when a license is the "first" one issued for a particular item and customer, and to then process later applications from other companies for the same item and customer in a timely way, rather than letting the first company gain an unfair advantage.

The bill also requires the government to report to Congress each year on how many of these "first" licenses were issued when other companies had competing applications pending, what happened to those other applications, and why the first license was granted ahead of others. Additionally, within 90 days of the law passing, officials must explain to Congress how they plan to carry out this new review process. Importantly, the bill makes clear that none of this can force officials to delay decisions or approve exports that would harm U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.

This bill mainly affects American technology and defense-related companies that export controlled goods, particularly smaller or newer firms that may have been at a disadvantage compared to whichever company happened to get the first export license to a given foreign buyer. It also affects the Commerce, State, Defense, and Energy Departments, which will need to coordinate more closely on these licensing reviews, and it gives Congress additional oversight through mandatory reporting.
ai_headline: Bill targets fairness in export license reviews for tech firms
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported by the Yeas and Nays: 44 - 0.
