title: KIDS Act
ai_summary:
# The KIDS Act (H.R. 7757), Explained

This bill combines multiple proposals into one large package aimed at protecting children and teenagers online. It requires websites, apps, social media platforms, online video games, and AI chatbots to build in safety features for users under 17, while giving parents more tools to monitor and control their kids' online activity. Key provisions include requiring "technology verification measures" to keep minors away from sexually explicit content, requiring social media platforms to offer safeguards like limiting who can contact minors, restricting location sharing, allowing opt-outs from personalized recommendation algorithms, and providing time-management tools. Companies would also need to let parents review privacy settings, restrict purchases, and monitor time spent on platforms.

The bill also targets specific features seen as risky for kids. Disappearing ("ephemeral") messages would be banned for minors, direct messaging would be blocked entirely for children under 13, and teens would need parental-approved contact lists for messaging. Online video games with chat functions would need similar parental controls. AI chatbots would be required to clearly disclose that they are not human, provide suicide-prevention resources when relevant, and encourage breaks after three hours of continuous use. The bill also orders government studies on topics like fentanyl sales to minors via social media and the mental health effects of chatbots on kids.

This bill would primarily affect large tech and social media companies, video game publishers, and AI chatbot developers, who would face new compliance costs and legal requirements enforced by the Federal Trade Commission. It would also affect parents (who gain new monitoring tools) and minors under 17 (who would experience more restricted, monitored online environments). Notably, the bill would generally override conflicting state laws on these same topics, meaning states would lose some ability to set their own, different rules in this area.
ai_headline: Bill would force new safety rules on tech platforms for kids under 17
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

title: FEC Administrative Improvements Act
ai_summary:
This bill would make two technical changes to federal campaign finance law, which is enforced by the Federal Election Commission (FEC). First, it would require people or groups who make "electioneering communications" (certain political ads that mention a candidate but don't explicitly tell people how to vote, often run close to an election) to file their reports with the FEC electronically, rather than allowing paper filings. This matches rules already in place for groups that report making campaign expenditures.

Second, the bill would change the rules for how political committees (like campaign committees or PACs) are allowed to spend money from their bank accounts. Currently, the law says these committees must make disbursements "by check." This bill would remove that requirement, allowing committees to pay for things using other common payment methods, such as debit cards, wire transfers, or electronic payments, as long as the money still comes from their official campaign accounts.

In practical terms, this bill mainly affects political campaigns, PACs, and other groups that spend money on political ads or federal elections, along with the FEC staff who process these filings. It doesn't change what activities are allowed or restricted in campaign finance law substantively — it updates outdated paperwork and payment rules to reflect modern practices, since many organizations already use electronic banking rather than paper checks. Everyday voters wouldn't be directly affected, but the changes could make campaign finance reporting more consistent and give campaigns more flexibility in how they pay their bills.

title: Eastern Mediterranean Gateway Act
ai_summary:
HR 3307, the "Eastern Mediterranean Gateway Act," is a foreign policy bill focused on strengthening U.S. cooperation with Egypt, Greece, Cyprus, and Israel, along with broader partnerships tied to the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC). IMEC is an international infrastructure initiative meant to connect Asia, the Middle East, and Europe through shipping routes, railways, and energy pipelines, seen partly as a counterbalance to China's Belt and Road Initiative. The bill declares Congress's support for this corridor and for existing diplomatic arrangements like the U.S.-Greece-Israel-Cyprus "3+1" format and the East Mediterranean Gas Forum, encouraging continued U.S. involvement in these groups.

In practical terms, the bill directs the Secretary of State to make the Eastern Mediterranean region a foreign policy priority, particularly around energy security and defense cooperation, and allows the State Department to set up formal recurring diplomatic dialogues with countries in the region. It also requires several government reports and studies: annual updates on energy and defense projects tied to the Act, a briefing on multilateral initiatives with IMEC countries, a review of a Cyprus-based security center as a possible model for cooperation, and a feasibility study on creating or expanding joint research and development programs (similar to existing U.S.-Israel science, agriculture, and industrial R&D partnerships) to include other Eastern Mediterranean nations.

This bill mainly affects U.S. foreign policy operations rather than everyday citizens directly. It would primarily impact the State Department, Energy Department, and Homeland Security officials who manage diplomatic and energy relations, as well as businesses or researchers involved in energy infrastructure, defense contracting, or scientific cooperation with these countries. It does not create new spending programs itself but sets policy priorities and reporting requirements that could shape future funding, diplomatic agreements, or energy projects involving the U.S. and its Eastern Mediterranean partners.

title: Great American Outdoors Act 250
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Great American Outdoors Act 250," updates and extends an existing federal program that pays for repair and maintenance backlogs on public lands. It renames the current "National Parks and Public Land Legacy Restoration Fund" as the "America's Legacy Restoration Fund" and continues funding it through 2030 using money from energy development on federal land (like oil, gas, and renewable energy leases), along with new visitor fees and private donations. The fund pays for fixing rundown buildings, trails, roads, and other infrastructure in national parks, wildlife refuges, national forests, lands managed by the Bureau of Land Management, and schools run by the Bureau of Indian Education. It sets specific percentages of money for each agency and requires priority to go toward projects that protect public safety, improve visitor access, or prevent more expensive repairs later.

The bill also creates new rules for how projects are chosen, tracked, and reported, requiring public online dashboards showing project costs, timelines, and progress, plus annual reports to Congress. It encourages partnerships with nonprofits and private donors to help pay for projects, sets up a small pilot program for outdoor recreation and hunting/fishing access improvements, and streamlines environmental review and contracting rules to speed up repairs. Separately, the bill requires foreign tourists (visitors on tourist or business visas) to pay new minimum fees—at least $100 per entry to federal recreation sites and at least $250 for an annual pass—with that money also going into the restoration fund.

This bill would primarily affect visitors to national parks, forests, and wildlife refuges, people living near or working for these federal land agencies, students in Bureau of Indian Education schools, hunters and anglers using public lands, and foreign tourists visiting U.S. federal recreation sites. It also affects private companies and nonprofits that might partner with agencies on funding or construction projects, as well as energy companies operating on federal lands, since some of their payments would help fund the program.

last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute (Amended) by Voice Vote.

title: Baltic Security Assessment Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 5543, the Baltic Security Assessment Act of 2025, would require the U.S. Secretary of State, working with the Secretary of Defense, to prepare a detailed report on security threats facing Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. The report would need to be delivered to relevant congressional committees within 180 days of the bill becoming law. It would cover military, cyber, political, and other "hybrid" threats to these three Baltic countries, and examine the roles that Russia, Belarus, China, Iran, and other countries play in creating those threats.

The report would also assess how U.S. and NATO military forces are currently positioned in the region to deter these threats, identify ways the U.S. could deepen defense cooperation with the Baltic countries, and offer recommendations for improving their defenses, cybersecurity, and democratic stability. The report would mainly be public, though it could include a classified section for sensitive information.

This bill doesn't create new military commitments, spending programs, or policy changes on its own—it simply directs executive branch officials to study and report on the situation. It would mainly affect government agencies (the State Department and Pentagon) by creating new reporting duties, and it would give Congress more information to use in future decisions about U.S. relations with the Baltic region, NATO, and foreign policy toward Russia and other countries named in the bill. Everyday Americans wouldn't be directly affected, though the report could influence future legislation or funding related to national security and foreign alliances.

title: Burma GAP Act
ai_summary:
The Burma GAP Act addresses the ongoing crisis facing the Rohingya, a Muslim minority group in Burma (Myanmar) who have suffered what the U.S. government has officially recognized as genocide and crimes against humanity at the hands of the Burmese military. The bill lays out official U.S. policy positions, including refusing to recognize the military junta that took power in a 2021 coup, supporting Rohingya civilian leadership, and working toward accountability for those responsible for atrocities. It authorizes the State Department to appoint a Special Representative for Burma to coordinate diplomatic efforts, sanctions, and humanitarian responses with other countries.

The bill directs the U.S. government to continue and expand support for Rohingya refugees, most of whom live in crowded camps in Bangladesh, as well as those still inside Burma. This includes funding for food, healthcare, education, legal aid, protection from violence and trafficking, and efforts to help refugees safely and voluntarily return home someday if conditions improve. It also pushes for accountability measures, such as helping international investigators collect evidence of atrocities for possible prosecutions, supporting a fund for victim compensation, and encouraging Burma's civilian leaders to eventually restore Rohingya citizenship and rights.

This bill mainly affects U.S. foreign policy and foreign aid spending rather than domestic programs, so it doesn't directly impact most Americans' daily lives. It would primarily affect Rohingya refugees and displaced people, the State Department (which would gain new responsibilities and reporting requirements), and U.S. relations with Burma, Bangladesh, and other regional countries. It authorizes specific funding levels—$5 million and $4 million annually through 2030—for investigation and documentation efforts, plus additional unspecified funds for broader humanitarian and accountability programs, meaning Congress would still need to approve actual spending in future budget bills.

title: A bill to amend the Mineral Leasing Act to provide for the payment of bonus payments of certain coal leases issued under that Act.
ai_summary:
This bill would change how companies pay the government when they win the right to lease federal land for coal mining. Under current law, coal leases sold through a competitive bidding process require the winning bidder to pay a "bonus payment," which is essentially the price paid upfront for the lease. This bill would allow that bonus payment to be spread out over time, specifically in 10 equal yearly installments, when a "deferred bonus payment" system is used, rather than requiring the full amount right away. The company would still need to submit the first installment along with its bid.

This change mainly affects coal mining companies that lease federal land for mining operations, as well as the federal government's revenue collection process. By allowing payments to be spread out over a decade instead of paid in one lump sum, it could make it easier and less financially risky for companies to bid on federal coal leases, potentially encouraging more coal leasing activity. It could also affect how quickly the federal government receives money from these leases, since the full payment would now come in over 10 years instead of upfront. States and local communities that receive a share of federal coal leasing revenue could also see changes in the timing of the funds they receive.

title: A bill to amend the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act to authorize the use of funds for certain additional Carey Act projects, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
**S. 1257** would change a federal infrastructure law so that more dams can qualify for repair funding. The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (the big 2021 infrastructure law) set aside money to fix aging, high-risk dams. This bill expands that funding pool to also include certain older dams built under the "Carey Act," an 1894 law that helped western states develop irrigation and water projects on public lands. These are typically dams that local irrigation districts or water users still operate today.

The bill requires the Secretary of the Interior to first make sure that dams already eligible under the current law have gotten the funding they need to complete their repair work. Only after confirming that, and confirming that money is still left over, can the Secretary use those remaining funds to rehabilitate, reconstruct, or replace Carey Act dams.

This mainly affects rural communities, farmers, and irrigation districts in western states (the bill was introduced by senators from Idaho) that rely on these century-old Carey Act dams for water supply. It does not create new spending—it simply widens the list of dam projects eligible for existing infrastructure funds, potentially helping more communities get access to federal dam-safety and repair money, though it may also mean funds are spread across more projects.
ai_headline: Bill would let older Carey Act dams tap federal repair funding

title: Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act, would create a new federal law requiring health care workers to give medical care to any infant who is born alive during or after an abortion attempt. Specifically, doctors and nurses present at such a birth would have to provide the same level of medical care they would give to any other newborn at the same stage of development, and then make sure the infant is quickly taken to a hospital. Health care workers or staff who know that this care wasn't provided would be legally required to report it to police or other authorities.

Under the bill, anyone who fails to provide this required care could face fines and up to five years in prison. If someone intentionally kills an infant born alive in this situation, they could be charged and punished the same as for murder under federal law. However, the bill specifically says the mother cannot be criminally charged under this law. It also allows the mother to sue for damages—including medical costs, emotional harm, and punitive damages—if a health care provider fails to give the required care, and courts could award attorney's fees to whichever side wins, depending on the circumstances.

This bill would mainly affect health care providers who perform abortions, particularly in the rare cases where an infant survives the procedure. Supporters and opponents disagree on how often this situation occurs and on the broader implications for abortion access and medical practice, but the text itself focuses narrowly on establishing legal requirements, criminal penalties, and civil lawsuit options related to the treatment of infants born alive after an abortion or attempted abortion.
ai_headline: Bill would require medical care for infants born alive after abortion

title: Route 66 National Historic Trail Designation Act
ai_summary:
This bill would officially designate Route 66 as a National Historic Trail under the National Trails System Act, the same law that governs trails like the Appalachian Trail. The designated trail would cover all the historic alignments of U.S. Highway 66 used between 1926 and 1985, stretching about 2,400 miles from Chicago, Illinois, to Santa Monica, California. The Secretary of the Interior would be responsible for managing the trail and would be required to consult with Native American tribes before taking actions that would significantly affect them.

The bill includes several limits on federal power to prevent the designation from interfering with private property or existing land uses. The government could not use eminent domain to acquire land for the trail, and any land it does acquire must be within a quarter-mile of the route and cannot extend outside existing federally managed areas without the landowner's permission. The law also makes clear that the designation does not create a "buffer zone" restricting nearby activities, does not interfere with energy development or transmission projects, and does not trigger new federal permitting requirements or classify the trail as part of the National Park System for mineral-leasing purposes.

This bill mainly affects federal land managers, Native American tribes along the route, property owners near historic Route 66, and communities in the eight states the route passes through (Illinois, Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California). It could also benefit tourism-related businesses along the route, since National Historic Trail status often increases public awareness, signage, and visitor interest, without changing existing land ownership or energy development rights.
ai_headline: Bill would make Route 66 a National Historic Trail across eight states
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

title: Canterbury Shaker Village National Heritage Area Study Authorization Act
ai_summary:
This bill, introduced by Senator Hassan with Senator Tillis, directs the Secretary of the Interior to conduct an official study looking into whether Canterbury Shaker Village in Merrimack County, New Hampshire, should be designated as a National Heritage Area. The bill itself does not create the heritage area; it only authorizes the research and evaluation needed to decide whether that designation would be appropriate.

Canterbury Shaker Village is a historic site founded in 1792 that was home to the Shaker religious community, a group known for celibate communal living, gender equality, pacifism, and distinctive furniture, architecture, and inventions. The site became a nonprofit museum in 1969 and was named a National Historic Landmark in 1992. The bill lays out this history to explain why Congress believes the site may deserve heritage-area status, which would recognize its cultural and historical significance and could support tourism, preservation, and educational programming.

The study would be conducted by the National Park Service (under the Secretary of the Interior) in consultation with New Hampshire state and local preservation offices, historical societies, and tourism agencies. This process mainly affects residents of Merrimack County and New Hampshire more broadly, as well as historians, museum operators, and tourism businesses connected to the Shaker Village. For most other Americans, the bill has no direct effect—it simply funds a feasibility study, not an actual designation or new federal program.
ai_headline: Bill orders study on Shaker Village becoming a national heritage area
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

title: Gateway Partnership Act
ai_summary:
This bill would let the Secretary of the Interior make a formal agreement with the Gateway Arch Park Foundation, a nonprofit partner group, allowing it to host private events inside buildings at Gateway Arch National Park in St. Louis, such as the Arch Visitor Center and the Old Courthouse. The agreement would set rules like how many events can happen each week, required staffing, and insurance the Foundation must carry to protect taxpayers from liability if someone is injured during one of these events.

The bill also requires that any private events not interfere with regular public access to the park, not damage or change the character of the park, and fit with the park's mission. The Secretary would be required to charge fees to cover wear-and-tear costs from these events and could recover other related costs, like staffing expenses. Importantly, the National Park Service would still be free to run its own events or issue permits to other groups, so this agreement wouldn't be the only way events could happen there.

This mainly affects visitors to Gateway Arch National Park, the National Park Service, and the Gateway Arch Park Foundation. Tourists might notice occasional private events (like weddings or receptions) in certain buildings, but the bill tries to make sure this doesn't block public access. Taxpayers are also affected because the bill's cost-recovery and liability provisions aim to make sure the federal government isn't stuck paying for damages or losing money from hosting these private functions.
ai_headline: Bill would allow private events at Gateway Arch buildings under new agreement
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

title: National Park System Long-Term Lease Investment Act
ai_summary:
This bill would let the National Park Service extend certain existing leases inside national parks without putting them up for competitive bidding. Right now, some leases within national park units (for things like private buildings, homes, or other facilities on park land) are governed by federal regulations that normally require a competitive bidding process when a lease term ends. This bill would create an exception, allowing the Park Service to simply extend a lease with the current leaseholder instead of reopening it to other bidders.

For this exception to apply, the leaseholder must have held the lease for at least five years and must be following all the rules and conditions of that lease. The Park Service would also have to determine that extending the lease is good for managing that particular park. If the bill becomes law, the Department of the Interior would have 90 days to update its official regulations to reflect this new authority.

This bill mainly affects people or businesses who hold long-term leases on facilities within national parks, such as lodges, concession buildings, or other structures on park land. It gives those leaseholders more certainty that they could keep their lease without competing against other bidders, as long as they've followed the rules. It could also affect the broader public and other companies interested in bidding on park leases, since it reduces opportunities for new competition once a lease is up for renewal. The National Park Service would gain more flexibility in deciding whether to renew a lease directly instead of running a new bidding process each time.
ai_headline: Bill would let Park Service renew leases without competitive bidding
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported with an amendment favorably.

title: MORE WATER Act
ai_summary:
The MORE WATER Act is a Senate bill that renews and expands several federal water infrastructure programs run by the Bureau of Reclamation, an agency that manages dams, canals, and water systems mostly in Western states. First, it reauthorizes a large-scale water recycling and reuse grant program, providing $450 million from 2028-2032 to help communities turn wastewater into usable water, extends project deadlines, and doubles the construction timeline allowed for projects. Second, it creates a brand-new "Water Conveyance Improvement Program" with $500 million to help build or repair canals, pipelines, and other systems that move water, with special rules encouraging projects that also benefit low-income communities' drinking water or the environment (like helping endangered fish or refilling shrinking lakes such as the Great Salt Lake).

The bill also increases funding caps and adjusts them for inflation for existing wastewater recycling projects, and provides $250 million for habitat restoration efforts tied to Reclamation water projects, including fish protection and monitoring programs in places like the Sacramento River basin. To help pay for these programs, it extends certain existing funding authorities for 15 years and creates a new process to identify and formally "deauthorize" old, inactive Reclamation projects that haven't received funding in years, clearing them from the books unless Congress, a funding sponsor, or the Secretary of the Interior steps in to save them.

This bill mainly affects Western and Southwestern states covered by federal reclamation law, including farmers, irrigation and water districts, Native American tribes, municipal water utilities, and low-income communities relying on public water systems. It could also affect taxpayers generally, since it authorizes over $1.7 billion in federal spending, and environmental groups and wildlife agencies interested in species protection and habitat restoration tied to water projects.
ai_headline: Senate bill would expand federal water infrastructure funding by $1.7 billion
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

title: Water Security and Drought Resilience Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Water Security and Drought Resilience Act, updates federal programs that help fund water storage and drought-related infrastructure projects in Western states served by the Bureau of Reclamation (known as "Reclamation States"). It expands the Secretary of the Interior's authority to provide financial assistance for water storage projects, requires that funding be spread across multiple states rather than concentrated in just one or two, and extends an existing small water storage grant program for an additional five years, authorizing $20 million per year through 2033. It also updates the size limits for projects that qualify for these small storage grants, covering things like reservoirs, groundwater recharge systems, and water conveyance infrastructure.

The bill also creates a new grant program for "natural water retention and release projects." These are projects that use natural materials and processes—like floodplains, wetlands, or aquifer recharge areas—to store water and manage its flow more effectively, rather than relying solely on traditional dams or reservoirs. States, tribes, municipalities, irrigation districts, and qualifying nonprofit organizations could apply for these grants, with the federal government covering up to 90% of project costs. This program would be funded at $15 million per year through 2031.

This bill mainly affects water managers, irrigation districts, tribes, and local governments in Western and Southwestern states dealing with drought and water shortages, as well as taxpayers who fund these federal grant programs. It does not change existing state or federal water rights laws, interstate water agreements, or treaty obligations—it simply creates more funding options for water storage and conservation infrastructure projects.

title: Geese House Site Conveyance Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Secretary of the Interior to transfer about 21,578 acres of federal land within the preserve area of Denali National Park and Preserve to Doyon, Limited, an Alaska Native regional corporation. The land, located in a specific township near a site called Geese House, was originally selected by Doyon back in 1978 under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, a 1971 law that gave Alaska Native corporations rights to select and receive certain federal lands. The transfer must happen within one year of the bill becoming law, and certain smaller parcels and lakes are excluded from the deal. Public access easements must still be preserved on the land.

The bill places some restrictions on how Doyon can use this land once received: the corporation cannot sell or transfer it to anyone other than the U.S. government, cannot allow mining or mineral extraction there, and cannot develop it in ways that would harm the cultural significance of the Geese House site, which appears to hold historical or cultural importance. The bill also requires Interior to officially redraw the boundary of Denali National Park and Preserve to remove this land from the park and match a proposed new boundary map.

This bill mainly affects Doyon, Limited, the National Park Service, and the Department of the Interior, since it changes land ownership and park boundaries. It could also matter to Alaska Native communities connected to the cultural site, as well as the public in terms of park boundaries and land access, though existing public easements are preserved. It's a narrow, location-specific bill rather than one with broad national impact.

title: Bay Area Ridge National Scenic Trail Feasibility Study Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Secretary of the Interior to study whether the Bay Area Ridge Trail, a roughly 550-mile trail circling the San Francisco Bay Area, should officially become a National Scenic Trail. The trail currently has about 415 miles completed, with another 140 miles still needed to finish the loop. It passes through diverse landscapes like marshes, grasslands, forests, and mountains, and connects more than 75 parks and open spaces, including well-known landmarks such as the Golden Gate Bridge area and the San Andreas fault.

The bill does not create the national trail itself. Instead, it amends the National Trails System Act to require a formal feasibility study, to be completed within one year of the bill becoming law. The Interior Department would need to work with the Bay Area Ridge Trail Council, along with federal and state agencies that manage land the trail crosses, to determine whether official designation makes sense.

This bill mainly affects residents of the San Francisco Bay Area who use or live near the trail, along with local and state park agencies, conservation groups, and hikers, bikers, and equestrians who use the trail network. If the study eventually leads to national scenic trail status, it could bring more federal attention, funding opportunities, and coordination for completing and maintaining the trail. However, at this stage, the bill simply starts the review process rather than granting new designation or funding.

title: Chiricahua National Park Act
ai_summary:
This bill would rename Chiricahua National Monument in southeastern Arizona as "Chiricahua National Park," making it an official national park rather than a monument. The physical boundaries of the site would stay exactly the same, and any money currently set aside for the monument would automatically continue to be available under the new park name. Any existing laws, maps, or documents that refer to the "monument" would now be understood to mean the "park" instead.

The bill also directs the Secretary of the Interior to keep protecting traditional cultural and religious sites within the park, working with Native American tribes to do so. It requires the government to give tribal members access to these sites for traditional and customary practices, and allows the Secretary to temporarily close small areas of the park to the general public, at a tribe's request, so those cultural or religious activities can take place without disruption. Any such closures must be kept as small and as short as possible.

This bill mainly affects visitors to and management of the site, Arizona residents and tourism-related businesses near the park, the National Park Service (which would administer it under standard national park rules), and Native American tribes with cultural or religious ties to the land. Redesignating it as a "national park" rather than a "national monument" is largely a status and branding change, though it could increase public recognition and visitation, since national parks often draw more attention than monuments.

title: Wintergreen Emergency Egress Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Wintergreen Emergency Egress Act, would require the Secretary of the Interior to approve a right-of-way (a legal permission to build and use a road) crossing National Park Service land along the Blue Ridge Parkway in Virginia. The purpose is to create an emergency exit route near Wintergreen, a mountain community, so residents could evacuate quickly during emergencies like wildfires, since the area's existing roads may not provide enough escape options.

Before the exit can be built, the bill requires the government to complete certain checks: studying whether other escape routes are possible without crossing federal land, including converting existing trails into roads, analyzing how a wildfire might behave in that area, and completing standard environmental and historic-preservation reviews required by federal law. Only after these steps are certified as complete would the Secretary be required to grant the right-of-way.

This bill mainly affects residents of the Wintergreen area in Virginia, who could gain a new emergency evacuation route, as well as the National Park Service, which manages the Blue Ridge Parkway land involved. It also has broader relevance for how the federal government balances land conservation and environmental review requirements with local public safety needs.

title: Fort Peck Water System Reauthorization Act
ai_summary:
This bill extends federal funding authorization for the Fort Peck Reservation Rural Water System, a project that was originally created by a law passed in 2000. That law authorized money to build and maintain a water system serving the Fort Peck Indian Reservation and surrounding communities in northeastern Montana. The funding authorization has been renewed several times over the years, and this bill would push the expiration date back again, from 2026 to 2028, allowing the project to continue receiving federal support for two more years.

In practical terms, the bill does not create new programs or change how the water system operates. It simply makes a technical update to the law by changing a date, so that federal agencies can keep authorizing money for construction, repairs, and operation of the water system without interruption. This mainly affects residents of the Fort Peck Reservation, including members of the Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes, as well as other nearby rural Montana communities that rely on this system for reliable drinking water. It would also matter to federal agencies, such as the Bureau of Reclamation, that oversee funding and construction for the project, and to Montana's congressional delegation, who introduced the bill to keep the water system funding authority from lapsing.

title: License to Drill Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the License to Drill Act, would change how the federal government handles fees for oil and gas drilling permits on public lands. Under current law, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) charges companies a fee whenever they apply for a permit to drill for oil or gas, and this fee arrangement is set to expire in 2026. The bill would extend this fee collection through 2037, keeping the program running for another decade.

The bill also changes what happens to the money collected from these fees. Right now, only a portion of the fees goes into a special account called the BLM Permit Processing Improvement Fund, which is used to help the agency process drilling permit applications more efficiently. Under this bill, all of the fees collected each year from 2027 through 2037 would go into that fund, rather than just part of them.

This bill mainly affects oil and gas companies that apply for drilling permits on federal lands, since they pay these fees. It also affects the BLM itself, since the agency would have more dedicated funding to speed up permit reviews. Indirectly, this could affect communities near federal drilling sites and taxpayers, since faster permit processing could influence how quickly energy development happens and how efficiently the agency operates.
ai_headline: Bill would extend drilling permit fees through 2037
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: The License to Drill Act would extend BLM oil and gas permit fees through 2037 and send all fee revenue to a permit-processing fund.
ai_sections.what: The bill extends the Bureau of Land Management's oil and gas drilling permit application fee, currently set to expire in 2026, through 2037. It also directs all fees collected from 2027 through 2037 into the BLM Permit Processing Improvement Fund, instead of just a portion as under current law.
ai_sections.who: Oil and gas companies that apply for drilling permits on federal lands pay these fees. The BLM itself is affected, since it would receive more dedicated funding for permit processing.
ai_sections.why: Directing all fee revenue to the fund could speed up how quickly the BLM reviews drilling permits, which could indirectly affect nearby communities and the pace of energy development on public lands.
ai_sections.cost: The bill changes how existing permit fees are allocated, routing all fees collected from 2027-2037 into the BLM Permit Processing Improvement Fund rather than only part of them; companies applying for drilling permits continue paying these fees.

title: Northern Border Security Enhancement and Review Act
ai_summary:
HR 5517, the Northern Border Security Enhancement and Review Act, updates an older law called the Northern Border Security Review Act. That original law required the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to study threats along the U.S.-Canada border once. This new bill changes that to require the study to be updated every two years, starting September 2, 2026, so the government has more current information about security risks along the northern border instead of relying on an old one-time report.

The bill also requires DHS to update its overall northern border security strategy within 90 days after each new threat study, or explain to Congress why no update is needed. It requires DHS to give Congress a classified (secret) briefing on the threat findings within 30 days of each report. Additionally, it directs U.S. Customs and Border Protection's Air and Marine Operations division to create performance measures within six months to better evaluate how well it is securing the border by air and water between official crossing points, addressing past recommendations from the Government Accountability Office (GAO).

This bill mainly affects DHS, CBP, and Congress by creating ongoing reporting and oversight requirements. It does not create new border patrol powers or funding directly, but it affects government planning and accountability processes. Indirectly, it could affect border communities, law enforcement agencies, and policymakers who rely on these reports to make decisions about border security resources and strategy.
ai_headline: Bill would require recurring DHS reviews of northern border threats
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported by the Yeas and Nays: 28 - 2.

ai_sections.tldr: DHS would update its Canada border threat study every two years instead of just once, starting September 2, 2026.
ai_sections.what: HR 5517 amends the Northern Border Security Review Act to require DHS to update its U.S.-Canada border threat study every two years, beginning September 2, 2026, instead of only once. DHS must also update its border security strategy within 90 days of each study or explain to Congress why not, and brief Congress on classified findings within 30 days. CBP's Air and Marine Operations must create performance measures within six months to evaluate border security between official crossing points.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects DHS, CBP, and Congress through new recurring reporting and oversight duties. Border communities, law enforcement agencies, and policymakers may be indirectly affected as they rely on these reports for security decisions.
ai_sections.why: The changes create ongoing reporting and accountability requirements rather than new enforcement powers or funding. This shifts government planning toward continuous threat assessment instead of a single outdated report.

title: A joint resolution disapproving the action of the District of Columbia Council in approving the D.C. Income and Franchise Tax Conformity and Revision Temporary Amendment Act of 2025.
ai_summary:
This bill, S.J. Res. 102, is a resolution in which Congress would formally reject a local law passed by the District of Columbia Council. The D.C. law in question, called the "D.C. Income and Franchise Tax Conformity and Revision Temporary Amendment Act of 2025," was approved by the D.C. Council on December 20, 2025, and dealt with updating D.C.'s income and business tax rules, likely to align them with recent changes in federal tax law or to make other technical revisions. Under the District of Columbia Home Rule Act, Congress has the power to review and overturn laws passed by the D.C. Council before they take effect, and this resolution is an exercise of that authority.

If passed by both the Senate and House and signed into law (or enacted over a veto), this resolution would block the D.C. tax law from taking effect, meaning the changes it proposed to income and franchise (business) tax rules would not happen. This primarily affects residents and businesses in the District of Columbia, since it concerns how they are taxed. It also touches on a broader, recurring debate about how much control Congress should have over local D.C. laws, since D.C. is not a state and its legislation is subject to congressional review in ways that state laws are not.
ai_headline: Senate resolution would block DC's new tax conformity law
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 314.

ai_sections.tldr: Congress is moving to block a D.C. tax law that updates income and business tax rules before it takes effect.
ai_sections.what: S.J. Res. 102 would formally reject a D.C. Council law called the "D.C. Income and Franchise Tax Conformity and Revision Temporary Amendment Act of 2025," passed December 20, 2025. If enacted, the resolution would prevent the D.C. tax law's changes to income and franchise tax rules from taking effect.
ai_sections.who: D.C. residents and businesses subject to income and franchise taxes; the D.C. Council; Congress, acting under its Home Rule Act review authority.
ai_sections.why: Blocking the law would stop D.C.'s planned tax rule updates from taking effect and continues a broader debate over congressional control of local D.C. legislation.

title: VA Fiscal Management Modernization Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) manages its money and budget. It officially designates the VA's Assistant Secretary for Management as the department's Chief Financial Officer (CFO), spelling out specific duties like preparing the budget, tracking spending, making sure the VA follows federal laws that prevent overspending, and reporting financial information to Congress. It also creates a new "Legislative and Congressional Budget Information Office" inside the VA, limited to 15 employees, whose only job is giving Congress accurate and timely financial information about the department. Additionally, it adds two new deputy positions focused on budget strategy and financial operations, and increases the total number of allowed deputy assistant secretaries from 19 to 21.

The bill also requires that VA employees who act as financial officers for specific VA divisions (like different hospital networks or administrations) report directly to the new CFO instead of local managers, and it bars these financial employees from also handling day-to-day program operations, to avoid conflicts of interest. It further prevents the VA from creating any duplicate office that does the same job as the new congressional budget information office. The Secretary of Veterans Affairs would have 180 days after the bill becomes law to put these changes into effect.

This bill mainly affects how the VA is internally organized and how it communicates financial information to Congress. It doesn't change veterans' benefits or services directly, but it could affect VA staff in financial and management roles, and it aims to give Congress clearer, more reliable information about how the VA spends its budget, which indirectly affects oversight of the VA's operations and, potentially, how efficiently veterans' programs are run.
ai_headline: Bill would give VA a formal chief financial officer role
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 13 - 9.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill formalizes a VA Chief Financial Officer and creates a small office to give Congress reliable budget data.
ai_sections.what: HR 7683 designates the VA's Assistant Secretary for Management as Chief Financial Officer with specific budget and reporting duties, and creates a 15-employee Legislative and Congressional Budget Information Office solely to give Congress financial data. It also adds two deputy positions and raises the cap on deputy assistant secretaries from 19 to 21.
ai_sections.who: Affects VA financial and management staff, including division-level financial officers who would report directly to the new CFO instead of local managers. Congress and VA oversight bodies are also affected through improved budget reporting.
ai_sections.why: The changes aim to centralize financial accountability and prevent conflicts of interest between financial oversight and program operations, potentially improving congressional oversight of VA spending.

title: Allied Defense Sales Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Allied Defense Sales Act, directs the U.S. Secretary of State to create a strategy that encourages groups of allied countries to jointly purchase American military equipment and services, rather than buying separately. Under this approach, one "lead" country would coordinate a purchase on behalf of several partner nations, who would then receive their share of the equipment afterward. The goal is to make U.S. arms sales to allies faster, cheaper, and more coordinated, while also strengthening military cooperation and interoperability among partner nations.

The bill requires the State Department to study which countries might be interested in this group-buying approach, which nations could serve as lead coordinators, and what legal or administrative obstacles (such as licensing rules under existing arms export laws) might slow the process down. It also specifically mentions supporting the AUKUS partnership (the security alliance between Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States) by identifying defense products that could be exported more easily under this system. The Secretary of State must report back to Congress every six months for three years, explaining progress, challenges, and any changes to law that might be needed.

This bill mainly affects U.S. defense contractors, foreign allied governments, and the State Department's arms sales bureaucracy. It does not directly affect everyday American citizens' daily lives, but it could influence U.S. foreign policy, defense industry jobs, and America's military relationships with allied nations by making it easier and faster for groups of countries to buy American-made weapons and equipment together.
ai_headline: Bill pushes group purchases of US arms among allied nations
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Foreign Relations.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill directs the State Department to develop a strategy letting allied countries jointly buy U.S. military equipment.
ai_sections.what: The Allied Defense Sales Act directs the Secretary of State to create a strategy encouraging groups of allied countries to jointly purchase American military equipment, with one lead country coordinating the buy for partner nations. It also requires studying which countries could participate or lead, identifying legal or licensing obstacles, and supporting the AUKUS partnership by easing exports of certain defense products.
ai_sections.who: This affects U.S. defense contractors, allied foreign governments, and the State Department's arms sales bureaucracy.
ai_sections.why: The change could speed up and coordinate U.S. arms sales while affecting foreign policy, defense industry jobs, and military relationships with allies; it does not directly affect everyday Americans.

title: Make the District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill sets up two things aimed at Washington, D.C.: a cleanup program and a new federal commission focused on crime and immigration enforcement in the city. The Secretary of the Interior would create a "beautification" program, working with local and federal officials, to keep monuments, parks, sidewalks, and other public spaces clean, remove graffiti, and restore damaged or altered federal monuments and statues. The program would also try to get businesses and private groups involved, and the Secretary would report to Congress each year on progress. This part of the law would expire in January 2029.

The bill also creates a "District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful Commission" made up of representatives from several federal law enforcement agencies (FBI, ATF, U.S. Marshals, Homeland Security, etc.) and U.S. Attorney's offices, led by a White House-appointed chair. This commission would recommend and review policies on topics like stepping up federal immigration enforcement in D.C., monitoring the city's "sanctuary city" policies, speeding up crime lab accreditation, helping recruit and support D.C. police officers, reducing fare evasion on the Metro system, reviewing pretrial detention rules for suspects seen as dangerous, and increasing law enforcement presence at places like the National Mall, Union Station, and city parks. It would also expire in January 2029.

This bill would primarily affect D.C. residents, visitors, and local government agencies, since it increases federal involvement in local policing, immigration enforcement, and maintenance decisions that are normally handled by D.C.'s own government. It could also affect federal agencies and their budgets, as they would need to assign staff and resources to both the cleanup program and the new commission. Because D.C. operates under a mix of local and federal authority, this bill reflects an increase in federal oversight of city functions rather than a nationwide policy change.
ai_headline: Bill would boost federal cleanup and crime commission for DC
last_action_text: Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 437.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 5103 creates a DC beautification program and a federal commission on crime and immigration, both expiring January 2029.
ai_sections.what: This bill creates a Secretary of the Interior-led "beautification" program to clean public spaces, remove graffiti, and restore federal monuments in Washington, D.C., with annual reports to Congress. Both programs would expire in January 2029.
ai_sections.who: D.C. residents, visitors, and local government agencies would be primarily affected, along with federal agencies like the FBI, ATF, U.S. Marshals, and Homeland Security who would staff the new commission.
ai_sections.why: The bill increases federal oversight of local D.C. functions—policing, immigration enforcement, and public space maintenance—that are normally handled by the city's own government.

press_names: Make the District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful Act

title: Foreign Military Financing Loan Authorization Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would let the U.S. Secretary of State give direct loans or loan guarantees to foreign countries or international organizations so they can buy American-made military equipment, defense services, or related construction services. Currently, the U.S. mostly provides military aid through grants or existing loan guarantee programs; this bill would create a more formal pathway for the government itself to lend money directly to foreign buyers of U.S. defense products, with the Secretary of State deciding interest rates and repayment terms. It also allows the State Department to use money from an existing fund (fees collected on foreign military sales) to help run these programs, and requires yearly reports to Congress detailing who received loans, how much, on what terms, and how it affects U.S. national security.

This bill mainly affects foreign governments seeking to purchase U.S. weapons and defense equipment, U.S. defense contractors who would benefit from increased sales, and the State Department, which would gain new authority and administrative responsibilities. Everyday U.S. residents wouldn't be directly affected in daily life, but the bill could influence U.S. foreign policy, defense industry jobs, and how taxpayer-backed financial tools are used to support allies' military purchases. Congress would maintain oversight through required annual reporting, and any loans would depend on funds Congress actually appropriates for this purpose.
ai_headline: Bill would let State Department directly loan money for U.S. arms purchases
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 37 - 9.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill creates a new direct-loan program letting the State Department finance foreign purchases of U.S. defense equipment.

The Secretary would set interest rates and repayment terms. It also lets the State Department tap existing foreign military sales fee funds to help administer the program.

title: Preventing Violence Against Women by Illegal Aliens Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Preventing Violence Against Women by Illegal Aliens Act," changes U.S. immigration law to make it easier to deny entry to or deport non-citizens connected to certain violent crimes. Specifically, it amends the Immigration and Nationality Act so that any non-citizen who has been convicted of, or who simply admits to committing, a sex offense, domestic violence, stalking, child abuse, child neglect, or violating a protective order becomes "inadmissible" (barred from entering the U.S.) and "deportable" (subject to removal if already here). Notably, the bill applies even if someone merely admits to the underlying actions rather than being formally convicted in court, which is a broader standard than a criminal conviction.

The bill also updates the legal definitions used for these offenses. It expands the definition of "domestic violence" for deportation purposes to match a broader federal definition from a 1994 crime law, regardless of whether the state or local jurisdiction involved receives certain federal grant money. It also adds "sex offense," as defined under the Adam Walsh Child Protection and Safety Act (a law focused on tracking sex offenders), as a distinct basis for deportation.

This bill would primarily affect non-U.S. citizens — including green card holders, visa holders, and undocumented immigrants — who have been convicted of or admit to these specific crimes. It does not affect U.S. citizens, since immigration law only governs non-citizens. Supporters frame it as strengthening protections against violent offenders; critics might raise concerns about the "admission" standard applying without a formal conviction. The bill has been introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee but has not yet become law.
ai_headline: Bill would deport non-citizens who admit to violent crimes, even without conviction
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 30 would make non-citizens deportable for admitting to certain violent crimes, not just being convicted.
ai_sections.what: HR 30 amends immigration law so non-citizens convicted of, or who simply admit to, a sex offense, domestic violence, stalking, child abuse, child neglect, or violating a protective order become inadmissible or deportable. It also broadens the legal definitions of "domestic violence" and adds "sex offense" as defined under the Adam Walsh Act as grounds for deportation.
ai_sections.who: Affects non-U.S. citizens, including green card holders, visa holders, and undocumented immigrants, who are convicted of or admit to these crimes. U.S. citizens are not affected.
ai_sections.why: The broader "admission" standard means someone could face deportation without a formal criminal conviction, raising questions about due process. The bill is still in committee and has not become law.

press_names: Preventing Violence Against Women by Illegal Aliens Act

title: Motor Vehicle Modernization Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill updates how the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) sets safety rules, tests vehicles, and communicates with the public. It requires NHTSA to create a public "priority plan" every two years listing upcoming safety rules and research projects, so the public and Congress can track progress and delays. It also overhauls the New Car Assessment Program (NCAP)—the government's 5-star safety rating system—by creating a dedicated office and a new advisory committee made up of safety groups, automakers, researchers, and consumer advocates to improve vehicle ratings and expand consumer education. The bill also directs NHTSA to periodically review existing vehicle safety standards to see if they should be updated or removed, and to speed up decisions on manufacturer requests for safety exemptions, including raising the number of vehicles eligible for certain exemptions from 2,500 to 90,000 per manufacturer.

Beyond rulemaking, the bill addresses several practical safety topics: it orders studies on why recalled vehicles often don't get fixed, on modernizing Vehicle Identification Numbers (VINs) to include information like electric vehicle battery specs, on wheelchair securement systems for accessibility, and on vehicle ownership costs and vehicle aging trends. It creates a working group on fire and battery safety to help first responders safely extract people from crashed vehicles (including electric vehicles), and another working group to help consumers understand the difference between partially automated vehicles (like adaptive cruise control) and fully self-driving vehicles. It also updates rules on how manufacturers must notify car owners about safety recalls, allowing email or other electronic notice instead of only mail, unless an owner requests mail specifically.

This bill mainly affects car manufacturers, NHTSA itself, and everyday vehicle owners. Manufacturers face new reporting, testing, and recall-notification rules along with expanded exemption eligibility. Consumers benefit from improved safety ratings, clearer information about self-driving technology, and better recall communication. First responders and people with disabilities are also specifically considered through the new working groups on vehicle fires and wheelchair securement systems.
ai_headline: Bill would overhaul how NHTSA sets vehicle safety rules and ratings
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 48 - 1.

ai_sections.why: Manufacturers face new reporting, testing, and recall-notification requirements alongside expanded exemption eligibility, while NHTSA takes on new planning, review, and coordination duties.

title: Kayla Hamilton Act
ai_summary:
This bill, named after Kayla Hamilton, changes how the federal government handles unaccompanied children who cross the border without a parent or guardian. It focuses on how these children are placed either in shelters/facilities or with sponsors (like relatives or family friends) while their immigration cases are processed.

The bill requires officials to check unaccompanied children over age 12 for gang-related tattoos or markings and to contact their home country's embassy for criminal history before placing them. If a child is found to have gang ties, a criminal record, or gang-related markings, they must be placed in a secure (locked) facility instead of a regular shelter or with a sponsor, and this decision would not have to be reviewed later. The bill also says children cannot be placed with sponsors who are in the country illegally, and it requires the Department of Health and Human Services to share detailed personal information—including names, Social Security numbers, immigration status, and background check results—about potential sponsors and everyone living in their household with the Department of Homeland Security before a placement happens.

This bill mainly affects unaccompanied immigrant children, the government agencies that care for them (HHS and DHS), and the families or sponsors who take these children in. Supporters would likely say it's meant to protect children from gang violence and unsafe placements, while critics might raise concerns about how it could affect due process, family reunification, and the privacy of sponsor households, especially those with mixed immigration status.
ai_headline: Bill would screen migrant children for gang ties before sponsor placement
last_action_text: Received in the Senate.

ai_sections.tldr: The Kayla Hamilton bill requires gang-tattoo checks on unaccompanied children over 12 and bars placement with sponsors who lack legal status.
ai_sections.what: The bill changes how unaccompanied immigrant children are placed in shelters or with sponsors while their immigration cases are pending. It requires screening children over 12 for gang tattoos, embassy checks on criminal history, secure detention for those with gang ties or criminal records without later review, a ban on placing children with sponsors who are in the country illegally, and detailed data-sharing between HHS and DHS on sponsors and their households.
ai_sections.who: Unaccompanied immigrant children, HHS and DHS, and prospective sponsor families are directly affected.
ai_sections.why: The changes could speed some placements into secure facilities while limiting review, and could reduce the pool of eligible sponsors and raise privacy concerns for mixed-status households.

title: Agent Raul Gonzalez Officer Safety Act
ai_summary:
This bill, named after Border Patrol Agent Raul Gonzalez, creates a new federal crime for intentionally fleeing from a Border Patrol agent or other law enforcement officer working with Border Patrol while driving a vehicle within 100 miles of the U.S. border. Under current law, evading law enforcement is typically handled under state laws, but this bill would make it a federal offense as well. Penalties would range from up to 2 years in prison for a basic offense, 5 to 20 years if someone is seriously injured, and 10 years to life in prison if someone dies as a result.

The bill also changes immigration law so that any noncitizen convicted of this offense—or who simply admits to committing the act, even without a formal conviction—would become inadmissible to the U.S. (unable to legally enter or gain status) and deportable if already in the country. It would also make such individuals ineligible for immigration relief, including asylum, essentially closing off legal pathways to stay in the U.S. for anyone who fits this description.

Finally, the bill requires the Attorney General and the Department of Homeland Security to report annually to Congress on how many people violate this law, how many are charged versus just apprehended, and what penalties are sought and given. This bill would primarily affect people driving near the border who flee from law enforcement, immigrants (including those seeking asylum) who could face harsher immigration consequences, and federal prosecutors and courts, who would gain new tools and responsibilities for handling these cases.
ai_headline: New federal crime targets fleeing Border Patrol agents near the border
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 35 makes fleeing Border Patrol within 100 miles of the border a federal crime with penalties up to life in prison.
ai_sections.what: This bill creates a federal crime for intentionally fleeing a Border Patrol agent or partnered officer while driving within 100 miles of the U.S. border. Penalties range from up to 2 years for a basic offense to 10 years-to-life if someone dies. It also bars noncitizens convicted of or who admit to this offense from legal status, entry, or immigration relief like asylum, and requires annual reporting to Congress on enforcement.
ai_sections.who: Drivers who flee law enforcement near the border, noncitizens including asylum seekers who could face harsher immigration consequences, and federal prosecutors and courts handling these new cases.

title: No Immigration Benefits for Hamas Terrorists Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "No Immigration Benefits for Hamas Terrorists Act of 2025," changes U.S. immigration law to specifically target people connected to the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks against Israel. It would make any foreign national who carried out, helped plan, funded, or otherwise supported those attacks automatically inadmissible to the United States, meaning they could not legally enter the country. It also adds Palestinian Islamic Jihad and Hamas to the list of organizations whose members are barred from entry under existing terrorism-related immigration rules.

The bill also closes off legal options for such individuals if they are already in the U.S. or facing removal. It states that anyone involved in the October 7 attacks cannot apply for asylum, withholding of removal (protection from being deported to a country where they might face harm), or other forms of immigration relief. It also updates the deportation rules so that these individuals can be removed from the U.S. on the same grounds.

Finally, the bill requires the Department of Homeland Security to report to Congress each year on how many people have been found inadmissible or deportable under these new rules. In practical terms, this bill mainly affects foreign nationals seeking to enter or remain in the United States who are found to have participated in or supported the Hamas attacks—it does not change immigration rules for the general public or other immigrants unrelated to that specific situation.
ai_headline: Bill would bar Hamas October 7 attackers from US immigration benefits
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill bars anyone tied to the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks from entering, staying in, or getting relief in the US.

It bars such individuals from asylum, withholding of removal, or other immigration relief, and allows their deportation on these grounds. title: Subterranean Border Defense Act
ai_summary:
This bill, known as the Subterranean Border Defense Act, changes an existing law about how the government tracks efforts to stop illegal tunnels built across the U.S. border. These tunnels are sometimes used for smuggling drugs, people, or other illegal goods between the United States and neighboring countries like Mexico.

Under a previous law passed in 2023, the Department of Homeland Security was required to create a one-time strategic plan and report on how it was working to detect and stop these border tunnels. This new bill changes that requirement so the report has to be produced every year instead of just once. This means Congress and the public would get regular updates on how well tunnel-detection efforts are working, what resources are being used, and whether the strategy needs to change over time.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies involved in border security, such as Homeland Security and Customs and Border Protection, by increasing their reporting responsibilities. It does not create new border policies or enforcement powers itself—it simply ensures that Congress receives consistent, ongoing information about tunnel-related smuggling threats and the government's response to them. Everyday residents wouldn't be directly affected, but the bill could improve government oversight and transparency regarding border security efforts.
ai_headline: Bill would make DHS report on border tunnels an annual requirement
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 495 changes a one-time DHS report on border tunnel detection to a required annual report to Congress.
ai_sections.what: The Subterranean Border Defense Act amends a 2023 law that required a one-time strategic plan and report on detecting and stopping illegal border tunnels. Under this bill, DHS would have to produce that report every year instead of just once, giving Congress ongoing updates on tunnel-detection efforts, resources used, and strategy changes.
ai_sections.who: This affects federal border security agencies, primarily the Department of Homeland Security and Customs and Border Protection, by increasing their reporting duties.
ai_sections.why: The bill does not create new border enforcement powers or policies; it only changes reporting frequency, aiming to give Congress more consistent oversight of tunnel-related smuggling threats.

title: Emerging Innovative Border Technologies Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Emerging Innovative Border Technologies Act, directs the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to create a detailed plan for finding and using new technology to improve border security. Within 180 days of becoming law, DHS and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) would have to give Congress a report explaining how they plan to use tools like artificial intelligence, drones, radar, sensors, and imaging systems to close gaps in current border security efforts. The plan would also need to cover costs, timelines, privacy impacts on border communities, and whether outdated technology should be replaced.

The bill also officially authorizes CBP to keep "Innovation Teams," which are small groups tasked with testing new commercial technologies before they are rolled out more broadly. These teams would need clear operating procedures, goals, and performance measures, and CBP would have to report yearly on what technologies they tested, whether those technologies worked, and how quickly successful tools move into full, funded programs.

This bill mainly affects how DHS and CBP plan and manage border security technology; it does not create new border policies or enforcement powers itself. It would affect government agencies (DHS, CBP, and its Science and Technology Directorate), companies that develop security-related technology (including small businesses and universities that might partner with CBP), and indirectly, people living in border communities, since the plan must assess how new surveillance tools could affect their privacy.

title: District of Columbia Federal Immigration Compliance Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, H.R. 2056, would stop the District of Columbia from having "sanctuary city" policies related to immigration enforcement. Specifically, it would prohibit D.C. from having any law, policy, or practice that blocks city officials from sharing a person's citizenship or immigration status with federal, state, or local governments, or from cooperating with federal immigration detainer requests from the Department of Homeland Security. A detainer request is when federal immigration authorities ask a local jail or police department to hold someone or notify them before releasing that person, so immigration agents can take custody.

The bill includes one exception: D.C. would not be violating the law if it has a policy protecting crime victims or witnesses who come forward, meaning officials could still decline to share immigration information about those individuals or honor detainer requests specifically for them.

This bill would primarily affect the D.C. city government, its police and other officials, and immigrants living in the District, particularly those without legal status who interact with local law enforcement. It would also affect how D.C. cooperates with federal immigration authorities. Because D.C. is not a state and Congress has specific authority to legislate for the District, this bill applies only to Washington, D.C., not to other cities or states with similar sanctuary policies.
ai_headline: Bill would bar D.C. from limiting cooperation with federal immigration agents
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

title: Save SBA from Sanctuary Cities Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Save SBA from Sanctuary Cities Act of 2025," would require the Small Business Administration (SBA) to move any of its regional, district, or local offices out of places the federal government labels "sanctuary jurisdictions." A sanctuary jurisdiction is defined as a state or local government that limits sharing immigration status information with federal authorities or refuses certain immigration enforcement requests, such as detainer requests, with some exceptions for crime victims and witnesses. The SBA Administrator would first have to publicly declare that an office is in such a jurisdiction, and then relocate it within 60 days to a location outside any sanctuary jurisdiction, preferably still within the same state if possible. The bill also bans the SBA from opening any new offices in sanctuary jurisdictions in the future.

If an office isn't relocated in time, it would have to shut down operations, and its employees would be reassigned to other SBA offices in non-sanctuary areas. The office's manager would need to explain the delay in writing, and could be removed from their position if they fail to do so or if their explanation is judged inadequate. This bill mainly affects SBA operations and employees, as well as small business owners in sanctuary jurisdictions who rely on local SBA offices for loans, counseling, and other services—since those offices could close or move farther away. It does not change immigration law itself but uses SBA office locations as a tool to pressure jurisdictions over their immigration enforcement policies.

title: American Entrepreneurs First Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the American Entrepreneurs First Act of 2025, would change who can qualify for two types of Small Business Administration (SBA) loans: 7(a) loans, which are the SBA's main general-purpose business loans, and loans under Title V of the Small Business Investment Act, which support small business investment companies. The bill requires anyone applying for these loans to submit their date of birth and to certify that they are a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, or lawful permanent resident (green card holder). If a business is applying, all owners of that business would need to meet this same requirement. Lawful permanent residents would also need to provide their alien registration number as proof of status.

The bill specifically blocks certain groups from qualifying for these loans, even if they are otherwise running a legitimate small business. This includes refugees, asylum seekers, people on temporary visas (such as work or student visas), DACA recipients (young immigrants brought to the U.S. as children who have deferred deportation status), and people living in the U.S. without legal immigration status. If any owner of a business—even a partial owner—falls into one of these categories, the whole business would be ineligible for the loan.

This bill would primarily affect small business owners and entrepreneurs who are not U.S. citizens or green card holders, including immigrants with legal temporary status, refugees, and DACA recipients, who currently may be eligible for these SBA loan programs. It would also affect banks and lenders that process these loans, since they would need to collect and verify additional documentation from applicants. Supporters and critics of this type of measure often disagree about its effects on immigrant-owned businesses and the broader economy, but the bill itself simply sets new documentation and eligibility rules for these specific federal loan programs.
