title: 21st Century Dyslexia Act
ai_summary:
This bill would update the main federal special education law, called the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), to specifically address dyslexia. Right now, dyslexia is often grouped under the broader category of "specific learning disabilities," and the law doesn't clearly define the term. This bill adds an official definition of dyslexia, describing it as an unexpected difficulty reading despite having the intelligence to read better, usually caused by trouble processing the sounds of spoken language. It also updates related sections of the law to make sure dyslexia is clearly recognized alongside other learning disabilities when schools identify and support students.

The bill also adds a new requirement that schools give all eligible children equal access to accommodations and services under this law, regardless of their background. This specifically includes children from low-income families, children from families with low socioeconomic status, and children who are still learning English. The goal is to prevent these groups from being overlooked or given fewer resources when it comes to identifying learning disabilities like dyslexia and providing the help they need.

This bill mainly affects public school students with dyslexia or reading-related learning disabilities, their parents, and school districts. Teachers, special education staff, and school administrators would need to follow the updated definition and rules when evaluating students and deciding what support or accommodations to provide, such as specialized reading instruction or extra time on tests. Families, especially those with lower incomes or limited English proficiency, could benefit from clearer guarantees that their children receive the same access to services as other students.
ai_headline: Bill would add clear definition of dyslexia to federal special education law
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 542.

title: Protect College Sports Act of 2026
ai_summary:
Congress is considering a bill called the Protect College Sports Act of 2026, which would create a comprehensive set of federal rules for how college athletes can be paid for their name, image, and likeness (NIL) and how college sports are run more broadly. It would guarantee that colleges, conferences, and organizations like the NCAA cannot block athletes from signing NIL deals or punish them for it, while also requiring athletes to disclose deals over $600 so there's more transparency. It sets up an agent registration system to crack down on shady sports agents, creates a public database to help athletes figure out fair market value for NIL deals, and establishes an independent "Ombudsman" office athletes can go to for help or complaints.

Beyond NIL, the bill adds several protections for student athletes: guaranteed medical coverage for sports injuries (including years after they stop playing), stricter concussion and heat-illness safety standards, protections against schools pressuring athletes about their choice of classes or major, rules limiting how easily scholarships can be pulled, updated transfer rules (letting athletes transfer once without penalty, with extra exceptions like a coach leaving), and a requirement that athletes hold at least one-third of seats on governing boards of athletic associations. It also has a specific rule stopping football coaches from taking a new head coaching job in the middle of the season while still working for their old team. A separate section of the bill addresses sports broadcasting, including rules about media rights and limits on conferences merging.

This bill would primarily affect college athletes, universities, athletic conferences, the NCAA, sports agents, and broadcasters. Student athletes would gain stronger legal protections, clearer financial rules, and new avenues for dispute resolution, while schools and athletic associations would face new compliance, disclosure, and funding requirements, including a multimillion-dollar fund for long-term injury costs. Everyday sports fans could see effects too, particularly through the broadcasting provisions, which could change how and where college football and basketball games are shown.
ai_headline: New bill would set nationwide rules for paying college athletes
last_action_text: Cloture motion on the motion to proceed to the measure presented in Senate. (CR S4449)

title: Home School Graduation Recognition Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal education law so that students who finish high school through homeschooling are officially counted as "high school graduates" for purposes of federal financial aid programs. Currently, the Higher Education Act has a section dealing with students who don't have a traditional high school diploma, and this bill would add specific language recognizing homeschool completion as equivalent to graduating high school, as long as the homeschooling was done in a way that state law recognizes as a legitimate home school or private school arrangement.

In practical terms, this matters mainly for students applying for federal student aid, like Pell Grants or federal student loans, to attend college or other higher education programs. To qualify for this aid, students generally need to prove they either graduated high school or have an equivalent credential like a GED. Homeschooled students sometimes face extra paperwork or uncertainty proving their "graduate" status, depending on how their state treats homeschooling. This bill would create a clearer, nationwide rule stating that a completed home school education counts as a high school diploma for federal financial aid eligibility purposes, as long as it follows the student's state homeschooling rules.

This bill would primarily affect homeschooled students and their families who plan to attend college, as well as colleges and universities that process federal financial aid applications and need to verify a student's educational credentials. It would not change how states regulate or approve homeschooling itself, since that determination is left up to individual state law.
ai_headline: Bill would count homeschool completion as high school graduation for aid
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 354.

title: Red Snapper Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Red Snapper Act of 2025, would temporarily stop the U.S. Secretary of Commerce from putting in place any new rule that closes off areas or the ocean floor to fishing in the South Atlantic for red snapper and related species. This restriction would stay in effect until a specific research project, called the South Atlantic Great Red Snapper Count, is finished and its findings are included in the official government assessment used to manage the fish population.

The bill points out that fishing is a big part of the economy in states like Florida, supporting billions of dollars in economic activity and thousands of jobs. It notes that red snapper populations have been recovering well in recent years, but this recovery has also led to more accidental catches of red snapper during times when fishing for them isn't allowed, which can still harm the population. Some fishery managers have discussed possibly shortening fishing seasons or closing certain areas to address this problem, but Florida officials are worried about the economic damage such closures could cause.

This bill would primarily affect recreational and commercial fishermen, coastal communities, and businesses connected to fishing in South Atlantic states such as Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, and North Carolina. It would also affect federal fishery regulators, who would need to wait for updated scientific data before making rules that limit fishing areas. Supporters of stricter fishing rules and environmental groups focused on conservation could also be affected, since the bill would delay any new closures until more complete data is available.

title: Brownfields Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews and updates the federal "Brownfields" program, which gives money to communities to help clean up and reuse contaminated properties like old factories, gas stations, or industrial sites. It extends funding for these grants through 2030 and increases how much money can go toward cleaning up each site, raising the cap from $500,000 to $1,000,000 per site. It also increases funding for state programs that manage their own contaminated-site cleanups, with amounts rising from $50 million in 2025 to $75 million by 2030.

The bill makes several changes aimed at helping smaller and lower-income communities access this money more easily. It reduces the local matching funds some communities must provide from 20% to 10%, and it waives that requirement entirely for small or disadvantaged communities. It also asks applicants to show plans for involving local residents in decisions about cleanup projects, expands which types of business associations can qualify for grants, and directs the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to study and simplify the grant application process, since it has been described as confusing. Additionally, it updates rules to make sure Alaska Native tribal corporations can qualify for these cleanup grants, correcting language that previously excluded them.

This bill would primarily affect local governments, tribal governments (including Alaska Native corporations), nonprofit organizations, and community groups that apply for federal help to clean up polluted land. It could also affect residents living near contaminated sites, since more funding and eased requirements may lead to more cleanup projects, especially in smaller or economically disadvantaged areas.

title: Youth Poisoning Protection Act
ai_summary:
S. 289, called the Youth Poisoning Protection Act, would ban the sale to consumers of products containing a high concentration of sodium nitrite, defined as 10% or more by weight. Under the bill, these products would be classified as "banned hazardous products" under existing consumer safety law, meaning they could not be sold to the general public. Sodium nitrite is a chemical that, in large amounts, is highly toxic and has been used in cases of self-harm, which is the concern driving this legislation.

The bill includes important exceptions. It would not affect industrial or commercial uses of high-concentration sodium nitrite where the chemical isn't meant for personal consumer use. It also would not apply to sodium nitrite used in food products, including meat, poultry, and eggs, where it is commonly used as a preservative in small, regulated amounts, nor to its use in drugs, medical devices, or cosmetics. This means grocery store meats and other food items with sodium nitrite as an ingredient would not be affected.

This bill would primarily affect companies that manufacture or sell concentrated sodium nitrite products for consumer purchase, such as those sold online for uses like pest control or metal treatment. Everyday consumers would be affected in that they would no longer be able to legally purchase these highly concentrated forms, though normal food shopping and use of typical household products would not change. The law would take effect 90 days after being signed, if passed.

title: Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill changes the debt limits that determine who qualifies for certain types of bankruptcy protection. First, it raises the debt cap for small businesses using the streamlined "Subchapter V" bankruptcy process (created to make bankruptcy faster and cheaper for small businesses) to $7,500,000 in total debt. This process is generally reserved for smaller, privately-held businesses, so the bill also clarifies that companies required to file reports with the Securities and Exchange Commission, or their affiliates, don't qualify, since those are considered larger, publicly-traded entities.

Second, the bill raises the debt limit for individuals filing Chapter 13 bankruptcy, which allows people with regular income to reorganize and repay debts over time rather than liquidating their assets. Under the bill, individuals (or married couples) with debts under $2,750,000 could use Chapter 13, combining what used to be separate limits for secured and unsecured debt into one single, higher threshold.

This bill mainly affects small business owners and individuals who are considering filing for bankruptcy. By raising these dollar limits, more businesses and individuals with higher debt loads would become eligible to use these faster, less complicated bankruptcy options instead of more complex Chapter 11 proceedings. The changes would apply to any bankruptcy cases filed after the bill becomes law, but would not affect cases already underway.
ai_headline: Bill would raise debt limits for small business and Chapter 13 bankruptcy

These changes apply only to bankruptcy cases filed after the bill becomes law.

title: Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal rules for colleges and universities that receive certain types of federal funding under the Higher Education Act. It targets schools that participate in "nonexpressive commercial boycotts" of countries considered major strategic partners of the United States, which under the bill's definitions would effectively include Israel. Each year, colleges receiving federal student aid (Title IV funds) would have to certify they are not engaging in such boycotts. The Department of Education would publish a public list of schools that fail to certify, and those schools could lose eligibility for this federal funding.

The bill also affects colleges that receive Title VI funds, which support international education and foreign language programs. To keep receiving that money, schools would have to certify that they let their students and faculty participate in academic exchanges, study abroad programs, conferences, and research collaborations with institutions in these partner countries on the same terms as they do with other countries. Schools would also have to allow students and faculty from these partner countries to participate in their own programs under equal conditions.

This bill mainly affects colleges and universities, particularly those with policies restricting academic or business ties to Israel, such as boycott movements sometimes seen on campuses. It could impact students, faculty, and administrators involved in study abroad programs, research partnerships, and international exchanges. Supporters frame it as protecting economic and academic cooperation with allies, while critics may see it as limiting how schools can respond to political or human rights concerns through boycotts. The bill does not ban personal or political speech—it focuses specifically on formal institutional actions tied to federal funding eligibility.

title: Bureau of Industry and Security License Administration Enhancement Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the federal government manages export control licenses, which are permits businesses need to sell certain sensitive products or technology (like advanced computer chips) to other countries. Currently, the Bureau of Industry and Security (part of the Commerce Department) sometimes uses informal letters or guidance to impose extra licensing requirements on companies, without going through the normal public rulemaking process. This bill requires that such informal guidance either go through the same interagency review as official licenses, or be formally published as a regulation within 60 days—otherwise it expires. It also requires the government to publicly explain the standards officials use when they lean toward denying an export license, and to share those standards with Congress beforehand.

The bill also strengthens the technical advisory committees that give the government expert advice on export controls. It requires the Commerce Department to maintain specific committees covering areas like computing and AI, biotechnology, robotics, aerospace, advanced materials, and weapons of mass destruction. These committees would include a mix of national security experts, industry specialists, and academics, meet regularly, and report their findings to Congress. Members would have to sign nondisclosure agreements to protect sensitive information discussed in meetings.

Finally, the bill directs the Commerce Department to review and report to Congress on how well a specific 2025 rule restricting exports of advanced computer chips is working, and whether it needs updates. Overall, this bill mainly affects companies that export sensitive technology (especially semiconductors, AI, and defense-related products), federal agencies involved in national security and trade policy, and members of Congress who oversee these programs. Everyday consumers would only be indirectly affected, mainly through how it shapes U.S. trade relationships with countries like China and Russia and the pace of innovation in controlled industries.
ai_headline: Bill would rein in informal export control rules on tech sales abroad

title: Health Data Access, Transparency, and Affordability Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal law to give employers and unions that sponsor health insurance plans for their workers much greater access to detailed claims data and pricing information held by insurance companies, third-party administrators, pharmacy benefit managers, and other middlemen involved in processing health claims. Currently, many of these service providers restrict how much information a company can see about what its own health plan is being charged, making it hard for employers to check whether they are being overcharged or whether care is priced fairly. The bill would require contracts between health plans and these service providers to guarantee fast, broad access to claims data, pricing formulas, fee schedules, overpayment information, and audit rights, in standardized data formats, generally within 15 days of a request.

The bill also bans "gag clauses" that prevent employers from reviewing or auditing this data, voids any existing contract terms that conflict with these new rules, and stops service providers from being shielded or reimbursed by the health plan if they are fined for violating these rules. The Department of Labor could fine companies up to $10,000 per day for noncompliance. Plans would also have to certify each year that they actually have this data access, with penalties for using outside administrators to falsely make that certification on their behalf.

This mainly affects employers and unions that sponsor group health insurance plans (often called "plan fiduciaries"), as well as insurance companies, pharmacy benefit managers, third-party claims administrators, and other health data intermediaries, who would face new transparency and compliance obligations. Indirectly, it could affect workers and their families covered by employer health plans, since better data access is intended to help employers negotiate lower costs and detect billing errors or fraud, potentially affecting premiums and health plan costs over time. The changes would take effect for plan years beginning at least one year after the law is enacted.

title: Stronger Engagement for Indian Health Needs Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would upgrade the top leadership position of the Indian Health Service (IHS) from "Director" to "Assistant Secretary for Indian Health" within the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). This is a change in rank and title, not a change in what the agency actually does day-to-day. The IHS is the federal agency responsible for providing healthcare to Native American and Alaska Native communities, and this bill aims to give its leader a higher-level position with more direct authority, including reporting directly within HHS's chain of command rather than through lower-level officials.

Practically, the bill also allows the new Assistant Secretary to appoint a Deputy Assistant Secretary and other staff, including attorneys, to help run the agency. It updates pay scales so the position is compensated at the same higher level as other HHS Assistant Secretaries, and it makes sure that any existing laws, rules, or documents referring to the old "Director" title automatically apply to the new "Assistant Secretary" title instead.

This bill mainly affects how the federal government is organized and how much authority and visibility the head of Indian health programs has within HHS. It would directly affect IHS leadership and staff, tribal governments and communities that rely on IHS services, and HHS's organizational structure. Everyday Americans who are not part of tribal communities or the IHS system would likely see no direct effect, though supporters argue that elevating the position could lead to better representation of Native health needs in federal policymaking.

title: Southcentral Foundation Land Transfer Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, S. 2098, directs the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services to transfer ownership of a specific piece of federal land in Anchorage, Alaska—about 3.372 acres—to the Southcentral Foundation (SCF), a nonprofit organization that provides health and social services, primarily to Alaska Native and American Indian people. The transfer must happen within two years of the bill becoming law, and the property must be used for health and social service programs. The land would be given for free, with no payment required and no strings attached, meaning the government could not later reclaim the property or impose extra conditions on how SCF uses it.

The bill also addresses legal and environmental details of the transfer. It specifies that the deed used will be a "warranty deed," which offers stronger legal protections than an existing quitclaim deed currently in place, and that the new deed will replace the old one. Importantly, SCF would not be held responsible for any pollution or contamination on the property that happened before the transfer date; that responsibility would remain with the federal government. However, if contamination occurs after SCF takes control of the property, SCF—not the government—would be responsible for it.

This bill mainly affects the Southcentral Foundation, the federal government (specifically HHS), and residents of Anchorage, Alaska, especially those who use SCF's health and social services. It does not have broad national impact but is a targeted, local land-transfer measure meant to help a specific healthcare provider expand or continue its operations on land it may already be using.

title: To require the Secretary of Agriculture to convey the Pleasant Valley Ranger District Administrative Site to Gila County, Arizona.
ai_summary:
HR 837 directs the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture, through the U.S. Forest Service, to transfer ownership of a piece of federal land known as the Pleasant Valley Ranger District Administrative Site to Gila County, Arizona. This property is about 232.9 acres located within the Tonto National Forest. The transfer would only happen if the county formally requests it within 180 days after the bill becomes law. The land would be given to the county for free, through a simple legal transfer called a "quitclaim deed," meaning the government isn't guaranteeing there are no legal issues with the property, just handing over whatever rights it has.

The county, not the federal government, would have to pay for any required surveys, environmental checks, or historical reviews needed to complete the transfer. Importantly, the bill requires that this land be used specifically to serve and support military veterans. If the county ever uses the land for something else, ownership could revert back to the federal government.

This bill mainly affects residents of Gila County, Arizona, especially veterans who might benefit from services or facilities built on this land. It also affects the Forest Service, which currently manages the site, and local officials who would take on new responsibilities and costs related to owning and maintaining the property.

title: To provide for the transfer of administrative jurisdiction over certain Federal land in the State of California, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
HR 8454 deals with a small land swap between two federal agencies in Tuolumne County, California, near Yosemite National Park. It transfers about 160 acres currently managed as part of the Stanislaus National Forest (under the Forest Service/Department of Agriculture) to the National Park Service (Department of the Interior), so it becomes part of Yosemite National Park. At the same time, it transfers about 170 acres currently managed as part of Yosemite National Park to the Forest Service, so it becomes part of Stanislaus National Forest. This is essentially a boundary adjustment known as the "Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange," matching land management to how the areas are actually used or connected geographically.

The bill also includes standard administrative provisions: it allows the two agencies to make small corrections to the land boundaries later if needed, requires them to identify and disclose any hazardous waste sites before the transfer, and states that whichever agency originally managed the land stays responsible for cleaning up any contamination there. It also protects existing rights, such as leases, easements, or permits, meaning people or companies who had agreements tied to the land can keep them, though the new managing agency will now oversee those agreements.

This bill mainly affects the U.S. Forest Service and National Park Service, since it changes which agency manages these specific parcels. It could also affect local land users, such as people with existing permits or easements on the affected acreage, though their rights are preserved. The general public is unlikely to notice major changes, since both agencies still protect and manage the land for conservation and recreation purposes.

title: Protecting Investors’ Personally Identifiable Information Act
ai_summary:
This bill would stop the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) from requiring stock exchanges and financial firms to collect certain personal information about everyday investors as part of a system called the Consolidated Audit Trail (CAT). The CAT is a massive database the SEC uses to track stock trades and detect market abuses like insider trading or fraud. Currently, this system can require reporting of details tied to individual investors, and this bill would ban the collection of personally identifiable information such as names, addresses, birth dates, Social Security numbers, phone numbers, emails, and IP addresses.

The bill defines personally identifiable information broadly, covering any data that could be used alone or combined with other information to identify a specific person. If passed, exchanges, associations, and their members would no longer be allowed to submit this type of information to the SEC under the audit trail reporting rules, even though the SEC could still collect other trading data needed for market oversight.

This bill mainly affects everyday investors who trade stocks, since it limits what personal information about them gets collected and stored in a large government-linked database. It also affects the SEC, stock exchanges, and brokerage firms, who would need to adjust their reporting systems to comply. Supporters of this kind of measure often cite data privacy and security concerns, since large databases holding personal information can become targets for hacking or misuse, while others may worry it could limit the SEC’s ability to track down individuals involved in specific instances of market fraud.
ai_headline: Bill would bar SEC's trade database from collecting investors' personal data
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 687.

title: Tyler’s Law
ai_summary:
Tyler's Law directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to look into how hospital emergency rooms handle drug testing for people who come in experiencing an overdose. Specifically, the government would study how often emergency rooms currently test for fentanyl (a powerful synthetic opioid) alongside other drugs like cocaine, marijuana, or amphetamines, what it costs to run these tests, and what benefits or risks patients might face from being tested. The study would also look at privacy concerns and how testing might affect the relationship between patients and their doctors.

After finishing this study within one year, HHS would have six more months to issue official guidance. This guidance would address whether hospitals should make fentanyl testing a standard part of overdose care, how to make sure doctors and nurses know exactly which drugs are being tested for, and how such testing might help prevent future overdoses or improve health outcomes.

This bill mainly affects hospitals, emergency room staff, and patients who experience overdoses. It doesn't require hospitals to change their practices right away—it only requires the government to study the issue and provide recommendations. Because fentanyl is a major driver of overdose deaths in the U.S. but isn't always included in standard drug tests, this bill could eventually shape how emergency rooms detect and respond to fentanyl-related overdoses, potentially affecting treatment decisions and follow-up care for patients nationwide.
ai_headline: Tyler's Law orders federal study of fentanyl testing in ER overdose cases
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

title: End Veterans Overdose Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the End Veterans Overdose Act of 2026, would require the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to give out opioid overdose rescue medications, such as naloxone, for free and without needing a prescription. This would be available at VA pharmacies to eligible veterans and to their caregivers who are enrolled in VA caregiver support programs. Anyone who receives the medication would also get information on how to use it properly.

The bill also sets rules to protect people's privacy and prevent misuse of their personal information. The VA could only collect information needed to provide the medication, and it could not use that information to deny someone a job, or as proof that they have a history of drug use or addiction. This is meant to reduce fear among veterans that seeking overdose-prevention medication could hurt their employment or reputation.

Finally, the bill requires the VA to report to Congress periodically on how the program is working—including how many people received the medication, whether it should be expanded to family members or non-VA healthcare providers, and how usage trends are changing over time. Overall, this bill mainly affects veterans, their designated caregivers, and the VA health system, aiming to make it easier to prevent fatal opioid overdoses within that community.

title: Advisory Committee on the Records of Congress Sunset Act
ai_summary:
This bill would eliminate the Advisory Committee on the Records of Congress, a small federal body that has helped oversee how Congress's historical records are preserved and managed. Sixty days after the bill becomes law, the section of federal code that created this committee would be removed entirely.

In place of the committee, the bill sets up a simpler reporting system. Each year, the Director of the Center for Legislative Archives at the National Archives would have to submit a report on how congressional records are being preserved to key officials, including the Archivist of the United States, the Secretary of the Senate, the Clerk of the House, and relevant House and Senate committees. After each report, those top officials would be required to meet and review how records are being handled. They'd also need to meet whenever a new Archivist, Secretary, or Clerk takes office, to make sure the transition doesn't disrupt recordkeeping.

This bill mainly affects how the federal government manages its own paperwork and historical archives behind the scenes—it doesn't directly impact everyday citizens. However, it could matter to historians, researchers, journalists, and others who rely on well-organized congressional records for studying government history. The change is essentially administrative: replacing a standing advisory committee with a simpler system of periodic reports and check-in meetings among key record-keeping officials.

last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by Voice Vote.

title: MATCH Act of 2026
ai_summary:
**HR 8183 — MATCH Act of 2026**

This bill updates federal job-training law to encourage states to build "talent marketplaces" — online platforms that help connect job seekers, students, employers, and training programs. These platforms would let people create digital records of their education, work history, and skills, and use standardized language so employers and schools can more easily match people to jobs or training opportunities. The bill also creates a "credential registry" (a public listing of what skills different certificates or degrees represent) and a "skills profile generator" (a tool to help people describe their own skills in standardized terms).

To make this happen, the bill directs the Department of Labor to set aside a portion of existing workforce program funding (5–10%) for grants to states or groups of states. States could use this money to build these online systems, link data across state education and employment records, improve job-market data collection, and train staff to use this data. States that haven't previously gotten this type of grant, or groups of states working together across state lines, would get priority. The bill requires privacy protections, since these systems would handle personal work and education history, and it requires grant recipients to report back on results.

This mainly affects state workforce agencies, job training providers, schools, and job seekers or workers using public employment services. It doesn't create a new mandate forcing every state to build these systems — it makes funding and guidance available for states that choose to. Everyday workers and students could eventually see more user-friendly government job-search and training websites, while state agencies and training providers would face new options (and some new administrative work) to participate in this data-sharing system.

title: USCP Empowerment Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the USCP Empowerment Act of 2025, gives the United States Capitol Police (USCP) new legal authority to deal with drones (unmanned aircraft systems) that might threaten the Capitol Building, its grounds, or other protected areas in Washington, D.C. Normally, federal laws make it illegal to intercept communications, interfere with aircraft, or disable someone else's equipment without permission. This bill creates an exception so Capitol Police can detect, track, warn, jam, seize, or even destroy a drone if it's judged to be a credible security threat. Any drone taken this way could be permanently confiscated by the government.

The bill requires the Capitol Police Board to work with the Department of Transportation and the Federal Aviation Administration to make sure these actions don't create dangers for other aircraft or interfere with normal air traffic. It also includes privacy safeguards: any communications intercepted from a drone can only be used for the specific security purpose, must generally be deleted within 180 days, and can only be shared with other agencies under limited circumstances. The Capitol Police must file regular reports to Congress explaining how these powers are being used, including any harm caused, privacy issues, and coordination efforts with other law enforcement agencies.

This mainly affects drone operators near the Capitol, who could have their devices tracked, disrupted, or destroyed if flying in a way seen as threatening. It also affects Capitol Police, who gain expanded enforcement powers, and federal aviation regulators, who must help ensure these actions don't disrupt broader airspace safety. Everyday citizens are affected mainly in terms of privacy protections and government transparency, since the law sets rules on how intercepted drone communications can be handled and reported.

title: Rural Hospital Cybersecurity Enhancement Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to create a nationwide strategy for building up the cybersecurity workforce at rural hospitals. Within one year, the Secretary must develop this strategy after consulting with other federal agencies (like the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the Departments of Education and Labor) and with at least two rural healthcare representatives from each of the nine census-designated regions of the country. The strategy must look at ways to build partnerships between rural hospitals, schools, and private companies, create training curricula for community colleges and vocational schools, identify challenges unique to rural hospitals versus hospitals in general, and recommend any new laws or rules needed. The Secretary would also have to brief Congress every year on how the strategy is working and how many people have been trained.

Separately, the bill requires the Secretary to create actual training materials that rural hospitals can use to teach their staff basic cybersecurity practices, and to run an awareness campaign so hospitals know these materials exist. This mainly affects rural hospitals, their employees, and patients who rely on these facilities, since cyberattacks on hospitals can disrupt patient care and expose sensitive medical records. It could also affect community colleges and vocational schools that might be asked to offer new cybersecurity training programs.

Notably, the bill explicitly states that no additional federal funding is authorized to carry out these requirements, meaning any strategy development, training materials, or awareness campaigns would have to be funded through existing budgets rather than new money from Congress.

title: Servicemembers and Veterans Empowerment and Support Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill aims to make it easier for veterans who experienced sexual assault, sexual battery, or sexual harassment during military service—known as "military sexual trauma" or MST—to get VA health care and disability benefits. It creates a clear legal definition of MST and lays out specific types of evidence the VA must consider when evaluating these claims, such as records from law enforcement, hospitals, or rape crisis centers, as well as behavioral changes like requesting a transfer, declining work performance, substance abuse, or unexplained anxiety. The VA would be required to tell veterans about these evidence options before denying a claim, and specialized, trained teams would handle these cases. Veterans could also choose to have their required medical exam done at an actual VA facility by a VA employee, rather than through an outside contractor.

The bill also requires the VA to review and improve how it communicates with people affected by MST, making sure letters and notices are respectful, include contact information for support services and crisis hotlines, and don't cause additional emotional harm. It orders several studies and reports—on training quality, claims accuracy, and how MST claims are processed—along with annual reviews to catch and fix errors, plus a workgroup focused on reducing repeat medical exams that can be re-traumatizing.

Finally, the bill expands who can get MST-related counseling and treatment, extending eligibility to all former reserve members regardless of duty status, and requires the VA to quickly connect veterans to support resources after they file an MST-related claim. It also directs the VA to work with the Defense Department, Homeland Security, and Transportation Department to make sure students who leave military service academies (like West Point or the Naval Academy) without graduating are told about their potential eligibility for MST care and can get copies of relevant records or investigation reports. Overall, this bill primarily affects veterans, current service members, reservists, and service academy students who have experienced sexual trauma, as well as VA staff who process these claims.
ai_headline: Bill would ease VA claims process for military sexual trauma survivors
last_action_text: Committee on Veterans' Affairs. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

title: Healthy Start Reauthorization Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would extend funding for the Healthy Start Initiative, a federal program that works to reduce infant deaths and improve health outcomes for mothers and babies in communities with high rates of infant mortality. The bill sets the program's funding at $145 million per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030, replacing the previous funding amount and timeline that had expired or was set to expire.

Healthy Start provides grants to local organizations and health departments to offer services like prenatal care support, health education, home visits, and case management for pregnant women, new mothers, and infants, particularly in areas where babies are more likely to die before their first birthday. This bill does not create a new program or change how it operates; it simply keeps the existing initiative funded and running for five more years.

This bill mainly affects low-income mothers, infants, and families in high-risk communities who rely on Healthy Start services, as well as the local health organizations, hospitals, and nonprofits that receive federal grants to run these programs. It also affects taxpayers, since it continues a specific level of federal spending, and healthcare workers and community health advocates who staff these programs across the country.

title: Lulu’s Law
ai_summary:
This bill, called "Lulu's Law," would require the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to add shark attacks to the list of emergencies that can trigger a wireless emergency alert. These are the alerts people receive on their cell phones for things like severe weather, missing children (Amber Alerts), or other dangerous situations. Under this bill, local authorities would gain the option to send similar alerts to warn people in a specific area if a shark attack has occurred nearby, such as at a beach.

The bill gives the FCC 180 days after it becomes law to officially make this change. It does not force any alerts to be sent automatically after every shark attack; it simply makes shark attacks an approved category of emergency for which officials could choose to send a wireless alert, similar to how other emergency categories work now.

This bill would mainly affect people who live near or visit coastal areas, beach communities, and popular swimming or surfing spots, since local emergency management agencies would be the ones deciding whether to use this new alert option. It could also affect wireless carriers and phone manufacturers, who are required to support the alert system, though the practical changes for them would likely be minor since shark attack alerts would simply become one more category within the existing wireless alert system.

title: HUD Transparency Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the HUD Transparency Act of 2025, would require the Inspector General of the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to appear before Congress once a year, by October 1st. The Inspector General is the official responsible for overseeing HUD's operations, catching fraud and waste, and making sure taxpayer money is spent properly. Under this bill, that official would have to testify before two specific committees: the House Committee on Financial Services and the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

During this yearly testimony, the Inspector General would need to report on several things, including efforts to detect and prevent fraud and misuse of funds, the office's ability to conduct audits and investigations, recommendations for improving HUD's programs, and whether HUD has enough resources and staff to do its job effectively. This is meant to create a regular, predictable checkpoint where lawmakers can ask questions and get updates on how well HUD is being run.

This bill mainly affects HUD's Inspector General's office, which would have a new annual reporting requirement, and members of Congress on those two committees, who would gain a formal yearly opportunity to review HUD's performance. Indirectly, it could affect the public and HUD program recipients—such as people receiving housing assistance—since increased oversight is intended to help ensure federal housing programs run efficiently and money is not wasted or misused.

title: Interagency Coordination in Export Controls Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Interagency Coordination in Export Controls Act of 2026, changes how the U.S. government decides which products and technologies can be exported to other countries for national security reasons. Currently, the Department of Commerce mainly controls this process. The bill would let the Secretaries of State, Defense, or Energy also submit proposed export control rules directly to the Export Administration Review Board, a government panel that reviews these rules. The Board would have 30 days to vote on any proposal, with a possible 30-day extension if a member needs more information and the original proposer agrees.

The bill also requires the Secretary of State to study how China's "military-civil fusion" strategy—where the Chinese government blends civilian and military technology development—affects U.S. export control policy and national security. This review must look at things like whether U.S. technology is being used to strengthen China's military, whether any Chinese companies can truly be considered "civilian," and whether current safeguards on U.S. exports are reliable. Within 90 days, the Secretary would need to consider proposing policy changes based on this review, such as adding companies to a restricted "Military End-User List." A detailed report on the findings and any proposed changes must go to Congress within 150 days.

Overall, this bill affects U.S. businesses that export sensitive technology (like semiconductors, AI, or biotech) by potentially creating new restrictions on sales to China. It also affects how federal agencies work together, giving Defense, State, and Energy officials more direct influence over export rules that were previously handled mainly through Commerce Department channels.

title: Northern Border Security Enhancement and Review Act
ai_summary:
This bill updates a 2016 law called the Northern Border Security Review Act, which requires the Department of Homeland Security to study security threats along the U.S.-Canada border and create strategies to address them. The new bill requires DHS to update its threat analysis by September 2, 2025, and then every three years after that, instead of just doing it once. It also adds a new requirement that the analysis include information about changes in the number and types of people apprehended at the northern border, broken down by region.

The bill also requires DHS to update its overall northern border security strategy by September 2, 2026, and then every five years after that, using the latest threat analysis as a basis. After each threat analysis is completed, DHS must brief relevant congressional committees on the findings within 30 days, using a classified (secure) briefing since the information may be sensitive. Additionally, the Customs and Border Protection agency must create ways to measure how well its Air and Marine Operations division is doing at securing the northern border by air and water.

This bill mainly affects DHS, Customs and Border Protection, and Congress by creating ongoing reporting and review requirements rather than changing how the border is physically secured. It does not authorize any new government spending, meaning agencies would need to carry out these requirements using their existing budgets. Everyday residents, especially those living in northern border states, may see indirect effects through improved oversight and planning, but the bill does not create new programs, change immigration law, or provide new funding for border operations.
ai_headline: Bill sets recurring schedule for northern border threat reviews
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

title: Space Commerce Advisory Committee Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new advisory group called the Commercial Space Activity Advisory Committee, run through the Commerce Department's Office of Space Commerce. Within 180 days of the law passing, the Secretary of Commerce would appoint 15 people to this committee, chosen from fields like space policy, engineering, law, science, and finance. These members would need real experience in the commercial space industry, and generally cannot be current federal employees. Each person would serve a four-year term and would have to wait two years before serving again.

The committee's job would be to advise the government on how private companies operate in space, such as satellites and spacecraft. Specifically, it would study challenges facing U.S. space businesses, including international rules, export controls, interference with space operations, and access to radio frequencies needed for communication. It would also look at best practices for avoiding contamination of the Moon and other celestial bodies, and for preventing harm to Earth's environment from material brought back from space. The committee would report its findings and recommendations to both the Secretary of Commerce and Congress, and it would automatically shut down 10 years after it's created unless further action is taken.

This bill mainly affects the commercial space industry (companies building or operating satellites, spacecraft, and related technology), as well as the federal government's role in overseeing and supporting that industry. Everyday Americans would only be indirectly affected, mainly through how this could shape future space-related policies, regulations, and business growth in the space sector.

title: DeOndra Dixon INCLUDE Project Act of 2025
ai_summary:

The bill requires the NIH to coordinate this research across its various institutes and offices to avoid duplicating existing work, and to provide technical support to researchers and organizations receiving grants. It also affects researchers, hospitals, and universities that may receive federal grants or contracts to conduct this work, as well as NIH staff who would oversee and coordinate the program.

title: A bill to amend the Help America Vote Act of 2002 to require voters to provide photo identification.
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal election law to require voters to show a photo ID before casting a ballot in federal elections. It would update the Help America Vote Act of 2002, which currently sets minimum standards for how elections are run and what identification can be requested at polling places. Right now, states have different rules — some require photo ID, some accept other forms of identification like a utility bill, and some don't require ID at all for voters who are already registered. This bill would create a stricter, uniform photo ID requirement that would apply nationwide for federal elections.

The bill would affect everyday voters, especially those who don't currently have a driver's license, passport, or other government-issued photo ID. This can include some elderly voters, people with disabilities, low-income individuals, rural residents without easy access to ID offices, and some minority voters who studies have shown are statistically less likely to possess photo ID. States and local election officials would also be affected, since they would need to adjust their voter verification procedures, poll worker training, and possibly provide ways for voters without ID to obtain one.

Supporters of photo ID laws generally argue they help prevent voter fraud and increase public confidence in election security. Critics argue such laws can make voting harder for certain groups and point to research showing voter impersonation fraud is rare. Because this is a short bill text without full details, specific provisions — such as what forms of ID would be accepted, whether free IDs would be provided, or how exceptions might work — aren't fully described here.
ai_headline: Bill would mandate photo ID for voting in all federal elections
last_action_text: Cloture on the motion to proceed to the measure not invoked in Senate by Yea-Nay Vote. 52 - 46. Record Vote Number: 231.

title: Indian Health Service Emergency Claims Parity Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes the rules for how long American Indian patients (or their health care providers) have to notify the Indian Health Service (IHS) after receiving emergency medical care from a non-IHS hospital or doctor. Currently, notification deadlines can vary, but this bill sets a clear 15-day window as the standard time limit for most patients to notify IHS that they received emergency care outside the IHS system. This notification is required for the IHS to cover or reimburse the cost of that emergency treatment.

The bill also preserves special rules that already exist for elderly and disabled Indian patients, meaning their notification requirements stay as they currently are under separate provisions of the law. In effect, this creates more consistency ("parity") between different groups of patients when it comes to emergency care billing deadlines, while still giving extra flexibility to elderly and disabled patients who may need more time or different rules.

This bill mainly affects Native American and Alaska Native individuals who rely on the Indian Health Service for health coverage, as well as hospitals and clinics that treat these patients in emergencies and need to bill IHS. It could also affect IHS administrators who process these claims, since a clearer, more uniform deadline may reduce confusion or disputes over late notifications and help ensure patients' emergency bills get paid.

title: Crow Revenue Act
ai_summary:
S. 239, the Crow Revenue Act, sets up a three-way land and mineral swap involving the federal government, the Crow Tribe of Montana, and the Hope Family Trust, a private family trust. The federal government would take back a coal lease in the Bull Mountains area of Musselshell County if the current leaseholder gives it up, and then transfer those mineral and surface rights to the Hope Family Trust. In exchange, the Hope Family Trust would give up its mineral rights on land within the Crow Reservation in Big Horn County, and those rights would be transferred to the Crow Tribe. If the Tribe requests it, the federal government would hold these new mineral rights in trust for the Tribe, meaning the land would have special legal protections and would not be taxed by the state of Montana or local governments.

Before this exchange happens, the Tribe and the Hope Family Trust must agree in writing on how they will share any future revenue if the Bull Mountains minerals are ever developed. The bill also makes clear that gaining these mineral rights will not cause the Tribe or its members to lose any other federal benefits or services they already receive. In short, this bill mainly affects the Crow Tribe, the Hope Family Trust, and federal land management in these two specific areas of Montana, giving the Tribe more control over mineral resources on its reservation while compensating the Hope family with different mineral rights elsewhere.
ai_headline: Bill sets up land swap giving Crow Tribe mineral rights on its reservation
last_action_text: Committee on Indian Affairs. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

The Tribe and Trust must first agree in writing on sharing any future revenue from the Bull Mountains minerals.

title: CHATBOT Act
ai_summary:
**S. 4407 — CHATBOT Act**

This bill would require websites and apps whose main purpose is offering an AI chatbot (like general-purpose conversational AI, not customer service bots or educational tools) to put special safeguards in place for young users. If a company knows a user is under 13, it must set up a "family account" that lets a parent control settings before the child can use the chatbot. If a user is a teen (13-17), the company must notify a parent and get verifiable parental consent before the teen can create an account, though parents can choose not to set up a full family account—in which case the strictest privacy and safety settings automatically apply. Existing accounts for kids and teens who haven't met these requirements must be shut down, and their personal data deleted (with a 90-day window to retrieve it first).

For accounts covered by parental controls, parents would get tools to limit screen time, turn off notifications and reward features, block financial transactions, view conversation logs, and control how long the chatbot remembers a child's data. Companies would also be banned from using kids' or teens' personal data for targeted advertising. Companies aren't required to demand ID or collect extra personal data just to verify someone's age—they only have to act on what they already reasonably know. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce the law, and it wouldn't override stricter state laws or existing laws like COPPA and FERPA.

This mainly affects companies that build AI chatbot products (like general-purpose AI assistants) and families with children or teens who use them. It gives parents more oversight and privacy protections for younger users while trying to avoid forcing broad age-verification systems on all users. The bill also calls for a government study on how chatbots affect kids' and teens' social development and mental health, plus a follow-up report on how well the law is working. It would take effect one year after being signed into law.
ai_headline: Bill would require parental controls for AI chatbot apps used by kids
last_action_text: Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

title: Youth AI Privacy Act
ai_summary:
The Youth AI Privacy Act is a Senate bill aimed at protecting minors who use AI chatbots. If a company knows a user is under 18, it would have to clearly tell that user they're talking to a computer, not a human, at the start of each session and every 30 minutes afterward. The bill also directs the Federal Trade Commission to write rules limiting how long companies can use a minor's personal data to personalize chatbot responses, and to ban design features that encourage compulsive use, such as push notifications, reward badges, unprompted messages, and fake "typing" indicators meant to mimic human conversation.

The bill also restricts how companies can use minors' data more broadly. It bans advertising to minors through chatbots, prohibits using their data to build psychological or behavioral profiles, and generally prevents companies from using minors' conversations to train their AI systems (with narrow exceptions for safety testing). It includes whistleblower protections for employees who report violations, funds federal research into how AI chatbots affect young people's mental health, and requires the CDC to start asking about chatbot use in national health surveys.

This bill would primarily affect companies that build or offer AI chatbots (like companion apps, virtual assistants, or general-purpose chatbots) when they know a user is a minor, requiring changes to how they design, disclose, and handle data for those users. It would also affect parents, who could sue companies directly for violations, and state attorneys general, who could bring enforcement actions. Everyday teenage users would be the main beneficiaries, gaining new disclosures, privacy protections, and design safeguards, while parents and regulators would gain new tools to hold AI companies accountable.
ai_headline: Senate bill would force AI chatbots to disclose they aren't human to minors
last_action_text: Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

title: Children's Artificial Intelligence Toy Safety Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Children's Artificial Intelligence Toy Safety Act of 2026, directs the federal government to study toys that use artificial intelligence to talk or interact with children. Specifically, it requires the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine to research how these AI-enabled toys and chatbots might affect kids physically, mentally, emotionally, and socially. The study would also look at how these toys affect learning, whether parents actually use safety controls built into the toys, whether marketing these products to children raises ethical or legal concerns, and whether the risks are serious enough that selling these toys to kids should be temporarily paused.

After the study, the Federal Trade Commission and the Consumer Product Safety Commission would have two years to create a joint action plan for Congress and relevant House and Senate committees. This plan would include recommendations for new laws or regulations, rules requiring companies to disclose when AI is built into a toy, safety guidelines or reviews for these products, and possibly restrictions on selling certain AI toys. It would also outline plans to educate consumers and the public about the risks and features of AI-enabled toys.

This bill mainly affects parents and children who use or might buy AI-powered toys, as well as toy manufacturers and AI developers who create these products. It does not immediately ban or regulate any toys — instead, it sets up a process to study the issue and develop future recommendations, which could lead to new rules or restrictions later on.
ai_headline: Bill orders federal study of AI-powered talking toys for children
last_action_text: Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

title: BEACON Act of 2026
ai_summary:
The BEACON Act of 2026 directs the Department of Veterans Affairs to create two new grant programs aimed at improving treatment for veterans with chronic mild traumatic brain injury (TBI), a common condition among service members exposed to blasts or head injuries during their service. The first program, called the TBI Innovation Grant Program, would award up to $5 million per year to nonprofits, universities, and health care providers to develop and test new, often non-drug-based rehabilitation treatments. The goal is to improve mental health outcomes, reduce suicide risk, and address long-term effects of mild TBI. This program would also coordinate with the VA's existing suicide prevention efforts and would run for three years, with $30 million total authorized through 2028.

The second program sets up a separate research grant system, managed with help from an independent research organization similar to the VA's National Center for PTSD. This program would fund smaller pilot studies (up to $625,000 each) and larger multi-site research projects (up to $1.5 million each) to study which TBI treatments work best, with the goal of eventually establishing a standard of care. It would be funded at $10 million per year through 2028, and results would be reported to Congress to help guide future VA policy.

Overall, this bill mainly affects veterans dealing with brain injuries, VA health programs, and the researchers, hospitals, and nonprofit organizations that study and treat TBI. It does not change veterans' benefits directly but instead funds research and pilot treatment programs intended to improve future care.
ai_headline: VA bill would fund new grants for mild brain injury treatment research

title: SAFE VISITS Act
ai_summary:
This bill, known as the SAFE VISITS Act, would require the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to help state, local, tribal, and territorial governments deal with security risks when foreign visitors want to meet with officials or gain access to government buildings, records, or computer systems. DHS would have to create yearly threat reports covering which government offices or facilities are considered high-risk targets, trends in foreign visitor access requests, and steps that can be taken to reduce security risks, including possible terrorism threats.

If DHS identifies a specific local or state office as a likely target, the bill requires DHS to reach out directly, share relevant threat information, help vet the foreign visitor, and offer guidance on how to handle the visit safely. After the visit happens, DHS would ask the local government for a debriefing to learn what happened and identify any suspicious behavior for future reference. DHS would also work on developing new technology to make sharing this security information easier and faster.

This bill mainly affects government employees and offices at the state, local, tribal, and territorial level, especially those who regularly interact with foreign delegations, since it gives them new resources and support from DHS. It does not directly affect ordinary citizens, but it could indirectly improve safety and security at public buildings and institutions where residents interact with local government services.
ai_headline: Bill would have DHS help local governments vet foreign visitor security risks

title: Veteran Infection Prevention Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires people who work as sterile processing technicians at Veterans Affairs (VA) hospitals to hold an official professional certification for that job. Sterile processing technicians are the staff who clean, disinfect, and prepare medical instruments and equipment so they are safe to use on patients. Properly sterilized equipment is critical for preventing infections, so this bill aims to make sure VA facilities meet the same certification standards often expected in other hospitals.

Under the bill, new hires (except those in entry-level positions) would need to get certified within two years of being appointed to the job. Current VA employees who already work as sterile processing technicians but are not yet certified would have two years after the law passes before the requirement applies to them. To help these current employees meet the new standard, the VA would be required to give them scholarships to pay for the certification training. In exchange, employees who receive this scholarship money would need to agree to keep working for the VA for two years after becoming certified.

This bill mainly affects VA employees who work in sterile processing roles and, indirectly, veterans who receive care at VA hospitals, since properly trained technicians play a role in preventing infections during medical procedures. It does not affect sterile processing staff outside the VA system or apply to other government agencies.

title: Civil Rights Cold Case Records Collection Reauthorization Act
ai_summary:
This bill updates a 2018 law that created a system for collecting and releasing government records related to unsolved civil rights-era cases, often involving violence or discrimination from decades ago. It strengthens the powers of the Civil Rights Cold Case Records Review Board, the group responsible for gathering these records and deciding when they can be made public.

Specifically, the bill states that Congress believes these records should generally be presumed open for release so the public can fully understand this history. It allows the Review Board to reimburse state and local governments for costs like digitizing, photocopying, or mailing records they submit. It also removes an exception that let state or local governments withhold certain records from being sent in, meaning they would now be required to transmit them like federal agencies do. Additionally, it changes privacy rules so that a specific privacy protection (which normally lets agencies withhold personal information that would invade someone's privacy) would no longer apply to records created on or before January 1, 1990, making older records easier to release fully.

Finally, the bill extends how long the Review Board can operate, changing its authorized lifespan from 7 years to 11 years. This affects historians, journalists, families of victims, and researchers who rely on these records, as well as state and local governments that hold relevant documents and may now get more support and clearer rules for submitting them.
ai_headline: Bill extends civil rights cold case records board and eases release rules
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 36 - 4.

title: National Fossil Act
ai_summary:
HR 9191, the "National Fossil Act," would officially designate the American mastodon as the national fossil mammal of the United States and the Tyrannosaurus rex as the national fossil dinosaur. It does this by adding a new section to an existing part of federal law (title 36 of the U.S. Code) that already contains other national symbols, such as the national bird. The bill also updates the chapter heading and table of contents to reflect this addition.

This is a symbolic, ceremonial bill. It does not change any laws related to fossil excavation, land use, funding, or research. It does not create new regulations, spending programs, or enforcement actions. In practice, it affects no one directly—no businesses, agencies, or individuals would need to change their behavior or follow new rules.

The main groups likely to care about this bill are paleontology enthusiasts, museums, educators, and science communicators, who might see it as a way to boost public interest in fossils and natural history. Similar symbolic designations (like the national bird or national flower) are often introduced to promote civic pride or educational themes rather than to solve a practical policy problem.

last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 22 - 1.

title: Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2026
ai_summary:
This bill sets the budget for the Department of Commerce, Department of Justice, and related science agencies for fiscal year 2026 (October 2025 through September 2026). It's one of the annual "appropriations bills" Congress passes to fund federal agencies. For Commerce, it provides money for things like the Census Bureau, the Patent and Trademark Office, NOAA (weather forecasting, ocean research, fisheries), the National Institute of Standards and Technology, export/trade programs, and economic development grants for communities. For Justice, it funds the FBI, DEA, ATF, federal prisons, U.S. Attorneys, U.S. Marshals, immigration courts, drug task forces, and victim assistance programs like those helping survivors of domestic violence and human trafficking.

In practical terms, this bill decides how many dollars each agency and program gets to operate for the year — for example, how much the FBI has for investigations, how much NOAA has for weather satellites and fishery science, how much goes to federal prisons, and how much supports patent processing or the census. It also includes detailed rules about how agencies can spend the money, such as limits on travel expenses, requirements to notify Congress before shifting funds between programs, and specific funding set-asides (like money for salmon conservation in Pacific states or methamphetamine lab cleanup).

This bill affects nearly everyone indirectly: businesses that rely on patents or trade programs, coastal communities and fishermen affected by NOAA programs, people going through federal courts or immigration proceedings, federal prisoners and staff, scientists using NIST research facilities, and taxpayers generally, since it determines how tax dollars are allocated across these agencies. It does not create new laws or policies on its own — it mainly funds existing federal programs and agencies for one year, with some specific spending conditions attached.

title: Stop Corrupt Trading Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Stop Corrupt Trading Act, would make it a federal crime for the President or Vice President to sell or trade nonpublic information they learn through their official duties for financial gain. "Nonpublic information" is defined broadly to include anything not available to the general public, such as material that's normally exempt from public records requests, marked confidential, or shared selectively rather than released to everyone equally. It also bans anyone else from buying, selling, or trading that kind of information for financial benefit, and it applies to businesses or entities controlled by or significantly owned by the President, Vice President, or their immediate family.

The bill sets up both criminal and civil penalties. Someone convicted could face up to 5 years in prison and fines up to double the value of the transaction, along with having to forfeit any profits gained. The Attorney General could also sue violators in civil court, seeking to recover profits, impose additional penalties (at least $250,000 or three times the financial gain, whichever is larger), and get court orders like injunctions. People or companies who knowingly participated in these deals could also be held financially responsible. The Office of Government Ethics would be required to report any credible evidence of this kind of misconduct to the Justice Department and to Congress's judiciary committees.

This bill mainly affects the President, Vice President, their family members, and any businesses connected to them, as well as anyone who might try to buy or profit from inside information tied to the presidency. Everyday Americans would not be directly affected unless they were knowingly involved in buying or trading this kind of nonpublic government information.
ai_headline: Bill would criminalize president trading on nonpublic government information

title: Federal Building Threat Notification Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Federal Building Threat Notification Act, would require the Federal Protective Service (the agency that provides security for federal buildings) to create official guidelines for warning people inside those buildings when there's a dangerous situation happening. This includes things like active shooter events, other weapons threats, terrorism, or suspicious packages found in the building or within about 150 feet of it. The goal is to make sure workers get clear, timely instructions on how to stay safe during these emergencies.

The bill also requires each federal building to have a designated safety official responsible for putting these guidelines into practice, and it directs the Federal Protective Service to regularly test whether employees are prepared to respond to these kinds of emergencies. Within one year, the agency must report back to Congress on what safety practices have been put in place and brief lawmakers on what additional resources might be needed.

This bill mainly affects federal employees and other people who work in or visit federal buildings protected by the Federal Protective Service, since it aims to improve how they are notified and instructed during security threats. It would also affect the agencies responsible for managing building security, since they would have new responsibilities for creating safety plans, appointing officials, and reporting to Congress.

title: Federal Program Integrity and Fraud Prevention Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Federal Program Integrity and Fraud Prevention Act of 2026, aims to keep people who commit certain federal fraud-related crimes from getting government contracts, grants, or loans for a period of time. It creates a new rule requiring that anyone convicted of specific federal felonies connected to a federal contract, grant, loan, or other financial assistance be automatically placed on a government-wide "exclusion list" for three years. This list, called the System for Award Management Exclusions list, is used by federal agencies to check whether a person or business is barred from receiving federal money or contracts. The covered crimes include things like fraud, bribery, identity theft, computer crimes, embezzlement, and false statements to the government.

The bill allows some flexibility: the head of a federal agency can grant a written exemption if they believe it's justified, but they must immediately report that decision to Congress. It also clarifies that agencies can still pursue other legal actions, like criminal charges or separate suspension/debarment proceedings, in addition to this exclusion. The Attorney General would be responsible for notifying the General Services Administration when someone is convicted, so that person can be promptly added to the exclusion list. Within a year of the law passing, the Department of Justice and General Services Administration would need to issue official guidance explaining how this new process should work.

This bill would mainly affect individuals convicted of federal fraud-related crimes tied to government programs, federal contractors and grant recipients, and the federal agencies that manage contracts, grants, and loans. Everyday taxpayers could be indirectly affected since the goal is to reduce fraud and misuse of federal funds, but the direct impact falls on people or businesses seeking or holding federal contracts and financial assistance.

title: PEACE Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the PEACE Act, would require the U.S. State Department to regularly update Congress on antisemitism and terrorism threats in Europe. Specifically, it directs a State Department official, the Assistant Secretary for European and Eurasian Affairs, to brief the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Senate Foreign Relations Committee within 180 days of the bill becoming law, and then once a year for two more years after that.

The bill also states Congress's opinion (called a "sense of Congress") that the State Department should treat rising antisemitism and terrorism in Europe as a serious foreign policy concern, and that U.S. diplomats should work with European governments to address these issues, especially where they might threaten American citizens or institutions overseas.

This bill mainly affects the State Department, which would take on new reporting duties, and members of Congress on the relevant committees, who would receive this information. It does not create new laws, funding, or programs affecting the general public directly; it is primarily about improving communication between the executive branch and Congress on this specific foreign policy issue.
