title: A bill to require the United States Postal Service to designate ZIP Codes for certain communities.
ai_summary:
This bill would require the U.S. Postal Service to give a specific list of towns, cities, and communities across the country their own unique ZIP Code within one year of the law being passed. The bill lists 75 named places across many states, including communities in California, Colorado, Florida, Texas, and others. Right now, these communities either share a ZIP Code with a neighboring area or use a ZIP Code officially assigned to a different town, even though they are their own distinct city or community.

Having a unique ZIP Code matters because it affects how a community is identified in mail delivery, government records, business listings, insurance rates, school district boundaries, and even how the community's identity is recognized on maps and by data systems. Communities without their own ZIP Code sometimes feel "invisible" in official records, since mail and address systems associate them with a different town's name.

This bill would primarily affect residents, local governments, and businesses in the 75 listed communities, giving them clearer identification through their own postal designation. It would also require the Postal Service to do the administrative work of creating and assigning these new ZIP Codes. Residents of other communities not on this list would not be affected, and the bill does not change any other Postal Service operations, rates, or services.

title: Combating Trafficking in Transportation Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Combating Trafficking in Transportation Act, changes federal transportation law to make it easier for states and local governments to put up human trafficking awareness signs at highway rest stops and welcome centers. It adds this signage as an approved use of certain federal transportation grant programs, meaning states can use existing funding streams to pay for these signs without extra red tape. It also removes some cost-sharing and matching requirements that would normally apply to these types of projects, making it simpler and cheaper for states to install the signs.

The bill also updates an existing federal advisory committee on human trafficking in commercial vehicles, which was created by a 2017 law. title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Department of Energy relating to "Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Consumer Gas-fired Instantaneous Water Heaters".

title: To require the Administrator of the Transportation Security Administration of the United States to develop guidelines to improve returning citizens' access to the Transportation Worker Identification Credential program, to assist individuals in custody of Federal, State, and local prisons in pre-applying or preparing applications for Transportation Worker Identification Credential cards, and to assist individuals requesting an appeal or waiver of preliminary determination of ineligibility, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) to make it easier for people leaving prison to get a Transportation Worker Identification Credential (TWIC card). A TWIC card is a security badge required for many jobs at ports, on ships, and in industries like oil and gas that need access to secure maritime facilities. Currently, people in prison cannot even begin the application process until after release, and the appeal or waiver process for those with certain past convictions can take up to 90 days, which can delay someone's ability to get a job right after leaving prison.

Under this bill, TSA would have one year to create guidelines helping incarcerated individuals start or prepare their TWIC card applications before they are released, and to help people navigate the appeals or waiver process if they are initially told they're ineligible due to their criminal record. TSA would also have to report back to Congress on what improvements have been made to access the program. The bill does not guarantee anyone a TWIC card or change the eligibility rules themselves—it focuses on speeding up and simplifying the application and appeals process.

This mainly affects people recently released from federal, state, or local prisons who want jobs in port-related or maritime industries, especially in states like Louisiana where many jobs depend on having a TWIC card. It could also affect TSA, which will need to create new guidance and procedures, and employers in the maritime and energy sectors who rely on a steady workforce with proper security clearance.
ai_headline: Bill would let inmates start port security card applications before release

title: A bill to require the Secretary of Agriculture to release a reversionary interest in certain land in the Black River State Forest in Millston, Wisconsin, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill deals with a specific piece of government-controlled land in the Black River State Forest near Millston, Wisconsin. Back when this forest land was given to Wisconsin, the federal government kept what's called a "reversionary interest," meaning the land would revert to federal ownership if it stopped being used for public purposes. This bill directs the Secretary of Agriculture to release that federal claim on about 31.83 acres of state forest land, but only if Wisconsin agrees to trade that land to a private company called Deli, Inc., a sphagnum moss producer in the area, in exchange for about 37.27 acres of land that Deli, Inc. owns or has the right to buy. Once the trade happens, the land Deli, Inc. gives up would become part of the state forest.

Practically, this bill lets a specific state-federal-private land swap move forward. Wisconsin's state government and Deli, Inc. have already worked out an agreement to trade parcels of land, but the federal government's old ownership claim on the state forest land needed to be officially lifted before the trade could be finalized. This bill removes that federal legal obstacle by having the Secretary of Agriculture issue a formal deed giving up any U.S. government claim to the land, once Wisconsin formally agrees to the exchange.

This mainly affects the state of Wisconsin's Department of Natural Resources, Deli, Inc. (a small business), and the federal Department of Agriculture, which manages this type of land arrangement. It does not affect people outside this specific local land deal, and it doesn't change any broader national policy — it is narrowly written to resolve one property transaction in Jackson County, Wisconsin.
ai_headline: Bill clears way for Wisconsin land swap with moss producer Deli, Inc.
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 209.

title: Skills-Based Federal Contracting Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the federal government can require college degrees or other education credentials when hiring outside contractors to do work for federal agencies. Under current rules, agencies can list a minimum education level, like a bachelor's degree, as a requirement for contractor employees who will work on a project. This bill says agencies generally cannot do that anymore unless the contracting officer writes a formal explanation showing why the agency's needs cannot be met without that education requirement and how it actually ensures the work gets done properly. The idea is to shift the focus toward skills and experience rather than degrees alone.

The bill also directs the White House's Office of Management and Budget to write guidance within 180 days telling agencies how to handle these justifications and encouraging them to consider alternatives to degree requirements, such as relevant work experience or demonstrated skills. It repeals an older law from 2000 that dealt with similar contractor education rules, once the new guidance takes effect. The new rules would apply to contract announcements issued about 15 months after the bill becomes law, giving agencies time to adjust. The Government Accountability Office would also study, after three years, how well agencies are following this new law.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies that hire contractors, the companies that bid on federal contracts, and workers seeking contractor jobs with the government. Workers without traditional four-year degrees but with strong experience or specialized skills could have an easier time qualifying for federal contract work. Companies bidding on contracts may have more flexibility in hiring, while agencies would need to more carefully justify any education requirements they still want to include.
ai_headline: Bill would limit degree requirements for federal contractor jobs
last_action_text: Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

This bill renames the United States Postal Service building located at 80 Prospect Street in Avon, New York, giving it the official name "Officer Anthony Mazurkiewicz Memorial Post Office Building." This is a common type of congressional action used to honor individuals, often local police officers, firefighters, veterans, or other community figures, by naming a federal building after them. The bill also specifies that any future official references to this post office in laws, maps, or government documents must use the new name.

This bill primarily affects residents of Avon, New York, and the surrounding area who use this particular post office, as well as the USPS, which will need to update signage and records to reflect the new name. It does not change postal services, operations, or funding in any way; it is a symbolic gesture honoring Officer Anthony Mazurkiewicz. Bills like this are typically non-controversial and are usually introduced by local representatives to recognize a person's service or sacrifice to their community.

title: Midnight Rules Relief Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Midnight Rules Relief Act of 2025, would change how Congress can reject federal regulations that are finalized near the end of a president's term, often called "midnight rules." Under current law, Congress has the power to review new federal agency regulations and pass a resolution disapproving them, which cancels the rule. However, current rules require Congress to vote separately on each regulation it wants to overturn, one at a time.

This bill would allow Congress to bundle multiple midnight rules together into a single resolution of disapproval, as long as those rules were reported to Congress during the final year of a president's term. Instead of holding a separate vote for each rule, lawmakers could vote once to reject several regulations at the same time, which would make the process faster and more efficient.

This bill mainly affects how Congress operates internally and how federal agencies' regulations get reviewed, rather than directly affecting individual citizens right away. However, it could have a bigger effect on regulations issued at the end of a presidential term, particularly if control of the White House or Congress changes hands. It would make it easier for the incoming Congress and president to overturn a wave of last-minute regulations from the previous administration, which could affect environmental rules, labor rules, health regulations, or other policies depending on which rules are targeted.
ai_headline: Bill would let Congress bundle late-term "midnight rules" into one vote
last_action_text: Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: The Midnight Rules Relief Act would let Congress reject multiple end-of-term federal regulations with a single vote instead of one at a time.
ai_sections.what: This bill, the Midnight Rules Relief Act of 2025, would let Congress bundle multiple "midnight rules" into one resolution of disapproval, as long as those rules were reported to Congress during the final year of a president's term. Currently, Congress must vote separately on each regulation it wants to overturn; this bill would allow a single vote to reject several at once.
ai_sections.who: This affects Congress's internal review process and federal agencies whose regulations are issued near the end of a presidential term. It could especially matter to an incoming Congress and president, particularly when control of the White House or Congress changes hands.
ai_sections.why: By speeding up and simplifying the disapproval process, the bill would make it easier to overturn a wave of late-term regulations at once, potentially affecting environmental, labor, health, or other policies depending on which rules are targeted.

title: Promoting Resilient Buildings Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Promoting Resilient Buildings Act, makes changes to federal disaster preparedness law to help homes and communities better withstand natural disasters like floods, hurricanes, tornadoes, earthquakes, and wildfires. It updates rules under FEMA's pre-disaster hazard mitigation program, clarifying that "latest published editions" of building codes means the two most recent versions of relevant safety standards. It also removes an outdated provision from FEMA's hazard mitigation revolving loan fund program, which helps states set up loan funds for disaster-resistant construction projects.

The main new element is a Residential Retrofit and Resilience Pilot Program, which FEMA must create within one year and run through September 2030. This program would give money to states and local governments, who would then provide grants directly to individual homeowners for projects that make their homes more disaster-resistant. Examples include elevating homes in flood zones, building tornado safe rooms, reinforcing roofs against wind damage, adding earthquake retrofits, and improving wildfire protection. FEMA can spend up to 10% of its existing pre-disaster mitigation funding on this program, and priority must go to homeowners who show financial need.

This bill primarily affects homeowners, especially those in disaster-prone areas and with lower incomes, by potentially giving them access to grants for home safety upgrades. It also affects state and local governments, which would apply for and distribute this funding, and FEMA, which must set up the program, oversee it, and report to Congress after four years on how well it worked, including costs, results, and lessons learned. Homebuilders, contractors, and disaster-preparedness advocates may also be affected as demand for retrofit work could increase.
ai_headline: New FEMA pilot would fund home upgrades against floods and storms
last_action_text: Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: FEMA must launch a pilot program giving homeowners grants for disaster-resistant home upgrades.
ai_sections.what: The bill updates FEMA's hazard mitigation rules, including clarifying building code standards and removing an outdated loan fund provision. It also creates a Residential Retrofit and Resilience Pilot Program, requiring FEMA to launch it within a year and run it through September 2030, funding home upgrades like flood elevation, tornado safe rooms, and wildfire protection.
ai_sections.who: Homeowners in disaster-prone areas, especially lower-income ones, would be eligible for grants distributed through state and local governments. FEMA, state and local governments, and homebuilders or contractors would also be affected.
ai_sections.why: The changes could increase demand for retrofit construction work and shift some federal disaster funding toward direct household-level grants rather than other mitigation uses.

title: Permitting Transparency and Accountability Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require federal agencies that issue permits to create a webpage showing the status of permit applications. Any business or individual applying for a federal permit—such as environmental, construction, or energy-related permits—would be able to check this webpage to see how their application is progressing.

The webpage would need to show specific details: which review stages have been completed, how many days each stage took, how long the application has been sitting at its current stage, contact information for the people reviewing it (including at other agencies involved in the review), what steps remain before a final decision, and an estimated timeline for when a decision will be made. This applies not just to the main agency issuing the permit, but also to any other agency involved in reviewing or processing that permit application.

The bill mainly affects federal agencies, which would have new administrative and technical work to set up and maintain these tracking webpages. It would also affect businesses, developers, and individuals who apply for federal permits, giving them more visibility into where their application stands and who to contact, rather than having to guess or repeatedly ask agency staff for updates. The bill does not change how permits are approved or denied—it only requires agencies to be more transparent about the process and timeline.
ai_headline: Bill would require agencies to post online trackers for permit applications
last_action_text: Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: Federal agencies would have to create webpages tracking the status of permit applications.
ai_sections.what: This bill requires federal agencies that issue permits to create a webpage showing each application's status, including completed review stages, time spent at each stage, reviewer contact information, remaining steps, and an estimated decision timeline. This applies to the main permitting agency and any other agency involved in reviewing the application.

title: GOOD Act
ai_summary:
**S. 252 — The GOOD Act** requires federal agencies to publish their "guidance documents" online in one central, easy-to-find location. Guidance documents are things like memos, bulletins, letters, or notices that explain how an agency interprets laws or regulations, even though they aren't official rules that carry the force of law. Right now, these documents can be scattered across different websites or hard to locate, making it difficult for businesses, lawyers, and everyday citizens to know how an agency actually intends to enforce or interpret the rules that affect them.

Under this bill, the Office of Management and Budget would pick a website within 90 days where all guidance documents must be posted. Each agency would then have to publish new guidance there as soon as it's issued, and post any existing guidance within 180 days of the law passing. Agencies would also need to organize the documents into clear categories and provide a visible link from their own websites. If a guidance document is later withdrawn or canceled, the agency must keep a record of it online, noting when and why it was rescinded, including any related court case.

This bill would mainly affect federal agencies, which would face new organizational and publishing requirements. It would also affect businesses, lawyers, journalists, and members of the public who rely on understanding federal guidance to comply with regulations or challenge agency actions, since it aims to make this information more transparent and centralized. Documents that are legally exempt from public disclosure, such as those protected under the Freedom of Information Act, would not be affected by this requirement.
ai_headline: Bill would force agencies to post all guidance documents in one place
last_action_text: Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: S. 252 would require federal agencies to publish all guidance documents on one central website within set deadlines.
ai_sections.what: S. 252, the GOOD Act, requires federal agencies to publish their guidance documents online in one central location chosen by the Office of Management and Budget within 90 days. Agencies must post new guidance as it's issued and existing guidance within 180 days, organized into categories with a visible link from agency websites. Withdrawn guidance must remain listed online with the date and reason for rescission.
ai_sections.who: Federal agencies must meet new publishing and organizational requirements. Businesses, lawyers, journalists, and the public who rely on agency guidance to understand or challenge federal rules are also affected.
ai_sections.why: The change is meant to make it easier to find how agencies interpret and plan to enforce laws and regulations, since such documents are currently scattered across different sites. Documents exempt from disclosure under laws like FOIA would not be affected.

title: CIPZIP Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the CIPZIP Act of 2025, creates a temporary program allowing the U.S. Postal Service to accept money, property, or services from state, local, or tribal governments to help cover the costs of changing or redrawing ZIP code boundaries. Normally, if a community requests a ZIP code change and the Postal Service says no because it would be too expensive, that request often just gets denied. Under this new program, the Postal Service would instead have to tell the requesting government about this cost-sharing option, provide an estimate of what the change would cost, and give the government at least 30 days to propose a way to cover that cost. If the only reason for denying the request was cost, and the community can pay for it, the Postal Service must approve the change.

This would mainly affect local, state, and tribal governments that want to adjust ZIP code boundaries—for example, to fix confusing mail delivery areas, align ZIP codes with city or county lines, or support economic development tied to certain postal addresses. It also affects the Postal Service, which would need to track these requests and report yearly to Congress on how many were approved, denied, or resolved through cost-sharing agreements. Everyday residents could be affected indirectly if their community pursues a ZIP code change, since this could affect mailing addresses, shipping costs, or local identity tied to ZIP codes.

The program would run for seven years and then automatically end unless Congress renews it. The bill is mainly about testing whether allowing local governments to help pay for administrative costs can make it easier to get ZIP code boundaries changed.
ai_headline: New law would let towns pay USPS to redraw ZIP code boundaries
last_action_text: Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: A seven-year pilot lets local governments cover ZIP code change costs so USPS can no longer deny requests solely over expense.
ai_sections.what: The CIPZIP Act of 2025 creates a temporary program letting the Postal Service accept money, property, or services from state, local, or tribal governments to cover the cost of changing ZIP code boundaries. If cost is the only reason for denial, USPS must disclose the cost estimate, allow at least 30 days for a funding proposal, and approve the change if the government agrees to pay.
ai_sections.who: Local, state, and tribal governments seeking ZIP code boundary changes, and the U.S. Postal Service, which must track and report on requests. Residents may be indirectly affected through changes to mailing addresses or local identity.
ai_sections.why: The change could make it easier for communities to get ZIP code boundaries adjusted for reasons like delivery confusion or economic development, but it also shifts some administrative costs onto local governments. The program expires after seven years unless Congress renews it.

title: Duplication Scoring Act of 2025
ai_summary:
The Duplication Scoring Act of 2025 would create a new check on Congress before it passes major legislation. Under this bill, the Government Accountability Office (GAO), a federal watchdog agency, would review bills that have been formally reported by a congressional committee to see if they create a new federal program, office, or initiative that duplicates or overlaps with something that already exists. GAO already publishes annual reports identifying wasteful duplication across the government, and this bill would require lawmakers to check new bills against those existing findings.

If GAO finds that a bill risks creating this kind of overlap, it would have to identify the new program, point to the specific section of the bill creating it, and note which past GAO report flagged the similar existing program. This information would be sent to the committee handling the bill and to the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), which could then include it alongside its usual cost estimates for the legislation. GAO would also have to post this information publicly on its website.

This bill mainly affects how Congress operates internally—it does not change any public benefits, taxes, or programs directly. It would primarily impact congressional committees, the CBO, and GAO, giving lawmakers more information to consider before voting on legislation. Everyday Americans would only be affected indirectly, through the possibility of more informed decisions about government spending and reduced duplication of federal programs over time.
ai_headline: New bill would flag duplicate federal programs before Congress votes
last_action_text: Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: GAO would review major bills for duplicate federal programs and report findings before Congress votes.
ai_sections.what: The Duplication Scoring Act of 2025 would require GAO to review committee-reported bills to check if they create federal programs that duplicate existing ones. If overlap is found, GAO must identify the new program, cite the bill section creating it, and reference the past GAO report that flagged the similar program.
ai_sections.who: This affects congressional committees, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), and GAO. Everyday Americans are only indirectly affected through potentially more informed spending decisions.
ai_sections.why: The change could give lawmakers more information before voting, potentially reducing duplication in federal programs over time. It does not alter public benefits, taxes, or existing programs directly.

title: Bonuses for Cost-Cutters Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Bonuses for Cost-Cutters Act of 2025," creates a system to reward federal employees who identify wasteful government spending. If a federal worker spots money in their agency's budget that isn't needed—money that's just sitting unused without hurting the agency's mission—they can flag it. The agency's Inspector General and Chief Financial Officer would then review the claim to confirm the funds really are unnecessary "surplus." If confirmed, that money would generally be sent back to the U.S. Treasury to help reduce the deficit or national debt.

As an incentive, agencies would be allowed to keep up to 10% of the identified savings instead of returning all of it to the Treasury. Part of that retained money could be used to pay cash bonuses to the employees who found the savings, and any leftover funds could be used elsewhere within the agency. Agencies would also have to file annual reports tracking how much money was saved this way and how many bonuses were paid out, and the Office of Personnel Management and Government Accountability Office would oversee and periodically review how well the program is working. Notably, top agency officials—like agency heads, certain high-level executives, and board members of independent agencies—would be barred from receiving these cash bonuses themselves.

This bill would affect federal employees across government agencies, giving lower- and mid-level workers a financial incentive to find and report wasteful spending. It could also affect taxpayers broadly, since successfully identified savings would help reduce the federal deficit or debt. The program includes a built-in expiration: unless Congress acts again, most of these new rules would automatically end six years after the law takes effect.
ai_headline: Bill would pay federal workers bonuses for flagging wasteful spending
last_action_text: Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: Federal employees who identify unneeded agency funds could earn cash bonuses under a new six-year program.
ai_sections.what: The bill lets federal employees flag unused, unnecessary funds in their agency's budget for review by the Inspector General and Chief Financial Officer. If confirmed as surplus, the money generally returns to the Treasury, but agencies can keep up to 10% to pay bonuses to the employees who found it and cover other agency needs. The program automatically expires six years after enactment unless Congress renews it.
ai_sections.who: Federal employees across government agencies, especially lower- and mid-level workers, would be eligible for bonuses; top agency officials, senior executives, and independent agency board members are excluded. Taxpayers are affected broadly since recovered funds would go toward reducing the federal deficit or debt.
ai_sections.why: The measure changes financial incentives inside federal agencies and creates new reporting and oversight requirements for the Office of Personnel Management and Government Accountability Office. Its effects on actual savings or bonus payouts would depend on how agencies implement and report the process.
ai_sections.cost: Agencies could retain up to 10% of confirmed surplus funds instead of sending it all to the Treasury, using part of that for employee bonuses and the rest for other agency purposes.
costChips: Agencies keep up to 10% of savings

title: Recognizing the Role of Direct Support Professionals Act
ai_summary:
This bill asks the federal government to consider creating a separate job category for "direct support professionals" — workers who help people with intellectual and developmental disabilities with daily tasks like bathing, cooking, shopping, communication, and community activities. Right now, these workers are often lumped together with home health aides or personal care aides in official government job classification systems, even though their work is different and requires different skills. The bill points out that this field has a very high turnover rate (39%), and creating a distinct job category could help track this problem more accurately.

Specifically, the bill directs the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to consider adding this new job code the next time it updates the Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) system, which is the system federal agencies use to collect labor statistics. If the OMB decides not to create this new category, it must explain its reasoning in a report to Congress. Importantly, the bill does not require the change to happen — it only requires that OMB consider it and justify its decision if it says no.

This bill would primarily affect data collection and labor statistics rather than pay, benefits, or working conditions directly. It could indirectly help direct support professionals, employers, and policymakers by providing better data on worker shortages and turnover, which could inform future funding or policy decisions. The bill explicitly states no new federal money is authorized to implement it, so it has no direct budget impact.
ai_headline: Bill asks OMB to weigh new job category for disability support workers
last_action_text: Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: S 3211 directs OMB to consider a distinct job code for direct support professionals, who face 39% turnover.

ai_sections.who: Direct support professionals, their employers, and federal agencies collecting labor statistics; indirectly, policymakers deciding future funding.

title: PEARL Act
ai_summary:
**S. 4079 – The PEARL Act** would require the Department of Homeland Security, through U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), to create a pilot program that adopts dogs from local animal shelters and trains them as support dogs. These support dogs would join CBP's existing Support Canine Program, which typically provides comfort and morale assistance to CBP employees rather than performing law enforcement duties like drug or explosive detection.

The bill sets a timeline: CBP would have 60 days after the law passes to get the program running, and the pilot program would automatically end after three years unless further action is taken to continue it. The bill is fairly short and does not specify a budget, number of dogs, or detailed training requirements, leaving those operational details to CBP to work out.

This bill would primarily affect CBP employees, who may benefit from having support dogs available in their workplaces, and local animal shelters, which could see some dogs adopted into this federal program. It does not affect the general public directly, nor does it change immigration, customs, or border enforcement procedures.
ai_headline: Bill would have CBP adopt shelter dogs as workplace support animals
last_action_text: Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. Ordered to be reported with an amendment favorably.

These dogs would join CBP's existing Support Canine Program, which provides comfort and morale support rather than detection or law enforcement work. CBP would have 60 days to launch the program, which ends automatically after three years unless extended.

title: Improving Access to Workers’ Compensation for Injured Federal Workers Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would change the federal workers' compensation system to allow nurse practitioners and physician assistants to provide official medical care and evaluations for federal employees who get injured on the job. Currently, the law mainly recognizes doctors (including osteopathic physicians) for these purposes, which can make it harder for injured workers to get timely care, especially in areas where doctors are scarce but nurse practitioners or physician assistants are available.

Under this bill, nurse practitioners and physician assistants would be treated as "eligible providers" under the Federal Employees' Compensation Act, meaning they could examine injured workers, provide treatment, and give medical opinions that count for compensation claims, as long as they are acting within what their state law allows them to do. The bill also updates related rules, such as those covering second opinions in disputed cases, to include these providers alongside physicians.

This mainly affects federal employees who are injured at work and rely on the workers' compensation system, as well as the medical providers who treat them. It could make it easier and faster for injured federal workers to get evaluated and treated, particularly in rural or underserved areas. The Secretary of Labor would be required to write official rules to implement these changes within six months of the bill becoming law.
ai_headline: Bill would let nurse practitioners treat injured federal workers
last_action_text: Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: S 3296 would let nurse practitioners and physician assistants handle official medical evaluations for injured federal workers.
ai_sections.what: This bill would expand the federal workers' compensation system to recognize nurse practitioners and physician assistants as "eligible providers" who can examine, treat, and give medical opinions for injured federal employees' claims. Currently the law mainly recognizes doctors, including osteopathic physicians, for these roles. Providers would act within limits set by their state's laws, and rules on second opinions would also be updated to include them.
ai_sections.who: Federal employees injured on the job and the nurse practitioners, physician assistants, and doctors who treat them under the Federal Employees' Compensation Act.
ai_sections.why: Requiring only doctors for official evaluations can delay care for injured workers in areas where doctors are scarce but other providers are available.

title: No Bonuses for Bad Service Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "No Bonuses for Bad Service Act," would stop the U.S. Postal Service from giving bonuses or other extra pay to its top two leaders — the Postmaster General and Deputy Postmaster General — in any year when mail delivery doesn't meet performance goals. Specifically, if the Postal Service fails to deliver mail on time at least 95 percent of the time for any of its main mail categories (like first-class mail), the Postal Service's governing board would be barred from approving bonuses or extra compensation for those two officials for that year, beyond their regular salary.

The bill also requires that a certain financial report the Postal Service already prepares be submitted to the Postal Regulatory Commission, an independent government agency that oversees postal rates and service standards, adding another layer of oversight.

This bill would mainly affect the Postmaster General, Deputy Postmaster General, and the Postal Service's governing Board of Governors, who set executive pay. Indirectly, it could affect everyday Americans who rely on mail delivery, since the goal is to create a financial incentive for postal leadership to prioritize timely and reliable mail service. It would not change mail rates, services, or delivery operations directly — it only ties executive bonuses to delivery performance.
ai_headline: Bill would tie postal executives' bonuses to on-time mail delivery
last_action_text: Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill would block bonuses for top USPS leaders in any year mail delivery misses the 95 percent on-time goal.
ai_sections.what: The "No Bonuses for Bad Service Act" would bar the Postal Service's governing board from approving bonuses or extra pay for the Postmaster General and Deputy Postmaster General in years when on-time delivery falls below 95 percent for major mail categories. It also requires an existing financial report to be shared with the Postal Regulatory Commission for added oversight.
ai_sections.who: The bill directly affects the Postmaster General, Deputy Postmaster General, and the Postal Service's Board of Governors, which sets executive pay. Everyday Americans who rely on mail delivery are indirectly affected.
ai_sections.why: The measure creates a financial consequence for postal leadership tied to delivery performance, without altering mail rates, services, or operations directly.

title: Tribal Forest Protection Act Amendments Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill updates the Tribal Forest Protection Act of 2004 to expand and clarify how Indian tribes can work with the federal government to manage forests and rangelands. It broadens the definition of "Indian forest land or rangeland" to include areas with grass or brush cover, land that could be restored to forest, and land in Alaska owned by Alaska Native Corporations. It also allows tribes to propose projects not just to "protect" land, as under current law, but also to "restore" it, and expands the type of federal land tribes can seek to work on beyond just Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management land to any federal land with special significance to the tribe.

The bill also changes the criteria federal agencies use to decide whether to approve tribally proposed forestry projects, adding "watershed" concerns alongside existing land and resource considerations. It could make it easier for tribes to partner with the federal government to manage, protect, and restore forests, rangelands, and watersheds that are important to them culturally or environmentally, potentially leading to more collaborative land management and wildfire prevention efforts on or near tribal lands.

title: Diversity Jurisdiction Inflation Adjustment Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes the rules for when people can sue in federal court instead of state court based on being from different states, a process called "diversity jurisdiction." Right now, to file this type of lawsuit in federal court, the amount of money at stake in the case must be more than $75,000. This bill raises that minimum to $150,000, and it also sets up a system to automatically increase that number every ten years starting in 2030, based on inflation (using the Consumer Price Index, a standard measure of rising prices). The dollar amount would be rounded to the nearest $25,000 each time it's adjusted.

The practical effect is that fewer lawsuits between people or companies from different states would qualify for federal court, since the case would need to involve more money to meet the new, higher threshold. Cases involving smaller amounts would generally have to be filed in state court instead. This affects individuals, businesses, and lawyers involved in civil lawsuits across state lines, since it changes where those cases can be filed. The bill also allows judges to penalize a plaintiff with court costs if they sue in federal court claiming a large amount but end up winning less than the required minimum, which is meant to discourage people from inflating their claims just to get into federal court.
ai_headline: Bill would raise money threshold for filing lawsuits in federal court

title: Common Cents Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Common Cents Act, would stop the U.S. Mint from making new pennies within a year after it becomes law. The Mint could still make a small number of pennies for coin collectors, but only if selling them covers the cost of making them. Pennies already in circulation would still count as legal money and could still be used to pay debts, taxes, or bills, just like today.

The bill also sets up a rounding system for cash purchases. Starting one year after the law passes, if a cash transaction's total ends in 1, 2, 6, or 7 cents, the amount would be rounded down to the nearest five cents. If it ends in 3, 4, 8, or 9 cents, it would be rounded up. Totals of exactly 1 or 2 cents would round up to 5 cents. This rounding rule only applies to cash payments—purchases made with credit cards, debit cards, checks, gift cards, or electronic transfers would not be affected and would still be charged the exact amount.

This would mainly affect everyday shoppers who pay in cash, retail businesses, vending machine operators, and employers who pay workers in cash wages, since they would need to adjust pricing and payment systems to round to the nearest nickel. It would also affect the U.S. Mint and Treasury Department, which would save money by not producing pennies, since each penny currently costs more to make than it's worth. Coin collectors would still be able to buy specially minted pennies through official numismatic sales.
ai_headline: Bill would end penny production and round cash sales to nearest nickel

title: A bill to expand the sharing of information with respect to suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade.
ai_summary:
This bill amends a section of the Tariff Act of 1930 that deals with how U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) shares information when it suspects imported goods may violate trademark or copyright protections (like counterfeit products). Currently, CBP can share limited details with rights holders (such as trademark or copyright owners) when it merely "suspects" a violation. The bill changes that standard to "reasonable suspicion," which is a more defined legal threshold, and expands what information can be examined and shared to include details about packing materials and shipping containers, not just the product and its packaging.

The bill also allows CBP to share additional nonpublic information gathered from online marketplaces, shipping companies, freight forwarders, and other businesses involved in importing goods. This means companies like Amazon, eBay, or shipping logistics firms could have information they provide to CBP passed along to rights holders investigating counterfeit goods. Finally, the bill broadens who can receive this shared information, adding "any other party with an interest in the merchandise" as determined by the CBP Commissioner, rather than limiting it to a specific list of parties.

This bill would primarily affect trademark and copyright holders (businesses trying to protect their brands from counterfeiters), importers, online marketplaces, shipping and logistics companies, and CBP itself. Everyday consumers could see indirect benefits if it helps reduce the flow of counterfeit goods into the U.S., though the bill mainly changes government and business procedures rather than creating new rules for individuals.
ai_headline: Bill would let CBP share more counterfeit goods data with brand owners

ai_summary:
This is a congressional budget resolution, which acts like a financial blueprint for the federal government. It sets overall spending and revenue targets for fiscal year 2027 and gives rough guidelines for the following nine years, through 2036. Congress uses this document to set limits on how much money can go toward broad categories like defense, healthcare, education, and other government programs before writing the detailed spending bills later in the year.

It's important to understand that this resolution itself doesn't create or cut any specific programs, taxes, or benefits. Instead, it's a planning tool that sets the stage for future legislation. It also doesn't require the President's signature, since it's a resolution between the House and Senate rather than a law. However, it can matter a lot politically because it can include special instructions allowing certain bills (through a process called "reconciliation") to pass the Senate with a simple majority instead of the usual 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster.

Because this bill only contains a general title without detailed provisions, it's impossible to know the specific spending levels, tax policies, or program changes it proposes. In practice, every American is affected by budget resolutions since they shape how much the government spends on programs like Social Security, Medicare, defense, and infrastructure, and whether taxes might rise or fall. title: To ban the sale of products with a high concentration of sodium nitrite to individuals, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Youth Poisoning Protection Act," would ban the sale of consumer products that contain highly concentrated sodium nitrite. Specifically, any product with 10% or more sodium nitrite by weight would be officially labeled a "banned hazardous product" under existing consumer safety law. Sodium nitrite is a chemical that has been misused in some suicide cases because pure, concentrated forms are dangerous if swallowed, even though it's commonly used in small, safe amounts as a food preservative (like in cured meats).

The bill makes clear that it does not affect sodium nitrite used in food products, such as bacon, deli meats, poultry, or eggs, since those already have separate safety regulations under food inspection laws. It also does not restrict sodium nitrite used for legitimate industrial or commercial purposes, where it's not being sold directly to individual consumers. This means grocery store food items and business/industrial uses would be unaffected.

The people most affected would be companies that currently sell concentrated sodium nitrite products directly to consumers, often marketed for uses like curing meat at home or, in rare cases, misused for self-harm. If enacted, these sellers would no longer be allowed to sell such high-concentration versions to the public. The law would take effect 90 days after being signed, giving businesses a short window to adjust their product lines.
ai_headline: Bill would ban consumer sales of concentrated sodium nitrite
last_action_text: Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 116.

title: Bonuses for Cost-Cutters and Fraud Preventers Act of 2026
ai_summary:
**HR 428 — Bonuses for Cost-Cutters and Fraud Preventers Act of 2026**

This bill changes federal law to encourage government employees to point out wasteful spending in their agencies. It expands an existing cash award program so that workers can be rewarded not just for reporting fraud or mismanagement, but also for identifying "wasteful expenses"—money set aside for salaries, operations, or similar accounts that isn't actually needed for its intended purpose. Each agency's Chief Financial Officer would decide whether flagged spending truly qualifies as wasteful. The bill also raises the maximum cash award an employee can receive, from $10,000 to $20,000.

The bill sets up a process where, if wasteful spending is confirmed, the agency head must notify the President so that the money can be proposed for official rescission (a formal process for canceling unused federal funds) through existing budget law. Agencies without a Chief Financial Officer would need to designate someone else to make these determinations. Agencies would also have to publicly report on these disclosures and how many awards were given out, and the Office of Personnel Management would monitor compliance and report to Congress annually. The Government Accountability Office would review how the program is working every three years for a total of six years.

This mainly affects federal employees and agency officials, particularly those in financial oversight roles, by giving them clearer incentives and procedures to flag unnecessary spending. It does not directly affect the general public, though it could indirectly reduce wasteful government spending over time. Inspectors General staff are excluded from receiving these awards, since identifying fraud and waste is already part of their normal job duties.

title: Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026, would create a broad new package of economic penalties against Russia in response to its war on Ukraine. It requires the President to sanction top Russian government and military officials, major state-owned banks (like Sberbank, VTB, and Gazprombank), and companies connected to Russia's defense industry or energy sector. It also blocks Americans from investing in Russia, buying Russian government debt, or trading Russian companies' stocks on U.S. exchanges. It bans imports of Russian uranium and energy products, and it slaps very high tariffs—up to 500%—on goods imported from Russia. Additionally, it punishes other countries that keep buying Russian oil or natural gas, or that help Russia dodge sanctions, by raising tariffs on their goods entering the U.S. by up to 100%.

The bill also targets the "shadow fleet" of tanker ships that move Russian oil around sanctions and price caps, and it penalizes foreign banks, insurers, and ports that help those ships operate. There are exceptions for humanitarian aid, food and medicine, nuclear cooperation for civilian energy use, NASA space activities, and U.S. government operations abroad. The President can waive certain sanctions if it's in the national interest, but must explain this to Congress, and Congress can vote to block the removal of sanctions through a special fast-track process. Sanctions would only be lifted for Russia once it signs a peace agreement acceptable to Ukraine's government and stops military action against it.

This bill would primarily affect large financial institutions, oil and energy companies, shipping companies, and businesses that trade internationally, since they would need to comply with new restrictions on dealing with Russia. It could also affect American consumers indirectly through changes in energy markets and global trade prices. Countries that buy significant amounts of Russian oil or gas, such as certain trading partners of the U.S., could face new tariffs, which could affect diplomatic and trade relationships more broadly.

title: Less Bureaucracy, Better Child Care for Student Parents Act
ai_summary:
This bill would move a specific federal program out of the Department of Education and into the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). The program in question, created under section 419N of the Higher Education Act, is called the Child Care Access Means Parents in School (CCAMPIS) program, which gives grants to colleges and universities to help low-income student parents pay for child care while they attend school. Under this bill, HHS—rather than the Education Department—would take over running this program, including all its staff, money, contracts, and paperwork.

The bill lays out the mechanics of how this transfer would happen: HHS would gain the same legal powers the Education Department had to run the program, existing grants and contracts would stay valid, ongoing legal cases would continue with HHS substituted in as the responsible agency, and the Office of Management and Budget would oversee the move to make sure it doesn't create extra federal jobs. The change would take effect six months after the bill becomes law, though early steps could begin sooner.

This bill mainly affects the federal government's internal organization rather than changing who qualifies for help or how much money is available. It would directly affect Department of Education and HHS employees who work on this program, as well as colleges and universities that receive these child care grants. Student parents relying on CCAMPIS funding likely wouldn't see changes to their benefits, but they might deal with a different federal agency handling the paperwork and oversight going forward.

title: Less Bureaucracy, Better Foreign Medical Accreditation Act
ai_summary:
This bill moves responsibility for accrediting foreign medical schools from the Department of Education to the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). Right now, the National Committee on Foreign Medical Education and Accreditation, which reviews whether medical schools outside the U.S. meet quality standards, operates under the Department of Education. This bill transfers that committee, along with its staff, funding, records, and legal authority, to HHS instead. The idea behind the change is that HHS, as the agency focused on health issues, may be a more logical home for overseeing medical school accreditation than the Education Department.

The bill includes standard legal provisions to make the transfer smooth: existing contracts, rules, and pending legal cases involving the committee will continue without interruption, and any ongoing accreditation reviews or applications will not be affected by the switch. It also requires the Office of Management and Budget to make sure the change doesn't result in more government employees overall, and to certify to Congress that the transfer follows the law. There is a transition period allowing the Department of Education to keep helping out temporarily, and the change would fully take effect six months after the bill becomes law.

This bill mainly affects U.S. medical students who attend medical schools abroad, since accreditation status affects whether their degrees are recognized for licensing and federal student loans in the U.S. It also affects the foreign medical schools themselves, which must go through this accreditation process, as well as federal employees at the Department of Education and HHS who work on these accreditation functions. The general public isn't directly affected, but the change could influence oversight quality and efficiency for international medical education programs.

title: Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act, creates a federal law requiring that if a baby is born alive during or after an abortion attempt, healthcare workers must give that child the same medical care they would give any other newborn at the same stage of development. It also requires that the baby be quickly taken to a hospital. Any doctor, nurse, or clinic employee who knows this care wasn't provided must report it to law enforcement. Healthcare practitioners who fail to follow these rules could face fines or up to 5 years in prison, and anyone who intentionally kills a baby born alive in this situation could face the same penalties as for murder.

The bill also allows the woman who had the abortion to sue for damages if these requirements aren't followed, including money for injuries, three times the cost of the abortion, and punitive damages. Importantly, the bill specifically says the mother herself cannot be criminally prosecuted under this law. It also renames the relevant section of federal criminal law from "Partial-Birth Abortions" to "Abortions."

This bill mainly affects healthcare practitioners (doctors, nurses, and clinic staff) who perform or are present during abortions, as it creates new federal criminal penalties and reporting duties for them. It also affects women who have abortions, since they gain a new legal right to sue if these rules are violated, while being shielded from prosecution themselves. The bill passed the House and was sent to the Senate, where it would need further action to become law.
ai_headline: House bill requires medical care for infants born alive after abortion attempts
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: Bill would mandate medical care for babies born alive during abortions and create new criminal penalties for noncompliance.
ai_sections.what: The bill requires healthcare workers to give any baby born alive during or after an abortion attempt the same medical care as any other newborn at that developmental stage, and to promptly transport the baby to a hospital. Practitioners who know this care wasn't provided must report it to law enforcement, and violations carry fines or up to 5 years in prison, with intentional killing treated like murder.
ai_sections.who: Doctors, nurses, and clinic staff who perform or are present during abortions face new federal duties and penalties. Women who have abortions gain the right to sue for damages but cannot themselves be prosecuted under this law.
ai_sections.why: The law would create new federal criminal liability and reporting obligations for healthcare practitioners involved in abortions. It also opens a new civil legal avenue for women to pursue damages if care requirements aren't met.

title: LACA
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Local Access to Courts Act (LACA), makes small technical changes to federal law that determine where federal district courts can officially hold sessions in two states. Specifically, it adds College Station, Texas, and El Centro, California, to the list of cities where certain federal district courts are authorized to conduct proceedings.

In practical terms, this means federal judges in those court districts could hold hearings, trials, or other legal proceedings in College Station or El Centro, in addition to the other cities already listed in the law. This does not create new courts or change how many judges serve those areas—it simply updates the legal list of approved locations where court sessions can take place.

This bill mainly affects people living in or near College Station, Texas, and El Centro, California, including residents, attorneys, and businesses who may need to interact with the federal court system. By allowing court sessions closer to home, it could make it more convenient for local residents to attend hearings without having to travel to a more distant courthouse. It does not affect the broader public outside these regions or change any other laws.
ai_headline: Bill would add two cities as federal court session sites

title: Chief Herbert D. Proffitt Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, named after Chief Herbert D. Proffitt, expands a federal program that pays benefits to law enforcement officers and their families when an officer is killed or permanently disabled in the line of duty. Currently, this program mainly covers officers who are actively serving. The bill changes the law so that retired law enforcement officers can also qualify for these benefits if they are killed or permanently and totally disabled because someone specifically targeted them due to their past work as a police officer.

To qualify, a retired officer must have left their job "in good standing," meaning they didn't retire under a cloud of misconduct or wrongdoing. The benefit only applies when the harm comes from a targeted attack connected to their former law enforcement service, not from unrelated causes like illness or accidents unrelated to their police work.

The bill also applies retroactively, meaning it covers qualifying attacks on retired officers going back to January 1, 2012, as well as cases already being reviewed by the Bureau of Justice Assistance. This means families of retired officers who were targeted and killed or disabled because of their former police service, even years before this law passed, may now be able to apply for benefits that weren't previously available to them.
ai_headline: Bill would extend line-of-duty death benefits to targeted retired officers
last_action_text: Received in the House.

ai_sections.tldr: S 911 would let retired law enforcement officers' families claim federal benefits if they're killed or disabled for past police work.
ai_sections.what: S 911 expands a federal program that pays benefits when officers are killed or permanently disabled in the line of duty. It extends eligibility to retired officers who are killed or permanently and totally disabled because someone targeted them specifically for their past police service. The bill applies retroactively to qualifying attacks going back to January 1, 2012, including cases already under review by the Bureau of Justice Assistance.
ai_sections.who: Retired law enforcement officers who left their jobs in good standing, and their families, would newly qualify for benefits. The Bureau of Justice Assistance administers the program.
ai_sections.why: Previously, this benefit program mainly covered actively serving officers, leaving retired officers targeted for past service without access to it. The change means more claims, including years-old cases, could now come before the Bureau of Justice Assistance for review.

title: Federal Law Enforcement Officer Service Weapon Purchase Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill would let federal law enforcement officers buy their old service weapons once those guns are retired from use by their agency. Within a year of the bill becoming law, the General Services Administration would have to set up a program allowing this kind of purchase.

To qualify, an officer would need to buy the weapon within six months after it was officially retired, and they would need to be "in good standing" with the agency that employed them. The price would be based on "salvage value," meaning the low resale value of a used, worn item rather than its original cost. Machine guns that weren't already legally owned before a 1986 law took effect would not be included in this program.

This bill mainly affects current and retired federal law enforcement officers (such as agents with the FBI, DEA, Border Patrol, and similar agencies), giving them a formal, legal way to purchase weapons they used on the job once those weapons are taken out of service. It does not affect state or local police, and it does not change any other federal gun purchase or background check laws.
ai_headline: Federal agents could buy their own retired service weapons under new bill
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

Officers must buy within six months of retirement, be "in good standing," and pay only "salvage value." Machine guns not legally owned before a 1986 law took effect are excluded.
ai_sections.who: Current and retired federal law enforcement officers, such as agents with the FBI, DEA, and Border Patrol. State and local police are not affected.
ai_sections.why: The bill creates a formal legal process for a purchase that previously had no established system, without altering other federal gun purchase or background check laws.

title: Improving Law Enforcement Officer Safety and Wellness Through Data Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Attorney General, working with the FBI and the National Institute of Justice, to produce three detailed reports for Congress within 270 days of the law being passed. It does not create new programs, funding, or crimes—it's purely a data-gathering and study requirement. The first report focuses on ambush and coordinated attacks against law enforcement officers, looking at how often they happen, how officers are trained to handle them, how well body armor programs work, and gaps in current crime-data systems. The second report examines "aggressive actions" against officers that don't rise to the level of a crime but still cause stress or harm, and whether a new reporting category should be created to track these. The third report covers the mental health of law enforcement officers, including available support programs, how often officers use them, and whether mental health screening should be expanded.

The bill mainly affects federal agencies like the Department of Justice and FBI, which would need to gather this information and consult with state, local, and tribal police departments, as well as outside organizations and experts. Indirectly, it affects law enforcement officers themselves, since the findings could shape future decisions about training, equipment funding, data collection methods, and mental health resources. Everyday residents wouldn't see immediate changes from this bill, but the reports it requires could influence future legislation or funding related to police safety and wellness.

last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.what: HR 2240 directs the Attorney General, with the FBI and National Institute of Justice, to produce three reports for Congress within 270 days. The reports cover ambush attacks on officers, non-criminal "aggressive actions" against them, and law enforcement mental health. The bill creates no new programs, funding, or crimes—it's strictly a study and data-gathering requirement.

title: LEOSA Reform Act
ai_summary:
HR 2243, the LEOSA Reform Act, updates a federal law called the Law Enforcement Officer Safety Act (LEOSA), which lets qualified active and retired police officers carry concealed firearms nationwide, even in states with stricter gun laws. This bill expands and clarifies those rights. It makes clear that officers covered under this law are exempt from the federal "Gun-Free School Zones" law, so they can carry near schools. It also extends their carrying rights onto public transportation (like buses, trains, and ferries) and other public property, and clarifies that National Park Service rules don't override their right to carry.

The bill also changes the training requirements retired officers must meet to qualify for concealed carry. Instead of only being tested by their old police department, they could now meet firearms qualification standards set by their state, a local law enforcement agency, or even a certified private firearms instructor, once a year (or up to every three years if their state allows it). Additionally, it updates the definition of "firearm" in this law to specifically include magazines, not just the gun itself.

Finally, the bill allows qualified current and retired law enforcement officers to carry firearms inside certain lower-security federal buildings that are open to the public, specifically ones rated "Security Level I or II" (lower-risk facilities like some federal offices, but not high-security buildings). This mainly affects current and retired police officers, federal building security policies, and rules about carrying firearms in public spaces like transit systems, parks, and federal offices. It does not change gun laws for the general public.
ai_headline: Bill would expand where off-duty and retired officers can carry guns
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 2243 would let qualified current and retired officers carry concealed firearms near schools, on public transit, in parks, and in some federal buildings.
ai_sections.what: HR 2243 updates LEOSA to exempt covered officers from Gun-Free School Zones restrictions, extend carry rights to public transportation and other public property, and clarify that National Park Service rules don't override those rights. It also loosens retired officers' annual firearms qualification requirements and lets qualified officers carry in lower-security federal buildings (Security Level I or II).
ai_sections.who: Affects current and retired law enforcement officers qualified under LEOSA, federal building security policy, and rules governing firearms in transit systems, parks, and federal offices. Does not change gun laws for the general public.
ai_sections.why: The changes would broaden the locations and conditions under which qualified officers can carry concealed firearms and relax how retired officers prove ongoing firearms proficiency.

title: PROTECT Our Children Reauthorization Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill renews and updates a 2008 law that funds and organizes efforts to catch people who exploit children online, especially through the Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force Program — a nationwide network of local, state, and federal law enforcement units that investigate child pornography and internet-based child exploitation crimes. It extends funding for these task forces through 2028, with amounts rising from $70 million in 2026 to $90 million in 2028. It also updates how the Justice Department must plan and report on this work, requiring a "National Strategy" report every four years instead of every two years, with more detailed information on staffing needs, arrests, prosecutions, and how many child victims are identified and rescued.

The bill also changes how task forces operate and are held accountable. It allows task forces to prioritize which tips or leads to investigate based on their own judgment and resources, and it gives them some legal protection ("limited liability") from lawsuits over those prioritization decisions — unless they acted with intentional misconduct, malice, or gross negligence. It expands task force partnerships to include tribal and military law enforcement, child protective services, and probation/parole agencies, and adds new duties like training judges on the connections between family-related abuse and online crimes. It removes an older provision about a specific Wyoming-based tracking system ("Operation Fairplay") in favor of more general language, and eliminates a section of the original law dealing with regional computer forensic labs.

This bill mainly affects law enforcement agencies (federal, state, tribal, and local), prosecutors, judges who handle these cases, and organizations like the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. Indirectly, it affects the public by aiming to improve how effectively the government identifies and rescues child victims and prosecutes offenders, and it affects internet and tech companies that report suspected child exploitation content, since the bill also tweaks legal requirements around how those reports must include supplemental data.
ai_headline: Senate bill renews child exploitation task force funding through 2028
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 80.

It changes reporting requirements to a four-year "National Strategy" report, lets task forces prioritize leads with limited legal liability protection, expands partnerships to tribal, military, and other agencies, and removes older provisions like the Operation Fairplay tracking system and regional forensic labs section.
