title: Honoring Our Fallen Heroes Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill makes it easier for police officers, firefighters, and other public safety officers to receive federal death and disability benefits when they get cancer from job-related exposure to harmful chemicals and substances. It creates a list of about 20 "exposure-related cancers" (including lung cancer, leukemia, melanoma, and others) and says that if an officer developed one of these cancers, it will generally be assumed to have been caused by their work, rather than requiring the officer or their family to prove it. This assumption applies if the officer served at least 5 years, was diagnosed within 15 years of leaving the job, and the cancer caused death or permanent disability. The government could still deny a claim if medical evidence shows the job exposure wasn't actually a contributing factor. The bill also sets up a process for federal officials to regularly review and add new cancers to the list based on scientific evidence, and allows any member of the public to petition to add a cancer to the list.

The bill affects public safety officers (police, firefighters, and similar workers) and their families who apply for benefits through the federal Public Safety Officers' Benefits program. It allows claims to be filed for deaths or disabilities going back to January 1, 2020, and gives people three years after the bill becomes law to file such claims. It also makes some technical changes to protect the privacy of information given to the Department of Justice in connection with these claims, and clarifies what counts as "line of duty" activity for a related 2020 law covering first responders. Overall, this is a benefits-expansion bill focused on recognizing cancer as an occupational hazard for emergency responders, without addressing any other unrelated policy areas.
ai_headline: Bill would presume first responder cancers are job-related for benefits
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 78.

ai_sections.tldr: S 237 would presume about 20 job-related cancers in public safety officers are work-caused for federal benefit claims.
ai_sections.what: S 237 creates a list of roughly 20 "exposure-related cancers" and presumes these were caused by job exposure to harmful substances for public safety officers seeking federal death and disability benefits. The presumption applies if the officer served at least 5 years, was diagnosed within 15 years of leaving the job, and the cancer caused death or permanent disability. Officials could still deny claims with contrary medical evidence, and a process would let the cancer list be updated over time, including through public petitions.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects police officers, firefighters, and similar public safety officers, plus their families, who apply through the federal Public Safety Officers' Benefits program.
ai_sections.why: The change shifts the burden of proof in benefit claims from officers and families to the government, which must now show job exposure wasn't a factor to deny a claim. It also allows retroactive claims for deaths or disabilities back to January 1, 2020, within a three-year filing window after enactment.

title: NORRA of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "No Rogue Rulings Act of 2025" (NORRA), changes how federal district courts can issue injunctions—court orders that block a law or government action from taking effect. Under current practice, a single federal judge can sometimes issue a "nationwide injunction" that stops a government policy for everyone in the country, not just the people who filed the lawsuit. This bill would generally stop that practice, limiting injunctions so they only apply to the actual parties (people or groups) who sued, plus anyone they're legally representing in a class-action-type case.

There's an exception: if a lawsuit is filed by two or more states from different judicial circuits challenging an action by the executive branch (the President or federal agencies), the case would go to a special panel of three judges instead of just one. These judges would be chosen randomly rather than picked by a senior judge, and this panel would have the power to issue a broader injunction if it decides that's needed—considering fairness, potential harm to others, and the balance of power between government branches. Decisions from this panel could be appealed either to a regular appeals court or directly to the Supreme Court, whichever the appealing party prefers.

This bill would affect anyone who relies on the court system to challenge federal government actions, including advocacy groups, businesses, and individuals. It would particularly change the strategy for lawsuits against presidential or federal agency actions, since single judges would lose the power to block policies nationwide except in narrow circumstances. Supporters argue it would prevent individual judges from having outsized power over national policy, while critics may see it as making it harder to quickly stop potentially harmful or unconstitutional government actions. The bill has passed the House and was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee for consideration.
ai_headline: House bill would limit judges' power to issue nationwide injunctions
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill would generally restrict federal injunctions to only the parties who sued, ending most nationwide blocks by single judges.
ai_sections.what: This bill would limit federal district court injunctions so they generally apply only to the parties who filed the lawsuit, not the whole country. An exception allows multi-state lawsuits against executive branch actions to go before a randomly-selected three-judge panel, which could issue a broader injunction and whose rulings could be appealed to an appeals court or directly to the Supreme Court.
ai_sections.who: This affects advocacy groups, businesses, individuals, and states that sue over federal government actions, as well as federal judges who currently issue nationwide injunctions.
ai_sections.why: Limiting single-judge injunctions would change litigation strategy against federal actions, making it harder to quickly block a policy nationwide except through the new multi-state panel process.

title: Stop STALLING Act
ai_summary:
This bill targets a specific tactic some drug companies use to delay competition from cheaper generic drugs or biosimilars. Under current law, anyone can file a "citizen petition" with the FDA raising safety or scientific concerns about a drug, which can pause approval of a competing product while the FDA investigates. The bill addresses situations where brand-name drug makers allegedly abuse this process by filing petitions that aren't based on genuine safety concerns, but are instead designed to slow down or block a rival's generic version from reaching the market.

The bill lets the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) sue companies that file these "sham" petitions, either a single baseless petition or a pattern of repeated petitions aimed at blocking a competitor rather than raising real concerns. If the Department of Health and Human Services determines a petition was mainly filed to cause delay and refers it to the FTC, there's a legal presumption that it was a sham, though the company can still defend itself in court. Companies found guilty could face significant financial penalties, either based on the money they made from sales during the delay or a flat fee of $50,000 per day the sham petition was under review, whichever is greater.

This primarily affects pharmaceutical and biotech companies, particularly those that make brand-name drugs, by making it riskier and costlier to file petitions purely as a delay tactic against generic or biosimilar competitors. Everyday consumers could benefit indirectly, since removing artificial delays to generic drug approval tends to bring lower-cost alternatives to market faster, potentially reducing prescription drug prices. The bill does not affect petitions filed in good faith over genuine public health or safety issues.
ai_headline: Bill lets FTC sue drug makers over sham petitions delaying generics
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 45.

ai_sections.tldr: The FTC could sue drug companies for filing sham FDA petitions to delay generic or biosimilar competition.
ai_sections.what: The bill lets the FTC sue drug companies that file "sham" FDA citizen petitions not based on real safety concerns but meant to delay generic or biosimilar competitors. If HHS refers a petition to the FTC as mainly delay-motivated, it's presumed a sham, though companies can still defend themselves in court. Petitions filed in good faith over genuine safety issues are unaffected.
ai_sections.who: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies, especially brand-name drug makers, are directly affected; consumers may see indirect effects on generic drug availability.
ai_sections.why: Making sham petitions costlier and legally riskier could reduce a tactic used to delay generic competition, though the summary does not quantify broader market effects.
ai_sections.cost: Companies found guilty face financial penalties: either the profits made during the delay or a flat $50,000 per day the sham petition was under review, whichever is greater.

title: Drug Competition Enhancement Act
ai_summary:
This bill targets a practice called "product hopping," where a drug company makes small changes to a brand-name medicine—like switching from a pill to a capsule, or tweaking a dosage—right around the time a cheaper generic or biosimilar version is about to enter the market. Companies sometimes do this to push patients and doctors toward the new "tweaked" version before the generic arrives, which can keep sales high and make it harder for the cheaper competitor to gain customers, even though the underlying drug works the same way.

The bill would amend the Federal Trade Commission Act to make certain product-hopping tactics illegal as an "unfair method of competition." This includes situations where a company pulls its older drug off the market (or lets its approval lapse) and steers business to a newer version ("hard switch"), or takes other actions that unfairly disadvantage the older drug to benefit the newer one ("soft switch"). Companies could defend themselves by showing they had legitimate reasons unrelated to blocking competition, such as genuine safety concerns or supply problems. The FTC would be given authority to investigate, sue in federal court, seek to stop the practice, and pursue financial penalties like forcing companies to give up profits gained through this behavior.

This mainly affects pharmaceutical and biotech manufacturers, particularly those that make brand-name drugs and biologics facing generic or biosimilar competition. It could also affect generic and biosimilar drug makers, who may find it easier to compete once their products reach the market, and indirectly affects consumers and insurers, since increased generic competition generally lowers drug prices. The FTC's enforcement powers would expand specifically in this area of drug-market competition.
ai_headline: Bill would ban drugmakers' tactics that delay generic competition
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 43.

ai_sections.tldr: S 1040 would make "product hopping" by drugmakers an illegal unfair competition practice enforced by the FTC.
ai_sections.what: S 1040 would amend the Federal Trade Commission Act to ban "product hopping," where drug companies tweak a brand-name drug to steer patients away from it right before a cheaper generic or biosimilar arrives. It covers both pulling the old drug entirely ("hard switch") and disadvantaging it while promoting the new version ("soft switch"), though companies could defend actions taken for legitimate reasons like safety or supply issues.
ai_sections.who: The bill mainly affects pharmaceutical and biotech companies making brand-name drugs facing generic or biosimilar competition, as well as generic and biosimilar manufacturers. It also indirectly affects consumers and insurers through drug pricing, and expands FTC enforcement authority.
ai_sections.why: The practice can keep brand-name sales high and make it harder for cheaper generic competitors to gain customers, even when the underlying drug is unchanged.

title: Bankruptcy Administration Improvement Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the bankruptcy court system is funded and how certain officials are paid. Chapter 7 bankruptcy (the type where a person's non-essential assets are sold off to pay debts) uses trustees who manage these cases. Those trustees have been paid only $60 per case since 1994, and this bill raises that payment to $120 per case, adjusting for the fact that costs and salaries have gone up significantly since then. The bill also adjusts how various bankruptcy-related fees are collected and distributed among different government funds to make sure the trustee pay raise and the overall bankruptcy court system remain funded without relying on taxpayer money.

The bill also extends the term length of certain temporary bankruptcy judge positions from 5 years to 10 years. These are extra judgeships that Congress created in past years to help handle heavy caseloads in busy bankruptcy courts; instead of letting those temporary positions expire and potentially disappear, the bill keeps them in place longer so courts have enough judges to handle current and expected bankruptcy filings.

This bill mainly affects people involved in the bankruptcy system: chapter 7 trustees (who would get a pay increase), businesses and individuals who file for bankruptcy (through fee adjustments, though personal filing fees themselves are not changed), and the federal courts that rely on these judgeships and funding structures. Everyday individuals filing for personal bankruptcy would not see their own filing fees change, and the bill specifically preserves the ability of courts to waive fees for people who cannot afford them.
ai_headline: Bill would double bankruptcy trustee pay and extend judge terms
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

title: Interagency Patent Coordination and Improvement Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill sets up a formal task force connecting the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) so the two agencies can share information about patents for prescription drugs and biological products. Currently, these agencies operate somewhat separately, even though decisions made by one often affect the other—for example, when a drug company gets FDA approval for a medicine, that can be relevant to whether a related patent should be granted. The task force would include staff from both agencies with medical, scientific, and legal expertise, and would create regular processes for sharing updates on drug approvals, label changes, scientific developments, and other information that patent examiners might need to properly evaluate patent applications.

The bill also requires the agencies to protect confidential business information when sharing it, including giving drug companies 30 days' notice before certain information about their products is shared between agencies. Additionally, USPTO must report to Congress within four years on how well this information-sharing is working, whether it's helping patent examiners do their jobs, and whether similar coordination should be set up with other federal agencies.

This bill mainly affects pharmaceutical and biotech companies that file both FDA applications and patent applications, since it changes how thoroughly their submissions may be cross-checked between agencies. It could also affect patent examiners, who may gain access to more information when reviewing drug-related patents, and potentially consumers and generic drug makers, since more accurate patent decisions could influence how long brand-name drugs keep exclusive market rights before cheaper generics can be sold.

last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 41.

It requires confidentiality protections, including 30 days' notice to companies before certain information is shared, and requires USPTO to report to Congress within four years on the program's effectiveness.

title: Preserve Access to Affordable Generics and Biosimilars Act
ai_summary:
This bill targets a practice called "pay-for-delay," where brand-name drug companies pay generic or biosimilar drug makers to keep their cheaper versions off the market longer. When a generic company challenges a brand company's patent, the two sides sometimes settle the lawsuit with a deal: the brand company gives the generic company money or other valuable things, and in exchange the generic company agrees to delay selling its cheaper version. This bill would make that kind of deal illegal, treating it as an unfair, anti-competitive business practice enforced by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC).

Under the bill, if a generic or biosimilar company gets something of value and agrees to hold off selling its product, regulators would automatically assume the deal is anti-competitive unless the companies can prove otherwise (for example, showing the payment was for a legitimate, separate service, or that the deal actually benefits competition more than it harms it). Companies that violate the rule could face lawsuits from the FTC and fines up to three times the value of the payment involved. The bill still allows normal, legitimate settlements, such as letting the generic company enter the market before the patent expires, paying for reasonable legal costs, or agreeing not to sue over patent infringement.

This bill mainly affects pharmaceutical and biotech companies, but its real-world impact would land on everyday consumers, insurers, and government health programs like Medicare and Medicaid. By making these delay deals illegal, the bill aims to help cheaper generic and biosimilar drugs reach the market sooner, which could lower prescription drug costs for patients and reduce federal health spending. It also adds new reporting and certification requirements so regulators can better track settlement agreements between brand and generic companies.
ai_headline: Bill would outlaw brand-generic deals that delay cheaper drugs
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 46.

Such deals would be presumed anti-competitive unless companies prove the payment was for a legitimate service or benefits competition overall. Normal settlements, like early market entry or covering legal costs, remain allowed.

title: Prescription Pricing for the People Act of 2025
ai_summary:
**S. 527 — Prescription Pricing for the People Act of 2025**

This bill directs the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to study companies that act as middlemen in the prescription drug supply chain, especially pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), which negotiate drug prices between drug makers, insurers, and pharmacies. Within 180 days of the bill becoming law, the FTC must give Congress a preliminary report, followed by a full report within one year. The full report needs to examine whether PBMs charge insurers more than they pay pharmacies, whether they push patients toward pharmacies they own, whether they misuse competitors' business data, and whether their drug-coverage lists favor higher-cost drugs. The FTC must also identify any legal obstacles preventing it from enforcing antitrust and consumer protection laws in this industry, and recommend changes to increase transparency and competition and make sure any savings from industry mergers actually reach consumers.

The bill also requires a separate FTC report on complaints about anticompetitive behavior by manufacturers of "sole-source" drugs—drugs made by only one company, often because of a patent or lack of generic competition. This report would look at how many such complaints the FTC receives, whether the agency has enough authority to act on them, and what new laws or policies might help.

This bill does not create new drug pricing rules or directly regulate PBMs or drug makers. Instead, it is a fact-finding measure meant to give Congress information and recommendations for possible future legislation. It would primarily affect the FTC, which would take on new reporting duties, and could eventually affect PBMs, drug manufacturers, pharmacies, insurers, and consumers if Congress acts on the findings later.
ai_headline: FTC would study pharmacy middlemen under new Senate bill
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 42.

title: DETERRENCE Act
ai_summary:
This bill increases the possible prison sentences for certain serious crimes when those crimes are committed under the direction of, or in coordination with, a foreign government or someone acting on its behalf. It applies to crimes already covered under federal law, including kidnapping, murder-for-hire, stalking, assaulting or threatening federal officials or their family members, harming federal employees, and threats against the President, Vice President, or their staff. For each of these crimes, judges would be allowed (but not required) to add extra years—ranging from about 5 to 10 years depending on the offense—if prosecutors can show the crime was tied to a foreign government's involvement.

The bill doesn't create new crimes; instead, it adds tougher potential punishments for existing crimes when there's a foreign government connection, such as evidence that a hostile country ordered, funded, or coordinated the criminal act. This is meant to address concerns about foreign governments using criminal proxies—such as hired criminals or intermediaries—to intimidate, harm, or kill people on U.S. soil, including public officials, dissidents, or their families.

This bill mainly affects federal prosecutors, judges, and defendants in cases involving foreign government-linked crimes. It does not change sentencing for ordinary criminal cases without foreign government involvement, and it does not affect state-level crimes, which are handled separately from federal law.

title: Strong Communities Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Strong Communities Act of 2025, changes how federal COPS grant money (funding used to support local police departments) can be spent. It creates a new "Strong Communities Program" that lets the Attorney General give competitive grants to local police departments so they can pay for officers or new recruits to attend police training academies or college-based law enforcement programs. The catch is that these officers must agree to work for a local police department close to where they live for at least 4 years within an 8-year period after finishing training. "Close to home" generally means within 7 miles of their long-term residence, or within 20 miles if they live in a smaller county (under 150,000 people).

If an officer or recruit doesn't complete the required years of service, they would have to repay the cost of the training benefits they received, unless the Attorney General has approved certain excused circumstances (like a medical issue). The bill also requires the Attorney General to send an annual report to Congress showing how many police departments received these grants, how many recruits they trained, and how many of those recruits stayed employed afterward.

This bill mainly affects local police departments, police academies, colleges with law enforcement training programs, and people hoping to become police officers in their home communities. The idea is to encourage people to become police officers where they already live, aiming to strengthen ties between officers and the communities they serve, while adding accountability and reporting requirements so Congress can track whether the program is working as intended.

title: Prison Staff Safety Enhancement Act
ai_summary:
This bill responds to a 2023 government watchdog report that found sexual harassment and assault of federal prison staff by inmates is a widespread problem, and that the Bureau of Prisons has failed to properly track this issue or fix it. The bill requires the Bureau of Prisons to fully carry out the recommendations from that 2023 Inspector General report within 90 days. If the Bureau can't complete all the fixes in time, it must explain to Congress why and provide a timeline for finishing the work.

After the Bureau implements these changes, the Inspector General must collect updated data on harassment and assault incidents from 2022 through 2025, analyze the numbers, and report findings to Congress and the Attorney General. This analysis must also look at how such incidents have historically been punished. Finally, the Attorney General is required to create new national rules for preventing, reducing, and punishing inmate-on-staff sexual harassment and assault within a year of receiving that analysis.

This bill mainly affects Bureau of Prisons employees, especially correctional officers, by aiming to improve their safety and working conditions. It also affects incarcerated individuals, since new punishment standards for this kind of misconduct will apply to them. The bill does not create new criminal penalties directly but sets up a process for the government to study the problem and eventually issue formal rules addressing it.

title: Strengthening Child Exploitation Enforcement Act
ai_summary:
This bill updates federal criminal laws dealing with kidnapping and sexual abuse of children to close some legal loopholes. It expands the kidnapping law so that tricking or deceiving someone to take them counts as kidnapping, not just physically grabbing them. It also says that for victims under 16, an offender cannot claim the victim "consented" as a legal defense unless the offender can show they reasonably believed the victim was 16 or older.

The bill also broadens child sexual abuse laws. It updates the law on abuse that happens while crossing state lines so it covers any travel involved in interstate commerce, not just physically crossing a state border. It creates a new specific crime for causing a child under 16 to touch someone's genitals directly (not through clothing) in federal jurisdictions like federal prisons or facilities, closing a gap where such conduct wasn't clearly covered before. It also expands laws around "abusive sexual contact" to cover attempts to commit these acts, not just completed acts, and reorganizes and renumbers sections of the law for clarity.

Overall, this bill affects federal prosecutors, law enforcement, and courts handling child exploitation cases, as well as anyone accused or convicted under these laws. Practically, it means more types of conduct—like deceptive kidnapping, attempted sexual contact, and certain forced touching—can be prosecuted under federal law, and it narrows the defenses available to people accused of abusing children under 16. Ordinary Americans are affected in that these changes are meant to strengthen protections for children and make it easier for prosecutors to bring charges in exploitation cases.

title: Preventing Child Trafficking Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Department of Justice's Office for Victims of Crime to keep working on recommendations that were made by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) in a December 2023 report about child trafficking. That GAO report identified gaps in public awareness efforts and in support services for child trafficking survivors, and it suggested specific improvements. This bill doesn't create new programs from scratch; instead, it requires the agency to follow through on fixes that were already recommended.

Specifically, the bill requires the Office for Victims of Crime to coordinate with the Office on Trafficking in Persons (part of the Administration for Children and Families) to develop joint strategies for preventing child trafficking and helping survivors. It also requires the agencies to set clear, measurable performance goals for anti-trafficking programs, using actual data from the organizations that receive government grants to run these programs. Within 180 days of the bill becoming law, the Director of the Office for Victims of Crime must send a report to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees explaining exactly what steps have been taken.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies and the organizations they fund to combat child trafficking, rather than everyday citizens directly. However, it could indirectly benefit the public by improving how effectively anti-trafficking programs are run, potentially leading to better identification of trafficking victims, clearer public awareness campaigns, and more consistent support services for child survivors of trafficking across the country.

title: Enduring Justice for Victims of Trafficking Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes federal law about extra fines charged to people convicted of certain crimes, mainly related to human trafficking and sexual abuse offenses. Under current law, courts already impose a special $5,000 assessment on convicted offenders who aren't considered "indigent" (too poor to pay). This bill removes a time restriction that was previously in the law, meaning the $5,000 fee will now apply regardless of when the offense occurred, rather than being limited to a specific starting date mentioned in the old version of the statute.

The money collected from these assessments typically goes into a fund that supports services for victims of human trafficking, such as housing, counseling, and legal assistance. This bill mainly affects people convicted of trafficking-related and certain sexual offenses, who would now be required to pay this fine without the previous timing limitation. It also indirectly affects trafficking victims and organizations that rely on this funding, since removing the restriction could mean more money flows into victim assistance programs over time. Everyday taxpayers are not directly affected, since the fee is paid by convicted offenders, not the general public.

title: Protect Children’s Innocence Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "Protect Children's Innocence Act," changes federal law about medical procedures performed on minors (people under 18). It expands an existing federal law that already banned female genital mutilation to also make it a federal crime, punishable by up to 10 years in prison, to perform certain gender-transition-related medical procedures on minors. This includes surgeries like mastectomies, hysterectomies, and various genital surgeries, as well as "chemical castration," which the bill defines as giving puberty blockers or hormone treatments (like testosterone or estrogen) at levels different from what's typical for a person's sex at birth, when done to change someone's body to match a gender different from their biological sex.

The law would apply nationwide if there's a federal connection, such as crossing state lines, using mail or the internet, or making payments through interstate commerce—which covers nearly all such procedures in practice. It does not punish the minors themselves, only the adults who perform, arrange, or facilitate these procedures. There are exceptions: the law does not apply to standard medical care, treatment of intersex conditions, medically necessary treatment for injury or illness, or treatment for a condition called precocious (early) puberty. The bill also states that religious or cultural tradition cannot be used as a legal defense for female genital mutilation.

This bill mainly affects doctors, medical providers, and parents or guardians involved in decisions about gender-transition treatments for minors, as well as transgender youth and their families, who would lose legal access to these treatments in the United States. It would not affect adults seeking the same treatments. The bill has passed the House and was received by the Senate, where it has been referred to the Judiciary Committee for further consideration; it is not yet law.
ai_headline: House-passed bill would criminalize gender-transition care for minors
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

title: To amend title 36, United States Code, to move the place of incorporation and domicile of the National Woman’s Relief Corps to Illinois, to move the principal office of such Corps to Murphysboro, Illinois, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill makes administrative updates to the federal law that governs the National Woman's Relief Corps, an organization that was originally chartered by Congress. The bill officially changes the group's legal home base from the District of Columbia to the state of Illinois, and it also moves the group's main office from Springfield, Illinois, to Murphysboro, Illinois. It updates the rules about who can legally receive official paperwork or lawsuits on the organization's behalf, switching that role from a D.C. official to the Illinois Secretary of State or another office designated under Illinois law.

This is a housekeeping bill rather than one that creates new programs or spends taxpayer money. Congress periodically passes bills like this to update the charters of federally recognized nonprofit and patriotic organizations, keeping their legal details accurate and matching where they actually operate. The National Woman's Relief Corps, which supports veterans and preserves Civil War-era history, is the only entity directly affected. Everyday residents won't be impacted by this bill; it simply keeps the group's official federal records current with its real-world location and operations.

title: DEFIANCE Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill lets people sue when someone creates, shares, or possesses fake "deepfake" pornographic images or videos of them without their consent. It updates an existing federal law that already allowed lawsuits over leaked real intimate photos, expanding it to also cover AI-generated or digitally altered images that falsely make someone appear nude or engaged in sexual activity, even if the image is labeled as fake. Victims could sue anyone who knowingly made, shared, or asked for and received such content, and could win money damages (either a fixed amount of $150,000–$250,000, or actual damages including any profits the creator made), plus court orders to have the images deleted or blocked. Courts could also let victims keep their identities private during the lawsuit, such as by using a pseudonym.

The bill affects several groups: people who might be victimized by having fake explicit images made of them can now more easily take legal action and recover damages; people who create or share such deepfakes, including websites or apps that knowingly distribute them, could face significant financial liability; and parents or guardians could sue on behalf of minors or incapacitated victims. Victims have up to 10 years to file a claim, or until they turn 18 if they were minors when the harm occurred. The bill does not replace or weaken any state, tribal, or other federal laws on this topic—it simply adds a stronger federal option—and it clarifies that it does not change intellectual property law.
ai_headline: Bill would let victims sue over fake AI-generated porn images
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

title: Drone Espionage Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Drone Espionage Act, updates an existing federal law that deals with spying on U.S. national defense information. That law, found in Section 793 of Title 18 of the U.S. Code, already makes it illegal to take or share certain sensitive materials, like photographs or sketches, of military bases, equipment, or other defense-related sites without authorization. This bill simply adds the word "video" to that list, meaning that shooting or transmitting video footage of protected defense information would now be explicitly covered by the same criminal penalties that already apply to photographs and other visual materials.

The change is likely a response to the growing use of drones, which can easily capture video footage of sensitive military sites from angles or distances that older laws may not have clearly addressed. By adding "video" to the law's language, the bill aims to close a potential gap and make sure that anyone using cameras or drones to record protected defense sites can be prosecuted just as they would be for taking photos.

This bill mainly affects people who might record video near military installations, defense contractors, or other government security sites, including drone operators, journalists, researchers, or foreign agents seeking sensitive information. It does not change how the law applies to ordinary photography or unrelated video recording; it only clarifies that video is treated the same as photographs under this specific espionage law.
ai_headline: Bill would add video to law banning capture of defense sites

title: Coercion and Sexual Abuse Free Environment Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Coercion and Sexual Abuse Free Environment Act (CSAFE Act), creates a new federal crime for forcing or manipulating a minor into harmful behavior. Specifically, it targets adults who use threats, blackmail, fraud, deception, or manipulation to pressure a child into self-harm (including suicide attempts), cruelty to animals, other abusive or degrading behavior that would be a crime, or sexually explicit conduct. This kind of coercion often happens online, where predators manipulate children through messages, social media, or other digital communication.

The bill sets penalties based on how serious the harm is: up to 10 years in prison for the coercion itself, up to 20 years if the victim suffers serious injury, and up to life in prison if the victim dies. It also updates related law so that this new crime is treated consistently within the federal system, including how it applies to juvenile offenders.

This law would primarily affect people who target and manipulate minors, often through the internet, into dangerous or abusive acts. It gives federal prosecutors a clearer, specific tool to charge people in these situations, rather than relying only on broader existing laws. Parents, children, schools, and law enforcement agencies dealing with online exploitation or coercion of minors would be the main groups impacted, since the law is meant to strengthen protections for children against manipulation tactics increasingly seen in cases of online abuse and exploitation.

title: Child Predators Accountability Act
ai_summary:
This bill updates federal child exploitation laws to close a gap related to digitally altered or fabricated images, such as "deepfakes." Currently, federal laws against producing child sexual abuse material focus on minors who actually "engage in" sexually explicit conduct, meaning they physically participated in creating the image or video. This bill expands that definition so that a minor is considered to have "engaged in" such conduct even if they never actually performed any act, as long as someone intentionally inserted or depicted that real minor's image into sexually explicit content, such as through digital editing or AI manipulation.

In practical terms, this means someone could be prosecuted under these federal child exploitation statutes for creating sexually explicit images that falsely depict a real child, even if the image was fabricated using technology rather than showing an actual event. The bill applies this change to two existing laws: one covering sexual exploitation of children generally, and another covering the importation of sexually explicit depictions of minors.

This bill would primarily affect law enforcement, prosecutors, and courts handling child exploitation cases, giving them clearer legal authority to charge individuals who create fake sexually explicit images using real children's likenesses. It could also affect people who create or distribute such digitally manipulated content, as they would now face the same federal charges as those who produce material involving minors who were physically present during the creation of the image.
ai_headline: Bill closes legal gap on deepfake child sexual abuse images

title: Tribal Warrant Fairness Act
ai_summary:
**S. 3041 — Tribal Warrant Fairness Act**

This bill expands the U.S. Marshals Service's authority to help Native American tribes track down fugitives and enforce arrest warrants. Currently, federal law allows the Marshals Service to assist with catching fugitives in matters involving federal, state, and local law enforcement, but it doesn't clearly include tribal law enforcement. This bill fixes that gap by explicitly stating that, if a federally recognized Indian tribe requests help, the Marshals Service can assist with tribal fugitive cases, just as it does for state and local cases.

The bill also updates a related law—the Presidential Threat Protection Act of 2000—to make sure tribal governments and tribal law are treated the same as federal, state, and local governments and laws when it comes to task forces that help catch fugitives. In practical terms, this means tribal police and courts would have better access to federal resources (like the Marshals Service's tracking and apprehension capabilities) when someone wanted on a tribal warrant needs to be found and arrested, including in cases where that person has left tribal land.

This bill mainly affects Native American tribes and their law enforcement agencies, giving them clearer legal ability to request federal help with fugitive cases. It also affects the U.S. Marshals Service, which would have expanded authority to work directly with tribal governments. For everyday tribal citizens, this could mean faster and more effective enforcement of tribal arrest warrants, since fugitives often cross jurisdictional lines that tribal police alone cannot pursue.
ai_headline: Bill would let US Marshals help tribes catch fugitives on warrants
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

It also updates the Presidential Threat Protection Act of 2000 so tribal governments and tribal law are treated the same as federal, state, and local governments on fugitive task forces.

title: Fighting Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill directs the U.S. Attorney General to study and propose a program that would help police officers, firefighters, EMTs, 911 dispatchers, and similar public safety workers get treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and acute stress disorder caused by their jobs. Rather than creating the program immediately, the bill requires the Department of Justice to research the idea and, within 150 days of becoming law, deliver a detailed report to Congress. That report must outline at least one possible treatment program, explain how confidentiality would be protected for officers who seek help, describe how the program could work at state, local, tribal, and federal levels, include draft legislation to formally create the program, and estimate how much money it would cost each year.

The bill points to research showing that public safety workers face PTSD and mental health struggles at higher rates than the general public, and that many police and fire departments lack the money or local resources to hire mental health professionals. It cites concerning statistics about suicide rates among firefighters and police officers as part of the justification for studying this issue.

This bill mainly affects public safety officers and dispatchers, the agencies that employ them, and federal officials at the Department of Justice, who will need to research options and produce a report. It does not create or fund an actual treatment program by itself—it's a required first step. Any real program would need separate future legislation and funding from Congress based on what this report recommends. In the meantime, no new services or benefits go into effect immediately for workers.
ai_headline: Justice Department told to study PTSD treatment program for first responders
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

title: NICS Data Reporting Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill requires the U.S. Attorney General to send Congress a yearly report about people who were denied the ability to buy a gun after failing a background check through the National Instant Criminal Background Check System (NICS). NICS is the system gun sellers use to check whether a buyer is legally allowed to purchase a firearm. The report would break down information about denied buyers by demographic categories such as race, ethnicity, national origin, sex, gender, age, disability status, average income, and English language proficiency, when that information is available. It would also separately track this same demographic information for people who appealed their denial and won, meaning their case was overturned.

The bill doesn't change who can or cannot buy a gun, and it doesn't alter how background checks are conducted. It simply creates a new reporting and data-collection requirement for the Department of Justice, aimed at giving Congress more detailed statistics about who is being denied firearm purchases and why. The first report would be due one year after the bill becomes law, with additional reports required every year after that.

This bill would mainly affect the Department of Justice, which would need to gather and compile this data, and members of Congress, who would receive the reports. Indirectly, it could affect privacy advocates, gun rights and gun control organizations, and researchers who study firearm policy, since the reports could become a public source of information used in future policy debates. Everyday gun buyers would not experience any direct change to the purchasing or background check process itself.
ai_headline: Bill would require yearly reports on gun buyers denied by background checks
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

title: Count the Crimes to Cut Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires the federal government to create a full list of every federal crime currently on the books. The Attorney General would have one year to submit a report to Congress listing all criminal offenses found in federal statutes, including details like the possible punishment, how many times each crime was prosecuted over the past 15 years, and what level of intent (mens rea) a person must have to be found guilty. Separately, dozens of federal agencies—such as the EPA, FDA-related departments, SEC, FTC, and many others—would have to compile similar lists of criminal offenses hidden within their own regulations, since breaking certain agency rules can also lead to criminal charges, not just fines.

After these reports are completed, the bill requires the Department of Justice and each listed agency to build a free, public online index of all these criminal offenses within two years. The idea is to make it easier for ordinary people, businesses, and lawmakers to actually see how many federal crimes exist, since many rules with criminal penalties are scattered across thousands of pages of law and regulation and are hard to track down. The bill does not create new crimes or repeal old ones—it simply forces a count and public listing of what already exists.

This mostly affects government agencies, who must do the work of compiling and publishing these lists. Indirectly, it affects everyday citizens and businesses by potentially making it easier to find out what federal actions could carry criminal penalties. It does not by itself change any laws, penalties, or enforcement practices; it only creates transparency and information that Congress could later use if it decides to change or reduce certain criminal laws.
ai_headline: Bill would force full public count of every federal crime on the books
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 370.

title: Lieutenant Osvaldo Albarati Stopping Prison Contraband Act
ai_summary:
This bill, named after Lieutenant Osvaldo Albarati, a federal corrections officer who was killed, increases the criminal penalty for smuggling cell phones into federal prisons. Under current law, providing a prohibited phone to an inmate carries a lighter punishment than smuggling other contraband like weapons or drugs. This bill changes that by setting a specific penalty of up to two years in prison for someone who illegally gives a phone to an inmate, closing what lawmakers saw as a gap in the law's severity.

The bill also requires the Federal Bureau of Prisons to review its policies within one year on how it handles inmates who make, possess, or try to obtain banned items like phones. Based on that review, the Bureau must update its rules if needed to better protect both incarcerated people and prison staff.

This bill mainly affects people involved with the federal prison system: inmates, corrections staff, visitors, and anyone who might attempt to smuggle a phone into a federal facility. Phones are considered dangerous contraband because inmates have used them to coordinate crimes, threaten witnesses, or communicate outside prison in ways that bypass security monitoring. Corrections officers and prison safety advocates are the primary group who benefits, since the bill aims to add a stronger deterrent against phone smuggling, which has been linked to safety incidents inside prisons.
ai_headline: Bill sets two-year penalty for smuggling phones into federal prisons
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

title: Voter ID Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Voter ID Act, would require people to show a valid photo ID before voting in federal elections, such as elections for President, Senate, or House of Representatives. Acceptable IDs include a state driver's license, state photo ID card, U.S. passport, military or veterans ID, or a tribal photo ID. If someone votes in person without an ID, they could still cast a provisional ballot but would need to show valid ID or sign a religious-objection affidavit within three days for their vote to count. People voting by mail would need to include a copy of their photo ID, or provide the last four digits of their Social Security number with a sworn statement explaining they couldn't get an ID, or have their ballot notarized. Military members voting from overseas and certain voters with disabilities are exempted from these rules.

The bill also requires states to tell voters about the ID requirement when they register, including during online registration, and to provide free public access to copy machines or scanners at libraries, courts, and government buildings so people can copy their ID. Separately, it creates a federal grant program to help states and Native American tribes cover the cost of issuing free photo IDs to people who say under penalty of perjury that they cannot afford the usual fee.

This bill would affect all voters in federal elections, since it sets a nationwide photo ID requirement, but it may have a bigger impact on people who currently lack photo identification, such as some elderly, low-income, disabled, or rural voters. It would also affect state and local election officials, who would need to update registration systems and polling procedures, and state and tribal governments, which could receive federal funding to issue free IDs.
ai_headline: Voter ID Act would require photo ID for federal elections nationwide
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 653.

title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services of the Department of Health and Human Services relating to "Medicare Program; Implementation of Prior Authorization for Select Services for the Wasteful and Inappropriate Services Reduction (WISeR) Model".
ai_summary:
This bill would cancel a Medicare rule created by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) called the "WISeR Model" (Wasteful and Inappropriate Services Reduction). That rule set up a program requiring prior authorization for certain Medicare services, meaning doctors or providers would need to get approval from Medicare before performing specific procedures, to try to cut down on unnecessary or wasteful medical spending. This bill uses a special congressional process, allowed under a law called the Congressional Review Act, that lets Congress vote to reject rules made by federal agencies. If passed, the WISeR rule would be treated as if it never took effect.

This matters to everyday people mainly if they or their family members use Medicare, the health insurance program for people 65 and older and some people with disabilities. Prior authorization rules can affect how quickly patients get certain treatments, since providers must first get government approval. Supporters of canceling the rule might argue it could create delays or added paperwork burdens for doctors and patients, while supporters of keeping the rule might argue it helps prevent unnecessary or costly procedures. Doctors, hospitals, and other Medicare providers would also be affected, since they would no longer need to follow the prior authorization requirements this rule created if the resolution becomes law.

This bill does not change other parts of Medicare and does not affect people who aren't enrolled in Medicare. It specifically targets this one CMS rule and the process for approving certain medical services under the WISeR Model program.

title: NO FAKES Act of 2026
ai_summary:
S. 4591, the NO FAKES Act of 2026, creates a new federal legal right for people to control the use of AI-generated "digital replicas" of their voice or likeness. This covers realistic computer-generated video, audio, or images that make it look or sound like a real person said or did something they didn't, including deepfake alterations of real recordings. Under the bill, using someone's digital replica without permission—or creating or distributing tools designed mainly to make unauthorized deepfakes of specific people—could lead to civil lawsuits, with damages of thousands of dollars per violation plus possible punitive damages for willful misuse. Importantly, this right doesn't expire when a person dies; it can be inherited and lasts up to 70 years after death, similar to how copyrights or estates work.

The bill affects everyday people, celebrities, actors, musicians, and their estates, giving them legal tools to fight back against unauthorized AI-generated fakes of themselves, including in explicit or misleading content. It also affects tech companies, social media platforms, and websites that host user-uploaded content: these companies get a "safe harbor" (protection from lawsuits) if they set up a system to promptly remove flagged deepfakes when notified, similar to how copyright takedown notices work online. There are exceptions for legitimate uses like news reporting, documentaries, parody, and criticism, so long as the content isn't presented as if it were real footage of the person or used in sexually explicit material. Filing false takedown claims or false counter-claims can also result in penalties.

The bill would take effect 180 days after becoming law and would generally apply only to conduct occurring after enactment, though the ownership right itself would apply even to people who died before the law passed. It also limits (preempts) most state laws on this topic going forward, while preserving some existing state laws already on the books before January 2025, particularly those addressing sexually explicit deepfakes or election-related fakes.

title: Cameras in the Courtroom Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require the U.S. Supreme Court to allow television cameras to record its public sessions, including oral arguments. Right now, the Supreme Court decides on its own whether to allow cameras, and it generally does not, though it sometimes releases audio recordings. This bill would change that by making televised coverage the default rule.

The only exception allowed under this bill is if a majority of the justices vote that filming a specific case would violate the due process rights of someone involved in the case. In that situation, the Court could block cameras for that particular case. Otherwise, all open sessions would need to be available for TV coverage.

This bill would primarily affect the Supreme Court itself, the lawyers and parties who argue cases before it, and the news media and general public who want to watch proceedings. Supporters of this kind of change generally argue it would increase transparency in how the Court operates, since millions of Americans could watch arguments directly rather than relying on written summaries or transcripts. It would not change how the Court rules on cases or how justices are selected; it only concerns whether the public can watch the Court's sessions on television.

title: Sunshine in the Courtroom Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Sunshine in the Courtroom Act of 2025, would let cameras and recording equipment into federal courtrooms under certain conditions. Right now, most federal court proceedings cannot be photographed, recorded, or broadcast. Under this bill, the judge in charge of a case—whether in a federal appeals court, the Supreme Court, or a district (trial) court—would get to decide whether to allow media coverage of their courtroom. Judges could still say no if they believe recording would violate a party's right to a fair trial.

The bill includes several protections. Jurors and the jury selection process could never be recorded or broadcast. Witnesses could ask to have their face and voice disguised so they aren't recognizable, and judges must tell witnesses about this right. Extra-strict rules would apply to protect vulnerable witnesses, such as crime victims, minors, undercover officers, and witnesses in protection programs, with detailed guidelines to be written by the federal courts' governing body within six months. Private conversations between lawyers and their clients, or between lawyers and the judge, could not be recorded even if cameras are otherwise allowed.

This would affect anyone involved in federal court cases—including witnesses, victims, lawyers, defendants, and judges—as well as news organizations and the public, who could potentially watch more court proceedings than before. The permission for district (trial) court cameras would automatically expire three years after the law passes unless Congress renews it, while appeals courts and the Supreme Court would have this option on an ongoing basis. Judges could also set their own rules for how media equipment is used in their courtrooms, and any costs to set up this equipment could be charged to the media rather than paid by taxpayers.
ai_headline: Bill would let judges allow cameras in federal courtrooms

title: Foundation of the Federal Bar Association Charter Amendments Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill updates the federal charter for the Foundation of the Federal Bar Association, which is a nonprofit organization that Congress officially recognized many years ago. A federal charter doesn't give an organization money or government power—it's more like an official acknowledgment of the group's existence and purpose, along with some basic rules it must follow. This bill changes those rules to give the organization more flexibility in how it runs itself.

Specifically, the bill lets the organization set its own rules about membership requirements, how its board of directors and officers are chosen, and where its main office is located, instead of having those details locked into federal law. Previously, for example, the group's headquarters had to be in Washington, D.C.; now the board can choose any location in the U.S. The bill also updates rules about legal processes (service of process) to follow state law instead of a fixed federal standard, and clarifies rules about handling money, banning political lobbying activity, preventing insiders from personally profiting, and how leftover assets would be distributed if the organization ever dissolved.

This bill mainly affects the Foundation of the Federal Bar Association itself and its members, officers, and directors. It does not affect the general public, taxpayers, or government spending in any significant way—it's essentially routine legislative housekeeping to modernize and simplify the legal rules governing this one specific nonprofit organization tied to the legal profession.

title: Federal Carjacking Enforcement Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes the federal law that makes carjacking a crime. Currently, prosecutors must prove that someone stole a vehicle "with the intent to cause death or serious bodily harm" in order to charge them under this federal law. This bill would lower that bar by changing the requirement to simply proving the person acted "knowingly" when taking the vehicle, meaning they intentionally took someone else's car by force or threat, without necessarily proving they meant to hurt or kill the victim.

The bill also adjusts the penalties. It sets stiffer punishment (up to 25 years in prison) for cases where the carjacker either intended to cause death or serious harm, or used a gun during the crime, and the victim suffered serious injury as a result. The toughest penalty, reserved for cases resulting in death, would still require proof that the person intended to cause death or serious harm when they took the vehicle—that stricter intent requirement stays in place only for the most severe outcome.

This bill mainly affects federal prosecutors, defense attorneys, and people accused of carjacking, since it changes what evidence must be proven in court and how harshly people can be sentenced. It could make it easier for the government to convict people under this federal law, since intent to harm no longer has to be proven for the base offense, while still requiring that stricter proof for cases resulting in death. Everyday drivers and carjacking victims may also feel effects indirectly, since supporters argue clearer, broader rules could support more prosecutions in armed carjacking cases.
ai_headline: Bill would lower intent standard needed to prosecute carjacking cases
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 404.

title: Retired Law Enforcement Officers Continuing Service Act
ai_summary:
This bill would let the U.S. Attorney General give grants to state, local, tribal, and territorial police departments so they can hire retired law enforcement officers for non-arrest, behind-the-scenes work. These retirees could help train civilian staff or directly assist with tasks like reviewing security camera footage, analyzing crime scenes, doing forensics work, helping with financial crime or homicide investigations, and providing computer or internet expertise. The bill specifically states these retired officers could not make arrests or use force, keeping their role limited to support tasks rather than active policing.

Before hiring anyone with grant money, police departments would have to make a genuine effort to check the retired officer's disciplinary history, either by searching a national database of decertified officers or by requesting records from their previous employers. The department's top officer would need to review any misconduct findings before finalizing a hiring decision. The bill also includes oversight rules: the Justice Department's Inspector General would regularly audit grant recipients, agencies with unresolved audit problems (misusing funds) would be barred from getting grants for two years, and the Attorney General would need to check for and report on any duplicate grants given to the same police department for similar purposes.

This bill mainly affects local and state police departments, which could receive new federal funding to expand their support staff, and retired law enforcement officers, who could find new paid opportunities using their experience without going back into frontline policing duties. It could also indirectly affect communities served by these departments, since freeing up funding for support tasks may let active officers focus more on direct law enforcement work.
ai_headline: Grants would let police hire retired officers for desk duty, not patrol
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 83.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill funds grants for police to hire retired officers for support work like forensics, barring them from arrests or force.
ai_sections.what: S 1563 would authorize the Attorney General to award grants to state, local, tribal, and territorial police departments to hire retired officers for non-arrest support roles, such as reviewing footage, forensics, financial crime and homicide investigation assistance, and computer expertise. These retirees could not make arrests or use force. Departments would also need to check hiring candidates' disciplinary histories before finalizing employment.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects state, local, tribal, and territorial police departments and retired law enforcement officers seeking non-frontline work; it may indirectly affect communities served by these agencies.
ai_sections.why: By shifting support tasks to retirees, active officers could redirect time toward direct law enforcement duties, though the summary makes no claims about effectiveness or outcomes.
ai_sections.cost: The bill establishes federal grants to police departments, with oversight including regular audits; agencies with unresolved fund misuse findings would lose grant eligibility for two years.

title: Improving Police CARE Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Improving Police CARE Act, sets rules for the quality of trauma first aid kits that police departments buy using a specific type of federal grant money, called Byrne Justice Assistance Grants. These grants help state and local law enforcement agencies pay for equipment and programs, and this bill makes sure that if that money is used to buy trauma kits, the kits actually meet solid medical standards.

Specifically, the bill requires the Bureau of Justice Assistance, working with trauma surgeons, emergency medical experts, and law enforcement groups, to create official performance standards for these kits within 180 days. The kits must include basic life-saving items such as a tourniquet, a bleeding-control bandage, gloves, scissors, instructional materials (like those from the "Stop the Bleed" campaign or the Red Cross), a carrying bag, and any other agency-approved supplies useful for treating serious injuries. Agencies can still buy individual parts separately and assemble their own kits, as long as the finished kit meets the standards.

This bill mainly affects police departments and other law agencies that receive Byrne grant funding, ensuring the trauma kits they purchase with taxpayer money are reliable and effective for treating severe bleeding injuries. It also indirectly affects police officers and the public, since better-equipped officers may be more prepared to respond to medical emergencies, such as shootings or serious accidents, before paramedics arrive.
ai_headline: Bill would set medical standards for police trauma kits bought with federal grants
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

ai_sections.tldr: The Improving Police CARE Act requires trauma kits bought with Byrne grant funds to meet official medical standards.
ai_sections.what: The bill requires the Bureau of Justice Assistance to work with medical and law enforcement experts to create performance standards for trauma first aid kits within 180 days. Kits bought with Byrne Justice Assistance Grant funds must include items like a tourniquet, bleeding-control bandage, gloves, scissors, instructional materials, and a carrying bag. Agencies may still assemble kits from separately purchased parts as long as the final kit meets the standards.
ai_sections.who: Police departments and law enforcement agencies that receive Byrne Justice Assistance Grant funding are directly affected. Police officers and the public are indirectly affected through emergency medical response.
ai_sections.why: The rules aim to ensure taxpayer-funded trauma kits meet solid medical standards rather than varying in quality across agencies.

title: Countering Threats and Attacks on Our Judges Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Countering Threats and Attacks on Our Judges Act, updates an existing law (the State Justice Institute Act of 1984) to help protect state and local judges and court staff from threats and violence. It allows the State Justice Institute, a federal organization that supports state courts, to give funding to qualified nonprofit organizations so they can set up a new "State Judicial Threat Intelligence and Resource Center."

This center would do several things: train judges, court staff, and local police on judicial safety; create security guides and conduct safety inspections of courthouses and judges' homes; watch for potential threats against judges; work with law enforcement agencies to respond to those threats; and build a national database to track and share information about threats against judicial officials. The organizations chosen to run this center must have real experience in courthouse security, court operations, and working with different types of courts, including rural and small-town courts.

The bill also requires the State Justice Institute to report annually to Congress on how many threats have occurred against judges and court staff, including details about the types and seriousness of those threats. This bill mainly affects state and local judges, court employees, and law enforcement agencies that work with courts, aiming to give them better tools and coordination to prevent and respond to safety threats. It does not directly affect the general public, though it reflects growing concern over increased threats against judges in recent years.
ai_headline: Bill would create national center to track threats against judges
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

This center would train judges and court staff, inspect courthouse and home security, monitor threats, coordinate with police, and build a national threat database. It also requires the State Justice Institute to report annually to Congress on threats against judges and court staff.

title: Opioid Overdose Data Collection Enhancement Act
ai_summary:
This bill updates an existing federal grant program, the Comprehensive Opioid Abuse Grant Program, to help states, cities, tribes, and local law enforcement track drug overdoses more effectively. It adds a new option under the program allowing these groups to apply for funding specifically to build or improve data-tracking tools, such as mobile apps or online maps, that record where fatal and nonfatal overdoses happen and where first responders use overdose-reversal medications like naloxone. The goal is to give communities faster, more accurate, real-time information about overdose trends so they can respond more effectively.

The bill also allows groups of law enforcement agencies working together (not just individual states or cities) to apply for these grants, but only for the purpose of building overdose-tracking systems. Any government or agency using the grant money for this purpose must first review what data and tools they already have, avoid duplicating existing systems, ensure their tool can share information with other federal, state, and local systems, and make the collected data available to relevant government agencies. The Attorney General is also required to consult with other federal agencies involved in drug policy, like the Office of National Drug Control Policy, when carrying out this program.

This bill mainly affects state and local governments, tribal governments, law enforcement agencies, and public health officials involved in responding to the opioid crisis. Indirectly, it could benefit the general public by improving how quickly and accurately communities can identify overdose hotspots and respond with resources like emergency medical services or public health interventions.
ai_headline: Bill adds overdose-tracking tech option to federal opioid grant program
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 127.

ai_sections.tldr: S 1098 lets states, tribes, and local police apply for existing federal grants to build overdose-tracking tools.

Recipients must review existing tools, avoid duplication, ensure data-sharing capability, and make data available to relevant agencies.

ai_sections.why: Faster, more accurate overdose data could change how communities allocate emergency medical and public health resources, though the summary notes this as an indirect effect.

title: TRACE Act
ai_summary:
The TRACE Act directs the Attorney General to add a new tracking feature to a national database called NamUs (the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System). This new feature would flag whether a missing person's last known location was on federal land, such as national forests or parks, or in U.S. coastal waters. It would also record specific details, like which forest, park, or coastal area was involved.

The bill also requires the Attorney General to send Congress an annual report showing how many missing persons cases in the database involve federal land or territorial waters as the last known location. This reporting would start about two years after the law takes effect and continue every year after that.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies that manage public lands and waters, such as the Forest Service, National Park Service, and Army Corps of Engineers, as well as law enforcement and families searching for missing loved ones. By tracking this information, officials hope to better understand how often people go missing on federal land or in coastal waters, which could help improve search efforts and resource allocation. The bill does not create new criminal penalties or change existing missing persons laws—it simply improves data collection and reporting.
ai_headline: Bill would track missing persons cases linked to federal land and waters
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

ai_sections.tldr: The TRACE Act would add a federal land and coastal waters tracking feature to the national missing persons database.

It also requires an annual report to Congress on how many cases involve these locations, starting about two years after enactment.

title: CHILD Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill updates a 1993 law called the National Child Protection Act, which allows certain organizations to request FBI background checks on people who work with children, the elderly, or people with disabilities. Currently, the law mostly covers direct employees and volunteers. This bill expands who can be checked by adding contractors, people who work for outside companies hired by these organizations, and individuals who are licensed or certified by these organizations to provide care.

In practical terms, this means organizations like daycare centers, nursing homes, or disability care agencies could now request background checks not just on their own staff, but also on contract workers they bring in, employees of companies they hire, and people they license or certify to provide care services. This closes a gap where someone could work closely with vulnerable people through a contract or licensing arrangement without going through the same background check process as a direct employee.

This affects businesses and nonprofits that serve children, elderly people, or people with disabilities, since they gain broader ability to screen the people who interact with those they serve. It also affects contractors, licensed caregivers, and certified individuals in these fields, who may now be subject to background checks that didn't previously apply to their specific working arrangement. The goal is to help these organizations better protect vulnerable populations by ensuring more of the people who have access to them have been screened for relevant criminal history.
ai_headline: Bill widens FBI background checks to contractors and licensed caregivers
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill lets organizations request FBI background checks on contractors and licensed caregivers, not just direct employees.
ai_sections.what: This bill updates the 1993 National Child Protection Act, which lets certain organizations request FBI background checks on people working with children, the elderly, or people with disabilities. It expands eligibility beyond direct employees and volunteers to include contractors, outside company employees, and individuals licensed or certified to provide care.

title: Less Bureaucracy, Better Workforce Development Act
ai_summary:
This bill would move career, technical, and adult education programs currently run by the Department of Education to the Department of Labor. Specifically, it transfers responsibility for the Carl D. Perkins Career and Technical Education Act, part of the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act, and adult literacy and adult education programs from the Education Department's Office of Career, Technical, and Adult Education to the Labor Department's Employment and Training Administration. Along with the programs themselves, the staff, budgets, property, contracts, and legal responsibilities connected to these programs would also move to the Labor Department.

The bill includes several technical rules to make this transition smooth: existing contracts, grants, and legal agreements stay valid; ongoing lawsuits and applications for benefits continue without interruption; and any reference to the "Secretary of Education" in other laws would now mean the "Secretary of Labor" for these specific programs. The Office of Management and Budget would oversee the transfer and must ensure it doesn't create new federal jobs overall. The change would take effect six months after the bill becomes law, though agencies could start preparing right away.

This bill would primarily affect state and local agencies, community colleges, and organizations that receive federal funding for career and technical education and adult literacy programs, since they would now work with the Labor Department instead of the Education Department. It could also affect students and adult learners in these programs, as well as federal employees who currently manage these programs at the Department of Education, since their jobs and functions would shift to a new agency. The stated goal is to reduce bureaucratic overlap by putting workforce-focused education programs under the same agency responsible for job training and employment services.
ai_headline: Bill would shift career and adult education programs to Labor Department
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 19 - 16.
