title: Tax Relief for Fraud Victims Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal tax rules to make it easier for people who lose money to theft or fraud to deduct those losses on their taxes. Currently, a 2017 tax law change generally blocks people from deducting personal casualty and theft losses unless they happened in a federally declared disaster area. This bill would repeal that limitation, so victims of theft in general could once again claim these losses as tax deductions.

The bill also adds special rules for people scammed through fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation, such as victims of romance scams, investment fraud, or con artists. These victims could choose which tax year to report the loss in (rather than being locked into the year the theft was discovered) and would get an extra year to file for a tax refund related to that loss. It also allows people who take early withdrawals from retirement accounts to cover fraud losses to avoid the usual tax penalty, and gives them extra time to repay that money or file refund claims.

Additionally, the bill includes a specific provision for homeowners whose houses were damaged by "pyrrhotite," a mineral that can cause concrete foundations to crumble. This is a known problem in parts of Connecticut and other states. These homeowners would get extended time to claim these tax deductions, dating back further than other filers. Overall, this bill mainly affects individual taxpayers who have been victims of theft, fraud scams, or deteriorating home foundations, giving them more tax relief and more time to file claims.
ai_headline: Bill would restore tax deductions for theft and fraud victims
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 39 - 0.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill lets theft and fraud victims deduct losses on taxes again, undoing a 2017 restriction.

It adds special rules for fraud and scam victims, letting them choose which tax year to report losses, giving extra time to file refund claims, and allowing penalty-free early retirement withdrawals to cover fraud losses. It also gives homeowners with pyrrhotite-damaged foundations extended, backdated time to claim deductions.

title: Title IX Clarification Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill would change the definitions section of Title IX, the federal law that bans sex discrimination in schools and colleges that receive federal funding. It adds specific legal definitions for "sex," "male," and "female" based on a person's reproductive biology—specifically, whether their body is naturally organized around producing sperm (male) or eggs (female). The bill states that "sex" under Title IX means this biological definition, rather than gender identity or other factors.

In practical terms, this bill would affect how schools, colleges, and universities apply Title IX rules covering things like school sports teams, locker rooms, dormitories, and other sex-separated programs or facilities. Because Title IX enforcement affects federal funding, this change would apply to essentially any public school district or college that receives federal money, which is nearly all of them. The bill would take effect immediately upon becoming law and would apply to any federally funded education programs going forward.

This bill is currently just a proposal that has been introduced in the House and referred to committee. It affects students, particularly transgender students, as well as school administrators who must apply Title IX rules, and it could influence ongoing legal and policy debates about how sex-based protections and accommodations are defined in education settings.
ai_headline: Bill would define sex in Title IX by reproductive biology
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 18 - 15.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8781 would define "sex," "male," and "female" in Title IX based on reproductive biology, not gender identity.
ai_sections.what: This bill would amend Title IX's definitions section to specify that "sex" means whether a person's body is biologically organized to produce sperm (male) or eggs (female). This legal definition would replace any interpretation based on gender identity. It would take effect immediately upon becoming law and apply to federally funded education programs going forward.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects students, particularly transgender students, and administrators at public schools, colleges, and universities that receive federal funding.
ai_sections.why: The change would reshape how schools apply Title IX rules to sports teams, locker rooms, dormitories, and other sex-separated programs, likely intensifying legal and policy debates over sex-based protections in education.

title: Data Infrastructure Energy Measurement and Standards Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), working with the Department of Energy, to create standardized ways of measuring how much energy and water data centers use, including the electricity and water consumed when training and running artificial intelligence models. Right now, there's no consistent method for tracking this usage, which makes it hard for utilities, researchers, and policymakers to predict future energy demand as data centers and AI systems continue to grow. The bill asks NIST to research measurement techniques, develop best practices and standard definitions, and account for factors like different cooling systems, workload types, and power sources.

Beyond measurement standards, the bill asks NIST to study gaps in data collection and availability, particularly around who can access information about data center energy use. It also directs NIST to help create shared data systems that let researchers and stakeholders track this usage over time, and to work with international partners to keep standards consistent globally. NIST would need to consult with industry, academic, and nonprofit groups, and report to Congress on its progress within one and two years.

This bill would primarily affect NIST and the Department of Energy, which would carry out the research and reporting. It would also affect companies that operate data centers (including major tech firms running AI systems), utility companies that supply them power, and researchers or policymakers who study energy demand. The bill authorizes $10 million per year from 2027 through 2029 to fund this work. It does not impose new regulations or reporting requirements on data center operators themselves—it focuses on building the measurement tools and standards that could inform future policy decisions.
ai_headline: NIST would develop standard measures for data center energy and water use
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 34 - 1.

NIST would research measurement techniques, develop best practices and definitions, study data access gaps, and help build shared data-tracking systems, coordinating with international partners.

title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Bureau of Land Management relating to Coastal Plain Oil and Gas Leasing Program Record of Decision.
ai_summary:
This bill cancels a decision made by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), a federal agency that manages public lands, regarding oil and gas drilling in the Coastal Plain area of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in Alaska. The BLM had issued a "Record of Decision" in December 2024 that set rules and terms for leasing this land to oil and gas companies. Congress is using a special law called the Congressional Review Act, which allows lawmakers to overturn certain federal agency rules through a simple majority vote, to reject this decision entirely. If passed, the BLM's plan would have no legal effect, essentially undoing that agency action.

This matters mainly to people involved in Arctic oil and gas development, including energy companies interested in leasing land in this remote Alaska region, as well as Alaska Native communities and residents who live near or depend on the Coastal Plain area. It also affects environmental groups and others concerned about wildlife and land protection in the refuge, since the leasing terms and conditions set by the BLM would be nullified. More broadly, this reflects how Congress can step in to block specific agency regulations it disagrees with, which affects the balance of power between federal agencies and lawmakers on land-use and energy policy.
ai_headline: Lawmakers move to void Arctic refuge drilling lease rules
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-52.

ai_sections.tldr: Congress could nullify BLM's December 2024 rules for oil and gas leasing in the Arctic refuge's Coastal Plain.
ai_sections.what: This bill uses the Congressional Review Act to cancel a BLM Record of Decision from December 2024 that set leasing rules and terms for oil and gas drilling in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. If passed, the BLM's decision would have no legal effect.

ai_sections.why: Nullifying the decision would eliminate the leasing terms and conditions the BLM had established, leaving the regulatory status of drilling in this area unresolved. It also illustrates Congress's power to override specific agency rules on land-use and energy policy.

title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "Waste Emissions Charge for Petroleum and Natural Gas Systems: Procedures for Facilitating Compliance, Including Netting and Exemptions".
ai_summary:
This bill cancels a federal regulation that the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) had put in place regarding the "Waste Emissions Charge" for oil and natural gas companies. That EPA rule was meant to explain how companies could comply with a fee charged on excess methane emissions from their operations, including details on how companies could offset emissions across different facilities ("netting") and qualify for exemptions from the charge. Congress is using a special law called the Congressional Review Act, which allows lawmakers to reject recently issued federal regulations with a simple majority vote.

If this resolution passes and is signed into law, the EPA's rule would be wiped out completely, as if it never existed, and the agency would be blocked from creating a very similar rule in the future unless Congress specifically allows it. This mainly affects oil and natural gas companies, since it changes the guidance they would have followed to calculate and pay fees related to methane leaks and waste from their equipment and operations. It could also affect environmental regulators and communities near oil and gas facilities, since methane is a greenhouse gas linked to climate change, and this rule was part of a broader effort to reduce those emissions from the industry.

This bill does not create new rules itself—it simply removes the specific EPA rule described, which dealt with compliance procedures for the methane fee, not the fee itself (which was created by a separate law).
ai_headline: Congress votes to scrap EPA rule on oil and gas methane fee compliance
last_action_text: Became Public Law No: 119-2.

title: Federal Workers’ Compensation Integrity and Care Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change how the federal government checks on people receiving workers' compensation benefits after being injured on the job as federal employees. The Federal Employees' Compensation Act (FECA) program, run by the Department of Labor, pays benefits to federal workers hurt at work. This bill lets the Secretary of Labor request earnings and employment information about benefit recipients from the Social Security Administration and the Department of Health and Human Services, including Social Security benefit payments and new-hire records. The goal is to catch cases where someone might be improperly receiving both a paycheck (or other income) and workers' compensation benefits at the same time.

Under this bill, the Secretary of Labor could get this information without needing to notify the employee or get their permission first. The Social Security Administration and HHS would be required to share the requested data quickly, for free, and following procedures spelled out in formal agreements that must be set up within 90 days of the law passing. The Department of Labor would also need to create internal procedures for matching up individuals' identities and job status with this newly available information.

This bill mainly affects federal employees who receive or apply for workers' compensation benefits through FECA, since their earnings and employment records could now be more closely monitored. It also affects the agencies involved—the Social Security Administration, HHS, and the Department of Labor—by creating new data-sharing responsibilities between them. Supporters would likely argue this helps prevent fraud and overpayments, while others might raise questions about privacy since data can be shared without an employee's knowledge or consent.
ai_headline: Bill would let Labor Dept check injured workers' pay data without consent
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 32 - 0.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill lets Labor check federal workers' comp recipients' earnings via SSA and HHS data without telling them first.

title: Congressional Records Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Congressional Records Protection Act, would create new legal limits on how government agencies can obtain records belonging to members of Congress and congressional staff. It would generally block agencies from using warrants, subpoenas, court orders, or similar tools to get records tied to a lawmaker's or staffer's official work, communications, or accounts—unless that specific person is the actual target of a criminal investigation and a judge has certified that probable cause exists. Records covered include written materials, emails, phone communications, and electronic devices used in official congressional duties.

If agencies do get permission to seek such records because a lawmaker or staffer is under criminal investigation, the bill requires them to notify that person before or shortly after collecting the material, though notice can be delayed up to 10 days if a judge agrees that early notice could endanger someone, let a suspect flee, destroy evidence, intimidate witnesses, or otherwise seriously harm the investigation. Even after collecting records, investigators generally must wait 30 days before reviewing them, unless there's an immediate risk to someone's life or safety.

The bill mainly affects federal, state, and local government agencies that investigate crimes, as well as current and former members of Congress and their staff. Its supporters describe it as a response to concerns about government surveillance of lawmakers, while the practical effect would be added legal hurdles and required court approval before investigators can access congressional records or communications.
ai_headline: Bill would require warrants and judicial sign-off to seize congressional records
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 22 - 1.

ai_sections.tldr: New bill would require probable cause and judicial approval before agencies can seize records of lawmakers or staff.
ai_sections.what: The Congressional Records Protection Act would bar agencies from using warrants, subpoenas, or court orders to obtain records tied to a lawmaker's or staffer's official work unless that person is the target of a criminal investigation and a judge certifies probable cause. If approved, agencies must notify the affected person before or shortly after collecting records, with notice delayable up to 10 days under certain conditions. Investigators must generally wait 30 days before reviewing collected records unless there's an immediate risk to someone's life or safety.
ai_sections.who: The bill applies to federal, state, and local agencies that investigate crimes, and to current and former members of Congress and their staff.
ai_sections.why: The change would add legal hurdles and court approval requirements before investigators can access congressional records or communications, affecting how criminal probes involving lawmakers proceed.

title: Congressional Authorization for Federal Building Names Act
ai_summary:
This bill would require that any renaming of federal property—such as buildings, monuments, or other government-owned sites whose names were set by federal law—can only happen through a new law passed by Congress. Currently, some federal officials, including agency heads or presidential appointees, have been able to rename certain federal properties through administrative action. This bill would close that option and make Congress the sole authority for changing these names.

The bill also creates a new crime for political appointees or Senate-confirmed officials who intentionally display an incorrect name on federal property or rename it without Congress's approval. Penalties would depend on the cost of the damage caused: up to 10 years in prison if the damage exceeds $1,000, or up to 1 year if it's less. This provision would take effect January 1, 2027, and violations could be prosecuted for up to 10 years after they occur.

This legislation would primarily affect federal agencies, political appointees, and Senate-confirmed officials who oversee federal buildings, parks, military bases, or other properties named by law. It would not affect ordinary citizens directly, but it could influence future disputes over renaming federal sites—such as buildings or landmarks named after historical figures—by shifting that decision-making power entirely to Congress rather than the executive branch.
ai_headline: Bill would give Congress sole power to rename federal properties
last_action_text: Referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, and in addition to the Committees on Transportation and Infrastructure, and Oversight and Government Reform, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

ai_sections.tldr: Only Congress could rename federal properties, and officials who defy this could face up to 10 years in prison.

The criminal provision takes effect January 1, 2027, with a 10-year window for prosecution.

title: I&A Mission Reorientation Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill changes the mission focus of the Office of Intelligence and Analysis (I&A), a part of the Department of Homeland Security that shares intelligence information. Congress found that this office is supposed to help state, local, tribal, and territorial governments, as well as private businesses, by sharing useful security information with them. However, Congress is concerned that the office may have shifted toward mainly collecting information from these local partners and sending it up to federal intelligence agencies, rather than sharing helpful information back down to the communities that need it.

To fix this, the bill officially requires I&A to treat support for local governments and businesses as equally important as support for federal intelligence agencies. It directs the office to actively watch for emerging threats, share information in both directions (not just collect it), stay closely connected with regional "fusion centers" (hubs where local and federal agencies share intelligence), and make sure that serving top DHS leadership doesn't come at the expense of serving local partners. The bill also requires DHS to report to Congress within 180 days on how it's making these changes and how it will measure success.

This bill mainly affects DHS operations and the way intelligence flows between the federal government and local police, emergency responders, tribal governments, and private companies involved in security. It does not change the office's watchlisting duties, meaning any current watchlist-related work stays the same. Everyday residents would likely feel the effects indirectly, through how well their local police and emergency agencies receive timely security warnings and threat information from the federal government.
ai_headline: Bill directs DHS intelligence office to prioritize local partners equally with feds
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 30 - 0.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 7443 requires DHS's I&A office to treat local and federal intelligence-sharing as equally important.

It directs I&A to watch for emerging threats, share information in both directions, stay connected with fusion centers, and ensure serving DHS leadership doesn't crowd out local support. DHS must report to Congress within 180 days on implementation and success metrics.

title: National Cemetery Administration Annual Report Act of 2026
ai_summary:
HR 7260, the National Cemetery Administration Annual Report Act of 2026, would require the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to send Congress a detailed yearly report on the operations of the National Cemetery Administration, which manages national cemeteries for veterans. The first report would be due within one year of the law passing, and updates would continue every year after that.

The report would have to include a lot of specific details, such as how many veterans and eligible family members were buried in each national cemetery, broken down by type of burial (casket or cremation) and category of eligibility. It would also need to cover customer satisfaction levels, maps of national and state/tribal veterans' cemeteries, available burial options, the number of headstones, markers, medallions, and presidential memorial certificates given out, construction projects completed or planned, unclaimed veteran remains interred, and information on grants given to states, counties, or tribal organizations to help run veterans' cemeteries. The Secretary would also have to post each report publicly online.

This bill mainly affects the Department of Veterans Affairs, which would have new reporting duties, and indirectly benefits veterans, their families, and lawmakers by making cemetery operations, burial services, and spending more transparent and easier to track over time.
ai_headline: Bill would require yearly public report on veterans' cemeteries
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by Voice Vote.

The first report is due within one year of enactment, with updates every year after, and each report must be posted publicly online.

title: Small Business Regulatory Flexibility Improvements Act
ai_summary:
HR 421 amends the Regulatory Flexibility Act, a law that requires federal agencies to study how new regulations will affect small businesses, nonprofits, and small local governments. The bill expands what counts as a "rule" that needs this review, requires agencies to consider indirect costs (not just direct ones) on small entities, and requires agencies to look at both harmful and beneficial effects of proposed rules. It also adds tribal organizations to the list of groups covered, requires review of certain land management plan changes by federal land agencies, and updates the definition of "small organization" for nonprofits. Agencies would have to produce more detailed written analyses explaining why a rule is needed, who it affects, and what alternatives were considered, and must publish plain-language summaries online.

The bill also boosts the power of the Small Business Administration's Chief Counsel for Advocacy, an official who represents small business interests in the rulemaking process. This office would gain authority to write binding rules for how agencies comply with the law, intervene in agency legal disputes, help set small-business size standards, and receive draft regulations early for review. It also creates a formal process where small businesses can be consulted before major rules are finalized, requires agencies to periodically review old rules for their impact on small businesses, and allows lawsuits challenging agency compliance to be filed after a final rule is published (not just during the proposal stage). Separately, the bill requires agencies to generally waive fines for a small business's first-time paperwork violation, with exceptions for serious harm, fraud, tax law, or public safety issues.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies that issue regulations, small businesses and nonprofits that must comply with those regulations, and organizations like the SBA's Office of Advocacy that represent small business interests. Everyday consumers could be indirectly affected since it changes how thoroughly agencies must weigh small-business impacts before finalizing rules on things like the environment, labor, health, or land use.
ai_headline: Bill would force agencies to weigh regulations' impact on small businesses more closely
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 13 - 12.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 421 would expand and strengthen small-business impact reviews before federal agencies finalize new regulations.

title: To direct the United States Postal Service to designate single, unique ZIP Codes for certain communities, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill requires the United States Postal Service to create a single, unique ZIP Code for each of about 66 named communities across the country, located in states including California, Colorado, Florida, Indiana, Texas, Wisconsin, and others. The Postal Service would have 270 days after the bill becomes law to complete this assignment. The bill lists each community by name and state, and includes cities, towns, villages, and townships of varying sizes.

The practical reason behind this kind of legislation is that many of these communities currently share a ZIP Code with a neighboring town or are grouped under a ZIP Code associated with a different city name. This can cause confusion with mail delivery, local identity, business addresses, emergency services coordination, and sometimes even how a community is perceived or classified for purposes like insurance rates, marketing, or local tax jurisdiction records. Residents in these areas have often lobbied for their own ZIP Code so their community appears correctly on mail, packages, and address-based systems.

This bill mainly affects residents, businesses, and local governments in the specifically named communities, since they would gain a distinct ZIP Code separate from whatever larger city or postal zone they currently share. It does not affect people outside these listed places, and it does not change any other postal rules, rates, or services nationwide.
ai_headline: Bill would give 66 named communities their own distinct ZIP codes
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.

The Postal Service would have 270 days after enactment to complete the assignments. Each affected community is listed by name and state.

title: Assuring the Future of Tibet Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Assuring the Future of Tibet Act of 2026, would direct the U.S. government to increase diplomatic support for the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), which is the Tibetan government-in-exile led by officials elected by Tibetan communities and historically tied to the Dalai Lama. The bill states that Congress views the CTA as the legitimate representative of the Tibetan people and criticizes a 2026 Chinese law that limits the use of Tibetan language and culture in favor of a unified national Chinese identity. It also states that the Gaden Phodrang Trust, a religious institution connected to the Dalai Lama, is the proper authority for recognizing future Dalai Lamas, which is relevant because China has separately claimed authority over that process.

To carry out these positions, the bill instructs the U.S. Secretary of State and U.S. representative to the United Nations to push for the CTA to gain observer status or participation rights in the UN and other international organizations. It also calls for senior U.S. officials to meet directly with CTA leaders, including its top elected official (the Sikyong), and to consider extending diplomatic courtesies such as security protection during visits to the U.S. The State Department would need to report to Congress each year for ten years on the progress made toward these goals.

This bill mainly affects U.S. foreign policy and diplomatic relations, particularly with China and Tibet-related organizations. It does not create new domestic programs or directly affect the daily lives of most Americans. It would likely affect U.S.-China relations, as China strongly objects to any international recognition of the Tibetan government-in-exile, and it could influence how the U.S. State Department engages with Tibetan advocacy groups and international bodies going forward.
ai_headline: Bill seeks stronger US diplomatic ties with Tibetan government-in-exile
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Foreign Relations.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill would push the US to boost diplomatic support for the Tibetan government-in-exile and seek it UN observer status.
ai_sections.what: This bill would direct US officials to increase diplomatic support for the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), the Tibetan government-in-exile. It calls for pursuing CTA observer status at the UN, direct meetings between senior US officials and CTA leaders, and possible diplomatic courtesies like security protection during US visits. It also states Congress's view that the Gaden Phodrang Trust, not China, should have authority over recognizing future Dalai Lamas.

title: Department of Homeland Security Appropriations Act, 2026
ai_summary:
This bill funds the Department of Homeland Security for the 2026 budget year, covering agencies like Customs and Border Protection (CBP), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), the Coast Guard, Secret Service, FEMA, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). It sets specific dollar amounts each agency can spend on staffing, equipment, buildings, vehicles, and technology, and includes disaster relief funding, flood insurance program money, and grants to state and local governments for emergency preparedness, firefighting, transit security, and nonprofit security. It also includes hundreds of detailed rules attached to the money—like requiring reports to Congress, limiting how funds can be reprogrammed, and restricting certain activities unless lawmakers are notified first.

Beyond the funding numbers, the bill contains many policy-related conditions. For example, it restricts ICE from performing or facilitating abortions or gender-related medical care for detainees, blocks new border-crossing fees, requires prioritizing detention and removal of immigrants with criminal or terrorism ties, limits when detention facilities can be inspected, and prevents defunding of 287(g) agreements allowing local police to help enforce immigration law unless serious violations are found. It also protects individuals importing small amounts of prescription drugs from Canada, bans admitting foreign drone systems from adversary nations, requires airport screening to apply equally to members of Congress and top officials, and restricts Coast Guard whale-protection speed rules not already in place before 2021.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies and their employees, government contractors, immigrants and asylum seekers, state and local governments receiving DHS grants, airports and airlines, ports, disaster survivors relying on FEMA aid, flood insurance policyholders, and taxpayers generally, since it determines how tens of billions of dollars in federal spending will be used for border security, immigration enforcement, disaster response, and homeland security operations over the next fiscal year.
ai_headline: DHS funding bill sets 2026 budget with new immigration policy riders
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 139.

title: Combatting the Persecution of Religious Groups in the People’s Republic of China Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Combatting the Persecution of Religious Groups in the People's Republic of China Act, lays out U.S. policy on religious freedom issues in China without creating new laws or spending money directly. It states that Chinese government officials responsible for abuses like arbitrary detention, forced sterilization, torture, or forced labor against religious and ethnic minorities—such as Tibetan Buddhists, Christians, Uyghur Muslims, and Falun Gong practitioners—should be evaluated for sanctions under the existing Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act, which allows the U.S. to penalize foreign officials for human rights violations. It also supports State Department programs that promote religious freedom in China and track repression of these groups.

The bill expresses Congress's views (called a "sense of Congress") that the U.S. should use diplomacy to pressure China on these issues, including raising specific cases of imprisoned individuals with top Chinese officials, calling for the release of political prisoners, and pushing for humane treatment of detainees, including access to family, lawyers, and medical care. It also encourages global religious communities to support persecuted groups in China and calls for better documentation of abuses and support for human rights defenders and dissidents.

Finally, the bill requires the U.S. Ambassador at Large for International Religious Freedom to give Congress an annual briefing on sanctions imposed, diplomatic efforts, and actions taken on behalf of political prisoners. This bill mainly affects U.S. foreign policy and diplomatic priorities rather than everyday Americans directly, though it could influence relations with China and shape how the U.S. responds to human rights concerns involving Chinese officials and international religious communities.
ai_headline: Bill sets US policy pressing China over religious minority persecution
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Foreign Relations.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill sets U.S. policy urging sanctions and diplomacy over China's treatment of religious and ethnic minorities.

It says Chinese officials responsible for abuses against groups like Tibetan Buddhists, Christians, Uyghur Muslims, and Falun Gong practitioners should be evaluated for sanctions under the existing Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act. It also expresses Congress's support for diplomacy, documentation of abuses, and an annual briefing to Congress on related actions.

title: Venezuela Democratic Transition Strategy Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Venezuela Democratic Transition Strategy Act, would require the U.S. Secretary of State to create a detailed plan within 180 days for helping Venezuela move toward democracy. The plan would need to cover several areas: U.S. diplomatic efforts to support democratic change, steps to help free people who have been unfairly jailed for political reasons, ways to reduce the influence of countries like Cuba, Russia, Iran, and China within Venezuela's military and government, how U.S. foreign aid could help ordinary Venezuelans through humanitarian assistance and support for basic services, and how the U.S. can support Venezuelan civil society groups such as independent media, journalists, and human rights organizations.

After submitting this strategy, the Secretary of State would have to report back to Congress once a year for two years, explaining what progress has been made and suggesting any changes needed. The Secretary would also have to regularly check in with relevant congressional committees—specifically the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Senate Foreign Relations Committee—twice a year to discuss how things are going.

This bill mainly affects U.S. government operations, particularly the State Department, by creating new reporting and planning requirements related to foreign policy toward Venezuela. It does not directly create new laws for individual Americans, but it could shape how U.S. foreign aid, diplomacy, and sanctions policy toward Venezuela are organized in the coming years. It may also indirectly affect Venezuelan citizens, political prisoners, journalists, and civil society groups who could benefit from increased U.S. attention and support.
ai_headline: Bill would require State Department plan for Venezuela's democratic transition
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported by the Yeas and Nays: 41 - 5.

title: Drug Shortage Compounding Patient Access Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill changes federal rules about "compounded" medications—drugs mixed or prepared by pharmacists or physicians for specific needs, rather than made by big pharmaceutical manufacturers. Right now, compounded drugs are generally supposed to be made for one specific, named patient with a prescription. This bill creates an exception: when a drug is on the FDA's official shortage list, pharmacists or physicians could compound it in small batches for hospitals or clinics to use urgently on patients, even before a specific patient is identified—as long as the prescriber tried and failed to get the drug from an approved "outsourcing facility" first, the product is properly labeled, and follow-up patient records and any bad reactions are reported to the FDA. The bill also updates how the FDA defines and tracks drug shortages, adding "surges in demand" (not just supply problems) as a reportable shortage cause, and requires manufacturers to report these surges to the FDA as soon as possible.

The bill also makes some technical changes to how "outsourcing facilities" (larger-scale compounding operations regulated separately) determine which drug ingredients they can use, requires the FDA to publicly post yearly updates on approved bulk drug substances, and standardizes the warning label required on compounded drugs to clearly state they haven't been FDA-approved.

This bill would primarily affect hospitals, pharmacists, physicians who compound medications, and drug manufacturers, by giving providers more flexibility to prepare and stockpile small amounts of shortage medications for urgent hospital use. Patients could benefit if it becomes easier for hospitals to have backup supplies of critical drugs during shortages, such as during a surge in illness or a supply chain disruption. It also affects the FDA, which would take on new reporting and transparency duties related to tracking drug shortages and demand surges.
ai_headline: Bill would let pharmacists pre-mix shortage drugs before a patient is named
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 5316 would let compounders pre-make small batches of FDA shortage-list drugs for urgent hospital use.

It also updates FDA shortage definitions to include demand surges and adds reporting requirements for outsourcing facilities and manufacturers.

title: Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe Project Lands Restoration Act
ai_summary:
This bill would transfer about 1,082 acres of federal land in Washington State, currently part of Olympic National Park, into trust status for the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe. Land held "in trust" means the federal government holds legal title, but the land is set aside for the tribe's use and benefit, and it would officially become part of the Lower Elwha Indian Reservation. The land involved is tied to the Elwha River area, where a major dam removal and ecosystem restoration project has been underway for years.

The bill skips certain standard federal procedures, such as requiring a formal appraisal or value equalization before transferring the land. It also specifies that part of the land along the Elwha River will continue to be managed under the Wild and Scenic Rivers Act, meaning environmental protections for that river will still apply. The bill explicitly says the land cannot be used for gaming purposes (such as building a casino) and that nothing in the act changes the tribe's existing treaty rights from an 1855 treaty with the U.S. government.

This bill mainly affects the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe, giving them expanded control over ancestral lands, as well as the National Park Service, which currently manages that part of Olympic National Park. It could also matter to Washington State residents and visitors interested in the Elwha River restoration project, environmental groups tracking land and river protections, and anyone interested in federal policy on Native American land and tribal sovereignty.
ai_headline: Bill would shift 1,082 acres of Olympic National Park to tribal trust land
last_action_text: Committee on Indian Affairs. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: S 1513 would place about 1,082 acres of Olympic National Park into trust for the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe.

It skips standard requirements like a formal appraisal or value equalization, keeps Wild and Scenic Rivers Act protections along the Elwha River, and bars gaming use on the land.

title: A bill to amend the Act of August 9, 1955 (commonly known as the "Long-Term Leasing Act"), to authorize leases of up to 99 years for land in the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe Reservation and land held in trust for the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah), and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal law to let two Massachusetts tribes—the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe and the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah)—enter into land leases lasting up to 99 years. Currently, a 1955 federal law called the Long-Term Leasing Act limits how long certain tribes can lease out their trust or reservation land, and some tribes have been given special permission for longer lease terms while others have not. This bill adds these two tribes to the list of those allowed the longer, 99-year leasing option.

In practical terms, this means the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe Reservation and land held in trust for the Aquinnah tribe could be leased out for much longer periods than shorter-term limits might otherwise allow. Longer lease terms can make it easier for tribes to attract businesses, developers, or other partners for housing, commercial projects, or economic development, since longer leases often provide more certainty and financial appeal to investors.

This bill mainly affects the two named tribes and anyone who might do business with them, such as companies or organizations looking to build housing, commercial buildings, or other projects on tribal land. It would not affect other tribes, non-tribal land, or the general public directly, but it fits into a broader pattern of Congress periodically updating leasing rules for individual tribes to support their economic development goals.
ai_headline: Two Massachusetts tribes could get 99-year land lease option
last_action_text: Committee on Indian Affairs. Ordered to be reported without amendment favorably.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill lets the Mashpee Wampanoag and Aquinnah tribes lease land for up to 99 years instead of shorter terms.

ai_sections.why: Longer lease terms can provide more certainty for investors and developers, potentially affecting how these two tribes pursue economic development. Other tribes, non-tribal land, and the general public are not directly affected.

title: Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill directs the federal government to transfer about 265 acres of land in California into trust status for the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians, a federally recognized tribe. It cancels an older 1964 federal order that had restricted use of one piece of land, and it requires the Secretary of the Interior to place two specific parcels — roughly 80 acres of Bureau of Land Management land and about 185 acres known as "Indian Creek Ranch" — into trust for the tribe within 180 days of the bill becoming law. Once in trust, this land would officially become part of the tribe's reservation and would be managed under the same rules that apply to other tribal trust lands nationwide.

Before finalizing the transfer, the Secretary must check whether a new land survey is needed and, if so, complete one, keeping the results available for public review. The bill also includes a specific restriction: this newly transferred land cannot be used for casino-style gambling operations (either "class II" or "class III" gaming, as defined under federal Indian gaming law).

This bill mainly affects the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians, who would gain expanded trust land tied to their reservation, and the federal Bureau of Land Management, which currently oversees the property. It could also matter to nearby California communities and local governments, since converting land to federal trust status can change how it's taxed, zoned, and regulated. It does not affect the general public directly, but it reflects a broader, common practice of Congress restoring or expanding tribal land holdings.

title: CRUISE Act
ai_summary:
**HR 7083 – The CRUISE Act** would change how the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) pays car dealers when disabled veterans use a VA benefit to buy specially equipped vehicles (such as cars with hand controls or other adaptive equipment for veterans with certain disabilities). Under current law, the VA provides this automobile purchase benefit, but payments to the dealers who sell these vehicles can reportedly be slow or inconsistent.

The bill would require the VA to make these payments on time, in line with existing federal prompt-payment rules, and to publicly report how long it takes to process any payment that isn't completed within 30 days. It would also require the VA to centralize this payment process within its main Central Office, rather than handling it in a scattered or decentralized way, and to create a system for tracking and resolving any payments to dealers that remain unpaid for more than 90 days.

This bill mainly affects disabled veterans who qualify for VA help buying adapted vehicles, and the auto dealers who sell them these cars. By speeding up and standardizing payments, it aims to make sure dealers get reimbursed reliably, which could also make dealers more willing to work with veterans using this benefit. It does not change who qualifies for the benefit or how much veterans receive—it focuses only on fixing the payment process itself.
ai_headline: Bill seeks faster VA payments to dealers for adapted veteran vehicles
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by Voice Vote.

title: To amend title 38, United States Code, to establish the Office of Congressional and Legislative Affairs in the Department of Veterans Affairs, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
HR 7950 would create a new office within the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) called the Office of Congressional and Legislative Affairs. This office would act as the main point of contact between the VA and Congress, handling things like preparing testimony for hearings, tracking congressional requests for information, and helping develop legislative proposals. The office would be led by a Senate-confirmed Assistant Secretary, with two deputies: one political appointee who shapes the VA's official positions on legislation, and one career civil servant who handles the actual production and delivery of documents to Congress. The bill requires that at least 65% of the office's staff be career employees rather than political appointees, aiming to keep day-to-day operations professional and less subject to political turnover.

A major part of the bill sets strict deadlines for how the VA must respond to information requests from the House and Senate Veterans' Affairs Committees—acknowledging requests within 2 days, giving a production plan within 5 days, and delivering materials within 45 days (with some flexibility for complex requests). It also bans VA officials from screening, delaying, or watering down information sent to Congress, and requires classified information to be shared securely with committee leaders rather than withheld. If the VA misses these deadlines, it must explain the delay, submit a corrective action plan, and the office's funding could be frozen until it complies; the VA's independent Inspector General would also investigate the cause.

This bill mainly affects how the VA interacts with Congress and would not change veterans' benefits directly. It affects VA employees and leadership (creating new job positions and staffing rules), members of Congress and committee staff (giving them clearer rules and faster access to information), and indirectly veterans and the public, who rely on effective congressional oversight of VA programs. A government watchdog agency (the Government Accountability Office) would also review how well this new system works two years after the law takes effect.
ai_headline: VA bill sets deadlines for answering Congress on veterans issues
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 13 - 10.

title: Kids Off Social Media Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Kids Off Social Media Act, would ban children under 13 from having accounts on social media platforms like Instagram, TikTok, or Snapchat. Platforms would have to delete accounts they know belong to children and remove the personal data collected from them, though kids could request a copy of their data for 90 days after their account is closed. The bill also bans social media companies from using personalized recommendation algorithms (the systems that suggest content based on someone's personal data) for any user under 17, though platforms could still use basic information like age, language, or general location to shape recommendations. Companies could still show chronological feeds of content a teen has chosen to follow. The bill defines "social media platform" carefully, excluding things like email, messaging apps, video games, online shopping sites, cloud storage, and news or educational sites.

The bill does not require companies to verify users' ages through ID checks; instead, enforcement relies on whether a company "reasonably should have known" a user's age based on available information. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce these rules, treating violations like deceptive business practices. Separately, the bill's "Eyes on the Board Act" section requires public schools that receive federal internet funding to block students from accessing social media on school networks and devices, with some exceptions for approved educational tools and teacher-led instruction.

This bill would primarily affect social media companies, who would need new systems to identify and remove underage users and adjust their recommendation algorithms for minors. It would also affect schools and libraries receiving federal internet funding, who would need to update their internet filtering policies. Parents, children, and teenagers would be affected by losing access to certain accounts and personalized content feeds until they turn 13 or 17, respectively.
ai_headline: Bill would bar under-13s from social media, curb teen algorithms
last_action_text: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 108.

title: Parents Opt-in Protection Act
ai_summary:
HR 4986, the Parents Opt-in Protection Act, would change an existing federal education law called the Protection of Pupils' Rights Amendment. Currently, schools that receive federal funding must get consent before requiring students to take certain surveys that ask about sensitive topics, like political beliefs, mental health, sexual behavior, or family income. This bill tightens that requirement by making clear that consent must be given in writing, and that this written permission must be obtained separately for each specific survey, rather than through a general one-time approval.

In practice, this means parents (or the student themselves, if they are an adult or legally emancipated) would need to sign off individually on each survey that asks for sensitive personal information before their child participates. Schools would no longer be able to rely on a blanket permission slip covering multiple surveys throughout the year. This affects public schools that receive federal funding, the teachers and administrators who run student surveys, and parents and students who fill them out, since it gives families more direct control and paperwork responsibility over which specific surveys their children take part in.
ai_headline: Bill would require separate written consent for each school survey
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 18 - 15.

That consent must be obtained separately for each specific survey rather than through a single general approval.

title: Stop Lawmakers From Predicting Act
ai_summary:
**HR 9367 — "Stop Lawmakers From Predicting Act"**

This bill would stop members of Congress, their spouses, and their dependent children from using "prediction markets" to make money. Prediction markets are betting-style platforms where people wager on the outcome of events, such as elections, government decisions, or policy changes. The bill bans covered individuals from entering into any bet or contract whose payout depends on a government policy, government action, political outcome, or any other event they learned about because of the lawmaker's job in Congress.

If a member of Congress, their spouse, or their child breaks this rule, the ethics office overseeing them can impose a financial penalty. The fine would be either $2,000 or 10% of the value of the bet, whichever is larger, plus any profit made from the illegal transaction. Lawmakers would not be allowed to pay these fines using official government office funds or campaign donations—they'd have to pay out of personal money. If a lawmaker leaves office without paying the fine, the ethics office can refer the matter to the Department of Justice for further action.

This bill mainly affects members of Congress and their immediate families, particularly those who might have access to insider knowledge about upcoming government decisions that could be used to profit from betting-style markets. It would not change laws for ordinary citizens using prediction markets. The rules would take effect 180 days after the bill becomes law, giving Congress and its ethics offices time to prepare guidance on how the new restrictions will be enforced.

last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 5 - 4.

title: AI-Ready Federal Data Guidelines Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to create voluntary guidelines that help federal agencies prepare their public data so it can be used to train artificial intelligence systems. The guidelines would cover things like formatting data so computers can read it properly, labeling and tagging information, checking data quality, documenting what the data means, keeping datasets updated, and making public data easier to access automatically. NIST would develop these standards working with other offices like the Office of Science and Technology Policy, the Department of Energy, and the Office of Management and Budget.

The bill also allows NIST to run up to two test programs, each lasting no more than a year, focused on specific fields such as biotechnology, to see how well these data guidelines work in practice and to identify problems before wider use. NIST would need to regularly update Congress on how this effort is going. Importantly, NIST cannot pull money from other existing programs to pay for this work, meaning it would need separate funding.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies that manage public data, NIST staff who would create and test the guidelines, and researchers, companies, universities, and national labs that might participate in the pilot programs. Indirectly, it could affect anyone who uses AI tools built on government data, such as researchers, businesses, and app developers, since clearer and better-organized federal datasets could make AI systems more accurate and reliable. Because the guidelines are voluntary, individual agencies would not be legally required to follow them, though they may choose to as a best practice.
ai_headline: NIST to draft voluntary rules for AI-ready federal data
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 29 - 0.

title: Oversight Access Act
ai_summary:
**H.R. 10111 — Oversight Access Act** would stop the Secretary of Homeland Security from blocking Members of Congress, or staff accompanying them, from entering any facility run by or for the Department of Homeland Security that is used to detain or house immigrants. This means members of Congress could visit these facilities to check on conditions without being turned away, and they would not have to give advance notice before showing up.

The bill also bars DHS from making any temporary changes to a facility just to affect what a visiting lawmaker sees — for example, cleaning up, moving detainees, or otherwise staging the site differently than it normally looks. If the DHS Inspector General finds that the Secretary failed to follow these rules, the Inspector General must report that failure to the Judiciary Committees in both the House and Senate within 30 days.

This bill primarily affects DHS leadership and staff who manage immigration detention facilities, as it limits their ability to restrict or control congressional visits. It also affects Members of Congress and their staff, giving them clearer legal authority to conduct surprise oversight visits. Indirectly, it could affect detained immigrants, since the law aims to ensure lawmakers see facilities under normal, unaltered conditions during oversight checks.

title: To make technical amendments to update statutory references to certain provisions classified to title 7, title 20, and title 43, United States Code, and to correct related technical errors.
ai_summary:
HR 5204 is a "housekeeping" bill that fixes outdated cross-references in federal law. Over the years, Congress has moved, renumbered, or reorganized sections of the U.S. Code (the official collection of federal laws), but many other laws still point to the old, now-incorrect section numbers. This bill goes through dozens of laws dealing with agriculture, education, land management, wildlife, taxes, and territories, and updates the citations so they correctly point to where those provisions now actually live in the law books. For example, it corrects old references to a 1965 agricultural extension law, updates citations related to student loan and higher education programs that were moved from one part of the code to another, and fixes references to laws about federal land grants and forestry programs.

Importantly, this bill does not change any actual policy, rights, benefits, or rules. It doesn't add new programs, cut funding, or alter who qualifies for anything. It simply makes sure that when one law refers to another law, it's pointing to the correct, current legal citation instead of an obsolete one. This kind of technical corrections bill mainly matters to lawyers, government agencies, and researchers who rely on accurate citations to interpret and apply the law correctly. For the average person, it has no direct practical effect — it's essentially legal bookkeeping to keep the U.S. Code accurate and easier to navigate.

title: Public Company Advisory Committee Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill creates a new group called the Public Company Advisory Committee inside the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Its job would be to give the SEC advice on rules and policies affecting publicly traded companies—things like corporate governance, shareholder voting procedures, stock trading rules, and how companies raise money. The committee would not weigh in on the SEC's enforcement actions against companies. It would have 10 to 20 members appointed by the SEC, mostly executives from public companies, along with representatives from business associations and professional advisers like lawyers and accountants. Members would serve four-year terms, and the committee would meet at least twice a year.

The bill mainly affects large publicly traded companies, their executives, and the professionals who advise them, since they would gain a formal channel to influence SEC policy decisions. It also affects the SEC itself, which would need to review the committee's recommendations and publicly respond to each one, though the agency wouldn't be required to follow any of the advice. Everyday investors are affected indirectly, since the rules this committee weighs in on—like shareholder voting and corporate reporting requirements—can shape how companies are run and how transparent they are to the public. Notably, the bill exempts this committee from the usual federal law (the Federal Advisory Committee Act) that normally requires such advisory groups to operate with certain transparency and public-access rules.

title: Repealing Big Brother Overreach Act
ai_summary:
HR 425, called the "Repealing Big Brother Overreach Act," changes the Corporate Transparency Act, a 2021 law that required many small businesses and companies to report information about their real owners (called "beneficial owners") to the federal government. This reporting was meant to help stop criminals, money launderers, and shell companies from hiding who actually controls a business. Despite the bill's title suggesting a full repeal, the version reported out of committee doesn't eliminate the reporting system entirely—instead, it narrows it so that only foreign owners and foreign-formed companies still have to report their ownership information to the government.

Under this bill, U.S. citizens and domestically formed companies would no longer be required to disclose their beneficial ownership information. The bill also directs the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the agency that collects this data, to delete within 90 days any ownership information it already has on file for U.S. individuals and domestic companies that no longer fall under the reporting requirement.

This bill mainly affects small business owners, entrepreneurs, and companies formed in the United States, who would be relieved of a paperwork and privacy burden many considered intrusive. It would also affect law enforcement and financial regulators, who use this ownership data to investigate financial crimes, since they would lose access to ownership records for domestic companies. Foreign-owned businesses and foreign individuals with U.S. business interests would still need to comply with the original reporting rules.

title: SAFEGUARDS Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the SAFEGUARDS Act of 2026, deals with the "9/11 Security Fee" that airline passengers pay when they buy a ticket. Congress states its intent that money from this fee should only be used for aviation security purposes, like screening passengers and bags, upgrading security technology, and paying security staff. The bill says that using this fee for other, unrelated government spending goes against its original purpose and should stop by 2027.

Starting in fiscal year 2028, the bill requires that at least $500 million a year from this fee go into the existing Aviation Security Capital Fund, which pays for security equipment and related grants. It also creates a new fund, called the Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund, and requires at least $250 million per year to go into it, specifically for testing, buying, installing, and maintaining security technology at airport checkpoints (such as scanners and screening equipment). The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) would manage both funds and decide how the money is distributed through grants or agreements.

This bill mainly affects airline passengers, who pay the fee through ticket prices, and the TSA, airports, and security technology companies, who would benefit from guaranteed, dedicated funding for security equipment upgrades. It does not create new taxes but changes how existing fee money must be spent, aiming to ensure it goes toward security improvements rather than other government uses.

title: Major Non-NATO Ally Terror Threat Assessment Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires the U.S. government to regularly study and report on terrorist threats coming from countries that are considered "major non-NATO allies" of the United States. These are countries like Israel, Japan, South Korea, Egypt, and others that have a special partnership status with the U.S. but aren't part of the NATO alliance. The Secretary of Homeland Security, working with the State Department and the Director of National Intelligence, would have to produce this report within 180 days of the law passing, and then every two years after that.

The report would need to identify any terrorist groups or individually designated terrorists operating in these allied countries, describe what those groups are doing (including whether they're using artificial intelligence or other advanced technology), and explain what each ally's government is doing to stop them. It would also assess how well U.S. agencies can track these threats, keep known terrorists from entering the U.S., and what additional resources might be needed. The report would be classified but available to any member of Congress who requests it, and Homeland Security would have to brief the relevant congressional committees each time a new report comes out.

This bill mainly affects government agencies and how they monitor and report on security issues—it doesn't directly change laws affecting everyday citizens. However, it could influence U.S. foreign policy and immigration screening practices involving these allied nations, and it increases oversight and information-sharing between the executive branch and Congress on terrorism-related matters.

title: China Exchange Rate Transparency Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 692, the China Exchange Rate Transparency Act of 2025, directs the U.S. government to push for more openness about how China manages the value of its currency, the yuan. Specifically, it instructs the U.S. representative at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to use America's voice and vote to press China to disclose more information about its exchange rate policies, including any behind-the-scenes efforts by Chinese banks or state-owned companies to influence the currency's value. It also calls for China's practices to be factored into IMF discussions about currency standards and into decisions about how much voting power and influence China has within the IMF.

The bill doesn't directly regulate businesses or individuals in the U.S. Instead, it's a foreign policy directive aimed at the Treasury Department and the U.S. official at the IMF, shaping how the U.S. engages internationally on this issue. The reasoning behind it, according to the bill's findings, is that past Treasury Department reports have criticized China for being unusually secretive about its currency management compared to other major economies, which makes it harder to determine whether China is manipulating its currency for trade advantages.

This law would automatically expire either seven years after it passes, or sooner if the U.S. reports to Congress that China has become transparent and compliant with international currency rules. In practice, this bill mainly affects U.S. diplomatic and economic policy positions rather than everyday Americans directly, though it relates to broader U.S.-China trade and economic relations that can influence things like the cost of imported goods and the competitiveness of American exports.

title: AI PLAN Act
ai_summary:
The AI PLAN Act (H.R. 2152) requires several top government agencies to work together and report to Congress on how artificial intelligence is being used by hostile actors to commit financial crimes. Specifically, the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of Homeland Security, and the Secretary of Commerce would have to jointly submit a report within 180 days of the law passing, and every year after that. This report would cover things like how agencies are coordinating with each other and with private businesses to fight AI-driven fraud, what tools and staff are currently available to combat these crimes, and what additional resources or funding would be needed. The report would include a classified section for sensitive details, with a public summary if possible.

The bill lists specific AI-related threats agencies must consider, including deepfakes, voice cloning, fake identities, election interference, stock market manipulation, phone number spoofing, and AI-assisted scams or cyberattacks. Many other financial regulators and officials—including the Federal Reserve, SEC, FTC, FCC, and banking regulators—would be consulted in preparing this report. After each report, the agencies would also have to send Congress recommendations for new laws and "best practices" that businesses and government offices can use to protect themselves from AI-enabled financial crime.

This bill mainly affects federal agencies, financial regulators, and law enforcement by creating new reporting and coordination requirements. Indirectly, it could affect banks, businesses, and everyday consumers, since the eventual recommendations might lead to new rules or industry guidance aimed at reducing AI-related fraud, scams, and identity theft. The bill itself does not create new crimes or penalties—it focuses on studying the problem and planning a government-wide response.

title: Fostering the Use of Technology to Uphold Regulatory Effectiveness in Supervision Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires major financial regulatory agencies to review and improve the technology they use to oversee banks and other financial institutions. It applies to agencies like the Federal Reserve, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the FDIC, the Treasury Department (including the Comptroller of the Currency and the financial crimes unit FinCEN), the Federal Housing Finance Agency, and the National Credit Union Administration. Within 180 days of becoming law, these agencies must evaluate whether their current technology—such as data systems, monitoring tools, and cybersecurity—is good enough to supervise banks effectively in real time, and also review their process for buying or building new technology to find ways to make that process faster and simpler.

After completing these reviews, the agencies must jointly submit a detailed report to Congress within 18 months, and then update it every five years. The report would cover things like what technology they use, how well they can hire tech experts, how they share information with each other, what upgrades they're planning, and what it might cost banks to adapt to any new reporting systems. The goal is to modernize government oversight of the financial system so regulators can better detect risks, prevent fraud, and keep up with new technology like artificial intelligence being used by banks.

This bill mainly affects the internal operations of federal financial regulators rather than the general public directly. However, everyday people could see indirect effects: banks and credit unions may face changes in how they report information to regulators, and improved technology could lead to better detection of financial risks, scams, or money laundering, which affects the safety and stability of the banking system that consumers rely on.

title: Price Stability Act of 2026
ai_summary:
HR 5396, the "Price Stability Act of 2026," would change the official instructions Congress has given to the Federal Reserve, the nation's central bank. Right now, the Federal Reserve Act requires the Fed to pursue a "dual mandate": both maximum employment (keeping as many people working as possible) and stable prices (keeping inflation low and predictable). This bill would remove the "maximum employment" goal, leaving stable prices as the Fed's main required focus when it sets policies like interest rates.

In practice, this means the Fed's decision-making could shift. Currently, when setting interest rates, the Fed tries to balance fighting inflation against supporting job growth—sometimes keeping rates lower to help employment even if inflation runs a bit higher. If this law passes, the Fed would legally be focused on controlling inflation and prices, without an explicit requirement to also weigh how its decisions affect jobs and unemployment.

This bill affects everyone who interacts with the economy, since Fed policy influences interest rates on mortgages, credit cards, business loans, and savings accounts, as well as overall job growth. Workers, particularly during economic downturns, could be affected if the Fed's focus shifts away from actively supporting employment. Businesses, borrowers, savers, and policymakers who rely on the Fed's dual approach would also see a change in how the central bank explains and justifies its decisions.
ai_headline: Bill would drop "maximum employment" from the Fed's official mandate
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 616.

title: Improving Travel for American Families Act
ai_summary:
This bill lets the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) create a test program at certain airports to make security screening easier for parents or guardians traveling with children age 12 and under. The goal is to speed up the process for families going through airport security, without lowering safety standards. Everyone would still be screened based on their existing risk status through TSA's Secure Flight program, and no one could use an expedited lane like TSA PreCheck unless their boarding pass already shows they qualify for it.

If TSA decides to run this pilot program, it would choose airports based on factors like how many families with young children travel through them and whether the airport has enough space and staff to add or expand screening lanes without weakening security elsewhere. Local TSA managers would have flexibility to open, close, or shift lanes based on how busy the airport is. The program would last two years, and TSA would have to brief relevant House and Senate committees on how it's going within about nine months of starting it.

This mainly affects families flying with young children, who may experience shorter or more convenient security lines at participating airports. It also affects TSA staff and airport operations, since the agency would need to manage staffing and lane space carefully to keep security effective while testing this new approach.

title: Science of Reading Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill changes how federal literacy grant money can be used in schools. It updates a law called the Elementary and Secondary Education Act to require that any reading instruction funded through federal "Comprehensive Literacy" grants follow what's known as the "science of reading" — an approach based on research showing that phonics, phonemic awareness, vocabulary, fluency, and comprehension are the key building blocks for learning to read. The bill specifically bans the use of the "three-cueing model," a teaching method where kids guess words using context clues, pictures, or sentence structure instead of sounding them out. States and school districts applying for these federal literacy grants would need to show their reading programs align with this science-based approach, and grants would give priority to programs that meet this standard.

This mainly affects state education agencies, school districts, and schools that apply for or receive federal Comprehensive Literacy State Development grants, as well as the teachers and reading specialists who design curricula using that money. It does not create a new nationwide curriculum mandate — the bill explicitly says the federal government cannot control a state's or school's specific teaching materials or lesson plans, and it doesn't change any special education or disability rights laws. In practice, the biggest impact would be on schools currently using reading programs based on the three-cueing/guessing approach, since they would need to shift toward phonics-based methods to remain eligible for this particular federal funding.
ai_headline: Bill would tie federal reading grants to phonics-based instruction
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 623.

title: Form 5500 Filing Simplification Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes the deadline and filing process for Form 5500, which is a report that employers and retirement/benefit plan administrators must file each year with the government about their employee benefit plans (like 401(k)s and pension plans). Currently, the deadline is generally about 210 days after the plan year ends. The bill would change this to a fixed deadline: 9 months and 15 days after the close of the plan year. It also allows for extensions if a plan or the people involved with it are affected by a disaster or similar emergency. A related deadline for a different annual report (filed under a section called 4065, dealing with pension plan terminations and insurance) is also changed from 6 months to the same 9-months-and-15-days timeframe, making the deadlines more consistent with each other.

The bill also directs the Treasury Department, Labor Department, and the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (which insures certain pension plans) to update their rules to match these new deadlines and to allow these forms to be signed electronically instead of requiring physical signatures. If a plan follows the new rules in good faith before the agencies formally update their guidance, it will still be considered in compliance.

This bill mainly affects businesses and organizations that sponsor employee benefit plans, such as employers offering retirement or health benefit plans, along with the accountants, lawyers, and administrators who prepare and file these reports on their behalf. It does not directly affect individual employees or plan participants, though it could make the reporting process smoother and less burdensome for the companies managing their benefits, potentially reducing administrative costs and paperwork errors.

last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 22 - 12.
