title: Truman Scholarship Clean House Act
ai_summary:
This bill overhauls the Harry S. Truman Scholarship Foundation, a federally chartered program that awards scholarships to college students planning careers in public service. It completely dissolves the current Board of Trustees 90 days after the bill becomes law and sets up a new 13-member board, with members appointed by House and Senate leaders from both parties and by the President with Senate confirmation. The bill limits how many board members can belong to the same political party, sets six-year terms with a two-term limit, and defines in detail what counts as being "affiliated with" a political party. It also changes how the Executive Secretary (the foundation's top staff position) is appointed, requiring a two-thirds board vote and setting four-year terms.

The bill also changes rules for who can receive and keep a scholarship. It sets clearer eligibility requirements for student applicants, and it says students cannot be picked if they were leaders of a student group that got suspended or expelled, were personally disciplined by their school, or have a felony conviction. Once someone has a scholarship, they can lose funding for similar reasons, or if they fail to report required information or don't start using the scholarship within four years. Recipients must eventually work in public service for at least three of their first seven years after finishing grad school, or they must repay the scholarship money plus 6% annual interest. The foundation must also give notice and a hearing before cutting off anyone's payments.

Finally, the bill requires the foundation to publicly post materials like press releases, program announcements, and scholarship recipients' biographies, and to keep an unaltered record if anything is later edited. These changes only apply to scholarships awarded after the bill passes; students who already have scholarships keep them under the old rules. This bill mainly affects current and future Truman Scholarship applicants and recipients, the foundation's leadership and staff, and college students interested in public service careers who might apply in the future.

title: Stop the Sexualization of Children Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change federal education law to stop schools from using money they get through the Elementary and Secondary Education Act to create, run, or promote programs, activities, or materials for anyone under 18 that contain "sexually oriented material." The bill defines that term broadly to include depictions of sexually explicit conduct, as well as any material that involves "gender dysphoria or transgenderism." It also specifically bars using these federal funds to expose kids to nude adults, stripping, or lewd dancing through school-funded programs.

The bill does carve out exceptions so schools can still teach certain things using federal funds: standard science classes like biology, anatomy, and human health; the texts of major world religions; classic literature (defined by specific reference lists, including the Great Books of the Western World collection and two reading lists from a company called Compass Classroom); classic artworks (defined by a specific art history textbook series); and safety lessons that teach kids to recognize and avoid child sex trafficking or grooming, including using real examples like the Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell criminal cases.

This bill mainly affects public K-12 schools and any school programs, teachers, or vendors that rely on federal education funding, since those funds could no longer be used for the newly restricted content. It would also affect students and families, since it could limit what school-funded materials or programs are available regarding topics like gender identity, sex education beyond basic biology, or certain LGBTQ-related content. Because it defines "sexually oriented material" to include anything involving gender dysphoria or transgenderism, it could specifically limit federally funded school programs, books, or activities that address transgender topics for minors.

last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 632.

title: To amend the Military Land Withdrawals Act of 2013 to withdraw and reserve certain public land in the vicinity of Yuma Proving Ground, Arizona.
ai_summary:
This bill would set aside about 22,000 acres of federal public land near the Yuma Proving Ground in Arizona for continued military use. The Yuma Proving Ground is an Army testing site, and this bill formally reserves the surrounding land so it cannot be claimed, sold, mined, or leased for oil, gas, or geothermal development under normal public land rules. Instead, the land would be set aside indefinitely for military purposes, unless the Army later decides it no longer needs it.

While the land is reserved for the Army, the bill allows some non-military activities to continue if they don't interfere with military operations. These include wildlife conservation, protecting historical or cultural sites, managing wild horses and burros, controlling problem animals, recreation and hunting, and fighting brush fires. The Department of the Interior would generally manage the land, but the Army could take over management duties later. The bill also creates a special rule allowing a specific utility corridor (used for power lines) to continue operating through the area without needing Army approval, though officials would try to reduce any interference with military activities.

This bill mainly affects people and businesses that use or depend on this land in southwestern Arizona—such as ranchers, recreational users, hunters, utility companies, and local communities near Yuma. It also affects the Army's ability to secure land for testing and training, and it clarifies how federal agencies will share responsibility for managing the area going forward.

title: Improving Travel for Military Members Act
ai_summary:
This bill allows (but does not require) the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) to create a pilot program that would speed up security screening at airports for active-duty military members and their traveling family members. If the TSA decides to start this program, it would have to begin within 60 days of the bill becoming law, and it could only expand quicker screening access if doing so does not weaken airport security.

The bill sets rules for how this would work: travelers would still be screened based on their existing risk status under the Secure Flight program, and no one could be allowed into TSA PreCheck or similar faster lanes without proper eligibility on their boarding pass. Local TSA managers would have flexibility to open or close screening lanes depending on how busy the airport is. When choosing which airports get this program, the TSA would prioritize airports located near military bases with significant numbers of active-duty personnel, and would also consider whether an airport has enough physical space for extra screening lanes.

This mainly affects active-duty military service members and their families who travel by air, potentially making their airport experience faster and less stressful. It could also affect airports located near military installations, since those airports might be chosen to test the program. The TSA would need to report to Congress about how the pilot is going within nine months of starting it, and if the program is created, it would run for three years before ending automatically unless further action is taken.

title: One-Stop Pilot Program Extension Act
ai_summary:
This bill extends and slightly modifies an existing airport security pilot program called the "One-Stop Program." Under this program, passengers and their checked baggage arriving in the U.S. on direct flights from certain approved foreign airports can continue on to connecting U.S. flights without having to go through additional TSA screening again, as long as their bags were already properly screened overseas using approved explosives-detection equipment and other security conditions are met. The bill updates the rules for re-screening checked baggage specifically, requiring that passengers can't access their bags until their final destination, that U.S. Customs and Border Protection receives clear images of the baggage before arrival, and that CBP hasn't flagged any passenger or bag for extra inspection. It also extends the length of the overall pilot program from six years to ten years.

This mainly affects international travelers connecting through U.S. airports after arriving from qualifying foreign departure points, since it can make their connections faster and more convenient by avoiding duplicate security screening. It also affects the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), which run and oversee the program, as well as airlines and airports participating in these arrangements. The extension gives the government more time to test whether this streamlined screening approach can work effectively and safely before deciding whether to make it permanent or end it.

last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

title: Reimbursable Screening Services Program Extension Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill extends and expands a Transportation Security Administration (TSA) program that lets certain airports pay to have private companies handle passenger and baggage security screening instead of using TSA employees directly. This program, known as the "reimbursable screening services program," allows airports to essentially purchase screening services on a private basis when they want faster approval or expanded access, rather than waiting for TSA's standard staffing process. The bill continues this arrangement, which was set to expire at the end of fiscal year 2026, through fiscal year 2031.

The bill also expands the program by increasing the maximum number of airports allowed to participate in the reimbursable version at any one time, raising the cap from eight airports to fourteen. This means more airports across the country could choose to pay for expedited or supplemental private screening services if they meet the program's requirements.

This bill mainly affects airports, airlines, and travelers who pass through TSA security checkpoints, especially at airports that opt into this program. It could also affect private security screening companies that contract with airports, and it has implications for how TSA manages staffing and resources at a larger number of participating airports. title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "Air Plan Approval; South Dakota; Regional Haze Plan for the Second Implementation Period".
ai_summary:
This bill would cancel a federal regulation approved by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) that dealt with South Dakota's "Regional Haze Plan." Regional haze rules are designed to reduce air pollution that causes hazy skies and reduced visibility in national parks and wilderness areas. The EPA had approved South Dakota's specific plan for the second round of these efforts (covering roughly the 2018-2028 period), and this resolution uses a special process under the Congressional Review Act to formally reject that approval, meaning it would no longer be legally in effect.

If passed, this would block South Dakota's approved haze-reduction plan from being enforced, which could affect industries like power plants and factories in the state that would have had to follow specific pollution-control requirements under that plan. It could also affect visibility conditions in nearby national parks and protected lands, since the plan was meant to limit the pollutants that cause haze. Additionally, canceling the rule this way would prevent the EPA from creating a substantially similar replacement rule in the future without new authorization from Congress.

This process, called a Congressional Review Act resolution, allows Congress to overturn recent federal agency regulations with a simple majority vote in both chambers, rather than the standard lawmaking process. The bill mainly affects South Dakota residents, businesses, and industries subject to the plan, as well as anyone concerned with air quality and visibility in the region's protected natural areas.
ai_headline: Resolution would void EPA approval of South Dakota's haze reduction plan
last_action_text: Motion to proceed to consideration of measure rejected in Senate by Yea-Nay Vote. 43 - 50. Record Vote Number: 4.

title: Promoting Opportunities for Non-Traditional Capital Formation Act
ai_summary:
This bill amends the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 to expand the duties of the Advocate for Small Business Capital Formation, an official position within the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The bill requires this office to create educational materials and host or participate in events aimed at helping small businesses understand their options for raising money from investors. It specifically focuses on businesses that have traditionally had a harder time accessing capital, including women-owned businesses, minority-owned businesses, businesses in rural areas, and businesses affected by hurricanes or other natural disasters.

The bill also requires the Advocate to meet at least once a year with representatives from state securities commissions to discuss ways federal and state officials can work together to help small businesses and the people who invest in them.

This bill mainly affects small business owners, especially those in the specified underrepresented groups, by potentially giving them better access to information about how to raise money for their companies. It could also affect small business investors who may benefit from increased outreach and education, and it creates additional responsibilities for the SEC office holding this role. There are no new penalties, taxes, or requirements imposed on the public; the bill is focused on outreach, education, and coordination between government agencies.

title: No Antisemitism in Education Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, called the "No Antisemitism in Education Act of 2026," would require public school districts and colleges that receive federal money to treat discrimination against Jewish students and staff just as seriously as they treat other types of discrimination already banned under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (a law that prohibits discrimination based on race, color, or national origin at institutions receiving federal funds). Schools would need to use a specific definition of antisemitism, based on one from a 2019 executive order, when investigating complaints and deciding whether incidents were motivated by anti-Jewish bias.

The bill points to data showing high rates of antisemitic incidents, including hate crimes and harassment reported by Jewish college students, and cites congressional reports claiming many universities have failed to enforce their own rules fairly when it comes to antisemitism. If passed, schools that don't comply could face the same enforcement actions used for other Title VI violations, which can include loss of federal funding. The bill also states that it shouldn't be read as limiting free speech rights under the First Amendment or overriding state anti-discrimination laws.

This would affect K-12 public schools, colleges, and universities that receive federal funding (which is the vast majority of them), as well as students, faculty, and staff at those institutions. Jewish students and employees would be a primary focus of the added protections, while schools would face new compliance obligations and potential legal exposure if they don't adequately address antisemitism complaints.
ai_headline: Bill would treat antisemitism as Title VI violation in schools

title: National Law Enforcement Officers Remembrance, Support, and Community Outreach Act
ai_summary:
HR 309 allows the Secretary of the Interior to give federal grants to the National Law Enforcement Officers Memorial Fund, which runs the National Law Enforcement Museum in Washington, D.C. If Congress provides the money, the Secretary would award a $6 million grant each year for seven years to help pay for the museum's operations. This money could be used for things like memorializing officers killed in the line of duty, creating educational programs and exhibits, training teachers, digitizing historical records, and expanding officer safety and wellness resources.

In exchange for receiving this funding, the museum would have to offer free admission to active and retired law enforcement officers and to family members of officers who died in the line of duty. It would also need to provide at least one day a week when the general public can visit for free. The museum would be required to undergo annual federal financial audits and submit yearly reports to Congress explaining how the grant money was spent and what progress was made on its programs.

This bill mainly affects the National Law Enforcement Museum and its funding, as well as law enforcement officers and their families who would benefit from free admission and expanded educational and wellness resources. It could also affect everyday visitors to the museum, who would get a weekly free-admission opportunity, and taxpayers, since the funding depends on Congress actually approving the money in future budget bills — the law itself doesn't create new spending, it just allows for it if funds are appropriated.
ai_headline: Bill would let Interior fund national police memorial museum for 7 years
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 658.

title: Fire Department Repayment Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Fire Department Repayment Act of 2025, aims to fix delays in how the federal government pays back local fire departments that help fight fires on federal land. When local fire departments assist with fires under existing agreements, they're supposed to be reimbursed for their costs, but the process can currently be slow and inconsistent depending on which federal agency is involved.

The bill requires the Secretaries of Agriculture, Interior, Homeland Security, and Defense to work together to create standardized rules for how and when these reimbursements happen. Within one year, they must review all existing cost-sharing agreements with local fire departments and update them to match these new standard procedures. The bill also says these payment agreements should line up with related cooperative fire protection agreements, and that the federal government should pay a fire department promptly once it submits a proper invoice. While the bill states that Congress believes reimbursements should generally happen within one year after a fire is fought, this is a "sense of Congress" statement rather than a strict legal requirement.

This bill mainly affects local and rural fire departments that assist with wildfires on federal land, as well as the federal agencies that manage that land. It aims to make sure these fire departments get paid back more quickly and predictably for their firefighting costs, which can help smaller departments—especially those with tight budgets—recover expenses without long delays.
ai_headline: Bill seeks faster federal repayment for local fire departments
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by Unanimous Consent.

Within one year, agencies must review and update existing cost-sharing agreements to match the new procedures, and payments should be made promptly after a proper invoice is submitted.

title: Valuing Employee Stock Today Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change a federal wage law called the Fair Labor Standards Act, which sets rules for calculating overtime pay. Under current law, when employers give workers stock options, stock appreciation rights, or let them buy company stock through an employee stock purchase program, the value of that stock doesn't count toward the employee's "regular rate" of pay used to calculate overtime. However, the law doesn't specifically mention restricted stock units (RSUs), a newer and now very common form of company stock compensation, which has created uncertainty about whether they qualify for the same treatment.

This bill would add restricted stock units to the list of equity compensation that's excluded from overtime pay calculations. Congress explains in the bill that RSUs weren't common back in 2000 when the original stock-related overtime rules were written, so they were left out simply because they didn't exist yet in their current form, not because lawmakers meant to exclude them on purpose. The bill also updates related language so that when an employee accepts RSUs (not just when they "exercise" stock options), that value still doesn't count toward overtime calculations.

This mainly affects employers who compensate workers partly through company stock, especially RSUs, and employees who receive that kind of compensation and also work overtime hours. If passed, companies would have clearer legal guidance that RSU value doesn't need to be factored into overtime pay math, similar to how stock options are already treated. The change would take effect 90 days after the bill becomes law.
ai_headline: Bill would exclude RSUs from overtime pay calculations
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 18 - 15.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8660 would exclude restricted stock units from overtime pay math, matching treatment already given to stock options.

It also updates the law so the value counts as excluded when RSUs are accepted, not just when stock options are exercised. The change would take effect 90 days after enactment.

title: End Tax Penalties on American Hostages Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the End Tax Penalties on American Hostages Act, would change federal tax rules to help Americans who are held hostage or wrongfully detained in other countries. Right now, if someone misses a tax filing deadline or payment while stuck overseas in such a situation, they could still face penalties and interest charges. This bill says that time period should not count against them—similar to how tax deadlines are already paused for people serving in combat zones. The pause would also apply to the detained person's spouse, and the IRS would be required to update its systems so penalties and collection actions automatically stop for these individuals.

The bill also sets up a way to fix past cases. If someone was wrongly charged penalties or interest while detained going back to January 1, 2021, they (or their spouse or dependents) could apply for a refund of those amounts. The State Department and the Hostage Recovery Fusion Cell (a government team that tracks hostage cases) would identify eligible people and notify them of their right to request money back, giving them extra time beyond the usual refund deadlines to file a claim.

This mainly affects Americans who have been designated by the U.S. government as wrongfully detained or taken hostage abroad, along with their families. It does not affect the general public's taxes—it's a narrow fix aimed at preventing people already dealing with a hostage or detention situation from also being penalized financially by the IRS for missing deadlines they had no control over.
ai_headline: Bill would pause tax penalties for Americans held hostage abroad
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 40 - 0.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill would stop tax penalties and interest from applying while Americans are wrongfully detained or held hostage overseas.

It also lets affected people, or their spouse or dependents, apply for refunds of penalties or interest wrongly charged since January 1, 2021.

title: Taxpayer Workforce Modernization Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Taxpayer Workforce Modernization Act, would require the IRS to create a fellowship program to hire data scientists from the private sector. The goal is to bring in tech and data experts who can work alongside the IRS's tax law specialists to handle complicated or new types of tax cases, improve how the agency uses data, and modernize tax enforcement and customer service. The IRS would need to set this program up by September 30, 2026.

Under the bill, at least 10 fellows would work in the program at a time, hired for terms of 2 to 4 years with the option of yearly extensions. These fellows, along with regular IRS employees, would form a task force responsible for building better tools to select audits, detect offshore tax evasion, train IRS staff on data analytics and artificial intelligence, and recommend ways to make audits more effective. Fellows would be paid at least as much as senior federal employees (GS-15 level) but no more than a capped amount tied to executive branch pay rules. At the end of their term, the IRS could hire a fellow permanently.

This bill mainly affects the IRS's operations and hiring practices, as well as data scientists interested in government work. Indirectly, it could affect taxpayers, since the program aims to make audits and tax enforcement more accurate and efficient using modern data analysis tools. The IRS would also have to report annually to Congress on how well the program is working, including its costs and benefits.
ai_headline: IRS would launch fellowship to hire private-sector data scientists
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 24 - 16.

title: Protecting Taxpayers from Ghost Preparers Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Protecting Taxpayers from Ghost Preparers Act, targets "ghost preparers"—tax preparers who fill out someone's tax return but don't sign it or take credit for it, sometimes altering documents improperly to avoid responsibility or to commit fraud. The bill expands the legal definition of a "return" for penalty purposes so that it covers not just official tax filings but also any document that looks like a tax return, adjustment request, or report, including ones that have been improperly altered. This closes a loophole that let some dishonest preparers escape penalties by claiming the altered document wasn't technically an official "return."

The bill also changes the rules about how long the IRS has to audit or assess additional taxes when fraud is involved. Normally, if there's fraud, the IRS can go back further than the usual three-year limit. This bill clarifies that this extended time limit only applies when the taxpayer themselves commits the fraud—not when a dishonest preparer commits fraud without the taxpayer's knowledge. This is meant to protect innocent taxpayers who were victims of a fraudulent preparer from facing extended IRS scrutiny through no fault of their own.

Finally, the bill makes a small technical fix to a separate, earlier law dealing with tax deadline extensions after disasters, essentially renumbering a section for organizational purposes. Overall, this bill mainly affects taxpayers who use paid tax preparers and the preparers themselves, aiming to hold dishonest preparers more accountable while shielding honest taxpayers from being penalized for a preparer's misconduct.
ai_headline: Bill targets unsigned "ghost" tax preparers while shielding their victims
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 40 - 0.

It also limits the IRS's extended audit time limit for fraud to cases where the taxpayer, not the preparer, committed the fraud, and makes a minor renumbering fix to an earlier disaster-extension law.

title: AI Tax Integrity Act of 2026
ai_summary:
**HR 9501 — AI Tax Integrity Act of 2026** would require the U.S. Treasury Department to set up a test program using artificial intelligence to help the IRS catch tax fraud. The AI would specifically look for tax returns that are inaccurate because of identity theft, false claims for tax credits or refunds, or returns that were improperly filled out by paid preparers who didn't properly identify themselves. Treasury would have 180 days after the bill becomes law to start this pilot program, which would run for at least 18 months but no more than 2 years.

After the pilot program ends, the Government Accountability Office (led by the Comptroller General) would have 180 days to write a report for Congress. That report would explain how much money was lost to fraud that the AI caught, how much money the government actually recovered, and how accurate the AI tools were at spotting fraudulent returns.

This bill mainly affects how the IRS operates internally — it doesn't change tax laws or require anything new from everyday taxpayers. However, it could indirectly affect people who file taxes, since AI-driven fraud detection might flag certain returns for review, including cases involving identity theft or improperly prepared returns. Tax preparers and companies that offer tax-filing services could also be affected, since the pilot program specifically targets fraud involving third-party preparers.
ai_headline: Treasury to pilot AI tool for catching IRS tax fraud
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 40 - 0.

The pilot must start within 180 days of enactment and last between 18 months and 2 years. Afterward, the GAO has 180 days to report to Congress on fraud caught, money recovered, and AI accuracy.

title: Tax Exempt Hospital Transparency Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Tax Exempt Hospital Transparency Act, requires nonprofit hospitals that don't pay federal income taxes to share more detailed financial and operational information with the government each year. Currently, tax-exempt hospitals already report some information, but this bill adds many new requirements, such as disclosing audited financial statements, how much charity care they provide, how many patients applied for financial assistance, and how they're addressing community health needs identified in required assessments.

Larger hospitals (those with more than 100 inpatient beds) and high-revenue hospitals (those earning more than $100 million in patient revenue per year) face even stricter rules. They must break down spending on quality improvement versus administrative or "nonclinical" costs, report advertising expenses, and provide detailed information about different medical service lines (like cardiology or oncology), including revenue and costs for each. Hospitals participating in the federal 340B drug discount program—which lets certain hospitals buy medications at reduced prices—would also need to report how much they make from that program and what it costs them to participate.

This bill mainly affects tax-exempt hospitals, especially large and high-revenue ones, by increasing their paperwork and disclosure obligations, while small, rural, or critical-access hospitals face lighter requirements. Patients and the public would gain more visibility into how nonprofit hospitals spend money and whether they're using their tax-exempt status to genuinely benefit their communities. The bill also requires a government watchdog study on the costs of these new rules and estimates of taxes the largest nonprofit hospitals would owe if they weren't tax-exempt.
ai_headline: Bill would force nonprofit hospitals to disclose more financial detail
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 25 - 15.

title: FEMA Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the FEMA Act of 2025, makes two major changes. First, it takes the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) out from under the Department of Homeland Security and turns it into its own independent, Cabinet-level agency, meaning its top official (the Administrator) would report directly to the President rather than to the Homeland Security Secretary. The bill spells out how this transition would happen, including moving staff, budgets, and legal responsibilities from Homeland Security to the new independent FEMA, setting up an inspector general to oversee the agency, and creating a new advocate specifically for veterans dealing with disaster assistance.

Second, the bill overhauls how FEMA handles disaster aid programs. It changes rules for "public assistance" (help rebuilding damaged public buildings, roads, and infrastructure after disasters), speeding up cost estimates and payments, and letting nonprofit organizations, including religious institutions, qualify for rebuilding grants. It also reforms "individual assistance" programs that help disaster survivors directly, such as simplifying applications, improving rental and housing assistance, and clarifying who can get temporary shelter. Additional sections address disaster mitigation (steps to reduce future damage, like stronger building codes and resilient utilities) and require more transparency, such as public dashboards tracking disaster aid and government reports on fraud, staffing, and the effectiveness of assistance programs.

In short, this bill would restructure how the federal government organizes and runs disaster response, aiming to make FEMA more independent and to make disaster aid faster, clearer, and easier to access. It would primarily affect state, local, and tribal governments dealing with disasters; nonprofit and religious organizations seeking rebuilding funds; individual disaster survivors applying for help; FEMA employees and leadership, who would work under a new agency structure; and taxpayers, since it changes how disaster funding is authorized and overseen.
ai_headline: Bill would make FEMA an independent Cabinet-level agency, overhaul disaster aid
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 57 - 3.

ai_sections.tldr: The FEMA Act of 2025 would separate FEMA from Homeland Security and reform how disaster aid is delivered.
ai_sections.what: The bill removes FEMA from the Department of Homeland Security and makes it an independent, Cabinet-level agency reporting directly to the President. It also overhauls public and individual disaster assistance programs, speeding payments, expanding nonprofit and religious group eligibility, and adding mitigation and transparency measures.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects state, local, and tribal governments, nonprofit and religious organizations, individual disaster survivors, and FEMA employees and leadership. Taxpayers are also affected through changes to disaster funding oversight.
ai_sections.why: The restructuring would change lines of authority and accountability for disaster response, shifting FEMA's oversight from Homeland Security to direct presidential control. It would also alter eligibility rules and processes for who can receive federal disaster aid and how quickly it is delivered.

title: To provide for the equitable settlement of certain Indian land disputes regarding land in Illinois, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill deals with an old land dispute involving the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma and land in Illinois that dates back to an 1805 treaty called the Treaty of Grouseland. The bill would give the U.S. Court of Federal Claims special authority to hear a land claim from the tribe based on that treaty, even though normal legal time limits (statutes of limitations) would otherwise block such an old claim. The tribe would have one year after the law passes to actually file that claim, or this special permission would expire.

At the same time, the bill would close the door on any other land claims. Except for the one specific claim allowed under this law, all other past, present, or future claims by the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma—or its members, descendants, or predecessors—to land in Illinois would be permanently ended ("extinguished"). This means the tribe could pursue this one legal case, but afterward would have no further legal ability to claim land in Illinois.

This bill mainly affects the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma, current landowners in Illinois whose property might otherwise be subject to old treaty-based claims, and the federal court system, which would gain a narrow, one-time authority to resolve this specific historical dispute. It does not affect the general public directly, but it could matter to people living on or near land historically covered by the 1805 treaty, as well as to tribal members seeking resolution of long-standing land claims.
ai_headline: Bill gives Miami Tribe one year to file old Illinois land claim
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 663.

The tribe would have one year after passage to file, or the special permission expires. After that one claim, all other past, present, or future tribal land claims to Illinois land would be permanently extinguished.
ai_sections.who: The Miami Tribe of Oklahoma, its members and descendants, current Illinois landowners, and the federal court system are affected.
ai_sections.why: The bill would resolve a long-standing historical land dispute while permanently closing off any further legal claims from the tribe over Illinois land.

title: AWRC Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 7889, called the Advancing Water Research and Collaboration Act of 2025 (AWRC Act), renews funding and updates rules for a long-running federal program that supports water research institutes, which are typically based at universities in each state. This program, first created under the Water Resources Research Act of 1984, funds scientific research into water supply problems, water quality, and related issues. The bill extends funding authorization through fiscal years 2026 through 2029, setting the funding level at $16 million per year, and reorganizes some of the technical rules about how that money is divided and used.

The bill makes a few notable changes. It adds language recognizing the "growing artificial intelligence industry" as one of the private-sector partners these water research institutes should collaborate with, reflecting AI's increasing role in water data analysis and management. It also clarifies that 20% of the program's funding must go specifically toward research on water problems that cross state lines or affect multiple states, rather than issues limited to just one state. Additionally, it reorganizes and clarifies existing rules about competitive grants and matching funds requirements for the institutes.

This bill mainly affects university-based water research institutes, state and federal water agencies, and researchers who study water supply, water quality, and related infrastructure issues. Indirectly, it could affect the general public by supporting research that informs decisions about drinking water safety, drought management, and water infrastructure — especially for problems that span multiple states, such as shared rivers or aquifers. It does not create new regulations for individuals or businesses; it primarily reauthorizes and tweaks an existing federal research funding program.
ai_headline: Bill would renew federal water research funding through 2029
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 665.

title: Lunar Landing Day Act
ai_summary:
S. 5123, the Lunar Landing Day Act, officially adds July 20 to the list of special observance days recognized in U.S. law. This is the same date that Apollo 11 astronauts first landed on the Moon in 1969. The bill doesn't create a federal holiday with a day off work or mandatory closures; instead, it's a symbolic designation encouraging citizens, organizations, and government bodies at all levels to acknowledge the day through proclamations, events, or educational activities that celebrate the Moon landing and promote continued U.S. involvement in space exploration.

Most of the bill's text is technical housekeeping. Because the U.S. law already lists dozens of similar observance days (like Mother's Day, Flag Day, and Veterans Day) in a specific numbered order, adding a new one requires renumbering many of the existing sections so everything stays in proper order alphabetically. That's why the bill contains a long list of section renumbering instructions—it's essentially reorganizing a legal filing cabinet to make room for the new entry, not changing what those other observances mean or how they're recognized.

This bill mainly affects how the federal law book is organized rather than affecting people's daily lives directly. It could matter to space enthusiasts, educators, museums, and organizations like NASA that might use the official designation to support events or educational programs around July 20. It does not create new federal spending, regulations, or requirements for individuals or businesses.
ai_headline: Bill would add July 20 as symbolic Lunar Landing Day in federal law
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

title: STAR Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the STAR Act, changes how Medicare pays long-term care hospitals (LTCHs). These are specialized hospitals that treat patients who need extended hospital-level care, such as people recovering from serious illness or on ventilators. Currently, Medicare uses a "site neutral" payment rule that pays these hospitals less for certain patients unless the patient meets specific criteria showing they need intensive, high-level care. This bill extends that site-neutral payment policy through 2032 instead of letting it expire in 2026.

The bill also adds a new category, called the "high acuity criterion," that would let more patients qualify for the higher payment rate. To qualify, a patient would generally need to have come directly from a regular hospital or a small rural hospital (called a "critical access hospital"), have a diagnosis considered serious enough under Medicare's coding system, and be treated at a long-term care hospital that already existed or was already being built before the bill becomes law. The bill also expands the existing rules for ICU-level and ventilator-dependent patients so that patients transferred from critical access hospitals can also count toward those higher-payment categories, not just patients from regular hospitals.

This bill mainly affects long-term care hospitals, the hospitals and rural facilities that transfer patients to them, and Medicare patients who need extended, intensive hospital care. It does not change coverage or costs for most everyday Medicare beneficiaries, but it could affect which hospitals get paid more for treating certain very sick patients, which in turn could influence hospitals' financial stability and decisions about which patients they admit.
ai_headline: Bill would extend Medicare's site-neutral hospital payment rule through 2032
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute by the Yeas and Nays: 40 - 0.

title: No Data Center NDAs Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the No Data Center NDAs Act, would stop members of Congress from signing nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) with state or local governments or private companies when those agreements are required to get information about data center projects. This includes details like planned investments, where a data center will be built, how it will be designed, and how much water or energy it will use. Data centers are large facilities that store and process computer data, and they are increasingly built with tax breaks or government involvement, which is why lawmakers sometimes seek information about them.

Under the bill, no federal money could be used to enforce any NDA that a member of Congress signs related to data centers, effectively making such agreements unenforceable if they involve federal funds. The House and Senate ethics committees would be responsible for writing specific rules to carry out this ban.

This bill mainly affects members of Congress (senators, representatives, and delegates), who would lose the option to sign these kinds of confidentiality agreements. It could also affect companies or local governments that build data centers, since they would not be able to require lawmakers to keep project details secret in exchange for access to information. The broader public could be indirectly affected because it may become easier for lawmakers to publicly discuss or share information about data center projects, including their environmental impact, in their districts or states.
ai_headline: Bill would ban lawmakers from signing data center secrecy agreements
last_action_text: Referred to the House Committee on House Administration.

No federal money could be used to enforce such NDAs, making them effectively unenforceable if federal funds are involved. House and Senate ethics committees would write rules to implement the ban.

title: HIRE Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the HIRE Act, would create a new federal tax on U.S. businesses that pay foreign workers or companies to perform services for American customers. Specifically, if a U.S. business hires someone overseas to do work that ultimately benefits people in the United States—like a call center answering customer questions or a company handling data processing—the business would have to pay a 25% excise tax on that payment to the government. If services are split between U.S. and foreign customers, only the portion serving U.S. customers would be taxed. The bill also says businesses cannot deduct these outsourcing payments from their income taxes, essentially taxing them twice: once through the new excise tax and again by disallowing the usual business expense deduction.

The money collected from this tax would go into a new "Domestic Workforce Fund." This fund would pay for job training programs, apprenticeships, and grants to states to help retrain workers in industries affected by outsourcing. The bill also increases penalties for businesses that fail to pay this new tax and requires companies to report detailed information about payments to foreign contractors so the IRS can enforce the rules.

This bill would mainly affect U.S. companies that outsource customer service, technology support, or other labor to foreign countries, potentially raising their costs and encouraging them to hire domestically instead. It could also affect consumers if businesses pass along higher costs, and it could affect workers in foreign countries who currently perform outsourced jobs for U.S. companies. American workers in industries that compete with outsourced labor could benefit from new job training resources and, potentially, more domestic hiring. The tax would apply to payments made after December 31, 2025.
ai_headline: New bill would tax US firms 25% for outsourcing work abroad
last_action_text: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.

ai_sections.tldr: The HIRE Act would impose a 25% federal tax on U.S. businesses paying foreign workers for services benefiting American customers.

If services serve both U.S. and foreign customers, only the U.S.-facing portion is taxed. Businesses also could no longer deduct these outsourcing payments from their income taxes, meaning the cost is taxed twice.

title: Workforce for AI Trust Act
ai_summary:
HR 9334, the Workforce for AI Trust Act, aims to grow the pool of skilled workers who can build and oversee trustworthy artificial intelligence systems. It updates the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020 to let the National Science Foundation (NSF) fund graduate and postdoctoral fellowships for students in a wide range of fields—not just computer science but also social science, ethics, law, and the humanities—so they can research AI safety, reliability, and trustworthiness. It also allows NSF to fund workshops, training programs, and certification opportunities to help students and researchers learn to apply AI responsibly across science and engineering fields, and requires that panels reviewing AI research grant proposals include people from diverse disciplines like ethics and law, not just technical experts.

The bill also directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to help build the AI workforce more broadly. NIST would create a standardized framework describing AI-related jobs, skills, and knowledge, similar to existing frameworks used in cybersecurity careers. This framework would help government agencies, schools, and employers identify skill gaps, train workers, and align hiring practices with clear, consistent AI job standards. NIST would work with the Department of Labor, the Office of Personnel Management, and other stakeholders, including industry and labor groups, to develop and publish this framework.

This bill would primarily affect universities, graduate students, and postdoctoral researchers who could receive new federal funding opportunities, as well as federal agencies and private employers seeking clearer standards for AI-related jobs. It does not regulate AI technology directly but instead focuses on training and preparing the workforce needed to develop and manage AI responsibly.
ai_headline: Bill would fund fellowships to train workers on trustworthy AI
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported in the Nature of a Substitute (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 35 - 0.

It also allows NSF to fund workshops, training, and certification programs, and requires grant review panels to include people from diverse disciplines. Separately, NIST must build a standardized framework describing AI jobs, skills, and knowledge, similar to existing cybersecurity frameworks.

title: China AI Power Report Act
ai_summary:
The China AI Power Report Act would require the U.S. Secretary of Commerce, working with agencies like the State Department, Defense Department, Energy Department, and intelligence officials, to write a detailed yearly report on China's artificial intelligence capabilities. This report would be sent to Congress starting 180 days after the law passes and continuing annually for three years. It would cover an enormous range of topics: China's AI computer chips and the companies that make them (like Huawei), semiconductor factories, memory chip makers, manufacturing equipment companies, chip design software, specific AI models developed in China, government funding for AI, computing power available to Chinese companies, humanoid robot makers, popular AI-powered apps, China's AI regulations, and how well U.S. export controls are working to prevent China from getting sensitive American technology.

The bill doesn't create new export restrictions itself; instead, it's meant to give Congress detailed, up-to-date information so lawmakers can decide whether to strengthen or adjust existing export control laws. Most of the report would be public, though sensitive information could be kept in a classified section attached to it. This bill mainly affects government agencies, who would take on new reporting duties, and indirectly affects semiconductor and AI companies (both American and Chinese) whose products and business dealings would be studied and referenced in these reports. Everyday Americans wouldn't be directly regulated by this bill, but the information gathered could shape future decisions about trade rules, technology exports, and national security policy involving AI and computer chips.
ai_headline: Bill would require annual Commerce Department reports on China's AI power
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by the Yeas and Nays: 47 - 0.

title: To amend the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 to provide for a ten-year statute of limitations for export control violations.
ai_summary:
This bill would change how long the federal government has to punish companies or individuals for violating U.S. export control laws. These laws regulate the sale or shipment of sensitive goods, technology, and services—like military equipment, advanced electronics, or certain software—to other countries, especially to prevent them from reaching adversaries or being misused. The bill sets a clear 10-year time limit, called a statute of limitations, for both civil penalties (fines) and criminal charges related to these violations.

Specifically, the bill amends the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 so that the government cannot start a civil enforcement action—such as issuing a fine or penalty—more than 10 years after the violation occurred. It also says that criminal charges (an indictment or formal accusation) must be filed within that same 10-year window. The bill defines the start of a civil case as including when the government sends an official "charging letter," which clarifies exactly when the clock begins.

This mainly affects businesses and individuals involved in international trade, especially those dealing with export-controlled items like technology, defense-related products, or dual-use goods (items with both civilian and military uses). It also affects the Commerce Department and other federal agencies responsible for enforcing export control laws, since it limits how far back they can look when pursuing violations. Supporters of clearer time limits often say it creates more predictability for businesses, while others may be concerned about how it affects the government's ability to pursue older cases.
ai_headline: Bill sets 10-year deadline for pursuing export control violations
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported by the Yeas and Nays: 44 - 0.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 8202 would give the government exactly 10 years to file civil or criminal export control violation cases.

title: To make technical amendments to update statutory references to certain provisions classified to title 2, United States Code, title 50, United States Code, and title 52, United States Code, and to correct related technical errors.
ai_summary:
This bill, HR 5210, is a purely technical "housekeeping" bill. Over the years, Congress has reorganized and renumbered parts of the U.S. Code (the official collection of federal laws), particularly sections dealing with Congress's own operations, national security and intelligence agencies, and election law. When laws get renumbered, older statutes that reference those sections by their old numbers become outdated or confusing, even though the underlying legal requirements haven't changed. This bill goes through hundreds of these old cross-references scattered across many other laws and updates them to point to the correct, current section numbers, while also fixing minor typos, wrong dates, and similar clerical errors.

The bill affects three main areas: laws related to Congress's own administration (title 2 of the U.S. Code), national security and intelligence laws such as the National Security Act and CIA-related statutes (title 50), and election laws such as the Voting Rights Act, campaign finance rules, and overseas voting rules (title 52). It does not change any actual policy, rights, benefits, or obligations for anyone—it does not add new rules, remove protections, or alter how these laws function in practice. It simply makes sure that when one law refers to another, it points to the right place in the code.

The people affected are mainly legal researchers, government agencies, courts, and anyone who needs to accurately trace which statute governs a given situation. For an everyday resident, this bill has no direct real-world impact on daily life, taxes, benefits, or rights; it's essentially legal maintenance to keep the U.S. Code internally consistent and easier to navigate.
ai_headline: Bill would fix outdated legal cross-references, not change any policy

title: Ensuring Casualty Assistance for our Firefighters Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Ensuring Casualty Assistance for our Firefighters Act, directs the Secretary of the Interior to create a formal support program for the families of federal wildland firefighters and support personnel who are killed, critically injured, or become seriously ill while on duty. Within six months of becoming law, the Department of the Interior would need to set up a "Wildland Fire Management Casualty Assistance Program" that standardizes how families are notified of a death or serious injury, helps cover travel costs for family members visiting an injured or hospitalized loved one, and ensures trained casualty assistance officers are available to guide families through the process.

The program would also create a one-stop source of information—available online and at no cost—explaining what federal benefits and financial assistance are available to survivors, and how to file complaints or request more help. It would require coordination between the Department of the Interior, the Department of Justice, and the Social Security Administration to make sure survivor benefits are handled accurately and quickly. The bill also collects data on how well this assistance is being delivered, working with fire safety and health agencies.

This bill mainly affects federal wildland firefighters, wildland fire support staff, and their families, particularly spouses, children, parents, and other next-of-kin who would receive support after a death, injury, or illness connected to firefighting duties. It does not change any existing death benefit programs but adds a structured support and communication system on top of them. It does not affect state or local firefighters unless they are part of federal wildland firefighting operations.
ai_headline: Bill would create casualty support program for wildland firefighters
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported by Unanimous Consent.

It would standardize death and injury notifications, help cover family travel costs to injured or hospitalized loved ones, and provide trained casualty assistance officers. title: To make revisions in title 51, United States Code, as necessary to keep the title current, and to make technical amendments to improve the United States Code.
ai_summary:
This bill is a "housekeeping" measure that updates and reorganizes Title 51 of the United States Code, which is the section of federal law dealing with NASA, space policy, and commercial space activities. It does not create new policy or change what the law actually means or does. Instead, it fixes outdated references (like replacing old committee names with current ones), renumbers chapters and sections so they're easier to find, removes duplicate or obsolete provisions, and consolidates various space-related laws that were passed separately over many years into a cleaner, more organized structure. The bill explicitly states that these changes are not meant to alter the substance of existing law, only to make it more current and readable.

Specific changes include renaming and reorganizing chapters covering NASA's budget process, facilities and infrastructure, aeronautics and space technology research, commercial cargo and crew transportation (like SpaceX and Boeing contracts with NASA), STEM education programs, orbital debris policy, and international space agreements. It also updates outdated legal citations, fixes cross-references between sections, and formally names some existing programs (such as the Commercial Crew Program and counterfeit parts detection efforts) within the official code.

This bill mainly affects how the law is organized and referenced rather than affecting people's daily lives directly. It matters most to NASA officials, government contractors, lawyers, and policy staff who rely on accurate, well-organized federal code to interpret space law and NASA's authority. Everyday Americans are unlikely to notice any practical difference, since the bill is designed specifically to preserve existing rules and programs while making the legal text easier to navigate.
ai_headline: Bill reorganizes NASA and space law code without changing its meaning

title: LIFT AI Act
ai_summary:
The LIFT AI Act is a bill aimed at helping schools teach kids about artificial intelligence (AI) from kindergarten through 12th grade. Congress states in the bill that AI is changing the world quickly, and that the United States needs to prepare young people with the skills to understand and use AI so the country stays competitive globally, including against rival nations. The bill directs the Director of the National Science Foundation to award competitive grants to colleges, universities, and nonprofit organizations to develop AI education programs for schools.

The grant money could be used for several purposes: creating classroom lessons about AI that are hands-on and age-appropriate, training teachers and school leaders on how to use and teach about AI responsibly, creating tools to measure how well students and teachers understand AI, and building professional development programs (in person or online) for educators. It also allows for updating existing school curricula to include AI-related lessons where it makes sense, rather than creating an entirely separate subject.

This bill would primarily affect K-12 public school systems, teachers, school administrators, and students across the country, since it aims to eventually reach classrooms nationwide. It would also affect universities and nonprofit organizations that could apply for and receive federal grant funding to design these educational materials. The bill does not create a specific mandate that all schools must teach AI, but it sets up a funding and support system through the National Science Foundation to encourage and expand AI education efforts nationally.
ai_headline: Bill would fund AI education grants for K-12 schools nationwide

Grant funds could support classroom lessons, teacher training, assessment tools, and professional development, or be used to update existing curricula with AI content.

title: Credit Access and Inclusion Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, the Credit Access and Inclusion Act of 2025, changes federal credit reporting law to make it clear that landlords, utility companies, telecommunications providers, and HUD can share information about people's rent, utility, and phone/internet bill payments with credit reporting agencies like Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. Currently, this kind of payment history is often left out of standard credit reports, even though it can show that someone reliably pays their bills. The bill also protects consumers who set up payment plans for overdue utility bills, stating that utility companies cannot report those balances as "late" as long as the consumer is keeping up with the agreed plan. Consumers can also opt out of having this information shared, if they choose.

For consumers, this could mean that people who pay rent and utility bills on time, but have thin or no traditional credit history (such as young adults, immigrants, or lower-income households), could build stronger credit profiles by having this positive payment history counted. However, it could also mean that missed or late payments on rent and utilities might now show up on credit reports, potentially lowering some people's credit scores. The bill limits legal liability for companies that report this data in good faith, and it requires the Government Accountability Office to study, within two years, how these changes affect consumers' credit scores and access to credit. This would affect renters, utility customers, telecom customers, landlords, utility and phone companies, and credit reporting agencies.
ai_headline: Bill would let rent and utility payments count toward credit scores
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 688.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 5402 lets landlords, utilities, and telecom firms report rent and bill payments to credit bureaus, with an opt-out.

It protects consumers on approved payment plans for overdue utility bills from being reported as "late," and lets consumers opt out of having this information shared.

ai_sections.why: Including this payment history could help people with thin credit files build stronger credit profiles, but it could also expose missed or late payments that weren't previously visible, potentially lowering some credit scores.

title: Words Matter Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 3420, the Words Matter Act of 2025, updates the language used in federal laws by replacing outdated terms like "mentally retarded" and "mental retardation" with more respectful, modern terms such as "intellectual disability" or "individuals with intellectual disabilities." This change applies across many different laws, including those dealing with military healthcare, nursing homes, criminal sentencing, Medicaid, school lunch programs, and civil rights protections for institutionalized people. The bill also directs federal agencies to update regulations to match this new language, while clearly noting the old terms for reference during the transition.

Importantly, this bill is purely about updating wording, not changing policy. It explicitly states that no one's rights, benefits, eligibility, or legal protections will change as a result of these edits. It also does not require states to update their own laws, even though it changes federal terminology. This bill mainly affects government agencies, legal documents, and regulations, rather than everyday people directly. However, it could indirectly benefit individuals with intellectual disabilities and their families by removing language many consider outdated or offensive from official U.S. laws.

title: Stop Stealing our Chips Act
ai_summary:
HR 6322, called the "Stop Stealing our Chips Act," aims to strengthen enforcement of U.S. export control laws, particularly to prevent advanced computer chips (like those used for artificial intelligence) from being illegally sent to countries considered national security threats. The bill does this by creating a whistleblower program at the Department of Commerce. People with inside knowledge of illegal chip exports or other export violations could report that information through a secure online portal, potentially anonymously, and receive a financial reward if their tip leads to a successful enforcement action resulting in fines over $1 million. Rewards would range from 10% to 30% of the money the government collects from the violator.

The bill also includes strong protections for whistleblowers. Employers would be barred from firing, demoting, threatening, or otherwise punishing employees for reporting export violations, whether they report internally or directly to the government. Whistleblowers who are illegally retaliated against could sue for reinstatement, double back pay, and legal costs. The bill sets rules about confidentiality (protecting the whistleblower's identity in most cases) and excludes certain people from receiving rewards, such as compliance officers who normally handle these issues as part of their job, or people who broke other laws to get the information.

This bill would primarily affect companies involved in exporting sensitive technology (especially semiconductor and AI chip manufacturers), their employees, and government agencies like the Department of Commerce that enforce export laws. It also creates a new government fund to pay for the whistleblower rewards and program costs, financed by fines collected from violators rather than new taxpayer spending. Ordinary consumers would likely not be directly affected, though the bill could help deter chip smuggling that raises national security concerns.
ai_headline: Bill would pay whistleblowers who expose illegal chip exports

title: To make improvements in the enactment of title 41, United States Code, into a positive law title and to improve the Code.
ai_summary:
This bill is a technical "housekeeping" measure that updates cross-references in federal law. Congress is in the process of rewriting title 41 of the United States Code (which covers federal procurement and contracting rules) into what's called "positive law," meaning the numbering and organization of that section of the U.S. Code is being reorganized and cleaned up. When that happens, hundreds of other laws that mention old section numbers from title 41 become outdated, since they point to citations that no longer exist or have moved. This bill goes through many other parts of the U.S. Code—covering everything from agriculture and housing to defense, small business, immigration, and education—and updates those old references so they correctly point to the new section numbers in the reorganized title 41.

In practical terms, this bill does not change any policy, rights, benefits, or obligations for anyone. It does not add or remove programs, funding, or rules. It simply corrects citations so that laws referencing old procurement statutes (like the "Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949," the "Office of Federal Procurement Policy Act," or the "Contract Disputes Act of 1978") now correctly point to their new locations in title 41. This mainly affects lawyers, federal agencies, and anyone who needs to look up or interpret these laws, ensuring that legal citations remain accurate and functional. Everyday residents are not directly affected, since the bill doesn't change what the laws actually require—only how they are labeled and cross-referenced within the U.S. Code.

title: A bill to provide for the equitable settlement of certain Indian land disputes regarding land in Illinois, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill deals with a land dispute between the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma and the state of Illinois, stemming from an 1805 treaty called the Treaty of Grouseland. Normally, old land claims like this can't be brought to court because too much time has passed (there are legal deadlines called statutes of limitations, plus other legal defenses based on delay). This bill creates a special, one-time exception: it allows the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma to file a land claim in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims, a special federal court that handles money claims against the government, without those usual time-limit rules blocking the case.

However, this permission doesn't last forever. The tribe has only one year from when the bill becomes law to actually file its claim in that court. If the tribe doesn't file within that window, the opportunity disappears. The bill also states that once this process plays out, all other claims the tribe (or its members, descendants, or predecessors) might have to land in Illinois are permanently ended, except for whatever claim gets filed under this new process.

This bill mainly affects the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma, the U.S. government, and potentially landowners or the state of Illinois if a claim is filed and decided in court. It essentially sets up a formal, limited legal pathway for resolving this specific historical land dispute, while making clear that once this window closes, the matter is considered settled for good.
ai_headline: Bill gives Miami Tribe one year to file 1805 land claim in court
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

title: SCALE Biology Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the SCALE Biology Act, directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to create a new research program focused on measurement science for engineering biology, biomanufacturing, and biotechnology. In plain terms, NIST would develop reliable, standardized ways to measure and test biological materials and processes—similar to how it already sets measurement standards for things like weights, time, or chemical purity. The goal is to help U.S. companies and researchers produce biology-based products (like lab-grown materials, engineered microbes, or biomanufactured goods) more consistently, safely, and competitively.

The bill lays out specific activities NIST would take on, such as researching how DNA translates into cellular function, creating shared scientific terms and definitions, building "biofoundries" (specialized research facilities), offering access to advanced lab equipment for outside researchers, and working with universities, nonprofits, and other federal agencies. It also requires NIST to report to Congress on its progress and to consider security risks tied to biological data and technology. Funding is authorized to grow from $55 million in 2026 to $85 million by 2030.

This bill would mainly affect scientists, biotech companies, universities, and government agencies involved in biological research and manufacturing. It does not create new regulations for the public but aims to strengthen the scientific infrastructure that supports the growing bioeconomy—industries built around biology-based products like medicines, biofuels, or lab-made materials. Everyday consumers could see indirect benefits over time through safer, higher-quality, and more efficient biotech products.

title: To make improvements in the enactment of title 54, United States Code, into a positive law title and to correct related technical errors.
ai_summary:
This bill is a technical housekeeping measure that fixes mistakes made when Congress converted a large body of laws about national parks, historic preservation, and public lands into "title 54" of the United States Code back in 2014. When laws get reorganized into these official code titles, small errors—like typos, incorrect cross-references, or accidentally repealed provisions—sometimes slip through. This bill corrects those errors so the law reads and functions the way it was originally intended.

Specifically, it fixes typos (like "Occcur" to "Occur" and "mimimum" to "minimum"), corrects section numbers that were mistakenly cited elsewhere in the law, restores a couple of provisions that were accidentally repealed, renumbers some sections to add missing "purpose" statements explaining why certain programs exist, and updates a few substantive details—such as extending a land-acquisition program's authorization from 2020 to 2025, adding a requirement that land can only be bought from willing sellers, and adding a rule barring use of certain funds for lobbying Congress. It also formally repeals a list of old, outdated laws that have already been replaced by title 54.

This bill doesn't change policy in a meaningful way for most people. It mainly affects government agencies like the National Park Service and the Bureau of Land Management, legal researchers, and anyone who relies on accurate citations to federal law regarding parks, historic sites, and conservation programs. Ordinary citizens are unlikely to notice any practical difference, since the bill's purpose is to clean up legal text rather than create new rules or spending.

title: Water Resources Development Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill, the Water Resources Development Act of 2026, is part of a regular series of laws Congress passes every couple of years to direct the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers on managing the country's rivers, harbors, dams, levees, and flood control systems. It doesn't create new taxes or major national policy changes; instead, it sets up new offices within the Corps (for example, to help communities access water-supply programs, speed up project reviews, and manage inland waterway construction), streamlines permitting processes, and adjusts rules for how projects are funded, studied, and approved. It also creates a "Levee Owners Board" to advise on levee safety, expands the Corps's ability to use electronic systems for permits and environmental reviews, and clarifies legal protections for cleaning up contaminated river or harbor sediment.

Beyond these general provisions, the bulk of the bill authorizes, modifies, or cancels ("deauthorizes") specific water infrastructure projects around the country—things like harbor dredging, flood control studies, reservoir management, and coastal restoration efforts in dozens of named states and communities. It also orders new studies and reports on topics like drought resilience, dam safety, disaster debris removal, and flood risk in specific river basins.

This bill mainly affects local governments, water utilities, port authorities, and communities that rely on the Army Corps of Engineers for flood protection, navigation, and water supply projects. It also affects Corps of Engineers operations internally, changing how it organizes staff, awards contracts, and communicates with the public and Congress. Everyday residents may notice effects indirectly, through improved flood protection, faster permit approvals for local infrastructure work, or new/canceled projects in their region, but the bill does not directly regulate individuals or businesses outside of these water infrastructure contexts.

title: AI Security and Innovation Act
ai_summary:
This bill would create a new "Center for AI Security and Innovation" inside the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), which is part of the Department of Commerce. The Center's job would be to study the risks that artificial intelligence systems might pose—especially to national security and the economy—and to help the U.S. stay ahead of other countries, particularly rivals like China, in AI research and development. It would evaluate powerful "frontier" AI systems (advanced models still to be formally defined), test them for security weaknesses such as hacking risks or misuse for chemical or biological weapons, and publish voluntary guidelines and best practices that AI companies could choose to follow.

In practice, this mainly affects AI developers, especially large companies building advanced AI models, since they could voluntarily submit their systems for government evaluation. It also affects federal agencies like the Departments of Energy, Defense, and Homeland Security, and the intelligence community, who would coordinate with this new Center. The bill specifically states that the Center would have no regulatory or enforcement power—it can't make companies do anything or create new rules. It's meant to be a research and information-sharing hub, not a regulator.

For everyday Americans, the bill wouldn't create new rules or requirements directly affecting individuals. Instead, it's a government effort to better understand AI risks and maintain U.S. competitiveness in AI development, funded at $20 million per year through 2032, with the Center set to automatically end after five years unless renewed. Information companies share with the Center would be kept confidential and could not be used by any government agency to regulate the company, and the Center would report to Congress annually on AI trends, competition with other countries, and staffing needs.
ai_headline: New NIST center would study AI risks without regulatory power
