title: SRBIJA Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the SRBIJA Act, lays out how the United States should respond to political problems in Serbia. Congress states its concerns about Serbia's government cracking down on protesters, weakening media freedom and judicial independence, and deepening ties with Russia, China, and Iran, even though Serbia is still officially seeking to join the European Union. The bill also references the deadly 2024 collapse of a train station canopy in Novi Sad, which many Serbians blame on government corruption, and calls for an independent investigation into that disaster and into the use of force against demonstrators.

To act on these concerns, the bill directs the State Department to write a report on Russian and Chinese influence in Serbia and to develop a strategy for U.S.-Serbia relations covering issues like corruption, media freedom, and the Serbia-Kosovo dialogue. It also says the U.S. should pause its official "Strategic Dialogue" talks with Serbia unless the Secretary of State certifies that certain topics—like elections, corruption, and civil liberties—will be addressed. The bill supports applying existing U.S. sanctions authorities against individuals in the Western Balkans, including Serbia, who undermine democracy, engage in corruption, or commit human rights abuses. If Serbia shows real progress on these issues, the bill allows for increased U.S. assistance, closer defense cooperation, and expanded academic and cultural exchanges. The law would automatically expire five years after being enacted.

This bill mainly affects U.S. foreign policy officials, particularly the State Department, and shapes how the U.S. government engages with Serbia's leaders. It could also affect Serbian officials or other individuals who might face sanctions, as well as organizations involved in U.S.-funded programs supporting media freedom, judicial reform, or civil society in Serbia. Everyday U.S. residents are not directly affected, though the bill reflects broader American interests in Balkan stability and countering Russian, Chinese, and Iranian influence in the region.

title: Harmful Algal Bloom and Hypoxia Research and Control Amendments Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill updates a 1998 law that deals with harmful algal blooms (sometimes called "red tide" or toxic algae outbreaks) and hypoxia (low-oxygen "dead zones" in water). It expands the government's focus from just coastal and Great Lakes waters to also include freshwater lakes and rivers. It requires federal agencies—mainly the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)—to research these problems, monitor and forecast outbreaks, and produce a public report every five years assessing the causes, health risks, and economic damage caused by algal blooms. The bill also creates a new national "incubator program" to fund and test new technologies for detecting and reducing algal blooms, and sets up a database tracking which prevention methods work best.

The bill also strengthens coordination requirements, directing agencies to consult with states, Native American tribes, Native Hawaiian organizations, local governments, fishing and farming industries, and rural or subsistence communities that rely on fish and water resources. It expands access to toxin testing for people in remote areas who fish for food, and requires that funding decisions consider impacts on public health, food security, and low-income or tribal communities. Finally, it authorizes federal funding—about $19.5 million per year to NOAA and $8 million per year to the EPA through 2030, plus $2 million per year for responding to major bloom events—and gives officials more flexibility to waive local cost-sharing requirements and to contract directly with tribes, states, and local governments for bloom response efforts.

This bill mainly affects government agencies, scientists, and coastal/freshwater communities—including commercial and recreational fishers, tribal nations, farmers (due to fertilizer runoff's role in algae growth), and residents near lakes, rivers, or coastlines affected by toxic algae or oxygen-depleted water. It does not create new regulations on businesses but focuses on research funding, monitoring, and coordination among existing federal programs.
ai_headline: Bill expands federal algae and dead zone research to lakes and rivers
last_action_text: Held at the desk.

title: Northeast Lobsterman Protection Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill changes a deadline in an existing law that deals with rules protecting the North Atlantic right whale, an endangered species, from getting entangled in fishing gear. Back in 2022, Congress had passed a law (part of a larger spending bill) that put certain whale-protection regulations on hold for a set period, giving the lobster and fishing industry more time before stricter gear rules would kick in. That pause was set to expire in 2028. This bill pushes that expiration date back to 2035, meaning the current, less restrictive rules would stay in place for seven more years than originally planned.

The bill mainly affects lobstermen and fishing businesses in the Northeast, especially in Maine, who use rope and trap gear that regulators have linked to whale entanglements. By delaying stricter federal rules, it gives these fishermen more time to keep operating under current practices without new restrictions or costs tied to updated whale-protection gear requirements. At the same time, the delay affects federal agencies like NOAA Fisheries, which oversee whale protection efforts, and it has implications for conservation groups and others concerned about the North Atlantic right whale, a species with a very small and declining population, since it postpones stronger protective measures meant to reduce deaths and injuries from fishing gear.

title: GPO Modernization Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill updates how the Government Publishing Office (GPO), the federal agency that produces and distributes official government documents, operates in the digital age. It shifts the agency's focus from primarily printing paper documents toward managing digital information, while still maintaining some physical distribution. Key changes include renaming the "Joint Committee on Printing" (the congressional committee overseeing GPO) to the "Joint Committee on Publishing," updating rules for the Federal Depository Library Program (which provides free public access to government documents at libraries nationwide) to better accommodate digital formats, and allowing libraries to be designated as "digital-only" depositories. It also creates a formal "National Collection of United States Public Information" to preserve government documents long-term, sets new privacy protections for people accessing government information online, and raises the dollar threshold for GPO's simplified purchasing procedures from $100,000 to $350,000.

The bill also makes changes to how certain congressional publications are produced. Notably, it eliminates the requirement that the Congressional Research Service produce the "Constitution Annotated" (a detailed legal reference guide to the Constitution) in printed hardbound form, making it digital-only going forward, and does the same for the Congressional Directory. It also adjusts GPO employee compensation and leave policies to align with other legislative branch agencies.

This bill mainly affects government agencies, libraries (especially the roughly 1,100 depository libraries that store federal documents), researchers, and legal professionals who rely on printed government publications. Everyday residents would be affected mainly through libraries: some government documents that used to be available in print may now only exist online, which could matter for people without reliable internet access. The changes are largely administrative and technical, aimed at modernizing an agency whose core printing-focused laws date back decades, rather than changing what information the public can access.
ai_headline: Government Publishing Office law overhaul shifts focus to digital documents
last_action_text: Ordered to be Reported (Amended) by Voice Vote.

title: Indian Health Service Emergency Claims Parity Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes a rule about how the Indian Health Service (IHS) handles payment for emergency medical care received outside its own facilities. Under current law, Native American patients who get emergency treatment from an outside hospital or doctor (not run by the IHS) must notify the IHS within a certain time limit for that care to be eligible for payment. Previously, this extended notification window applied only to elderly or disabled patients. This bill expands that same protection to all Native Americans receiving emergency care, not just those who are elderly or disabled.

Specifically, the bill sets a minimum 15-day window for notifying the IHS after receiving emergency treatment from a non-IHS provider or facility. This gives patients and their families more time to complete the required paperwork before the IHS can deny payment based on late notification. Emergency situations are often chaotic, and patients or their families may not immediately think about notifying a government health program while dealing with a medical crisis.

This bill primarily affects Native American and Alaska Native individuals who rely on the Indian Health Service for their healthcare and who may need emergency treatment at hospitals or clinics outside the IHS system. It also affects the IHS itself, which administers these payment rules, and outside healthcare providers who treat IHS-eligible patients and seek reimbursement. By standardizing and extending the notification deadline for everyone rather than just elderly or disabled patients, the bill aims to reduce situations where emergency claims are denied simply because notification paperwork wasn't filed quickly enough.
ai_headline: Bill extends 15-day emergency care notice rule to all IHS patients
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 679.

title: Rural Jobs and Hydropower Expansion Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes an older law, the Reclamation Project Act of 1939, to make it easier for private companies and local organizations (not the federal government) to build hydropower projects at facilities owned by the Bureau of Reclamation. The Bureau of Reclamation manages dams, canals, and reservoirs mostly in western states for irrigation and water supply. Currently, the law mostly allows this kind of non-federal hydropower development on small water pipes ("conduits") and reservoirs used for pumped storage. This bill expands that permission to cover hydropower development on any Bureau of Reclamation facility, not just those smaller or specific structures.

The bill also updates the technical rules for how these projects work. It clarifies terms like "transferred works facility" (a facility run day-to-day by a non-federal group under contract) and "reserved works facility" (one still run by the Bureau of Reclamation itself). It also addresses what happens to federal permits, called "authorizations," issued by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) for these hydropower projects — allowing them to stay active and be renewed, and specifying that if a permit becomes inactive, control of that project site returns fully to the Bureau of Reclamation. The bill states it does not expand any leasing authority beyond the existing project boundaries.

This bill mainly affects companies and organizations interested in developing hydropower using federal water infrastructure, especially in rural western areas where Bureau of Reclamation projects are common. It could open up more opportunities for local economic development and clean energy production tied to existing dams and canals, while keeping oversight authority with federal agencies like the Bureau of Reclamation and FERC.
ai_headline: Bill would let private firms build hydropower at more federal dam sites

title: National Wildlife Refuge System Invasive Species Strike Team Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Secretary of the Interior, through the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, to create a nationwide program called the "Invasive Species Strike Team Program" to fight harmful non-native plants, animals, and other organisms on or near National Wildlife Refuge lands. Each regional office of the Fish and Wildlife Service would have at least one trained team that finds invasive species early, responds quickly, and works to control or remove them before they spread and cause lasting damage to native wildlife, habitats, or local economies. These teams would use modern tracking tools and databases, coordinate with state, tribal, and local governments, and can also provide help—money, expertise, or equipment—to landowners and organizations dealing with invasive species near refuge areas.

The bill affects wildlife refuge managers, conservation groups, state and tribal agencies, and nearby private landowners who may deal with invasive species problems. It could also indirectly benefit farmers, outdoor recreation businesses, and communities near refuges, since invasive species often damage crops, fisheries, and natural areas. The Fish and Wildlife Service would be required to report to Congress and the public on the program’s progress after two and five years.

Financially, the bill authorizes—but does not guarantee—$10 million per year from 2027 through 2033 for this effort, meaning Congress would still need to approve the actual funding each year through the regular budget process.

title: Safe Beaches, Safe Swimmers Act
ai_summary:
HR 5063, the "Safe Beaches, Safe Swimmers Act," addresses lifeguard shortages at swimming areas managed by federal agencies, including the National Park Service, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bureau of Land Management, and Bureau of Reclamation. If the Secretary of the Interior determines that a federally managed beach or swim location is facing a real staffing shortage—meaning it can't be adequately covered by federal lifeguards during its normal operating season—the bill allows the Secretary to arrange for local government lifeguards to fill in. This would help ensure these swim spots stay monitored for safety, rescues, and first aid rather than being left unwatched.

The bill specifies that any local government agency providing lifeguards under this arrangement must be reimbursed for reasonable costs. It also clarifies that this only applies to more serious, ongoing staffing shortages, not short-term gaps caused by things like an employee taking vacation or sick leave.

This bill would primarily affect visitors to federally managed beaches and swim areas, who could benefit from more consistent lifeguard coverage. It would also affect local governments near these federal lands, since they could be asked to supply lifeguards and would receive federal funding to do so. Federal land management agencies would gain a new tool for addressing lifeguard shortages without needing to hire more federal staff directly.

title: Enhancing Geothermal Production on Federal Lands Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the federal government reviews small-scale geothermal exploration projects on public lands. Geothermal energy comes from heat inside the earth, and companies that lease federal land to explore for it currently have to go through detailed environmental reviews before drilling test wells to check underground conditions. This bill says that certain small, temporary exploration projects—those using narrow well casings, disturbing less than 8 acres of land, finished within 180 days, and restored within 3 years—will no longer count as "major federal actions." That means they would skip the lengthy environmental review process normally required under the National Environmental Policy Act, though companies would still have to notify the government at least 30 days before drilling starts.

The bill also covers related activities like geological studies, off-road travel on approved routes, and maintenance of access roads used for geothermal work. It does not change rules for actual large-scale geothermal energy production, only the early exploratory phase used to determine whether a site is worth developing.

This mainly affects energy companies that lease federal land for geothermal exploration, allowing them to move faster and spend less on paperwork and permitting for small test projects. It also affects the Bureau of Land Management and Forest Service, which oversee these leases and environmental reviews, and indirectly affects nearby communities and environmental groups, since faster approvals could mean less opportunity for public environmental scrutiny before drilling begins. Supporters say it speeds up clean energy development, while others may be concerned about reduced environmental oversight, but the bill itself simply changes the review process rather than mandating any particular outcome.
ai_headline: Bill would exempt small geothermal test wells from environmental review
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 674.

title: Crow Tribe Water Rights Settlement Amendments Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill updates a 2010 law that settled water rights claims for the Crow Tribe in Montana. The original law set up a system for the federal government to help build a rural water system providing drinking water and other water services to the Crow Reservation. This bill changes how that project is managed and funded, replacing an older approach (a federally built "MR&I System") with a new setup where the Tribe itself takes the lead on building, running, and repairing its own water infrastructure using money from a dedicated account. It also makes clear that once the Tribe builds these water projects with this funding, the Tribe owns and controls them, and the federal government won't be responsible for future maintenance or repair costs.

The bill also extends a deadline related to hydropower revenues from the Yellowtail Dam, giving the Tribe 20 years instead of 15 to receive certain payments tied to the dam. Additionally, it updates outdated legal references in the original law and cleans up some technical language so the law is easier to apply correctly.

This bill mainly affects the Crow Tribe, since it changes how they receive and use federal funds for water infrastructure on their reservation. It could also affect the U.S. Department of the Interior, which manages the settlement funds and trust accounts involved, and it may have modest effects on the federal budget by adjusting how and when certain payments are made.

title: LACA of 2026
ai_summary:

The bill mainly affects people in these two specific regions of Texas and California, including local residents, attorneys, and litigants who use the federal court system there. It could make it more convenient for people living near College Station or El Centro to attend court proceedings without traveling long distances to another city. The bill does not change what cases federal courts can hear or how they are decided; it only addresses the physical locations where court sessions may take place.

title: FACE Act Repeal Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the FACE Act Repeal Act of 2025, would eliminate a federal law known as the FACE Act (Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act). That existing law, passed in 1994, makes it a federal crime to use force, threats, or physical obstruction to block people from entering or leaving reproductive health clinics (including those that provide abortions) or places of religious worship. It also protects people who provide or receive services at these clinics, as well as clergy and worshippers at religious sites, from violent or obstructive interference.

If this bill passes, Section 248 of the federal criminal code would be completely removed, meaning these specific federal protections and criminal penalties would no longer exist. The bill also states that this repeal would apply to any ongoing or future prosecutions, meaning cases currently being prosecuted under this law could be affected once the repeal takes effect.

This bill would primarily affect abortion clinics and their staff and patients, anti-abortion protesters, and houses of worship. Supporters of repeal often argue the law has been used to unfairly target and prosecute pro-life demonstrators for nonviolent protest activities, while opponents of repeal argue the law is necessary to prevent violence and harassment at clinics and places of worship. Without this federal law, protection against clinic blockades and related violence would depend more heavily on state laws, which vary significantly from state to state.

title: NDO Fairness Act
ai_summary:
**HR 6048 — NDO Fairness Act** deals with situations where the government secretly obtains someone's emails, cloud files, or other online records from companies like Google or Microsoft without telling that person right away. Under current law, prosecutors can get a court order forcing tech companies to stay silent about these requests ("nondisclosure orders" or NDOs) so a suspect doesn't find out they're being investigated. This bill tightens the rules for how long that secrecy can last and what the government has to prove to get it. Generally, gag orders would be capped at 90 days (with possible extensions), except in child exploitation cases, which could get up to a year. Courts would need to write detailed findings explaining why secrecy is truly necessary—such as protecting someone's safety or preventing evidence destruction—rather than granting these orders routinely.

The bill also strengthens protections for the person being investigated and for tech companies. Companies could challenge gag orders in court, and their obligation to hand over data would pause while that challenge is being decided. Once a gag order expires, the government would be required to notify the affected customer, explain why they were investigated, and tell them how to request copies of the records that were shared—except in child exploitation cases or when it would compromise an ongoing case. Finally, the Department of Justice would have to publish an annual public report detailing how many of these secret orders were requested, granted, or denied, including how many affected journalists.

This bill mainly affects three groups: everyday internet and email users who could eventually learn if their data was secretly searched; tech and telecom companies that must comply with these orders while gaining new rights to push back in court; and federal prosecutors and judges, who would face stricter standards and more paperwork when seeking secrecy in criminal investigations.
ai_headline: Bill would cap secret gag orders on tech firms at 90 days

title: Hershel ‘Woody' Williams National Medal of Honor Monument Location Act
ai_summary:
This bill allows a monument honoring Medal of Honor recipients to be built in a special protected area of the National Mall in Washington, D.C., known as "the Reserve." Normally, federal law restricts new monuments from being built in this particular area because it's considered largely complete and reserved for the most significant national memorials. This bill creates a specific exception so this monument can be placed there.

The monument itself was already approved in an earlier law (Public Law 117-80), which allowed the National Medal of Honor Museum Foundation to build a commemorative work honoring the courage and sacrifice of Medal of Honor recipients—the highest military award for valor in combat. This new bill doesn't create the monument; it simply changes where it can be located, letting it be placed within the Reserve instead of elsewhere on or near the National Mall. title: CORE Act of 2025
ai_summary:
**H.R. 2556 – CORE Act of 2025**

This bill directs several federal agencies—including the Departments of Energy, Interior, and State—to study and report on offshore oil and gas resources near the United States. It requires a detailed report on "transboundary" oil and gas deposits that cross maritime borders with countries like Canada, Mexico, Cuba, and the Bahamas, including how disputed ocean boundaries might be resolved (potentially through international courts) and how the U.S. could cooperate with neighboring countries on shared drilling projects. The bill also calls for using advanced technology, such as AI and improved mapping tools, to get better estimates of how much oil and gas exists in U.S. coastal waters.

The bill updates an existing law (the Energy Policy Act of 2005) to require the Interior Department to regularly review and improve the models it uses to estimate offshore energy resources, and to study how restricting drilling in certain protected areas (like marine sanctuaries) affects jobs, national security, and government revenue. It also requires a periodic comparison of how the U.S. offshore leasing and drilling process stacks up against other major oil-producing countries in terms of efficiency, output, and competitiveness.

This bill mainly affects government agencies, energy companies, and coastal communities involved in offshore drilling. It doesn't authorize new drilling itself, but it sets up studies and reporting requirements that could shape future decisions about where and how offshore energy development happens, as well as U.S. relations with neighboring countries over shared ocean resources.

title: To require the Secretary of State to submit a notification to Congress prior to obligating funds for certain art-related purchases, and for other purposes.
ai_summary:
This bill would require the U.S. State Department to notify Congress before spending money on certain art-related purchases costing more than $37,500. This applies to three specific programs: the Art in Embassies Program (which buys or displays artwork at U.S. embassies and diplomatic buildings), residential design programs (which furnish and decorate official homes used by ambassadors and other top diplomats overseas), and the Cultural Heritage Program (which preserves or restores historic artwork and architecture at diplomatic properties). The bill doesn't stop the State Department from making these purchases—it simply adds a reporting requirement so that Congress, specifically the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Senate Foreign Relations Committee, knows about big art and design expenses in advance. This mainly affects the State Department's internal operations and oversight process; it doesn't directly affect everyday citizens' lives, taxes, or services. It's aimed at increasing transparency and congressional oversight of how taxpayer money is spent on art, furnishings, and historic preservation at U.S. embassies and diplomatic residences abroad.

title: Preshevo Valley Discrimination Assessment Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Preshevo Valley Discrimination Assessment Act, would require the U.S. Secretary of State to write a detailed report on how Serbia treats its ethnic Albanian minority, particularly those living in the Preshevo Valley region. The report would need to be finished within 180 days of the bill becoming law and sent to foreign affairs committees in both the House and Senate.

The report would look into a wide range of specific issues, such as whether Serbian authorities are canceling the official residency status of ethnic Albanians (which can block them from renewing ID cards or voting), whether Albanian-language education, media, and cultural activities are being restricted, whether diplomas earned in Kosovo are recognized, whether government funding is distributed fairly to Albanian-majority towns, and whether police mistreat or intimidate ethnic Albanians without cause. It also asks whether Serbia is considering mandatory military service for this group or taking steps that make daily life harder for Albanians in the region.

This bill would not change any laws or provide funding for programs—it simply directs the State Department to research and report on these issues. It primarily affects U.S. foreign policy information-gathering and could influence future discussions about U.S.-Serbia relations. It does not directly impact everyday life for most Americans, though it could affect diplomatic relations and inform future U.S. government actions or foreign aid decisions related to Serbia and its treatment of the ethnic Albanian minority.

title: Moab UMTRA Project Transition Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill deals with a former uranium mill site near Moab, Utah, which the federal government has been cleaning up for years because of radioactive tailings left behind from old mining operations. The bill changes an existing law to say that once the Department of Energy determines the cleanup has reached a point safe enough for the land to be transferred, the government must give the site to Grand County, Utah, at no cost. Right now, the law does not clearly require this local transfer, so this bill sets up a specific legal path for it to happen.

The bill includes several conditions. The Department of Energy would keep certain water rights needed to continue monitoring or cleaning up groundwater contamination, even after the land changes hands. The government could also place restrictions on how the land is used if needed to protect public health and safety. Additionally, Grand County would be barred from selling or transferring the land to any private company or nonprofit organization, meaning it would have to stay under public (county) control.

This bill mainly affects residents of Grand County, Utah, and the surrounding area, since it determines who will own and manage this land once environmental cleanup is complete. It could also matter to state and local governments involved in land use planning, as well as environmental regulators overseeing the safety of the site. The broader public may be indirectly affected through implications for how contaminated federal sites are transferred to local communities in the future.
ai_headline: Bill sets path to give cleaned-up Moab uranium site to Grand County
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported with an amendment favorably.

title: American Voices in Federal Lands Act
ai_summary:
This bill would change how the federal government collects public opinions before creating rules for managing federal public lands, such as those overseen by the Bureau of Land Management. Currently, agencies gather input from "citizens" broadly when writing land management rules. Under this bill, when the Bureau of Land Management is developing regulations, officials could only formally consider comments submitted by citizens of the United States, rather than input from any interested member of the public, including foreign individuals or organizations.

The bill also requires the Bureau to use CAPTCHA technology (the "type the letters you see" or similar verification tools) during public comment periods to block automated bots or artificial intelligence programs from submitting comments, ensuring that feedback comes from real people rather than computer-generated submissions.

This bill would primarily affect how public land management agencies conduct their official rulemaking process. It could impact environmental groups, industry organizations, land-use advocates, researchers, and international stakeholders who currently participate in commenting on federal land policies, since some may no longer have their input formally counted if they aren't U.S. citizens. It would also affect the Bureau of Land Management and Department of Agriculture, which would need to update their public comment systems to include identity verification and citizenship-screening tools when writing new land management rules.

last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

title: Chugach Alaska Land Exchange Oil Spill Recovery Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill sets up a large land swap in south-central Alaska between the federal government and the Chugach Alaska Corporation, an Alaska Native regional corporation. The swap is meant to fix a problem left over from cleanup efforts after the 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill. Back then, a fund created from Exxon's settlement money bought surface land and conservation easements from Alaska Native village corporations to protect wildlife habitat, but it didn't buy the underground mineral rights, which by law belonged separately to Chugach Alaska. This left the government owning the surface of the land while Chugach Alaska still owned the resources beneath it, creating conflict between conservation goals and the corporation's right to develop those resources for its Native shareholders.

To resolve this, the bill directs Chugach Alaska to give up its underground mineral rights on about 231,000 acres where the government already controls the surface, in exchange for the government transferring about 65,000 acres of full ownership (both surface and subsurface) of other federal land to Chugach Alaska. This includes specific parcels of national forest, park, and other federal land identified in an earlier government study. Small areas already set aside for village development or Native shareholder home sites are excluded from the trade.

The bill mainly affects Chugach Alaska Corporation and its Alaska Native shareholders, several Alaska Native village corporations, the U.S. Forest Service, Bureau of Land Management, and National Park Service, and residents or businesses connected to land and resource use in the Chugach region of Alaska. For everyday Americans outside that region, the impact is indirect—it affects how federally protected conservation land is managed and how Native corporations can use their land and resources, but does not have direct effects on the public elsewhere.
ai_headline: Bill would swap Alaska land to settle Exxon Valdez cleanup dispute
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

title: Western Wildfire Support Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Western Wildfire Support Act of 2025, makes a series of changes aimed at improving how the federal government prevents, fights, and recovers from wildfires, especially in Western states. It requires more detailed public reporting on how much money is spent fighting major wildfires, directs the Department of Defense to reimburse states when military training exercises accidentally start fires, and requires federal land agencies to create updated wildfire-risk plans for specific high-risk forest areas ("firesheds"). It also calls for several studies, including one on training gaps for local firefighters responding to wildfires, one on how private drones interfere with firefighting aircraft, and one on modernizing radio communication and predictive fire-modeling technology used by firefighters.

The bill also promotes new technology for detecting and responding to fires, such as expanding sensors, cameras, satellite data, and drones for early fire detection, and funding research into using unmanned aircraft for firefighting. It expands a grant program to help local governments and Native American tribes buy portable water tank units for firefighting trucks. For recovery after fires, it supports state websites that help residents find disaster assistance, creates permanent emergency response teams to stabilize burned land and prevent erosion, and establishes a new funding account (up to $100 million per year) for long-term rehabilitation of burned areas, such as replanting trees and restoring watersheds. It also creates a cash prize competition to encourage new technology for controlling invasive plant and animal species that spread after wildfires.

The people most affected would be residents of Western states prone to wildfires, firefighters and emergency responders (federal, state, local, and tribal), landowners near federal forests, and communities recovering from fire damage. Federal agencies like the Forest Service, Department of the Interior, FEMA, and the Department of Defense would have new reporting, planning, and coordination responsibilities. The bill does not create new taxes but does authorize additional federal spending, mostly through existing programs and new studies, reports, and support programs related to wildfire prevention and recovery.

last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

title: Historic Roadways Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Historic Roadways Protection Act, would block the Secretary of the Interior (acting through the Bureau of Land Management) from spending federal money to finish or carry out certain travel management plans on public lands in Utah. Travel management plans are documents that decide which roads and trails in a given area can be used by vehicles, and which ones are closed off, often to protect wildlife, land, or historic sites. The bill lists ten specific "travel management areas" across Utah, including places like the Henry Mountains, San Rafael Swell, and Book Cliffs, where new plans could not be finalized or put into effect. It also names four already-developed plans, such as the Labyrinth/Gemini Bridges and San Rafael Desert plans, that could not be implemented.

The freeze would stay in place until a specific set of long-running lawsuits, known as "R.S. 2477 cases," are fully resolved. These lawsuits involve Utah counties and the state government suing the federal government over old rights-of-way claims to roads that cross federal land, based on an 1866 law (R.S. 2477) that allowed roads to be built across public lands before they were formally protected. Many of these disputes stretch back over a decade and involve questions about who legally controls certain roads and trails.

This bill would primarily affect rural Utah counties, ranchers, off-road vehicle users, environmental groups, and federal land managers. Supporters of blocking these plans might argue that road ownership should be settled in court first before new restrictions are imposed. Opponents of the bill might argue that delaying travel plans could postpone environmental protections or clarity on public land use. The bill does not change the outcome of the lawsuits themselves; it only pauses federal spending on the affected travel plans until those cases are decided.
ai_headline: Bill would freeze BLM travel plans on Utah lands until road lawsuits end
last_action_text: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Ordered to be reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute favorably.

title: HEIRS Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the HEIRS Act of 2025, aims to help families who inherit property from relatives without a formal will, which often creates a messy legal situation called "heirs' property." This happens when someone dies without a will, and the property automatically passes to multiple relatives who then jointly own it. This can make it hard to sell, use as collateral for loans, or pass down further, and has historically led many families, especially in underserved and rural communities, to lose land or homes.

The bill directs the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to create grant programs with three main parts. First, it would give money to states, local governments, territories, and tribal governments that adopt a specific model law (the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act) designed to protect heirs from being forced into unfair property sales. States receiving these grants would use the money to help residents with costs like title searches, land surveys, legal fees, and estate planning. Second, it creates a separate grant program for housing counseling agencies, legal clinics, and nonprofits to directly help property owners clear up title issues and stay in their homes. Third, it requires housing counseling organizations that already receive federal funding to explain heirs' property risks to their clients and refer them to legal help when needed.

This bill would affect families dealing with inherited property, especially those without wills, as well as state and local governments, nonprofits, and housing counselors who could apply for these new grants. Both grant programs are temporary, ending seven years after the law takes effect, unless renewed later.
ai_headline: New bill offers grants to help families untangle inherited property disputes
last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 693.

title: Whistleblower Protection Act of 2025
ai_summary:
HR 4646, the Whistleblower Protection Act of 2025, is a short bill that extends existing federal whistleblower protections to more people working on projects funded by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). Under current law, there's a federal rule (found in title 41 of the U.S. Code) that protects employees of government contractors and grant recipients from being fired, demoted, or otherwise punished for reporting fraud, waste, or abuse. This bill makes clear that this protection applies to anyone working under a HUD-funded contract, subcontract, grant, subgrant, or personal services agreement, no matter when that agreement was signed, including ones that existed before the law changes.

In plain terms, this means employees and contractors working on HUD-related projects, such as public housing programs, community development grants, or housing assistance initiatives, would have legal protection if they report problems like mismanagement, fraud, or illegal activity connected to that funding. It affects people who work for companies, nonprofits, or agencies that receive HUD money, ensuring they can safely raise concerns without fear of retaliation. It also affects HUD itself and its contractors, since the agency and its funded partners would need to comply with these whistleblower protection rules more broadly than before.

last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 686.

title: STOP Payments Fraud Act of 2026
ai_summary:
This bill changes federal rules about how quickly banks must make deposited money available to customers, specifically to help banks fight check and wire transfer fraud. Currently, banks generally must make deposited funds available within set time limits. This bill lets banks delay access to funds longer than usual when they have a "reasonable suspicion" that a check or wire transfer is fraudulent. Banks could hold funds for an initial period (up to 10 days) and an extended period (up to 45 days) while they investigate, following rules that the Federal Reserve and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would need to create. The bill also allows longer holds on new or risky accounts and requires banks to notify customers when they delay funds and why.

The bill also addresses fairness and oversight. If a bank delays a wire transfer for suspected fraud but fails to properly notify the customer, the bank can't charge overdraft fees caused by that delay. Regulators must also study how well current fraud protections work, including comparing federal and state rules, and report back to Congress with recommendations. Separately, the bill gives regulators power to speed up availability of certain check types (making them available as fast as local checks) during periods of high fraud losses, rather than being locked into current slower timelines.

This bill mainly affects everyday bank customers, especially those who deposit checks or receive wire transfers, since their money could be held longer than under current law if a bank suspects fraud. It also affects banks and credit unions, who would gain more flexibility to delay suspicious deposits but would face new recordkeeping, notification, and regulatory compliance requirements. Regulators like the Federal Reserve and CFPB would be responsible for writing detailed rules and reporting to Congress within set deadlines before these changes take effect.

last_action_text: Placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 692.

title: Earned Wage Access Consumer Protection Act
ai_summary:
This bill creates federal rules for "earned wage access" companies—apps and services that let workers get paid a portion of wages they've already earned before their official payday, often for a fee or "tip." It requires these companies to always offer a free option alongside any paid option, clearly disclose fees, limits, and tipping terms before and during transactions, and prevent tips from having a suggested default amount above zero. Companies must also let customers cancel recurring service without penalty, set up a process for handling consumer complaints and errors, and reimburse customers if a mistimed withdrawal causes an overdraft fee. The bill bans certain aggressive collection tactics, such as suing consumers, using debt collectors, or selling debts to third parties, except in cases of fraud by the consumer.

The bill also states that, if these companies follow the new federal rules, their services should not be legally treated as loans or credit, and the companies should not be treated as lenders under federal law. It limits states from passing their own laws that would classify earned wage access as a loan or interfere with these services, though states can still enforce general consumer protection laws like those against fraud. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) would be responsible for writing detailed rules to implement the law within six months of passage.

This bill mainly affects everyday workers who use paycheck-advance apps (a fast-growing industry, especially among hourly and gig workers), the companies offering these services, employers who may partner with such providers, and state regulators who currently oversee some of these products under existing lending or licensing laws. Supporters and critics disagree over whether the bill's provisions represent strong new consumer protections or whether the federal preemption of state law would limit oversight of an industry some regulators currently treat similarly to payday lending.

title: Promoting Cross-border Energy Infrastructure Act
ai_summary:
This bill changes how the government approves pipelines and power lines that cross the U.S. border with Canada or Mexico. Currently, companies building these "border-crossing facilities" for oil, natural gas, or electricity often need a Presidential permit, a process that can take years and depends on executive branch discretion. Under this bill, instead of a Presidential permit, companies would apply for a "certificate of crossing" from either the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (for oil and gas pipelines) or the Department of Energy (for electric transmission lines). These agencies would have to approve the certificate within 120 days after required environmental reviews are finished, unless they find the project isn't in the public interest. The bill also sets a strict 30-day deadline for approving natural gas import/export applications with Canada or Mexico, and it removes a similar approval requirement for electricity transmission to those countries. Existing pipelines, power lines, and permits already in place would be unaffected, and the President would no longer be allowed to revoke previously issued permits without Congress's approval.

This bill mainly affects energy companies that build or operate cross-border pipelines and power lines, as well as federal regulators like FERC and the Department of Energy, who would gain new responsibilities and deadlines. It could also affect communities near the border where these facilities are built, environmental review processes, and the broader relationship between the U.S. and its energy trade partners, Canada and Mexico. Everyday consumers might see indirect effects through energy prices, supply reliability, or environmental impacts of expedited pipeline and transmission projects, since faster approvals could mean quicker construction but less time for review or public input.
ai_headline: Bill would replace presidential permits for border energy lines with agency review
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 3062 shifts approval of cross-border pipelines and power lines from presidential permits to agency certificates with set deadlines.

Agencies must decide within 120 days after environmental review, and natural gas import/export applications with Canada or Mexico get a 30-day deadline. Existing facilities and permits stay unaffected, and the President can no longer revoke past permits without Congress's approval.
ai_sections.who: Energy companies building or operating cross-border pipelines and power lines, plus FERC and the Department of Energy, which gain new approval duties and deadlines.
ai_sections.why: Faster, more predictable approvals could speed construction but leave less time for environmental review and public input, affecting border communities and U.S. energy trade relations with Canada and Mexico.

title: Understanding Cybersecurity of Mobile Networks Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires a federal official, the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information, to study how secure U.S. mobile phone networks are against hacking and spying. Within a year of becoming law, that office—working with the Department of Homeland Security and other agencies—must give Congress a detailed report on cell phone network cybersecurity. The report has to cover things like how well phone companies are fixing known security weaknesses, whether customers care about cybersecurity when choosing phone plans or devices, how strong the encryption used in phones and networks actually is, and how common "cell site simulators" (fake cell towers sometimes used for surveillance) are and who uses them.

The report will look specifically at older mobile technologies, not 5G, and will focus on real-world security problems rather than theoretical ones found only in labs. It must be written so the public can read it, though sensitive details can be kept in a separate classified section, and any information that could help hackers exploit weaknesses will be removed from the public version.

This bill doesn't create new regulations or requirements for phone companies. It mainly affects government agencies, who will need to research and prepare this report, and indirectly affects mobile carriers, device makers, and software developers who may be asked for information during the study. For everyday people, the bill itself doesn't change anything immediately, but the resulting report could help lawmakers decide whether new cybersecurity rules for mobile networks are needed in the future.
ai_headline: Bill orders federal study on cell phone network security risks
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

title: Charlotte Woodward Organ Transplant Discrimination Prevention Act
ai_summary:
This bill aims to stop hospitals, doctors, and transplant centers from denying someone an organ transplant just because they have a mental or physical disability. It says that if a person otherwise qualifies medically for a transplant, a healthcare provider cannot refuse them, refuse to refer them to a specialist, or leave them off a transplant waiting list solely because of their disability. Providers would also be required to make reasonable accommodations—such as considering a person's support network of family, friends, or caregivers who can help them follow post-transplant care instructions—rather than assuming a person cannot manage on their own.

The bill does allow disability to be considered in one specific situation: if a doctor determines, after an individual evaluation, that the disability is medically relevant to whether the transplant would work or be safe. However, if a patient has help available (from family, paid caregivers, or other support) to manage medications and follow-up care, their inability to do those tasks entirely by themselves cannot be used as a reason to deny them the transplant. The national organ transplant board is also barred from creating policies that would block disabled patients' access to transplants.

This bill mainly affects people with disabilities who need organ transplants, as well as the hospitals, transplant centers, and healthcare providers who evaluate and treat them. It gives patients or their advocates a way to file complaints with the Department of Health and Human Services if they believe they were discriminated against, while also preserving any stronger protections already available under other disability rights laws or state laws.
ai_headline: Bill would bar organ transplant denials based on disability alone
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 1520 would stop hospitals from denying qualifying patients organ transplants solely because of a disability.

Providers must make reasonable accommodations, including counting help from family, friends, or caregivers when assessing whether a patient can manage post-transplant care. Disability can only factor into decisions when a doctor's individual evaluation finds it medically relevant to transplant safety or success.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects people with disabilities needing organ transplants and the hospitals, transplant centers, and providers who evaluate and treat them.
ai_sections.why: The change would shift how providers weigh disability and support networks in transplant eligibility decisions, and creates a complaint process through the Department of Health and Human Services for alleged discrimination.

title: Romance Scam Prevention Act
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Romance Scam Prevention Act, requires online dating apps and websites to warn users if they've been messaging with someone who gets banned for suspected fraud. If a dating service bans an account because it believes that person was trying to scam others out of money, the app must alert anyone who exchanged messages with that banned account. The notification must include the banned person's username, when the messages happened, a warning that the person may have used a fake identity, a reminder not to send money or financial information to other users, tips for avoiding scams, and customer service contact information.

Dating services generally must send this warning within 24 hours of the ban, though they can wait up to 3 days if needed, or longer if law enforcement asks them to delay it for an ongoing investigation. Companies that follow these rules properly are protected from being sued over the notifications themselves. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce this law, treating violations as deceptive business practices. The bill also sets one national standard, meaning individual states can't create their own separate or conflicting notification requirements for dating services.

This bill mainly affects people who use online dating apps and websites, as well as the companies that run those services, such as major dating platforms. Users would benefit from earlier warnings about potential scammers they've interacted with, potentially helping them avoid financial losses from romance scams. Dating service companies would need to build systems to track bans and send these notifications, and would face legal consequences if they fail to comply once the law takes effect, one year after being signed.
ai_headline: Dating apps must warn users after banning suspected scam accounts
last_action_text: Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 438.

ai_sections.who: Affects users of online dating apps and websites, and the companies operating those platforms, including major dating services.
ai_sections.why: Companies must build tracking and notification systems and could face enforcement action for noncompliance, while the law sets a single national standard overriding conflicting state rules.

title: Promoting United States Wireless Leadership Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill directs a federal official, the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information, to help boost America's influence in the international groups that set technical standards for 5G and future wireless networks. These standards-setting bodies (like the International Organization for Standardization, 3GPP, and the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) decide the technical rules that wireless devices and networks worldwide must follow, so having strong U.S. participation can help American companies and technology stay competitive globally.

Specifically, the bill requires this official to work with the National Institute of Standards and Technology and the State Department to encourage U.S. companies and other stakeholders to participate in these standard-setting groups, and to offer them technical help to do so effectively. However, companies or organizations officially identified as national security threats, such as those already flagged by security agencies or under existing laws targeting risky foreign telecom equipment, would be excluded from this support. Within 60 days of becoming law, the official must also brief relevant congressional committees on the strategy for carrying this out.

This bill mainly affects U.S. telecommunications and technology companies, government agencies involved in tech policy and national security, and indirectly, everyday consumers who rely on wireless networks, since the standards set in these bodies shape how future phones, devices, and networks work. It does not create new regulations for consumers directly but focuses on strengthening America's voice in global tech policymaking.
ai_headline: Bill directs US push for bigger role in global 5G standards bodies
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

title: Critical Infrastructure Manufacturing Feasibility Act
ai_summary:
HR 1721, the Critical Infrastructure Manufacturing Feasibility Act, directs the Secretary of Commerce to study whether products used in America's critical infrastructure could be made in the United States instead of imported. Critical infrastructure sectors include things like energy, water systems, healthcare, transportation, communications, and financial services—16 areas the government has identified as essential to keep the country running. The study would identify which important products in these sectors are currently imported because of manufacturing, material, or supply chain problems in the U.S., and then evaluate whether those products could realistically be made domestically instead.

The bill requires the study to look at costs and benefits, including effects on jobs, wages, and working conditions, as well as how manufacturing domestically might change the price of these products. It also specifically asks the Commerce Department to examine whether such manufacturing could happen in rural areas or industrial parks, which could matter for economic development in less urban parts of the country. The Secretary would have one year to complete the study and 18 months to report the results and recommendations to Congress, with the report made public online.

This bill does not require any company to actually build factories or change their supply chains, and it does not give the government power to force businesses to share information. It mainly affects the Department of Commerce, which must carry out the study, and could eventually influence future policy decisions on manufacturing, trade, and rural economic development. Everyday residents wouldn't see immediate changes, but the findings could shape future legislation affecting jobs, product costs, and where certain goods are manufactured.
ai_headline: Bill orders study on making critical infrastructure goods in the US
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

ai_sections.tldr: HR 1721 requires Commerce to study whether imported critical infrastructure products could instead be manufactured domestically.

The study must identify products currently imported due to domestic manufacturing, material, or supply chain problems, and assess whether they could realistically be produced domestically, including in rural areas or industrial parks.

title: NTIA Policy and Cybersecurity Coordination Act
ai_summary:
This bill officially creates an "Office of Policy Development and Cybersecurity" within the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), which is the federal agency that advises the President on telecommunications and internet policy. The bill essentially takes an existing office at NTIA (currently called the Office of Policy Analysis and Development) and reorganizes it, giving it a new name and an expanded set of responsibilities focused heavily on cybersecurity, in addition to its existing work on internet and communications policy.

The new office would be led by an "Associate Administrator for Policy Development and Cybersecurity," a position filled automatically by whoever currently holds the equivalent job, so there's no disruption in leadership. This office's duties would include studying how Americans use the internet and communication services, developing policies to encourage competition and innovation in tech and media markets, coordinating with industry and researchers on cybersecurity and privacy standards, and advising Congress and other federal agencies on cybersecurity issues affecting phone and internet networks. It would also pay particular attention to the needs of small businesses and rural communities when it comes to access to technology and communications infrastructure.

This bill mainly affects how the federal government is internally organized to handle telecommunications and cybersecurity policy; it doesn't create new laws or regulations for the public or businesses to follow. The people most directly affected are NTIA staff and leadership, other federal agencies that coordinate with NTIA on cybersecurity, and businesses (including telecom companies and internet service providers) that interact with the government on these policy issues. Everyday internet and phone users could see indirect effects over time if this office's work leads to new cybersecurity standards or policies affecting internet and communication services.
ai_headline: NTIA to create new office focused on cybersecurity policy
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

title: To direct the Secretary of Commerce to submit to Congress a report containing an assessment of the value, cost, and feasibility of a trans-Atlantic submarine fiber optic cable connecting the contiguous United States, the United States Virgin Islands, Ghana, and Nigeria.
ai_summary:
This bill directs the Secretary of Commerce to study and report to Congress on whether it makes sense to build a new undersea fiber optic cable connecting the continental United States, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Ghana, and Nigeria. Rather than actually authorizing construction of the cable, the bill only requires a detailed feasibility report within one year, covering things like the cost, security benefits, economic opportunities, and how ready the Virgin Islands' infrastructure is to support such a project. The report would also look at how old the existing cables serving the Virgin Islands are, how secure current telecommunications links are, and which companies could be trusted partners for a project like this based on national security screening standards already used by the government.

The report must also examine a related idea: building a secure data center and cloud computing facility in the Virgin Islands with its own power supply, meant to support U.S. military communications (specifically for Africa Command and Special Operations Command) and other national security needs. The bill says the Secretary cannot force any company to hand over data for this study, and the final report must be public (unclassified), though sensitive details could be included in a separate classified section.

This bill mainly affects government agencies, since it creates a study requirement rather than immediate action. It could eventually affect telecommunications companies, U.S. Virgin Islands residents and infrastructure planners, and U.S. national security operations in West Africa if a cable and data facility are eventually built. Everyday Americans wouldn't feel direct effects now, but the results could shape future decisions about internet infrastructure, security, and U.S. relations with Ghana and Nigeria.
ai_headline: Bill orders feasibility study on undersea cable to Virgin Islands, West Africa
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

title: ITS Codification Act
ai_summary:
This bill formally establishes the Institute for Telecommunication Sciences (ITS) as an official part of the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), a federal agency that manages communications and spectrum policy. ITS already exists as a research lab, but this bill writes its role into law. Its job is to study radio waves, test how different users can share the same airwave frequencies, and help the government figure out how to free up or share government-controlled spectrum for private companies, such as wireless carriers, to use. This matters because spectrum (the invisible radio frequencies used for cell phones, Wi-Fi, radios, and other wireless devices) is limited, and decisions about who gets to use it affect phone service, internet access, and new technology development.

The bill also directs NTIA leadership to create a new initiative focused on emergency communication and tracking technology, specifically tools that could help find people trapped in places like collapsed buildings, mines, or other areas where normal radio signals don't reach. The agency would work with private companies and other federal agencies to assess what's needed to make these tools work better and more reliably, and would have to report its findings to Congress within 18 months.

This bill mainly affects government agencies, wireless and telecom companies, and emergency responders. Everyday Americans could see indirect benefits, such as better cell service due to more efficient spectrum use, and improved technology for search-and-rescue operations during disasters. It does not create new taxes or direct payments to individuals; it mainly reorganizes and formalizes existing government research and adds a new focused research effort.
ai_headline: Bill formalizes federal telecom research lab and adds rescue tech study
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

ai_sections.tldr: The bill writes ITS into law and orders a report on emergency tracking tech for trapped people within 18 months.

It also directs NTIA to launch an initiative on emergency communication and tracking tools, such as technology to find people trapped in collapsed buildings or mines, with a report to Congress due within 18 months.
ai_sections.who: The bill affects NTIA, ITS researchers, wireless and telecom companies, other federal agencies, and emergency responders.
ai_sections.why: Spectrum is limited, so decisions about sharing it between government and private users affect phone service, internet access, and technology development. Formalizing ITS and adding the emergency tech initiative could shape future spectrum policy and disaster response tools.

title: National Coal Council Reestablishment Act
ai_summary:
This bill requires the Secretary of Energy to bring back the National Coal Council, an advisory group within the Department of Energy. The council would be reestablished using the same rules (charter) it operated under as of November 19, 2021. Its job is to study issues related to coal and the coal industry and give advice and recommendations to the Secretary of Energy, but it would not have any power to create laws or regulations on its own.

The bill also addresses how the council fits into existing government rules for advisory committees. Normally, a federal law called the Federal Advisory Committee Act requires these kinds of advisory groups to follow certain transparency rules and also sets time limits on how long they can exist before needing to be renewed. This bill says most of those transparency-related rules still apply to the National Coal Council, but it exempts the council from the usual automatic termination requirement, meaning it wouldn't need to be periodically renewed to keep existing.

This bill mainly affects the coal industry, energy policymakers, and the Department of Energy. Coal companies, miners, and related businesses could benefit from having a formal channel to advise federal officials on coal-related policy. It does not directly change any regulations, taxes, or funding—it simply restores an advisory body that previously existed before being allowed to lapse.
ai_headline: Bill would revive National Coal Council as DOE advisory body

title: Consumer Safety Technology Act
ai_summary:
This bill directs several federal agencies to explore new technologies and report back to Congress. First, it requires the Consumer Product Safety Commission (the agency that protects people from dangerous products) to create a one-year pilot program testing artificial intelligence. The AI could be used to spot injury trends, identify hazardous products, catch recalled items being resold online, or flag unsafe imports at the border. The agency must consult with tech experts, retailers, manufacturers, and safety groups while running the program, then publish a report on how well it worked.

Second, the bill has the Secretary of Commerce, working with the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), study how blockchain technology could help protect consumers from fraud and scams. This study would look at current and emerging uses of blockchain for fraud prevention, industry trends, public-private partnership models, potential benefits and risks, and whether any federal rules should change to encourage its use. The public would get a chance to weigh in, and the findings would be reported to Congress.

Third, the bill requires the FTC to report on its actions against fraud and deceptive practices involving "tokens" (digital assets recorded on blockchains, such as cryptocurrencies or NFTs). This report would cover enforcement actions already taken, ongoing efforts to prevent token-related scams, and any recommendations for new laws to better protect consumers in this market. Overall, this bill doesn't create new regulations or penalties itself—it mainly directs agencies to research, pilot-test, and report on how AI and blockchain technology affect consumer safety and protection, which could inform future legislation. It affects consumers broadly, as well as businesses in retail, manufacturing, and the cryptocurrency/blockchain industry who may see new rules down the road.
ai_headline: Bill directs agencies to pilot AI and study blockchain for consumer safety
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

title: Awning Safety Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the Awning Safety Act of 2025, directs the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) to create a mandatory safety standard for retractable awnings, including both fixed and freestanding types. The goal is to reduce the risk of death or serious injury from these products, particularly the danger of an awning suddenly springing open and striking someone while they are removing the bungee cords that hold the cover in place. The CPSC would have 18 months after the bill becomes law to finalize this standard, and it would also decide exactly which types of retractable awnings fall under the new rule.

Once created, this safety standard would be treated the same as other official consumer product safety rules, meaning manufacturers would be legally required to follow it. This affects companies that make or sell retractable awnings, since they would need to redesign or test their products to meet the new federal safety requirements. It also affects everyday consumers who buy or use retractable awnings, such as homeowners or business owners, since the rule aims to make these products safer and reduce accidents. Awning retailers and installers may also see changes in the products they are able to sell once the standard takes effect.
ai_headline: New bill orders federal safety standard for retractable awnings
last_action_text: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

title: L’Ouverture Economic Development Plan for Haiti Act of 2025
ai_summary:
This bill, called the L'Ouverture Economic Development Plan for Haiti Act of 2025, would create a new organization called the Haitian American Enterprise Fund to support economic development in Haiti. The President would designate a nonprofit organization to run this fund, which would be overseen by the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and a 9-person oversight panel made up of Americans, Haitian-Americans, and Haitian citizens with business experience. The fund would invest in Haitian businesses, infrastructure projects (like electricity, roads, water systems), agriculture, manufacturing, and job training programs, using tools like loans, grants, equity investments, and technical assistance. The bill also lays out U.S. policy goals for Haiti, including supporting democracy, reducing corruption, improving security, and addressing the root causes of migration from Haiti to the United States.

The bill authorizes Congress to provide $1 billion per year from 2026 through 2031 (up to $6 billion total) to fund this effort. The fund would be required to repay any government money it received by the end of 2031, at which point it would shut down. Regular audits and reports to Congress and the public would track how the money is spent and whether the investments are working.

This bill would primarily affect people and businesses in Haiti, especially small and medium-sized businesses, farmers, and workers who might benefit from new jobs, infrastructure, and investment opportunities. It would also affect Haitian-Americans, who make up about 1.2 million people in the U.S. and who send billions of dollars home to family members each year; the bill specifically encourages this diaspora community to invest in and partner with Haiti's economy. U.S. taxpayers would be affected as funders of the program, and U.S. government agencies like the International Development Finance Corporation and USAID would be involved in managing and coordinating the effort.

title: AIDA
ai_summary:
This bill, called the African Diaspora Investment and Development Act (AIDA), aims to make it cheaper and easier for people in the United States with family ties to Africa or Caribbean countries to send money home and invest in those regions. It would create programs where the U.S. government matches diaspora investments (up to $5,000 per taxpayer) in projects related to health, education, agriculture, clean energy, or job creation. It also directs regulators to loosen certain investment rules so more people can invest in approved projects, sets up support for "diaspora bonds" issued by African and Caribbean governments, and creates a fund to help fintech companies owned by diaspora members offer lower-cost money transfer services.

The bill also changes federal tax law. It would let individuals deduct up to $3,000 per year for remittances sent to family in Africa or Caribbean countries if the money is used for things like housing, education, healthcare, or small business support. It would exclude up to $12,000 in dividend or interest income from certain certified diaspora investments from being taxed. It also repeals an existing excise tax on remittance transfers. Finally, it requires the Treasury Department and other agencies to report annually on progress in reducing remittance costs and boosting diaspora investment, with a bigger review after ten years.

This bill mainly affects people in the U.S. who send money to or invest in African or Caribbean countries, especially African and Caribbean immigrants and their families, as well as banks, fintech companies, and investment funds that handle these money transfers. It also affects federal agencies like the Treasury Department, the SEC, and the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, which would take on new responsibilities to carry out these programs.
ai_headline: Bill would match diaspora investments and cut remittance costs to Africa, Caribbean
last_action_text: ASSUMING FIRST SPONSORSHIP - Mr. Jackson (IL) asked unanimous consent that he may hereafter be considered as the first sponsor of H.R. 4586, a bill originally introduced by Representative Cherfilus-McCormick for the purpose of adding cosponsors and requesting reprintings pursuant to clause 7 of rule XII. Agreed to without objection.

It also affects the Treasury Department, SEC, and U.S. International Development Finance Corporation.
ai_sections.why: The changes would alter how remittances and diaspora investments are taxed and regulated, shifting federal revenue and creating new compliance and reporting duties for agencies and financial firms.
